https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: This is how we do it: ‘Leaving our cult has made sex more intimate’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: As told to Olivia Ladanyi
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Jude, 43
 By the time we got married, we had done everything but kiss and have penetrative sex
Our first kiss was on our wedding day, in front of all our family and friends. It was long and deep, and felt like lightning. That was 22 years ago, but Tess and I had met nine years before as we grew up in the same Christian cult.
Chastity was a fixation in the church, and there was a culture of fear, but we pushed (nearly) every boundary. By the time we got married, we were pretty comfortable with each other sexually, having done everything but kiss and have penetrative sex – things we knew our parents would explicitly ask about.
A few years into our marriage, before I took over from my dad as pastor, I was working at a university when I became attracted to a colleague. It felt like God was testing me – to see if I would be faithful before handing me a congregation. The last thing my dad said to me before he died was: “If you ever commit adultery, you’re finished.” I felt I had passed God’s test, as things never became physical between us, although the attraction still felt like infidelity. When I told Tess how I felt, even though it hurt her, we faced it together. But it cast a shadow over our sex life for three years. Tess would worry: “Is he thinking about her when he’s having sex with me?”
Three years ago, Tess and I broke away from the cult. We’re doing things we weren’t allowed to do before: listening to music, drinking wine. It feels as if we’re dating again. Whereas before, Tess was my “wife” rather than her own person, because in God’s eyes we were one, now, as two individuals, as equals, our connection is stronger than ever. Sex is more intense because we’re free to be ourselves.
We left the church amid a growing disillusionment with the things we had been conditioned to believe. I went from a leadership role I was groomed to do since childhood to being unemployed. I struggle with depression as a result, but as a couple we’re much closer. Lying on Tess’s chest, I feel so safe. Just the scent of her arouses me. But her friendship is the most important thing, especially now it’s just the two of us and our kids, without the community we have known our entire lives.
Tess, 40
 I’m considered an abomination. As a woman, I was supposed to be submissive
I met Jude after my family moved from the Caribbean to the US. As the pastor’s son, he was expected to become a church leader; as a woman, I was expected to be a virgin. But we couldn’t keep our hands off each other. Being sexually intimate before marriage meant we understood what turned each other on. When we tried to have penetrative sex on our honeymoon it was too painful, but Jude was patient.
I was in my early 20s when Jude became the pastor. People looked up to our relationship, and as the pastor’s wife I was expected to listen to their problems, though I had relationship issues of my own. When Jude developed an attraction to a colleague, I remember thinking I had two options: he could hide what he was feeling from me and go through it alone, or I could be open to those conversations, where Jude would tell me in detail how he felt. Despite how much it hurt, I was willing to do that to protect our relationship. We saw it as a test from God – one that Jude would overcome.
Since leaving the church, we have been learning who we are as individuals. The excitement of watching Jude discover who he is makes me more attracted to him. Having my own identity makes me feel more desirable. I can wear trousers, pierce my ears, or take Jude out for coffee. But Jude’s family won’t let me into the house. My mum doesn’t talk to me. I’m considered an abomination. As a woman, I was supposed to be submissive, but Jude and I have always been friends, which has made the transition to partners easier.
We’re all each other has. That closeness has made sex more intimate. Sometimes we pause during sex just to look at our hands touching. That’s when I feel closest to him – in those moments where time stands still.
Names have been changed

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Train crash kills seven, injures dozens near Egypt’s Cairo city
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Train crash kills seven, injures dozens near Egypt’s Cairo city
The passenger train was travelling from Egypt’s capital to Aswan in the south when it derailed, overturning carriages.
At least seven people have been killed and more than 125 others injured in a train crash on the outskirts of Cairo in Egypt’s Giza province, according to the country’s Health Ministry.
A train travelling between Giza and Fayoum on Sunday ran into the back of another train on the Cairo-to-Aswan route, causing the latter to derail from its tracks onto a countryside road in the district of al-Ayyat, authorities said.
Emergency rescue teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, Egyptian National Railways said.
Authorities say more than 70 ambulances were involved in transport and evacuation operations at the scene of the crash, with casualties taken to nearby hospitals.
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi said he was following the accident “with great concern”, and had directed authorities to conduct an urgent investigation to “hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent”.
Witnesses described chaotic rescue efforts after the collision, as villagers, first responders and railway workers scrambled to reach passengers trapped inside overturned carriages.
Abdel Wahed Mohamed, 31, who was sitting at a nearby cafe when the collision occurred, said the Aswan-bound train had stopped, when the Fayoum-bound train crashed into it.
“The train overturned at around 1:30 pm [11:30 GMT]. Six carriages overturned,” he said, adding that victims suffered a range of injuries, including head wounds and broken limbs.
Another witness, Ahmed Moussa, 25, said rescuers dug beneath one overturned carriage to reach trapped passengers.
“There were people piled on top of each other inside,” he said, adding that he saw two women among the dead.
Taha Abdel Tawab, 43, said he “saw a young man leaving the train carrying his dead father”.
Previous accidents
Al-Ayyat district, where the collision happened, is also the site of Egypt’s worst-ever rail disaster.
In 2002, more than 370 people were killed when a fire swept through a train carrying holiday travellers south of Cairo. In 2009, multiple train crashes in the area killed dozens.
Egypt’s 110 million people depend heavily on rail transport, but the cross-country network – one of the largest in Africa – is in need of modernisation.
Over the past decade, Egypt has poured billions of dollars into updating its transport infrastructure, including new highways and high-speed rail lines, but has yet to overhaul much of its dated train services.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/accueil-de.title: Sénégal : au moins 21 personnes meurent lors du naufrage d’une pirogue transportant des migrants
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/accueil-de.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/accueil-de.text:
Le naufrage d’une pirogue transportant des migrants au large de Kébémer (nord-ouest du Sénégal) a causé la mort d’une vingtaine de personnes, a annoncé le gouvernement ce samedi 7 novembre. Un drame qui alourdit le bilan général du nombre de victimes ayant perdu la vie en tentant de rejoindre l’Europe.
Au moins vingt et une personnes sont mortes lors du naufrage d’une pirogue transportant des migrants au large de Kébémer, dans le nord-ouest du Sénégal, ont indiqué ce samedi 7 novembre dans la soirée les autorités.
« Au soir du 7 novembre 2026, le bilan provisoire fait état de 21 corps sans vie et d’un rescapé », a indiqué le ministère sénégalais de l’Intérieur dans un communiqué, qui ne précise pas le jour du drame. « Les services compétents de l’État sont mobilisés pour poursuivre les recherches, porter secours aux éventuels rescapés et accompagner les familles », est-il précisé.
Un bilan dramatique qui s’alourdit sans cesse
Des milliers de personnes originaires d’Afrique de l’Ouest, en majorité des jeunes, tentent depuis des années de gagner clandestinement l’Europe en empruntant la route de l’Atlantique, principalement vers l’archipel espagnol des Canaries, à bord d’embarcations surchargées, souvent vétustes. Selon le quotidien national Le Soleil, le naufrage s’est produit au large des côtes de la localité de Loumpoul, dans la région de Louga (département de Kébémer), entre Dakar et Saint-Louis.
« La plupart des victimes seraient originaires des communes de Léona et de Thiéppe », dans le même département, ajoute le quotidien. Samedi également, la gendarmerie sénégalaise a annoncé avoir intercepté au large de Dakar 142 migrants clandestins, dont plusieurs femmes et des enfants, qui tentaient de rejoindre l’Espagne à bord d’une pirogue.
Au cours de la semaine, la Crète a également été le théâtre de deux drames concernant des embarcations transportant des migrants. Ce mercredi 4 novembre, 59 personnes ont été portées disparues après un naufrage. Aucune d’entre elles n’a été retrouvée, indiquent les garde-côtes à l’AFP ce dimanche.
Un autre homme a été retrouvé mort au sein d’une embarcation en détresse dans la même zone ce 8 novembre. Les 28 autres passagers ont quant à eux été pris en charge, deux d’entre eux ont été hospitalisés.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘I’ve seen people in my neighbourhood pulled out of their cars’: Ava DuVernay on the cruelty and brutality of Trump’s America
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Ellen E Jones
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
When I ask Ava DuVernay how she kept her focus while making her new film – or how anyone does, when the onslaught of news, fake news and disputed facts seems designed to overwhelm – she starts to answer, then stops. Her eyes have filled with tears.
“I just got emotional, as you said that, because it was the film that saved me,” she says. “It’s been a very tough two years. I live in Los Angeles, and I’ve seen people in my neighbourhood pulled out of their cars. The lady who sells flowers next to my office was there one day, and the next day she wasn’t. People I know personally are literally hiding in their houses, like Anne Frank vibes … So when I would feel the rage and the fear, I put it into the film … And I just … I was doing something.”
The film that saved DuVernay, titled 14th, takes a little history to explain. In early 1864, as the civil war raged on in the battlefields of Jonesville, Virginia and Dandridge, Tennessee, and with President Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address still ringing out across the nation, work began on what would become the first addition to the US constitution for 61 years. The 13th amendment ended slavery, with one exception, “as a punishment for crime”, and thus a loophole was created, which – as explored in 13th, Ava DuVernay’s Oscar-nominated documentary of 2016 – has allowed for the continued oppression of Black Americans to this day.
Now, 10 years on from 13th’s release, DuVernay has made another rousing documentary exploring how a different Reconstruction-era constitutional amendment, drafted in pursuit of that “more perfect union”, has come under sustained attack. A sequel of sorts, then – though 13th is hardly the sort of film you’d expect to birth a franchise. “Oh no. I never thought I’d do 14th until I heard they were trying to rescind birthright citizenship,” says DuVernay, referring to President Trump’s executive order of January 2025. “I mean, one of the bedrocks of America is that if you were born in America, you’re an American. Now it was going to change? Just the sheer audacity and absurdity of that propelled me to look deeper into how we got here.”
For a full year she thought she was making a film about birthright citizenship, the first and best known of the 14th amendment’s five sections, but as DuVernay travelled the country, meeting experts and conducting further research, the plan changed. “We started to see that, systematically, the other parts were also being attacked. It felt like such a design, so purposeful, that I thought there’s something here …”
At 54, and with eight feature films, six TV shows and numerous prestigious awards to her name, Ava DuVernay is an established film industry leader and a Black American icon, who counts Oprah Winfrey and the Obamas among her friends. She looks the part too, dressed today in an Oxford blue shirt and tailored taupe trousers; her nails short but manicured, and her hair styled in pristine, waist-length locs. She could pass for a senator, exuding warmth with engaging eyes and ready answers to tough questions.
DuVernay’s work has always been powered by a fiery sense of justice. After graduating from UCLA, she interned at CBS News, then worked in PR for many years before becoming a film-maker. Her 2014 feature film Selma was, incredibly, the first Hollywood biopic made about civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, and also the first film directed by a Black woman to be nominated for a best picture Oscar. She followed up with another Oscar nomination, for 13th, then When They See Us, an Emmy-winning drama series about a racially charged, Trump-exacerbated miscarriage of justice in 1980s New York.
Some of DuVernay’s accumulated expertise was already on show 10 years ago in 13th, which digested 100 years of American history into 100 cogent minutes, but this new film is her masterpiece. The sheer amount of information it delivers, and the galvanising clarity with which it does so, add up to an astounding feat of documentary film-making. Not only is the 14th amendment a more complex and unwieldy piece of legislation – memorably described by one contributor as “the everything bagel of democracy” – but every day in Trump’s US provides fresh examples of the human rights rollback and, for those watching closely, glimpses of an overarching strategy behind it.
“People think I’m some kind of legal mind or political junkie,” says DuVernay, between sips of hot chocolate. “I’m not. I’m just a regular lady who wants to understand.” This attitude informed the documentary and its structuring round 50 interviews, every one of which she conducted personally. Those featured include celebrity New York congresswoman Alexandria “AOC” Ocasio-Cortez, the internet’s favourite socialist sex symbol Hasan Piker, and David W Blight, Yale professor and the Pulitzer prize-winning author of several impressive tomes on slavery and the civil war.
But what’s even more notable than the quantity and quality is the diversity. We hear, as you might expect, from historians and constitutional experts, but also – as you might not expect – from a 22-year-old livestreamer: “I wanted the full ideological spectrum,” says DuVernay, nodding vigorously when I mention some of the more surprising names. “And that’s not just Republican and Democrat; far-right, far-left. We have all that, but it’s also generational. Dean Withers [the streamer] and his generation are thinking of it much differently than David Blight is … Or are they?”
The conservative perspective is articulated by figures including Anna Paulina Luna, a Mexican-American, ICE-defending congresswoman, who argues that – contrary to the 14th amendment – immigrants aren’t entitled to due process. The author Dr Donald Critchlow at one point forwards that favourite canard of “lost cause” revisionists: that the Confederate general Robert E Lee was not a slave owner (he was, and this claim is swiftly factchecked). Meanwhile, the staunch Republican-but-never-Maga viewpoint is represented by US senator turned ambassador to Turkey Jeff Flake.
DuVernay says she has “a lot of respect” for all three, and regrets she didn’t include more shades of conservative thought in the film. Not for lack of trying, though. More than 300 requests went out to “every sitting congressperson, every sitting senator, every sitting Republican governor, every sitting Republican mayor of a major city”, making clear there was no intention to embarrass or even debate contributors. Still, only a handful said yes. Why so camera-shy? “To me, it really speaks to the strategic choice by Republicans to preach to the choir. These are not conversations they see any reason to have outside a certain sphere.”
And while all men are created equal (according to another of the US’s founding documents), all Netflix documentary interviewees are not. DuVernay’s film evinces clear favouritism towards the prominent legal scholar Sherrilyn Ifill, whom we hear from first and most in the film. That’s logical: Ifill is the woman who in 2025 founded the 14th Amendment Center for Law and Democracy at Howard University, Washington DC. She’s “the Meryl Streep of 14th”, says an awed DuVernay, “the grande dame of it. I talked to her for six hours straight. I was just riveted by her.”
DuVernay became aware of Ifill and her work during Trump’s second presidential campaign, when the law professor was among a small group trying to draw attention to section 3 of the 14th amendment and its relevance, after the 6 January 2021 attack on the Capitol. Section 3 bars from office anyone who’s “previously taken an oath … to support the Constitution of the United States [and then] engaged in insurrection or rebellion against the same” (attempts to disqualify Trump on these grounds were effectively shut down by a 2024 supreme court ruling).
DuVernay admits she didn’t take Ifill seriously back then. “I even remember thinking: ‘Hmmm, she’s a little kooky,’” she says. “She was coming out on television saying: ‘Use section 3 of the 14th amendment!’ And it was like: ‘Look at this crazy lady!’ There were a few other people saying it – David Blight, I believe, wrote a piece – but it was truly seen as a very outsider take. Now you just look back and you’re like: ‘What were we doing?’” Section 3 was written with former Confederates in mind. “We had been through this before and forgotten,” says DuVernay, before correcting herself. “Or had we forgotten? Or had [this history] been purposely put to the side?”
The deep admiration DuVernay now feels for Ifill is evident in the film: “I just wanted to put the camera so close and she’s like – “Um … it’s really close!” Ifill and many of the other participants are also interviewed amid the imposing columns, marble and monuments of campus or federal buildings, implying, perhaps, that people – just as much as neoclassical architecture – can embody democratic values and act as ballast against their wanton destruction.
That idea is further explored by the story of Devon “the Statue Slayer” Henry, the lone contractor brave enough to remove Confederate monuments – that is, essentially, pro-slavery monuments – from public places across the south, at the official behest of local government. DuVernay’s documentary also utilises and examines the power of pop culture in other forms, with music from Kendrick Lamar and Fleetwood Mac, clips from 1939’s Gone With the Wind, and standup routines from George Carlin and Paul Mooney. “I don’t see the comedians as much different than the monuments,” says DuVernay. “In that there’s this commemorative landscape all around us, which signposts what to think and carries messages through time.”
Another, potentially more controversial technique in the film was jointly inspired by a moving camera illusion known as “the Ken Burns effect” and some 19th-century stereoscopic photography DuVernay saw at the Smithsonian. It involves using traditional animation and AI to bring archive photography vividly to life, and it’s incredibly effective. It’s also, on occasion, deeply moving, particularly with regard to images of Black American life in the Reconstruction era. This is the often forgotten – or deliberately obscured – period from 1865 to 1877, when the provisions of the 14th amendment allowed previously enslaved people to take elected office and build thriving businesses and communities. All this was then brutally destroyed by a decades-long backlash of white supremacist violence characterised by public lynchings, massacres and Ku Klux Klan arson attacks, referred to by historians as “the Nadir”.
The brief, shining promise of Reconstruction is powerfully conveyed in DuVernay’s film, but the use of AI is contentious in Hollywood. Concerns about the technology prompted some of the town’s longest ever labour strikes in 2023, and many big names have publicly spoken out, for and against. Did that aspect give her pause? “No, because we didn’t do any prompting. We didn’t say: ‘Hey Claude, make up some people in the civil war for us.’ It’s all real images that we were moving. Right now, people have a real allergy to AI. I do too. I think it’s dangerous. I’m also sober enough to know it’s embedded in [editing software] Pro Tools, Avid and Resolve … Every film-maker is using it, unfortunately.”
And if it comes down to ends justifying means, then these “ends” could hardly be more dire. “I think America is sitting in a dark, dangerous room and you can’t get out of a room if you can’t see the door or where the furniture is. All I’m trying to do is just turn on a little light. It’s not a big light, it’s not the overhead. It’s a little something to get you around these obstacles and to an exit.”
This is true, she says, not just for African Americans, but for all Americans. And not just for Americans, but for the rest of the world, too. “Authoritarianism is on the rise everywhere and we know where it leads. There’s no country that hasn’t been touched by this at some point in its own history. We just need to remember. And so the hope is that this film could be not a lesson, but a reminder.”
What Ava DuVernay has done with 14th is turn the light on. Now it’s up to others to make a move towards the door marked “freedom”. “And I really think that’s what I would tell people to do,” she concludes. “You may not be a film-maker, but, if it’s just on your block, talking to your neighbour – do something.”
14th is in cinemas from 27 November, and on Netflix from 4 December.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: NWSL playoffs: Rodman’s brace leads Spirit rout while Gotham sneak into semi-finals
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Agencies and Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Trinity Rodman scored twice and the host Washington Spirit overwhelmed the Portland Thorns 4-1 on Sunday in the quarter-finals of the NWSL playoffs.
The third-seeded Spirit scored twice in two minutes to take a 3-0 lead into half-time against the sixth-seeded Thorns at Audi Field. Washington will face the seventh-seeded Utah Royals in the semi-finals next weekend.
Rodman helped open the scoring in the sixth minute. She stripped Portland defender Carolyn Calzada of the ball deep in the Thorns’ end, dribbled into the penalty area and slipped a low pass through traffic to Mélissa Bethi, who beat goalkeeper Mackenzie Arnold.
Clara Luvanga doubled the lead in the 34th minute when Arnold hesitated over a back pass from defender Isabella Obaze. Luvanga closed down Arnold and scored. A minute later, she raced into the box and crossed for Rodman, who finished for her first goal.
Pietra Tordin pulled one back for Portland in the 51st minute. The ball came out to Jessie Fleming after a corner kick, and Fleming sent it back into the box for Tordin to finish.
Luvanga and Rodman answered seven minutes later. Luvanga drove a grounded pass across the penalty area, and Rodman met it with her left foot to restore Washington’s three-goal lead.
Portland’s Jayden Perry was booked in the 47th minute for a tackle on Rodman and was sent off with two minutes left in regulation after earning a second yellow card for pulling Rodman’s arm during another tackle.
Luvanga was booked in the 62nd for shoving Thorns defender Reyna Reyes in the back, and teammate Esme Morgan saw yellow in the 82nd for a rough foul.
Gotham advance after own goal, zero shots on target
Ann-Katrin Berger made three saves and top-seeded Gotham FC protected a one-goal lead for most of the game, defeating the eighth-seeded Seattle Reign 1-0 in their quarter-final in Harrison, New Jersey.
Gotham got on the board in the fourth minute on an own goal credited to Seattle’s Jordyn Bugg. Jaedyn Shaw sent a corner kick toward the near post and Bugg misplayed it, sending it straight past her goalkeeper, Claudia Dickey.
The Shield winners took five shots during the game, but none of them were on target. They had 54% of possession but just 0.16 expected goals (xG) and zero big chances created.
Berger made one save in the first half and two more after half-time. One of the best goalkeepers in the sport, Berger led the league with a 0.85 goals-against average this season.
Seattle appeared to equalize in the 59th minute when veteran Reign midfielder Jess Fishlock found Nérilia Mondésir in the box. Mondésir finished past Berger, but the goal was ruled out because Fishlock was offside when Maddie Mercado played the ball to her.
Shaw received a yellow card in the 76th minute for grabbing Reign midfielder Sam Meza to stop a Seattle counterattack. In the 90th minute, Gotham defender Leila Ouahabi took a yellow card for a tactical foul that denied Brittany Ratcliffe a clear chance to equalize.
Players and coaches from both Seattle and Gotham criticized the state of the Sports Illustrated Stadium pitch, which was patchy and sandy on Sunday after several weeks of heavy wear-and-tear for soccer and rugby matches.
Gotham, who edged the San Diego Wave by three points for the NWSL Shield and home-field advantage in the first two rounds of the playoffs, will face the fourth-seeded Kansas City Current in the semi-finals next weekend.
Semi-final sites remain uncertain
The dates and venues for the semi-finals have yet to be announced. ESPN reported earlier this week that Gotham and Washington could play their semi-final matches away from their home venues because of scheduling conflicts. MLS’s New York Red Bulls, the primary tenant at Sports Illustrated Stadium in New Jersey where Gotham regularly play, have a friendly scheduled for 14 November. A Division III college football game is scheduled for that same afternoon at Audi Field in Washington.
The league will soon announce the dates and venues for the matches.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Washington state passes ballot measure banning trans girls from school sports
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levin
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voters in Washington state have passed a ballot measure banning transgender girls from playing on girls’ sports teams, a major loss for LGBTQ+ rights in a solidly Democratic state.
The measure says students in elementary, middle and high school who want to join girls’ athletics must first submit statements from their healthcare providers verifying their “biological sex”. Opponents have raised alarms the measure may force girls to endure “invasive and extreme” genital exams to participate in school sports.
Initiative 638 passed with support from nearly 57% of voters as of Thursday morning, though votes were still being counted.
More than 25 states across the US have adopted similar bans on trans youth athletes, mostly through legislation pushed by Republican lawmakers. Voters in Arizona and Nebraska approved similar ballot measures this week, and a ban proposed in Colorado was leading in early results, but that race has not yet been called.
Prohibiting trans youth from sports has become a major priority of conservatives and anti-LGBTQ+ groups who argue that they are protecting “fairness” in women’s athletics. But civil rights advocates say the policies are discriminatory and unnecessary, noting that trans youth have long played sports and that the restrictions target a small group of students already facing extreme prejudice and exclusion.
The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association said earlier this year that it was aware of only about 10 trans middle and high school sports players, a tiny fraction of the more than 200,000 students competing statewide. The state has for nearly two decades allowed trans students to play on teams that match their gender identity.
Critics of the sports bans argue they subject all girls to harmful scrutiny of their bodies, with opponents of Initiative 638 warning it could “force tens of thousands of Washington girls each year to undergo invasive, embarrassing, and potentially harmful genital exams just to play sports”.
More than 140 healthcare providers issued a statement opposing Washington’s measure, with Kelsey Gellner, a Seattle-based pediatric nurse, saying last month: “I tell my kids and patients that my No 1 job is to keep them safe. I can say with confidence that girls do not want to have an unnecessary exam that creates an unsafe barrier.”
The initiative was introduced in 2025 by a political action committee called Let’s Go Washington, which was founded by Brian Heywood, a hedge fund manager who has funded conservative measures. The measure was considered the most restrictive of the four trans youth sports bans on state ballots this year, as it mandates that girls prove their sex through hormone or genetic tests, or genital examinations. The measure only applies to women’s sports, and boys are not required to undergo any similar procedures.
Medical professionals have also criticized the measure for not allowing doctors to rely on birth certificates to confirm a patient’s eligibility to play on girls’ sports teams, with Libby Loft, a family physician in Spokane, saying: “I have to examine someone’s reproductive anatomy – that seems inappropriate to me for a sports physical.”
In an interview last month, Loft said sex-verification requirements created additional barriers for girls to participate in athletics, noting they were already twice as likely as boys to drop out of sports by age 14: “I don’t see this as a way to level the playing field for girls, and we’re making a villain out of trans girls who are children.”
Civil rights advocates have also argued that Washington’s ban was unconstitutional, violating students’ rights to privacy and equal protection rights. The initiative is due to go into effect in December, though it could face legal challenges.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Iran threatens to ‘rain down hell’ if US escalates war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Iran threatens to ‘rain down hell’ if US escalates war
US President Donald Trump warns that United States forces are ‘locked and loaded’ and ready to strike if necessary.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the United States resumes attacks, serving Washington with an ultimatum in an attempt to end the two countries’ eight-month war.
“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Araghchi wrote in a post on X on Sunday.
“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened warriors rain down hell,” he said.
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that renewed strikes on Iran are “highly unlikely” if negotiations progress over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
‘Locked and loaded’
“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said when asked about continued US strikes on Iran during a phone interview reported by CNN. “I would [continue], if necessary, but we hit them really hard,” he added.
Trump warned that US forces have three aircraft carriers stationed in the region “fully locked and loaded”, ready to continue strikes if need be. He also said that the US has 38 bridges in Iran’s crosshairs that US forces “can knock down in literally one hour”.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry also quoted Araghchi in an earlier statement on Sunday that said Iran would “not go easy on American targets” in the region.
Araghchi’s statements came after reports by state media that an oil tanker caught fire earlier that morning after hitting a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz, citing Iran’s navy.
The navy claimed the ship’s identification systems were turned off and it was travelling in the no-go zone of the strait.
‘Devastating and severe’ response
An adviser to Iran’s commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Aerospace Force made threats that echoed those of the Iranian foreign minister and said that weapons have been “secured for years to come”.
“The armed forces are at the ready, and if the enemy makes a mistake, Iran’s response will be devastating and severe,” warned IRGC Brigadier-General Ali Belali in a statement on Telegram.
“As senior commanders of the armed forces have pointed out, we have upgraded our capabilities in the post-Ramadan War period,” Belali said.
The back-and-fourth between Iranian and US leaders comes following US midterm elections in which the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress, soundly defeating Trump’s Republican Party.
Araghchi alleged that negotiations have been delayed as a result of the elections, but he awaits the path forward, Iranian state media reported.
“It will take some time for things to settle down and for the atmosphere to become conducive to the mediators resuming their visits,” the foreign minister said. “We have to wait.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Trump’s shattered ‘mirror world’: American voters roundly reject president’s alternate reality
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Rachel Leingang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
A new “golden age of America” is under way, Donald Trump repeatedly declared in his final pitch to voters before the US midterm elections.
The war in Iran was not really a war, because “we’ve done very little fighting”, the US president stressed. The stock market had hit 88 all-time highs. “They’re saying,” he said, that on his watch the US has become “the hottest country anywhere in the world”.
“We’ve achieved more in less than two years than any administration in American history, and I’ve kept every single promise I made – except far more,” he claimed in an extraordinary speech at Washington’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool on the last day of the campaign. “I’ve actually kept far more promises than I made. We’ve done much more than I promised.”
As Americans prepared to cast their vote in hundreds of congressional races across the country, Trump implored them to “pretend I’m on the ballot”, and vote on the policies he had enacted.
This “mirror world” – Trump’s constructed reality, casting his enemies as democracy-stealing villains and himself as the savior – was a central pillar of his victorious bid to reclaim the White House two years ago. As votes were counted on Tuesday night, though, it became clear the mirror had shattered.
Americans, including those who went for Trump in the past, weren’t buying his narrative. They didn’t approve of the Iran war, and weren’t experiencing a “golden age” as they filled up their cars and paid for groceries.
Across the US, however, the Guardian spoke to voters who made clear they accepted one element of Trump’s alternate reality as they entered polling places: they did consider his administration, and agenda, to be on the ballot – much to the devastation of Republicans running for office up and down the ballot.
“One by one,” said Tom Galvin, a Republican on the Maricopa county board of supervisors in Arizona, “everything that was important” to the coalition of voters that carried him back to power in 2024 fell by the wayside.
“For example, if you wanted the Epstein files, that didn’t happen,” said Galvin. “If you wanted to address inflation because Biden had runaway inflation, well, that didn’t happen. If you wanted to see a relief in gas prices, that didn’t happen. If you didn’t want us to get into‘foreign wars or senseless wars’, that didn’t happen.”
Later in the week, Trump remained defiant about his role in his party’s collapse. He elevated Stephen Miller, one of the most controversial figures in his administration, to chief of staff.
“I JUST WASN’T ON THE BALLOT,” he wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. “IF I WERE, WE WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE!”
The reflecting pool election?
Voters in Tuesday’s election explained the economy – particularly their inability to afford their lives – was central to their decisions. But corruption under Trump, the Iran war, tariffs, datacenters, healthcare costs and the administration’s aggressive deportation scheme weighed into their votes.
“There’s a war that nobody wants right now,” Jim Conrad, a voter in Ohio, told the Guardian. Ron Miller, in Kansas, said he was for Trump, but acknowledged that the president “hasn’t done anything” to lower the cost of living. Todd Cox, in Maine, cited “the disregard for the rule of law”, while Linda Olson, in Kansas, a previous Trump voter, said the president was now working to “make himself richer instead of really helping the people”.
Voters who usually split their tickets between the two parties’ candidates said they wanted to send a message. As Stacey, a voter in Iowa, told the Guardian: “I wanted to vote for no Republicans.”
Rather than acknowledge voters’ woes, Trump tried for months to explain, or dismiss, them. Affordability, he said last year, was a “con job” perpetrated by Democrats. Fuel prices may be high for consumers, but “the United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars”, he said in October. People who don’t want datacenters in their communities will end up “backwards and poor”, he said this summer. He was “willing to do tariffs” and they have helped US companies, he said in Kansas just before the election.
“You don’t see the stock market on the side of the road. But you drive down a street, you see the gas prices,” said Paul Bentz, an independent pollster and strategist at HighGround, an Arizona public affairs firm. “The tone-deaf nature of his approach on things, talking about issues that other folks don’t care about, ignoring and pretending like there aren’t struggles going on, just was not the right strategy.”
Bentz’s colleague described it as the reflecting pool election. Trump delivered his final speech before an algae-beset pool of water he spent 14m renovating that showed him his own reflection: “Narcissism 101”, a metaphor for the midterms.
Trump was on the ballot
Jim Abeler, a Republican state senator in Minnesota who lost his reelection bid this month, knocked on the doors of about 80% of the homes in his district. He encountered a lot of “outright hostility” toward Trump over gas prices and the Iran war, and some voters refused to talk to him because of it.
He didn’t hear voters saying that Trump’s rhetoric or his attempts to explain away economic concerns were the problem; it was the economics themselves. Half of the people he talked to were “unforgiving”, he said.
One woman who said she usually voted for Democrats but also had voted for Abeler in previous elections said she couldn’t do it this year. “She said, ‘I’m sorry, it’s just a bad year to be you,’” he recalled.
Chris Madel, a Minneapolis attorney who was running in the Republican primary for Minnesota governor until he dropped out and criticized his party over the deportation onslaught into the state, said he knew in January – amid the Operation Metro Surge crackdown – that this would end poorly for Republicans.
“The people that were showing that fealty towards him and towards this one person,” Madel said. “The tone deafness was really without equal.”
Madel said he asked his Trump-supporting family members whether they “think it’s OK” for the US president to accept “a 747 for free” from Qatar, for example. The attorney never thought the US would look like “a banana republic with respect to corruption”, he added.
Democratic candidates said for months that voters, including those in red-leaning areas, just wanted to feel heard. They centered their campaigns around in-person town halls, went to county fairs, and returned to retail politics.
People “don’t feel that the federal government really gives a damn about them”, Rebecca Cooke, a Democrat running for a Republican-held congressional district in western Wisconsin, said just before the election. She won.
Erin Klaus, who owns a small business in Cooke’s district that will close at the end of this year after weathering economic pains the last two years, said it has felt like the message from the government was that her problems weren’t really happening.
“The federal government can say that the prices are going down, and inflation is going down. But, I mean, that’s just not true in our daily lives,” she told the Guardian in October. “I think it’s really hard to continue to be told these things that we know aren’t true and feel almost like we’re getting mocked for the hardships that we’re enduring – both as business owners and as just regular folks, trying to live their lives.”
Bob Brooks, a Democrat who flipped Pennsylvania’s 7th congressional district, said voters were “frustrated with a guy who was promising them one thing” but gave them “something completely different”.
In short, “they felt lied to by the Trump organization, anybody that supported him, and they’re looking for change”, he added. “The status quo is not OK.”
No daylight between Trump and his party
After epic losses, Republican party leaders are searching for what comes next – and considering how tied their futures are to Trump.
Galvin, the Maricopa county supervisor, said the people in his party who either stayed home, or voted the other way, were trying to send a message: stop excusing corruption and trafficking in election lies, and get to work on real issues that matter to voters.
Republicans didn’t seriously attempt to distance themselves from Trump. Breaking with him would have been a major political risk in the Republican primaries, where the party faithful remained supportive of Trump. But by the time polls closed on 3 November, Arizona Republicans lost handily up and down the ballot - both chambers of the state legislature flipped, and the Democratic governor won her reelection bid by nearly 13 points – a stomping victory in a battleground state.
But “there is a lane to do the right thing” in the Republican party, according to Galvin. He had argued that tariffs were wrong. He heard from voters concerned about corruption in Washington after seeing what looked like pay-to-play pardon schemes. “I didn’t see any federal officials in Arizona, or federal candidates in Arizona on our side, say anything about that,” he said.
“Federal candidates in Arizona did not fully convey that they appreciate people’s pain,” he said. “I think they they whistled past the graveyard.”
Joe Pitts, a Republican who leads Arizona think tank 1912 Institute, said he’s not ready to count out Trump, or his influence in the party. A lot of the quick conclusions offered this week will look wrong in a few months, he suggested. “So long as Trump is president and frankly, so long as Trump is alive, he will exercise significant influence over the Republican Party.”
Pitts also warned that the significant shifts do not signal broad approval for Democrats, but that these demographics are all up for grabs and willing to change their minds. The massive losses could, in time, mean there opportunities for Republicans, he said.
Abeler, the Minnesota state senator who lost his race, predicted that the presidential election could go better for Republicans because people got protest votes off their chests.
Democrats, too, have been careful not to interpret the results as a broad endorsement of their party, but a sign that people are sick of politics as usual – including the way the president talks about the issues that affect them directly.
“People are just tired of nonsense. They’re tired of people performing in front of them,” said Brooks, the Pennsylvania Democrat. “People are tired of the show. I don’t want to be a show. I just want to help people.”
Christine Hunschofsky, a Florida state representative and the incoming House Democratic leader in the state, said in a media call this week that elected officials in both parties should see the election results as a call to listen to voters and address their concerns, or they will be voted out, no matter how safe a seat seems for either party.
People no longer trust that their government will respond to their needs because they keep hearing from candidates who say they care and then not seeing any action when those candidates take office, she said,
“Every elected official has such a responsibility right now to restore that trust,” Hunschofsky said. “Because once that trust is gone, I have even bigger concerns for our country.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Healthcare, tariffs – but not Trump impeachment: Democrats chart next two years of power
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
“Costs, chaos, corruption”: after almost two years spent relentlessly criticizing Donald Trump for failing to address those three, broad political concerns, Democrats won a monumental return to power in Tuesday’s midterm elections that will give them potent new leverage over the president.
Now the question becomes: what will they do with it?
While party leaders say their exact strategy remains under discussion, all signs point to Democrats embarking on aggressive campaigns of both investigating and lawmaking, with the aim of giving their eventual nominee the ammunition they will need to win the 2028 presidential election.
“We are going to make sure that those candidates running for president of the United States aren’t getting asked about plastic-straw bans. Instead, we should be talking about all of the legislation that we pass out of the House, pass out of the Senate, and force to Donald Trump’s desk,” Greg Casar, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told reporters on Wednesday.
He envisioned “passing bold legislation that people called for, every single week, off of the floor of the House and the Senate”, pointing to bans on price gouging, Super Pacs and stock trading by lawmakers as priorities. “If [Trump] vetoes it, then that is the platform upon which candidates can run in 2028, and then we can get signed into law in 2029,” Casar said.
That election is still two, long and unpredictable years off. And despite flipping seats across the country, the Democratic party brand remains deeply unpopular.
But Democrats have reason to feel confident: Republicans suffered such a cataclysm Tuesday that they lost Senate seats they’d held for decades, and House seats drawn specifically to elect only Republicans.
It was the biggest midterm defeat for an incumbent party in more than 50 years, but the power Democrats have gained in Congress is not unlimited. Trump is still set to inhabit the White House until January 2029, and can veto bills that do not pass with overwhelming support.
And the Senate filibuster – which Democrats used to block many bills that Republicans attempted to pass along party lines over the first half of Trump’s second term – remains in place. Now the shoe is on the other foot: Republicans can use it to stop any incoming Democratic legislation that does not have 60 votes in a chamber. Ballot counting is still ongoing, but if the two outstanding Senate races are won by their candidates, Democrats and their allies will have 56 seats.
Congress’s incoming leaders have made clear those obstacles will not stop them from at least trying to enact legislative solutions to the problems they campaigned on fixing.
“We made a promise to the country that we would fight for an affordable America, and we intend to keep it,” said Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become speaker of the House of Representatives when the new Congress convenes after the new year.
He named as priorities reimplementing premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act (ACA) health plans as well as undoing the cuts to the Medicaid insurance program that Republicans approved last year. Jeffries also promised legislative action to make Trump undo his tariffs, and end the conflict with Iran.
“Everything we do maps onto three promises, the very same three we ran on, turning from a critique into a to-do list: lower costs, make your government work for you, clean up the corruption,” Chuck Schumer, who is expected to be the next Senate majority leader, said during an appearance at the Center for American Progress, a liberal thinktank.
One thing that does not seem to be on the table: impeaching Trump, for a third time. During his first term, Senate Republicans rescued the president after two impeachments, first on charges of leveraging aid to undermine his political rivals, and then again after his supporters attacked the Capitol on January 6.
While Democrats have accused Trump of violating the law and the constitution regularly during his second term, they appear clear-eyed about Republicans’ willingness to force the president from office.
“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” Jeffries said. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability.”
When it comes to the latter, Democrats have no shortage of ideas. After publicly issuing a warning to potential targets to “lawyer up,” Robert Garcia, who will lead the investigative House oversight panel, told reporters this week to expect inquiries related to allegations of corruption in Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracting, stock trading by lawmakers, corporate profiteering and the government’s release of files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Noting he’d sent more than 200 demands for information to the Trump administration and others, Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House judiciary committee, said “go back and read my letters” when discussing who he would investigate next year. His letters carried no legal force, because he was in the congressional minority, but that will soon change – once the Democrats take committee gavels next year, they can issue subpoenas.
The party also doesn’t lack for ideas when it comes to addressing concerns about affordability, a major issue for voters in the elections.
It was Democrats’ demands to extend the ACA subsidies that led to the record-long government shutdown last year, and their candidates made warnings about the impending Medicaid cuts prominent in their campaigns.
The outgoing Republican congressional majorities have so far rejected attempts to address either issue, but Democrats did have some luck coaxing the majority to vote for war powers resolutions intended to end the conflict with Iran – one measure did pass, but the president has thus far ignored it.
“Trump has the ability to block our efforts to lower costs for American families, root out corruption in Washington, end the chaos in our streets and overseas,” Schumer acknowledged.
“But if he does that, I have no doubt the American people will rebuke him and his party just like they did in the election.”
So far, Trump, who cannot run again in 2028, has oscillated between saying he’d be willing to work with Democrats, and defiantly posting on social media an image of a red cap with the word “Veto” written on it.
The Democratic victories in the midterms came only after at-times anguished primaries that underscored the divides between the left and centers in the party, and over contentious issues like aid to Israel.
In the wake of their wins, leaders of the party’s ideological factions have taken tones of unity and cooperation – which could be aided by the fact that the Democratic majorities in both the Senate and House are expected to be so large that intraparty fights could be less impactful.
Kristen McDonald Rivet, who leads freshman lawmakers on the centrist New Democrat Coalition, acknowledged that when it comes to healthcare – a marquee issue for everyone in the party – “people want big change”.
“Some people’s approach to that is Medicare for all. Others are talking about Medicare for all who want it,” McDonald Rivet told reporters.
“There’s all kinds of ways to solve the solution, but I actually do not see that as a place of combat with other members of the caucus. It’s actually an incredibly hopeful thing that we are going to debate what big thing we can do around healthcare.”

https://projects.propublica.org/american.title: Search More Than 500 Cases of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
https://projects.propublica.org/american.author: Nicole Foy, Ruth Talbot, Cengiz Yar, Bianca Fortis, Mariam Elba, Kahlie Wray
https://projects.propublica.org/american.text:
ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes
corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms. Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.
Experts have long warned that immigration dragnets will inevitably result not only in the erosion of rights for immigrants but also for citizens. Since the start of this Trump administration, we've watched those warnings come true.
So we have once again done what the government won’t: We have tallied and cataloged every case we can find of an immigration agent reportedly detaining a citizen during the current administration — more than 500 cases from Inauguration Day through Oct. 21, 2026.
We compiled our list by scouring social media, court records and local media, and we included an incident only if we could find at least two sources for it. We asked the Department of Homeland Security about each incident, and we searched for any federal criminal charges that were brought in relation to each incident. (DHS has repeatedly said it is not arresting U.S. citizens.)
Since the government itself does not track these cases, our list is almost certainly an undercount. Below, we're showing you every case we found — the reality that the administration denies — along with the receipts. Read more about how we reported this project.

Santa Maria, California.
A citizen riding a bike was tasered, injured and handcuffed after colliding with an ICE vehicle in Long Beach, California. Video footage shows the ICE vehicle driving the wrong way down a one-way street then swerving toward the cyclist. DHS denied hitting the citizen and accused him of smashing the vehicle’s mirror, which is not captured on available video.
One citizen was injured and detained by ICE agents who were looking for someone who matched his description in Evanston, Illinois. A responding Evanston police officer said one agent had blood on his hands and the citizen was taken to the hospital. DHS claimed the man didn’t cooperate with “lawful commands” and agents detained him until he identified himself.
A citizen leaving a coffee shop in Annapolis, Maryland, was handcuffed, denied a phone call and held for almost two hours. DHS said it took the citizen to another location to interview him because “agitators” had gathered.
A citizen mother of four was detained in Lafayette, Louisiana, at a local law enforcement checkpoint outside her apartment, then transferred to ICE custody and booked into a detention facility before her attorney won her release. ICE and the local law enforcement agency that detained her still dispute her citizenship.
Jeury Concepcion, a 19-year-old citizen, was walking in front of a barbershop in the Bronx when three masked agents tackled him, mistaking him for someone else. The teen said that they released him far from home with his head bloodied, and that an agent apologized to him. A DHS statement said agents temporarily detained the teen to safely finish their questioning. A video associated with this incident appears in our main story.
A citizen was accused of assaulting an officer during the arrest of her husband in Asbury Park, New Jersey. She was detained for eight hours in Delaney Hall, an ICE detention facility, before being released without any known charges. Videos showed her 9-year-old daughter and toddler left crying alone in her vehicle, with ICE agents standing guard until family arrived to pick them up.
A 25-year-old citizen from Denver, Colorado, was detained and deported after a traffic stop in Fredericksburg, Texas, when he was unable to provide identification or proof of citizenship. He was held without access to his phone or a lawyer for several days before he agreed to leave the country. He was allowed to cross back into the U.S. using his Colorado birth certificate in August.

https://www.propublica.org/article/krono.title: Detroit Could Block Billionaire-Owned Concrete Plant From Further Neighborhood Expansion
https://www.propublica.org/article/krono.author: Jena Brooker
https://www.propublica.org/article/krono.text:
After years of community opposition, Detroit city officials have taken steps to stop a concrete mixing facility from further expanding into a residential neighborhood.
City Council members, acting on a recommendation last week from planning officials, will soon consider a rezoning measure that would restrict industrial activity at the site of the Kronos concrete plant and surrounding area. The concrete facility at its current size could stay and continue to operate as normal.
The planning recommendation comes after a BridgeDetroit and ProPublica investigation this year revealed how city officials helped Crown Enterprises, a real estate company owned by Detroit’s wealthy Moroun family, obtain property in Cadillac Heights and then provided latitude when its Kronos facility violated environmental laws. Residents have been filing complaints and protesting Kronos for years, frustrated by the dust, noise and other issues created by the concrete operation.
The City Planning Commission voted Oct. 22 to recommend a change to some of the zoning in the neighborhood from heavy to light industrial, which allows buildings such as warehouses but excludes facilities like concrete plants. The commission also recommended that other lots be zoned for residential and commercial purposes. Earlier this month, the commissioners unanimously voted to exclude industrial zoning in the area adjacent to Kronos, but they stepped back from that last week.
Crown has objected to any zoning change.
Sharon Buttry, who helped organize residents to protest against the Kronos plant, said she is glad the lots would be rezoned but was disappointed that the earlier recommendation, which was more pedestrian- and transit-friendly, didn’t stand.
Buttry said she fears that the latest zoning recommendation would make it easier for Crown to expand eventually. “We still want them to shut down or move,” she said.
The zoning plan was revisited at the request of City Planning Commissioner Fred Russell Jr., who said the adjustment would create a buffer between residents and the existing concrete plant.
The City Council, which will ultimately decide on the rezoning, has scheduled a public hearing for Nov. 19.
Over the last seven years, Crown has obtained dozens of parcels in Cadillac Heights — some through a land deal with the city in 2019 and others after residents sold their parcels and left. In all, the company now owns more than 160 lots in the neighborhood, most of which are barren.
How a 2019 Land-Swap Deal Accelerated the Morouns’ Foothold
The Moroun family spent decades, from 1966 to 2018, records show, gradually acquiring lots in Cadillac Heights through their various companies, eventually putting the parcels all under the ownership of Crown Enterprises. A May 2019 deal with the city of Detroit allowed Crown to acquire dozens of additional parcels during the next seven years.
In a letter to Detroit officials in mid-September and Oct. 22, a law firm representing Crown threatened legal action if city officials change the zoning, arguing that doing so would devalue the property and create uncertainty about future development.
Attorney Melvin Butch Hollowell also said if the rezoning goes through, the city would be backtracking on its commitment to support Crown’s development in Cadillac Heights. Crown obtained the land there in exchange for the company swapping property in another part of the city, which allowed automaker Stellantis to open the first new car plant in Detroit in three decades.
City officials have said they didn’t know Crown’s plans included a concrete facility. Crown did not present a specific plan at the time of the land transfer. But after the concrete plant opened, the city in 2022 signed a first-of-its-kind agreement with Crown that gave the company time to fix issues before being penalized. The agreement has allowed the company to avoid fines on several occasions, the news organizations have documented.
In response to questions from BridgeDetroit and ProPublica, a Crown spokesperson said the company has invested more than $10 million to develop the concrete operation based “on the City’s promises and actions of approving our plans for this facility.”
“The property was traded to us for the express purpose of redevelopment,” the spokesperson, Kenneth Dobson, wrote.
Dobson said that if the zoning changes, the company will not make the improvements it has promised, including new landscaping and sidewalks. He claimed the improvements would not be allowed under the new zoning and that they also wouldn’t be a sound business decision. City planning staff, however, said the company can still make the improvements.
The neighborhood surrounding Kronos has been zoned to allow heavy industry since the 1940s, when a rail line operated there. Before the concrete operation, the land was occupied by a trucking depot for decades.
Despite the zoning designation, the neighborhood attracted working-class families who lived in modest single-family houses. Buddy’s Pizza, famous as the birthplace of Detroit-style pizza, was founded there and drew crowds from across the city.
The City Planning Commission’s votes this month were four years in the making and part of a broader evaluation of land near the proposed Joe Louis Greenway, a walking and biking trail that will traverse the city and is already under construction.
Scott Benson, the council member who represents Cadillac Heights, asked the planning commission in 2023 to consider whether the industrial zoned areas along the greenway should be rezoned to a use that better supports safety and public health. He said the request at first was unrelated to Kronos, but then community input further influenced the desire for change.
“That did play a role here,” he said in an interview. “The community came out and said, ‘Yes, we especially want this part done and it abuts the Joe Louis Greenway.’”
More than 30 people — some in favor of a zoning change and some against — spoke out at recent commission meetings. Kronos employees and others told the commission that the company has created jobs for Detroit residents and said Crown has invested in the neighborhood with new paving.
Terrell Daniel, whom the city identified in meeting minutes as a Kronos employee, urged the commission at its Oct. 1 meeting to continue to allow industry in the neighborhood.
“It’s bringing back the backbone of Detroit,” he said. He said the concrete plant has provided an opportunity “for guys who never had a chance to work in the city.”
Those in support of rezoning expressed concerns about the dust, air quality and Crown’s track record of not taking care of the neighborhood, which has included leaving vacant homes unsecured and messy.
Residents have filed about 80 complaints to both city and state environmental offices, according to records obtained by BridgeDetroit and ProPublica. They have described “literal whiteout conditions” and “dust clouds” that blanket their neighborhood and irritate their eyes.
The city has issued several tickets to Kronos for violating Detroit’s fugitive dust ordinance, passed in 2024 to limit pollution. The law requires businesses such as concrete plants and scrapyards to submit plans to limit dust and prevent it from spreading into neighborhoods.
On Oct. 7, the city received a complaint about Kronos and an inspector found the company had spread dust in the neighborhood and had piles of materials that should have been blocked from view, according to city spokesperson Georgette Johnson.
Kronos wrote in a letter to the city that it swept and watered the streets and reduced the height of the piles. Johnson said Crown corrected the problems.
Dobson said readings from its air monitors have never exceeded the city’s pollution limits and that a small number of people regularly complain. He previously said that the company planned to demolish a vacant home littered with trash but was waiting on utilities to be disconnected.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New research reveals original colours of Ancient Egyptian shrine at Oxford museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A shrine built almost 3,000 years ago in northern Sudan will regain its original glowing colour later this month. Housed at the Ashmolean museum in Oxford, and the only freestanding building in Britain dating back to the time of the pharaohs, the Shrine of King Taharqa (690BC-654BC) will be recoloured through a digital projection that has been made after extensive research on surviving scraps and traces of pigment.
Fragments of red paint survive in crevices of the sandstone carvings, but microscopic analysis and hyperspectral imaging—combining photography and spectroscopy—also revealed evidence of colours now invisible to the naked eye, including yellow and “Egyptian blue”, a brilliant pigment used to depict divine figures.
According to Liam McNamara, the Ashmolean's keeper of antiquities, the carvings and inscriptions tell the story of the construction of the shrine: how the young Taharqa, later the king of Kush in Nubia and Pharaoh of Egypt, saw the ruins of the earlier brick temple to Amun-Re, built by Tutankhamen, with “the sand drifted to its roof”, as he journeyed north towards Thebes. At Taharqa's coronation he vowed to restore it and went on to build the shining new shrine within a new temple. Scorch marks on the stones of the shrine, also revealed in the project, bear witness to its eventual destruction in turn.
The relief carved sandstone blocks were originally plastered and brightly painted, showing Taharqa with the gods of Memphis, Heliopolis and also Amun-Re represented as both a Theban and a local Gematen deity. Taharqa himself is depicted both as an Egyptian pharaoh wearing the Double Crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, and in other scenes as a Kushite king with a ram’s head and sun disc earrings and the Kushite crown surmounted by two cobras.
The Shrine of King Taharqa came to Oxford from Khartoum in 150 crates 90 years ago as a gift from the Sudanese government to the Oxford University Excavations in Nubia, which had excavated it and other monuments over several seasons. It was given to the museum in 1936 by Nora Griffith, in memory of her husband Francis Llewellyn Griffith, who had led—and largely paid for—the expeditions. He had taught himself Ancient Egyptian at Oxford since there was no department, and went on to become the first professor of Egyptology and a renowned scholar.
McNamara describes the monument itself as a fascinating insight into the art and archaeology of ancient Sudan.“The new projection—and the scientific research behind it—will allow visitors to appreciate and understand the shrine’s original painted decoration like never before,” he adds
The project has been supported by James Lupton, the Ashmolean's chair of the board of visitors and his wife Béatrice. The projection onto the shrine will be free for all visitors to the Ashmolean’s Ancient Egypt and Sudan galleries, from 13 November.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Lula’s Victory! Bolsonaro’s Defeat! What’s Next for Brazil?
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: James N. Green
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Lula’s Victory! Bolsonaro’s Defeat! What’s Next for Brazil?
A leading Brazil scholar predicts that Trump will continue to meddle in Brazilian politics.
On October 25, Brazil’s incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a momentous, come-from-behind victory over the candidate of authoritarianism, Flávio Bolsonaro. The dramatic electoral outcome has generated a wave of hope in Brazil and beyond; Lula’s win is widely perceived as a rebuke to the march of ultraconservative forces throughout Latin America and to the Trump administration’s flagrant attempts to bolster Bolsonaro and assert US control over Brazil’s political and economic future. Referencing US interference, Lula declared in his acceptance speech that his victory demonstrates that “this country does not accept being anybody’s backyard.”
Flávio is the 45-year-old son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup to stay in power when he lost the presidency to Lula four years ago. Like his father, Flávio has refused to concede his loss. Under investigation for corruption and money laundering, this week he fled Brazil and, on Trump’s order, was allowed free passage into the United States. Hoping for US support to install him in power, Bolsonaro promptly declared himself “president-elect” of Brazil, even though he lost the election by over 4 million votes. The mainstream Brazilian media has accused Bolsonaro of “coup-mongering.”
To understand the implications of these dramatic events, The Nation placed a call to one of the leading international experts on Brazil, Brown University professor emeritus James Green, in São Paulo. This, with a bit of editing for clarity, is what he told us.
—Peter Kornbluh
The Nation:  Lula’s win is being heralded as historic. How do you interpret this unexpected and extraordinary victory for the first Brazilian to be elected president for a fourth time?
James Green: It is historic. I think it solidifies Lula as the greatest politician in Brazilian history. But there are reasons for this historic victory.
It is important to note that the first round of voting on October 4 took place amid one of the biggest corruption scandals in Brazilian history—the discovery that the head of a major bank, Banco Master, was bribing numerous Brazilians in the political world, including members of the Supreme Court. [Bolsonaro himself has been implicated in this scandal.] This caused tremendous distraction from the electoral process, and Lula’s campaign was quite lackluster; consequently, he lost the first round of voting by 1.9 points to Bolsonaro, leading to the runoff election on October 25.
After the October 4 vote, Lula’s campaign was in shock for a day, and then they turned it around. In less than three weeks, they did three key things to win the final election runoff.
The first was to carry out massive demonstrations in all the major cities of the country—huge, big demonstrations. This created a feeling of energy and community, and the possibility of winning with massive numbers of people in the streets.
The second was building a very effective social-media campaign. A pro-Lula congressman, André Janones, who is a very energetic and dynamic person, transformed his WhatsApp channel into a “Lula’s Army” website, which quickly garnered 10 million followers. This allowed the campaign to reach out through the Internet and to circumvent the algorithms that Meta was using to favor Bolsonaro’s campaign. For the first time, the left dominated the right on social media.
And the third initiative started spontaneously but then became a key part of Lula’s electoral campaign: asking supporters to draw up a list of friends and relatives whom they could convince to flip their vote or just get out and vote. The campaign targeted 16- to 18-year-olds, who can vote but don’t, as well as people over 70 who are not required by law to vote. There were wonderful videos on social media of people bringing their grandmothers to the polls, wearing their red Workers’ Party shirts and voting, of course, for Lula. This campaign helped bring 4 million people who had not voted in the first round to the polls for the runoff. And Lula won by about 4.5 percent, or about 4.5 million votes.
The night he won, there was just a huge, amazing celebration. It was as if Brazil had won the World Cup! It was that amazing.
TN: As you know, the defeated candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to concede and then fled into exile in the United States with the help of the Trump administration. (President Trump personally ordered that Bolsonaro be given “a pass” so he could enter the country.) As soon as he arrived in Miami, Bolsonaro cried “electoral fraud” and declared that he was the “president-elect” of Brazil—Brazil’s true “leader.” What do these political machinations mean for the aftermath of the election?
JG: It is still too early to know what Trump’s plan is with Flávio Bolsonaro, but I think Marco Rubio is interested in creating an exile government to pressure and weaken Lula’s administration. I imagine that they will impose more sanctions against Brazil, including on members of the government—performative sanctions against Brazil and some actual economic sanctions on the country.
But it is all going to backfire. There is a tremendously strong nationalist sentiment in the country. People are really questioning Bolsonaro’s commitment to Brazil since he refused to concede the election results and left the country. And because of the mass mobilization around the elections, I think there will be a lot of energy around mobilizing against any serious US measures to punish Brazil for this situation.
That said, Trump’s plan appears to consist of applying pressure from the United States, creating an alleged exile government in the United States, and also pushing the new Brazilian Congress, in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party now has a majority, to pressure Lula’s government—including efforts to impeach him. So it is going to be a very rough time for the new Lula administration. There is going to be tremendous pressure from the far right against it.
TN: Trump tried to put his thumb on the Brazilian election and engineer a victory for Bolsonaro. What, in your opinion, has motivated him to take such a keen interventionist interest in Brazil?
JG: The answer to that question lies in the Trump administration’s broader strategic plan for Latin America. Trump wants to return to a neocolonial time when there are spheres of influence and Latin America clearly belongs to the United States. He wants to put Latin America—Central and South America and the Caribbean—under the thumb of the United States again, reassert the Monroe Doctrine and US hegemony in the region.
Popular

That means controlling the economies of Latin America to provide markets and materials to the United States. And in Brazil’s case, also guaranteeing US access to rare earth minerals, which Trump has fixated on controlling. Brazil has the second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals in the world. Trump wants that. And Flávio Bolsonaro offered that to him.
There is also the issue of Cuba. At the end of the day, I think the big goal of both Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio is to destabilize and bring down the Cuban government. One of the major countries in Latin America that has maintained diplomatic relations and an open and friendly relationship with Cuba has been Brazil.
TN: Lula’s reelection has generated attention all over the world. Beyond Brazil’s borders, what are the regional and global implications of this very important victory over Bolsonaro?
JG: After a period of time when left-oriented, social-democratic governments were elected to power, there has been a counterwave of the far right throughout the region. And that has demoralized the Latin American left, leaving it weakened and disunited.
Now Brazil offers an inspiration. There is a possibility that Brazil could mark the beginning of a new dynamic, a counterswing away from the far right that now dominates countries like Argentina, Chile, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia. Lula’s victory, I think, will inspire others to stay in the fight for social justice and equality, environmental protection, etc., rather than being demoralized about the future. That is an element of this dynamic that will be important.
