https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: CUNY Students Won on Investment Disclosure. Now They’re Demanding Divestment.
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Ana Agudelo
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
CUNY Students Won on Investment Disclosure. Now They’re Demanding Divestment.
The records reveal that the public university was invested in companies—including Lockheed Martin, Caterpillar, and Elbit—that are linked to Israeli military operations in Gaza.
After battling for two years to obtain the City University of New York’s (CUNY) investment records, student divestment activists won a big victory on September 9. A Supreme Court decision ruled in favor of the students, who argued that under New York’s Freedom of Information Law, the university could no longer withhold its records from the public.
Despite the ruling, CUNY, which operates 26 colleges across all five boroughs of New York City, has failed to disclose the full cache of materials students have requested, including purchase order histories for the 30 companies whose financial ties to CUNY organizers sought to investigate. Of these, the university only provided records for two—the American technology companies Dell and IBM. Through these holdings, organizers were looking to identify the university’s financial ties to companies they believed profited from Israeli military actions.
Since 2024, CUNY4Palestine, an organization of CUNY students and workers, has been the force behind calls for the university to disclose investments in companies that are connected to Israeli military operations in Gaza. Across all 26 schools, CUNY4Palestine has organized divestment efforts for years, connecting this investment campaign to broader demands for institutional change.
The newly released forms reveal that from 2020 until 2025, CUNY was invested in companies, including Boeing, Raytheon, Lockheed Martin, Elbit Systems, and Caterpillar, that have provided Israel with weapons and military equipment used in its decimation of Gaza. CUNY also held stock in mass detention and surveillance companies such as Palantir, Geo Group, and CoreCivic.
For many students, the newly released information raises another question: What should CUNY do now?
A draft resolution, a collaboration by Hunter College’s student government and Hunter SJP members, demands that CUNY “immediately divest from these harmful holdings” and instead “adopt an ethical investment policy.”
For many students, the university has failed to uphold its mission as a university “for the whole people of New York.” They believe the university has profited from genocide, displacement, and incarceration, which stands at odds with the values and goals of the larger CUNY community.
“Students have become passive actors in mass violence without their knowledge” by paying tuition that may find its way into the university’s invested fund, said one Hunter SJP member, who asked to remain anonymous for safety reasons. “CUNY is merely a facade of a public institution that instead perpetuates harms to the very communities it claims to serve.”
Corinna Mullin, an adjunct professor in the political science and economics department at John Jay College and Brooklyn College and a member of CUNY4Palestine, said the fight goes beyond CUNY’s investment practices.
“We have always linked divestment—as we did in the encampment—to broader systemic change at CUNY: cops off campus, demilitarization, a fully funded CUNY with free tuition, fair contracts for CUNY workers, and solidarity with the Palestinian liberation struggle,” Mullin said. The group has also advocated to keep Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) away from CUNY campuses.
For Mullin, the disclosure of CUNY’s investments marks a new stage in the group’s organizing efforts.
Mullin participated in the Gaza Solidarity Encampment at Columbia University in 2024. In 2025, four Brooklyn College adjunct professors, including Mullin, were removed from their positions due to ongoing support for Pro-Palestinian protests and movements. Three have since been reinstated; Mullin continues to advocate for the last member to regain their post.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Mullin said that one of the organization’s mantras, borrowed from the Black feminist movement, is “None of us is free until all of us are free.”
Many of these student- and faculty-run organizations share one goal: to hold the university accountable and to ensure its representatives accurately reflect the people who make up the university community.
CUNY is known for the wide undergraduate racial and ethnic representation of its student body. For Mullin and other members of CUNY4Palestine, campuses should represent the larger New York City community.
“Now that we’ve won disclosure, we’re building a broad coalition because we recognize that CUNY investments are connected not only to settler colonialism and genocide in Palestine,” Mullin said, “but also to the US imperialist war machine and to repression at home.”
“We want a university run by and for its students, workers, and community members,” she said.
To some CUNY professors, the disclosure story is significant not just for what the records reveal but also for what the university’s refusal to release them says about the school and its true priorities.
Anthony Alessandrini is a professor of Middle Eastern Studies at the CUNY Graduate Center and chair of the Professional Staff Congress’s Academic Freedom Committee. The committee is dedicated to protecting CUNY faculty and staff and ensuring freedom throughout the university.
Alessandrini explained that faculty members have tried to defend students’ right to organize long before this phase of the divestment movement started. He traces CUNY’s Palestine solidarity organizing to a 2013 Brooklyn College panel on the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions.
For decades,“the message being given to students [has been], we’re here to teach you critical thinking, we want you to question things, we want you to look and analyze things, but not your own university,” Alessandrini said.
He also points out that the university’s refusal to disclose these records is part of a broader pattern of restricting academic freedom and student activism, not only at CUNY but also in schools worldwide. Alessandrini looked to France, where high school students and teachers are leading protests over poor educational facilities and staff shortages. For him, these demonstrations highlight the importance of holding educational institutions accountable.
He said the university’s response to student protests and its treatment of workers involved in the movement also raises questions about its role as a public institution.
“If you’re arresting your students, if you’re refusing to disclose your investments to students, if you’re firing workers for being against genocide,” Alessandrini said, “you’re not a functioning university.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/trum.title: Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/trum.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/trum.text:
The United States will stop providing $4 billion in annual aid to Israel starting next year, President Donald Trump claimed in an Election Day interview. While the U.S. will continue to sell arms to its closest Middle East ally, Trump’s announcement — should it actually hold true — could represent a seismic shift in American foreign policy.
Still questions remain and experts are dubious that the claim is what it seems.
Trump told Fox News during a phone call on Tuesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him with the idea years ago. He did not state specifically why he waited to announce the decision in the midst of a midterm vote in which his party is expected to lose its lock on Congress, but noted that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point, singling out Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” said Trump.
An August 2026 Fox News poll found 55 percent of Michigan voters oppose continued military assistance to Israel, including 70 percent of Democrats, 66 percent of Independents, and 35 percent of Republicans.
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats, as Netanyahu’s government has slaughtered civilians with impunity. Almost 75,000 Gazans have been killed and nearly 176,000 wounded, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza. A recent U.N. report said, “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
Amid the slaughter, sympathy for Israel among all Americans fell from roughly 50 percent to 36, while sympathy for Palestinians rose to 41 percent, according to a February Gallup poll. Among Democrats, support for Israel plummeted from more than 50 percent in 2001 to roughly 17 percent this year. October 2026 polling from the Institute for Middle East Understanding’s D.C.-based IMEU Policy Project and YouGov found a majority of voters in six key swing states — Georgia, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas — support halting the transfer of bombs to Israel.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Experts cautioned not to take Trump at his word, especially as his administration pushes a pending $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act that would embed Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.
“President Trump is a serial liar who has announced over $20 billion in weapons giveaways to Israel since taking office and launched a war at Israel’s request that has already cost every U.S. household over $2,000 — the equivalent of $262 billion,” said Hamid Bendaas, IMEU Policy Project’s communications director. “He and other politicians realize our taxpayer funding for Israel is a liability. That’s why he and his allies in Congress are at this very moment trying to advance legislation to conceal support for Israel by integrating Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon. This is a bait and switch that would result in Americans funding Israeli weapons makers in record amounts.”
Others expressed skepticism about Trump‘s claim of an immediate end of annual aid in 2027. “It’s not plausible there will be a total cut-off starting January 1,” said Josh Paul, who spent more than 11 years as the director of congressional and public affairs at the State Department bureau that oversees arms transfers to foreign nations before resigning in 2023 over U.S. military assistance to Israel, noting that funding is baked into existing and pending legislation. “My guess is that he was speaking off the cuff with the next 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel in mind, but did so in a way that is at best inaccurate or imprecise.”
A decade ago, President Barack Obama signed an unprecedented MOU with Israel to give its military $38 billion between 2019 and 2028, amounting to almost $4 billion a year.
Paul was hopeful, however that Trump’s statement would allow Republicans license to join Democratic colleagues in paring down future funding. He said it was a recognition of the bipartisan demand by the American people for an end to that military aid.
Trump’s announcement did not address the proposal in the National Defense Authorization Act, which would inextricably link the U.S. armed forces and the Israeli military, giving Israel leverage over the Pentagon.
“Initial reporting on Trump’s statement omits a crucial fact: that the National Defense Authorization Act contains a provision intended to protect U.S. tax dollars flowing to Israel from the massive shift in U.S. public opinion against funding Israeli aggression,” Annelle Sheline, who served as a foreign affairs officer in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, told The Intercept. “The provision would move U.S. funding out of security assistance under the purview of the State Department — which carries legal provisions like the Leahy Laws, transparency requirements, and an annual congressional vote — into the Pentagon procurement process, which has none of these.”
Sheline added, “Insulated from public opinion and away from public visibility, U.S. funding to Israel is likely to grow exponentially.”
With his popularity in free fall in the U.S., Trump teased the possibility of decamping for Israel and taking Netanyahu’s job as the Israeli prime minister battles for his political life after an inconclusive election last week. “In fact, if people ever got tired of me in the U.S., I’ll move to Israel, become prime minister,” Trump declared during his Fox appearance.
The White House did not immediately respond to requests for further details.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
A photograph showing thousands of satellites cross-hatching the night sky over New Zealand appeared so extraordinary the astrophotographer who captured it is fighting accusations it was created by AI.
To create his spectacular image – now viewed millions of times online – Brendan Larsen spent two hours in September snapping hundreds of photographs of the night sky over Mount Taranaki in the North Island.
Larsen, 51, says he set his camera up to take an unlimited number of eight-second-long shots, with a two-second gap in between each photo. “I left her running for two hours and captured 578 photos … That was the easy part.”
The hard part came next. Larsen spent about 40 hours layering the individual photos – each of which contained about 25 satellites – over one another, using Adobe Photoshop. Much of the time was spent painstakingly erasing stars, to reveal the satellites.
“I could start to see the pattern emerging and realised: ‘Wow, this looks really awesome.’ I knew if I carried on it would look even better and more impressive in terms of satellite numbers.”
The resulting image shows the sky inundated with about 1,400 satellites and 14,000 trails forming a dense crisscrossing pattern above the mountain.
When Larsen uploaded the image to his social media channels in mid-October, it quickly went viral, gaining him 15,000 new followers, clocking up tens of millions of views and igniting thousands of comments.
Some viewers dismissed the photo as AI – but Larsen understands why. “AI generating software is becoming so good it is becoming difficult to tell AI images from real images … especially if you’re not familiar with the location or with astrophotography,” he says. Still, it is “frustrating”.
It is also exasperating, he says, to see his image downloaded and recreated by AI, with obvious flaws.
In anticipation of the AI accusations and backlash, Larsen documented his creative process on video, which he hopes will also allow viewers to form an emotional connection to the landscape.
As a child Larsen was “absolutely blown away” by the number of stars over parts of rural New Zealand. But he has noticed an increase in light pollution and the number of satellites over the six years he has been photographing the sky.
“It’s interesting and fascinating seeing satellites, but it’s also disturbing,” he says.
“I’ve got about 10,000 comments on my Facebook page … nine out of 10 of the comments are like: ‘Wow, beautiful photo, but horrifying, terrifying and really concerning about what’s happening to the night sky.’”
About 16,000 working satellites are circling the planet, alongside tens of thousands of defunct spacecrafts, rocket parts and debris from payloads breaking up.
Studies have warned that metal particles from space activities – such as rocket launches and satellite reentries – could affect atmospheric chemistry and the ozone layer, while the UN has warned increased space activity poses risks to ground safety, darkness and astronomy.
While satellites don’t yet overwhelm the sky to the naked eye, Larsen worries about the future state of the night sky. He hopes his image will ignite debate and reflection over how satellites can be used responsibly.
“We can raise awareness, and through that get a groundswell of support for protecting the night sky.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Kathy Hochul Sails to Re-Election
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte, Katie Honan, Kaitlyn Schwanemann, and Jose Martinez
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York’s governor won reelection over Trump ally Bruce Blakeman as national Democrats hoped disaffection with the president would hand them control of Congress.
Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul locked down a second full term as the leader of New York State on Tuesday with a double-digit defeat of Republican Bruce Blakeman, the challenger backed by President Donald Trump, in a contest centered on affordability.
Within minutes of polls closing at 9 p.m., the Associated Press called the race for Hochul, who was leading with 77% of the vote over the Nassau County executive, with 12% of votes counted. That margin was expected to tighten as more votes are tallied.
Her easy win could be an early sign of what Democrats are hoping will be a blue wave for the party nationally, with voters revolting over soaring costs under Trump, who had trashed Hochul as a “disaster” who “may be the worst governor in the history of New York State.”
The first woman to serve as New York’s governor spent the last days of the campaign stumping for votes alongside Mayor Zohran Mamdani at the Queens Night Market and at an Astoria bar. But the alliance will now be tested by the mayor’s continuing push to raise taxes on the wealthy to fund housing and childcare in the city, hikes that Hochul has in part resisted.
At a West 166th Street polling place in Washington Heights, voter Marlon Feliz, 35, said she was influenced by the relationship between the mayor and the governor.
“Hochul is not my favorite, but I appreciate the partnership she has with Mamdani and I think it’s productive,” Feliz said.
Doorman Ricardo Guzman, 50, also said he was backing Hochul.
“We don’t have nobody else to be honest and she’s an intelligent woman,” said Guzman, who voted at Alianza Dominicana, a cultural center on West 166th Street. “And power to the women too, we need more women in powerful positions.”
Jose is The City Reporter's transportation reporter, covering the latest developments and policies impacting traffic and transit in New York.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Ballot Proposals on Public Space, Street Safety and More Pass in NYC
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Kaitlyn Schwanemann
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
In a sweep, all five proposals on the back of New Yorkers’ ballots passed by a large margin Tuesday evening, giving a boost to Mayor Zohran Mamdani in his first year in office.
With a majority of precincts reporting, each ballot proposal received at least 60% of the vote.
The questions, drawn up by the Mamdani administration’s government efficiency commission over the summer, concern use of public space, city contracting, street safety, building permitting and the city’s rainy day fund.
Each proposal is an amendment to the City Charter — the local constitution defining the powers of government. This year, most of them involved cutting some aspects of public review processes to get city projects approved quicker. The last proposal sets up a rainy day fund for the city.
Overall, city voters had cast close to 1.7 million Election Day ballots across the five boroughs as of 6 p.m., according to the city Board of Elections, on top of the nearly 700,000 votes recorded during nine days of early voting that ended Sunday.
Of all five boroughs, only one voted the five proposals down: Staten Island.
Among the five proposals, voters approved an amendment, Proposal 1, that will shorten the process of getting approved for projects using public space, including outdoor dining structures such as roadside cafes and street sheds. Applying for one can take up to eight months currently, but through the new application system, the process should be cut down to approximately two months.
They also said yes to Proposal 2 that gives a new power to the mayor to approve contracts over $5 million more quickly.
Proposal 3 concerns transportation projects and city-owned property.
Currently, the city Department of Transportation must notify local elected officials, community boards and the police department before implementing transit projects. Now, in some urgent situations, and when the DOT finds that the project is necessary, the agency can start working before notifying other groups.
Selling or leasing some city-owned property will also require less public reviews with the goal of speeding up sales: Instead of the seven-month process of getting transactions approved through multiple agencies, they’ll go through an expedited one, allowing different reviewers to go over it concurrently. The final review by the City Council is also removed from the process.
That proposal faced opposition from preservation groups who urged New Yorkers to vote against it for fear that it would take land away from the public with minimal review processes. Washington Heights resident Ken Roberts told The City Reporter outside of his poll site on Tuesday that he voted against it.
“I understand a lot of proposals were looking out for small businesses, but I know that if a big corporation wants something, they come in and they take it,” he said.
A Flatbush native, the 31-year-old added he’s especially skeptical about the public land aspect of the proposal after seeing deed theft strip people of their homes in Central Brooklyn.
Proposal 4 creates a centralized permitting hub for New Yorkers looking to get a construction project approved, among other changes aiming to speed up approvals for building projects.
And with Proposal 5, Mamdani’s giving the city a piggy bank, containing 12% of the city’s previous year’s tax revenue in the event of a recession.
Under the change, by May 2027, the Office of Management and Budget, alongside the Comptroller, will have to publish a plan for making deposits if the fund is below target.
The city can’t withdraw more than 50% of the fund, unless the mayor has a “compelling fiscal reason,” according to the efficiency commission.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-appeals-co.title: NY appeals court strikes down Nassau County's ban on transgender athletes
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-appeals-co.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-appeals-co.text:
A New York appeals court on Wednesday struck down Nassau County's ban on transgender girls and women participating in certain sports competitions at county-owned facilities, marking a turning point in a years-long legal battle.
The local law prohibited teams designated for women and girls from using county-owned sports facilities if they allowed transgender women and girls to compete.
The ban, backed by Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, had been subject to multiple legal challenges.
Both the New York Civil Liberties Union and Attorney General Letitia James filed separate lawsuits, arguing that the ban violated state laws protecting against discrimination based on gender identity.
Wednesday's ruling reversed a lower court decision that had upheld the ban. The appellate court found that Nassau County could not enact a local law that conflicted with the state's antidiscrimination protections.
The ban had already been temporarily blocked by the same appeals court in October 2025 while litigation continued.
But Nassau County did not consider the legal battle over.
“We are reviewing the decision with the intention to continue the appeals process,” county attorney Thomas Adams said.
That may be easier said than done, according to Gabriella Larios, an attorney at the NYCLU, which filed its lawsuit on behalf of the Long Island Roller Rebels, a women's roller derby league.
“The court made it abundantly clear that any attempt to ban transgender girls from public spaces across our state is prohibited by New York's anti-discrimination laws,” Larios told Gothamist. “So this is a massive victory, not just for trans people in sports, but for trans people everywhere.”
Larios said Nassau County could seek to appeal to New York's highest court, but there is no guarantee the court would agree to hear the case.
“It is an uphill battle for them, and they would be flying in the face of very clear state law in pursuing that appeal,” Larios said.
The Roller Rebels said they continue to welcome transgender women to join their league.
The appeals court also ruled in favor of the attorney general in a separate lawsuit challenging the same ban.
“Transgender athletes have the right to play on the court or field like everyone else,” James wrote on X Wednesday.

https://gothamist.com/news/four-takeaway.title: 4 takeaways after Democrats’ big night in New York
https://gothamist.com/news/four-takeaway.author: Walter Wuthmann, Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/four-takeaway.text:
Tuesday night’s blue tsunami fortified Democrats' dominance in New York — and boosted their influence around the country.
Gov. Kathy Hochul cruised to re-election over Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman with the widest margin for a New York governor since 2018, according to unofficial results. Democrats expanded their already large majorities in both the state Senate and state Assembly. And Mayor Zohran Mamdani saw his “affordability” message successfully deployed by Democrats to score historic wins from Texas to Maine.
Here are four takeaways from election night:
1) Hochul quieted the naysayers
The governor has spent the last four years dogged by criticism that she dragged down the Democratic ticket with her narrower-than-expected win in 2022, when she defeated Lee Zeldin by just six points. But Hochul silenced those critics Tuesday night, with unofficial results showing a 20-plus-point drubbing of Blakeman. That included winning Blakeman’s own Nassau County.
Hochul bet big on her key alliance with Mamdani, that delivering on their shared promise to expand free childcare would energize the party’s young, progressive base. At the same time she cast herself as a moderate and level-headed foil to President Donald Trump, pushing back on his hardline immigration enforcement and trade war with Canada.
Hochul now goes into her second full term with goodwill, a robust fundraising machine and a mandate. It remains to be seen whether her margin of victory changed her political calculus on top progressive priorities like taxing the rich.
2) The night also belonged to Mamdani
Over at Hochul’s victory party in midtown Manhattan, the star speaker of the night wasn’t the governor, but Mamdani.
Mamdani praised Hochul for embracing progressive policy ideas like universal childcare, and for her willingness to partner with him. But he drew a direct connection between Democrats’ triumphs across the country on a message of affordability and his own election last year.
“We have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to working people once again,” he said.
3) NY Republicans will be looking for a fresh playbook
There was an obvious sign New York Republicans knew they were in for a bad night at the Long Island banquet hall where Blakeman held his election party: no TVs broadcasting election results. Instead, Frank Sinatra’s “My Way” blasted over the speakers.
Afterward, Blakeman delivered a brief concession speech, and some attendees continued to chat and order drinks at the bar as if nothing happened. Others sank into denial. “There had to be some shenanigans,” said Rosalie Cancellarich of Floral Park. “Am I saying it was rigged? I don’t know.”
The party has a steep uphill climb back to power — Republicans haven’t won statewide office in New York since Gov. George Pataki was re-elected in 2002. The GOP playbook focused on crime and illegal immigration — which Rep. Mike Lawler and Blakeman both used — was a dud. The party is in for some soul-searching ahead of 2028.
4) All eyes on AOC
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said she would wait until after the Midterms to decide whether to run for president or Senate. Tuesday night’s blue tsunami undoubtedly strengthens a case that she has a path to the White House. The congresswoman previously said that Abdul El-Sayed’s election in Michigan would portend a huge win for progressive movement, and that it could "break open the entire political calculus in America.”
Adding to the intrigue, Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign released a memo on Tuesday touting her accomplishments and concluding that the congressmember has “proven herself to be one of the most effective voices in the country for America’s working class.“
Ocasio-Cortez stayed out of the spotlight on election night, but she’ll now be fielding a lot of questions about her future. She won her fifth term in office with a commanding margin over her Republican opponent Diamant Hysenaj.
Some of her constituents were already mulling whether it might be the last time she asks voters to return her to the House.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-wins-cour.title: NYC wins court fight over rollout of pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-wins-cour.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-wins-cour.text:
New York City has won a legal battle over its new tax on luxury second homes, potentially clearing a hurdle for Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to collect hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenue.
On Wednesday, a state appeals court reversed a lower court's ruling that had given property owners temporary relief from the new surcharge and dismissed their lawsuit against the tax.
The new pied-à-terre tax is intended to raise revenue from certain high-value properties used as second homes. While Mamdani has said the tax would help fulfill a campaign promise to tax the rich, its rollout has faced significant political and legal hurdles.
The tax has been subject to three separate legal challenges, including claims that the city's rollout would cause “mass confusion” for property owners and that the surcharge unfairly discriminates against wealthy residents.
In September, a Staten Island judge ordered the city to redo notices it had mailed to property owners who might be subject to the surcharge.
Wednesday's ruling marked a victory for the Mamdani administration against the lawsuit, filed by property owners who argued that the new pied-à-terre tax hadn't been properly rolled out.
The appeals court found that the property owners lacked standing to sue because they hadn't shown they suffered a concrete injury from the city's actions. The judges said receiving a tax notice or appearing on a public list of properties potentially subject to the surcharge was not enough to establish such harm.
The court did not determine whether the city had followed every procedure correctly, and the decision does not resolve separate legal challenges to the tax.
In a statement Wednesday, Mamdani celebrated the decision, saying the appeals court had rejected an attempt by wealthy property owners to avoid paying their fair share.
“The pied-a-terre surcharge asks those who can afford luxury second homes to contribute toward the safer streets, cleaner parks and essential public services that every New Yorker deserves,” Mamdani said.
He added that the city would continue defending the tax against ongoing legal challenges.
But Mamdani's claim that the tax will bring in $500 million a year remains in question. The city's Department of Finance has already granted more than 8,800 exemption requests.
Earlier this year, city Comptroller Mark Levine estimated that the tax could generate up to $380 million from roughly 11,200 properties.
David Brand contributed reporting.
This story has been updated with new information.

https://gothamist.com/news/cornell-alum-.title: Cornell alum, ‘Diddy’ prosecutor tapped to investigate allegations of campus gang rape
https://gothamist.com/news/cornell-alum-.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/cornell-alum-.text:
A former federal prosecutor who oversaw the sex trafficking case against Sean “Diddy” Combs is now leading an investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Wednesday that Jacqueline Kelly will serve as outside counsel in the high-profile case.
“The Office of the Attorney General is committed to a thorough investigation guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law,” James said in a statement, describing Kelly as a “seasoned prosecutor who has overseen numerous cases from investigation through trial.”
She added: “With her criminal legal experience, commitment to public service and judicial experience, I am confident that she will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
An unnamed former student filed a lawsuit in September accusing seven men of pressuring her to consume drugs and alcohol, then raping her while she was intoxicated. The civil complaint prompted protests at Cornell and reignited a decades-long debate about how to prevent sexual assault on college campuses, as well as how to address the limitations of New York’s sexual assault laws.
A spokesperson for the university said the administration fully supports a special prosecutor’s appointment and is committed to an independent review of how it has handled the case. The spokesperson, who declined to be named, also said the university supports efforts to change the state’s rape laws.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said last month she would remove Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten from the case after he declined to bring criminal charges. The governor signed an executive order that appointed the attorney general’s office to investigate the woman’s allegations. Kelly will lead that team, which James said is tasked with gathering evidence, reviewing records from previous investigations, interviewing witnesses and assessing whether any laws were broken.
“All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case,” Kelly said in a statement. “I look forward to lending my years of experience as a federal prosecutor to the Office of the Attorney General as we examine all available evidence.”
Kelly is a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, where she represents sexual assault victims, as well as companies facing investigations, according to a biography on the firm’s website.
Before going into private practice, she served as the first chief of the civil rights unit in the criminal division of the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York. In that role, she supervised the prosecutions of Combs, a doctor accused of sexually abusing dozens of patients, and the CEO of a clothing company charged with sex trafficking.
Kelly is a Cornell University alum and went to law school at Columbia University.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/france-polic.title: France’s Police Unions Are Throwing Their Weight Around
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/france-polic.author: Harrison Stetler
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/france-polic.text:
France’s Police Unions Are Throwing Their Weight Around
Amid protests in France, police unions are pushing for wage hikes and special legal privileges to cash in on the political capital they’ve built under Emmanuel Macron’s rule.
“The proportionate use of force should never be an obstacle to the job of restoring order,” French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote in a September 30 message to police chiefs. High schoolers across the country had only just launched a wave of campus blockages over poor learning conditions, in demonstrations that would soon morph into a full-fledged social crisis. In an October 6 government questions session, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu dismissed as “slander” any claims of systemic violence in policing and crowd-control tactics.
In the weeks since then, little has punctured the pressure for similar deference to the police. Certainly not the persistence of intense protests — and, in some cases, rioting — which have instead strengthened the reflex among France’s political class to celebrate muscular policing as the lone rampart against disorder. Nor have the numerous examples of people, often minors, being maimed or otherwise severely injured by the arsenal of “nonlethal” weapons at the police’s disposal.
Then again, political authorities have ample reason to be wary. “I accuse!” wrote Fabien Vanhemelryk in a statement published after the most intense day of protests and looting on October 17, reprising the famous declaration from Émile Zola’s 1898 public letter on the Dreyfus affair. For Vanhemelryk — leader of France’s largest police union by membership, the hard-right Alliance Police Nationale — the deepening crisis was the result of “years of permissiveness, political cowardice, and concessions.”
From the police’s point of view, the turbulence of recent weeks will most likely stand as a reminder that the state’s reliance on them gives them leverage. As Emmanuel Macron’s presidency enters its twilight, police unions are waging their own offensive, demanding salary increases and bonuses and looking to secure a raft of other pet projects. They hope to reap the rewards of their importance not only within the powerful Interior Ministry but also in the practice of government that has come to define Macron’s near-decade in office, as policing has become a key crutch during critical periods of political and social tension.
It’s an understatement to say that French organized labor has seen better days. Police unions offer perhaps the most notable exception. But the Interior Ministry is not your average employer, and police unions aren’t your average professional constituency.
Material Demands, Symbolic Rewards
In a dramatic show of force this past September 15, upward of ten thousand off-duty police officers descended Paris’s Champs-Élysées to the National Assembly, with protesters hauling dummy coffins along the capital’s central artery in protest of low wages and strenuous work conditions. The demonstration was called by the hard-right Alliance Police Nationale and UN1TÉ, the two largest unions among rank-and-file officers. They are pushing for some €500 million in new funding, allowing for salary increases and bonuses in addition to around a thousand new hires.
The Interior Ministry has already been among the winners of the Macron years in financing terms.
In 2023, police unions won special carve-outs in Macron’s unpopular increase in the pension age to sixty-four, a reform suspended during last winter’s budget negotiations in parliament. Adopted in 2023 and designed to extend over five years, a special budgeting law earmarked €15 billion extra funding to the Interior Ministry, adding to the baseline annual appropriations, which rose from some €22 billion in 2022 to over €34 billion in 2026. (Compare that to the €4 billion in low-rate loans to local authorities for school renovations, which the government rolled out in late October as a concession to student protests.)
Still, with Macronist Premier Lecornu vying for tens of billions of euros worth of savings for the 2027 budget, Interior Minister Nuñez can only go so far in his attempt to satisfy police unions’ demands.
But the police want more than just financial concessions. In a controversial bill currently awaiting final approval from parliament, police unions hope to claim a strategic win in one of their long-running campaigns: erecting legal shields to protect police officers who use their firearms from investigation and eventual criminal scrutiny.
The title of the proposed law calls it a “presumption of legitimate defense,” but to the bill’s critics it’s better known as the “permit to kill.” According to the legislation, which sailed through the lower-house National Assembly in July, police who use their firearms “are presumed to have acted” in accordance with the law, unless evidence can be shown to justify an investigation. To critics, that amounts to a tautology opening major holes in the rule of law, hamstringing oversight by putting the onus on victims of police violence to prove possible wrongdoing.
For Laurent Bonelli, a sociologist of security policy, the government finds itself in a genuine structural dilemma, caught between stretched resources, an acquired dependence on stiff policing in moments of social unrest, and palpable frustration among average troopers.
“There’s only so much money to give, so what can be done?” Bonelli told Jacobin. “That’s where symbolic rewards come in. And a classic example of that is this bill on so-called legitimate self-defense.”
Presumed Guilty
Will a “legitimate defense” bill be rolled into an eventual postcrisis compromise for a police force exhausted as this fall’s social unrest stretches on? The current push for greater immunity for the police first gained momentum during a series of events not wholly unlike the current one. Over summer 2023, the fatal police shooting of seventeen-year-old Nahel Merzouk in the Paris suburb of Nanterre kicked off days of protests and rioting that fanned accusations of systemic racism and violence among the police.
In several respects, the Nahel crisis provided the template for this fall’s conflict over law and order. In an incendiary public declaration that summer, the Alliance Police Nationale and UNSA police unions referred to rioters as “wild hordes” and “pests,” demanding a swift restoration of order. In less-than-veiled threats to political authorities, they also called for “concrete measures of legal protection” for the officer responsible for Merzouk’s killing.
While the legislation does not make an explicit principle of police irresponsibility, Nathalie Tehio, president of the Ligue des droits de l’Homme, warns that the greater risk is in raising the threshold needed to obtain an investigation into police wrongdoing. “So long as the [use of a firearm] is presumed to be legal, there will quite simply be no investigation,” she told Jacobin. “What that means is that the victim, or the family of the victim, will have to bring proof to the contrary.”
Shielding police from scrutiny has been a leitmotif of security policy for some time. During Macron’s first term, his government tried to ban the filming and photographing of active-duty police officers. Legislation approved this past spring authorizes turning off video cameras during temporary police custody, a change that legal observers fear could weaken oversight over interrogation practices. The law also sought to anonymize the identities of police officers appearing in judicial proceedings, though that was struck down by the Constitutional Council.
All signs are pointing toward what Tehio called the “construction of police immunity.” The contrast could not be more striking when compared to the evolution of the law as it applies for everyone else.
One piece of legislation to emerge out of this fall’s social crisis is the “rioters-pay” law, which is currently being fast-tracked through parliament thanks to consensus support between the Macronist center and the far right. The bill stipulates legal responsibility — and potential financial liabilities — for individuals accused of having “wittingly participated” in a grouping that including acts of rioting and vandalism. A presumption of guilt, you might say, for participating in demonstrations that turn awry.
Magical Solutions
One-upmanship between the police forces and political authorities eager to satisfy a critical arm of the state is a dynamic that long predates Macron’s presidency.
Part of this power is due to the nature of the force itself. France’s National Police is rigidly centralized, making it practically immune to local control and oversight. Concrete practices have also helped drill in the clientelist influence of police unions with a staunch ideological bent. “Comanagement,” granting unions considerable say over things like internal promotions, hardens their influence over the workforce — and marks the Interior Ministry off from many other state administrations.
One immediate bugbear among the lower echelons is that superiors were granted a considerable salary increase this year. Police unions are looking to shore up support among their bases before public sector workers hold professional elections in December, with the police counting among the most unionized workforces in the country.
But the greatest leverage that hard-line police unions have is structural, drawing on their position as a critical state service in a society on edge. Macron and his predecessors have long developed a dependence on muscular policing to contain conflicts over political decisions, whether the labor law reforms of the mid-2010s, the 2023 pension drive, or the anger with the education system that erupted these last few weeks. From enforcing immigration law to handling more quotidian social problems like drug use and extreme mental health cases, the “forces of order,” as France’s police are often called, offer a one-size-fits-all solution.
“To many in the political class, the police has come to appear as something of a magic solution for resolving the consequences of an increasingly unequal society,” said Bonelli, the sociologist. “It should come as little surprise that the police as an institution would try to capitalize on its weight in the ongoing battles within the state itself.”
Tensions over policing are so fraught that it’s barely ever asked whether an institution that separates itself so dramatically from the surrounding society is acting in its own best interests.
“Promising impunity is in reality to abandon the police — which is indeed in need of many urgent reforms — to those who are pushing for permanent confrontation with the general public,” the minority Interior Ministry branch of the national Confédération Générale du Travail (CGT) union warned in a January press release, when the government threw its support behind the “legitimate defense” law.
Doubts like these are increasingly inaudible, however, as a radicalized majority goes on the offensive. In doing so, they’re also pulling back the veil on what is starting to look to many like a state within the state.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Christie’s first Abu Dhabi art auction makes $8.9m
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Razmig Bedirian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Christie’s first fine-art auction in Abu Dhabi has realised more than $8.9m, with several works fetching six figures and surpassing their original estimates.
The auction, titled Mawasim, was held last week (1 November) at The Abu Dhabi Edition. It marked the 20th anniversary of Christie’s first auction in the United Arab Emirates.
Topping the sale was Variations on the Hexagon (2006) by Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian. The work was estimated between $150,000 and $250,000. It sold for $844,800, after almost seven minutes of bidding.
The mirror mosaic panel was commissioned for the opening of the Jameel Gallery at the Victoria and Albert Museum.
“It is a magnificent work of exceptional historical significance,” said Ridha Moumni, chairman of Christie’s Middle East and Africa.
“Farmanfarmaian is undoubtedly one of the most talented female artists in the region. This particular work, however, is especially spectacular.”
Other works that led the sale included Fahrelnissa Zeid’s Composition (1948-1949), which fetched $524,800. Her Endless Thoughts, painted in the late 1970s, sold for $486,400.
Ali Banisadr’s Homo Deus (2018), meanwhile, sold for $512,000, as did Faisel Laibi Sahi’s Baghdad Café (The Coffee Shop) (2016), which set a record for the artist. The painting, which measures six metres in length, is the largest by the Iraqi painter to go under the hammer.
Mahmoud Saïd’s Portrait de Princesse Fadia (Portrait of Princess Fadia)(1952) was sold for $486,400. Paul Guiragossian’s Noces (Wedding), an oil-on-masonite work created between 1958 and 1959, fetched $486,400. The sale marked a record for the medium for the artist, as did Samia Halaby’s Yesterday (1978), which sold for $358,400. The painting is a prime example of Halaby’s work from the 70s, when she developed her idiosyncratic approach to geometric abstraction.
Overall, Christie’s announced nine auction records, including for Jellal Ben Abdallah, whose Les Musiciennes (The Female Musicians) (1973) sold for $204,800 against an estimate between $100,000 and $150,000. Juliana Seraphim’s Femme Fleur (Flower Woman) (1973) also set a record, selling for $83,200. It had been estimated between $25,000 and $35,000.
Mawasim also marked the auction debut for several artists, including Nabil Kanso, Rami Farook, Fatma Lootah and Afra Al Dhaheri.
Moumni said that the fine-art auction of modern and contemporary works from the Middle East and North Africa was “the strongest results since 2015.
“It sends a very strong signal to the market and underscores the growing demand for art from the [region],” he said. “The results also demonstrate the significant presence of artists of Iranian origin in the market. We witnessed particularly spirited bidding for these artists, which was very exciting to see.”
Works by Emirati artists, such as Najat Makki and Hassan Sharif, have also “performed exceptionally well,” Moumni said.
Makki’s Emirates of Love (2025) sold for $28,160, whereas a painting from Sharif’s celebrated Press Conference series sold for $83,200.
“We were delighted to see works by all these UAE artists supported by both local and international collectors,” Moumni said. “There is still work to be done in further developing their market value, but the results were a truly wonderful surprise and a testament to the vitality of the UAE’s creative art scene.”
The auction, Moumni said, attracted a “healthy mix” of private collectors and institutional buyers. Interestingly, 30 per cent of participants were Generation Z and the millennial generations. There were also several first-time bidders.
“Thirty-seven per cent of participants were new to Christie’s, representing an encouraging expansion of our collector base,” Moumni said.
Sunday’s auction was the climactic conclusion to a week-long exhibition at The Abu Dhabi Edition, which presented the works featured in the Mawasim auction. The works came from private as well as institutional collections, such as from the Dalloul Collection and the Trad family collection in Beirut and the Barjeel Art Foundation in Sharjah.
Christie’s first auction in the UAE was held in 2006 in Dubai, at a time when the city’s arts scene was at a pivotal moment. New galleries and institutions were opening up and the city was preparing to host the DIFC Gulf Art Fair, which would then be rebranded at Art Dubai.
As a 20th anniversary auction, Mawasim was held in Abu Dhabi during a similar landmark moment. The UAE capital is preparing to host its first Frieze in November and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is meanwhile gearing up for its December opening.
“It was particularly important for us to present this anniversary auction here in Abu Dhabi, a city that is home to some of the region’s most significant museums, with several more important cultural institutions set to open in the coming years.”

https://hyperallergic.com/shape-your-art.title: Shape Your Artistic Future at UC Davis: The Maria Manetti Shrem Art Studio MFA Program
https://hyperallergic.com/shape-your-art.author: University of California, Davis
https://hyperallergic.com/shape-your-art.text:
Shape Your Artistic Future at UC Davis: The Maria Manetti Shrem Art Studio MFA Program
Generously funded, renowned faculty and visiting artists, spacious studios, and an exhibition at the Manetti Shrem Museum of Art.
Supported by a $14 million endowment from Maria Manetti Shrem, the critically engaged Art Studio Program at UC Davis offers generous funding for incoming graduate students. With exceptional opportunities for fellowships and awards, the recently renamed Maria Manetti Shrem Art Studio MFA provides students with spacious private studios so they can thrive in a vibrant, creative community as they work closely with internationally renowned faculty and visiting artists.
As a research university, UC Davis provides MFA students with the opportunity to engage in intensive artistic work and interdisciplinary research while interacting with artists and scholars across campus. The program is committed to delivering an innovative educational curriculum to prepare graduates for professional public engagement in the arts, including arts education, exhibition and curatorial practices, and community-based work. The culmination of two years of study is presented in a thesis exhibition at the Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art.
Three visiting artist programs offer students first-hand exposure to artists, critics, and curators of note: The California Studio, Betty Jean and Wayne Thiebaud Lecture, and Visiting Artist Lectures Series. A select list of recent speakers includes Njideka Akunyili Crosby, Cecilia Alemani, Xu Bing, Helen Molesworth, Wangechi Mutu, Tania Candiani, Raúl De Nieves, Latoya Ruby Frazier, Lynn Hershman Leeson, Kota Ezawa, Sky Hopinka, Amelia Jones, and Hito Steyerl, among other innovative artists.
The Maria Manetti Shrem Art Studio MFA Program provides substantial financial support through paid teaching assistant positions, awards, and fellowships. UC Davis partners with prestigious professional programs, including the Headlands Center for the Arts, the Dedalus Foundation, Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture, and Tropical Lab residency in Singapore.
For more information, visit arts.ucdavis.edu.
RSVP for the Virtual MFA Open House at 12pm (PST) on Friday, December 4, 2026.
The deadline to apply is January 5, 2027. Submit an application to arts.ucdavis.edu.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ba.title: Art Collector Barbara Jakobson’s Famous Upper East Side Townhouse On the Market for $9 Million
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ba.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ba.text:
Barbara Jakobson was a monumental force in the New York art world for over 60 years, serving as an influential collector, a fierce patron, and a longtime trustee of New York’s Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). She also had a sharp, curatorial eye and a truly singular style. That is perhaps best evident in her home on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, which doubled as her own ever-evolving gallery from the mid-1960s until her death in 2025.
“I see the house as a vessel for an ongoing autobiographical exercise,” Jakobson told Curbed in a 2021 interview. “I keep the transformation as proof of life.”
The five-story townhouse along East 74th Street in the Lenox Hill neighborhood was built in 1910 and later expanded by architect John Kingsland in 1956. Prior to Jakobson, filmmaker Elia Kazan lived in the 20-foot-wide abode while directing East of Eden (1955) and Splendor in the Grass (1961). Hollywood stars including James Dean, Natalie Wood, and Marlon Brando reportedly visited then.
	Jakobson, a native New Yorker, bought the pad in 1965 and lived there for nearly six decades. During that time, she welcomed New York’s creative set, such as artists Jasper Johns, Andy Warhol, Cy Twombly, and Robert Rauschenberg. After her death last summer, the property was brought to market in April 2026 for $9.8 million. It received a price cut of over $800,000 before reaching its current asking price of $8.99 million. Leslie Hirsch, Edward Joseph, Howard Morrel, and Benjamin Anderson of Christie’s International Real Estate New York hold the listing.
Nicknamed “the Squirrel House” on account of the bronze squirrel sculptures at the entrance, the home is whimsical yet refined. Red lacquered doors open to 6,000 square feet of stylish interiors, with eight bedrooms and six full bathrooms spread throughout.
A grand entry hall with triple arches and custom wallpaper by artist Peter Halley leads to a parlor floor featuring a formal living room, a gallery, and a salon with a wood-burning fireplace. A staircase—on which Jakobson was photographed for Vogue—spirals down to a spectacular double-height great room, where an outline of Frank Stella’s 1971 Felsztyn III remains. It once hung there but was sold in 2005 at a Christie’s auction featuring works from Jakobson’s collection. Glass doors lead out to a private 350-square-foot garden.
The guest bedrooms, including two junior suites with dressing rooms and en suites, sprawl across the next two levels. The primary suite, meanwhile, covers the entire top floor, offering a light-filled private lounge for reading, relaxing, or even pondering art.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Mais de 6 mil mulheres procuram Defensoria Pública no DF; violência continua após fim de relacionamentos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Cruz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Às vésperas do Dia Internacional pela Eliminação da Violência contra as Mulheres, celebrado no dia 25 deste mês, dados da Defensoria Pública do Distrito Federal (DPDF) mostram como a violência doméstica pode continuar mesmo depois do fim de um relacionamento. Disputas pela guarda dos filhos, falta de pagamento de pensão alimentícia e retenção de patrimônio estão entre as situações enfrentadas por mulheres que procuram assistência jurídica no DF.
Entre janeiro e julho de 2026, o Núcleo de Promoção e Defesa dos Direitos das Mulheres (Nudem) realizou 6.683 atendimentos e protocolou 276 ações judiciais. Do total de atendimentos, 1.945 foram relacionados ao Direito de Família, equivalente a 29,1%. Outros 1.628 envolveram medidas protetivas de urgência e situações de descumprimento, correspondentes a 24,4%.
Os dados fazem parte do relatório de atividades do Nudem, divulgado pela Defensoria nesta sexta-feira (6). O levantamento mostra que o enfrentamento à violência também passa por garantir condições de sobrevivência, autonomia financeira, moradia e proteção aos filhos.
Para a coordenadora do Nudem e defensora pública Rafaela Mitre, as demandas acompanhadas mostram que a violência está associada a diferentes situações de vulnerabilidade. “Os casos apresentados no relatório mostram como a violência se combina com falta de renda, insegurança de moradia, adoecimento e ausência de apoio para cuidar dos filhos. Por isso, proteger uma mulher também significa criar condições para que ela possa se sustentar e reconstruir sua vida com segurança”, explica a coordenadora.
Violência que continua
Entre os atendimentos relacionados ao Direito de Família, as ações de alimentos lideraram os registros, com 503 casos, seguidas pelas demandas de guarda, com 502. Também foram contabilizados 235 atendimentos relacionados a divórcio, 142 a união estável e 123 a execução de alimentos.
Na avaliação de Mitre, essas demandas não podem ser compreendidas apenas como conflitos familiares. “As demandas de guarda, pensão alimentícia e divórcio são parte fundamental da proteção das mulheres, porque a violência pode continuar mesmo depois da separação. Os vínculos familiares e econômicos podem ser utilizados para praticar novas violências, como deixar de pagar a pensão para comprometer a subsistência da mulher e dos filhos, usar a convivência com as crianças para ameaçar ou vigiar a mãe, reter patrimônio ou criar obstáculos ao encerramento da relação”, afirma.
A defensora destaca que a formalização do divórcio e a regulamentação da guarda, da convivência e da pensão alimentícia são medidas importantes para reduzir os espaços de controle e estabelecer regras que considerem a segurança da mulher e dos filhos.
O relatório também apresenta casos acompanhados pelo Nudem que ilustram a relação entre violência patrimonial e dependência econômica. Em um deles, uma mulher que havia criado uma empresa de locação de brinquedos infantis teve equipamentos e veículos retidos pelo ex-companheiro, que descumpriu uma medida protetiva patrimonial. Os bens eram a principal fonte de renda da família.
Sem recursos para manter a própria subsistência, a mulher sofreu um Acidente Vascular Cerebral (AVC) enquanto relatava as violências na Delegacia da Mulher. A Defensoria ingressou com pedido de alimentos compensatórios. A liminar concedeu o pagamento provisório de 1,5 salário mínimo mensal, e a decisão foi proferida cinco dias depois do ajuizamento da ação.
Dependência econômica
O relatório aponta que a atuação do Nudem envolve demandas que ultrapassam o atendimento jurídico. Entre janeiro e julho, foram registrados 325 atendimentos psicossociais e 308 encaminhamentos à rede de proteção e a outros setores.
A equipe própria do núcleo é composta por uma assistente social e uma psicóloga, que trabalham de forma integrada à assistência jurídica. Entre as atividades estão acolhimento, avaliação de vulnerabilidades, identificação de fatores de risco, elaboração de relatórios técnicos e encaminhamento para serviços de saúde, assistência social e acolhimento institucional.
Para Rafaela Mitre, a dificuldade de romper o ciclo de violência está relacionada à combinação de diferentes fatores, que muitas vezes atingem as mulheres simultaneamente. “Os obstáculos envolvem medo, ameaças, dependência econômica, sofrimento psicológico, isolamento e preocupação com os filhos. Muitas mulheres precisam enfrentar tudo isso ao mesmo tempo, sem moradia segura, renda própria ou uma rede de apoio”, diz a defensora.
A defensora também chama atenção para as formas de violência que não envolvem necessariamente agressões físicas. “É fundamental ampliar a compreensão de que a violência não começa com a agressão física. Humilhações, isolamento, controle do dinheiro, vigilância e ameaças muitas vezes são naturalizados ou confundidos com ciúme e cuidado, mas já são formas de violência e podem se agravar ao longo do tempo”, afirma.
Rede de proteção e acesso aos serviços
Além da assistência individual, o Nudem desenvolve ações para aproximar os serviços de proteção das mulheres em regiões periféricas e rurais. Uma das iniciativas é o projeto Entrelace, realizado desde março de 2025, que já alcançou aproximadamente 500 mulheres no Distrito Federal.
O projeto promove rodas de conversa, atividades de educação em direitos, orientação jurídica e atendimento psicossocial. As ações são organizadas a partir de demandas identificadas por lideranças comunitárias, com participação de instituições parceiras. A iniciativa busca facilitar o acesso à informação sobre a Lei Maria da Penha, medidas protetivas, direitos familiares e autonomia econômica. O núcleo também realiza capacitações para profissionais da Defensoria e da rede de atendimento, com o objetivo de qualificar o acolhimento.
Para a coordenadora, um dos principais desafios é garantir que os diferentes serviços funcionem de maneira integrada e que os encaminhamentos resultem em atendimento efetivo.
“A mulher não pode ser responsável por articular a própria proteção, percorrendo sozinha diferentes instituições para conseguir segurança, moradia, assistência social, saúde e orientação jurídica”, afirma Rafaela Mitre.
O relatório também registra o monitoramento de decisões de indeferimento de medidas protetivas e reclamações relacionadas ao atendimento. A partir desse acompanhamento, o núcleo busca identificar obstáculos à proteção, aperfeiçoar os pedidos judiciais e reunir informações para fundamentar a atuação institucional.
A avaliação de risco é outra frente de trabalho. O Nudem utiliza o Formulário Nacional de Avaliação de Risco (Fonar) para identificar fatores associados ao feminicídio e à reincidência da violência, subsidiando pedidos de proteção e estratégias de segurança construídas com as mulheres atendidas.
“As medidas protetivas salvam vidas. Garantir sua efetividade exige acesso rápido, avaliação cuidadosa do risco, acompanhamento e resposta aos descumprimentos. Essa proteção deve estar articulada às políticas de moradia, renda, saúde e cuidado com os filhos, criando condições concretas para romper o ciclo de violência”, conclui a coordenadora do Nudem e defensora pública Rafaela Mitre.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Indígenas denunciam corte de água que abastece comunidade no Parque do Mate, em Campo Largo
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Karina Ernsen
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O curso de água que abastece a comunidade indígena do Parque do Mate, em Campo Largo (PR), na Região Metropolitana de Curitiba, está seco há cinco meses. As famílias da retomada indígena kaingang, que ocuparam o espaço desde 2022, denunciam a irregularidade do abastecimento hídrico. Esse córrego existe desde o antigo engenho, no fim do século 19.
O Parque Histórico do Mate, também conhecido como Antigo Engenho de Mate da Rondinha, é um remanescente da economia ervateira paranaense. Construído por volta de 1870, o conjunto preserva a tecnologia dos engenhos hidráulicos que utilizavam a água do Rio Rondinha, desviada por um canal, para movimentar a roda d’água e acionar o maquinário.
Tombado pelo Estado do Paraná em 10 de julho de 1968 (Processo 19/68) e pelo Instituto do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico Nacional (IPHAN) em 1985, o local é um patrimônio histórico. Após anos de abandono pelo poder público, encontrou na comunidade indígena kaingang da aldeia Kógunh Já Má seus atuais guardiões.
O açude que abastecia o parque e a comunidade está seco. A água vem do Rio Rondinha, através de um desvio artificial que abastecia o antigo engenho. Esse desvio, que alimentou o desenvolvimento econômico do Paraná, foi interrompido, deixando a comunidade indígena sem acesso à água.
Omissão que enfraquece a luta indígena
O cacique Jafé Cassemiro, liderança da aldeia, relata que, quando chegaram, o açude estava cheio de peixes e o rio alimentava não apenas a comunidade com comida, mas também com lazer. “A água descia para o açude. As crianças se banhavam, pescavam, a gente irrigava as hortas. Agora não dá nem para jogar uma linha de anzol”, lamenta.
Ele conta que a interrupção não é a primeira, mas tem sido a mais longa e dolorida. Vivem ali 38 famílias, incluindo mais de 60 crianças.
O abandono do Parque do Mate antecede a ocupação indígena. De acordo com a professora Emi Lorenzetti, do curso de Tecnologia em Agroecologia do Instituto Federal do Paraná (IFPR) – campus Campo Largo, o local estava inativo e sem manutenção há mais de uma década, com a estrutura se deteriorando.
Desde 2022, os indígenas que ocuparam o local têm mantido o território. A comunidade realiza a limpeza da área, o plantio árvores nativas, como as araucárias, e a manutenção do espaço. Jafé relata o acordo feito com o governo para assumir o cuidado com o espaço: “A gente fez várias reuniões com o estado, com o município, em que eles afirmaram [a permissão] de ficar aqui, com um termo de compromisso, de cuidar aqui do Parque do Mate”, explica.
Enquanto cuidam do território, sofrem com o corte de água, que atinge diretamente a segurança alimentar e nutricional da comunidade. “Sem essa fonte, fica inviável qualquer projeto, até mesmo para a sustentabilidade do local”, afirma a professora Lorenzetti, que acompanha a retomada indígena desde o início. Ela lembra que os peixes que habitam o lago estão morrendo na lama: “Onde há água, há vida. E hoje a comunidade está sendo privada disso.”
O que diz o poder público?
Em janeiro de 2026, o Centro de Apoio Operacional das Promotorias de Justiça de Proteção aos Direitos Humanos do Ministério Público do Paraná (MPPR) fez uma visita institucional à aldeia Kókhun Já Má, no Parque do Mate, a convite da própria comunidade. A visita teve como objetivo conhecer as condições de moradia e planejar ações futuras de infraestrutura coletiva, incluindo saneamento, iluminação e acesso à água e energia elétrica.
Na ocasião, foi produzido um relato formal ao órgão com a necessidade de regularização do fornecimento de água e energia elétrica para as moradias. As demandas foram registradas pelo MPPR para análise e eventual articulação institucional.
Procurado pelo Brasil de Fato Paraná, o MPPR esclareceu que a 4ª Promotoria de Justiça de Campo Largo, responsável pelo acompanhamento da questão hídrica, tem um procedimento administrativo em curso para monitorar os impactos ambientais na aldeia. No entanto, segundo o órgão, “até o momento não chegou à Promotoria notícia relacionada ao citado esvaziamento de um açude devido ao bloqueio de um desvio do Rio Rondinha.”
O MPPR informou ainda que, na 1ª Promotoria de Justiça, tramita o Procedimento Administrativo nº MPPR-0023.23.000778-5, que acompanha as tratativas de formalização da reivindicação territorial e outras diligências estruturantes.
A prefeitura de Campo Largo informou que o caso é de responsabilidade do governo do Paraná e do Instituto Água e Terra (IAT), entidade autárquica vinculada à Secretaria do Desenvolvimento Sustentável e do Turismo.
Procurado, o IAT respondeu, em nota, que localizou no sistema oficial três “Declarações de Uso Insignificante” para captação superficial no Arroio Rondinha, afluente do Rio Verde, destinadas à irrigação de olerícolas. Segundo o IAT, a licença é para “pequenas parcelas de água” e uma equipe de fiscalização deve ir ao local verificar irregularidades. O órgão não explica como captações “insignificantes” teriam o poder de secar um açude histórico e deixar a comunidade sem água.
A atuação da Funai e o Grupo de Trabalho
O indigenista Mauro Leno Silvestrin, servidor da Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) e que acompanha o caso, esclarece que a situação do Parque do Mate é tratada por um Grupo de Trabalho (GT) interinstitucional, que reúne diversas secretarias estaduais, órgãos federais (como o próprio IAT, a Funai e a Defensoria Pública da União), o MPPR, a Defensoria Pública do Paraná, a Universidade Federal do Paraná (UFPR) e o IFPR. Segundo ele, todas as decisões relativas ao parque e à comunidade indígena passam por essa instância colegiada.
Silvestrin explica que é necessário um processo de desassoreamento do rio para restabelecer o fluxo da água — o que já foi encaminhado pelo GT. A execução dos mutirões de limpeza depende da compra de Equipamentos de Proteção Individual (EPIs) para garantir a segurança dos voluntários.
Segundo ele, a Secretaria de Cultura do Estado e o IAT ficaram responsáveis por tentar adquirir esses equipamentos, e a Defesa Civil foi consultada sobre a possibilidade de doação. “Estamos aguardando a compra desses equipamentos de proteção para poder fazer os mutirões e desassorear o rio”, afirma o indigenista.
Jefé conta que as famílias já subiram o córrego para desassorear o curso em duas ocasiões, mas que, dessa vez, o poder público pediu para a comunidade aguardar medidas do Estado.
Como se deu a denúncia
A denúncia sobre a seca do açude que abastecia o parque foi feita pelos próprios indígenas durante um encontro da Rede EcoAção Socioambiental RMC, projeto executado pelo Centro de Formação Urbano Rural Irmã Araújo (Cefuria), em parceria com a Itaipu Binacional.
A rede aplica questionários e se reúne com catadores, agricultores familiares, povos originários, comunidades tradicionais, organizações da sociedade civil e instituições de ensino. A partir dos dados, um dos objetivos da iniciativa é consolidar “diagnósticos participativos” e articular comunidades e grupos da Grande Curitiba.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘As plataformas digitais são dos bilionários, mas temos que disputá-las’, diz Sandra Bitencourt
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Como as plataformas digitais mudaram a disputa política, o jornalismo e a democracia no Brasil? A pergunta atravessa “Redes e rumos: jornalismo e sociedade transformada na era dos distúrbios informacionais”, livro de Sandra Bitencourt lançado na Feira do Livro de Porto Alegre.
A obra, organizada em seis partes, discute as transformações nas relações entre jornalismo, política e democracia no momento de expansão das plataformas digitais. Entre os temas estão as plataformas como arena pública, a “política das emoções” e a “batalha pela verdade” em tempos de desinformação.
Na conversa, a entrevistada analisa o Brasil que saiu das urnas em 2026. Ela comenta a atuação do “Exército do Lula”, comandado pelo deputado André Janones, e a ocupação das redes na reta final da eleição. Também fala sobre o papel do jornalismo na cena política.
Sandra Bitencourt é jornalista e doutora em Comunicação Social pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).
O podcast De Fato é uma produção do Brasil de Fato RS em parceria com o SindBancários de Porto Alegre e Região. Todo sábado, um entrevistado ou uma entrevistada debaterá os principais fatos em destaque no Rio Grande do Sul, no Brasil e no mundo.
