https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Why Trump wants UFC chief Dana White as his new White House press secretary
The two have business ties going back decades, and White has helped Trump reach out to younger voters.
Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) chief executive Dana White is set to meet United States President Donald Trump on Monday to discuss taking the job of White House press secretary.
Trump announced the offer on Saturday, days after his Republican Party suffered record losses in midterm elections. In a post on Truth Social, the president praised White as “a violent Fighter and Warrior” who would bring along leading UFC fighters as “assistants” to “defend us against the Lunatic Left”.
But it remains unclear how serious the offer is. In a news conference on Saturday, White confirmed he would travel to Washington, DC, to meet with Trump. But he also signalled concerns about his existing workload.
“I got a lot of jobs already,” White, a Trump ally and donor, said. “We have a meeting on Monday, so I’m sure I’ll have more to talk about after that.”
White also posted a photo to Instagram Stories of himself standing behind the White House podium. Its caption read, “On to the next chapter.”
Trump, too, posted his own AI-generated memes about the potential hire.
On Sunday, he shared an animated cartoon of White in the White House briefing room, flanked by a row of fighters. One of them body-slams a reporter who asks, “Is Trump a threat to democracy?”
The press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia’s brief tenure ended last month. She left the post within five days of being hired after facing criticism that she presented herself as a lawyer without being licensed in the US.
Zacharia succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down from the role at the end of August, citing the needs of her growing family.
But why is the head of a mixed martial arts franchise being considered for the new public face of the Trump administration? Al Jazeera explains that and more in this brief explainer.
Who is Dana White?
A former bouncer and small-time boxer, White began his career as a businessman by opening a boxing gym in Boston where he trained other fighters.
He later moved to Las Vegas, where he continued to run gyms and manage emerging fighters.
The UFC was founded in 1993, at about the time White resettled in Las Vegas. The organisation sought to offer an arena for fighters from different disciplines – from boxing to wrestling to jujitsu – to face each other in “no-holds-barred” competition.
In 2001, White convinced two casino magnate friends to buy the UFC for $2m and name him president. Since then, he has built the company up through big fights and lucrative pay-per-view television deals.
He has been a fixture in the UFC in the more than two decades since. White has been credited with turning the fledgling franchise into a global business that brought mixed martial arts into the mainstream.
In 2016, the UFC was sold for $4bn, and in 2023, White became its CEO after a merger with World Wrestling Entertainment valued at some $21bn.
How do Trump and White know each other?
White has been a longtime supporter of Trump, appearing by his side at campaign events for nearly a decade.
Trump, in turn, has a history of hosting UFC fights as far back as 2001. At the time, UFC was struggling against criticism that the sport was too violent.
White had just taken up his position as UFC president, and he and Trump came to an agreement to host that year’s UFC championship at Trump’s Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey.
The next year, the UFC returned to the Taj Mahal.
Speaking in support of Trump at the 2016 Republican National Convention, White recalled how the early collaboration helped open doors for the UFC, making other venues more accessible.
“No arenas wanted us,” White said at the time. “This guy reached out, and he’s always been a friend to me.”
The 2016 election cycle would mark Trump’s first successful bid for public office. In 2018, White was invited to visit the White House during Trump’s inaugural term as president.
During the 2020 elections, White again endorsed Trump as he sought a second term as president. White also donated $1m to Trump’s campaign and was a key speaker at the Republican Party’s national convention that year.
“I’ve known this man for 20 years. We’ve actually become even closer since he’s become the president of the United States,” White told supporters at a rally in Colorado. “He’s a fighter. He loves this country. He’s doing great things for this country, and we’ve got to win this election again.”
Trump lost the 2020 race to Democrat Joe Biden. But four years later, in 2024, he launched another re-election bid, and successfully won a second term.
During that campaign, Trump credited White with helping him connect with younger voters.
“He introduced me to people I never heard of, young kids,” Trump told Time Magazine in May. “I was being interviewed by 20-year-old kids. I’m saying, ‘Where the hell did you meet these people?’ They’re called influencers.”
How has UFC shaped Trump’s second term?
Experts say Trump’s 2024 campaign benefitted significantly from his UFC connections.
Ahead of his victory, Trump courted influencers like UFC fan Theo Von and UFC host Joe Rogan, whose podcast boasts about 11 million listeners per episode.
Trump has also used his second term as president to elevate the UFC’s profile, weaving one of its events into plans to celebrate the 250th US Independence Day.
Dubbed “UFC Freedom 250”, the tournament was given unusual access to national monuments for a commercial event.
White, for instance, hosted a weigh-in for fighters on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, with uniformed military personnel standing as an honour guard. The fights themselves were held on the lawn of the White House.
Trump called the event “one of the most exciting days in the history of our fabled White House”.
But critics warned the event could constitute a conflict of interest: In the months before the fight, Trump reportedly bought up to $50,000 of stock in TKO Holding, the UFC’s parent company.
A lawsuit also challenged the UFC’s use of public facilities, calling the event “deeply corrupt”.
How is the announcement being received?
Some opposition figures have dismissed Trump’s idea of appointing White as press secretary as a way to distract attention from the midterm elections.
During the November 3 elections, Trump’s Republican Party suffered record losses, losing majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Melat Kiros, a Democrat elected to represent Colorado in the House, said on Saturday that Trump’s offer to White “demonstrates how deeply unserious this man is, how ridiculous this administration is”.
Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, meanwhile, said Trump’s choice raised questions about the president’s wellbeing.
“It would be really funny if it wasn’t dangerous, if he wasn’t the president,” Kelly said. “Countries around the world are continuing to laugh at us because of what he’s doing.”
There has also been some speculation that Trump may have tapped the wrong Dana White.
A woman by the same name formerly worked as a Pentagon spokesperson during Trump’s first term. She has denied being approached for the press secretary role.
“To everyone texting me congratulations: thank you, but you have the wrong Dana White,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: NFL roundup: Cowboys stun Colts with late comeback as Bengals roll in Madrid
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Dak Prescott threw for 335 yards and CeeDee Lamb caught 10 passes for 195 yards before the Dallas defense made the decisive play to help the Cowboys escape Indianapolis with a 27-23 victory on Sunday.
Cowboys rookie safety Caleb Downs intercepted Daniel Jones with 35 seconds remaining to seal the victory for Dallas.
The Cowboys outgained the Colts 508-271 but were nearly undone by a series of self-inflicted mistakes.
Trailing by three points with 97 seconds remaining, Dallas needed less than 30 seconds to drive 65 yards and take the lead.
Prescott went deep for Ryan Flournoy on first down, with the receiver making the catch despite Sauce Gardner grabbing his left arm to move the ball to the Colts’ 19-yard line. Javonte Williams powered his way to the 11 before a penalty on defensive tackle Grover Stewart gave Dallas first-and-goal at the six. Williams scored from a yard out to put the Cowboys ahead 27-23 with 1:08 remaining.
Williams finished with 101 yards on 20 carries while Tyler Goodson added 77 yards on 12 attempts. Dallas rushed for 179 yards, averaging 5.3 yards per carry.
The Cowboys were penalized 14 times for 153 yards.
New York Giants 19-11 Philadelphia Eagles
Jameis Winston replaced the injured JJ McCarthy long enough to throw a go-ahead touchdown pass and help the New York Giants maintain their grip on the NFC East with a 19-11 victory over Philadelphia on Sunday, handing the Eagles their seventh straight loss.
The Eagles (2-7) are on their longest losing streak since dropping eight straight games in Andy Reid’s final season in 2012.
With Jalen Hurts likely out for the season with blood clots and a playoff berth all but out of reach, the Eagles could undergo a roster makeover ahead of Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline.
The Giants (5-2-1) are the only team in the division with a winning record.
The Eagles had beaten the Giants in 13 straight home meetings – including one playoff game – since New York’s previous victory in Philadelphia on 27 October 2013.
Denver Broncos 26-21 Carolina Panthers
Bo Nix threw for 237 yards and two touchdowns as the Denver Broncos benefited from a momentum-shifting coach’s challenge to beat the Carolina Panthers 26-21 on Sunday for their fifth straight victory.
Jonah Coleman ran for 57 yards and a touchdown, while Courtland Sutton and Pat Bryant each caught touchdown passes for the Broncos.
Denver (7-2) came up with a late defensive stop when Nik Bonitto strip-sacked Bryce Young and recovered the ball near midfield with 1:24 remaining. The Broncos picked up a first down to seal the victory.
Young completed 28 of 39 passes for 276 yards, three touchdowns and an interception for Carolina. He was sacked three times after going down six times in last week’s loss to Green Bay.
Los Angeles Rams 20-13 Washington Commanders
Matthew Stafford found star receiver Puka Nacua early and often, Myles Garrett had three sacks and a forced fumble in his return, and the Los Angeles Rams held on for their third straight victory, beating the Washington Commanders 20-13 on Sunday.
Seemingly open all afternoon, Nacua was targeted 19 times by Stafford and finished with 14 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown as the Rams (5-4) moved above .500 for the first time this season. Stafford threw for 219 yards and an interception, completing 26 of 43 passes.
Nacua made a leaping, contested catch in the corner of the end zone for a seven-yard touchdown that broke a 13-13 tie early in the fourth quarter.
Garrett gave the Rams’ defense a lift in his first action since Los Angeles’ season-opening loss to the 49ers in Australia. The All-Pro defensive end had missed seven games with a knee injury.
Detroit Lions 19-9 Miami Dolphins
Jahmyr Gibbs ran for a touchdown, Jared Goff threw for 170 yards and the Detroit Lions beat the Miami Dolphins 19-9 on Sunday for their fourth straight victory.
Jake Bates kicked four field goals on an underwhelming day for Goff and the Lions’ top-ranked offense, which entered the game averaging 29 points and 395.4 yards but finished with just 271 yards.
Goff completed 17 of 25 passes and was sacked three times as Miami’s defense pressured him throughout. He was intercepted by rookie cornerback Chris Johnson on a tipped pass in the first quarter – just his second interception of the season.
Gibbs averaged just 3.7 yards per carry, finishing with 74 yards on 20 attempts and an eight-yard touchdown run that put the Lions ahead 16-6 entering the fourth quarter. All-Pro receiver Amon-Ra St Brown had 86 yards receiving for Detroit, who are trying to keep pace in a competitive NFC North.
New York Jets 12-35 Kansas City Chiefs
Patrick Mahomes threw for 242 yards and two touchdown passes to Kenneth Walker, who added 102 yards and a score on the ground, as the Kansas City Chiefs got back on track with a 35-12 rout of the hapless New York Jets on Sunday.
Walker finished with 143 yards from scrimmage and the Chiefs sacked Geno Smith five times while keeping the Jets out of the end zone, allowing Kansas City (6-2) to bounce back from consecutive losses to the Seahawks and Broncos.
Smith finished with 165 yards passing for the Jets (2-7), who lost their fourth straight game. They managed minus-nine yards of offense in the third quarter as Kansas City scored two touchdowns to turn a narrow 14-12 halftime lead into a comfortable victory.
The Chiefs have beaten the Jets in each of their last three meetings.
Cleveland Browns 22-23 New Orleans Saints (OT)
Tyler Shough threw a 15-yard touchdown pass to Juwan Johnson on the opening possession of overtime as the New Orleans Saints held on for a 23-22 victory over the Cleveland Browns on Sunday.
Shough threw for 265 yards for the Saints (3-5), while Shedeur Sanders, starting in place of the injured Deshaun Watson (concussion), passed for 297 yards and two touchdowns for the Browns (5-4).
After New Orleans took the lead in overtime, Sanders found Harold Fannin Jr for a 39-yard touchdown, but his ensuing two-point conversion attempt fell incomplete.
The Saints opened the scoring on their first possession with a 30-yard field goal from Charlie Smyth.
Cincinnati Bengals 34-17 Atlanta Falcons
Joe Burrow threw for three touchdowns and rushed for another and the Cincinnati Bengals’ offense kept rolling to defeat the Atlanta Falcons 34-17 in Madrid on Sunday for their fourth straight win.
Ja’Marr Chase had eight receptions for 142 yards in the first half, and Tee Higgins added two touchdown catches at Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabéu stadium. Chase finished with 10 catches for 155 yards and a touchdown.
After his 47-yard touchdown catch in the first quarter, Chase celebrated with Higgins in bullfighting style, with Higgins mimicking a bull by putting his hands on his head and Chase playing the matador with an imaginary cape.
The Bengals (6-2) have scored 30 points or more in four straight games for the first time since 1997. It was the second consecutive defeat for the Falcons (3-6).
Burrow, who completed 24 of 29 passes for 271 yards Sunday, had thrown five touchdown passes and rushed for another in overtime in the team’s 43-36 win over the Tennessee Titans last week.
Playing under the closed roof of the Bernabéu, Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr played better than in the rain in a 16-0 loss to the Buccaneers in Tampa Bay last week, but threw a late interception to go along with his opening-drive touchdown to tight end Charlie Woerner. Penix was 20 of 31 for 162 yards with a touchdown and interception and added 50 yards rushing.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Oxford years: PhD, political influences and sporting distinction
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In the cold, twilight days of 2008, inside the University of Michigan’s fortress-like Fleming administration building, one student was given a particularly adulatory sendoff.
Mary Sue Coleman, president of the university at the time, convened a ceremony for the latest Rhodes scholar heading to the University of Oxford: Abdul El-Sayed. “There is no doubt among anyone who crosses his path that he will achieve all he sets out to accomplish and more,” she declared to a room full of the university’s leaders, calling the medical PhD student the “epitome of the engaged intellect”.
She even recalled Bill Clinton’s response to a speech made by El-Sayed in 2007, with the former US president remarking: “I wish every person in the world could have heard you speak today.”
For those who ran into El-Sayed months later in autumn 2009 when he finally crossed the pond, these words of praise rang true. “He always seemed very driven,” says Elias Rothblatt, who played lacrosse alongside Michigan’s senator-elect more than 15 years ago. El-Sayed was captain of Oxford’s lacrosse team and student journalists at the time described him as a “defensive master” in the sport.
Rothblatt, 36, who works in fintech, says El-Sayed was a “very fierce competitor” on the field and a “wonderful” captain. “He had a great sense of humour. He struck a really good mix of being friends with other people on the team but also setting the tone and helping lead the team and keep things, keeping serious.”
Off the field, Rothblatt says, El-Sayed was equally “fun and friendly”. He says: “It was always a pleasure to run into him. He was with his wife sometimes and she was wonderful too.” El-Sayed also had a fixation on a resolutely British sandwich: coronation chicken. Speaking to the Times, Ricardo Chasebi, owner of a now-closed cafe in Oxford’s covered market, recalled El-Sayed’s order as a grilled ciabatta filled with coronation chicken, cheddar, peppers and red onion that was topped with lettuce and tomato.
He eventually placed El-Sayed’s version on the menu, naming it “the Abdul”. The senator-to-be was so keen on Chasebi’s sandwiches that he would call ahead from the airport and say: “I’ll be in Oxford in two hours, don’t shut until I get there.” El-Sayed even handed Chasebi a copy of his doctoral thesis, where he thanked the cafe owner in the acknowledgments for “nourishing my stomach and my soul”.
Rothblatt has tried the Abdul sandwich. “It’s good,” he says. El-Sayed also had a penchant for Nando’s, organising meetings there with his fellow Rhodes scholar cohort.
While he eventually settled into Oxford life, things didn’t start smoothly for El-Sayed. He did not enjoy his course at first and flew back to Michigan two weeks before his first term ended. And based on a recent outburst, where he told a Sky News reporter: “You know how many votes I want to get in the UK? Zero,” you might assume he was, at best, apathetic about his time in Britain. But that is not the case. In his memoir, Healing Politics: A Doctor’s Journey into the Heart of Our Political Epidemic, El-Sayed wrote: “My classmates in Oxford taught me more than I could learn in any classroom.” And in several articles El-Sayed wrote for the Guardian, he expressed an appreciation for Britain and, in particular, its political system.
In one piece, where he declared that UK democracy had the “upper hand” on the US, El-Sayed expressed his awe at a parliamentary hustings in Tower Hamlets, east London before the 2010 general election where all of the candidates were of Bengali heritage, reflecting the demographics of the local area. He opined: “As an Arab-American, the likelihood of ever having the opportunity to vote for an Arab-American candidate for national office during my lifetime is minimal.”
But this week, he did have the opportunity to do so, being able to cast the ballot for himself. He was joined by more than 2.5 million others who followed suit and elected El-Sayed as the country’s first Muslim senator.
Rothblatt is “very excited” to see what El-Sayed will do in the Senate. “I think he’s going to do a fantastic job. Back then, he was a talented, ambitious person who had some really good ideas about what he wanted to do in the world. Now he’s continuing to bring those to life,” he says.

Turkiye pushes electrification top of climate agenda as COP31 set to open
Ankara aims to make electricity account for 35 percent of global energy demand by 2035.
The United Nations climate conference COP31 is set to open on Monday in Antalya, Turkiye, against the backdrop of the US-led war on Iran, which has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels.
Turkiye has said it would centre electrification on the COP31 agenda, launching the non-binding 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to make electricity account for at least 35 percent of global energy demand by 2035.
Electricity currently accounts for about one-fifth of global total final energy consumption, according to the International Energy Agency.
Turkiye says the “35 by 35” will speed up the shift to renewable sources of energy while strengthening energy security.
“This year’s energy crisis has shocked us… everyone now understands that energy that you import is energy that you do not control,” the COP31 president and Turkiye’s environment minister, Murat Kurum, said on Thursday.
“Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions.”
COP31’s aim is “to usher in the age of electricity”, he said.
The climate conference’s priority areas also include zero waste, methane reduction, climate-resilient cities, green industrialisation, education and implementation of national climate plans.
However, climate advocates have criticised the pledge, arguing it does not require that additional electricity come from low-carbon sources.
This has set up a debate on whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.
A coalition of countries, including South Pacific island nations most vulnerable to sea level rise, is pushing more generally for a clearer global roadmap away from fossil fuels.
Many oil and gas producing countries, including Saudi Arabia, argue that fossil fuels can form a substantial part of the global energy mix, provided they are paired with technologies that reduce or capture emissions.
US-Israel war on Iran
The US-Israel war on Iran has severely disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, raising fuel prices around the globe and leading governments to scramble for alternative sources.
US President Donald Trump has encouraged policies maximising oil, gas, and coal production to address the Middle East disruptions.
South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations have increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.
At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean technology from China.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
A joke or test? Why Trump floated UFC’s Dana White as his press secretary
White is a close friend of Trump and has endorsed him for president, but has never held a government position.
For a brief period over the weekend, it looked like United States President Donald Trump had zeroed in on a new White House press secretary: Dana White.
A stocky former fighter with a shaved head and a penchant for wearing black, White currently serves as the chief executive of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), a mixed martial arts company that counts Trump among its fans.
But on Sunday night, after hours of speculation, Trump put an end to the rumours he himself started.
“I was only kidding. But Dana loves the idea,” Trump said from an airport tarmac in West Palm Beach, Florida. “And there’s only one Dana. He’s great.”
Just a day earlier, Trump had posted a message to his Truth Social platform, purporting to offer White the press secretary job.
“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote on Saturday.
He proceeded to explain – in seemingly tongue-in-cheek style – that he had asked White to bring along fighters like Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov as “assistants”.
The post was accompanied by images of the muscle-bound fighters, several of them baring their teeth.
“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” Trump continued in his post. “Dana, please take the job!”
Testing ideas in public?
Trump has a history of unconventional picks for public office. The press secretary role remains vacant after Trump briefly appointed political commentator Katie Zacharia to the job in October.
Zacharia lasted five days, the shortest tenure of any White House press secretary in history.
Critics questioned her legal credentials and her job performance. At her inaugural briefing, she struggled to deliver her opening remarks, and the meeting ended within 15 minutes.
White would likewise have been an out-of-the-box choice to serve as press secretary. But political insiders say Trump has an affinity for pushing the envelope of what is acceptable in Washington, DC.
“Knowing President Trump as I do, I believe he was partly serious,” Rob Arlett, a Republican strategist and former Delaware campaign manager for Trump, told Al Jazeera.
“He and Dana White share a longstanding friendship and business relationship dating back more than 25 years, when Trump supported the UFC by hosting events at his Atlantic City casino. Their mutual loyalty and trust remain strong.”
Arlett believes Trump often floats ideas publicly to gauge reactions before deciding his next move.
It’s also part of the president’s strategy, he said, to generate headlines, test public opinion and assess the response.
Who is Dana White?
Born on July 28, 1969, in Manchester, Connecticut, White is a two-time college dropout and former boxer who turned a passion for fighting into a billion-dollar enterprise.
He is also one of Trump’s longtime political supporters. In December 2015, White endorsed the Republican leader’s bid for the presidency, even though Trump was considered a long shot at the time.
“You will never hear me say a negative thing about Donald Trump,” White told TMZ Sports. “Donald will get my vote.”
Trump went on to win the 2016 presidential election in his first successful bid for public office.
The two men’s careers have been intertwined for decades, though. White began his career running gyms in cities like Boston and Las Vegas, and eventually, he started to manage champion fighters like Tito Ortiz and Chuck Liddell.
It was the 1990s, and both men were competitors in a new competition circuit known as the Ultimate Fighting Championship.
The tournament was designed to bring different martial arts, like jujitsu and wrestling, together in one arena.
White would ultimately be credited with transforming the sport into an international commercial success.
He became president of the UFC in 2001, after the businessmen Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta bought the company for $2m.
But the sport was struggling at first, according to White’s own account. Critics slammed its tournaments as too violent and unregulated.
“It was basically considered a blood sport,” White told the Republican National Convention in 2016, as he rallied on behalf of Trump’s campaign. “State athletic commissions didn’t support us. Arenas around the world refused to host our events. Nobody took us seriously. Nobody – except Donald Trump.”
During the first year of White’s leadership at the UFC, Trump arranged to host the tournament at his Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey. He did so again the following year.
White credits the move with helping the UFC gain mainstream acceptance.
“Donald was the first guy that recognised the potential that we saw in the UFC and encouraged us to build our business,” White said.
He has since campaigned for Trump in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections, donating tens of thousands to his campaign. In 2020, for instance, White donated $1m to America First Action, a pro-Trump political action committee.
A tale of two men
Trump and White have continued to enjoy a close relationship since the Republican leader’s return to office.
In June, Trump hosted a UFC tournament on the White House lawn as part of the festivities for the 250th anniversary of US independence.
And over the weekend, White acknowledged he had plans to meet Trump in Washington, DC, on Monday.
“I’m flying to Washington, DC, right now,” White told reporters at a news conference. However, he appeared dismissive of the prospect of joining Trump’s administration.
“I’ve got a lot of jobs already,” he quipped. Since 2023, White has served as the CEO of the UFC, as well as its president.
White has no previous government experience. But some experts say that might not be disqualifying under Trump’s leadership.
“Trump likes to think outside the box and be the first to do something to stand out from the others,” Ihsan Alkhatib, a lawyer and political science professor at Murray State University in Kentucky, told Al Jazeera.
“But the position requires a set of skills that Dana White doesn’t have,” Alkhatib added.
The lack of experience prompted some critics to question Trump’s decision-making abilities when he first floated the idea of naming White as press secretary.
Still, Alkhatib explained that other presidents have likewise faced pushback over decisions to appoint unconventional candidates to public office.
The scenario is “not as unusual as it might sound”, Alkhatib said, offering an example. “George W Bush wanted to elevate his personal lawyer and White House counsel, Harriet Miers, to the US Supreme Court, and she was definitely not qualified for the position.”
White’s appointment, however, would likely have generated further controversy had Trump pursued it.
White has been married to Anne Stella since 1996, but in 2022, a video posted on social media showed White slapping her during an argument at a New Year’s Eve party in Mexico.
White later apologised for his behaviour. In a statement to the media at the time, he said, “There’s no defense for this, and people should not be defending me, no matter what. All the criticism I’ve received this week is 100% warranted.”
Trump had four White House press secretaries during his first term, from 2017 to 2021. So far, during his second, he has had two: Karoline Leavitt and Zacharia.
The post has been vacant since October 16. Trump is still without a chief spokesperson.

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.title: ‘Thicky thicky dumb dumb’ satirist Cody Dahler on his viral videos: ‘my material is presented to me on a silver platter!’
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.author: Interview by Liam Pape
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.text:
Why did you get into comedy?
  
My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform. Given that I have zero rhythm, comedy was my other option. She wrote me a poem called Mrs Brown’s Moggy, about a cat that was often very soggy, for my school’s talent show. Because you can’t tell the difference between real and polite laughter at the age of six, I assumed I’d killed my first gig and convinced myself I was born to do nothing else.
Where do you find your material? 
  
In a world where Robert Jenrick claims Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism”, the answer is that my material is presented to me on a silver platter each morning.
When did it click that you might be on to something with your “thicky thicky dumb dumb” videos? 
  
When Donald Trump captured the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro. Up until that point I was covering four or five stories in each video. But obviously Trumpty Dumpty’s top-class diplomacy meant that people only really wanted one story breaking down for them. That was the video that really exploded online. If you look closely at the picture of the blindfolded Maduro in that US military helicopter, you can see my career taking off with him.
What can readers expect from your new book?
  
An attempt to help them understand why everything is so crap, written in a way that won’t make them feel like a thicky thicky dumb dumb in front of all their mates. Partly because the book answers questions that my followers sent in to me. While researching it, I was pretty shocked by how inaccessible books about British politics were. Everything seemed to be Margaret Thatcher 1973-74: The Pre Policy Years and Governed! – A Battle for the Soul of Britain’s Fiscal Policy Within the Bank of England. No disrespect to the fiscal policy nerds but I’m pretty sure even they don’t want to read that. I know from doing political videos online how interested and engaged people are about politics – it’s just that nobody is talking about it using language they actually understand.
What’s a topic you’ve found particularly difficult to explain?
  
I genuinely believe that things are made to sound more complicated than they are to exclude people from engaging with politics. And often to get politicians off the hook for not knowing what the hell they’re doing. So basically, my big-headed answer is once I’d waded through the academic guff that’s used to make people feel cleverer than you, most things were actually very simple to explain.
You’ve got more than two million followers online. What’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had?
  
At the live recording of my podcast, The Truth (In My Opinion), at the Bedford pub in Balham, an audience member called Bethany came up to me to say she’d travelled from Chicago that day specifically to see the show. Given that many of my north London friends thought south London was too far for them, I thought that was pretty amazing.
Any bugbears from the world of comedy?
  
Oh God, absolutely – but I’d like to keep my career for now, thank you very much!
Best advice you’ve ever been given?
  
Make your own stuff.
Worst advice you’ve ever been given?
  
Say yes to everything.
What’s next for you?
  
Frostbite. I’ve made the mistake of basing my entire brand around wearing shorts in all weathers. Now winter and El Niño are on the way …

Iran mocks US military initiative to disrupt supply routes
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has dismissed a new US military initiative to restrict the movement of goods through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea as “merely wordplay”, as tensions over shipping routes and Washington's blockade continue.
“The Iron Gate plan is merely wordplay. The Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing severe economic pressure to cause economic collapse in Iran through this approach,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Mohebbi said Washington had previously predicted that Iran would suffer economic collapse within two weeks, but that this had not happened.
Tehran had prepared for economic pressure and maintained close relations with neighbouring countries, he said.
The response came after US Central Command (Centcom) announced the establishment of Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Asian stock markets climb after earlier tech rout
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Asian stock markets climb after earlier tech rout
Markets rebound after tech rout triggered by Democrats’ sweeping victory in US midterm elections.
Asian stock markets have rebounded after last week’s tech rout triggered by the Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the US midterm elections.
Key indexes in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong made substantial gains on Monday, following a rebound on Wall Street on Friday.
In Tokyo, the benchmark Nikkei 225 was up 3.45 percent as of 04:00 GMT.
In Taipei, the Taiex was 5.72 percent higher, while the Kospi in Seoul was up 1.68 percent.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index was up 0.19 percent.
Futures for Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 index and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 were up 0.60 percent and 0.59 percent, respectively.
They had dipped earlier following US-based chip giant Nvidia’s announcement that it would investigate its CEO over a romantic relationship he conducted with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
Nvidia’s board of directors said that while it had confidence in CEO Jensen Huang and had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised, an independent inquiry would examine “all available information”.
The board said Huang supported the inquiry and pledged his full cooperation.
“The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said.
The stock market rebound comes after the US midterm results prompted a $2.5 trillion sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday amid concerns that Democratic-controlled legislatures could slow the rollout of data centres used to power AI.
The tech rout spilled into Asia on Friday, with the Nikkei 225 and Kospi plunging about 6 percent and 9 percent, respectively, and the Hang Seng Index dropping more than 1 percent.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Rubio says war on Iran unpopular but ‘necessary’ to stop nuclear threat
US secretary of state says Iran’s negotiation demands are ‘outrageous and ridiculous, and really not realistic’.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran to safeguard the world from Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.
Rubio told reporters in Florida on Sunday that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and had worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon.
Trump addressed “difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary”, Rubio added.
On diplomatic efforts to end the war, Rubio said, “I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough”. He added that although Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, Iranian demands are “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.
Rubio comments came after Trump had said that “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President JD Vance recent comments blaming the US-led war on Iran for the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in last week’s US midterm elections.
Trump said that although he mostly agreed with Vance, he did not regret the decision to go to war against Iran. It “will go down as one of the best things we ever did”, he said, adding that if Tehran were to have a nuclear weapon, “they would blow up the world”.
Trump also told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday that as long as Washington sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a “strong agreement”, it is “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” for the US to resume strikes.
For Iran’s part, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that it was “time for the White House to make its own” decision on the war.
“American voters have made their choice,” Araghchi wrote on X, referring to the midterm election results.
He added that Tehran’s “2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results”.
“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”
Iran has offered to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within two days if the United States meets its conditions.
Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule.
Tehran is reviewing proposals presented by Qatar aimed at addressing differences with Washington, according to the Associated Press news agency.
In recent days, Rubio has also denied “unfounded” speculation that he was quitting as the top US diplomat to run for higher office in 2028.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: New Zealand’s Opportunity party takes aim at populist politics as it prepares to enter parliament
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
A history-making centrist party that could influence New Zealand’s political direction has taken aim at populism as lawmakers arrived at parliament on Monday.
A nail-biting election failed to hand either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc a strong winning hand on Saturday. New Zealanders will now need to wait until 27 November for the final result, which includes the addition of about 400,000 “special votes” – those cast overseas or outside the voter’s electorate.
The Opportunity party, led by businesswoman Qiulae Wong, secured 5.9% of the party votes, clearing the hurdle to enter parliament, and becoming the first new party not born of an existing MP, or party, to enter parliament since the formation of New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996.
Wong, who is of Chinese and European descent, also becomes the first leader of a party who has Asian ethnicity.
With the left and right blocs separated by just a few seats, after the official results are released, Opportunity could be in a position to decide who governs.
On Monday, newly elected lawmakers descended on Wellington for their induction into parliament, including Opportunity’s seven MPs. From parliament’s steps, Wong said it was “a huge day” for the party, whose nearly 150,000 supporters wanted a more pragmatic approach to politics.
“We’ve seen that populism doesn’t deliver results,” she said. “It is paper thin, it doesn’t have substance around taking countries forward. So it’s really encouraging to have had that support.”
Opportunity will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats, but its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.
“Ultimately, we need to align on that future vision for New Zealand,” Wong said.
Leader of the centre-right National party, Christopher Luxon, had previously ruled out working with Opportunity but he extended an olive branch on Monday. Speaking to RNZ, Luxon said he would call Wong “shortly” and discuss the need for cross-party collaboration.
“I intend to build a relationship with her and try and find common ground with her, too,” Luxon said.
National, and Labour – the centre-left mainstream party – experienced a near photo-finish on Saturday, with neither party clearing 30% of the vote. The two parties recorded their worst combined vote in MMP history.
In contrast, minor parties hoovered up support, amid public frustration with persistently high living costs and incrementalist policymaking. The Greens and Act both claimed their highest ever results, while New Zealand First jumped nearly 4% from its 2023 result. Te Pāti Māori also managed to retain five electorate seats, despite major challenges and in-fighting over the past year.
But while the minor parties celebrate their successes, New Zealand is reckoning with the aftermath of the messy election result, which is not only on track to deliver the second lowest voter turnout ever, but has triggered questions about the future of New Zealand’s voting system.
In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote. However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
 
As it stands, New Zealand’s parliament could have an additional eleven overhang seats, because National and Te Pāti Māori gained more electorates than their share of the popular vote.
Political scientists say the complexities around overhang seats raise serious questions about MMP.
“It kind of starts to defeat the purpose of MMP,” says Dr Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, who edited a textbook on MMP.
Te Pāti Māori had campaigned for people to only give them their electorate vote, to engineer an overhang in the seven Māori electorates. So far, they’re on track for five seats.
Meanwhile, various right wing groups, including one backed by wealthy businessman Harry Mowbray, had asked supporters to party vote for the Act of NZ First parties, while backing National electorate MPs to engineer overhangs on the right. So far, National could have six overhang seats.
Greaves said such campaigns undermined the spirit of MMP, which New Zealanders voted for in the 1990s after a string of skewed results under the first past the post system.
“I am concerned these sorts of issues could create further polarisation,” Greaves said.
“The possibility is some people will be quite unsettled by this result … there might be questions as to the legitimacy of this whole parliament and this government.”
- Additional reporting by Jamie Tahana

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Mexico arrests alleged major leader of Jalisco cartel
Rafael Alvarez, alias ‘R2’, was captured with intelligence shared by the US Drug Enforcement Administration.
Authorities in Mexico have announced the arrest of an alleged leader in the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), one of the country’s two main criminal groups.
Rafael Alvarez, alias “R2”, who is suspected of heading CJNG’s “Los Rs” cell, was arrested in an operation in the city of Zapopan, in the Guadalajara metropolitan area, on Sunday, as a result of intelligence shared by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), according to Mexico’s Navy.
“This cell is mainly linked to extortion, drug trafficking, homicide, illegal deprivation of liberty, kidnapping and attacks against authorities,” Mexico’s Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said.
He added that victims of the group’s extortion included “business owners and avocado producers”.
Harfuch said on X that Alvarez was wounded in a shootout that broke out during the arrest and is receiving medical care.
Alvarez has an outstanding arrest warrant in Mexico for aggravated homicide and another warrant for extradition to the US, Harfuch also said.
Authorities, including those from Mexico’s National Intelligence Center, also took part in the operation, which captured 19 other people.
Alvarez is linked to the killing of at least 19 people, including last year’s murder of Carlos Manzo, the popular crime-fighting mayor of Uruapan in Mexico’s avocado-producing Michoacan state.
The CJNG, which operates in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan, was designated a “foreign terrorist organisation” by the US government in 2025 and is known for violent tactics and attacks on authorities.
It competes with the Sinaloa Cartel for drug trafficking into the US.
Since the death of the CJNG founder, Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, in a military operation in February, several of its top leaders have been apprehended.
But there are still reports of kidnapping for ransom in the areas where the cartels are active.
An estimated 134,000 people are believed to be missing across Mexico, with Jalisco recording the country’s highest numbers of disappearances.

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.title: Wanted review – generic crime musical lacks outlaw grit
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.author: Richard Lawson
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/n.text:
The new retooled musical Wanted, from writer Angelica Chéri and composer Ross Baum, opens with a blare of excitement: a Greek chorus of sorts, clad in billowing white garments like spirits from the great beyond, lay their scene in 1890s Texas. There, we meet two Black sisters, Mary and Martha Clarke, who will become wanted criminals. The tone of Baum’s music is portentous, its volume high, suggesting that an epic journey is about to unfold. What ensues from there is, sadly, not quite as suspenseful, moving or grand as advertised.
Chéri based this “mostly true” story on two of her great-great aunts, daughters of an emancipated sharecropper whose absent father was white. Mary and Martha are light-skinned and thus figure they can pass in the white world, at least long enough to earn some money that might allow their mother, Tallulah, to buy the cotton-field land she’s been working for decades. It’s a dangerous gambit, and soon devolves into a gun-wielding crime spree in which the sisters rob various deserving targets. But that potentially invigorating spree is reduced to a mere montage, a quick flurry of activity that saps these daring acts of their inherent tension, of any true sense of risk. Despite its dynamic subject matter – marginalized people violently asserting themselves in a repressive time and place – this is a dismayingly tame production, albeit a more muscular one than was staged at New Jersey’s Paper Mill Playhouse in 2024.
That version was far flatter, well-intentioned but clumsy. The tweaks made for the Broadway transfer were mostly smart ones. The pacing is tighter (though, maybe too tight in places), the orchestrations are lusher and the design is more robust. Lauded scenic designer Beowulf Boritt houses most of the action under the weathered-wood framing of a barn, affording director Stevie Walker-Webb the chance to create some levels in his stage pictures. Stefania Bulbarella’s video projections are tasteful more often than not, effectively employing patterned color washes to establish changes of location. We at least see the intended grit and passion of the piece, even if we don’t always feel it.
Disappointingly lacking in levels are Chéri and Baum’s songs, almost all of which are pitched as belting showstoppers. Wanted is a musical near entirely built out of pop- and gospel-inflected 11 o’clock numbers; even the romantic ballads and duets whip themselves up into a frenzy after a verse or two. Everyone in the cast has the pipes to pull off all this maximalism, but one craves a softer song here and there. More specifically story-driven numbers might have helped flesh out characters that are otherwise underdeveloped.
As Mary – who is drawn into a new life as the presumed-white wife of a shady landowner – the actor Solea Pfeiffer has at least some nuance to play. But we don’t fully understand why she in particular becomes so committed to this con, or why it (rather quickly) transforms into something much more meaningful than that. One would think that playing Martha, who is the fiercer and more rebellious outlaw, would give Liisi LaFontaine (reprising the role from the Paper Mill production) lots of dynamic stuff to do. And yet, only a costume change that makes Martha look a little like Joan Crawford in Johnny Guitar really communicates her evolution into a true renegade.
Both actors have gorgeous, powerful voices, but they seem somewhat stranded, searching for characters that have not been sufficiently provided for them. As Martha’s love interest, Elijah, Luke James deftly deploys his silky tenor and forlorn sex appeal, but his storyline is truncated. Wanted is not without its arresting performances, though. I was most taken by Awa Sal Secka as Flo, one half of the show’s gossipy-housemaid double act. Whether singing or speaking her lines, Sal Secka brings sorely needed vim and detail to all her scenes; if only she was a more central figure in the story.
Perhaps in the next iteration of Wanted, wherever and whenever that might be, that story will be more sharply realized. As is, this is a western that’s not wild enough, a melodrama lacking heat, a song showcase that grows repetitive in all its smooth and unsurprising melody. In a scene toward the end of the show, Martha stands defiant on a high perch with an enormous projection of an American flag behind her. We are meant in that moment to feel the rumble of something enormous – of history, and of individual lives and adventures that went mostly unrecorded, but have endured nonetheless in the passing-down of family lore. That’s a lovely, potent sentiment, particularly about Black experience in this country. But it’s one smothered by a too-heavy lacquer of generic Broadway pomp.
- Wanted is at James Earl Jones theatre, New York City, until 31 March 2027

Moldova launches new power line to Romania to cut reliance on Russia
Moldovan President Maia Sandu says ‘two more power lines to Romania are on the way’.
Moldova has officially launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid to reduce its reliance on Russian energy.
“For decades, Moscow used energy to blackmail us,” Moldovan President Maia Sandu said on X on Sunday.
“No more: Moldova buys zero Russian gas,” she added.
Moldova, a country of 2.6 million people wedged between Romania and Ukraine, received most of its gas from Russia via its pro-Moscow separatist region of Transnistria and pipelines running through Ukraine.
“Thanks to this project, we are strengthening our electricity transmission capacity, diversifying our means of supply and reinforcing the connection of the Republic of Moldova to the European energy system,” Sandu said during the power line’s inauguration ceremony on Sunday in the capital, Chisinau.
She also said that “two more power lines to Romania are on the way”.
European Commissioner for Energy Marta Kos, who was at the ceremony, said Moldova could now “buy energy where it is cheapest”.
The 400-kilowatt extra-high-voltage line, which runs from the city of Vulcanesti to Chisinau, allows Moldova to cut reliance on the Cuciurgan thermal power plant in Transnistria.
“Every time Moldova dares to choose something other than what Moscow wants, they threaten to cut our electricity,” said Sandu.
Dubbed the “energy independence line”, the power grid was launched two years after the date Moldovan authorities initially promised.
Last month, Moldova’s parliament approved a government-requested state of emergency until November 20 as it tries to ease gas shortages amid soaring world energy prices.
Some in Europe have blamed Moscow for the skyrocketing gas prices, accusing it of withholding additional supplies to put pressure on the continent.
European-aligned states in the Black Sea region say they are experiencing renewed attacks allegedly carried out by Russia.
Last month, Romania blamed Russia for a drone strike that sank a cargo ship off Romania’s Black Sea coast, killing one crew member and leaving three others missing.
Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to “fast-track the additional surveillance capabilities” to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea, as fighting in Russia’s war on Ukraine escalates.
NATO said it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield
The strike leaves more than 70 percent of northern Iraq’s Kurdish region without power.
A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials.
The Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power.
It was not clear who was responsible for the attack or whether it was related to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad has verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in the Sulaimaniyah governorate.
Omid Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Electricity, said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in the cities of Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.
The strike knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of electricity generation off the grid, he said.
He added that the ministry would provide electricity to critical facilities, such as hospitals and water treatment plants, by operating hydroelectric power stations and other plants that run on alternative fuel.
Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, cited security sources as saying the explosive-laden drone struck the Khor Mor gas storage facility, reducing the energy grid’s capacity by 70 to 80 percent.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said there were no casualties as a result of the attack, based on an initial assessment, the INA reported.
Al-Zaidi also directed that a joint investigative committee be formed with the relevant authorities in the Kurdish region to investigate the circumstances surrounding the attack, INA reported.
The attack comes amid heightened regional tensions. A drone strike hit the same facility last year, with no group having claimed responsibility.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Jeffries backs Hegseth impeachment as Democrats vow probes of Trump allies
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Jeffries backs Hegseth impeachment as Democrats vow probes of Trump allies
Democratic lawmakers are mapping out their post-midterm agenda with pledges to lead committee investigations into Trump and his officials.
United States House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has thrown his support behind impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, as the Democratic Party prepares to use its incoming congressional majorities to probe President Donald Trump’s administration.
In a Sunday appearance on the Television show This Week with George Stephanopoulos, Jeffries weighed in on the upcoming impeachment resolution, anticipated for the coming days.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.”
The impeachment resolution has been spearheaded by outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a vocal critic of the US-Israel war on Iran.
“Pete Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries added. “I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution.”
Investigating ‘unprecedented corruption’
Jeffries is poised to become the next speaker in the House of Representatives after Democrats notched a historic victory in the November 3 midterm elections.
Both the House and the Senate flipped into Democratic control, with the left-wing party making some of its biggest gains in the lower chamber in more than half a century.
Democrats are expected to use their new congressional majorities to launch investigations into the Trump administration.
There have also been concerns, voiced by Trump himself, that he and other top officials could face impeachment.
In Sunday’s interview, Jeffries said the Democratic majority would move “aggressively” in its first 100 days in office, both to address affordability and “unprecedented corruption” under Trump.
“We are committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found,” Jeffries said. “That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court, and with respect to this administration.”
Currently, Republicans hold a government “trifecta”, with control of both chambers of Congress and the presidency. The Supreme Court also boasts a conservative supermajority, shaped by three Trump appointees.
But a new Congress will be sworn in on January 3. In the coming weeks, Democrats will choose their party leaders for both chambers.
Representative Robert Garcia formally announced his bid to lead the House Oversight Committee in a letter to colleagues on Thursday.
The committee is the chamber’s principal investigative panel, with the power to subpoena witnesses and documents.
‘Very serious’ allegations
On Sunday, Garcia told CNN that Stephen Miller‘s influential role in the Trump administration warranted investigation.
Miller, who was named last week as White House chief of staff, has been closely associated with Trump’s hardline immigration policies since his first term as president.
“What we think is that Stephen Miller is the architect of this horrific, unjust policy happening across the country,” Garcia said, pointing to policies of separating immigrant families and accusations of due process abuses.
“Stephen Miller is at the centre of major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and it does deserve oversight and investigation.”
Garcia also signalled interest in questioning businessman Elon Musk over his leadership in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a federal initiative that led to widespread federal workforce cuts at the start of Trump’s second term.
DOGE also sought access to sensitive government data, including Americans’ personal information.
“What happened with DOGE, in particular, and the federal employees losing jobs the way they did and people’s data likely being compromised, I think, is very serious,” Garcia said.
Congressional committees have the power to hold hearings, subpoena witnesses, and demand documents, giving lawmakers a constitutional check on the executive branch.
The House can also impeach administration officials if a simple majority votes in favour.
Conviction and removal, however, require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a high bar even with Democrats controlling the chamber.
Trump’s camp bites back
The White House was quick to draw its own battle lines.
Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said there could be investigations into Democratic lawmakers over their “threatening” rhetoric.
He added he was ready to counter Democratic efforts to probe and impeach Trump officials.
“If that’s what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready,” said Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump. “If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It’s me.”
Trump, meanwhile, made similar remarks in a Truth Social post on Saturday.
He called on the Justice Department to investigate Democrats over their plans to haul his allies before congressional committees, branding them as “SLEAZEBAGS” who “should go to jail”.
“The threats being made by the Democrat Party against innocent Republican Donors and Party Members are absolutely unprecedented, and totally illegal,” the president wrote.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Mexican mayor found alive after hours-long abduction
Rio Bravo mayor freed by captors after being abducted in Zacatecas state, known for violence linked to cartel activity.
The mayor of the Mexican border town of Rio Bravo has been found alive after being abducted in the violence-ridden Zacatecas state in northern Mexico.
Federal officials said Miguel Angel Almaraz was released by his captors on Sunday, hours after being taken to the city of Zacatecas.
He was abducted while travelling with family and friends in a region that straddles the states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosi on Saturday, when his car was intercepted by armed men, who let the others go.
Almaraz’s relatives were able to reach a town in San Luis Potosi, where they alerted authorities about the incident, according to the state’s Security Department.
Almaraz is the mayor of Rio Bravo, a municipality of about 110,000 people in Tamaulipas state, 11km (7 miles) from Mexico’s border with Texas, United States.
He was acquitted of money laundering charges in 2015, after being imprisoned for six years.
He is a member of the conservative National Action Party, but was previously associated with the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution.
It is unclear why Almaraz was taken. Authorities say they are investigating the case, including who might be involved in the abduction.
Zacatecas state is known for activity involving the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Sinaloa Cartel, both accused of attacking civilians and politicians.
A car bomb exploded outside a municipal police headquarters in Ojo Caliente, Zacatecas state, in August, injuring 11 people and damaging about 30 homes. Officials said the attack may have been retaliation by an organised crime group after a recent arrest.
In June 2021, police discovered the bullet-ridden bodies of 18 men after an apparent gun battle between suspected drug cartels in Zacatecas state.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Chancellor Merz to nominate Aigner as Germany’s first woman president
Ilse Aigner, speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, belongs to the Christian Social Union in Bavaria (CSU) party.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will nominate Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner for Germany’s next president, which would make her the country’s first female head of state.
Merz made the announcement at a dinner for leaders of his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party on Sunday.
Aigner, speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, belongs to the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the CDU.
If her nomination is confirmed at a CDU and CSU meeting on Monday, she would almost certainly be formally elected.
According to German political practice, coalition parties must agree on a common candidate. The governing coalition is made up of the CDU, the CSU and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
The SPD has frequently voiced its support for Aigner as president.
The German president is elected by the Federal Convention, convened solely to choose the president. It will decide on incumbent Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s successor on January 30.
Steinmeier, a Social Democrat, took office in 2017, and will reach the limit of two five-year terms in March 2027.
Germany’s president holds a largely ceremonial position, signing legislation into law and formally appointing ministers.
But the president can play the role of a neutral arbiter, above party politics, and acts as a symbol of national unity.
The CSU put forward Aigner’s name earlier this year, but the CDU held back from endorsing her while Merz considered alternatives, straining relations between the parties.
Aigner, 61, began her political career in local politics before being elected to federal parliament in 1998.
She served as agriculture minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel before returning to her home state of Bavaria, where she became speaker of the state parliament in 2018.

https://www.propublica.org/article/sport.title: Federal and State Officials Ramp Up Scrutiny of DraftKings, Other Sports Betting Apps
https://www.propublica.org/article/sport.author: Jake Pearson
https://www.propublica.org/article/sport.text:
State and federal officials have ramped up scrutiny of online sports betting companies in recent weeks, launching inquiries, demanding information and, in one case, proposing a new rule that would limit when companies like DraftKings can pitch their users to bet more.
The moves — by gaming regulators, government lawyers and federal lawmakers — follow an investigation last month by ProPublica that tested the guardrails DraftKings and other sports betting companies have in place to protect users from spiraling out of control. That system is called responsible gaming, and executives say it’s integral to their companies’ long-term success.
The ProPublica article showed how DraftKings bestowed VIP status on a reporter who deliberately bet like a problem gambler. The report detailed the ways in which the app’s user design and promotions encouraged more betting — even after the reporter opted into responsible gaming tools designed to slow users down. A week earlier, The New York Times reported that DraftKings had used machine learning and artificial intelligence to target promotions to losing bettors.
Those articles were the focus of an Oct. 15 meeting of the Louisiana Gaming Control Board, which, partly in response to the stories, tabled the renewal of DraftKings’ five-year license. Instead, the board granted the company a temporary four-month permit while investigators look into the issues raised in the reports as well as other paperwork concerns.
The board’s chair, Christopher Hebert, said the Times had raised some “very serious questions” and called ProPublica’s reporting “very troubling.”
While news stories “are not findings of regulatory violations,” Hebert said, “as regulators we have a responsibility to examine these matters that could affect the integrity of gaming operations and the protections of our citizens here in Louisiana.”
State health officials say the number of Louisianans believed to have a gambling disorder has risen in recent years amid the surge in popularity of online gambling and prediction market sites. One top official reported this summer that gambling addiction was among the health department’s “top three priorities.”
What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out.
If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files.
Paul Liberman, who co-founded DraftKings and serves as its president of operations, told the regulators: “We do not use artificial intelligence to target losing gamblers by any means.”
DraftKings previously told ProPublica that it proactively closes the accounts of suspected problem gamblers “all the time” but declined to provide specific figures. Yet when asked by a Louisiana board member for those same specifics, Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, said 175 accounts in the state had been shut down this year. She told the board she didn’t know how many total users DraftKings had in the Pelican State.
“We’re not physicians, we’re not clinicians and that’s not our role, but we certainly want to help people enjoy the service, the platform that we’re offering them,” Kalani told the board. “I know that we’re doing our job and that when we see something, we say something and we engage. I just can’t tell you if 175 is the right number. I wish it was zero.”
In a statement, a DraftKings spokesperson said: “As a legal, regulated operator, DraftKings values an open and ongoing dialogue with regulators and regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business.”
In response to ProPublica’s original investigation, Kalani said DraftKings’ responsible gaming system — which consists largely of in-app messages about the company’s tools — “worked the way it was supposed to.” She cautioned against “drawing broad conclusions” from one user’s experience.
The day after the Louisiana meeting, regulators in Ohio proposed an amendment to the state’s sports gaming rule that would bar companies like DraftKings from sending direct ads or marketing to bettors for 48 hours after they’d opted into responsible gaming tools or updated their current settings.
The proposed amendment speaks directly to a finding in ProPublica’s reporting: After blowing nearly $4,500 betting on tennis in 24 hours, the reporter used such tools to limit the amount of time and money he could spend on the app. Just 30 minutes later, though, he received the first of four push notifications promoting new betting opportunities. It wasn’t until he opted into a far more restrictive tool, called a “cool-off,” that the notifications temporarily stopped.
Andromeda Morrison, the interim executive director of the Ohio Casino Control Commission, said that though her office had been working on its proposal for some time, ProPublica’s story illuminated the issue. “Hopefully this is something that is fairly easy for the industry to see as a common sense restriction to make sure those consumers are making good choices without those push notifications,” she said.
But Keith Whyte, a former director of the National Council on Problem Gambling who now consults for industry and nonprofit groups, said the proposed amendment could unintentionally disincentivize users from using tools like deposit limits. “I think the implication is that using a responsible gaming tool is a sign of a gambling problem,” he said. The measure faces a long rulemaking process, including more rounds of public hearings and comments.
Sports betting operators are also feeling the heat at the federal level.
Citing ProPublica’s reporting, three Democrats who have long called for industry reforms are now demanding more information from major sports betting and prediction market companies about how the businesses entice their customers.
The letters are signed by Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, New York Rep. Paul Tonko and North Carolina Rep. Valerie Foushee. They asked the companies to answer a series of questions, including how many customers are enrolled in their VIP programs and how much revenue is generated by them.
“As repeated stories from exploited gamblers and media reports have vividly documented, VIP programs are driving the gambling industry’s most susceptible customers into debt and addiction through rewards tied to waging ever increasing amounts of money,” the lawmakers wrote.
DraftKings conferred VIP status on a ProPublica reporter after he lost close to $6,000 in three weeks on the app by chasing losses with long-shot bets, playing late into the night and firing risky wagers on fast action, like whether a major league baseball player will take a strike, a ball or connect for a hit — betting behavior that experts say are clear red flags of problem gambling.
In a statement, DraftKings said it would “respond accordingly once we have had a chance to review” the letter. Its biggest competitor, FanDuel, which has been trading letters with the lawmakers for months, wrote on Oct. 20 that the company was committed to responsible gaming and said “the VIP program is intended to provide enhanced service and encourage customers who chose to wager to use FanDuel rather than another platform.”
The companies are likely to face further scrutiny.
In New York, investigators for the state’s attorney general have contacted former DraftKings employees about issues raised in the Times’ story, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the probe and messages it had reviewed. A spokesperson for the office declined to comment.
That inquiry follows proposals earlier this month by state gaming officials that they say will strengthen New York’s own standards governing the use of artificial intelligence and responsible gaming guidelines.
Regulators in Maine, Massachusetts and Michigan have also said that they’re reviewing some of those same issues.
DraftKings, the spokesperson said, “does not market to customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming.”
Still, there are signs that yet more states may be interested in vetting those claims.
Jennifer Davenport, New Jersey’s attorney general, recently told the RG Journal, a publication that focuses on responsible gaming and industry matters, that “we are monitoring recent press reports alleging certain sports books are ignoring our consumer safeguards and chasing customers who are clearly exhibiting signs of problem betting.”
“Let them be warned, our office stands ready to take action against anyone who violates our gaming regulations and tries taking advantage of New Jerseyans and those who gamble here,” she said.
A spokesperson for Davenport declined to comment.
