https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Haley Stevens’s Betrayal Is a Fiasco for the Democratic Establishment
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Haley Stevens’s Betrayal Is a Fiasco for the Democratic Establishment
Centrist, pro-Israel Democrats helped Stevens undermine Abdul El-Sayed for months. Now they are reaping the consequences.
Michigan Representative Haley Stevens likes to tell the world what she’s dreaming about. Sometimes, she even overshares a little bit, as in her notorious December 2023 statement that “Israel comes to me in my dreams.”
On Saturday, Stevens dipped into her well of nocturnal visions in a bid to calm the waters she’d started churning up over her clear antipathy toward Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Michigan Senate nominee who defeated Stevens in a bitter primary in August. Responding to concerns that she might break with her party and endorse El-Sayed’s Republican rival, Mike Rogers, Stevens reportedly texted a Michigan Democrat, “I am voting straight Dem!!!! I had a dream last night we won. And I believe he will win! P.S. it was a happy dream.” She reportedly said much the same thing to multiple friends and congressional colleagues up until early Sunday morning—until, without warning, she appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church and announced that she was endorsing him.
The drama of Stevens’s life over the last few weeks has been a battle between these competing dreams. Her pro-Israel politics were in tension with her partisan identity after she lost the primary in August to El-Sayed, who is strongly critical of Israel. AIPAC spent more than $30 million supporting Stevens. After her loss, AIPAC and allied groups such as the United Democracy Project have continued to pour tens of millions of dollars into the effort to defeat El-Sayed, although the full spending on the race hasn’t yet been tabulated. Stevens, meanwhile, kept insisting that her dream of a Democratic Senate outweighed her dreams of Israel, even as she demanded that El-Sayed denounce anti-Israel ads he had nothing to do with. (El-Sayed complied.)
Now we know which dream ultimately won out. When Stevens made her announcement, one of the people in the background was Abigail Ronson, described by Drop Site News as not only a Rogers spokesperson but also “a registered foreign agent for the state of Israel.” Not surprisingly, AIPAC repeatedly posted celebratory retweets of Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers.
Stevens has a personal connection to Zionism as well. Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, is strongly pro-Israel and a megadonor to both political parties. He has donated more than $24,000 to the campaign of Maine Republican Susan Collins. Last week, Turkish announced that he is voting for Rogers. (A friend of Stevens told The Washington Post on Sunday that Turkish had been “really working her over” to endorse Rogers, including by saying that she was betraying Jewish voters by backing El-Sayed.)
In declaring her own support for Rogers, Stevens claimed, “Who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and it is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.” This claim is absurd, since El-Sayed has not been running a hateful campaign, while Rogers and other Republicans have targeted the Democrats with vile Islamophobia. In fact, after welcoming the support of Stevens, Rogers referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist.”
The journalist Ray Wert, who is married to Mallory McMorrow, who was also bested by El-Sayed in Michigan’s Democratic senatorial primary, offered some insights into Stevens in a long post on X.com that emphasized her personal flakiness and speculated on the role her fiancé might have played in the decision. According to Wert:
I’ve known Haley Stevens for a long time. Until now, she has always had staff to protect her, prop her up, and keep her safe from her own irrational behavior. What we’re seeing now? This is just raw, unfiltered Haley. 
The Haley who flip-flops and goes from thought to thought without rhyme or reason. The Haley that calls you at 3 AM to yell at you, and then calls you back at 5 AM oblivious to the fact that she even spoke with you at 3 AM. The Haley who bends to the last and loudest voice that tells her something. 
More often than not that last voice is now her fiancé. And…that appears to potentially be a really troubling relationship.
This account of Stevens’s personal instability is plausible enough, and other emerging accounts reinforce this narrative. So too will the train wreck of an interview that Stevens gave to CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Sunday night, in which she appeared erratic in the extreme and failed to give any coherent reason for her last-minute endorsement of Rogers.
But Stevens’s personality is only part of the story. Donald Trump is also weird, but his weirdness is amplified and given direction by his ideology as well as pressure from those around him.
In Stevens’s case, hardline pro-Israel ideology is key to understanding her decision. Danielle O’Byrne, a political strategist who has worked for Stevens as well as Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, wrote bluntly about the ideological dimensions of Stevens’s actions:
In 2022, I worked for Haley Stevens’ campaign. Over my time working there I quickly learned that she was bought and sold by AIPAC. A Democrat from the middle of America, obsessed with foreign interests and willing to sell herself and us out for it. We won that race by 20 points. With over $10 million in outside spending by AIPAC to oust another Jewish Democratic member, @andylevin, all because he wasn’t kowtowing to them.
It’s precisely because Stevens was a fierce pro-Israel warrior that she had the support of the Democratic Party establishment. In the primaries, she was the preferred candidate of Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader. After she lost the primary, Stevens started making comments that were clearly designed to sabotage El-Sayed. But this didn’t put her beyond the pale, since other party leaders such as former House speaker Nancy Pelosi and Neera Tanden (head of the Center for American Progress) were saying much the same thing.
In retrospect, centrist Democrats such as Pelosi and Tanden were playing a dangerous game. They were clearly intent on reducing El-Sayed’s margin without fatally wounding his campaign. The goal was to make sure that even if El-Sayed won, they could argue that he underperformed because his version of progressive politics—particularly when it came to Israel—was too extreme, thus making it easier to ideologically discipline him in office.
Stevens was playing the same game, but on Sunday, she went too far by actually endorsing Rogers. This robbed establishment Democrats of their plausible deniability in hamstringing the El-Sayed campaign.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Stevens also made herself toxic among Democrats. She still has a few defenders, such as Todd Richman, head of Democratic Majority for Israel. But her longtime chief of staff Justin German has quit and says many of his colleagues are also resigning. Party leaders—notably Schumer, Pelosi, and Tanden—who previously supported Stevens are now decrying what Schumer described as a “despicable betrayal.”
But the lamentations of these powerful centrist Democrats ring hollow. They sound like Dr. Frankenstein wringing his hands over the havoc wreaked by the monster he created. The monster, of course, deserves punishment—and there is already a move to expel Stevens from the Democratic Party’s congressional caucus—but so do the doctors.
The best-case scenario for the Democrats might be that they win a large enough supermajority that they can afford to expel a few wreckers within the party, not just Stevens but also Senator John Fetterman.
But Stevens is merely a symptom of a deeper problem. Even as voters are becoming more wary of the US alliance with Israel, Democratic Party elites are top-heavy with figures closely aligned to the pro-Israel lobby. Any reckoning with the Stevens fiasco has to also include radically weakening this lobby.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Ilhan Omar: “Trump Has an Unhealthy and Creepy Obsession With Me”
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
In the predawn hours of October 12, Department of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents raided the home of US Representative Ilhan Omar, DFL-Minnesota. The raid was reportedly part of a criminal fraud investigation that was focused on decades-old immigration and citizenship paperwork that was filed by Omar’s father when she was a child. Omar, an outspoken progressive, is a refugee from Somalia who came to the United States at age 12. She has been the target of attacks by Trump, his Republican allies, and right-wing media for the better part of a decade. She denied any wrongdoing and decried the raid as “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
That sentiment was echoed by former president Barack Obama, along with many other prominent Democrats and defenders of civil liberties. For his part, Trump claimed he had nothing to do with the raid. Yet, on the same day that it occurred, the president ripped into Omar as “totally crooked personally” and “a terrible person.” He also endorsed Minnesota Republican US Senate nominee Michele Tafoya, who is mounting a high-stakes challenge to DFL candidate Peggy Flanagan in Tuesday’s midterm election. With Republican prospects fading in Senate battleground states such as North Carolina and Georgia, Tafoya’s bid was on Trump’s radar to such an extent that, just hours after the raid on Omar’s home, he was telling Minnesotans, “You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who’s a very respected person.”
The Nation recently asked Omar to discuss the raid and the politics surrounding it. Here’s what she had to say.
—John Nichols
John Nichols:  There was an immediate show of support from your constituents after the raid. You can’t be too worried about your own reelection prospects. But do you think that the president and his allies are trying to stir up anti-immigrant and anti-Somali sentiment in the broader context of the midterms?
Ilhan Omar: Absolutely. This is political, and it’s a deliberate attempt to distract the American people from the failures of this administration. Republicans don’t want to talk about the soaring cost of living, the Epstein files, the war in Iran, Trump’s shady diesel deal with Russia, or a healthcare system that is spiraling out of control. So instead, Trump sends DHS to raid my home. This is what authoritarianism looks like: weaponizing the federal government against anyone he sees as an opponent, scapegoating immigrant communities, and using racism and fear to divide us. He is reaching for the same tired playbook because he knows his party is in trouble. Trump thinks he can turn our neighbors against one another to win an election. I believe the American people are better than that.
JN: Why do you think the president and so many Republicans are obsessed with you?
IO: Trump has an unhealthy and creepy obsession with me. I represent everything Trump and today’s Republican Party seem to despise. I’m a woman, an immigrant, a refugee, a Muslim woman who wears a hijab, and someone who refuses to be intimidated into silence. I know who I am and why I do this work.
The Republican Party has chosen to serve billionaires and powerful corporations over working people. They know that our vision of healthcare for everyone, an economy that works for working families, and a country where everyone can live with dignity is popular with the American people. So they resort to racism, Islamophobia, conspiracy theories, and lies. They want to make me the story because they don’t want to answer for their own failures. But I will not let their hatred define me, and I will not let it distract me from the people I came to Congress to serve.
JN: Many Minnesotans have complained about being targeted by the administration—with last winter’s Operation Metro Surge, and with all the focus on you. Why do you think this is happening?
IO: Trump has said that this is political retribution. I believe Minnesota is a target because we represent everything his politics of division cannot understand. We are a community that chooses solidarity over fear and care over cruelty. We welcome immigrants and refugees. We don’t just welcome them into our neighborhoods—we send them to Congress. When our neighbors are threatened, we show up, even in below-zero temperatures. We deliver meals, give children rides to school, check on one another, and organize mutual aid. We understand that when one family is hurting, our whole community has a responsibility to help. I have seen that love firsthand in the outpouring of support from my constituents. In moments when this administration tries to make people feel afraid and alone, Minnesotans have reminded me what this country can be at its best. Their courage and compassion mean more to me than I can put into words.
That is what Trump cannot stand. He wants us to believe that our differences make us weaker, that some people belong here more than others, and that fear is the only way to lead. Minnesota proves otherwise. Our strength comes from looking out for one another, recognizing our shared humanity, and refusing to abandon our neighbors. The antidote to authoritarianism is community. It is love. It is solidarity. It is the belief that every person deserves dignity and that none of us are free until all of us are free. Those are Minnesota’s values. Those are American values. And no raid, no threat, and no amount of hatred will take them away from us.
JN: You have often spoken about your patriotism and your pride at being an American. How does the raid—and the president’s very personal attacks on you—make you feel about your country and the people who are currently leading it? Do you think Trump is out of touch with American values and ideals?
IO: Trump’s behavior echoes some of the darkest chapters in our nation’s history. But I believe deeply in the promise of this country because generations of Americans have fought, sacrificed, and organized to make it a more just and equal place. That’s why I ran for office.
My family and I have endured death threats, relentless harassment, and years of personal attacks from this president. It has been painful, but it has never shaken my love for this country or my belief in its people. Trump may be out of touch with our values, but I know the best of America is found in people who stand up for one another, refuse to give up, and keep fighting for a country that lives up to its promise. I will never stop fighting for an America where everyone can see a doctor, afford a safe home, and put food on the table.
JN: What can Congress do to hold Trump and DHS to account?

IO: Congress has a constitutional duty to stand up to this abuse of power. We must defend our rights under the Speech and Debate Clause [outlined in Article I, Section 6, Clause 1 of the United States Constitution] and make clear that no president gets to use the power of the executive branch to intimidate or target members of Congress for political reasons.
This is bigger than party. It is about defending our democracy and protecting the independence of Congress. When we allow one branch of government to intimidate another, we weaken the very foundations of our republic.
[House Speaker] Mike Johnson has failed to meet this moment. But I promise you this—when Democrats retake the majority in November, we will stand up, hold this administration accountable, and defend the institution and the constitutional rights that every member of Congress is sworn to uphold.
JN: President Obama offered a powerful statement in your defense. It is notable that he was also a target of Trump’s conspiracy theories and a questioning of his citizenship. Were you struck by that?
IO: President Obama knows the world of right-wing conspiracies better than anyone. In many ways, the conspiracy world I find myself in was created around him. That is why he can so clearly see the purpose and contradictions of the lies being told about me. He knows that no amount of evidence or facts will ever be enough for these trolls, because they are not after the truth. The conspiracy itself is what drives them. It meant so much to me to know that President Obama sees this for what it is and was willing to speak out.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Russia’s security service detains teen over alleged terror plot targeting Moscow museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sophia Kishkovsky
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Russia’s FSB security service has detained a teenager on charges of threatening Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve via TikTok after an unusual warning from US officials of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” on 31 October. The alert was posted on the website of the US embassy in Moscow and social media. Der Spiegel reported that German citizens in Russia had received a similar warning.
On 1 November, the FSB distributed a video, published on sites such as Tass, the official state news agency, showing an unidentified young man being detained, footage of a knife, camouflage and neo-Nazi content on his phone, and his confession to posting “propaganda of Nazism” on his TikTok page. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee posted the same footage to its YouTube channel.
The US issued a similar alert several days before an attack that killed at least 149 people in March 2024 during a concert at Crocus City Hall in Moscow. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack; before it occurred, Russian President Vladimir Putin denounced the warnings as “outright blackmail”.
In a change reflecting US President Donald Trump’s cooperation with Russia, the FSB in a statement on 1 November, posted on the agency’s website, credited “US law enforcement agencies” for warning of an impending attack at Tsaritsyno: “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”
The FSB statement added that “in the interest of public safety, planned cultural events at the museum-reserve have been cancelled, and security measures in the surrounding area have been stepped up”. The museum is typically closed on Mondays, while the surrounding park, known for its rolling hills, fountains and wooded paths, is open daily. Russian media reported that the park reopened on Sunday.
The FSB’s statement claims the detained minor had posted images on TikTok “showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, cap, eyewear and headset—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon” as well as “photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, accompanied by the caption: ‘I found a place’”.
The complex, which was originally intended as a summer residence for Catherine the Great in the 18th century, is consistently ranked as one of Moscow’s most visited tourist sites. Tsaritsyno’s website states that over 7 million people visit the museum and park in southern Moscow annually. The Grand Palace, its centrepiece, is known for its neo-Gothic design by the architect Matvey Kazakov, which remained unfinished after Catherine’s death. Many other buildings on the grounds were designed by Kazakov’s teacher, Vasily Bazhenov, Catherine’s court architect, who was initially commissioned to design the palace before falling out with the Empress.
Some preservationists denounced the glitzy completion of the palace, inaugurated in 2007 with Putin present. It was carried out under Moscow’s mayor at the time, Yury Luzhkov, who was known for monumental construction projects. Although some attempts have been made to show contemporary art at Tsaritsyno, its exhibitions are primarily focused on the tsars and historic Russian folk crafts.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Richard Kreitner
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The False Promise of Bob Woodward
He’s always been known as an intrepid journalist. But critics in The Nation, throughout decades, identified ways he held important stories for his own gain.
The False Promise of Bob Woodward
He’s always been known as an intrepid journalist. But critics in “The Nation,” throughout decades, identified ways he held important stories for his own gain.
“Sometimes people have a vision of themselves that just doesn’t fit with reality,” Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward writes in his new memoir, Secret. For example, he does not feel the public’s understanding of him as “‘all business’ and cold” is quite right. But the problem is deeper than that. Woodward has always presented himself as a fearless and committed truth-teller, intent on getting to “the center of what was really going on.” Repeatedly, however, Woodward’s books, purporting to bring readers into the inner operations of the US government, have obscured more than they revealed.
Decades of reviews in The Nation of Woodward’s books show the consistent flaws and oversights that have marked the journalist’s work, not least a habitual reliance on the tropes and trivialities of inside-the-Beltway access-mongering. Jefferson Morley spotted the tendency early, reviewing Woodward’s 1987 book, Veil: The Secret Wars of the C.I.A., 1980-1987, which largely focused on Reagan’s CIA director, William Casey. “Woodward has not so much misreported his story as misinterpreted it,” Morley argued. Training his attention on minute “power struggles” between top officials, Woodward “tends to neglect the more fundamental and important news,” such as the Agency’s support for the contras in Nicaragua, which became international news while Woodward was reporting his book. Instead of telling readers about what the US government was actually up to—including the crimes that high officials were committing—the journalist focused on petty personal squabbles: “Because there was not much dispute among Woodward’s high-level sources about routine C.I.A. support for contra operations, he had no controversy to report on. No high-level controversy, no story.”
The excerpt of Woodward’s new memoir that recently ran in The New Yorker purports to recount a time when he courageously chose to publish the unvarnished truth about infighting within the George H.W. Bush administration, at the cost of losing a close friend who had been his source for the story. But Morley’s review highlights a consistent thread throughout Woodward’s career: His closeness to sources has often won out over a commitment to printing the truth. “Woodward probably has more access to top government officials than any other Washington reporter,” Morley noted. “But access always—always—has a price. Veil confirms that the more access a reporter has, the higher price he or she pays.” Indeed, Woodward himself acknowledged that he did not have the time to pursue the contras story because he was busy talking to Casey for the project that turned into Veil.
Reviewers have often pointed to the glaring lack of background information in Woodward’s supposedly immersive political narratives. Assessing 1991’s The Commanders, framed as an unparalleled glimpse into the (first) Bush administration’s deliberations on the eve of the (first) invasion of Iraq, Jon Wiener observed that “the book’s fatal flaw is that it contains virtually nothing about the political context in which Bush made up his mind in favor of war”— for instance, that his decision to invade was motivated by a sluggish economy and slumping poll numbers ahead of an important midterm election.
But Wiener identified an even worse problem with Woodward’s book, one that would keep cropping up throughout the journalist’s career: his tendency to keep a lid on important stories until the moment was right for him. In the run-up to the first Gulf War, it would have been useful for the public to know that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff was opposed to an invasion. Wiener asked, “What did Woodward know and when did he know it?… Why did that information become Woodward’s private property, which Simon and Schuster would sell to us months later for $24.95? The information Woodward possessed would have been a powerful weapon for the antiwar movement…. Woodward has privatized the news.”
As the Reagan era segued seamlessly into the reign of Clinton, Nation critics objected more strenuously to Woodward’s customary tricks and tics. Reviewing The Agenda, in 1994—a “work of intensive stenography,” about the early years of the Clinton administration—Christopher Hitchens wrote, “The portentous vacancy of neoliberal argot has met its chronicler in one who takes it seriously.”
Woodward’s next book was The Choice, a nearly 500-age tome about the 1996 election, which happened to be published months before that election. Republican challenger Bob Dole “cooperated readily” with the author, as Lynn Phillips wrote in her Nation review, while neither President Clinton nor first lady Hillary Clinton agreed to do so, an imbalance that Woodward never quite managed to rectify, as Phillips wrote: “And when a reporter gets so close to his candidates that he speaks from inside their mouths (Bob Dole, c’est moi!), his reportorial glasses fog up.”
Woodward’s glasses were especially foggy in the early years of this century. His 2003 book Bush at War, about the months after the September 11 attacks, was appraised in The Nation by Washington editor David Corn: “Woodward stuck with what has become in recent years his standard MO: Approach each power player and say, ‘All the other power players are telling me their side of the story, so you should do so as well.’ Woodward then weaves the various self-serving versions—supplied, of course, on background—into a quasi-official chronicle, with little overt sourcing.” While his Watergate investigations “excavated a story the big shots didn’t want public,” Woodward’s later work related only “what the powerful do want known.”
And so on, through the Obama, Trump, and Biden years, and into our own abysmal present. Most recently, in 2025, Matthew Duss, executive vice president at the Center for International Policy, assessed Woodward’s book, War, about the Biden administration’s handling of conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine. As Duss wrote, “Woodward consistently fails to interrogate any of what he is told, choosing instead to simply record and relay it and allow his readers to assemble the picture as they wish, as if the real journalistic feat was just getting the decision-makers and insiders to talk to him in the first place.”
Despite the self-serving accounts in his memoir, Woodward remains, as he has long been, a conduit for largely meaningless internecine battles among elites, a glorified stenographer haplessly doing the bidding of the powerful even while he presents himself as a heroic crusader for the vitality of the Fourth Estate. It’s a vision of himself that doesn’t fit with reality, even if Woodward’s first-draft accounts of history have done all too much to shape it.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Objects reinstalled at Museo Nacional de Colombia following removal by right-wing government
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Mercedes Ezquiaga
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Bogotá’s Museo Nacional de Colombia has reinstalled the 63 objects previously taken down from its permanent galleries over claims of “political indoctrination”. The move followed a court order that reversed the national government's removal of the items on 15 October.
On the evening of 28 October, César Enrique Osorio Ortiz—a judge at Bogotá’s 24th Family Court—ordered Colombia’s cultural ministry and the museum to return the works to their original locations within 48 hours. The ministry complied with the order on Friday (30 October).
The decision came in response to a constitutional-rights case filed by cultural groups and political opponents who had accused the government of the country's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella of censorship. The judge also ordered both institutions not to remove works based on their content or the views they express.
Among the removed pieces were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo, a pen made from a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 peace agreement between the state and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.
The removals came amid calls by De la Espriella for a “cultural war” and a “direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture”, an offensive that affected the country’s main museum.
The government’s decision sparked a series of protests during which hundreds of people gathered outside the museum, as well as a joint statement by six museums expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of their professional autonomy. The signatories included the Modern art museums of Bogotá, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellín and Tolima, as well as the Museo Rayo.
Marielsa Castro Vizcarra, the chief curator of the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (which signed the joint statement), tells The Art Newspaper that the cultural sector responded quickly, from street protests to the statement and the involvement of the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art. Castro described the incident as “a precedent we need to take into account” and “an authoritarian way of spreading fear”.
According to the judge's ruling, the artefacts had been removed “without a documented curatorial justification” in a decision that “disregarded the constitutional protection of cultural expressions”. The court did not rule out future changes to the exhibitions, provided they are properly justified and not based on the authorities’ objections to the works’ content.
“No government owns our history!” wrote Gabriel Becerra, a left-wing lawmaker behind the constitutional-rights case, in a post on X welcoming the court’s decision.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | There is cautious optimism surrounding the contemporary art market—but will it last?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Tim Schneider
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
There is an irony to trying to gauge the health of the art market, as so many in the industry are doing now, with New York’s marquee auctions, the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi and the latest Art Collaboration Kyoto ahead this month. On the one hand, the trade is endlessly driven by emotion. On the other, few broad-based, rigorous read-outs can be found of how the participants actually feel about the state of play.
But one exception that proves this rule was published recently: the September edition of ArtTactic’s report on confidence in the contemporary art market. It adds quantitative heft to the sentiment that has emerged from more and more reporting since the spring. Although the market has not caught fire yet, the findings indicate that significant segments of it have certainly thawed. More importantly, a cross-section of experts with skin in the game expect the (modestly) good times to continue for the foreseeable future.
Confidence game
So what is the Contemporary Art Market Confidence Report? Twice a year, the study asks a cross-section of collectors, advisers, auction house professionals and other market participants whether they feel positive, negative or neutral about aspects of the art trade and the wider economy in the US and Europe. ArtTactic then converts the ratings into a single score, from zero (essentially, no confidence) to 100 (essentially, absolute confidence), for each question, offering a quantified, collective evaluation.
The main takeaway is encouraging but measured. The overall confidence indicator rose from 43 (slightly pessimistic) in March 2026 to 56 (slightly optimistic) in September. It marks only the third time the rating has reached positive territory in more than four years.
However, both previous moments of optimism were short-lived. After hitting a rowdy 75 in February 2022, the rating dropped to 42 that July. And the January 2025 score of 54 plunged to a frightening 30 six months later.
Anders Petterson, the founder and chief executive of ArtTactic, thinks the current bout of positivity is more durable than the last one. In January 2025, he points out, 39% of the survey respondents expected Donald Trump’s return to the White House to produce economic policies that would boost the art market. “Instead, he introduced tariffs and a significant amount of uncertainty, which pulled down confidence for the July 2025 reading,” Petterson says. The difference now is that the “confidence seems to be grounded in a real recovery in sales, rather than just a belief”.
Steady state
Still, the experts polled by ArtTactic are nearly as wary as they are optimistic. Asked whether sales would rise, fall or stay flat over the six months to come, 60% chose the last of these options.
That may not sound great, but it isn’t bad. Remember, a confidence indicator of 56 means most of the respondents believe things are good right now, even if only just. In this context, Petterson says that a flat outlook for the next half year “suggests stability rather than deterioration”.
Some parts of the market appear steadier than others, however. Confidence in the auction market—up to 78 from 69 in March, spurred on by results at the top end—far surpassed confidence in the primary market, which nudged up to 51 from 45. Although this is good news for the trade at large, the visibility of strong hammer results tends not to boost all sellers equally.
“Most of the recovery at auction is still concentrated in the above $1m segment, which is likely to benefit galleries/artists operating at the top end,” Petterson says. “What is less clear is whether, and how quickly, that confidence will make its way down to lower-price-point galleries and artists.”
Galleries may need to do more to help themselves. On the eve of Frieze week, the American adviser Adam Green said he has seen “a noticeable shift” among many of his clients. Offputtingly high and persistent prices for new works have pushed several collectors who often used to buy from primary market dealers toward auction houses and private resellers, both of which “can provide a better opportunity to acquire works closer to their true fair market value”.
Although Green believes market recovery is “broadening to some degree”, he also suspects its full reach will take until the end of the year to become clear. If you wanted to translate the ArtTactic report data into one simple sentiment, it would be hard to do it more efficiently than in that sentence. Now we know this sentiment really is shared by more than just a few industry figures that we journalists happened to ask for comment.

https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.title: New York City SNAP Participants Will Get Extra Funds for Fresh Produce in 2027
https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.text:
Share This Article
The city is expanding its Health Bucks program, which matches every $2 a SNAP participant spends on fruit and vegetables at farmers markets and other select vendors. The change comes as inflation and rising food costs has more households struggling.
With food costs on the rise, the city is expanding a program that offers low-income New Yorkers extra money to spend on local produce, the Mamdani administration announced Thursday.
Starting in January, participants in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP or food stamps, will have greater spending power under the city’s Health Bucks program, which matches every $2 they spend at farmers markets and farm stands with coupons they can use to purchase additional fruits and vegetables.
The city is raising the daily Health Bucks cap from $10 to $14, meaning SNAP participants can qualify for an extra $4 a day for fresh produce at more than 100 locations across the city—what officials say will offer a boost to both households’ budgets and local farmers.
“Every day, New Yorkers walk into a store hoping prices haven’t gone up again,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement announcing the change. “As food insecurity rises, far too many families are forced to skip the fruits and vegetables.”
From 2021 to 2024, the number of city residents at risk of food insecurity—meaning their households sometimes or often struggled to afford food—increased by 18 percent, from 2.2 million to 2.6 million, according to Health Department data released last month.
For certain demographic groups, the numbers were even starker: some 59 percent of Latino and 50 percent of Black New Yorkers were at risk of being food insecure in 2024, the same report found, compared to 40 percent of the city’s population overall. Food insecure households were more likely to forgo fresh produce, the report found.
The city says it expects to distribute nearly $2.3 million in Health Bucks benefits next year with the expanded matching cap.
The change comes as inflation and rising food costs have more SNAP households stretching their monthly dollars to make ends meet. A recent Urban Institute analysis found that for many counties across the country, maximum SNAP benefits fall far below the average cost of a “modestly priced” meal in that area.
In Manhattan, for example, that average meal is approximately $6.07—109 percent more than the $2.90 per meal that a maximum SNAP benefit covers, the analysis found, one of the largest gaps in the country.

Election day is finally here, and amid national chatter about the big blue wave, the balance of power in Congress could all come down to New York.
No pressure, right? Early voting numbers have reportedly slowed since 2025, particularly in the Commie Corridor, which saw a 34 percent drop in early voting this election, but early voting increased in majority Black districts across the city, including Central Brooklyn (a 50 percent jump) and parts of Southeast Queens. (By the way, if you live in New York City and procrastinated on voting—and who would do something like that, especially if they had to work overtime on election night, ha ha ha—here's where to find your polling site.)
Tonight, we will learn if North Country voters choose a dairy farming executive, Democrat Blake Gendebien, over a guy with an AI rap album that lobs Islamophobic slurs at Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Republican Anthony Costantino. We'll find out if Republican incumbent Mike Lawler can smirk his way past Democratic candidate Cait Conley in NY-17. We'll see if Governor Kathy Hochul prevails over Bruce Blakeman, the sentient haircut slash would-be militiaman who is taking a run at Albany from Nassau County, and whose name could have hypothetically been Blake Bruceman. And although we promise we're not actually putting any money on this, we're pretty sure we'll be witnessing Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Brad Lander, and various leftist candidates across the city ride the Mamdani wave to electoral victory.
But before all that happens, Hell Gate will be doing our usual live blog dance: running all around the city all day, talking to voters, catching up with candidates, and generally taking the temperature on whether New Yorkers consider this weird and wild midterm to be a referendum on Trump 2.0. (And don't forget about those ballot proposals!)
We'll be updating this post all day and into the early evening with dispatches from the team. Then, we'll keep the party going on our LIVE Hell Gate Election Night 2026 Podcast. The live pod starts at 9 p.m. on the dot on our YouTube channel and at select watch parties around the city (including the one you throw at your apartment, if you're a real fan).
Until then, keep refreshing, and we'll keep reporting.
And don't forget to subscribe to Hell Gate to support independent worker-owned journalism, from live blogs like this one, to features, to columns and newsletters, to our podcast, to our events, and more! We can't do any of this without you.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: A collection of intimate interviews with the late Jo Spence provides further texture to her life and legacy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Beth Williamson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Jo Spence (1934-92) was a London-born and based British photographer, writer, class and health activist and educator. She is best known for challenging the assumptions of what photography could be, for example, by using her own image to question common tropes around female beauty, health, identity and societal expectations. Spence’s achievements centred on the small home and studio on Islington’s Upper Street that she shared with her partner and collaborator Terry Dennett (1938-2018).
The Unknown Recordings is an intimate self-portrait in text form. There are pictures, but surprisingly few. Still, in that respect, Spence’s disarmingly frank autobiography Putting Myself in the Picture (1986) could not be surpassed. Forty years on, this publication makes sense of a textual account largely in the form of transcripts of key historic recordings made with the artist.
The verbatim transcript of Spence’s interview for the British Library’s Oral History of British Photography, recorded in 1991, extends to more than 100 pages. It covers every aspect of her life from childhood experiences to early working life, before progressing to her photographic work, collaborations and politics, as well as her experience of breast cancer and leukaemia.
The conversation between Spence and the interviewer flows, with few fragments and diversions, in a manner that allows us (almost) to hear it. Generous in her sharing of extremely personal ideas and experiences, Spence does not shy away from difficult topics, least of all her own experience of chronic illness and her attempts to regain power over her own body and identity. Her friendship with artist Rosy Martin and their development of phototherapy, a form of psychological therapy centred on photography, is especially raw.
Distress, tears and self-analysis
The transcript of a short personal recording made in 1982, after the breast cancer diagnosis, is more unsettling. This is Spence recording her own thoughts, filled with distress, tears and self-analysis: while it became part of her archive and she often blurred the line between private and public, it does feel a little like eavesdropping. Recorded over two days, it is intensely emotional, as Spence struggles to process and come to terms with the various stressors in her life. In a particularly poignant moment, Dennett is recorded shouting words of support, presumably from another room.
Spence’s interview with visual activist and educator Andrew Dewdney and curator Shirley Read has a political slant. Recorded in the Cockpit Arts Workshop in London in 1989, this conversation gives acute insight into Spence’s commitment to a political as well as photographic practice. It ranges across her ideas relating to different areas of her work, such as the Photography Workshop, Hackney Flashers, Half Moon Photography Workshop and Camerawork magazine. Ultimately, these projects perhaps coalesced around Spence’s focus on people’s right to speak and be seen. It is a powerful conversation.
A series of four appendices act as a kind of postscript to Spence’s voice. There is the documentation of Spence’s sacking from Half Moon over ideological differences; recently discovered images of Spence’s retrospective of 1994; photographs, thoughts and exchanges with artist Pru Clements; and Spence’s CV from March 1987.
This section also includes Dennett’s reworked introduction to Spence’s Putting Myself in the Picture. Here, he makes it clear that Spence’s work was done under difficult circumstances but that she remained focused on the importance of empowering others. Rather than concluding in some fashion or other, together these last documents point the reader to other rich visual and textual archival material that surrounds Spence’s life and legacy. She extended the possibilities of photography to speak about the unspeakable and photograph the unphotographable. Spence was not within the cultural elite, but found a way to tell her own story and hoped it would be a model for others to follow.
• Jo Spence: The Unknown Recordings, Museums etc, 256 pp, 30 colour and 8 b/w illustrations, £35 (pb), £25 (e-b), 1 January

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: An expert’s guide to Pierre-Auguste Renoir: five must-read books on the French Impressionist
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: José da Silva
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
• Click here for more reading lists on the world's greatest artists
The French Impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir is a surprisingly divisive artist, from some of his peers denigrating him to the so-called Renoir Sucks at Painting movement a decade ago and a critic recently labelling him “the chocolate boxiest” of the Impressionists. But the recently opened exhibition Renoir and Love at the National Gallery in London (which debuted at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris earlier this year and will travel to Boston in 2027) has had—for the most part—rave reviews and robust ticket sales. Its co-curator Christopher Riopelle, who is also the author of Renoir: The Great Bathers (1990), has selected five key books for anyone wanting to go beyond first impressions.
Renoir, My Father (1962) by Jean Renoir
“Father and son, both artistic geniuses—a rare combination. That the great cineaste Jean Renoir should have penned an idiosyncratic, anecdote-filled life of the father is more than we deserve. Moreover, it is a film-maker’s biography, countless scenes set up visually, in flowing time. No surprise to learn that the loving son wrote it in far-off Hollywood!”
Renoir’s Portraits: Impressions of an Age (1997) by Colin B. Bailey
“Colin B. Bailey is our leading Renoir scholar. It is invidious to choose which of his several publications to include; I settle on this study of 69 portraits. Bulging with new information, it is every bit as indispensable to social historians as to art historians. As Renoir studies resurge, let us hope it returns to print.”
Renoir in the 20th Century (2010) with essays by Roger Benjamin, Claudia Einecke, Guy Cogeval, Isabelle Gaëtan, Emmanuelle Héran, John House, Virgine Journiac, Martha Lucy, Laurence Madeline, Monique Nonne and Sylvie Patry
“Late Renoir: Marmite. But the period includes among its admirers Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso and the collector Albert C. Barnes. Sylvie Patry guides us through the final two decades with concision, deep respect and an unfailing eye for bravura painting. More than that, she demonstrates why the allusive Classicism of the late works played a key role in Modernism.”
Renoir in the Barnes Foundation (2012) by Martha Lucy and John House
“The Renoir scholar John House wrote this assessment of the largest and greatest of all Renoir collections with a passionate and utterly engaged eye. Martha Lucy was with him all the way; it’s as if we eavesdrop on a wickedly clever conversation between receptive student and brilliant, probing master.”
Auguste Renoir: Lettres choisies (2026), edited by Augustin de Butler and Anne Distel
“At last, a meticulous scholarly edition of 314 key Renoir letters tracing his career from 1865 to 1919. Helped in shaping by the consummate Renoir scholar Anne Distel, finally we can ‘hear’ the master’s voice. The wit is clear but so, too, the anxiety. Let us have a translation soon, to stand beside the newly translated Claude Monet letters.”
• Renoir and Love, National Gallery, London, until 31 January 2027; Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 28 February 2027-13 June 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Italy set to create restitution panel for Nazi-looted art
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Italy’s parliament is considering legislation that would, for the first time, establish a formal process for restituting art and cultural property seized by the Nazis and Italian authorities from victims of racial persecution during the Holocaust era.
Introduced by a lawmaker from Brothers of Italy, the party led by the country’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni, the proposal has been hailed by as “an act of civilisation” by representatives of heirs of those whose property was stolen, and would bring Italy in line with Germany, Austria, France, the Netherlands, the UK and Switzerland, the latest European country to establish its own restitution mechanisms.
The bill grants the government powers to establish a five-member committee to examine the provenance of works that were confiscated, looted or sold under duress as a result of racial persecution between 1933 and 1945. The committee would assess individual cases and issue decisions on restitution to the original owners, their heirs or—if no living heirs are identified—the broader Jewish community in Italy.
If enacted, the bill, which is currently being examined by the lower house’s culture committee, would give the government six months to establish the restitution system.
“Introducing this bill does not merely mean finally bringing Italy into line with the highest international standards... but means, first and foremost, fulfilling a historic duty,” Federico Mollicone, a key Meloni ally who introduced the bill in March, tells The Art Newspaper.
“We are not merely talking about property claims, but about restoring human dignity, memory and the fundamental principles of our constitution,” says Mollicone, who is the president of the culture commission in Italy’s lower house of parliament.
Seized works in state museums
State-sponsored looting, confiscation and forced sale of Jewish-owned art and cultural heritage became increasingly commonplace following the fascist dictator Benito Mussolini’s 1938 introduction of racial laws that prohibited Jewish books, excluded Jews from public office and introduced limits on Jewish property ownership. The dispossessions increased from 1943, when Italian and occupying German Nazi forces began arresting and deporting Jews to concentration camps.
Some of the seized works subsequently entered the collections of Italian museums, where four publicly known disputed works are currently displayed, according to Katharina Hüls-Valenti, an expert in provenance research at Parma University. They include Edouard Manet’s Portrait de M. Arnaud à cheval (1875), which Hüls-Valenti says was sold under duress in 1935 by its owners, the family of German painter Max Liebermann, and donated to the Galleria d’Arte Moderna in Milan in 1958. Hüls-Valenti says that Liebermann’s heirs had sought restitution but had encountered resistance from the museum.
Asked to respond to those allegations, Paola Zatti, a curator at the Galleria d’Arte Moderna, said in a statement to The Art Newspaper: “The painting was sold by Liebermann’s wife in 1935 (incidentally, to a Jewish antiques dealer), but there is no evidence that she was forced to do so.”
Zatti added that, in accord with a lawyer representing Liebermann’s heirs in Germany, the museum had agreed to display a label explaining the work’s ownership history. The text, Zatti said, “clearly highlights the tragic moment when the work was sold by its Jewish owners” and helps visitors appreciate the “circumstances under which [the work] left Germany”.
Another painting, Cristo portacroce (around 1508-09) by Girolamo da Romano, was requisitioned by France’s pro-Nazi Vichy government in 1941 from the family of Federico Gentili di Giuseppe, an Italian Jewish businessman and art collector living in Paris. It was auctioned to a private collector and then bought by Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera museum in 1998. Following a request by the heirs, US authorities seized the work while it was on loan to a Florida museum in 2011.
The real number of Holocaust-era seizures currently held by museums, Hüls-Valenti suggests, could be closer to dozens. “We really don’t know for sure,” she says. “Better research is required.”
Italy endorsed the 1998 Washington Principles, which established guidelines for the restitution of Nazi-looted art. A 2001 enquiry led by Tina Anselmi, a former Italian government minister, found evidence of systematic expropriation from Jews. It found evidence of 7,847 seizure warrants issued up to April 1945 for property including houses and land, businesses, bank deposits, insurance policies, jewellery, paintings and furniture.
Despite the report’s findings, Italy, a global leader in securing the restitution of its own national heritage, has been slower than other European countries to seek justice for dispossessed Jews. France created a commission for restitutions and compensation in 1999. The UK established the Spoliation Advisory Panel in 2000 to evaluate claims to works held by British national institutions.
Delay due to several factors
“Italy is obviously a central country in the world of art... and yet on this issue of the Holocaust restitution it had barely scratched the surface in addressing it,” says Gideon Taylor, the president of World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO).
Experts point to various reasons for the delay in Italy’s response, including a national reluctance to confront the country’s fascist past, insufficient political will to prioritise the restitution of Jewish-owned cultural heritage, and a lack of transparency about provenance in museums. They say poor cataloguing has contributed to an assumption that few works would be affected by a law.
Complicating matters, Italian law recognises works held in Italian museums as inalienable parts of the national heritage. The bill addresses this hurdle by indicating that the final restitution decision would automatically remove the work from the public domain. Further, restituted works would no longer be subject to the protections of Italy’s heritage code, meaning they could permanently leave the country. The bill also indicates that existing statutes of limitations would not prevent restitutions.
The commission would accept claims from legitimate owners, their descendants or heirs, and the Union of Italian Jewish Communities (UCEI) or individual Jewish communities. It would include a member nominated by Italy’s art police and have to rule within 180 days of a claim. The bill is intended to help heirs seeking restitution from both public and private collections.
Italy’s parliament adopted the bill following the submission of a report evaluating the country’s restitutions record commissioned by the WJRO and written by the lawyer Lorenzo Casini, a former chief of staff at the culture ministry who now heads a public research institution in Lucca. It was written with the support of six leading experts, including Hüls-Valenti, the Parma professor.
“Museums don’t necessarily hide their works, but there isn’t full understanding of just how important transparency is and how helpful it would be for all these works to come to light,” Casini says. “Besides addressing the tragic wounds left by looting and filling the legislative gap in Italy, the law is specifically designed to bring those artworks to light.”
Speaking to parliament’s culture commission in June, Casini praised the bill but suggested areas for improvement, proposing widening the commission’s remit from art to other cultural heritage—including manuscripts, books, archives and ceremonial objects—and advising that the commission and researchers would require additional funds to carry out their work.
“The next step could hopefully be to seek funding once the law has been passed,” Casini tells The Art Newspaper.
Federico Mollicone says lawmakers will “ensure” the culture ministry’s upcoming funding plans include “adequate resources to support research projects on provenance, the digitisation of archives, and the training of dedicated experts”. He highlights culture minister Alessandro Giuli’s “strong commitment to this issue”.
He also predicts the bill will have a smooth passage into law, noting that there is “wide political consensus” on redressing injustices from racial persecution. Brothers of Italy has roots in the post-fascist parties that rose from the ashes of the Second World War.
“Our goal is to complete the parliamentary review and pass the bill in the coming months,” Mollicone says. “We want to bring this historic reform to a successful conclusion within this legislative session.” A general election is due to take place before the end of next year, with analysts suggesting it may be brought forward to the spring.
Paolo Gnignati, UCEI’s head of legal affairs, says the bill’s arrival in parliament is significant. “The regulations on restitution are something that can be meaningful to specific individuals because they have financial and personal implications,” he says. “But they are also, fundamentally, an act of civilisation.”

https://citylimits.org/opinion-washingto.title: Opinion: Washington is Making It Harder for People Like My Grandparents to Keep Their Health Insurance. I Won’t Let That Happen.
https://citylimits.org/opinion-washingto.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-washingto.text:
Share This Article
“As the federal government abandons the people it is meant to serve, New York City is leaning in to protect public goods like health coverage.”
A few years ago, I was working in a doctor’s office scheduling colonoscopies and endoscopies—screenings that can detect cancer early, when it is most treatable. Each appointment I booked felt like a small act of prevention against a disease that has claimed the lives of so many.
One day the doctor stepped into our office with new instructions: Stop scheduling appointments for patients insured through Medicaid. The reimbursement process was too slow and cumbersome, he said. It simply wasn’t worth the hassle.
The room went quiet. We were handed a list of Medicaid-allied insurance carriers we were to no longer accept. As I scanned the list, my heart dropped. On it was the plan that covered my grandparents.
If my own grandparents called to book a cancer screening, I was expected to turn them away.
After that, I was determined to do something that would serve everyone in my community, not just those who can afford it. I wanted to help others who, like my grandparents, have been abandoned by our broken healthcare system.
Problems like this inspired me to work at the New York City Health Department. I’ve joined a new team of highly trained community health workers with a mission to help all New Yorkers access health insurance and other services they deserve. The new Health and Affordability Resource Team, or HART for short, is designed to protect struggling New Yorkers at risk of falling through the ever-widening holes in our country’s social safety net.
Created by the Health Department together with Mayor Zohran Mamdani, HART deploys dozens of community health workers like me into the neighborhoods where we’re needed most, and where many of us are from. 
Through neighborhood outreach in 13 languages, we accompany people through each step of the process, from screening and applications to enrollment and follow-ups. Our primary goal is connecting people to health coverage and other essential benefits, housing stability and eviction prevention resources, and financial assistance for hospital bills.
We’re specially trained to help New Yorkers navigate the latest federal cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, including expanded work requirements and red tape that put as many as 900,000 New Yorkers at risk. These are people who could lose their health insurance—not because they don’t qualify, but because the federal government has made keeping it prohibitively complicated and confusing.
We’re not going to stand for that. Because as the federal government abandons the people it is meant to serve, New York City is leaning in to protect public goods like health coverage.
Years after leaving my job at the cancer screening clinic, it hit me: this wasn’t a one-time decision or one bad provider. It was an entrenched, systemic problem. The cards have been stacked against so many New Yorkers who deserve the care they are being denied.
People are sorted not by their medical need, but by how quickly and conveniently a payment arrives. And the patients who can least afford to miss a cancer screening are the ones being quietly refused. Many will never know why.
That day in the doctor’s office, I could have looked away. I had a steady job and the decision wasn’t up to me. But once you see people losing critical health care like that, you carry it with you.
I left that job and went back to school, this time for public health. I wanted to understand not just how a system fails people, but how it can be redesigned so that it improves people’s lives at scale. I am continuing my studies to receive a master’s in public health, learning about program design and evaluation.
As I’ve studied, I continued working alongside New Yorkers. I held a case management role supporting people with disabilities who needed home health aides. That work taught me what the paperwork could not: Navigating benefits and approvals is exhausting for anyone, and for people already managing a disability or a chronic illness, it can be overwhelming. I have sat with clients as they navigated hurdles that never should have been there.
Today with the Health Department, I’m building on what I’ve learned in classrooms and through my lived experience to help others understand and navigate the barriers in their lives.
As part of the Health and Affordability Resource Team, I get to take meaningful action every day to make life better for my fellow New Yorkers. And now, if my grandparents were to call, there are many ways I can assist them, too.
Jasmine Taylor is a community health worker on the Health and Affordability Resource Team at the NYC Health Department.

https://citylimits.org/hold-it-mamdanis-.title: Hold It: Mamdani’s Public Restrooms Plan Underwhelms
https://citylimits.org/hold-it-mamdanis-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/hold-it-mamdanis-.text:
Share This Article
A plan to double the number of public restrooms in New York City is scant on commitments, advocates for the homeless say.
New Yorkers excited about the city’s goal to double the number of public restrooms by 2035 will have to hold it a bit longer.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani quietly released a City Council-mandated plan to expand the number of public restrooms in the city Friday—but flushed many of the concrete commitments.
The plan they delivered underwhelmed, according to advocates who have been fighting for more restrooms. That includes Homeless New Yorkers—either those living on the street or living in city shelters that often close their doors during the day—who could stand to benefit the most from increased access.
“This isn’t really where it needs to be, but I do feel hopeful that they’re committed to it,” said Councilmember Sandy Nurse, who sponsored last year’s legislation mandating that City Hall come up with a plan to double the number of public restrooms, to over 2,000 citywide. “We need more meat on the bone here.”
The administration already asked for more time to work on the report, which was originally due Sep. 1.
Nurse’s legislation called on the city to accelerate the pace of bathroom building, both publicly owned and through public-private partnerships.
Everyone wants more places to pee. But building more toilets is logistically complex and sometimes prohibitively expensive.
“Delivering high-quality public restrooms for New Yorkers and visitors requires a range of strategies, milestones, and resources across many City Agencies,” Jeremy Edwards, deputy press secretary at City Hall, said in a statement.
While the administration’s plan identifies possible strategies to expand public restrooms—by incentivizing businesses to include them, requiring it of developers, or mandating them in privately owned public spaces—it did not specify how many more the city hopes to yield, or by when.
Instead, it punted those commitments to a forthcoming “action plan” that the administration says will come out by the end of 2027.
“The action plan should have been the report,” said Adolfo Abreu, housing campaigns director at VOCAL-NY, a grassroots group that organizes New Yorkers impacted by homelessness, incarceration and other issues.
Advocates with the “Free to Pee” coalition, of which VOCAL is a member, were supportive of the administration’s aims, but called on City Hall to do “more than the current trickle.”
“The City must still make concrete commitments,” the coalition said in a statement Tuesday.
The fuss over the report illustrates just how challenging it is to build restrooms in New York City, a process that requires coordination between numerous agencies. The report suggested reforms to city procurement and siting processes, regulations, and building code—rules that can slow down planning and drive up costs.
The majority of the 1,100 existing bathrooms the city identified were in parks and libraries.
“Most of those operate on limited hours,” said Alison Wilkey of Coalition for the Homeless “There are very few bathrooms that are open during the evening.”
Around 100 of the 1,100 restrooms were not currently operational, the report found.
Building a single restroom in a park can cost the city $3.6 million dollars on average, according to the City Reporter, which found that dozens of park restrooms have been closed for over a decade and would cost at least $5 million each to repair.
“The need to use the bathroom is 24 hours a day, and one thing that we’ve heard, especially from unsheltered New Yorkers over the years, is that they do things that are contrary to their health because of the lack of bathroom access, like not drinking water after certain hours, so that they won’t have to use a bathroom overnight,” added Wilkey.
It can also put them at risk of a ticket: the New York City Police Department issued a record 10,003 summonses for public urination during the most recent fiscal year, according to VOCAL-NY.
Without any additional funding or reforms, the report says the city is on track for 46 new bathrooms by 2030, and five new restrooms each year after, bringing the total to 1,210 by 2042. “These benchmarks are a starting point, not the limit of the City’s ambition,” the report reads.
Nurse’s legislation calls for at least half of the goal of 2,120 bathrooms by 2035 to be publicly owned.
More public restrooms will require leaders to “put your money where your mouth is,” said Abreu, who said that it was helpful to see strategies the city might employ to build bathrooms, but wanted to see firmer commitments.
Getting to 2,000 will require scaling up the city’s public private partnerships, like a recent pilot with potty-tech company Throne Labs at 17 locations around the city.
But some homeless New Yorkers had concerns about accessing those facilities, which require a cell phone or tap card, to be made available at nearby businesses, for access.
“People who have privilege and don’t look homeless or of a particular race have a lot easier time walking into a business and asking to use the bathroom and getting a favorable response,” said Wilkey. “What we wouldn’t want to see happen is as the city moves forward with some of these public-private partnerships that we run into these same problems of inequitable access.”
City Hall promised more to come: “The forthcoming action plan will be developed in consultation with agencies, elected officials, and advocates and will build on the work done to-date to identify challenges, mitigate barriers, and expand the tool-kit of public restroom options for all New Yorkers,” said Edwards in a statement.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/main.title: Polls Close in Maine as Democrats Make Final Push to Oust Sen. Susan Collins
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/main.author: Noah Hurowitz, Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/main.text:
The toughest reelection campaign of Republican Sen. Susan Collins’s career is over, as Mainers await results of whether their longtime senator effectively portrayed herself as an independent force in Washington or was weighed down by the baggage of a Republican Party entering the midterms at a severe disadvantage.
Polls closed at 8 p.m. ET Tuesday night in a race that could see the 30-year incumbent lose her powerful Senate post to challenger Troy Jackson, a progressive who was virtually unknown on the national stage until his rushed elevation just over three months ago as the Democratic replacement candidate.
Tuesday night’s election results could change the control of the Senate chamber, with Maine as one of the seven critical states likely to determine whether Democrats can overcome the Republican majority in D.C.
But Maine voters may have to wait far later to learn who won. The state’s ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates by preference rather than being forced to select just one candidate, could delay results significantly.
“I think it’s possible results will take us past midnight,” Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows told reporters in Lewiston on Tuesday.
Bellows said municipalities have two business days to submit their results to the state, although election officials have requested that towns share their vote counts Tuesday night.
Collins, who has represented the state since 1997, campaigned on her record of securing federal investments for state infrastructure, such as rural hospitals, and prided herself as being a moderate Republican who breaks ranks with President Donald Trump.
However, an analysis by Congressional Quarterly Roll Call found that her votes aligned with Trump 90 percent of the time in both the president’s first and second terms.
Still, Collins’s split support among some Democratic voters was evident Tuesday in Lewiston, where several residents told The Intercept they were supporting the Republican senator despite filling their ballots out to Democrats otherwise.
“I am Susan Collins all the way,” said Anne Marie Hastings, a voter who also expressed strong support for Matt Dunlap, a progressive running against former Republican Gov. Paul LePage in a closely watched race in the state’s 2nd Congressional District.
“I’m a registered Democrat, but when it comes to things like this, I go with what I feel is right, not the party that they belong to,” Hastings said.
Another Lewiston voter, Ouellette Bertram, said he voted blue across the board, with the exception of “the Republican lady,” who he said he just plain likes.
“She’s been doing a good job, I think,” Bertram said.
Other Maine residents didn’t share the sentiment toward the Republican incumbent and the Republican Party’s decadelong legacy within the state.
One all-Democrat voter was Bryan Golay, who said he wished the Democratic Party would move to the left but voted against what he described as the GOP’s “enshittification” of America, much of which, he said, has come during Collins’s time in Washington.
“If you can’t get shit done in 30 years, why are we gonna give you another term?” Golay said.
Mags Krantz, a master’s student of social work who works with children with disabilities, said she voted for all Democrats, including Dunlap and Jackson, citing GOP-backed cuts to social services.
“They just cut funding for my job, and for my career,” Krantz told The Intercept outside a polling site in Lewiston on Tuesday. “I really voted for my future, but I also voted for every vulnerable child that I work with every single day that really wishes adults would vote for them over money.”
Speaking to a crowd of supporters on the eve of the election, Jackson toasted the grassroots organizing that has powered his rapidly assembled campaign into the most serious challenge yet to Collins’s hold on her seat.
“This government is fundamentally broken, and it only works for the wealthiest people in this country — that’s what we’re up against right now,” Jackson said. “They are going to outspend the hell out of us. There’s no doubt about it. But they don’t have people like you in rooms like this across this state and across the country.”
Jackson, who spent nearly 20 years in the state legislature, ran on a platform focusing on lowering costs for working-class families, expanding healthcare access, and combating the influence of wealthy donors and corporate PACs in Washington. He entered the race somewhat hastily in late July, after former Democratic nominee Graham Platner withdrew from the Senate race following a rape allegation, which Platner denied.
Maine is one of the two critical swing states determining control of the Senate to use ranked-choice voting. The other is Alaska, where the last polls won’t close until 1 a.m. ET on Wednesday.
The Collins–Jackson race has been one of the top targets for national attention this cycle — most of it on purpose. In October, The Intercept reported that Defending Main Street, a Republican-aligned super PAC associated with Collins spent between $20,000 and $25,000 attacking Jackson on topics such as cost-of-living and taxes. The ads mistakenly were targeted to audiences in Portland, Oregon, rather than the intended Portland, Maine.
This is a developing story that will be updated. Noah Hurowitz reported from Lewiston and Portland, Maine.

https://gothamist.com/news/brace-for-bus.title: Brace for bus and bike lane boom following NYC ballot approval
https://gothamist.com/news/brace-for-bus.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/brace-for-bus.text:
Bus and bike lanes in New York City are now on the fast track.
Advocates said Wednesday that a ballot measure that passed Tuesday night reforming the process for construction of bus and bike lanes means more street safety projects throughout the five boroughs.
The measure will amend the city charter to “simplify the review of street safety projects to reduce construction timelines,” according to the text of the ballot question. The measure passed with 65% support, or 1.1 million voters.
“This really just defangs some of the opponents who have sought to slow down and stop these street safety projects,” said Ben Furnas, executive director of Transportation Alternatives.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office estimated construction timelines on major bus and bike lane projects could be reduced by at least 33%.
Furnas and other street safety boosters said the ballot question came in response to the extensive delay of bus and bike lanes under former Mayor Eric Adams.
“These delays are deadly,” Furnas added, referring to Vision Zero data that shows 205 recorded traffic deaths last year.
Mamdani has resumed several high-profile projects that stalled under Adams, a protected bike lane on McGuinness Boulevard in Greenpoint, busways on Manhattan’s 34th Street and Fordham Road in the Bronx, and a redesign of Grand Army Plaza.
Hartley Bernstein, an attorney who sued the city to suspend street redesign plans on 31st Street in Astoria and W. 72nd Street in Manhattan, said the question means more bike and bus lanes are on the horizon.
“My interpretation is quite simple: This proposition essentially grants the authority to an unelected individual, the commissioner of transportation in the city of New York, to make any changes that he feels in his specific and individual opinion is necessary for safety,” Bernstein said.
The measure still requires the city to solicit input from community boards before moving forward with any street redesign.
“ I have no doubt you're going see a lot more of these projects. If that wasn't the purpose, we wouldn't have the proposition,” Bernstein added.
Sara Lind, co-executive director at the transportation advocacy group Open Plans, agreed.
“[Mamdani] clearly understands he’s using all the levers at his disposal to help speed up these critical safety projects and these projects that will help all New Yorkers get around more quickly and have different options,” Lind said.

https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.title: Brooklyn fire kills 6 people, injures 7 others in Sunset Park, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.text:
Six people were killed and seven others were injured after a fire ripped through a two-story home in Sunset Park early Thursday morning, police and fire officials said.
Fire department officials said they received calls about the blaze around 1:40 a.m., and found an intense fire burning on multiple floors of the home on 58th Street and 7th Avenue in Brooklyn. It took more than 200 first responders and almost three hours to bring it under control.
Four people were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the FDNY and NYPD, while two more people died after they were taken to a local hospital with critical injuries. Both agencies said they did not immediately have identifying information for any of the victims.
Four other civilians were also hospitalized — one with serious but non-life threatening injuries, and the others with minor injuries, officials said. The three firefighters were also being treated for minor injuries, according to the department.
Officials said a lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it’s too early to tell whether it caused the fire.
Fire marshals on Thursday morning were looking closely at what appeared to be a charred stand up scooter that firefighters brought outside the house, along with debris that firefighters were shoveling through the home’s blown-out windows.
Luis Ramos, 54, who said he lived across the street from the fire, said the house looked like “a bonfire that was out of control” where flames were “coming out of everywhere,” including the roof, windows and door.
“Whoever was in there, they didn’t even have time to get out,” he said, adding that he witnessed a body that was black and charred. “There wasn’t a spot in that building that didn’t have a flame coming out.”
Ramos said he felt for the family who lived there, especially with Thanksgiving coming in a few weeks. “Instead of, you know, of happiness, they gotta bury their family members.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who spoke at the scene of the fire on Thursday morning, said helping people recover from this fire will take time and resources.
"Because we know that fires are not only devastating in the moment, but also they displace New Yorkers from their home,” he said. “And they require help and support not just from their community, but from the city at large."
Mamdani said the Red Cross has moved all the displaced people into hotels.
Jimmy Juoguo, a neighbor, said the fire was very scary.
“It’s so sad because even we [didn’t] know each other, but it’s six people, it’s too much,” he said.
The incident comes less than a week after four family members, including 11-year-old Zion Maine, died when a lithium ion battery caught fire in the Bronx.
This is a developing story and has been updated with new information.
