A Staten Island man on Wednesday was arrested for striking and killing a woman in Brooklyn while driving a Department of Sanitation garbage truck last week, according to the NYPD.
Timothy A. Mcvey, 41, was charged with failure to yield to a pedestrian and failure to exercise due care, the NYPD said.
Siobhan Lynch, 30, of Brooklyn, was crossing the parkway at Cropsey Avenue around 6:35 p.m. on Oct. 28 when the garbage truck, heading east, turned right onto the parkway and hit her, police said.
Emergency services took Lynch to NYU Langone Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Mcvey stayed at the scene, police said.
“This is a terrible tragedy, and our thoughts are with the family of the victim,” Department of Sanitation spokesperson Joshua Goodman told Gothamist in an email last week.
Information on Mcvey’s attorney was not immediately available.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-pledg.title: Mamdani pledged support for NYC street vendors. Now they’re facing a crackdown.
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-pledg.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-pledg.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has pledged to support street vendors, but under his administration tickets for people illegally hawking trinkets and merch have reached new highs, data shows.
Tickets issued by Parks Enforcement Patrol for unlawful vending reached 2,237 by the end of September, jumping 671 tickets — or 43% — from the same time in 2025.
Data shows parks officers are also issuing many more tickets for the relatively obscure offense of “unattended personal belongings.” In 2025, parks enforcement officers issued just 55 such tickets. They’ve issued 429 summonses for unattended belongings so far this year.
The trend comes after Mamdani created an office of street vendor services in March, which is led by longtime vendor advocate Carina Kaufman-Gutierrez. "Our street vendors are not a problem to solve, they are a community to support," Mamdani said at the time.
“This increase reflects several factors, including higher park attendance, increased vending activity and events in parks, and additional PEP staff on patrol," said Jeremy M. Edwards, deputy press secretary of the parks department.
The department will continue to work with vendors to ensure they understand the rules and regulations, he added.
The mayor’s office did not return a request for comment about the expanded enforcement.
Licensed Vendor John Golden said he’s getting slapped with violations for unattended personal belongings even though he has a license to sell merchandise at City Hall Park. Data shows he’s been hit with at least three violations.
“They give us the tickets and tell us to go fight in court, and we beat them, and they still come back. It’s harassment,” he said.
He said understood that unlicensed vendors are just trying to earn a living, but was frustrated he was also being caught in the crackdown.
“I understand that unlicensed guys gotta make money 'cause they got a family to feed too... I'd rather see you come out and work in the streets than rob and steal,” he said.
Parks enforcement patrol officers have issued 98 tickets for unattended personal belongings so far this year at City Hall Park.
DC37 Local 983 President Joe Puleo, who represents the roughly 350 parks enforcement officers in the city, said his members are addressing a problem that surged after the pandemic.
“ If you don't address it, it's just gonna get worse and worse,” he said. ”Foot traffic equals dollar signs.”
The City Council passed a bill last year ending jail time and criminal charges for breaking street vending rules.
Data shows Parks Enforcement Patrol officers have issued more tickets overall compared to last year. PEP officers typically crack down on unleashed dogs, drinking or smoking in parks, unlicensed operation of pedicabs and public urination.
Parks officers issued 6,591 tickets through September of 2026 according to city data, a surge of 59% compared to the same period last year.
Mayor Eric Adams banished vendors from the Brooklyn Bridge near City Hall Park in 2023, citing crowding concerns.
Mamdani has long supported efforts to increase the number of permits issued to street vendors. He filmed an early viral video for his campaign at a halal cart. He called vendors “the heart of New York City” in a tweet in December, shortly before taking office.
A press release on Kaufman-Gutierrez's appointment in March said she would "reduce unnecessary penalties and advance fair enforcement."
The city will begin distributing 10,500 new vending licenses in January.

https://gothamist.com/news/mind-boggling.title: ‘Mind-boggling’ killings show persistence of NYC’s domestic violence problem
https://gothamist.com/news/mind-boggling.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/mind-boggling.text:
A 44-year-old man doused his wife with rubbing alcohol, set her on fire and then threatened their 11-year-old daughter with a knife on a recent Saturday afternoon in Crown Heights, officials said.
Several hours later, in a quiet corner of the Rockaways, police said they discovered the body of another woman buried in a shallow grave near a cricket field.
Two days after that, officers responded to a report of an assault at a home in Flushing, Queens, and found a woman stabbed nearly 40 times, police said. She died at a local hospital shortly after.
Vanessa Edmonds, 38, Seraphina Pereira, 35 and Tania Morales, 24, were all attacked by their male partners, according to the NYPD. Detectives arrested all three men in the following days, charging them with offenses ranging from murder and attempted murder to assault and child endangerment. Their lawyers either declined to comment or did not respond to inquiries on the pending cases.
New York City’s violent crime rates have dropped to historic lows, but violence against women remains a persistent outlier. Domestic violence assault reports went up by roughly 3% from 2024 to 2025, even as murders and shootings dropped by 19% and 23% in the same time period, according to police data.
So far this year, reported domestic violence incidents are down by only 1% while shootings and murders are down by 11% and 17%, respectively.
Police and experts say there’s no single reason for the recent rash of violent attacks, but advocates and community leaders are demanding that more be done to get the situation under control.
“ Within the past three months, we have buried six women that have been victims of domestic violence,” said Bishop Boyde Y. Singletary, who leads the grassroots organization Brothers in Purple. “It’s mind-boggling.”
The three deadly incidents were not the city's only cases of violence in the home in October, which is Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Authorities say a 23-year-old woman died when her partner pushed her and their infant daughter off a 15th-floor balcony in the Bronx. Dozens of other domestic violence incidents were reported to police as well.
NYPD data shows reports of domestic violence across the city have stayed relatively consistent with last year. There have been 48 homicides tied to domestic incidents so far this year, which is even with the same time last year, according to the police department. There have been 24,829 reported domestic violence assaults, which is down by 273 assaults from this time last year, according to the data.
Experts point to a variety of factors as to why reported rates of domestic violence remain stubbornly high.
Sharon Gandarilla-Javier, a professor at CUNY’s John Jay College of Criminal Justice and a former NYPD officer who worked on domestic violence cases, said those factors could include including increased awareness among police officers when deciding whether to categorize particular incidents as domestic in nature.
“When something bad happens, like what happened [last] month with these cases, commanding officers are pressured to say, ‘Hey, no, we’ve got to figure out what's going on here.’ And so now more eyes and ears are into those types of calls,” she said. “ We have to improve reporting, but we also have to follow through in the efficiency of that report."
According to the NYPD, Commissioner Jessica Tisch revamped domestic violence enforcement efforts through the October 2025 creation of the Domestic Violence Unit — the largest unit of its kind in the country. The initiative has helped centralize these cases under the Detectives Bureau, assigning more tha 450 officers to focus on domestic violence in precincts across the city.
Gandarilla-Javier pointed to more sophisticated technology that helps police make arrests in these cases, including AI and better tracking capabilities. But she also said tech has been a “double-edged sword” for victims, because abusers are better able to track the movements and activities of their partners.
Lives lost and changed forever
When Seraphina Pereira went missing from her home in the Ocean Bay Apartments on Oct. 19, her ex-boyfriend was not the first person her family suspected.
“At the time we were thinking, because she was a little depressed, we thought maybe she walked into the water or … everybody was talking about sex trafficking and stuff, so we thought maybe she was kidnapped,” Pereira’s sister Davonna Gray told Gothamist. “Never once did we think murder.”
Police released Seraphina Pereira’s photo in the hopes that someone would tip them off about her whereabouts. At the same time, Gray said, Pereira’s ex, 26-year-old Rogelio Lozano-Garita, took their two children and her older son from a previous marriage and brought them to his mother’s house.
Gray said Lozano-Garita hid out there until Oct. 26, when police arrested him after discovering Pereira’s body. The medical examiner said she had been shot several times, and the Queens District Attorney’s office alleged that Lozano-Garita carted her body out of the apartment in a wagon, then buried it and reported her missing after claiming a surfer had found her belongings on the beach.
“She actually broke up with him and he just wouldn't leave. He wouldn't just take no for an answer,” Gray said, adding that her sister never mentioned any physical abuse in the relationship. “That's why we're just like, ‘How can you just go from never putting a hand on her to just taking her life like that?’”
Gray said her sister lived for her four children, who are 14, 12, 6 and 5, and her two step-children. The three younger kids are currently living with another aunt as the family tries to pick up the pieces.
“They’ve been breaking down here and there,” Gray said. “We're trying to keep their minds off of things. We're still sending them to school, trying to keep it as normal as possible for them.”
Children factored into almost all of the severe domestic violence cases in October. According to Queens prosecutors, Tania Morales’ estranged husband, Angel Apodaca, stabbed her dozens of times while the couple’s 2-year-old child was home. Police found the toddler with blood on his clothes, but doctors later confirmed he was not harmed in the attack, according to the District Attorney’s office.
Gandarilla-Javier said the presence of children in an abusive relationship often adds tension and can make it harder for women to leave.
“ I think they use the children as bait a lot of times in terms of divorce court, in terms of the order protection,” she said.
Morales’ mother, Aidee Garcia, told Gothamist that her daughter was fiercely protective of her son, but had never outwardly expressed any concerns about her safety, even when they spent time together the Sunday before her death.
“This should be an example for all women who keep quiet — they need to speak out,” Garcia said. “No one imagined this [would happen]. No one.”
Prevention and resources
City officials and advocates alike have been working to remind New Yorkers about the resources on offer to help prevent, escape from and cope with the aftermath of domestic violence.
The Mayor’s Office to End Domestic and Gender Based Violence has Family Justice Centers in each borough, providing access to case management, counseling, mental health services, legal services and immigration help, according to Commissioner Saloni Sethi. The office also runs workshops in housing complexes and high schools across the city to better educate residents on the signs of domestic abuse and the actions they can take to help prevent it.
“ We are really fortunate to have a robust set of resources for survivors and children who might be impacted by domestic violence, or people who might have witnessed this type of abuse or harm,” Sethi said, though she emphasized that no group of agencies can be physically present all the time to address the issue.
New Yorkers can also turn to organizations like We All Really Matter, also known as WARM, or Sisters and Brothers in Purple, which work to prevent gun violence and domestic violence across the city through outreach, education, counseling and housing support.
“ We also teach and raise up the men who've also been in the situation as well,” Singletary said, adding that they do a bulk of their work through the Alpha and Omega Church of the Lord Jesus Christ.
On the enforcement side, Gandarilla-Javier said, the NYPD needs to continue to make sure officers are trained to identify and respond to domestic incidents before the violence can escalate.
“ What's the underlying issue of this verbal abuse that's going on? Is it tension within the family? Is it child custody? Is it a divorce? Is it a breakup? Because those are important indicators that you as an officer can use to make choices about how this is going to go, in terms of arrests, in terms of court, in terms of compliance,” she said.
Mayoral spokesperson Sam Raskin called the attacks “horrific.”
“Every New Yorker should be able to walk anywhere in our city at any time of day or night without fear of violence. The Mamdani administration is committed to ensuring that survivors are heard and supported — and that those responsible are held accountable,” he wrote in a message to Gothamist.
Davonna Gray broke down in tears when asked whether her family had received any help from the community or the city.
“I can't explain how helpful they've been. If it wasn't for them, I don't know how me and my sister would've got through this week out here,” she said, explaining Safe Horizon had provided the family with a hotel room to stay in, several of the kids’ schools had donated clothes, shoes and vouchers for food, and several local elected officials had shown up at a vigil for Pereira to extend further support.
“I didn't know a city like this can actually come together as a community and be so helpful,” Gray said.
If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence and needs support, call 1-800-621-HOPE, or 1-800-621-4673. Support is also available online through the NYC Hope Resource Directory.

https://hyperallergic.com/met-galas-new-.title: Met Gala's New Theme Is the Biggest Recession Indicator Yet
https://hyperallergic.com/met-galas-new-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/met-galas-new-.text:
Met Gala's New Theme Is the Biggest Recession Indicator Yet
Brace yourself for A-listers strutting down the red carpet in everyday garb like jeans, T-shirts, and "humble, even 'disposable' materials."
Two months after British fashion designer John Galliano bowed out of his 2027 Met Gala and Costume Institute exhibition due to backlash over his racist past, organizers have decided to play it safe with the new theme announced today, November 5.
In perhaps the biggest recession indicator yet, extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday will see A-listers and Hollywood's finest strutting down the red carpet in everyday garb like jeans, T-shirts, and "humble, even 'disposable' materials."
When The Met announced the Costume Institute exhibition John Galliano: Horizons in July, intense scrutiny resurfaced around the designer, who was convicted of antisemitic and anti-Asian hate speech directed at a French couple in February 2011, and fined for a torrent of antisemitic slurs against a woman the same year. A separate video of Galliano declaring “I love Hitler” caused Dior to fire the designer from his post as creative director in March 2011. Amid the renewed backlash, Galliano withdrew his exhibition on August 31.

The Museum Wiesbaden will repatriate ten human skulls held in its collection to Indonesia, marking the first instance of a German institution returning items taken during the country’s Dutch colonial era. The skulls will be presented to representatives of the Indonesian government in a formal ceremony on November 10, and will be covered with black cloth to preserve the dignity of the dead.
Timon Gremmels, the Hessian Minister of Culture, said in a statement that the restitution “is part of the efforts of the Hessian state institutions to systematically examine their collections for unlawful acquisitions during the colonial period and to assume responsibility for the history of their holdings.”
The remains were removed from Indonesia by Ernst Albert Fritze, a Hessian military physician who worked for the Dutch East India Company in Southeast Asia in the early 19th century. According to research by Andy Reymann, the museum’s curator of cultural anthropology, Fritze donated several natural history objects to the Nassau Society for Natural History (the Museum Wiesbaden’s predecessor) beginning in 1833.
Reymann—who has been researching the provenance of Fritze’s human skull collection for several years—noted that little has been discovered about Fritze or the origins of his collection, despite the fact that he was well-known in his time and was mentioned in the writings of German botanist and geologist Franz Wilhelm Junghuhn.
Another Fritze-acquired skull in the museum’s collection was restituted in 2023. That item, a Toi Moko, or tattooed Māori head, was returned to a delegation of Māori and Moriori representatives through New Zealand’s Karanga Aotearoa repatriation program.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.title: The Democratic Coalition Still Has a Class Problem
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.author: Jared Abbott
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.text:
The Democratic Coalition Still Has a Class Problem
The blue wave was undeniable. But early survey data suggest the party rode on a backlash against Donald Trump and a midterm electorate tilted toward college graduates, not a return of the working-class voters the party will need in 2028.
Democrats won a massive victory in the 2026 midterms, performing so well that Republicans’ best-laid gerrymandering plans actually backfired in a number of states, most notably Texas and North Carolina. There, Democrats held most of the seats Republicans had targeted and even flipped some districts drawn to be safely Republican. Democrats flipped Senate seats in places like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina that were considered virtually unimaginable reaches in the very recent past.
That’s of course very good for the party, and, I would hasten to add, for our fight against the ever-present threat of the far right. But Democrats’ stunning upset also brings a strong temptation for moderates and progressives alike: to read the result as proof that the party has finally turned the corner with working-class voters and can ride carefree into the 2028 sunset.
But provisional data suggest otherwise. Unless noted, the figures in this piece come from the AP Voter Poll, a large survey of voters conducted for the Associated Press around Election Day, and from its predecessor, AP VoteCast, for earlier elections. We won’t know the true shape of the 2026 electorate for months, until validated voter data becomes available, but the AP poll gives us a helpful initial look. It shows Democrats gaining real ground since 2024 with college graduates and voters without degrees alike.
But measured against 2018, the last Democratic midterm wave, the party is still deep in the hole with working-class voters, and its coalition is more lopsided by class than ever. That leaves Democrats exposed to another 2024-style loss in 2028. It also keeps out of reach the broad working-class supermajority progressives would need to deliver real change for working Americans.
It’s the (Trump) Economy, Stupid
Few doubted heading into November that Democrats would take the House of Representatives. The president’s party has lost the national House vote in each of the last five midterms. This year followed a similar script as past midterms, but it was amplified by several additional factors.
First, Donald Trump is deeply unpopular. Only 38 percent of 2026 voters approved of his job performance, and 75 percent said the economy was in poor or not-so-good shape. Some 43 percent said they voted to express opposition to Trump, against 16 percent who voted to support him.
The second factor follows from the first. Trump’s unpopularity reached into his own coalition, especially the less partisan, less habitual voters who backed him in 2024 because they were pissed off with the Democrats on affordability and immigration. With the economy still souring and Trump himself not on the ballot (despite his many exhortations that voters imagine he was), however, many saw little reason to turn out for Republicans. As a result, according to a rough estimate from the AP data, depressed turnout among Trump supporters alone was worth around 5 points to Democrats.
Third, Democrats now have a stronger midterm coalition than Republicans. For most of the twentieth century, Democrats depended on working-class voters who turned out less reliably, so low-turnout midterms tended to favor Republicans. That pattern has flipped. Democrats now draw more of their support from college graduates and other highly engaged voters who tend to show up even in off years. Republicans, meanwhile, rely increasingly on less engaged, lower-propensity voters, many without degrees, who turn out mainly when Trump is a candidate. The upshot is that the lower the turnout, the better Democrats now tend to do.
The danger for Democrats is that these advantages are temporary and unlikely to reappear in 2028 when Trump will no longer be the Republicans’ national standard-bearer, and many of the low-propensity conservative voters who sat out this year will flock back to the polls.
The Class Divide Grew in 2026
The divide between college and noncollege voters grew again in 2026, even as Democrats gained among both groups. Democrats’ margin among college graduates jumped 12 points from Kamala Harris’s 2024 showing, while their margin among noncollege voters improved by about 8 points and remained negative.
If we compare 2026 with 2018, the last time Democrats rode a midterm backlash against Trump, we see that while the party’s national margin was 2 points better in 2026, Democrats actually won voters without college degrees by 3.5 points in 2018, whereas this year they lost noncollege voters by about 5 points. Meanwhile, Democrats’ margin among college graduates grew from 14 points to 26 during the same period. The result is a yawning class gap of over 30 points, up from about 10 points in 2018.
That gap matters, because the road to the White House and sustained control of the Senate still runs through voters without college degrees. Noncollege voters remain a majority of the electorate, and in 2020 they made up a majority of voters in every one of the key swing states. With class-based support remaining so lopsided, Democrats remain vulnerable in the key presidential battlegrounds, let alone expanding their reach further into red territory in a durable way that outlasts the political manna Trump delivered to them in 2026. Relying on larger margins among college-educated suburbanites alone is arithmetically insufficient and politically unsustainable.
Democrats’ problems with noncollege voters are hardly limited to white voters. Among voters of color without college degrees, Democrats won by 57 points in 2018 but by only 34 in 2022 and 2024. This year’s rebound to 40 points, especially among Latino voters, is real, but it recovers only about a quarter of the ground the party has lost with these voters since 2018. Voters of color without degrees are now less Democratic than voters of color with them, a reversal of the 2018 pattern.
Do Democrats Even Need Noncollege Voters After 2026?
AP’s data suggest that college graduates supplied most of the national swing toward the Democrats in 2026. Based on my calculation from AP’s published breakdowns of the vote by education, voters with a four-year college degree likely accounted for more than half of the roughly 11-point move toward Democrats from Harris’s 2024 margin to 2026. This invites a tantalizing conclusion: that the party’s future lies mainly with college graduates, and that the noncollege gains are a bonus rather than a necessity. But that idea is clearly belied by the results of the red-state Senate races.
In the five red-state Senate upsets, the national pattern did not hold. There, Democrats’ margins among noncollege voters improved by 15 to 24 points over Harris’s 2024 showing, far more than the roughly 8-point gain they made with this group nationally. The figure below estimates what would have happened if each educational group in these states had shifted only as much as it did nationally.
Had noncollege voters in these states moved only at the national pace, three of the five Senate Democratic hopefuls in red states would have lost, and the other two would have won by less than 2 points. Had college graduates moved only at their national pace, four of the five would still have won. In other words, red-state Democrats did not win by riding the national wave. They won by outrunning it among noncollege voters.
Democrats Are Still Unpopular
Democrats won a landslide, but not because Americans suddenly warmed to them. In Pew’s polling of all adults, 40 percent of Americans viewed the Democratic Party favorably a month before the election, and 58 percent unfavorably. That is a recovery from a low of 36 percent in August 2025, but it is still well below the 46–47 percent Democrats drew during Trump’s first term. Gallup tells a similar story: 43 percent favorable in September 2026, up from 37 percent a year earlier but below the party’s 49 percent average since 1992.
A good share of Democrats’ 2026 margin also came from voters whose support came grudgingly. About 16 percent of voters viewed neither party favorably, and Democrats won them by 25 points, which works out to roughly 4 points of the party’s national margin.
Trust in Democrats on the issues is also thin. Asked which party could better handle the economy, 43 percent said Democrats, 38 percent said Republicans, and 19 percent said neither. That is a 6-point edge in a year when three in four voters rated the economy poorly. Republicans still led on immigration, and the parties were tied on taxes. Recent research I conducted with Joan Williams, based on a February 2026 survey, shows how shallow Democrats’ gains on immigration are. Fifty-six percent of working-class respondents agreed that Trump “has gone too far, with masked men arresting ordinary hardworking people instead of just deporting criminals.” Yet only 36 percent preferred Joe Biden’s immigration policies to Trump’s. Many working-class voters are uneasy with how Trump’s policies are carried out, but they still prefer them to Biden’s by nearly two to one.
The Dealignment Carousel
American politics over the past decade has settled into a self-reinforcing cycle of backlash that virtually guarantees heightened polarization and increasing voter disaffection. The White House has changed parties in three straight elections, and control of the House has now flipped in three consecutive midterms. After each of these elections, the winning party has claimed a mandate to finally address Americans’ growing sense of economic dislocation and political disenchantment, and each time it fails to deliver.
This is what dealignment looks like. Neither party has a stable majority coalition, so outcomes swing with the national mood and with which party’s voters turn out. In the current arrangement, that produces a reliable rhythm. In midterms, the electorate is smaller and more educated, which now favors Democrats, and the president’s party is punished, so Democrats win big when a Republican holds the White House. In presidential years, the electorate grows by tens of millions, and the added voters are disproportionately noncollege, less attached to either party, and now lean slightly Republican.
But even as each election ping-pongs back and forth between the parties, the education gap has continued to grow from 10 points in 2018 to 27 points in 2024, and now 31 in 2026. The electoral carousel goes up and down, but class dealignment continues apace.
That is why even a midterm landslide like this one does little to change the underlying shape of American politics. A wave lifts the party’s fortunes with nearly every group at once, so on election night the gains among college graduates and the modest recovery among working-class voters blurred together into a single triumphant story. But when the tide goes out, Democrats are left with the same lopsided class coalition that has plagued them for more than a decade, and Americans are left in a seemingly endless limbo where neither party can govern for working people.
Rather than overreading this year’s victory, Democrats should look closely at where they won on hostile terrain, and how they did it. The red-state Senate races offer the clearest model: as we saw above, James Talarico, Sherrod Brown, Adam Hamilton, Annie Andrews, and Josh Turek won by outrunning the national swing among noncollege voters, not by running up the score in the suburbs. The question for 2028 is whether Democrats can keep making gains like these with noncollege voters through an affirmative economic message that cuts through even without the assistance of a historically unpopular chief executive.
There is plenty raw material to work with. Seven in ten voters in the AP Voter Poll said the US economic system favors the wealthy, and those voters backed Democrats by more than 50 points in 2026. That is a ready-made audience for an economic populist message aimed at working-class voters, many of whom agree that the system is rigged but don’t yet trust Democrats to fix it. Democrats again won lower-income voters by more than higher-income voters this year, and union households backed them by 20 points, compared with 8 among nonunion voters. Those are signs that a class-based appeal can still work. But they will not add up to a durable majority unless Democrats also find a way to maintain and expand their margins among voters without college degrees.
Trump has handed Democrats a reprieve, not a realignment. They can spend the next two years taking credit for a blue wave delivered largely by outside forces, or they can use it to figure out how to build lasting support among the working-class voters they will need when the wave recedes.

https://hyperallergic.com/mfa-boston-to-.title: MFA Boston to Allow Visitors to Watch Live Conservation of Dutch Painting
https://hyperallergic.com/mfa-boston-to-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/mfa-boston-to-.text:
MFA Boston to Allow Visitors to Watch Live Conservation of Dutch Painting
Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy’s 17th-century group portrait of an Amsterdam wine guild will be the star of a pop-up restoration studio that museumgoers can peer into.
Visitors to the Museum of Fine Arts (MFA) in Boston can soon watch the year-long restoration process of Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy's "The Founders of the Amsterdam Wine Merchants Guild" (1625).
Beginning on December 9, museumgoers can watch as conservators, scientists, art historians, and curators cycle through a pop-up studio in the MFA's Center for Netherlandish Art's Innovation Gallery.
Acquired last year, the group portrait depicts the six founding members of the lucrative Amsterdam Wine Merchants Guild, which operated until the late 18th century.

https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.title: Queens Public Library online system downed by ransomware hack, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.text:
A ransomware attack Wednesday on the Queens Public Library resulted in a system-side network outage that continued into Thursday and could take some time to be fixed, library officials said.
In posts on social media, the library said while all branches are open to the public, several services including the website, on-site computers, check out and return machines, and free Wi-Fi were unavailable. The library’s app and digital media services were also down.
Services remained affected as of Thursday afternoon. CEO Dennis Walcott told Gothamist the library was working closely with law enforcement including the NYPD and the FBI to rectify the problem.
“ Unfortunately, it's part of the world that we live in right now,” he said. “So the Queens Public Library is a victim of the type of world that we're living in, where people are launching cyber attacks against various types of entities, large corporations, and now Queens Public Library.”
Walcott said the investigation is ongoing, and it’s not yet clear who is behind the attack, why the Queens Public Library was targeted or if users’ data was vulnerable.
“ We're getting information in on a regular basis, we have regular meetings with, the authorities and always getting updated information as far as the next steps that we need to take and also what the law enforcement authorities are doing as well,” he said.
In the meantime, library users will be able to check books in and out in person at their local branches, Walcot said. They should check with their local branches about virtual and in-person programs, which may be limited as the library works to get systems back up, he said. While renewals aren’t available, those who have books or other media due won’t be charged late fines, library officials said.
The Queens Public Library system includes 66 branches across the borough library system, including seven adult learning centers, teen centers, bookmobiles, and book bicycles.
This story has been updated with more information.

The Studio Museum in Harlem on November 5 announced curator, writer, and historian Ade Omotosho as associate curator. Omotosho will take up his post on November 16, reporting to chief program officer Natasha Logan and joining the museum as it celebrates its first year in its new purpose-built home. He will be tasked with shaping and overseeing the institution’s permanent collection, which comprises more than nine thousand objects—including works by more than eight hundred artists—dating from the present back to the nineteenth century.
“The Studio Museum in Harlem is delighted to welcome Ade Omotosho, an accomplished and adept curator whose thoughtful approach and breadth of experience will greatly enhance our mission to support and amplify artists of African descent through the care and growth of our permanent collection,” said Logan in a statement.
Omotosho, a 2025 participant in the museum’s Art Leadership Praxis, arrives to the Studio Museum from the Dallas Museum of Art, where he was assistant curator of contemporary art. Previous roles include those in the curatorial departments at Pérez Art Museum Miami and the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. Omotosho holds a BA in art history from the University of Texas at Austin with a certificate in African studies, and an MA from the Williams Graduate Program in the History of Art. He has contributed writing to exhibition catalogues including those published by the Studio Museum in Harlem as well as those accompanying the 2024 Venice Biennale, Made in LA 2023, and Prospect.5.
Omotosho in a statement acknowledged that he was “thrilled” to be joining the museum at a “pivotal moment” in its history. “From its inception, the Museum has championed the range of practices of artists of African descent,” he continued, “supplying a way of seeing that remains vital and necessary in our cultural landscape.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-pales.title: Elections in a Genocidal State Are Not Democratic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-pales.author: Raz Segal
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-pales.text:
Elections in a Genocidal State Are Not Democratic
The defining feature of Israeli “democracy,” including its elections last week, is its operation according to a Jewish supremacist logic, intensifying the discrimination, oppression, apartheid, mass violence, and genocide against Palestinians.
The recent Israeli elections are a grotesque spectacle. They are grotesque because Israel is a state perpetrating genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, cheered on by most of its Jewish citizens. They are grotesque because they peddle the lie of democracy in a state subjecting millions of Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip to a brutal military occupation for nearly six decades, without basic rights, dispossessing them to settle more than 750,000 Jews in crude violation of basic international law. And they are grotesque because they promote the illusion, both within and outside Israel, that nearly two million Palestinian citizens of Israel somehow hold the key to saving the state from itself. A genocide state and society, however, will do what a genocide state and society does: destroy the people it considers its enemies, especially those it sees as the enemy within.
These elections, in other words, should trigger alarm and open our eyes: we have not seen the worst of Israel’s genocidal assault against Palestinians, against all Palestinians under Israeli rule.
Instead we are drowned in reporting about the Israeli election results as a divide between a bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu against a bloc opposing him, averting our gaze from the obvious and overwhelming majority bloc of ninety-three mandates (out of 120) that support Jewish supremacy and genocide. That very real majority includes the opposition party Yachad (in English: “Together”) that two former Israeli prime ministers lead, Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett, the latter of whom on October 12, 2023, shouted at a Sky News anchor: “Are you seriously asking me about Palestinian civilians? What is wrong with you? We’re fighting Nazis.”
Supporters of Jewish supremacy and genocide on the anti-Netanyahu side also include Avigdor Lieberman, a far-right politician and leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu (“Israel Is Our Home”) party who, as defense minister in April 2018, praised an Israeli sniper who had shot an unarmed Palestinian man during the Great March of Return in Gaza. A soldier nearby caught the sniper’s war crime on video. As the Palestinian man falls to the ground, either the shooter or the soldier recording the act says in Hebrew, “Wow. What a video! Yes! That son of a b-tch.” Lieberman had this to say about the sniper: “He deserves a medal.”
So much change awaits us with Bennet and Lieberman. But the greatest promise for something new comes from Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief of staff and leader of Yashar (in English: “Straight”), the main opposition party. Yes, the same Eisenkot who in 2008, as a general and chief of Northern Command, explained the Dahiya Doctrine, his method of mass murder of civilians in Beirut two years earlier:
What happened in the Dahiya quarter of Beirut in 2006 will happen in every village from which Israel is fired on. . . . We will apply disproportionate force on it and cause great damage and destruction there. From our standpoint, these are not civilian villages, they are military bases. . . . This is not a recommendation. This is a plan. And it has been approved.
Planned, approved, and implemented — and then, also morphed into the Gaza doctrine, already well before October 2023, and back again to Lebanon in the last two years for more of that “great damage and destruction” that we can expect in the unlikely event of an Eisenkot-led, post-Netanyahu Israel.
It is, however, that longtime leader of Israel’s opposition, Yair Lapid, the poster boy of Israeli secular liberalism, who perhaps most signifies the danger of Israel’s genocide now escalating further. Lapid rose to political prominence in Israel’s elections in January 2013. Palestinian political parties then received eleven mandates, significantly less than the unprecedented success in the form of nineteen mandates that they won in the recent elections. Netanyahu was the sitting prime minister then too, and his Likud party gained thirty-one mandates in 2013 (it secured twenty-seven now). Lapid’s party then, Yesh Atid (in English: “There is a Future”), trailed behind with nineteen.
It was thus clear that any challenge to Netanyahu would require a coalition with Palestinian parties. But Lapid quickly clarified that such a scenario is “off the table.” Lapid proceeded to delegitimize all Palestinian political parties and, by implication, more than 1.6 million Palestinian citizens of Israel then, 20 percent of the state’s citizens. Lapid had promised his voters, in the name of his party then, a future, a different future. Clearly he assumed that all his voters were Jews, and that the Israeli future he envisioned belonged to them and them alone.
All Israeli governments since then, including the one led by Lapid in 2022, operated according to this Jewish supremacist logic, intensifying the discrimination, oppression, apartheid, mass violence, and, after October 2023, genocide against Palestinians. This is the defining feature of the charade of Israeli democracy: the extremely violent urge to eliminate Palestinians that Netanyahu, Lapid, Bennet, Eisenkot, and Lieberman share, together with the vast majority of Israeli Jews who voted for them in the past and now.
Par for the Course
This should surprise no one who knows anything about the Israeli state. In 2018, the Knesset (Israeli parliament) passed the Jewish Nation-State Law — one of the state’s basic laws, which function as a de facto constitution — that relegates Palestinian citizens to second-class status. Then, in May 2021, as many Israeli Palestinians came out to protest an attack on Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem and a related Israeli attack on Gaza, the Israeli police responded with massive repression and violence, arresting hundreds. The situation deteriorated quickly, as Jewish and Palestinian citizens clashed across Israel — in some places, as in Haifa, with Jewish citizens attacking Palestinian citizens on the streets and, aided by the police, breaking into houses of Palestinians and attacking them there.
The attack on Israeli Palestinians intensified significantly in the weeks following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and Israel’s subsequent genocidal assault on Gaza: Israeli police arrested over 250 Israeli Palestinian for any expression of identification with Palestinians in Gaza, with then–Israeli Police Commissioner Yaakov “Kobi” Shabtai threatening to expel them to Gaza. A large-scale poll among Israeli Jews a year and a half later, in March 2025, confirmed that many of them would approve of such action: 56 percent supported the expulsion of all Israeli Palestinians. Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right settler who serves as Israeli minister of national security, compounded Shabtai’s threat by distributing thousands of weapons to Israeli Jews to form hundreds of civilian “self-defense” units within Israel and in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli media and society added fuel to this fire, with Israeli journalists calling for large-scale killing and destruction in Gaza, as David Mizrahi Wertheim did already on October 7 when he suggested on social media to “turn the [Gaza] Strip into a slaughterhouse.. . . . we are facing human animals.” As Israeli American Pennsylvania State University sociologist Tamir Sorek has shown, this crude dehumanization and bloodlust persisted well beyond the days following October 7. A bit more than two months later, on December 26, 2023, former soccer star and TV commentator Danny Neuman said that “in Gaza, without exception, they are all terrorists, sons of dogs. They must be exterminated, all of them killed.” On February 8, 2025, to take another example, Kinneret Barashi, a lawyer and a television host, tweeted that “every trace of the murderous mutations in Gaza must be erased, from the delivery rooms to the last elderly person in Gaza.” The list goes on and on.
The Israeli elections, in other words, took place in the context of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, in an Israeli society immersed in genocidal discourse, and with Palestinian citizens considered second-class and suspected as dangerous. Netanyahu amplified this discourse on election day when he raised the false charge that Palestinian political parties are “stealing the elections.” As the success of Palestinian political parties became clear, he said that they were plotting the destruction of the Jewish state and, without evidence, that Qatar and Turkey somehow bribed Palestinians to vote.
While many Israeli Jewish politicians in the anti-Netanyahu camp reject these accusations, they nevertheless reproduce their rationale by calling to create a Zionist government without Palestinian political parties. It may happen that the Jewish religious Orthodox and ultra-Orthodox parties agree to join a coalition led by Eisenkot, even though they fiercely oppose his plan to recruit them into the Israeli army. Alternatively, a “unity government” with both Eisenkot and Netanyahu might emerge, even though Eisenkot has promised he would not go down that path.
What is highly unlikely to happen, in any case, is a government that would challenge Netanyahu’s dangerous anti-Palestinian discourse by including Palestinian politicians as equals, not to mention that Eisenkot is committed to continue Israel’s violent occupation and settler policies in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
An exclusionary political discourse depicting millions of citizens as essentially disloyal should raise alarm wherever and whenever it emerges. In the case of the Israeli state that is perpetrating genocide in Gaza, such a discourse, advanced by the prime minister, points both to the abysmal failure of governments, the United Nations, and the international legal system to stop Israel’s ongoing genocide and to the acute danger of its looming escalation and spread beyond Gaza.
Looking at the history of twentieth-century genocides gives a horrific indication of what might await Israeli Palestinians. The Ottoman Empire destroyed Armenian communities and murdered around a million and a half Armenian citizens during World War I on the baseless charge that their loyalty lay with the Russian enemy. In 1994, the Hutu-controlled Rwanda state murdered about eight hundred thousand Tutsis and their Hutu supporters following the invasion in 1990 of the Rwanda Patriotic Front, a Tutsi armed force that sought to topple the government.
Israel’s genocide in Gaza has already led to a murderous and destructive escalation of Israeli state and settler violence in the occupied West Bank, with Israeli leaders now speaking explicitly about treating Palestinians in the West Bank like Palestinians in Gaza. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, for instance, referred to the killing and injuring of Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen outside Hebron on October 23, saying that “every clan neighborhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents.. . . . Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.” Netanyahu spoke even more directly: “We will act to destroy this place,” also announcing plans for the largest Israeli military operation in the entire West Bank since 1967. “The [Israel Defense Forces are] prepared to carry it out, and we will determine the timing, but it is on the way.”
Israel’s election results in the context of the genocide in Gaza, the intent of Israeli leaders to expand it to the occupied West Bank, and the widespread genocidal discourse among Israeli Jews together place all Palestinians under Israeli rule, including Israeli Palestinians, in great danger. The record performance of Palestinian political parties has rendered them, in the eyes of many Israeli Jews in both blocs, particularly problematic in the way they undermine, if not outright threaten, the dominance of Jews in the Israeli state.
The sixteen years of the Israeli siege on Gaza before 2023 — the longest siege in modern history — provided clear indications of the impending genocide. To paraphrase Netanyahu, it was on its way. Those who recognize and oppose genocide when the perpetrators declare it openly, in our faces, should resist the temptation to treat the Israeli elections — election in a genocide state — as anything other than a warning sign of even worse to come.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-glimchers-.title: The Glimchers Can’t Keep Up the Pace
https://hyperallergic.com/the-glimchers-.author: Lakshmi Rivera Amin
https://hyperallergic.com/the-glimchers-.text:
The Glimchers Can’t Keep Up the Pace
The mega gallery is struggling, Ebony L. Haynes joins Marian Goodman Gallery, longtime Manifesta director steps down, and more in Art Movements.
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Rich People Problems
The beleaguered Pace Gallery is in the news again, this time after its United Kingdom tax filings revealed that it lost $5.4 million last year and has a $19.2 million debt-for-equity swap in the works with its US parent company. The filings also outlined plans made in 2025 to cut costs and reduce full-time positions.
The reports come in the wake of an abrupt downsizing over the summer, when the gallery laid off 50 workers and slashed 50 artists from its roster in one fell swoop. (Multiple Pace employees told Hyperallergic that they learned of the cuts only when the New York Times broke the story in early June; one artist said the gallery demonstrated "a callous breach of trust.") Additionally, Pace closed its Hong Kong gallery last October after 12 years and is still looking for a smaller space for its London outpost, which put its 8,600-square-foot location on the rental market in June.
Ebony L. Haynes Departs Zwirner
Nine months after Marian Goodman's passing at age 97, her namesake gallery has appointed Ebony L. Haynes as its inaugural senior director and global head of curatorial affairs. Haynes steps into the role after six years at David Zwirner, where she founded and led 52 Walker as a space run entirely by Black staffers. Under her leadership, the Tribeca gallery exhibited work by artists including Arthur Jafa, Cauleen Smith, Pope.L, and Gordon Matta-Clark. Marian Goodman Gallery also announced Rose Lord and Junette Teng, two of its longtime partners, as co-presidents.
What Else Happened?
- Estrellita B. Brodsky, Michael Govan, and Hank Willis Thomas received the annual Cultural Leadership Awards from the American Federation of Arts (AFA).
- Hedwig Fijen stepped down as director of Manifesta after 33 years at the biennial's helm. Emilia van Lynden and Catherine Nichols, appointed general director and artistic director, respectively, will jointly organize the next edition in 2028.
- Ade Omotosho, former assistant curator at the Dallas Museum of Art, was named associate curator at the Studio Museum in Harlem.
- Nolan Jimbo, former assistant curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago, was appointed Arnhold associate curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art.
- Ido Radon won the Betty Bowen Award, which includes a solo show at the Seattle Art Museum in 2028.

- The Vilcek Foundation awarded a total of $212,000 to 12 nonprofits across the United States, including the Japanese American National Museum in Los Angeles and Rhode Island Latino Arts. See the full list here.
Wildcard: A Blue Wave in Brooklyn
It has indeed been a beautiful week in the neighborhood. Brad Lander spent Halloween in a house costume made by his daughter, Rose, days before securing New York District 10’s House seat in the midterm elections on Tuesday; Queens-based organizer and artist Claire Valdez also won her race, becoming the first Native person to represent the state in Congress.
