https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Bowling, burgers and civilian housing: Life on the Fort Hamilton Army installation
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
Back in the spring, when people across the city were making summer vacation plans and debating where to find the best beach along a commuter rail line, I started hearing murmurs in my neck of southern Brooklyn about one specific priority: Everyone was jockeying for a seasonal membership at the pool club on the Fort Hamilton Army installation.
We didn’t bite — we’re a beach family — but the idea of getting a little R&R on a military compound happened to be a familiar thrill. I grew up about 10 miles south of a major Marine Corps base in Southern California, and my hockey coach, an active-duty sergeant, used to bring us on base for parties on their beach, which was essentially empty.
So the “Looped In” team decided last week to cross through the gates of Fort Hamilton — passports in hand — to see what else a civilian can get up to on base, and the answer is: a lot, starting with renting a home.
“We have approximately 212 leases, and of that, probably 40% are what we call ‘waterfall’ residents,” said Tony Mercante, the administrator in charge of the privatized housing on the installation.
“Waterfall residents” — cool code name — refers to the civilians who live on base, and at rates that are pretty competitive compared to the city’s median rent.
For $3,800 a month, Mercante said, you can get a 1,700-square-foot three-bedroom garden apartment, complete with a washer/dryer hookup, a dishwasher, a garbage disposal, most utilities included and one parking spot.
“This is a very idyllic installation,” he added. “When you come through those gates, we basically have no crime. It's a tiny, self-contained community where a lot of people know each other.”
“Idyllic” is a more-or-less fair descriptor. Walking around Fort Hamilton, a 176-acre rolling plot at the foot of the Verrazzano Bridge, feels like being on a Hollywood backlot version of an American suburb. The trees are tall and mature, the roads are windy, the SUVs actually obey the speed limit. There’s a chapel, a Post Office, a gas station and a Burger King.
But “self-contained” isn’t the same thing as “trapped.”
Garrison Command Sgt. Major Eric Riding, who moved to Fort Hamilton about a year ago from Fort Sam Houston in Texas, said the access to the city has been incredible.
“You walk out about a block and a half, you're on the [R train],” Riding said. “I think the public transportation in this city is the best I've ever seen, and I've been all over.” (He said he’s going with his family to see the Rockettes this Christmas; the R train can get them right there!)
Susan Blair, the chief of public affairs for Fort Hamilton, told us the installation’s relatively small size — and its location within the largest city in the country — means it actually relies on local civilians to keep it up and running.
“When you go to a base like Fort Bragg or Fort Hood, the entire surrounding community almost relies on the base — the base supports a lot of the economy. Where it's almost the inverse here,” she said.
And the outside community has plenty of ways to support the base’s economy, hence the private apartments, the pool club, the clubhouse bar (where Thursdays at 4 p.m. are reportedly bumpin'), the wedding and events venue space, the Harbor Defense Museum and not least, the bowling alley. (Civilians looking to visit the installation unescorted are required to fill out background check forms and submit them in-person or via fax 24-48 hours prior to visits.)
Stephen Ramosa, who lives next door in Bensonhurst, said he started working at the Fort Hamilton Bowling Center about a year ago and sees a mix of civilian bowlers and servicemembers and their families.
“ We have a senior league Tuesday mornings. That's the one that I run, and they're pretty chill,” he said. “They're pretty old, and they still bowl better than me.”
Things we didn’t see on our tour: tanks, humvees, helicopters, firearms or any kind of weaponry that wasn’t a historical artifact. Blair said that Fort Hamilton was used as a staging ground for law enforcement after 9/11, but generally, much of its significance now is related to its history.
“One of the unique things about Fort Hamilton is it's one of two bases where a Revolutionary War battle was actually fought,” Blair said.
In August of 1776, British troops landed on the beach outside what’s now Fort Hamilton and kicked off one of the largest battles of the war, one that ended with General George Washington retreating up to Manhattan.
“We did not win that one,” Blair said. “But we won the big thing.”

https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.title: A View From the Easel: Natali Bravo-Barbee
https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.author: Lakshmi Rivera Amin
https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.text:
A View From the Easel: Natali Bravo-Barbee
“As a mother, there are so many spaces in my life that are organized around other people’s needs. The studio is a space where I get to return to myself.”
Welcome to the 362nd installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Natali Bravo-Barbee moves between modes of motherhood and making while testing the limits of what photography can be.
Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.
Natali Bravo-Barbee, Governors Island and South Street Seaport, New York
How long have you been working in this space?
Three years (the spaces change every year).
Describe an average day in your studio.
An average day in the studio is rarely average. As an artist and mother, I have learned to build flexibility into my studio practice. My days usually start once my children are in school, around 8:30 or 9am. I start by making a to-do list. There is an incredible amount of administrative work that is part of being an artist and maintaining a studio practice, so I usually try to get those tasks out of the way first.
Once I clear that list, I can pick up where I left off creatively. I usually have my mate and a thermos of hot water with me, and I sip as I settle back into whatever I was working on. Sometimes that means exposing cyanotypes that I coated the day before. Most recently, it has meant going through the photographs I selected to print and spending time with the images before deciding how I want to move forward with them. I’m constantly moving between making, looking, researching, and organizing. For me, all of those things are part of the studio practice.
How does the space affect your work?
The space affects my work quite a bit, particularly because I move between my home studio and my studio on Governors Island. They create two very different conditions for working.
When I’m working from home, the day is much more fragmented. I’m able to work around my family’s schedule, but I’m also surrounded by everything that comes with running a household: laundry, groceries, dinner, and the general visual noise of home. Sometimes I’ll be in the middle of something and realize I need to switch gears completely. There is always another task waiting for me.

Intermedia + Digital Arts MFA Program at UMBC Now Accepting Applications
Funding for tuition, healthcare, and stipends is available. Apply to the University of Maryland, Baltimore County program by Feb 1 to be considered for financial support.
The Intermedia and Digital Arts (IMDA) MFA Program at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC) invites applications from interdisciplinary artists seeking to expand or reinvent their practice. IMDA is a three-year, 60-credit graduate program with private studios in Baltimore’s progressive art community. IMDA faculty are nationally and internationally recognized artists, filmmakers, designers, and scholars with active exhibition and publication records.
IMDA offers a multidisciplinary program with one on one feedback from world-renown visiting artists, independent teaching opportunities, professional exhibition venues, and dedicated fabrication, media, and physical computing labs. UMBC is a top-ranked R1 Research University with an inclusive culture that provides students with access to research centers and broad interdisciplinary opportunities. Graduate Assistantships that include full tuition remission, health insurance, stipends, and other merit based financial support are available.
IMDA supports a broad range of interdisciplinary creative practices including socially-engaged, community-based, interactive, and studio-based artworks made using cutting edge and traditional methods and technologies. Alumni present their work at distinguished venues around the world, receive prestigious grants and residency awards, and are academic leaders at internationally recognized art academies and universities.
Visiting artists include: Janine Antoni, Zoe Beloff, Lynda Berry, Paul Chan, Annica Cupetelli and Cristobal Mendoza, Paul DeMarinis, Tony Dove, Hasan Elahi, Karen Finley, Guillermo Gómez-Peña, Guerrilla Girls, Barbara Hammer, Nina Katchadourian, Alison Knowles, William Pope.L, LoVid, Matmos, Michael Rakowitz, David Rokeby, Paul Rucker, Frances Torres, Mark Tribe, Levester Williams, Stephanie J. Williams, Fred Wilson, Martha Wilson, Krzysztof Wodiczko, Karen Yasinsky, and The Yes Men.
Applications are due February 1, 2027.
To learn more, register for the IMDA Online Info Session on Friday, November 13, 12:00 - 1:00 pm (EST).
To schedule a tour, visit imda.umbc.edu, or email imda@umbc.edu.

https://hyperallergic.com/met-galas-new-.author: Hyperallergic
https://hyperallergic.com/met-galas-new-.text:
Met Gala’s New Theme Is So Basic
Brancusi at MoMA, trouble at Pace, a rediscovered Georgia O'Keeffe painting, and The Met presents the biggest rescission indicator yet.
Jackson Pollock at The Met, Roy Lichtenstein at the Whitney, and Constantin Brancusi at the Museum of Modern Art — our critic Aruna D'Souza is tired of this dead-White-men fest. That said, she still has a soft spot for Brancusi. She went to see the Romanian artist’s solo show at MoMA, and she has some thoughts.
Speaking of dead White blokes, visitors to the MFA Boston will soon be able to watch a live conservation of Dutch painter Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy’s “The Six Founders of the Amsterdam Wine Guild” (1625). Watching paint dry never sounded so appealing.
In living-White-men news, Pace Gallery, owned by father-and-son duo Arne and Marc Glimcher, has reported steep losses. Meanwhile, a recently rediscovered Georgia O'Keeffe painting is heading to auction and might sell for millions.
But if that’s all too exciting, get a load of the Met Gala's new “everyday” theme.
—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief
At MoMA, Brancusi Is Lost in Space
Let’s get one thing out of the way first: For all my weariness about how canonical dead White men are STILL. CONSISTENTLY. CENTERED in museum exhibitions — even after said museums have publicly taken pains to expand collections, hire curators with broad expertise and interests, and invite new audiences into their spaces — I have ZERO complaints about putting on a Constantin Brancusi exhibition. Even in fall 2026, when the city’s three major museums have turned themselves over to Brancusi, Lichtenstein, and Pollock simultaneously. (I will go to my grave insisting that it should have been a Krasner show.)
That said, the work of this particular canonical dead White man is glorious, and continues to resonate with contemporary artists: His name has come up consistently in interviews with sculptors this past year, whether Rodney McMillian or Martin Puryear or a number of others I’ve talked to. Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio at the Museum of Modern Art is a great reminder of why.| Aruna D’Souza

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.title: President Trump Moves to Make Oval Office a Public Monument
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.text:
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday seeking to designate the Oval Office and the adjacent Cabinet Room national monuments, saying that the new designation would prevent future administrations from making major modifications without Congressional approval. In his second term, Trump made it a priority to redecorate both, turning the previously restrained presidential working spaces into extravagantly gilded interiors in the style of Louis XIV.
In the wake of this week’s midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered historic defeats, Trump appears to be self-soothing by focusing on the many renovation projects he has initiated at the White House and across Washington, D.C. At the White House, in addition to his makeover of the Oval Office, these have included the construction of a granite helipad on the White House’s South Lawn and, most notoriously, the demolition of the building’s East Wing to make way for a 90,000-square-foot, $600 million ballroom. (On Wednesday, in his first public appearance after Tuesday’s Republican wipeout, Trump led a media tour of the ballroom construction site.)
Around the nation’s capital, Trump has embarked on a fraught, $14 million repair of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, begun the redevelopment of a popular public golf course by cutting down hundreds of trees, and proposed a 250-foot-high triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Apparently worried that incoming Democrats would block construction of the arch, Trump asked for hastened approval of the project, which was granted Wednesday by his hand-picked planning commission; that evening, Judge Tanya Chutkan stopped construction for fourteen days.
It is not clear how designating the Oval Office a national monument will prevent another president from simply revising, or ignoring, the designation—the White House is already designated a National Historic Landmark, which has not stopped Trump from building his ballroom. Nevertheless, speaking from the now gold-saturated Oval Office, Trump told reporters, “When completed, and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it’ll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.title: Andy Warhol’s ‘Camouflage’ Portraits Inspired Piaget’s New Limited-Edition Watch
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.text:
Andy Warhol amassed quite the watch collection during his life—including a piece or two from Piaget (around seven, to be exact). And now, the maison has collaborated with the Andy Warhol Foundation for Visual Arts to bring an homage to the artist to your wrist.
Meet the Camouflage watch, a creation inspired by Warhol’s Camouflage self-portraits, which the artist crafted in 1986. As such, just 86 pieces of this iteration of the Andy Warhol watch will be made. Piaget takes the bold colors splashed across the American creative’s face in the series and plops them right on the dial. Here, sodalite and turquoise stones are the stars in waves of blue, paired alongside satin-finished gold and polished rose gold to add texture and dimension to that camouflage look. Piaget uses 27 pieces in all to make the dial, which it took over 100 hours of R&D and craftsmanship to come to life, into a blend of blue and warm hues.
Beating away inside the gadrooned white-gold case lies Piaget’s 501 P1 caliber, an automatic movement that powers those dauphine hands and offers up a 40-hour power reserve. Flip the watch over, and you’ll catch a glimpse of Warhol’s engraved signature, as well as the number of watches in the series.
“Our objective is to take inspiration from Andy Warhol’s creations without strictly reproducing each of his works on a dial,” Stéphanie Sivrière, artistic director of Piaget, said in a press statement. “The direct connection between Andy Warhol and Maison Piaget is color, particularly through the use of ornamental stones, which remains the common thread of this very distinctive timepiece.”
This isn’t the first time the duo has teamed up, either. In 2024, Piaget was given the go-ahead by the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts to rename its Black Tie watch (itself a reinvention of the iconic Ref. 15102, a 45 mm cushion-shaped timepiece Warhol owned) in Warhol’s honor. Under the new license, the maison was also able to craft one watch annually that pulled from the artist’s oeuvre. As a result, Piaget dropped the limited Collage timepiece back in 2025, home to blocks of pink opal, green chrysoprase, and yellow serpentine on the dial, now followed by the 2026 iteration (price available upon request). We’ll just have to wait and see what’s in the cards for 2027, then.
	As part of Art Week NYC, a citywide gathering celebrating contemporary art, Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, is speaking with ARTnews senior editor Maximilíano Durón about Warhol’s love of timepieces and the watchmaker’s collaboration with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts that grew out of it. The talk takes place at the PMC Studio on Saturday, November 14. RSVP here.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ga.title: Miami Beach Dealer Faces Another Lawsuit from Artist Alleging Non-Payment
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ga.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ga.text:
Gabriel Kilongo, the dealer behind the Miami Beach–based gallery Jupiter, is facing another lawsuit from a third artist who alleges that he is withholding money from the sales of her art.
Yirui Jia, a young painter who had a solo show at Jupiter’s Miami Beach location in 2025, sued Kilongo in September in the Supreme Court of the State of New York, alleging that he had only paid her $2,000 of a $42,000 sum owed for the sales of five paintings.
It is one of four lawsuits filed in the past two years against Kilongo, whose gallery also formerly operated in New York. Others, as first reported by Urgent Matter, have centered around allegations of nonpayment, damage to art, and withheld artworks. The lawsuit regarding the damaged artwork appears to have been settled, while the others appear to still be pending.
According to Jia’s lawsuit, she received written assurances from Kilongo that he would pay her. He told her that he was “managing a very tight cash flow,” per an exchange quoted in the lawsuit, and stated that he was “waiting for a few things to clear on the gallery’s end” in order to remit payment. But he did not do this, the suit alleges, and therefore defied the consignment agreement they had signed.
The suit includes a sales report produced by Jupiter that notes that all five paintings had sold for values between $2,000 and $32,000. Two went to a Vancouver-based buyer named Bing Zhang, the document states, while the other three went to Bradley Chubb, the Buffalo Bills linebacker who was traded from the Miami Dolphins earlier this year.
“The complaint speaks for itself,” said a lawyer for Jia in a statement to ARTnews. Kilongo has not responded to the complaint at this time of writing.
He did not respond to ARTnews’s request for comment on Jia’s lawsuit specifically. But, responding to the four lawsuits facing the gallery, he said, “These are distinct proceedings, involving different circumstances and procedural histories, and should not be presented as a single narrative of wrongdoing.”
The dealer founded Jupiter in 2022, having previously worked at New York’s Mitchell-Innes & Nash gallery as an associate. The gallery has regularly shown at notable art fairs, including Untitled, Expo Chicago, and Zona Maco, and has even continued doing so as Jupiter has faced lawsuits, most recently appearing in the Independent New York art fair this past May.
Kilongo has previously touted his relationship with Jia, whose work was the subject of a solo show at Mitchell-Innes & Nash in 2024, the second to last exhibition there before the gallery transitioned to an advisory. “We have successfully placed works by artists—like Yirui, for instance—in prominent collections, including those of some museum trustees,” Kilongo said in an interview for Artnet’s Gallery Network program. “It’s always incredibly gratifying to see how her work holds up along other historical artists while still maintaining Yirui’s distinct and recognizable identity.”
Urgent Matter reported in May that Kilongo surrendered his New York gallery to his landlord and agreed to pay $25,000. It is unclear, however, whether Jupiter continues to operate in Miami Beach. The gallery’s website states that the most recently staged exhibition, a two-person show for George Clinton and Gerasimos Floratos, closed in Miami Beach this past February.
In Artnet News, Kenny Schachter reported that Jupiter was administratively dissolved on September 25, exactly one day after Jia’s lawsuit. Kilongo told ARTnews that this was not true and “does not accurately reflect [the gallery’s] current standing.”
Schachter’s column also stated that Kilongo, who was born in Democratic Republic of Congo and was raised in Israel, was detained by ICE and has since been released. Schachter attributed confirmation to James Snyder, director of New York’s Jewish Museum, but ARTnews could not establish a clear connection between Kilongo and that institution beyond the dealer having served on a host committee for a young collectors event held at the museum this past October. A database on ICE’s website that allows users to track detainees does not contain an accessible record for Kilongo.
Schachter did not mention in his column that he had himself exhibited with Jupiter in 2025. Others to have exhibited with the gallery include Emmanuel Louisnord Desir, Baseera Khan, Marcus Leslie Singleton, and Travis Fish.
The first of the lawsuits against Kilongo’s business was filed in 2025 by Jade Thacker, who alleged that she was owed $204,000 because he failed to pay her out for one sale and return works shown in 2024 that did not sell. Kilongo has not responded to Thacker’s lawsuit.
That lawsuit was followed by one in February 2026 from Location Incorporated, a New York entity based in the East Village that claimed Kilongo’s gallery had inflicted $1.6 million in damage to a sculpture shown at the Untitled Art, Miami Beach fair in 2024. Though the lawsuit did not identify the artist or work, Jupiter brought a work that year by New York–based artist Izhar Patkin. That lawsuit was dismissed and later settled, according to Urgent Matter.
And in March 2026, artist Stephanie Pierce sued Kilongo, echoing Thacker’s allegations by claiming that she was owed money for works sold in 2023 and that he withheld artworks. She sought $100,000 in damages. In this case, Kilongo responded by denying the allegations. Serving as his own legal representative, he said that “payment relating to the works has been made and that the return of the remaining works is actively in progress, with a majority already returned.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ca.title: Carsten Höller’s Spiraling Silver Slides Appear in Mexico City as a Permanent Installation
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ca.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ca.text:
Belgian artist Carsten Höller’s giant, spiraling silver slides have made their way to Arte Abierto Polanco in Mexico City as part of a permanent installation.
The large-scale installation, titled Mexico City Slides (2026), features four spiral slides integrated into Antara, an upscale open-air shopping mall that houses retail, dining, entertainment, offices and public space. Höller’s installation was commissioned by Arte Abierto and Sordo Madaleno Arquitectos and can be seen from Antara’s gardens, plazas and pedestrian promenade.
The Mexico City Slides installation ranges from 39 to 125 feet in height and 102 to 295 feet in length. All four spiral slides are open to the public and allow four people to ride simultaneously from various entrances such as the family-style restaurants, the Google offices, the Rosewood Hotel, and the Arte Abierto Art Space. All four slides end at the same exit. The artist said he wanted the installation to be an “equalizer” and a “voluptuous panic upon an otherwise lucid mind” for participants and viewers. In 2015, Höller told The Guardian that it’s “impossible to travel down a slide without smiling.”
Höller’s installation is part of a work-in-progress franchise that he started in 1998. Different variations of the slides have appeared across the world, from Test Site (2006) at Tate Modern in London, Victoria Slide (2011) at the New Museum in New York, Vitra Slide Tower (2014) at the Vitra Campus in Weil am Rhein, Florence Experiment Slides (2018) at Palazzo Strozzi in Florence and DAC Slide (2020) at the Danish Architecture Centre in Copenhagen.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ro.title: Rome’s Galleria Borghese’s $11.15 M. Extension Is Moving Forward Despite Pushback
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ro.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ro.text:
Rome’s Galleria Borghese is getting too popular for its own good. The 17th-century villa museum has launched an architectural competition for an extension, reports Le Figaro.
The decision is a result of an influx of tourists. Each year, the museum has 700,000 visitors, 60 percent of which are international. The museum houses paintings, sculptures, and antiquities from works by Bernini and Caravaggio to Canova and Raphael.
“Until now, we have had to cap daily attendance at 2,000 people, allowing entry only to those who have booked online,” Francesca Cappelletti, the museum’s director, told the French newspaper. “Yet, every day, we see groups of international visitors in the park who are disappointed to find they cannot enter because there are no spots left.”
The new extension is being created with support from Rome’s Ministry of Cultural Heritage and the municipality. It estimated to cost $11.15 million (€10 million). The space will span 3,000 square meters and will help the museum exhibit work that’s sitting in storage, as well as stage exhibitions, open a restaurant or bookstore, and a laboratory. “We cannot alter the existing heritage; the solution must involve a contemporary structure. After all, look at the Louvre pyramid in France—it works perfectly,” said Cappelletti in regard to the extension. The structure is meant to blend in with the villa’s distinct white style and surrounding park.
The competition for the extension is being organized by the Italian engineering firm Proger Spa, also a patron of the museum. The deadline for candidates to express their interest in the competition is November 13. “Naturally, it is not the company, but rather a jury of independent experts and renowned international figures that will select the winner in mid-May 2027. We have no intention of relinquishing our role; the final decision rests with us. That said, every effort must be made to ensure that Italian public funds remain protected,” said Cappelletti.
But not everyone is a fan of the plan. “It is a grotesque proposal. It is blasphemy,” Alix van Buren, president of the Friends of the Villa Borghese association, told the Times of London. “The villa is one of the most perfect, unalterable artistic ecosystems that human genius has ever created. Not a single pin can be moved without upsetting the balance.”
Michele Campisi, the general secretary of the Italia Nostra heritage group, joined in on the fury, calling the plans “bizarre” and arguing that the museum is trying to compete for popularity with the Colosseum. Tomaso Montanari, an art history professor at the Universita per Stranieri di Siena, described the extension as “moronic” in the Italian newspaper Il Fatto Quotidiano, adding that it was like “building an extension on Brunelleschi’s dome” at Florence Cathedral.
Fabio Rampelli, the vice-president of Italy’s lower house of parliament and a key ally of Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Cappelletti to resign in a Facebook post. “Treating a space like this as if it were your own back garden is dismal,” he said.

NPR reports that less than two hours after a federal planning commission granted final approval to Trump’s arch, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order barring the government from any construction work for fourteen days.
The order, which granted a request filed days earlier by the governments of Washington, D.C. and Virginia, took effect minutes after the decision, halting work on the project that the administration had planned to begin immediately.
Chutkan issued a thirty-three-page memorandum and opinion that cited a litany of competing and contradictory claims from the Trump administration, including sudden declarations from Secretary of War Peter Hegseth and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullen filed late in the ongoing litigation that describe the Arch as a potential platform for supporting “coordinated protective operations.”
In their complaints, D.C. and Virginia claim that the construction of the arch “will inflict immediate and irreparable harm on the District and Virginia,” as it is “slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the District has a statutory responsibility to protect.” Judge Chutkan agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by the construction of the arch.
The National Park Service (NPS) environmental assessment found that the arch would adversely affect surrounding historical properties, including Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. It also projects two to three months of site preparation and excavation, four to five months of foundation work, and two to three years of construction in total.
“Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box,” former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi said during a night of public testimony on Thursday. “They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Primeiro passo para regular big techs é exigir transparência, afirma especialista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
As eleições brasileiras de 2026, sobretudo a disputa presidencial, foram marcadas por evidências de interferência das big techs, como a própria Meta acabou admitindo, além de decisões controvérsias do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) referentes às plataformas.
No cenário global, o tema da inteligência artificial (IA) ganhou força máxima em outubro e novembro de 2026, impulsionado por fortes correções no mercado financeiro global e, em especial, pelo estouro de uma bolha de IA na China.
A conjuntura tem feito diversos analistas políticos e o próprio governo federal sinalizarem para a urgência do debate de regulação das big techs.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Paulo Rená, especialista em constitucionalismo digital, que participou da elaboração do Marco Civil da Internet, avalia que o maior nó nesse tema é a questão da falta de transparência. “O mais importante é a transparência. As plataformas operam hoje com uma opacidade que não é possível saber, auditar, avaliar se estão funcionando bem ou mal, as regras de funcionamento, e isso dificulta muito para a sociedade e até para as autoridades avaliar o que está funcionando”, afirma. “A gestão dos algoritmos, das publicações que a gente recebe ou não recebe, que foram desequilibradas nas eleições, ou como a inteligência artificial vai funcionar, a regulação mais importante é exigir que as plataformas sejam mais transparentes”, resume.
Rená destaca que a sociedade tem “a informação na ponta dos dedos” e lembra que, antigamente, quando uma pessoa telefonava para a outra, caso não houvesse resposta, a vida seguia normalmente. “Hoje, se a gente mandar uma mensagem direta e a pessoa não responder, a gente já começa a pensar que algo aconteceu”, avalia.
“Esse tipo de percepção afeta tudo ao nosso redor e muda a forma como o direito se realiza, a política, a economia. E isso afeta também o nosso psicológico, a dificuldade que a gente tem de tomar decisões, inclusive na questão da aposta online”, argumenta.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/br.title: A New Hudson Valley Art Space Promises to Be As Accessible as It Is In Flux
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/br.author: Maximilíano Durón
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/br.text:
Less than two blocks from the Katonah train station stands a nondescript, gray two-story building on one of the main drags of this Hudson Valley town. Emblazoned in a kerned-out serif font, its name, Branchline, belies what awaits inside: a public-facing exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection (GFC).
Established just five years ago, the GFC has already become one of the world’s leading collections of contemporary Indigenous art, with more than 850 works. Until now, works from the GFC have primarily hung in the New York apartment of Becky Gochman, the collection’s founder and custodian, and her family, though some 200 works are typically on loan to institutions around the world at any given time. The GFC has generously opened the home to museum groups, schools, and artists for tours and events as a way to bring more attention to Native artists, but the organization’s ambition has always been to make its holdings as accessible as possible.
“It’s one thing to articulate a mission, but what matters to me,” GFC creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) said Thursday during a press preview, “is if I’m putting that language out into the world [then] I’m making sure that our organization is following that with action.” She added that she sees Branchline as a place for “bringing community together, which means making the Native community feel like they are very much a part of what the decision-making parts of this are, and then also inviting the community of Katonah to come in and learn about new artists that they might not have heard of.”
Anticipating that many visitors will arrive via Metro-North, the GFC named the space after the rail term “branch line,” or the place “where paths diverge and new paths begin,” as GFC director Laura Phipps put it. “We were excited about all the sort of ideas that ‘branch line’ conjures—both thinking about the metaphor of the train and the metaphor of trees—and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”
Free to the public, Branchline is taking its time to grow into its new digs, which will eventually total 10,000 square feet across four buildings. Friday evening’s inauguration will show off the first completed space, as well as plans for expansion in the coming months across an L-shaped plot that runs from the main building’s entrance on the Parkway to Katonah Avenue. The building houses a three-room gallery on the ground floor, two bedrooms upstairs for invited artists to determine how they want to spend the time, and a nearly operational ceramics studio downstairs.
Architectural renderings on view Thursday afternoon show that the building’s back door will open onto a small sculpture deck leading to a yet-to-be-built barn, where large-scale works will go on view. (The original barn was in such bad shape that it had to be torn down to make way for an exhibition space.) The barn will in turn lead to the Annex, which will take a more experimental approach (more on that later). From there, visitors will turn left onto a patio and eventually reach the back entrance of Twig, a retail store and café.
For now, visitors will get a taste of Branchline’s ambitions through a more traditional offering. Inaugurating the modest, nearly 2,000-square-foot gallery is “Line Break,” curated by GFC assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee + Diné) with collection associate Nicole van Brugge. “Lines are a core facet of all visual language,” the exhibition’s introductory wall text begins, but Begay and van Brugge look past the formal qualities that a line and its breaks contribute to a work. Instead, they treat the line as a metaphor for lineage and bloodlines, borders and cartographic marks, horizons and sound barriers.
A tight show of 28 works by 18 Indigenous artists, “Line Break” offers visually compelling juxtapositions of artists from different generations working in a range of mediums and styles. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s The Spaniard (1988), a semi-abstract aerial view of the Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana, hangs next to Sara Flores’s Untitled (Shao Pei Maya Kené), 2024, a painting rendered in the geometric abstract visual language of the Shipibo-Conibo people, whose designs, according to an exhibition brochure, “map the community’s local worldview, environmental understanding, and cosmology.” Farther along are Teresa Baker’s Echoes (2024) and George Morrison’s Night Shadows. Red Rock Variation: Lake Superior Landscape (1994). Both are brightly colored abstract meditations on landscape made in very different mediums: acrylic, yarn, willow, and artificial sinew on AstroTurf for Baker; acrylic on canvas on board for Morrison.
Even the most seemingly formal works reveal their secrets as you delve deeper into how these artists use lines to make meaning. Across from the Quick-to-See Smith and Flores works are two pieces from Nadia Myre’s “Code of Construction” series, in which the artist arranges strung ceramic cylinders into squares depicting the ground-to-air distress signals for “Require Map and Compass” and “Not Understood.” Myre’s choice of medium draws on the tradition of wampum belts, used by Indigenous communities of the Northeast Woodlands to communicate political relationships. Myre’s work finds an analog in Faye HeavyShield’s the red line II (2025), a strand of red beads that the artist strung by hand. Here it is displayed in a coil, though its configuration is flexible—perhaps a metaphor countering the seeming immutability of shape, form, and even time.
The exhibition reaches its crescendo at its center with Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021–24), a handwoven wool textile accompanied by a multichannel sound piece whose low hum visitors have been hearing since entering the gallery. In 2016, Chacon noticed the sounds made by drones flying over the Oceti Sakowin camp at Standing Rock, where protesters had gathered to oppose the Dakota Access Pipeline. Ranging from loud and piercing to soft and soothing, the sounds of police surveillance drones mingled and merged with those of the protesters’ countersurveillance drones. In that harmonious dissonance, Chacon saw a score, which he recorded and also translated into the woven textile, charting the drones’ erratic flight patterns in a traditional Diné weaving style and structure.
Rounding out “Line Break” are two elements that will likely look drastically different in a few months. The GFC commissioned Matthew Kirk to make a site-specific work for an exterior wall of the building along an alleyway. Across three plywood panels, Kirk has collaged painted tar paper in various abstract forms and shapes. The work was already showing its ephemeral quality on Thursday morning, the paper having warped in the light rain.
A few steps down the alleyway is the Annex, which is still under construction: the plywood is exposed, and power cords run to jerry-rigged lightbulbs that illuminate its two floors. Rather than hide this rawness, the GFC team has decided to embrace it. For now, the Annex is home to a small show of drawings by Shuvinai Ashoona, who maps imagined scenes—ones that could perhaps one day come true—onto the Arctic landscape where she lives in Nunavut, Canada. The team acknowledged that it hasn’t quite figured out how the space will look in the near term, even once the build-out is complete. That will depend on how artists interpret a prompt that gives them the autonomy to do what they want.
“What GFC is doing is not trying to become an institution,” Martin said. “It’s trying to just meet where things are needed, and a space is definitely needed for art that is outside of the white box that you’re used to seeing, so that’s what we’re offering.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Apoio do PT a Alcolumbre precisa de acordo político, diz senador Humberto Costa
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Apesar de apontar para o apoio do PT à reeleição do presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), o senador Humberto Costa (PT-PE) disse que ainda é preciso fechar um acordo político com o senador.
“Devemos apoiar, mas isso precisa ser dentro de um acordo político. Queremos uma posição mais clara, de entendimento com o governo. Nós não queremos que as relatorias, por exemplo, fiquem concentradas nas mãos de uns poucos que, na maioria das vezes, se colocam contra o próprio governo. Nós precisamos construir uma agenda em cima de questões que são fundamentais para o governo, que possam ser encaminhadas pelo presidente do Senado”, disse Costa ao Conexão BdF 2º Edição, da Rádio Brasil de Fato.
Para Costa, Alcolumbre poderá ser também importante para “barrar algumas questões que são absolutamente inaceitáveis do ponto de vista de pautas da extrema direita”.
O senador considerou o resultado da última legislatura bastante positivo para o governo. “Foi uma grande proeza, porque nós não temos maioria no Congresso Nacional, nem na Câmara, nem no Senado, mas a capacidade de articulação do presidente Lula, a capacidade de articulação do governo, dos integrantes do partido no Congresso Nacional permitiu que os acordos viessem a ser feitos e pontos extremamente importantes para o Brasil terem sido aprovados”, disse, apontando para pautas como reforma tributária, isenção do imposto de renda para quem ganha até R$ 5.000, o arcabouço fiscal do governo e o fim da escala 6×1.
Nesse sentido, o senador acredita também que é possível que haja alguns acordos com os bolsonaristas para aprovação de pautas. “Apesar de a bancada bolsonarista ser grande, não é absolutamente homogênea. Então, diante de certos temas, certos interesses, é possível construir alguns acordos políticos”, avalia.
Em relação à Medida Provisória (MP) das bets, que baniu os jogos eletrônicos de azar do país, Costa disse que vai trabalhar para que a vire lei rapidamente e criticou a decisão da Justiça Federal de São Paulo, que liberou três empresas, classificando-a como “inconstitucional”.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Senado aprova impeachment e presidente do Paraguai é preso
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O ex-presidente do Paraguai, Santiago Peña, foi preso, nesta sexta-feira (6), após o Senado aprovar por unanimidade seu impeachment. Peña vai cumprir prisão domiciliar. 
Com a saída de Peña, o vice-presidente Pedro Alliana assumiu a presidência, cargo que deve ocupar até agosto de 2028, ano de eleições no Paraguai. Alliana e Peña são do mesmo partido, o Colorado.
A destituição e prisão de Peña acontecem em meio ao escândalo envolvendo o fechamento do banco Ueno, que provocou uma crise financeira afetando cerca de três milhões de pessoas, quase metade da população, além de atingir diversas contas públicas. Peña foi sócio da holding do banco até março de 2025.
Foram 44 votos pelo impeachment; apenas um senador não estava presente. Desde terça (3), o país passa por uma onda de protestos que aumentou a pressão sobre os parlamentares. 
Numa manobra, Peña anunciou sua renúncia na quinta (5), que, se aprovada pelo Congresso Nacional, teria o livrado da prisão. Os parlamentares decidiram manter o julgamento. Ele então afirmou que iria comparecer ao Senado, mas tentou uma nova manobra na manhã desta sexta para adiar o julgamento. 
Além do presidente, o Ministério Público pede a prisão do ex-presidente do Banco Central do Paraguai (BCP), Carlos Carvallo Spalding.
Entenda
A quebra do banco digital Ueno Bank mergulhou o Paraguai em uma crise financeira e política. Em dois dias, o colapso levou centenas de pessoas às ruas da capital, Assunção, derrubou o presidente do Banco Central do Paraguai (BCP), deixou grandes redes varejistas praticamente sem vendas e fez o Congresso correr para mudar a lei e acelerar a devolução do dinheiro bloqueado dos clientes.
O Ueno tem 2,9 milhões de clientes, cerca de 40% da população paraguaia, e processa perto de 3 milhões de transações por dia. Por ele, passam dois terços dos pagamentos eletrônicos das grandes redes de varejo, e a Associação de Importadores e Comerciantes do Paraguai (Asimcopar) já alerta para uma semiparalisação do mercado.
Os manifestantes reivindicam a devolução integral dos depósitos, incluindo os recursos do Instituto de Previdência Social (IPS) e das caixas de aposentadoria aplicados no banco. Os protestos também cobram responsabilidades do presidente Santiago Peña, que foi acionista do grupo controlador do banco até 2025.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Uruguai dá aula de democracia em recepção ao Papa Leão XIV
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A recepção ao Papa Leão XIV no Uruguai transcorreu em um clima de união institucional democrática. O atual presidente uruguaio, o esquerdista Yamandú Orsi, convidou para a solenidade na Plaza de la Independencia três ex-mandatários de direita.
Em seu discurso de boas-vindas, o presidente Orsi destacou a estabilidade geopolítica do país e a convivência pacífica entre os diferentes espectros políticos uruguaios. “Recebe-o este país, Uruguai. Um país onde o governo, os cidadãos que foram presidentes por diferentes partidos políticos, junto com o nosso povo, podemos nos sentar todos juntos, em paz e com alegria, para oferecer-lhe este abraço de boas-vindas”.
Por sua vez, o Papa Leão XIV elogiou a maturidade democrática e as conquistas socioambientais da nação sul-americana. “Em 2025, completaram-se quarenta anos ininterruptos de democracia no Uruguai, durante os quais, por decisão dos cidadãos, se sucederam diferentes governos. A autoridade pública encontra a sua razão de ser no serviço ao bem comum e é chamada a ser exercida no âmbito da ordem jurídica, respeitando a liberdade e a responsabilidade dos cidadãos”, declarou o pontífice.
Meio ambiente e inteligência artifical
Os discursos do pontífice e do presidente convergiram em diversos pontos, como ao falarem da importância de questões ambientais. Leão XIV ressaltou a transição energética do país como exemplo global: “Nas últimas décadas, o Uruguai transformou profundamente a sua matriz de produção de energia elétrica, que hoje se baseia quase inteiramente em fontes renováveis. Trata-se de um resultado notável que exigiu decisões sustentadas ao longo de anos e a participação de diversos setores.”
Ambos trataram ainda dos possíveis impactos da inteligência artificial sobre o mercado de trabalho. Orsi citou a encíclica Magnifica humanitas (2026) para alertar sobre limites éticos. “O avanço tecnológico não pode ir contra o inerente à nossa condição humana; e, quando afeta negativamente o emprego, não podemos apenas pensar em termos de porcentagens, reconversão ou em chave de mera subsistência. Estamos diante de um dilema antropológico-social que o senhor identificou claramente”, apontou o presidente uruguaio.
Alinhado a essa preocupação, Leão XIV enfatizou o valor central da dignidade humana frente às inovações técnicas. “O desenvolvimento destas tecnologias deve ampliar as capacidades humanas, facilitar as tarefas e criar possibilidades, procurando garantir que a pessoa que trabalha não seja reduzida a uma mera peça dispensável em meio ao processo produtivo”, pontuou o Papa, citando ainda o ensinamento da encíclica Laborem Exercens (1981): “Convém recordar que ‘o trabalho é para o homem e não o homem para o trabalho’”.
Por fim, a defesa da diplomacia e da cooperação global encerrou a fala de Orsi, que defendeu a mediação como único caminho para o equilíbrio global. “O multilateralismo é muito mais que uma opção, é o convite permanente para nos sentarmos à mesa e evitarmos confrontos que, a esta altura, sabemos que podem adquirir dimensões catastróficas. Para a humanidade, a paz, o diálogo e a negociação são o único caminho possível”, concluiu.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Entramos na história’: lançamento de documentário do BdF sobre alfabetização popular traz debate com educandos e educadores em SP
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Lucas Estanislau
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Ao ver educadores e educandos retratados no novo documentário do Brasil de Fato, “Mãos que Educam, Mãos que Alimentam”, é possível entender como “entramos na roda da história”. A percepção é da pedagoga e militante do MST Paula França, que foi uma das debatedoras durante o lançamento do filme exclusivo do BdF realizado no Sesc São Bento nesta sexta-feira (6).
“Nas jornadas de alfabetização, nós víamos filmes da década de 1960, quando alunos do método cubano liam cartas para o presidente, como foi na Nicarágua. Hoje, são os educandos que podem se ver nesse filme. Nós vemos como entramos na roda da história”, disse.
O evento marcou a estreia do documentário que retrata histórias de vida impactadas pelas jornadas de alfabetização e das cozinhas solidárias promovidas pelo Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST) por meio do projeto Mãos Solidárias.
Também fizeram parte da mesa de debates a educanda Janeide Barbosa, o membro da coordenação nacional do Mãos Solidárias David Zamori, e o deputado estadual Eduardo Suplicy.
“É um projeto muito rico de saberes e de histórias”, contou Janeide. Ela foi uma das pessoas alfabetizadas nas jornadas em São Miguel Paulista, no estado de São Paulo. Além disso, ela coordena uma cozinha solidária e foi daí que veio a oportunidade de retomar os estudos.
“Eu sou do Nordeste, venho do Agreste de Pernambuco, onde não havia muita familiaridade com a escola. A emoção foi demais. Só quem vive que sabe o momento que a gente passa e teve no nosso dia a dia, na nossa vida”, disse.
As jornadas nasceram no seio do programa Mãos Solidárias, que tinha como centro inicialmente as cozinhas solidárias, iniciativa encabeçada pelo MST durante a emergência sanitária da Covid-19. Com o aumento da fome e da pobreza, diversas cozinhas foram abertas para produção de refeições que eram distribuídas à população vulnerável.
“A jornada de alfabetização chega da necessidade de fazer mais”, explicou David Zamori. “A alimentação é uma parte, há muito mais para ser feito. Hoje, além de fortalecer os trabalhos das cozinhas, o Mãos Solidárias busca formas de fazer mais, entrar com outros projetos para fortalecer a organização nos bairros”.
Para o militante do MST e um dos coordenadores do projeto, o personagem principal da jornada “são os educandos, os que se propuseram a todo dia ir fazer aula”.
“Esse método depende da pessoa ir todo dia às aulas. Isso é um esforço enorme, a gente sabe. Para pessoas idosas, avós e avôs, há muita demanda em casa, então foi um esforço grande”, afirmou.
Ao longo de um ano, a iniciativa reuniu cerca de 18 mil educandos e 1,5 mil educadores em mais de 1,3 mil turmas de alfabetização espalhadas pelo país. O documentário percorreu territórios de Pernambuco, Paraíba e São Paulo, onde cozinhas populares, garagens e associações de moradores se transformaram em espaços de aprendizagem.
Método cubano
Um dos destaques do projeto é a utilização do método cubano “Sim, eu posso”. Criado por Cuba na década de 1990, ele já foi aplicado em vários países e é responsável pela alfabetização de mais de 10 milhões de pessoas em todos os continentes.
Paula França explicou as raízes do método e lembrou que, no Brasil, o responsável por guardar o projeto é o MST.
“A primeira experiência foi em 2006, no Piauí. O método se mostrou eficaz, com 80% de êxito, então decidimos espalhar. As experiências principais no início foram nos assentamentos do MST e só depois passamos a atuar junto com o poder público”, contou.
A pedagoga também explicou que o método é totalmente pensado e voltado para a formação de pessoas adultas, pois conta com vídeos em formato de “novelas” e “com a associação entre letras e números”, por isso tem pouca evasão e muita eficácia. “Isso faz com que esse aprendizado seja mais rápido.
Um exemplo bom, lembra França, foi na Venezuela. “Eles conseguiram erradicar o analfabetismo em várias edições da Missão Robinson, no período do ex-presidente Hugo Chávez”, disse.
‘Bom documentário’
O deputado estadual Eduardo Suplicy elogiou o documentário e disse que ele “retrata boa parte da vida do povo que vive em dificuldade social”.
“O documentário é bom para conhecermos as dificuldades dos personagens dessa história. Ele contribui para que tenhamos melhor consciência da situação socioeconômica de muitos brasileiros”, destacou.
Suplicy ainda lembrou do seu projeto de criação de uma renda básica de cidadania e disse que “se [o projeto] já estivesse em vigor, a condição de vida dos personagens do documentário teria mudado completamente”.
Produzido pelo Brasil de Fato e pelo Centro Popular de Mídias, o documentário tem realização do Instituto Federal do Paraná e do Ministério da Educação (MEC), por meio da Secretaria de Educação Continuada, Alfabetização de Jovens e Adultos, Diversidade e Inclusão (Secadi). A direção é de Afonso Bezerra, com produção executiva de Ana Rosa Carrara e Cibele Lima. A direção de fotografia é de Vitor Shimomura, a direção de arte, de Beatriz Zupo, e a montagem, de Gabriela Peres.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: ‘Possibilidades políticas da guerra no Irã continuar são quase nulas’ após onda azul nos EUA
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: BdF Entrevista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
As eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos impuseram derrota ao presidente Donald Trump. Com a maioria Democrata no Senado e na Câmara, existe uma expectativa de mudança na condução política de temas sensíveis, como a guerra no Irã, as tarifas (que também têm impactado a economia interna) e a imigração.
Ao BdF Entrevista, Jana Silverman, professora e secretária de Relações Internacionais dos Socialistas Democráticos dos EUA (DSA), destaca que, além de modificar a correlação de forças, a derrota republicana proporcionou como grande novidade a ascensão de candidaturas abertamente de esquerda. “É a eleição de uma bancada não apenas progressista, mas socialista pela primeira vez na história dos Estados Unidos. Nós, como DSA, dos nove candidatos a deputado federal, ganharam oito. Dos oito, seis mulheres e dois homens”, afirma.
A dirigente enfatizou que os candidatos endossados pela organização precisavam cumprir critérios rígidos, devendo “ser explicitamente anticapitalistas, não receber e não aceitar dinheiro, nenhuma fonte empresarial” e manter um posicionamento abertamente anti-imperialista. “É uma coisa muito importante, porque nos Estados Unidos, diferente do Brasil, o que a gente chama aqui de Caixa 2 é totalmente liberado por lei”, conta.
Outro aspecto central que foi colocado em debate nas eleições estadunidenses diz respeito aos rumos do conflito provocado pelos EUA contra o Irã. Silverman lembra que Trump atropelou o Congresso ao declarar guerra ao país persa e precisará passar pela aprovação do parlamento para a sua continuidade. “As possibilidades políticas de guerra se estenderem mais são quase nulas hoje em dia. Eu tenho certeza absoluta de que o novo Congresso vai chamar essa votação, que se chama War Powers Authorization, ou autorização para ir à guerra. E, se não ganhar essa votação, que vai ser altamente provável, o Trump, por lei, teria que já retirar as tropas e cessar a ação bélica na ação referida no projeto de lei”, aponta. “Penso que será uma prioridade altíssima, já que até republicanos estão rejeitando a política externa de Trump com relação ao Irã.”
Jana Silverman também ressaltou que o fator econômico teve um peso importante para o eleitorado, já que a perda no poder de compra e o encarecimento do custo de vida transformaram o pleito em um referendo contra as promessas econômicas não cumpridas. “A inflação nos EUA nem é tão alta para os padrões latino-americanos. Mas o problema é que o poder de compra está baixando porque os salários reais não estão subindo. É um país em que você não tem um aumento real do salário mínimo nacional desde 2008”, enfatiza.
Além disso, a truculência das operações do órgão de imigração (ICE) em portas de escolas e comunidades causou indignação pública e provocou uma expressiva virada no voto dos eleitores latinos. “Esse grande tsunami azul, sobretudo no estado do Texas e outros estados como Arizona, Novo México, foi com base na mudança do padrão do voto latino. O voto latino, sobretudo dos homens, foi quase a maioria para o Trump em 2024. E vimos uma mudança de quase 30% desses eleitores, sobretudo homens latinos, mudando do Trump para o partido Democrata”, conta.
Diante dessa conjuntura, Silverman defendeu posições contundentes sobre a reestruturação da política migratória. “Eu tenho muito medo de que o setor mais moderado do partido, que, no final das contas, é o que ganhou a maioria das cadeiras no novo Congresso, vai tentar uma solução muito meio-termo.” Ou seja: ‘Vamos dar mais treinamento, vamos dar aquelas câmaras nos uniformes, etc’. Mas nossa posição é abolir totalmente o ICE”, defende.
A professora também avaliou com otimismo a capacidade de organização social, não apenas no Brasil, como nos EUA, frente à onda conservadora global. “Não é inevitável o crescimento da extrema direita, mas o poder do povo, o poder da classe trabalhadora, ainda está muito vigente”, conclui.
