https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) agradeceu neste domingo (08) a mobilização popular nas ruas e nas redes sociais durante as eleições presidenciais que garantiram a sua reeleição.
Em sua primeira fala em rede nacional após a vitória eleitoral para o quarto mandato, Lula também prometeu criar condições para reduzir a taxa de juros, defendeu a soberania nacional e afirmou que o “Brasil não é lugar para quem foge”, em uma declaração interpretada como referência a Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que fugiu para os EUA após ser derrotado nas urnas.
“Nunca fugi dos compromissos, nunca fugi das críticas, nunca fugi da luta e jamais abandonei meu país. O Brasil não é lugar para quem foge das suas responsabilidades”, disse.
Ao agradecer os mais de 64 milhões de votos recebidos, o presidente destacou a participação popular no processo eleitoral e classificou o resultado das urnas como “uma vitória da democracia”.
“Antes de ir às urnas, o povo brasileiro foi às ruas e às redes defender seus direitos, suas causas e suas esperanças”, afirmou o presidente.
Lula elogiou especialmente o protagonismo da juventude nas manifestações e a participação dos idosos, afirmando que a mobilização popular seguirá tendo papel no próximo governo.
“É com a força da mobilização popular que vamos conduzir o governo daqui para frente, conectados com os anseios da população, ampliando a escuta e o diálogo”, disse.
Lula também associou a mobilização popular à defesa da soberania nacional e criticou a atuação das grandes plataformas digitais durante a disputa eleitoral. Segundo ele, as chamadas big techs tentaram interferir nas eleições brasileiras ao ampliar o alcance de conteúdos de desinformação e notícias falsas, que receberam milhões de visualizações.
Lula afirmou que pretende governar para todos os brasileiros, independentemente das posições assumidas durante a disputa eleitoral.
Redução dos juros e investimentos
Na economia, Lula apontou a redução dos juros como uma das prioridades do próximo mandato, ainda que tenha indicado preocupação com a dívida pública e prometido responsabilidade fiscal.
“Um dos principais objetivos do nosso governo é elevar o investimento do país para mais de 20% do PIB, em parceria com o setor privado. Para tanto, vamos criar as condições para reduzir a taxa de juros”, prometeu.
O presidente não detalhou quais medidas serão adotadas para alcançar a redução dos juros nem estabeleceu um prazo para que isso aconteça.
Também anunciou iniciativas voltadas à diminuição do endividamento das famílias, incluindo a compra de dívidas junto aos bancos e o perdão de débitos de microempreendedores individuais (MEIs) com o governo federal.
Entre os compromissos econômicos, Lula mencionou ainda a implementação do programa Prospera MEI, voltado ao fortalecimento dos pequenos negócios, e a ampliação das oportunidades de emprego, especialmente para os jovens.
O presidente também comemorou os efeitos econômicos que atribuiu ao fim das apostas eletrônicas, as chamadas bets. Segundo Lula, a interrupção das apostas permitiu que as famílias ampliassem o consumo, estimulando o comércio, a indústria e a atividade econômica.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Godzilla Minus Zero takes US box office by storm in opening weekend
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Japan’s most recognisable film star shows no sign of losing its ability to captivate global audiences, after Godzilla Minus Zero – a foreign language film - swept to the top of the US box office on its opening weekend.
The film – the 39th in a franchise stretching back to 1954 – generated $63m worldwide, including $31.6m in the US and Canada, where it set a record for opening weekend receipts for the biggest live-action foreign-language film. It is shown in Japanese with English subtitles.
Filmgoers were just as enthralled in Japan, where the sequel to the 2003 Oscar-winning film Godzilla Minus One set a domestic record for a live-action film, according to the Kyodo news agency.
In Godzilla Minus Zero, set in Japan in 1949 – two years after it lay “dead” at the bottom of the ocean – the creature resurfaced to respond to a new threat to the country’s attempts to rebuild after the second world war: a dragon-like beast called Ghidorah.
The film, directed by Takashi Yamazaki, shows a radioactively regenerated Godzilla confront its three-headed nemesis – which destroys buildings with lightning bolts fired from its mouth – with the help of human intervention.
“This historic opening shows how deeply audiences around the world connect with Godzilla and with Takashi Yamazaki’s vision,” Koji Ueda, president of Toho Global, which produced the film, said in a statement. “Our first near-simultaneous global release was built on that belief.”
In Japan, Godzilla earned ($5.75m) on its opening day on 3 November, setting a box office revenue record for the first day of a live-action release in the country and, according to Toho, more than double the opening day earnings generated by Godzilla Minus One.
Minus Zero qualifies as a live-action film as it was principally shot on-location, including at a sports park in Ibaraki, northeast of Tokyo, that was used for large crowd scenes and at a temple in Maizuru, Kyoto prefecture.
Industry experts said the success of its global release on Imax and regular screens worldwide had easily exceeded expectations.
“This weekend’s opening takes the Japanese production to a new level – it’s nearly three times the previous opening [of Godzilla Minus One] in December 2023,” industry analyst David A Gross wrote.
The latest Godzilla film faces competition from the Indian epic Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, which earned $55.7m on its opening weekend. The Hindi-language blockbuster – the most expensive Indian film ever made – made $8.7m in the US and $32m in India.
Godzilla Minus Zero and Ramayana were produced in the Imax format, with the former receiving an early Imax-only release last week. The large-format screens appear to have driven audience interest, generating 34% of Godzilla’s box office take on its opening weekend.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘I can’t bear it’: young family takes refuge in bedroom as choking haze engulfs Indonesian city
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Garry Lotulung in Palangkaraya, and Oliver Holmes in Bangkok
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Every day in Palangkaraya starts with an air quality check. For people who can afford one, a handheld device can test the air for toxic particles floating into their lungs. For others, a look out the window will reveal skies turned orange with smoke.
But for those closest to the fires ravaging this part of Indonesia, the check is done before they even open their eyes, with the acrid smell and the hacking cough that comes as they wake.
On the island of Borneo, people are facing life where the air itself is a threat. Windows are sealed with plastic sheeting, children are locked in bedrooms and families spend evenings inhaling oxygen from tanks.
At the centre of the crisis sits the city of Palangkaraya, home to about 300,000 residents, who have been besieged for months by wildfires engulfing its surrounding forests. Here, Apri Dona Yusmelita sits on the floor with her five-month-old son. She encourages him to take breaths from a nebuliser – a machine that will transport medicine to the infant’s tiny lungs. He has been sick for most of his short life.
“The cough is phlegmy, so he always has to vomit,” says Yusmelita, who also has a four-year-old. “So it’s like he struggles to catch up to his target weight. Because he’s constantly sick. So whatever he drinks, he vomits it all up, because he coughs so often.”
Since the fires started in July, Yusmelita has regularly had to keep her children in the bedroom where she has an air purifier. The 27-year-old moved the television from the living room to keep them occupied, but rotating power outages can make the days feel longer. Smoky air seeps into the rest of their home.
“Even eating had to be in the bedroom for the kids because their lungs are different from ours,” she says. “We moved everything here, especially when the smoke turned yellow yesterday … So it’s only safe in the bedroom.”
Over the past four months, her family has spent roughly half their time inside that single room. When her mother briefly took the children outside to play, their symptoms flared immediately. “I can’t bear it,” she says. “It’s so pitiful.”
Smoke from annual fires has become a way of life here. Many blazes were started intentionally using the “slash and burn” method of clearing land for crops such as palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.
This year has been exceptionally bad, with close to 2m hectares of forest and peatland burned in Indonesia. A “godzilla” El Niño has brought drier-than-usual conditions.
‘They come just to breathe’
Authorities have been unable to cope with the scale of the catastrophe, meaning it is often local volunteers who monitor air pollution. The Ranu Welum Foundation, a local Indigenous organisation, has been fundraising for smoke “safe houses” equipped with air purifiers, oxygen tanks and nebulisers.
Roro Ardya Garini, 35, a co-founder, says they cater for vulnerable populations – the children and elderly – although on severe days anyone is welcome. “They come just to breathe,” she says. There are now 14 of these so-called haze shelters, often in rooms donated by churches or public buildings. The best ones have air-tight concrete walls and minimal ventilation.
The shelters are not a replacement for hospitals, Garini says, and sometimes volunteers have to send people away. Once, a baby arrived blue from acute oxygen deprivation and was quickly sent to the emergency room.
At another shelter operated by the volunteer group JPIC Kalimantan, Sabrina Alfiana supervises her four-year-old son, Fahreza Alfarizqia, as he inhales mist from a nebuliser. Air purifiers are lined up and plugged into the wall, as well as oxygen tanks.
Sabrina, 26, says she keeps her children inside, but sealing her home is a lost cause. “It’s smoke, right? Whether it seeps in through the cracks, the windows, you can still feel it,” she says. “Even inside the bedroom, we can smell the smoke.”
While Palangkaraya is on the frontline of the haze crisis, millions of people across south-east Asia have been breathing air that could be damaging their bodies in ways they cannot predict.
Thick smoke has drifted into Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Timor-Leste, even reaching as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Schools have been closed, tens of thousands have been hospitalised with respiratory issues, and residents have been sharing images of rainwater turned black with ash.
In Singapore the government has set up its own air-conditioned haze shelters while Malaysia’s capital, Kuala Lumpur, has seen an uptick in pets brought to the vet. Toxic air has spiked demand for oxygen tanks and air purifiers across the region, manufacturers say.
The Indonesian government has dispatched firefighters and says it will pursue the companies accused of arson, but decades of promises to address the fires have failed.
In Palangkaraya, volunteer Melodyna Adhesiva, 23, is in charge of taking air quality readings and posting the results on social media for the public. The readings monitor levels of PM2.5, particulate matter small enough to enter the bloodstream and cause lung damage.
The World Health Organization recommends a 24-hour average of 15 micrograms per cubic metre, and in Palangkaraya it regularly reaches 300. The worst reading Adhesiva took last month was above 3,000.
Her team has several devices, but the air quality is so bad they’re ineffective. “This one can only reach a maximum of 999,” she says, holding a monitor high up in her hand. “So we rarely use it for going out. We sometimes just use it for checking indoors.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump tells 60 Minutes that deportation policy was ‘too tough’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump has admitted that his deportation policy was “too tough” and has offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats in a concession following the Republicans’ disastrous defeat in the midterm elections.
In an interview on the CBS network’s 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, the president acknowledged that the aggressive crackdown had hurt him politically and said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.
Trump was asked by 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether his deportation policy had gone too far. “I think it was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”
The president’s comments offered an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.
Since Trump returned to office, sweeping Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids at workplaces, homes and public spaces have ensnared people with no criminal records, separated families and spread fear in immigrant communities. Federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during operations in Minneapolis earlier this year.
The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”
Trump added that there were competing views within the country about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported or allowed to remain if they were working and paying taxes. He said some people believed that “they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company” and “in some cases, paying taxes”.
Trump said he believed an agreement with Democrats was achievable, allowing some long-term undocumented residents to stay while continuing to remove people convicted of serious crimes. He proposed targeting killers, rapists and drug dealers while making an accommodation for people who had been in the country for 10 or 15 years.
“Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said. He described the proposal as something that could be negotiated, saying: “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”
Trump suggested Democrats were receptive to a compromise, saying some had already contacted him. Asked whether he could refrain from name-calling for six months to secure an agreement, he replied: “Very easily.”
Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat, agreeing with an assessment by his vice-president, JD Vance, that the conflict had been a major factor. He also cited what he described as growing dislike of Israel.
He maintained, however, that the military campaign had been justified and said he would make the same decision again. “My answer is an emphatic yes because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Trump insisted the war had been won and predicted that Tehran would eventually negotiate a deal. He acknowledged that the military campaign might not have been popular in the short term, saying: “I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.”
He said he was not looking to escalate the conflict after the midterms.
On the economy, the president conceded that his administration had failed to communicate its achievements effectively, despite repeatedly claiming that employment, investment and stock market figures were at record levels. “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me,” he said.
Trump signalled an openness to safeguards for artificial intelligence, despite having previously favoured allowing technology companies to police themselves rather than imposing sweeping government restrictions. “I don’t mind guardrails,” he told 60 Minutes. “But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position.”
The interview also raised questions about the substantial increase in Trump’s personal wealth since his return to the White House.
Douthat cited a Forbes estimate that Trump’s net worth had increased by $3bn from the autumn of 2024 to the autumn of 2025. Trump initially suggested that the increase reflected the general performance of the stock market and said his finances were managed by his son.
Asked about his family’s cryptocurrency business, World Liberty Financial, in which he is a co-owner and which has attracted investment from people connected to the United Arab Emirates, Trump defended the arrangement by saying: “I know nothing about it.”
But Dan Alexander, a Forbes senior editor who calculates the net worth of wealthy individuals for the magazine, challenged Trump’s explanation in a lengthy thread on X, arguing that the president’s increased fortune could not be explained simply by stock market gains.
Alexander identified several sources including cryptocurrency ventures that generated more than $1bn in proceeds and the appreciation of tokens retained by Trump, overseas licensing agreements that expanded the value of his branding business, and the removal of an almost $500m financial penalty in his New York civil fraud case.
Trump also offered a glimpse of the Republican succession battle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, saying he might endorse a candidate but had not decided whether to intervene. Asked whether he expected to endorse a successor, Trump replied: “Probably. Not necessarily.”
He described the Republican party as having a strong field of potential candidates and praised secretary of state Marco Rubio while declining to rule out other contenders.
The president said his endorsement would carry considerable weight but suggested he might be better off staying out of the contest. He also expressed confidence that the “Make America great again” movement could survive without him as its leader, describing its defining principles as strong borders and a strong military.
At the end of the interview, Trump was asked whether he could forgive political opponents including former FBI director James Comey and former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, even before the judgment of God. Trump said: “The answer is no. I want to be honest, no.”
Douthat followed up: “Mr President. You have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime and you are telling me that before the judgment throne of God you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies? After all that’s been given to you? Come on. Help me out here.”
But Trump remained adamant, insisting: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”
Douthat then noted that many presidents are remembered with a single line such as “He freed the slaves” or “He won the cold war” and asked what line will Trump’s presidency be remembered with.
The president said simply: “That I made America great again.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Pope Leo delivers stinging rebuke of Milei’s austerity measures during Argentina visit
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier Milei’s harsh austerity measures, insisting growth must benefit all in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.
“The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy,” he said on Sunday, shortly after landing in Argentina on the second leg of a Latin America tour.
Leo stressed the plight of those who, “despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household’s needs”.
He spoke out in defence of the poor and pensioners, insisting that “particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability” – a veiled reference to the government’s controversial cuts to disability assistance.
He also told Milei, known for his foul-mouthed diatribes, that strengthening democracy required a “willingness to listen” and the “careful use of words”.
Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 12-day tour of the continent, just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
The visit is the first by a pontiff to Argentina in nearly four decades, and Leo was met with calls to help mend deep divisions in the country after three years of austerity under Milei.
Argentina is the home country of the late pope, Francis, who Milei famously insulted for his pro-poor teachings.
Leo said he was “retracing” Francis’s steps.
Argentines are hoping the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics will help unite the country, which is bitterly divided between supporters and opponents of Milei.
“Just like the World Cup unites us, hopefully the pope will too,” said Liliana Deblauwe, a 68-year-old retired teacher who waited with hundreds of people to see the pope visit a monument to liberation hero Jose de San Martin.
Hundreds more chanting “Papa Leon” (Spanish for Leo) gathered outside the presidential palace, where he was hosted by Milei.
Brian Inacio Rodriguez, a 26-year-old job seeker, spent five days travelling overland from Ushuaia, at the very tip of South America, to see the pontiff.
He said he hoped he brought “much peace to Argentina”.
Leo arrived in Buenos Aires from Uruguay, where he began his first trip as pope to Latin America, the world’s most Catholic continent which is becoming increasingly secular.
In Uruguay, he condemned drug violence and urged an end to child poverty.
In Buenos Aires, he insisted on the importance of “personal integrity” in public office, stressing that “corruption undermines the confidence of citizens in their institutions.”
The Argentine stage of his visit aims to boost the flagging faith of a country left disappointed by Francis’s failure to visit during his papacy.
It will also act as a litmus test of support for the church. In a recent University of Buenos Aires poll, 57.7% of people identified as Catholic, down from about 90% in the 1960s.
Leo will visit a home for disabled people and a prison and celebrate three open-air masses.
The church has said it expects 7 million to attend the various events.
Milei came to office on a promise to revive Argentina’s ailing economy and tame runaway inflation by shrinking the welfare state, targeting public hospitals, universities and pensioners in particular.
The poverty rate has swung wildly since he came to power – increasing to 32.3% in September.
A close ally of US president Donald Trump, with a similar combative style, Milei had a tense relationship with Francis.
On the campaign trail the cost-cutting economist called his countryman an “imbecile” for championing social justice.
Once in office, however, he softened his tone, but he continues to heap insults on the press and opposition.
His relationship with Leo has so far been cordial, but the local Catholic church has heavily criticised him for treating key social services solely as a budgetary constraint.
Milei has also been criticised for restricting several democratic freedoms, including the right to protest. But he maintains a loyal supporter base for drastically reducing inflation.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making UFC’s Dana White next press secretary
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Mackey
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump said on Sunday that he “was only kidding” when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).
Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.
“So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump added. “Of course, I was kidding. And you could see that because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with him … It was just a little fun.”
Earlier on Sunday, the president shared an animated AI cartoon made by one of his supporters on social media, which showed UFC fighters beating up journalists and one, Josh Hokit, repeating the racist remark about Michelle Obama he made during the UFC event at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June.
The president said that his mock announcement that White would become his spokesperson, in a social media post on Saturday, “was an example of something where I was kidding, and then people said, ‘You know, that’s actually a pretty good idea’”.
He did not say who, exactly, supported the idea.
The first in a series of taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads broadcast by the White House in the run-up to the recent midterms closed with images of the UFC fight on Trump’s birthday and remarks about him from White, who could be heard saying: “He is the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life.” White used that formulation to describe Trump multiple times during the 2024 presidential election campaign, most notably to sing Trump’s praises at the Republican national convention.
The role of White House press secretary has been vacant for three weeks, since Trump’s previous pick, the far-right commentator Katie Zacharia, was forced to resign after trying, and failing, to dodge questions about why she described herself as an attorney despite having failed the bar exam.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Kyle Larson joins Nascar’s all-time greats with third Cup title in six years
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Kyle Larson is now a three-time Nascar champion.
Larson clinched his third Cup Series title in six years early in Sunday’s 400-mile season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway, becoming the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010. Johnson won five consecutive titles beginning in 2006.
The 34-year-old Larson also became the 11th driver in Nascar history to win three Cup titles, joining an exclusive club that includes seven-time champions Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt and Johnson. Jeff Gordon won four titles, while Lee Petty, David Pearson, Cale Yarborough, Darrell Waltrip, Tony Stewart and Joey Logano each won three.
Ryan Blaney won the race for Team Penske, passing Tyler Reddick of 23XI Racing with just over a lap remaining as NBA legend Michael Jordan watched from pit road. Reddick finished second, followed by William Byron, Christopher Bell, Bubba Wallace and Denny Hamlin.
But the biggest celebration belonged to Larson, who finished 12th. He stopped near the start-finish line for a smoky burnout before exchanging high-fives and hugs with his team and children. He then climbed atop his No 5 Chevrolet with the championship flag and all three of his children to celebrate.
Larson had been the overwhelming favorite to lift the Bill France Cup long before the green flag dropped.
He entered the weekend with a 67-point lead over Bell and needed only nine points to secure the championship. He earned one point for starting the race and seven more by finishing fourth in the opening stage. When Bell failed to win that stage, he was mathematically eliminated from contention.
Larson responded to crew chief Cliff Daniels breaking the news over the radio with a deadpan assessment: “That was anticlimactic.”
Hendrick Motorsports owner Rick Hendrick, celebrating his team’s 16th Cup championship, radioed Larson to congratulate him during the ensuing caution period.
“Now you can go ride the wall,” Hendrick joked.
Larson obliged, only to cut a right-rear tire and be forced to pit out of sequence, effectively ending his hopes of winning the race.
“I got the word that we clinched it, and I started driving like an idiot,” Larson said. “I’m more mad at myself.”
The mishap mattered little after a remarkable postseason in Nascar’s Chase for the Championship. Larson ended a 51-race winless streak by winning three of the previous nine playoff races and finished in the top 10 in eight of them.
He produced a similarly dominant finish in 2021, his first season with Hendrick, winning four of the final five races, including the championship finale at Phoenix Raceway.
His second title came in dramatic fashion last year at Phoenix. Taking advantage of a late caution, Larson’s crew opted for two new tires rather than four, allowing him to leapfrog sentimental favorite Denny Hamlin on pit road with two laps remaining. Hamlin could not catch him.
This year’s championship was considerably less suspenseful. Larson’s advantage was so commanding that he was the only Cup driver invited to Nascar’s championship media day on Thursday, an experience he described as awkward.
Any concerns about how Larson and his No 5 Hendrick Motorsports team would handle the pressure appeared unfounded by Saturday’s qualifying session.
“They were debating on if a hot dog is a sandwich and if cereal is a soup,” Larson said. “So I would say they were pretty relaxed. I was surprised by all that.”
With three Cup championships secured, Larson’s place among motorsport’s most versatile drivers is becoming increasingly difficult to dispute.
Parnelli Jones, Mario Andretti, AJ Foyt and Stewart are widely regarded among the greatest American drivers for their success across multiple disciplines.
Jones won in sprint cars and stock cars around the time he captured the 1963 Indianapolis 500. Andretti won four IndyCar titles, the 1967 Daytona 500 and the 1969 Indianapolis 500. Foyt won four Indianapolis 500s and the 1972 Daytona 500, while Stewart claimed the 1997 IndyCar championship and three Cup Series titles before moving into top-level NHRA drag racing.
Larson has twice competed in the Indianapolis 500 and has won the Rolex 24 at Daytona, three Chili Bowl Nationals and four Knoxville Nationals. His third Cup title further strengthens his case for a place alongside those legends.
“He wins in everything he does, and they’re all completely different cars and tracks,” said retired driver and NBC Sports analyst Jeff Burton. “And he’s racing against the best in every discipline.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ch.title: Chicago Crowds Try and Fail to Move Anish Kapoor’s Bean, Art Lawyer Michael Ward Stout Has Died, Louvre President Says Mona Lisa’s Move Will Be Sad, and More
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ch.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ch.text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.
Good Morning!
- Hundreds in Chicago tried and failed to push the Bean, Anish Kapoor’s iconic Cloud Gate sculpture, seven inches.
- Michael Ward Stout, a lawyer who ran Robert Mapplethorpe’s foundation and represented Salvador Dalí, has died at 83.
- Two oil studies by Peter Paul Rubens, lost for over 80 years, will join three others by the artist to be exhibited at the Ducal Museum in Gotha, Germany.
The Headlines
WHOSE BEAN CALLING? “Push the Bean!” shouted hundreds of people gathered Sunday in Chicago’s Millennium Park. They were there to answer a call to do just that: push Anish Kapoor’s iconic sculpture titled Cloud Gate (popularly referred to as the Bean) seven inches to the left of its location, reports CBS News. Legend and good-excuse-for-gathering-in-person has it that a man is stuck inside the bean and to free him, the sculpture could use a little nudge. The event has gone viral, with videos showing a crowd of outstretched hands reaching toward, trying and failing to push the 110-ton stainless steel sculpture, albeit mostly with just one hand, which arguably reduces their chance of success in half. Their other hands were busy recording with smartphones held high. After all, if a bean moves seven inches, but there is no one there to film and later post it, did it really move? Either way, concerned citizens should know that City Council member Brendan Reilly has long confirmed there is no man trapped inside the Bean. And also, please stop calling him about it.
IN MEMORIAM. Michael Ward Stout, a lawyer who ran Robert Mapplethorpe’s foundation and represented Salvador Dalí, has died at 83, reports The New York Times. Stout handled artist licensing, contracts, exhibitions, and his other clients included the estates of Jean-Michel Basquiat and dealer Barbara Gladstone. We’ve also learned that French video artist Fred Forest died at 93, as reported by Le Monde. In 2017 and 2024, the Centre Pompidou dedicated retrospectives to his video, “sociological art,” and “Net art.” In a message sent by his son, the artist himself announced his own death. “Thanks to the affectionate complicity of my son Adrien, I have the pleasure of announcing my own death,” reads the statement. “Lying in this hole dug in the earth at Anserville [north of Paris], I will now have all the time to reflect calmly on what I will be doing tomorrow, my friends …” signed, Fred Forest.
The Digest
Two oil studies by Peter Paul Rubens, lost for over 80 years, will join three others by the artist to be exhibited at the Ducal Museum in Gotha, Germany, where they had been part of the collection for centuries before their disappearance. [The Art Newspaper]
French investigators have arrested four people in connection with the July thefts of jewelry at the Musée Lalique, and ancient coins at the Archaeology Centre in Montans. [Le Monde]
Following news that The Hole gallery in New York is being sued over back rent and not paying artists and workers, the gallery is facing eviction from its Bowery space and is $102,823 in the hole for owed rent and late charges. [Artnet News]
More than 50 protesters gathered last week in Washington, D.C., to oppose President Trump’s planned triumphal arch. project. [Hyperallergic]
The Grand Rapids Art Museum is staging a powerful survey of art by or about people once incarcerated within the United States, from a 1,000-piece ceramic installation by Julie Green of plates depicting the final-meal choices of people on death row, to quilted appliquéd works by artist Gary Tyler, who was wrongly convicted at seventeen years old. [ARTnews]
The Kicker
LONELY MONA LISA. Will the Mona Lisa’s smile feel lonelier if she’s removed from her current gallery in the Louvre and placed in a new one by herself? To Louvre president Christophe Leribault, at least, the prospect is decidedly triste, despite it being a key part of the museum’s major new, over $1-billion-dollar renovation plan for which he is actively fundraising. As he told the Wall Street Journal, Leribault explained that moving the Mona Lisa to her own room will control crowds, but “is sad,” because it “will separate the Mona Lisa from the other Leonardo da Vinci paintings.” For now, and despite planned protests, the Louvre remains open, and visitors can try to catch a glimpse of the Mona Lisa in the good company of other Da Vinci paintings and throngs of selfie-wielding tourists.

A quick recap of the arguments both sides have made. Brand’s lawyers are looking for a more lenient sentence, the prosecution has called for serious category one term.
Karmy-Jones KC pushed for Brand to receive a sentence of 10-15 years for the rape conviction, arguing that his crimes warranted such a level of punishment because of how he had abused his position, and then further degraded and humiliated his victims.
She said Brand had the view that he could abuse without impunity and he must bear some responsibility for the culture around him which enabled his offending for years.
Karmy-Jones read out three victim impact statements from the women abused by Brand. All described the debilitating impacts of his violence, and how it had damaged their relationships, careers, their feelings of self-worth and confidence and their day-to-day existence.
One woman delivering her statement in person to the judge. She said she had carried around “that undeserved feeling of shame” for 20 years.
All of the victims said they still carried the trauma with them to this day, and relayed the stressful experience of going to court to bring him to justice.
Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter KC, argued that Brand was a fundamentally changed man these days.
He said the crimes had occurred 17 years ago, and had been “isolated incidents”. He described the rape that Brand has been convicted for as a “short and momentary failure” of consent.
Winter said any major sentence given out to Brand would have a “catastrophic” impact on his young family and urged Judge Bennathan to show mercy.
'You thought fame meant you could act however you liked'
The judge, laying out the crimes, notes Brand’s “staggering arrogance” and how his entourage regularly indulged Brand’s actions.
Three of the four crimes took place in public settings, in front of other people – at a bar, radio station and a setting where an advert was being filmed. Others in the room laughed after the assaults, the women said.
These insults in front of an audience, said after the assault amount to an additional humiliation.
The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect, and your belief that fame meant you could act however you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live.
The judge is relaying the sexual assaults Brand committed against the women.
He starts with the attacks on one woman in a pub in London where Brand groped the breast of a fellow party attendee.
“The effect on her had her wandering the streets of London, phoning a friend in the middle of the night, tearful and distressed.”
He outlines another assault, where Brand, visiting a radio station with an entourage launched himself at a woman, groping and kissing her in front of her colleagues and his entourage.
He notes the attack’s impact on her, how it damaged relationships with her male colleagues.
“There was the added humiliation of you assaulting her in front of an audience and the laughter afterwards”.
Judge Bennathan is about to begin his sentencing remarks, having considered the submissions from the prosecutor and Brand’s defence lawyer this morning.
A reminder that Russell Brand, once one of Britain’s most high-profile actor-comedians, was convicted last Thursday of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.
A jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six women on allegations dating back to 2004. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand has sat upright and remained remarkably composed throughout the trial, but he was seen looking down at his lap towards the end of this morning’s hearing.
When he left the dock, he could be seen clutching prayer beads in his right hand and nodding at his wife, Laura.
She seemed emotional when Ian Winter KC told the court she was standing by him.
“Words are completely inadequate… to convey the total devastation she’s experiencing,” he said.
Channel 4 worker assaulted by Brand said attack was 'brushed under the carpet'
Brand was convicted last week of forcing himself onto a woman in a Channel 4 radio studio, kissing her and groping her.
In her victim impact statement the woman says she spoke up immediately after the attack but it was “brushed under the carpet by senior management”.
“This really affected me and had something similar happened again at that time, I know I would not have had the confidence to speak up again. There was a culture at the time which meant I felt I had to just carry on and not talk about it anymore.”
She said she felt powerless in the moment. “It had a knock-on effect on my confidence because I felt like I had no control on that day and there was nothing I could do about what he did to me.”
She said giving evidence in court “to a room full of strangers and Russell Brand took me right back to how I felt on the day of the assault. It was a hugely distracting and overwhelming process and it took an awful lot out of me.”
“I am eternally grateful to the police and prosecution team for their support and for allowing my voice to be heard.
“I finally feel believed but I am still so anxious. I worry that there will be repercussions for telling the truth. This was and is being spoken about so much by the world media and social media, it’s left me feeling exposed and exhausted.”
Victim says Brand has 'no remorse' for his behaviour
One of Brand’s victims was assaulted by him at her workplace, attacked in a small room at the offices of Capital Radio in 2009.
Her victim impact statement was read out by Karmy-Jones:
Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse for how his behaviour has impacted my life. I just hope that he is not allowed to hurt any more women.
She relayed how Brand had “managed to move on and even forget that he sexually assaulted me violently in a very public place and in front of people.”
“This has had a lasting impact on my life even if I thought that I had successfully buried what happened.
“I recognise this now but I tried for so long to be strong and carry on- business as usual. However over the years hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump. I had a strong adverse reaction, especially to his voice.”
She was diagnosed with severe anxiety 20 years later, after the first published reports about Brand’s actions against women were published.
“It was the first time in 20 years that I had spoken to anyone about what had happened. I almost decided to withdraw from the case as I did not think I was strong enough emotionally to proceed with my allegation.” But she persisted with bringing a case to police, with the support of the detectives and officers who took her case seriously she said.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC has asked Judge Bennathan for a category one sentence – where prison terms begin at 12 years, but have a range of 10-15 years depending on aggravating or ameliorating factors.
But she noted too that if the court didn’t agree with that category, the next level down, a category two sentence would have a starting point of eight years, with a range of seven-nine years.
Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter KC, pushed for a much more lenient punishment, a sentencing between category two and three.
Another detail revealed during Brand’s lawyers argument earlier was that one of the character testimonies given to the court came from the woman at the centre of the ‘Sachsgate’ scandal.
Brand built a career, partly based on this image where he would brag about his sexual exploits and pursuits of women.
In 2008, he was the host of a BBC show where and Jonathan Ross left voicemails on Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs’ phone, saying that Brand had slept with Sachs’ grand-daughter Georgina Baillie.
Brand subsequently left the BBC after the disgraceful prank and Ross was suspended.
Now, it’s been revealed that Baillie was one of six people who gave character references in support of Brand. She said he had helped paid for her alcohol rehab programme.
Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter read out some of her statement:“I still choose to support him as a person I know him to be.”
I’m just going to run through some other details the prosecution highlighted as “aggravating” factors, when presenting the case to the judge that Brand should receive the most serious category one level of sentencing.
In the case of the rape – where Brand removed his condom and anally penetrated a then-21-year-old fan at his home and then dismissed her afterwards, calling her “dirty” in follow-up messages – the prosecutor argued Brand knew of the young woman’s idolisation of him and abused that position of trust.
His victim was worried for months afterwards that she may have contracted HIV from him.
Karmy-Jones KC noted how he had pursued conversations with the “vulnerable young woman,” offering her advice on the problems she was having with her boyfriend at the time.
When Brand learned that she and her boyfriend had separated, he told her he would look out for her, that he would hold her.
“The court will wish to consider whether this introduces an element of abuse, of trust and manipulation”, said Karmy-Jones.
