https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Former High Museum of Art executive sentenced to 12 months in prison for embezzlement
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Matthew Terrell
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Brady Lum, a former chief operating officer at Atlanta's High Museum of Art, was sentenced to 12 months in federal prison on Monday (2 November) for embezzling more than $600,000 from the institution. The sentencing comes as the High celebrates its centennial and its parent organisation, the Woodruff Arts Center, conducts a major corporate fundraising campaign.
Federal prosecutors said Lum diverted museum funds to pay for personal purchases, including guitars, music lessons and woodworking equipment. He concealed the expenditures through falsified invoices, reimbursement requests and accounting adjustments. The scheme began in September 2019, less than nine months after Lum joined the museum, and continued until its discovery in November 2025.
Lum paid full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High and voluntarily paid approximately $500,000 more to cover costs the museum incurred while uncovering and investigating his criminal activity.
During Monday's hearing, US District judge Michael L. Brown focused extensively on the deterrent purpose of sentencing. Although Brown said he did not believe Lum was likely to reoffend, he emphasised the court's responsibility to discourage similar financial crimes by others in positions of trust.
The judge acknowledged similarities between his own professional and socioeconomic background and Lum's, discussing how sentencing structures have historically been shaped by educated, professionally successful individuals whose circumstances resemble those of many white-collar defendants.
Brown also considered Lum's prompt restitution after the misconduct was discovered, distinguishing between voluntarily returning stolen funds before detection and repaying them after being caught. The latter, he indicated, carried less weight in assessing accountability.
Lum addressed the court and apologised for his conduct, expressing regret for disappointing his family and community. The gallery appeared to consist largely of relatives, friends and supporters of Lum.
Contacted for comment following Monday's sentencing, a spokesperson for the Woodruff provided the following statement: "We respect the court’s decision and remain focused on fulfilling our mission, responsibly managing our resources and connecting deeply with the audience we serve."
Both the Woodruff and the High declined to provide substantive information about financial safeguards introduced following Lum's misconduct, or whether they intend to publish a remediation plan addressing financial controls, governance reforms and oversight procedures.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Mummy in Glasgow may be repatriated to Egypt following removal from display
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A mummy removed from display last month at Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum could be returned to Egypt. According to the Scottish newspaper The Sunday Post, Egyptian authorities have asked for the mummified remains of the priest Nekht to be repatriated.
Glasgow Life, the charitable organisation which operates the museum, confirmed to The Art Newspaper that it had received a request to send remains of Nekht back to Egypt. The organisation has not confirmed the origin of the request.
Last month, officials at the museum removed the coffin and mummified corpse of the ancient Egyptian priest from public view. A spokesperson for Glasgow Life said: “Glasgow Life Museums’ draft Human Remains Policy proposes human remains should only be displayed where there is documented and informed consent from the deceased individual or, in appropriate circumstances, their descendants. In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals.”
The move comes after the International Council of Museums (Icom) revised its code of ethics in June, recommending the “inherent dignity” of human remains be upheld; Icom does not state however that all remains should be removed from display.
Meanwhile the Hunterian gallery in Glasgow confirmed to Museums Journal that it had covered an open sarcophagus containing the mummified remains of Lady Shep-En-Hor following an internal ethical review, although the sarcophagus itself remains on display.
The removal of the mummified remains at Kelvingrove and other museums feeds into current debate in the UK museums and heritage sector over the care and display of human remains. In response to the museum's policy on the lack of consent by the deceased, Stuart Robertson, the former director of the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society in Glasgow, wrote on LinkedIn that “applying modern, 21st-century bureaucratic consent standards retrospectively to ancient history is an absurd and impossible standard. It completely undermines the educational mission of public museums”.
Last year, officials at the Manchester Museum asked visitors if the mummified remains of an Egyptian woman should remain on display. The mummy, known as Asru, was subsequently taken off public view.
“Asru now lies in the museum’s stores within her outer coffin, which will remain closed, but this is not intended to be her permanent resting place. We are thinking about how we better care for ancestors, in line with the wishes of the dead and of living communities,” says the museum's website.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Why Mary Cassatt was more than just a painter of the 'modern Madonna'
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Annabel Keenan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
As the centennial of the death of Mary Cassatt (1844-1926) brings renewed attention to the US-born Impressionist, a new publication challenges the image of her as a sentimental painter of mothers and daughters. In Cassatt Reconsidered, Mary G. Morton uses her expertise as a curator and head of French paintings at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, to examine how the art world shaped Cassatt’s reputation, and posits a broader view of her within radical French Modernism.
The book coincides with major exhibitions on Cassatt, including at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris (until 31 January 2027), the Art Institute of Chicago (until 3 January 2027) and the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut (7 November-14 February 2027). Looking closely at the artist’s work and framing her within the experience of women in a modern Paris, Morton shows why Cassatt deserves another look.
The Art Newspaper: What prompted your reassessment?
Mary G. Morton: I thought I knew enough about Cassatt until a 2014 exhibition at the National Gallery on Cassatt’s artistic pas de deux with Degas emphasising their radical technical experimentation. A few years later, an encounter with the PhD candidate Nicole Georgopulos transformed Woman with Sunflower (1905) in my mind from a generic mother and child image to a complex realist allegory, a kind of feminist manifesto responding to and supporting the contemporary suffrage movement. The public recognises Cassatt’s name but associates her with images of maternity. There is so much more to her art, to her story.
How did the art market contribute to the narrowing of Cassatt’s reputation?
Her dealer essentially marketed her as a painter of motherhood, the painter of the “modern Madonna”, hiring critics to write about her in this vein. And while he had success selling her work, the strategy did not serve her well in art historiography. Another dynamic is the burgeoning field of American art history in the 20th century, when Cassatt became an asset to curators as an Impressionist. In most major US museums, her work hangs with US artists, depriving her of the aesthetic context in radical French Modernism. She looks loud, garish, awkward, whereas if you put her with Degas, Renoir and Morisot, she fits in.
What would you like museums, scholars and the public to see differently about Cassatt?
It would be great if Cassatt could exit the limited box she has been put into. Cassatt was the most successful avant-garde artist of the 19th century to represent the lived experience of women in modern urban Paris. She created a fresh visual vocabulary for women’s interests and concerns, refusing the oppressive social norms of her class and producing an extraordinary body of work. Cassatt brings us women’s side of the story.
The primary aim of this book is to provoke readers who might be familiar with Cassatt as a misty-eyed painter of mothers and children to look again. My hope is that the book compels people into museums to find Cassatt’s art and experience what I have: brilliantly expressive, innovative objects that relay a unique vision of humanity and of women’s lives as they were lived more than 100 years ago.
• Mary G. Morton, Cassatt Reconsidered, Getty Publications, 208pp, $35 (hb)

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: The story behind Grant Wood’s American Gothic and what made it go viral
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Grant Wood’s painting American Gothic (1930)—the realist depiction of an austere rural man and woman posed stiffly before a modest white house with a gothic-styled window—has seeped into the public consciousness on a par with Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa and Edvard Munch’s The Scream. “I never stopped watching the ways American Gothic has transitioned into the iconic ‘couple with the pitchfork’ over the past six decades,” says the US art historian Wanda Corn, whose new book The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon delves into the cultural history of the painting.
Over the decades, Corn says she accumulated an “immense archive of reimagined couples” and her publication “sheds critical light on the cultural forces that transformed an image with humble roots into a global icon whose reach and charisma extend far beyond the world of art”, according to the publisher, Princeton University Press.
Grant Wood today is seen as a far more complicated and tragic figure than he presented and for many years was understood to be Wanda Corn
Corn, professor emerita of art history at Stanford University, outlines in detail how Wood picked his sitters: his 30-year-old sister, Nan Wood Graham, and his 62-year-old dentist, Byron McKeeby. “The two men shared a sense of humour, often chuckling over their ‘bridge for a bridge’ exchange; the dentist had provided the artist with a dental bridge and Wood paid him with a painting of a Paris bridge,” Corn writes.
Crucially the image has been misconstrued over the decades, with viewers interpreting the couple as married when in reality the pair represented a father and his daughter, according to the artist’s sister. “In Wood’s mind, the two people in front of the house represented a father and his aging daughter—a spinster—living in small-town America,” writes Corn. Wood and his closed circle described it this way repeatedly, she adds.
“Yet when the painting went out into the world, not one person saw the couple as a parent and child, nor did they see them as from a small town … this is one of the best examples in the history of art of how an artist’s intentions in a work can differ from the public’s reception of a painting.”
The person who corrected Corn about this widespread misconception was Wood Graham herself. “I too thought it represented a married couple,” Corn says. She explains that when she was photographed as the pitchfork couple with her husband in the 1970s, for a feminist work called Joe and Wanda Corn, Holiday Card (1975) by Keith M. Jones Sr, she was “under the assumption that [Wood’s sitters] were a married couple. But when I went to see [Wood Graham], I talked about them as a couple and she said in no uncertain terms: ‘They’re not a couple. It’s a father and daughter.’”
The image, and Wood’s achievements as an Iowa-based artist, were consistently lambasted and dismissed though. Early art historical texts initially ignored him, such as A History of Art (1962) by H.W. Janson, which only included the work in its seventh edition published in 2006. Corn’s survey of such texts establishes, she says, “how passive-aggressive the coverage of American Gothic was in this literature”.
The critical reaction to a Wood show Corn curated in 1983 was also brutal. “A writer of a Wall Street Journal article in May 1983 … labelled it the ‘Great Grant Wood Redemption Campaign’ and quoted the reaction of a well-known art dealer in town: ‘Flush it down the drain. It’s just cornball, provincial, nationalistic propaganda and it has nothing to do with art!’”
Corn’s 1983 exhibition of Wood’s work, Grant Wood: The Regionalist Vision, which launched at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, toured to other venues such as the Minneapolis Institute of Art (Yale University Press published an accompanying book). “The last landing of the exhibition was in San Francisco [at the de Young museum], and what better place to launch the first gay Gothic [work] on the walls of a major museum than in San Francisco,” she says, referring to the 1983 front cover of the gay magazine Frontiers that was included in the show.
Sexuality under scrutiny
The author unpicks the thorny issue of Wood’s sexuality, which has come under the microscope in recent years. “The upshot is that Wood today is seen as a far more complicated and tragic figure than he presented and for many years was understood to be,” she writes, acknowledging that two art historians, Tripp Evans and Sue Taylor, have contributed the most to recent psychosexual interpretations of Wood’s life and “the uncovering of his homosexuality”.
“I can see his struggles constantly,” Corn says. “But on the other hand, I also know people who found him just boundless fun to be with, lovable and endlessly creative, not dark and gloomy … we have to get a more balanced view [of him].”
How American Gothic came to be assimilated into the art history canon, across high and low popular culture is also explored through a wide variety of images including Obama Gothic (2012) by Mario Piperni, which shows Michelle and Barack Obama in front of the White House as the pitchfork couple, and Barry Kite’s photocollage Gothic Wave (2010) that draws on Hokusai’s famous 19th-century woodblock print.
“I actually could not have written the book I wrote now back then [in 1983] because I didn’t have the raw data,” Corn says. “I didn’t have this notion of the episodic uses of [the image] for everyday transient events and political events. I didn’t have any sense of what the computer was going to do to the image: the way it was going to translate it but also just make it a resource anybody could tap into.”
• Wanda Corn, The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon, Princeton University Press, 312pp, $49.95/£42 (hb)

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Women behind the lens: ‘I learned early what I was meant to become: a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home’
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Remofiloe Nomandla Mayisela
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
MilkMaid is part of my photographic series Lipservice, which stars Mrs Martha May, a contemporary makoti (a colloquial South African term for a wife). Mrs May is always dolled up, poised, ready to serve. Here she stands before a wall of long-life milk, face painted in the patches of a dairy cow, a crate balanced on her head. Rubber gloves, a frilled apron over shweshwe (coloured fabric). Milkmaid and milk, server and served, in one body.
The idea grows from the old line: the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach. In Lipservice the kitchen is a stage with food the script women are handed. Milk felt like the most intimate ingredient, the first thing a woman gives and the easiest to package and sell back. The carton reads like a job description: long life, full cream, UHT process. Made to last on a shelf. Stacked in repetition, the cartons speak to how women are consumed: branded, endlessly replaceable.
I was raised in a strong matriarchal household. I learned early what a woman is meant to become: a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home. My work began there, with coming of age and the quiet curriculum of the perfect woman. Who wrote it?
Mrs May is less an alter ego than an extension of that role I was raised to rehearse, played out loud.
I direct, style and do my own makeup, gather the props, set the self-timer and step into frame. Kitsch and pop colour keep it playful, so humour invites people close before they notice what they are looking at. The pinks are sweet. The idea underneath is not.
The term Makoti is popularly traced to the Afrikaans maak ons tee – “make us tea” – naming the wife as the one who serves.
Self-portraiture is how I tell this story honestly. The work speaks to many women, but I can only testify from my own body. It is auto-ethnography in a costume. She watches you watch her, and the gaze turns back to ask who the performance is really for.
Lipservice was the entry point. My practice is an ongoing investigation into the performance of womanhood, and the makoti is the role on a pedestal, held up as the ultimate goal, or so they say. That inquiry continues through my current research and a new body of work, Aftertaste.
MilkMaid laughs, but it also asks you to taste what you are being served. A bite of truth.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: ‘We’re in Charge’: What the Blue Wave Means for New York City
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
At an Election Day eve party at a bowling alley in Williamsburg on Monday night, Gov. Kathy Hochul laid out her dream scenario for the midterms.
The event, headlined by the statewide Democratic ticket, predicted a blue wave of voter unrest that would catapult two New Yorkers to the top of the House and the Senate and provide a check on the second administration of President Donald Trump.
“I cannot wait when I call up Hakeem Jeffries and say, ‘Mr. Speaker, I kind of need a few more billions of dollars for New York,’” Hochul said. “Then I call Chuck Schumer: ‘Mr. Majority Leader, I need a few more billions of dollars for New York State.’”
“Get used to it, America,” added Hochul. “Because we’re in charge.”
Hochul got her wish. Democrats captured Congress in a seismic realignment of the electoral map, gaining at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House seats, including a crucial pickup in the New York suburbs, with critical funding for the five boroughs on the line.
Now, there is renewed hope that federal dollars will flow for infrastructure projects like the $16 billion Gateway Program, the Penn Station overhaul and the Second Avenue Subway, and that Republican cuts to health care and food stamps might be softened.
Meanwhile, a new crop of state legislators on the left flank of the party — the Democratic Socialists of America doubled its representation in Albany — is eager to hold the governor’s feet to the fire on signature issues like taxing the rich, expanding childcare and raising the minimum wage.
Grace Mauser, the DSA’s local co-chair, said its contingent in the Legislature and its base will push the governor harder for a progressive income tax and higher taxes on the ultra-wealthy. Hochul thanked Mamdani Tuesday night for his support — and now the democratic socialists want to see her deliver.
MORE: How Every Neighborhood in New York City Voted for Governor
“I’m hopeful that Hochul has seen the energy, the excitement that can come from the masses of people who want and deserve a better government, and she takes those lessons and brings them to Albany, and is braver than she has been in past years in terms of standing up for working class New Yorkers,” Mauser said.
Other leaders of the Democratic party’s left echoed DSA’s demands.
“As soon as we’re done here we’re going right back into the state budget fight,” Jasmine Gripper, the co-executive director of the Working Families Party, told The City Reporter. “We will only accept a budget that is equitable and taxes the ultra-rich so that working families can thrive and children have what they need.”
As voters delivered strong results for Democrats in New York and elsewhere, politicos gathered at the Midtown Hilton for Hochul’s election night party were positively giddy at the prospect of two of their own leading both chambers of Congress.
“Before this night is over, we are going to say the words out loud ‘Speaker Jeffries takes the gavel,’” Sen. Kristen Gillibrand said Tuesday.
The previous night, at the Democratic unity event, Jeffries vowed to use his perch as Speaker to tackle Americans’ high cost of living and hold members of Trump’s cabinet accountable, name-checking Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and vowing to “stop this reckless and costly war of choice over in Iran.”
“Here in New York, and all across the country, we’re gonna run these MAGA extremists out of town,” he said.
House Democrats are musing over how they will use their majority to grill key members of the Trump administration under oath and slash Immigration Customs and Enforcement funding.
MORE: Mamdani Ballot Proposals on Public Space, Street Safety and More Pass in NYC
“Everything” is on the table, U.S. Rep. Grace Meng of Queens told The City Reporter. “We have to act fast. This is a mandate, not just a promotion or a change in title, but people want to see Democrats move fast and to hold the administration accountable.”
U.S. Rep.-elect Micah Lasher of Manhattan said that he talks to his predecessor Jerrold Nadler, the top Democrat on the powerful judiciary committee, “every day” about how to use the levers of Congress to reverse the worst of the Trump administration’s impacts on New Yorkers.
“We’re going to have robust oversight powers, and we need to use them, to shine a white hot light on the grift and the graft of this administration.”
For Hochul, Tuesday night was an opportunity to vindicate herself after she was partly blamed for Democrats’ poor showing in the 2022 midterms — the first time she ran at the top of the Democratic ticket — a year that cost state Democrats five House seats and the party its slim House majority.
Hochul spent the last few weeks of the race criss-crossing the state and in New York City touting her record, palling around with left-wing standard-bearers Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and boosting Hudson Valley House candidate Cait Conley.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/m.title: Mamdani Continues Crackdown On Illegal E-Motos With Brick-And-Mortar Sweep
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/m.text:
Illegal e-motos are common on city streets. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Dozens of businesses were hit with more than 130 violations for selling illegal e-bikes and scooters in a two-month enforcement blitz to protect consumers against fire-prone and overpowered micromobility devices.
Inspectors for the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection visited 229 retail shops across the five boroughs between Aug. 1 and Sept. 20 and found 136 individual violations that resulted in more than 75 summonses, each carrying a $1,000 fine. Three stores were shuttered.
“New Yorkers deserve to feel safe knowing that the devices they see in their communities meet the City’s safety requirements,” said DCWP Commissioner Sam Levine, whose agency ensures that stores sell only UL-certified e-bikes and batteries, display e-bike fire safety materials in their storefronts, and don’t sell illegal e-motos and scooters that have too much power and speed capability. “Our citywide sweep sends a clear message that businesses cannot put New Yorkers at risk just to make a profit.”
In addition to the three closures, Levine’s agency worked with another five shops to bring them into compliance with the law, the agency said. Stores remain closed until all outstanding fines are paid to DCWP, the department said.
Since e-bikes and scooters started growing in popularity during the pandemic there has been misplaced ire from politicians. Confusion over which devices are legal on city streets and bike lanes led to a fervent backlash to all electric bikes.
E-scooters are illegal in New York City if they exceed 20 miles per hour or weigh more than 100 pounds. E-bikes are legal if their motors don’t exceed 750 watts and their top speed is 25 mph.
The law defines a “motorized scooter” as a two-wheeled powered device that can’t be registered with the Department of Motor Vehicles, like, say a legal moped, and also doesn’t fit the city’s street-legal definitions of an e-bike or stand-up scooter. DCWP can give summonses to businesses selling these out-of-class devices, known as e-motos.
These devices, which far exceed the city’s limits for power and speed, are often sold online and in stores as legal devices.
But the tides are shifting. Two high–profile deaths involving New Yorkers riding non-street-legal e-motos and scooters sparked long-overdue action from city and state politicians.
In August, the city Law Department sent cease-and-desist letters to 42 online retailers selling the so-called e-motos, which are illegal to ride on city streets and bike lanes.
The cease-and-desists brought large retailers like Amazon, Temu, and Walmart into compliance. Such companies now block orders by geography so consumers can’t ship these devices to their New York City homes. But many small direct to consumer brands are still shipping flagrantly illegal e-motos and scooters and marketing them for city use. Aniioki, a brand that Streetsblog sees out on the streets daily, sells bikes online that can hit over 50 miles per hour.
DCWP said it also issued more than 85 cease-and-desist orders and 41 summonses to online sellers for battery safety violations.
And in July, Attorney General Letitia James issued a consumer alert to warn perspective buyers of the shady market. So far her office has received three relevant complaints.
State lawmakers are also pushing legislation to officially bar the sale of e-motos online and in stores, closing a loophole that has allowed retailers to sell devices that are illegal to ride on roadways but are legal to own for private use.
State Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D-Long Island City) introduced the bill to establish a clear definition for these overpowered vehicles, and explicitly prohibit companies from not only selling them, but from falsely advertising them as legal, a common practice that results in unsuspecting consumers purchasing devices they can’t legally use.
The driver, Timothy McVey, 41, of Staten Island, turned himself in at the 62nd Precinct station house and was booked for failure to yield and failure to exercise due care

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.title: Sunset Park Blaze Kills 6 As Lithium-ion Battery Fire Crisis Rages On
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.text:
The fire left lives and homes ruined. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Six Brooklynites were killed in an early morning fire that engulfed an entire wooden row house — and authorities are investigating whether the blaze is linked to this year’s 68 percent rise in fires sparked or intensified by highly flammable lithium-ion batteries.
It took smoke-eaters three hours on Thursday to extinguish the 1:40 a.m. fire, which sent flames shooting out of every window. When the smoke cleared, four people were dead on the scene and two died later in the hospital. Four others remain hospitalized, officials said at a press briefing.
Fire marshals are still investigating, but early reports linked the fire to a lithium-ion battery, though it is unclear if the battery sparked the blaze or was simply consumed by it. Two burnt-out electric bike frames were spotted outside the building on Thursday.
The Sunset Park incident comes weeks after a family of four was wiped out in the Bronx when an e-bike caught fire in their apartment.
The story behind the story
After a peak in deaths associated with the batteries in 2023, officials were quick to pass legislation banning the sale of uncertified lithium-ion batteries and e-bikes, but they are still easy to obtain online on sites like Facebook Marketplace. In addition, after-market modifications make batteries unstable.
Many batteries bought during the pandemic — when the delivery industry fueled by e-bikes boomed — are nearing the end of their useable life. The decay of lithium-ion batteries is one reason why there have been fewer deaths this year from fires, even as there have been more blazes, because more fires are occurring outside of homes when batteries are discarded.
So far this year there have been 406 fires determined by FDNY to be caused by the batteries compared to 241 last year. But, the largest increase is in non-structural fires, up to 252 from 100, meaning blazes that occur outside of a home or business. Through mid-October, as Streetsblog reported exclusively, there were 87 lithium-ion fires in garbage trucks, up from 55 in all of last year, according to the Department of Sanitation.
“There’s no comprehensive plan to deal with the battery life cycles,” Baruch Herzfeld, who co-founded the battery charging company Popwheels, told Streetsblog last month. “There’s a fictitious belief that battery fires don’t happen unless batteries are charging. People are basing their safety guidelines on something that’s not true.”
The city’s efforts to promote outdoor battery storage and charging have largely fallen flat. After a successful pilot in 2024, the city has yet to install any public charging infrastructure and companies who provide battery subscription services are hindered by a web of ever-changing safety regulations that make it nearly impossible to grow. As of last month, the city hadn’t approved any permits that would allow landlords or business owners to set up charging cabinets on the sidewalk. The application will now be streamlined since New Yorkers overwhelmingly passed the mayor’s charter revision ballot proposals on Tuesday.
Sunset Park is filled with e-bikes — on the street, inside restaurants, within the gates of the many row houses, inside apartments. Elected officials want to see outdoor charging options.
“We have had multiple trainings from FDNY that ask people, do not store your battery inside, and also do not charge when you are sleeping. So that has been an ongoing issue,” said Council Member Susan Zhuang (D-Sunset Park) at the scene on Thursday. “I am going to look and see if we can set up some stations so people can just charge outdoors, that will be helpful to the community. It’s not just the delivery people that use the bikes, it’s everyone.”
A neighbor who has lived on the block for 42 years told Streetsblog she lives in fear of battery fires.
“I am angry as hell right now. We need control of these lithium batteries coming from China,” said Rukmin DeGaray. “They are no good for neighborhoods; they shouldn’t be allowed in any building that people live in. They just blow up and these old wooden buildings, they go up like lightning.”
The driver, Timothy McVey, 41, of Staten Island, turned himself in at the 62nd Precinct station house and was booked for failure to yield and failure to exercise due care

https://gothamist.com/news/feds-accuse-f.title: Feds accuse former FBI agent of Brooklyn hit and run, leaving victim on a bench
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-accuse-f.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-accuse-f.text:
A former FBI special agent hit a man in a Brooklyn crosswalk with his government car February, then dragged him unconscious onto a bench and left him there without calling for help, federal prosecutors alleged in an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Andrew Reyes, 30, of Brooklyn, was arrested Thursday morning and charged with violating the man’s civil rights as an FBI agent by moving him and driving off without getting him help. He also faces charges with lying to investigators about the crash, prosecutors said.
The crash happened around 6:20 a.m. on Feb. 3 at Ocean Parkway and Beverley Road in Kensington, according to the indictment. Prosecutors said Reyes was driving his FBI-issued Chevrolet Impala north in the southbound lane of Ocean Parkway, emergency lights on, when he went through a red light at Beverley Road.
The charges come nine months after the crash, and the court papers don’t say why Reyes’ emergency lights were on, how the victim is doing now or how investigators tied the crash to Reyes. Prosecutors have not identified the man, whom they described in a release as “severely injured.”
Reyes got out of his car after striking the man, dragged him from the street across the sidewalk and onto a bench, then went back for the man’s bag and set it next to him, according to the indictment. He then drove off with his emergency lights still on, prosecutors said. He did not call for medical help or report the crash to the FBI, according to the indictment.
On May 1, agents from the Justice Department’s Office of the Inspector General asked Reyes whether he had ever hit someone with his FBI car and not reported it, according to the indictment. He said he had not, prosecutors alleged.
“The defendant’s alleged conduct demonstrated a shocking disregard for human life and his sworn oath to uphold the law,” Joseph Nocella Jr., the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said in a statement.
Reyes had been an FBI agent since about 2023 and was assigned to the bureau’s New York Field Office, according to court records. Prosecutors described him as a former agent but did not say when he left the FBI.
He was scheduled to be arraigned Thursday afternoon before a federal magistrate judge. His attorney declined to comment.
If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison, prosecutors said.

https://gothamist.com/news/battery-found.title: Battery found at deadly Sunset Park fire days after similar blaze in Bronx
https://gothamist.com/news/battery-found.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/battery-found.text:
The discovery of a lithium-ion battery at the scene a house fire in Sunset Park that killed six people Thursday comes as city officials struggle to regulate the booming e-bike and e-scooter industry.
Last week, an e-bike fire at the Patterson Houses in Mott Haven killed four people, including an 11-year-old boy.
Delivery services became hugely popular in the pandemic, leading New Yorkers to buy e-bikes and e-scooters for app-based services. But the FDNY has said many of the batteries on the market do not meet safety standards and are prone to catch fire while charging.
The city has dedicated significant resources to addressing the problem, but lithium-ion fires, injuries and deaths so far this year are already much higher than last year at this time.
“ These fires are primarily due to low-cost, cheaply, poorly made, lithium-ion battery packs coming from various sources that are coming in without complying with suitable regulations,” Mike Fritz, a consultant for e-bike technology, said.
He added that the risk is substantially lower for a battery with proper safety requirements.
As firefighters continued working the scene of the fire in Sunset Park, Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protections released the details of a citywide crackdown on businesses selling illegal electronic micromobility devices.
Between August and September of this year, the agency reported it inspected more than 200 shops across the city and issued more than 130 violations for failing to meet safety requirements.
Violations included selling battery-powered devices without proper safety certification standards or failure to display safety information.
“Investigators are working to determine the cause of the fire,” City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in a statement. “The presence of lithium-ion batteries at the scene is a serious concern, and more must be done to encourage and mandate safe storage practices. Enough is enough.”
If a battery is confirmed as the cause of Thursday’s fire, 10 people will have died in battery fires in just eight days. The FDNY said it investigated 292 lithium-ion battery fires in 2025, causing 51 injuries and one death. That number was down from 6 deaths in 2024, and 18 in 2023, according to the FDNY.
The department had pointed to last year’s low death toll as a sign that a combination of enforcement and a public awareness campaign about the dangers of low-quality batteries and proper storage was working.
But this year is trending back in a deadly direction with the death toll through October already surpassing all of 2025, according to FDNY stats. There have been 406 fires caused by lithium-ion batteries this year, the FDNY said, resulting in 70 injuries and 9 deaths. Through roughly the same period last year, the city had 241 fires, with 42 injuries and 1 death.
At the scene outside the home in Sunset Park, FDNY firefighters removed a charred e-scooter found inside the home.
State Senator Steve Chan — who represents the neighborhood — said he spoke to neighbors who said many people in the neighborhood use e-bikes. He said many parents use e-bikes to take their kids to school.
“They seem to think that there’s some e-bikes in the location,” Chan said. “Of course, there’s lithium batteries present in every one of these homes over here, there’s a tremendous hazard.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

https://hyperallergic.com/jordan-poorman.title: Jordan Poorman Cocker’s Vision of Global Indigeneity
https://hyperallergic.com/jordan-poorman.author: Petala Ironcloud
https://hyperallergic.com/jordan-poorman.text:
Jordan Poorman Cocker’s Vision of Global Indigeneity
The curator, who just organized a major rehang of Indigenous art at Crystal Bridges, reflects on the ways institutions can create space for Native artists to flourish.
BENTONVILLE, Ark. — On October 16 and 17, before a room full of Indigenous artists, curators, and scholars at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art’s symposium on contemporary Native art, Jordan Poorman Cocker opened with a land acknowledgment. Founded by Walmart heiress Alice Walton, the museum sits on the ancestral homelands of the Osage Nation, Quapaw Nation, and Caddo Nation, who were forcibly relocated in the 19th century. Poorman Cocker, a Kiowa and Tongan citizen, was hired as the museum’s Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) officer and first full-time curator of Indigenous art in 2023. She makes the hour-and-a-half drive in from Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the Cherokee Nation’s capital and home to several nations coerced there during the removal era.
The two-day gathering coincided with the reinstallation of contemporary Native art in the museum, which Poorman Cocker spearheaded alongside Ashley Holland (Cherokee Nation) as a way to showcase the diversity of style, medium, and living Native artists across Indian Country, including works by citizens of the ancestral Tribes in Arkansas. Choctaw and Cherokee multi-disciplinary artist Jeffrey Gibson delivered a keynote address, and later spoke to an audience with Poorman Cocker while beading; Diné weaver Melissa Cody traced the lineage of her work in dialogue with her mother Lola Cody; and Lehuauakea delivered a workshop based in her traditional kapa practice.
Poorman Cocker’s own curatorial practice draws on her background in museum studies at Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand and the global spirit of Indigeneity, which rejects the divisive borders of colonial nation-states. Like many Native curators, she cites the groundbreaking 2019 exhibition Hearts of Our People: Native Women Artists at the Minneapolis Institute of Art as a major source of inspiration. That sentiment was echoed by Kiowa beadwork artist Terri Greeves, who spoke at the symposium alongside other Kiowa Tribe members and matriarchs. Poorman Cocker is also a beadwork and textile artist herself, rooted in Kiowa and Tongan beadwork and textile conventions.
In an email correspondence with Hyperallergic, Poorman Cocker shared more about a recent landmark commission, telling a fuller history of Native art, and what it means to bring Kiowa voices into the museum. The interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.
Hyperallergic: Tell me more about what the reinstallation at Crystal Bridges represents for Indigenous art in this moment. What is it trying to change? How did the 114,000-square-foot expansion inform the museum’s capacity to provide ongoing opportunities to collaborate with the featured artists?
JPC: The impetus is to recenter two primary areas: the Indigenous art collection and the craft collection. Native American and Indigenous art are foundational to every American art collection. Over the years, I have written acquisition proposals for artworks sourced from the gallery system and annual markets, with an emphasis on artist commissions. Crystal Bridges is better positioned to nourish the art ecosystem, including many artists — particularly those whose work aligns with intergenerational art forms, who need financial support for artist apprenticeships, community classes, and other art education efforts that sustain artist communities and knowledge systems.
Indigenous and Native art makes up about 3% of Crystal Bridges’s permanent collection. The museum sector writ large has a long way to go to better present Indigenous artists and stories.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Washington Spirit avert scheduling crisis, keep NWSL semi-final at Audi Field; Gotham venue TBD
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Ella Brockway and Pablo Iglesias Maurer
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The Washington Spirit will play their NWSL semi-final at Audi Field after the club reached a deal to avoid playing a playoff game at Northwest Stadium, home of the NFL’s Washington Commanders.
The club announced late Sunday night that they will play their semi-final against the Utah Royals on 14 November (Saturday) at noon.
Audi Field has been the NWSL team’s full-time home since 2023, and it has hosted raucous crowds for the team’s playoff runs, including Sunday’s 4-1 win over the Portland Thorns to advance to the semi-final.
A Division III college football game between the Coast Guard Academy and the Merchant Marine Academy was previously scheduled for that same afternoon at Audi Field. ESPN reported earlier this week that the NWSL had been preparing scenarios that would see the Spirit play their playoff game on Saturday at Northwest Stadium, a 64,000-seat venue in Landover, Maryland, roughly 10 miles north-east of downtown Washington where the team have never played a game in their 13-year existence, in the event that both the Spirit and top-seeded Gotham advanced in this weekend’s quarter-finals.
The Spirit, as is the case with many teams across the NWSL with their respective stadiums, are not the primary tenants at Audi Field. The stadium is owned and operated by MLS team DC United. The Spirit would not confirm if the college football game has been moved to a different location or date.
The league also announced that Gotham’s semi-final against the Kansas City Current will take place at 3pm on 15 November (Sunday), but it did not announce a location. The Shield winners usually play at Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, New Jersey, and with the Spirit’s home semi-final set for Saturday, they are cleared to play in the Sunday late-afternoon broadcast window.
The issue now, though, is the conditions of the field at Sports Illustrated Stadium. It has taken much wear-and-tear after hosting soccer and rugby matches in recent weeks, and would host the semi-final just one day after MLS’s New York Red Bulls, the stadium’s owners, play a friendly against Liga MX side Club América.
During Gotham’s 1-0 win over Seattle in their quarter-final on Sunday afternoon, the venue’s field was patchy and sandy, with many visible brown spots. Reign captain Jess Fishlock described the field as “atrocious”. Gotham coach Juan Carlos Amoros apologized for the conditions and said the club – which is a tenant at and not an owner of the stadium – attempted to mitigate the circumstances without success.
“Let’s be real, there’s no way a playoff game should be played on that shit,” Reign head coach Laura Harvey told ESPN. “I just can’t believe they’ve allowed it. They knew it last week.”
The league reportedly fined Gotham $10,000 for the poor conditions in their regular-season finale game on 4 November.
Gotham’s semi-final could be played at Icahn Stadium, a 5,000-seat stadium on Randall’s Island in New York City where the club has played several games in recent years. Icahn Stadium mostly hosts track events and is not well-trafficked but has a natural grass pitch funded by MLS club NYCFC in 2024.
“While some circumstances are outside our control, we’ve proactively evaluated multiple scenarios and their tradeoffs to prepare for every potential matchup, with the goal of minimizing disruption to players, clubs and fans while protecting competitive integrity,” the league said in a statement before the quarter-finals. “These challenges also reinforce why stadium infrastructure and meaningful control or influence over venue availability have been central to our growth strategy for years.”

https://taz.de/DFB-Slogan-vor-Nations-Le.title: DFB-Slogan vor Nations-League-Spielen: „Verdammt noch mal für Deutschland“
https://taz.de/DFB-Slogan-vor-Nations-Le.author: Frank Hellmann
https://taz.de/DFB-Slogan-vor-Nations-Le.text:
DFB-Slogan vor Nations-League-Spielen: „Verdammt noch mal für Deutschland“
Vor den Länderspielen gegen Serbien und die Niederlande will Bundestrainer Klopp den Teamgeist auch mit etwas mehr Patriotismus bestärken.
Es liegt in der Natur eines Jürgen Klopp, mit wortgewaltigen Vorträgen zu überzeugen. Doch nicht jeder Nationalspieler ist für ellenlange Monologe empfänglich, insofern ist das neuerdings öffentliche Motto des Bundestrainers eher prägnant gehalten. „Für dich. Für uns. Für Deutschland.“ Ein Plakat mit diesem Leitspruch hängt neuerdings nicht nur in der Kabine, sondern auch beim Eintreffen der Nationalspieler am Montag in Herzogenaurach im Innenhof des Home Ground.
Vor dem Doppelpack in der Nations League gegen Serbien in Belgrad (Freitag 20.45 Uhr/RTL) und gegen die Niederlande in Berlin (Montag 20.45 Uhr/ARD) hat der Deutsche Fußball-Bund (DFB) den Slogan publik gemacht, der bereits bei der ersten XXL-Maßnahme benutzt wurde.
Klopp will damit eine in der Vergangenheit wiederholt unliebsame Debatte einfangen. „Nationalhymne singen, bedeutet mir viel. Ich erwarte aber nicht, dass es jedem was bedeutet“, sagte der 59-Jährige. „Also habe ich überlegt, wie kriegen wir das hin.“ Für ihn ist der Leitspruch schlüssig, weil er außen vor ist: „Weil Nationalmannschaft nicht für mich ist. Nationalmannschaft ist für dich, ist für uns alle und es ist verdammt nochmal für Deutschland!“ Der gerne in Bilder denkende Klopp-Berater Marc Kosicke wird gewiss seinen Anteil an den Überlegungen haben.
Jede Gruppe, sagte Klopp in einem weiteren vom Verband veröffentlichten Video, ob Fußballmannschaft, Firma oder Familie, müsse „auf eine bestimmte Art geführt werden“. Mittels „klarer Regeln, gesundem Menschenverstand beim Anwenden dieser Regeln, Empathie und im Idealfall Liebe“. Er möchte damit die jüngere Generation gewinnen, vor allem jene Talente, die wie der erstmals berufene Wael Mohya auch für eine andere Nation antreten könnten.
Der 17-Jährige absolviert auf dem Adidas-Gelände im Frankenland nur einen Schnupperkurs, die Verantwortung tragen die erfahrenen Nationalspieler. Das Gerüst bilden Marc-André ter Stegen im Tor, Jonathan Tah und Nico Schlotterbeck in der Abwehr, Joshua Kimmich in der Mittelfeldzentrale, Florian Wirtz als Taktgeber, Kai Havertz als Mittelstürmer. Kann diese Zusammensetzung an die alten Erfolge anknüpfen, die auch Klopp so herbeisehnt?
Anstehendes Kontrastprogramm
Beim Jubiläumstreffen auf dem DFB-Campus der Europameister von 1996 sprach der Bundestrainer von Kindern, die „waren 2015 geboren und haben noch nie eine deutsche Nationalmannschaft einen Pokal in der Hand halten sehen“. Das wolle er gerne wieder ändern. Nächste Möglichkeit wäre die EM 2028 in Großbritannien, für die sich der dreimalige Europameister aber erst einmal qualifizieren muss. Der Weg wäre einfacher, wenn die DFB-Elf noch das Viertelfinale der Nations League erreicht, wobei das Unterfangen bei erst fünf Punkten aus den ersten vier Spielen knifflig ist.
Klopps Team steht zum Abschluss ein Kontrastprogramm bevor: erst ein trostloses Geisterspiel im Stadion Rajko Mitić in Belgrad, weil die Gastgeber wegen rassistischer und diskriminierender Vorfälle bei den Nation-League-Partien gegen Griechenland (1:2) und die Niederlande (1:2) sanktioniert worden sind. Danach ein stimmungsvoller Härtetest gegen die Niederlande im Berliner Olympiastadion, das bis auf wenige Restkarten ausverkauft ist. Am liebsten würde er sich ein „Endspiel“ gegen den früheren Erzrivalen wünschen, erklärte Klopp, um den Entwicklungsprozess im März 2027 mit weiteren K.-o.-Spielen zu beschleunigen. Er habe auf den Klassiker gegen Holland schon heute eine „Riesenlust“.
Zuerst aber steht die Pflichtaufgabe gegen Serbien an. Er wisse genau, was auf einen zukomme, witzelte Klopp im Nominierungsvideo. „Entschuldigung Mainz 05, aber als ich gespielt habe, waren noch keine Zuschauer da. Das hatte sich auch angefühlt, als wären wir allein.“ Eine Anspielung auf die grauen Zweitligazeiten der Nullfünfer im alten Bruchwegstadion. Woraufhin ihn Mainzer Anhänger in den sozialen Medien daran erinnerten, dass es so schlimm doch auch nicht gewesen sei: Bis Mitte der 90er Jahren pendelte der Schnitt bei 3.000 bis 5.000 Besuchern, die laut Klopp einen Fußball sahen, „den ich mir auch nicht angeschaut hätte“.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Parents and teachers decry Google pledge to yank Search if schools block AI: ‘This threat is nothing but extortion’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google’s announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search.
Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google’s AI tools will also lose access to its search engine.
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” said Chris Phillips, vice-president for education at Google. “After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”
Parents and teachers across the country raised concerns to the Guardian about AI’s potential to weaken students’ critical-thinking skills and the growing influence of big tech in education.
Some called on schools to consider alternative search engines, while others argued that students should be taught how to use AI responsibly rather than prevented from accessing it altogether.
Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, lambasted Google’s approach, saying: “When the software is free, you are the product, and it is inappropriate for Google to test or develop AI with minors. This should not be allowed at all.”
A 44-year-old father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said he worries that “AI will weaken people’s ability to think critically. I use AI in my work, but it would not be effective if I did not have well over a decade of experience under my belt. Even the best models are often flat-out wrong in their responses.”
“These tools are not something that should be introduced to children at such a young age. I’m hopeful that a Democratic Congress will force the adoption of legislation that will protect our schools from corporate malfeasance such as this. This threat from Google is nothing but extortion and it should be treated as such,” he added.
Similarly, Eyla Whitemoon, a mother and educator based in Kernville, California, said: “By infiltrating or ‘partnering’ with our institutions, Google and Meta et al, created a false dependency and our starved public education system happily merged with their ilk. And just like any good mob boss, drug dealer or capitalist minion, these companies got society hooked on their products and now are raising the cost of their supply … My heart aches for what our children won’t experience in a future where AI is in charge and the mega technoautocrats sit in their bunkers and hide.”
Meanwhile, a 64-year-old educator based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, said: “Thankfully, after having to revamp all teaching in response to AI, Gen Z has begun appreciating what they stand to lose on account of surrendering their cognitive skills to AI. There are alternative search engines to Google and those will now be what we turn to. Teachers and students alike detest the tech industry’s demand that we kiss their feet and give ourselves up to be their peons.”
Others questioned why schools should depend on Google at all.
An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland, said: “Google decided to follow the evil path to riches. When they started, they were great. Today they are simply evil money grubbers … Schools should tell Google to go pound sand and simply have kids use DuckDuckGo or one of the other search engines … There is nothing Google offers that is not available from some other source.”
Rachel Dominguez, a 42-year-old parent in Minneapolis, Minnesota, also suggested that schools turn to academic databases instead of relying on Google Search.
“Seeing as how Google Search has turned into an AI slop-first service, maybe it’s better that the kids learn how to use databases such as Academic Search Premier, JSTOR, and arXiv. Most school districts have subscriptions to these services, and students learning to use them would be better prepared for college. A trip to the media center is not some abnormal chore … That is, if the librarian still has a job in the first place,” she said.
Not everyone believes blocking AI is the answer. Some argued that schools should focus on teaching students how to use the technology responsibly.
A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said: “I do not blame Google. AI is not going away. I’ve been very frustrated this year trying to teach AI literacy with AI blocked. Schools need to teach how to properly use AI, not block it.”
A California resident echoed that view, arguing that schools could use Google’s AI tools to teach students to question the information they receive.
“Google Search has existed since the 90s and it’s crazy of them to completely remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That being said, I would like to see schools actually permit the use of Gemini and use it as an opportunity to show students how its sources aren’t always valid and you can’t trust everything an AI tells you,” they said.

https://taz.de/Was-Nvidia-so-wichtig-mac.title: Was Nvidia so wichtig macht: Die Hardware hinter KI
https://taz.de/Was-Nvidia-so-wichtig-mac.author: Svenja Bergt
https://taz.de/Was-Nvidia-so-wichtig-mac.text:
Was Nvidia so wichtig macht: Die Hardware hinter KI
KI-Chatbots wären in ihrer heutigen Form nicht denkbar ohne die Chips von Nvidia. Auch Deutschland will dem US-Konzern nahe sein.
Erst kürzlich hat Deutschland ein bisschen was abbekommen, vom großen Nvidia-Hype. Das Unternehmen hielt seine Hausmesse GTC, die sonst meist im kalifornischen San José stattfindet, in Berlin ab. Jensen Huang, Mitgründer und Unternehmenschef sprach und Fans jubelten ihm zu wie einem Popstar. Beim Investorengipfel der Bundesregierung gab es dann auch etwas Glamour für die Politik: Wirtschafts- und Forschungsministerium unterzeichneten eine Absichtserklärung mit Nvidia zur Kooperation in Sachen künstliche Intelligenz.
Nvidia, 1993 gegründet, ist der global wichtigste Hersteller von KI-Hochleistungschips und einer der am höchsten bewerteten börsennotierten Konzerne. Der aktuelle Börsenwert liegt bei rund 5 Billionen US-Dollar. Obwohl Nvidia schon 1999 an die Börse gegangen ist, lief es in der öffentlichen Wahrnehmung lange etwas unter dem Radar. Der Fokus lag eher auf den Tech-Unternehmen, mit deren Produkten die Kund:innen in direkten Kontakt kommen: Google, Amazon, Facebook (später als Teil von Meta), Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft.
Einen Schub sowohl was die wirtschaftliche Bedeutung angeht als auch in Sachen Bekanntheit, erhielt Nvidia mit der Popularität von großen Sprachmodellen aus dem Bereich künstliche Intelligenz. Diese Modelle sind die Basis für KI-Chatbots wie ChatGPT oder Claude. Und gerade für das Training der Modelle sind spezielle Hochleistungschips nötig. Nvidia ist bei der Herstellung dieser Chips Marktführer, zur Liste der Geschäftspartner zählen unter anderem Anthropic, Google, Meta und Microsoft.
Für sorgenvolle Blicke auf die Branche sorgt jedoch, dass Nvidia eben nicht nur Zulieferer ist für Chips – sondern auch Investor in KI-Unternehmen, zum Beispiel in Anthropic, und auch Kunde für KI-Dienste. In derart eng verflochtenen Konstellationen kann schon eine umstrittene Unternehmensentscheidung, eine Fehlinvestition oder eine Änderung der politischen Rahmenbedingungen Rutschbewegungen in der gesamten Branche auslösen.
Heilsame Kursverluste
Branchenbeobachter:innen zufolge könnten daher die jüngsten Kursverluste nach den Zwischenwahlen in den USA eine heilsame Kurskorrektur sein. Wenn die Bewertungen der KI-Unternehmen tatsächlich flächendeckend zu hoch sind und damit eine Blase entstanden ist, könnten schrittweise Kurskorrekturen ein abruptes Platzen verhindern.
Und Deutschland? Die jüngst vereinbarte Kooperation mit Nvidia sehen Expert:innen zwar grundsätzlich positiv, weil sie der hiesigen Industrie Zugriff verschafft auf die marktführende Chip-Technologie. Gleichzeitig aber birgt sie ein Abhängigkeitsrisiko: Eine solche Kooperation dürfe nicht mit technologischer Souveränität verwechselt werden, warnte Patrick Glauner, Professor für künstliche Intelligenz an der Technischen Hochschule Deggendorf, gegenüber dem Science Media Center: „Europa muss parallel eigene Anbieter bei Hardware, Infrastruktur und Software stärken.“

- Körperhygiene
Sex auf unserer Haut
Schrubben, reiben, abspülen: Sich zu waschen, ist langweilig. Doch davon, was sich auf ihrer ungewaschenen Haut abspielt, ahnen viele nichts.
Kaum jemand spricht darüber, aber: Unter den alltäglichen Verrichtungen, die unvermeidlich sind, gehört das Waschen des eigenen Körpers zu den bei Weitem stumpfsinnigsten. Immer wieder Wasser über die Haut laufen lassen, mit der Seife hantieren, schrubben, reiben, abspülen. Morgen für Morgen, Abend für Abend. Es ist eine durch und durch nervtötende Angelegenheit. Das Waschen ist zeitraubend und infolge der repetitiven Handlungen, die man dabei täglich auszuführen genötigt ist, vor allem langweilig: Haare, Gesicht, Oberkörper, unter den Achseln, Bauch, Beine, Po. Es ist so öde. Bitte auch die Zwischenräume zwischen den Zehen, die Perianalregion und die Interglutealfalte nicht vergessen, wo sich im Laufe eines anstrengenden oder ereignisreichen Tages so einiges ansammelt.
Man hat sie so satt, die immergleichen kreisenden Handbewegungen, diese idiotische Schufterei am eigenen Körper. Wenn es nur der Schweiß und der Talg wäre. Aber man hat es mit weitaus mehr Material zu tun, das entfernt werden muss: den ganzen abgestorbenen (und unerbittlich weiter jede Minute absterbenden) Hautschuppen, den öligen Kosmetika-Resten, dem Staub, einem dicken Film aus Großstadtschmutz und Fetten. Nicht zu vergessen: die ganzen Fettsäuren, die für unangenehme Gerüche sorgen. Offiziell nennt man diese Säuren in verniedlichender Absicht »mikrobielle Stoffwechselprodukte«, das klingt schön wissenschaftlich und neutral, in Wirklichkeit handelt es sich hierbei um den Kot der auf unserer Haut lebenden Bakterien. Ja, da staunen Sie – darüber wird in der Fernsehwerbung und bei »Lanz« und »Maischberger« nun mal nicht gerne geredet.
Nur der tapfere Mitteldeutsche Rundfunk greift das Tabuthema Haarbalgmilben auf (»sie leben auf uns, mit uns, von uns … diese kleinen Milben haben Sex auf unserer Haut«) und spricht in einem Wissenschaftsartikel dankenswerterweise Klartext. Die Haarbalgmilbe, so erfährt man darin, ist extrem scharf auf Melatonin, »einen Stoff, der kleine wirbellose Tiere nachts aktiv werden lässt«, den das geile kleine Krabbeltier selbst aber nicht produzieren kann.
Doch die Natur hat, wie gewohnt, alles perfekt organisiert: Menschen geben nachts, wenn sie schlafen, über die Haut großzügig Melatonin ab, das Koks der Milbenwelt. Eine perfekte natürliche Symbiose aus Gebern und Nehmern ist so entstanden, bei der, betrachtet man sie genau, der letztgültige Sinn und Zweck unserer Gesichtsbehaarung enthüllt wird: »Mit dieser Melatonin-›Fütterung‹ ermöglichen wir den kleinen Tierchen ihr nächtliches Sexualleben. (…) Die Männchen haben einen Penis, der von der Vorderseite des Körpers nach oben ragt, was bedeutet, dass sich das Männchen beim nächtlichen Stelldichein unter dem Weibchen positionieren muss und sich beide ans menschliche Haar klammern, während sie kopulieren.«
Thomas Blum ist grundsätzlich nicht einverstanden mit der herrschenden sogenannten Realität. Vorerst wird er sie nicht ändern können, aber er kann sie zurechtweisen, sie ermahnen oder ihr, wenn es nötig wird, auch mal eins überziehen. Damit das Schlechte den Rückzug antritt. Wir sind mit seinem Kampf gegen die Realität solidarisch. Daher erscheint fortan montags an dieser Stelle »Die gute Kolumne«. Nur die beste Qualität für die besten Leser*innen! Die gesammelten Texte sind zu finden unter: dasnd.de/diegute
Lange Zeit verbreitete sich der Mythos, diese sexbesessenen Parasiten hätten keinen After, würden ihren Kot wochenlang in ihrem Körper ansammeln und im Moment ihres Ablebens explosionsartig auf unserer Haut verstreuen. Die moderne Forschung soll das mittlerweile jedoch widerlegt haben: »Die Milben besitzen eine funktionierende Ausscheidungsöffnung und geben kontinuierlich winzige Mengen Kot ab«, wie es auf einer Milbenspezialisten-Webseite heißt. Das ist beruhigend.
Sicher, man hat nach so und so vielen Jahren Routine bei der Körperpflege und beim Duschen, muss nicht mehr über die Reihenfolge der Verrichtungen nachdenken: Soll man sich morgens zuerst das Barthaar und die Wimpern waschen, um die auf der Hautoberfläche haftenden Rückstände des nächtlichen Milbengeschlechtsverkehrs loszuwerden? Ist es sinnvoller, mit der Kopfhaarwäsche zu beginnen, um das teure medizinische Shampoo erst ein wenig einwirken zu lassen? Oder soll man sich als Erstes um die Mulden zwischen Hodensack und Oberschenkelinnenseiten kümmern, damit es dort nicht mehr »riecht wie ein Suppenwürfel« (Martin Puntigam)?
Der eine oder die andere kann sich vielleicht noch daran erinnern, dass es früher – bis in die 80er und 90er Jahre hinein – in vielen Familien, die nicht zu den begüterten zählten, einen sogenannten Badetag gab. Als ich, in der finstersten Provinz aufgewachsen, noch ein Kind war, wurde in der Familie an Samstagen gebadet: Vormittags wurde der Badeofen angeheizt, damit es für mehrere Stunden heißes Wasser gab, dann nahm einer nach dem anderen jedes Familienmitglied ein Bad. Wochentags behalf man sich mit dem, was allgemein als »Katzenwäsche« bezeichnet wird. In Zeiten, in denen die Energiekosten permanent steigen und die Regionen, in denen sauberes Wasser verfügbar ist, permanent schrumpfen, werden die weniger Privilegierten wohl früher oder später wieder zu solchen oder vergleichbaren Arten der Körperreinigung zurückkehren müssen. Eine maßvolle Körperreinigung ist obendrein hautschonend: weniger Allergien, weniger trockene Haut, intakte Hautflora (Milben-Sex). Und man spart viel Zeit, die man bislang mit einer extrem öden Tätigkeit verschwendete.
Dennoch bin ich mir nicht sicher, ob, um einer besseren Zukunft willen, nicht via gelingender Weltrevolution und durch die sich zwingend anschließenden Fortschritte in der wissenschaftlichen Forschung Entscheidendes erreicht werden könnte. Dann nämlich wäre irgendwann gesichert, dass ausnahmslos alle Menschen Zugang zu Strom und ausreichend sauberem Wasser haben.
Sicher ist jedenfalls: Die Mühen der Körperreinigung übernähme dann das in ausnahmslos jedem Haushalt installierte vollautomatische Badezimmer, in dem, sobald man morgens schlaftrunken hineintrottet, in Nullkommanichts geübte Roboterhände jeden nötigen Handgriff ausführen, vom Einseifen bis zum Abtrocknen.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

Trilaterales Treffen in Abu Dhabi: Europäer mit am Tisch? Von wegen!
Der Kreml besteht auf Gesprächen zwischen Washington, Moskau und Kyjiw. Ohnehin geht es Wladimir Putin nicht um die Ukraine, sondern Geopolitik als Ganzes.
Miteinander zu sprechen ist besser, als übereinander zu sprechen. Aus dieser Warte betrachtet ist es durchaus positiv, dass am 10. und 11. November in Abu Dhabi wieder Gespräche stattfinden, um Russlands Angriffskrieg gegen die Ukraine perspektivisch auf dem Verhandlungsweg zu beenden. Die Ankündigung von US-Präsident Donald Trump, dort das Thema Sicherheitsarchitektur in den Vordergrund zu stellen, hat indes eine unerwartete Dynamik in Gang gesetzt.
Mehrere europäische Länder und die Nato sollen daraufhin ihre Absicht erklärt haben, sich in das Treffen einzubringen. Kremlsprecher Dmitrij Peskow reagierte am Montag mit einer kategorischen Absage: Es bleibe beim geplanten trilateralen Format unter Beteiligung Russlands, der Ukraine und den USA.
Russlands Präsident Wladimir Putin hatte am Samstag seinerseits die Zusammensetzung der russischen Delegation aufgewertet. Erstmals sollen auf russischer Seite mit dem stellvertretenden russischen Außenminister Sergej Rjabkow und Armeegeneral Jurij Schigarlowskij zwei ausgewiesene Experten für europäische und globale Sicherheitsfragen an einem solchen Treffen teilnehmen.
Gleichzeitig gibt man sich in Moskau angesichts der innenpolitischen Turbulenzen, mit denen sich Trump angesichts der Wahlniederlage seiner Partei bei den Midterms herumschlagen muss, betont zurückhaltend.
Auf den Putz hauen
Maria Sacharowa beispielsweise, die als Sprecherin des russischen Außenministeriums gerne auf den Putz haut, scheint keine signifikanten Änderungen zu erwarten. Als Reaktion auf die US-Wahlen bescheinigte sie dem alten US-Kongress „offene Sabotage von Ideen und Initiativen“, die auf eine „relative Normalisierung der bilateralen Beziehungen“ abzielten. Als Grund nannte sie einen klaren „antirussischen Konsens“.
Eine Möglichkeit mit Menschen auf der Straße über politische Themen zu diskutieren, waren früher Kundgebungen aller Art. Weil das Privileg, sich zu versammeln, längst nur noch wenigen Auserwählten zugestanden wird, darf man heutzutage nicht allzu wählerisch sein. Also einfach mal am Karl-Marx-Denkmal vorbeischauen, wo am 7. November die Kommunistische Partei KPRF den 109. Jahrestag der Oktoberrevolution feierte.
Dort bietet an diesem Tag ein Mann die letzten beiden Ausgaben der „besten linken Zeitung“ feil – kostenlos. Ob Hammer und Sichel schon auf Trumps Wahlniederlage reagiert habe? Der Mann verneint, hat zu dem Thema aber eine eigene Meinung. Gegen Trump als US-Präsidenten habe er nichts einzuwenden, aber er findet es gut, dass die Demokraten jetzt ein Gegengewicht zu Trump bildeten: „Jetzt können sie uns nicht mehr einfach so erpressen.“
Glänzendes Peace-Zeichen
Von der improvisierten Bühne hinter Marxens Rücken ertönen kämpferische Stimmen. Vom „Siegesprogramm der Partei“ ist da die Rede, vom „Sieg über Faschismus“ – damals und heute. Das Wort Ukraine fällt kein einziges Mal. Ein Kundgebungsteilnehmer hat ein nicht zu übersehendes silbern glänzendes Peace-Zeichen an seinen Mantel geheftet, in der Hand hält er ein handgeschriebenes Plakat mit der Aufschrift „Iran – sozialistische Solidarität“.
Nach der kurzen Abstimmung über die für solche Veranstaltungen obligatorische Resolution pilgern rund 200 Menschen zum Lenin-Mausoleum. Auf dem Weg dahin bittet ein älterer Herr ein junges Paar, ihre Uhren mit der auf dem Kremlturm zu vergleichen. Die zeigt 12 Uhr an, tatsächlich ist es schon zehn Minuten später. „Die Zeit ist stehen geblieben – was für ein Zufall!“, ruft der Herr aufgeregt. Viele legen Blumen an den Gräbern der sowjetischen Anführer nieder. Auch am Grab Stalins.
Kommunistenchef Gennadij Sjuganow sagt im Anschluss vor laufenden Fernsehkameras: „Trumps Frist ist abgelaufen.“ Ob Wladimir Putin diese Ansicht teilt, ist schwer zu sagen. Zumal Trump ja weiter im Amt bleibt und die Geschäfte mit ihm, insbesondere der vereinbarte Export von russischem Dieseltreibstoff, weiterlaufen werden, hofft jedenfalls Peskow.
Aber das sind Nebensächlichkeiten. Putin bekommt in Abu Dhabi genau das, worum es ihm geht: Er will nicht über Frieden, sondern über Geopolitik diskutieren. Mit einem vermeintlich ebenbürtigen Gegenüber, nicht mit Vertreter:innen einer Riege politisch uneiniger Staaten.
