https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Time to fight back: five leading thinkers on what Democrats should do post-midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert Reich, Wajahat Ali, Katie Phang, Judd Legum and Charles Blow
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Welcome to a special edition of How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Sign up here to receive future editions in your inbox.
Bust up the broligarchy
Democrats should use their mandate to be Democrats again. That means taking on concentrated wealth and economic power – the oligarchy – with a wealth tax on multimillionaires and billionaires. Campaign finance reforms to get big money out of our democracy. Labor law reforms to make it easier for workers to form unions and harder for employers to fire them for doing so. And tough new anti-monopoly laws to give government authority to bust up concentrations of economic power, especially in tech.
– Robert Reich, former US secretary of labor and a Guardian US columnist
Smoke out the ghost of the Confederacy
The majority of voters repudiated the corrupt, racist Republican party that made life unaffordable and committed crimes with impunity. To keep people from their pitchforks, Democrats need to use this singular power for transformation, not restoration. Preach and practice affordability and accountability. (Talking to you, Hakeem Jeffries.)
We’re not going to just move forward, hold hands and get along. We have to vanquish the Maga spirit to ensure the ghost of the Confederacy can no longer haunt and terrorize our country.
First, Democrats should unleash hell in the name of justice. This means investigations of the Jeffrey Epstein class, Elon Musk, Pete Hegseth, Jared Kushner, Robert F Kennedy Jr and Stephen Miller. Second, Democrats must end the trade wars and the failed, disastrous war in Iran while not getting outflanked by Republicans in rejecting Israel’s interference in our politics. Restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse the $1tn cuts to Medicaid. And how about Medicare for All?
– Wajahat Ali, editor of The Left Hook and co-host of The Democracy-ish Podcast
Make the lawyers pay
One of the most insidious aspects of Trump’s second term has been his aggressive destruction of the rule of law. Trump’s weaponization of the Department of Justice to instill fear in his political opponents has eroded the public’s trust in our system of justice.
With their clear mandate from voters, Democrats must immediately launch investigations into the actions of Trump’s former lawyer Alina Habba, former US attorney Lindsey Halligan, US attorney Jeanine Pirro and other US attorneys and federal prosecutors who furthered Trump’s intimidation campaign. US attorney general Todd Blanche, who allegedly quarterbacked several of these illegal and unethical prosecutions, should be investigated first.
After the 2021 attack on the Capitol, at least 20 million people tuned in to watch the first hearing of the January 6 select committee. Public hearings would allow Americans to witness the extent of these lawyers’ complicity in following the whims of the president to pursue vindictive indictments and prosecutions. The all-out assault on the rule of law by Trump and his justice department must be stopped. It should be a top priority for the Democrats as they begin the 120th Congress.
– Katie Phang, independent journalist, trial lawyer and political analyst
Root out corruption
The most crucial issue for 2026 voters was not grocery prices, or the Iran war or immigration. It was corruption. And that’s exactly the issue Democrats should start on when they gain control of Congress in January.
The first order of business should be to pass a law banning all members of Congress and the president from trading individual stocks. (Trump has made more than 25,000 individual stock trades since returning to the White House.) Such a bill should pass with overwhelming – and potentially veto-proof – bipartisan support. What better way for Democrats to begin their majority than to deliver real reform on an issue of importance to voters?
Next, subpoena Jared Kushner. Trump’s son-in-law is a top US negotiator on every key foreign policy issue while reportedly remaining on the dole of foreign governments. It’s one of the biggest corruption scandals in history. Kushner claims he is a volunteer, not a government official. That makes it difficult for him to assert executive privilege.
– Judd Legum, founder and author of Popular Information
Do the work
First, I would caution Democrats not to consider this victory a mandate, but rather an assignment. Voters were repulsed by Trump and his actions, but they were not writing Democrats a blank check. They want accountability for corruption and affirmative action toward greater equality and economic relief.
However, the “blue wave” delivered neither a filibuster-proof nor a veto-proof majority in Congress. The goal now is to keep expectations aligned with actual opportunity and ability.
– Charles Blow, author, political analyst and contributing writer to the Guardian
Want to hear more from our contributors?
Follow them on Substack and elsewhere: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum, Wajahat Ali, Margaret Sullivan, and Charles Blow.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump is humiliated and angry – and Europe is where he’s free to lash out | Nathalie Tocci
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Nathalie Tocci
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Europeans have greeted the blue wave that crashed down on Donald Trump and his Republican party with jubilation and relief. Jubilation, because Trump’s second presidential administration has been the most destructive in the history of the transatlantic relationship. His disdain for Europe and his evident delight in attacking its governments – in particular that of Ukraine – have been hard to swallow.
Relief, because the midterm election results confirm that Europeans are not unique in being appalled by Trump’s actions: a large majority of Americans are too. I was in Washington immediately after the vote, and the mood was one of excitement and a newfound confidence. And like many Americans, in these results Europeans see hope that US democracy can be saved, American foreign policy moderated and the transatlantic partnership revived.
They are both right and wrong. Despite recent backsliding, democracy is alive and kicking in the US. The Democratic party, which for a long time seemed stunned and paralysed by Trump’s return to the White House, is bubbling with fresh energy and ideas. Its claim to be a big tent is no longer an abstract ideal but a reality, with a remarkable array of diverse and charismatic figures shining through – from the Christian progressive James Talarico in Texas to the democratic socialist Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who will be the first Muslim in the US Senate, and Georgia’s moderate Jon Ossoff.
The political power of a big tent is a lesson European liberals and progressives should heed, as many European countries head into crucial elections in the coming months facing strong headwinds from the far right.
The resounding defeat of Trump’s agenda – and in particular Americans’ stark rejection of the war on Iran, acknowledged explicitly by JD Vance and implicitly by Trump himself – could also lead Washington to soften its stance in the Middle East. Before the US midterms (and elections in Israel), the region had seemed set on a ladder of escalation; the Republicans’ drubbing could now force Trump to climb down. That will be good news if it happens. And European leaders, though largely sidelined, should do their utmost to encourage de-escalation by backing the diplomatic outreach of Gulf states such as Qatar.
But Europeans would be badly mistaken to think this mellowing will extend to US policy towards Europe and the war in Ukraine. Regarding Europe, the lesson Trump is likely to draw from the midterms is that his mistake – if he can bring himself to conceive of making any – was not being Trumpy enough, not lashing out hard enough at the continent’s liberal democracies.
After all, while Trump’s Maga base is sceptical of the Iran war, it applauds the normalisation of ties with Moscow and the withdrawal of support for Kyiv, and would be happy to see a more decisive US military disengagement from Europe. Trump’s decision to promote Stephen Miller to chief of staff points in that direction. While Miller has not played a prominent role on Ukraine so far, he is among the foremost proponents of the Maga worldview that might makes right. In the European context, this predatory approach often translates in the belief that Russia will (and therefore should) prevail. Over the past two years, Trump has humiliated and insulted Europeans, imposed punitive tariffs on them and threatened Greenland. In fairness, though, the US military disengagement from Europe and Nato has so far been limited.
Hemmed in on his Middle East adventurism, and having achieved most of what was within reach in Latin America – from the toppling of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro to a string of rightwing electoral victories across the region, blunted only by Lula’s unexpected comeback in Brazil – Trump is left with Europe to lash out at. It would be surprising if he didn’t. While little can be expected from the resumption of Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, Europeans should brace for dirty tricks from the Trump-Putin-Xi Jinping trio, which may meet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen later this month, and from a Trump-hosted G20 in Miami in December. And it would be surprising not to see a further, uncoordinated US military pullback from Europe.
Trump and Maga have always seen Europe as the mirror image of their domestic foes: a bunch of presumptuous, woke, emasculated liberals. Now that those foes have made a comeback at home, Trump’s rancour towards Europe is likely to grow.
To imagine that the worst is over and that the transatlantic partnership will settle back to the good old days would be more than wrong. It would be delusional. The midterms may mark the beginning of the end for Trump, putting the US on track for a Democratic victory in the 2028 presidential election. But that road is long and strewn with obstacles. And even if a Democrat victory is achieved and the two sides of the Atlantic seek to pick up the pieces of their broken relationship, what they rebuild will look quite different. For a start, the US’s betrayal of Europe over the past two years can’t be quickly forgotten, but also the new class of Democrats emerging from this election lacks the commitment to Europe held by older generations.
The transatlantic relationship can and will be rebuilt. But it will be narrower, more interest-based and less sentimental. Europeans should not look to the US midterms for a past to be revived. The time for transatlantic nostalgia is over.
- Nathalie Tocci is a professor of practice at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, Europe, and a senior fellow at Bocconi University’s Institute for European Policymaking

50. Duisburger Filmwoche: Betreutes Sehen als Erkenntnismethode
Von Assads Toten bis zu Jugendlichen, die Jugendliche spielen: Die 50. Duisburger Filmwoche hat viele verschiedene deutschsprachige Filme diskutiert.
Zum 50. Mal fand die Duisburger Filmwoche in diesem Jahr statt. Neben dem regulären Festivalprogramm, das wie stets eine Auswahl von etwa 20 Filmen aus dem deutschsprachigen Raum präsentierte, gab es aus diesem Anlass einige Sonderveranstaltungen.
Die nachhaltigste dürfte die Präsentation eines Sammelbands gewesen sein, der unter dem Titel „Arbeiten für das Kino“ auf knapp 500 Seiten Erinnerungen und Reflexionen über 50 Festivaljahrgänge versammelte. Sichtbar wurde in dem Band nicht nur eine Vielzahl von Themenfeldern und thematischen Linien, sondern auch, welch vielstimmiges Umfeld die Duisburger Filmwoche immer schon prägte.
Wie kaum ein anderes Festival lebt das in Duisburg davon, dass Menschen Jahr für Jahr aus weiteren Entfernungen dorthin reisen und sich mit einem Publikum mischen, das aus der Gegend kommt. In diesem Jahr scheint es einen ganzen Schwung neuer Besucher_innen des Festivals gegeben zu haben. Ungewöhnlich viele Vorführungen waren ungewöhnlich voll und teils mussten Filme in Zusatzräume übertragen werden.
Die Duisburger Filmwoche ist ein Ort der Traditionen und der Neuerungen. Zu den Neuerungen gehört, dass seit letztem Jahr jeweils zwei Menschen aus dem Umfeld des Festivals ein Thema mit einer Auswahl von Filmausschnitten vertieft betrachten. Betreutes Sehen als Erkenntnismethode.
Alle schauen und reden dann drüber
Zu den Traditionen zählt einerseits der grundsätzliche Ablauf – alle gucken einen Film, dann reden alle über diesen Film und ganz am Ende steht ein Protokoll, das die Grundlinien und einige Aussagen der Diskussion festhält. Dieser Ablauf und die Grundhaltung, das Reden und den Austausch über Film ebenso wichtig zu nehmen wie das Sehen der Filme, ist der unveränderte Kern des Festivals über alle 50 Jahre hinweg.
Es gibt aber auch kleinere, neuere Traditionen. So wird jedes Jahr einmal das Stück „Aufregung über hybride Formen“ aufgeführt. Der Ablauf ist in etwa so: Ein Film, der formal eher nach Spielfilm als nach Dokumentarfilm aussieht, wird im Rahmen der Filmwoche gezeigt. Im Anschluss sitzt die vereinte Dokumentarfilmkompetenz, die bei der Filmwoche das Publikum ausmacht, im Diskussionssaal und versucht zu verstehen, warum sie diesen Film sehen sollte. Auf dem Podium wiederum sitzt ein_e Regisseur_in und versteht nicht, woher die Aufregung kommt und wie dem Film geschieht.
Das Potenzial von Realität
In diesem Jahr fand diese Aufführung nach Julian Rabus’ Film „Sunstrokes“ statt, der Jugendliche Jugendliche spielen lässt. Rabus hat sich für seinen Film eine Anordnung überlegt, die den jugendlichen Darsteller_innen Raum geben soll, „das Potenzial von Realität“ zu erkunden.
Auf weitere Versuche, die Grenzziehungen und Verortungen in der Dichotomie Dokumentarfilm–Fiktion einfordern, nimmt Rabus für seinen „Hybrid-Slackerfilm“ in Anspruch, „ein Bild manchmal nicht Realität abbilden muss, sondern es reicht zu wissen, ‚dass es Realität sein könnte‘“, wie das Protokoll der Diskussion vermerkt. Die diesjährige Diskussion über hybride Formen war gegenüber früheren Jahren vergleichsweise lebendig. Ganz konnte man sich aber auch dieses Mal nicht des Eindrucks erwehren, dass aneinander vorbeikommuniziert wurde.
Die Filme bildeten auch in diesem Jahr eine große Bandbreite von Formen ab. Almourad Aldeeb setzte in seinem an der Kölner Kunsthochschule für Medien entstandenen Film „Estahbes“ seinen in syrischen Foltergefängnissen gestorbenen Freunden ein Denkmal. Ende 2013 werden Aldeeb und ein Freund nach einem Geburtstag in Damaskus in ein Gefängnis verschleppt. Wenig später folgen sieben weitere Freunde.
Nach dem Sturz Assads sind zwei noch am Leben. Aldeebs Film ist über weite Strecken an eben jenem Ort gedreht, an dem er und seine Freunde gefangengehalten wurden. Zu kargen Bildern der Räume rekonstruiert Aldeeb seine Erlebnisse. Am Ende besucht er mit weiteren überlebenden Freunden, die Familien der Toten. Die Wohnzimmer sind leer. Aldeeb bekam für seinen beeindruckenden Film den Nachwuchspreis des Landes NRW.
Die österreichische Künstlerin Heidrun Holzfeind porträtiert in ihrem Film „The 49th Year“ den militanten Aktivisten Toshihiko Kamata, der nach einer Reihe von Bombenanschlägen, die die Schwarzhelm-Gruppe ab 1971 verübt hat, seit 1980 in Japan in Haft ist. Der berühmteste Anschlag galt einem Weihnachtsbaum neben einer Wachbox der Polizei in Tokio. Die Bombe verletzte den Polizisten schwer und mehrere Passanten. Holzfeinds Film geht ausgehend von Briefen Kamatas aus dem Gefängnis auf Spurensuche. Der Film wurde mit dem 3sat-Dokumentarfilmpreis ausgezeichnet.
Jeden Tag sechs Stunden
Philipp Hartmann steuerte den schönen und intimen halbstündigen Dokumentarfilm „Auf der Rückseite der Landschaft“ zum diesjährigen Festivaljahrgang bei. Hartmann besucht seinen ehemaligen Filmprofessor, während der auf einem Parkplatz auf seine Partnerin wartet, die an einer örtlichen Schule Kunst unterrichtet. Jeden Tag sechs Stunden. Hartmanns Film gewann den Preis der Stadt Duisburg.
„Übergang“ von Peter Badel und Chris Wright wurde nach der Goldenen Taube beim Dokumentarfilmfestival in Leipzig und dem Publikumspreis bei der Viennale in Duisburg sehr zu recht erneut ausgezeichnet und erhielt zwei Wochen vor dem Kinostart den Arte-Dokumentarfilmpreis. Auch in diesem Jahr musste man nicht allen Redebeiträgen zustimmen, um die Diskussionen insgesamt dennoch als Reflexion über dokumentarisches Arbeiten zu schätzen. Die 50. Duisburger Filmwoche zeigte sich quicklebendig, gut besucht und wortreich wie immer.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: The rise and rise of the family farm
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Stephen Starr in Bellbrook, Ohio
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
On any given Saturday at this time of year in south-west Ohio, the Lucas Brothers Fall Festival is the place to be.
There’s a hayride into the woods, an inflatable obstacle course, a go-kart track and a corn maze linked to a game that visitors can play on their phones.
At the center of the farm is a quaint barn store filled with jars of jams, honey and other items, and customers lining up for grilled food and drinks. Outside, there’s a wood-burning fire ring billowing smoke into the crisp fall air.
“The barn was initially going to be a machine barn, but then 10 years ago we changed gears, just decided to do a fall thing,” says Susan Lucas, whose husband, Mark, and his brother own the fall fest. The brothers also grow around 1,500 acres of corn, soybeans and wheat, and raise 200 acres of produce every year.
“Definitely, having extra income from the venue helps, the costs are going up, but the price of grain is not. We need that income to pay our bills and support two families,” says Lucas.
With net farming income set to fall by 5.5% after inflation this year, fuel prices at record levels and commodity grain prices stagnant, more farming families are turning to fall festivals and “agritainment” to make a living.
The financial crisis facing family farms is nothing new, with more than 140,000 farms lost in the US from 2017 to 2022.
But in recent years, it has become even worse. Billionaires including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos are snapping up millions of acres of agricultural ground, and since the Covid-19 pandemic, farmland values have increased 44%.
Worth an estimated $1.3bn in 2022 or $4.5bn when off-farm and non-edible goods are included, agritourism is increasingly being seen as a lifeline for landowning families.
In the midwest, some farm festivals are reporting record numbers of visitors this fall and for farmers present a fast income revenue stream when, by contrast, payments for crops and cattle can take months, even years, to come through. Some venues have gotten so popular that they’ve had to issue online tickets to manage the crowds.
The boom in income has prompted farmers to double down by building farm stores and even conference and wedding spaces.
In Ohio, the number of farms operating an agritourism business grew 27% in the five years to 2022.
“Agritourism is a way to diversify. However, it takes entirely different skills,” says Lisa Chase, a professor at the University of Vermont and co-author of a US Department of Agriculture-sponsored national study of agritourism published in August. The study found that 75% of participants saw an increase in income after adding an agritourism arm to their farming business.
“Often, it’s the [grown] kids coming back to the farm, but milking cows is not what they want to be doing – they want to be in the education, marketing, hospitality side of things,” says Chase.
The survey of 911 farmers found that in 2024, 24% of participants made from $25,000 to $99,999 in gross revenue from agritourism-related sales and services, while 5% made from $1m to $5m.
For Pam Nelson, who with her husband runs Nelson Produce Farm outside Omaha, Nebraska, agritourism was a route to achieving a long-held dream of running their own farm.
“Neither of us inherited any ground and it’s very hard to get into conventional farming if you don’t have any of those assets,” she says.
She and her husband first grew vegetables for local stores and had two roadside markets before opening their business in 2019.
Now, the farm has experienced extraordinary growth, with close to 100,000 visitors expected this year who come for tulip festivals, a corn maze after dark and a host of other seasonal attractions, such as farm-to-table dinners.
“We hold one every month [from June to October], with different themes and foods,” Nelson says of the latter event.
“We sell tickets in March, and I think this year they sold out in less than an hour.”
Today, the farm employs 70-100 part- and full-time people during its busiest season.
“Every year we have truck and tractor days where we actually give kids truck and combine rides,” she says.
But while agritourism has emerged as an important way to fill in for losses in conventional farming, it’s by no means a silver bullet.
The University of Vermont study found that 45% of participants made less than $25,000 in 2024 from their agritourism ventures.
“One of the biggest challenges we’re facing is getting access to data that shows what the agritourism trends are,” says Claire Whitehouse, a researcher at the University of Vermont and co-author with Chase of the report.
“[The US] Food and Drug Administration figures do not include sales for inedible foods such as pumpkins, wool and decorative gourds.”
What’s more, signs suggest that investment firms may be targeting small farms as a revenue source.
For the past two years, Hidden Valley Orchards, one of the most popular fall festival farms in south-west Ohio, has been operated by a company called Endurance Farm Partners, a limited liability entity run by California-based real estate and business investors with ties to a San Francisco-based investment firm. Emails sent to Endurance Farm Partners by the Guardian asking whether the business owners reside locally were not responded to. The farm had previously been owned by a local business.
For others, growing competition has become a challenge.
“Last year and this year, we noticed a lot more places are opening up and doing what we’re doing,” says Lucas.
“A lot of the local cities and townships are having free fall events, which compete with our market share.”
Still, Lucas says, since the farm has been in her husband’s family for five generations, the fall fest is unlikely to change anytime soon, especially as she sees opening up her farm to the public as a kind of mission.
“Part of the reason it sits on a working farm [is so visitors can connect with rural life],” she says of the business.
“They see the machinery, the barns and the buildings; they see that it’s a lot of work and there’s a lot involved in farming.”

https://taz.de/Boxhandschuhe/!6228672/.title: Boxhandschuhe: Die Unze macht alles weicher
https://taz.de/Boxhandschuhe/!6228672/.author: Martin Krauss
https://taz.de/Boxhandschuhe/!6228672/.text:
Boxhandschuhe: Die Unze macht alles weicher
Je länger die Sportgeschichte fortschreitet, desto schwerer werden die Fäustlinge, mit denen geboxt wird. Gefährlich bleibt die Sache dennoch.
N eulich gab es bei Günther Jauch diese Frage: „Was wird für Erwachsene üblicherweise in den Größen 10, 12, 14 oder 16 oz angeboten?“ Antwort B war „Boxhandschuhe“, und was mich zumindest am meisten verblüffte: Die richtige Antwort war 64.000 Euro wert.
Was „oz“ ist, lässt sich leicht erklären: Unzen. Schwergewichtsprofis, männlich wie weiblich, pflegen mit 10-Unzen-Handschuhen zu kämpfen. Die sind 283,5 Gramm schwer, und das Gewicht drückt aus, wie gepolstert sie sind. Als 1936 und 1938 Joe Louis gegen Max Schmeling kämpfte, waren es schon 8 Unzen. Die Schlagwirkung soll halt immer besser absorbiert werden.
Was sich so technisch anhört, hat viel mit einer Zivilisierung des Boxsports zu tun. Er wird immer ungefährlicher, was, wenn man den Satz genau liest, bedeutet: Gefährlich ist er immer noch, und der Zwang, ihn ungefährlicher zu machen, besteht fort.
Ein Blick in die Geschichte der Boxhandschuhe gibt Auskunft in die Entwicklung der menschlichen Beziehungen. Die Fäustlinge, die wir heute kennen, gibt es seit Mitte oder Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts. Richtig durchgesetzt haben sie sich mit dem 7. September 1892.
Dass man ein derart genaues Datum nennen kann, liegt schlicht daran, dass James J. Corbett („Gentleman Jim“) und John L. Sullivan an diesem Tag um die Schwergewichts-WM kämpften – und zwar mit 5-Unzen-Handschuhen. Sullivan, der verlor und seinen Titel abgeben musste, hatte zuvor auch des Öfteren ungepolstert gekämpft. Der Fachausdruck lautet „bare knuckle“, und das gibt es tatsächlich bis heute; es ist allerdings nur in wenigen Communitys populär.
Zur Kriminalität des Fäustlings
Boxhandschuhe gehören also zur bürgerlichen Gesellschaft, genauso wie Parlamente, Kinos oder die Eisenbahn.
Apropos: Tatsächlich stellen Boxhandschuhe die historisch zu begrüßende Einhegung brutaler individueller Macht dar. Und das bedeutet im Umkehrschluss, dass, wer sich nicht daran hält, einen Wettbewerbsvorteil hat. Das kann verbrecherisch sein.
1983 boxten Billy Collins Jr. und Luis Resto gegeneinander. Ein nicht weiter wichtiger Weltergewichtsfight im New Yorker Madison Square Garden. Nach Runde fünf hatte Collins zu seinem Vater, der ihn betreute, gesagt: „Daddy, es fühlt sich an, als habe er Steine in seinen Handschuhen!“ Resto gewinnt, Collins ist benommen, der Stern schreibt, sein Kopf sehe aus „wie eine Wassermelone, seine Augen erinnern an matschige Pflaumen“. Sein Vater greift nach Restos Handschuhen und protestiert.
Die Ermittlungen ergeben: Die Handschuhe waren manipuliert. Das Rosshaar, das für die Fütterung sorgt, war durch zwei Löcher herausgezogen worden. Luis Resto und sein Trainer werden lebenslang gesperrt. Sein bis dahin als großes Talent geltender Gegner Billy Collins Jr. erlitt irreversible Augenschäden, wurde depressiv und starb später bei einem Autounfall.
Die Sache mit dem Gips
Streitereien um Handschuhe und Bandagen gab und gibt es immer. Dass sie derart dramatisch enden wie 1983 im Madison Square Garden, ist zum Glück selten. Aber die Planung der Manipulation kann durchaus noch verbrecherischer sein.
Beim Weltergewichtskampf Antonio Margarito gegen Shane Mosley 2009 stellte sich heraus, dass die Handschuhe nicht leichter, sondern härter gemacht worden waren. Es ist gute Tradition, dass ein Vertreter des Gegners beim Bandagieren des anderen Boxers dabei ist. Mosleys Trainer bemerkte dabei, dass in Margaritos Bandagen eine weiße Substanz war. Sie wurde untersucht und stellte sich als Gips heraus. Bei Kontakt mit feuchtem Schweiß wären Margaritos Hände steinhart geworden.
Boxhandschuhe müssen gut gefüttert sein. Und das hat nichts damit zu tun, dass es draußen wieder kalt ist.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Diversity, decency and a new south: who were the real winners in the US midterms? |
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Robert Reich
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Rather than regurgitate the particular wins and losses that occurred on Tuesday, I thought it more useful, at this point, to look at the big picture and identify the largest overall winners and losers for the country as a whole.
Biggest winner: a diverse, equitable and inclusive America. It’s Donald Trump’s DEI nightmare. Georgia voters elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in the country. Texas chose Gina Hinojosa, the state’s first Latina governor and first Democratic governor in more than 30 years. California elected Xavier Becerra, the state’s first Latino governor. New Mexico chose Deb Haaland, the country’s first female Native American governor. Florida elected Byron Donalds, the first Black governor in Florida’s history (a Republican).
For the US Senate, New Hampshire chose Chris Pappas, that chamber’s first out gay member. Minnesotans picked Peggy Flanagan, the first Native American woman elected to the Senate. Michiganders chose Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate.
These are remarkable wins. Some are attributable to a surge in voting by Black people, many of whom were understandably incensed at efforts to push Black representatives out of Congress through overt racial gerrymandering. And by Latinos, enraged at ICE’s wanton arrests and detentions. Women upset by Republican efforts to outlaw abortion in their states. And LGBTQ+ people, angry about the blatant bigotry of Trump and his Republican enablers.
But many straight white men and women also disagree with Trump’s narrow definition of America. It turns out that the nation is far more diverse, equitable and inclusive than Trump or his Republican enablers want (or believe) it to be. They tried to make us fear and hate one another over our many differences. They indubitably failed.
Another winner: the new south. For as long as anyone can remember, the states that comprised the Old Confederacy have been regressive, conservative, intolerant and, at least since the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Republican.
No longer. On Tuesday, three of the four most populous southern states (Texas, North Carolina and Georgia) voted for Democrats up and down their tickets. Texas Democrats carried every statewide office from governor through lieutenant governor, attorney general, and even railroad commissioner. North Carolina and Georgia Democrats also scored stunning victories.
The biggest surprise was Annie Andrews’ win over Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate contest. As I write this, another possible gobsmacker: the Democrat Scott Colom may actually win the Mississippi Senate seat held by the Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Even Democratic losers in the south came remarkably close to winning: the Democratic Senate candidate Jamie Davis was within a hair’s breadth of victory in Louisiana. Florida’s Angie Nixon almost won the Senate seat there.
What accounts for this new south? Partly a large and growing professional class (in metro Atlanta, North Carolina’s “research triangle”, and Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth and Austin) combined with an increasing flow of young workers and their families from other states, seeking more affordable housing. Add to this, an abundance of Latino and Asian immigrants. All told, the new south is more tolerant than the old. Much of it is also more more educated.
A third winner: decency. During the run-up to the 2026 midterms, American voters were inundated with Republican attack ads, inflamed rhetoric, and personal smears against Democratic rivals. Those efforts backfired. Americans soundly rejected the politics of hate and fear, and embraced common decency.
Trump, JD Vance and RFK Jr did their worst to fuel Islamophobia against Michigan’s Dr El-Sayed. Trump claimed if El-Sayed won, he’d “invite hordes of jihadis to our shores”. RFK Jr baselessly linked El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood. Their fear-mongering obviously didn’t work.
Vance suggested that the Texas Democratic senatorial candidate James Talarico is gay. Another backfire.
Ohioans were so turned off by the Trump-endorsed billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against his Democratic opponent Dr Amy Acton – using Acton’s mother, whom Acton hadn’t seen since she was 12, when her stepfather was accused of raping her – that the ad may have helped fuel Acton’s win, making her the first Democrat to win Ohio’s governorship since 2006. (Trump thought the ad was just fine, and Vance even blasted fellow Republicans who spoke out against the ad, calling their criticism “disgusting” and telling them to “stop whining” because “politics is a tough business.”)
Since Trump came on the scene, many Republicans have eagerly imitated his scurrilous character assaults. Such smears have become so common that we tend to forget that most Americans don’t particularly like this form of politics. They prefer Barack Obama’s tempered rhetoric and the late John McCain’s dignified and respectful way of disagreeing. Now, after the 2026 midterms, perhaps decency is back.
So who were the biggest losers? Besides Trump and his Republican sycophants, the biggest losers are the mega donors and Super Pacs that poured record amounts of money into failed Republican candidacies.
Top awards for strategic stupidity go to the crypto industry (which tried unsuccessfully to derail Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio); Aipac (which did everything it could to block El-Sayed and prevent any mention of Israel’s genocide in Gaza); the AI industry, which spent loads of cash trying but failing to allay voter’s concerns about datacenters; and Elon Musk, who sought, singlehandedly, to save Ken Paxton’s doomed Senate campaign in Texas.
Musk deserves his own special place in the loser’s circle. The richest person in the world became the poster child in the 2026 midterms for billionaire greed, legalized bribery, and corporate welfare. He sunk almost a half billion dollars into failed Republican campaigns, the most that any single human being has ever spent on elections – and for naught. After Tuesday’s blowout, shares in Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla dropped off a cliff.
Once they’re in control of Congress, Democrats will want to know what personal data and information Musk might have obtained when he ran his ill-fated “department of government efficiency”; what, exactly, happened with Ukraine’s Starlink access; and why the US government should continue to grant him an effective monopoly on satellites anyway rather than nationalize Starlink. To say Musk will be on the hot seat understates the temperature where he’ll be sitting.
In sum, considering the overall winners and losers from the 2026 midterms, I’d say America came out way ahead.
- Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Black girls in LA keep seeing women around them getting killed. They’re driving change
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Abené Clayton in Los Angeles with photographs by Julien James
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
As a child, Tioni Theus was a ball of energy. After school she liked to play golf and dance. On weekends, she’d go to the movies and the mall with her older cousin. Driving back home at the end of the day to her family’s apartment in South Los Angeles, California, she’d ask: “What are we doing next?”
Everything changed when Tioni was 13. Her mother was hit by a car and critically injured, leaving her unable to take care of her daughter. While her mom recovered, Tioni lived with other family members. But the accident left Tioni angry, her older cousin Nafeesah Kincy said, and she struggled to understand that her life had permanently changed.
Tioni started talking to strangers online, Kincy noticed, and hung out with unfamiliar people, including older teen boys and young men. Then she left her family’s care and would bounce between random people’s houses, Kincy said, or spend nights with a boyfriend at a hotel. Each time she saw Tioni, Kincy would implore her to come back to her family.
Over the next two years, Tioni stopped going to school and became “lost in the streets”, said Kincy, who would take her cousin to get food, or meet at another family member’s house to drop off care packages with deodorant, clean underwear and tampons. Family members pleaded with Tioni to stay with one of them permanently.
“It was devastating because I couldn’t protect her,” she said. “We did everything we knew to do.”
Then, on 8 January 2021, Tioni’s body was found on a stretch of highway with a gunshot wound to her neck. She was 16. How she ended up there remains unknown.
Tioni’s killing shocked many in Los Angeles, but it outraged LA’s Black community. In the weeks following her death, there were repeated calls for a swift investigation, for compassion from local leaders, and tangible measures to curb the violence. Black women and girls make up about four percent of the population in the LA region, but represent an outsized share of female homicide victims.
Local and state leaders said they heard their calls. They put together a $115,000 reward for information, and the city commissioned a report to better understand why Black women are killed more often than women of other races. But five years later, there have not been any arrests for her killing, and families, community organizers and violence prevention workers say not enough has changed to prevent future deaths.
Families and organizers want local governments and police to be more outspoken about the harms Black women and teen girls face, to study the dynamics more deeply, to fund programs that address the intersection of domestic and community violence, and to make gender-based violence a key component of the region’s general violence prevention strategy.
“We are in a climate where Black women are the most unprotected species,” Kincy said. “We’re not looked at as human. Even our own men don’t feel the need to protect, and it’s scary, it’s sad and disheartening.”
At the same time, some of the root causes of this violence, including misogyny and long-held stereotypes about Black women and girls, can’t be legislated or policed away. So Black women in LA are doing it themselves, using taskforces, rallies, summer programs and podcasts to share their stories. Doing this, they say, can grow the number of people who are looking out for them – which is particularly important right now after the Trump administration cut millions in federal funds for gun violence prevention.
“It feels like people just don’t care,” said Ken’Niyia, 15. “It feels like Black women are not seen as something that should be protected.”
‘We talk about things that are important to know’
Ken’Niyia, a 15-year-old track-and-field athlete who sports two long french braids, lives in Inglewood, one of several Black- and brown-majority cities in LA county. Over the summer, she enrolled in a program that gave teen girls a place to connect with each other, share their experiences and learn about systemic racism, gender-based violence, rape culture, and the myriad ways generations of Black women have overcome them.
The program has given the girls the rare opportunity to talk about their shared experiences of feeling unsafe in their neighborhoods, and understanding the ways stereotypes about Black women and girls influence their lives, they said.
“We talk about things that are important to know when you’re a teen trying to navigate life,” said 17-year-old Laniyah. “It gives us Black girls a chance to be vulnerable with each other.”
The girls say they’re regularly followed by men in cars and on the streets while they walk home, to school or the store. They’ve witnessed shootings and lost loved ones to gunshot wounds. They’ve heard stories of girls their age being killed on the streets and in domestic violence incidents.
“Even if it’s not happening to me specifically, just to know that it is happening makes me feel unsure,” Ken’Niyia said.
In addition to not feeling safe, several of the girls said they felt left behind, or that the rest of the city was judging them. “It feels like anything that happens to us, Black women in Los Angeles, is our fault,” said Dalila, 17.
There have been several shootings outside Dalila’s home, including one two years ago, when her cousin was shot in the mouth. The cousin survived.
All of these girls live in the areas that have long seen an outsized share of the city’s violence and systemic neglect, where people live on meager incomes and access to grocery stores and thriving business corridors are scant.
Living here puts girls like Dalila at a higher risk of violence compared to their peers of other races and income brackets. And when they are harmed, Dalila said, they don’t get the same compassion white women do.
“People say, ‘She lived in South Central. She’s a product of her environment,’” she said.
The workshops the girls attended were organized by the Women’s Leadership Project (WLP), a nonprofit that offers mentorship to teen girls and queer youth and educates local high-schoolers on gender-based violence and the social issues that contribute to it.
Though the organization was founded 15 years before Tioni’s death, her short life has galvanized the group, said its director, Sikivu Hutchinson. “I don’t like to say [Tioni’s] a symbol, but she is unfortunately representative of so many things. It’s really just symptomatic of the lack of protection, lack of harm reduction, and the lack of prevention and care,” Hutchinson said.
WLP has been pressuring local officials to focus on the violence Black women and girls face in their schools, homes and neighborhoods. The group is calling for the creation of a youth center in Tioni’s name that would give young people in South Central a safe place to hang out, do homework, and take classes.
“In South Central, we see boarded-up buildings, vacant lots, pot shops and liquor stores, but no youth spaces. All of that is a symptom of the disinvestment in the so-called inner city,” Hutchinson said. “We want all of those resources and services in our community because of the high rates of harm and victimization that young people are experiencing.”
Race and gender disparities
The city of Los Angeles and its police department have touted strong decline in overall homicides in recent years, but domestic violence killings, which overwhelmingly claim the lives of women, have remained a persistent issue. In 2022, LA recorded 392 homicides, according to LAPD’s annual homicide report, but by 2024 that number had declined to 284. The number of domestic killings remained consistent, though, with 32 murders in 2022 and 33 in 2024. Black women are disproportionately the victims of domestic homicides. Black women make up about 13.5% of the city’s female population, but a third of its female domestic homicide victims.
This trend also extends to the rest of the county. Black women had the highest homicide rate of any racial group in 2024, according to California department of health data. The only other demographics with high rates are Black and Latino men, who historically have made up most of the region’s homicide victims.
It’s not just LA. Black women across the US have long had a higher risk of being killed than women of other races, according to a 2024 analysis of homicide data by the Violence policy center. That year about 700 Black women and about 1500 white women were killed by men. Black women make up 13% of the US female population, white women make up 55%. Black women were most often killed with a gun, by a man they knew.
The city of LA says it’s working to address the high rates of violence by bolstering its response network for domestic violence victims, and by funding programs that can prevent gun violence in the neighborhoods where Black women and girls die most frequently.
The office of the mayor, Karen Bass, pointed to investments the city has made in its nearly 20-year-old gang reduction and youth development (GRYD) program, which operates programs throughout the city, including South Central. Though GRYD is mostly geared toward pulling Black and Latino men and teens out of the cycle of violence, staff also refers families to supportive programs. The program has helped bring down homicides in the city’s hardest-hit neighborhoods throughout South Central by almost 30% in 2025, the mayor’s office said.
California has tried to address the issue at a state level, when in 2023 lawmakers created the Ebony Alert, a first-in-the-nation emergency notification system specifically geared towards finding missing Black women and girls. Since the alert became law in 2024, it has been activated for 182 people. Of those, 175 have been found alive, one was found deceased, according to California highway patrol data.
Still, the racial and gender disparities in victims of violence remain.
Some cities and states have come up with frameworks to address the issue with more fervor. Minnesota created a taskforce made up of elected officials, nonprofit leaders and representatives from law enforcement agencies to specifically look into the killings and disappearances of Black women and girls. The group advises the state’s department of public safety on ways to reduce violence against them, and how to work with service providers to give tailored support to Black victims’ families and domestic violence survivors.
The Minnesota taskforce was in part created in memory of Brittany Clardy, an 18-year-old who was murdered in 2013. Clardy’s family reported her missing after she left to go to a nearby store but then stopped answering calls and texts. She was found dead in her car two weeks later.
The man who ultimately pleaded guilty to her murder was also convicted of murdering another woman, 24-year-old Klaressa Cook, who was found dead in the trunk of a car just months after Clardy.
In the years following Clardy’s killing, her sister, Lakeisha Lee, spoke in front of the state legislature and started a foundation to help support girls who are at risk of being sex-trafficked.
It’s not uncommon for these kinds of efforts to be spurred by people who’ve lost a mother, daughter or sister to violence, said Dr Brittany Lewis, founder and CEO of Research in Action.
“This happens because families endure going to committee hearings to convince people that the death of their family member matters,” she said. “And that what they need is much bigger than the band-aid solutions we’re producing.”
Cases left unsolved
Not only do Black women and girls face disproportionate rates of violence, but when they’re killed, their cases are less likely to be solved. In 2022, the Los Angeles police department solved all killings of Black female victims. But the next year, that rate declined to 90%. In 2024, it plummeted to 67% and in 2025, at a time when the number of homicides in the city was plummeting, just half of the killings of Black women and girls were solved, according to the LAPD’s annual homicide reports.
LA sheriff’s department numbers?
Shalissa Collier, whose daughter Mikeona Johnson was found dead in the trunk of her car in Los Angeles in September 2020, was determined to beat this trend.
After Mikeona’s death, Collier learned that she had long been abused by a former partner and that her daughter had filed for three separate restraining orders against the man.
Collier says she brought these findings to Los Angeles police, but six months later they came to her home to tell her that the department didn’t have any leads and would be closing the case, Collier said. “LAPD pissed me off. I can’t even sugarcoat it,” she recalled.
Collier began organizing candlelight vigils and press conferences in front of the LA county’s district attorney’s office. She also spoke with independent journalists and on the podcast Misogynoir Murders, which highlights the stories of missing and murdered Black women.
In February 2024, the roommate of Johnson and her partner, Phillip Charles Howze, went to police with new information, and Howze was arrested. He was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to 15 years to life.
With her daughter’s killer sentenced, Collier in October was finally ready to bury her daughter’s ashes, and she held a burial ceremony.
“I felt like it would be fitting to do it, especially after he got his time. Now she can finally rest,” Collier said.
Misogynoir Murders started out as an attempt to center the stories of Black women and girls in the true-crime genre. Now, host Ronnetta Rideout says she sees it as a community service for the families that want to keep the stories of their daughters, sisters and mothers alive.
“[Black women] were still very underrepresented even in stories, even though we’re overrepresented in the actual data,” Rideout said.
LAPD declined to respond to questions about its initial decision to close Mikeona Johnson’s case. When asked about the department’s approach to solving the homicides of Black women and girls specifically, public information officer Jeff Lee said LAPD “takes all acts of violence seriously, and every homicide is thoroughly investigated. Detectives follow all available leads and work to identify those responsible, leaving no stone unturned in the pursuit of justice.”
He did not offer specifics on whether or not the recommendations from the 2023 city report have been implemented within the department.
California highway patrol said it is still actively investigating Tioni Theus’s murder.
‘We can’t be silent any more’
While Tioni’s family awaits answers from law enforcement, they say members of the South Los Angeles community, too, have a role in preventing violence against Black women and girls, whether it’s reporting underage girls on sex-trafficking corridors to police or supportive services, calling out predators who are grooming teens online, or sharing information that can lead to an arrest.
“I feel like as a community we can’t be silent any more,” Kincy said. “We can’t wait for politicians, lawmakers or even the police. We have to stand up and make people accountable.”
Michael Dolphin, Tioni’s great-uncle, agreed. “This is not a white folks problem, it’s not an LAPD problem, it’s not a Mayor [Karen] Bass problem. It’s a community problem, because someone knows what happened,” he said.
He wants the city to pour resources into programs that can rehabilitate young people who have been repeatedly arrested or are currently incarcerated. These investments, he hopes, can stop teen boys from becoming violent.
“We need to figure out ways to catch these kids earlier,” he said. “We need to figure out how to get involved sooner and provide alternatives to hanging out on the street.”
Dolphin remembers his niece as a smart, loving teenager. He saw her often in the mornings, on her way to school, when she would come by to visit her great-grandmother, whom Dolphin was caring for. They would share breakfast and go over her homework together. “She liked her schoolwork,” he said. “And big mama’s house was a quiet, peaceful refuge for her.”
Kincy says she hopes that the story of her bubbly, sometimes clumsy teen cousin who walked on her tiptoes can lead to greater awareness around the increased risk of violence and exploitation Black teen girls and young women face and shed light on stories that received less news coverage than Tioni’s.
“When Tioni’s story hit, it resonated with people because it happened to their kid as well and they didn’t get the exposure,” Kincy said. “We can bring light to these stories through her.”

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: It’s not too late to get it: what to know about getting the flu vaccine this year
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Adrienne Matei
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
Influenza arrived early this year, popping up on the west coast “about two and a half months earlier than normal”, says Dr Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota – a timeline not seen since the 2010 season.
And while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) still considers flu activity overall to be low, with 16,000 recorded flu-related hospitalizations so far, it expects infections to keep rising in the coming weeks as the virus spreads through the midwest and east coast.
While factors like travel patterns may have contributed to this early season, “there’s not a completely ironclad explanation for why this has occurred,” notes Dr Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease specialist at Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.
Timing isn’t the only unusual thing about this year’s flu – here’s what you need to know.
What’s different about this year’s flu: a mutated H1N1 virus
This year’s dominant flu strain is an H1N1 virus carrying a mutation known as G155E. According to Adalja, there’s no evidence that the mutation makes the virus more likely to cause severe illness, though it resembles features of H1N1 strains that circulated before 2009.
Early research suggests that teens and young adults under 25 “have less immunity” to this strain, Adalja says – the virus may be “more able to get around some of the immunity that people have from prior infections and prior vaccinations”, he says.
So far, there has been one reported US pediatric influenza-associated death this season, of an elementary-aged child from outside the Denver metro area. An estimated 24,000 people, 198 of them children, died of flu-related illness in the 2025-26 season.
According to Dr Alex L Greninger, head of the division of infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington, differences in how people respond to the flu have more to do with the individual infected – people with diminished cardio respiratory capacity, for example – than with the virus itself. “If you’ve recently had heart disease, when the flu comes it can push you over the edge in terms of heart and lung function,” he says.
The vaccine was developed before this mutation – but is still worth it
Every February, the World Health Organization (WHO) brings together experts who review global flu data and create an informed, but not completely certain, forecast as to which three flu variants they expect to see dominate the northern hemisphere in the coming winter.
“We make vaccines for flu the same way we made them in the 1940s; we use very old technologies that require a long lead time,” says Adalja.
This year, their forecast was off. “This particular variant really emerged after we already had chosen what was in the vaccine,” notes Osterholm, meaning that this year’s vaccine is a weaker match against infection.
But, Osterholm says, the question is not about whether the vaccine works or doesn’t work, but about it being less protective. Being vaccinated is like “having your seatbelt attached against the flu. It protects you against severe disease, hospitalization, and death.”
This year’s weak vaccine-flu match is not related to the US leaving the WHO. “Even though the US left the WHO, which is the wrong decision for a number of reasons, the CDC did participate in the WHO strain selection process,” says Adalja. “So it wasn’t as if they were not part of that decision-making … The strains that are used in the northern hemisphere that are being administered in the United States are identical to the ones being administered in Canada and Mexico, for example.”
This is the first year that an mRNA-based flu vaccine, developed by Moderna, is also available to the public. Called mFlusiva, the vaccine is recommended for adults 50 and older, a group that faces the highest risk from flu, and has been shown to produce milder reactions than mRNA Covid vaccines, Osterholm says.
While mFlusiva was also developed prior to the flu’s mutation, Adalja hopes that mRNA technology will help future vaccine strain selections occur closer to the start of flu season, improving the quality of the match.
When should people get vaccinated this year?
Because it takes about two weeks after a vaccine for your body to create enough antibodies to protect you, the time is near to guard yourself before the holiday season.
“Now is the time to get your vaccine,” says Osterholm. “Especially those under 25 should be encouraged to get vaccinated earlier than usual, meaning now.”
Osterholm encourages everyone to get both a Covid booster and their flu shot, saying he got his on the same day. It’s “not unexpected” to feel unwell for a day or two after your shots, he says. “Just know it’s a lot better to have a reaction, than to get the flu.”
If you get sick, at-home antigen tests for influenza, flu A, flu B and respiratory syncytial virus are all available. Experts agree that testing is worthwhile because knowing what strain you have can help your doctor prescribe useful antivirals like Tamiflu or Xofluza, which can reduce serious illness, hospitalizations and recovery time.
When ill, it’s important to stay at home to mitigate flu spread and to protect vulnerable people; if you must leave your home, Osterholm recommends wearing an N95 mask.
Where can people find trustworthy guidance on the flu?
While once people could reliably find information about the flu vaccine on the CDC’s website, this year, it’s a bit more complicated. In 2025, health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr fired every member of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and appointed his own picks. A federal court has since halted the new panel’s votes. As a result, the systems that normally advise Americans have stalled, with the CDC relying on last year’s flu recommendations.
“There is no [Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices]. It doesn’t exist in a sense,” says Osterholm.
Other major medical groups have stepped in to provide reliable information to the public. In September, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America issued coordinated recommendations. They drew on an evidence review by the Vaccine Integrity Project, an initiative at Osterholm’s research center. All four groups advise a flu shot for everyone six months and older, including pregnant people in any trimester.
Adalja advises people to start with those groups rather than the CDC. “Some of the data from the CDC is valid and can be trusted, but some of it can’t,” he says. For a layperson, “it’s hard to know whether this is something that’s been tainted by RFK Jr.”
And while this year, America’s exit from the WHO didn’t make a difference in the flu vaccine’s makeup, Adalja worries the break “will likely pose a problem when novel strains of flu arise outside the United States” in the future, he says.
It’s impossible to predict the trajectory of any flu season, though holiday travel is often linked with a boost in flu infections. Still, experts aren’t ruling out “a normal season in January and February”, Greninger conjectures. What’s clear is that precautions against the flu, from vaccination to hand-washing, masking, and staying home when sick, are as critical as ever.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he has spoken to Huang on Monday as the scandal reverberated across Silicon Valley and the Nvidia CEO faced an uncertain future.
“I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” Trump said during a White House briefing.
Trump said that the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) was “looking into” the issue, but provided few details. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said.
The remarks came after Trump threw his support behind Huang over the weekend, telling reporters on Sunday: “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.”
“I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump added, saying he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.
Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the US, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.
Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government, according to the New York Times. Trump was reportedly briefed on the relationship last year, the Times reported, but took no action. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are unrelated, with the latter being one of the world’s richest men and CEO of Nvidia, worth more than $4tn, for the past 33 years.
US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.
The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility. Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.
As news of the scandal broke over the weekend, Musk and prominent investors shared their support of Huang. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.
“Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted.
“Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post.
Bill Ackman, the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.
“He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Ackman posted. “He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward.”
Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.
China has meanwhile denied allegations of an intelligence operation targeting Huang, with the Associated Press reporting that foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations as “entirely baseless vilification and smearing”.
Nvidia and its chips have been an integral part of the AI boom in recent years, with hundreds of billions of dollars committed to building out projects such as datacenters and chip factories. In August, Nvidia agreed to provide a $105bn guarantee to help OpenAI lease an Ohio datacenter.
As Nvidia has grown in prominence, Huang has also become one of the world’s richest people and most influential figures in tech. He has taken calls from Trump in the middle of an all-hands company meeting and on stage at a conference, and attended state dinners with the president and accompanied him on a trip to China. Huang has also been a powerful voice on tech policy, weighing in on issues such as export controls of chips to China and regulation of open-source AI models.
Nvidia’s stock price fell on Monday as speculation swirled around the extent of damage from the affair. Shares of Nvidia, the second-most valuable company in the world, tumbled 4.2% and closed at their lowest level since 7 April as investors questioned Huang’s future.
Agencies contributed reporting
