https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.title: Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ after talks with Qatar PM
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ after talks with Qatar PM
Iranian officials dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as ‘fake news’ after the US president suggested a close to the war.
United States President Donald Trump has signalled that he considers the US-Israeli war against Iran “effectively” at an end, after meeting with mediators from Qatar.
In a surprise briefing on Monday, Trump reiterated his position that the US had destroyed Iran’s military. But his remarks suggested he faced pressure from allies in the Middle East to bring hostilities to a close.
“Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We’re just keeping it the status quo,” he said. “We’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”
The US president clarified that the “status quo” would involve continuing the US naval blockade against Iranian ports, as well as the newly announced Task Force Iron Gate, which seeks to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.
“Much was discussed with respect to the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said.
“Most importantly, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others would prefer the status quo, that we remain as is — in other words, a continuation of the greatest naval blockade in the history of our country. Probably in the history of the world.”
Trump’s comments come shortly after he and Vice President JD Vance hosted Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House to discuss the Iran war.
The prime minister posted on social media that he was “grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region”.
It is unclear whether Trump’s latest statements significantly change US posture in the war. Trump himself declined to commit to any long-term ceasefire.
“I don’t guarantee anything,” he told the White House briefing room. “But if we do have to go back in, we are locked and loaded and ready to go.”
Iranian officials, meanwhile, dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as a distraction. Both sides have claimed victory throughout the conflict.
“The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler,” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote in a post on social media.
“FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.”
Separately, through Iran’s state-aligned Tasnim News Agency, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to the situation, which he described as “neither war nor peace”.
Pezeshkian added that Iran was open to further negotiations but would not be coerced. “We will not surrender to force and bullying,” he said.
Since the war on Iran began on February 28, the conflict has spilled into surrounding countries and roiled international trade.
Almost as soon as the US and Israel began their attacks, Iran moved to shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for fossil fuels and fertiliser, among other goods.
Iran has also responded to US and Israeli strikes with missile and drone fire in countries like Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE, with many of the attacks targeting US military installations.
Other, related conflicts have since emerged. Saudi Arabia has renewed its fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis, and Israel began its occupation of southern Lebanon, as well as deadly airstrikes.
In the nearly nine months since the war began, the US offensive against Iran has grown sporadic, with intermittent exchanges of fire. In recent days, for instance, the Trump administration announced “minor strikes” against Iran’s Qeshm Island.
It also offered a $20m reward for the “information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel”.
After the Twelve-Day War in June 2025, Trump had claimed that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been obliterated. But he has since made curtailing Iran’s nuclear programme a central premise for the ongoing war.
Iran has long denied seeking a nuclear weapon, maintaining its uranium enrichment programme is for the purposes of civilian energy generation.
Officials in Iran, meanwhile, have pushed for the US to accept seven conditions in order to end the war.
They include lifting the US naval blockade, reparations for war-related damage, an end to sanctions against its economy and a cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon and Gaza.
Qatar has served as one of several key mediators in the conflict. Sheikh Mohammed, the prime minister, also serves as foreign minister and has been known to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.
In Monday’s closed-door meeting, he reportedly presented Trump with a two-day framework from Iran to end the war.
Afterwards, reporters asked Trump in the briefing room, “Why not just declare an end to the conflict and be done with it?”
Trump framed the continued US blockade as a question of regional security. He also called for a “long-term solution”, rather than a short-term one.
“We have some great allies there, and we have to make sure they’re not hurt, and they would be hurt,” he said.
“They are right now a lot safer than they were six months ago because Iran’s been very much decapitated. But there’s still the bully of the Middle East a little bit.”

https://taz.de/Die-Muellmetropole-Adana/.title: : Die Müllmetropole Adana
https://taz.de/Die-Muellmetropole-Adana/.author: Derya Türkmen
https://taz.de/Die-Muellmetropole-Adana/.text:
: Die Müllmetropole Adana
In der Millionenstadt in der Türkei wird ein goßer Teil des europäischen Plastikabfalls zu Geld gemacht. Natur und Bevölkerung profitieren davon nicht
I n der Luft von Adana hängt ein unerträglicher Plastikgeruch. So, dass es fast in der Nase brennt. Umut Özşimşek hockt am Rand eines Wasserkanals und fotografiert. Das Wasser ist dunkelbraun und wirkt eher dickflüssig. An der Oberfläche treiben weiße Schlieren. „Das kleine weiße Zeug da auf der Oberfläche, das ist Plastik. Mikroplastik“, sagt der 27-Jährige.
„Hier liegt alles dicht beieinander“, sagt Özşimşek und zeigt nach links. Dort steht das Fabrikgebäude von SASA, einem der größten Polyesterproduzenten der Türkei. Sein Finger wandert nach rechts, zum Recyclingareal Kemal Deniz, auf dem zahlreiche Betriebe Plastikabfälle sortieren und verarbeiten. Und dazwischen der Wasserkanal, in dem sich die Plastikreste sammeln. Ein Hirte zieht mit seiner Schafherde vorbei. Die Tiere grasen zwischen den Pflanzen und Plastikabfällen.
Özşimşek ist in der Millionenstadt im Süden der Türkei aufgewachsen. Seine Familie lebt seit Generationen in Adana. Heute ist er Generalkoordinator der Çukurova Ekoloji Hafıza Derneği, einer Umweltinitiative, die die Zerstörung der Natur in der Region dokumentiert. Sie nennt sich auch „Çukuravo“. Eine Anspielung auf den in Adana verbreiteten Ausruf „Aboooo!“. Den hört man hier, wenn jemand etwas kaum glauben kann.
Plastik: Der Kreislauf, der keiner ist?
Recycling oder Downcycling?
Aus einer Plastikflasche wird nicht automatisch eine neue. Häufig entstehen aus recyceltem Kunststoff andere Produkte, etwa Textilfasern, die später nur schwer wiederverwertet werden können. Das nennt man Downcycling. Selbst beim Recycling entstehen Abfälle und verschmutztes Abwasser. Ein geschlossener Kreislauf ist das nicht.
Nur neun Prozent
Weltweit wurden 2019 laut OECD lediglich neun Prozent des Plastikabfalls tatsächlich recycelt. Rund 19 Prozent wurden verbrannt, fast die Hälfte landete auf regulären Deponien. Weitere 22 Prozent wurden nicht ordnungsgemäß entsorgt.
Plastik und die Klimakrise
Kunststoff besteht überwiegend aus Erdöl und Erdgas. Förderung, Herstellung, Verarbeitung und Entsorgung verursachen Treibhausgase. 2019 war Plastik laut OECD für rund 3,4 Prozent der weltweiten Treibhausgasemissionen verantwortlich – etwa 1,8 Milliarden Tonnen CO₂-Äquivalente. Rund 90 Prozent davon entstanden bei Herstellung und Verarbeitung. (dt)
Das dürfte sich auch Özşimşek beim Anblick der Müllberge immer wieder denken. Die Initiative will eine Art Landschaftsgedächtnis der Region festhalten. Fotos, Videos und Forschungsberichte dokumentieren verschmutzte Gewässer, brennende Müllberge, die Zerstörung landwirtschaftlicher Flächen. Derzeit beschäftigt sich Çukuravo vor allem mit importiertem Plastikmüll. Für Özşimşek ist das Problem längst nicht auf die Recyclingareale begrenzt. Wenn dort Abfälle brennen, zieht der Rauch bis in die umliegenden Wohngebiete.
Ein großer Teil des Plastiks kommt aus Europa. Laut einer Auswertung des Basel Action Network exportierten die EU-Staaten 2025 rund 503.000 Tonnen Plastikabfälle in die Türkei, aus Großbritannien kamen weitere 139.000 Tonnen hinzu. Zusammen waren das fast 650.000 Tonnen. Und Deutschland war mit rund 154.000 Tonnen der größte einzelne Lieferant. Die Türkei ist damit der größte Abnehmer von Plastikmüll aus der EU.
Weltklimakonferenz in der Türkei
Politiker*innen und Expert*innen aus aller Welt treffen sich zur 31. UN-Klimakonferenz im türkischen Antalya. Vom 9. bis 20. November beraten Vertreter*innen aus rund 200 Staaten über den Kampf gegen die Erderhitzung. Die taz ist mit einem Team vor Ort. Verfolgen Sie unsere Berichterstattung auf unserem Schwerpunkt auf taz.de, auf klima.taz bei Instagram, im Podcast klima update°, im Newsletter TEAM ZUKUNFT, im werktäglichen E-Paper und in der Wochentaz.
Warum landet dieser ganze Müll ausgerechnet in Adana? Yaşar Gökoğlu kennt die Antwort. Der 78-Jährige hat einen weißen Schnurrbart, nennt sich selbst einen Sozialisten und stammt ebenfalls aus der Stadt. Heute engagiert er sich in der Adana Ekoloji Platformu, einem Zusammenschluss von Umweltaktivist:innen, der sich gegen die Umweltzerstörung in der Region einsetzt. Schon als er Kind war, habe es Recyclingbetriebe hier gegeben, erzählt er. Damals verarbeiteten sie vor allem Papier und Plastik, das örtliche Müllsammler zusammentrugen.
Doch als China 2018 wegen der Umwelt- und Gesundheitsbelastungen durch die Verarbeitung importierter Abfälle weitgehend aus dem Müllgeschäft ausstieg, musste Europa neue Abnehmer finden. Die Türkei bot sich an. Zwar gibt es auch in Istanbul, Izmir oder Gaziantep zahlreiche Recyclingbetriebe, doch in Adana konzentrieren sich besonders viele. Neben der bereits bestehenden Recyclingindustrie liegt das auch an der Nähe zum Hafen von Mersin. Dort kommen die europäischen Abfälle mit Containerschiffen an, Lastwagen bringen sie anschließend nach Adana.
Gökoğlu schätzt, dass inzwischen mehr als die Hälfte der türkischen Plastikmüllimporte hier landet. Genaue Zahlen gibt es jedoch nicht, da die türkischen Behörden die regionale Verteilung der importierten Abfälle nicht transparent offenlegen.
In den Betrieben würden Arbeiter ohne ausreichenden Arbeitsschutz Plastikabfälle von Hand sortieren und zerkleinern, erzählt Gökoğlu. Gegen den Plastikstaub verhüllten sie ihre Gesichter mit Tüchern, Atemschutzmasken hätten sie nicht. Schon 2022 dokumentierte Human Rights Watch ähnliche Zustände in Adanas Recyclingbetrieben. „Früher haben dort vor allem Kurd:innen gearbeitet“, sagt Gökoğlu. Heute seien es zunehmend Geflüchtete aus Syrien und Afghanistan, teils ohne Arbeitserlaubnis.
Was hinter den Toren geschieht, bleibt für Außenstehende weitgehend verborgen. Wie riskant Recherchen werden können, zeigte sich ebenfalls 2022: Zwei Journalist:innen wurden nach eigenen Angaben auf einem Recyclinggelände in Adana angegriffen und zeitweise festgehalten.
Yaşar Gökoğlu, Umweltaktivist
Besonders beschäftigen Gökoğlu die wiederkehrenden Brände in den Recyclingvierteln. Im September 2025 brannte es in Küçükdikili 48 Stunden lang, weitere Brände gab es im April 2026 in Sarıhamzalı und zuletzt am 2. November im Stadtteil Onur Mahallesi. Die Brände sind längst keine Seltenheit mehr. Einen Tag nach dem Feuer in Sarıhamzalı veröffentlichte die Adana Ekoloji Platformu eine Erklärung. Darin stellte sie zwei Fragen: Werden die Betriebe nicht ausreichend kontrolliert? Oder werden manche Brände absichtlich gelegt?
Die Initiative fordert seit Langem Aufklärung über die Brandursachen. Gökoğlu erzählt, dass er mit seinen Mitstreiter:innen versucht habe, die Berichte der Feuerwehr einzusehen. Die Stadtverwaltung habe die Herausgabe verweigert. Gökoğlu vermutet, dass manche Brände absichtlich gelegt werden, um nicht verwertbare Abfälle loszuwerden. Beweise dafür gibt es aber bislang nicht.
Während Gökoğlu und andere in Adana seit Jahren vor den Folgen des Müllhandels warnen, weist die türkische Regierung die Kritik zurück. Am 20. Oktober bezeichnete das staatliche Zentrum zur Bekämpfung von Desinformation Medienberichte über europäische Plastikmüllexporte und die Verschmutzung in der Türkei als „schwerwiegende Manipulation“. Importiert werden dürften nur saubere, sortierte und wiederverwertbare Abfälle. Die Einhaltung der Vorschriften werde streng überwacht. Eine Anfrage an die Stadtverwaltung in Adana blieb unbeantwortet.
22 Organisationen, darunter die Adana Ekoloji Platformu, forderten die Behörden in einer gemeinsamen Erklärung auf, sich die betroffenen Viertel selbst anzusehen und mit den Bewohner:innen zu sprechen.
Dass so viele die Erklärung mit ihrem Namen unterzeichneten, überraschte selbst Gökoğlu. Auch sein Name stand darunter. Am nächsten Tag saß er zu Hause und rechnete damit, dass die Polizei auftauchen könnte. „Doch die kam zum Glück nicht“, sagt er lächelnd.
Auch die Europäische Union nehme sich zu leicht aus der Verantwortung, findet Gökoğlu. Ab dem 21. November 2026 verbietet die EU nämlich den Export von Plastikmüll in Staaten außerhalb der OECD. Die Türkei aber gehört zu den Mitgliedstaaten der Internationalen Wirtschaftsorganisation und ist deshalb von dem Verbot ausgenommen. Für Malaysia, Indonesien und Vietnam, die bislang ebenfalls europäischen Plastikmüll aufnehmen, gilt das nicht. Gökoğlu befürchtet, dass die Abfälle, die Europa künftig nicht mehr dorthin exportieren darf, stattdessen noch häufiger in der Türkei landen.
Sedat Gündoğdu, Meeresbiologe
Mit dem Müll lässt sich nämlich Geld verdienen. Und dafür muss die EU der Türkei nicht einmal etwas bezahlen. Das Geschäft läuft zwischen Unternehmen: Europäische Firmen können ihre Plastikabfälle verkaufen und Entsorgungskosten sparen. Türkische Recyclingbetriebe bekommen günstig Rohstoff, den sie aufbereiten und weiterverkaufen. Allein 2024 importierte die Türkei Plastikabfälle im Wert von rund 194 Millionen US-Dollar aus aller Welt. Das ist der Wert des Mülls, nicht der Gewinn der Betriebe.
Eine vom ifo-Institut publizierte Untersuchung von Wirtschaftswissenschaftlern zeigt jedoch, dass die Rechnung für die Türkei nicht aufgeht. Zwar profitieren Unternehmen von den Plastikimporten: Sie kommen günstiger an Rohstoffe und können mehr produzieren. Den wirtschaftlichen Vorteil für das Land schätzen die Forschenden auf höchstens 116 Millionen US-Dollar. Das klingt nach viel Geld, ist aber kein Gewinn einzelner Betriebe, sondern ein geschätzter Nutzen für die gesamte Wirtschaft. Die Schäden durch Luftverschmutzung beziffern die Forschenden dagegen auf 558 bis 655 Millionen Dollar. Fast fünf- bis sechsmal so viel.
Gökoğlu holt mehrere Karteikarten aus seiner Tasche hervor, die er aus einer alten Papierverpackung in gleich große Stücke geschnitten hat. Auf einer hat er die Programmpunkte der bevorstehenden Weltklimakonferenz COP31 in Antalya notiert, die am Montag beginnt. Er liest sie laut vor: Klimafinanzierung. Investitionen in erneuerbare Energien. Grünes Wirtschaften. Hoffnung auf Veränderung macht ihm das nicht. „Der Kapitalismus versteht es, aus den Krisen Profit zu schlagen, die er selbst verursacht.“
Seine Hoffnung richtet sich stattdessen auf den alternativen Klimagipfel, die Halkların İklim Zirvesi. Dort sollen die Betroffenen der Klimakrise zu Wort kommen. Gökoğlu freut sich besonders auf den Austausch mit Kohlegegner:innen aus Kolumbien und Aktivist:innen aus Großbritannien. „Schulter an Schulter“ wolle man dort gemeinsam kämpfen. Schon beim vergangenen Klimagipfel im brasilianischen Belém hätten sich Umweltbewegungen international vernetzt, mit indirekter Unterstützung von Präsident Lula da Silva, erzählt er. Von der türkischen Regierung erwarte er solche Unterstützung allerdings nicht.
„Was hat die COP in Aserbaidschan verändert? Oder in Katar, den Vereinigten Arabischen Emiraten und Ägypten?“, fragt Sedat Gündoğdu rhetorisch. Auf seinem Schreibtisch steht eine weiße Metallflasche mit der Aufschrift „COP17“. Der Meeresbiologe forscht an der Çukurova-Universität seit Jahren zu Plastikverschmutzung und internationalem Müllhandel. Klimakonferenzen könnten durchaus Veränderungen anstoßen, sagt er. Doch freiwillige Verpflichtungen reichten längst nicht mehr aus.
Wie stark die Recyclingbetriebe das Wasser belasten, zeigen Gündoğdus Untersuchungen. In einem Kanal am Recyclingareal Kemal Deniz, wo zuvor auch Umut Özşimşek die weißen Schlieren fotografierte, fanden die Forscher unterhalb der Anlagen zehnmal so viel Mikroplastik wie oberhalb. An anderen Stellen in Adana war die Belastung sogar bis zu 132-mal so hoch. Beim Zerkleinern und Waschen der Plastikabfälle entsteht verschmutztes Abwasser, das nach Gündoğdus Angaben teilweise illegal in die Kanäle geleitet wird.
167 Recyclingbetriebe soll es offiziell in Adana geben. Doch als Gündoğdu und seine Kolleg:innen selbst durch die Viertel zogen und nachzählten, kamen sie auf mehr als 500. Viele davon arbeiteten ohne Lizenz, sagt er. Und nur etwa 70 Betriebe hätten eine Genehmigung, ihr Abwasser in die Kanalisation einzuleiten. Stattdessen lande verschmutztes Wasser immer wieder illegal in den Kanälen und Flüssen der Stadt, berichtet Gündoğdu.
Und über genau diese Kanäle gelangt das verschmutzte Wasser in den Seyhan-Fluss und schließlich ins Mittelmeer. Dort tragen Meeresströmungen die Plastikpartikel weiter, entlang der Küste von Mersin bis nach Antalya und darüber hinaus. Vor der Küstenstadt Alanya fanden Gündoğdu und seine Kolleg:innen an der Meeresoberfläche bis zu 65-mal höhere Mikroplastikkonzentrationen als die üblichen Vergleichswerte. Auch vor Zypern seien Plastikpartikel beobachtet worden, berichtet er.
Dabei ist Mikroplastik nur ein Teil des Problems. Denn Plastik wird überwiegend aus Erdöl und Erdgas hergestellt und enthält zahlreiche chemische Zusatzstoffe. Beim Zerkleinern und Waschen können diese ins Abwasser gelangen. Gündoğdu warnt vor den Folgen für Böden und Pflanzen, wenn belastetes Wasser zur Bewässerung genutzt wird. Ob und in welchem Umfang kleinste Plastikpartikel von Pflanzen aufgenommen werden, müsse überhaupt erst noch untersucht werden.
„Deutschland verhält sich in dieser Frage widersprüchlich“, sagt Gündoğdu. Das Land gebe sich umweltbewusst, verbrenne jedoch große Mengen Müll und exportiere Plastikabfälle in die Türkei. Für ihn ist das eine neue Form des Kolonialismus. Denn die europäischen Müllimporte verschmutzten nicht nur die Umwelt, sondern untergrüben auch die heimische Abfallwirtschaft, betont auch er.
„Null Abfall“ auf der COP31
Währenddessen präsentiert sich die Türkei international als Vorreiterin in Sachen Abfallvermeidung. „Sıfır Atık“, auf Deutsch „Null Abfall“, heißt das 2017 unter der Schirmherrschaft von First Lady Emine Erdoğan gestartete Programm. Bei der COP31 ist ihm sogar ein eigener Tag gewidmet. Landesweit sollen Behörden, Schulen und Betriebe ihre Abfälle trennen und recyceln.
Aber ist Zero Waste überhaupt möglich? „Natürlich ist null Abfall möglich“, sagt Gündoğdu. In der Natur diene das, was ein Organismus ausscheidet, einem anderen als Lebensgrundlage. Bei Plastik sei das anders. Nicht jeder Kunststoff lasse sich wiederverwerten, und selbst beim Recycling blieben Reste zurück. Das Problem lasse sich deshalb nicht allein durch Recycling lösen. Statt immer mehr Plastik herzustellen, müsse vor allem der Verbrauch von Einwegkunststoffen und Verpackungen sinken. Dafür brauche es wiederverwendbare Verpackungen und Alternativen zu Kunststoff.
Doch die Entwicklung geht in eine andere Richtung. In Ceyhan und Yumurtalık, nicht weit von Adana, sind neue Anlagen zur Kunststoffproduktion und zur Herstellung petrochemischer Rohstoffe geplant. Schon jetzt exportiert die Türkei Kunststoffprodukte unter anderem nach Deutschland und Großbritannien. Aus denselben Ländern importiert sie wiederum Plastikmüll. Und nun soll noch mehr Kunststoff hergestellt werden. „Wie soll so weniger Abfall entstehen?“, fragt Gündoğdu.
Und was ist mit dem Mikroplastik, das längst in Gewässern und Böden steckt? Lässt es sich wieder entfernen? „Unmöglich. Dafür ist es zu spät“, sagt Gündoğdu. Einmal in der Umwelt, verteilen sich die winzigen Partikel immer weiter. Ein Teil sinkt auf den Meeresgrund und lagert sich dort ab. „Wir hinterlassen den kommenden Generationen ein verschmutztes und giftiges Erbe“, sagt er.
In Şakirpaşa ist Umut Özşimşek zwischen Bergen aus Plastikabfällen unterwegs. Zerfetzte Folien, Polyesterpullover und Verpackungsreste liegen auf dem Boden. Dazwischen eine kleine Taschenwaage und Waschmittelverpackungen mit britischem Logo. Auf vielen Verpackungen: das Recyclingzeichen. Ein Großteil der Abfälle hier in Şakirpaşa stamme aus Großbritannien, sagt Özşimşek.
Viele Kurd:innen betroffen
Eigentlich sollten sie wiederverwertet werden. Und was die Recyclingbetriebe nicht verwerten können, landet offenbar auch anscheinend einfach am Straßenrand. Er habe sogar schon Krankenversicherungskarten gefunden, mit Namen und persönlichen Daten der Versicherten. Özşimşek schüttelt den Kopf: „Solche Karten kann man doch gar nicht recyceln!“
Doch Şakirpaşa ist auch ein Wohnviertel, in dem nach seinen Angaben überwiegend kurdische Familien leben, die in der Türkei in vielen gesellschaftlichen Bereichen benachteiligt werden. Kurd:innen sind oft Repressionen und Diskriminierungen ausgesetzt, etwa auch bei der Wohnungs- und Arbeitssuche. Hinzu kommt, dass vielen Familien schlicht das Geld fehlt. Wegziehen aus dem Müllviertel könnten viele deshalb nicht. „Wohin sollen diese Menschen gehen? In ein Hotel?“, fragt Özşimşek sarkastisch.
Ein paar Kilometer weiter, in Küçükdikili, türmt sich hinter dem Metallzaun eines Recyclingbetriebs ein riesiger Müllberg. Der Geruch nach verbranntem Kunststoff ist kaum auszuhalten. Gleich nebenan spielen Kinder vor einer Grundschule. Was mit dem Müllberg geschehen soll, weiß auch Özşimşek nicht genau, doch er befürchtet, dass die Abfälle irgendwann verbrannt werden.
Plötzlich tauchen zwei Männer auf. Sie schauen misstrauisch und kommen näher. Für Özşimşek ist klar: schnell weg hier. „Mit diesen Leuten ist nicht zu spaßen. Mit denen will man nichts zu tun haben“, sagt er.
Nicht weit entfernt erzählt eine Bewohnerin, die anonym bleiben möchte, von dem Gestank, der manchmal den ganzen Ort erfülle. Immer wieder habe sie Kopfschmerzen. Ob es Migräne sei oder die Beschwerden mit der Verbrennung von Plastik zusammenhingen? Sie zuckt mit den Schultern. Eines aber sei für sie klar: Wenn es so weitergehe, sehe die Zukunft ihrer Kinder düster aus.
Für Özşimşek ist die Verschmutzung auch eine Frage grundlegender Rechte: Sie beeinträchtige die Gesundheit der Menschen, ihr Wohnen und die Bildung der Kinder. „Die einen machen Gewinn. Und die andern müssen eben den Preis zahlen“, sagt er. Für ihn gibt es deshalb nur eine Lösung. „Und die heißt Systemwandel“, sagt Özşimşek.
Einmal, erzählt er, habe er eine britische Person nach Şakirpaşa begleitet. Angesichts der Müllberge habe diese ihn gefragt, wie er sich denn dabei fühle. Özşimşek habe dann die Frage zurückgegeben: „Wie fühlt es sich denn für dich so an?“

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Pope meets with clergy abuse survivors in Argentina
During private meetings with survivors, Pope Leo XIV pledged to reinforce safeguards and listen to victims.
Pope Leo XIV has met with five survivors of clerical sexual abuse on the second day of his historic visit to Argentina.
The private meetings in Buenos Aires on Monday were the first of several talks the pope is planning to hold with abuse survivors during his 12-day tour of Latin America, according to the Vatican.
“The Pope spoke individually with each of them, listened to their words and to the painful stories of their experiences, as well as to their proposals for strengthening paths towards healing within the Church,” the Vatican said in a statement.
The closed-door meetings followed a historic open-air mass that drew an estimated 2.5 million people to Avenida del Libertador, a major boulevard in the capital, at the Monumento de los Espanoles. It was the country’s first papal liturgy in nearly 40 years.
The meetings with survivors respond to the pope’s desire to “express his closeness to those who have suffered”, build paths to healing and ensure the church is a safe and “spiritually healthy” place, the Holy See Press Office said in October.
Leo, the first pope born in the United States, has consistently met with survivors during foreign visits as part of a wider outreach aiming to repair global relations and restore the Catholic Church’s credibility. Lawsuits, widespread sexual abuse and cover-ups have sullied its reputation over the last three decades.
While clergy abuse cases are difficult to track globally, a 2021 independent inquiry found there were an estimated 216,000 victims of the French Catholic Church’s clergy alone between 1950 and 2020. Earlier research found more than 10,600 people were abused by Catholic priests in the US between 1950 and 2002, while Australia counted 6,875 victims of Catholic clergy, religious and lay church workers between 1980 and 2015, according to a 2019 German study.
During the meeting, which lasted more than an hour, Leo, 71, listened to victims’ testimonies and reiterated his pledge to strengthen safeguarding in the Catholic Church. Before being named pope, Leo served as president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America.
Argentina is the second stop on Leo’s three-country tour, which began in Uruguay and will wrap up in Peru.
His visit was the first by a pontiff since Pope John Paul II’s trip in 1987.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says US war in Iran ‘effectively over’ as he plays down escalation concerns
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump has said that the war in Iran is “effectively over” as he played down concerns that the US would escalate its military campaign against Tehran after the midterm elections.
During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and that an escalation was not needed.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House.
The remarks followed talks in the Oval Office with the Qatari prime minister, Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who has lobbied Trump alongside other Gulf countries not to resume the fighting against Iran.
“We’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon,” he added.
Trump has frequently exaggerated claims about the status of negotiations with Iran, saying a final peace deal was imminent dozens of times during the nearly nine-month long war.
The US had continued to move troops to the Middle East in the run-up to the midterm elections. There was speculation that the Trump administration was waiting for the elections to take place before resuming a military campaign, in order to prevent a backlash at the polls.
Republicans were nevertheless routed in a historic defeat in which they lost both houses of Congress, with the vice-president, JD Vance, declaring soon after that the Iran war was a key reason for the defeats.
Trump earlier on Monday said on Truth Social that the leaders of Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, and Kuwait would prefer the “status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History”.
He repeated a mantra that Iran would not be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon, and added that if the situation changed then the US was ready to resume full-scale military action against Iran.
“At this point, however, that seems to be quite unlikely,” he continued. “Israel, and the entire Middle East, are protected from Iranian danger and threats. We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected. At the conclusion of this Military Engagement, the American People, and the World, will be far safer and more secure.”

Le 17 octobre, en fin de manifestation, elles ont été violemment blessées par des grenades de désencerclement projetées par des CRS sur le boulevard Dugommier, dans le premier arrondissement de Marseille.
En l’espace de trente minutes, le 17 octobre, trois femmes ont été blessées par des CRS, dans le premier arrondissement de Marseille. Stationnés vers la station de métro Noailles, les fonctionnaires ont procédé à plusieurs tirs de gaz lacrymogène et de grenades de désencerclement en direction du boulevard Dugommier, tandis que la foule se dispersait.
Deux de ces victimes ont déposé plainte contre X ce lundi 9 novembre pour des faits de « violences volontaires ayant entraîné une mutilation ou une infirmité permanente »....

Hungarian police reportedly detain brother of ex-PM Viktor Orban
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban has accused the country’s new government of “political persecution” after the reported arrest of his younger brother.
Hungarian police arrested Aron Orban on Monday on suspicion of people smuggling, among other offences, according to a press report shared by Prime Minister Peter Magyar. Viktor Orban’s staunch opposition to immigration defined his 16 years in power that ended in defeat at elections in April.
News of the arrest was first reported by Kontroll, a news site owned by Magyar’s brother, Marton. Police carried out raids involving Aron Orban’s business associates but did not confirm whether he was among those detained, local media reported.
Viktor Orban accused the government of arresting his brother as a way to “divert attention” from other issues.
“I am the real target. My younger brother is simply being used to get to me,” he wrote on X.
Like other members of the Orban family, Aron built several successful businesses during his brother’s rule.
Last year, an investigation by news site Telex linked Aron Orban and his business associates to an alleged scheme involving visas for foreign guest workers.
Authorities said they had detained four people suspected of people smuggling.
Pro-EU conservative Magyar won a landslide election victory in April, ending 16 years of Orban’s rule, after promising to investigate his predecessor’s alleged corruption and abuse of power while in office.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Michael Carrick facing Manchester United axe amid review by Jason Wilcox
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Exclusive by Jamie Jackson
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Manchester United are moving towards sacking Michael Carrick, though no final decision has been made by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, who is leading the review after the head coach was given the Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa games to turn results around.
Wilcox has been consulting with Omar Berrada, the chief executive, before a recommendation regarding Carrick is made to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy.
If Carrick is removed, Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a potential candidate as it is understood the USA head coach is open to the position, while sources indicate that Eddie Howe also remains on the radar of Wilcox too.
The former Newcastle manager is taking a break from the game but would consider the job if offered it. United are in the Premier League relegation zone and have three victories in 15 games in all competitions. Carrick came close to being removed after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October. But after Wilcox and Berrada met the following day at the training ground to discuss his position, Carrick was given the three games until the international break to prove he and the players could reverse a dismal start.
A defeat, a win and a draw in those matches plus the team’s displays in each compounded with the overall run of form has moved Wilcox and Berrada towards a position where they are minded to remove Carrick. There is a growing expectation within the club that he will lose his job.
The final decision is yet to be made, though. When contacted on Monday night by the Guardian the club declined to comment.
In what may prove Carrick’s final three games in charge, United lost 2-0 at Chelsea, beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford and drew 4-4 at home against Villa on Sunday. In each game United were uneven. At Chelsea, Carrick’s side impressed in the first half but failed to convert chances before conceding twice after the interval, the second from a penalty after Lisandro Martínez was sent off.
In the Roma victory they were 2-0 behind in a poor opening 45 minutes before three goals in a rousing second one. On Sunday United twice trailed by two goals and entered added time 4-2 down, strikes from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu rescuing a point.
After the Roma game Carrick urged his team to build momentum but within four minutes against Villa they were 2-0 down, continuing a pattern of conceding very early. In the 4-1 defeat at Como> last month, Nico Paz scored after two minutes. This followed Pablo Barrios’s opener one minute into the 2-0 defeat at Atlético Madrid> the previous week.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/9.text:
Saudi Arabia reports new attack on key East-West pipeline
The oil pipeline runs through the desert to the coast and is essential for bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia’s critical East-West oil pipeline has suffered another attack, according to state media.
An official at the Saudi Ministry of Energy said that the pipeline was targeted in the Medina region in the west of the country on Monday, causing a “limited fire” that was extinguished, the Saudi Press Agency reported.
“No injuries or fatalities were reported, and pipeline operations were unaffected,” it said.
The report did not identify the party behind the attack, but fighting continues to intensify between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government coalition that it backs, and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
The pipeline is essential for bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, which remains tightly constricted by the US-Israel war on Iran. It has come under attack several times as the war on Iran fuels a global energy crisis.
The Houthis have also repeatedly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, including refineries and storage facilities, with drones and missiles.
The 1,200km (745-mile) pipeline runs through the desert across the Arabian Peninsula. It was shut down for several days in September after drone attacks, which Saudi Arabia said were launched from Iraq.
Since the conflict disrupted oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, Riyadh has rerouted about 4 million barrels per day of crude via the East-West pipeline to Yanbu, equivalent to about 4 percent of global supply.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: M John Harrison becomes first science fiction author to win the Booker prize
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Emma Loffhagen
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.
Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.
Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.
The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.
Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”
Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.
This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.
Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.
His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”
Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.
The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.
The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.
It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.
- The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.title: Placé en redressement judiciaire, le BHV ferme ses portes à cause d’un problème d’assurance
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
L’enseigne, placée en redressement judiciaire depuis le début du mois, a temporairement fermé ses portes ce lundi 9 novembre à 16 heures pour une régularisation d’assurance.
Le BHV, emblématique grand magasin de Paris, a fermé ce lundi à 16 heures pour une « régularisation administrative » temporaire, en raison d’une question d’assurance, a indiqué l’Agence France presse (AFP).
La fermeture concerne le BHV Marais, au centre de Paris, et celui de Parly 2, dans le centre commercial des Yvelines, qui « doivent fermer ce soir par précaution pour nos équipes et nos clients : une de nos polices d’assurance n’a pas pu être transférée dans le cadre du redressement judiciaire en cours », a indiqué le président de l’enseigne, Karl-Stéphane Cottendin, dans un message aux salariés ensuite transféré à l’AFP.
Un magasin vide de son personnel et de ses clients
La société SEGM BHV avait été placée en redressement judiciaire par le tribunal des activités économiques de Paris le 2 novembre dernier. Le chiffre d’affaires quotidien de l’entreprise avait chuté de 95 % en un an. La procédure, qui intervenait après la reconnaissance de la faillite et était souhaitée par les représentants du personnel, permet l’ouverture d’une période d’observation de six mois, renouvelable six mois, afin de déterminer si le magasin peut être sauvé.
Un plan de continuation du groupe peut ensuite être présenté au tribunal. Un plan de relance avait été présenté à l’été par la direction du BHV Marais, mais un manque de trésorerie en avait empêché la réalisation.
Le 9 novembre, une journaliste de l’AFP avait constaté la fermeture du magasin parisien avant 18 heures, vide de son personnel et de ses clients, sans pour autant qu’une information ait été affichée à destination de ces derniers.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: M John Harrison’s Booker prize-winner is weird, challenging and strikingly topical
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Justine Jordan
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
A Booker prize for M John Harrison, at 81 the oldest ever winner, symbolises an extraordinary 60-year journey from the margins into the limelight, without ever compromising on a literary vision that remains deeply weird and unique. The End of Everything is baffling, unnerving, confusing – very purposefully so. It follows two lost souls on the Kent coastline, beachcomber Phillip and his artist aunt Marnie, decades after alien entities called the iGhetti have leaked into our world and triggered a slow-motion social collapse. The City of London is a battle zone; strange biological “artefacts” are washing up from the sea; people are unpredictably affected by episodes of psychic rupture that they call, with classic British understatement, a “bad patch”.
But in the midst of catastrophe, what can one do but try to keep calm and carry on? In the real world, we’re currently supposed to be gathering our government-mandated three-day stockpile, though we’re not sure for what emergency – take your pick. And you can take your pick as to what the iGhetti might symbolise – late-stage capitalism? We are told they became more forceful in the 1980s, and cluster around the financial district. Brexit? In this novel, the continent does indeed appear to be cut off from England. Climate degradation? AI? The artefact that Phillip pulls out of the sea, hoping to sell it on the black market, shows the mimicry and uncanny self-actualisation of a large language model.
Some have balked at a novel where none of the characters knows what’s going on, and the prose scrupulously refuses to make things any clearer for the reader. “None of this made any sense to Marnie. In that, she shared the situation of around 8 billion other human beings on the planet.” Harrison has always traded in unknowing: in Climbers, his brilliant 1989 novel about his passion for rock climbing, by the end all the main character has learned is that “I didn’t know anything about anything”.
But Harrison’s own description of The End of Everything – “What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?” – is a strikingly topical question for 2026. It’s precisely the uncertainty, the sudden violence, the sense that something incomprehensible is happening out of the corner of one’s eye, that makes it resonate so deeply. In the postwar period, writers such as JG Ballard and Nevil Shute channelled fears of ecological breakdown and nuclear armageddon. Now, it’s Everything.
Harrison started out in science fiction – a genre famously overlooked by the Booker – publishing his first short story in Science Fantasy magazine in 1966, and becoming part of the 70s SF New Wave with Ballard and Michael Moorcock. You can find the operatic wonder and alienation of space opera in The End of Everything, though here trained on Earth: in the wake of the iGhetti, “the night was crawling with new constellations”. (A sentence that made me think of Elon Musk’s thousands of satellites.) Phillip the beachcomber – the broken man looking for revelation and a change of fortune in his shoreline discoveries – is reminiscent of the noirish space wanderers in Harrison’s back catalogue.
From the beginning, though, Harrison butted at genre conventions, having more in common with the mavericks of modernism and existentialism: Olivia Laing put it perfectly, describing him as “the missing evolutionary link between William Burroughs and Virginia Woolf”. (Moorcock had him as “an anarchist aesthete”.) The SF Kefahuchi Tract trilogy in the noughties, and 2020’s Goldsmiths-winning The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again – an uneasy prequel to The End of Everything – brought rising acclaim for the delicate control of his understatedly beautiful prose as well as his visionary ideas.
Harrison is also a wonderful landscape writer, and in this novel his style is more visual and cinematic than ever. There’s a great depth of experience here – eight decades of seeing – with the effects of certain scenes closer to paintings than prose.
The most capacious pigeonhole for his work over the decades is the one titled “Weird literature”, taking in elements of SF, fantasy and horror, often through a politically aware lens. As Harrison declared in his 2023 “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here, “The Weird is a way of writing about the real” – however unreal it may feel. This Booker win is an unexpected but fitting reward for a spectacular novel and career. Harrison may not have courted success, but it’s found him.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/cyberattaq.title: Cyberattaques contre des congélateurs : l’Iran responsable, pointe Jean-Noël Barrot
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/cyberattaq.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/cyberattaq.text:
Des juges d’instruction ont été chargés, ce lundi 9 novembre, d’enquêter sur les cyberattaques d’ampleur ayant visé des réfrigérateurs connectés de supermarchés en octobre, les investigations s’orientant vers l’Iran, selon le ministère des Affaires étrangères.
Plusieurs supermarchés en France, mais aussi en Belgique, en Estonie, en Finlande, en Irlande, en Italie, au Luxembourg, aux Pays-Bas, au Portugal et en Suède ont subi, ces dernières semaines, une hausse des températures des réfrigérateurs et congélateurs commandée à distance, provoquant d’importantes pertes alimentaires.
Des chambres froides d’un prestataire de l’Établissement français du sang contenant des stocks de sang avaient aussi subi une cyberattaque. Deux groupes de hackers russes l’ont revendiquée, sans que ça ne soit confirmé par les autorités françaises. Le Kremlin a démenti le 5 novembre 2026 être impliqué dans ces cyberattaques, estimant qu’accuser Moscou était « absurde ».
L’ambassadeur d’Iran convoqué
Le parquet de Paris dirige en ce moment ses investigations vers une autre piste, incriminant directement l’Iran, et a ouvert une information judiciaire visant notamment « le chef du groupe iranien Shahid Kaveh, unité cyber offensive affiliée au Centre électronique et cyber du Corps des Gardiens de la Révolution (CGRI-CEC) » et « ses deux adjoints », a précisé la procureure Laure Beccuau dans un communiqué publié ce 9 novembre.
L’Iran est « responsable » de l’attaque contre les frigos connectés en France, confirme de son côté le chef de la diplomatie française. « Je suis en mesure de confirmer que la responsabilité de cette attaque revient au corps des Gardiens de la révolution de la République islamique d’Iran. C’est une attaque d’une ampleur inédite et d’une agressivité inédite », a déploré Jean-Noël Barrot.
« Nous avons évidemment, c’est la moindre des choses, convoqué lundi l’ambassadeur d’Iran en France pour protester très vivement contre cet acte extrêmement grave. Nous prendrons des sanctions à l’échelle européenne contre tous les responsables de cette attaque », a ajouté le ministre.
Le journal des intelligences libres
« C’est par des informations étendues et exactes que nous voudrions donner à toutes les intelligences libres le moyen de comprendre et de juger elles-mêmes les événements du monde. »
Tel était « Notre but », comme l’écrivait Jean Jaurès dans le premier éditorial de l’Humanité, le 18 avril 1904. 122 ans plus tard, il n’a pas changé.

"We’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon," he said during a news conference.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Auckland hit by swarms of bees after milder than usual New Zealand winter
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Engulfing parked cars and blanketing inner-city street signs – New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland, is in the midst of an unusually large bee swarming season, that experts say has been exacerbated by a milder than usual winter.
The Auckland Beekeepers Association says it is fielding five to 10 calls a day, requesting assistance to remove swarms of bees – with individual members of the association being contacted for help as well.
“In past years, it was under five a day,” said Bryan Lang, the association’s swarm control coordinator, adding the team has now dealt with at least 100 call-outs.
In October, a swarm plastered the back of a parked car in Birkenhead for two hours according to witnesses. A woman inside was napping at the time, Lang understands.
“I’m surprised she didn’t hear them because they’re pretty loud,” he said.
A month earlier, a swarm took over a sign at a busy intersection on Auckland’s major commercial thoroughfare, Queen Street, forcing pedestrians to reroute.
During spring and early summer, bees can “swarm” – a natural occurrence which sees part of a colony that has outgrown its hive abandon it in search of a new home or extra food. The mass of insects will temporarily find a place to land away from their hive, while scout bees search for an appropriate dwelling.
“As a beekeeper, you don’t want them to swarm because you’re losing two-thirds of your bees, and right at the time when they should be bringing honey in for you,” said Lang. “And it’s not great for your neighbours either.”
Public awareness is growing over why bees swarm, and what to do should one happen to take over part of your garden or street, and according to Lang, many are taking to social media bee swarming pages and local beekeeping clubs to appeal for help.
The association’s president, Ken Brown, says when bees swarm in the countryside, no one really notices, but “townies” are not so familiar.
“If you don’t know about bees – how they’re only defensive – then you might be intimidated with thousands of venomous insects flying around,” he said, adding that a colony of bees is at its most placid when swarming.
Brown believes a much milder winter and start to spring has led to bees swarming weeks earlier than usual, and larger numbers of bees splitting off from their hives. New Zealand experienced its third warmest winter on record in 2026, according to Earth Sciences NZ. Other parts of the world are seeing similar behavioural shifts in bees, including in North America, as global warming leads to hotter winters and spring.
“Beekeeping is much more unpredictable nowadays because you do have the extremes of weather and the different patterns. Every year is slightly different, but it’s actually even more different in recent times,” said Brown.
Milder temperatures over winter might mean a colony develops a larger brood of eggs, larvae and pupae. If they don’t succumb to varroa mite, a tiny and deadly parasite that attaches to honeybees and their brood, then the survivors will be “much stronger and ready to swarm sooner”, said Brown.
Prof Phil Lester, an entomologist and ecologist at Victoria University, said beekeepers have been active catching swarms in other parts of the country, including Wellington.
Unmanaged bee swarms that cannot be captured pose a risk to other honeybees or native bees if they are carrying varroa mite. Further, it can be a pain for beekeepers to lose their bees right when they are readying to produce honey.
Still, it could be a positive signal for this year’s bee populations, Lester said.
“It means they have been able to build up numbers and populations, earlier than perhaps they normally would do … its probably a good indication that it is a good bee year.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Saudi Arabia downs missiles fired at Riyadh after Houthi attack on pipeline
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Saudi Arabia downs missiles fired at Riyadh after Houthi attack on pipeline
Saudi forces intercept two missiles fired towards Riyadh, hours after reporting damage to key East-West pipeline.
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has announced it intercepted two missiles fired towards the kingdom’s capital, Riyadh, and another aimed at its southern region.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition, blamed the Iran-backed Houthis for Tuesday’s attacks.
In a series of posts on X, he said a ballistic missile and a cruise missile were intercepted and destroyed over Riyadh, while a second ballistic missile was downed over the southern part of the country.
Multiple explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to the AFP news agency, and residents received text-message alerts instructing them to take shelter due to an “aerial threat”.
A subsequent message from the country’s civil defence agency said the danger had passed.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
The strikes were the latest in a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia as fighting rages in Yemen between the Houthis and the country’s internationally recognised government, backed by Riyadh.
The coalition has supported a Yemeni government offensive to retake territory with air strikes, while the Houthis have repeatedly struck Saudi oil infrastructure, including refineries and storage facilities, with drones and missiles.
On Monday, the East-West oil pipeline in the Medina region was attacked again. A Saudi Energy Ministry official told the state-run SPA news agency the strike caused a “limited fire” that was extinguished. The official said that “pipeline operations were unaffected”.
No injuries or deaths were reported.
The pipeline is a vital route for Saudi oil exports due to Tehran’s restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war against Iran. The pipeline has come under attack several times as the war on Iran fuels a global energy crisis.
On Sunday, the Houthis also said they attacked Riyadh’s business district.
Saudi officials said falling debris from an “attempted attack” had caused minor damage to the Aramco Tower.
Images released by the SPA showed the deputy governor of the Riyadh region and other officials inspecting the building, with damage visible on several floors.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/colleges.title: Exclusion temporaire, intervention de la gendarmerie… Dans le Tarn, un collégien sanctionné pour avoir porté un tee-shirt aux couleurs de la Palestine durant un cross
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/colleges.author: Léa Paredes
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/colleges.text:
Omar, élève de 5ème d’origine palestinienne scolarisé dans un collège du Tarn, a été exclu huit jours pour avoir arboré un tee-shirt aux couleurs de la Palestine lors d’un cross de son établissement, le 13 octobre. Près de 300 personnes se sont rassemblées devant le collège ce lundi 9 novembre pour le soutenir, alors qu’un conseil de discipline était censé se prononcer sur une éventuelle exclusion définitive.
Ils sont près de 300 devant les grilles du collège de Cordes-sur-ciel (Tarn), ce lundi 9 novembre. Parents d’élèves, collégiens, élus locaux et citoyens se sont donné rendez-vous pour soutenir un jeune collégien de 12 ans et dénoncer la sanction qui lui a été infligée. Dans ce petit établissement rural, qui compte à peine 230 élèves, le rassemblement fait masse.
Quelques semaines plus tôt, le 13 octobre, avait lieu le traditionnel cross de l’établissement. À quelques centaines de mètres de la ligne d’arrivée, le jeune Omar1 et trois de ses camarades retirent leurs sweats et leurs chemises, laissant apparaître des t-shirts aux couleurs de la Palestine. Selon les témoignages, plusieurs professeurs tentent alors de les rattraper pour leur faire remettre leurs vêtements.
Prévenue, la directrice de l’établissement appelle les gendarmes qui arrivent vite....

Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
Nearly four in five Britons see Israel as a serious threat to world peace, according to a survey published last week by the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen).
The figure rose from 48 percent in 2005 to 78 percent this spring, two-and-a-half years into the genocide in Gaza and just after Israel and the US had attacked Iran.
In July, a YouGov opinion poll commissioned by the Council for British-Arab Understanding found that only 17 percent of the British population believes that Israel is not committing genocide in Gaza.
The war on Iran has hit the UK economy, leaving households paying more for energy, food and mortgages. The rising bills have brought the cost of Israel’s wars in the Middle East home to British households.
Last week, the Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75 percent to 4 percent, its first increase in more than three years. The rise pushes up payments for borrowers on mortgages and adds to the cost of taking out or renewing a home loan.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Senate advances bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Hilary Beaumont
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja).
The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73-25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward.
Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.
Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.
Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them.
“This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.
Protesters rallied outside Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer’s building on Friday over concerns that the bill could boost datacenters. “It would be highly ironic if, having won an election where datacenter opposition was at the front and center, the first act of Congress was to make it easier to build datacenters,” said Bill McKibben.
Democrats elected in the blue wave will not take their seats until January, so the bill’s proponents still have time to rush it through the Senate, and technically there is time for it to pass in the House before new Congress and go to Trump.
But midterm success for the Democrats is dialing up the political friction. House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the House speaker in the new Congress, said the bill “falls short in several areas”, including failing to protect tribal sovereignty, and he would not “rubber-stamp legislation without more constructive involvement with our caucus”.
Earlier on Monday, the bill’s Democratic sponsors, Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, said they had the votes to pass the bill. Heinrich said they had made last-minute changes to ensure tribal consultation, and they believed the bill would favor renewables over fossil fuels. “If we can create an open, competitive level playing field, clean is cheap, and cheap wins in the marketplace,” Heinrich said.
Whitehouse, who wore a tie with wind turbines on it, argued that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on clean energy policies next year with majorities in the House and Senate. “People should just cool their jets and have a little faith that this is not the end of the story,” he said.
Proponents of Baaja say it is needed because it takes too long to build large projects in America and the bill shortens timelines. It simplifies federal rules for building interstate transmission lines, it narrows what gets reviewed under the National Historic Preservation Act and limits tribal consultation, it limits the use of the Clean Water Act, shortens timelines for the Endangered Species Act, limits how the executive branch can interfere with federal permitting, and makes big changes to Nepa such as changing what requires Nepa review and who has standing to sue.
Baaja would expand fossil fuels
The fossil fuel industry is backing Baaja. The American Petroleum Institute (API) hailed the bill as “a historic opportunity” and called on congress to “finish permitting reform this year”.
“It creates a very accelerated fast track for gas pipelines,” said Earthjustice Action’s president, Abbie Dillen. “The gas industry is extraordinarily excited about this because they are interested in expanding existing pipeline capacity to get more liquefied natural gas out for export, and to be feeding power-hungry datacenters with gas.”
The bill could help pave the way for the Constitution gas pipeline that Williams Companies is trying to build through New York. The state denied the project’s water quality permit in 2016, but the company has revived the project under the Trump administration. The proposed pipeline could benefit from the bill’s changes to the Clean Water Act.
Baaja could also enable construction of gas pipelines in the west. Fossil fuel advocacy group Western States and Tribal Nations wants to build gas pipelines to feed domestic datacenters and export LNG from the west coast. During a 3 November election day meeting with Wyoming’s Sweetwater county board of commissioners, the advocacy group’s president, Andrew Browning, said he was talking to lawmakers about the bill: “The permitting bill’s a huge thing … We’re going to need that for everything we’re envisioning and building out.”
How the bill would increase clean energy
Some clean energy advocates want the bill to pass because it would connect renewables to the grid. Wind, solar and battery storage are now cheap to build, but the country lacks the necessary transmission lines to bring clean energy where it’s needed.
Interstate transmission lines can take a decade to get built, and energy projects also face a bottleneck in connecting to the grid. At the end of 2025, 2,060 GW of total generation and storage capacity were waiting in a queue to connect to the grid.
Ben King, energy and climate director at Rhodium Group, said Baaja would reform the interconnection queue process and unlock the ability to build the transmission that is needed. “We’re at a pretty low point for policy support for clean [energy],” he said, referring to Trump’s repeal of clean energy tax credits. “[Baaja] sets up the ability to build stuff more quickly for when the next wave of climate policy happens.”
Many experts have modeled what the bill would do to emissions, but there is a lot of uncertainty on that question. Rhodium Group’s analysis found that domestic emissions go down if Baaja passes. But another model by the Purdue engineering professor Kevin Kircher found it would increase domestic emissions.
Kircher said the optimistic case for Baaja is that there’s a huge amount of clean energy ready to go, and if we get rid of the long queues and regulations, “level the playing field and let it rip”, then clean energy wins on the economics. “I think that understanding is outdated,” he said.
What the bill does to emissions partly depends on what type of energy gets connected to the grid. Rhodium Group assumed, based on a report from 2025, that 85% of the capacity added to the grid would be renewables. But Kircher said some grid operators have updated their queues this year to remove redundant and speculative offers. (PJM’s queue as of 3 August looks quite gassy.)
King said the economics show an impressive decrease in the cost of renewables, while fossil fuels are not getting any cheaper. “Some of it is just a bet on what’s going to win out in the future,” he said. “Our modeling suggests that clean stuff is going to dominate energy expansion for the foreseeable future, and there might be people who have a different view on that. API might have a different perspective – they might bet that there’s more room for them to grow.”
Kircher emphasized that the various models have not had time for peer review since the bill was first introduced on 30 September. “We need to have some humility in recognizing that the process of taking that 417 pages of super dense legal text and mapping it … is extremely complicated and full of uncertainties,” he said.
What the bill would do to Nepa
The bill would significantly reduce the scope of Nepa. It would narrow the definition of a “major federal action” that would trigger Nepa review, and effectively eliminate the authority of courts to enforce Nepa compliance.
Nepa is the powerful law that attorneys used to block the Trump administration’s plans to convert 11 mega-warehouses into massive ICE detention centers. If the bill passes, it could accelerate the development of ICE detention centers, according to a letter the American Civil Liberties Union sent to senators. “As written, this bill would hamper, if not altogether thwart, critical work by the ACLU and our partners to halt ICE’s dangerous expansion of immigrant detention,” the letter said.
Baaja’s passage would be “the single biggest overhaul” of American environmental laws since the 1970s, said Dillen of Earthjustice. “There are legitimate concerns that Nepa has been weaponized to slow down important projects, but people have recognized this problem for years, and the law has been reformed, and it’s also been weakened very significantly by the supreme court. What this bill does is take the last pieces of it that are very relevant in an administration like this,” she said.
Trump has pushed a “drill, baby, drill” fossil fuel agenda, and Baaja’s weakening of environmental regulations would further embolden him, Dillen said. She pointed to Trump’s plan to allow drilling near Chaco Culture national historic park, a Unesco world heritage site. “Chaco Canyon is in the crosshairs,” she said.
“At Earthjustice, we are deeply committed to building clean energy and to do it in a time frame that is meaningful, given the threats that we face. But the way to do this, the way to build our country better and even faster, is not by running over tribes and by emboldening a president who voters have just come out in a historic turnout to push back on,” Dillen said.

https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/fin-du-direc.title: Fin du direct
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/fin-du-direc.text:
C’est la fin de ce direct consacré à la conférence sociale de ce 9 novembre, merci à toutes et tous de l’avoir suivi. Retrouvez nos analyses sur l’humanite.fr
Bonne soirée !
L'essentiel
- Dans la matinée, Sébastien Lecornu a reçu organisations patronales et syndicales pour une conférence sociale sur les salaires et le pouvoir d’achat. Le premier ministre doit rendre compte de ce échange à 13h30 lors d’une conférence de presse.
- Un appel à la mobilisation et à la grève a été lancé par l’intersyndicale de la fonction publique pour le mardi 17 novembre 2026, afin d’exiger une hausse immédiate de la valeur du point d’indice, gelé depuis quatre ans.
- La hausse du Smic qui pourrait être annoncée à l’issue de la conférence sociale en cours lundi matin à Matignon serait comprise entre « 1,5 % et 2 % », selon le président de la CFTC Cyril Chabanier.
HIER À 18h41
HIER À 16h46
Le prix repère de vente de gaz (PRVG) augmentera de 5,8 % au 1er décembre, vient d’annoncer la Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE). Il passera à 206,26 euros TTC le mégawattheure en moyenne, contre 194,90 euros au 1er novembre.
« La hausse du SMIC sera donc entièrement absorbée par la hausse du prix du gaz. À ce niveau de foutage de gueule, c’est de l’art ! », a aussitôt réagi le sénateur communiste de Paris Ian Brossat.
Selon la CRE, cette hausse s’explique par la montée des prix sur les marchés du gaz en octobre par rapport à septembre. « On subit un prix de marché international, on importe 95 % de notre gaz », a rappelé sa présidente, Emmanuelle Wargon, qui y voit le reflet d’une offre réduite « depuis la crise dans le détroit d’Ormuz ».
Le PRVG avait déjà augmenté de 5,6 % en septembre, de 6,3 % en octobre et de 6,6 % en novembre. Pour les ménages dont l’offre est indexée sur ce prix, la CRE estime le surcoût à 16 euros TTC en moyenne pour le seul mois de décembre. Sur l’année, la facture 2026 serait supérieure de 11,8 % à celle de 2025, soit 143 euros TTC de plus en moyenne.
Environ 6 millions de ménages sont concernés, soit près de 60 % des abonnés résidentiels au gaz. Les offres à prix fixe ne bougent pas. Depuis la fin des tarifs réglementés en 2023, le PRVG sert de repère aux fournisseurs pour fixer leurs prix, et aux consommateurs pour comparer les offres.
HIER À 16h25
Le gouvernement a également annoncé à l’issue de la conférence sociale, un décret qui obligera les entreprises « à transmettre au CSE (comité social et économique) la liste de toutes les aides publiques dont elles bénéficient ». L’exécutif reprend ainsi une recommandation de la commission d’enquête sénatoriale sur les aides publiques aux entreprises, dont le sénateur communiste Fabien Gay était le rapporteur.
Dans un communiqué, l’élu de Seine-Saint-Denis et directeur de l’Humanité salue « une nouvelle victoire pour la transparence et pour le rapport sur les 211 milliards ». Selon lui, le texte doit être publié d’ici à la fin de l’année. Il obligera les entreprises à transmettre au CSE l’ensemble des informations sur les aides perçues, et les élus du personnel devront rendre un avis. « Les élus du personnel auront enfin les cartes en main pour vérifier l’usage de l’argent public perçu, exiger des contreparties et empêcher que ces aides ne servent à financer des plans de licenciements, des délocalisations ou le versement de dividendes excessifs », écrit-il.
Publié en 2025, le rapport de la commission d’enquête chiffrait à 211 milliards d’euros par an le montant des aides publiques aux entreprises, versées selon Fabien Gay « sans véritable contrôle, sans contreparties » et sans que les représentants des salariés en aient une vision claire. Le sénateur rappelle que ses travaux ont déjà débouché sur le remboursement de 4,3 millions d’euros par Michelin et sur la mise en place d’un suivi des aides publiques par le Haut-Commissariat.
Il voit dans cette annonce « le fruit d’un travail collectif, parlementaire et syndical, gagné grâce à la mobilisation sociale ». Fabien Gay promet de rester « vigilant quant à la rédaction et à l’application de ce décret ». Il entend continuer à se battre « pour conditionner plus largement ces aides à des garanties sur l’emploi, les salaires et la transition écologique ».
HIER À 16h08
Le secrétaire national du Parti communiste français (PCF) a vivement réagi sur X à la hausse du SMIC annoncée par le gouvernement à l’issue de la conférence sociale. « Même pas 2 % de plus sur le SMIC, aucune augmentation sur les salaires. Des miettes », a écrit Fabien Roussel. « Personne ne doit s’en satisfaire, ils nous méprisent : on se mobilise. Tous dans la rue, demain et le 17 novembre », ajoute le dirigeant communiste.
Dans une autre publication, le candidat à l’élection présidentielle réclame un « SMIC à 2 200 euros bruts », avec une hausse proportionnelle de « tous les salaires au-dessus ». Il propose aussi d’« accompagner les entreprises, notamment les plus petites ». « C’est par la relance de la consommation que l’on va relancer l’économie », fait-il valoir.« Tout ce que nous demandons c’est que le capital paie, et le travail reçoive. il faut inverser tout ce qui a été fait ces dix dernières années », a t-il poursuivi.
HIER À 15h07
Le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste a réagi lundi après-midi sur X à la hausse du SMIC annoncée par le gouvernement à l’issue de la conférence sociale. « Le compte n’y est pas ! », a-t-il écrit. Pour Olivier Faure, il s’agit surtout d’une anticipation de la revalorisation automatique du 1er janvier, à laquelle le gouvernement ajoute « cinq petits euros ». « On ne convoque pas une conférence sociale pour en sortir avec une mesure qui relève du trompe-l’œil », estime-t-il. Et d’ironiser : « 5 €, c’est un petit déjeuner avec une baguette, du lait et une motte de beurre. »
« Comment expliquer aux travailleurs mobilisés que c’est là l’unique réponse pour faire face à la vie chère ? », interroge le député de Seine-et-Marne, avant d’ajouter : « Ils ne demandent pas de privilèges mais une vie digne. »
HIER À 14h13
« On apporte une mauvaise réponse à un vrai problème », a réagi Patrick Martin, président du Medef, sur Franceinfo après l’annonce de la hausse du Smic de 1,6 % le 1er décembre. Prêt à tout pour détruire le modèle social français, le représentant des patrons affirme que « plus personne ne parle d’emploi, d’investissement et de croissance », ce qu’il estime être « la vraie réponse » à apporter à la perte de pouvoir d’achat des Français.
Le patron du Medef ajoute que « si on veut répondre à ces attentes légitimes de pouvoir d’achat, il faut créer des emplois là où on est en train d’en détruire. Il faut de la croissance là où on frise la récession. Il faut investir alors que sur le dernier trimestre, l’investissement a plongé d’une manière effrayante » en France.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ja.title: Rare Jan van Huysum Pendant Paintings Head to Christie’s for $10.7 M.
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ja.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ja.text:
Dutch Golden Age artist Jan van Huysum’s pendant paintings A Vase of Flowers and Fruit with Flowers, will lead Christie’s Old Masters Evening Sale in London on December 8 with an estimate of $8 million to $10.7 million (£6 million to £8 million).
The two paintings are the only known large-scale fruit and flower pendants by the artist dating back to 1731 to 1733. The pendants have a rich provenance, moving from the ownership of the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel, the Barings, and the Rothschilds.
They are now coming to auction from a private collection. The first still life, A Vase of Flowers, depicts a terracotta vase overflowing with flowers: roses, hyacinths, gentians, peonies, blossoms, and others. In Fruit with Flowers, fruits and flowers are spilling on top of each other, from peaches, grapes, figs, plums, red currants, and a pomegranate to hollyhocks and poppies.
A Vase of Flowers and Fruit with Flowers will tour New York until November 16 ahead of going on public view in London on December 4. “In terms of quality, condition and visual impact these are amongst the finest 18th century still lifes I have come across and they perfectly exemplify the refinement and ambition of Van Huysum’s mature style,” said Andrew Fletcher, Christie’s global head of the Old Masters department in a statement.
In June, Christie’s sold van Huysum’s Peaches and Grapes in a Wicker Basket for $8.65 million (£6.52 million) after carrying an estimate of £3 million to £4 million during the Old Masters Evening Sale in London, while another painting from the artist, an elaborate bouquet of roses, peonies, narcissi, poppies and orange blossom, totaled $7.35 million (£5.54 million).
