https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Harare demolitions leave families homeless after years of building
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Harare demolitions leave families homeless after years of building
Residents who say they legally bought land have seen their homes demolished.
Harare, Zimbabwe – At around 5am on Friday, August 14, Methro Masunga, 28, was jolted awake by the sound of bulldozers and shouting municipal police officers. Outside, earth-moving vehicles were preparing to demolish homes in St Martins Extension, a suburb of Harare.
At first, Masunga thought the machinery had arrived for roadworks. Then she realised her home was among those marked for destruction.
“I thought they were here for some other business, probably land development or road grading; alas, they had been sent to destroy our homes. We tried to understand, but no one would hear us,” Masunga told Al Jazeera.
A single mother of three, Masunga had spent years saving to own a home. She worked part-time cleaning other people’s houses, putting aside what she could to buy a residential stand.
“I worked part-time jobs doing laundry and washing dishes in people’s houses for five years, saving where possible. So, when I came here, I paid the deposit and started monthly contributions,” she said, standing among the remains of her house.
Years of sacrifice reduced to rubble
Masunga began paying for her stand in 2015 and received an allocation in 2019. She says the arrangement was formalised through the city council in 2020, when residents began receiving official documents.
Her experience reflects a wider dispute over land allocations in Harare. Residents say they bought stands through council-linked processes and invested their savings in building homes. The municipality says it is enforcing planning regulations against structures built without the necessary approvals or on land not designated for housing.
The full number of people displaced by demolitions across Harare in 2026 has not been independently established. However, city council records seen by Al Jazeera list more than 5,000 houses facing demolition under 37 outstanding High Court orders. These figures concern properties targeted under the wider programme, not homes already demolished. A council task force has separately inspected 22,255 sites to identify structures on prohibited or unauthorised land.
Authorities say the demolitions are intended to address illegal construction, disputed land sales and development on sites reserved for public infrastructure. Residents argue that enforcement has also affected people who say they obtained allocation letters and agreements of sale through municipal processes.
Memory Chengeta, whose house in St Martins was also demolished, said residents were bewildered by the operation because of an earlier court order.
“There was a court order for them to stop demolitions. The municipal authorities came with no court order that overturned the previous judgement, but went ahead to destroy the properties,” she said.
A former street food vendor, Chengeta had saved to build a more stable life. She is now homeless. Some affected residents have returned to renting, while others, including Chengeta and Masunga, have remained in St Martins, putting up makeshift shelters rather than leaving the area.
Joachim Nhete also lost his home after using his retirement package to buy land and build a house. He estimates his investment at more than $10,000.
The legal question behind the demolitions
The dispute has raised questions about how residents acquired their stands and whether the council complied with existing court orders.
On October 29, 2025, Justice Happias Zhou issued a consent order in case HCH5444/25, setting aside demolition notices issued to named applicants in St Martins Extension. It barred the City of Harare from evicting those applicants or demolishing their homes without a valid court order. It also prohibited further development without written council approval.
The order did not automatically protect every property in St Martins. The available information does not establish whether Masunga, Chengeta or their specific properties were among those covered.
The council has maintained that it did not demolish properties protected by the order. Its spokesperson, Stanley Gama, told local media that the municipality was targeting structures whose owners had repeatedly been warned against building illegally.
“We are only demolishing structures built illegally whose owners were told and warned many times not to proceed with construction,” Gama said.
Harare Mayor Jacob Mafume told NewsDay on August 15 that residents with approved building plans should produce them during council inspections. He said the municipality had repeatedly warned residents to obtain the necessary documents but declined to comment on the legality of the specific demolitions in St Martins.
Harare’s principal housing director, Edgar Dzehonye, later said residents had been warned against building in the area because it had not been adequately serviced.
These explanations raise a separate question: whether residents who received council allocation letters and agreements of sale also had valid planning and building approvals. An allocation to occupy a stand does not necessarily establish that a house was authorised for construction. The status of the residents’ documents, the approved layout, and individual building permits are therefore central to determining whether the demolitions were justified.
Precious Shumba, director of the Harare Residents’ Trust, said the demolitions were particularly troubling because of the court order protecting residents allocated stands by the municipality.
“Despite that, the town planning department and legal officers in the Chamber Secretary’s Department issued directives to the Municipal Police to demolish the houses of St Martins Extension residents,” he said.
Zimbabwe’s Constitution, under Section 74, prohibits the eviction of people from their homes or the demolition of their homes without a court order made after considering all relevant circumstances. The National Human Settlements Policy also calls for alternative accommodation to be prepared before relocations and demolitions. Residents say they were not offered alternative housing.
Residents demand accountability
The controversy reflects long-standing problems in Harare’s land administration. A 2019 commission of inquiry chaired by Justice Tendai Uchena identified unauthorised land sales, weak administration and poor record-keeping by local authorities. It found that land barons had sold state land without authority, sometimes allegedly working alongside council officials.
Shumba said the Harare Residents’ Trust wrote to the president on July 22, 2026, calling for the publication of the report of the commission of inquiry into the financial affairs of the city of Harare. The organisation also wants the findings of the Justice Maphios Cheda commission of inquiry into the city’s governance crisis implemented.
David Jenje, chairman of the St Martins Residents Association and the St Martins Housing Happiness Pay Scheme, said residents had paid for their stands years before receiving allocation letters.
He said the council’s Education, Housing and Community Services Committee resolved in 2019 to expedite the allocation and servicing of the land.
“Most of the members had paid deposits of $5,000 as far back as 2018 … Allocations were made in July 2019 after completion of payment of intrinsic land value. All the allocation letters and agreements of sale were signed in February 2020. These demolitions were illegal,” Jenje said.
ZimRights, a human rights organisation, said the demolitions raised questions about the rule of law and accountability.
Harare South MP Trymore Kanopula called for a halt to further demolitions until the land allocations had been audited and investigated. He also urged the government to present the findings of the commission of inquiry into state land sales to Parliament.
Parliament’s speaker referred the matter to the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works for action.
Minister Daniel Garwe said the government did not carry out demolitions and could not interfere with court processes. He acknowledged that the Harare City Council had approximately 5,000 demolition orders and said the government had sometimes tried to delay demolitions while seeking solutions.
For Nhete, however, official interventions offer little comfort. His house is gone, and he says he has no insurance to recover his investment.
“Unlike some who had home insurance, I didn’t have one,” he said. “I cannot recover the loss and pain. My hope is in the courts of law that Harare City Council must be held accountable and pay us back.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Police investigate as nearly 30 Santa Barbara half-marathon runners fall ill with ‘unusual symptoms’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Abené Clayton
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Police in southern California are investigating the circumstances that led to the hospitalization of nearly 30 runners who participated in the Santa Barbara Half on Sunday.
Santa Barbara police said in a statement to the Associated Press that they had opened an investigation after receiving reports from Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital about multiple half-marathon participants seeking medical treatment for “unusual symptoms”.
Cottage Health said in a statement it had a “larger than expected number of emergency visits … a number of them with similar symptoms of undetermined cause”.
Race organizers say they believe any illness is attributable to heat or dehydration. The high on the day of the race was 88F (31.1C), an unusually high temperature for this time of year.
Neither the hospital nor police have detailed the symptoms beyond calling them unusual. Cottage Health said on Monday that 27 participants came to emergency rooms in Santa Barbara and Goleta, a small city about 10 miles west.
More than 4,640 people competed in the half-marathon, which spanned about 13 miles, according to the Santa Barbara Half Marathon website.
Of those who were either taken to the hospital or arrived there on their own, 24 patients had been treated and discharged as of Monday morning. The three others were in stable condition, the company told the Associated Press.
Event director David Monico said organizers transported 15 people from the medical tent to local hospitals. He said the event’s medical team treated numerous runners for dehydration and overheating both on the course and at the finish line.
The half-marathon’s event director, David Monico told the Guardian that they have “no additional information to suggest that the issues some of the participants experienced were caused by anything other than endurance event exertion-related symptoms”.

Teddy Riner candidat : le macronisme a son nouveau champion ?
Publié le 9 novembre 2026
Mais à quoi joue Teddy Riner ? Onze fois champion du monde, triple champion olympique, le judoka a annoncé sa candidature à l’élection présidentielle. Celui qui se présente comme un renouveau politique a pourtant très bien adopté le vocabulaire et le discours libéral. Alors pourquoi se présente-t-il ? Que défend-il, qui défend-il ? A-t-il déjà le semblant de début de projet politique ?
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.title: The World’s Best Biennial Is in St. Louis
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.author: Emily Feldman
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.text:
A sign of the times: Shortly after St. Louis’s Counterpublic triennial chose sites for its third edition, climate disaster and civic disintegration plucked them off one by one. First was the International Institute, a nonprofit for immigrants and refugees selected after the last census showed that migrants made up the region’s only population growth. Originally, the team behind Counterpublic had hoped to highlight and celebrate the Institute’s vital work. But on Trump’s first day back in office, an executive order suspending refugee admissions decimated the organization’s budget, forcing it to furlough 60 percent of its staff.
Then, a tornado ripped through The Ville, a redlined neighborhood, tearing the shingles off Sumner High School’s roof—which, despite being the first Black high school west of the Mississippi and boasting alumni such as Tina Turner, Dick Gregory, and Arthur Ashe,was already suffering from civic neglect. Next, a historic warehouse—one of the show’s main sites—caught fire: It smoldered all Black Friday weekend long, even through the snow, until its roof collapsed.
The question for the organizers of Counterpublic, a civically minded public art exhibition, became not only one of how to create site-specific, civically engaged artworks in the age of the poly-crisis, but why? Then, the existential threat wrought an existential reckoning that meaningfully reimagined what a recurring exhibition of the biennial/triennial variety might be.
The team titled the 2026 edition “Coyote Time,” after a video game that artist Alice Bucknell made for the show. The titular term refers to the grace-period moment after a character in a game runs off a cliff but before gravity catches up, when the player can still jump. It’s named for Wile E. Coyote, who hovers over the canyon until he looks down and clocks the height.
INFRASTRUCTURE HAS BECOME a central topic in art and politics of late, a theme of the most recent Whitney and Medina biennials and a focus of the Mamdani administration in New York. That’s largely because infrastructure becomes most visible when it isn’t working as it ought to—or when you’re not the person it’s designed to work for—as the curators of Counterpublic experienced vividly while selecting sites. For their exhibition, infrastructural critique became both subject and method.
At the International Institute, the curatorial cohort installed several new commissions thematically related to the Institute’s work. On the façade, Petrit Halilaj’s metallic monumentalization of children’s drawings from Kosovo harks back to his childhood as a refugee during the Yugoslav wars. Inside, Rachel Youn’s kinetic sculpture sees fake flowers move mechanically like the brushes of a car wash; theirs is an homage to immigrant labor (including their own family’s). To steward these artworks, Counterpublic also raised funds to hire back some furloughed staffand covered building upgrades, too: fresh paint, a new ceiling.
The artworks at the Institute are not simply a means to an end, nor a mere reversal of the art washing, tax evasion, and money laundering that have become part and parcel with art institutions. They also bring levity, dignity, and warmth to a space where migrants often spend hours waiting for legal counseling and paperwork help. The Institute is a life-giving center that nevertheless could have a perfunctory, bureaucratic feel. Counterpublic hoped to change that in a gesture that feels honest about the reality of what art can meaningfully bring forth, and also what it can’t. Material change and symbolic gestures are not the same, but they can work hand-in-hand.
One artwork, by Rirkrit Tiravanija, ties these threads together. It’s a continuation of his famous communal Thai food meals—quintessential biennial art—but the most delicious and most meaningful version I’ve encountered. The recipes were developed using native fruit, pawpaws, and with the help of the Institute’s clients, who in the process received training for potential careers in hospitality. Running through Counterpublic’s threemonths, the temporary restaurant offers free food and a space to gather. Counterpublic also helped support a new ventilation system and brought the Institute’s kitchen up to code, which set up Tiravanija’s project for success—and will also be useful for more cooking to come.
Tiravanija’s is a familiar project given new meaning by its context, much like the reimagined triennial format itself. While the artist’s original meal, first served in 1990, became a hallmark of relational aesthetics—a critique of the white cube’s reification of static objects through art that expanded to include social encounters—this version responded to a different kind of site and its needs. In so doing, it swapped institutional critique for infrastructural intervention. Here and throughout its three editions, Counterpublic has married art and action, always careful to parse activism from organizing.
AS IF DIRECTLY COUNTERING the criticism political art often (and rightly) gets for confusing virtue-signaling with substantive change, several artworks in Counterpublic aremore or less invisible: You could enjoy a free meal at the Institute without realizing you were consuming art at all. That is the trouble or the triumph—depending on who you ask—of systems artworks like these: The art part can be hard to see once the world around it gets blended in. In the exhibition’s catalog, artist Margaret Honda states outright that she wants her work to “be kind of invisible”: She installed two Noguchi-inspired benches and a brick path in The Ville alongside newly planted trees in response to the community’s request for parks.
Another inconspicuous artwork, Brianna Leatherbury’s Appreciation (2026), sees sculptures buried underground: Made of phosphate reclaimed by an agritech company from the city’s wastewaters, the works absorb lead and cleanse the soil. Without a Counterpublic sign, Leatherbury’s intervention would surely go unnoticed—and yet, it is among the projects that stayed with me most vividly. However invisible it may be, the work is also both a pollution solution and a symbol: Foursculptures are planted in The Ville, a Black neighborhood that bears traces of St. Louis’s disinvestment, and five morerun along the riverfront, home to a reserve of development ambitions. Both sites have been deemed “unoccupied” by the city, and Leatherbury’s project scrambles notions of waste and value: Fine art made from feces makes each lot less toxic and turns it into better real estate, but redlining and racism keep their market value uneven.
Two other works of latter-day Land art effect bioremediation, but blink and you’ll miss them: Chris Carlinstalled a garden of largely native plants and a subtle soundscape near Counterpublic’s main hub, and Lynne Smith rewilded a postindustrial pond at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC)—home to the nation’s largest collection of architectural artifacts, just across the Mississippi River in Illinois. NBAC inhabits a decommissioned steel foundry in what was once the company town of Monsanto—the chemical corporation we have to thank for DDT, Agent Orange, Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, and so much more. Foraging there for sumac berries one day, Smith came across a loading dock that had been converted into a retention pond for managing runoff, where frogs were laying eggs as young tadpoles slithered along. In an effort to make the site even more frog-friendly (and rehabilitate an arguably apocalyptic chemical crime scene), the artist installed a three-chamber structure—designed after the amphibian’s hearts—to filter rainwater and sediment, used to cultivate ancient native American lotus plants to mitigate both algae growth and the distinct chemical smells of the city.
Clearly, sustainability is a major theme of “Coyote Time,” but in more than just the ecological sense: The scale of the exhibition is considered and refreshingly humane for visitors, and every work by a living artist is a new commission. That means the organization does not take on more than it can meaningfully support, or give visitors more than they can meaningfully consume. Too often, biennial-goers leave beleaguered and artists end up in debt—suspended past the edge of the cliff in coyote time, wondering if it all will pay off.
Other memorable commissions include Li-Yi Fan’s absurdist video rating mirror renderings in various video games and Glenn Ligon’s riff on Thomas Jefferson’s famed feats of engineering—undulatingbrick walls that could stay sturdy with just one buttress-free layer—behind which he hid enslaved laborers. Titled Who Builds Anything In This Country (2026), Ligon’s work speaks to the enslaved labor that built St. Louis and its brick business, too;it is memorably installed just past St. Louis’s iconic Gateway Arch. Fan’s commission is sure to have afterlives in future exhibitions; Ligon’s is in St. Louis to stay.
Counterpublic’s models of redistribution, of art-as-infrastructure, and of sustainability find precedent, of course, in artists’ practices. Take duo Ryan Trecartin and Lizzie Fitch, who are part of the show: Whenthe sculptor and video artist received a major commission from Fondazione Prada for a 2019 exhibition, they used the funds to build a set—including a prefab barn with an amusement-park-like “lazy river”—where they now live and work. For “Coyote Time,” they created a similar structure blurring performance and life: A stage for the city that offers space for civic gathering, performing arts, and play. The duo’s signature frolicsome use of color and scale joins an equipment library with projectors, speakers, and microphones. The stage is one of 15 works—among them Honda’s, Ligon’s, Halilaj’s, Smith’s, and Carl’s—that is a permanent gift to the city.
ANYTHING THIS AMBITIOUS raises hard questions—in fact, that’s part of the point. One involves the slippery slope between well-meaning efforts to improve urban infrastructure and the gentrification that too often ensues. Where the displacement of poorer urban residents was once considered an unfortunate side effect of biennials and their ilk, we’ve now seen developers and municipalities enlist artists strategically for the purpose of increasing property value. Indeed, on opening night, I saw a lone protester with a sign that read our communites are not your brand.
But one could argue—indeed, Counterpublic seems to—that if we know art and real estate are now bedfellows, perhaps this can be wielded to a community’s advantage if organizers and not developers are at the helm. Certainly, this does seem worth a try. Notably, community partners—like The Ville’s 4theVille, on behalf of Sumner High School—reached out to Counterpublic to collaborate rather than the other way around. The school had nearly closed several times, but to remind the city of its cultural significance—which can seem at odds with its material neglect—Counterpublic commissioned Tony Cokes to craft a memorable homage to alumna Tina Turner, installed in a church nearby. And Timmy Simonds—whose ongoing project Miss Othmar School for Teachers imagines a school without students—made flags that pay homage to the first Black teachers college west of the Mississippi, once housed on the same site. A clever nod to how teachers—like the titular Miss Othmar, of Peanuts fame—are often only seen from the waist up, these pant-shaped former parachutes evoke their full personhood, while also dressing down the classroom’s hierarchy and the teacher’s authority. We’re all teachers and all students sometimes.
Where Counterpublic does make efforts to offer solutions to civic issues of varying scales, these gestures stand out for the way they never attempt to cover up the seams. Artworks lay issues bare as much as they attempt to ameliorate them, occupying an honest middle ground between critique and repair. Art, we all know, is hardly the ideal fix for civic issues, but still, solutions start somewhere. As Rebecca Solnit says, “revolution takes place first in the imagination,” or as (choose your fighter) Andrew Breitbart said, “politics is downstream from culture.” And yet, in “Coyote Time,” art is more than a start, because the exhibition is always thinking about what it leaves behind: a place to sit, a kitchen to cook in, a spot of shade, a stage to scream from, soil to grow in.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Russia, Ukraine and US to meet as Zelenskyy claims battlefield successes
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Russia, Ukraine and US to meet as Zelenskyy claims battlefield successes
Zelenskyy claims Russia ‘suffering record losses’ as Trump says US seeing ‘strong inclination’ to end war in Ukraine.
Negotiators from Russia and Ukraine are set to meet for peace talks brokered by the United States in Abu Dhabi, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that recent gains on the battlefield had strengthened his country’s hand.
The meeting in the capital of the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday will be the third round of talks there this year, following security consultations in January and February. The US side is led by US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded Washington’s mediation.
The three delegations last met in Geneva on February 18.
“Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating position,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was “suffering record losses”, a claim Moscow disputes, and urged Washington to persuade the Kremlin to end the war.
Zelenskyy said General Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented a report on Ukraine’s military positions that pointed to heavy recent Russian losses, and that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including oil facilities, were having an effect.
“We are responding to Russia’s war in a fully justified manner and demonstrating that this war must end,” he said. “Russia can do this. It can end its war. It is important that the United States convince Russia of precisely this.”
‘Strong inclination’
In Washington, DC, Trump told reporters that he saw a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.
“We’re having a very good conversation about that in Abu Dhabi,” he said.
Trump had promised to end the war quickly when he took office in January 2025, but a settlement has remained elusive nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
A US official, briefing reporters on the condition of anonymity, said on Monday that both Russia and Ukraine had privately shown some flexibility on a possible exchange of territory. Security guarantees for Ukraine would be a central topic, the official said, including the possibility of a defence commitment modelled on Article 5 of NATO’s founding treaty.
Both Ukraine and Russia have been adamant about territory.
Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to obtain all of the Donbas region.
Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea and parts of the eastern Donbas region. The Russian move has not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has previously urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war.
The US official said any territorial agreement would most likely come at the end of the negotiations, once other issues, including a post-war security framework, had been settled.
‘Ways to go’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio meanwhile struck a cautious note, saying that the process to end the war still has “a ways to go”.
“We’ll keep trying. And that’s what we’ve been trying to do the whole time is try to be creative and find ways that we can help bring that conflict and that war to an end,” Rubio said.
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, will again lead the country’s delegation, according to The Kyiv Independent. Russia’s team will be headed by Vladimir Medinsky, a Kremlin aide, and will include Sergei Ryabkov, a deputy foreign minister, as well as Yuri Zhigarlovsky, a senior military officer.
European powers, including France, Germany and the European Commission, will send officials to the talks in Abu Dhabi, but Russia has made it clear it doesn’t want the Europeans to take part in negotiations.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said the talks would focus on security guarantees. European officials would not take part, he added, because the negotiations had been agreed to as a three-way format.
“What will take place in Abu Dhabi in the coming days is trilateral negotiations between Russia and Ukraine with US mediation,” Peskov said. “As for the presence of Europeans, you know that the Americans have their own channels of communication with Europeans, and Ukrainians with Europeans.”

https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.title: Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya: Staaten streiten schon jetzt übers Geld
https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.author: Nanja Boenisch
https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.text:
Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya: Staaten streiten schon jetzt übers Geld
Am Montag hat die UN-Klimakonferenz begonnen. Geprägt von Aufrufen zu mehr Tempo beim Klimaschutz – und zu einer gerechten Klimafinanzierung.
Es muss schneller gehen mit dem internationalen Klimaschutz – und fairer. Das machten am Montag zum Auftakt der zweiwöchigen Weltklimakonferenz im türkischen Antalya (COP31) sowohl UN-Klimachef Simon Stiell als auch UN-Generalsekretär António Guterres deutlich.
Guterres forderte die politischen Machthaber weltweit auf, „Ernst zu machen mit einer schnelleren Verringerung der Emissionen und der Abkehr von fossilen Brennstoffen“ – also von Öl, Gas und Kohle. Fortschritte beim Klimaschutz würden lange nicht schnell oder gerecht genug gemacht, sagte Klimasekretär Stiell. Die diesjährige UN-Klimakonferenz müsse deshalb mehr als nur Warnsignale liefern: „Bestehende globale Ziele und nationale Pläne müssen auf konkrete Schritte heruntergebrochen werden“, betonte Stiell.
Eines dieser Ziele ist, die Finanzmittel für Klimaanpassung bis 2035 zu verdreifachen – darauf hatte sich die internationale Gemeinschaft bei der letzten Weltklimakonferenz vor einem Jahr in Belém in Brasilien verständigt. Allerdings wurde dort kein Vergleichswert festgelegt, und bisher liegen viele Staaten hinter ihren eigenen Versprechen zurück. In Antalya machte Guterres deshalb Druck: „Besonders verwundbare Staaten müssen die Gelder und den Schutz erhalten, den sie benötigen.“
Die Frage, wer für die Folgen der Klimakrise zahlen muss, sorgte allerdings auch in diesem Jahr bis kurz vor Beginn der Konferenz für Streit. Staaten des Globalen Südens hatten sich dafür starkgemacht, Verhandlungen über konkrete Finanzierungsschritte ins offizielle Programm aufzunehmen.
Klimafinanzierung offiziell im Programm
Industriestaaten wehrten sich; die Europäische Union hatte schon im Vorhinein ausgeschlossen, neue Gelder zuzusagen. Auch Deutschland hat seine Finanzierungsversprechen zuletzt gebrochen. Trotzdem haben es die Beratungen über eine konkrete Ausgestaltung des Belém-Beschlusses nun offenbar ins Verhandlungsprogramm geschafft, jedoch nicht als eigener Tagesordnungspunkt.
Auch der türkische Umweltminister Murat Kurum, der am Montagmorgen offiziell zum Präsidenten der diesjährigen COP gewählt wurde, mahnte Tempo beim Klimaschutz an. „Verzögerungen verursachen einige der höchsten Kosten im Klimaschutz.“ Zusammen mit Co-Ausrichter Australien wolle die türkische Präsidentschaft „helfen, Lösungen für die Herausforderungen besonders verwundbarer Länder zu finden“.
Schon in diesem Jahr haben die Folgen der Klimakrise mehrere Regionen der Welt erschüttert – mit Dürren und Waldbränden wie im Sommer in Südeuropa, mit Fluten wie in Teilen Chiles oder Nepal. 2027 drohen neue Katastrophen: Das Jahr könnte das wärmste seit Beginn der Messungen werden, wie die Weltwetterorganisation WMO zu Beginn der Konferenz mitteilte.
Das Klimaphänomen El Niño, das in regelmäßigen Abständen natürlicherweise vorkommt, in diesem Jahr aber besonders stark ausfällt, erhöhe das Risiko für Hitzewellen, tropische Wirbelstürme und Unwetter mit Starkregen deutlich. So wirken El Niño und die Klimakrise wie Brandbeschleuniger füreinander: Die Klimakrise verstärkt das natürliche Phänomen El Niño, und El Niño lässt die globalen Temperaturen weiter steigen.
Fentje Jacobsen, WWF
Laut der WMO waren die vergangenen zwölf Jahre jeweils die wärmsten, die jemals gemessen wurden. Wie das UN-Umweltprogramm Unep vor Kurzem bekannt gab, wird das 1,5-Grad-Ziel, das sich die Staatengemeinschaft noch 2015 mit dem Pariser Klimaabkommen gesteckt hatte, demnach mit Sicherheit zumindest zeitweise überschritten.
„Wenn Land und Meer sich weiter aufwärmen, hat das drastische Konsequenzen für unser Leben auf der Erde“, warnte Fentje Jacobsen, Klimachefin der Entwicklungsorganisation WWF. „Stärkere Extremwetterereignisse führen zu massiven ökonomischen Kosten – und kosten Menschenleben.“ Auch Jacobsen fordert daher etwa Fortschritte bei der Abkehr aus fossilen Energien, bei der Elektrifizierung auf Ökostrombasis und bei der Klimafinanzierung.
Elektrifizierungs- und Finanzierungsfragen stehen noch in dieser Woche auf dem offiziellen COP-Verhandlungsplan.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. https://www.humanite.fr/monde/catastroph.title: Turquie : 10 morts dans l’explosion d’une usine sidérurgique près d’Izmir et la police arrête… Des syndicalistes
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/catastroph.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/catastroph.text:
Dix ouvriers ont été tués et une quinzaine d’autres travailleurs ont été blessés dans l’explosion d’un site de sidérurgique survenue ce lundi 9 novembre aux alentours de midi. Le sujet tourne à la polémique nationale car les conditions de travail sont régulièrement dénoncées par les employés et les syndicats. Selon « Evrensel », un quotidien turc, il s’agit du troisième accident mortel en seulement trois semaines.
Dix personnes ont été tuées et une douzaine d’autres blessées dans l’explosion d’une usine sidérurgique, survenue aux alentours de midi lundi 9 novembre, près de la ville portuaire d’Izmir, dans l’ouest de la Turquie, a indiqué le gouvernorat local. Le gouverneur d’Izmir, Süleyman Elban, a annoncé que 10 ouvriers étaient morts et 15 blessés. Les médias turcs ajoutent que quatre d’entre eux sont dans un état critique.
« Les opérations de recherche et de sauvetage se poursuivent pour atteindre nos travailleurs piégés sous les décombres », a déclaré le ministre de la Justice, Akin Gürlek, annonçant l’ouverture d’une enquête. La puissante déflagration, suivie d’un incendie, s’est produite vers midi à l’usine Habas Demir Celik à Aliaga, à environ 60 kilomètres au nord d’Izmir.
Selon l’agence de presse DHA, l’explosion se serait produite à la suite de l’effondrement d’une grue-portique dans un grand four industriel, en plein processus de coulée d’acier liquide. Sur les images et vidéos diffusées dans la presse turque, un épais nuage de fumée foncée s’élève au-dessus de l’usine Habas Demir Celik à Aliaga.
Deux syndicalistes qui dénonçaient les conditions de travail arrêtés
Deniz Ulker, un témoin qui passait à proximité, a décrit des vibrations ressemblant à un séisme. « Le sol bougeait sous nos pieds, j’ai cru que c’était un tremblement de terre. Quand j’ai regardé l’usine de l’autre côté de la rue, une épaisse fumée noire en sortait. Un incendie s’est déclaré au niveau de la cheminée », a-t-il raconté à l’agence de presse d’État Anadolu. Pour un autre employé du site, Turan Ilbay, « C’était comme une bombe qui explosait ». Toutes les victimes sont des ouvriers de l’usine.
Des policiers antiémeutes ont été déployés devant l’hôpital d’État d’Aliaga, où ont été admis les ouvriers blessés lors de l’explosion, selon le quotidien Evrensel. Deux porte-paroles de l’Union des travailleurs d’Égée, Yücel Memiş et Sonay Tezcan, ont été arrêtés alors qu’ils s’exprimaient devant l’établissement.
Yücel Memiş a toutefois eu le temps de dénoncer les conditions de travail : « Depuis des jours, nous répétons sans cesse : prenez des précautions ! Trop c’est trop. Vous produisez des milliers de tonnes de fer, vous employez des dizaines de milliers de travailleurs, vous gagnez des fortunes. Est-ce si difficile de prendre des précautions ? »
Le Parti du travail (EMEP) a également dénoncé un accident lié au non-respect des mesures élémentaires de sécurité. « Depuis des années, les ouvriers dénoncent le report des opérations de maintenance et de révision afin de ne pas perturber la production », a-t-il pointé.
« Les géants du fer et de l’acier, qui se vantent de leurs résultats à l’exportation, ne sont pas inquiétés et les inspections rigoureuses nécessaires ne sont pas effectuées », a ajouté le parti, exigeant que le propriétaire de Habas, ses dirigeants et responsables soient « traduits en justice ». Selon Evrensel, il s’agit du troisième accident mortel dans l’entreprise en trois semaines.
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?  
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Cameroon sets date for twice-delayed legislative and local elections
President Paul Biya, the world’s oldest leader, sets February 7 for Cameroon’s delayed legislative and local polls.
Cameroon’s President Paul Biya has announced that legislative and local elections will be held in the country on February 7 next year.
Biya, who is 93, made the announcement in a decree read on public radio on Monday.
The decree comes at a tense moment for Cameroon, with authorities cracking down on the opposition, roughly a year after an election that handed Biya another term.
Biya, who has ruled Cameroon since 1982, is the world’s oldest head of state.
His re-election in October last year set off widespread protests that the authorities met with a violent crackdown.
Lawyers cited by Human Rights Watch said security forces detained up to 2,000 people, and some of those detained remain in custody, according to the AFP news agency.
Biya’s government has already postponed Cameroon’s legislative and local elections twice, forcing the extension of lawmakers’ terms to December 20 and those of municipal councillors to February 28, 2027.
The country is also awaiting a government reshuffle announced nearly a year ago and the appointment of a vice president. A constitutional reform reintroduced the post in April, and its holder would be expected to succeed Biya in the event of his death.
Questions about the president’s health have continued to swirl, with his frequent stays abroad fuelling debate over his ability to govern. Media debate about the president’s health, however, has been banned since 2024, when rumours circulated about his death.
In late August, Biya returned to Yaounde after more than two months in Geneva, drawing sharp criticism from the opposition.
Last month, the authorities suspended the Cameroon National Salvation Front (FSNC), the party of defeated opposition presidential candidate Issa Tchiroma Bakary.
Bakary went into exile in the Gambia after declaring himself the election winner and calling on supporters to defend his “victory”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US supreme court clears way for Trump’s border wall in Texas’s Big Bend
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US supreme court has allowed Donald Trump to continue his administration’s construction of a border wall in Texas’s Big Bend region, including parts of Big Bend national park.
In an unsigned, five-page ruling, the nation’s highest court granted the Trump administration’s emergency request to suspend a lower court order that had temporarily stopped the project last month.
Liberal justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only member of the nine-member court to dissent from the ruling.
The justices wrote that the case’s plaintiffs, which include the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend river guide and a church preservation group, “claim that construction in the Big Bend sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area”.
However, they noted: “But Congress’s enactment of [immigration law] – which permits the secretary [of homeland security] to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws – reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert.
“The government’s interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents,” the justices said.
The Trump administration plans to construct more than 300 miles of six-foot-tall vehicle barriers and supporting roads, relying on a 1996 law that authorizes the homeland security secretary to “waive all legal requirements”, including environmental and conservation protections, in areas designated as having high levels of illegal border crossings.
The plaintiffs argue that the project threatens wildlife and public lands, could destroy “iconic sections” of the Rio Grande’s protected river corridor, and would undermine the “carefully wrought web of laws meant to protect a vast universe of biological, historic, cultural, and other interests”.
The border wall plans have also faced bipartisan opposition from local residents, many of whom warn that construction could threaten their livelihoods and disrupt their communities.
A Customs and Border Protections map shows plans for barriers and patrol roads across Big Bend national park, including remote areas that would require extensive dynamite blasting. Construction is also planned in isolated canyons where there have been no documented unauthorized vehicle crossings and where vehicles cannot reach the US-Mexico border, the Center for Biological Diversity noted.
According to Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, the wall, which is being built out at about 12 miles a week, is expected to be completed by the end of Trump’s second term.
The Center for Biological Diversity condemned the supreme court’s decision, saying: “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.
“The destruction we’ve already seen in Big Bend unleashed a firestorm of outrage so severe that the administration was forced to pause its plans. If the bulldozers return now, public opposition will only grow … The damage done to Big Bend will be felt for future generations of Texans and Americans, and this administration will bear responsibility for the natural heritage we lose,” the center added.
CBP has awarded five contracts worth more than $6bn for border security upgrades in Big Bend, including 30-ft steel fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology, which the agency calls its “smart wall”.
Following a federal judge’s ruling that temporarily halted the construction in October, CBP said at the time: “We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region.”
The Guardian has reached out to CBP for comment on the supreme court’s latest ruling.

https://www.humanite.fr/sports/ministere.title: « C’est pas le ministre qui marque les buts », la dernière idée de génie de Sarah Knafo pour réduire la dette : supprimer le ministère des Sports
https://www.humanite.fr/sports/ministere.author: Éric Serres
https://www.humanite.fr/sports/ministere.text:
Pour réduire la dette de la France, l’eurodéputée du parti Reconquête d’Éric Zemmour propose de supprimer le sport des postes ministériels. Toujours plus éloignée des revendications populaires, l’extrême droite démontre une fois de plus sa volonté de mettre hors jeu l’action et les services publics.
Dans une espèce de course à l’échalote, où chacun y va de sa recette miracle afin de réduire la dette de la France, Sarah Knafo, du parti Reconquête d’Éric Zemmour, a expliqué sur BFMTV/RMC vouloir supprimer non seulement 800 000 postes de fonctionnaires, mais aussi mettre fin à l’existence du ministère de Sports : « C’est pas le ministre des Sports qui marque les buts de l’équipe de France, on n’a pas besoin du ministre des Sports pour ça. » Mince alors, nous qui croyons que si… !
Petit rappel à l’eurodéputée, qui semble avoir découvert qu’il existait un ministère dédié dans notre pays : les premières structures étatiques dédiées aux sports remontent à 1921, avec la création d’un premier sous-secrétariat d’État chargé de l’Éducation physique. Ces structures n’ont cessé d’évoluer depuis, au gré des Républiques et des gouvernements.
« Le sport est un ciment de notre société »
Elles ont permis très souvent, n’en déplaise à Sarah Knafo, de mettre, même avec des budgets en perte de vitesse, le sport au centre des préoccupation des Français. Ce qu’a rappelé l’actuelle ministre Marina Ferrari : « sans cette action publique, au service d’une politique qui constitue l’un des ciments de notre société, le sport en France ne serait plus qu’une machine économique réservée à celles et ceux qui peuvent se l’offrir. Le sport est un droit. Et c’est la responsabilité de l’État de le garantir. » Avec plus de moyens ce serait encore mieux, madame la ministre !
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Republican Thomas Massie moves to force vote to impeach Pete Hegseth
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: George Chidi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A Republican lawmaker has moved to force a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, setting the stage for a showdown over one of the most divisive figures inside Donald Trump’s administration.
Thomas Massie, of Kentucky, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers.
Massie, an outgoing Republican congressman from Kentucky and vocal critic of the president, argued from the well of the House of Representatives that Hegseth had committed “high crimes and misdemeanors” and “has executed unlawful orders” in office.
Massie is expected to have some Republican support for a vote on articles of impeachment. Under House rules, the vote would have to occur no later than Wednesday.
Massie first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on 15 September, but House speaker Mike Johnson called US Congress into recess before it could be heard.
Republicans retain control of the House until new members are seated in January, but House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York – widely expected to ascend to speaker – has said he is a “hard yes” on impeaching Hegseth. “Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries told ABC News on Sunday.
Hegseth spent the morning on Monday at the Naval War college, announcing an array of changes to military education that he said would enable US military officers “to wage war with such devastating speed, precision and lethality that no adversary dares test American result that’s deterrence – and if they do that, they are completely and utterly destroyed: that we achieve victory”.
But it is the failure to deliver victory that has placed a target on Hegseth’s back.
Trump, vice-president JD Vance and other Republican leaders quickly attributed last week’s historic US midterm election losses by Republicans to the Iran war and its pocketbook effects on otherwise-conservative voters.
Hegseth fired back at his critics in a short video released on Thursday, describing the threat of his impeachment as “all about the politics of personal destruction”, insisting that it “won’t work with me”.
Watchdogs Common Cause and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington argued that the video is a violation of the Hatch Act, which bars the use of government funds for partisan political purposes.
Massie’s impeachment resolution holds that Hegseth has subverted the power of Congress to declare war with unauthorized attacks on Iran and Yemen; systemically violated laws meant to minimize civilian casualties with the killing of more than 100 children at a school in Iran; and engaged in extrajudicial killings when ordering suspected drug boats in the Caribbean to be sunk and their crews left without rescue.
The resolution also argues that Hegseth’s investigation and threatened prosecution of Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat, and others for calling for troops to disobey illegal orders was an unconstitutional violation of the first amendment, and alleges that the kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela was illegal and unconstitutional.

https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-polnis.title: Ermittlungen gegen polnischen TV-Sender: Hat TV Republika Falschinformationen verbreitet?
https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-polnis.text:
Ermittlungen gegen polnischen TV-Sender: Hat TV Republika Falschinformationen verbreitet?
Er ist Polens reichweitenstärkster Sender: TV Republika sendete live vom Anschlag in Krakau und soll dabei Falschinformationen verbreitet haben.
kna | Wegen seiner viel kritisierten Berichterstattung über den tödlichen Anschlag in Krakau drohen dem polnischen Privatsender TV Republika Konsequenzen. Die nationale Rundfunkbehörde eröffnete am Montag ein Verfahren gegen den meistgesehenen Nachrichtenkanal des Landes, der als Sprachrohr der rechtskonservativen Opposition gilt. Während und nach dem Attentat berichtete der Sender am Samstagnachmittag live vom Anschlagsort, dem Hauptmarkt; dort habe es keine Polizisten gegeben.
Bei dem schwersten Attentat in Polen seit dem Ende des Kommunismus 1989 hatte ein 24-jähriger Pole in Krakaus Altstadt sechs Menschen erschossen. Unter den Todesopfern sind auch eine Österreicherin und ein Brite. Elf weitere Opfer sowie zwei Polizisten liegen weiter schwer verletzt in Kliniken. Der von der Polizei mit Schüssen gestoppte Täter erlag am Montagmorgen im Krankenhaus seinen Verletzungen.
„Sender meldete Falschinformationen“
Der Landesrat für Rundfunk und Fernsehen teilte mit, seine Vorsitzende habe aufgrund der bei ihm eingereichten Beschwerden Maßnahmen zur Klärung der Vorwürfe eingeleitet. TV Republika müsse der Behörde nun die Aufzeichnung der umstrittenen Sendung zur Verfügung stellen und zu den gegen ihn erhobenen Vorwürfen Stellung nehmen.
Auch Kulturministerin Marta Cienkowska beschwerte sich bei der Behörde über TV Republika. Der Sender habe unüberprüfte Informationen verbreitet, schrieb sie auf der Plattform X. Sie warf dem Kanal eine Berichterstattung vor, „die Panik potenzieren kann“. Solch ein Anschlag dürfe „kein Brennstoff für politische Propaganda“ sein, so die Ministerin. Sie forderte die Behörde auf, Gesetzesverstöße zu ahnden.
Der Chef von TV Republika, Tomasz Sakiewicz (58), war zum Zeitpunkt des Anschlags auf dem Hauptmarkt, weil er von einer rechten Demonstration gegen die Regierung berichtete. In der Live-Sendung hatte er auch suggeriert, es mangele in Krakau an Polizisten, weil örtliche Beamte in Warschau eingesetzt würden.
In der Hauptstadt sichern seit Tagen viele Polizisten unter anderem das Verfassungsgericht. Um das Gericht tobt ein Machtkampf zwischen der Mitte-Links-Regierung und dem von der rechtskonservativen Opposition unterstützten Staatspräsidenten Karol Nawrocki. Der Nachrichtensender soll zudem behauptet haben, der Attentäter sei ein Ausländer.
Senderchef spricht von Hetzjagd
Sakiewicz sprach von einer „beispiellosen Hetzjagd“ gegen sein TV-Programm. Die Kritiker wollten die Zensur wiedereinführen, behauptete er. Die größte Oppositionspartei, die rechtskonservative PiS, verteidigte die Berichterstattung von TV Republika. Ihr Vorsitzender Jaroslaw Kaczynski erklärte, Journalisten wie Sakiewicz hätten das Recht zu fragen, ob Krakau angemessen gesichert gewesen sei, „selbst wenn es der Regierung nicht gefällt“.
Der Landesrat für Rundfunk und Fernsehen kann wegen der Verletzung von Vorschriften Geldstrafen verhängen und in extremen Fällen Sendelizenzen entziehen. Laut einer Sprecherin gingen bei der Behörde seit Samstag mehr als 5.000 Beschwerden gegen TV Republika ein. Auch der „Rat Polnischer Medien“, ein Organ der Selbstkontrolle vergleichbar dem Deutschen Presserat, protestierte gegen den Sender.
In dem 2023 gegründeten Gremium sind Zeitungen, Radio- und Fernsehstationen und Online-Medien vertreten. Es warf TV Republika eine „inakzeptable Instrumentalisierung der Tragödie zu politischen Zwecken“ vor. Das habe nichts mit Journalismus zu tun, so der Rat.
„Unverantwortliche Informationen“
Er kritisierte besonders Sakiewiczs' Behauptung, am Anschlagsort seien keine Polizisten gewesen, weil „alle Reserven nach Warschau abgezogen wurden“. Dies sei umso verheerender, als bei der Verfolgung und Festnahme des Täters zwei Polizisten schwer verletzt worden seien und weiter um ihr Leben kämpften.
Der „Journalistenverband der Republik Polen“ äußerte ebenfalls „Empörung über die unverantwortlichen und unwahren Informationen“, die der Sender verbreitet habe. Sakiewiczs Verhalten sei skandalös und „geprägt von Lügen und politischer Unverfrorenheit, wie sie für diesen Sender typisch sind“.
Der Sender Telewizja Republika, so sein vollständiger Name, war im Oktober laut der nationalen Rundfunkbehörde mit einem Marktanteil von 5,9 Prozent und mehr als 300.000 Zuschauern der meistgesehene Nachrichtenkanal in Polen. Das ebenfalls private Programm TVN24 liegt demnach mit einem Marktanteil von 5,1 Prozent auf Platz zwei, gefolgt von der öffentlich-rechtlichen Station TVP Info (2,1 Prozent). Gegründet wurde TV Republika 2012 von Sakiewicz und weiteren Journalisten.
Trotz aller Aufrufe: Der schreckliche Anschlag scheint Polen nicht zu einen, sondern die Spaltung des Landes weiter zu vertiefen. Und TV Republika spielt dabei mit drastischer Kritik gegen die Regierung eine zentrale Rolle.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Poll finds Americans less likely to back pro-war candidates by 3-1 margin
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Poll finds Americans less likely to back pro-war candidates by 3-1 margin
Voters say they want government to prioritise an end to price increases over achieving Trump's military goals in Iran.
A YouGov poll completed on the eve of the 2026 midterm elections has found that Americans were far less likely to back candidates who supported the US-Israel war on Iran.
The poll, released on Monday, found that 44 percent of people said they were less likely to support candidates who backed the war, while just 13 percent said they were more likely.
That means a candidate’s support for the war was more than 3 times as likely to put people off as to win them over.
Another 26 percent, meanwhile, indicated the Iran war would not make much of a difference in their vote.
The economics of the war also factored into people’s choices. Some 56 percent of those surveyed said that the US should prioritise avoiding higher prices domestically over achieving US President Donald Trump’s military goals in Iran.
Meanwhile, 22 percent said the opposite: that the Trump administration should prioritise the war over higher costs.
The poll also asked who should decide when the war ends. A majority, 53 percent, said Congress should have the final say, while 29 percent said that the president should decide.
The US and Israel jointly launched the war against Iran on February 28. But Trump’s decision to bypass congressional authorisation for the war has raised constitutional concerns in the US.
Jonathan Guyer, the programme director at the Institute for Global Affairs at Eurasia Group, a risk consultancy firm, told Al Jazeera that the poll – which was conducted on his organisation’s behalf – indicated Americans were looking to Congress to be more assertive.
“The story of the [economic] tradeoff is really important, and then there’s this other story of where Congress has been: Why haven’t lawmakers, not just over the last year but over the last decade, played a bigger role as a backstop on reckless wars launched by presidents?” said Guyer.
“And I think these numbers show the public really wants Congress to play a bigger role and expects their lawmakers to hold power to account.”
Anti-war lane
The survey is the latest to underscore the unpopularity of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has killed thousands of people in Iran and contributed to surging prices, a top issue in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump’s Republican Party suffered one of the most significant electoral setbacks in modern US history, with Democrats reclaiming both chambers of Congress with strong majorities.
Democrats also flipped key offices in states like Texas, once seen as a conservative stronghold.
Those results have advanced a debate over the war that is playing out in both parties, often pitting more hawkish establishment figures against newcomers opposed to foreign intervention and support for Israel.
In the wake of the “blue wave”, analysts have argued that Democratic voters may expect the party’s leadership to take firmer steps to rein in the president and bring the fighting with Iran to an end.
On Monday, Trump himself said “Iran militarily is effectively over”, though he declined to rule out any further military action. A US naval and land blockade around Iran also remains in effect.
Guyer said he anticipates that foreign policy and, in particular, US support for Israel is likely to emerge as a key dividing line for candidates in future elections, particularly the upcoming 2028 presidential election.
“I think it does create a lane for people like Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, for the wing of the [Democratic] party represented by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who have a very strong position on this war and on the role of the US in the world that traditional Democrats have been largely silent on,” said Guyer.
A similar debate is also taking place on the political right.
Following the midterms, US Vice President JD Vance shared a lengthy social media post blaming his party’s implosion on the war.
Figures such as Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor Greene have also criticised the war as a betrayal of Trump’s promise to end conflicts around the world.
While the YouGov poll found that Republicans were the only group more likely to vote for a candidate if they supported the president’s war, Guyer says that support has been “softening”.
“A third of Republicans say that backing the war made a candidate appealing, so it’s kind of small,” he said. “And 40 percent shrugged and say it made no difference.”

Meeting du Bourget : LFI réunit 20 000 personnes pour présenter son programme
Publié le 9 novembre 2026
Depuis le parc des expositions du Bourget (Seine-Saint-Denis), Jean-Luc Mélenchon et son mouvement ont présenté les grandes lignes de « L’Avenir en commun » devant 20 000 personnes. Un moment présenté comme une invitation à se projeter dans une France de l’après-Macron et un monde débarrassé des « suprémacismes ».
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: John Fetterman to be challenged for Senate seat by democratic socialist born in Gaza
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Tait in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
John Fetterman, the maverick Democratic senator who has provoked widespread anger by increasingly siding with Republicans, is to be challenged for his Pennsylvania seat by a democratic socialist candidate who is originally from Gaza.
Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American, said he would run in a primary to be the Democratic nominee in 2028, when Fetterman’s seat is up for re-election.
The move is the first sign of Fetterman’s weakened position in the party since the Democrats won back control of the Senate in last week’s US midterm elections, when the party won at least 54 of the upper chamber’s 100 seats.
The prospect of a comfortable Senate majority in effect eliminates the possibility of Fetterman’s vote being decisive, a relief to Democratic strategists who feared he could no longer be relied on for support on contentious issues.
Fetterman had already caused widespread disillusionment among many Pennsylvania Democrats, who campaigned for him in the 2022 midterms when he ran as a progressive outsider.
But he has sparked anger by, on occasion, speaking out in support of Donald Trump, who in turn has praised Fetterman as “a great guy” and said he would “love” him to become a Republican.
Moor, 42, a writer and journalist who was born in the southern Gaza city of Rafah and has previously written for the Guardian, told the Philadelphia Inquirer that he was “not really running against Fetterman”.
“I’m running for good government. I’m running for the rule of law. I’m running because I believe in America,” he said.
But his Palestinian background throws down the gauntlet to Fetterman’s vocally pro-Israel stance, which has become increasingly strident since the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas that left about 1,200 people on the Israeli side dead. More than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza – most women and children – have been killed in Israel’s retaliatory military response.
Fetterman has said he has no intention of leaving the Democrats but strongly suggested would change his mind if the party became “anti-Israel”.
“That’s my red line,” Fetterman said last July. “If the Democratic party becomes official anti-Israel, then that’s when I would force me out. If they make it the official platform of the party, then that’s a much different situation.”
Fetterman has met more often with Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, than with Philadelphia’s mayor, Cherelle Parker, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer.
Moor, by contrast, said he supports withdrawing US aid from Israel and imposing sanctions aimed at securing equal rights for Palestinians.
Democrats say Moor is unlikely to be the only challenger to Fetterman, who provoked outrage in his own party in September by sending a video message to the Republicans’ midterm convention in Texas in which he praised Pennsylvania’s Republican senator, Dave McCormick.
“I’m pretty confident that you’ll see some bigger, mainstream kind of names, involved,” said Mike Weidinger, a veteran Lancaster county Democrat with state-wide connections, who cited Chris Deluzio, a representative from the Pittsburgh area, and Malcolm Kenyatta, a Pennsylvania state legislator, as likely challengers.
“Generally, people think [Fetterman] either misrepresented himself when he ran the first time, or he changed completely from what he said he was,” said Weidinger.
“We just had an election here in Pennsylvania where a lot of us busted our ass for [Pennsylvania governor Josh] Shapiro and a lot of other people, and he didn’t spend one penny or do one thing for a single Democrat candidate here last week.”
On the possibility of Fetterman joining the Republicans, he added: “If he wants to switch, he can switch. If it would have been 51 to 49, it would have mattered. But it doesn’t matter now.”

https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/gaz-le-prix-.title: Gaz : le prix de référence augmente encore de 5,8 % au 1er décembre, la hausse du SMIC sera donc « absorbée » selon Ian Brossat
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/gaz-le-prix-.text:
C’est la fin de ce direct consacré à la conférence sociale de ce 9 novembre, merci à toutes et tous de l’avoir suivi. Retrouvez nos analyses sur l’humanite.fr
Bonne soirée !
L'essentiel
- Dans la matinée, Sébastien Lecornu a reçu organisations patronales et syndicales pour une conférence sociale sur les salaires et le pouvoir d’achat. Le premier ministre doit rendre compte de ce échange à 13h30 lors d’une conférence de presse.
- Un appel à la mobilisation et à la grève a été lancé par l’intersyndicale de la fonction publique pour le mardi 17 novembre 2026, afin d’exiger une hausse immédiate de la valeur du point d’indice, gelé depuis quatre ans.
- La hausse du Smic qui pourrait être annoncée à l’issue de la conférence sociale en cours lundi matin à Matignon serait comprise entre « 1,5 % et 2 % », selon le président de la CFTC Cyril Chabanier.
HIER À 18h41
HIER À 16h46
Le prix repère de vente de gaz (PRVG) augmentera de 5,8 % au 1er décembre, vient d’annoncer la Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE). Il passera à 206,26 euros TTC le mégawattheure en moyenne, contre 194,90 euros au 1er novembre.
« La hausse du SMIC sera donc entièrement absorbée par la hausse du prix du gaz. À ce niveau de foutage de gueule, c’est de l’art ! », a aussitôt réagi le sénateur communiste de Paris Ian Brossat.
Selon la CRE, cette hausse s’explique par la montée des prix sur les marchés du gaz en octobre par rapport à septembre. « On subit un prix de marché international, on importe 95 % de notre gaz », a rappelé sa présidente, Emmanuelle Wargon, qui y voit le reflet d’une offre réduite « depuis la crise dans le détroit d’Ormuz ».
Le PRVG avait déjà augmenté de 5,6 % en septembre, de 6,3 % en octobre et de 6,6 % en novembre. Pour les ménages dont l’offre est indexée sur ce prix, la CRE estime le surcoût à 16 euros TTC en moyenne pour le seul mois de décembre. Sur l’année, la facture 2026 serait supérieure de 11,8 % à celle de 2025, soit 143 euros TTC de plus en moyenne.
Environ 6 millions de ménages sont concernés, soit près de 60 % des abonnés résidentiels au gaz. Les offres à prix fixe ne bougent pas. Depuis la fin des tarifs réglementés en 2023, le PRVG sert de repère aux fournisseurs pour fixer leurs prix, et aux consommateurs pour comparer les offres.
HIER À 16h25
Le gouvernement a également annoncé à l’issue de la conférence sociale, un décret qui obligera les entreprises « à transmettre au CSE (comité social et économique) la liste de toutes les aides publiques dont elles bénéficient ». L’exécutif reprend ainsi une recommandation de la commission d’enquête sénatoriale sur les aides publiques aux entreprises, dont le sénateur communiste Fabien Gay était le rapporteur.
Dans un communiqué, l’élu de Seine-Saint-Denis et directeur de l’Humanité salue « une nouvelle victoire pour la transparence et pour le rapport sur les 211 milliards ». Selon lui, le texte doit être publié d’ici à la fin de l’année. Il obligera les entreprises à transmettre au CSE l’ensemble des informations sur les aides perçues, et les élus du personnel devront rendre un avis. « Les élus du personnel auront enfin les cartes en main pour vérifier l’usage de l’argent public perçu, exiger des contreparties et empêcher que ces aides ne servent à financer des plans de licenciements, des délocalisations ou le versement de dividendes excessifs », écrit-il.
Publié en 2025, le rapport de la commission d’enquête chiffrait à 211 milliards d’euros par an le montant des aides publiques aux entreprises, versées selon Fabien Gay « sans véritable contrôle, sans contreparties » et sans que les représentants des salariés en aient une vision claire. Le sénateur rappelle que ses travaux ont déjà débouché sur le remboursement de 4,3 millions d’euros par Michelin et sur la mise en place d’un suivi des aides publiques par le Haut-Commissariat.
Il voit dans cette annonce « le fruit d’un travail collectif, parlementaire et syndical, gagné grâce à la mobilisation sociale ». Fabien Gay promet de rester « vigilant quant à la rédaction et à l’application de ce décret ». Il entend continuer à se battre « pour conditionner plus largement ces aides à des garanties sur l’emploi, les salaires et la transition écologique ».
HIER À 16h08
Le secrétaire national du Parti communiste français (PCF) a vivement réagi sur X à la hausse du SMIC annoncée par le gouvernement à l’issue de la conférence sociale. « Même pas 2 % de plus sur le SMIC, aucune augmentation sur les salaires. Des miettes », a écrit Fabien Roussel. « Personne ne doit s’en satisfaire, ils nous méprisent : on se mobilise. Tous dans la rue, demain et le 17 novembre », ajoute le dirigeant communiste.
Dans une autre publication, le candidat à l’élection présidentielle réclame un « SMIC à 2 200 euros bruts », avec une hausse proportionnelle de « tous les salaires au-dessus ». Il propose aussi d’« accompagner les entreprises, notamment les plus petites ». « C’est par la relance de la consommation que l’on va relancer l’économie », fait-il valoir.« Tout ce que nous demandons c’est que le capital paie, et le travail reçoive. il faut inverser tout ce qui a été fait ces dix dernières années », a t-il poursuivi.
HIER À 15h07
Le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste a réagi lundi après-midi sur X à la hausse du SMIC annoncée par le gouvernement à l’issue de la conférence sociale. « Le compte n’y est pas ! », a-t-il écrit. Pour Olivier Faure, il s’agit surtout d’une anticipation de la revalorisation automatique du 1er janvier, à laquelle le gouvernement ajoute « cinq petits euros ». « On ne convoque pas une conférence sociale pour en sortir avec une mesure qui relève du trompe-l’œil », estime-t-il. Et d’ironiser : « 5 €, c’est un petit déjeuner avec une baguette, du lait et une motte de beurre. »
« Comment expliquer aux travailleurs mobilisés que c’est là l’unique réponse pour faire face à la vie chère ? », interroge le député de Seine-et-Marne, avant d’ajouter : « Ils ne demandent pas de privilèges mais une vie digne. »
HIER À 14h13
« On apporte une mauvaise réponse à un vrai problème », a réagi Patrick Martin, président du Medef, sur Franceinfo après l’annonce de la hausse du Smic de 1,6 % le 1er décembre. Prêt à tout pour détruire le modèle social français, le représentant des patrons affirme que « plus personne ne parle d’emploi, d’investissement et de croissance », ce qu’il estime être « la vraie réponse » à apporter à la perte de pouvoir d’achat des Français.
Le patron du Medef ajoute que « si on veut répondre à ces attentes légitimes de pouvoir d’achat, il faut créer des emplois là où on est en train d’en détruire. Il faut de la croissance là où on frise la récession. Il faut investir alors que sur le dernier trimestre, l’investissement a plongé d’une manière effrayante » en France.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.title: Kommunalpolitik | Freiberg wappnet sich zum Abwahlkampf
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.author: Hendrik Lasch
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.text:
- Politik
- Kommunalpolitik
Freiberg wappnet sich zum Abwahlkampf
Stadtrat ebnet Weg für Amtsenthebung des seit Wochen abgetauchten Oberbürgermeisters Philipp Preißler. Die Hürde ist allerdings extrem hoch.
Das neue Jahr wird für das sächsische Freiberg mit einem freudigen Ereignis beginnen. Beim Neujahrsempfang am 8. Januar wird der Schriftstellerin Sabine Ebert die Ehrenbürgerwürde überreicht. Die 68-Jährige habe die Bergstadt mit ihrer Saga um die Hebamme Marthe weit über die Grenzen Sachsens hinaus einem Millionenpublikum bekannt gemacht, hieß es zur Begründung. Ebert ist die erste Frau überhaupt, der in Freiberg diese Ehre zuteilwird.
Als Ebert im vergangenen Frühjahr bei einem literarischen Stadtrundgang persönlich zu einigen Schauplätzen ihrer historischen Romane führte, schritt ein Mann an ihrer Seite, über dessen politisches Schicksal ebenfalls im Januar 2027 entschieden werden soll: Oberbürgermeister Philipp Preißler. Der 41-Jährige war im Oktober 2025 zum Rathauschef gewählt worden, konnte sein Amt wegen eines Einspruchs gegen die Wahl und einer folgenden Klage aber erst Ende Juni 2026 antreten. Vier Monate später hat der Stadtrat beschlossen, dass Preißler es wieder verlieren soll. Bei zwei Enthaltungen stimmten 32 von 34 Mitgliedern für die Einleitung eines Abwahlverfahrens, deutlich mehr als die erforderlichen drei Viertel. Am 31. Januar haben die Bürger das letzte Wort.
Grund dafür, dass der Rathauschef aus dem Amt entfernt werden soll, ist die Tatsache, dass er es seit Monaten nicht mehr ausübt. Kurz nach der Vereidigung ging Preißler in den Urlaub. Anfang August berichtete die Polizei in Leipzig dann über einen Mann, der in einem Hotel randaliert, Gegenstände aus dem Fenster geworfen, Beamte angegriffen und zwei von ihnen leicht verletzt haben soll. Als sich herausstellte, dass es sich um den Freiberger Oberbürgermeister gehandelt hatte, wurde diesem durch das Landratsamt die Führung der Amtsgeschäfte untersagt und später ein Disziplinarverfahren eingeleitet. Über die Hintergründe für Preißlers Ausraster ist wenig bekannt. Ob gesundheitliche Probleme der Auslöser waren, ist offen. Die Ermittler äußern sich unter Verweis auf Persönlichkeitsrechte nicht. Der OB selbst ist abgetaucht.
Sein monatelanges Schweigen bewog schließlich die Freien Wähler dazu, eine Abwahl zu beantragen. Eine Erklärung Preißlers sei »längst überfällig«; sein Verhalten stelle »seine Eignung für das Amt infrage«, hieß es. Pikanterweise waren es die Freien Wähler, die Preißler als OB-Kandidat nominiert hatten. Zuvor war er Büroleiter des seit 2015 amtierenden Rathauschefs Sven Krüger gewesen, der zum Landrat von Mittelsachsen gewählt worden und zum 1. Mai 2026 aus dem Freiberger Rathaus in die Kreisverwaltung gewechselt war.
Die Freiberger Kommunalpolitik liegt trotz Preißlers Abwesenheit nicht brach. Die Verwaltung arbeite »eingespielt und reibungslos«, sagt Baubürgermeister Martin Seltmann, der 2023 auf den Posten kam und seit Krügers Weggang fast ununterbrochen auch als Vertreter des Oberbürgermeisters agiert. Weil Krüger einst zudem das Amt des Finanzbeigeordneten abschaffte und die Aufgaben dem OB zuschlug, »erledigt er praktisch sogar drei Jobs«, sagt Jana Pinka, Stadträtin des Bündnisses Freiberg für alle. »Das hält man nicht auf Dauer durch.« Sie merkt zudem an, dass der gewählte Oberbürgermeister Preißler trotz seiner Abwesenheit die vollen Bezüge kassiere. Der Rathauschef im gut 41.000 Bürger zählenden Freiberg wird nach Besoldungsstufe B5 bezahlt, was in Sachsen ohne Zuschläge rund 11.500 Euro im Monat entspricht.
Ende Januar können die Bürger entscheiden, ob dieser Zustand beendet werden soll. Allerdings sind die Hürden extrem hoch. Nicht nur muss es eine Mehrheit für Preißlers Abwahl geben. Die Anzahl derjenigen, die für die Abwahl stimmen, muss zudem mindestens der Hälfte der Wahlberechtigten entsprechen. So regelt es die sächsische Gemeindeordnung. Im zweiten Durchgang der OB-Wahl im Oktober 2025 hätten 30.245 Bürger abstimmen dürfen; das Quorum für die Amtsenthebung Preißlers läge damit bei gut 15.100 Stimmen. Das wären mehr als doppelt so viele wie die 7125 Stimmen, die diesem damals zum Sieg gegen drei Mitbewerber reichten, darunter den von Freiberg für alle aufgestellten und am Ende zweitplatzierten Christian Pudack. An der damaligen Wahl nahmen insgesamt nur 15.564 Freiberger teil.
Um überhaupt eine Chance zu haben, das Drama an der Stadtspitze zu beenden, müsse man sich also um eine ungewöhnlich hohe Wahlbeteiligung bemühen, sagt Pinka. Einfach wird das nicht an einem Sonntag im Winter, an dem keine andere Wahl die Bürger zum Urnengang animieren könnte. »Wir müssen uns für einen Abwahlkampf wappnen«, sagt die Stadträtin und weist auf eine bittere Ironie hin: Abgesehen von den Freien Wählern müssen die meisten Parteien und Wählervereinigungen nun viel Geld und Energie investieren, um einen Mann wieder loszuwerden, den sie von vornherein nicht in dem Amt sehen wollten.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.
