https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Jensen Huang’s affair: why did Trump ignore the warnings? | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
It could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice.
Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers.
Democrats, buoyed by their midterms’ success, will be looking for answers. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “No, I don’t think so.” That makes the question of his reasons unavoidable. There could be trouble at Mr Trump’s commerce department if it backed Mr Huang’s policy agenda and loosened export controls despite knowing of his affair with a Chinese spy. Reports suggest that the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia called investigators. Congress clearly has grounds to investigate whether the Trump administration knowingly disregarded a foreign intelligence threat. Whatever happens next, Mr Huang’s admission is likely to be the beginning, not the end, of the saga.
Rumours had swirled for months that Nvidia’s boss had been in a “special relationship” with Ms Huang – an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that in 2025 was revealed to be under investigation for suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. What makes this extraordinary is the possibility that Mr Huang’s romantic and commercial relationship exposed him to a Chinese intelligence operation. In May, analysts at Culper Research argued that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenues, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. Then Nividia’s boss publicly defended Megaspeed while secretly conducting an affair with its top executive. More than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation as soon as Wall Street opened.
Industrial espionage is nothing new. Richer nations often block the export of their commercial secrets to prevent others from catching up. These challengers often go to extraordinary lengths to obtain new technology. Historically, diplomatic or military so-called honeytraps – spies sent to seduce victims to gain confidential information – have been more common than commercial ones. But in 2008, British spy agencies accused Beijing of a campaign to target businesses, using sex to pressure targets into cooperating. Whether that has happened here is unknown. But a president who promised to get tough on China needs to explain why his administration eased chip export controls despite warnings that the businessman lobbying for it might be compromised.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/hongrie/le.title: Le frère de Viktor Orban aurait été arrêté pour trafic d’êtres humains
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/hongrie/le.author: Gaël De Santis
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/hongrie/le.text:
Selon le premier ministre, Péter Magyar et un média qui lui est proche, le frère de Viktor Orban aurait été arrêté et placé en garde à vue pour des soupçons de trafic d’être humains, ont-ils annoncé ce 9 novembre. Une information que ne confirme pas, pour l’heure, l’agence anti-corruption.
Dans la famille Orban, il y a Viktor, ancien premier ministre qui a fait son beurre en pourfendant l’immigration. Et il y a Aron, dont les entreprises ont prospéré durant ses seize années au pouvoir.
Ce même Aron « a été placé en garde à vue pour des soupçons de trafic d’être humains », affirme sur Facebook l’actuel premier ministre Péter Magyar ce 9 novembre. Une information dévoilée tout d’abord sur Kontroll, un site possédé par son propre frère, Marton Magyar.
Une accusation qui n’a pas pour l’heure été confirmée par Anna Róza Unger, la présidente de l’Agence nationale de récupération et de protection des avoirs (NVVH), organisme anti-corruption fondé à son arrivée par le gouvernement de Péter Magyar pour démanteler la « Mafia Orban ».
Une enquête pour trafic d’influence
Selon plusieurs médias, cette agence aurait lancé quatre enquêtes, dont une pour trafic d’influence. Un groupe de responsables politiques aurait promis des visas en échange d’argent par un contournement des procédures.
Ainsi, une compagnie d’Aron Orban aurait par exemple facilité l’entrée de Vietnamiens sur le territoire en les faisant participer à des cours de secourisme de deux jours à l’université de Pecs, indique le site Daily News Hungary.
Depuis sa défaite aux élections de mai dernier, le Fidesz, parti de Viktor Orban, qui avait alors obtenu 36,7 % des suffrages, perd en influence. Selon un sondage de l’institut Median, il ne lui est plus accordé que 16 % d’intentions de vote.
« C’est moi la cible, mon frère n’est qu’un outil », a réagi l’ancien premier ministre d’extrême droite Viktor Orban dont trois anciens ministres sont actuellement détenus suite aux enquêtes du NVVH.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.title: Kommunalwahlen in Südafrika | Südafrika: Debakel für Mandelas Erben
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.author: Martin Ling
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.text:
- Kommentare
- Kommunalwahlen in Südafrika
Südafrika: Debakel für Mandelas Erben
Bei den Kommunalwahlen in Südafrika hat der Afrikanische Nationalkongress (ANC) eine desaströse Niederlage eingefahren. Ein Kommentar.
Der Niedergang des Afrikanischen Nationalkongress (ANC) setzt sich fort. Nie hatte er seit dem Ende der Apartheid 1994 weniger Zuspruch und Kredit bei der südafrikanischen Bevölkerung als heutzutage. 15 Prozentpunkte weniger als bei den Kommunalwahlen 2021 heimste die einst unangefochten dominierende Partei am Wochenende ein. Die stärkstedes Landes ist sie aber immer noch – mit 30,76 Prozent im Landesschnitt.
Doch in vielen Kommunen verfehlte die Partei des verstorbenen Nationalhelden Nelson Mandela klar die Mehrheit und verlor Stadt- und Gemeinderäte, die sie seit Jahrzehnten dominiert hatte. Überraschen konnte maximal das Ausmaß der Stimmenverluste, dass der ANC der vielen Probleme im Land nicht Herr und deswegen bei Wahlen immer weiter abgestraft wird, ist ein seit Jahren anhaltendes Phänomen. Den ANC als kleinstes Übel zu wählen, wird als Option öfters denn je verworfen.
Auf nationaler Ebene hatte der ANC 2024 zum ersten Mal die absolute Mehrheit verloren. Die Regierung der nationalen Einheit unter seiner Führung mit der konservativen Demokratischen Allianz als Juniorpartner nebst einer Handvoll kleinerer Parteien hat bisher keine Wende zum Besseren gebracht. Südafrika ist laut Weltbank das Land mit der größten sozialen Ungleichheit weltweit und weist eine offizielle Arbeitslosenquote von über 30 Prozent. Die Wirtschaft stagniert seit einem Jahrzehnt, flankiert von hohen Kriminalitätsraten und maroden öffentlichen Einrichtungen, angefangen von den regelmäßigen Stromabschaltungen.
Der ANC hat nicht das geliefert, was nach dem Ende der Apartheid versprochen und erwartet wurde. Das hat zu einer tiefen sozialen Unzufriedenheit geführt, die Bewegungen wie die 2025 gegründete fremdenfeindliche »March and March« gegen die Einwanderer*innen gerichtet haben. Darauf reagiert Südafrikas vom ANC geführte Regierung mit Verständnis, nur Lynchjustiz lehnt sie ab.
Dass der ANC noch die Kurve kriegt und das macht, was nach dem Ende der Apartheid einst versprochen wurde, nämlich die bestehenden Eigentumsverhältnisse generalzuüberholen und für soziale Gerechtigkeit zu sorgen, ist nicht zu erwarten. Aber auch nicht von der Opposition jeglicher Couleur. Für Südafrika heißt das weiter wachsende soziale Konflikte – einschließlich wachsender Fremdenfeindlichkeit.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Verdict delayed in Honduras sex-trafficking case linked to disappearance
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Verdict delayed in Honduras sex-trafficking case linked to disappearance
Angie Pena’s disappearance in 2022 exposed what prosecutors called a sex-trafficking network and state corruption.
A court in Honduras has delayed a verdict in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Pena, a case that has raised concerns about impunity in transnational crimes.
On Monday, Honduras’s judiciary cited the need to review evidence and wait for the return of a court interpreter, who was out of the country. The decision has been delayed until November 20.
The verdict was expected that same day. Critics framed the unexpected delay as yet another hurdle in a case that has drawn comparisons to the crimes of the late Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender in the US accused of running a sex-trafficking ring.
Four men, including two US citizens, are on trial for crimes related to Pena’s disappearance four years ago.
Harold Green and William James Murdock, both from the US, face human-trafficking charges. Another US citizen, Gary Lee Johnston, and Honduran citizen Gustavo Trejo are accused of criminal association.
Honduran authorities have also sought an Interpol notice for another suspect, US citizen Antony Frank Grayson.
The Honduran public prosecutor’s office said the suspects are part of a network involved in crimes including drug trafficking and sex trafficking involving minors.
It alleges police and at least one judge helped facilitate the criminal network, without naming the officials.
Defence lawyers, however, have denied the men’s involvement and requested an acquittal.
Pena went missing on January 1, 2022, after setting out on a jet ski from West Bay on the Honduran island of Roatan, while vacationing with her family.
Authorities initially focused on a rescue mission at sea, treating her disappearance as a possible accident.
But the case expanded into a trafficking investigation after Pena’s jet ski was found in Belize, some 170km (90 nautical miles) away.
In August 2022, authorities investigating the disappearance found a minor in the Roatan house occupied by Johnston, who was later sentenced to 32 years for commercial sex trafficking and child pornography in a separate case.
An analysis by Honduran media found that the country was mentioned more than 100 times in the Epstein files, including multiple references to Roatan, from where Pena disappeared.
“There are many more women and girls who have been victims of trafficking networks, and those cases are silenced, they go unpunished,” said Kenia Paz, a lawyer for the Legal Team for Human Rights, which represents Pena’s family.
Lawyers representing the family have questioned the lack of transparency in the investigation and in the trial, which was not open to the press or the general public.
Postponing the verdict “fuels the perception of impunity, increases public distrust in state security institutions, and prolongs the suffering and vulnerability of affected families”, said former Honduran Vice Minister of Security Julissa Villanueva in a post on X.
Dereck McNeil, a key protected witness, was killed in August, spurring further concerns about the case.
In videos made public after his death, McNeil alleged corruption within a special unit of the public prosecutor’s office known as the ATIC.
He accused the unit of leaking information about the case and being linked to drug-trafficking networks.
The ATIC director has denied any corruption and said that the unit has not been involved in investigating Pena’s disappearance.
Villanueva, the former vice minister, told The Associated Press that she believes prosecutors mishandled the case from the start, pushing a “tunnel vision” explanation of what happened.
“There are connections with other larger networks, and only by making them public will this family be able to get justice,” said Villanueva.
“It’s not just Angie. It’s all those women around Angie. There are many.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Rebecca Bailey
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
There is little public information available about Alice Huang, the woman reportedly at the centre of the Jensen Huang honeypot allegations, a fact that has only added fuel to claims she is a Chinese intelligence asset.
She was the chief executive of a Singapore-based datacentre company reportedly suspected of evading US export controls and routing Nvidia chips to China.
US officials then came to believe she was also a spy for Beijing who was having an affair with Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, the chip company critical to US ambitions of staying ahead of China in the AI race.
People briefed on the US intelligence told the New York Times they believed Alice Huang was recruited as part of efforts to learn more about American AI chips, and to try to persuade Nvidia to push for its advanced chips to be made available to China.
China has denied the allegations, calling them “nothing but smears”.
It is unclear exactly when the two Huangs, who are not related, first met.
Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected within the upper echelons of the global AI chip industry, the New York Times wrote, citing people who had met her.
Megaspeed, the datacentre company for which she was previously listed as chief executive, still describes itself as “a premier business partner of Nvidia” on LinkedIn.
It was in this capacity that the businesswoman was pictured in Jensen Huang’s company several times in 2024 and 2025.
One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted by another attending company on LinkedIn, shows the two sitting next to each other on a couch in Taipei.
The year after, they were filmed together again in Taipei at a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.
Press outside livestreamed footage of the two, seemingly comfortable in each other’s company, with Jensen Huang at one point putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kissed him on the cheek.
The two later left the restaurant in the same car, the footage showed.
A New York-based short-selling firm first raised concerns publicly about their “uncomfortably close relationship” six months ago.
Earlier this year, US officials wrote a memo saying the two Huangs had been romantically involved, the Financial Times reported on Saturday, citing sources who had seen it.
On Sunday the Nvidia chief executive sent a company-wide email apologising for an affair.
He did not name Alice Huang but said he would cooperate with an investigation “regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports”.
Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unknown, and she has not given a public statement about the allegations.
It is unclear what her current relationship is with Megaspeed. Culper Research, the short-selling firm, quoted an employee in May as saying that contrary to public reporting, Alice Huang was “actually still our boss”.
The details of her career before that are difficult to ascertain.
Several media outlets have cited a profile matching her name and picture on a Chinese fund database, which listed previous jobs at banks including HSBC and CITIC, as well as roles at Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.
However, reporters have been unable to confirm any of the details listed.
Megaspeed is among a number of south-east Asian firms that buy chips to build facilities and then rent their computing power to companies in China.
According to Singapore’s Straits Times, it was previously known as 7Road International – a Chinese gaming company with ties to state-backed investors.
At the time of the rebrand, it was owned by Huang Le Limited and led by Alice Huang, the newspaper said, before the ownership was transferred to another company in 2023.
Since late 2024, the US government has reportedly been investigating Megaspeed for helping companies in China sidestep American export restrictions.
The New York Times said Singapore questioned Alice Huang during its own investigation into the company, but released her.
Nvidia has previously said it has looked into Megaspeed but found no cause for concern.
The Guardian has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

Depuis le 20 octobre, une trentaine de salariés du restaurant des Champs-Élysées sont en grève contre un management brutal qui licencie à tour de bras. Présents dans toutes les manifs, ils incarnent à merveille un mouvement qui entend aussi se faire respecter.
C’est une mousse au chocolat qui n’aurait pas été fabriquée dans les règles. Pour l’utilisation d’un « mauvais » fouet, la punition tombe : mise à pied de cinq jours pour un cuisinier qui la confectionne pourtant ainsi depuis des décennies. C’est un passe-plat entre le rez-de-chaussée et le premier étage du restaurant. Il est en rade depuis des lustres, et la direction ne fait plus semblant de vouloir réparer, contraignant le personnel en salle à trottiner dans les escaliers.
Ce sont les sous-traitants pour le nettoyage qui sont écartés par pur esprit de lucre, poussant à envoyer tel ou tel commis en urgence aux toilettes. C’est ce bac à graisse dont les « cavistes », chargés de toute la logistique...

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.title: Bewegungen | Gen-Z-regelt – Zwischen Solidarität und Vereinnahmung
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.author: Patrick Lempges
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.text:
- Politik
- Bewegungen
Gen-Z-regelt – Zwischen Solidarität und Vereinnahmung
Luisa Neubauer, die Interventionistische Linke und die Junge Union zeigen Verständnis für »Gen-Z-regelt«. Wer ist Unterstützer, wer Ausbeuter?
Am 20. November wird wieder demonstriert. In mehr als 30 Städten ruft die Initiative »Gen Z regelt« erneut zu Protesten auf, gleichzeitig wollen Studierende an mehreren Hochschulen den Lehrbetrieb bestreiken. Der erste bundesweite Aktionstag Ende Oktober hatte mehr als 100.000 Menschen auf die Straße gebracht. Die meisten demonstrierten friedlich für bessere Bildung, Bezahlbarkeit, Klimaschutz und gegen die Wehrpflicht. Anschließende Ausschreitungen, insbesondere in Frankfurt am Main, bestimmten allerdings die politische Debatte.
Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) sprach von »gewaltbereiten linken Gruppen und migrantischen Chaoten«, die sich unter die Demonstrierenden gemischt hätten. Auch andere Unionspolitiker warnten vor einer Unterwanderung der Proteste. Grünen-Politiker und SPD-Verteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius hatten vor pauschalen Zuschreibungen gewarnt. Die Linke kritisierte die Kriminalisierung der Proteste und beantragte eine Aktuelle Stunde im Bundestag.
Wie aber blicken diejenigen Bewegungen auf Gen-Z-regelt, die schon länger für Klimaschutz, soziale Gerechtigkeit und linke Politik auf die Straße gehen? Und wer versucht, die Proteste tatsächlich für sich zu nutzen?
Fridays for Future
Bei Fridays for Future (FFF) hält man sich bislang organisatorisch aus den Demonstrationen heraus. Inhaltlich gibt es allerdings durchaus Überschneidungen. Die Klimabewegung erklärt, solidarisch mit den friedlichen Protesten für Klimaschutz, bessere Lern- und Lebensbedingungen und gegen die Wehrpflicht zu sein. Gerade in Krisenzeiten würden die Interessen junger Menschen besonders leicht übergangen. Während Politiker*innen immer wieder bessere Schulen und Generationengerechtigkeit versprächen, werde am Ende über die Köpfe der Jugendlichen hinweg entschieden: »Wir brauchen jetzt konkret eine Politik, die auch junge Menschen in den Mittelpunkt stellt: Gelder für bessere Schulen, echte Beteiligung, Zukunftschancen und ein gutes Leben für alle.«
Auch Luisa Neubauer, eine der bekanntesten Stimmen von Fridays for Future, sieht die Wut der jungen Generation als berechtigt an. In einem Gastbeitrag für die »Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung« beschreibt sie einen brüchig gewordenen Generationenvertrag: Das Versprechen, dass es der nächsten Generation einmal besser gehen werde, lasse sich angesichts von Klimakrise, marodem Bildungssystem und möglicher Wehrpflicht kaum noch aufrechterhalten. »Dass sich junge Menschen nun in Deutschland und ganz Europa zu Wort melden, ist nicht nur ihr gutes Recht – es ist regelrecht überfällig«, so Neubauer.
Zugleich hat Neubauer einen strategischen Rat an die Organisator*innen. Im RBB-Inforadio empfahl sie, die Forderungen stärker zu bündeln. Die vielen Krisen machten es zwar nachvollziehbar, dass die Bewegung möglichst viele Probleme gleichzeitig angehen wolle. Politischen Druck aufzubauen werde aber leichter, wenn die Ziele klarer umrissen seien. Neubauer sieht außerdem die Gefahr, dass die Ausschreitungen nach den Demonstrationen dazu benutzt werden, eine ganze Generation zu diskreditieren.
Linke Perspektive
Deutlich offensiver positioniert sich die Interventionistische Linke (IL), die bedeutendste linksradikale Gruppe auf Bewegungsebene in Deutschland. Gegenüber dem »nd« erklärt die IL, sie teile die Wut über die politischen Verhältnisse. Die Generation habe einige ihrer wichtigsten Jugendjahre im Lockdown verbracht und erlebe nun eine Politik, die ihr Wehrdienst abverlange, während gleichzeitig ein großer Teil der öffentlichen Daseinsvorsorge gekürzt werde. Die IL sieht in der zunehmenden Wut keinen Grund zur Distanzierung, sondern eine Folge davon, dass die herrschenden Verhältnisse jungen Menschen kaum Perspektiven böten.
Dass die Proteste wütender würden, sei deshalb kein Zufall. »Diese Generation hat in den bestehenden Verhältnissen keinen Platz. Auch deshalb ist dieser Protest so unversöhnlich und das mit Recht!«, heißt es von der IL. Die Organisation sieht darin nicht bloß einen Protest gegen einzelne politische Entscheidungen, sondern einen grundsätzlichen Konflikt mit den herrschenden Verhältnissen.
Auf die Frage, wer hinter der Bewegung stehe, antworte die IL: »Das ist keine geplante und von Aktivist*innen erdachte Kampagne, sondern Teil einer weltweit sich artikulierenden Jugendrevolte.« Auf der Straße seien sowohl Menschen gewesen, die bislang kaum demonstriert hätten, als auch erfahrene Aktivist*innen. Auch Eltern hätten demonstriert, aus Sorge, ihre Kinder könnten von der Bundesregierung in den Krieg geschickt werden.
Die IL will sich daher an der Bewegung beteiligen und bestehende Strukturen bei Bedarf unterstützen: »Wir sind in einigen Städten schon mittendrin und natürlich wollen wir dort, wo es Sinn ergibt, die entstehenden Strukturen stärken und unterstützen.« Dabei sei es besonders wichtig, ein paternalistisches Verhältnis zu vermeiden. Am Ende zähle, dass sich die Menschen selbst organisieren und für ihre Interessen eintreten, doch Bewegungen seien immer Bewegungen verschiedener Gruppen, die jeweils ihren Teil der Arbeit zur Veränderung beitragen. »Wir werden unseren Teil der Arbeit leisten und unser Bewegungswissen gerne mit neuen Leuten teilen.«
Versuchte Vereinnahmung durch die Junge Union
Während sich die IL, FFF aber auch Die Linke und ihre Parteijugend in Pressemitteilungen mit den Protesten solidarisch zeigen, bemüht sich die Union um eine andere Deutung des Protests. Besonders deutlich wird dies bei der Jungen Union. Deren Bundesvorsitzender Johannes Winkel (CDU) erklärte im ARD-»Bericht aus Berlin«, er könne die Unzufriedenheit junger Menschen nachvollziehen – die junge Generation werde von der Politik vernachlässigt, so der 35-jährige Bundestagsabgeordnete.
Winkels Erklärung für die Proteste fällt allerdings bemerkenswert aus: Er führt die Enttäuschung der Jugend von der Politik vor allem auf die Rentenpolitik der Bundesregierung zurück. Die geplante Rentenreform sei katastrophal für die junge Generation, und wenn die Regierung die Vorschläge der Rentenkommission umsetze, könne sie Vertrauen zurückgewinnen, so Winkel. Damit versucht der JU-Chef, den Protest in die eigene politische Auseinandersetzung mit der Bundesregierung vom letzten Jahr einzubetten. Damals rebellierte die Junge Gruppe unter seiner Führung gegen die Rentenpläne der Regierung und verlangte geringere Renten und Rentenbeiträge. Dass die Demonstrierenden gegen Wehrpflicht, Sozialkürzungen und Aufrüstung protestieren und bessere Bildung sowie Klimaschutz verlangen, spielt in seiner Deutung überhaupt keine Rolle.
Dabei hatten Unionspolitiker im Vorfeld noch vor einer politischen Unterwanderung der Demonstrationen durch linke Gruppen gewarnt. Nun ist es ausgerechnet der Vorsitzende der eigenen Jugendorganisation, der versucht, den Protest für die eigene Agenda zu vereinnahmen. Schon zuvor hatte Bundesbildungsministerin Karin Prien (CDU) versucht, die berechtigte Frustration der Jugend mit zu hohen Rentenbeiträgen in Verbindung zu bringen, Zuspruch gab es keinen.
Während eher sicherheitsaffine Teile der Union vor den vermeintlichen Gefahren der kommenden Demonstrationen warnen, versuchen andere Teile der Union, den Jugendlichen eigene politische Anliegen zuzuschreiben. Die Linke und die außerparlamentarische Bewegung wiederum sehen in den Demonstrationen das Potenzial für einen breiteren gesellschaftlichen Aufbruch. Was die Bewegung tatsächlich fordert, ist auf ihrer Website und auf ihren kommenden Demonstrationen zu sehen.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Trump says FBI probing Nvidia CEO Huang’s affair with alleged spy
US president says he believes CEO Jensen Huang had no knowledge of woman’s alleged work for Chinese intelligence.
United States President Donald Trump has said the FBI is probing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman accused of working for Chinese intelligence services.
Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump said law enforcement had begun inquiries following Huang’s admission that he engaged in an extramarital relationship with a Chinese executive named Alice Huang.
“We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else,” Trump told reporters at a news conference. “I think he will be in good shape.”
Trump said Huang told him earlier that he had “absolutely no idea” that the woman was an alleged intelligence agent.
“He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” Trump said.
Asked by a reporter when he first became aware of concerns about the relationship, Trump said it was “not too long ago”.
“I have been hearing about it and I have been reading a little bit about it over a period of time,” the US president said.
Nvidia, which dominates the market for high-end chips used to power artificial intelligence, did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Nvidia on Sunday announced that it had opened a probe into its CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, following media reports that cited US intelligence claiming she worked for China’s Ministry of State Security.
Nvidia’s board of directors said it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised, but that an independent inquiry overseen by outside counsel would examine “all available information”.
In a separate statement admitting to an extramarital relationship, Huang apologised to his family, colleagues and shareholders, and pledged to cooperate fully with the board’s inquiry.
Huang’s admission came after the New York Times and the Financial Times last week reported that unnamed US officials had authored a memo alleging that he had been targeted by Alice Huang for intelligence-gathering activities.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday rejected the allegations, with spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying the reports were “groundless speculation, and a smear against China”.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Nvidia, based in Santa Clara, California, is a critical player in the global AI race, controlling an estimated 80 to 90 percent of the market for graphics processing units (GPUs) used to run frontier models.
Shares of Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable companies, fell 4.27 percent on Monday to close at $178.67.

https://www.propublica.org/article/midte.title: Trump Has Tried to Exert More Control Over Elections. Here Are the Key Findings From Our Reporting.
https://www.propublica.org/article/midte.text:
Ahead of next week’s midterm elections, President Donald Trump has systematically demolished institutional guardrails that prevented him from overturning the 2020 presidential election, ProPublica’s reporting has shown.
Trump has empowered his loyalists to try to transform the voting process. He launched an unprecedented — and largely unsuccessful — effort to find noncitizen voters. And he tried to restrict mail-in voting.
Our reporters have spent much of this year covering Trump’s efforts to exert more federal control over elections. Here are five takeaways from their reporting.
1. The Trump administration has sought greater federal control over elections.
In April, Doug Bock Clark and Jen Fifield reported on Trump’s efforts to “take over” the midterm elections, detailing how the administration has discarded or diminished endeavors across the federal government to protect the voting process or block foreign interference. Those efforts have included cutting staff on election-related teams at federal law enforcement agencies and finding ways to exert greater federal control over voting.
Our reporting led by Peter Elkind revealed that the Trump administration harnessed Homeland Security Investigations’ personnel, technology and legal authority to try to back up Trump’s unproven claim that illegal voting by noncitizens is tilting elections toward Democrats. Administration officials insisted the effort spearheaded by HSI was producing meaningful results. Our analysis of Justice Department data found, as of May, 41 alleged noncitizens were charged with voting illegally or other election-related crimes. Earlier this month, CBS reported 156 people have been charged since the beginning of the second Trump administration.
“Paper Trail” Podcast
Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “Paper Trail.”
As part of that effort, the Justice Department has demanded states turn over unredacted voter rolls, which contain confidential information on millions of Americans and have historically been managed by states. Since September 2025, the department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for the confidential data. Wary of federal overreach, state officials — including some Republicans — have fought back, and so far every DOJ lawsuit that’s been decided by a federal judge has been dismissed. (The Trump administration has appealed most of its losses to federal appeals courts and has said it will consider taking its fight to the Supreme Court. A Justice Department spokesperson said its “attorneys are skilled, principled advocates who argue every case honestly and in good faith.”)
In a March executive order, Trump instructed the U.S. Postal Service to create new regulations for mail voting. The rules would have put the Postal Service in the unprecedented role of deciding whether to send or deny the delivery of voters’ mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court in September blocked the rules, at least until after November.
The Trump administration has said its actions will make U.S. elections fairer and more secure — and keep those prohibited from voting, such as noncitizens, from doing so. Spokespeople for the DOJ and Department of Homeland Security emphasized that their departments are focused on ensuring elections are free and fair, and that they are working closely with the states to achieve those goals. Contentions to the contrary, they say, are false.
2. Trump has pushed out career officials — and is coordinating with a conservative grassroots organization to transform elections.
At least 75 nonpartisan career officials who’d held roles at federal agencies related to election integrity and safety have been fired or left the government.
Two dozen Trump appointees — including many from the election-denial movement — have been hired. Ahead of the midterms, current and former government officials and election security experts have expressed concerns that once-fringe actors who’ve espoused debunked conspiracy theories about elections are now in positions to control the narrative around the voting process. (A DHS spokesperson said it hires “experts with diverse backgrounds who go through a rigorous vetting process.”)
At least 25 administration appointees have close ties to Cleta Mitchell, a lawyer who leads Election Integrity Network, a grassroots conservative group focused on transforming America’s voting system. This month, Clark profiled Mitchell — and detailed how, despite not holding a formal role in the White House, she’s played a key role in shaping the Trump administration’s elections agenda. The White House has appointed her associates to help hunt for noncitizen voters and investigate accusations of voting fraud in 2020. (Mitchell declined multiple requests to speak with ProPublica, but wrote in an email: “You’re my opponent. … You’re never going to write in any objective, non-judgmental way about the election integrity movement.”)
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
Mitchell, who played a role in helping Trump challenge his loss in the 2020 presidential election, has been leading efforts to pass state and federal iterations of the SAVE Act. The 2026 version of the bill, known as the SAVE America Act, would require voters nationwide to provide proof of citizenship to register and present a photo ID to vote, and would compel states to turn over their voter rolls to DHS. Trump has repeatedly called the measure his top legislative priority, but it has been blocked in the Senate.
In July, Trump also pushed out the remaining members of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission, a four-member board designed to be evenly split between Republicans and Democrats that sets standards for state voting systems. (At the time, a White House official wouldn’t confirm the moves but said the president “reserves the right to remove individuals that may not be totally aligned with the important task of securing America’s elections and ensuring every legal vote is counted.”)
3. Trump officials asked a cybersecurity agency to secretly acquire a voting machine — and hack it.
A few months into Trump’s second term, political appointees at DHS asked its Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure a voting machine, hack it and report the findings so they could be given to the White House, two former administration officials with knowledge of the request told Clark and Andy Mannix.
CISA employees told the political appointees their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. (One of Trump’s first actions when he returned to the White House was to dismantle the agency’s election security work.)
Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems. Since CISA became an agency in 2018, it has come to provide crucial support to thousands of local election officials grappling with increasingly sophisticated attacks.
But some state election officials said CISA provided them with little help as they planned for the 2026 midterms. And other state authorities told Clark and Mannix that they no longer trusted the agency and feared it had been compromised by the Trump administration. (A DHS spokesperson told us in April the “claim that DHS has a broken partnership with states and made our elections less secure is simply false.”)
DHS did not respond to questions for our October investigation, but a DHS spokesperson previously told ProPublica that the changes at CISA were in response to “a ballooning budget concealing a dangerous departure from its statutory mission,” which included “electioneering instead of defending America’s critical infrastructure.” A White House spokesperson declined an interview request but said, “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”
4. The White House floated an idea that would’ve shut down virtually all mail-in voting.
The White House initially proposed a change for the Postal Service that would’ve been even more disruptive than the rule the Supreme Court rejected in September.
As Fifield and Elkind reported, the Trump administration suggested all ballots be delivered through certified mail, meaning voters would need to be home to sign for delivery of their ballots. The Trump administration dropped this plan after the USPS said it would be too difficult to execute. It instead proceeded with the executive order that would’ve forced postal workers to serve as gatekeepers, deciding which ballots would be delivered and which wouldn’t.
In an emailed statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied the administration had interfered improperly with the Postal Service, an independent agency whose governance structure is specifically designed to protect it from political influence.
The Supreme Court’s order in September means that voting by mail can proceed as planned for the midterms, with states left to decide the rules for mail-in ballots.
5. The Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have led to delays and more rejected ballots in rural areas.
Amid the increased attention on the Postal Service’s role in elections, a ProPublica analysis found that delays resulting from the agency’s cost-cutting measures in recent years have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas.
The Postal Service has consolidated processing of first-class mail into regional hubs, and the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from those processing plants. The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and pushed back postmarking, an official mark confirming an envelope has been received by the Postal Service.
Across five states where the best data was available — Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon — the delays during this year’s primary elections have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024.
Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts in place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Peggy Flanagan Makes Her Closing Argument Against Trump’s “Cruelty and Chaos” in the Minnesota Senate Race
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Joan Walsh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Peggy Flanagan Makes Her Closing Argument Against Trump’s “Cruelty and Chaos” in the Minnesota Senate Race
Flanagan opponent Michele Tafoya’s extreme and erratic stands on Operation Metro Surge may well cost her the Senate seat.
Minnesota GOP Senate candidate Michele Tafoya has had nearly a year to take a solid stand on Donald Trump’s “Operation Metro Surge,” which sent ICE and other federal agents into her state to seize immigrants, snatch children from parents, and murder two Minneapolis citizens, poet and mother Renée Good and nurse Alex Pretti. The former NFL sideline reporter has failed to do so, and now it’s Minnesota’s turn to weigh in on Tafoya. Her extreme and erratic stands on Metro Surge may well cost her the Senate race, against consistent surge critic Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan.
Just to recap: As the siege began in December, Tafoya defended it on her podcast. “Look, Immigration and Customs Enforcement is a law enforcement group and they are trying to enforce the law and they’re trying to do it in cities that have major issues. They’ve determined that Minneapolis is one such city.” In her campaign rollout video, she included glowing footage of ICE operations. Maybe most outrageously, she blamed Good for her own murder.
Related Article
“I’m sure you guys are seeing on the Internet this car that was driving right toward an agent,” she said the day Good died, on The Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show. “You can’t run people over with a car. The car is a deadly weapon.” When multiple forensic examinations showed decisively that Good was driving her car away from Customs and Border Patrol agent Jonathan Ross, Tafoya shifted blame to Minnesota Democrats she claimed were leading people like Good, and later Pretti, to interfere with Metro Surge.
“They have created an environment where people think, ‘Oh my gosh, I have to go resist,’” she told The Will Cain Show. “‘I can’t just peacefully protest. I’ve gotta put my body, my car… This is what I have to do in order to stop this.’”
Pretti’s gruesome killing—video captured ICE agents shooting him multiple times in the back, while he knelt on a Nicollet Avenue sidewalk subdued by other agents—turned public opinion sharply against Metro Surge. So Tafoya calibrated, a little, applauding the departure of Department of Homeland Security director Kristi Noem and praising Trump for putting “border czar” Tom Homan in charge in February. But she quickly returned to blaming Minnesota Democrats, and protesters she repeatedly called “violent,” for the clashes in the streets of Minneapolis. And in her October debate with Flanagan, Tafoya bizarrely blamed Minnesota protesters, and Flanagan herself, for worsening Operation Metro Surge.
“This was not about peaceful protesting. This was about violence and criminal conduct. And she should know because she has participated in illegal protests in the past as well,” Tafoya said. Flanagan countered by noting that Tafoya accused Good of causing her own death, and Tafoya replied, “That is a hideous statement.” The debate moderator didn’t follow up.
I began putting together this brief recap of Tafoya’s many defenses of Operation Metro Surge when I saw multiple reports that, at least 10 days before the election, Minneapolis’s early vote totals had already reached 101 percent of its early vote in the 2024 presidential election. The New York Times noted that the city was “the heart of Operation Metro Surge.” That seemed like bad news for Tafoya. A few days later a Times/Siena College poll showed Flanagan up 54–40 percent over her GOP challenger.
I caught up with Flanagan, while she was on a last-weekend bus tour of her state, to discuss the role she thought Operation Metro Surge was playing in her contest with Tafoya.
The early voting numbers, she told me, “are incredibly encouraging and hopeful. But what I also know is that it matches the energy that we are feeling on the ground. People are fired up to vote. I think this is the biggest opportunity that people who’ve been impacted by Donald Trump and Operation Metro Surge have, to push back on this administration, and to send folks to Washington, DC, to be a check on the cruelty and chaos that we have experienced firsthand.”
Flanagan went on: “I think this has really been the arc of this campaign, right? From Operation Metro Surge, and how people showed up to march, and to feed their neighbors, and to drive kids home from school who weren’t even their kids. Then going to precinct caucuses, to becoming delegates to the state convention, to a 20-point win in the primary.” Flanagan beat Democratic rival Angie Craig, who has since endorsed her, by that much in August.
“And now headed into the general election, where Donald Trump has endorsed my opponent multiple times in the last couple of weeks.”
I asked Flanagan how she’d chart Tafoya’s evolution on Operation Metro Surge. “There’s no evolution,” she said flatly. “The thing you can count on her to do is be two-faced. She has said that ICE should be called ‘NICE.’ She said that ICE treated children really, really well, in response to 5-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos’s being detained.
“I just think that every time she opens her mouth to express outrage about this,” Flanagan continues, “she tells on herself, that she does not know the people of Minnesota, and frankly, they do not know her. What I witnessed in Operation Metro Surge: literally packing bags [of groceries] to feed my neighbors. It was marching in negative 30-below, bundled up with 50,000 people. It was simply telling the truth about what it is that we have experienced. For me, it was Christmas Eve, at Mass.” Flanagan attends the multiracial, bilingual, activist Catholic Church of the Ascension in northern Minneapolis, whose Latino members were hard hit by Metro Surge. ”And there were maybe 40 people, when usually that night you can’t even get a seat, because people were so afraid.” She sounds increasingly fed up with Tafoya. “Give me a break, lady. You have no idea what you’re talking about.”

But Flanagan insists that her base of support goes well beyond Minnesotans outraged by Operation Metro Surge. She had just finished an energetic tour of Indian Country, including her own home base of White Earth, where she’s an enrolled member of the Ojibwe tribe (her Irish Catholic mother signed her up, even though she’d separated from Flanagan’s father, the late Ojibwe leader Marvin Manypenny). She ticked off the issues she says are propelling her campaign.
“We’ve done 340 events in 125 communities, and every single place I go, people talk about affordability, specifically around healthcare. This is the thing. that I hear about in every community, urban, rural, suburban. And I did not start off in this campaign supporting Medicare for All, but having these conversations with Minnesotans I was like, oh, this is what we have to fight for, and this is what we’ve got to do.” As we hang up, I ask Flanagan about Tafoya’s calling the NYT-Siena poll that showed her 14 points behind “an outlier.” She laughs.
“Listen, I’ve always run for office like I’m 10 points behind. I’m not taking anything for granted. We are gonna run it through the tape.” Her staff signals to both of us that it’s time to get back on the bus and continue her final-weekend travels, and we say goodbye.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Donald Trump Has Lost It
At one of his final midterm rallies, the president showed just what a spent political force he has become—and what little grip on reality he still has.
Dubuque, Iowa—“It’s pure fricking genius.”
Donald Trump was, of course, describing himself—or rather his rhetorical stump style, which had been trained on the crowd of MAGA faithful assembled here at Dubuque’s Five Flags Center for more than an hour. He’d been complaining about how his wife, Melania, wants him to be less demonstrative at the rally podium—less dancing, no more impersonations of female weightlifters getting bested by transgender competitors. The first lady, Trump protested, wants him to be “more presidential,” which prompted him to do an impersonation of a typical campaign stiff: “Ladies and gentlemen of Iowa, it is a great honor to be with you this evening.” (The impression came across a good deal like House Speaker Mike Johnson, who did a cameo turn at the podium during Trump’s performance.)
Trump then gleefully went through a series of weird angular gesticulations to simulate his slantwise narrative style—the string of non sequitur grievances and resentful old-rich-guy refrains that he dubbed “the weave” during the 2024 campaign. But that descriptor has graduated, midway through his second term, into the work of a maestro.
This was one of the last Trump rallies in the 2026 midterm cycle—which is to say, one of the last Trump rallies we will ever need to care about, given that the president is hurtling toward lame-duck status. The president’s stylings on the stump had revolutionized American politics a decade ago. Now, like a good Midwest county fair touring band, Trump had revived many of his oldest MAGA hits. He laid into the “sick people” on the press risers at the back of the room, insisting that “they are the biggest threat to our country.” He railed against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, dubbing him a “jihadist” and “Communist” and proudly explaining why he’s repeatedly given his first name as “Mohammed.” (It’s something he does for “certain reasons,” he said, in a strained effort to make gutter bigotry sound somehow cagey, before gleefully announcing that he does it “because I’m the president.”) He lobbed kindred racist attacks against Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar, whom his Justice Department has targeted with a bogus authoritarian raid and investigation, as well as Somali immigrants; like any washed-up anti-woke comic, he said, “I hope I don’t say anything too controversial” to set up his pet anti-Somali refrain: “We don’t want them here.” There were also extended riffs, even now, about Joe Biden’s cognitive failings, the de rigueur reminder that Trump has “aced” three cognitive exams himself, and some talk about Kamala Harris’s woeful turn as overseer of immigration policy at the White House—all key issues for him and essentially nobody else.
It was hard to see how any of this translates into fricking genius, though. I was in the upper levels of the stadium, and several of my seatmates were straining to make out just what Trump was talking about—especially when he went into digressive genius mode, dilating on optimal flagpole design and golf masters as models for political achievement (yes, really).
Last week, the GOP briefly canceled the rally in favor of a virtual gathering, which would ostensibly be a bigger draw (an objective that makes zero sense for an event meant to generate excitement and boost turnout for state and local politicians). Then the party reversed course, perhaps understanding how weak the move would make Trump look. Five Flags is a small facility—it boasts ads in the corridors for a February performance of a Pink Floyd Tribute band, “Think Floyd”—and it was reasonably full, despite the event’s bait-and-switch scheduling..
Trump came on stage 90 minutes late—long after all the GOP candidates in this suddenly purplish battleground state had delivered their own versions of the stiff-politician election-eve pitches. During the protracted stretch of dead air, the crowd began to get restive and bored; the playlist of classic rock standards began repeating, and at one point, people began swaying their phones in flashlight mode in time to Sinead O’Connor’s “Nothing Compares 2 U”—a singularly odd spectacle after the state’s gubernatorial GOP nominee, Zach Lahn, inveighed against the depraved and murderous character of liberal culture warfare; this was, after all, a performer best known for tearing a photo of the pope in half on live television. There was a palpable mood of the agitprop starting to lose interest in itself.
A very different brand of Kulturkampf was announced, in any event, ahead of Trump’s appearance. There was a video of white-jumpsuit Vegas-era Elvis—a performer the crowd had already heard at least a half-dozen times over on the soundtrack—delivering a demented medley of “Dixie” and “The Battle Hymn of the Republic.” Near the end of the mashup, the camera lingered uncomfortably on a Black flautist in the Elvis ensemble delivering the closing strains of “Dixie.” A nearby diehard MAGA supporter must have noted my goggle-eyed expression and volunteered, “That was really weird.”
Not as weird as the next video entry: the 2024 rally chestnut called “God Made Trump,” delivered as a riff on radio Paul Harvey’s address “God Made a Farmer,” but shot through with the militant messianic imagery of the New Apostolic Reformation. The video starts with an AI-manipulated version of Harvey’s voice announcing “On June 14, 1946, God looked down on his planned paradise and said, ‘I need a caretaker,’” and goes rapidly downhill from there, depicting Trump as an axe-wielding mortal foe of wolves, vipers, the deep state, and the fake news.
It all made for an abrupt shift of tone from the autopilot classic rock playlist, but it didn’t really come anywhere near a closing campaign argument. Iowa is facing many pressing economic and political challenges—from the soaring price of diesel and fertilizer in the wake of Trump’s war in Iran to overlapping crises in cancer and water quality to the declining standing of the state’s formerly distinguished public education system. Senate GOP nominee Ashley Hinson has belatedly positioned herself as an opponent of the Iran War, after voting in favor of it seven times in the House, in order to stay competitive with her upstart Democratic rival, state Representative Josh Turek. Lahn has broken ranks with deregulatory Republican orthodoxy to demand investigations into the cancer and water crises.
Trump, not surprisingly, didn’t mention any of these problems, or GOP proposals to address them; his prescription for electoral victory in Iowa appeared to be Worship me harder. So he stayed firmly and gleefully within his comfort zone of deriding Democrats as “lunatics” hell-bent on spreading communism and forcing sex changes on the children of unwitting God-fearing parents. He made desultory promises that gas prices would come down shortly after the midterms—presumably by resuming the same large-scale attacks on Iran that have already caused those prices to skyrocket while completely failing to defeat the Islamic Republic. He reprised his bribery pledge of $5,000 to every voter who will preserve and expand the GOP majorities in Congress. But he relied mostly on more video footage to drive home the theme of the GOP 2026 campaign: “craziness versus common sense.” One scattershot set of supercuts sought to dramatize the socialist orthodoxy and transgender fetishes of the Democrats, while another highlighted the alleged open-border excesses of the Biden White House, and dwelled on lurid details of murders and sexual attacks from undocumented immigrants. By the time the second video kicked in, people in my section and many on the main floor began to leave. They’d seen this show before—and besides, they could watch Fox News in the comfort of their home, without having to see Elvis hymn the Confederacy or Donald Trump cosplay as Jesus.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Hochul and Mamdani Teach Democrats a Vital Lesson in Party Unity
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Bill de Blasio
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Hochul and Mamdani Teach Democrats a Vital Lesson in Party Unity
New York State’s governor and New York City’s mayor are illustrating how ideologically diverse Democrats can build winning coalitions.
To paraphrase a classic work, there is a specter haunting the Democratic Party, and its name is “socialism.” Or at least that’s what the mainstream American media would have you believe.
Whichever network I appear on, I’m sure to get a breathless question about the looming civil war between the progressive and moderate wings of my party.
It is treated as an article of faith that peaceful coexistence is an impossibility, and that any chance of unity will inevitably be subverted by the wily and newly empowered Democratic Socialists of America.
This narrative is oh-so-clean and fulfills the normal journalistic desire for conflict.
But the facts on the ground in 2026 suggest a far different reality, one that has been consistently developing over the last decade and that in truth offers new possibilities for the growth of the party.
The most powerful example is on display in my state: New York. Here, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul have formed a mutually beneficial and strikingly cohesive alliance. In the New York context, we are getting an object lesson in the ways both wings of our party actually need each other.
On many of the issues that matter, it is Mamdani who often sets the tone ideologically and moves Hochul leftward, a phenomenon we will see more frequently around the country.
The recent adoption by the state legislature of a pied-a-terre tax for NYC—asking a little more from those with expensive second homes—is an example of a progressive policy that Albany would never have passed on its own but felt it had to because of the grassroots energy created by Mamdani’s movement.
To be clear, this is not an entirely new reality. When I was elected mayor in 2013 on a platform of higher taxes on the wealthy to fund Universal Pre-K, my campaign created inexorable pressure on then-Governor Andrew Cuomo to act.
The difference now is that rather than resisting Mamdani at every turn (which was my experience with Cuomo), Hochul understands that the best way to both win elections and to govern is with the mayor by her side.
The governor has taken positions on taxation and on Mamdani’s enlightened Universal Childcare Plan that she otherwise might not have. But instead of the sky falling for her politically because she worked with a democratic socialist, she is arguably in a stronger position to lead than ever.
In the run-up to today’s midterm elections, the Democratic Party’s Washington-based organs began to embrace the general election campaigns of progressive primary-winners in ways they wouldn’t have in the past. It may be grudging and not generous enough, but it has been happening.
DNC chair Ken Martin has more genuine affinity for the progressive wing than almost any of his predecessors, and Democratic congressional leaders Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have clearly been changing their tune about the new voices emerging around them.
Have we seen a seamless and elegant transition to a new political reality? No, as has been illustrated by the drama surrounding defeated centrist Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens, and her late-stage withdrawal of support for the party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.
But Stevens is the exception, not the norm. In most states, open warfare is rare. For the most part, the two tendencies are working together.
Even in Michigan, after arguably the nastiest primary fight in the nation, the vast majority of the mainstream Democratic establishment, led by centrist Senator Elissa Slotkin, quickly united behind El-Sayed. Indeed, Slotkin had been a steady and effective campaigner for El-Sayed.
Were there entirely practical motivations for Democrats such as Hochul and Slotkin to embrace unity and enlightened approaches to the 2026 campaign?
Absolutely!
But what’s striking is the growing recognition that moderates now need the energy and mobilization and new ideas that progressives bring.
And these examples also remind us that progressives can benefit from the resources (in Hochul’s case) and the access to important constituencies (in Slotkin’s case) that moderates often bring to the table.
Although I don’t want to overstate the notion that a productive modus vivendi is developing between the two wings of the party, it’s fair to say nationally there has been a striking change in recent years.
If 2016 was an extraordinary growth moment for the left because of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders’s campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination, it also marked a low point for party unity. The Clinton campaign and the Democratic establishment simply couldn’t forgive Bernie’s audacity and didn’t want to embrace his movement. I had a front-row seat in Philadelphia as this huge mistake of arrogance and underestimation unfolded at that year’s Democratic National Convention. As I watched Bernie take the microphone and call for Hillary to be nominated by acclamation, I thought surely this was the beginning of the coalition we needed to win. But that fleeting moment was followed by a spurning of progressive ideas and energy that may well have cost Democrats the White House in 2016.

A scenario like that may not be unthinkable today, but it is much less likely.
Progressives have gained strength and won elections to such a degree that the Democratic mainstream now broadly understands they no longer have the party to themselves. Increasingly, they recognize that mainstream Democrats must work with the powerful movement that progressives have built.
Could this end up being a 1932- or 1964-like moment, when a new and bigger Democratic coalition developed accompanied by a more progressive vision?
It’s certainly possible, especially given the increasing openness of American voters to solutions that address the more glaring failures of the capitalist system.
As the discourse opens up, and proposals for real change begin to emerge, we Democrats should understand that Donald Trump—and the real threat of authoritarianism he poses—has inadvertently played a major role in sparking a long-overdue renewal in our party.
For while his disruption of the Republican Party has surely led it rightward—and badly damaged his party’s prospects in this midterm election season—his broader disruption of American politics, and of the American economy, has led to a disruption of the Democratic Party.
That disruption, along with decades of hard work by Sanders and the recent victories of a new generation of candidates, has brought Democrats closer to our New Deal and Great Society roots and begun to forge a party that is ready to win again. And when Democrats regain power, to build a future than does not just reject Trump but that builds a progressive future for our country.

Kamala Harris Has Her Eye on Today’s Gubernatorial Races
The former vice president reminds The Nation that, even if government is divided in DC, “a governor, as the chief executive of a state, can actually make things happen.”
Today’s midterms will mark the end of one election cycle and the beginning of another. As soon as the votes from 2026 are counted, the 2028 presidential race will take center stage. But that’s just a formality.
For all intents and purposes, the 2028 contest began during the course of the midterm campaign. Several dozen prospective contenders for the Democratic nomination hit the midterm trail to boost their national profiles—campaigning in states across the country and positioning themselves as allies of the candidates who could flip control of Congress and check President Trump in the last two years of his term.
Most of these 2028 hopefuls zeroed in on Senate races, which grabbed the spotlight in final weeks of the 2026 campaign. Nobody doubts the importance of these contests, whether in Michigan, which saw a chaotic close to the race between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Trump Republican Mike Rogers, or in Texas, where Democratic James Talarico could become the first Democratic senator from the state in more than three decades.
But the front-runner in several surveys that tested the strength of 2026 Democratic presidential prospects has placed an emphasis on today’s gubernatorial races, which will define the direction of states across the country.
That prospect is former vice president Kamala Harris, who, in a national Harvard-Harris poll released one week ago, garnered 34 percent support among likely Democratic presidential primary and voters—16 points ahead of the second-place finisher, California Governor Gavin Newsom. It was the same story in two other polls that were released in October—one for the Financial Times and one by the Echelon Insights firm—both of which gave the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee a clear lead.
Harris—whose 75,017,613 vote total in 2024 was the highest in history for any candidate except for the Republican who narrowly beat her that year, Donald Trump (77,302,580), and for the Democrat with whom she served as vice president, Joe Biden (81,283,501) in 2020—told The Nation that she has not decided whether to mount a new bid for the presidency. That’s a genuine response, as is Harris’s insistence that the top factor in making that decision will be her family. But she has little doubt that she could do the job, as someone with significant White House experience who recalls that she has “spent a lot of time with foreign leaders, thinking about America’s responsibility and role globally, as well as our responsibility as a government to our own people.”
To a greater extent than many prominent political figures, Harris thinks about the duties of executives—in Washington and in statehouses across the country. So while Harris made plenty of 2026 campaign appearances with Senate candidates—including El-Sayed in Michigan, late-surging Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff—she also focused on some of the 36 gubernatorial races that will be decided today.
For Democrats, the chance to win control of statehouses is especially important. Even if they secure majorities in the House and Senate, they will still have to operate with divided government at the federal level—given that Trump is still in the White House. Democratic governors and legislatures can move far more immediately and far more effectively to address economic concerns, expand access to healthcare, invest in education, regulate data centers and artificial intelligence, and protect the rights of women and the LGBTQ+ community. They can also defend democracy by moving to address gerrymandering and to defend against voter suppression in the run-up to the 2028 election.
This understanding led Harris to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in the days before the midterm election, where she campaigned with David Crowley, the Milwaukee County Executive who this year is the Democratic nominee to replace outgoing Democratic Governor Tony Evers.
Harris appeared on October 26 with Crowley—who’s in a tight race with MAGA Republican US Representative Tom Tiffany—at a packed Democratic campaign headquarters in a neighborhood on Milwaukee’s northwest side and then at a huge “Women for Crowley” event in a downtown hotel. As always, Harris came prepared, with plenty of insights regarding the Democrat she was supporting and plenty to digs at the Republican he was opposing. And the crowds loved it.
Harris has her share of critics, and there are certainly Democrats who would rather she sit out the 2028 race. But her fans are ardent, and they have been out in force this fall as she hit the trail on behalf of Democratic candidates from Michigan to Mississippi to New Hampshire and Georgia. That was certainly the case in Milwaukee, where Harris was greeted by enthusiastic crowds of Democrats who held cameras aloft, waved posters, and cheered her every remark.
“She’s a huge mentor of mine,” declared Crowley.
For her part, Harris was effusive in her praise of the candidate, whom she described to The Nation as someone who is “in it for all the right reasons.”
“He is a true public servant,” she said of Crowley, who grew up in a Milwaukee neighborhood that is one of the poorest in the country. “He has had the experience of being hungry and knowing that you can’t assume that the very basic needs that you have will be fulfilled—without the government playing its part to help those in need, at a time when they need it most.”
In the closing days of a campaign where candidates on both sides of the partisan aisle are talking about affordability, Harris recognized Crowley’s authenticity.
“It’s not lip service. It is a lived experience for him—in a way that he sees the pain that people are experiencing right now. There’s a whole lot of pain right now. It is about affordability of the basic needs that people have. And that pain is compounded with a real legitimate belief [on the part of so many Americans] that their needs are unimportant, as compared to the powerful and the rich.”
Crowley, she said, “gets it. He understands what the priority should be.”

Crowley is one of eight Black gubernatorial candidates who are running in states across the country today. Five of them are Democrats: Maryland Governor Wes Moore, who is seeking reelection, and former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, state Attorney General Aaron Ford in Nevada, state Representative Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina, and Crowley. Three are Republicans: US Representative Byron Donalds in Florida, US Representative John James in Michigan, and state Representative Lisa Demuth in Minnesota.
“The eight Black nominees in governor’s races this year are seeking to force change that has been slow in coming, long after the ends of slavery and the Jim Crow era,” noted CNN. “While some carry favorable odds and others are long shots, taken together, they represent a record number of candidates in one cycle.”
Harris, the first Black person to serve as vice president and the first Black woman to be nominated for president, simply said, “It’s about time.”
She has campaigned not just with Crowley but with Ford and Lance Bottoms too—all three of whom would make history if they’re elected as the first Black governors of their states. “I am a witness to her grace and her greatness as a leader,” said Harris when she traveled to Georgia to appear with Bottoms. “Georgia has Keisha Lance Bottoms who will be the first Black woman governor in the history of the United States.” With Ford in Las Vegas, she urged Black voters to “honor the ancestors” by electing the attorney general as the first Black governor of Nevada and the first Black governor of a state located west of the Mississippi River.
While Harris made reference in campaign stops with the gubernatorial candidates to the civil rights era and to contemporary struggles for justice, she also spoke with fervor about the economic pain and chaos created by the Trump administration, which she describes as “the most callous, corrupt, and incompetent presidential administration we’ve ever experienced.” At every turn, she spoke of the candidates she has endorsed as uniquely qualified. And she reminded people of the power of governors to get things done.
“I was campaigning for Aaron Ford, and he’s been attorney general for two terms. So he knows the state, he knows it from the perspective of fighting for consumers, law enforcement, and all that,” she explained to The Nation. “I think there’s an obvious point, which is that a governor, as the chief executive of a state, can actually make things happen—and these really outstanding candidates want to make things happen in their state.”

I Am a UMich Student From Texas. Choosing Where to Vote Was Impossible.
Despite Michigan being a battleground for one of the most contentious midterm races this cycle, I couldn’t help but feel a draw to my native Texas.
These days at the University of Michigan, it is virtually impossible to walk through central campus without being reminded of the midterms. Blue and red tables line the walkways, and student organizers will literally chase you down to offer their spiel about which candidate deserves your vote.
It is not uncommon for professors to invite student organizations to give voter registration and election information presentations before class starts. As early voting began in Ann Arbor, on-campus voter hubs frequented classrooms to help Michigan-registered students cast their ballots. Even as I open my laptop and scroll through social media, advertisements for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers flash across my screen.
The visibility of the midterm elections in purple Michigan has been a striking contrast to my first 18 years growing up in solidly red Texas. There, I seldom encountered campaign advertisements and often questioned whether casting a ballot had any effect on electoral outcomes. But in Michigan, there is no doubt about it: Every vote matters.
University of Michigan student Britta Pingree, president of Turn Up Turnout, a nonpartisan organization that promotes civic engagement, said she has seen more political messaging and student advocacy during this “big election.”
“It definitely does seem like an energetic and important time,” Pingree said. “Students are aware of candidates and the specific offices that they’re voting for. They are knowledgeable about the ballot proposals that are available on the Ann Arbor and Michigan ballot.”
Despite Michigan’s being a battleground for one of the most contentious midterm races this cycle, I couldn’t help but feel drawn to my native Texas. The result of the tight race between Texas Senate candidates James Talarico and Ken Paxton may well be a litmus test for whether Democrats can make gains in red states.
Medha Kristipati, a student of government at the University of Texas at Austin, said she has noticed greater political engagement among students in recent years.
“I definitely do think people are more invested in politics now than when I was a child in Texas,” Kristipati said.
At the relatively liberal UT Austin, Kristipati has particularly noticed Democratic campaign outreach surrounding the Texas elections. She told me there’s an energetic effort to flip Texas blue—and that there’s a real sense that this might be possible.
“People are really pushing to make that happen.”
Experiencing these two political environments has led me to reconsider what makes voting feel meaningful. Although Michigan is a swing state where individual votes can carry significant weight, my connection to Texas shapes my decision to vote there instead. Having spent most of my life in Texas, I feel a personal responsibility to contribute to the state’s future, especially as it appears to be on the precipice of significant change.
Rather than viewing the state’s political leanings as a reason to disengage, the possibility of flipping Texas further encourages me to vote there and help shape a different political future for the place I call home.
