The Valkyries’ WNBA Finals Win Was a Triumph Against Fox News Bile
As Fox News whips up anti-trans, anti-WNBA hysteria, the Valkyries’ win is a victory for the sane.
The first Game Seven in WNBA Finals history took place on Saturday, and the Golden State Valkyries, in just their second year of existence, were ready. Playing at home, in front of a sold-out crowd crackling with enough energy to raise the roof, the Valkyries won the whole damn thing, 68–63, against the Atlanta Dream.
Earlier this year, the Valkyries rechristened their San Francisco arena Ballhalla, after the grand dining hall—called Valhalla—where the female warriors of Norse myth would bring only the bravest fallen soldiers. The true Valkyrie on Saturday was the team’s general manager, Ohemaa Nyanin, who built a championship team in two years by gathering together a disparate group of players who became the true “warriors” in the Bay. They claimed Ballhalla as their own and, suffice it to say, Halloween in the Bay was lit.
The Most Valuable Player of the finals was Gabby Williams, who, after a tepid two-point first half, scored an astounding 28 second-half points and played her brand of stellar defense all the way through. She’s a leader, a charisma-bomb, and the sort of player anyone would be proud to call “the face of the WNBA.”
Even more gratifying, given the recent anti-trans hysteria that has overtaken professional sports, Williams has always shown solidarity with the trans community, saying in August, “I would welcome a trans athlete on my team or against my team, anytime. I don’t think it’s a problem in the world. It’s just another way to kind of attack trans people.”
Such a basic statement of solidarity took great courage, given that far-right-wingers and a viciously obsessed Fox News spent much of the 2026 season attacking the WNBA by whipping up its rapidly aging viewership into a frenzy over the thought of a—currently nonexistent—trans hooper playing in the WNBA.
Media Matters reported that Fox News—in a time of war and a spiraling energy crisis—spent 13 and a half hours of airtime across over 200 segments on the WNBA from late June to early August. The stories were not about the incredible players and stories emerging from the league’s most successful season in its 30 years of existence. Instead, they incessantly denounced the WNBA’s unwillingness to condemn and vilify trans athletes, even though—again—there is not one trans player in the WNBA.
Fox News also whipped up another nonexistent controversy, whining and whinging that the league was permissively and violently racist against white players because athletes like the white and straight Caitlin Clark were being fouled too hard. They even sang the praises of a rump group of congresspeople willing to hold hearings on the matter. Fox News never gave a hot damn about the WNBA until it could become a stalking horse to attack Black women—particularly Black queer women. They also went after any white player not willing to play the aggrieved victim. To have the great Gabby Williams stand against anti-trans hate mattered. After the game, when Williams looked into the camera, amid the confetti and hugs, and said, “This is for the gays,” that warmed the heart.
It all speaks to a team that seems to really understand the rhythm and the passion of a city that has claimed them as their own. They stand with San Francisco and Oakland, and unlike so many athletes who live in rarified air and gated mansions, they are the community. Because of that, the Bay has adopted the Valkyries like few others in the rich history of sports in the region. When I was in San Francisco and Oakland during the playoffs, I saw violet everywhere: from uniforms on the street to banners in the urgent care unit (burned hand, spilled tea). Then, after the victory on Halloween, the two cities erupted into the kind of rapturous celebration that takes place when the home team not only wins a championship Game Seven—nothing like it—but does so on the Bay’s infamous night of all parties. A friend in the Mission neighborhood of San Francisco told me that the streets were flooded with Valkyrie vampires, Valkyrie zombies—everyone was out for Valkyrie-themed Halloween. October 31, he told me, has always been special in the Bay Area. “But this time it was a different level,” he said. “It is really something I haven’t experienced before, with women taking center stage.”
In the Bay Area this Halloween, the only appropriate color to wear was violet. And though the costume may come off on November 1, the feeling goes on.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New York Studio School revamp unearths long-forgotten murals
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Julie Belcove
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Back in 1907, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney established her sculpture studio in a converted stable and hayloft on MacDougal Alley in the heart of Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The heiress and artist then proceeded to procure four neighbouring brownstones one by one, with the Lincoln Memorial sculptor Daniel Chester French being the last holdout.
The five buildings that now comprise 8 West 8th Street are some of the New York art world’s most storied. It was here that Whitney promoted US artists at a time when they were widely denigrated, and where she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1931. After the museum relocated uptown, the nascent New York Studio School (NYSS) moved into the compound in 1967.
Over the past century Edward Hopper sketched, John Cage lectured and Philip Guston taught within these walls. Countless other greats practised, exhibited or, in the case of Marianne Faithfull, lived in what is now a National Historic Landmark. “This building has been the incubator for American art for 120 years,” says the artist Matthew Ritchie, sitting in a bare-bones conference room on a warm September afternoon. It has also been sorely in need of a makeover at least since he was a student here in the 1990s.
Leaks and hazards
When Ritchie was named the school’s director last year, the roof and studio skylights—coveted by students for their diffused natural light—leaked, the nearly century-old cloth-wrapped wiring had deteriorated dangerously and wheelchair access was extremely limited. His priority was renovation. The first phase—including doubling the public exhibition space and creating a new accessible lecture and performance hall in wood with stepped seating—is set to be completed this autumn, and phase two will begin in the spring.
Prior to Ritchie’s arrival, the school had obtained public grants for the necessary work, but they required matching funds and their expiration date was fast approaching. He quickly marshalled forces. The board agreed to donate the required money, he says, and the school tapped Matthew Baird of Baird Architects to helm the overhaul.
Ritchie and Baird’s history of collaboration dates back 17 years and across two other local institutions. In 2009, they teamed up to consider the effects of rising sea levels on the built environment as part of the interdisciplinary Rising Currents project at the Museum of Modern Art. Just a few years later, they put their theories into practice after Hurricane Sandy tore through the city, its storm surge flooding much of downtown. Ritchie was on the board of the beloved alternative art space The Kitchen when it enlisted Baird to rehabilitate its waterlogged lobby and black-box theatre.
The architect’s sensitive execution on that project—he preserved visual evidence of flood damage, for example—made him an obvious choice for the NYSS project, which presented a similar challenge. “You have this really cool building that’s got this patina of great artists that have moved through it,” Baird says. “How do you not erase that?”
Buried treasure
Thanks to Baird and Ritchie’s handle-with-care edict, the construction crew was on the lookout for treasures buried beneath layers of plasterboard. The artist Cecily Brown had told Ritchie that she painted her first mural on a school wall when she was a student in the 1990s but could not remember where. And the school archives held numerous photos of murals Whitney had commissioned from the artist Robert E. Locher for the original carriage house.
Sure enough, the crew uncovered the work of both artists within a 24-hour period. Brown’s piece—featuring disembodied penises, two of them appearing to kiss—is in the newly expanded gallery space on the main floor. To prevent it from potentially distracting from exhibitions, the design team installed a shallow cabinet in front of the mural.
Ritchie jokes that the set-up resembles a gabinetto segreto, or secret room, the most famous of which was a locked vault of erotic artefacts from Pompeii and Herculaneum. “Who doesn’t want a Cecily Brown mural? And then, who doesn’t want pornography in your brand-new public gallery?” he says with a laugh. “It’s the perfect combination.”
Workers discovered the two Locher murals where a bathroom and a hallway leading to it will be built. Intended to be viewed in the candlelight of Whitney’s dining room, one is a glimmering green, the other a trompe l’oeil image of doric columns. Baird tweaked the layout but not the location of the restroom. “Now it will be the most historic bathroom in New York,” Ritchie says.
A less fortuitous surprise: the beams beneath Robert Winthrop Chanler’s flame-motif fireplace in Whitney’s original second-floor studio were cracking, requiring emergency shoring up to stop the ceiling from collapse—together with the priceless fireplace. “This is the urgency of renovation,” Ritchie says. “You can wait too long, and then you lose it all.”
Super-tight deadlines
Because of the grant deadlines for the first phase of the project, Baird needed to work at warp speed, condensing three years of planning, permitting, bidding and execution into one. Owing to New York City’s complex building code, he approached the $2.2m renovation as “100 small projects” rather than gutting the 59,000 sq. ft building. The landmark-restoration specialist Jonathan Raible is overseeing the new roof.
In addition to enhancing the first floor’s public spaces, Baird rewired the building, renovated the wreck of a kitchen and improved accessibility by adding a wheelchair lift to the performance hall. “You can’t have a public programme if you don’t provide correct facilities for the public,” Ritchie says. “You’re not really welcoming them.”
Climbing the narrow staircases to the maze of studios where the school’s 27 full-time, in-person students work, Baird speaks enthusiastically about the second phase of renovations, which will include a student coffee bar. In keeping with his preservationist instincts, he plans to relamp with LED bulbs the elegant Fresnel recessed box lighting that Whitney installed for evenly washed walls, and he hopes to restore the system of baffles that modulated direct light in the studios as well as undertake other restoration while safeguarding the landmark’s character.
Ritchie already has his eye on another, likely longer-term fix for the school: free tuition. “That would require a very large endowment from extremely generous single or multiple donors,” he says, giving his best impression of a silver-tongued salesman, “which we’re eagerly awaiting with an entirely unique naming opportunity.”

https://citylimits.org/nine-homeless-new.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nine-homeless-new.text:
Share This Article
The remains of the nine unhoused people, who died of hypothermia on the city’s streets, were initially slated for mass graves on Hart Island—until a group of fellow New Yorkers stepped in.
Last winter, a brutal stretch of cold weather and lingering snowstorms killed at least 18 people in New York City, including several who were homeless and on the street at the time of their deaths.
Months later, nine of those unhoused New Yorkers’ remains had yet to be claimed by friends or family, despite what one advocate described as “diligent searches” on the part of the medical examiner’s office to locate next of kin. Their bodies were headed for Hart Island, the city’s desolate potter’s field off the shore of City Island in the Bronx, which for more than a century has served as the final resting place for those without someone to plan or pay for their burial.
Instead, after several fellow New Yorkers stepped in, the nine late residents were honored with a funeral mass Monday night at Saint Thomas Church Fifth Avenue, where their ashes—contained in square golden urns, their names inscribed on the front—were interred in the cathedral’s columbarium.
“We believe that those who have been homeless deserve dignity in death, even if they did not receive it in their lives,” Charles King, CEO of the homeless services nonprofit Housing Works, said during the service, where the robed church choir sang “Amazing Grace” and other hymns set to booming organ music.
“We want our fellow New Yorkers to appreciate the cost of our collective decision to throw away human lives, as evidenced by our lack of meaningful shelter and care for the least among us,” King said.
Few details are known about the nine people laid to rest, organizers said. All of them died from hypothermia, found in different parts of the freezing city—one in the doorway of a building in the East Village, another along the Van Wyck Expressway in Queens—between November 2025 and February 2026. They ranged in age from 38 to 74, and came from South Carolina, Puerto Rico, Russia, and India; two were born in the city.
Their names were James Paul Smith, Manjeet Singh, Harold Hemphill, Tomeka Ryeshera Gibson, Jorge Elias Rivera Torres, Jeffrey Costa, Edward “Eduardo” Adames, Jose M. “Joseph” Pena, and Igor Zapevalov.
“We know little of these nine neighbors, but we do know this: they are beloved,” Rev. Mark Schultz of Saint Thomas Church said during the service.
The ceremony and interment were arranged by Community Burial Project, a new initiative founded by artist Rhonda Roland Shearer to provide memorials for New Yorkers experiencing street homelessness at the time of their deaths.
Shearer, who spent the months after 9/11 distributing supplies to first responders at Ground Zero, said she was struck by the ceremonial process for handling recovered remains there, which she described as “dignified and very emotionally present.”
She’d previously partnered with Housing Works to raise memorial funds for unhoused New Yorkers who died during the COVID-19 pandemic. She was distressed, she said, at the prospect of those killed during last winter’s deadly cold being sent to Hart Island, where the dead are buried in mass graves.
“No one’s allowed to be there to pray,” she said of burials on the island, which for years were largely inaccessible to the public.
Shearer reached out to Housing Works, which connected with the city’s Human Resources Administration and Medical Examiner’s Office to make arrangements for any victims of the cold snap who went unclaimed. A local funeral home provided the funeral services and urns, and Saint Thomas’ offered the columbarium space. Additional expenses were covered by a donation from the author Amy Tan and her husband, Shearer said.
“The ability of community to just come together on this is the big message here,” she said. Going forward, the Community Burial Project will make similar arrangements for other street homeless New Yorkers at risk of being “forgotten,” she added.
“These nine, I believe, are not only being treated with dignity and getting the respect that all humans deserve, but I think they’re going to serve, in this case, the larger effort…to continue this,” Shearer said. “That will also add another layer of what meaning was conveyed by their lives.”
King, of Housing Works, said he and the organization have pushed for years for the city to cease its use of Hart Island for burials, and to come up with a “dignified way to deal with people who don’t have anyone to claim their remains.”
“They bury people in pine boxes, often five deep in these big anonymous holes,” he said.
The public memorial service, he explained, was also a way to “to make the public aware of the homeless people we walk around all the time,” and the need to treat them with respect, both during life and after it.
He called for the city to invest in more drop-in centers to offer “humane and comfortable spaces” for unhoused people, with fewer restrictions and better conditions than the often crowded—and sometimes dangerous—city shelters that street homeless New Yorkers are reluctant to enter.
“The truth of the matter is, we tend to look at homeless people in a very one-dimensional way, forgetting that they have their own hopes, their own dreams, their own aspirations,” King said.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/mich.title: Michigan Senate Race Closes as a Referendum on Israel Policy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/mich.author: Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/mich.text:
For the left, it’s been the marquee race of the midterm cycle. Either a Republican former U.S. representative known for pushing domestic spying powers or an outspoken progressive who forced a reckoning over U.S.–Israel policy among Democrats will emerge from Election Day as the next senator from Michigan.
Abdul El-Sayed would be the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected Tuesday night, capping off a race that’s been viewed as a referendum on swing-state appeal for the Democratic Party’s left flank. If he defeats Mike Rogers, a loyal Trump ally whose campaign often peddled Islamophobic tropes against the Democratic nominee, the results will all but certainly embolden progressives ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
If El-Sayed loses, it will likely trigger a centrist backlash — and cost the Democrats a critical Senate seat as the party fights to take back the upper chamber.
Polls across Michigan closed by 9 p.m. ET on Tuesday, with anxious voters across the state awaiting the returns.
In the heavily Arab and Muslim city of Dearborn, voters across party lines said they were outraged at the Islamophobic attacks ads targeting El-Sayed that became a staple of airwaves and social media feeds in the campaign’s final days.
“I am a Muslim. And I’ve seen a lot of ads, and it’s disgusting, because we are good people,” said Gus Tarraf, a Republican running for a state House seat. “I love this country.”
Although Donald Trump carried many precincts in Dearborn two years ago due to voter frustration over the Biden administration’s support of Israel, Tarraf said his community is turning on the Republican Party this year.
“Not a lot of Arab Americans are happy with the Trump administration,” he said. “So it doesn’t matter if they know you, as soon as they know you are on the Republican ticket.”
El-Sayed’s willingness to criticize U.S. policy on Israel animated soap-opera-level drama in the final days of the race, when his former primary opponent, centrist Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, announced she would switch her endorsement to support Rogers.
After demanding an apology from El-Sayed for an outside PAC’s ad, Stevens said on social media that she came to the decision after feeling “shut out” by El-Sayed’s campaign, adding that she’s heard from “Black voters, Jewish voters, and others about how deeply these messages hurt.” Rogers, she said, gave her “the hope that he can serve in the tradition of John McCain: a senator willing to put country before party and stand up to his own side when conscience requires it.”
Stevens’s late-breaking endorsement of Rogers drew a mix of eye-rolls and outrage from voters at three precincts in Detroit and Dearborn. None of the voters interviewed by The Intercept said it had swayed them to vote for Rogers.
“People have already early voted. People have already absentee voted,” said Noora Iskander. “I don’t think many people change their minds. So I think it’s just hypocritical.”
Stevens’s decision to make the endorsement while inside a Black church in Detroit may also have generated backlash from the Black voters that Rogers was hoping to win over, according to some who spoke to The Intercept. One said the church community has been buzzing — and not positively — about the weekend’s events.
“Unfortunately, she went to a Black church to use it as a backdrop,” said Dearborn voter Dorothea Sharon. “It really was a slap in the face for the Black community that that happened.”
While El-Sayed has had to face intense scrutiny over accusations of conflating opposition to U.S. aid to Israel with antisemitism, little accounting has been made of the blatant Islamophobia and xenophobia from the Rogers campaign, the Republican Party, and Trump. But in Dearborn, the rhetoric had clearly hurt several voters who spoke to The Intercept.
The father of state Senate candidate Abbas Alawieh, a Democrat who played a prominent role in the 2024 Uncommitted movement, grew visibly upset when asked about the ads targeting Muslims.
“These are weak people who don’t have anything to do — they don’t have any programs for our economy, for our health, for our future,” Zouheir Alawieh said. “That’s why they are attacking us as Muslims and as human beings. It’s never been like this. This is a shame. America is a place where the Black with the white with the yellow, the Muslim with the Christian with the Jews, can live freely. Don’t try to tear up our society.”
Outside Dearborn, El-Sayed has tried to defuse the anti-Muslim smears against him by joking that he is only in favor of “shawarma law.” However, the Islamophobic attacks convinced at least one voter to cast her ballot for Rogers.
“I don’t want to live under Sharia law,” said Joann, a law firm employee who declined to give her last name after she voted in Detroit.
The fear of Islamic rule was the main issue for Joann, she said, although she also worried about El-Sayed’s campaign pledge of Medicare for All.
“I’ve worked my whole life, put all my stuff into the Medicare, but then I’ve got to let other people get it for free? It doesn’t seem fair to me when I’ve worked my whole life for it, and we’re not even sure that it’s going to be there when we really get ready to retire,” she said.
Yet it was that very messaging from El-Sayed’s campaign that excited many other residents in Michigan. Many voters who spoke to The Intercept said they were more focused on pocketbook issues.
“It’s the gas prices, the food. I mean, money is running out your pocket so fast,” Leigh James said after voting at Tabernacle Missionary Baptist Church in Detroit.
James said she had walked to the polling place to avoid using gas. “I’m trying to save,” she said. “So thank God I live in the neighborhood.”
Other voters said they were inspired by El-Sayed’s personality, with one woman describing him as a “fighter.”
Noora Iskander, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, said she approved of his stance in favor of Medicare for All, his affordability platform, and his solidarity with Palestine.
“I think he’s going to make a lot of change. He’s going to scare a lot of people — which I believe is a good thing, because you can’t really change for the better if you don’t scare a few people,” she said.
This is a developing story. Matt Sledge reported from Dearborn and Detroit, Michigan.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Vienna Recession? Four galleries in Austrian capital shut shop amid a tougher market
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melanie Gerlis
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Vienna’s contemporary art scene seems to be collapsing. Three of its galleries—Layr, Exile and Zeller van Almsick—are either closing or “evolving”, all citing the unsustainability of running increasingly costly businesses in an unpredictable market. Meanwhile Eva Presenhuber, who opened a space in Vienna in 2022, has confirmed she is also leaving the Austrian capital amid a downturn in sales.
Those that have confirmed they are closing for good—Exile after 18 years and Zeller van Almsick after nearly ten—are clear-eyed. “There is no point in sugarcoating the fact that the past two years have been financially extremely challenging,” says Magdalena Zeller, a co-founder of Zeller van Almsick. For Christian Siekmeier, the founder of Exile, “there are simply no new collectors emerging”.
Emanuel Layr, who is closing his corner-hugging Layr gallery in favour of a more nomadic, project-based business (including a smaller, by-appointment space in Vienna), says: “The gallery model as we know it is increasingly reaching its limits.” The relentless commitments, to art fairs and the customary six-weekly exhibition, are not paying off. “It’s harder to sell some things, costs are getting higher, then there’s a big art fair coming and taking another €100,000,” he says. “I had to be more realistic, and think, ‘How much profit do I get? How much does the artist get?’.”
Yet Layr and his Viennese counterparts identify a groundswell of enthusiasm from younger generations. September’s new Astoria Artshow, an event held in Europe’s oldest garage (founded in 1918), was a hit, and notably from a young crowd. Its cash tills might not have been ringing, but galleries paid only €500 to participate so had much less to lose. The gallery-led gathering, which returns as a “fair” next year, seemed a breath of fresh air in the slot of previous events, such as Viennacontemporary, which is not showing any sign of returning.
A unique month-long festival
Long-time collectors were also fans of Astoria Artshow. “This will be the future,” says Eva Frey, who with her husband Manfred has been buying contemporary art for more than 30 years, and who sits on the board of Mumok, another bright spot in Vienna’s cultural offerings. Frey points out that the gallery closures will come after the city’s unique, month-long Curated By festival, supported by the city and state and which has been a boon to the contemporary art scene since it launched in 2009.
Frey says that the issue for Vienna’s cutting-edge galleries is that collectors of her vintage (which she defines as “over 70”) are not enough to keep business going. The problem, she says, is not so much the youngest generations, but that “there are fewer people between 45 and 55, who are established in a profession, and who used to be the main collectors in the market”. Layr finds too that “for middle-income professionals, there is less money around, so they are more careful”.
The middle-income strains seem a microcosm of what is happening in the wider art market
Many of the issues might be Vienna-related. It’s a small market and Zeller identifies “a significant gap between the cultural importance of the city and the depth of its local collector base”. But the middle-income strains seem a microcosm of what is happening in the wider art market, namely plenty of enthusiasm from the younger generations and a relative handful of older buyers keeping the top end just about managing. This requires a holding pattern of flexibility, at best, from the galleries who stick it out. For those that do, and can, hope rests on the juniors, but we just might have to wait a while to know if they can fill the gaps.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/vill.title: In California’s Central Valley, ICE Might Swing a Red District Blue
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/vill.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/vill.text:
In California’s Central Valley, some surprising voters are lining up behind a progressive upstart: A law enforcement officer who calls for the abolition of ICE. A millennial who once voted for a Republican congressman.
They found themselves among supporters of Randy Villegas, a Democrat poised to oust longtime incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao in a district dominated for decades by conservatives in California’s Central Valley.
With Democratic victories across the nation, California’s 22nd Congressional District is the kind of historically red stronghold where progressive policies may find new purchase.
Villegas’s path to the general election mirrors that of other progressive candidates charting a new identity within the party. Running on policies such as Medicare for All, addressing affordability, rejecting corporate donations, and halting the flow of weapons to Israel, the 31-year-old defeated a moderate Democratic state assembly member backed by the party’s establishment in the June primary.
Villegas’s opposition to ICE in a district that is 70 percent Latino or Hispanic marked the sharpest point of contrast with Valadao, who defended the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant campaign and famously uttered “It is what it is” on the debate stage last month when pressed on the issue. Valadao claimed “a lot” of the individuals captured by ICE in the Central Valley in recent weeks have criminal records, despite research showing the majority of those detained by ICE lack criminal convictions.
It was Valadao’s stance on immigration that most animated Central Valley voters who spoke with The Intercept.
“I’ve never seen him stand up to something I feel is egregious,” said Raul Castro, 53, a Fresno County probation officer who is upset with Valadao’s lack of willingness to oppose Trump on the ICE raids surging through the area in recent weeks. “I just don’t respect people like that.”
While standing on the front porch of his house in a middle-class suburb in northwest Fresno, Castro lamented ICE’s targeting of immigrants based on their appearance, language, or jobs. He spoke out against immigration agents pulling people from the street and into labyrinthine detention centers where civil rights advocates have reported a lack of access to basic necessities such as clean water and adequate healthcare. Though Castro once supported ICE, when asked whether he would support abolishing the agency altogether, he said yes.
“If you asked me that same question, ‘Hey would you abolish ICE?’ I’d say, ‘No, ‘cause they’re doing things to make sure our country is safe. I want to live in a safe Fresno, safe county, safe city,’” Castro told The Intercept. “But now, wait a minute, maybe that’s not what I thought it was going to be.”
Villegas told The Intercept he wasn’t surprised to hear he had won the support of an anti-ICE law enforcement officer.
“I don’t find it surprising because I think ICE has made it much more difficult for local law enforcement to carry out their jobs and their work — and everybody is seeing the indiscriminate profiling going on,” Villegas said at a Fresno park rally to support last-minute canvassing efforts.
Villegas himself does not support abolishing ICE but instead has called for wide-ranging reforms of the agency. The policy position makes Villegas somewhat an anomaly among his progressive peers, who are riding a wave of leftist energy into Congress, some of whom include “Abolish ICE” among their campaign platforms.
While holding key endorsements from high-profile democratic socialists Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Villegas has also rejected the socialist label, preferring “populist,” despite attempts by the Republican national party to weaponize the term against him. Unlike many of his fellow progressives, Villegas is also one of the few who is running in a historically red district. And he’s confident voters are not caught up in the ideological nuances and hopes to instead cut through them.
“People are fed up with an agency who is unaccountable, people are fed up with a member of Congress who is unaccountable, who doesn’t even have public town halls,” Villegas said. “We deserve better than that in the Central Valley, and I think that’s why our messaging is resonating across the political spectrum.”
Such reach across the political spectrum is also evidenced in voters like Aram Easter, 33, who was born and raised in Fresno. He doesn’t vote in every election, but cast a ballot for Valadao a decade ago when his district previously covered Fresno, largely because he bought the vision of someone with local Central Valley roots (Valadao was born and raised in the nearby Hanford). He also agrees with some aspects of Trump’s agenda, such as building the border wall. But he drew the line on immigration enforcement.
“You got people tearing people’s families apart,” Easter said. “My family immigrated here — I have Black and Mexican family — I’m not with them overly-aggressively doing it.”
Since early October, ICE raids have become more prevalent in the region, with more than 200 people detained by authorities throughout the surge, according to the local newsroom Fresnoland. Similar upticks in ICE have taken place recently throughout the state, including Los Angeles and San Diego. Voter rights organizations in the Central Valley have taken notice and are viewing the raids as an effort by the Trump administration to suppress the vote, especially in a key race in the 22nd District.
“This timing of the uptick in ICE is not a coincidence,” said Marisa Moraza, political director at PowerCA Action, which is doing independent expenditure work to support Villegas’s campaign. “It’s not a coincidence that this started at the beginning of October when voters received their ballots in the mail.”
The raids have also suppressed get-out-the-vote efforts, Moraza said. Last month, the group had to pause in-person canvassing operations for several days amid the surge in ICE activity, electing to instead do phone banking.
The ICE activity is also keeping would-be voters from dropping off their ballots, as recent arrests of U.S. citizens struck fear among voters, said Cirilo Ordaz, a canvasser with PowerCA supporting Villegas.
“With going out to vote, I think a lot of them haven’t done it yet because of that fear,” said Ordaz, who was one of dozens of Villegas supporters who fanned out across the region on the Monday before Election Day to urge residents to vote.
Sylvia Ramirez, another Fresno native canvassing with PowerCA said she’s noticed far fewer people outside in recent weeks, including a lack of crowds at the popular annual event Big Fresno Fair. For voters, she and her group offer to drop off people’s ballots for them if the fear is keeping them inside.
“Offering the services of dropping off a ballot for somebody really helps out with the fear that people have of leaving their houses,” she said, adding that she has told her family to stay at home as much as possible in recent days to avoid interactions with ICE.
The Central Valley, known for its significant agriculture production, has been the seat of high-profile Republican lawmakers, such as former Rep. Devin Nunes and former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy.
But after a Democrat-led redistricting in the state last year in response to Texas’s partisan redistricting effort, the district now includes the northwest sections of Fresno, a city with more Democrats.
Early voting across the state has outpaced recent midterm elections, according to a recent survey. It’s unclear how much of that is anti-Trump animus or having a candidate voters are excited to support.
Castro, the probation officer, was among those who voted early. In recent weeks, he said he noticed residents looking at him with concern while on the job in uniform, showing up at areas where ICE had previously conducted raids. It’s a fear he acutely understood. As a child, he lived in labor camps with his mother and father, who were both undocumented immigrants working in Fresno as farm laborers. He recalled similar indiscriminate sweeps by Border Patrol in the 1970s.
“When I was small, back then it was Border Patrol, and they used to show up in a van,” Castro recalled. “All the agents used to get out and run after these guys. And they used to round them up and take them out,” he said.
Seeing video and hearing of recent ICE raids targeting farmworkers in the area conjured such painful memories.
“I never thought I’d see that again,” he said.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/jame.title: Even Anti-Trans Panic Couldn’t Save Republicans in Deep-Red Texas
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/jame.author: Akela Lacy, Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/jame.text:
On an election night handing Republicans a beating in critical House and Senate races across the country, the GOP fell short even in once deep-red Texas after a campaign run on a go-to outrage tactic: fearmongering over the rights of transgender people.
Democrats escaped the political wilderness in the Longhorn State on Tuesday night, when Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton — despite the far-right attorney general’s relentless attacks on the trans community and his party’s claims that Democrats would enforce so-called “transgenderism” as a kind of ideology.
The massive upset was paired with a victory for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, who beat Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott shortly after the Senate race was called for Talarico.
In Dallas, Paxton voter Rachel Fuller told The Intercept she was alarmed by what she believed was Talarico’s support for “far-fetched” ideas, like “giving children the right to decide — and making parents, calling them abusive for not letting them have transgender changes.”
Her comments suggested some of the $78 million Republicans spent on anti-trans attack advertisements in Texas were working. But they weren’t enough to help Republicans hold onto power in Texas, which hasn’t had a Democratic senator since the 1990s.
The ads made up almost half of all ad spending in support of Paxton, according to an analysis from Puck using data from AdImpact.
By and large, the ads spread blatant misinformation about Talarico’s record.
One infamous $29 million ad created by Texas PAC, a political action committee primarily funded by billionaire Elon Musk, claimed that Talarico supported jailing parents who did not support gender-affirming surgeries for minors. “Every mom in Texas should be worried about James Talarico putting parents in jail if they do not support surgically transitioning their children,” a woman in the ad warned ominously.
That attack, which according to Puck received 1.9 billion views as of October, does seem to have caught the attention of Texans — even with voters who ultimately supported Talarico.
Julius Ishola, a canvasser for Black TOP, an operation under Texas Organizing Project that targets Black voters, told The Intercept he had frequently heard Black voters raise concerns that Talarico intended to jail parents.
“I’ve been getting a lot of bad feedback regarding James Talarico,” Ishola told The Intercept, saying many voters cited concerns of “gender sex change and possibly prosecuting parents who go against that … and allowing transgenders into female restrooms.”
As a state legislator, Talarico fought bans on transgender athletes’ participation in youth sports, and famously said that God is “nonbinary,” earning him ridicule from Republicans, who nicknamed the Senate candidate “Talafreako.” In the face of those attacks this cycle, Talarico appeared to backtrack on the issue, telling Fox News in September that he supported bans on transgender children’s participation in sports if it risks “safety or fairness” — without clarifying what that meant.
His wavering does not seem to have reached many voters.
“I voted Republican all the way. And that’s my fear of Talarico going in,” said Carol Billings, a voter who cast her ballot for Paxton at the Living Waters Church in Dallas County. Like Fuller, she cited her perception of the Democratic nominee’s trans policies as a major source for concern.
Still, many voters in Black districts, which were vital to Talarico’s victory, barely mentioned Talarico.
“At the end of the day,” said Dallas Jones, a Houston-based Democratic political strategist whose firm focuses on African American voter engagement and backed Talarico, “the results show that people care more about their everyday lives than they do about trans Americans who just want to get by.”
Some voters told The Intercept they were far more concerned with issues of affordability. “ I just hope we can get these gas prices down,” said Darryl Moore, a Fort Worth voter.
This is a developing story and will be updated. Akela Lacy reported from Dallas, Texas.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘I put a smoke bomb in a road cone and stuck it on my head’: Delton Barrett’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Chris Broughton
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
I grew up on New Providence in the Bahamas, and still live on the south side of the island. After leaving school, I worked with my dad in construction, and that’s where I started taking photos. For the first couple of years, I used my flip phone, playing with images of nature and flowers on the sites we were working on, but in 2010 I bought my first DSLR (digital single-lens reflex) camera and started teaching myself about photography.
I started doing a lot of landscapes. I tended to shoot at sunrise or sunset, and became interested in taking photos of people in vacant spaces. Because I didn’t have a model, I used a tripod and a timer to include myself in these very fantasy-looking naturescapes.
This shot came about on a day when I woke up feeling I needed to try out something new. I took three or four different outfits to the western part of the island along with a few props, one of which was this cone. I often keep random items I find, sometimes incorporating them into images.
The road I was on leads to a dead end, so cars don’t drive along it much. It was a pretty safe space – I almost felt like I was in my own back yard. I’d been playing with ideas, and putting the cone on my head was the last one I tried that day. I just liked the way it looked but, as you can imagine, it was quite suffocating.
Then I remembered I had a smoke bomb in the car and it just happened to fit into the tip of the cone. Looking back, it’s a wonder I survived. I’d tried many shots and was getting tired. But it occurred to me that this shot really did look like someone losing their mind, going ballistic. The way I’m gripping the cone makes it unclear whether I’m trying to throw it off or hold it on. Perhaps I’m trapped inside, perhaps I’m in there intentionally because there’s something I don’t want to see.
Either way, there’s some kind of struggle happening. Maybe the smoke is giving a signal, calling people nearby for help, like: “Hey, something’s up here!” I call the image Stop the Madness. We pass people every day who give off signs that they are struggling, or not in their right mind. Maybe we walk past, maybe we help.
The island inspires me a lot. It’s the only backdrop I’ve ever really known. In 2024, I went to Madrid, which is highly developed compared with the Bahamas. When I came back to Nassau after, I thought: “Wow, we have so much more colour, so much more green.” I hadn’t really understood that until then. As an artist and photographer, what stimulates me are my surroundings. The beaches are a five-minute drive away – my images tend to have seas or a sunset or some type of bush involved. I use the elements around me to express my ideas.
Some of my images are manipulated to fit the concept or tell the story I want. If I need a seagull to be in a precise spot, for example, I won’t spend all day waiting for that to happen. One of my favourites shows me standing on top of the sea opposite another version of me in a different costume – and our fingers are almost touching, like in Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam. It’s an image I’d thought about for a long time, so when everything came together it was like a mother who’d waited nine months to have her baby. But often a scene is perfect as it is – all I need to do is frame it and adjust the lighting and maybe the contrast. That’s all that was needed for Stop the Madness.
Delton Barrett’s CV
Born: Manchester, Jamaica, 1991
 
High point: My first solo show in 2018 at D’Aguilar Art Foundation in Nassau. The Bahamas has been a lasting high point. It set the sail for me to continue to create great images that can inspire others in a way I’d also want to be inspired
 
Top tip: Create what makes you feel. Sit with your ideas and think about them until you’ve found the right way to execute them. We can become so excited in photographing the idea that we miss out the small details that make the image worth taking in the moment. In a nutshell I would say: “Take the pressure off shooting and focus more on what you want to shoot and how you want it to feel”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Abdul El-Sayed Triumphed. Trump and Islamophobia Lost.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
On Tuesday night, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim ever elected to the United States Senate—delivering the most direct and profound of the many rebukes that Republican President Donald Trump suffered as the American people thunderously transformed the country’s electoral and political landscape.
Yes, voters handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, creating a vital check on Trump’s presidency that substantially disempowers him in the last two years of his second term.
Yes, Republicans experienced substantial setbacks in states such as Iowa, Ohio, Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas, where Trump won with ease just two years ago—confirming the American public’s fundamental break with a historically unpopular, and now unmistakably lame-duck, president.
Yes, unprecedented wins in gubernatorial and legislative races have given Democrats the ability to turn states into laboratories of democracy that counter Trump’s pro-corporate agenda on everything from AI regulation to monopoly power, labor rights, and access to healthcare.
But the election of El-Sayed—a progressive, pro-labor, anti-racist doctor who advocated for Medicare for All, boldly called out genocide in Gaza and Trump’s war in Iran, and proudly defended his Muslim faith—struck a blow in the heart of the relentless Islamophobia that has long been a core part of the president’s political identity.
Trump did everything in his power to defeat the American-born son of immigrants from Egypt. He labeled El-Sayed a “jihadist” and “a Muslim Brotherhood guy,” and claimed that the Democrat “would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”
“We’ll have a hundred senators, and most of them will go directly [into the chamber],” said Trump, who at an October rally invited Republicans to laugh along with his bigotry. “We’re gonna have to get a special metal detector for Abdul.”
El-Sayed’s winning campaign against Republican Mike Rogers countered Trump’s hateful rhetoric with the most inspiring and reconciling statement of the midterms—a digital ad where El-Sayed spoke of his faith, saying:
My name is Abdul, it means “servant.”
I pray every day.
I reflect on my role in this life, on this earth.
How we leave it better than we found it.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
To serve God.
To serve our neighbors.
All across Michigan, families pray.
They feel hopeless.
Faith is a thing there’s just too little of in Washington.
We don’t have faith in our future.
We don’t have faith that we can actually fix things.
So yeah, we need a few more people of faith in Washington.
I’m Abdul El Sayed, man of faith, that’s a good thing, and I approve this message.
Michiganders heard the worst of Donald Trump’s Islamophobic hate-mongering. And they heard the best of Abdul El-Sayed’s faith-based hope. They chose hope, and sent a Muslim man of faith to the United States Senate.
So it was, early on Wednesday morning, that Abdul El-Sayed finished his campaign by saying, “to all the parents who struggled to explain to their kids why the president openly mocks someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Scenes From a Democratic Earthquake In Iowa
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Scenes From a Democratic Earthquake in Iowa
The state was a MAGA citadel. Not anymore.
Des Moines, Iowa—“All along I’ve said Iowa was the center of the political universe,” Josh Turek, the Hawkeye State’s newly elected Democratic senator, told a giddy election-night crowd on Tuesday. “And man, did we prove that tonight.”
Some hyperbolic Hawkeye pride was more than a little pardonable on a night when the so-called “blue tsunami” swept Democrats into power across the country. But Turek was not wrong to highlight what was happening in Iowa. This is a state that Donald Trump carried by 13 points just two years ago, and that, thanks to a GOP-dominated statehouse and legislature, had earned the moniker “Florida of the North” for its firmly DeSantis-like lurch into a regressive, deregulatory, and woke-baiting governing agenda. It was supposed to be a firewall in the Republican Party’s doomed fight to hold on to its Senate majority. Millions in super PAC donations and vicious attack ads had flooded the state. And Turek still won.
Not only that: Rob Sand, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, captured the statehouse for the party for the first time since 2010, and Democrats also took three of the state’s four congressional seats. All those winning candidates were women—another historic breakthrough in an evening full of them.
At the same time, Iowa’s repudiation of the MAGA disease in American politics was very, well, Iowan—which is to say, humble, neighborly, and civically optimistic. I grew up in eastern Iowa, and when I moved to the West Coast, I soon learned that greeting passersby on the street was regarded not as welcoming but creepy. The obsessive punctuality and the usage of honorifics that had been drilled into me as a kid likewise were regarded as quaint throwback rituals—virtual stage directions in a community-theater production of Our Town.
But Turek, like most Iowans, is still very much at home in these traditions. Even after the bruising campaign he waged against GOP Representative Ashley Hinson, he stressed that “I have deep respect for anyone who steps up to run.” (Some Iowans in the crowd were admittedly less generous, greeting the mention of Hinson’s name with a smattering of boos.) In his speech—delivered at the ur-Iowan venue of the state historical society—Turek addressed the state in the familiar second person, as in “Now, Iowa, let us be the city on the hill—the Iowa we grew up in that was the envy of the nation…. Iowa, this is where our comeback begins.”
At the same time, Turek also channeled the capital-P Populist tradition that has decisively shaped the state’s politics over the past century. Near the end of his speech, he called former US senator Tom Harkin to the podium, telling the crowd how Harkin had “changed my life” by working to secure passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act (Turek is wheelchair-bound, having contracted spina bifida in the womb after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in the Vietnam War). Harkin also embodied the crusade to secure fair and equal representation to working-class Americans, Turek explained—a cause that now served as “the North Star” of his own politics.
In this register, the patina of Iowa niceness became something more righteous and confrontational. Turek toned down his congenital niceness when he addressed the parlous state of our politics; in lieu of the amorphous indictments of “a broken system” that many lawmakers favor, he denounced a moneyed oligarchy—not exactly the sort of bipartisan overture he was chided on social media for earlier in the day when he said he’d cast his ballot in some local races for GOP candidates. One of his biggest applause lines was “Tonight, Iowa, we outvoted the billionaires,” and he made the same point in a much more personal idiom later, saying, “In Iowa, Elon Musk does not decide elections.” And he vowed to “end the corruption we’re seeing on both sides of the aisle,” adding, “I am going to DC to overturn Citizens United.”
If Turek is a prairie populist in the Harkin vein, the state’s governor-elect Rob Sand, who celebrated at the same Des Moines gathering, is something closer to Jimmy Stewart’s title character in Mr. Smith Goes to Washington. Sand is the incumbent state auditor and has relied on a long roster of endorsements from Republicans and independents in a campaign that he described as dedicated to “the straight and narrow path of public service, not politics.” When Iowans send their children off to school, he announced, “We don’t tell them to be red or to be blue. We tell them to be good, to be kind, to tell the truth.” Sand’s campaign distilled that sentiment into another typically Iowan slogan: “Not redder and bluer, but better and truer.” Midway through his speech, he paused to revive the civic ritual that he made the signature moment in his town halls across the state, leading the crowd in “America the Beautiful.”
But Sand also went on to explain that this is more than simple goo-goo sentiment. As a matter of basic political math in a state where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by 180,000, “the smallest party has to appeal to reasonably minded people in the other party.” And in governing a state with GOP majorities in both houses of the legislature, Sand has little choice but to seek some workable common ground with a MAGA-fied GOP.
Speaking of the loyal opposition, Sand said, “I hope you will kindly tell me why you didn’t vote for me—and since I’ll be here for a while, you’ll get to know me better, and maybe change your mind next time.” It’s a pragmatic, improbably wholesome start at charting a path out of the MAGA darkness that’s engulfed the state, but it’s again not without precedent. Throughout much of the 20th century, Iowa had some of the most liberal and most conservative members of the Senate—Harkin and the state’s now super-senior nonagenarian Senator Chuck Grassley, John Culver and Roger Jepsen, Harold Hughes and Jack Miller. This, too, was a legacy of Populism, which in its Upper Midwest iteration found later expression in left-wing movements like North Dakota’s Nonpartisan League and Minnesota’s Farmer-Labor Party. Tuesday’s results supplied a strong confirmation of the argument that the best rejoinder to the phony mogul populism of the Trump era is actual economic populism; it could be that Iowa’s incorrigibly neighborly contribution to that project is to make civic populism a going concern once again. Who’s up for a chorus of America the Beautiful?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Jon Ossoff Showed Democrats How to Channel Voters’ Anger About Corruption and Corporations
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Joan Walsh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Jon Ossoff Showed Democrats How to Channel Voters’ Anger About Corruption and Corporations
The Georgia senator was considered the most vulnerable incument this cycle. He cruised to a commanding victory, with lots of lessons for 2028.
Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff came into his reelection contest judged the most vulnerable incumbent in the Senate, the only Democratic senator running in a state Trump won two years ago. On election night, Ossoff was the first Senate candidate called a winner. At 7:18 pm—yes, just 18 minutes after the polls closed—the respected Decision Desk declared him the victor over Republican Representative Mike Collins, 59–41 percent. What happened?
Shortly before the midterm vote, we saw polls showing that 90 percent of voters considered political corruption their top issue, while just behind were voters who said it was the cost of living. That explains Ossoff’s win. Throughout the campaign, he led the way in showing Democrats how to link the grifting of Donald Trump, as well as the white supremacy and self-dealing of his Trump-loving opponent Representative Mike Collins, to Georgia voters’ own struggles.
The link wasn’t necessarily obvious at first, but once Ossoff did it, I was surprised no one else figured it out.
Related Article
I have been covering Ossoff since his unsuccessful but close congressional race, and his victorious 2020 Senate race. I’m on the record as an admirer. But in the last year, I’d become a big Instagram fan—his staff clips the greatest hits of his campaign talks. But it was more powerful seeing him in person in Savannah, watching him twin the two devastating effects of the Trump era, elite corruption and middle-class immiseration, and put it to voters in a way that they got it.
“I don’t know if you saw the mess in Washington last week. The president was so humiliated in [the Strait of] Hormuz, he threw his toys out the stroller,” Ossoff told the Savannah crowd. “That’s after he gave some felon donor a no-bid contract for the Reflecting Pool, and it filled up with algae.”
But then he hit Trump’s domestic agenda. “He promised to bring down prices on day one,” Ossoff said. “Y’all know what today is? Today is day 524, and groceries, rent, and healthcare are at their all-time highs in American history. Donald Trump and his puppet Mike Collins—they doubled health-insurance premiums for more than a million Georgians and threw 300,000 Georgians off their insurance altogether. I heard from a woman with cancer who waits tables for a living and said she was going to lose her health coverage in the middle of chemotherapy. And they did this to pay for a tax cut that went overwhelmingly to the rich and to corporate America. Did you know that, Savannah?” Savannah knew, indeed.
Ossoff went on: “While hundreds of thousands of Georgians lose their healthcare, Mike Collins builds Trump a ballroom. They worked harder burying the Epstein files than they ever worked to lower your grocery bill. And while you pay more for everything, the Trumps are raking in billions. from all over the world. Illegal tariffs, failed war, healthcare cuts, and unmatched corruption.”
But I found myself most drawn in by the most everyday stories Ossoff tells: how most of us, even those who aren’t in crisis, feel the walls of corporate power closing in. “The corporate disrespect is suffocating,” he told the Savannah crowd. “Instead of reading to your child, that precious spare hour after work is spent on the phone, fighting your bank, or the cable company, or the insurer that’s denied your claim and dared you to fight back while you’re sick. A toddler’s ambulance is followed by a $3,000 bill. Hedge funds buy up houses till there are none left to afford, then rip off the renters. We were promised a political system that delivers for the public, but instead, it delivers for the donors.”
Maybe not surprisingly, Ossoff returned to those themes in his victory speech Tuesday night, with new polish and conviction. “While the wealthy and well-lobbied feast on inside information and official favors, America’s forgotten families are treated to systemic corporate disrespect and official indifference, working harder and harder while the treadmill just gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher,” he told the Atlanta crowd.
“Instead of reading your daughter her favorite book, that precious spare hour after work, you’re on the phone begging the insurance company to cover the medicine that prevents her seizures. You report the black mold to your landlord, who doesn’t fix the leak, and the ambulance for your toddler’s asthma attack is followed by a $3,000 bill.” The senator just a year ago judged the most vulnerable found new power in channeling the growing vulnerability of American voters.
Ossoff told me back in June, as he tells everyone, that he will not run for president in 2028. I chose to believe him, since he is a 39-year-old senator running for his second term, with two small daughters and a wife with a medical practice. I still believe he has plenty of time and plenty of crossroads ahead. But he ran such a flawless campaign, he’s going to face this question incessantly.
For now, I’m going to leave him with his own summary of what his victory, and the stunning wins by Democrats from the Senate to the House to state legislatures, have to say about the country’s political health. “In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame-duck president, Donald J. Trump.” Indeed. Ossoff’s overwhelming victory Tuesday night makes him a major player in deciding what comes next, whether he decides to run or not.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: November Book Bag: from a book about broken art to a collection of Zanele Muholi’s LGBTQ+ portraits
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture, C. D. Dickerson III and Andrew Sears, Chicago University Press, 240pp, £40 (hb)
The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture explores the enduring fascination with fractured statues, focusing on the “power dynamics of iconoclastic dismantling and defacement, and how various cultures treat broken statues”, says a publisher’s statement. Highlights include Michelangelo’s terracotta Model of a Nude Woman (around 1533), which new research suggests may have been intentionally created incomplete. The publication accompanies a wide-ranging and eclectic exhibition spanning more than 4,500 years of global history, which opened in September at the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence before it travels to the National Gallery of Art in Washington DC next year.
Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Nancy Spector, Phaidon, 352pp, £39.95 (hb)
This newly revised and expanded edition assesses the relevance today of the influential conceptual artist Felix Gonzalez-Torres who died from an Aids-related illness in 1996. “Almost two decades after its original publication, the monograph accompanying Gonzalez-Torres’s 1995 retrospective at the Guggenheim Museum is still the canonical text on the artist,” says a publisher’s statement. Gonzalez-Torres is known especially for his famous sweet installations, which are usually mounted in piles in the corner of rooms. “The candy pieces, like all his works, encourage a wealth of meanings, and can be everything from stridently political to gently lyrical,” writes the critic and host of The Art Newspaper’s podcast, Ben Luke.
The Voice of the Artist(s): another vocabulary, Gabriela Galcerán (editor), Sternberg Press, 360pp, £23.50 (pb)
This publication grew out of a video project devised by the cultural producer Gabriela Galcerán in which 26 artists chose a word, one for each letter of the alphabet, and responded to it in their own way. The five thematic chapters, including “Power + Politics” and “Agency + Language”, subsequently draw connections between their ideas. Contributors include Lynn Hershman Leeson, Lawrence Abu Hamdan and Gary Hill. “They all made me flinch, each for a different reason. I love the wide range of tones and registers that make up this choral effort. Some are intimate, some political, some humorous or oblique,” says Galcerán in a statement.
Faces and Phases, Zanele Muholi, Renée Mussai (editor), Mack, 464pp, £65 (hb)
For more than 20 years, the South African artist and activist Zanele Muholi has been documenting Black lesbian and bisexual women, along with queer, trans, non-binary, and gender fluid people for the project Faces and Phases. This new volume of the work, released to mark the project’s 20th anniversary, has been updated to include new sitters in locations such as São Paulo, Salvador, London, Porto and Los Angeles. “These striking photographs are often accompanied by participants’ testimonies, sharing their personal stories, feelings, and lived experiences,” says a publisher’s statement. Muholi was born in Durban in 1972 at the height of apartheid in South Africa. In the early 2000s, the photographer began to raise awareness of the hypocrisies and hate crimes that remain prevalent against the LGBTQ+ community within the country.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: 8 Takeaways From Progressives’ Biggest Night in a Generation
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
8 Takeaways From Progressives’ Biggest Night in a Generation
Polls did fail to capture something: the scale of the Democratic wave.
In the days leading up to Tuesday’s election, prognosticators issued the obligatory warning that polls could be subject to systematic error. And indeed, polls did fail to capture something: the scale of the Democratic wave.
Not only did Democrats win the House (as expected), and the Senate (as seemed possible), but they secured a majority of governorships for the first time in 20 years. They swept at least five of the six Senate seats rated as toss-ups by The Cook Political Report (with votes still being counted in Alaska), and even picked off a seat in South Carolina that had been in Republican hands since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964.
Not since the waning days of George W. Bush’s disastrous second term has there been a Republican collapse of this scale, nor such a clear set of opportunities to lead for the Democratic Party. The results have upended much of the conventional wisdom that has dominated American politics since Donald Trump himself tore up the rulebook a decade ago.
While the meaning behind the results will surely be debated through the next election, it was a decisive enough evening for a few stories to come into focus almost immediately.
Democrats can—and should—compete everywhere. The party swiftly picked up Senate seats in five states—Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas, and South Carolina—where Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024. But perhaps more remarkable were the states where Democrats came unexpectedly close: In increasingly ruby-red Florida, democratic socialist Angie Nixon fell short of winning a Senate seat by just three points. Even closer was Jamie Davis in hyper-polarized Louisiana—and, as of writing, Scott Colom’s race in Mississippi is still too close to call. All three were Black candidates who put up historic results despite limited investment from the national party. As successful a night as the party had in deep-red territory, Democrats may have approached a supermajority with a little more investment in races dismissed as unreachable.
The generational shift in the Democratic Party is here, and it’s populist. Seven battleground states elected Democratic senators under the age of 50, in Peggy Flanagan (47), Josh Turek (47), Chris Pappas (46), Annie Andrews (46), Abdul El-Sayed (42), Jon Ossoff (39), and James Talarico (37). And it’s not just the candidates themselves that are fresh and new; it’s their ideas. In Colorado’s First Congressional District, 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros became the first woman from Generation Z elected to Congress. And in Montana, it looks like Sam Forstag, a union leader and former wildland firefighter, will flip MT-1. It’s a far cry from the Democratic Party that, two years ago, hoped to invigorate the youth vote with the vim and vigor of Joe Biden. And the depth of the bench is no accident: It was cultivated by organizations like Run for Something, which not only notched nearly a hundred local victories and counting Tuesday but planted the seeds for statewide wins by backing candidates like Talarico starting nearly a decade ago.
The GOP’s gerrymandering gambit backfired. In Texas, Florida, North Carolina, and Ohio—all of which redrew their maps mid-decade to marginalize Democratic voters—Democrats held on to seats they were projected to lose, and in some cases even picked up seats. What’s more, in another blow for disenfranchisement, Black voters showed up in droves in the wake of the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act. Among other victories, they helped elect the first Black woman governor in American history. In spite of everything, voters continue to choose their politicians; not the other way around.
Americans do care about foreign policy. President Trump made a surprising final pitch to voters on Election Day, with a dubious vow to suspend $4 billion in aid to Israel and an admission that his administration’s financial support of the country is “a bad talking point” for Republicans. It was an acknowledgment of Americans’ deep opposition to his international agenda—and, with more strikes on Iran potentially coming after the midterms, it’s also a reminder to newly empowered Democrats that voters are demanding a break with the foreign policy status quo. It was just under 20 years ago that Senator Barack Obama launched a presidential campaign built around his opposition to the Iraq War; that could be instructive.
Voters vented their AI agita. Voters weighed in on at least 40 data center measures nationwide, and, overwhelmingly, communities from Maine to Ohio to Kansas voted to regulate and restrict data center construction. Data center industry darling Darline Graham and infamous AI flip-flopper Greg Abbott faltered. Meanwhile, Big Tech already has its eyes on the presidential matchup ahead: “We already know the number-one issue of the 2028 presidential election,” reads a memo by a leading industry lobbyist: “AI.” (One potential candidate—Jon Ossoff—directly addressed those risks in his victory speech.)
Money doesn’t change everything. This was the most expensive midterm election in US history—and no single donor gave more than the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, who funneled huge sums to Republicans in his home state of Texas. Democratic hopefuls James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa made Musk’s attempts to buy their races a centerpiece of the joint rally that closed their campaigns. “Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people?” asked Hinojosa, “Or this is the billionaires’ world and we just live here?” In the end, Texans picked the people, not the plutocrat.
MAGA may have reached the end of the line. Many of the issues top of mind for voters amounted to a referendum on Trump’s governance. Gas prices, affordability, and national security have been squeezed by the profoundly unpopular Middle East war he promised he’d never start. His naked self-dealing has thrown the wealth gap into stark relief and made political corruption one of voters’ chief concerns. And with countless jobs and the health of the economy riding on the whims of a few increasingly unaccountable tech companies, Trump’s failure to regulate AI has sounded yet another sour note with the public. He also handpicked a number of disastrous candidates who fumbled winnable races: the corrupt Ken Paxton, the shameless Vivek Ramaswamy, the grossly underqualified Darline Graham, and on and on. In stripping his party of both the House and Senate in such dramatic fashion, Americans may have just rendered their final verdict on Trump—and the MAGA movement at large will stand trial in 2028.
Every party faction had something to celebrate. It remains to be seen if that unity can last. From the insurgent left to the moderate middle, hardly any candidate up or down the ballot underperformed on Tuesday. The factional divides faded away in favor of an unambiguous rebuke of Donald Trump; a rising blue wave lifted all boats. But for a Democratic Party that remains historically unpopular, approaching what will be the first presidential election in 13 years without Trump on the ballot, hard work lies ahead. As one of the new progressive House members texted me late last night, “Wow Wow! I hope Hakeem and Chuck understand how much this is anti-establishment, populist, fed-up energy for change.”
As Robert Reich said before any votes were counted, “We’re going to have to continue to organize, mobilize, and energize everyone around us to put pressure on Congress—even a Congress controlled by the Democrats—to protect and strengthen our democracy.”

The American People Just Kicked Donald Trump’s Ass
An epic defeat turns the president into a lame duck—and hopefully marks the beginning of the end of the MAGA era.
Donald Trump wants to make one thing perfectly clear: The epic defeat suffered by the GOP in Tuesday’s midterms wasn’t his fault.
As it became clear that the GOP was not only losing both houses of Congress, as well as countless local races, but doing so at levels not seen in generations, Trump posted on Truth Social: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”
Trump spent much of the evening that way—searching for anything that could explain the humiliation he was suffering. He blamed Fox News for having too many Democrats on. He blamed far-right Republican politicians like Texas Governor Greg Abbott, resoundingly defeated in his bid for a fourth term, for supposedly straying from the righteous path of Trumpism. He proclaimed to Fox News that the results weren’t actually about him. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he said, adding, “It was a point in time. I shouldn’t feel guilty.”
Almost nobody believed the man who has now morphed from a onetime political colossus to a widely loathed lame duck. (As if to underscore his newfound irrelevance, the White House posted a picture of Trump on Wednesday morning with the desperate-sounding caption, “PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT.”) That’s because the verdict of the American people was as unmistakable as it was accurate. Across the country, voters said the same thing: Trump’s entire second term has been a catastrophe, and he deserves to be punished, along with the party that has aided and abetted him for the last 10 years.
It is not hard to understand how we got here. Trump won in 2024 only because he faced a fatally weak opposition. The Democrats nominated Joe Biden, who was visibly in cognitive decline, committed to supporting a genocide in Gaza that revolted many Democratic voters, and maddeningly indifferent to the affordability crisis caused by Covid and the Ukraine War. By the time Biden finally ended his campaign, the damage had already been done (particularly since the new Democratic nominee, Kamala Harris, was unwilling to distance herself from Biden). Trump told voters he would focus on lowering the cost of living and keep the United States out of new wars overseas. That was enough to get him a second stint in the Oval Office. But instead of sticking to the promises he’d made, Trump misinterpreted the election as a mandate for a hard-right, untrammeled MAGA presidency, with himself as an imperial, untouchable king. He unleashed ICE to deploy gestapo tactics on American streets, enriched himself and his friends with corruption that dwarfed the graft of the Gilded Age, and launched a ruinous tariff war. Then, to top it all off, he launched an illegal war of choice in Iran that destabilized the global economy and sent the price of just about everything soaring.
Voters were rightly fed up. Given a chance to express themselves in the midterms, they handed the GOP a defeat that is truly historic. Metaphors of a blue wave or blue tsunami hardly do the midterms justice. The scale of the Democratic Party’s victory was far larger than other modern midterm defeats, even the “thumping” suffered by George W. Bush in 2006, Barack Obama (a “shellacking”) in 2010, or Donald Trump in 2018.
Instead, the 2026 midterms were the type of wipeout that a party suffers once in a generation. In terms of scale, it is comparable to the 1974 midterms, where the GOP was devastated by the Watergate scandal and the resignation of Richard Nixon.
Sean Trende, one of the smartest Republican political strategists, noted, “If you are watching this and just have a passing familiarity with elections, just understand you’re seeing something special, a 100-year flood. Easily the worst election for a party since 1974.”
The Democrats are on track to win the popular vote in House races by 13 percentage points. As New York Times columnist David Wallace Wells notes, “The 2010 margin was 6.8 points, an election remembered as a generational wipeout. Tonight is expected to almost double that. 2008 was 10.5 and 2006 was 8.0. A thirteen point win would be the biggest congressional margin in fifty years.”
Even more impressive than the size of the victory was where the Democrats won. They didn’t just sweep the swing states but also made unprecedented incursions into red states—or what should now be seen as formerly red states. The Solid South is no longer solidly Republican. Texas now has a Democratic senator and governor. Georgia has two Democratic senators and a Democratic governor. South Carolina has a Democratic senator. Mississippi is too close to call but could have a Democratic senator. Angie Nixon, who wasn’t supported by the national Democratic Party, came agonizingly close to flipping Florida.
The victories in the South inaugurate a new era of politics: If Texas is a purple state, then Democrats have many more paths to forging a national victory in presidential elections.
It’ll take a few more weeks to have a full vote count, but Democrats are looking at roughly 255 seats in the House and 54 or 55 Senate seats.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The Democratic victory is all the sweeter because Republicans ran a disgracefully bigoted campaign, playing to racism, Islamophobia, transphobia, and homophobia. Despite this, Keisha Lance Bottoms, who won in Georgia, will become the first Black woman governor in American history. Abdul El-Sayed, who won handily in Michigan, will be the first Muslim senator in American history. Chris Pappas, who won in New Hampshire, will be the first openly gay male senator in American history.
These victories also bode well for the future: The Democrats, if they can address the economic problems that have fueled voter rage, have a chance to govern as a multiracial, multicultural, and socially liberal majority party.
One of the bizarre features of the election was how focused Donald Trump was on the human posterior. He repeatedly praised the “ass” of Ohio Senate candidate Jon Husted (who lost his race) and singer Nicki Minaj. Republican operative Todd Gillman told Politico: “Honestly, we need to move as far away from Trump as we can. I think Republicans might be screwed all the way until ’30. Talking about Nicki Minaj’s fat ass. All that stuff is just wearing people out.”
Trump’s crude way with words perhaps gives us the best metaphor for the midterms. Trump and the GOP have received a once-in-a-lifetime ass-kicking.
