https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Brooklyn Asylum Seeker Breaks 30-Day Hunger Strike in ICE Detention in Georgia
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Gwynne Hogan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
A Russian asylum seeker who lives in Brooklyn ended a monthlong hunger strike in a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Georgia on Wednesday.
Andrei Gerdiukov, who’s been in ICE detention since February, and the group of 10 strikers were demanding their releases — or in his case, at least a transfer to a facility in New York so he can be closer to his wife.
He and the other remaining hunger strikers broke their fast Wednesday, 30 days after they stopped eating on Oct. 6, according to Polina Chertushkina, 27, Gerdiukov’s wife, who spoke with him over the phone.
“His hands and legs were shaking,” Chertushkina said Gerdiukov told her, as he took his first bites of a pastry, his first solid food in a month. Chertushkina lost more than 30 pounds over the course of the month, she said.
Andrei Gerdiukov, 31, was among dozens of detainees at the Folkston D. Ray James ICE processing center in Georgia who launched a hunger strike last month. As the weeks dragged on, the strike dwindled to 11 participants, including Gerdiukov, who were then sent to another ICE detention center across the street.
In recent days, the remaining participants have been threatened with being force fed, Gerdiukov told The City Reporter in a phone call from the facility earlier in the week when the fast was ongoing
“I cannot sleep at all because of hunger,” he said.
“We’re waiting for them to start force feeding,” Gerdiukov said. “They told us every day.”
“I can see my ribs,” he said.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return a request for comment.
As the Trump administration has detained historic numbers of people as part of its mass deportation agenda, detainees across the country have turned to hunger strikes to protest the conditions of their confinement. The Guardian has reported on how ICE has force fed hunger strikers with the approval of federal courts. Force feeding is a practice widely condemned by human rights groups as a form of torture.
Gerdiukov has been in ICE detention since Feb. 22, when he and his wife were pulled over by Border Patrol agents during a traffic stop while they were on vacation in Florida with another Russian asylum-seeking couple.
All four were arrested, and the men were held in ICE detention while the women were released under orders of supervision, Chertushkina said in an interview.
In the months since, Gerdiukov has tried to win his freedom in every way he could think of. He tried to get bond in immigration court and filed a habeas corpus petition. He was denied bond and then ordered removed, a decision he’s appealing. His habeas corpus petition seeking release is still pending before a federal judge in Georgia, seven months after he filed.
He and other detainees raised grievances about food, lack of medical care and poor conditions at the facility. He and his wife requested a transfer through formal channels, reaching out to their local Congressmember Yvette Clarke (D-Brooklyn), whose office also requested he be transferred on their behalf, according to correspondence shared with The City Reporter. None of it went anywhere, he said.
“We tried every legal process. Every issue we tried to solve it here, but they didn’t listen to us,” he said. “They leave us only one choice, that’s to protest, hunger strike.”
Chertushkina said that staff approached Gerdiukov this week offering to transfer him to another facility in Georgia, but not one closer to New York. Now that the strike was over she wasn’t sure what they would do.
“Maybe other people can forget about it,” she said. “Everything will be as it was before.”
Fleeing Putin’s Russia
The couple entered the United States seeking asylum in 2024, after fleeing Russia ahead of the landslide re-election of President Vladimir Putin.
They were caught by Russian police distributing pamphlets in favor of the opposition and arrested, Chertushkina said in an interview, and Gerdiukov was beaten up.
When they were released and told to return the next week, they understood that to mean they would be put in prison if they didn’t get out of the country. They bought plane tickets right away.
“We came home, and we understood, we have to leave Russia. You have another choice, or we will be in prison,” Chertushkina said.
The couple settled in Midwood, Brooklyn, applied for asylum, got work authorization and were going through deportation proceedings, immigration court records show. Gerdiukov was working as a handyman, while Chertushkina was teaching English to Russians, Belarusians and Ukrainians in Southern Brooklyn, she said. They were settling into life in New York City.
“Everybody was very kind. In New York City I feel a lot of people support immigrants, and I thought all Americans were like New Yorkers,” Gerdiukov said. “But I was wrong. Right now, I can see the difference.”
When they decided to go on vacation with their Russian friends, they thought with their asylum claims and deportation cases pending, they were not at risk of arrest by ICE or border patrol.
“They gave me all [the] documents, I thought I was legal,” Gerdiukov said. “I brought it with me. I have nothing to hide. I’m clear.”
All four of the Russians were arrested by border patrol. The women were released on orders of supervision, which means Chertushkina cannot leave the state to visit her husband in detention.
The two men were handed off together to ICE custody and spent a week at Alligator Alcatraz before they were sent to Folkston. Gerdiukov’s friend, Andrei Mikhailov, is also partaking in the hunger strike at Folkston, while Chertushkina and Mikhailov’s wife, Ksenia Volkova, have been advocating for their detained husbands, calling elected officials and reporters across the country.
Spokespeople for Rep. Clark, Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, Senator Chuck Schumer and Governor Kathy Hochul haven’t returned requests for comment.
Gerdiukov has already faced retaliation for his protest, disciplinary records shared with The City Reporter show. He was cited with the “prohibited acts” of “engaging in group demonstration” and “conduct that disrupts” after staff said he helped orchestrate a video call with other detainees that was put online and published by several media outlets “to generate public and media attention.”
After the charges, Gerdiukov spent two weeks in solitary confinement, he and his wife said.
When Gerdiukov spoke to The City Reporter earlier in the week, he said he felt weak, exhausted and hungry all the time. Still, he said the separation from his wife hurts most.
“I’m trying not to think about that,” he said. “It’s the hardest part.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uaw-michigan.author: Alex N. Press
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uaw-michigan.text:
The UAW Bet on Abdul El-Sayed and Won
The United Auto Workers backed Abdul El-Sayed in a close Senate primary, then mobilized members across Michigan. Its sights are set on the next fight with the Big Three.
Three Rivers, Michigan, is a factory town in a county where Donald Trump won 66.2 percent of the vote in 2024. Its biggest employer is American Axle, whose workers belong to United Auto Workers (UAW) Local 2093. In 2008, the company demanded major concessions, arguing that it needed lower labor costs to remain competitive and keep the plant open. Workers spent nearly three months on strike before accepting a contract that halved some workers’ pay, from $29 an hour to $14.50. The plant survived, but by this spring, production workers still topped out at only $22 an hour.
Workers spent years trying to recover what they had lost. Yet when members voted to authorize a strike in 2021, the international union did not support them walking out, according to Rosemary Dodge, a machine operator and trustee of Local 2093. Members were angry at the company and at the union leaders who wouldn’t back a strike.
“People’s attitudes toward our international union were very negative,” she told Jacobin.
This year, Dodge took time away from the plant to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed in his run for Senate. Her local had struck with the international’s backing in June, and El-Sayed had spent hours on their picket line.
“I had not seen that kind of solidarity in our union up until that point,” she said of the contract fight.
The UAW, Michigan’s largest union, counts more than 350,000 members, active and retired, in the state. It backed the Medicare for All advocate in a primary where Governor Gretchen Whitmer and retiring Senator Gary Peters supported Haley Stevens, El-Sayed’s opponent, and other major unions stayed neutral or backed Stevens. El-Sayed’s campaign called the UAW’s backing “critical” to his 1 point primary victory.
Dodge, sixty-four, works on the paint line and has been at American Axle for almost eleven years. “The starting wage was not enough for people to both have a place to live and have a vehicle to get to work,” she told Jacobin, describing what coworkers faced before this year’s contract fight. “There were people that were either walking or riding bikes to work, or people that were living in their cars.”
But by the time Local 2093 prepared to bargain again this year, things had changed inside the international union. Two former UAW presidents were among the officials convicted in a federal corruption investigation. Members subsequently won direct elections of their top officers and elected Shawn Fain president in 2023. That fall, the UAW struck all three major US automakers.
In the lead-up to the 2026 contract fight at American Axle, the local bargaining committee had spent a year preparing, including tracking parts shipments and the company’s efforts to build inventory. Members began “working to rule” to resist management’s stockpiling efforts, and hundreds attended the local’s meetings.
“We had a really strong bargaining committee that was very well prepared, and when the international saw that, it was on board and helping us,” Dodge said. “Since we’ve had the change at the top of the international with Shawn Fain and one member, one vote, the international leadership and its willingness to back us changed a lot of people’s minds.”
Fain and Michigan Lieutenant Governor Garlin Gilchrist attended a rally to kick off contract negotiations at Axle, she recalled. “We were like, ‘All right, the lieutenant governor’s here, and we’ve got the president of the international here.’” Members could see that people had their backs, she said. “That made a big difference in people’s attitudes.”
On June 1, nearly one thousand American Axle workers walked off the job. They wanted a $30 hourly rate by 2030, no increases in out-of-pocket health care costs, and stronger protections for their personal time.
Four days later, the UAW endorsed El-Sayed’s primary campaign for Michigan’s open US Senate seat. The candidate joined Local 2093 members on the picket line that day.
“Abdul was the one who spent hours on our line, talking to the people of our union, walking with us, while there were so many other politicians who came and showed up just for a photo op,” Dodge said.
“We are going to make sure that they hear you nationwide,” El-Sayed told the strikers at the time, pointing to the concessions workers had made to keep the plant open and accusing the company of failing to share the gains from their work.
In mid-June, Axle’s workers ratified a contract with a $30 top rate by 2030, with additional paid time off and no concessions on existing health care costs. Those hired before May 31, 2012, received an immediate $8 hourly increase.
“[El-Sayed] genuinely cared about how we were doing, and he was one of the first ones to call and congratulate us when we got a great contract,” Dodge said.
In a September Abdul for Senate television ad, Local 2093 Bargaining Chair Josh Jager contrasted his more than twenty years on the line with Rogers’s political career. “Mike Rogers has been in office for over twenty years — not good years,” he said. “Every day, I show up on the line and build stuff. Every day, Mike shows up for his corporate donors.”
Dodge joined the UAW’s political program before the August primary, taking release time from the plant to knock doors, make calls, and rally her fellow members to back the progressive challenger. Despite the barrage of attacks on El-Sayed — including from Trump, whom some members had supported — Dodge said the majority of the union households whose doors she knocked on were polite even when they disagreed (though one did call them communist sympathizers and order them off his property).
“I believe that Abdul is someone who does respect working people, and that’s what earned my respect for him,” she said.
“We were pleasantly surprised when we started at how many people were really receptive to hearing the information we had to share about Abdul,” Dodge said.
El-Sayed won both of the city’s precincts. Unofficial returns show him receiving 1,318 votes to Republican Mike Rogers’s 1,060, or 53.6 percent to 43.1 percent. Two years earlier, Rogers beat UAW-endorsed Democrat Elissa Slotkin in the city, while Trump beat Kamala Harris.
Choosing Their Candidate
The union’s endorsement of El-Sayed in the primary mentioned his stance on Medicare for All, banning stock buybacks, and May Day 2028. Its Big Three contracts expire April 30 that year, allowing a strike on May Day; the UAW has urged other unions to align their contracts so they can strike together.
The endorsement decision came through Michigan’s member-elected Community Action Program (CAP) board, following candidate forums and member surveys. Endorsement required a two-thirds majority of the board, where a plant representative’s vote carried the same weight as that of the international president.
Three Democrats — Stevens, El-Sayed, and Mallory McMorrow — participated in a candidate forum at the UAW’s national CAP conference in Washington in February. Fain said the union had invited Rogers too, but the Republican candidate “didn’t even bother to respond.” The union invited the candidates to another forum in Detroit. “Again, Rogers didn’t show up, didn’t bother to respond,” Fain recounted.
Members quickly warmed to El-Sayed, who secured the endorsement on the board’s first vote.
“When he talks to people, they understand who he is, and they understand that he cares about working-class issues,” Fain said. “Our members really drove this decision, and that’s what I’m really proud of.”
Back in Three Rivers, rising costs were eating into the contract’s hard-won gains, leaving members open to what El-Sayed had to say. “People were frustrated by that,” Dodge said. “They said we worked so hard to get this better contract, and it’s not really showing. I think they were willing to hear other options.”
At a Wednesday press conference after El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers, Fain recalled hearing from Three Rivers members at the union’s June convention.
“There were so many people coming up to me from Three Rivers, Michigan, saying, ‘This guy speaks my language. He understands me,’” Fain said. “This was an area where they were Trump supporters in ’24.”
To turn that support into votes, fifty Michigan UAW members left their workplaces to serve as full-time political organizers, the union’s “power squad.” Fain put the program’s totals at more than half a million calls made and more than one hundred thousand doors knocked.
The political program emphasized shop-floor conversations, with coworkers talking about wages, health care, retirement, and time off. Those conversations were also meant to get more members organizing inside their plants ahead of a possible strike in 2028.
James “Jay Jay” Jewell has worked at Ford’s Sterling Axle plant for fourteen years and is a district committeeman in Local 228. He began working full-time on the election in early September. As a recruitment lead, he made calls and organized one-on-one to get members to volunteer. “This was very structured,” he said. “This is very intentional work happening.”
“Money out of politics; money in your pockets; Medicare for All,” Jewell said of El-Sayed’s appeal, echoing the now-senator-elect’s key campaign slogan. “We have a lot of faith that the political structure and system in this country might be ready to turn around if regular working people have it in their hands. It’ll take time and work and more organizing, but the tools are there now.”
“It was far from lukewarm,” he said of volunteer recruitment among his fellow UAW members. “It was amazing how many people were raising their hands to do it, how many people were picking up the phone when I was calling.”
Jewell lives and works in Macomb County, where Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024 and Rogers beat Slotkin 53.3–43.6 percent. This year, unofficial returns there put El-Sayed just 7,526 votes behind Rogers, fewer than 2 percentage points.
Jewell had seen how a contract win could change members’ expectations of their union. For him, talking with conservative members about the election meant pointing to those gains. “When we have progress and wins, we just have to name it and make it clear and simple,” he said.
The 2023 Ford agreement had eliminated wage tiers at Sterling Axle and Rawsonville, bringing substantial raises for workers on the lower wage scales. Jewell himself had benefited from the union’s more aggressive bargaining. “My plant got rid of two tiers, so more than half my plant got a $12 raise overnight,” he said. “Made whole, including myself.”
“It’s no coincidence,” he said of the union’s bargaining and electoral victories. “They’re going to feed off each other: we get policy and legislation out of the people that got elected.” Better contracts, in turn, build confidence in the leadership and in collective solidarity. “It’s going to be self-perpetuating if we do this right.”
Building Power for 2028
“What we win at the bargaining table can be taken away in the halls of power the next day,” Fain said Wednesday. “The days of us blindly endorsing people because of party affiliation — those days are way behind us.”
The UAW put money behind that choice, with its V-CAP political action committee giving Fighting for Michigan PAC, an independent expenditure group backing El-Sayed, $300,000 in July and another $600,000 by October. The union still gave to Senate Majority PAC, but it broke with Democratic Party leaders in Michigan’s primary and put its money and members behind El-Sayed.
“We’re going to target races. We’re going to target people. We’re going to put our resources behind candidates that want to carry that agenda and want to stay with working-class people,” Fain said. “And I don’t care if you’re Democrat, Republican, independent. If you’re not with us, we’re not going to be there for you.”
Fain described the political program as part of the changes he had run to make inside the union.
“I was very frustrated with where we were politically: how we approached politics, how we approached bargaining, how we approached organizing, pretty much every aspect of our union. That’s why I ran for president,” he said Wednesday. “Right out the gate, it was about Big Three bargaining, going into new organizing, winning at places like Volkswagen, and the next stage of that is controlling our politics.”
El-Sayed won amid a broader Democratic sweep in Michigan. Unofficial returns showed El-Sayed led Rogers 52.5 to 45.5 percent as of November 5. Slotkin had beaten Rogers by just 19,006 votes (0.3 percent) two years earlier. Democrats also won back the state house, giving them control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office.
El-Sayed ran about 2 points behind Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who received 54.5 percent in the governor’s race. His campaign faced repeated Islamophobic attacks, with Trump labeling him a jihadist and advertisements falsely suggesting he had ties to terrorist organizations. He will be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
“Corporate Democrats are as big of a problem as any right-wing Republican,” Fain said when asked whether the election results nationwide vindicated the party’s moderates or progressives. “I do believe that the progressive people in the party are speaking more the language that resonates with working-class people.”
He warned Democrats against assuming the results showed confidence in the party. “They’re voting Democrat because they’re pissed off, because they’re frustrated with where they are in life right now, and they can’t afford to live,” he said. “If the Democrats do not heed that warning and come out with a platform and go to work to fix the problems in this country,” he warned, “they’ll be voting the other damn way.”
Jewell said the objections he heard while canvassing concerned El-Sayed’s race and religion; there was little disagreement over his platform. “I did not have a single member in two months who really wanted to argue against anything that he wanted to deliver,” he said.
In Three Rivers, Dodge did hear concerns about Medicare for All from some members who had just fought to preserve their insurance. But she supported El-Sayed’s health care politics. Even with union coverage, she said, a catastrophic illness could leave a worker in debt.
Tielece Perry, a thirty-year worker at Detroit Assembly Complex–Jefferson and a member of Local 7, chairs the union’s Region 1 CAP Council. She said conversations with coworkers often concerned their parents and the cost of their care.
“We’re raising our kids, but we’re also taking care of our elderly parents, and we still have to work full time,” she said. “So when someone like that has to make a choice between whether they’re going to have medication or groceries, that’s a real challenge.”
Asked what she wanted El-Sayed to do in office, Perry said, “We’re going to hold him accountable. I would like to see him be successful with Medicare for All.”
“He understands that when you work hard, you want to have a life outside of work,” Dodge said. At American Axle, she said, departments were still being placed on “critical status,” allowing management to mandate up to seven days of work a week. “We tried to get that language improved in our contract; it’s not as strong as we wanted it to be.”
El-Sayed had included “the freedom to spend time with your family” among the promises of his campaign. “These principles aren’t radical,” he said. “They’re the baseline for a more equitable Michigan and America.”
When Michigan’s new legislature convenes in January, passing unemployment insurance for striking workers will be among the UAW’s priorities ahead of its 2028 contract fight, Fain told reporters Wednesday.
“We plan to carry the power that we built in 2026 into our next major fight, which is the 2028 Big Three contract negotiations,” Fain said.
“We don’t do this much organizing and winning to get unemployment for striking workers and that’s it. No, we need a whole revamp of the system,” Jewell said. His priorities included the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act, which would make employers pay fines for breaking labor law and prevent them from indefinitely stalling negotiations for a first contract, and finding a way to undo Citizens United.
Asked by Jacobin whether he saw a path to passing the PRO Act or similar legislation, Fain stressed the need for stronger enforcement of workers’ rights. “We would love to see the PRO Act pass,” he said. “They fire people. They threaten people. They intimidate people,” he said of employers. “And there’s zero repercussions for corporate America when they do this.”
Jewell expected the candidates the UAW had helped elect to strengthen workers’ rights and curb corporate influence in politics. “I need them to go be aggressive as f — ,” he said. “They already know what we need. It’s not a secret.”
In his election night victory speech, El-Sayed mentioned Local 2093 bargaining chair Josh Jager and the strike he and his fellow members had waged at American Axle. “And they won that fight,” he said. “His hope?” the senator-elect continued, referring to Jager. “An America where every single worker gets the right to a union.”

https://gothamist.com/news/20-rent-contr.title: $20 rent-control cap coming to Elizabeth, New Jersey
https://gothamist.com/news/20-rent-contr.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/20-rent-contr.text:
Rent-controlled tenants in Elizabeth, New Jersey won a years-long legal battle on Election Day after voters approved a measure that restores a $20 cap on future rent increases, at least for a year.
City leaders have tried to eliminate the cap for years, saying it was outdated, but affordability advocates in a city with a where roughly half the population is foreign-born said the cap is still needed for a community struggling in the margins.
“The rents continue to climb and are just incredibly unaffordable,” said Nedia Morsy, the director of Make the Road New Jersey, a group that advocates for immigrants and the working class.
Elizabeth voters agreed, approving the measure with 68% support, according to unofficial election returns.
“ We talked to thousands of tenants. We organized tenants to come to tenant meetings. We connected this issue to the broader affordability crisis sweeping everywhere,” said Isaac Jimenez, an organizer with the Freelizabeth campaign, which pushed for the $20 cap. “And tenants showed out.”
Morsy said the cap will restore critical protection for Elizabeth residents at a time when the city is seeing “explosive” rent increases.
Elizabeth’s local law requires the city to reevaluate its rent control rules every two years, according to Jimenez. The regular review means the voter-approved cap will only be in place for 2027. It will be up to city leaders to decide on renewing it for the longer term.
“ Whatever they choose to do after is up to the [city] council,” Jimenez said.
The dispute originates with a decades-old city ordinance that once capped annual increases on rent-controlled units to 3% or $20, whichever was less. The median rent in Elizabeth is $1,523, according to U.S. Census data. A 3% increase for that rent would be about $45.
Elizabeth leaders in 2022 changed the ordinance to remove the $20 limit, allowing 3% rent increases annually regardless of dollar amount. City Councilmember Manny Grova told NJ Advance Media at the time that the $20 limit was “outdated.” Grova did not respond to requests from Gothamist for comment.
The North New Jersey Democratic Socialists of America and Make The Road New Jersey, which partnered to organize the Freelizabeth campaign, responded with a petition drive in 2025 to force a referendum on restoring the $20 cap.
“We knew that rents were going to creep up, that developers were going to start moving into Elizabeth, and that we would need to make an intervention,” Jimenez said.
A group of landlords went to court to challenge the signatures that were collected on the petition. A judge ultimately validated the petition, but only after the deadline for getting the question on the 2025 ballot had passed. As the fight over the petition signatures played out, the city council attempted to restore the $20 cap. Landlords sued to block that effort as well. A judge rejected the landlords’ claim that the cap was unconstitutional, but did rule that the council’s vote on the ordinance was invalid because it came at a meeting that did not have proper public notice.
Matthew Moench, a lawyer representing the local landlords in court, did not respond to requests for comment.
David Brogan, the executive director of the New Jersey Apartment Association, called the $20 cap arbitrary and said it ignored the financial challenges facing landlords.
“Property owners face rising taxes, labor, insurance, utility, and maintenance costs, yet their ability to recover those expenses is severely restricted,” Brogan said. “Ignoring these economic realities risks discouraging investment, undermining property maintenance and ultimately diminishing the quality and availability of rental housing for the very residents this policy is intended to protect.”
Brogan said the cap would hurt apartment property values in Elizabeth, which would increase the tax burden on local homeowners.
“Ignoring the financial realities of providing rental housing doesn't solve the affordability problem,” Brogan said. “It simply kicks the can down the road.”
Morsy said the $20 cap was more important than ever amid the ongoing affordability crisis.
“ Meeting the bills that your money has already been assigned to at the top of the month is incredibly difficult,” Morsy said. “ If we want to maintain the fabric of people's communities, which is beneficial for all of us, then no [it’s not outdated.] It's responsive to a system that just continues to exploit working people with, at least for the interim, no end in sight.”
The small city, which sits just south of the Newark Airport, has been a favorite target of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which detained 1,138 people in Elizabeth during the first 18 months of President Donald Trump’s second term, according to a Gothamist analysis. When one person is detained or deported, there’s often a family that relied on that person left behind, Morsy said.
“ What we've experienced even more so in the last year has been people who have been separated from their breadwinners,” Morsy said. “ Folks that were already struggling to make ends meet because of abusive and negligent landlords now had even more of a difficult time trying to make it to the end of the month while simultaneously also trying to support a loved one who was trying to fight their case.”
Elizabeth’s rent increase cap was the main focus this election season for North New Jersey DSA, according to Jimenez, who is also on the executive committee of the chapter. Jimenez said expanding and strengthening rent control in the state is top priority for local socialists.
“ Rent control in whatever form, whether it's temporary rent freezes, whether it's universal rent control, is definitely something that we're going to try in other cities,” Jimenez said.
Mayor Christian Bollwage’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

https://gothamist.com/news/better-days-a.title: Better days ahead for NYC commuters with Democrats in control of Congress, MTA chair says
https://gothamist.com/news/better-days-a.author: Stephen Nessen, Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/better-days-a.text:
MTA Chair Janno Lieber said Thursday that he’s optimistic the end of the “anti-city” movement has arrived and that more federal funding for public transportation projects is on the horizon after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm election.
Since President Donald Trump took office in 2025, his administration has repeatedly withheld funding from New York and the MTA. The Trump administration attempted to shut down congestion pricing, threatened to pull funding for the Second Avenue Subway extension project and took over the redesign of Penn Station.
“Obviously, having a Democratic Congress led by two New Yorkers and with the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee led by (Sen.) Kirsten Gillibrand, we are hopeful that we can do much, much better than that historical short-changing,” Lieber said during a special appearance on WNYC’s On The Way.
He was referring to Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer, who are frontrunners to serve as House speaker and Senate majority leader, respectively.
“I think we have more confidence that the existing projects will be funded, and we would like to now start pursuing money for new big projects,” Lieber said.
“But the bigger issue is is a mandate in Congress right now to stop this anti-city campaign that has been in effect in Congress and in Washington for the last couple of years,” Lieber added.
Lieber will speak about the future of mass transit in New York in a special event at WNYC’s The Greene Space on Nov. 17.
One pool of funding MTA officials are seeking to tap is the Surface Transportation Reauthorization bill, which expired in September. Some $256 million went to the MTA through former President Joe Biden’s infrastructure bill. Lieber said he’ll be looking to the Democratic Congress to reauthorize that money to fund vital accessibility signal upgrade projects.
The MTA has other major projects in the works that will require further federal funding, like the extension of the Second Avenue Subway west across 125th Street and building the Interborough Express, a light rail line connecting Brooklyn and Queens together that is only half-funded.
Tom Wright, the president of the Regional Plan Association, said with new pro-transit New York representatives headed to Washington, securing funding for bigger projects should be a priority.
“If through the new Congress there is money for mass transit, the IBX ought to be at the front of the line because it is such an excellent project,” Wright said. “And I think that that's what our delegation needs to be focused on.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-wor.title: Working-Class Democratic Candidates Won Big in the Midterms
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-wor.author: Jared Abbott
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-wor.text:
Working-Class Democratic Candidates Won Big in the Midterms
After this week’s elections, Democratic congresspeople from working-class backgrounds are set to grow their numbers by 75%. They have a chance to push the party’s agenda in a pro-worker direction. Organizing in a congressional caucus can help them do that.
In January, a logger from Maine’s North Woods will take a seat in the US Senate. Troy Jackson spent his adult life cutting timber before he ran for office, and he will be the only Senate Democrat whose working life before politics was spent mostly in a working-class job. But he won’t be alone on Capitol Hill. Across the House, a union ironworker from suburban Cleveland, a Bethlehem firefighter, a Wisconsin waitress, an emergency room nurse, a Montana smoke jumper, a Rochester math teacher, and a former Trader Joe’s worker from Queens are heading to Washington too.
By my count, twenty-one Democrats in the next Congress will have spent at least half of their working lives before politics in working-class jobs. Today there are just twelve. Working-class Democrats will still represent a woefully small fraction of the party caucus in the new year, but the 2026 midterms have swelled their ranks fast, and that gives them a real opportunity to come together to lead on a pro-worker agenda.
Having more workers in Congress isn’t just a matter of symbolism; it can meaningfully change what government does and how ordinary people feel about their elected officials. Political scientists Nicholas Carnes and Noam Lupu have shown that when workers don’t hold office, economic policy tilts toward the haves and away from the have-nots. Their work demonstrates that when working-class people are underrepresented in office, legislatures are less likely to pass pro-worker policies, governments tend to build less generous welfare states, and citizens have lower trust in their elected officials.
A Working-Class Wave
Of the over 250 Democrats serving in the current Congress (counting both the House and the Senate), just twelve (4.6 percent) spent most of their pre-political careers in working-class jobs. Meanwhile, roughly half of American workers hold working-class jobs.
I count a member of Congress as working class only if they spent at least half of their working life in working-class jobs before entering public office. That means jobs like factory work, waiting tables, office support, teaching, nursing, firefighting, and enlisted military service. A summer job or a few years of college shifts doesn’t count. That rules out many Democrats with real but limited working-class history, whose time in those jobs was too short or too uncertain to count.
The ten newcomers who clear that working-class bar mostly won hard-fought, highly competitive races. Indeed, nine of them won or lead in still-uncounted races for seats that Republicans hold today: Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th District; Bob Brooks and Bob Harvie in two Pennsylvania districts; Rebecca Cooke in western Wisconsin; Mitchell Berman in southern Wisconsin; and JoAnna Mendoza, Jake Johnson, and Sam Forstag lead in Arizona, Minnesota, and Montana, respectively. Troy Jackson took a Republican-held Senate seat in Maine. The tenth, Claire Valdez, won an open seat in Brooklyn and Queens, one of the most heavily Democratic districts in the country.
These candidates’ résumés read like a cross section of the American working class:
Many of these working-class candidates are also union members, and several have held union office: Poindexter as an organizer and apprenticeship instructor, Brooks as president of Pennsylvania’s firefighters’ union, Forstag as a vice president of his Forest Service local, and Valdez as a unit chair in the United Auto Workers. They join eleven returning members with similar backgrounds, from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the former bartender, to Stephen Lynch, the ironworker who ran his union local, and Norma Torres, a former 911 dispatcher.
Working-Class Democrats Span Every Wing of the Party
The working-class Democrats come from a wide range of the party’s caucuses. Among current members, they include Congressional Progressive Caucus stalwarts like Ocasio-Cortez and Maxine Waters, New Democrats like Lucy McBath and John Mannion, and Blue Dog Jared Golden.
The incoming class is just as mixed. Valdez was backed by Justice Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Jackson was Bernie Sanders’s pick. Harvie was endorsed by the New Democrats’ PAC, Johnson and Berman by both the New Democrats and the Blue Dogs. And Poindexter, Brooks, and Forstag managed something that should be impossible under the party’s factional logic: they were endorsed by both the Progressive Caucus PAC and the Blue Dog PAC.
But despite their ideological range, this crop of new working-class Democrats is more progressive on economics than it might at first appear. When I coded the campaign positions of the nine newcomers who ran in swing seats, five came out progressive or leaning progressive, including three the Blue Dogs endorsed. Troy Jackson and Bob Brooks both ran on Medicare for All. Sam Forstag proposed a 5 percent wealth tax on fortunes over $1 billion, Bob Harvie backs the PRO Act and a $15 federal minimum wage, and Brian Poindexter wants to make it easier to join a union and to make the wealthy pay their fair share to shore up Social Security funding. Claire Valdez, who ran in a safe seat in New York City, made Medicare for All one of her three platform pillars, alongside “unions for all” and “housing for all.”
Even the newcomers who lean moderate or show no clear lean hold robust pro-worker positions. Rebecca Cooke supports a $15 minimum wage and expanding Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing. Mitchell Berman calls for a living wage of about $21.54 an hour and joined striking nurses on the picket line. Jake Johnson wants a new top tax bracket for the highest earners and to break up big corporations that exploit workers. JoAnna Mendoza backs the right to unionize and expanding Medicare as well.
Whatever wing of the party they come from, this group’s shared working-class background grounds them in the bread-and-butter, kitchen-table issues that working people care about most and makes them ideal tribunes for working people’s interests on a national stage. They share an experience: of hourly pay, of shift work, of what a health insurance deductible means when you’re living paycheck to paycheck, and of the value of a union contract to families’ financial stability.
We Need a Working-Class Caucus in Congress
Congress has caucuses for nearly every region, industry, and ideological tendency. The Democrats’ main ideological blocs in the House are the Progressive Caucus, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs. But Congress doesn’t have a caucus by and for working people, dedicated purely to delivering material gains that improve the lives of ordinary Americans. The Labor Caucus does important work championing workers’ rights on the job and the priorities of the labor movement, from the PRO Act to a higher minimum wage. A working-class caucus would build on that work with a broader vision: raising the standard of living for all working people and making sure every working family has what it takes to thrive. Such a caucus, of course, wouldn’t need to police who does or doesn’t count as working class, but lawmakers with strong working-class backgrounds, who know firsthand the pressures that working families face, would play a central role. That would give working people not only allies in Congress but a voice of their own.
A working-class caucus could do things the existing ones cannot. To start, because working-class lawmakers already sit in caucuses across the party’s ideological spectrum, a working-class caucus could build coalitions across factional lines on bread-and-butter issues like wages, labor law, health care costs, and housing. Each faction supports progress on many of these issues in principle, but an organized bloc would be better placed to push back when party leaders are tempted to let those priorities slide down the agenda. Nick French has made a similar case for the record number of socialists heading to Congress: even a small minority can exert meaningful leverage when it organizes as a bloc.
Second, the issues that shape working people’s daily lives would sit at the top of the caucus’s agenda: making sure a full-time job pays enough to support a family; bringing down the cost of housing, health care, and childcare; protecting retirement security; strengthening workers’ right to organize; and investing in the towns and regions that decades of bad economic policy have left behind.
Finally, there is the bench of future working-class candidates to build. The 2026 results showed that working-class Democrats can win the competitive seats that decide control of the House, and a caucus could recruit, train, and fund more of them, so that a waitress or an electrician thinking about running knows there is a bloc in Washington that wants her to be there.
Organizing twenty or so working-class members of Congress into an organized caucus obviously won’t remake the Democratic Party into a party of the working class on its own. It can’t fix the deeper problem that working people have too little organized power in American politics. But it would give workers more leverage inside the party, because an organized group of pro-worker champions in strategic positions across the party can keep its leadership focused on working people’s priorities and hold the party brass accountable when it strays.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.title: Trump Hurt Average Americans, So They Voted Against the GOP
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.text:
Trump Hurt Average Americans, So They Voted Against the GOP
Populism isn’t just a switch the GOP could have chosen to flip on in this election but didn’t. Its governing record under Donald Trump has been one of harm and contempt for working people. Voters knew that and punished Republicans for it.
You didn’t even have to look at the numbers on Wednesday to know the election was a rout. You could have just guessed it by the fact that Donald Trump didn’t deny the results, call the whole thing “rigged,” or vow to fight the cheaters to the bitter end. Instead he meekly congratulated the Democrats, insisted none of it was his fault, and offered to work with his opposition before getting back to the truly important work of his ballroom.
In a two-week period that saw right-wing leaders across the world refuse to concede and try to find ways to deny election results, Trump, the man who first gave them the playbook to do it, was the only one to accept his defeat. It’s a measure not of any change in the president but of how emphatically he was rejected by the country.
By now, everyone knows this past Tuesday was a generational calamity for Republicans, and the party is of course now yelling over each other to explain what went so badly wrong.
“We forgot that we’re a populist party,” one GOP operative told Politico about the party’s lack of an affordability message.
“President Trump’s message won. Unfortunately he wasn’t the messenger,” Trump’s former campaign deputy communications director told Fox News, complaining that his team had “allowed his winning message in 2024 to be co-opted by his opposition.”
The issue was just that the GOP “forgot how to win,” wrote outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn, blaming the poor “character and integrity” of its candidates and urging the party to be more “likeable.”
For Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, now eagerly positioning himself as captain of this shipwreck, the problem was that Republicans were too obsessed with fighting “wokeness,” which was “yesterday’s battle.”
It’s not surprising that a party that would allow itself to get destroyed so thoroughly would in the aftermath still be completely oblivious about why they lost. Technically, yes, it was many of these things: the lack of populism, the bad candidates, the ignoring of affordability, the obsession with wokeness.
But that’s really underselling it. The reason the Republicans have been decimated is that the party did everything they could possibly do to make almost everyone in the country’s lives dramatically worse for the past twenty-two months: it pushed four hundred thousand people out of their jobs, it is throwing millions of people off of their health care, it wrenched Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits — also known as food stamps — from 5.5 million people, and raised their insurance premiums by 26 percent, with another 13 percent to come next year.
This was part of the party’s genius idea of slashing federal support for health care more than anyone had ever done in US history, to the tune of $1 trillion. This is all before you factor in the average of $471 per person in fuel costs alone added to US households’ expenses by the Iran war and the $1,745 more per family they’ve had to pay because of Trump’s blanket tariffs.
Mind you, all this was as Trump and the GOP shoveled a trillion dollars in tax cuts — the same amount they had cut from most people’s health care — to the top 1 percent, in a cut that gave 70 percent of its benefits to the wealthiest fifth of Americans. At the same time, it presided over record-high wage theft by employers and actively decided to let hundreds of corporate crooks who gave money to Trump off the hook for a variety of alleged wrongdoing, including price-fixing, workplace discrimination, and forced labor — all while the president and his family lined their own pockets in a way that’s never been seen before in US (or really, human) history, with the president alone growing his net worth by $3 billion through crypto scams that tricked his own voters into buying and being stuck with worthless Trump-themed digital currency.
We’re not even getting into the way Trump’s deportation crusade has caused terror, havoc, and death even among US citizens while directly hurting the farming communities that had lent him their support.
You will note the problem here is not that Trump and the Republicans were not talking about affordability. Trump could have spent the final weeks of the campaign actually talking about the high cost of living instead of droning on about his reflecting pool and men’s asses, and the reality is people’s lives still would have been significantly, materially worse off because of the policies they sunk untold months, energy, and political capital into to pursue — the same decidedly anti-populist policies Republicans have pushed for decades.
Those policies are not the ones desired by ordinary Trump voters, who — if you look at polling and the election results for ballot measures and candidates — want things like a higher minimum wage, a clampdown on price gouging, affordable childcare, and more generous employer benefits. Instead they got the bog-standard neoliberal agenda that the GOP’s donors and corporate sponsors promote, lobby for, and force onto the legislative agenda, because it benefits their bottom lines.
It’s not that Republicans suddenly forgot to be populist going into the election. It’s that they had nothing to be populist about.
The problem for the GOP here is the same one that the similarly corporate-backed Democratic Party has been wrestling with for decades: the interests of its working-class voters are fundamentally at odds with the interests of the people who fund its campaigns, who bankroll the think tanks they rely on for their policy ideas, and who are often the 1 percenters who make up its roster of elected officials.
The Democratic Party is, thanks to the left insurgency in its ranks, currently in the middle of a battle to try and resolve that contradiction. The GOP appears completely oblivious that that contradiction even exists — and as a result, has no real idea why voters just gave it a historic rebuke.

https://gothamist.com/news/manhattan-sho.title: Health aide, elderly man died in East Harlem senior center shooting, NYPD said
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattan-sho.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattan-sho.text:
A man and a woman were shot to death Thursday night at an East Harlem senior center, police said.
Officials said they responded to a 911 call from the Gaylord White Senior Center on East 104th Street and 2nd Avenue, part of a New York City Housing Authority complex, around 8:30 p.m. When they arrived, they found a 55-year-old woman, a home health care aide, and a 66-year-old man, both with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Police said it was still unclear whether the incident was a murder-suicide, or whether there was another suspect. They did not have a description of a possible perpetrator early Friday, and had not yet publicly identified the victims.
Shooting incidents in the 23 precinct – which serves East Harlem north of East 96th Street – are down by more than 37% this year compared to last year, according to NYPD data. There has been one other murder in the precinct so far this year.
Though gun violence is also down compared to last year in East Harlem’s public housing complexes, police data shows there have been two other murders in the sector this year, whereas last year by this time there were none.
This is a developing story and has been updated.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/european-ste.title: The Steel Disaster in Taranto, Italy, Is a Warning to Europe
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/european-ste.author: Valentin Vogl
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/european-ste.text:
The Steel Disaster in Taranto, Italy, Is a Warning to Europe
Italy’s top court has shut down the ILVA steel mill in Taranto, recognizing that it has become a disastrous health hazard. While European authorities boast about green investment plans, the site’s demise reflects the failure of their industrial policy.
For decades, labor unions and residents of the southern Italian city of Taranto have been mobilizing around the toxic emissions churned out by the local steel mill. A dedicated group fought for their right to good health through a yearslong legal battle that reached all the way to Italy’s top court. On October 29, the court finally ruled: the blast furnaces, which for decades have blanketed Taranto with fine particulate matter, dioxins, benzene, and asbestos emissions, must close with immediate effect. It represents a bitter-tasting victory after one of the great struggles of European industrial history.
ILVA, as Europe’s nominally largest steel mill is still called, stands right in the center of Taranto, a city with a population of nearly two hundred thousand. The steel mill was built in the 1960s, when Italy’s capitalist class dreamed of finally industrializing the South of the peninsula. The company is now called Acciaierie d’Italia (“Italy’s Steelworks”) and has been operating under state-imposed emergency measures since 2024.
The history of ILVA is one of Europe’s biggest environmental scandals. Local residents, unions, the mayor, and even the local soccer club have all demanded the closure of the blast furnaces. These efforts have consistently failed for want of government plans for financing alternatives.
In statistical terms, the people of Taranto suffer from pleural mesothelioma (a cancer caused by asbestos exposure) four times as much as the general population. In addition, the steel mill has been proven to cause elevated levels of particulate matter and emissions of micropollutants such as benzopyrene and dioxins, as determined by official health-impact assessments. Fans of the local Taranto soccer club have also been fighting against the plant for many years. They have written books, sold scarves with slogans such as “Fabbrica assassina, vergogna tarantina” (“Murderous factory, Taranto’s shame”), and rented public ad space to express their discontent.
With the abrupt closure of its largest employer, Taranto faces the threat of social crisis. More than ten thousand jobs depend on the steel mill; enormous health care costs and the cleanup of a toxic wasteland are deterring investors. The situation is fertile ground for the authoritarian right and its ability to turn disappointment, uncertainty, and frustration into votes.
The much-heralded return of European industrial policy also bears responsibility for ILVA’s demise.
In recent years, governments around Western Europe tried to coax “green” investments out of private capital through generous handouts. And yet, oligarchs and steel tycoons were in no hurry to comply. Although the plant is currently state owned, the government has no concrete plan for continuing production. The site’s future appears to be a painful choice between a complete sell-off to oligarchs or else outright collapse.
Europe’s Rusty Steel Empire
In an age of (sort of) flying cars, steel mills seem like relics from a bygone era. Appearances are not deceiving. The blast furnace process, used worldwide to produce steel for infrastructure, buildings, cars, and weapons, was developed in China over two thousand years ago. Steel truly took off thanks to the self-accelerating economic model of fossil capitalism: machines needed steel and coal; growing coal mining required more machines; and these, in turn, required more steel and coal. Today’s imperial core then began burning ever more fossil coal in ever-larger blast furnaces to produce pig iron — and greenhouse gases, too.
Starting in the 1970s, Europe lost ground to Japan’s rising steel power. Japanese steelmakers dared to build blast furnaces of unprecedented size and, in the process, created a global market for fossil metallurgical coal. Today more than one billion metric tons of coal are burned annually to produce steel. This makes the global steel industry responsible for one-tenth of all human-caused greenhouse gases, more than the EU as a whole.
By the time they were privatized in the late 1980s and early ’90s, European steelmakers were already lagging behind the competition, particularly their Japanese rivals. Global steel tycoons also took advantage of the wave of privatizations to snap up plants that were being sold off at bargain prices following the collapse of the Soviet Union. They downsized the plants’ workforces, established companies in tax havens, closed unprofitable sites, and generally generated good returns for themselves and minority shareholders.
Today Europe’s steel mills are outdated. No new blast furnace plants have been built since the 1970s, and only two blast furnaces have opened in the EU since 2000. From Eisenhüttenstadt to Fos-sur-Mer, Gijón, Kraków, IJmuiden, and Taranto, in a long list of former steel hubs, local residents suffer from air pollution and health problems. Investments to modernize these facilities and curb emissions are long overdue.
Derisking Has Failed
In Italy, at the height of the European Green Deal investment projects in the early 2020s, the prime minister was none other than Mario Draghi. He had previously been a key figure at Goldman Sachs and, as president of the European Central Bank throughout the 2010s euro crisis, a key figure in the troika that imposed austerity on the Greek government. Since 2024, Draghi’s name has come to symbolize EU competitiveness and the associated watering down of European environmental and human rights policies.
In the meantime, in 2021–22, Draghi served as Italian premier and developed a climate road map for the steel plant in Taranto. Beginning in 2019, Europe’s steel manufacturers successively announced decarbonization plans to transition from coal to hydrogen and electric furnaces in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In Taranto, according to Draghi’s plan, €4.7 billion in largely private capital was to be invested to achieve full employment and increase production by 2025.
The political ideology in which economic policy levers are adjusted so that unattractive investments like “green steel” become viable business cases is called “derisking.” The European Green Deal aims to make the steel industry climate neutral and competitive again through such means. Specifically, this meant free emissions allowances, billions in state aid for steel and hydrogen, protective tariffs against China, public procurement of “green steel,” energy price subsidies, and more lenient reporting requirements.
In an attempt to make green investments attractive to private capital, several EU countries dealt with ArcelorMittal. The world’s second-largest steel company holds a de facto monopoly on blast furnace production in Spain, France, Belgium, and Poland and operates additional blast furnaces in Germany (Bremen and Eisenhüttenstadt). From 2018 to 2024, ArcelorMittal also operated the plant in Taranto. Yet governments underestimated the steel giant’s negotiating position; it abruptly announced that it could not invest at all locations, thereby provoking a subsidy race among member states.
Up to €15 billion in low-carbon subsidies has since been awarded to steelmakers, but even that is not enough. As a result of high energy prices following the invasion of Ukraine, ArcelorMittal put all hydrogen projects on hold at the end of 2024. Seven lost years after the Green Deal, only a few Swedish and German steelmakers in the EU are still pursuing significant decarbonization projects. Meanwhile, many locations are in an even worse economic position than before. The EU’s “derisking” project appears to have failed, at least for now.
Draghi is quite right to blame the industry’s struggles to a lack of competitiveness. Raw materials and energy mostly have to be imported. Labor costs are comparatively high due to Europe’s past imperial might but also its historic labor struggles. Europe’s historical advantage in innovation has long since been squandered; the innovation hubs of the steel industry are now in Japan, Korea, and above all China. Added to this are persistent global overcapacity and higher returns in the financial sector, which is why ArcelorMittal prefers to carry out share buyback programs rather than make forward-looking investments.
Yet instead of EU member states pursuing alternative and more democratic economic models, the lack of competitiveness serves as a pretext to pursue austerity measures and the upward redistribution of wealth. Europe’s steel-producing regions are thus kept in a state of perpetual crisis, which further exacerbates health and climate damage. The authoritarian right skillfully exploits the resulting uncertainty about people’s jobs and the economic survival of their hometowns. This too is a result of timid industrial policies. In turn, these same right-wing parties, building on neoliberal ideological assumptions, further undermine democracy.
Socialization Is Not Enough
A bold democratic alternative is urgently needed to ensure a stable supply of raw materials. The good news is that we’re not starting from scratch. In June, the French National Assembly voted for the second time to nationalize the French division of ArcelorMittal, but the measure has so far failed to gain Senate approval. In Germany, in a recent position paper, Die Linke advocates for state involvement in the steel industry. Some steel manufacturers, such as the German companies Saarstahl and Salzgitter, are either part-publicly owned or bound to social interests. In Austria, Voestalpine employees own 15 percent of the company.
Recent developments in France and Germany make it clear that momentum is finally building around the issue of ecosocialist industrial policy. Yet socialist parties are running late, and nationalization alone is not enough. Rather, the direction of these plants must be anchored in a solid transformation strategy.
Democratic management of industry requires that we wrest the systems of provision we need to meet our basic needs from the logic of capital accumulation. Such transformative supply systems must be protected from capital and structured in such a way that social participation has a self-accelerating effect.
This presents two fundamental challenges for the democratization of the steel industry. First, solutions are needed to protect socialized steel mills from the capitalist market. Only in this way can economic leeway be created for radical experiments in Europe’s outdated and contaminated facilities. Long-term offtake agreements with public infrastructure operators (such as water or energy utilities) could be a first step. Further socialization of major steel consumers could be the next.
The second is that the EU obtains most of its energy and raw materials through imports. Dependence on raw materials makes socialist experiments vulnerable to crisis-induced market fluctuations and acts of economic sabotage. Increased use of scrap steel and renewable energy within the EU can mitigate these risks. In the spirit of “resilience by cooperation,” solidarity-based alliances can be built beyond the EU, with the goal of dismantling colonial patterns in value chains and organizing the procurement of more socially and environmentally sustainable primary raw materials in the longer term.
In Taranto, the state and private capital are leaving behind a toxic wasteland that hangs over the future generations. Even beyond the enormous costs of repairing this situation, hopes of industrial transformation are also complicated by the presence of organized crime in every stage of the waste cycle and its frequent involvement in public-procured construction projects, as documented by Italian NGO Legambiente in its No Ecomafia campaign. Given these obstacles, democratizing production is likely the only way for Taranto to retain the site in the long term. Unions and the local population have already mobilized and have the only concrete plan for the plant’s future.
For the rest of Europe, Taranto remains a cautionary tale: a foretaste of what might come next.
