https://gothamist.com/news/skeletal-rema.title: Skeletal remains found in backyard of West Village building, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/skeletal-rema.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/skeletal-rema.text:
Construction workers discovered part of a 19th-century human skeleton behind a building in the West Village on Thursday, according to the NYPD.
Officials said a construction crew excavating the backyard of 79 Christopher St. called 911 around 11 a.m. after finding several bones and part of a skull, buried 4 to 7 feet below the ground.
The city medical examiner determined that the bones were historic, and likely buried when the plot of land was used as a cemetery for the neighboring church in the mid-1800s, according to the NYPD. The property is adjacent to St. John’s Lutheran Church, which dates back to 1855.
Police said no foul play was suspected, and that it was not immediately clear if the remains belonged to a woman or a man.

https://gothamist.com/news/supreme-court.title: Supreme Court case could affect admissions reforms for NYC specialized schools
https://gothamist.com/news/supreme-court.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/supreme-court.text:
As Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces mounting pressure to boost the numbers of Black and Latino students gaining admission to New York City’s specialized public high schools, a new case before the U.S. Supreme Court could sharply narrow his options, education experts say.
The high court recently agreed to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a challenge to the test- and lottery-based admissions system used by the Maryland county for its public magnet middle schools.
The case comes amid the recent rekindling of decades-old debates over integration of New York City Public Schools, one of the most racially segregated school systems in the country. Many of the calls for reform have centered on the city’s prestigious and highly selective specialized high schools, where Black and Latino students are sharply underrepresented.
As with his predecessors, Mamdani has been pressed to articulate a specific plan to address underrepresentation of Black and Latino students to the specialty schools, with students, parents, past school officials and members of the City Council sounding the alarm.
But the Supreme Court, which has steadily eroded affirmative action initiatives, even those where race receives no mention, could further narrow and define what options are available for policymakers in New York City and other school systems facing similar challenges.
“It might freeze in time the racial makeup of every screened program in New York City,” said David Bloomfield, an education professor at Brooklyn College and the CUNY Graduate Center, who has publicly opposed the entrance exam for the city’s specialized high schools.
Here’s what to know about the Montgomery County case and its potential ramifications for New York City.
What is the issue before the Supreme Court?
The admissions lottery under scrutiny, based on successful test-takers in specific neighborhoods, was added during the pandemic and with an eye toward increasing the enrollment of Black and Hispanic students in the magnet schools.
Policy experts said the case centers on a narrow but consequential question: How do challengers of an admissions policy prove harm to a particular race when the policy makes no mention of race?
Under Supreme Court precedent, a so-called race-neutral policy can be found to be racially discriminatory — and a violation of the constitution’s equal protection guarantee — if challengers can prove two things: that the intent of the policy and its effect are discriminatory.
The challengers there are arguing that the lottery admissions policy is racially discriminatory in part because the share of Asian and white students admitted to the county’s magnet schools decreased after it was implemented. The challengers argue that individual Asian and white students were harmed.
“If a program is racially discriminatory and it hurts a single student of that race, that should be enough to bring a lawsuit to challenge it,” said Dean McGee, a lawyer for the Pacific Legal Foundation, who has brought similar cases in the federal courts.
But lower courts found that the lottery admissions system for Montgomery County magnet schools isn’t racial discriminatory, because the share of Asian American students admitted to the schools is still larger than the share of Asian American students in the applicant pool. In similar cases elsewhere, the First and Fourth Circuit courts of appeal have arrived at similar conclusions.
Why is this case being watched beyond Maryland?
The Supreme Court’s decision guidance could affect outcomes in similar admissions cases in the federal pipeline, including an action brought by a parent in New York who alleges a special admissions initiative discriminates against Asian American students.
If the Supreme Court sides with the parent challengers in the Montgomery County case, the justices could broaden what constitutes racial discrimination, opening the door for similar challenges of school admissions policies.
Liberal and progressive education experts say such a ruling could also deter education officials from pursuing admissions reform for selective schools, out of fear of incurring more lawsuits.
The court’s guidance could also affect reforms not just aimed at changing the racial makeup of selective schools, but also the economic diversity of such schools, said Richard Kahlenberg, an education and housing researcher for the Progressive Policy Institute, who has opposed race-based affirmative action programs but supported economic-based affirmative action.
A ruling for the plaintiffs, Kahlenberg said, could make it easier for conservatives to sue school districts over economic race-neutral affirmative action programs.
He added: “That’s the worry — that you freeze in an unfair status quo, and any reform that negatively impacts white or Asian students would be cause for concern among those on the right.”
But McGee, the Pacific Legal Foundation lawyer, said a ruling for the challengers wouldn’t necessarily halt admissions reform.
Policymakers, he said, would have to ask, “How do we benefit individual students? How do we fix failing schools? It would prohibit them from viewing (reforms) through a strictly racial lens and implementing policies for specific racial goals.”
How are admissions to New York City’s specialized high schools determined?
New York City has eight specialized high schools that currently determine entrance offers based on a student’s score on the Specialized High Schools Admissions Test, or SHSAT.
A portion of seats are also allocated to students who score slightly lower on the exam and attend a summer preparatory program.
At the eight test-based specialized high schools only 3.5% of students admitted this year were Black and 6.5% were Hispanic. The majority, 56.5%, were Asian and 23.5% were white, according to city education department data.
At Stuyvesant High School, only three of the 777 admitted students were Black. At Staten Island Tech, only one of the 294 admitted students was Black.
State law requires the SHSAT be the sole determinant for admissions to three of the city’s top specialized high schools.
What has Mamdani said about the situation in NY?
On the campaign trail, Mamdani promised to keep in place the SHSAT, after previously opposing it. At once, he has also vowed to address school segregation.
After the writer Nikole Hannah-Jones recently published a widely discussed article about the fallout from her decision to send her daughter to the city’s segregated public schools, Mamdani has repeatedly been asked how he plans to address the issue. He has vowed to tackle the issue, but offered scant specifics.
“We are exploring every single tool that we have at our disposal to ensure that this is going to be a very different school system moving forward than the one that we have inherited,” Mamdani said on The Brian Lehrer Show.
When pressed about the specifics of any integration plan at a recent town hall with Hannah-Jones, the schools chancellor Kamar Samuels promised to improve integration but offered no specifics or timeline for acting.
City council members have also urged the Mamdani administration to act.
Specifically, the members have pushed changes to the admissions policies at the five other specialized schools not explicitly cited in the state law, suggesting the schools instead rely on other factors in addition to a student’s SHSAT score, such as essays, teacher recommendation, and an applicant’s “background.”
But the policy experts said those reforms, if enacted, could also be the target of future racial discrimination lawsuits.

https://gothamist.com/news/south-bronx-e.title: South Bronx, East New York lead NYC in littering and panhandling tickets, analysis finds
https://gothamist.com/news/south-bronx-e.author: Ben Feuerherd, Carol Chen
https://gothamist.com/news/south-bronx-e.text:
NYPD officers are issuing criminal tickets for low-level offenses like loitering, panhandling and littering in the South Bronx and in East New York, Brooklyn at higher rates than anywhere else in the city, according to a new data analysis.
In 2025 and the first half of this year, more than 60% of the criminal summonses the NYPD issued for loitering were written by officers in just one of the city’s 78 police precincts — the 40th, in the South Bronx — according to an analysis published earlier this week by the Data Collaborative for Justice at John Jay College.
Audrey Martin, a spokesperson for the New York Legal Aid Society, said the new data shows that police are unfairly targeting neighborhoods where many low-income people of color live.
"Policing strategies like saturating neighborhoods with summonses fail to change anything except for how much time our neighbors spend fighting tickets or how much money they pay out of their pockets,” Martin said.
Residents of the neighborhoods who spoke to Gothamist had mixed opinions about such enforcement, with some supportive of the NYPD and others critical of low-level ticketing.
The analysis comes as Mayor Zohran Mamdani has faced intense criticism about his handling of policing issues, including for allowing the NYPD to continue a crackdown on what the NYPD calls quality-of-life crimes and violations. As a candidate for mayor, Mamdani said police should focus on solving more serious crimes, but quality of life enforcement has continued at a similar rate as the final year of the Eric Adams administration.
NYPD spokesperson Bradley Weekes said in a statement that NYPD officers in the South Bronx and East New York precincts are responding to increasing numbers of 311 calls. He said in the 40th precinct, in the South Bronx, 311 calls have increased 215% since 2015. In the same period, they’ve increased 556% in the 75th precinct. He did not immediately say whether there are disproportionately more 311 calls about low-level offenses in those precincts than in others.
Weekes added that the number of summonses citywide has not grown over time. The overall number of criminal summonses currently being issued by officers is at similar levels to what they were during Bill de Blasio’s administration, not counting the years during the pandemic, he said.
He said that in the South Bronx and East New York, the number of criminal summonses being issued by officers is down this year compared to the same period last year. Officers in the 40th precinct in the South Bronx have written 20% fewer criminal summonses, and officers in the 75 precinct in East New York have issued 15% fewer, he said. The analysis notes criminal summonses are on track to decline slightly in 2026, with officers on pace to issue 101,192 in 2026.
Police officers issue criminal summonses for violations that could be covered by lesser civil tickets — like open container violations — for a variety of reasons, according to the NYPD patrol guide. If someone is a recidivist, has a warrant or if an officer finds a "legitimate law enforcement reason” to do so, they can issue the more serious criminal summons.
Few are convicted
The vast majority of the criminal tickets that NYPD officers issue wind up being dismissed, according to a previous study by the same John Jay College group. In 2024, judges who heard criminal summons cases threw out 65% of them because of paperwork issues or because they were legally insufficient.
In the end, only 9% of the criminal tickets issued in 2024 ended in convictions, according to the study. The researchers found that even if people end up getting their tickets dismissed, they are punished anyway because they often lose time and wages fighting a ticket in court.
Racial disparities in summons enforcement have also persisted for years, according to the most recent analysis. In the first half of 2026, nearly 82% of criminal summonses were issued to Black and Hispanic New Yorkers, according to the data.
Michael Rempel, a researcher at the Data Collaborative for Justice and an author of the dashboard, said violations like having an open container of alcohol or loitering, are ones where police officers have the most discretion.
They are not the kind of offenses officers respond to after getting 311 complaints, Rempel said. “Clearly it's a choice to issue those types of summonses in large numbers,” Rempel said.
Residents have mixed feelings
More than a third of the city’s panhandling complaints from 2025 through the first half of this year were issued in the 40th precinct, in the South Bronx.
Antigone Raynaud said she comes to a busy shopping district called The Hub in that area regularly to make extra cash selling her blood plasma at a medical office. Raynaud said drug use and homelessness seem like understandable reasons for police to patrol the area. But, she added, a criminal summons for loitering could turn into an arrest warrant if the person doesn’t pay it — and she said that seems like too severe a punishment for a low-level offense.
“To be standing somewhere and get a ticket, not show up, and then now you're getting arrested, I think that's a bit excessive,” Raynaud, 30, said when she heard the area led the city in such tickets.
Malaika Holder, 32, is a lifelong resident of the Bronx who lives in Mott Haven, another neighborhood in the 40th precinct. In an interview earlier this week, she said she was not surprised residents there are ticketed at high rates for something like loitering — but said she found it sad.
“I do feel like the residents of the Bronx do have this very tense relationship with police and law enforcement, especially because in the Bronx, a lot of the community and what the culture is just loitering and just hanging out in different spaces,” she said. “A lot of our third spaces are stoops.”
Holder added that even though there may be an issue with people using drugs in the area, she thought that should be addressed with resources other than the police department.
“I don't think we should be criminalizing people who are looking to substitute their hard times with vices,” she said.
In Brooklyn, officers in East New York issued 855 criminal summonses for alcohol in public in 2025 through the summer of 2026, the most out of any precinct in the city. The tickets accounted for 8% of the citywide total, the data shows.
East New York residents offered a variety of opinions on the enforcement.
Das Angshu, 57, a plumber who lives in the neighborhood, said he welcomes the police presence.
“I see the police all the time right around here. They are doing a public service. I don’t see them doing a lot of ticketing,” Angshu said. “ I see them, I feel more safe. They are very fair.”
Kenneth Willis, an 18-year-old student, said he supports the police in stopping serious crimes, but said he’s concerned low-level enforcement will pit police against residents.
“ It's gonna create tension within the neighborhood, especially you already have people that don't like cops,” he said. “You're making it so people have to go to court, people have to pay money, people have to pay money that they don't have, it's gonna cause problems.”

https://hyperallergic.com/pablo-helguera.title: Pablo Helguera to Helm the New School’s Vera List Center
https://hyperallergic.com/pablo-helguera.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/pablo-helguera.text:
Pablo Helguera to Helm the New School’s Vera List Center
Upon his appointment, the artist reflected on the urgency he feels to “make sense of rapidly unfolding events, question prevailing narratives, and imagine alternative futures.”
Artist, educator, and writer Pablo Helguera has been appointed as the new director of the New School's Vera List Center for Art and Politics (VLC), succeeding Senior Director and Chief Curator Carin Kuoni, who steered the arts-driven research center for 22 years. Helguera was also tapped as the director of the university's art collection, which consists of over 2,000 postwar and contemporary works.
Having entered the new role this Monday, November 2, Helguera takes the reins after six years of serving as an assistant professor and director of the Arts Management and Entrepreneurship graduate program at the New School's College of Performing Arts. Helguera was previously the director of adult and academic programs at the Museum of Modern Art for over a decade.
As an artist, Helguera centers social engagement through public performance and installation, archival findings, pedagogical practices, and traditional media. Among his most famous projects is “The School of Panamerican Unrest” (2006), a cross-continental road trip from Anchorage, Alaska, to Ushuaia, capital of Argentina's southernmost Tierra del Fuego province, that culminated in over 100 public engagement events across 25 cities in 20 countries. Helguera is also known for developing Librería Donceles, a traveling used bookstore with thousands of Spanish-language texts that visited 13 countries.
The social, ideological, and cultural frameworks of language are prominent themes that Helguera explores in his practice, which coalesces with his roles in education and public programming. He became a Guggenheim Fellow in 2008, and additional recognitions include support from the Franklin Furnace Archive, Art Matters, and Blade of Grass; a Creative Capital grant; and an honorary doctorate from the Kansas City Art Institute.

https://hyperallergic.com/meg-onli-and-z.title: Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial
https://hyperallergic.com/meg-onli-and-z.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/meg-onli-and-z.text:
Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial
Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company.
Meg Onli, an organizer behind some of the Whitney Museum of American Art's signature exhibitions, and Zack Winokur, a performing arts director and co-founder, are the co-curators for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, the museum announced today, November 6.
“Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art," Scott Rothkopf, director of the Whitney, said in a statement. "Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial."
The news comes just two months after the 2026 Biennial closed and a month after unionized staff at the museum dodged a full-blown strike ahead of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, a blockbuster retrospective co-curated by Onli. The Whitney union was one of four New York City museum unions under United Auto Workers 2110 — along with the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum — that voted to strike amid drawn-out contract negotiations over low compensation, benefits, and workplace conditions. Hours before the planned strike, unionized staffers ratified their second contract and secured a new wage floor, increased parental and bereavement leave, and stronger safety provisions, among other amendments.
First joining the museum as curator-at-large in 2023, Onli co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, Even Better Than the Real Thing, with Chrissie Iles. That same year, Onli was promoted to Nancy and Fred Poses Curator to lead the Whitney’s painting and sculpture acquisition committee, bringing her previous experience as director and curator of the Underground Museum in Los Angeles and associate curator at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania.
“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about," Onli said in a statement. "I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead."
Winokur is the co-founder of the American Modern Opera Company, an interdisciplinary collective comprised of 17 singers, musicians, dancers, and other performing artists. He also served as artistic director for Little Island on Pier 55 and NYPopsUp, a statewide initiative aimed at opening performing arts spaces after COVID-19.
“I’m honored to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur added in a statement. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring."
Dating back to 1932, the Whitney Biennial remains the longest-running survey of American art, with more than 3,600 artists participating in the exhibition to date. The 83rd edition is slated to open in March 2028.

Art Basel Miami Beach has unveiled a “Premium Discovery” pass. Available for one- and two-day increments, and priced at $3,600 and $4,500, respectively, the pass promises a “Signature Experience” at the event, which will launch in previews December 2–3 before opening to the general public December 4–6. Despite its many perks, the Premium Discovery pass will not gain visitors entry to the fair’s inaugural preview day, and will only get them into the three-hour vernissage on the second preview day.
Those purchasing the single-day pass may attend the December 3 vernissage, from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m., and enjoy a “curated journey” on December 4 or 5. Buyers of the two-day pass can expect the “ultimate Art Basel Miami Beach Immersion” on both December 4 and 5 and may also attend the vernissage. Holders of both single- and two-day passes can attend all three public days with early entry. Other benefits include concierge service during the public days, access to the collectors’ lounge, invitation to select VIP events, a guided tour of the show conducted by director Bridget Finn, and an “exclusive Art Basel gift.”
Those seeking a slightly less expensive experience can purchase the “Premium Connection” pass ($2,600) or a “Premium” pass ($1,250). The former comes with concierge service and the aforementioned gift; the latter does not, but both guarantee entry to the vernissage and the collectors’ lounge.
For those of more modest means, a single-day standard ticket will get you into any one of the public days for $92—one forty-ninth (1/49th) the price of the Premium Discovery pass.

https://hyperallergic.com/dc-protesters-.title: DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch
https://hyperallergic.com/dc-protesters-.author: Emma Cieslik
https://hyperallergic.com/dc-protesters-.text:
DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch
A group of 50 used puppets and a fake arch to deliver the point that Americans are against the "Arc de Trump."
WASHINGTON, DC — South of Memorial Circle, within eyeshot of the Lincoln Memorial and John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, more than 50 protesters gathered yesterday, November 5, to oppose Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch ahead of the National Capital Planning Commission’s (NCPC) final meeting to vote on the project.
Hours after the NCPC approved the arch in an 8–4 vote, a district court judge granted the District of Columbia and Virginia a 14-day restraining order to halt construction.
At the event organized by Third Act DC, an environmental and pro-democracy action group for area residents aged 60 and up, two Virginia Congressional representatives, an Arlington County Board member, and Greg Werkheiser, an attorney with Cultural Heritage Partners, spoke about how the arch would infringe on the architectural and spiritual purpose of the space. He was one of two people associated with lawsuits that the District of Columbia and Virginia, the Arlington County Board, as well as Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed against the National Park Service and Department of the Interior in opposition to the arch.

The Whitney Museum of American Art has named Meg Onli and Zack Winokur as the curators of the 2028 Whitney Biennial.
Onli, who currently serves as the museum’s Nancy and Fred Poses Curator, co-organized the 2024 Biennial, “Even Better Than the Real Thing,” as well as the blockbuster retrospective “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New,” on view at the Whitney through spring 2027. She is the founder of the Black Visual Archive project, which documents and reviews contemporary Black culture.
Winokur, the onetime artistic director of New York’s Little Island, is a director of theater, dance, and opera widely known for his genre-defying productions. Winokur also cofounded AMOC* (American Modern Opera Company), and served as the artistic director of NYPopSUp, a statewide initiative aimed at resurrecting the performing arts post-Covid.
“Every Whitney Biennial springs from a distinct curatorial alchemy, and I couldn’t be more excited to bring Meg and Zack together to lead the 2028 edition,” said Whitney director Scott Rothkopf in a statement. “Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art. Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial.”
In a statement, Onli described herself as “thrilled” to be co-curating the event. “From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about,” she said. “I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead.”
Winokur was equally enthusiastic about partnering with Onli. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration,” he said. “It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring. As an artist, what excites me most is being in service to other artists, and I’m delighted to have the opportunity to do so in the context of the Whitney.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anderson-phi.title: Equality Is About Who Rules
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anderson-phi.author: Matt McManus
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anderson-phi.text:
Equality Is About Who Rules
What do we actually mean by “equality”? Few thinkers have answered that question better than Elizabeth Anderson: not identical outcomes but a society where no one gets to dominate anyone else, including at work.
There is a complex debate about the extent to which socialists prioritize equality above the full flowering of each person’s individuality. But you’d have to be quite the contrarian to deny that socialists take equality very seriously; perhaps more seriously than any other major political ideology. Prominent socialist thinkers like G. A. Cohen and Thomas Piketty have dedicated much of their work to defending the philosophical and economic merits of egalitarianism. Socialist Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech put equality at the core of his vision: “that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: ‘We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.’”
That said, the commitment of socialists and other egalitarians to equality can often seem frustratingly vague. It invites accusations of ill-defined “social justice” advocacy or even pursuing the much dreaded “equality of outcomes” through a Harrison Bergeron–like willingness to cut everyone down to size. Of course, many of these charges are lobbed in bad faith, and even the more refined versions ignore how other core principles — like liberty or order — are equally contestable and vague until explicitly defined. But having a firmer grasp on what we mean by equality and what we want would help the Left understand itself better.
Equality of What?
Few living thinkers have done more to answer this question than University of Michigan philosopher Elizabeth Anderson. A former doctoral student of John Rawls, Anderson made her name in the 1990s criticizing contemporary egalitarian philosophy and developing her own version of relational equality. More recently, Anderson has become a vigorous proponent of workplace democracy, contending that there is something deeply tyrannical about the forms of work that exist today. Her most recent book, Hijacked: How Neoliberalism Turned the Work Ethic Against Workers and How Workers Can Take It Back, argues for rehabilitating the tradition of social democratic and socialist political thought as a counter to the Right’s moralizing about work.
From the beginning, Anderson was fiercely critical of many dimensions of contemporary capitalism and its inequalities. Her early book Value in Ethics and Economics (1993) is a careful critique of how market relations and their distinct ways of reasoning about ethical questions are increasingly colonizing many spheres of society. She insisted that realizing many forms of “freedom, autonomy and welfare demands that certain goods be produced, exchanged, and enjoyed outside of market relations or in accordance with non-market norms.” While in this book Anderson typically appeals to ideas of autonomy and welfare rather than strict equality, there is a clear egalitarian undercurrent. She criticizes libertarians’ “fetishism” of property and markets as the sole site of freedom, and how this leads them to be blind to the “social relations of domination that exist prior to market transactions and that condition the choices individuals make there.” For instance, a long history of patriarchal subordination means that women may feel compelled to enter into exploitative contracts, say, in the sex industry, to get by day to day.
In her important paper “What Is the Point of Equality?” Anderson clarifies the role equality plays in inhibiting domination. It opens with a sardonic question: “If much recent academic work defending equality had been secretly penned by conservatives, could the results be any more embarrassing for egalitarians?” She chastises both Marxists like G. A. Cohen for trivializing equality by reducing it to debates about whether we ought to compensate people for being temperamentally gloomy or easily bored, and liberal egalitarians like Ronald Dworkin for proposing an envy-free distribution of resources — implying conservatives are right that the push for equality is ultimately about nothing more than resentment.
Anderson wanted egalitarians to finally get serious and realize that we aren’t, in fact, all that interested in building a society where people get the same bundle of goodies. Inegalitarian societies have built hierarchies whose social relations enabled some people to dominate others, often by insisting that those atop the social hierarchy were intrinsically worth more than those at the bottom. Egalitarians, Anderson argued, are fundamentally committed to undoing those forms of social hierarchy that enabled domination and oppression:
Egalitarian political movements oppose such hierarchies. They assert the equal moral worth of persons. This assertion does not mean that all have equal virtue or talent. Negatively, the claim repudiates distinctions of moral worth based on birth or social identity — on family membership, inherited social status, race, ethnicity, gender, or genes. There are no natural slaves, plebeians, or aristocrats. Positively, the claim asserts that all competent adults are equally moral agents: everyone equally has the power to develop and exercise moral responsibility, to cooperate with others according to principles of justice, to shape and fulfill a conception of their good.
In The Imperative of Integration, Anderson further defined the parameters of what she called the “relational theory” of equality and inequality. It located the “causes of economic, political, and symbolic group inequalities in the relations (processes of interaction) between groups, rather than in the internal characteristics of their members or in cultural differences that exist independently of group interaction.” Anderson emphasizes that in our society what makes people unequal often isn’t intrinsic to them but the result of the social relations in which they are embedded. But to invoke Karl Marx’s language of fetishism, this is very often obscured by ruling ideologies, which redirect the source of inferiority from social relations onto the individuals and groups themselves. Someone sold into slavery is described, in Aristotle’s terms, as a “natural slave” rather than someone who has been trapped in an oppressively hierarchical social system. Moreover, to reinforce hierarchy we often impute still worse forms of inferiority upon those at the base of the pyramid. For instance, when Senator John C. Calhoun called slavery a “positive good” because slaves were racially inferior, and the best thing for everyone was their paternalistic subordination to the superior race.
There is a lot to commend in Anderson’s relational equality. It helped steer egalitarians away from arguing about whether people with highfalutin tastes should be supplied with plovers’ eggs and truffle oil and back toward the hierarchies of oppression that it is the Left’s job to confront. If there is a limitation to her approach, it’s an enduring ambiguity about what a flourishing life ought to look like. This is a necessary part of making the case for equality; namely, why and how would people live better lives if they were more equal through being free of domination. Here Marx provides us with a helpful clue in the third volume of Capital, where he posits that under socialism the cooperative development of human powers and capabilities will become an end in itself for the first time, rather than just a means of training more efficient workers. The development of human powers to foster a rich individuality in community with others ought to be on our horizon, and doing so will mean transcending capitalism.
The Tyranny of Private Government and the Conservative Work Ethic
In her more recent work, Anderson has become one of the sharpest critics of both capitalist practices and ideology. In Private Government, she asks us to imagine “a government that assigns almost everyone a superior whom they must obey.” This government offers routines but no rule of law: orders can be arbitrary, can change without notice, and can’t be appealed. Worst of all, the bosses answer to no one below them. “They are neither elected nor removable by their inferiors.” Most of us, Anderson point out, don’t have to imagine this. It’s what most of us encounter every day when we go to work. And yet, despite the oppression it entails, we are often told that not only is there no alternative, but that such a system is nothing less than freedom itself.
Anderson’s point is well taken. If we were told that tomorrow the federal government was going to tell most Americans when to wake up, what they were going to wear, when they could go to the bathroom and eat lunch, how and when they were going to talk to others, there would be riots in the street. Everyone with a “Don’t Tread on Me!” flag would be making liberal use of their Second Amendment rights, Rand Paul would be weeping on live television, and the Daily Wire would proclaim this the Communist States of America. And yet Anderson observes this is the reality for millions of Americans subject to “private government” every day. She rejects the claim that that the modern commercial firm is a realm of individualism, as opposed to the collectivism of the state. Anderson notes that in the “great contest between individualism and collectivism regarding the mode of production, collectivism won, decisively. Nearly all production is undertaken by teams of workers using large, indivisible forms of capital equipment held in common.” Firms are collective enterprises, where the social relations grant capitalists and managers enormous domineering powers at the expense of their workers. She recommends that the way to respond to these forms of domination is to extend the liberal and democratic norms we already apply to statist collectives to private government: allow workers more democratic rights, greater protections, and the right to assemble and check unaccountable private power.
In Hjjacked, Anderson examines some of the ideological reasons many on the Right consider this unacceptable. She points out how from the beginning of the modern era there have been fierce debates over the work ethic and who deserved greater power and rewards: workers or capitalists. Anderson shows how socialists and a surprising number of liberals argued a “progressive work ethic” holding that, since workers did most of the work under capitalism, they were getting a raw deal. But they were always confronted by capitalists advocating a “conservative work ethic” that “stressed discipline, frugality, and asceticism for workers, while reaping the lion’s share of productivity gains for themselves in their capacity as capital owners.” The spirit of this conservative ethic was well captured in Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises’s letter to Ayn Rand, congratulating her on the publication of Atlas Shrugged:
You have the courage to tell the masses what no politician told them: you are inferior and all the improvements in your conditions which you simply take for granted you owe to the effort of men who are better than you. If this be arrogance, as some of your critics observed, it is still the truth that had to be said in the age of the Welfare State.
Anderson thinks that there are several ways we can confront this ideology. One is by reconstructing and re-canonizing the work of socialist and social democratic thinkers who tried to conceive of better ways to organize the economy. Anderson quips that it is “telling that in the history of political thought, no social democrat has been canonized, despite the huge influence of social democracy in many wealthy capitalist countries.” This is something of an exaggeration outside the United States, where left-wing economic thought has gained more traction, but her point still stands. A major goal of left-wing philosophers ought to be reintroducing large numbers of people to the rich and thoughtful tradition of socialist and social democratic thought, to help inspire thinking about where to go in the future.
Anderson is esteemed in academic circles but deserves a much wider popular audience. The times are certainly ripe for her message: in his second administration, Donald Trump has gone on a warpath against workers’ rights and needs, making it harder for public sector employees to engage in collective bargaining. Recently, he even went as far as to adopt an explicit “Let them eat cake” attitude toward rising costs to pay for his siege of Iran: “We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare.” Anderson offers us ways to both criticize these forms of domination and think through how to envision a better future where workers take back the world they built.
But above all else, Anderson reminds us that equality is about more than who gets what. Fundamentally, it’s a question of who rules and who is ruled. For most of us, for most of our waking hours, the answer is that the boss rules and we are ruled. Anderson’s work is an invitation to change that answer.

The journal Antiquity has published a new study on a collection of engravings discovered in 2019 within Cova de la Font Major, a cave located near Barcelona in northeastern Spain. The find is one of the largest collections of cave art on the Iberian Peninsula; its 280 Paleolithic engravings include 55 animal figures, as well as nonfigurative designs.
Although more than half of the Paleolithic cave-art groupings recorded in Europe are located in the Iberian Peninsula, the study notes that the northeastern region has generally yielded only fragmentary evidence. The discovery of this extensive collection came as a surprise, particularly since the cave was first excavated in 1957 and it has been part of a tourist route since 1993.
Míriam Salas-Altès, a co-author of the paper, believes these engravings went unnoticed for so long because the cave is dark and, as Scientific American reports, it may have been more difficult to spot the carvings than it would have to see paintings. Additionally, the walls are covered in modern-day graffiti, making it even trickier to make out the etchings.
The study reveals that the majority of markings are nonfigurative: “Among the most frequent representations are straight, parallel lines, arranged in groups of two, three or four, sometimes superimposed over zoomorphic figures … Other, less common motifs include convergent lines, circular or semicircular forms and quadrangular shapes.” One panel contains hundreds of “loop-shaped” etchings.
Representations of fauna include horses, deer, wild oxen, and at least one bear, though identification is difficult due to the limited depiction of details such as eyes, nostrils, hooves, manes, and coats. Most are rendered through simple body outlines.
Tourists’ access has been curtailed in order to protect the engravings, and researchers believe that clearing the years of sediment that has settled in the caves may reveal more art.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/benyamin-n.title: Israël : « Notre priorité absolue est d’écarter Benyamin Netanyahou du pouvoir », affirme Yousef Jabareen, à la tête de la Liste unifiée
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/benyamin-n.author: Jean Dorval
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/benyamin-n.text:
Yousef Jabareen, à la tête de la Liste unifiée, analyse les conditions d’un changement politique après la désignation de Gadi Eisenkot pour former un gouvernement. Avec une participation record et une représentation inédite à la Knesset, la gauche et les Palestiniens d’Israël s’imposent comme acteurs centraux de la séquence politique ouverte par l’échec de la coalition conduite par Benyamin Netanyahou aux élections législatives du 27 octobre.
La percée électorale des citoyens palestiniens d’Israël a rebattu les cartes de la vie politique israélienne. Avec une participation record et une représentation parlementaire sans précédent, la Liste unifiée, formée par le Hadash (les communistes et leurs alliés), Ta’al et Balad, s’impose comme un acteur incontournable dans l’équation politique ouverte par l’affaiblissement de Benyamin Netanyahou. À la tête de cette liste, Yousef Jabareen analyse les ressorts de cette mobilisation historique, détaille les conditions d’un éventuel soutien à un gouvernement dirigé par Gadi Eisenkot et plaide pour un changement de cap politique à l’égard des Palestiniens, en Israël comme dans les territoires occupés.
Que pensez-vous des résultats des élections du 27 octobre ?
L’évolution la plus importante, qui constitue un changement majeur par rapport aux élections précédentes, c’est la participation électorale des Palestiniens. Elle est historique, sans précédent. Le taux de participation est de 80 %, alors que lors des dernières élections, il était de 53 %. En conséquence, la représentation parlementaire est elle aussi sans précédent. Nous disposons désormais de 19 députés, 11 pour la Liste unifiée et 8 pour la Liste arabe unie (Ra’am).
Nous avions 10 députés lors des dernières élections. La conséquence immédiate, c’est la défaite de Benyamin Netanyahou. Il disposait d’une majorité de 68 sièges et n’en a désormais plus que 53, sans majorité parlementaire. Et pour la première fois depuis des années, il existe désormais une majorité claire contre Benyamin Netanyahou. Sans cette forte mobilisation électorale de notre communauté, il serait peut-être aujourd’hui en train de célébrer sa victoire. Ce n’est pas le cas.
Comment expliquez-vous cette forte hausse de la participation électorale palestinienne ?
Je pense que cela résulte d’une combinaison de plusieurs facteurs, mais le principal est que, ces dernières années, Benyamin Netanyahou, Itamar Ben Gvir et Bezalel Smotrich ont mené une politique terrible, extrêmement dure et cruelle envers notre communauté. Le taux de criminalité dans les villes arabes est désormais l’un des plus élevés au monde. Il y a également eu les démolitions de maisons, et même de villages entiers dans le Sud....

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Na Argentina de Milei, Papa defende sindicatos, um Estado regulador e diz que o desemprego ‘fere a dignidade’
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Rodrigo Chagas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O papa Leão XIV defendeu nesta segunda-feira (9), em Buenos Aires (Argentina), o papel dos sindicatos na proteção dos trabalhadores, a capacidade reguladora do Estado e políticas públicas de geração de empregos. Diante de dirigentes das centrais sindicais CGT e CTA e de movimentos populares como a União dos Trabalhadores da Economia Popular (UTEP), o pontífice afirmou que “o desemprego é um verdadeiro drama na vida de quem o sofre” e advertiu que a falta de trabalho compromete a dignidade humana.
“Privar uma pessoa do trabalho não é simplesmente negar-lhe um rendimento econômico; é ferir gravemente a sua dignidade, anular a sua capacidade de contribuir para a sociedade e mergulhá-la na exclusão social”, declarou durante o encontro na Universidade Católica Argentina (UCA), que reuniu dirigentes sindicais, empresários, movimentos populares e representantes do meio acadêmico.
O discurso ocorre em meio às reformas econômicas do presidente Javier Milei, que incluem a flexibilização da legislação trabalhista e a redução da intervenção estatal na economia. A reforma trabalhista aprovada em fevereiro ampliou a flexibilidade das contratações e jornadas, modificou regras de indenização e restringiu o direito de greve. O governo sustenta que as mudanças favorecem investimentos e a formalização do emprego, enquanto as centrais sindicais denunciam perda de direitos.
“O sindicato é uma instituição indispensável quando defende aqueles que não têm voz e quando se opõe à mercantilização da força de trabalho”, afirmou Leão XIV. O Papa também pediu que as organizações sindicais incorporem trabalhadores precarizados, informais e excluídos do mercado formal.
Um levantamento do Centro de Economia Política Argentina (CEPA) aponta que o país perdeu 437.611 postos de trabalho registrados em unidades produtivas entre novembro de 2023 e julho de 2026. A informalidade alcançou 45% dos trabalhadores.
Em setembro, dirigentes dos movimentos populares entregaram ao Vaticano um relatório de 72 páginas denunciando a precarização do trabalho, o endividamento das famílias, a repressão aos protestos e o enfraquecimento das políticas sociais durante o governo Milei.
Leão XIV também defendeu a atuação do Estado na economia, embora tenha ressaltado a importância da iniciativa das comunidades. “O Estado não tem de fazer tudo, mas cabe-lhe a tarefa de favorecer a ação dos organismos intermédios”, afirmou, acrescentando que o Estado deve manter “o poder regulador para o bem comum”.
O pontífice reconheceu o protagonismo de catadores de materiais recicláveis, camponeses e artesãos, recuperando a reivindicação de Francisco por “terra, teto e trabalho”.
A posição contrasta com o programa de desregulamentação econômica de Milei, uma das principais bandeiras de atual governo argentino. Segundo o Ministério da Desregulamentação e Transformação do Estado, comandado por Federico Sturzenegger, até outubro de 2026 foram editadas 842 normas desregulamentadoras, responsáveis por modificar ou eliminar 2.937 normas anteriores e alterar ou revogar 18.001 artigos.
A passagem de Leão XIV pela capital argentina foi marcada por uma missa multitudinária no Monumento dos Espanhóis, no bairro de Palermo. Segundo o Vaticano, cerca de 2,5 milhões de pessoas acompanharam a celebração e a passagem do papamóvel, na maior concentração de fiéis registrada durante seu pontificado.
Antes da missa e do encontro com trabalhadores, Leão XIV visitou o Pequeno Cottolengo Don Orione, em Claypole, instituição que atende mais de 400 pessoas com deficiência e enfrenta dificuldades de financiamento associadas aos cortes do governo Milei. “O progresso de uma nação também se mede pelo acolhimento que sabe dispensar a todas as pessoas portadoras de deficiência e com necessidades especiais”, declarou o pontífice.
Cortes sociais e defesa dos mais vulneráveis
As declarações desta segunda-feira ampliaram o posicionamento apresentado pelo Papa no domingo (8), diante de Milei e de autoridades argentinas, durante cerimônia no Palácio Libertad. Na ocasião, Leão XIV afirmou que “a economia deve estar ao serviço da pessoa, não a pessoa ao serviço da economia”.
Também pediu atenção aos idosos, às famílias que enfrentam dificuldades financeiras e aos trabalhadores cuja renda não é suficiente para cobrir as despesas domésticas.
O pontífice defendeu ainda o fortalecimento das universidades, da educação e da pesquisa científica, além da proteção dos recursos naturais argentinos, incluindo água, energia e minerais. Alertou que a exploração dessas riquezas deve preservar os ecossistemas e beneficiar as comunidades locais.
Mineradoras globais avançam sobre áreas de glaciares na Argentina que fornecem água para 20% da população.
Ao abordar a inteligência artificial e a automação, cobrou responsabilidade dos poderes públicos diante dos riscos ao emprego. Também ressaltou a importância do diálogo democrático, da cooperação entre países e do reconhecimento dos limites do poder político.
As declarações do Papa provocaram reações divergentes na política argentina. O governador da província de Buenos Aires, Axel Kicillof, defendeu que o governo colocasse suas recomendações em prática. Já o chefe de gabinete, Diego Santilli, afirmou que as palavras do pontífice eram compatíveis com as políticas adotadas pela administração Milei.
Papa se reúne com vítimas de abusos sexuais
Leão XIV também recebeu nesta segunda-feira cinco vítimas de abusos cometidos por integrantes do clero e de instituições eclesiásticas argentinas. Segundo o Vaticano, o encontro durou mais de uma hora. O pontífice ouviu individualmente os relatos e propostas para fortalecer os mecanismos de proteção e acolhimento dentro da Igreja Católica.
A reunião ocorreu em meio a cobranças por maior transparência e responsabilização nos casos de violência sexual. Organismos argentinos de direitos humanos aproveitaram a visita para reivindicar a expulsão do estado clerical de Christian von Wernich, ex-capelão policial condenado à prisão perpétua por crimes contra a humanidade durante a ditadura militar.
Leão XIV permanece na Argentina até quarta-feira (11). Nesta terça (10), viajará a Córdoba para celebrar uma missa e se reunir com representantes da Igreja local, retornando a Buenos Aires para um encontro com jovens. Na quarta, visitará uma unidade penitenciária federal e celebrará uma missa no Santuário de Nossa Senhora de Luján, antes de partir para o Peru.
A Argentina é a segunda etapa de sua viagem pela América do Sul, iniciada na sexta-feira (6), no Uruguai. No país vizinho, o pontífice passou por Montevidéu, Paysandú e Florida, onde celebrou missas e participou de encontros com comunidades populares, estudantes e autoridades. A viagem será encerrada no Peru, em 17 de novembro.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.title: Bad Hersfeld | Kein Vorlesen mehr: Omas gegen rechts an Schulen unerwünscht
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.text:
- Politik
- Bad Hersfeld
Kein Vorlesen mehr: Omas gegen rechts an Schulen unerwünscht
Die Initiative las in Bad Hersfeld in Grundschulen vor. Damit ist Schluss. Die Grünen kritisieren die Auslegung des Neutralitätsgebots.
Die Omas gegen rechts im hessischen Bad Hersfeld dürfen nach einer anonymen Beschwerde keine Bildungsarbeit mehr an Schulen leisten. Der Schulleiter habe »Ärger bekommen«, erklärte Petra Gromann, eine der sechs Frauen aus dem Organisationsteam der Initiative, der »Frankfurter Rundschau«. Dabei liege die Entscheidung über die Einladung externer Gäste in der Verantwortung der Schulleitungen. »Daraufhin wurden alle weiteren Termine gestrichen.«
Bis dahin hatten die Frauen unter dem Motto »Vorlesen für Toleranz und Vielfalt« Vorlesegruppen an Grundschulen in der Stadt geleitet. Ende März 2026 organisierten sie außerdem einen Projekttag für die neunten Klassen einer Gesamtschule, bei dem sie über Rechtsextremismus aufklärten. Darüber berichteten auch Medien. Die Berichterstattung hatte jedoch Folgen für die Initiative: Beim Schulamt ging eine Beschwerde ein. Es reagierte laut Gromann umgehend und drastisch. Weitere Projekttage der Bürgerinitiative seien untersagt worden.
Einen Monat später kam die nächste Einschränkung. Nachdem auf einer Schulleiterkonferenz vor einer Zusammenarbeit mit den Omas gegen rechts gewarnt worden war, wurden demnach schließlich auch die Vorlesegruppen untersagt. Weil die Initiative bislang keine zufriedenstellende Begründung für den Ausschluss erhalten habe und sich auch von politischen Vertreterinnen nicht gehört fühle, habe sie beschlossen, am Wochenende noch einmal an die Öffentlichkeit zu gehen, so Gromann.
Inzwischen hat auch der CDU-Stadtverband Bad Hersfeld Stellung genommen. Er begrüßt die Entscheidung des Schulamts, Auftritte der Omas gegen rechts an Schulen zu untersagen, und sieht auch die Aktivitäten der Initiative in Kitas kritisch. Es gehe ausdrücklich nicht darum, demokratisches Engagement oder die Auseinandersetzung mit Extremismus, Rassismus und Diskriminierung infrage zu stellen, heißt es in einer Mitteilung. Diese Themen seien wichtige Bestandteile der demokratischen Bildungsarbeit. Entscheidend sei jedoch, wer diese Inhalte vermittle und mit welcher politischen Zielsetzung.
Auf Anfrage der Grünen-Landtagsfraktion in Wiesbaden stellte Kultusminister Armin Schwarz (CDU) klar, dass »zivilgesellschaftliche Akteure wie die ›Omas gegen rechts‹ grundsätzlich in den Unterricht eingebunden werden können – solange sie in einer Rolle als Unterrichtsgäste auftreten«, wie es in einer Mitteilung der Fraktion heißt.
Schule müsse parteipolitisch neutral sein, betonen die Grünen im Landtag, sie dürfe aber nicht wertneutral gegenüber den Prinzipien der liberalen Demokratie sein. Die Fraktion fordert das Kultusministerium dazu auf, eine zu enge Auslegung des Neutralitätsgebots zu verhindern und den Omas gegen rechts sowie ähnlichen Akteurinnen und Akteuren Zugang zu Schulen zu gewähren. »Das Neutralitätsgebot darf nicht als Vorwand dienen, um demokratisches Engagement gegen Rechtsextremismus aus unseren Schulen herauszuhalten.« nd
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.title: « Des miettes » : après trois semaines de manifestations contre la vie chère, Sébastien Lecornu vente un coup de pouce de même pas dix euros par mois
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Cyprien Boganda
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
La montagne a accouché d’une souris : la conférence sociale convoquée à Matignon, ce lundi, a lâché des clopinettes : un mini coup de pouce au Smic et le relèvement de la prime carburant. Une nouvelle date de mobilisation est déjà fixée le 17 novembre.
Les syndicats n’en attendaient pas grand-chose mais ils ont quand même été déçus : la grande conférence sociale annoncée au débotté par le premier ministre pour tenter d’assécher le mouvement de contestation a, comme prévu, tourné court. Faute d’ambition politique et de volonté de faire pression sur un patronat rétif au dialogue, la rencontre a accouché de quelques mesures de faible envergure.
Un coup de pouce anticipé au Smic qui, associé à la revalorisation automatique du salaire minimum, devrait porter ce dernier à 1 502 euros net par mois environ dès le 1er décembre (contre 1 477,93 euros aujourd’hui) ; le relèvement du plafond de la prime carburant de 300 euros à 1 000 euros et, enfin, la hausse des exonérations sur les heures supplémentaires. Loin, très loin, des revendications des syndicats, qui réclamaient entre 100 et 150 euros net de hausse du salaire minimum.
Trois petites heures de discussion pour acter des non-mesures
Il y avait de toute façon quelque chose d’un peu lunaire dans cette initiative convoquée à la surprise...

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Assassinato de japonesa causa revolta e reacende debate sobre presença militar dos EUA em Okinawa
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Bruno Falci
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A morte de uma mulher japonesa, pela qual um militar estadunidense foi indiciado, voltou a colocar em evidência os conflitos em torno da presença militar dos Estados Unidos em Okinawa, no sul do Japão. O caso provocou indignação na ilha e levou o governador Genta Koja a anunciar, nesta segunda-feira (9), que defenderá uma revisão fundamental do acordo bilateral que estabelece as condições de permanência das forças militares dos EUA no país.
Anna Yagi, de 39 anos, foi encontrada morta em 3 de outubro em um hotel de Naha, capital de Okinawa. O fuzileiro naval estadunidense Devin Jacob Ballard, de 20 anos, lotado na estação aérea militar de Futenma, foi indiciado em outubro sob acusação de roubo com resultado morte. Segundo a imprensa japonesa, ele nega as acusações.
Durante uma coletiva de imprensa em Tóquio, Koja classificou o episódio como um crime extremamente grave e afirmou que ele provocou grande preocupação entre os moradores da ilha.
O governador anunciou que pretende solicitar mudanças no Acordo sobre o Estatuto das Forças dos Estados Unidos no Japão, conhecido pela sigla SOFA. Entre as medidas reivindicadas está a transferência de suspeitos sob custódia militar estadunidense para as autoridades japonesas sempre que houver solicitação, inclusive antes da apresentação formal de acusações.
O que estabelece o acordo entre Japão e Estados Unidos?
Assinado em 1960, o SOFA estabelece as regras que regulam a presença das forças militares estadunidenses em território japonês. O documento trata de questões como jurisdição criminal, custódia de militares suspeitos, circulação de tropas e utilização das instalações militares.
Um dos pontos mais controversos está no artigo 17. O dispositivo estabelece que, quando o Japão tem o direito de exercer jurisdição sobre um militar estadunidense que permanece sob custódia dos Estados Unidos, a transferência para as autoridades japonesas ocorre, em regra, após a apresentação formal da acusação.
Na prática, essa regra pode impedir que investigadores japoneses tenham acesso imediato a suspeitos mantidos sob custódia militar estadunidense. O acordo, entretanto, não concede imunidade geral aos integrantes das Forças Armadas dos EUA: o Japão mantém o direito de julgar crimes cometidos em seu território, conforme as regras estabelecidas pelo tratado.
A entrega de suspeitos antes da formalização das acusações foi objeto de uma negociação específica em 1995. Naquele ano, após o estupro de uma menina de 12 anos por três militares estadunidenses em Okinawa, Washington concordou em considerar favoravelmente pedidos japoneses de transferência antecipada em casos específicos de assassinato e estupro.
O compromisso, porém, não tornou a transferência automática ou obrigatória. Segundo informações do Ministério das Relações Exteriores japonês, o Japão solicitou a transferência antecipada de suspeitos em seis casos no período coberto pelo balanço oficial. Em cinco deles, os Estados Unidos atenderam ao pedido.
Para Koja, as medidas adotadas até agora não foram suficientes. O governador afirmou que Okinawa apresenta repetidos protestos às forças militares dos Estados Unidos e aos governos de Tóquio e Washington após incidentes envolvendo militares e funcionários civis vinculados às forças estadunidenses.
“Após cada incidente ou acidente envolvendo militares ou funcionários civis das forças estadunidenses, Okinawa apresentou repetidos protestos contundentes às forças militares dos Estados Unidos e aos governos do Japão e dos Estados Unidos”, declarou.
Koja também criticou a insuficiência de ajustes pontuais no acordo. “Para resolver crimes tão graves — assim como outros problemas envolvendo as bases militares dos Estados Unidos —, não são suficientes ajustes operacionais no SOFA que deixam determinadas questões à discricionariedade dos Estados Unidos”, afirmou.
Além da transferência antecipada de suspeitos, o governador defende a aplicação de normas japonesas, como a Lei de Aviação, às atividades militares dos Estados Unidos. Também reivindica que as autoridades de Okinawa tenham acesso às instalações militares para realizar inspeções ambientais.
Uma ferida histórica: a concentração militar em Okinawa
O episódio que marcou a relação entre a população de Okinawa e as forças militares estadunidenses ocorreu em setembro de 1995. Na ocasião, três militares dos Estados Unidos sequestraram e estupraram uma menina japonesa de 12 anos.
O crime provocou uma onda de indignação e mobilizações populares na ilha. Tornou-se um símbolo das tensões relacionadas à presença militar estrangeira e fortaleceu as reivindicações por mudanças no SOFA e pela redução das instalações militares estadunidenses.
A repercussão levou a negociações entre Washington e Tóquio sobre a entrega de suspeitos às autoridades japonesas, resultando no entendimento de outubro de 1995 que estabeleceu a possibilidade de transferência antecipada em determinados crimes graves.
No ano seguinte, os dois governos anunciaram um acordo para devolver a base aérea de Futenma ao Japão. A medida, entretanto, foi condicionada à construção de uma instalação substituta na própria província de Okinawa.
A proposta de transferência para Henoko, no município de Nago, no norte da ilha, tornou-se outro foco de conflito. Moradores e movimentos contrários às bases questionam a construção de uma nova instalação militar no território da província, argumentando que a mudança não elimina o peso da presença estadunidense sobre a população local.
Mais de três décadas depois do crime de 1995, a morte de Anna Yagi voltou a expor a permanência dessas tensões.
O peso da presença militar também aparece na distribuição territorial das instalações. Okinawa representa aproximadamente 0,6% da superfície do Japão, mas concentra 70,3% da área ocupada pelas instalações militares estadunidenses de uso exclusivo no país, segundo dados do Ministério da Defesa japonês referentes a 1º de janeiro de 2026.
A ilha abriga bases aéreas, campos de treinamento e estruturas de apoio logístico. A concentração dessas unidades em uma área relativamente pequena afeta a vida cotidiana dos moradores, com ruído de aeronaves, restrições ao uso do território, preocupações ambientais e riscos associados a acidentes.
O barulho provocado por aeronaves militares é uma reclamação recorrente nas comunidades próximas às bases. As autoridades japonesas mantêm sistemas de monitoramento nas regiões de Kadena e Futenma, enquanto o governo de Okinawa também realiza medições e divulga relatórios sobre os níveis de ruído. O problema está entre as preocupações apresentadas pelo governador.
Acidentes e incidentes envolvendo aeronaves e outros equipamentos militares também fazem parte das reivindicações locais. Na coletiva de imprensa, Koja citou o barulho das operações aéreas, a contaminação ambiental e os episódios envolvendo militares estadunidenses entre os problemas associados às bases.
A questão ambiental ganhou destaque especialmente por causa da presença de substâncias químicas persistentes conhecidas como PFAS, entre elas o PFOS, em águas subterrâneas, rios e nascentes próximos a instalações militares.
Segundo o governo de Okinawa, levantamentos de água e estudos sobre o fluxo subterrâneo indicam alta probabilidade de que as bases aéreas de Kadena e Futenma sejam fontes importantes da contaminação. No entorno de Camp Hansen, a administração local também aponta a possibilidade de origem dentro da instalação militar.
A investigação enfrenta, porém, obstáculos relacionados ao acesso às áreas militares. Desde junho de 2016, o governo de Okinawa apresentou quatro pedidos de autorização para realizar inspeções em Kadena, Futenma e Camp Hansen. Três solicitações, feitas entre 2019 e 2021, continuavam sem resposta em novembro de 2025. Em 19 de dezembro daquele ano, as autoridades japonesas divulgaram a recusa dos Estados Unidos.
Em 12 de junho de 2026, o governo de Okinawa apresentou novos pedidos de acesso, adaptados às justificativas utilizadas na negativa anterior. A dificuldade de realizar inspeções diretamente nas instalações militares continua sendo um obstáculo para identificar as fontes da contaminação e definir medidas de controle.
Futenma é um dos exemplos mais conhecidos dos conflitos em torno da presença militar. Localizada em uma área densamente povoada do município de Ginowan, a instalação está cercada por áreas residenciais e comerciais. A transferência para Henoko é apresentada pelo governo central japonês e pelos Estados Unidos como uma forma de reduzir os riscos para a população que vive nas proximidades da atual base.
O governador Genta Koja apoia essa transferência, diferentemente de seus antecessores, Denny Tamaki e Takeshi Onaga, que se opunham ao projeto de construção da instalação substituta em Henoko.
Na coletiva de imprensa, Koja defendeu que o governo central estabeleça um cronograma para a transferência de Futenma e a posterior devolução dos terrenos atualmente ocupados pela base. Também reivindicou a liberação mais rápida de áreas militares localizadas em regiões comerciais, argumentando que sua devolução poderá contribuir para o desenvolvimento econômico da ilha.
A posição de Koja evidencia uma divisão no debate político local. O governador defende mudanças nas condições da presença militar estadunidense e a devolução de terrenos, mas não se opõe à transferência de Futenma para outra área de Okinawa.
A importância estratégica de Okinawa para Washington
A presença militar estadunidense na ilha também está relacionada à sua localização geográfica. Situada no sudoeste do Japão, Okinawa está próxima de Taiwan, da China continental e de importantes rotas marítimas do Pacífico ocidental.
Essa posição confere à província um papel relevante na estratégia militar dos Estados Unidos no Indo-Pacífico. Suas instalações permitem o deslocamento de tropas, aeronaves e equipamentos para diferentes áreas do leste asiático.
O governo japonês também considera a localização de Okinawa importante para a aliança de segurança com Washington. A presença de forças estadunidenses na ilha integra a estrutura de cooperação militar entre os dois países.
É nesse contexto que se encontra uma das principais contradições do debate: a importância estratégica atribuída por Washington a Okinawa para sua atuação militar no Indo-Pacífico convive com uma concentração de instalações que impõe à população local uma parcela desproporcional dos custos territoriais e sociais dessa presença.
Enquanto Tóquio e Washington apresentam as bases como parte central de sua arquitetura de segurança regional, moradores e movimentos locais questionam a distribuição das instalações, os impactos sobre suas comunidades e os limites impostos à atuação das autoridades japonesas.
O debate também envolve a ampliação das estruturas de defesa japonesas no sudoeste do país. Koja pediu que o governo central explique quais capacidades militares considera necessárias para a defesa da região e por que determinadas instalações e funções precisam ser concentradas nas ilhas de Okinawa.
A reivindicação de uma revisão fundamental do SOFA, portanto, vai além das circunstâncias de um caso criminal. Ela expõe um problema que atravessa décadas: a dificuldade de as autoridades japonesas exercerem controle efetivo sobre diferentes aspectos da presença militar estadunidense e a permanência de uma distribuição desigual dos custos dessa presença. Para os moradores de Okinawa, a discussão sobre segurança regional também passa pelo direito de decidir sobre o futuro de seu próprio território.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ge.title: Getty Pitches In on First-Ever Conservation of an Earthquake-Damaged 17th-Century Church in the Andean Highlands of Peru
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ge.author: Brian Boucher
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ge.text:
The Getty will work with local authorities on the first-ever conservation project on a 17th-century earthen church in the Andean highlands of the Cusco region of Peru. The Church of Santo Tomás de Aquino, locally known as the Church of Rondocan, is a sacred cultural heritage site. Over the years, earthquakes have damaged the church, and not only the structure but also the church’s collection of more than 300 cultural objects is under threat.
The Peruvian government has allotted $5 million to a multi-year initiative that will strengthen the earthen site and support the conservation and care of both building and collection, which includes 17th- and 18th-century paintings, gilded wooden retablos and associated sculptures, ecclesiastical textiles, and more. The Getty will contribute expertise from staffers across various departments.
In a Baroque style and with thick adobe brick walls, the church, Getty says, is one of many remote earthen sacred sites that have gone without regular maintenance while suffering damage from earthquakes. The Getty Conservation Institute’s Seismic Retrofitting Project (SRP) employs high-tech analytical techniques to strengthen earthen heritage sites against quakes and create long-term plans to monitor and maintain them. A regional office of the Ministry of Culture of Peru will work in partnership with SRP to develop a comprehensive conservation and seismic retrofitting project, with construction to begin in 2027.
“Since 2011, the Conservation Institute has worked across Peru with local conservation professionals to conserve some of the country’s most significant earthen architectural buildings,” said Claudia Cancino, principal project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute, and project lead for the Sacred Heritage in the Andes Project, in press materials. “These are the buildings in which so much of daily life in these regions takes place, but they require specialized efforts for their protection. With this collective effort, we will be able to provide expertise and support for the Rondocan community, who have been the primary caretakers of the church and its incredible collections for generations.”
Among the most notable works in the collection is a series of eight large easel paintings by the Italian Jesuit priest and painter Bernardo Bitti (1548–1610), “Principales Misterios de la Vida y Muerte de Cristo Nuestro Salvador y de la Virgen Santísima” (“Principal Mysteries of the Life and Death of Christ our Savior and the Holy Virgin Mary”), painted in Cusco, likely in the later 1590s. When Getty staffers visited the church in 2010, they were surprised to find the works, thought at the time by most art historians to be lost. One painting from the series, La Oración en el huerto (“Prayer in the Garden”), will be transferred to the Getty in 2027 to undergo scientific analysis and conservation treatment.
Per Britannica, Bitti is credited with introducing Mannerism to Peruvian art after training in Rome as an artist and then becoming a Jesuit. He went to Cusco in 1583, remaining there for a year, constructing the high altar of the Jesuit church. His travels in Juli, La Paz, and Lima, as well as numerous visits to Cusco, positioned him as an influence on painters throughout the Andes.
“What makes the church’s collection unique, beyond its richness for such an isolated church, is that no evidence suggests it has ever been restored,” said Stéphanie Auffret, senior project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute, in press materials. “As such, it represents a rare opportunity to document the artifacts, generating knowledge useful to a variety of stakeholders. The study of the decorative surfaces of the lateral altarpieces, for instance, with their rarely preserved original materials, will inform the interpretation of similar decorative surfaces in other churches in Peru.”
The work involves objects that are in regular use, added Auffret: “This project also provides a wonderful opportunity to interact with the local community, who care deeply about the site and all its cultural objects, such as the sculptures they carry as part of processions during the Semana Santa. Preserving a collection in use presents challenges as well as valuable exchanges with community members, something not experienced in a museum’s context.”

https://taz.de/Umstrittene-Plastiksteuer.text:
Umstrittene Plastiksteuer : Mogelpackung für Klima und Umwelt
Die Koalition streitet über die geplante Steuer für Hersteller von Kunststoffverpackungen. Die SPD hat der Union den Kampf dagegen leicht gemacht.
W ir essen Plastik. Wir trinken Plastik. Wir atmen sogar Plastik ein. Kunststoff macht uns krank, verdreckt die Umwelt. Die Herstellung ist auch ein Klima-Desaster, vergleichbar mit dem globalen Luftverkehr.
Insofern kann man es fahrlässig finden, wenn Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei im ZDF einfach sagt: „Die Plastiksteuer machen wir nicht.“ Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) plant schon mit den Einnahmen, Umweltminister Carsten Schneider (SPD) hat den Gesetzesentwurf vorgelegt. Unklar, ob es bis Donnerstag noch eine Einigung geben kann. Dann trifft sich der Haushaltsausschuss des Bundestags zur entscheidenden Bereinigungssitzung zum Bundeshaushalt 2027.
Leider hat die SPD es der Union aber leicht gemacht, die Plastiksteuer abzusägen. Das Konzept hat einen großen Mangel: Die Steuer dürfte dem Staat zwar Geld einbringen, aber Klima und Umwelt kaum nützen.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Natürlich ist es auch gut, wenn der Staat sich Geld von den Herstellern von Plastikverpackungen zurückholt. Sie kosten ihn nämlich viel: Seit 2021 müssen EU-Länder für jedes Kilogramm an nicht recyceltem Plastikverpackungsmüll 80 Cent an den EU-Haushalt abführen. Deutschland zahlt dafür jedes Jahr rund 1,4 Milliarden Euro. Das wäre doch aber gerade ein guter Grund, das Problem gleich an der Wurzel zu packen.
Expert*innen warnen: Die Höhe der geplanten Steuer reiche nicht aus, um Recycling-Material attraktiver zu machen. Weil sie nur für Verpackungen mit einem Kunststoffanteil von 5 Prozent aufwärts gelten soll, könnte sie sogar negative Effekte mit sich bringen. Denn das könnte schließlich ein Anreiz sein, auf Pappe mit dünner Plastik-Beschichtung zu setzen. Solche Verbundstoffe lassen sich nur schwer wieder trennen und werden deshalb kaum wiederverwertet.
Auch Unionsfraktionschef Frei hat unter anderem mit der mangelnden ökologischen Wirkung argumentiert. Dass ihn das mehr interessiert als der Protest vieler Lobby-Verbände, kann man getrost infrage stellen. Wenn ihm das Argument aber in die Karten spielt, nutzt er es natürlich. Das hätte die SPD vermeiden können und sollen.
