https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya and Rebecca Bailey
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.
Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.
“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”
For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. “They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”
He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”
China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.
Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way: “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
China as a ‘doer and go-getter’
The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows.
Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.
The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue. “Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed.
Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.
The need for trust
China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.
Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”
If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.
Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … So no major drama.”

https://taz.de/Verdaechtiger-im-Fall-Lis.title: Verdächtiger im Fall Lisa T.: Schon früher im Visier der Ermittler
https://taz.de/Verdaechtiger-im-Fall-Lis.text:
Verdächtiger im Fall Lisa T.: Schon früher im Visier der Ermittler
Der Tatverdächtige im Fall des ermordeten Mädchens aus Marzahn stand schon früher im Fokus der Justiz – wegen Kinderpornografie.
dpa | Nach dem Gewaltverbrechen an der 13-jährigen Schülerin Lisa aus Marzahn und dem Fund ihrer Leiche in Brandenburg geht die Auswertung von Spuren weiter. Gegen den 22 Jahre alten Tatverdächtigen ermittelten Staatsanwaltschaften schon vorher wegen des Erwerbs und Besitzes kinderpornografischer Inhalte.
Wie das Mädchen starb, ist weiterhin unklar. Nach einer Obduktion wurden weitere Untersuchungen in Auftrag gegeben. Der mutmaßliche Täter und die 13-Jährige hatten sich zuvor nicht gekannt, wie die Staatsanwaltschaft Berlin mitteilte.
Der Mann mit deutscher Staatsangehörigkeit wurde am Sonntagmittag mit einer lebensgefährlichen Schussverletzung im selben unbewohnten Haus im brandenburgischen Bad Freienwalde gefunden, wo die Polizei auch das tote Mädchen entdeckte.
Der Verdächtige werde intensivmedizinisch behandelt, hieß es in einer Mitteilung der Staatsanwaltschaft vom Montag. Ermittler durchsuchten inzwischen seine Wohnung in Marzahn-Hellersdorf. Es seien „potenzielle Beweismittel“ sichergestellt werden, hieß es.
Kinderpornografisches Material sichergestellt
Die Staatsanwaltschaft Berlin ermittelte seit Januar 2025 gegen ihn wegen des Verdachts des Erwerbs und Besitzes kinderpornografischer Inhalte. Es geht dabei um Auswertungen von Zahlungen an eine Darknet-Plattform. Im März 2025 seien im Zuge einer internationalen Aktionswoche gegen Kinderpornografie die Wohnräume des Mannes durchsucht und Datenträger sichergestellt worden. „Auf diesen sollen über 900 inkriminierte Dateien enthalten sein, die er sich im Jahr 2023 beschafft haben soll“, erklärte die Staatsanwaltschaft.
Zudem übernahm die Berliner Justizbehörde im April dieses Jahres ein Ermittlungsverfahren von der Staatsanwaltschaft Passau. Auf einem Mobiltelefon des Beschuldigten, der sich seinerzeit in Bayern aufgehalten habe, sei ebenfalls eine Vielzahl mutmaßlich kinderpornografischer Inhalte entdeckt worden, hieß es. Vorbestraft ist der Tatverdächtige nicht.
Lisas Tod machte bundesweit Schlagzeilen und löste große Anteilnahme aus. Eine Mordkommission des Berliner Landeskriminalamtes ermittelt zu Ablauf und Hintergründen des Tötungsdeliktes. Am Fundort nahe der Grenze zu Polen sicherten Einsatzkräfte am Montag weiter Spuren.
Spurensicherung am Fundort
Ungeklärt ist weiterhin, wann und wie Lisa in das Haus in einem Ortsteil von Bad Freienwalde rund 50 Kilometer nordöstlich von Berlin gebracht wurde. Die 13-Jährige hatte die Wohnung ihrer Familie am Dienstag vergangener Woche morgens gegen 7.15 Uhr verlassen, um von einer Bushaltestelle in der Nähe zu ihrer Schule zu fahren. Dort kam sie nicht an.
Die Polizei suchte mit Hunderten Beamten, Spürhunden, einem Hubschrauber und einer Unterwasserdrohne. Letztlich führte ein Hinweis wegen Hausfriedensbruchs dazu, dass die Polizei zu dem leerstehenden Haus ausrückte. Dort entdeckten Beamte dann Lisas Leiche und den schwer verletzten Tatverdächtigen.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/gers/on-.title: « On n’a absolument aucun élément » : la justice contredit les affirmations de Laurent Nuñez sur l’incendie de la maison d’un policier à Auch
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/gers/on-.author: Tom Demars-Granja
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/gers/on-.text:
Le procureur par intérim du Gers, Claude Derens, a démenti lundi 9 novembre les accusations du ministre de l’Intérieur, qui a affirmé que « tout laisse à penser » que l’incendie de l’habitation d’un policier à Auch « a été commis en raison de (sa) profession ». Selon la justice, il est « vraiment absolument prématuré de l’indiquer ».
Laurent Nuñez a de nouveau tordu la réalité pour conforter son agenda politique. Quelques heures après qu’un incendie a ravagé le domicile d’un policier d’Auch (Gers), dans la nuit du vendredi 6 au samedi 7 novembre, le ministre de l’Intérieur a affirmé, sur X, que « tout laisse à penser que cet acte criminel intolérable a été commis en raison de la profession » de la victime.
À peine deux jours plus tard, le procureur par intérim dans le Gers, Claude Derens, tempère ces affirmations. « C’est un incendie dont les experts confirmeront vraisemblablement l’origine volontaire, mais y a-t-il un lien avec l’activité du policier, pour l’instant, c’est vraiment absolument prématuré de l’indiquer », a-t-il rétorqué auprès de l’Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Une mise à feu volontaire
« On n’a absolument aucun élément permettant de rattacher cet incendie volontaire à l’activité professionnelle de la victime », a poursuivi le procureur. « La mise à feu a vraisemblablement une origine volontaire puisqu’il y a deux départs distincts de feu », a précisé le magistrat, ajoutant que les investigations étaient « en cours ».
L’enquête est menée par la circonscription de police nationale (CPN) et le service interdépartemental de la police judiciaire (SIPJ) de la Haute-Garonne. Si l’habitation incendiée était bien la propriété du policier, elle n’était pas son domicile familial mais lui permettait de dormir quand il terminait tard son service.
L’agent a découvert son habitation en flammes à son retour. Selon France 3, « le policier aurait été menacé à plusieurs reprises par des individus de la ville. Des tags, affichant son numéro de matricule et proférant des menaces auraient été découverts sur des murs du quartier Garros à Auch ».
Avant de partir, une dernière chose…
Contrairement à 90% des médias français aujourd’hui, l’Humanité ne dépend ni de grands groupes ni de milliardaires. Cela signifie que :
- nous vous apportons des informations impartiales, sans compromis. Mais aussi que
- nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers dont bénéficient les autres médias.
L’information indépendante et de qualité a un coût. Payez-le.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: In uneasy times, Bangladesh launches its first art fair
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Rebecca Anne Proctor
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Bangladeshi capital of Dhaka is set to stage its first commercial art fair this month, which aims to transform the city’s private art sector and encourage a new generation of Bangladeshi collectors.
Art Dhaka, staged under the tagline “Art for All”, will take place at Aloki, a popular multidisciplinary cultural hub and former garment factory.
Though Dhaka is increasingly recognised on the global stage for its non-commercial exhibitions, the city has a limited number of traditional commercial art spaces, with only a few private galleries.
The fair’s founding members—Durjoy Rahman, Nahar Khan, Aumia Khundkar and Fahd Sattar—are addressing the city’s lack of commercial infrastructure by staging a curated fair of emerging and established Bangladeshi artists. Those whose work will feature in the first edition include Dhali Al Mamoon, Mojahid Musa, Najmun Nahar Keya, Bishwajit Goswami, Ayesha Sultana and Dinar Sultana Putul.
The new fair is being curated by Najmun Nahar Keya and fellow Dhaka-based artist and curator Zihan Khan, both of whom have guest curated Dhaka’s international festival for photography, Chobi Mela. The fair will feature gallery presentations, public programming and dedicated spaces for emerging artists.
“This is not like Frieze or Art Basel—it is with the ambiance of an art biennial,” says Rahman, a collector and the founder of the Durjoy Bangladesh Foundation (DBF). “We wanted to stage an event to showcase the art, culture and architecture in Bangladesh through a platform which caters to a wider ecosystem, with a commercial aspect.”
Bangladesh, emphasises Rahman, is a country of around 178 million people, making it the eighth most populous nation in the world, and one in which art has long played a key role. “Culture and art have always been important to everyday life,” Rahman says. “Craft is a part of everyone’s household. We grew up going to cultural events. But over the years, because of industrial development, art became a subject for just a few. Art Dhaka attempts to fill this gap.”
Only a handful of galleries
“We don’t have a strong gallery system,” Rahman says. Besides his own foundation, Dhaka is home to a handful of other private foundations, including the Bengal Foundation, Brihatta Art Foundation, Cosmos Foundation and the Samdani Art Foundation. The latter was founded in 2012 and has organised the Dhaka Art Summit (DAS) since 2012, arguably the most influential event in attracting international attention to Dhaka’s art scene.
The handful of commercial art galleries include Drik, internationally known for championing photography and multimedia storytelling; Galleri Kaya and Gallery Chitrak, showing Modern masters and contemporary Bangladeshi painters; and Abinta Gallery of Fine Arts, a non-profit cultural centre that opened in 2012 and shows established and emerging Bangladeshi artists.
“In a city with 36.6 million people, how do we stage something that will lure even 2% of the population when we have such few art spaces?” asks Rahman. “We want to balance the display of both Modern and contemporary art and encourage new and younger Bangladeshi collectors to invest in art.”
“For the first edition, I think we want to establish the fact that we have local patronage. We do have the calibre of artists and we have the organisational ability within ourselves and our curators to put on this show,” says Fahd Sattar, the founder of Aloki.
“We need to have cultural infrastructure between South Asian countries,” he adds, emphasising how future editions of the fair will incorporate the wider region. “This year we are focusing on Bangladeshi artists and the diaspora. Next edition, we could also venture out of Aloki to other areas of the city, and may open to international galleries and artists.”
While there is much hope the new hybrid-format fair will provide a needed boost for Dhaka’s art scene, it is taking place as the country continues to navigate a challenging socioeconomic and political landscape.
Following a historic general election on 12 February—which marked the first contested presidential election since October 1991 and resulted in a landslide victory for Tarique Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)—the nation is still finding its footing. The last few years in Bangladesh have been characterised by intense political turbulence and economic strain, particularly during the challenging democratic transition under an interim government following the ousting of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in 2024. Against this backdrop, Bangladesh’s art scene is undergoing a profound post-uprising transformation. Following the fall of Hasina’s government, the creative community has experienced a surge in politically engaged expression, alongside institutional restructuring and the formation of new international partnerships.
Globally, the Bangladesh art scene garnered much international interest due to the DAS, a biennial event staged by Bangladeshi collectors and patrons Nadia and Rajeeb Samdani. But the country’s challenging political landscape has created difficulties in staging the summit, with the last edition taking place in 2023.
“We have never censored any artist; you can’t censor artists,” says Rajeeb Samdani, emphasising that DAS cannot be staged in Bangladesh’s current political climate.
Most recently, transgender and feminist human rights activist Ho Chi Minh Islam was dropped as a speaker from the fifth Bay of Bengal Conversation in Dhaka, scheduled to take place on 5 October, following an intense online backlash. The event is an international forum on geopolitics, technology and governance, organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS).
A return for the summit
Rajeeb Samdani, who praises the inaugural Art Dhaka for the wealth of opportunities to be had for the Bangladeshi art scene, says he and Nadia hope to return to Bangladesh with the DAS in the next few years, once the challenging political landscape dissipates.
“It’s great an art fair is taking place in Dhaka as I think it is important for the city’s art ecosystem and the wider development of the art scene,” he says.
In the meantime, the Samdanis have been busy maintaining their programming abroad. This includes a multi-year partnership with the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, which includes a solo exhibition of Soma Surovi Jannat and the appointment of Munem Wasif as the inaugural visiting artist at the UK museum.
On 27 November the Kunsthalle Basel will present works by eight shortlisted finalists for the Samdani Art Award from Bangladesh alongside 16 artists from the wider Basel region in the exhibition Far Reach (until 2 January 2027).
The Samdanis’ much anticipated permanent space, Srihatta Samdani Art Center and Sculpture Park in Sylhet, will include permanent galleries and residency facilities. “We haven’t announced it publicly yet, but we started operations at the beginning of this year,” says Rajeeb.
During a period of uncertainty in Bangladesh, Samdani is hopeful. “It’s wonderful everyone is coming together during this period of transition,” he said, “We are looking forward to doing the summit sometime soon.”
• Art Dhaka, Aloki, Dhaka, 6-10 November

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.title: Democrats, Don’t Mess This Up
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: Natasha Lennard
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.text:
For two years, Donald Trump’s Republican Party has worked to push the United States further and further into a state of fascist rule. Trump’s regime has turned the federal government against ideological enemies, enriched and entrenched the power of billionaire allies, and done its utmost to decimate any checks and balances on the actions of the despotic leader and his loyalists.
It is, then, an extraordinary and overdue moment of relief to see the processes of democracy — however flawed in our barely representational system — offer the opportunity to take an off-ramp away from technocapital-backed fascism. Across the nation, Democrats secured historic victories. Even in Republican strongholds including Texas, Georgia, and South Carolina, voters delivered a rebuke to Trump’s GOP.
Democrats in Congress now have a mandate to do two things: Stop Trump, and improve the welfare of the U.S. working class. This should be understood as no less than a moral imperative to act immediately to curb the regime’s fascism in every possible way.
Americans are above all furious at the dire economic conditions in which they’re expected to struggle. The midterm results reflect a limit of Trumpian false consciousness: People know when they are poor, and they can see when billionaires, federal armed forces, genocidal governments, and presidential family members are profiting.
Despite their newfound congressional majority, Democrats now face an uphill battle to deliver legislation that will improve people’s material conditions. But that is not an excuse for inaction, mealy-mouthed gestures, or nods to bipartisanship. Democrats must push legislation that Republicans cannot stop, as well as legislation that Trump is all but sure to veto.
For one, Democrats must immediately roll back cuts to programs like Medicaid and supplemental nutritional programs. They must go further, too, and deliver on campaign promises for robust healthcare provisions, welfare spending, and restrictions on the ruinous depredations of Big Tech.
Trump bypassed Congress to prosecute his illegal war of choice on Iran, which has cost over $47 billion to date. But Congress has the power to curb military spending. Democrats must pass further resolutions to end the war, and they must pull the plug on military budget, directing funds instead to healthcare, housing, and investments in green infrastructure, to name a few urgent priorities. Though a flailing Trump finally announced that he would end military aid to Israel on Monday, it is Democrats who must pass further legislation to end all U.S. complicity in Israel’s apartheid regime and genocide.
Democrats must also propose laws to defund and abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement. This is no outlandish proposal; the impunity-drenched militia was only founded in 2003, and it is only by virtue of Congress that it now receives more funding than any other federal law enforcement agency. It is in Congress’s power to dismantle the agency and pass legislation to nullify the $170 billion-plus allocated to the border regime in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill.
Democrats should do whatever possible to roll back and end political prosecutions and the Trump administration’s brazen efforts to criminalize dissent.
The Democratic program must, in short, reject the austerity logics that have dominated the party for four decades. As sociologist Melinda Cooper has pointed out, and Trump’s Republicans have again and again proven, such austerity is not even austere: Pro-austerity governments since the Nixon administration in the 1970s have overseen lavish public spending in the shape of tax cuts and subsidies for holders of financial wealth (which does not trickle down), as well as funding for policing, border enforcement, prisons, and war machines. These are choices, and Democrats have been given a mandate to make choices that instead benefit — to revive a classic — the many, not the few.
Democrats such as Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., have stressed that their focus will be on the “affordability agenda” on which the party has run. This must include taking swift action to investigate and impeach the president and the worst offenders in his Cabinet, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In no way does insisting on accountability for Trump and his acolytes’ lawlessness distract from an economic focus. No affordability agenda can be achieved with an authoritarian executive in place. Challenging Trump’s despotism and self-dealing with every possible tool goes hand in hand with legislating to deliver on so-called kitchen-table issues.
Will Democrats in Congress, many of whom continue to reject the progressive and left-wing energies that have helped drive this blue wave, succeed in this anti-fascist political and economic agenda? No doubt, they will be thwarted at every turn by a desperate and dangerous executive and an embattled Republican minority. That is no reason to compromise, and constant pressure must be kept on Democrats who pretend otherwise. As the votes tonight make clear, in their millions, Americans know who to blame.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://citylimits.org/new-latino-democr.title: New Latino Democrats Group Aims to Build Political Power Across Five Boroughs
https://citylimits.org/new-latino-democr.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-latino-democr.text:
Share This Article
The new club aims to increase Latino representation in local politics, develop future leaders and strengthen community involvement across New York City, founder Jamey Battle said.
After years of participating in Democratic clubs, women’s organizations and professional networks, Jamey Battle said she often found herself asking the same question.
“I kept thinking, where are the other Latinos?” said Battle, who previously worked in the New York State Assembly and for a lobbying firm. “How can I bring them into this space? How can I get us involved in this political movement?”
Rather than continuing to search for Latino representation within existing political organizations, Battle decided to help create that space, centered on Latino voices and experiences.
Last month, Latino Democrats of New York City (LDNYC) celebrated its official launch as a 501(c)(4). Founded in October 2025 as a volunteer organizing group, LDNYC now has nearly 200 members, according to a press release.
The club aims to increase Latino representation in local politics, develop future leaders and strengthen community involvement across New York City’s five boroughs.
“I came up with the idea for Latino Democrats about a year ago. I texted my vice president, Evelyn Norris Pez, and we reached out to people in the network that we knew that shared two values: integrity and community centeredness,” said Battle, the group’s president.
“I finally came to a realization of, why am I spending so much time trying to have Latinos fit into a space that was never made for us, that isn’t led for us by us, and that doesn’t serve us?”
The group celebrated its new nonprofit status on Oct. 21 with an inaugural “Primera Noche” reception at Lighthouse Rooftop in Long Island City, Queens.
The evening brought together elected officials, community leaders, organizers and supporters for a celebration featuring speeches, award presentations and conversations about Latino political participation.
Attendees included Claire Valdez, who will head to Congress in January to represent Brooklyn and Queens’ 7th District; Brian Romero, newly elected to the State Assembly in Woodside and Jackson Heights; plus Queens Assembly members Catalina Cruz and Steven Raga, among others.
Throughout the reception, speakers shared personal stories about their families, careers and the experiences that shaped their involvement in public service.
One recalled growing up with a Salvadoran mother who arrived in the United States undocumented at age 12, and described hearing family stories about workplace exploitation, wage theft, policing and immigration enforcement—experiences that they said continue to shape their approach to community advocacy.
In New York State, Latinos account for 2.2 million eligible voters, making them the largest ethnic and racial group after white voters, according to the Pew Research Center.
For Battle, the group’s launch marks an opportunity to bring more Latino New Yorkers into political spaces and develop a stronger network of community leaders.
It comes as Democrats celebrate sweeping wins across the country in Tuesday’s midterm election, including victories for several candidates Latino Democrats NYC endorsed.
“I’m really excited for the next few years, really mobilizing and energizing the Latino community in New York City and building political power for all Latino communities in New York City,” Battle said.

Voters across New York City, the state, and the country turned out in droves Tuesday to cast their ballots in what is already looking like one of the most dramatic midterm elections in living memory. Some of the implications are obvious. Others are more subtle. Let's dig in to who comes out ahead after Tuesday and who has been laid low.
WINNER: Zohran Mamdani
Boring but true. Aside from one ill-advised endorsement of Lindsay Boylan for City Council in the spring, Mayor Zohran Mamdani can't lose! His three Congressional candidates—Brad Lander, Darializa Avila Chevalier, and Claire Valdez—swept their races over the summer and cemented their victories Tuesday night. https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: After the ‘Blue Tsunami’: Dems Await Mamdani and Hochul in Puerto Rico as Taxes Take Center Stage
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Katie Honan, Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — The “blue tsunami” celebrations swelled onto the beaches of San Juan on Wednesday, less than a day after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate and Gov. Kathy Hochul easily won reelection.
The annual SOMOS convention, held by the New York Democrats in Puerto Rico after every Election Day, has seen the ebbs and flows of politics.
“Two years ago, this looked like a funeral,” outgoing Rep. Nydia Velazquez told The City Reporter at the conference’s opening reception, remembering President Donald Trump’s 2024 reelection. “Two years ago, we were here agonizing. And tonight, we are celebrating.”
Democrats routed their Republican opponents across the country, which state Attorney General Letitia James, who also waltzed to victory on Tuesday , said was “about a course correction.”
“It’s a rejection of all the chaos, confusion, and corruption,“ she told The City Reporter.
The other contrast to 2024: New York City is now led by a socialist, Zohran Mamdani, whose historic mayoral election and win seemed far off two years ago. He’s now riding some of the highest favorability numbers of any mayor in decades and has used his popularity to help elect members of the Democratic Socialists of America to Congress and the state Legislature — doubling the number of members heading up to Albany next year, from eight to 16.
When Mamdani and Hochul visited SOMOS last year, he was a freshly elected phenomenon while she was facing a potentially difficult reelection battle.
While Mamdani made an early endorsement of Hochul this year and barnstormed with her across the city, she is now the target of his next campaign: for higher taxes on the wealthiest people and corporations.
MORE: Hochul Made Big Gains in NYC’s Blue Wave — Except in These Neighborhoods
Grace Mausser, co-chair of the DSA’s New York chapter, said a more progressive tax structure is a top priority — and she hopes Mamdani was able to persuade Hochul during their time together on the trail.
“The wealthy elite don’t necessarily like Zohran, large businesses in the real estate industry don’t necessarily like Zohran. A lot of those special interests are allies of Hochul,” Mauser said.
Both Hochul and Mamdani are set to arrive in San Juan later this week for SOMOS.
State Sen. Zellnor Myrie (D–Brooklyn) told The City Reporter conversations around more progressive taxes will start happening over the next few weeks.
The governor has been reluctant to say whether she’ll push for a tax on the rich, although groups like the DSA and newly-elected state lawmakers have made it a priority.
“There’s a philosophical question about who has the mandate. And the governor just won by 20 points — that is a mandate by any person’s stretch,” Myrie said.
“But there were also very spirited primaries where voters chose them as well,” Myrie said of the new legislators. “And that is also a mandate.”

https://gothamist.com/news/service-upgra.title: Service upgrade coming to On The Way: An hour-long radio show on all things NYC transit
https://gothamist.com/news/service-upgra.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/service-upgra.text:
This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
For three years, this newsletter and weekly radio segment on All Things Considered have dug into the nitty gritty of the subways and streets.
Now, much like an old A train getting upgraded to a sleek R211, we’re improving service for our audience. On The Way is launching an hour-long pop-up radio show on Thursdays. Starting next week, on Nov. 12, tune into WNYC 93.9 FM from 1 to 2 p.m., listen on the WNYC app, or check out our YouTube channel for the show hosted by me, Stephen Nessen. I’ll be speaking with my fellow transportation reporter Ramsey Khalifeh and editor Clayton Guse, bringing you analysis of the latest transportation news.
We’ll have special guests, including decision makers and the sharpest thinkers in the transit world. We’ll take your calls and welcome questions about your daily commutes, as well as your hopes and dreams for mass transit. Write me at [email protected].
It’s going to be a gas — consider this your invitation.
As we do in this newsletter each week, we’ll discuss the most important transportation topics of our time, from the redevelopment of Penn Station and the antiquated elements of the subway system, to the new projects like the Interborough Express and Penn Access. We’ll look at the ongoing issues in the transit system like fare evasion, subway signals, and the future of the taxi industry.
We’ll also look at the subway bottlenecks that slow your commutes, and share tips on how to legally avoid paying for the AirTrain, or navigate Exit 31 on the BQE without pulling your hair out.
Speaking of the BQE, you can bet we’ll get into that too.
The Curious Commuter segment will continue, so please keep the questions coming!
As always, we welcome your thoughts on our coverage on the web, on the air and in your inbox. Talk to you on the airwaves.
NYC transportation news this week
Bus and bike lanes galore to come. Advocates say that a ballot measure that passed on election night will reform the process for the construction of bus and bike lanes and means more street safety projects throughout the five boroughs. The measure will amend the city charter to “simplify the review of street safety projects to reduce construction timelines,” according to the text of the ballot question.
“This really just defangs some of the opponents who have sought to slow down and stop these street safety projects,” said Ben Furnas, executive director of Transportation Alternatives.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office estimated construction timelines on major bus and bike lane projects could be reduced by at least 33%. But the measure still requires the city to solicit input from community boards before moving forward with any street redesign.
SoHo basketball court set to leave MTA construction purgatory. The refreshed Grand Canal Court at Sixth Avenue, set to open at the end of November, will feature new benches, a water fountain, upgraded lighting and fencing. The courts were originally ripped up in 2022 so workers could build a new substation that provides electricity to trains.
Scary good ridership for the MTA over Halloweekend. On Halloween Saturday, 3.27 million riders got on the subway, the most on a Saturday since 2016. And during the New York City Marathon, the subway saw its highest Sunday ridership on record.
NYPD seizes e-bikes along a clogged East Village street. Eleven e-bikes parked along East 11th Street and First Avenue were confiscated by police last week. Neighboring business owners and residents have been complaining for months about idle delivery bikes clogging sidewalks and curbs, sometimes by the hundreds.
Watchdog says MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes. The budget watchdog Citizens Budget Commission recommends the MTA should make sweeping cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete as the agency could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
Question from Charles in Brooklyn
Charles from Brooklyn asks: Why on earth did the MTA eliminate over half of the seats on the new D trains?! We have long commutes and need those seats!
Answer
The MTA has been slowly replacing some of the oldest subway cars (in lines like the A, C and now D) with new R211 trains. They’re noticeably different from the trains of yore with “conversational” yellow-and-orange seats. The newer subway cars have wider doors to allow for more people to easily get on and off the trains. And yes, there are notably less seats. More standing room means more space for people in a single subway car than previous models with more seats. While riders with longer commutes have a lower chance of snagging a seat on one of these new train cars, the modern equipment is less likely to break down, meaning better service all around.
Join us for a conversation with MTA Chair Janno Lieber
Lieber joins WNYC’s “On The Way” at The Greene Space on Nov. 17 for an in-depth conversation on the country’s largest mass transit system. Lieber is the 14th person to run the transit agency, but only the fourth person to hold the job for more than five years. He joins WNYC Transportation and Infrastructure Editor Clayton Guse in The Greene Space to discuss what the transit agency means to New York and the future of the transportation networks used by millions of people every day. “On The Way” subscribers can use promo code “OTW” for 20% off tickets. Information and tickets are available here.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-s.title: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-s.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-s.text:
Google is locked in a standoff with the nation’s largest public school system as the debate over AI’s place in the classroom pits parent groups against the tech behemoth.
Earlier this week, Google said schools that ban artificial intelligence will lose access to Google search, prompting cries of blackmail and a swift rebuke from Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani wrote on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”
In September, Mamdani announced a one-year ban on most AI programs in city schools and tighter limits on screens, especially for the youngest students. The moratorium was a major win for city parents who oppose the use of artificial intelligence in public school classrooms.
But Google’s threat to pull the plug on search in classrooms underscored how deeply the technology’s products are woven into the fabric of education.
This is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of students
Google products are ubiquitous in schools. Since the pandemic, many students have been issued individual Chromebooks for schoolwork and remote learning. City officials said the school system has 1.3 million Chromebooks, with about 500,000 assigned to students, and another 800,000 in schools. Teachers post assignments to Google Classroom, and students, like many adults, rely heavily on Google Docs and search.
“It would be incredibly difficult for us to disentangle our school system entirely from Google, and that's what they're betting on,” said Kelly Clancy, part of the coalition calling for a total ban on AI in the city’s public schools. She said all three of her children are required to use Google Classroom for remote learning and homework.
“But I think what they're not counting on is the fact that parents across the country have mobilized against this,” Clancy said. “And this is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of students.”
Google has insisted it’s impossible to separate the company’s search function from AI.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that “search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” so turning off AI will also mean turning off the search engine. The company said the new policy would go into effect early next year. It did not respond to Gothamist’s requests for comment.
But over the past year, an influential movement of parents, educators and lawmakers have sought to beat back the creep of artificial intelligence in schools. They argue AI summaries and bots enable cheating, short-circuit learning and seduce children into inappropriate and even dangerous relationships. This week, parents of a North Carolina 13-year-old sued Google alleging she made plans to end her life after interacting with its AI Mode.
Education officials said they were still trying to figure out how Google’s new policy would affect search in schools.
Officials are “reaching out to Google to discuss this update further,” public schools spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said.
She said the city has disabled the Gemini chatbot and AI mode on Google Chromebooks issued to students, and they’ve made requests to Google to disable the AI Overview that continues to appear in search results.
“We will keep students and school communities updated as we continue to place student safety and wellbeing above all other interests,” she said.
Following the Times report, Google posted additional information about its plans on X.
It said the announcements give schools "more choice, not less" and that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will be off by default, and schools will be in charge of which service, if any, is turned on.
The company emphasized the changes were made in response to feedback from K-12 schools. Google said it’s also changing how AI will function within search “to make it better for learning.” The company said both AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guidance through problems” rather than just “quick answers to schoolwork.”
Assemblymember Alex Bores noted that Google has made “deep investments” into its educational offerings over the years, aggressively and successfully marketing its suite of products to schools.
“This is a product choice that Google is making, and it's a profit maximizing one,” said Bores, who worked at Palantir and recently co-founded Who Decides, an advocacy group for AI safety and regulation.
“Competitors like Duck Duck Go let people opt in or opt out of AI search. And Google could do the same. They could also do the same only when it comes to children if they wanted. But they're making an intentional choice not to, and I think that's a disappointing one,” he said.
Anti-AI parents and educators said Google’s threat should encourage the city to cut ties with the company, and invest in other search engines instead. Naveed Hasan, a member of the Panel for Educational Policy, which votes on education contracts, said the city should consider writing limits into contracts to prevent tech companies from unilaterally changing the software the school system has already purchased without permission.
“We should revisit how we look at technology contracts when companies change their features mid contract,” he said.
Zephyr Teachout, professor at Fordham Law School, said the company’s move may also face legal challenges. “What Google is doing is illegal under antitrust law and I expect there will be investigations from the Attorney General’s office and other places soon,” she said. “It’s simply not credible to me that Google cannot provide search without AI overviews.”
Clancy saw an opening for the school system to rethink how it teaches students to do their work.
“This is an exciting opportunity for us to figure out [how] to teach kids the fundamentals of research,” she said.
Maybe instead of spending so much on Google, Clancy added, the city could invest in school libraries and books.

“Across the line, then in line, then out of line: This was my progression through WAR”
MILES GREENBERG ONCE walked without respite on a conveyor belt for twenty-four consecutive hours, save for a twenty-three-minute loss of consciousness around hour eighteen. This durational performance, Oysterknife, 2020, had been an outlier in the Canadian artist’s body of work, its staging and premise owing less to the canon of Western sculpture Greenberg typically engages than to the conventions of performance art itself (think of Senga Nengudi and David Hammons’s collaborations, or Pope.L’s crawls). It had been an outlier, that is, until the debut of WAR at the former Eighty-Sixth Street Cinema on October 29, Greenberg’s first performance in New York City in more than three years and his largest to date. Entailing forty performers walking for six continuous hours, it was also the first piece since Oysterknife to feature the motorized belt.
As I passed under the marquee and into the erstwhile theater turned active construction site, I was already expecting Greenberg to deviate from the sculptural sensibility for which he is best known. “It does what a painting does,” the artist had written in announcement of WAR on his Instagram, setting his iron sights on sculpture’s sister art, away from things like Roman marbles. In my mock Michael Fried voice, I thought, “Surely it does what a bad painting does”—though at that point, I did not yet know that Greenberg had taken as his model precisely the kind of French history painting that Fried disparaged for being overly posed, chief among such works Jacques-Louis David’s The Intervention of the Sabine Women, 1799. Armed with the absorption/theatricality paradigm, I was simply curious to discover how Greenberg would bring painting and performance together in this crumbling cinema.
I went up some stairs, through a kind of foyer done up with an open bar, and then entered the theater proper to join a crowd of onlookers beneath the projection booth soffit, all gazing out at the spectacle occupying the rest of the hall. I saw four rows of ten semi-undressed performers, two flanking a central runway, each performer striding barefoot on a conveyor belt. At the far end of the room, a mirrored backdrop extended the phalanxes indefinitely, and where the runway intersected with the backdrop was an LED screen glowing a cold white light. A stone lay directly in front of the screen. Altogether, the arrangement formed a kind of tableau vivant: Greenberg had staged two opposing factions on the verge of battle. I noticed the music next, an original score by Chino Amobi composed of atmospheric chanting, intermittent sirens, and explosive percussion like something out of a violent video game. Every ten or so minutes, in phase with the looping score, the white light flashed red. This was Greenberg’s cue to break ranks, hop off his treadmill, and strut fiercely down the runway in surveillance of his company. Throughout the six hours, he acted as an overseer.
There was more to describe—for instance, the team of stagehands running around in boiler suits, switching out exhausted performers like spent bullets, or the various video cameras and photographers documenting every detail—but what struck me was the audience. For a start, it was the kind of fashionable crowd that made me keenly aware that I should have worn more black. This sense of being out of place was heightened by the fact that, little by little, people were stepping out onto the runway, crossing the implicit proscenium between performance and world. They would walk to the stone and back, gawk at the performers, and maybe take some photos, all the while looking terribly self-conscious themselves. If the timing was right, the light would flash red and Greenberg would have to march through the people clotting his path.
It took a tequila or two from the bar to steel me for a turn down the runway. When I reentered the theater, Greenberg was patrolling the rows of performers with a 3D scanner in hand, wielding it over body after body, capturing the shapes of future sculptures. With the thought in mind that the word per-formance signifies a passage through form, I set foot into the scene. Suddenly, the opposition between absorption/theatricality seemed utterly to dissolve, if only for a moment. The sensation was something like I imagine it would be to walk through Walter De Maria’s Mile-Long Parallel Walls in the Desert, 1961–63, when the visual field suddenly flattens into a diagram of linear perspective. “I wanted it to feel like you were standing in a gigantic oil painting,” as Greenberg put it to me the following day. “It’s about the physical relationship between the viewer and the artwork, being able to traverse this straight through the panel.” I found the extent to which WAR was successful along this line to hinge on the stone at the end of the runway. Walking directly toward it, straining to keep my focus on its silhouette against the effulgent screen behind, it appeared as a vanishing point, impossibly distant, everything converging there.
And then the illusion was gone, for I was standing there myself, looking back through the rows of performers to the crowd I had abandoned. Now among the all-Black cast, my pallor felt a great deal more conspicuous than my clothing had at the other end of the room, especially as I had to step out of the way of Greenberg’s patrol. Indeed, the knowledge of being an object in everyone’s sight was so overwhelming, I could not be certain that I had ever really felt absorbed into the scene, even as I played an active part in it. Across the line, then in line, then out of line: This was my progression through WAR, and it gave me to understand just how, in posing as painting, the boundary between presence and representation becomes an irresolvable problem: “I wrote WAR as a response to the news, but I didn’t feel like I could make an artwork about one particular conflict or genocide which doesn’t physically affect me,” Greenberg said. “This was a kind of petri dish to put the feelings that do apply to me in, and to see what happens.”
Traipsing back up the runway, I knew that neither rejoining the audience nor drinking any more tequila would dispel my confusion between definite responsibility and limited agency. After all, what could be a better emblem of this tension than the motorized belts all around, demanding as they did one step after another, only to foreclose forward movement? Compared with the Covid-era Oysterknife, though, the difference here was that WAR implicated cast, crew, and crowd equally in the performance of this confusion, even while thematizing the very difficulty of sharing it—a vital reminder, especially when getting the news or looking at a painting can feel like such a private experience.
Julian Stern is a critic who lives in New York.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-arrested-.title: Man arrested in NYC on accusations of sexual assault, rape on Cape Cod, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/man-arrested-.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/man-arrested-.text:
A former rowing coach was arrested Thursday in the Bronx on allegations of sexual assault and rape stemming from his time coaching on Cape Cod, according to law enforcement officials.
Guy Monseair, 57, was taken into custody on City Island around 7 a.m. by officers from the NYPD and Homeland Security Investigations Human Trafficking Task Force, officials said. According to the Barnstable, MA Police Department, he is charged with four counts of aggravated statutory rape of a child and one count of indecent assault and battery on a child under 14.
Police said all of the alleged incidents took place between 2008 and 2011 while Monseair was a rowing coach at several different clubs on the Cape. Barnstable Police said they were made aware of the allegations last month.
It was not immediately clear when Monseair moved to the Bronx. NYPD officials said he started the City Island Rowing group between 2012 and 2014, though officials couldn’t say if he was still involved in the organization. There have not been any allegations against Monseair from his time in New York, according to the NYPD.
An undated online profile page lists Monseair as the head coach and executive director of City Island Rowing. The profile says that he grew up in Zimbabwe and moved to the U.S. to pursue his coaching career full time.
“At City Island Rowing, Monseair’s coaching philosophy emphasizes both athletic and personal growth, with a focus on resilience, teamwork, and discipline. Under his leadership, the program has grown to support a large team of athletes, many of whom have achieved national and collegiate success,” the page reads.
The organization did not immediately respond to several messages seeking comment.
In a statement, a spokesperson for USRowing said the organization revoked Monseair’s membership rights as soon as they learned about the allegations on Thursday. That means he is prohibited from participating in all competitions and activities under their jurisdiction.
USRowing also reported the matter to the U.S. Center for SafeSport, and urged other abuse survivors to come forward either online or by phone at 833-5US-SAFE (833-587-7233).
According to the Barnstable Police Department, Monseair will be extradited back to Massachusetts, where the case will be prosecuted by the Cape and Islands District Attorney's Office.
Information for his lawyer was not immediately available.
This is a developing story and was updated with new information.

The ICA Miami has selected Gensler as the architect to renovate the building they acquired in 2024. The 30,000 square foot building will house the museum’s permanent collection and increase public-programming space. The new wing is scheduled to open at the end of 2027.
Formerly the home of the De la Cruz collection, a private museum that closed after the death of its co-founder, Rosa de la Cruz it has since 2024 been the site of the museum’s educational programs. The renovation is expected to cost $40 million, paid for by private donors. Eight galleries will occupy the first and second floors dedicated to exhibiting the ICA’s permanent collection of over 2,000 works. The third floor will be dedicated to hosting public programming, including lectures, performances, and symposia. “We intend to enhance the museum’s story-driven narrative approach to the collection and exhibitions,” Alex Gartenfeld, the ICA’s director and chief curator, told The Art Newspaper.
“Beyond adding galleries, this renovation will strengthen the ICA’s ability to support artists, expand learning and create a platform for exchange and belonging in one of the world’s most dynamic cultural cities,” said Bevin Savage Yamazaki, Gensler’s global culture and museums leader. The renovation will also include a redesigned lobby, reconfigured outdoor space, and an expanded cafe. “We are aiming to create a more collective experience,” said Gartenfeld.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-jewish-sis.title: The Jewish Sisters in Renoir’s “Pink and Blue”
https://hyperallergic.com/the-jewish-sis.author: Eurídice Arratia
https://hyperallergic.com/the-jewish-sis.text:
The Jewish Sisters in Renoir’s “Pink and Blue”
Author Catherine Ostler follows the lives of the two cherubic girls, whose rarefied lives in an elite, artistic French family would be toppled by the horrors of the Holocaust.
In 1881, at the dawn of the Belle Époque, Pierre-Auguste Renoir steps into the ritzy Parisian townhouse of the Cahen d’Anvers family to paint a double portrait of four-year-old Alice and six-year-old Elisabeth, daughters of the Antwerp-born Jewish banker Louis and salonnière Louise. In the finished canvas, “Pink and Blue, the Misses Cahen d’Anvers” (1881), the two cherubic girls with rosy cheeks and reddish-golden hair stand in a sumptuous salon, holding hands, enveloped in a cloud of lace and satin.
This “duet of sugared-almond-colored-sweetness,” as author Catherine Ostler puts it, and “La Petite Irène” (1880) — a portrait of their older sister, painted by the artist a year earlier — are the springboard for her book The Renoir Girls.
From the opening pages, Ostler’s exhaustively researched, deftly structured book conjures the gilded world of fin-de-siècle Paris, leading the reader through the brocade curtains of the Cahen d’Anvers family’s dazzling life as members of the Jewish elite to their tragic end in the Holocaust. At center stage is the art patron Louise; Marcel Proust was a close friend, and her famed salon drew artists, writers, and members of the conservative Catholic aristocracy alike. And there was her lover, the collector and art critic Charles Ephrussi, who had arranged for Renoir to paint the girls and was suspected of being Alice's biological father. But alongside this world of opulence and privilege, in which every ball and horse race the Cahen d’Anvers women attended made it into the newspaper columns, ran another Paris, one divided by inequality and political instability, which fueled antisemitism and punctured the sisters’ rarefied lives.
Ostler captures the collision of these two worlds with the dreadful inevitability of a train derailing in slow motion. Despite the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Code having ensured equal rights for France’s Jewish population, antisemitism was insidious across the country. It took the form of resentful grumbles “aligned with the times”: “I really give up with the Jews,” wrote Renoir to a friend complaining about Louis’s “stingy” payment. It took the form of the anti-Jewish venom of diarist and, perversely, frequent visitor to Louise’s salon, Edmond de Goncourt. And it reached its peak with the Dreyfus Affair of 1894 to 1906, in which a Jewish French army officer was framed for treason. While the Cahen d’Anvers and their close circle belonged to the Dreyfusard camp, some members of the Jewish elite — the haute Juiverie — seemed to waltz through this moral and political crisis, which polarized the nation. Amid political assassinations and anarchist bombs, Louise and Louis went on worshiping the 18th century and restoring Château Champs-sur-Marne to its ancient regime glory. Meanwhile, the girls continued on their path to assimilation, not without puzzling twists and heartbreaks.
In 1895, at the height of the Dreyfus Affair, a 21-year-old Elisabeth converts to Catholicism and marries a penniless aristocrat, whom she later divorces. In 1897, the adventurous, anglophile Alice meets the ambitious British Colonel Charles Townshend in Egypt and, a year later, ties the knot in an Anglican ceremony at her parents' chateau. And Irène, the only one to enter into an arranged marriage, leaves her husband, Moïse de Camondo, for the head of his stable. But in the 1930s, the glittering carousel comes to a screeching halt, and Ostler’s account of the Nazis’ occupation descends into a harrowing tale of persecution.
The Cahen d'Anvers’s love for France and desire to belong run deep throughout the book. Their forebears adapted their surname to sound more aristocratic; Irène’s son, Nissim de Camondo, fought for France and died in World War I. They gave generously to philanthropic causes, restored dilapidated historical properties, and later donated them to the French state. But neither their wealth nor their belief in the values of the Enlightenment could shield them from the catastrophe to come, and four members of the family perished in concentration camps, including Elisabeth, who, in 1944, old and infirm, was betrayed by the mayor of the village where she was hiding and died in or on the way to Auschwitz.
As for the paintings, “Pink and Blue” now hangs at the Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, where it is one of the institution’s most popular works. “La Petite Irène,” on the other hand, was looted by the Nazis, restituted to Irène, and then was subsequently bought by the Swiss arms dealer and war profiteer Emil Georg Bührle. It is now on view at the Kunsthaus Zürich, its sweetness belying a story of devastation and betrayal amid one of the darkest chapters of European history — a story Ostler’s engrossing, kaleidoscopic chronicle vividly brings to life.

The Vera List Center for Art and Politics (VLC) at the New School, New York, has announced artist and educator Pablo Helguera as its new director, effective November 2. He succeeds Carin Kuoni, who has led the center since 2004 as its senior director and chief curator. Alongside his appointment as director, Helguera was named director of the school’s art collection. He arrives to the VLC from the school’s College of Performing Arts, where he has served on the faculty since 2020. Helguera previously spent thirteen years as director of adult and academic programs at the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
“Pablo Helguera brings an extraordinary combination of artistic vision, intellectual curiosity, and institutional experience to the Vera List Center for Art and Politics,” said VLC board chair JK Brown in a statement. “His commitment to socially engaged art and the role of artists in shaping public life aligns deeply with the VLC’s mission.”
Helguera is known for his socially engaged practice—he founded and directed the School of Panamerican Unrest, a nonprofit public art project connecting different parts of the Americas, as well as Librería Donceles, a traveling Spanish-language used bookstore of 25,000 titles. Before joining MoMA, he worked at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, and the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago. A midcareer retrospective of his work is slated for 2027 at the Sheldon Museum of Art in Lincoln, Nebraska.
“We are living through a moment of profound political and cultural transformation, when the need to make sense of rapidly unfolding events, question prevailing narratives, and imagine alternative futures has become especially urgent,” said Helguera in a statement. “I believe artistic practice has a vital role to play in this process, not only by responding to the issues of our time, but by creating new spaces for inquiry, exchange, and collective reflection.” Helguera further note that he was looking forward to working with the center’s team to develop “initiatives that can help us navigate the complexities of this pivotal moment.”

https://hyperallergic.com/please-dont-si.title: Please Don’t Sit on the Flowers
https://hyperallergic.com/please-dont-si.author: Hakim Bishara
https://hyperallergic.com/please-dont-si.text:
Please Don’t Sit on the Flowers
Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape goes to auction, Brancusi gets lost at MoMA, interview with Doris Salcedo, and is showing at documenta worth it?
Sitting at September Cafe, I watch the autumn leaves separate from the trees and get carried away gently by the wind. They swirl and twirl, performing a merry little dance in the air before falling to their final resting place.
News has just come in about a sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections, as fierce and awesome as a Gustave Courbet wave. But I see nobody popping champagne bottles in the streets. A pregnant black cat with a hanging belly saunters by.
Lying back in the dentist’s chair, a TV screen in front of me shuffles picturesque views from exotic places. They're idyllic to the point of not looking real. My doctor, a Lebanese, shows me an X-ray of my mouth, which looks like Beirut at the height of the Civil War.
The sky over the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge is gray, and the Harlem River is brooding as I make my way to Taryn Simon’s exhibition Father Country I Do Love You at the Guggenheim Museum. The show tells the heroic tales of an FBI agent whose alleged career intersects with major events in American history. Cold, antiseptic photographs encased neatly in plexiglass make up a detective story linking the protagonist to the explosion of TWA Flight 800, the 9/11 attacks, the bombing of the United States embassy in Nairobi, Bill Clinton’s impeachment, and more. Trudging up the Guggenheim’s spiraling galleries, I wonder whether this patriotic show is organized and sponsored by the US State Department. Simon makes you read a lot, but all that reading is just meant to distract you from thinking.
Jodie Foster narrates the audio guide for those who don’t have the patience to read long-winded wall texts. At the cafeteria, while eating a bikini sandwich, I see a woman who looks exactly like Judi Dench, another actress. “I love storytelling,” she tells a friend before plunging her teeth into a chocolate croissant.
On my way out, I once again resent how this museum forces everyone to exit through the gift shop to encourage commerce, but I buy myself a $5 Guggenheim bag anyway. Outside, in one of the manicured gardens of the Upper East Side, a small sign pleads, “Please don’t sit on the flowers.”
I cross the street into Central Park through Engineers’ Gate, climb the steps past a gilded bust of John Purroy Mitchel, NYC mayor between 1914-1918, and look out over the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir. I think of the Kennedys, of Trump, and of Simon. A worker collects brown leaves in plastic bags and tosses them into a truck wrapped in a photo of green leaves. A mother tries to snap a photo of her child, but the unruly kid refuses to pose for the camera. He throws a fit, falls, and, to her shock, ends up sitting on the flowers.
—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

The People Against the Arch
Protesters in DC roast the Arc de Trump, plus the Whitney Museum announces the next curators of its blockbuster biennial.
Rise ’n shine! No sooner had the last Whitney Biennial closed than we got news about the next one — or its curators, at least. Staff Writer Anna Lee has the details on the appointment of Meg Onli, co-curator of the 2024 edition, and Zack Winokur, opera director and producer, for the blockbuster American art exhibition’s 2028 iteration.
Speaking of museums of American art, we caught up with pathbreaking Kiowa and Tongan curator Jordan Poorman Cocker, who just organized a major reinstallation of contemporary Indigenous art at Crystal Bridges. She talks with Petala Ironcloud about approaching Indigeneity as a global framework and telling a “more honest story of American art” through her community-driven work.
Protesters in DC rally against Trump’s ill-fated triumphal arch, a new book chronicles the tragic lives of the Jewish sisters in Renoir’s beloved painting “Pink and Blue," and more must-reads below.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mo.title: Moab Petroglyphs Discovered Vandalized: ‘Irreplaceable Cultural Resources’
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mo.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mo.text:
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Utah is seeking the culprits behind two incidents of vandalism that left protected petroglyphs near Moab riddled with crude carvings, including that signature and another, less distinct marking.
The vandals reportedly struck one site along Highway 279, a scenic stretch parallel to the Colorado River, and one by Hell’s Revenge, a well-known off-road slickrock trail. Photos taken by the Bureau, and first published by SF Gate, show clear damage to the petroglyphs that decorate the rock fave: In one photo, an investigator is seen measuring huge letters—spelling “Craig W”—that now cover a portion of petroglyph depicting animals.
Writing on social media, the BLM described the petroglyph as “irreplaceable cultural resources” which are protected under the Archaeological Resources Protection Act.
“Our cultural resources are part of our shared heritage,” the Bureau said. “Once damaged, they cannot be restored to their original condition. We ask visitors to respect these resources and help protect them for future generations.”
Petroglyphs near Moab and beyond are a frequent target for criminal mischief and looting, amid more existential threats posed by recent government rollbacks of their protections. In 2021, a series of sacred, 300-year petroglyphs along the cliffs of Hawaii were defaced with a paintball gun, marking one in a string of incidents involving the artworks. A group of petroglyphs located at the Volcanic Tableland in Bishop, California, carved into the rock by the Paiute-Shoshone before European colonization, have faced multiple episodes of vandalism, including desecration and even theft: Criminals reportedly used power saws to remove large sections of rock featuring the carvings. The BLM managed to recover the stolen petroglyph, though the suspects remained at large.
Whoever they are, they’ll find little mercy from locals. “The minimum sentence for this crime should be life without parole,” wrote one user on the r/California subreddit at the time. “If you disrespect historical artifacts of great significance you should be labeled an enemy of the public. Zero tolerance.”

https://hyperallergic.com/wexner-center-.title: Wexner Center for the Arts to Keep Name Despite Founder’s Epstein Ties
https://hyperallergic.com/wexner-center-.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/wexner-center-.text:
Wexner Center for the Arts to Keep Name Despite Founder’s Epstein Ties
Hundreds had urged Ohio State University to remove Les Wexner's name from campus buildings over his connections to Jeffrey Epstein.
Ohio State University (OSU) has called off the school's review process to consider removing billionaire benefactor Les Wexner's name from campus buildings, despite hundreds of renaming requests citing Wexner's connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Interim Provost Trevor Brown's decision, made public last Friday, November 6, overrides the advisory committee conducting the review.
It also comes as a blow to the university's Wexner Center for the Arts staff, who told Hyperallergic they've been “directly affected” by public discontent with the Center's association with Wexner.
“Workers will bear the brunt of this decision, fielding angry and hostile comments from the public and having the work we do questioned for its association with the Wexner name,” said a representative of the Wexner Center's staff union, Wex Workers United (WWU), in a statement. Wexner funded the art institution's creation and remains the center's board chair.
In June, the Wexner Center's Executive Director Cat Predmore told WOSU that one artist and one grantmaking organization have withdrawn from showing art at and funding the Center, respectively, over Wexner's connections to Epstein.

https://hyperallergic.com/six-stolen-pic.title: Six Stolen Picassos Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Home
https://hyperallergic.com/six-stolen-pic.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/six-stolen-pic.text:
Six Stolen Picassos Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Home
Seven suspects were arrested in connection with the theft of the prints from L’Amandier restaurant in the south of France.
French authorities discovered six stolen Pablo Picasso prints under a pile of clothes in a home on the French Riviera on Tuesday, November 3, and arrested seven suspects for the theft, the French National Gendarmerie said in a press release. Details and images of the works have not yet been made public.
On the night of October 1, two masked intruders broke into L'Amandier, a restaurant in the village of Mougins, while a getaway driver remained on the lookout. The duo made away with six of the artworks on display in the restaurant's Salon Picasso lounge. The prints, which have an estimated worth of over €100,000 ($112,208), were reportedly found in perfect condition behind clothes and toolboxes in one of the village houses they searched, according to Le Monde.
Picasso first visited Mougins in 1936 and returned decades later to live out his last 12 years of life in Notre-Dame-de-Vie. L'Amandier's Salon Picasso lounge pays tribute to the Spanish artist and his impact on the former farming village, which became a tourism hotspot after his arrival.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: É preciso politizar o sofrimento, mas sem perder o singular das pessoas, diz psicólogo e escritor
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: Conversa Bem Viver
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
A experiência de mais de dez anos em seu consultório, ouvindo, sistematicamente, seus pacientes relatarem repetidamente episódios de racismo, foi o incômodo necessário para que o psicólogo e escritor Lucas Veiga investigasse o impacto cotidiano da violência racial e os caminhos para promover um cuidado psíquico fortalecido.
É isso que propõe o livro “Clínica do Impossível: como pessoas negras podem cuidar da saúde mental em um mundo racista”. Para o autor, o título da obra deriva de um duplo sentido da palavra impossível. “Os episódios de racismo exatamente não param de acontecer. Então é impossível, numa primeira camada de sentido, porque o fim imediato do racismo não está posto como possível”, explica.
Por outro lado, ele ressalta o caráter da resistência negra como um caminho de cuidado. “Ao mesmo tempo que é impossível a resolução total desse problema, é impossível também que nós, pessoas negras, que a comunidade negra seja totalmente devorada, seja totalmente capturada pelo problema do racismo”, pondera.
Diante desse cenário, Veiga convoca a criação de estratégias no presente, inspiradas na tecnologia ancestral dos quilombos. Ele enfatiza a urgência de construir “espaços de aquilombamento” na vida cotidiana e propõe investigar “por quais caminhos cada pessoa negra pode praticar a liberdade em relação à colonialidade”. O psicólogo defende o afastamento das narrativas racistas para a construção de um eu autônomo, permitindo que “cada pessoa negra possa ser negra à sua maneira”.
Na prática clínica, o autor desenvolve o conceito de “dupla escuta”, que articula de forma inseparável as dimensões políticas e individuais do sofrimento psíquico. “Eu preciso escutar ali as marcas da coletividade. A gente precisa poder politizar o sofrimento. E, ao mesmo tempo, é preciso escutar aquilo de radicalmente singular, que também aparece, que também está presente no discurso, na fala daquele paciente. Para que quando eu escutar o João, e ele é um homem negro, eu possa escutar ao mesmo tempo o João enquanto homem negro e o João enquanto João”, argumenta.
Nessa relação entre o coletivo e o individual, segundo Lucas Veiga, é que o consultório pode se transformar em um “território livre para expressão, para elaboração e para experimentação” do cuidado.
Apoiado no pensamento de Frantz Fanon, Lucas Veiga combate a tendência do racismo de homogeneizar os sujeitos e recorda a máxima de que “não há um preto, há pretos”, evidenciando a singularidade da experiência negra. Por essa razão, o escritor defende que a busca pela saúde mental envolve ultrapassar as amarras coloniais em direção à afirmação da própria vida. “O objetivo final é descobrir por quais caminhos a pessoa pode quebrar essa máscara branca para poder viver a sua negritude e viver a sua vida no seu maior grau de potência possível”, conclui.
