Para encerrar estes comentários que sugerem a disputa popular politizada e organizada em relação ao binômio renda e poder, nada mais justo que o governo Lula e a direção nacional do PT encaminhem esforços para propor estudos de adoção do Orçamento Participativo (OP) articulado com as mobilizações Rua-Rede.
Desde já, sugerimos examinar dois segmentos, ambos com polpudos valores disputando o orçamento público:
1) Emendas Parlamentares (total reservado): 61 bilhões de reais.
2) Renúncias Fiscais federais (incluindo todos os tipos de benefícios tributários) está estimado em R$ 903,3 bilhões para 2026, segundo levantamento da Unafisco.
A sorte está lançada. A luta é irrenunciável.
*Cristóvão Feil é sociólogo.
*Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Explosões de aviões e equipamentos pelo Ibama também impactam o crime organizado na Amazônia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Luís Indriunas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Vídeos de equipamentos e aviões usados no garimpo ilegal sendo destruídos por explosões realizadas por agentes do Ibama na Amazônia, viralizaram nas redes sociais na semana passada. Representando apenas 4% ou 5% dos totais das ações de fiscalização, essas operações contra o desmatamento têm forte poder simbólico e atingem estruturas que também são usadas pelo crime organizado para outras práticas ilícitas, como tráfico de drogas, madeira e armas, além de trabalho escravo e grilagem de terras.
Um balanço do Ministério Público Federal (MPF) sobre as 1.313 operações feitas, de março a outubro, na Terra Indígena Sararé, na região de Pontes e Lacerda, a 483 km de Cuiabá (MT), aponta um prejuízo estimado de R$ 111,5 milhões ao crime organizado. Entre os equipamentos destruídos, estavam duas escavadeiras hidráulicas avaliadas em cerca de R$ 1 milhão cada. A Polícia Federal (PF) prendeu 72 pessoas em flagrante.
Investigações da PF divulgadas em junho apontam que o território tem túneis escavados para apoiar a exploração do ouro e que são utilizados pelo Comando Vermelho (CV) para esconder armas e munições. A facção criminosa, originária do Rio de Janeiro, atua na região desde 2023, oferecendo proteção armada para garimpeiros.
Segundo o relatório Cartografias da Violência na Amazônia, do Instituto Mãe Negra, 22 grupos criminosos e facções diferentes estão presentes em pelo menos 178 municípios da Amazônia Legal brasileira.
“O tráfico encontrou na Amazônia e no ouro do garimpo não só uma oportunidade de lavar o dinheiro, mas também de ganhar muito dinheiro”, disse, ao Brasil de Fato, o agente de fiscalização do Instituto Brasileiro do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Naturais Renováveis (Ibama) e representante da Associação Nacional dos Servidores da Carreira de Especialista em Meio Ambiente e Pecma (Ascema), Wallace Lopes.
Lopes, que atua na fiscalização ambiental desde 2009, destaca que, além do crime organizado, o garimpo ilegal está envolvido com grandes grupos de interesse, como figuras políticas, lideranças religiosas, grileiros de terras e madeireiros.
As destruições que viralizaram, apesar de pequenas dentro do universo de atribuições do órgão, são importantes do ponto de vista simbólico e também porque pegam no bolso do crime.
“É importante dizer que a gente tem um percentual reduzido de destruições, mas que aparecem nos jornais, nas redes sociais. O Ibama trabalha muito mais do que aparece. Mas as ações contundentes contra esses crimes são importantes para desestimular outras pessoas a cometerem a mesma infração pelo risco, pelo medo de serem punidas. Para que outras pessoas falem assim: ‘Se eu quiser garimpar em algum lugar, se eu quiser colocar um maquinário, tem o risco disso acontecer’”, explica Lopes.
“Na hora que a gente destrói um avião, incomoda, porque o avião é um investimento caro, por pior que ele seja. Prender o garimpeiro não incomoda, porque normalmente ele é um laranja explorado”, aponta a presidente da Ascema Nacional, Tânia Maria de Souza, que já atuou como fiscal para o estado do Rio de Janeiro e para a União.
“O mais comum é que o cara que vai se ferrar, porque ele está lá no meio da floresta, ganha uma miséria, muitas vezes fica doente, não consegue nem ser socorrido”, lembra Souza.
Condições análogas à escravidão são comuns nos garimpos, como exploração por dívidas, acampamentos insalubres e violência. Em um vídeo, Lopes mostra a barraca com cobertores no chão batido como cama, sem nenhuma proteção, em uma operação em 2021, na Terra Indígena Apyterewá, no Pará.
As condições precárias também são muitas vezes vistas pelos equipamentos. Em outro vídeo, na Terra Indígena Yanomami, Lopes mostra a falta de condições do avião apreendido. “Seria um risco enorme, não só para o piloto, mas para qualquer um que tivesse embaixo daquela coisa ao voar.”
Além dessas questões, a destruição é também uma opção baseada na logística e na proteção dos fiscais. Em várias ocasiões, é possível disponibilizar para prefeituras tratores e outros equipamentos que são apreendidos, mas, nessas operações, os perigos de emboscadas e a certeza de que os delitos continuariam assim que os fiscais saíssem fazem a destruição ser uma solução extrema, mas mais eficaz para o problema.
Por isso, Lopes destaca que não são os garimpeiros os principais alvos da fiscalização. “Não são essas pessoas, embora elas claramente estejam cometendo um crime também, participando de uma rede criminosa, que focamos. Elas estão ali porque não têm condições. Por isso, a gente foca em encontrar os grandes responsáveis, quem realmente financia, quem realmente ganha dinheiro com essas atividades ilegais”, destaca.
19 mil km² por fiscal do Ibama
Com 750 agentes de fiscalização em atividade no Ibama atualmente, segundo a Ascema, é como se cada fiscal do órgão fosse responsável por uma área média de 18.945,81 km², contando biomas terrestres e marinhos, o equivalente a mais de três vezes a área de Brasília.
Nesse sentido, a Ascema aponta um déficit de cerca de 8 mil servidores para o Ibama, para o ICMBio, que é responsável pelas unidades de conservação, e para o próprio Ministério do Meio Ambiente e das Mudanças Climáticas (MMA).
Nos últimos concursos públicos, cerca de mil novos ingressantes tomaram posse. “É muito boa a chegada dos colegas, mas obviamente está muito aquém”, aponta a presidente da Ascema.
Mesmo com essa escassez, os resultados ambientais têm tido recordes. Em maio, o desmatamento na Amazônia Legal teve redução de 61,4% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2025, a maior redução percentual de desmatamento já registrada na região.
Parte desse resultado é a aposta do Ibama tanto em trabalho de inteligência policial quanto em mecanismos eficazes a partir de cruzamento de dados.
No primeiro caso, o Ibama e o Instituto Chico Mendes de Conservação da Biodiversidade (ICMBio) fazem parte do Sistema Brasileiro de Inteligência (Sisbin), que compartilha dados que garantem um planejamento coordenado. Como são operações complexas e perigosas, os fiscais contam com apoio de agentes da PF, das Forças Armadas ou da Polícia Militar Estadual.
Os fiscais do Ibama têm um forte treinamento para atuar em campo e contam ainda com o Grupo Especial de Fiscalização (GEF), um grupo de elite que é treinado com táticas militares.
Sobre o cruzamento de dados, o Ibama tem um sistema eficiente que procura autorizações estaduais e federais de áreas onde são detectados desmatamentos. “A partir daí, quando não dá match, quando você tem um desmatamento que não tem uma autorização correspondente na internet, eles fazem embargos remotos”, explica a coordenadora de Políticas Públicas do Observatório do Clima, Suely Aráujo, que já foi presidenta do Ibama.
Os embargos remotos são muito criticados pela bancada ruralista, já que o indício de crime paralisa o crédito. Os bancos param de emprestar. “O embargo é muito mais eficaz do que aplicar multa, porque esse pessoal não paga multa. Contrata advogado e vai recorrendo. Mas, enquanto ele fica embargado, ele não tem crédito rural. O pessoal fica assim, mas muito bravo”, detalha Araújo.
Durante o governo Bolsonaro, houve 13.207 embargos realizados pelo Ibama. No governo Lula 3, foram 18.158 embargos, um aumento de 38% dos casos. Em área embargada, o aumento foi de 44%, passando de 1,3 milhão de hectares para 1,9 milhão.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.title: NFL trade deadline 2026: Vikings reunite with Kirk Cousins in blockbuster, Bengals-Eagles deal collapses – live updates
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.author: Ella Brockway (before) and Bryan Armen Graham (now)
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
The Denver Broncos have acquired linebacker Daiyan Henley from their AFC West rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers, in exchange for a fourth-round pick in the 2027 draft and a fifth-rounder in 2028, according to multiple reports.
Henley, a former third-round pick out of Washington State, has developed into one of the NFL’s most promising young linebackers. The move strengthens Denver’s defense as they look to create separation from a logjam of teams atop the AFC standings, where the top six teams are within a game of the No 1 seed.
The Broncos expect to receive a fourth-round compensatory pick in 2027 for the departure of defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers, allowing them to part with their own fourth-round selection in the deal, according to Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer.
Kirk Cousins’ return to Minnesota comes with an unusual statistical wrinkle. The veteran quarterback has played through the first part of the season without a week off in Las Vegas, but the Vikings have already enjoyed their bye. That scheduling quirk means Cousins could theoretically start 18 regular-season games – a first in NFL history for a quarterback – if he takes over immediately and remains under center for the rest of the season. You like that?
A total of 19 players in NFL history have appeared in at least 18 regular-season games in a single year, and none have been quarterbacks, according to Josh Dubow of the Associated Press. Fifteen achieved the feat between 1925 and 1930, while four have done so since the league adopted a 17-game schedule in 2021: Leonard Williams (2023), Mike Williams (2024), Rashid Shaheed (2025) and Dre’Mont Jones (2025).
Cousins rejoins Vikings as Raiders launch Mendoza era
Kirk Cousins is heading back to Minnesota. The Vikings have acquired the veteran quarterback from the Las Vegas Raiders in a blockbuster exchange for a third-round pick in the 2027 draft, according to multiple reports, including ESPN’s Adam Schefter and NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport.
The move reunites Cousins with the franchise where he spent six seasons from 2018 to 2023 and gives Minnesota an experienced option under center as they look to salvage their season.
For Las Vegas, the trade clears the way for No 1 overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza to take over as starting quarterback. The Raiders, who sit at 4-5, will throw the rookie straight into the deep end, with his first two NFL starts coming against two of the league’s toughest defenses in Seattle and Denver.
Tennessee are building quite the war chest. The Titans now hold two first-round picks and two second-round picks in the 2027 draft, plus another two first-rounders in 2028. That gives them six picks in the first two rounds over the next two years and a golden opportunity to reshape their roster.
The 7-1 Bills were in need of safety help and it appears they’ve gotten it. Buffalo have acquired safety Amani Hooker from the Tennessee Titans, according to Tom Pelissero of the Ringer, bolstering their secondary amid their push for the AFC’s top seed.
Hooker, 28, is the NFL’s joint-interceptions leader this year and has established himself as one of the league’s most versatile safeties.
Buffalo are sending back a second-round pick in the 2027 draft to Tennessee in exchange for Hooker and a 2027 fifth-rounder, according to reports.
The 49ers are sending a sixth-round pick in the 2027 draft to Indianapolis in exchange for Allen, according to reports. With San Francisco getting healthier at wide receiver, the 34-year-old provides experienced depth at a relatively modest price.
The San Francisco 49ers have acquired six-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Keenan Allen from the Indianapolis Colts, according to multiple reports, giving Brock Purdy another experienced target for the stretch run.
Allen, who had been seeking a move to a contender, joins a San Francisco team with inside track on the No 1 seed looking to bolster their passing attack ahead of the playoff push. The 34-year-old veteran brings more than a decade of NFL experience and one of the league’s most reliable pairs of hands. Terms of the deal have yet to emerge.
The NFL reinstated Brandon Aiyuk on Monday and gave the 49ers a two-week roster exemption to determine their next step with the disgruntled former All-Pro wide receiver.
Aiyuk had been on the reserve/left squad list since December 2025, when he stopped reporting to the Niners while rehabbing a knee injury.
It doesn’t sound like Aiyuk will be making any return to San Francisco – coach Kyle Shanahan said on Monday that the status change “means absolutely nothing to our team” – and they could attempt to trade him before today’s deadline. Will teams want to sign him given the fact that he hasn’t played a game since December 2024, and even during that season, he had just 374 receiving yards in seven games? The league also told Aiyuk and the players union last week that it believes he must repay the Niners $13m in already-paid bonuses for failing to participate in team activities.
His agent, Drew Rosenhaus, seems to believe a team will take the chance. On the Pat McAfee Show today, he said: “I think that in all likelihood Brandon will probably sign with a team that knows him, somebody that has somehow been affiliated with him either in college or the 49ers. That’s just my guess.”
The Falcons are signing kicker Jake Moody off the Ravens’ practice squad and releasing fellow Nick Folk, according to insider Jordan Schultz.
Moody had a 53-yard field goal and an extra point in his debut for the Ravens last Thursday. Folk, a 19-year veteran of the league, missed his fifth field-goal attempt of the season in Atlanta’s loss to the Bengals in Madrid on Sunday.
Who are the Vikings’ options on the quarterback market?
They have the best defense in the NFL and an excellent group of position players, headlined by wide receiver Justin Jefferson. A competent quarterback could be the difference between wasted windows and Super Bowl contention. Some of the names being thrown around:
Eagles-Bengals trade for DE Arnold Ebikeite falls through
With just under four hours until the deadline, we’ve gone from one trade on the day to minus-1. NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Jordan Schultz report that the Bengals’ trade with the Eagles for Arnold Ebikeite has been called off.
Rapoport says it was scratched by the Bengals “with an eye toward keeping a future compensatory draft pick they would’ve lost with this deal” and that the agreement had not been finalized. That compensatory draft pick would have been the one the Bengals were to receive for former edge rusher Trey Hendrickson signing with Baltimore this year in free agency.
The Jaguars have reportedly received calls about wideout Brian Thomas Jr, but ESPN says they have told teams they aren’t interested and have no plans to trade him.
Thomas was the 23rd overall pick in the 2024 draft and had a breakout season as a rookie, with 87 catches for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns plus Pro Bowl honors. His production has dramatically dropped since: he has 10 catches for 117 yards and two touchdowns. He received zero targets from Jacksonville quarterback Trevor Lawrence in Thursday’s loss to the Ravens.
Not a trade, but an NFL development nonetheless: Dolphins defensive tackle Zach Sieler will undergo season-ending surgery on his ruptured biceps, per ESPN.
Sieler was hurt during Miami’s loss to the Lions. He had recorded 24 tackles and two sacks in eight games this season.
The Dolphins are 1-7 and stuck at the bottom of the AFC East standings. Sieler’s absence leaves a hole in their defensive line.
Jordon Hudson is suing two Airbnb hosts over a Ring doorbell camera video of a shirtless Bill Belichick. Hudson says that the 2023 clip invaded her privacy by prompting public disclosure of her relationship with the former Patriots coach.
The Lions strengthened their depleted secondary on Monday, trading for Jets safety Andre Cisco in exchange for a 2028 sixth-round pick. Cisco has played in nine games this season for New York but wasn’t a regular starter. Detroit are down two safeties in star Kerby Joseph, who is out with a knee injury, and Thomas Harper, who is on injured reserve.
I’m sure you’ll hear more on this topic later today from the Guardian’s resident Philadelphian Bryan Armen Graham, but for now! After trading Arnold Ebiketie to the Bengals, the Eagles now up to 10 owned picks in the 2027 draft.
Philadelphia are in the middle of a seven-game losing streak, the franchise’s worst skid since 2012. General manager Howie Roseman is stocking up.
The Colts have had a busy few weeks. After a 2-4 start, they fired longtime GM Chris Ballard. They traded eight-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.
The big question is how much that fire sale continues today. There’s speculation Indianapolis could trade away star running back Jonathan Taylor or quarterback Daniel Jones – or even the both of them.
Several insiders around the NFL have said Taylor would command a high package – perhaps similar to what Christian McCaffrey went for when he was traded from the Panthers to the 49ers in 2022 for a second-, third- and fourth-round pick in the 2023 draft, plus a fifth-round pick in 2024. The Giants have been floated as a potential landing spot, but it’s unclear if they could give the Colts what they want.
The Eagles are still making moves, trading edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie to the Bengals for a 2027 sixth-round pick, per multiple reports.
A second-round pick by Atlanta in 2022, Ebiketie has 16.5 sacks in his career. He spent four seasons with the Falcons and then joined the Eagles this offseason on a one-year, $7.3m contract.
A team to watch today: the Minnesota Vikings. If you watched them on Monday night, you’ll know about their messy quarterback situation. Regular starter Kyler Murray is out with a hamstring injury; Carson Wentz, the 33-year-old veteran backup, was dreadful against the Bills, going 8-for-25 for 81 yards and three turnovers. His completion percentage was the worst by a quarterback with at least 10 attempts in a game this season.
Murray is considered week-to-week, but the offense has been mediocre even with him. Minnesota traded away JJ McCarthy, the player they had selected just two years ago with the No 10 overall pick, in September. The Vikings still have the NFL’s leading scoring defense, but their offense is an obvious weakness. After a 6-0 start, they have lost two straight.
Could a reunion with Kirk Cousins be in store? The 38-year-old is the starter for the Raiders, but they also have top draft pick Fernando Mendoza waiting in the wings. Do they try for Daniel Jones, who had a short stint as the Vikings’ third-stringer in 2024?
ESPN’s Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport report that the Vikings have begun making calls around the league about trading for a quarterback.
AFC South leaders Jacksonville went all-in on Monday, adding defensive tackles Jordan Davis in a blockbuster trade with Philadelphia. The Eagles got a 2027 first-round draft pick and a 2029 second-round pick in return.
Davis has just 1.5 sacks with one interception in nine games this season, but he had career highs in 2025 with 4.5 sacks and 72 tackles. He was a first-round draft pick in 2022 and helped the Eagles beat the Chiefs in Super Bowl LIX, receiving a three-year, $78m contact on the heels of that win.
Monday’s trade capped a trio of defensive moves by the Jaguars, who have won five of their last six games. They also traded for Falcons safety Jessie Bates III and for Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux.
In total, the Jaguars gave up six future draft picks. If the season ended today, they would be the No 3 seed in the AFC. They clearly think they can go higher.
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the 2026 NFL trade deadline. After weeks of splashy moves, swirling rumors and increasingly frantic speculation, we’re finally approaching the moment of truth. The clock is ticking and all 32 teams have until 4pm ET (9pm GMT) to get their affairs in order.
It’s already been an eventful trading season. The Chicago Bears made the biggest splash by acquiring All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans for a package including two first-round draft picks. The Jacksonville Jaguars made a trio of moves to bolster their defense, headlined by a trade with Philadelphia to land defensive tackle Jordan Davis. The Indianapolis Colts have been busy dismantling their roster, shipping eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to Seattle and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to San Francisco. Meanwhile, Marvin Harrison Jr has landed in Houston, Joey Porter Jr has joined Dallas and the injury-ravaged Baltimore Ravens have brought in veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett.
But plenty of questions remain unanswered. Will Indianapolis continue their fire sale by parting with star running back Jonathan Taylor? Which contenders will make one last push for reinforcements? And could another blockbuster deal emerge before the window slams shut?
We’ll be following every confirmed trade, credible rumor and last-minute development throughout the day, with instant analysis of what the moves mean for the playoff race and beyond.
Strap in. Deadline day has arrived and there’s plenty still to play out.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: F1 star Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Bilge Kotan
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
F1 star Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border
Formula One star Lewis Hamilton visited Egypt's Rafah border crossing on Tuesday and met aid workers delivering assistance to the war-battered Gaza Strip, according to an Egyptian government statement.
North Sinai governor "Khaled Megawer took Lewis Hamilton on a visit to the Rafah land crossing to learn about the Egyptian efforts to support the Palestinian brothers in the Gaza Strip", the statement read.
Video shared by Megawer's office showed the seven-time world champion greeting aid workers and learning about their efforts to get supplies into Gaza, where this week heavy rains swept away tens of thousands of tents.
According to a truce struck by Israel and Hamas last year, at least 600 trucks of aid per day should enter Gaza, where more than two million people are facing a severe humanitarian crisis.
Aid workers say only a fraction of that amount is being allowed through by Israeli authorities, who control all entry into the territory.
Over 74,500 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/mi.title: Michigan election: How Abdul El-Sayed's critics smeared his defence of Palestinians as 'hate'
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/mi.author: Murad Idris
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/mi.text:
Michigan election: How Abdul El-Sayed's critics smeared his defence of Palestinians as 'hate'
In his victory speech last week, Abdulrahman El-Sayed, the first Muslim American elected to the US Senate, said "hate" or "hateful" five times, and each time the word did something different.
He recalled supporters asking why he never called his opponents hateful. Those opponents, he said, "hate the idea" of an America big enough for people who pray differently.
He told Mike Rogers, the Republican he had just beaten, "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope." Then he turned to those who call people hateful for believing that Palestinian children should not be killed with American tax dollars: "That's not hate. It's love."
In one speech, Sayed declined the word "hate", turned it around, used it as a weapon and refused it as a name. The rhetoric of hate is the currency of American politics. It gets minted, exchanged and spent, and it buys moral standing, which converts into votes and endorsements.
Everyone trades in it, including the man it was aimed at, but its real value is sorting groups into those accused of hate and those who make the accusation.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Follow its circulation through Michigan. "Hate" hounded Sayed throughout his campaign. Rogers regularly denounced his "hateful ideology". One Democrat told CNN he could not vote for Sayed "because I'm against hate".
Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens, whom Sayed beat in the primary, switched her endorsement to Rogers, "choosing country over hate". She announced it after attending services with Rogers at a prominent Black church in Detroit, as his party courted Black and Jewish voters.
Hours before the polls opened, US President Donald Trump posted: "Abdul El-Sayed Hates Jews and Hates Blacks." A year earlier, as New Yorkers voted, he had called Zohran Mamdani, the Muslim candidate for mayor of New York, "a proven and self professed JEW HATER".
The word comes back around. In Vanity Fair, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates noted that Stevens, having accused Sayed of hate, had joined "the campaign of hate, of which El-Sayed is the latest victim". Its purpose, he wrote, is "to render Muslims and Arabs more killable".
Minted in Michigan
See how it gets minted. The fight's last round began with an ad from Rebellion PAC, an outside group not connected to Sayed's campaign. It ties grocery prices to US military aid to Israel. It is guns versus butter, one of the oldest arguments in American politics.
Stevens nonetheless said the ad blamed "Israel and Jews". Those last words turn a dispute over funding a state into a people's guilt. This was, for her, "hate".
Researchers at the Washington-based Center for the Study of Organized Hate counted 38,280 Islamophobic posts naming Sayed between January and August, which they called "anti-Muslim hate". The Michigan office of the Council on American-Islamic Relations reported three death threats in three days after an anti-Muslim protest in Dearborn.
Aimed at Rogers, hate means bigotry and fear-mongering. Aimed at El-Sayed, it means bigotry, too, plus terrorism and radicalism: a threat
Sayed spoke at a "Hate Has No Home in Michigan" event in the city in August. A month later, when Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas named him at his party's midterm convention in Dallas, a man in the crowd shouted: "He should be shot!" The word "hate" circulates in every direction, but it does not trade at the same value.
Rogers settled his own account cheaply. He asked his opponent at their last debate: "Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Spoken in the name of national security, the accusation cost him nothing.
His earlier claim that Sayed supported the Muslim Brotherhood had cost him one line from a spokesperson, who told a fact-checker that he "vehemently condemns hate against all religious groups". To win Stevens's support, Rogers had to disavow nothing, including the multiple ads that racialised Sayed as "dangerous" and "radical".
Aimed at Rogers, hate means bigotry and fear-mongering. Aimed at Sayed, it means bigotry, too, plus terrorism and radicalism: a threat.
Whether Sayed disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, a group no evidence ties him to, or disclaimed an ad he did not make, the accusation stuck. A Muslim candidate is handed a text to recite, and yet whatever he says is not quite it.
Balancing the books
Even the ostensible peacemakers balance the books. Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Dingell found hate on all sides: in the ads targeting Arab-American Muslims, in the grocery ad, in a country being torn apart.
Every community's account gets credited, and an ad about an appropriation, no matter how crude, is entered at the same value as one casting a Michigan-born doctor as a Brotherhood loyalist.
The framing also misnames the culprit. A feeling and heated rhetoric did not tear the world apart.
Wars, the budgets that fund them, the campaigns and institutional norms that have long treated Muslims as suspects, the conflation of Jews with Israel to justify sending military aid to a foreign state that stands accused of genocide and apartheid - that is what is doing that work. Calling all of it hate discounts those choices.
Sayed, too, traded in this currency. "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope" might be a satisfying line, especially after an anti-Muslim and anti-Arab racist campaign that featured more foghorns than dog whistles, but it misnames the problem. The speech itself offers a better name.
Sayed described a corporate advertising campaign "built to deceive and distract", and put the pro-Israel lobbying group Aipac's spending against him at $42m. That is a description of power: who paid, for what, and to whose benefit? Calling it hate turns a strategy into a feeling, which can be deplored but not explained. Spending the word keeps the currency in circulation.
His sharpest line refuses the currency outright. To say "that's not hate" is to say the word misnames the thing, and here he is right. Hate asks what is in a speaker's heart, not whether the claim is true.
It turns a political claim into an emotion - the wrong emotion - or into how other people's supposed emotions make us feel. If it is about hate, nobody has to debate aid or Gaza, and Palestinian children vanish from the account.
Sayed brought them back and then went straight to the budget: what Michigan's taxes should buy here, and what they should not fund abroad. That is the argument the accusation exists to prevent.
The morning after his victory, the first question put to the senator-elect on MS Now was what he would do to protect Jewish voters "in this era of antisemitism": the text to recite, handed to him once more.
He answered that standing up against the killing of Palestinian children "is not about hate for anybody", and that he would hate for anyone to assume he accepted the abuses of Egypt's government because he shares the ethnicity of most Egyptians.
The price of unity
In Michigan, the accusation of hate failed to buy the Senate seat, but the currency itself still circulates. "Hate" will outlive the ballot. It is the keyword of American politics around Muslim candidates, Arabs and Palestine. In practice, its working opposite was not "love", as Sayed claimed. It was unity.
Democrats staged unity events, and Sayed called former Vice President Kamala Harris's visit a matter of unity, standing with a leader of the administration that armed Israel's genocide in Gaza. Former President Barack Obama, whose drone wars killed Muslims from Pakistan to Yemen, came too.
Neither of them carries the word that stuck to Sayed. Against hate, unity asks only who stands together. It demands erasing what they have done. The first Muslim senator will now be welcome as proof that the country is big enough, never mind what it keeps doing.
The point is not Sayed as a person, or his commitments, convictions or compromises. It is not to take away from the historic nature of his victory or what he might be able to accomplish. In fact, he likely understands the hate currency, how it works, and how and when to use it best.
The point, however, is the structural conditions under which some kind of "victory" alongside Democrats who stand "against hate" is possible. This was the price to be paid: continuing to accept "hate" as the framework and permitting unity to displace critical analysis and accountability.
Ask of every transaction: who minted it, where it is accepted, what it bought, and who paid. This time it did not buy a Senate seat. Arabs and Muslims in Michigan paid anyway.

Welcome to Worth it, where Filter editors spotlight one genuinely good discount on something we have tested and loved. Each week, we filter endless sales so you don’t have to.
At the Filter, we’re on a mission to reduce microplastics and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (Pfas) in our kitchens. It is a gradual process, but even small amounts of some Pfas are unsafe to consume. And though we don’t entirely know how bad microplastics are for our health, their growing prevalence everywhere (even the soil) is causing concern.
This past year we have tested plastic-free cutting boards, non-toxic pans, food storage containers and other kitchen tools to help you make well-informed decisions.
 
Items free of Pfas and microplastics are investments, so we like to spotlight good deals when we find them. This week, we’re sharing two non-toxic cookware discounts worth a look. Both ranked highly in our testing.
The big deal
Our Place Titanium Always Pan Pro 8.5in $129 $155
After testing 13 non-toxic pans, Our Place’s Titanium Always Pan Pro emerged as our “best overall” winner.
“It heated up quickly, eggs slid off the pan smoothly, and proteins got an even sear despite the micro-dot ridges on the pan’s surface (that help with the non-stick effect),” write the scientists at Drexel’s Food Lab.
It’s worth it if … you’re ready to invest in a Pfas-free, non-stick pan or need a pan that can withstand high heat (this one is safe for temperatures up to 1,000F or 537C).
Other non-toxic kitchen deals we recommend
These products are also all Pfas-free and reviewed by us here at the Filter US.
- Material Kitchen Mk Free Board for $40 $59: The MK free board was a top performer in our best cutting boards testing, working particularly well with raw meat. It’s made from a plant-based bioplastic that leaves behind “no permanent microplastics”. “It’s slim, but has a small juice groove that held exactly the amount of liquid expressed from a whole, raw chicken while I stuffed and trussed it for roasting,” wrote Marian Bull, a food writer and tester. “It didn’t pick up any smells, and I really loved the color options.” (Sale ends 2 December 2026)
- Our Place Ceramic Cookware set for $189 $240: After testing to find the best induction cookware sets, Our Place’s two-piece set was ruled as the “best designed”. Its lid can lock or let out steam, wooden utensils have set spots to rest and more.
- Caraway Baking & Cooling ceramic baking sheet and rack for $93 $115: Emily Farris, a veteran kitchen product reviewer, recommended Caraway’s sheet and rack in our guide to Caraway products. She’s a fan of the large baking sheet’s ability to handle high heat and produce perfectly browned food. However, she did note that its non-stick coating will wear off over time.
- Our Place Wonder Oven Pro for $275 $325: This summer, we partnered with scientists at Drexel’s Food Lab, who cooked with 10 air fryers to help us find the best-performing models. Our Place’s Wonder Oven stood out for its non-toxic, Pfas free stainless steel interior and food surfaces – along with its ability to produce crispy fries and evenly baked chocolate chip cookies.
- Anyday Anydeli containers for $39 $46: Last week, we highlighted a sale on Anyday’s round glass containers. While those are still on sale, its plastic-free deli containers are also marked down. As Farris wrote, Anyday’s containers are “endlessly versatile, lightweight and durable enough to send in my kids’ lunchboxes without worry”.
Why you should trust our recommendations
after newsletter promotion
We work for our readers, rather than the brands we write about. Every item we recommend is something a Filter editor or contributor has personally tested and can vouch for. On occasion, we may present a close substitute from the same brand and explain any differences from the original.
We scour competing retailers for the lowest prices on any item, and we use price-tracking tools such as Camelcamelcamel to check price history and ensure the discounts are truly good value, rather than a faux markdown. (So, while we love sharing good deals, we also aren’t afraid to call out the unimpressive ones.)
Our mission at the Filter US
Our mission is to help you filter out junk products and buy fewer, better things.
At the Filter US, we test the products we recommend ourselves and never take your trust for granted. We also consider possible impacts on your health or the environment in our coverage and companies cannot purchase a spot in our product rankings because we are here to serve you, not corporations.
Our dedicated testing, editing and production teams are based across the United States and Canada. We are a part of the Guardian’s US editorial team and our journalists follow its strict ethical standards. Learn more about us here.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/gcc-e.text:
GCC to establish joint forward-command centre in Kuwait
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) has approved a new joint forward-command centre to deepen military integration among members, as doubts rise about the US’s commitment to regional security amid the war on Iran.
The command centre will be built in Kuwait, a Gulf state that endured thousands of missile and drone strikes from Iran and Iraqi militias aligned with Tehran.
GCC secretary general Jasem al-Budaiwi said in a statement on Tuesday that the deployment of "appropriate" forces to the centre would take place, but did not provide additional details.
The GCC body representing six Gulf states established a joint defence agreement in 2000, stating that an attack on one member is an attack on all.
The GCC’s commitment to self-defence, however, is not as ironclad as that of the Nato military alliance.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The move could be seen as an effort to address the GCC's lack of a joint military command structure. The organisation has failed to respond to attacks on members from several fronts.
The GCC did not respond when Israel attacked Hamas negotiators in Doha, Qatar, in September 2025. The organisation has also failed to respond to devastating Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The decision to base the command centre in Kuwait may also raise questions about its practical viability.
Kuwait’s geography at the hook of the Gulf made it especially vulnerable to missile and drone attacks from both Iran and Iraqi militias during the war.
Kuwait hosted around 14,000 US troops before the war, more than any other country in the Middle East. It is home to two large bases - Camp Arifjan and Ali al-Salem Air Base - both of which came under intense attack from Iran.
It's unclear how the GCC could defend a command centre when the US could not defend its bases.
US security guarantees in doubt
Gulf states have turned to external partners for security. Saudi Arabia has activated the Mecca Pact with Pakistan and Turkey amid Houthi attacks.
Meanwhile, the UAE has doubled down on its security relationship with Israel.
The US has been the security guarantor of the Gulf states for over half a century. But that relationship has been called into question as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE lobbied the US against attacking Iran, but their pleas went unanswered. In retaliation, Iran attacked Gulf states that are home to US military bases.
The presence of US troops on their soil has been perceived by some Gulf analysts as making them a target.
Oman, for example, which has one of the oldest diplomatic relationships with the US, has no permanent US military presence and was the least hit Gulf state.
The US Department of War’s inspector general said in a report published in September that “hundreds of buildings and structures” at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan were damaged or destroyed by Iranian strikes.
Current and former US officials say the Iran war exposed vulnerabilities in the US’s strategy of establishing bases close to Iran and that some facilities are unlikely to be rebuilt.
“The truth is that we are not as inclined to occupy these bases now that we have seen what the Iranians can throw at them,” David Petraeus, a former director of the CIA and head of Centcom, told Bloomberg in May.
“This is much more than when I was commander at Central Command,” he added.
Another former head of Centcom, General Frank McKenzie, said in July that the US needs to relocate its bases in the Gulf to Israel and neighbouring countries to better protect its assets from Iran’s missiles and drones.
“No one in their right mind would ever put the Centcom forward headquarters, you know, 100 miles away from Iran, [in Qatar], yet that’s where it is,” he told the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, referring to al-Udeid.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Where to start with: John Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Henry Eliot
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
John Berger was born a hundred years ago today. He was an artist, critic, novelist, poet, polemicist and playwright who made impassioned, idiosyncratic, fiercely attentive and deeply humane contributions to a swathe of artistic and intellectual disciplines across six decades. In fact, the diversity of his output can make it “difficult to grasp,” as Geoff Dyer observes, in his introduction to the Selected Essays. “Even admirers tend to know him in only one or two of his many incarnations.”
I hope the recommendations below provide a somewhat representative handle on Berger’s range. I have limited myself to books he assembled himself, which means I haven’t allowed myself to include anthologies, such as the excellent Understanding a Photograph, edited by Dyer, or Tom Overton’s collections Landscapes and Portraits, or the recent selection Across a Frontier, chosen by the similarly interdisciplinary critic, photographer and novelist Teju Cole.
There are many ways to approach Berger, but wherever you choose to start, you will be encountering, as Susan Sontag said of him, “a wonderful artist and thinker”.
The entry point
Berger is best remembered for Ways of Seeing, his 1972 BBC television series and accompanying Penguin paperback. Radically, he combined art and social criticism, discussing artworks in relation to advertising, mass reproduction, the female nude, the male gaze and social status. The book’s format is equally revolutionary: the text appears to begin on the front cover, and three of the seven chapters are made up of images only. Ways of Seeing is a sui generis design classic and a swift introduction to Berger’s enduring preoccupations with art, sex and politics.
The prizewinner
The same year that Ways of Seeing was published, Berger won the fourth Booker prize with G. (1972). The novel itself has been somewhat overshadowed by Berger’s acceptance speech, in which he pilloried the sponsor Booker McConnell Ltd for their “extensive trading interests” in the Caribbean, announcing that he would be donating half his prize money to the British Black Panther movement. This experimental novel follows a young man (G) and his vigorous sex life as he travels across Europe on the eve of the first world war. G is mostly oblivious – but inextricably connected to – the world-historical events taking place around him.
The quiet masterpiece
Another excellent place to start would be A Fortunate Man (1967), the first collaboration between Berger and the Swiss photographer Jean Mohr. It is a deceptively simple portrait of a country GP in the Forest of Dean, told through stark photography and haunting prose. Word and image interweave to powerful effect: the minutiae of one man’s vocation reflect compellingly on the whole of society. Berger and Mohr became close friends working on this project and collaborated several times over the following 50 years.
The one for writers
One of Berger’s lesser-known titles is Photocopies (1996), which presents a series of exquisite prose vignettes, titled as if they were photographs. Berger captures real moments, reproducing them – photocopying them – with pinpoint attention to detail. The book has an air of delicate stillness: it is a masterclass in clarity and an inspiration for prose stylists.
The one for artists
Ways of Seeing may have made his name, but much of Berger’s best art criticism is collected in About Looking (1980), which includes essays on Turner, Giacometti, Magritte, Francis Bacon and Walt Disney. It also includes his famous essay Why Look at Animals?, which considers the fact that we rarely interact with animals today, despite living in a world full of animal imagery.
The best on photography
Berger’s third collaboration with Mohr was Another Way of Telling (1982), a revelatory investigation into the art of photography. Despite its diffident subtitle – “A Possible Theory of Photography” – this landmark work stands alongside those of Walter Benjamin, Roland Barthes and Susan Sontag. A photograph is “a meeting place,” writes Berger, “where the interests of the photographer, the photographed, the viewer and those who are using the photography are often contradictory”.
The best on politics
To some extent, everything Berger wrote was political; he was always concerned with the human experience in relation to society. One topic he wrote about repeatedly was migration, most memorably in A Seventh Man (1975), another remarkable collaboration with Mohr. This galvanising book intimately documents the experience of migrant labourers seeking work in western Europe in the early 1970s, but it remains soberingly topical today.
The one that will make you cry
G. may have won the Booker prize, but To the Wedding (1995) is Berger’s greatest novel. Through fragments of conversations, songs and silences, we follow a mother and father, estranged for many years, travelling across Europe to the wedding of their daughter Ninon. It’s both a heartbreaking story and a triumphantly optimistic celebration of love and life. Colum McCann calls it “one of the greatest and most honest love stories of our time.”
The one that deserves more attention
The wonderful Here Is Where We Meet (2005) is fiction – or is it? In 8½ chapters, “John” has a series of encounters with people who are dead: he meets his mother sitting on a park bench in Lisbon, he meets his childhood mentor in Krakow market, he stands above the grave of Jorge Luis Borges in Geneva. This is Berger at his most playful, seamlessly blending novel, essay, criticism, memoir and travelogue. It’s a brilliant, unclassifiable achievement.
The one to carry in your pocket
“This is a book I carry with me everywhere,” writes the actor and director Simon McBurney, in his new introduction to And Our Faces, My Heart, Brief as Photos (1984). “It fits into the inside pocket of my jacket, a little larger than a passport.” This slim, numinous work contains scraps and scenes about mortality, art, sex and belonging. It is organised into two halves – “Once”, about time, and “Here”, about space – and manages to condense a lifetime’s wisdom into little more than a hundred pages.
- Henry Eliot edited the 2026 Bloomsbury reissues of John Berger’s work. He is the author of five books, including The Penguin Classics Book

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/s.title: Some of NYC’s Worst Super Speeders Are City Marshals (You Know, The Guys With Badges)
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/s.author: Sammy Sussman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/s.text:
They get justice for private citizens — yet they endanger them at the same time.
City marshals — private citizens appointed by the mayor to secure civil court judgments on behalf of victorious plaintiffs — are among the city’s worst super-speeders, with just 30 of them racking up 647 speed-camera infractions and 102 red-light tickets, virtually all since 2020, city records show.
Streetsblog obtained a list of 30 city marshals who have been issued parking placards and found that all but one had racked up camera-issued tickets for reckless driving. And 12 of these law-enforcement officials — or 40 percent — have gotten at least 10 school-zone speeding tickets since 2020.
Two of these officers have gotten over 120 camera-issued school-zone speeding tickets:
- One marshal, who drives a vehicle with the license plate LEG6496, has received 125 camera-issued speeding tickets and 13 red light tickets since 2023. This marshal’s driving is only getting worse — between July 2025 and June 2026, they received 68 speed-camera and 10 red-light tickets.
- Another marshal, whose license plate is W857KP, has received 132 speeding tickets and 13 red lights tickets in a saga of unmitigated dangerous driving going back to 2014. That reckless driving remains a problem: Since January 2025, this driver has gotten 19 camera-issued tickets for speeding or running red lights.
Both drivers racked up enough tickets in different 12-month periods to be declared a “super speeder” under New York State law. Such drivers will soon be required to install speed-limiting devices inside their cars to prevent recklessness.
City pols were appalled to hear that marshals who are appointed by the mayor to enforce civil judgments won by private citizens in court are themselves law-breakers.
“No one is above the law,” said Council Member Kayla Santosuosso (D-Bay Ridge). “The most reckless drivers must be reined in, no matter who they work for or what they do.”
Meanwhile, the Department of Investigation, which oversees the marshals, admitted that it hasn’t tracked the officers’ driving patterns, but after told of Streetsblog’s findings, a spokesperson for the agency said it would now be “following up on these allegations.”
“DOI will be issuing a memo to all city marshals reminding them of their obligation to obey traffic laws,” Diane Struzzi, the department’s director of communications, told Streetsblog. “They are required to obey the law in both personal and official capacities.
“Any marshal found to display a pattern of reckless or dangerous driving could be subject to disciplinary action,” Struzzi added.
Who are these people?
City marshals occupy an often-overlooked niche in New York City’s sprawling law enforcement world: Marshals can seize assets on behalf of private citizens who won judgments in civil court. In exchange, the marshals can collect a bounty of up to 5 percent.
These officers are given city-issued placards, and they are granted broad powers to tow vehicles with more than $350 in unpaid fines, though it is unclear how often marshals actually do this work.
Given their role in the city’s law-enforcement ecosystem, it was especially hard to street safety advocates to accept that private individuals with quasi-police powers were abusing that power so flagrantly.
“City marshals can’t keep New Yorkers safe if they’re speeding recklessly around the five boroughs,” said Ben Furnas, the executive director of Transportation Alternatives. “We can’t accept repeat speeding in New York City.”
Soon, we won’t have to: Under the Stop Super-Speeders law passed by state lawmakers last year and making its way through the City Council, drivers with at least 16 camera-issued school-zone speeding tickets in a 12-month period will be forced to install a speed-limiting device in all their vehicles.
Had the law been in place already, at least three of the 30 placarded marshals in Streetsblog’s data cache would have been forced to install a speed-limiter — and two marshals cleared the super-speeder threshold in at least three different 12-month periods. The worst marshal, according to this data, has actually qualified as a super-speeder in four separate calendar years.
At that egregious rate of ticketing, this driver is over 50 times more likely to be involved in a fatal or serious crash than an average driver, according to a 2024 study by DOT. This reckless driver’s speeding history puts them among the 400 worst drivers across the approximately two million drivers of personal cars in New York City — and yet the city still vests them with the power to enforce judgments and tow other cars.
It’s an eerie reminder that people in official positions — i.e. New York City employees who should know better — are occasionally caught by the press for flagrant violations of the public trust. Earlier this year, Streetsblog identified a Staten Island cop with 547 speed-camera tickets. He received 187 camera-issued tickets in 2025 alone — an average of one every other day. The only discipline he has received from the NYPD is that he no longer drives a squad car on duty.
The latest records obtained by Streetsblog do not include the name of any specific marshal, rendering it even more difficult to pressure the political system for change.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/m.title: Mamdani Administration Battling Yet Another Suit By Delivery Apps Fighting Worker Protections
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/m.text:
Two delivery workers pass each other on Chrystie Street in Manhattan. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
City officials and advocates are outraged that the tech giants behind the exploitive delivery gig economy have yet again sued to block a city law that protects delivery workers from random deactivations — a key workplace improvement that also keeps streets safer.
Last week, Uber, Instacart and Amazon sued to block new requirements to give workers “deactivation” protections — that is, giving workers 120 days’ notice before kicking them off the platform permanently and providing a reason for the deactivation; creating a progressive discipline structure so that deactivation is a last resort; and creating an independent appeals process.
The law builds on the success of the delivery worker minimum pay standard and is seen as essential for street safety because it would eliminate the constant threat of deactivation that leads to workers to put street safety on the back burner in order to keep their precarious jobs. The city vowed to defend it in court.
“The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection will not back down from protecting the rights and safety of all New Yorkers,” agency Commissioner Sam Levine said. “New York City deserves safe streets and delivery workers deserve dignity and due process.”
One progressive lawmaker slammed the corporations for the latest suit, which follows an earlier effort to defeat the minimum wage law.
“Every single time we’ve passed a piece of legislation to protect these workers, the [delivery companies] have spent a ton of money to stop the bill. They lose, and then they spend a ton of money on legal challenges that they ultimately lose and end up having to settle,” said Council Member Sandy Nurse (D-Bushwick). “They have a lot of money to burn, and instead of burning it, they should just pay their workers and find ways to work with the city and DCWP to protect them and come up with fair agreements. It’s not hard, but they don’t want to jeopardize their bottom line.”
In the latest case, Amazon, Uber, and Instacart are making a federal case of their opposition, suing on Oct. 28 in the Southern District of New York to stop the law from taking effect in January. The complaint alleges that Local Law 34, which passed last year, violates the constitutional rights of the companies because it undermines their “ability to exercise their own respective business judgments about who is allowed access to their applications.”
The companies also argue that sharing details about deactivations with workers would put customers at risk and could give so-called “fraudsters” information on how to better defraud the system.
“Uber also does not disclose details of its decision when it has deactivated a courier based on fraudulent activity because doing so would provide couriers with information they could exploit to evade Uber’s fraud-detection mechanisms in the future,” the complaint reads.
Instacart had a similar rationale. The company said that even “limited detail” can allow one of its contracted workers to “identify the customers who filed the report.” The company claims around 5 percent of its workers were deactivated in the past year, thats around 600 of the 12,000 grocery delivery workers the company claimed in its city-mandated reports.
Amazon said it contracts around 73,400 “flex” workers, who use the company’s app to do deliveries with their personal cars. The Bezosian behemoth said its deactivation rate was around 2.9 percent, which translates to about 2,100 human beings.
Instacart said in a statement that the law “would make it harder to protect against fraud, theft, harassment, and unsafe conduct” and that it joined the lawsuit “to protect the safety and trust that shoppers, customers, and retail partners expect us to uphold.”
Amazon concurred, but also argued that the law is unconstitutional.
“Amazon Flex enables tens of thousands of New Yorkers to earn money on their own terms, and deactivations are rare, reserved for serious issues such as theft, fraud, safety, and service violations,” said company spokesperson Steve Kelly. “This law would put customers at risk by hampering our ability to act quickly against misconduct and uphold the standards that keep deliveries safe and reliable. A federal court has already blocked the nearly identical companion law for ride-share drivers, concluding it’s likely unconstitutional.”
Kelly was referring to a ruling earlier this year by a different Southern District judge that blocked a city law that sought to protect Uber and Lyft drivers from the same types of deactivation. That law, indeed, has yet to take effect as a result of the judge’s injunction.
Cutting through the legalese, the city’s delivery workers are adamant that deactivations lead to unsafe streets.
“These corporations use the threat of deactivation to pressure delivery workers to move faster and complete more orders, putting workers’ lives and livelihoods at risk,” the Worker’s Justice Project’s Los Deliveristas Unidos said in a statement. “Worker safety is public safety.”
That echoed a recent report by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection that identified worker protections “essential” for street safety.
For its part, the City Council defended its work to protect the large delivery workforce.
“It is the Council’s responsibility to ensure that all working New Yorkers are safeguarded from worker exploitation and are given the opportunity to earn a sustainable living wage,” said the Council’s spokesperson Sophia Saidi. “Speaker [Julie] Menin has made worker protection a top priority, especially vulnerable and low-wage workers, as New Yorkers across the board continue to face rising costs of living.”
Uber did not respond to Streetsblog’s request for comment. It is unclear why DoorDash and Wonder, which owns Seamless and Grubhub, are not part of the suit; neither company responded to Streetsblog’s request for comment.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/o.title: OPINION: New York City’s Trash Revolution Should Be an Accessibility Revolution, Too
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/o.author: William Juhn, Anna Humphrey, Sharon McLennon Wier
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/o.text:
Our narrow and crowded sidewalks have always created an obstacle course for disabled New Yorkers. The city’s ubiquitous practice of piling trash bags on sidewalks is one of the biggest reasons why. Many residents consider the resulting mountains of garbage as mere eyesores, but they are a matter of life and death for people with disabilities. Huge mounds of refuse force the disabled community into moving traffic, block curb cuts and create unpredictable hazards that lead to injury and death. 
Formally known as the Citywide Containerization Program, New York City’s so-called “trash revolution” is an overdue step toward cleaner streets. The program will require residential buildings with up to nine units to use individual bins, while buildings with 10 to 30 residential units can choose between individual bins or stationary on-street receptacles known as Empire Bins. Buildings with more than 30 residential units will use Empire Bins.
Done right, the program can also serve as an “accessibility revolution” by delivering cleaner sidewalks, safer streets and a more accessible city for all New Yorkers. Unless the city designs the program with accessibility in mind, however, its leaders risk replacing one kind of barrier with another. 
Unbroken lines of bins placed on sidewalks make navigating the street difficult for low-vision or blind New Yorkers who use orientation and mobility canes to negotiate sidewalks. Rows of bins interrupt otherwise continuous building lines, creating unpredictable and hazardous obstacles that increase the risk of tripping or veering into moving traffic. 
In densely populated neighborhoods with narrow sidewalks, clusters of bins shrink the clear path needed by wheelchair users, individuals using walkers, and people using other mobility devices. Overturned bins, loose lids and misaligned containers can easily block curb cuts, bus stops and building entrances.
Empire Bins and moveable dumpsters can address these problems because they clear sidewalks of bins and bags. The city can encourage smaller buildings to share bins rather than use individual ones. To advance the City’s climate and zero waste goals, Empire Bins must be able to collect recycling and compost, too — keeping even more bags away from walking paths. 
This is a promising approach, but it will require careful planning to execute. Empire Bins can also obstruct curb access — a dangerous outcome for Access-A-Ride and taxi users who may be forced to board within, or disembark into, active traffic lanes. And Empire Bins placed too close to crosswalks or curb cuts can obstruct sightlines between shorter pedestrians or wheelchair users and oncoming traffic, increasing the risk of injuries and deaths. 
New York City can and should ensure that its waste management goals benefit all New Yorkers. We cannot sacrifice the rights, safety, and independence of pedestrians with disabilities. Accessibility must be a foundational requirement, not an afterthought. 
To accomplish all of this, the Department of Sanitation must:
1. Make sidewalks truly waste-free 
Sanitation should expand the use of Empire Bins to smaller buildings and begin working on a way to accept recycling and compost. While the agency deserves credit for launching a pilot in Brooklyn that allows smaller buildings to share Empire Bins, the larger program must formally replace individual bins and bags with Empire Bins. Sidewalks must be clear of all bins and bags. 
2. Partner with the disability community 
For decades, siloed New York City agencies stalled containerization. Now that the program is underway, Sanitation must proactively partner with the disability community and agencies such as the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities. Together, they can develop clear and enforceable placement guidelines consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act and state and local accessibility laws. 
For example: Empire Bins should never be placed within 20 feet of curb cuts, crosswalks, Access-A-Ride pickup zones or bus stops. On dense residential blocks that will receive large numbers of bins, Sanitation must consider the construction of additional mid-block crosswalks and loading zones to accommodate people with disabilities.
3. Create real oversight and accountability 
DSNY must develop transparent mechanisms for oversight and accountability, including accessibility and safety reviews for every Empire Bin location. The agency must also establish a formal process to allow people with disabilities to request relocation of bins that impede access or create safety concerns, and those requests must be addressed promptly. 
Containerization is one of the most significant changes to New York City’s streetscape in decades, and this is the rare chance to solve two long-standing problems at once. The trash revolution must also be an accessibility revolution, precisely because we want a city that every resident can access. This opportunity must not go to waste.

Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
