Gen Z Postcards From a Stunning Election Night
We asked students coast to coast to describe what it felt like to witness the 2026 midterms blue wave.
Gerrymandering—the process of manipulating election maps in ways that are likely to produce particular outcomes—has long been either a feature or a bug in the United States, depending on whom you ask. In either case, it’s been pervasive. Due to a series of recent Supreme Court rulings, it got much more severe and frequent this past election cycle.
The results were said to be foregone. There was talk of GOP incumbency lasting generations. But it was not to be. In one illuminating example, North Carolina Democrat LaKesha Womack defeated incumbent Republican Tim Moore in North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District, a seat widely viewed as safe for Republicans. The upset was stunning: Moore was one of the most powerful politicians in the state and helped draw his own district while serving in the General Assembly. NC’s 14th, however, includes many students. And yesterday young voters in North Carolina joined an unprecedented wave of their peers in a decisive rebuke of Republicans and their redistricting tricks.
Nationally, young people overwhelmingly voted for Democratic candidates in the 2026 midterm elections: An estimated 72 percent of those aged 18–29 voted for a Democrat for the US House of Representatives, compared to 25 percent for a Republican. According to Tufts’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE), a nonpartisan research organization focused on youth civic engagement, “the strong 47-point youth preference for Democrats in 2026 is the highest we have ever seen in a national election.” Meanwhile, in key Senate races, the 18–29-year-old demographic also voted blue in droves—Florida (74 percent), Kansas (80 percent), Maine (74 percent), and Michigan (67 percent).
This is historic stuff and StudentNation correspondents were out in force reporting from polling sites, watch parties, and campus events. From coast to coast, our writers reflected young people’s undeniable appetite for change. Written from Alaska, Texas, Michigan, Indiana, Kansas, New York, Rhode Island, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and overseas, these postcards from a stunning election night offer a glimpse into the hope and rage animating young voters today.
—The Editors
Nome, Alaska—Wind kicked dirt into mini-tornadoes as it made its way to the ocean. By 9:30 am, the sun had burned its mark onto the horizon over the subarctic beach town. Nome residents pulled into the parking lot of Old St. Joe’s leaving their trucks running, as they went in to cast their vote. Inside, election workers ask “How’s your auntie?” before checking IDs.
“I didn’t vote for the current president, but I did hear what he had to say, and it sounded all good,” electrical lineman Perry Saito said.“It was all the great promises that everybody wanted, but none of them came true. I’m tired of the lies.”
Locally, voters seemed unbothered by rumors of ballot stacking by Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign. “It doesn’t faze me one bit,” Adam Lust said while picketing for Democrats.
Old St. Joe’s, a Gothic revival church built in 1901 now serves as a community gathering space and election site for all of Nome. Inside, bright lights and parabolic ceilings cultivate a sense of duty. Voters shuffled forward in lines. A first-time voter received a standing ovation from the pollsters.
An Alaskan Native from rural Alaska, Peltola is the obvious choice for many in the region.
“I’m an Alaska Native. I would trust another Alaska Native over who’s been in office,” Terra Abbott said as she waited for friends to finish casting their vote.
In rural Alaska, day-to-day issues, like fishing and hunting rights, or the exorbitant costs of extremely rural living, aren’t understood by many in the Lower 48—the US mainland.
Amanda Van Vliet’s family just bought a woodstove, she explained while picketing across the street from one of two gas stations in town. The price of unleaded fuel is now $7.39.
“We paid like $10,000 for diesel to heat our house last year,” Van Vliet said. “And now we have a bunch of foster kids and that cost is going up.
Guadalupe Callahan, a recent college graduate, grew up in Nome, hunting, fishing, and frolicking in Alaska’s natural playground. This year, her and her friends are voting for candidates who don’t see the state as “a land sack of soil and oil.”
“I’ve grown up here my entire life. I fish all the time, I go out hunting all the time, and I think the only way to keep doing that is if we preserve the land we’re on,” Callahan said.
“People always say, ‘Oh Alaska, that’s a red state’ but I don’t know why there’s that idea that you are what you are,” Callahan said. “If Texas can be blue, sure enough, Alaska can too.”
Anna Lionas, University of Alaska, Fairbanks ’26/
Reporter, Nome Nugget
Boston, Massachusetts—At the Boston College Democrats midterm watch party, every election had a sound. When Amy Acton won the governor’s race in Ohio, the AI-generated, meme-ified song “We Are Charlie Kirk” played over the speakers. When Chris Pappas won a Senate seat in nearby New Hampshire, air horns blared. When Angie Nixon faltered in Florida, a fart noise followed.
At a school that students say “isn’t political,” memes like this are how the midterms wormed their way into public discourse.
Boston College was among the lowest-ranked schools in the Foundation for Individual Rights and Free Expression “free speech” rankings due to administrative censorship of protests and rampant self-censorship among students. So what does the campus speech climate really feel like?
Junior Connor Moquin put it this way: “It’s like, if you’re at the Thanksgiving dinner table with all your relatives, you’re not gonna bring up politics in front of your Trump uncle and then start a huge fight, right?” Moquin said. “It’s the vibe that I get coming to campus.”
So even in a room like this one, where attendees were decked out in blue and most people shared political views, humor became the way to sidestep controversial conversations and cut through students’ broader alienation from politics.
“They have to keep people engaged in, like, a culture of—or at least a projection of—apathy,” freshman Finn Kerns said.
The use of humor was accompanied by a broader push to appeal to a wide range of students. Freddy Osborne, president of BC College Democrats, said that he has tried to steer away from activism related to specific issues, like Gaza. Instead, he thinks focusing on democratic participation and political discussions more broadly will help widen the tent, even to those who don’t consider themselves Democrats.
“There are people I know who, like, probably didn’t vote, or probably didn’t vote for a Democrat who are here right now,” Osborne said. “I really wish BC had more of these spaces.”
As for the fart noises, those are just to make the news more entertaining for the people in the room. “Well, politics is crazy now, right? It’s really stressful,” Aalok Bhattacharya said. “And so, I think the more joy we can bring to politics, the better.”
When James Talarico flipped the Texas Senate, the air horns blared again as Bhattacharya added his own complementary commentary.
“It’s confirmed, God has six genders now.”
Genevieve Morrison, Boston College
New Haven, Connecticut—The campus wasn’t fully awake when the alarm went off—out of Sterling Memorial Library came students, librarians, and the families of hopeful applicants, spilling onto the grassy quadrangle.
Then the white fire trucks—two of them—ripped through High Street from opposite directions and idled there, shoulder to shoulder, before the main branch of the third-largest academic library in North America. In went the firefighters—to evacuate people, to keep at least one campus tour from glimpsing the nave, and, if it could be managed, to save the 4 million books.
No. No fire. False alarm!
The firefighters left in quick succession. And the tour group was already onto the next Gothic attraction.
It was Tuesday, and there were signs that it was Tuesday. Monterey Jack quesadillas. Beef tacos! Some students knew it was Election Day. Their professors, it appeared, did not—there were still classes. It was the midterms, or what a particularly funny person, feeling optimistic, might call Liberation Day.
By nightfall, there were watch parties and 30 members of the Yale Political Union’s Progressive Party, gathered in Saybrook College’s TV Room.
I met with the union to ask them about the possibility of another false alarm—was this a blue wave? Or a blue mirage?
Savan Parikh, the president of the Yale Political Union and a member of the Progressive Party, went into the night more pessimistic than the polls, “because I felt so betrayed by the polls” the last few cycles. Had he feared that their predictions were a false alarm?
“Certainly. Certainly.”
And now?
“Better. Yeah, better. A lot better.”
Then NBC called Texas for Talarico—72 percent of voters under 30, the exit polls were saying! The room erupted—AAAAAHHHH!
“What I’m seeing tonight is a lot of screaming,” said Massimo Mejia, chair of the Yale Political Union’s Progressive Party. “Some of our people have already lost their voice.”
Mejia cast his first vote in 2024 and remembers “such a crushing lack of hope.” But Tuesday night, he said, felt like “something new.”
There was no second false alarm Tuesday. By the time results from all over came in, the campus, like much of the country, was engulfed in a real blaze.
“It’s a kind of fire,” Mejia said, “that we haven’t seen on the left for a long time.”
Zachary Clifton, Yale University
Ann Arbor, michigan—At 2:15 pm, I rounded the corner to the campus polling site and was greeted by a swarm of students and local news stations gathered on the adjacent road.
Cars struggled to pass through the street while students and reporters tried to get a sense of what was happening. Soon it became clear: At the center of the commotion was the man himself, US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Students rushed to get a photo with him while cameras rolled and local stations clamored for interviews. University of Michigan sophomore Kamya Jariwala was one of the many students in the crowd.
“I have never seen that many people so excited to be involved in politics,” Jariwala said. “There was a long line just to see him. Just to get a glimpse of him.”
El-Sayed’s connection to the University of Michigan as an alumnus has resonated deeply with students. “It’s very important to have politicians who are in touch with the student body—elected officials who have roots in the state that they’re running in so they understand how to represent their electorate,” Jariwala said.
Beyond the bustle surrounding El-Sayed, Election Day was marked by long lines stretching outside polling locations, volunteers encouraging students to cast their ballots, and voters preparing to wait hours for their turn. When I returned to a polling site later in the day, lines continued to wrap around buildings, with some students reporting estimated wait times of up to two hours.
Despite the lengthy waits, students such as sophomore Alexa Sohn remained committed to casting their ballots in person on Election Day. “Everyone’s on the same page that we should all vote, especially because this is a really big time for our generation,” Sohn said. “That’s why I waited until Election Day to vote, so I could experience the best atmosphere possible.”
Sarayu Bongale, The University of Michigan
Houston, Texas—Thunder cracked over Sewall Hall at Rice University in Houston all Tuesday afternoon. I watched students line up to vote between classes, some waiting nearly half an hour, others taking shelter from the rain. The storm came in bursts, the voters in a steady flow.
Shem Brown had brought his notes. On one side of the page was material for class. On the other, a list of candidates he wanted to remember in the voting booth.
Brown, a Rice University senior, had read voter guides and followed the campaigns closely. He was confident about James Talarico’s prospects, less so about Gina Hinojosa’s. He had seen plenty of advertising for the former and far less for the latter.
Hinojosa was seeking to become the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990. “I really want Gina Hinojosa to win,” Brown said. “But I really think that Talarico is gonna win,” he continued, knocking on a wooden bench outside the polling station. “I just have so much faith in his campaign.”
“Texas is ready for this kind of change,” Brown averred.
Not everyone shared his enthusiasm.
Stefano Marchisio, an 18-year-old, had voted for Abbott, Paxton, and Republicans down the ballot. He had done little preparation, relying partly on the judgment of his parents and mentors, “the wisest people I know.”
He wanted Abbott to remain in power, he said, “so that I have no doubts nor questions about the future government.”
Alissa Ferguson, 22, had carefully researched choices. She voted Democratic at the national level and wanted Abbott, Paxton, and Dan Patrick out of office.
For her, the stakes ranged from her rights as a woman to the future of her high school.
“My high school in far West Texas is at risk of closure and will likely shutter its doors at the end of this year,” she said. She blamed state education policies and cuts to public school funding. The alternative of private education meant little where she grew up.
“There aren’t any private schools, and even if there were, they aren’t affordable; the vast majority of the people in this area barely get by.”
She had come to vote wearing a Texas flag shirt. Behind her, a sign directed voters toward the polls in English, Spanish, Vietnamese, and Chinese.
Brown, meanwhile, was preparing to graduate. He wanted to stay in Houston but wasn’t sure he could.
“I love Texas so much,” he said, “and a lot of the time it feels like Texas does not love me back.”
Brown had been in middle school during the 2016 election. In 2024 with Trump’s election, he felt “really blindsided.” This time, he had allowed himself to believe something different might happen.
“I’m gonna lose a lot of faith in humanity if this does not work out,” he told me.
By 10:17 pm, the rain had passed and the blue surge had swept across Texas. Talarico defeated Paxton, becoming the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Texas since 1988. Hinojosa unseated Abbott and Democrats also led races for lieutenant governor, attorney general, and railroad commissioner.
After 2016, Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 defeat, which voters brought up all day, and 2024, young Texans like Brown had learned to hedge their hopes. For a trained, cynical Gen Z Texan, Tuesday night was its own version of 2006—the year of an unusually competitive, five-way gubernatorial election. They were feeling their very own version of millennial optimism.
Lajward Zahra, Rice University
Providence, Rhode Island—Students packed the lobby of Friedman Hall election night as a Ben & Jerry’s stand began handing out free scoops. With two floors of games, pizza, analysis, and midterm-themed crossword puzzles, the Brown Political Union’s election party kicked into high gear around 8 pm when the Associated Press called the Massachusetts Senate race for the incumbent Democrat.
“Ed Markey, baby!” a student shouted from Friedman 102, the lecture hall hosting the event’s main watch party.
Students scavenged for makeshift seats in aisles and on windowsills as a lanky boy in a donkey onesie flipped the stream between the Kornacki Cam and ABC. The donkey in charge, a sophomore named Indy Singh, gushed over the turnout, both in the room and across the country. “Tonight shows that this big orange guy in office isn’t invincible,” he said.
In addition to relentless cheers for upsets in Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina, the room showed school spirit for Hannah Pingree and Rob Sand, two Brown alumni who triumphed in their gubernatorial races in Maine and Iowa. With Brown alum Matt Meyer already in office in Delaware, their wins will leave Brown tied with Harvard for the most alumni serving as governor come January.
Down the hall, professor of public policy and political science Eric Patashnik fielded live updates from the audience as he lectured on election analysis. Also on the ballot Tuesday night was one of Patashnik’s former students, David Morales, the democratic socialist state representative who won decisively after beating Providence Mayor Brett Smiley in a contentious Democratic primary.
“He brings a lot of passion. He’s an amazing communicator. And he’s a part of a new generation that wants to be involved in government. So I think that’s terrific,” Patashnik said.
Meanwhile, the state’s Democratic Party was having a ball of its own downtown. What it lacked in free ice cream, it made up for at the open bar.
Hundreds crowded the 17th floor of the Hilton Providence and cheered as Morales, who at 28 will be the youngest mayor in the city’s history, took the stage. Among the many students working the room, I met Brady McCarthy, a sophomore at Roger Williams University who wants to go into politics.
“Tonight gives me a lot of hope,” he said, “especially knowing that I’m in a state that is gonna give me a lot of opportunities by having such a large Democratic majority.”
Paul Hudes, Brown University
Berkeley, California—In the first November rain, hundreds of voters lined up outside of UC Berkeley’s Eshleman Hall to cast their ballots.
From the outdoor screening of the midterm race on Memorial Glade to the watch party inside the Institute of Governmental Studies library, morale was high. Half-eaten pizzas on paper plates and T-shirts adorned with “I Voted” stickers were proof that young voters were reluctant to experience democracy alone.
Berkeley, of course, had little reason to doubt its own Democratic political inclinations. But the rest of the country was another matter. Nobody could stop talking about the notorious Ramaswamy campaign ad, or the racist attacks on El-Sayed. Young Californians had turned their eyes outward, running headlong into a collective, jittery anxiety.
“I am just looking forward to seeing humanity in this country tonight,” commented a graduate student who sat at the forefront of the IGS library, repeatedly refreshing the real-time vote tallies with evident unease.
The evening began with a guided meditation, as well as a reminder of the late John Lewis’s call to “be hopeful, be optimistic” in this “struggle of a lifetime.” Attendees closed their eyes to drink in the words.
Xavier Becerra won the less politically risky race and became the state’s first elected Latino governor. The crowd cheered more out of comfort than elation. But California’s Proposition 40, the billionaire wealth tax that had enjoyed considerable attention on social media, provoked more angst.
In an informal poll conducted by the host, few attendees expressed confidence that California could effectively “tax the rich.” Some recalled signing the petition months before on our very own Sproul Plaza to put Proposition 40 on the ballot. Despite the shared sentiment that “nobody needs a billion,” one Berkeley freshman questioned the proposition’s ambiguous definition of assets and whether it could affect middle-class families. Another raised concerns about the campaign waged by California’s tech titans and mega-rich to sink the bill.
At 6:42 pm, Democrats flipped the House. As the blue wave washed over Texas, Ohio, and South Carolina, cheers erupted across the room. By the time Texas flipped blue, some attendees headed for the exit, seemingly satisfied that the night’s work was done.
The blue wave reflects a national desire to perform a check on power. But, amid the euphoria and complacency that it may breed, Californian voters must ask themselves: How do we confront concentrated wealth and its ability to change political tides in our backyard?
Dorothy Huang, The University of California, Berkeley  
Edinburgh, Scotland—I walk up an alleyway that stinks of piss, before being bathed in green lights that make me wonder if I’m about to be dissected by aliens.
“Great,” I think. “I’m here!”
Dropkick Murphy’s is an Irish pub and dance club that’s as authentically Irish as a union jack. This is where the University of Edinburgh’s Democrats’ Overseas society is hosting its election night party.
Upstairs, it’s American dance night, and beautiful young women dressed as farm animals dance to Ella Langley with guys in plastic cowboy hats. Downstairs, there’s an election party, and lacy tops turn into sensible sweaters and collared shirts. “Last time, when Trump won, it was Chappell Roan night,” a local reporter for The Herald also covering the party informs me.
The partygoers clap as the BBC announces that polls have closed. Five people on television sit around a crescent table in a blindingly bright studio and discuss the night reasonably. Compared to Fox, it’s almost academic.
As I sit, a girl in red flannel and a cowboy hat descends from the dance floor, trips down the stairs, and tramples a young woman watching the midterms results. The cowgirl is drunk and mumbles an apology before darting out.
Forbes, an 18-year-old working-class Scot with a serious mullet and a beige flannel over-shirt is here with his English friend.
Why have they come? “It’s something to do,” his English mate says.
“The Dems will win, right?” Forbes asks.
“What makes you say that?” I reply.
“All my favorite comedy podcasts switched up from the Trump bandwagon,” Forbes says. “I just think it makes sense as well because the world’s pretty fucked right now. And that Iran shit was insane, lads.”
I ask him what comes to mind when he thinks of America.
“It’s gotta be one of the most beautiful countries in the world, ’cause it’s so big, it’s got everything, you know? I know you can’t really anymore, but I’d like to think I could move over there one day and have a cool life,” he says.
The BBC projects Maine will go to the Democrats. The room absolutely erupts.
“I would like to move to the South,” Forbes says. “Like, where was True Detective filmed? Louisiana? Yeah. I’d love to see Louisiana. It looks so cool over there. Those willow trees and shit.”
The BBC projects Jon Ossoff will win Georgia after 5 percent of the vote comes in. People cheer. Less loudly than Maine, but they still cheer.
“I like how they’re saying it so decisively after only 5 percent,” a girl behind me comments.
The guy sitting next to the young woman leans in so close to her face I’m sure she could tell me a great deal about his teeth. “Welcome to American democracy!”
Henry Fernandez, University of Edinburgh
(Study Abroad via Cornell University)
Kansas City, Kansas—Hundreds of Kansas Democrats huddled in the Marriott Ballroom, eagerly anticipating a potentially historic midterm election. A deep-red state like Kansas usually doesn’t have this much optimism, yet something felt different.
The Adam Hamilton election watch party in Kansas City personified his campaign—attracting the same motley voting coalition that propelled him into power: Democrats, Republicans, independents, young, old, wealthy, working-class, you name it.
As The Guardian noted, “Hamilton, who branded himself as a centrist with the slogan, ‘leading from the middle,’ joined several other ‘prairie populists’ this year to win over Republican strongholds by leaning on populist messaging and vowing to stand up to corruption and corporate interests.”
The energy in the ballroom was similar to a major sporting event. There were hardly any empty tables or chairs. Every time a Democrat took a lead or projected a win, the crowd cheered as loudly as they could.
Then Hamilton won. And spectators erupted into applause—chanting “U-S-A” and “Adam” over and over.
But Hamilton, with all reason to gloat after upsetting a deep-red Senate seat that hadn’t been held by a Democrat since 1932, did not. The longtime pastor kept to his humble Christian values. During his victory speech, he evoked scripture—among them, the Parable of the Good Samaritan. The story goes: A traveler is beaten by robbers and left for dead. Two religious men pass him and do not help. But, then the Samaritan, from an enemy group, treats his wounds and helps him recover. This allusion tied back to Hamilton’s campaign and his promise of going across the aisle to work for all Kansans.
Hamilton did not mention his opponent, incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, at any point in the evening. He was sick of the mudslinging of electoral politics. “You can get a whole lot done if you don’t care who gets the credit,” Hamilton said. This message fired up the crowd once more.
Kansans walked out of the ballroom with a belief that things would get better. It was once impossible to imagine a Democrat in the Senate during our lifetimes. But state Democrats, after witnessing a two-term Democratic governor and now an incoming blue senator, are choosing to think differently. Kansans just made history, and they aren’t planning on stopping.
Madden Rausch, The University of Kansas
Ithaca, New York—On the first day of early voting in Ithaca, Cornell Votes president Erik Lapidus was eighth in line at the Crash Fire Rescue Center when the ballot scanner stopped working.
The first voter received an error. A technician tried to fix it, and poll workers began directing ballots into an emergency ballot box instead. By 9:28 am, Lapidus said, nearly everyone was using it. But when his turn came, he flipped his ballot over and tried the scanner again.
“When I scanned my ballot a second time, it went in perfectly well,” Lapidus said.
As rumors began circulating online that ballots placed in the emergency box would not count, Lapidus pushed back, confirming that those ballots would still be counted, even if not until after Election Day polls closed.
For Lapidus, correcting misinformation was only one part of a semester spent trying to get Cornell students to vote. Cornell Votes began by distributing registration forms in every student dorm. The organization helped nearly 500 students register this semester, compared with just over 300 during the 2024 presidential election, and saw more than four times as many absentee-ballot forms taken.
On Election Day, members were at Robert Purcell Community Center, Cornell’s on-campus polling place, from 5 am to 9 pm, helping students navigate the voting process. By then, the challenge was no longer getting students to show up—it was getting them to wait in a 90-minute line.
“There could definitely be more polling places, because there is more than one community center on campus, to avoid the long wait,” Cornell student Osiel Faez told me while waiting. “But at the same time, this means that there is a really good turnout.”
By night, voting lines gave way to an election-watch party hosted by the Cornell Democrats.
“Especially with two years of not too much hope, it’s nice to have a place as isolated as Ithaca to come together and be hopeful,” Cornell Democrats president Nash Wickremeratne said.
For political director Alex Blue-Baron, from Texas, the hope was for a celebratory night—and for her home state to flip blue.
“It makes me super happy to see how many students are politically and civically engaged,” Blue-Baron said.
Jeannine Chiang, Cornell University
New York City—Sounds of Brazil, located in Hudson Square, hosted a midterm election-watch party titled “The Revolution Will Be Televised.” Across the room, people of all ages sat surrounded by six televisions displaying polling percentages. Attendees watched the screens with excited smiles as everyone waited for the clock to strike 9 pm.
“We need to take the Senate, take the House. We are in very bad shape,” Larry Gold, owner of Sounds of Brazil, said to the audience as we awaited results. He emphasized how New York City developed a strong sense of community throughout the summer, from the Knicks’ games to the World Cup, and he said his goal for this event was to help New Yorkers come together again.
This seemed to resonate. Attendees clapped in unison as the six television screens showed a new state turning blue; little by little, Democrats took over the majority of the House of Representatives, and the Senate and cheers quickly erupted in the room.
Ana Agudelo, Hunter College
Los Angeles, California—The Regent Theater in Los Angeles was packed at 8 pm on election night. The Democratic Socialists of America LA were hosting their watch party. People were feeling “cautiously optimistic.”
The old theater sits right in the heart of Downtown and was filled with Angelenos of all ages talking, eating, and walking around as they watched the tight race between current LA Mayor Karen Bass and DSA-endorsed City Council member Nithya Raman unfold.
For many young LA residents, Raman was an obvious choice. “Driving around Downtown makes me so sad,” said Nikki Kobrick, who recently moved to LA after graduating from college. “And I’m thinking, this is not what the downtown of one of the greatest cities in the world should look like.”
For many young DSA members, choosing to support Raman ultimately came down to her pledge to fix the city. Twenty-three-year-old William Prince is a LA native and grew up frequently visiting Downtown. He first joined DSA in 2021, when Raman won her City Council race, and has since grown excited about her policies on transportation and housing. “I want a city that loves me back,” Prince said. “For Nithya to say just so unabashedly, ‘I love LA, but LA doesn’t love us back, and I want it to,’ was very powerful.”
Supporters of Raman seemed confident that she would win the mayoral race—but slightly less so in what that would mean for the future of LA. Several watch party attendees acknowledged that they were politically to the left of Raman, and that they voted for her with the intention of pushing her office further while using this election as a stepping stone to further their future goals.
Kobrick said she’s looking ahead to 2028 and hopes that a socialist mayor in LA will set the stage for Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to win the presidential election.
As the watch party stretched late into the night, voters remained hopeful that a new socialist mayor would soon transform LA. As of this writing, Raman holds a narrow lead over Bass.
Sarah Soroosh Moghadam, UCLA
Bloomington, Bndiana—At a local bar in Bloomington, Indiana, in the heart of a reliably red state, local Democrats buzzed, invigorated by the potential “blue wave.” To much of the country, Indiana may seem irrelevant, a flyover state and Republican stronghold. But to the college students and recent graduates who made up some of the crowd, the midterms were an opportunity to prove that Indiana can once again be a competitive state politically.
One group of young people—Ben Baranko, 19; Finn Nowacki, 21; Izzy Frieze, 22; and Jackson Lythgoe, 19—called out vote percentages in key races in different counties across the state, incredulous and heartened by the early momentum. They laughed in disbelief, thrilled, before someone chimed in with the sobering reminder that it was still early. Things could change.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
That person was right, it was still early. But the early blue trickle was, in fact, a harbinger of the blue tsunami to come. Before the night was over, Democrats would flip several seats for the state House, breaking the Republican supermajority that had held steady for 14 years, and Beau Bayh would win secretary of state, the first Democrat in statewide office since 2012.
At another table, 19-year-old Talan Buell, wearing a cross necklace, toggled between 10 different computer tabs while listening to Steve Kornacki’s election commentary through his left AirPod.
A speaker for the county Democratic Party got on the microphone and started speaking to the crowd. “Prices are too damn high,” he said and, without looking up from his computer, Buell called out, “Amen!”
C.J. Miller, 23, might have been the most expressive of the bunch, banging on the table with excitement and gesturing wildly when he heard promising results for races in other states. “That means AOC is viable!” he crowed when he heard that democratic socialist Angie Nixon in Florida was polling well. He’s thinking ahead to potential Democratic presidential nominees for 2028.
Back in Indiana, a Bayh win for secretary of state, Miller said, sets an example for how Democrats can succeed in deep-red areas. They need to “define themselves,” he says, and avoid letting Republicans control the conversation.
Despite attempts to convince voters that people in the Midwest and on the coasts are wildly different, Miller thinks the wave of blue he sees sweeping across the country is evidence that voters across the country want the same things.
“We’re all frustrated,” he said. “We’re all broke and we’re all trying to figure out why.”
Samantha Camire, University of Indiana Bloomington

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.title: The Progressive Agenda: End Iran War, Rein in AI, Get Dems to Actually Do Something
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.text:
Now that Democrats have secured earth-shattering wins in both chambers of Congress, the party’s progressives are sending a message to their more moderate leaders: It’s time to deliver for voters who are demanding meaningful action.
“Even where the candidate wasn’t a self-described progressive, progressives won big last night,” said Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar, D-Texas, during a press call on Wednesday. “Across the country, so-called moderate candidates ran on ending forever wars,” he added, pointing out that Democrats went after the GOP for voting down congressional attempts to stop President Donald Trump’s unpopular military actions — efforts that the progressive caucus had organized.
With comfortable majorities in both chambers — 54 seats in the Senate and 237 in the House, as of 4:30 p.m. ET Wednesday — Democrats now have the legislative breathing room to deliver on their promises to reduce the cost of living, root out government corruption, and end Trump’s failed war in Iran.
But they’ll have to notch these achievements under an angry lame-duck president who vowed last night — via a Truth Social post of one of his signature red hats — to wield his veto against the new class of Democrats. The current Democratic leaders in each house of Congress, Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, both have long track records of sparring with the left. And which of their goals will progressives prioritize when their ranks swell come January?
“We will have an H.R. 1 through 10 that focuses on costs and healthcare and corruption,” Casar said Wednesday, referring to the first 10 House resolutions he wanted to see his party push. “Every single week, we should now be sending a bill to Donald Trump’s desk that is overwhelmingly popular with the American people, that cracks down on corporate greed, that cracks down on price gouging, that cracks down on big money and politics.”
To Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement and a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America who beat Republican incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett in a Michigan swing district on Tuesday, the Democrats’ historically successful night translates into a responsibility to achieve transformative change.
“It’s undoubtable that this was a sweeping mandate around the entire country,” said Lawrence, who ran a campaign focused on his opposition to data centers, a notoriously unpopular area of tech development that the left has pushed Democrats to oppose.
The outsized influence of the artificial intelligence industry is another critical area for progressives to tackle, Rep. Summer Lee, D-Pa., told The Intercept. She said that she and other progressives will push legislation to end the outside influence of billionaire and super PAC money in elections, including her bills to ban super PACs and overturn the Citizens United Supreme Court decision.
“Every year, we see record-breaking numbers for the most expensive races in history by the millions,” Lee said. “In the 120th Congress, I look forward to our party recognizing the detrimental impact of special interests and billionaire influence in our politics, whether it be from crypto or AI or AIPAC.”
Other progressive priorities include passing policies like Medicare for All, ending corporate corruption, and investing in affordable housing. The ideas are tenets of the redistributive platform popularized by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who rallied voters across the country to “fight oligarchy” earlier this year and helped elevate many of this cycle’s upstart candidates.
On Wednesday, progressives did not yet seem prepared to commit to which single issue they would push for first. Asked by The Intercept about their Day-One priorities when they return to Congress, Casar said progressives planned to keep up the legislative pressure throughout the two years of the coming congressional term.
The Working Families Party, which backed Lawrence and often works to push Democrats to the left, saw Tuesday’s results as a sign that “voters want Democrats to stop the buildout of data centers and rein in the AI industry,” said Ravi Mangla, the group’s spokesperson. Like the congressional progressives, WFP cited a range of priorities for the years to come: guaranteeing healthcare and low-cost childcare, lowering housing costs, and providing more union jobs to American workers.
In fact, candidates who signed onto a promise to push a suite of pro-labor policies organized by labor leaders in swing states were among the Democrats’ biggest winners on Tuesday night. Signatories to the “Contract with Working America” included Troy Jackson, who toppled three-decade incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine; James Talarico, who flipped the Texas seat for the first time in almost 40 years; and Gina Hinojosa, who ousted 10-year incumbent Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.
Jackson pointed to the pledge during his victory speech in Maine on Tuesday night and thanked the union members who canvassed for him.
“On Labor Day, brothers and sisters, I stood before you and I made a pledge to working Mainers,” Jackson said to cheers at his election night party in Portland. “And I’m going to keep that promise. Because I am a union member tonight. I’ll be a union member when I walk into that Senate chamber.”
“The way things are set up in our economy right now, the money is just moving up and concentrating at the top, and squeezing the people at the bottom,” said Maine AFL-CIO President Cynthia Phinney. Her organization helped develop the labor platform Jackson signed onto, and she said they “fully anticipate that we’re going to need to continue to organize around these issues that matter to the folks who voted for him, and a lot of folks who didn’t vote for him.”
Referring to Hinojosa, Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., noted that Latino voters “delivered a gubernatorial seat in Texas,” as well as a U.S. senator. Ramirez, who has introduced a bill to abolish the Department of Homeland Security, argued that her party should not lose sight of outrage over violent immigration enforcement.
“Shame on us Democrats if we again do not meet the moment when it comes to immigration and when it comes to justice as it pertains to ICE and CBP and DHS,” Ramirez told The Intercept.
Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., pointed out that the issues that defined this cycle were often first championed by progressives.
“We were the first to fight back against the war in Iran. We were the first to call out corruption on so many levels. We were the first to push to rein in ICE and CBP, a shift that really drove a lot of Latino voters across the country that mattered in this election,” said Jayapal. “Hopefully, this puts to rest the idea that you can’t be a progressive and win with your ideas in any district in the country.”
If history is any guide, it won’t. As the wins rolled in on Tuesday night, Jeffries, the next likely speaker of the House, threw cold water on the idea that the vote marked a seismic rebuke of the Republican Party’s way of doing things, saying the results were “patriotic,” not “partisan.”
On Wednesday, Jeffries said voters had chosen Democrats “because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”
“I agree, and I’ll go one step further,” Casar said. “The American people delivered a demand for bold change.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: As it expands, Provincetown’s Fine Arts Work Center prioritises access and affordability
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Osman Can Yerebakan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Provincetown, the harbour community perched on the tip of the Cape Cod peninsula in Massachusetts, has a well-earned reputation as a haven for artists, but that status is under threat due to a lack of affordable housing. Geographically secluded and aesthetically distinctive, the town, which experienced an influx of Portuguese sailors in the 1850s, has attracted artists for almost a century, particularly queer painters, writers and poets.
Provincetown’s Fine Arts Work Center(FAWC) has been at the heart of this creative community since it was founded in 1968 by a group that included the painters Robert Motherwell, Myron Stout, Jack Tworkov and Fritz Bultman. The painter Sam Messer and Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Mary Oliver were among the centre’s early residents, followed in ensuing decades by artists including Lisa Yuskavage, Jack Pierson, Ellen Gallagher, Jeffrey Gibson, Firelei Báez, Elliot Hundley, Jacolby Satterwhite and Jennifer Packer.
Today, the non-profit grants artists access and community in a town that is among the most expensive in New England during the summer season. Providing room and support for queer artists remains a priority. The Venezuelan artist Miguel Braceli, for instance, completed his 2024 residency by orchestrating the public performance True Love’s Kiss, in which strangers were invited to lock lips at the granite breakwater on the shore’s very western tip.
Located in the Provincetown’s residential east end, the FAWC is best known for its residency programme, which provides ten artist fellows and ten writers with lodging and studio space for seven months every year, between October and April. Among this year’s artist residents are Abigail Dudley, Alina Perez, Nasim Hantehzadeh and L.J. Roberts.
“People have come here for generations to live their identities to the fullest and they have heavily contributed to the artistic creativity that makes Provincetown what is,” Sharon Polli , the centre’s executive director, tells The Art Newspaper. “The unique experience residents feel the second they drive down Route 6 or step off the ferry comes out in the work created here.”
The centre has been in a continuous state of expansion and renovation for much of its 58-year history. What was once the longtime Provincetown resident Hans Hoffman’s studio is now a fraction of the centre’s main grounds, named Days Lumberyard, which includes multiple living units, studios, offices, an auditorium, a gallery space, an outdoor area and a printshop that still houses Motherwell’s own press. The centre acquired a heating supply building in 1972 for around $120,000 and has gradually transformed its coal bins and other disused or dilapidated areas into its main hub.
Polli says the lumberyard’s growth and importance to the community are proof of “Provincetown being a place where there has always been room for artists and writers who maintain the town’s cultural identity” since the middle of the 20th century. The centre operates on an annual budget of around $3m, $600,000 of which this year was raised at its annual summer gala at the Pilgrim Monument at the Provincetown Museum.
The centre’s core role in maintaining the town’s artistic and intellectual identity has recently been officially acknowledged. The municipal board made a pledge this past summer to grant the centre $1.5m toward a planned $12m transformation of its 4 Brewster Street building. Located around the corner from the main FAWC complex, the lot the centre acquired in 1997 is in line for a totally new build. The Boston-based firm Hacin Architects was selected to double the housing square footage for fellows and staff, while adding a community space and a rooftop garden.
“We are hoping that the municipal support will help us leverage private funding,” Polli says. She and her team of 12 full-time employees keep the conversation and cultural exchange active throughout the off-seasons by offering a community-oriented programming. The year-round calendar includes FAWC Fridays, group exhibitions with past fellows, Queer Week, workshops and public talks with artists such as Catherine Opie, Ilana Savdie and Doron Langberg.
Polli says the centre’s off-season programming is even “more important than anything we do rest of the year because we give people a place to engage with high-calibre dialogues where many locals have working practices”.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: This Midterm Election Just Burst Republicans’ 2028 Bubble
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sasha Abramsky
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
This Midterm Election Just Burst Republicans’ 2028 Bubble
Yesterday’s results showed a full-throated rebuke of Republican dominance—so what does that mean for 2028?
There are an overwhelming number of once-in-a-generation stories coming out of Tuesday’s elections. One could focus on the improbable outcome of the South Carolina Senate race, or the nail-biter in Mississippi, or the restructuring of the Midwest’s political architecture. The sheer number of flipped House and Senate seats is its own story, with many races producing Democratic wins so overwhelming that—as was the case in Hungary this past April—the autocrats simply had no wriggle room to challenge their defeat.
But to my mind, the biggest story, by far, is Texas, where James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton by more than a million votes in the Senate race, and where Gina Hinojosa knocked long-time Governor Greg Abbott off of his perch. This has been the Democrats’ holy grail for 30 years—and on Tuesday they finally grabbed it.
Up and down the ballot in Texas, Democrats won. They won every statewide race—including the contest to replace Paxton as attorney general; it’s likely they won enough state House seats to control one chamber of the legislature and make inroads into the Senate majority. And they won all four of the state Supreme Court justices’ positions that were up for election, meaning a 9–0 hyper-right Supreme Court is now split 5–4. In one brutal night, the GOP’s decades-long dominance over Texas politics evaporated. The Lone Star State, long the dominant force amongst a coalition of diehard red states, is now tinted blue.
Texas in 2026 is California in the late 1990s, post–Prop 187, or Arizona after state legislators passed a string of venomously anti-immigrant measures in the 2000s. In both of those states, the political backlash, and the organizing of Latino communities to push back, transformed politics and broke GOP dominance. So, too, in Texas, massive voter mobilization efforts—in the valleys along the Rio Grande, in particular—transformed the makeup of the state’s electorate. After years of false starts, Talarico and Hinojosa ushered into power a truly multiracial coalition in the country’s second-most-populous state.
Speaking of Arizona’s decade-and-a-half-long quest to turn blue: Yesterday the Democrats won both the state House and Senate, meaning that Arizona now has a democratic trifecta, joining California, neighboring Nevada—whose voters ousted GOP Governor Lombardo and replaced him with Aaron Ford—New Mexico, Colorado, Oregon, and Washington. New Mexico will be governed by Deb Haaland, the country’s first Native American governor. California and Texas will both be governed by people of Latino descent. Though Xavier Becerra’s victory in the governor’s race in California was a comprehensive win that in a normal election year would have merited national headlines, it barely registered among commentators, so vast were the shifts occurring all around the country yesterday.
It’s possible that the results were a one-off fluke, a product of the unique fissures and furies running through the nation’s electorate in 2026, and that come 2028 Texas will revert to being a red bastion. But I doubt it. If the Democrats can consolidate their position, implementing policies on wages, housing affordability, healthcare access, and humane immigration reforms that meaningfully impact Texans’ lives for the better, and if they can keep engaged the vast numbers of people who in 2026 made the leap into political participation for the first time, the consequences will be far-reaching. The Texas revolt will, in the long run, likely have an impact on national politics as profound as California’s transformation away from Pete Wilson–era GOP dominance in the 1990s. It will alter the national calculus on everything from abortion access to environmental policies, from immigration enforcement strategies to minimum-wage policies. And it will make it infinitely more difficult for the next Republican presidential candidate to get the Electoral College to break in his or her favor.
Four of the five biggest states in the country are now firmly Democratic, and the fifth, Florida, came within a whisker of joining the club. Had the Democrats invested in Florida even a fraction of what they poured into Texas, Floridians would, today, also be waking up to a new political reality. Increasingly, as these elections have shown, Republican dominance can be guaranteed only in the most rural of Midwestern, Mountain-Western, and Southern states. And no matter how you slice and dice it, that is simply not enough to form the core of an electoral coalition capable of winning on the national level.
A decade ago I wrote, optimistically, that Donald Trump would become Lonesome Rhodes, the silver-screen demagogue portrayed so powerfully by Andy Griffith in the 1957 movie A Face in the Crowd. Shunned by his own fans, spurned by the people who had previously cheered his every word, and ultimately left bellowing into the rafters of an echoing, empty mansion, Rhodes collapses into his own narcissistic madness. It didn’t happen to Trump in 2016; it did happen this week, in 2026. MAGA’s coalition was shattered beyond repair, and Trump’s hold on his audience was finally, irretrievably, obliterated.
All evening long, Trump bellowed and ranted into a social-media void. His insanity flowered as, perhaps, it has never flowered before. He blamed Fox News. He blamed Greg Abbott. He blamed the RNC. He blamed the pollsters. He announced that “I wasn’t on the ballot, and if I was we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J TRUMP”
At one point, after the addled president had spent hours blaming everyone but himself for the electoral debacle, one of his own followers replied on Truth Social that it wasn’t “them” who were to blame but Trump himself. “You fucked us,” his follower wrote in a message that flashed on my screen but that, alas, I forgot to save before it disappeared. It may well have been the most accurate commentary of the evening.

Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
Abdul El-Sayed handily defeated Republican Mike Rogers for Senate in Michigan early Wednesday morning, retaining Democratic control of the seat and solidifying the party’s Senate majority. To become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, the former public health official overcame rampant, bipartisan Islamophobia and bigotry. For the country, and the Democrats, to move forward, we must cast it out of public life forever.
The Michigan Democrat’s victory felt almost like an afterthought compared to the upset Senate victories won by Democrats in South Carolina and Texas. The 2026 midterms were a referendum on President Donald Trump and his control of the GOP, and voters delivered their verdict, turning control of both houses of Congress over to the opposition party.
But we should neither forget nor forgive how we got here. El-Sayed faced an uphill battle from the beginning, which included a protracted, venomous primary, and the call was often coming from inside the house.
No detractor was as vicious as his former primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens, whose eleventh-hour betrayal of her party’s nominee — she formally switched her endorsement to Rogers on Sunday — was a transparent attempt to turn the seat red.
Backlash was swift and harsh and came from all corners of the party. Sen. Chuck Schumer, the powerful leader of the Senate who has made little secret of his disagreements with El-Sayed on Israel, called Stevens’s actions “a despicable betrayal.” Michigan Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who finished third in the primary, went as far as to express personal concern for Stevens.
And Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., just days after implying El-Sayed and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani were antisemites for opposing ethno-supremacy in Israel, said Stevens chose “to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms, and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers.”
In the 48 hours-plus since she threw in with Rogers — which increasingly seems like it was motivated primarily out of spite when she was boxed out of a Sunday campaign event with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., in Detroit — Stevens embarked on a media tour of justification that got weirder and weirder.
A 15-minute, rambling interview with Anderson Cooper on CNN Sunday night didn’t provide insight into her motivations, or much else; on Monday evening, Stevens followed up with a long statement posted on X owning the decision to destroy her political career with the Democratic Party. She also denied that her fiancé, political donor Jason Turkish, played any role in the endorsement: “I made this decision, and I am proud of it. Do not question my independence simply because you disagree with my conclusion.”
Congressional staffers to Stevens resigned en masse on Sunday, and former campaign aides told the Washington Post that they had to run defense to keep Turkish — who had endorsed Rogers before Stevens did — out of the spotlight and marginalize his influence.
“Any campaign staff being directly quoted in this article, I was made miserable by working with them,” Stevens told the Post in response, adding, “I have nothing else to say about the campaign at this time.”
But a singular explanation of Stevens’s decision lets Democrats off the hook far too easily for the anti-El-Sayed campaign waged by leaders in the House and Senate. For the party to move forward after the midterms, the Democrats need to take a hard look in the mirror and purge institutionalized Islamophobia from their ranks.
They can start with their friends in the media. The Atlantic’s Jonathan Chait, in a screed published Sunday, whined that “during the same period of time that El-Sayed has been winking at a political movement inflected with anti-Semitism, he has been targeted by a political message that is not merely inflected with racism but saturated with it.”
Political commentator Van Jones noted on X ahead of Election Day that “the Republicans are conducting a campaign of blatant anti-Muslim fear mongering.” But in the same post, he also argued El-Sayed’s “refusal to outright denounce” a little-seen ad produced by an outside PAC — an ad which El-Sayed distanced himself and his campaign from — tying the rise of grocery costs to U.S. support for Israel was comparable.
“Something is going horribly wrong in the Senate race in Michigan,” Jones added huffily. “And I am going to keep calling it out.”
After last night’s massive blue wave, it should be undeniable that the left was a major factor in flipping the House and Senate. That means the party’s progressive wing can now credibly claim a seat at the governing table without compromising on domestic or foreign policy. We should get ready for a long overdue, but almost certainly painful, intraparty debate on how Democrats policed dissent in their own ranks in this election, and how to disentangle leadership from unconditional support for Israel.
There’s always the possibility that the party’s centrist wing comes together with the left and repairs the damage. A good first step would be for leadership to make clear that Stevens, and anyone else who indulged in anti-Muslim arguments to score political points, has torched any possible future in the Democratic Party. Any advocacy or lobbying group that offer Stevens or her ilk safe political harbor should also be blacklisted.
Party discipline applied to the treacherous center doesn’t appear to be the top priority for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the presumptive next speaker, who devoted his first remarks after the election to downplaying partisanship in this “patriotic moment.”
But without backup from party leadership, El-Sayed will continue to be met with hostility. On Wednesday morning, CNN asked fellow incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico if he would “stand up” to El-Sayed and other, unnamed left-wing members of his caucus. To his credit, Talarico demurred from directly challenging his fellow future senator. Still, it’s a sign of a long battle to come.
The question for “unity”-caping Democrats remains: Who will they rally around — and who will be left out in the cold?

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.title: How Democrats Changed Everything
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.text:
The size of the Democrats’ victory Tuesday night shattered records and even the most optimistic expectations, handing the party a governing mandate with a clear demand for change.
But what do voters want that change to look like? This week on The Intercept Briefing, politics reporter Jessica Washington and managing editor Maia Hibbett break down Tuesday night’s election and hear from voters in Maine, Michigan, and Texas about what drove them to the polls in the midterms that saw a so-called “blue tsunami.”
“The rich get richer, the poor get poorer,” said one voter in Maine. In Michigan, a voter told The Intercept that politics “feels like a game that the rich play sometimes.” A Texas voter expressed anger that President Donald Trump was “spending taxpayer money to renovate the White House and turn it into this gold sanctuary.”
Frustration with wealth inequality and money in politics came up again and again in The Intercept’s conversations with voters. So did a desire for more social welfare spending, Medicare for All, freedom for Palestinians — and responses to transphobic and Islamophobic fearmongering on the campaign trail.
“When Democrats win so far across the board, you can make an argument that any faction of the Democratic Party has the mandate,” said Hibbett, “because Democrats of all stripes won Tuesday night.”
In any case, the results indicated a clear disapproval of the way the Trump administration is governing and the use of fearmongering as a tactic of distraction.
“One lesson maybe for Democrats is there’s no point in attempting to placate people when it comes to bigotry,” said Washington. “The thing that’ll motivate voters is if you can convince them that you’re going to make their lives better, not if you can convince them that you’re playing the middle on an issue of civil rights.”

Despite an unceremonious, sudden, and possibly illegal eviction, it seems like the young barn owls of upper Manhattan will be OK.   
A parliament of barn owls had been nested in a hole in the roof of the rickety water tower of an Upper West Side apartment building—but late last week, birders noticed workers doing construction on the roof of the water tower, destroying the nest that the owls had built.  
Birder David Lei told Hell Gate that the fledglings being raised in the disrupted nest began roosting out in the open on nearby buildings last week, which was unusual, he explained. 
"That owl should have been roosting in a more sheltered location, like on an air conditioner windowsill, something like that," Lei said. "But it was out in the open, fully exposed. Songbirds had been bothering it during the day, just natural behavior. But you know, a hawk could have seen it and attacked it."
Lei said that management at 15 West 75th Street had told the residents that they were doing "scheduled maintenance" on the water tower. The building's management did not respond to Hell Gate's request for comment by publication time, but we will update this story if they do.

https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.title: Trump’s State Department Is Giving $1 Million to Controversial Group to Study Crimes Against White South Africans
https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.author: Sharon Lerner, Anna Maria Barry-Jester
https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.text:
After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.
The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “God-given calling,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “document hateful rhetoric and violent acts” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.
The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.
Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”
Samuel Samson Speaks at Lex Libertas Event
There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”
AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement.
South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics, and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.
But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.
AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”
The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. Now, with Black South Africans governing the country, white people — of which Afrikaners are the majority — remain one of the wealthiest segments of the population.
The support has caused dismay among several former high-level diplomats, who spoke to ProPublica anonymously because they fear retribution from the administration.
Two former senior U.S. officials responsible for Africa policy said that they would never have met with AfriForum, let alone funded the group, because it was considered to be politically extreme and not credible. They described the organization as cherry-picking crime statistics to create a misleading narrative. “We would certainly not have funded what we would see as a racially incendiary initiative,” said one of the officials.
The decision to direct money toward the group comes after the Trump administration halted programs that advocated for the end of violence in African countries such as Sudan, where the Biden administration determined in 2025 that there was a genocide, calling it “the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe.”
“It’s offensive to provide funding solely to this one group after we’ve cut off funding in countries undergoing real documented crises,” said David Jandura, who managed the Africa portfolio for the State Department’s human rights bureau for several years and lost his job during the mass layoffs in 2025.
Congress has also raised questions about how the award was made. A Senate aide to Democrats told ProPublica that despite repeated requests to State Department officials, they had not received a briefing outlining the recipients of funds earmarked for democracy and human rights, which they described as “highly unusual.”
“The Trump Administration proceeded with funding fringe right-wing causes internationally despite objections from Congress,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a New Hampshire Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, who described the lack of transparency as “unacceptable.”
In response to a series of questions about the AfriForum funding, a senior State Department official wrote in an email that the department does not comment on funding deliberations and that they routinely keep Congress informed of their actions, consulting extensively on this year’s programming. “The Administration has been clear about its concern about the abhorrent race-based discrimination and violence in South Africa,” the unnamed official wrote. “Human rights protections do not depend on a person’s income or ethnicity.”
In July, ProPublica revealed that the State Department originally intended to give the $1 million research award to Lex Libertas, a small organization founded last year by a former AfriForum executive named Ernst Roets. Trump officials later expanded the potential awardees to a small pool of handpicked organizations. The plan drew outrage from Congress over the content of the award as well as plans to bypass the typical competitive bidding process. After ProPublica’s reporting, the State Department released an open call for the funding opportunity, offering $986,500 to a nonprofit organization to “create a comprehensive record of violence affecting Afrikaner and other South African minority populations.” It’s this grant that is now being awarded to AfriForum.
Both AfriForum and Lex Libertas advocate for Afrikaner rights and have developed relationships with the Trump administration. Trump’s ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III, visited AfriForum’s headquarters in September, praising the organization for its neighborhood watch programs while criticizing the South African government for not enacting policies requested by the Trump administration. AfriForum has also met with Trump officials in Washington, D.C., drawing public criticism from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. And in September, Roets met with administration officials.
AfriForum was founded 20 years ago and, with some 300,000 members, claims to be the biggest civil rights organization in South Africa. It says it aims to “establish self-dependence and growing self-governance” and provides some local civic services, such as garbage collection and systems for reporting pot holes and broken traffic lights. The group has said it distances itself from “white supremacist and extremist groups” and that it disagrees with Trump’s assertion that white South African farmers are experiencing a “white genocide.” But it has also said the South African government is “targeting the continued existence of Afrikaners” through racial legislation and the downplaying of farm murders, among other things. Academics and former U.S. diplomats have repudiated some of the ideas the group promotes as racist.
It unsuccessfully challenged a ban on the “gratuitous display” of the national flag flown during apartheid, which a South African court has found to be a form of hate speech. And while the group’s leader, Kallie Kriel, has said apartheid “was wrong,” he has also said it did not constitute “a crime against humanity” as the U.N. has determined, on the grounds that not enough people were killed during that time.
AfriForum has been focusing on farm attacks since at least 2009. In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Kriel and Roets, who was then his deputy, met with government officials in Washington, D.C., about the issue, and Roets spoke about it with Tucker Carlson on Fox News, as the chyron below him announced in all caps, “White farmers brutally murdered every week in SouthAfrica.”
Additional research on crimes against white South Africans is an unnecessary and confusing use of U.S. taxpayer dollars, said Carolyn Holmes, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who studies democracy in southern Africa. Holmes noted that AfriForum already produces annual reports on crimes against farming communities. “These data already exist,” she said. “You don’t need a new study. You don’t even need a far-right study, we have those.”
The U.S. support offers more than a financial boost to the organization. “For some time, AfriForum has been campaigning for recognition of their claim that white people face discrimination and persecution,” said Alex Dyzenhaus, a lecturer in international relations and African politics at the University of St. Andrews. “Before, they were only getting the Tucker Carlsons and the far right of the news ecosystem. Now they have the U.S. government on their side.”
The Trump administration has made the plight of white, rural South Africans a key foreign policy issue. In addition to the early executive order, Trump held a contentious meeting with Ramaphosa in the White House last year where Trump claimed white farmers were being executed. The administration has also considered an ad campaign focused on encouraging more Afrikaners to come to the U.S.
In September, Roets of Lex Libertas met with the White House to discuss what he sees as the crisis facing the Afrikaner community and, along with the New York Young Republican Club, placed 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall to commemorate South African farm murders.
Roets declined to answer specific questions from ProPublica but, in a text message, described the murders of several Afrikaners that he knew personally. He also wrote, “I see the suffering of black people in South Africa, I am deeply moved by it, and I spend every day of my life campaigning to make things better for us all.”
Appearing at a press conference for the Lex Libertas event, Samson, the State Department official, showcased the sharp shift the administration has made in U.S. relations with South Africa. While apartheid has been understood globally as a symbol of racist oppression, Samson described the current South African government as having discriminatory “race-based” policies and a cautionary tale for the rest of the world.
At the end of apartheid, in 1994, South Africa was a “flourishing, prosperous society,” Samson said. Since then, the country has gone to “ruin.” He blamed the fall on a “radical ideological leftist movement that wears human rights, that wears tolerance and inclusivity, as a skin suit to advance their Marxist communist worldview.”
Part of the Trump administration’s solution to this perceived crisis, he said, was to provide the research funding.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Kamala Harris on Expanding Democratic Power in the South
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Kamala Harris on Expanding Democratic Power in the South
A conversation with the former vice president about the fight for Democrats in the too-long-neglected South.
Kamala Harris made a big return to the campaign trail in the fall of 2026, heading to such battleground states as Michigan, where she boosted US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and Georgia, where she campaigned with Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. But Harris also visited places that rarely see former vice presidents, such as Columbus, Mississippi, where she appeared in a packed high-school gymnasium on behalf of Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom. This campaigning, which she referred to as her “freedom tour,” has also taken the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee to Arkansas and Louisiana. Harris says she hasn’t decided whether to run for president again in 2028. But no matter what her own next step may be, she tells The Nation, she’s committed to boosting Democratic prospects in the too-long-neglected South.
—John Nichols
John Nichols:  Let’s talk about the fight for Democrats in the South.
Kamala Harris: One of my favorite subjects.
JN: You have been appearing at party events and with candidates across the region.
KH: And for my book tour. The publisher [of the book, 107 Days] was like, “Well, we don’t normally do a lot of book tours in the South.” And I was like, “Well, we’re going to do that, and people will come.” And they did—often a thousand people.
JN: There has been a lasting debate within the Democratic Party about how to approach deep-red states. A lot of strategists make the mistake of arguing, usually behind closed doors, “Let’s just write them off.”
KH: That is a mistake…. There are people in the South who have profound needs for the things the Democratic Party says we stand for: affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, a meaningful job that leads to the ability to have opportunity for your children. The dignity of all people—equality, fairness.
That point being number one.
The other point I would raise is that if you look at what’s happening demographically in the country, there is a reverse migration happening toward the South—both in terms of families who, historically, were from the South as well as a lot of young families, because it’s more affordable. And the South, you know, in terms of topography, is beautiful.
