“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
JN: There’s also a political side to this. In several Southern states in 2024, you ran as well as or better than you did in several Northern states that were historically identified as more competitive. There’s a base to build from in the South, right?
KH: That’s right. And I feel so strongly that you have to be able to do battle, instead of sitting back and implicitly accepting the notion that you can’t win there. You certainly won’t win if you don’t do battle. And that requires, as we know, being present. And it requires an investment. And that is part of the failure [for national Democrats], which is a failure to invest in the infrastructure that would allow us to win. And then it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Then what do we do? We abandon the people of those states who want clean drinking water? Who want the freedoms we say we fight for? Who want Medicaid, because their rural hospitals are shutting down because of a lack of federal funding? Who, as I was saying in Mississippi, know they deserve better? And who know it doesn’t have to be that way?
Well, the Democratic Party’s got to get hip to that, too: It doesn’t have to be that way.
JN: When Democrats aren’t hip to that, it narrows the party’s path to governing majorities, right?
KH: That’s my point—absolutely right. It’s about: Are we gonna play small ball?
Look, everything worthwhile requires investment. And investment, by its very nature, includes planting some seeds for a return that might be a little ways down the road but will be well worth the investment.
JN: There may also be an opening now, because of widespread disdain for the GOP administration. Have you been surprised by the implosion of Trump’s approval ratings this year?
KH: I’m not surprised. I say it publicly because I mean it: This is the most callous, corrupt, and incompetent presidential administration we’ve ever experienced.… What has happened also is [Trump] has created a party—and they’ve allowed it—in his own image. This is not Ronald Reagan’s party. That’s so cliché; everybody says it. But he has created a party in his own image, including the callous nature. So am I surprised about that? No.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: One museum visit a month could improve health, new report finds
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Joe Ware
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Visiting a museum or art gallery for just one hour a month could significantly improve people's physical and mental health, according to a new report which calls for cultural engagement to become as routine as exercise and healthy eating.
The research, commissioned by the charity Art Fund in partnership with University College London professor Daisy Fancourt, recommends that people spend at least 60 minutes with art in museums and galleries every month.
However, the survey of 2,000 UK adults found that 89% fail to meet this proposed target, equivalent to an estimated 49.5 million people.
The report, “The Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing”, draws together scientific evidence suggesting that regular cultural engagement can reduce stress, improve cognitive health and potentially extend life expectancy.
Previous studies have shown that regular museum and gallery visits could nearly halve the risk of developing depression over the following decade. Other studies have linked cultural participation with reduced dementia risk and lower levels of loneliness.
Viewing original artworks in galleries was also associated with a 22% greater reduction in the stress hormone cortisol compared with viewing reproductions.
Fancourt, whose book Art Cure on the scientific benefits of art came out earlier this year, says regular engagement with art should be considered a health-promoting behaviour alongside exercise, a balanced diet and spending time outdoors.
“Guidelines like eating our 5-a-day of fruit and vegetables and getting our 10,000 steps have proven effective in helping us to prioritise other health-promoting behaviours in our busy lives,” she says in a statement. “Adding regular arts engagement to this list could be a simple and joyful way of investing further in our health and wellbeing.”
But the findings also raise questions about whether Britain's struggling museums have the resources to encourage more frequent visits. Jenny Waldman, the director of Art Fund, tells The Art Newspaper that the research strengthens the case for sustained public investment in museums, including protecting free admission at national institutions and supporting local and regional collections.
“We want to see sustained, long-term public investment across the museum sector, so that all museums have the resources to care for their collections and welcome the widest possible audiences,” she says.
Waldman acknowledged that removing admission charges alone would not overcome barriers to visiting museums, including accessibility and the resources available to institutions.
She says Art Fund's research among museum directors found that 36% of museums had reduced their opening hours because of insufficient funding and staffing.
“If we want museums to play a greater role in supporting public health, we must invest in the sector and give them the means to do so,” she adds.
Waldman also points to international developments, including Greece's introduction of arts prescribing into its national healthcare system and growing recognition of cultural organisations as public health assets. She also notes efforts closer to home: “Scotland's Chief Medical Officer, Sir Gregor Smith, recently published a report recognising arts organisations as important public health assets and calling for arts and culture to be embedded more widely in Scotland's approach to public health.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/safes.title: SafeSport Will Now Alert Schools, Clubs if Coaches Sanctioned for Abuse Continue to Work With Kids
https://www.propublica.org/article/safes.author: Molly Hensley-Clancy
https://www.propublica.org/article/safes.text:
The U.S. Center for SafeSport is taking steps to stop coaches banned over allegations of sexual abuse from working with children, part of an initiative that the organization said it is launching because of reporting by ProPublica and The Washington Post about gaps in the child protection system in youth sports.
Charged by Congress with investigating allegations of sexual abuse in sports, SafeSport has the power to suspend or permanently bar coaches from contact with athletes and place their names on a public disciplinary list. But the center has authority only over the country’s national sports governing bodies, which are overseen by the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee. Elementary and high schools, colleges and many independent youth sports leagues are not required to follow SafeSport’s bans, though some opt to do so. Parents and other caregivers only know if a coach has been sanctioned if they check the list.
SafeSport’s new initiative encourages people to find and report banned coaches who are continuing to work with children, SafeSport said, with a publicity initiative that includes a video with its CEO.
It is also launching a new “internal process” to notify schools and other organizations that coaches are on the SafeSport list. Hilary Nemchik, SafeSport’s vice president of external affairs, said the organization would send a form letter when it learned coaches were still working with kids, either as a result of its own investigation or in response to a report.
“When SafeSport imposes a sanction for abuse or misconduct, the community should be aware,” Benita Fitzgerald Mosley, SafeSport’s CEO, said in a statement. “Someone could be on the SafeSport Database for abuse but go on to work at a school or coach for a league outside of our jurisdiction.”
ProPublica and The Post discovered several coaches who had been banned by SafeSport but continued to work with children. One story highlighted the case of a volleyball coach, Ryan Richardson, who SafeSport found to have committed sexual misconduct with a minor but who has continued coaching teenage girls in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. An independent volleyball league allowed Richardson to coach at several of its tournaments even after his name appeared on SafeSport’s database. Videos posted online showed Richardson on the sidelines.
The reporting showed that Richardson continued coaching in part by allowing a former assistant, Gavin Rudder, to take over the volleyball club after Richardson was banned by USA Volleyball, the sport’s governing body, in 2024. ProPublica and The Post found that Rudder allowed Richardson to coach the teams for years after the ban, a violation of the SafeSport code.
After the story was published, SafeSport added Rudder’s name to its public database, listing him as temporarily restricted from unsupervised coaching or training.
Rudder is currently listed as the coach at Weslaco High School, near McAllen. Abel Aguilar, the Weslaco district’s deputy superintendent, said in an email that the district “does not comment on personnel matters.”
In a text message, Rudder said the SafeSport ban “has nothing to do with high school volleyball” and that he had not “done anything wrong.” He said he was no longer associated with Richardson’s club volleyball team following the end of the 2026 season.
Read More
Richardson has not responded to requests for comment on ProPublica and The Post’s reporting. When he was first suspended in 2024 by Lone Star Region Volleyball, the organization overseeing volleyball in South Texas, Richardson told the local news website MyRGV that complaints about him were an effort to “retaliate and defame someone’s character,” and said he “would never do anything to risk the physical or mental wellbeing of these strong young ladies.”
In announcing the changes, SafeSport also nodded to a bipartisan inquiry into a major youth sports organization launched last month by the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee, which also oversees SafeSport.
The lawmakers said they were launching a probe of the Amateur Athletic Union after ProPublica and The Post reported that the nonprofit does not follow SafeSport bans and has become a haven for coaches who are banned for abuse. The committee asked AAU President Jo Mirza for details on its child safety policies and training, setting a deadline of Oct. 21.
Committee representatives this week didn’t respond to questions about the status of the investigation. The AAU, which has said in a statement that it is “committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection policies overseen by our Compliance Department,” said it would “cooperate fully” with any inquiry.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Women Are the Real Story of the Midterm Elections
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Michele Goodwin
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Women Are the Real Story of the Midterm Elections
In a rebuke of the Trump administration and its cataclysmic decisions and policies, voters elected record numbers of women into office.
The 2026 midterms were historic. The Democrats prevailed, taking control over both the House and the Senate and gaining five governor’s offices. Pundits and political analysts will spend the coming days, weeks, and months analyzing the election results, examining why Americans voted as they did. But what message did voters send?
Two messages are clear. First, the 2026 midterms were a resounding, blistering rebuke of the Trump administration and its cataclysmic decisions and policies. The administration has blatantly abused the powers of the executive branch, mishandled foreign affairs, slashed essential programs that helped the poorest Americans and farmers, disregarded and destroyed beloved institutions and sites, and gutted essential environmental regulations, to say nothing of its grifting, bullying, and attacks on women in power and through its disastrous policies and actions.
On one hand, in just two years, the Trump administration has undone decades of American progress. On the other, America was already failing so many of its people and Trump only intensified their suffering.
Despite promises in 2024 of making Americans better off or “great again,” the Trump administration failed its working- and middle-class constituents. Its erratic and arbitrary financial policies, including unlawful tariffs and baffling war in Iran continue to hurt American families, dramatically raising the costs of gas across the country. In the outer regions of Alaska, gas prices exceeded $25 per gallon. The high costs of food now make it difficult for Americans to feed their families. And despite Trump supporters’ rallying around tougher immigration laws in 2024, the mass detention of their neighbors and community members and the murdering of their fellow Americans by ICE agents were not part of their agenda.
Trump’s exploitation of office is at a breaking point. At every turn, he has financially benefited during this term in office, trampling the Emoluments Clause and presidential norms. The president has hawked not only Bibles and sneakers but literally hundreds of items. Visit the so-called Trump Store—an online bazaar, selling everything from branded footballs, honey, hoodies, roasted coffee, vests, shot glasses, candles, cookies, jellybeans, and chocolates. There is no arms-length dealing here. Trump is selling a pricey “Presidential Gold Aurum Note” and a “President Donald J. Trump ‘We The People’ Silver Medallion” and one in gold too. He’s also faced accusations of selling access to the White House.
Yet the midterms were not only about fighting back against an administration that shows little regard for the concerns of Americans. The second message they delivered was about women claiming their space and expanding political leadership. In a historic showing, pro-choice women leaders across the country secured House and Senate seats and prevailed in gubernatorial races—a powerful response to both Trump’s policies and the Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade.
Keep in mind, since January 2025 when Donald Trump took office for a second term, his administration has targeted women with political harassment, pulling grants that focused on women’s health, demoting women leaders in the military, firing scores of Black women in government positions, and seeking to disenfranchise women voters through the SAVE Act, which “would make it harder to vote for 69 million women.” The National Partnership for Women and Families issued a report shortly after Trump returned to the White House, identifying “35 ways the Trump Administration has harmed women and families in its first 100 days.” That list has only grown since then.
Trump has frozen family-planning funding—gutting programs that provided breast cancer screenings, contraception, and STI testing. The administration has revoked efforts to raise the minimum wage, which would directly affect women workers, many of whom are the main provider and head of their household. Rather than prioritizing family leave or childcare initiatives, this administration decimated the Department of Education and invested in war, while turning its keys over to the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). According to congressional oversight letters, the administration canceled minority health grants, diverting the money to “support things like treatment for erectile dysfunction in the name of family values.” Trump also terminated the federal diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility offices, which tracked gender disparities.
Voters responded by electing record numbers of women into office. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, made history by becoming the state’s first woman governor, and the first Black woman to ever be elected governor in US history. Bottoms beat out Rick Jackson, an anti-abortion billionaire who invested $200 million of his personal resources in the campaign. Audio recordings of Jackson surfaced where he was heard expressing “support for further restrictions beyond Georgia’s current six-week abortion law,” which ProPublica investigations have found contributed to the preventable deaths of women in the state.
In Ohio, Dr. Amy Acton resoundingly defeated Vivek Ramaswamy, who describes himself as “unapologetically pro-life.” Ramaswamy, a Trump loyalist, ran deeply disturbing, disgraceful ads against Acton, featuring her estranged mother calling her a liar. Notably, Acton was raped as a child by her stepfather. Nevertheless, Ramaswamy doubled down—as did Vice President JD Vance and Donald Trump, who criticized Republicans who urged Ramaswamy to not run the ad.
In a stunning victory, Representative Gina Hinojosa (D-Austin) defeated Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the first Latina governor of Texas. Hinojosa, who campaigned on the vision that “this is our last best chance to take back Texas for the people,” has shared her personal story of pregnancy loss. In contrast, Abbott played a critical role in rolling back reproductive freedom in Texas. The state was the first to implement an extreme abortion ban, nine months before Roe was overturned. And now in Texas doctors risk 99 years of incarceration, $100,000 fines, and the possibility of losing their licenses to practice medicine if they violate the state’s total abortion ban.
Deb Haaland, the former US secretary of the interior, will be New Mexico’s next governor. She will be the first Indigenous woman governor in US history. In Minnesota, a state that has felt the devastating brunt of Trump’s domestic immigration policies, voters have elected Senator Amy Klobuchar as their next governor. Klobuchar has consistently criticized the US Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade. And, in Illinois, Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton has been elected to the Senate. Stratton helped spearhead in the state the ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment, which would prohibit sex discrimination.
As Trump’s lame-duck presidency comes into clear view, Americans are rejecting policies that keep them vulnerable and threaten their future, entangle them in wars, and make a mockery of the rule of law. There is a momentum building with historic wins across the nation, including in Texas, Ohio, and Iowa. As the Democrats return to power in Washington, DC, they should look not only to rebuild what was lost but to lay the groundwork for a third Reconstruction.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | John Berger at 100: why the writer and artist's legacy is as vital as ever
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: John-Paul Stonard
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
John Berger was born on 5 November 1926, making this year his centenary. Next year will be the tenth anniversary of his death. It seems a good time to look back and take stock of one of the 20th century’s most persuasive and challenging voices in art and literature, and one of only two writers on art who also wrote a Booker Prize-winning novel (the other was Anita Brookner).
The story of Berger’s 1972 Booker Prize speech, after winning for his novel G., is told by Tom Overton in his thoroughly engaging biography, John Berger: From Life, published in August this year. To a stunned and affronted audience at the prize ceremony, Berger announced he was donating half the considerable prize money to a British chapter of the Black Panthers, as a protest against the labour exploitation in British Guiana that had made the Booker McConnell fortune. It is hard to imagine an acceptance speech nowadays without acknowledgment of the reputation-laundering that is still widespread in cultural sponsorship. Berger’s bravery in making such a stand, which can hardly have been easy, is one aspect of his legacy worth remembering.
This legacy—why Berger matters—is the subject of the smattering of centenary events but is also brought into focus by their dearth. The only anniversary exhibition in Britain devoted to Berger is a small display of his drawings at Mandell’s Gallery in Norwich (until 21 November), co-curated by the artists John Christie and Martin Battye. Berger’s drawings are those of a writer intent on seeing the world around him, gathering images and experiences, but also of an artist who knows that the best way to look is to draw.
Berger’s popular legacy lies with his 1972 book Ways of Seeing, which remains, quite remarkably, a bestseller—“one of the most stimulating and influential books on art in any language”, says its publisher, Penguin. Anyone rereading the book now might pause at such a description. Berger was hardly the first to show how images are constructed by viewers, and reflect their prejudices, but he was the first to publish a book that communicated this idea so effectively, combining relentless polemic with brilliant design (thanks to Richard Hollis). It also helped that the book was based on a successful television series and contained numerous pin-up images to back up the argument that Old Master painting, through patterns of privilege and possession, relates directly to contemporary advertising.
Yet the arguments feel dated and even slack, quite unlike Berger’s later writing on art. His attacks on Seymour Slive’s interpretation of Frans Hals, and on Kenneth Clark’s book The Nude, are grounded in a personal dislike of art historians. What Gen Z art students will make of his attack on the “disingenuousness that bedevils the subject of art history”, picking apart Lawrence Gowing’s nitty argument that the figures in Gainsborough’s Mr and Mrs Andrews (around 1750) are not just enjoying nature but being philosophical about it, is anybody’s guess.
Art against the profit motive
And yet the questions Berger asks about how we value works of art, and how they exist as part of our lives and the world in which we live, are still utterly relevant. They are part of what Overton describes as the idea central to all his writing: how we live with the dead, how the past surrounds us and keeps us company. Berger spent his life tilting against a world “ordered with the logic of profit, always looking forward, never back”, Overton writes, a world therefore bent on neglecting the past and forgetting the dead.
It is an idea explored in Berger’s short story The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol, from the novel Pig Earth, about peasant life in France at the turn of the 20th century. And it appears in the leaps of imagination and connections he draws between art from different periods in the writings collected in Portraits: John Berger on Artists: on Fayum portraits seen from a century of exile and emigration, or his description of drawing Antonello da Messina’s astonishing 1475 Christ Crucified in the National Gallery, while recalling hearing pianist Myra Hess playing in the same gallery in 1942 (before being thrown out for swearing at a security guard), or his account of Jean-François Millet, “a moralist in the only way a great artist can be, by the power of his identification with his subjects”, in his case the experience of peasants working the land.
Berger’s legacy is his remarkable ability to link art with the most important questions of our time, and so to redeem it from the clutches of the market and specialists alike.
• John-Paul Stonard is an author and art historian

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: How These Midterms Can Guide Us Into a Post-Trump Political Future
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Faris
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
How These Midterms Can Guide Us Into a Post-Trump Political Future
The historic repudiation of the MAGA right at the ballot box opens up new avenues to democratic revival.
The 2026 midterm elections were a genuine earthquake—an across-the-board, unspinnable drubbing that left the 2024 Trump coalition in smoking ruins. Democrats made massive gains in once-impenetrable Republican strongholds like Texas and South Carolina and acquired vast new power in state legislatures. Tuesday was the night that liberals and progressives have been waiting a decade for: a long overdue and richly deserved repudiation of President Trump’s MAGA movement, everything it represents, and everyone who enabled it.
The scale of the GOP’s defeat is almost unfathomable, with significance beyond simply running up the score in both chambers of Congress. Democrats will have at least 54 Senate seats and are now projected to win as many as 260 seats in the House for a 43-seat gain, numbers that went far beyond consensus forecasts and came very close to 99th percentile, best-case-scenario outcomes. Those gains will make the lives of the party’s senior leadership dramatically easier, but they are hardly the most far-reaching outcomes of the evening.
First, Democratic gains in state legislatures look like they will rival the GOP’s 2010 midterm rout, when Republicans flipped more than 700 seats in a critical election before what was then once-a-decade redistricting. On Tuesday, Democrats captured a coveted trifecta—both chambers of the state legislature and the governor’s office—in the battleground of Wisconsin, wiping out the devastating post-2010 gerrymander that locked them out of power in the state legislature even when they won clear majorities of the popular vote.
They did the same in perennially purple Pennsylvania, where incumbent Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro won by nearly 22 points, his coattails sweeping Democratic majorities into both chambers of the state legislature. Not only can Democrats now draw fairer maps for House districts both states; they can also unrig the state legislatures so that they don’t need a sweeping national tsunami to win bare majorities.
Democrats flipped North Carolina’s House and nearly captured its Senate, which means that extremist GOP supermajorities will no longer be in a position to deny power to Democratic governors. They also finally broke the GOP’s stranglehold on Georgia state politics, making Keisha Lance Bottoms the first Black woman to win a race for governor in American history, and appear to have flipped the Georgia House.
They easily recaptured trifectas in Michigan and in Minnesota, where Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan won by double digits, throwing cold water on the GOP’s years-long quest to use a minor welfare scandal to ratchet up fear and loathing of the state’s Somali American minority. Perhaps even more shocking are new Democratic trifectas in Arizona, a GOP stronghold just a decade ago, and Nevada, which had been trending to the right. In both states, significant Latino minorities shifted hard to the left—a trend that will make it hard for the GOP to come back unless and until it purges r the racist nativists from the party.
The impact of these wins will go far beyond the ability to prevail in the mid-decade redistricting war that Trump stupidly started last year. Democrats now control enough states to put the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact into practice—a kind of back-door abolition of the Electoral College that has twice this century delivered a Republican popular-vote loser into the White House. That agreement, which has already been passed by states possessing 222 electoral votes, would go into effect when it clears the electoral vote threshold of 270.With the new Democratic trifectas in Pennsylvania (19 Electoral Votes), Michigan (15), Arizona (11) Wisconsin (10) and Nevada (six), states now have more than enough to get it done.
States that have passed the NPVIC agree to give their electoral votes to the national popular vote winner regardless of who wins the state’s popular vote. That would be extraordinarily messy in practice, but some advocates of the plan argue that the threat alone could compel a bipartisan compromise capable of making it through the constitutional amendment process.
In many ways, though, the most unexpected and momentous outcomes of the 2026 midterms were the Democratic gains across the Deep South, starting in the Lone Star State. The debased political style and lurid policy agenda of the Texas Republican Party had long been the bedrock of the national GOP, and that arid fortress of mean-spirited extremism is now in complete ruins. Democrat James Talarico inflicted an astonishing 12-point drubbing on the profoundly repellant Ken Paxton, a morally bankrupt and politically talentless hack who personifies every awful thing imaginable about the Trump-era Republican Party.
Paxton ran one of the most inept and disgusting campaigns that has ever been mounted in American politics, wasting tens of millions of dollars on anti-trans attack ads, including a repulsive spot with an AI-generated Talarico talking about how God is nonbinary and believes there should be “six genders.” But Talarico’s victory was resounding enough to suggest that outgoing Senator John Cornyn would have gotten clobbered too—-the fate that greeted the three-term incumbent Governor Greg Abbott, who lost decisively to state Representative Gina Hinojosa.
It’s hard to overstate the centrality of Texas to the national Republican project. If Democrats can maintain the inroads they clearly made with the state’s now fervidly anti-Trump Latino plurality, it will be difficult for a Republican presidential candidate to win there, making the party’s Electoral College math very difficult. But it wasn’t just Texas.
As of this writing, Democratic challenger Scott Colom leads incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 65 votes out of nearly a million ballots in Mississippi, a state that Trump won by almost 23 points in 2024. In deep-red South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews didn’t just win but easily knocked off appointed incumbent Senator Darline Graham Nordone—one of the many laughably inept candidates that Trump was personally responsible for elevating in Republican primaries. Even a tiny national investment of time and energy could likely have put Democrat Jamie Davis over the top in Louisiana, where the hapless Republican Julia Letlow (you guessed it: a Trump pick who primaried a sitting senator) prevailed by fewer than two points. Senate candidate Angie Nixon in Florida—yes, Florida—also came close to winning, despite the complete absence of support from the national Democratic Party.
These results mean that the backlash to the Supreme Court’s final demolition of the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais was a vastly underrated factor in the region. Black voters in the South made their power and fury known—effectively signaling that they would not allow the work of generations to be erased by these unconscionable Republican goblins. Incredibly, with Don Davis leading in North Carolina and Shomari Figures winning in Alabama, it looks like Republicans only successfully redrew a handful Black Democrats out of their seats. The biggest drop in Black representation in Congress will actually come from several GOP Black House representatives who sought higher offices rather than from the neo-Confederate gerrymanders that Trump unleashed in the region.
These are all paradigm-shifting upsets that promise to revive the fortunes of the Democratic Party in the Deep South. This midterm cycle marks the last time that Republicans could afford to take these states for granted—or that national Democrats starve great Southern candidates like Jamie Davis of resources and support. If Democrats can win in Mississippi and South Carolina, they can win anywhere.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But they could not have done it by increasing Black turnout alone. We don’t yet have exit polls or data for individual states, yet it seems possible that several of the pillars that have propped up Republicans in the region may have crumbled. In the rest of the country, college-educated white voters have become a core Democratic constituency, but in the Deep South they remained a sharply Republican group. That looks like it changed on Tuesday night. New York Times data shows that college-educated white voters shifted left by 18 points in the South Carolina Senate race, 17 points in Texas and 16 points in Louisiana. If that holds beyond this election, the consequences would be far-reaching for long-term Republican control of this region.
And in Texas, Latino voters who had long been redder than their counterparts in the West, Midwest, and Northeast clearly broke decisively for Democrats. The magnitude of that shift in Texas (42 points according to The New York Times) is staggering. If it lasts beyond this election—and it’s hard to imagine Latinos forgiving and forgetting the GOP’s inhumane, disastrous mass deportation campaign anytime soon—that would lead to a longer-term collapse of the GOP’s position in Texas reminiscent of how California Republicans committed collective political suicide in the 1990s by turning Latino voters against them. Ask the California GOP how that’s going 30 years later.
The scale of this once-in-a-generation wipeout is already forcing Republican media outlets to genuinely come to terms with a crushing defeat for the first time since 2012. Party elites famously did not conduct any kind of autopsy after 2020, throwing their lot in instead with Trump’s sore-loser election denialism. And the Republicans’ broad but shallow victory in 2024 led virtually every elected Republican to believe that nasty authoritarianism overseen by clueless edgelords was a winning formula. It was not.
Republicans looking for a silver lining in last night’s results have a harder task than the grunts tasked with finding those mythical weapons of mass destruction in Iraq. The truth is that Trumpism was repudiated up and down the ballot as comprehensively as anyone could possibly have hoped. Popular anger about stupid wars, high energy prices, brownshirt vigilantes in our cities, rising costs, corruption and attempted election-rigging is the real vibe shift before us now.
Each of these calamitous policy outcomes was tied directly or indirectly to the MAGA authoritarian project, and none of them would have happened with a functioning Congress even remotely interested in upholding its role in the constitutional order or pushing back against the Mad King unraveling by the hour in the White House. On Tuesday night, Americans revolted decisively against this indecent, flailing autocrat, sending scores of his pathetic congressional enablers into retirement. In the process, they’ve given Democrats their first glimmers of real hope in many years and affirmed, at long last, that voters still have enough decency to reject the profound, disorienting ugliness of the past two years.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Art Collaboration Kyoto fair celebrates five years of matchmaking galleries
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
This year marks the fifth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto (ACK), the fair that pairs Japanese commercial galleries with international peers to collaborate on shared stands. The fair will take place from 7 to 9 November at the Kyoto International Conference Center. The event has become known for its distinctive exhibitor model, which has proved popular with exhibitors and fair attendees alike.
“We thought, ‘If we are going to do this, why not create a fair that galleries and artists themselves would find exciting and genuinely want to be part of?’” Miho Doi, ACK’s director of experiences, tells The Art Newspaper about the fair’s founding.
This year’s edition includes a number of high-profile Western galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Jeffrey Deitch and Carlos Ishikawa, alongside Asian galleries such as Seoul’s Gallery Hyundai.
The collaborative format is intended to give both Japanese and international galleries an opportunity to work together and introduce their artists and programmes to new audiences. Pairing domestic and foreign galleries has been key for the success of the fair, organisers say, especially for dealers without experience in Japan.
“For an overseas gallery, participating independently in an art fair in a country it is entering for the first time is by no means easy,” Doi says. “We have heard from participating galleries that, for a variety of reasons, taking part in a Japanese fair entirely on their own would not have been realistic.”
The fair’s main section will bring together 52 galleries. Taro Nasu from Tokyo will join forces with Hauser & Wirth for a presentation focused on text in contemporary art, including works by Louise Bourgeois, Jenny Holzer, David Horvitz and Glenn Ligon, among others. Nanzuka from Tokyo will work alongside Jeffrey Deitch, while Tokyo Gallery + BTAP will team up with Gallery Hyundai for a presentation pairing post-war Japanese and Korean experimental practices, including the Korean artist Seung-taek Lee in dialogue with the Japanese artist Kishio Suga.
“Some participating galleries have even described ACK as a ‘fair built on friendship’ rather than a place for competition,” Doi says.
Another section of the fair is dedicated to presentations from 11 individual galleries with strong connections to Kyoto. Mendes Wood DM, for instance, will present works by Tomie Ohtake—who was born in Kyoto and later relocated to São Paulo, which is home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan—among other artists. Hong Kong’s Kiang Malingue will show works by Yang Chi-Chuan and Faye Wei Wei, whose sculptures and paintings respond to Kyoto’s landscapes and urban environment.
The fair also coincides with a programme of special exhibitions and projects across Kyoto. This year, the Scottish painter Andrew Cranston will present an installation at Ryosokuin Temple, a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto’s historic Gion district. The exhibition is organised by Modern Art and Ingleby. Elsewhere, Carlos Ishikawa will stage a presentation of work by Evelyn Taocheng Wang and Issy Wood at Korin-in Temple.
This edition of ACK takes place under a new leadership committee structure, introduced earlier this year. Rather than being led by a single fair director, ACK is now guided by a seven-member committee with expertise spanning art consulting, cultural foundations, Kyoto cultural policy, fair production, education, partnerships and collector relations. The former fair director, Yukako Yamashita, now leads the fair’s ambassador programme.
As for ACK’s next five years, Doi says the leadership committee aims to develop the fair into a platform that “connects the art scenes of Japan and the world and generates a virtuous cycle between cultural and commercial value”.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: After the Celebration, Some Key Lessons From Election 2026
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Robert L. Borosage
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
After the Celebration, Some Key Lessons From Election 2026
Populist messages and populist candidates won.
Last night, voters delivered a stunning repudiation of Donald Trump, his Republican congressional enablers, and his reign of chaos, corruption, and calamity. Democrats won Senate seats in Texas, South and North Carolina, Kansas (for the first time in nearly a century), Iowa, and more. They won races where their candidates were outspent 10 to one and more. They elected the most diverse and populist candidates in memory—the first Gen Z woman in Congress, a DSA populist, and, to the Senate, the first Muslim, the first Native American woman, and the first openly gay male, as well as the first African American female governor ever, in Georgia of all places, the first Hispanic female governor in Texas, and more. They triumphed over Trump’s midterm reapportionment gambit and a record flood of money from billionaires and crypto, AI, and AIPAC lobbies.
In his sad and delusional closing argument to voters, delivered before the Reflecting Pool, the president boasted about his renovations of the pool, the golf course, the ballroom, and more, then asserted that “I’ve kept every single promise I made, except far more. I’ve actually kept more promises than I made.”
In fact, the stunning Democratic sweep was directly the result of promises broken—Trump’s campaign promises of no more wars, that prices would come down on day one, that tariffs would be paid by foreigners, that the crackdown on immigrants would target criminals, that he’d clean the swamp, that he’d protect Medicare and Social Security, and more.
Compared to 2024, the swing in votes toward Democrats went across the board, led by young men, plus 38; young voters generally, plus 32; Hispanics, plus 22; African Americans, plus 16; and white women, plus 11. MAGA hopes of a new enduring majority were shattered.
As Democrats recover from the celebration, there are clear lessons that should not be forgotten.
Movements matter. In this election, mobilization beat money; aroused and organized citizens beat billionaires. That began not with party operatives and pollsters but with citizen mobilizations. The No Kings marches that galvanized energy in the wake of Trump’s victory in 2024. The stunning Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez “Fighting Oligarchs” tour that set the frame for campaigns from Texas to Maine. The courageous citizen response to the masked ICE thugs, most dramatically in Minneapolis, where citizens organized to protect their neighbors, doubling down even after ICE murdered two protesters.
Second, populism unites and galvanizes. For months, establishment Democrats took potshots at the left, even at the risk of reinforcing Trump’s poisonous assault on socialists, lunatic communists, and jihadist radicals taking over the Democratic Party. Bernie was too extreme; radicals were alienating Democratic donors. James Carville, featured on Democratic Party fundraising appeals calling this the most important election of our lifetimes, even opined that he’d rather Republicans have a small majority in the House than Democrats, who otherwise would have to deal with the left.
In any event, populist messages and populist candidates won—and defined the election. Democrats across the country argued that Trump and his cronies were cleaning up while people were hurting. It was James Talarico, now the youngest senator from Texas, framing his race as a question not of left or right but of bottom or top, people against billionaires. It was Dr. Annie Andrews, newly elected senator from South Carolina, running with the promise to indict Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for his assault on public health. It was Gina Hinojosa, newly elected governor of Texas, making unaccountable AI and data centers and the money behind them a centerpiece of her campaign. It was Abdul El-Sayed, newly elected senator from Michigan, remaining focused on working people, campaigning unapologetically for Medicare for All and more. It was Troy Jackson in Maine campaigning on Medicare for All and on abolishing ICE.
“Affordability” was a Democratic mantra, dramatized by rising gas and crippling diesel fuel prices. Trump’s war of choice on Iran was largely the cause. Trump’s broken promise of no more wars was the modern equivalent of George H.W. Bush’s broken promise of no more taxes. Once more, Americans have voted overwhelmingly against foreign misadventures. Just as Vietnam destroyed Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society, and the horrors in Gaza cost Biden and Harris in 2024, the Iran debacle was Trump’s most costly folly.
Democrats should not ignore this reality. Democrats would be wise to become the anti-war party. Americans overwhelmingly want their leaders to focus attention and resources at home and not continue to wage wars across the globe. The foreign policy establishment—the “Blob”—that constantly prioritizes America’s imperial role over the needs of its citizens needs to be retired from the halls of power, dispatched to monasteries and colleges to meditate on the error of its ways.
The media is already speculating on how Democrats will divide, how the newly empowered left will face off against the leaders in the House and Senate. In fact, on domestic policy, Democrats are likely to be largely unified, building on the groundwork laid by the Congressional Progressive Caucus. They will launch investigations into the brazen corruption, abject incompetence, and lawlessness of the Trump claque. They will unite around a commonsense agenda to roll back the cuts in healthcare and food stamps, to raise taxes on billionaires and impose excess-profits taxes on Big Oil, to lift the minimum wage and increase overtime pay, to have the government dispense generic drugs at cost, to end surveillance pricing, and more.
Their big divisions are most likely to come over foreign policy and the forever wars. Democrats should move to end the war in Iran, to stop military aid to Israel, to block Trump’s grotesque hike in the already bloated military budget, and return funds to vital domestic needs. They should curb Trump’s illegal efforts to force regime change in Cuba and what will probably be an intense effort to undermine the da Silva government in Brazil. These commonsense measures will face fierce resistance from the military-industrial complex, the neocons, AIPAC and the Israeli lobby, the tech companies increasingly feeding on military contracts, and more.
Faced with the historic sweep, Trump announced that he would accept the election results and promised to work with the new Democratic leadership, while claiming to have led “the most successful two-year period in the history of any president.” He is, of course, the lamest of lame ducks. But he still has veto power to block reform, a politicized bureaucracy to do his bidding, and foreign policy and national security prerogatives that give him immense power. The big money that lost so dramatically last night will reorganize, hire Democratic lobbyists and consultants, and lay plans for the 2028 presidential race, which now will begin in earnest. To sustain the new sense of hope, Democrats will have to continue to mobilize, to challenge the entrenched powers that be, to become truly an anti-war party—even as the presidential race opens a big argument about the fundamental reforms and reconstruction needed to make this economy work for working people once more.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Guillaume Cerutti named president of the Palace of Versailles
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexandre Crochet
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
After eight months without a president, the Palace of Versailles finally has a new leader. Guillaume Cerutti, 60, has been named the president of the prestigious institution, according to the newspaper Politico. A graduate of France’s elite École nationale d’administration (ENA) and a former senior civil servant in the finance ministry, he succeeds Christophe Leribault, who was appointed president and director of the Louvre in February following the abrupt departure of Laurence des Cars.
The appointment marks Cerutti’s return to public service after two decades in the private sector. In a twist of fate, he is following in the footsteps of his former mentor, Jean-Jacques Aillagon, who headed the Palace and National Estate of Versailles from 2007 to 2011. Cerutti worked closely with Aillagon for many years, first at the Centre Pompidou, where Aillagon was the president from 1996 to 2002, and later as his chief of staff when Aillagon became France’s culture minister in 2002. “Having worked alongside Guillaume [Cerutti] for decades, I know he has all the experience and qualities needed to lead Versailles,” Aillagon told Le Monde.
Cerutti went on to put his management skills to work in the art market, becoming head of Sotheby’s France in 2007. In 2015, he was poached by François Pinault, who appointed him president of Christie’s operations in Europe, the Middle East, Russia and India. Just months later, he was promoted to global chief executive of the auction house. At both Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Cerutti built a reputation as a formidable cost-cutter. He also proved adept at steering Christie’s through difficult market conditions.
His next move within the Pinault empire, however, was less successful. In January 2025, Cerutti was appointed president of the Pinault Collection, which oversees the Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice, as well as the Bourse de Commerce in Paris. Once again, he was following in the footsteps of Aillagon, who had held the same position in the 2010s. But, as Le Monde reports, Cerutti’s efforts to impose the kind of financial discipline he had introduced at Christie’s, coupled with his wish to slow the pace of acquisitions, brought him into conflict with Pinault, who was used to running his collection on his own terms. Barely a year later, Cerutti was forced to step down.
He now assumes one of the most coveted positions in French cultural life, taking charge of a historic palace, museum and gardens that welcomed 8.4 million visitors in 2025 and employ around 1,000 people. His extensive connections in the worlds of business, culture and politics could prove particularly valuable as Versailles faces mounting budgetary pressures and an ever-greater need to secure support from wealthy patrons.
- This article was originally published in The Art Newspaper France

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Rare Altdorfer landscape previously unknown to scholars to be auctioned next month
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A rare landscape by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Altdorfer will be offered at auction at Sotheby’s Old Masters Evening Sale in London on 9 December, with an estimated price of between £3m and £5m.
The painting of a thickly wooded landscape and a rainbow against a densely clouded sky, dating from around 1520, surfaced in a Swiss private collection. It was previously unknown to Altdorfer scholars and does not feature in the artist’s catalogue raisonné. It is one of only three known oil landscapes by Altdorfer, who is considered one of the first landscape artists. The other two are both in museums—one is in Munich’s Alte Pinakothek, and the other in London’s National Gallery.
“To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field,” says George Gordon, the chairman of Sotheby’s Worldwide Old Masters Department.
The current owner of the painting inherited it from his father, who purchased it in 1957 from the collection of a noble Austrian family, the House of Harrach. Painted on parchment, it was later glued to a wooden panel support. It is the smallest of Altdorfer’s known landscapes. A distant castle perches on a rocky outcrop beyond the rain-wettened forest and undergrowth that dominates the painting, which is signed.
Altdorfer was born in 1480 in Regensburg in southern Germany, spent most of his career there, also working as a politician, and died in the city in 1538. His densely wooded landscapes are drawn from the mixed deciduous and evergreen forests either side of the Danube downstream from Regensburg, Gordon says.
He says it was difficult to give a price estimate for the painting because no Altdorfer work has been offered on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery paid the reported sum of £2.4m for Christ Taking Leave of His Mother (around 1520). It was one of the highest prices ever paid for a work of art at that time.
“We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon says. “It could fetch more than our estimate. I think it’s quite likely that museums will be interested.”
Sotheby’s will exhibit the painting in New York from 7-19 November and in London from 4-9 December.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Charles Dickens’s writing chalet and Hastings Castle added to list of English heritage sites at risk
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The cabin where Charles Dickens spent the last day of his life, the home in Stratford-upon-Avon of William Shakespeare’s daughter Susanna and the castle built by William the Conqueror high on the cliffs above the town of Hastings are among 197 buildings and sites added to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register today (5 November).
The list identifies sites such as buildings, parks, battlefields and shipwrecks that are threatened by decay, neglect or inappropriate development. There are now 4,991 entries on the register, all of which are labelled as of national importance. This encompasses 197 sites that were added this year.
The miniature Swiss chalet which became the writing retreat of Charles Dickens was a Christmas gift to the author in 1864, arrived flat packed in 94 pieces, and was put together by a theatre carpenter after Dickens and his house guests failed. Dickens placed it at the furthest end of the garden, reached by a tunnel he built under the road at his last home, Gad’s Hill, near Rochester in Kent. He spent much of 9 June 1870 working in the chalet on The Mystery of Edwin Drood, before returning to the house where he died that night, aged just 58.The house, now a school, and tunnel survive, but the chalet was moved in the 1960s to the garden of Eastgate House in Rochester, where it is now too fragile for public access.
Hall’s Croft, an imposing timber-framed building dating from 1613, was the home of Susanna Shakespeare and her husband John Hall. After many uses, and residents including the playwright George Bernard Shaw and the bestselling Victorian romantic novelist Marie Corelli, it was acquired by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and opened to the public in 1951. It had already been closed for several years for extensive conservation work when, in October 2025, a car reversed into the facade and caused further serious damage. The playwright Ken Ludwig has donated £1m to the work but major fundraising will still be needed.
Hastings Castle was one of the first three such sites built by William the Conqueror after his victory in the famous battle—and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. The site, with a sweeping view across a stretch of the coast, has a long history, with remains of an Iron Age fort having been discovered there. The castle’s commanding site has made it very vulnerable to storms and coastal erosion and there have already been urgent works to stabilise its ruins. Future plans for the site include the creation of a new visitor centre and cafe.
Along with the sites that have been added this year there is good news: 85 sites for which solutions have been found, and which have now been removed from the register. They include the storm-lashed Newlyn Harbour in Cornwall and a little hut in the Gloucestershire garden of Edward Jenner, in which, in 1796, he performed the first-ever vaccinations.
A pair of elegant Georgian houses in east London, built around 1715 and Grade II* listed, had an unusual saviour: Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, which has converted them—with help from the Lottery Heritage Fund—into artists studios, gallery spaces, and a cafe. The space is run by Sarabande Foundation, which was founded by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen.
Rescue grants available include the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund and the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, both funded by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and administered by Historic England, and the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service.
The UK’s heritage minister Baroness Twycross said in a statement that the register has a crucial role in identifying historic places in need of support. “Every part of the UK is bursting with history, so it is vital we protect the heritage sites at the heart of communities which help tell the stories of our nation.”
Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire, the joint chief executives of Historic England, said the most effective way of protecting the sites was to bring them back into use.“The sites saved and removed from the Register this year show what can be achieved when partners and communities work together to deliver positive lasting change.”
