Ernstige kwetsbaarheden blootgelegd in software voor gebruik eID
door Jan Walraven
Een Amerikaanse onderzoeker heeft veiligheidsproblemen ontdekt in de browser-extensie van Connective. Met dat stukje software van Nitro Software Belgium kunnen Belgen met hun eID online inloggen, documenten ondertekenen of ook Itsme activeren. De extensie in de Google Chrome-webbrowser telt twee miljoen gebruikers. Nitro heeft de problemen intussen opgelost, weliswaar bijna 150 dagen na de eerste melding door onderzoeker James Arnott van het Amerikaanse cyberveiligheidsbedrijf Bay Area Labs.
Arnott stelde zijn bevindingen voor op DEF CON, een jaarlijkse conferentie in het Amerikaanse Las Vegas, en in een uitgebreide blogpost. Via de door Arnott ontdekte kwetsbaarheden kon in principe elke website toegang krijgen tot de gegevens van de identiteitskaart − inclusief de pincode − wanneer die via de kaartlezer ingelezen werd. Arnott legde ook bloot dat een potentiële aanvaller via de Connective-extensie vanop afstand computercode kon uitvoeren op de computer van gebruikers, ook als de kaartlezer niet verbonden was. De potentiële impact hiervan is moeilijk in te schatten, want zo “kan het bijvoorbeeld gaan om spyware of ransomware die al wordt geladen door simpelweg de verkeerde webpagina te bezoeken”, schrijft Arnott in een e-mail aan Apache.
Onder meer bij de ingebruikname van Itsme, de authenticatie-app in handen van vier Belgische grootbanken en drie telecomoperatoren, moeten gebruikers de extensie van Connective gebruiken. Hetzelfde geldt ook voor onder meer het gebruik van je eID met Doccle, de tool waarmee particulieren, zelfstandigen en bedrijven online hun administratie kunnen regelen, en die naar eigen zeggen gekoppeld is aan meer dan 150 bedrijven en overheidsinstellingen.
In zijn blogpost legt Arnott uit dat de veiligheidsfout het in principe mogelijk maakte dat een aanvaller bijvoorbeeld een vals Itsme-account op naam van een slachtoffer kon aanmaken en dus in diens naam transacties en dergelijke zou kunnen uitvoeren, met alle mogelijke gevolgen van dien. Dat een stukje software dat zo belangrijk is voor Belgische burgers dergelijke kwetsbaarheden vertoont, noemt Arnott reden om de wettelijke veiligheidsvereisten te verstrengen.
In een officieel statement benadrukt Nitro dat het om “een kwetsbaarheid, geen inbreuk” ging. “We hebben geen aanwijzingen gevonden dat er misbruik is gemaakt van deze kwetsbaarheden. De kwetsbaarheden zijn gemeld aan het Centrum voor Cyberveiligheid België en we hebben gedurende het hele proces nauw met hen samengewerkt.” Volgens Nitro is het probleem nu verholpen en zijn klanten die de huidige versie gebruiken beschermd. Een woordvoerder van het Centrum voor Cyberveiligheid België benadrukt dat niet Nitro, maar wel de onderzoeker het Centrum op de hoogte bracht.
Aan Apache bevestigt Arnott dat ook hij geen aanwijzingen heeft dat er misbruik van de kwetsbaarheden is gemaakt, “maar dat komt alleen omdat we geen manier hebben om dit te controleren”. Hij voegt er nog aan toe dat het bij Nitro “ontzettend lang heeft geduurd” om deze problemen op te lossen, ondanks zijn aandringen en hoewel een oplossing volgens hem veel sneller geïmplementeerd had kunnen worden. Na de eerste melding duurde het volgens hem 146 dagen totdat Nitro de problemen effectief opgelost had. Nitro vroeg hem om zijn bevindingen pas wereldkundig te maken zodra ze de oplossing hadden doorgevoerd. Hij vroeg een ‘beloning’ (bounty) voor zijn werk en Nitro zou hem 200 dollar hebben aangeboden, maar hij wil die niet aanvaarden.
Om Apache te kunnen lezen moet je niet inloggen via eID, gewoon jaarlijks of maandelijks je abonnement betalen volstaat. Oef! En dat geld proberen we zo goed mogelijk te besteden. Bijvoorbeeld door niet langer elke maand een pakje euro’s over te maken aan Google. We hebben het er in deze blog al enkele keren over gehad, maar nu komt het stilaan in een stroomversnelling: de migratie van onze cloudopslag naar Nextcloud.
Wat we nu al zeker kunnen zeggen, is dat Google op dat vlak een beetje op Donald Trump gelijkt: het maakt migratie allesbehalve gemakkelijk. Om het overzetten van ruim 600 gigabyte aan documenten, e-mails, … toch zo vlot mogelijk te laten verlopen, rekenen we op de expertise van Tactic asbl. Deze vzw zal ook onze Nextcloud-omgeving ‘hosten’ en onderhouden.
Maar maakt Apache zich dan niet afhankelijk van Tactic, vraag je je misschien af. En dat is een terechte vraag. Hier ligt net het voordeel van opensourcesoftware als Nextcloud: als we niet meer tevreden zijn over de ene aanbieder kunnen we gewoon aankloppen bij een andere. Of kunnen we zelf de opensourcesoftware hosten op een eigen server – nu al doen we dat voor sommige zaken. De software blijft dezelfde, enkel de aanbieder verandert.
Rekening houdend met de vakantieplannen van onze ploeg, mikken we erop dat we vanaf midden september in Nextcloud aan onze artikels en nieuwsbrieven schrijven en schaven. Daarna openen we meteen enkele andere werven. Zo willen we onder meer het Amerikaanse Mailchimp, het programma waarmee we nieuwsbrieven versturen, vervangen door het opensource-alternatief CiviCRM.
En volgende week hebben we een videogesprek gepland met de mensen van Bonfire. Zij ontwikkelen opensourcesoftware waarmee we hopelijk de Apache-community een boost kunnen geven. Het Duitse magazine Jacobin toont nu al de mogelijkheden van dit “eigen sociale netwerk”. Daarover later hopelijk meer!
Om zijn afhankelijkheid van big tech af te bouwen werkt Apache aan een eigen app. Wil jij ons een zetje geven? Dat kan met een donatie op BE55 5230 8045 8444, of door een aandeel in onze lezerscoöperatie te kopen via apache.be/bouw-mee. Bedankt.
Ludieke luddieten maken verzet tegen big tech weer leuk
door Jan Walraven
“Fuck, fuck, fuck AI.” Veel duidelijker wordt een slagzin niet. Begin juli vierden actievoerders in New York een week lang The Summer of Ludd. En ‘vierden’ is wel degelijk het juiste woord, als we het verslag van Janus Rose voor technologieniewssite 404 Media mogen geloven.
Het festival was niet gewoon een zoveelste protestmars, maar wou eerst en vooral aantonen dat we geen sociale media en dominante techplatformen nodig hebben om elkaar te ontmoeten én plezier te maken.
De Luddite Renaissance kondigde de acties niet aan op sociale media, wel via affiches en mond-aan-mondreclame. Van het theatrale tribunaal en de vele getuigenissen tegen pakweg de “criminele praktijken” van OpenAI werden geen korte video’s voor TikTok of Instagram gemaakt. Want: The Event is the Medium, zoals de titel van het enkel op papier verkrijgbare manifest duidelijk maakt.
Ja, er verschenen wel nieuwsartikels met enkele foto’s, maar je moest er vooral écht bijzijn. Bijvoorbeeld om te zien dat de nieuwe generatie luddieten, die al enkele maanden onder verschillende namen actief zijn in New York, niet enkel haar inspiratie haalt bij de originele brekers van machinale weefgetouwen in het negentiende-eeuwse Engeland, maar ook bij de Nederlands-Belgische ‘kabouters’. Deze geweldloze, anarchistische protestbeweging voerde begin jaar 70 ludieke acties tegen onder meer consumentisme en voor natuur en milieu.
(Terzijde: als iemand ‘luddiet’ als scheldwoord gebruikt omdat je niet zomaar Claude gebruikt om te weten hoe je een potlood slijpt, laat die persoon dan dit artikel uit ons archief lezen.)
Zal een als kabouter verklede New Yorker die een iPhone aan grut slaat Mark Zuckerberg doen twijfelen of hij wel nog een giga-datacenter moet bouwen? Wie weet! Janus Rose ziet alvast in de kolderieke en absurdistische sfeer het onderscheidende karakter van deze nieuwe luddieten: geen cynisme, wel het pure plezier van protesteren tegen iets dat onontkoombaar lijkt. En een oude smartphone symbolisch offeren, is eens iets anders dan AI-ontwikkelaars als Anthropic die massaal tweedehands boeken opkopen om die in te scannen en tegelijk te vernietigen (de rug wordt ervan gesneden om ze makkelijker te kunnen scannen). Hoe ouder het boek, hoe liever, want daar staat zeker geen door AI gegenereerde nonsens in, in tegenstelling tot wat tegenwoordig op het wereldwijde web verschijnt. Zeldzame boeken zijn het meest gegeerd. Kwestie van hun taalmodel nog “slimmer” te maken. En eenmaal vernietigd, worden ze nóg zeldzamer.
Maar terug naar de nieuwe luddieten. Zij willen voorbijgangers geen complex aanpraten of veroordelen omdat ze werkelijk alles aan Google Gemini vragen of soms te lang door hun Instagram-feed scrollen, maar vooral tonen dat we ook zonder big tech kunnen. En dat dit verzet geweldig plezant kan zijn. Dat is misschien de beste overredingstactiek om zich bij deze onafhankelijkheidsbeweging aan te sluiten en mee te werken aan offline ontmoetingsplekken.
Het is een les die we bij Apache ook ter harte kunnen nemen. Uiteraard geven we onze onafhankelijkheidsstrijd tegen big tech niet op, maar dit gaat om meer dan technologie. Onze Franstalige collega’s van Médor en ook van het Portugese Fumaça hebben dat al langer begrepen: zij organiseren op regelmatige tijdstippen ook échte, offline ontmoetingen met hun lezers, zoals we in een artikel voor Apache Magazine schreven.
Ook de Europese Commissie lijkt er (althans soms) op gebrand om big tech het lachen te laten vergaan. De Commissie heeft Google (nogmaals) twee boetes opgelegd van in totaal 890 miljoen euro omdat de techgigant zijn machtspositie misbruikt. Ten eerste door in zijn zoekmachine voorrang te geven aan eigen producten en diensten, en ten tweede door het voor app-ontwikkelaars te moeilijk te maken om gebruikers naar goedkopere aanbiedingen buiten de Google Play Store te leiden.
Die nieuwe boete is Donald Trump wel (weer) in het verkeerde keelgat geschoten. Hij heeft al gedreigd met hogere importtarieven voor de EU, waarmee hij nogmaals de nauwe banden tussen de Amerikaanse techsector en het Witte Huis in de verf zet.
Het is lang niet de eerste (noch laatste) keer dat de Commissie Google aanpakt wegens oneerlijke praktijken. Begin juli bevestigde het Hof van Justitie een boete van ruim 4 miljard euro voor het misbruik van de dominante positie van zijn smartphone-besturingssysteem Android. Het beroep van Google mocht dus niet baten.
Ik schreef deze blogpost trouwens op een Lenovo Thinkpad X240, bouwjaar 2013, die stof lag te vergaren op onze redactie. Aangezien we met Apache op zoek zijn naar alternatieven voor de diensten van big tech en daarbij zoveel mogelijk willen kiezen voor opensourceoplossingen, moeten we ook af en toe experimenteren, bijvoorbeeld met een alternatief op Linux gebaseerd opensourcebesturingssysteem. Dat we zo een dertien jaar oud toestel nieuw leven kunnen inblazen, is mooi meegenomen.
Ik koos ervoor om Linux Mint te installeren ter vervanging van Windows 10. En dat ging verbazend vlot. De naar hedendaagse normen oeroude laptop doet weer wat hij moet doen. Gezien zijn ouderdom verwondert het niet dat hij soms wat hapert, maar dat is niet erg als je het toestel als een prikkelvrije computer beschouwt en gebruikt. Ideaal om zonder al te veel afleiding deze blogpost te schrijven.
Eerst had ik trouwens de meest geavanceerde versie van Linux Mint geïnstalleerd. Die bleek echter te zwaar voor de dertien jaar oude hardware. Met de lichtere Xfce-versie van Linux Mint loopt alles veel vlotter. Linux Mint wordt aangeraden als de beste Linux-optie voor gebruikers die Windows gewend zijn. Als Mac-gebruiker is het dus wel wat aanpassen aan de interface, maar door enkele simpele aanpassingen kan je de gebruikerservaring iets meer op die van een Apple Macbook laten lijken. Een simpel voorbeeld: de knoppen om een venster te sluiten of minimaliseren kan je links bovenaan zetten zoals op een Macbook.
Het zal nog even duren voor alle collega’s op een laptop werken die draait op Linux, maar dit experimentje toont alleszins dat het niet onmogelijk is. En dat opensourcetoepassingen ook een ecologische optie kunnen zijn: alweer een laptop van de schroothoop gered.
Vlaamse Microsoft-factuur verdubbeld tot 22,6 miljoen euro
door Jan Walraven
De Vlaamse overheid gaf vorig jaar ruim 22,6 miljoen euro uit aan Microsoft-diensten. Dat is een verdubbeling ten opzichte van 2023. Dat blijkt uit een antwoord van Vlaams minister-president Matthias Diependaele (N-VA) op een parlementaire vraag van Kris Verduyckt (Vooruit). De voorbije drie jaar spendeerde de Vlaamse overheid net geen 50 miljoen euro aan Microsoft.
Van de 22,6 miljoen euro die Vlaanderen in 2025 betaalde, ging bijna 8 miljoen naar clouddiensten. De resterende 14,6 miljoen euro ging vorig jaar naar de licenties om de programma’s van Microsoft te mogen gebruiken.
In die 14,6 miljoen euro zit ook de kost van 5.000 Copilot-licenties verrekend. In 2025 bedroeg het totaalbudget voor de uitrol van Copilot binnen de Vlaamse overheid 1,93 miljoen euro. Zoals Apache eerder schreef, komt daar dit jaar nog eens 3,65 miljoen euro bij voor de uitrol van 5.000 extra Copilot-licenties.
De uitgaven voor Microsoft gebeurden binnen de bestaande raamovereenkomsten, die nog lopen tot 2029, geeft minister-president Diependaele aan.
Terwijl Digitaal Vlaanderen een nieuwe aanbesteding voor de ICT-raamovereenkomsten voorbereidt, zet de Europese focus op digitale soevereiniteit de keuze voor Amerikaanse technologieleveranciers op scherp. Daar zit het bruuske optreden van Donald Trump voor iets tussen, maar ook een recente uitspraak van het Amerikaanse Hooggerechtshof zorgt voor onrust.
Is op vlak van gegevensbescherming het gebruik van Amerikaanse clouddiensten nog te verantwoorden, nu er eigenlijk geen onafhankelijke Amerikaanse toezichthouder meer is?
De geopolitieke context, maar ook de modus operandi en de daaruit vloeiende machtsconcentratie die big tech zo big maakt, noopt Apache tot een koerswijziging.
Zoals we een maand geleden hebben aangekondigd, wordt een overstap naar de opensource-toepassing Nextcloud in plaats van Google Workspace ons eerste wapenfeit. We gebruiken al een tijdje beide oplossingen naast elkaar, maar in de komende weken bereiden we een volledige migratie voor.
Dat zal wat voeten in de aarde hebben – en dat terwijl collega’s van welverdiende vakantie genieten – maar het is ook een goed moment om ons overstromende digitale archief op te ruimen. Hebben we echt nog een kopie van een draft van een artikel uit 2017 nodig?
De cloud mag dan wel efemeer klinken, het gaat wel degelijk om fysieke, energie- en waterslurpende infrastructuur, zoals ze onder meer in Henegouwen maar al te goed beseffen.
We gebruiken sinds kort de opensource-berichtenapp Signal om dagelijkse updates over onze onderzoeken te versturen. En dat wordt blijkbaar gesmaakt, want het aantal leden in onze Signal-groep groeit razendsnel. Op deze pagina leggen we graag uit hoe jij je ook kan aanmelden.
Verandering doet meestal wel een bitje pijn – pun intended – maar het helpt om te weten dat we er niet als enige mee bezig zijn.
Voor een artikel dat in het herfstnummer van Apache Magazine zal verschijnen, mocht jouw verslaggever langsgaan in de Brusselse hackerspace, waar digitale doe-het-zelvers tonen dat technologie ook leuk kan zijn en dat een door een AI-chatbot gegenereerde afbeelding niet het toppunt van digitale creativiteit is (alsof dat nog bewezen moest worden).
Ja, opensourcetoepassingen zijn plezant. Wie experimenteert nu niet graag met een robotstofzuiger?
Bij de meeste Belgen doet de naam Hyves wellicht geen belletje rinkelen. In Nederland ging de nostalgiemeter wél in het rood bij de aankondiging dat het sociaal netwerk een tweede leven krijgt. De Telegraaf had de primeur: met Hyves gaat moederbedrijf Mediahuis de concurrentie aan met de Facebooks en Tiktoks van deze wereld. Hyves was in Nederland begin jaren 2000 nog de populairste socialenetwerksite, maar gaf dertien jaar geleden de strijd tegen de Amerikaanse concurrenten op. Drie jaar eerder, in 2010, had Telegraaf Media Groep (TMG) nog 43,7 miljoen euro veil voor het platform. TMG werd inmiddels opgeslorpt door Mediahuis, de Belgische uitgever van onder ander Het Nieuwsblad en De Standaard.
Mediahuis ontkent dat de reanimatie door nostalgie werd ingegeven, maar probeert het te verkopen als ethisch alternatief voor big tech. De uitgever plaatst Hyves’ herrijzenis nadrukkelijk binnen twee trends. Enerzijds speelt het in op toenemende kritiek op de schadelijke effecten van de verslavende algoritmes van grote platformen, anderzijds surft het mee op de golven van de beweging die pleit voor meer Europese digitale autonomie.
“Hyves wil het anders doen”, klinkt het. Maar wie de gebruiksvoorwaarden en privacyverklaring leest, ziet meteen dat je dit best met een korrel zout neemt. Hyves wordt een zoveelste advertentieplatform voor Mediahuis, zoals elke ‘mediamerk’ dat eigenlijk is. De gegevens die Mediahuis over gebruikers van Hyves binnenhaalt, kunnen gebruikt worden om ook de advertenties op andere sites van Mediahuis op maat van gebruikers te snijden.
Of het nu van Mediahuis of DPG Media is: op basis van de gegevens die de uitgevers verzamelen, krijgen gebruikers ‘gepersonaliseerde’ reclame te zien: surveillance capitalism in de Lage Landen. Op kleinere schaal, maar in essentie blijft het hetzelfde verdienmodel als dat van Facebook, Instagram, … (Moederbedrijf Meta lanceerde tot grote tevredenheid van de beurs een ‘persoonlijke’ AI-agent voor zijn gebruikers en daarmee wil Meta uiteraard ook gebruikersgegevens opslurpen en gebruiken.)
Het Nederlandse platform voor onderzoeksjournalistiek Follow the Money ontdekte bovendien dat gebruikersgegevens van Hyves gewoon verwerkt worden via Amerikaanse software. Ondanks de belofte van “een overwegend Europese technische architectuur”.
Een commercieel mediabedrijf dat gebruikers wil insluiten op een commercieel sociaal medium. Denken we echt dat dit een oplossing is? Een stukje macht van vooral Amerikaanse big tech afknijpen en overdragen aan commerciële bedrijven van ‘eigen bodem’? Nochtans toont een andere krant van Mediahuis dat het ook anders kan. Lezers van NRC konden de voorbije weken de queeste van techjournalist Marloes de Koning volgen om de krant aan het open sociale web toe te voegen. Het leidde tot een plan om een NRC-server te openen op Mastodon, waarop “mensen van binnen en buiten NRC met elkaar in gesprek kunnen gaan, onder onze eigen voorwaarden en op onze infrastructuur”.
Mastodon is onderdeel van het fediverse, een verzameling van alternatieve sociale netwerken die onderling verbonden zijn. Zoals bij e-mail maakt het niet uit of je nu een account hebt bij NRC of bij een andere dienstverlener: je kan met anderen in gesprek gaan. (En van dienstverlener wisselen als je ontevreden bent.) Om dit mogelijk te maken, rekent dat fediverse op het ActivityPub-protocol; een set van regels over hoe systemen met elkaar moeten communiceren.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Inside France’s Biggest Uprising Since 1968
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Marlon Ettinger
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Inside France’s Biggest Uprising Since 1968
Despite harsh reprisal from the government, students show no sign of stopping.
In the middle of September, blockades set up by high-school students protesting the abysmal educational and sanitary conditions in their schools swept France. Galvanized by a wave of actions in the Paris suburbs, the movement quickly spread across the country. At its peak in the beginning of October, more than 1,000 schools were blockaded, and the government was scrambling.
The national police responded with a spasm of extreme repression, arresting around 7,000 minors—a third of whom were detained on the nebulous charge of participating in an “unauthorized assembly.” Law enforcement deployed shocking violence; social-media feeds and TV screens overflowed with videos of students as young as 14 being strangled, beaten, and tear-gassed. By the middle of October, the police had fired 145 crowd-control grenades at children and injured 215 middle- and high-schoolers. Two teenagers were partially blinded, seemingly after being hit by crowd-control weapons. A 15-year-old had his hand torn off by a grenade, and another grenade broke a 14-year-old’s jaw and shattered his teeth.
There were also widespread reports of children being mistreated in police custody. One 16-year-old arrested in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis told the online news journal Mediapart that police officers dragged him by the hair into a police car and pulled his arm so hard he thought it would break. Like many others, he was detained for 48 hours and served a single meal each day. In another case, a lawyer told a reporter from the independent newsroom Off Investigation about a severely diabetic teenager who was arrested and held without being medically evaluated properly. The teenager suffered a hypoglycemic attack, then slipped into a diabetic coma that required hospitalization.
“The goal of this strategy was to scare the students and their parents into stopping the uprising as soon as possible,” one police commissioner told the weekly paper Le Canard enchaîné.
Instead, this harsh repression prompted popular anger, which drew more segments of French society into the movement. One poll at the end of the first week of October found that over 80 percent of the country believed the police violence against the high-schoolers was unjustified. In the second and third weeks of October, hundreds of thousands of people across the country joined large demonstrations against the high cost of living and soaring fuel prices.
On October 17, over 100,000 people marched in Paris alone. The demonstration had been planned for weeks. In Paris, the police were well aware of the expected turnout, as well as the fact that there was a threat of large-scale looting from some groups. During the day, marches full of righteous anger bloomed as half a million people protested across the country. Most places where the riot police didn’t intervene stayed calm; in others, the police used tear gas early and indiscriminately, diverting the orderly processions into cramped side streets and sowing chaos.
The Interior Ministry later admitted that it had lost control of the streets at night, a situation likely exacerbated by the heavy-handed response during the day. The ministry has not yet explained why it deployed only 42 riot-police units and left 14 units inactive. In the Southern Marseille region, where hundreds of businesses were looted, only three units were deployed, while seven were left inactive. And in Le Touquet and Amiens, special riot police were mobilized to protect the artisanal-chocolate shops owned by the family of President Emmanuel Macron’s wife.
After fiery images from the night’s riots spread across the world, the international far right, including the president of the United States, joined France’s home-grown racists in Islamophobic attacks blaming French Arabs and Africans. Those with no answers for popular demands also blamed immigrants and outside agitators for the October 24 riots following housing protests in Barcelona, Spain, and high-school demonstrations in Belgium, both partially inspired by the French blockades.
President Macron told citizens not to march at all, as the Senate accelerated legislation introducing harsh penalties for protesters who are merely present near acts of violence and looting, and the government has drafted plans to cut off access to social media at the discretion of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. The government has also blamed the left, including Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the presidential candidate of the left-wing party La France Insoumise, whom Lecornu reportedly explored prosecuting for “inciting rebellion.” Similar charges were being considered for the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko.
On October 24, when protesters defied the government’s warning and came out in nearly the same numbers as they had the week before, I talked with Ozana, a 20-year-old who was marching in the rain with a friend and was angry about the government’s response. “We’re in France—we have the right to make demands, we have the right to protest!” she said. On October 26, the Education Ministry announced that some of the high-schoolers’ demands would be met. Student unions and organizations responded with calls to increase the pressure on the government and to continue the protests during the coming weeks.
“We got crumbs compared to what we are asking for,” one student organization’s representative, Clément Vieillot, told BFMTV, a major news channel.
Ozana vowed to me that they would continue to come out to protest for as long as they needed to. “Even in the rain?” I asked.
“Even in the snow!” she replied.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Jonathan Jones
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Exhibition of the week
Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires 
  
From the tulips and silks of the Ottoman court, back in time to the Emperor Constantine’s palace, this is a sumptuous and haunting mystery tour.
 
V&A South Kensington, London, 7 November to 9 May
Also showing
Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant 
  
Two modern painters, one complex relationship in an exhibition that takes you to the heart of the early 20th century Bloomsbury Group.
 
Tate Britain, London, from 12 November
Ida Applebroog 
  
Angry Birds of America, a series of animal images that updates Audubon for the Trump era, and naked portraits of people that celebrate human variety.
 
Fruitmarket Gallery, Edinburgh, until 11 February
Glenn Brown 
  
The superbly decadent contemporary painter takes on the luscious genius of Thomas Gainsborough.
 
Gainsborough’s House, Sudbury, until 18 April
Alexis Kyle Mitchell 
  
An exhibition about health inequalities and the way people’s bodies are judged.
 
Site Gallery, Sheffield, until 21 March
Image of the week
The aficionados among you will immediately recognise this screenprint: Marilyn Monroe was recreated countless times with infinite variety by Andy Warhol. Only the very keenest cognoscente, however, will recognise that pop art’s king of reproduction has himself been reproduced here. Elaine Sturtevant’s Warhol Black Marilyn (2004) is just one example of a feedback loop the conceptual forger has created with artists such as Jasper Johns, Keith Haring and her beloved Warhol, by copying their work to such a degree that it makes us reflect on how meaning is created around art. Her exhibition is at Raven Row in London until 20 December.
What we learned
Comedian Andy Field drew a horse a day until he mastered it
Visiting art galleries is good for you but we do we need another self-optimisation prescription?
A rare Renaissance masterpiece hidden for 70 years could fetch £5m at auction
British modernist painter Wilhelmina Barns-Graham is finally getting the recognition she deserves
CJ Reay is fighting the system with quilts
You can make great art by putting a traffic cone on your head
The Bloomsbury Group helped shape how we think about mental health – and illness
Art imitates life imitating art imitating life … if you consider Rocky art
Masterpiece of the week
The Virgin and Child by Giovanni Bellini, c1480-90
The Bellinis not only dominated Venetian art in the later 15th century but spanned east and west, linking Italy with Istanbul. Giovanni’s brother Gentile travelled to the capital of the Ottoman Empire and portrayed its Sultan – as seen in the V&A blockbuster Constantinople to Istanbul – as well as other places and people he saw in the eastern Mediterranean. Giovanni was more of a homebody but you couldn’t entirely avoid global influence in Venice, capital of a great trading empire, with its golden Byzantine mosaics in St Mark’s. Is there perhaps a hint of a Byzantine icon about this painting with its eerie spiritual calm and the subtly luxurious hanging behind the Virgin? You feel the air warming and vibrating around her, the stillness of those clouds, the rich veined purple marble of the parapet in front of her. Bellini makes you meditate with his music of colour.
 
National Gallery, London

This weekend, Powerhouse Parramatta, a vast new arts and technology museum, opens in Sydney, Australia. But its unveiling is shrouded in allegations of misconduct relating to the chief executive who had led the project, Lisa Havilah, who stepped down in August. Ben Luke speaks to The Art Newspaper’s Australian reporter, Elizabeth Fortescue, about the building and the scandal.
In southern Lebanon, despite a supposed ceasefire in the war between Hezbollah and Israel, heritage continues to be damaged by Israeli military activity. Ben talks to Sarvy Geranpayeh, who has been talking to politicians, heritage professionals and artists about the destruction.
And this episode’s Work of the Week is greens crossing greens (to Piet Mondrian who lacked green) (1966) by Dan Flavin. A landmark work for the US artist, first shown at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, it is one of the highlights of the exhibition Dan Flavin: Some Light at the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain, which opens next week. Ben discusses the work with Lauren Hinkson, curator for collections at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, who is organising the Bilbao show.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Crushed Trump. Here’s What They Should Do Next.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel, John Nichols, The Nation
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Crushed Trump. Here’s What They Should Do Next.
Seeking facile compromises with Trump is a fool’s mission—and voters who are hungry for change will not accept half-measures.
Donald Trump made one thing crystal clear to Americans who have been suffering because of his failed economic policies, disastrous wars of whim, and rampant corruption: that the 2026 midterms should be seen as a referendum on his presidency. Time and time again, on campaign swings to try and boost hapless Republicans from Ohio to Texas, the president told voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”
The voters listened—and on November 3, they delivered an epic rebuke to Trump and his scandal-plagued party.
Democrats did not just win the House, where they are projected to win as many as 258 seats as this issue goes to press—a majority similar to the one a newly elected Barack Obama enjoyed when he and then–House Speaker Nancy Pelosi enacted the Affordable Care Act. They flipped at least seven seats in the Senate as well, taking control of a chamber that, during the first two years of Trump’s second term, had rubber-stamped such noxious cabinet picks as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. And they made these gains not just in reliably blue territory, but with dramatic victories in state after state where Trump had prevailed just two years ago—including Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas—and in at least one state (Kansas) where they hadn’t won a Senate seat since the 1932 election that saw Franklin Roosevelt defeat Herbert Hoover.
Coupled with statehouse wins that put Democrats in charge in all seven of the swing states that backed Trump in 2024, and the victories of a multiracial, multiethnic slate of Democratic governors in states where the party has not prevailed in decades—including Texas and Georgia—this is truly a national mandate. It gives congressional Democrats the authority at the federal and state levels to check and balance a historically unpopular president—the Pew Research Center put Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 30 percent just before the election—and to develop a robust alternative to Trumpism, that toxic blend of authoritarianism, bigotry, corruption, unnecessary wars, tax cuts for the rich, surrender to AI oligarchs, and a cruel neglect of human needs.
The winners tell the story. From coast to coast, voters backed Democrats who called for more than just status-quo politics with a little blue coloring. Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who overcame Trump’s vicious attacks on his Muslim faith, won with a motto of “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All”—as well as an outspoken opposition to the genocide in Gaza and AIPAC’s influence on American politics. James Talarico beat Trump’s “Talafreako” labeling and a $158 million attack campaign by Elon Musk to become the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988. In his victory speech, Talarico called for “a new kind of politics: a politics rooted in a deep love—for our state, for our country, and most importantly, for all of our neighbors,” one that “requires that we stand between the bullies and the bullied.” The senator-elect wasn’t alone; Lone Star voters, long known for dashing Democrats’ hopes, went straight-ticket blue, handing Democrats every statewide position on the ballot and electing Texas’s first-ever Latina governor, the anti-corruption campaigner Gina Hinojosa.
In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation’s first Black woman to win a governorship. In Ohio, Amy Acton triumphed over the hateful politics of the Republican right. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the country’s first Native American woman governor, while Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan will go to the US Senate as a proud member of the White Earth Nation in northwestern Minnesota, as well as a former head of the Children’s Defense Fund–Minnesota and—along with El-Sayed and Troy Jackson in Maine—a close ally of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders.
Many newcomers to the House are unapologetic progressives who ran with support from Sanders and the surging Democratic Socialists of America, including New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros in Colorado, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. And a proud economic populist, Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, will return to the Senate as an unabashed advocate for breaking up monopolies, regulating banks, strengthening unions, taking on Big Tech, regulating data centers, and going after Trump’s corruption.
The scope and character of this rebuke to Trump is vitally important: It gives the new Congress a mandate to check and balance “the most dangerous president in the history of the United States,” as Sanders referred to him during the midterm campaign.
Trump is indeed dangerous, and he will remain so in the last two years of his presidency. He retains the much-abused powers of his office—including the ability to unilaterally launch wars abroad—and he will no doubt redouble his efforts to bypass Congress, ignore the courts, target enemies, and obstruct meaningful progress.
But he will do so now as a more diminished and discredited figure than ever before. Voters everywhere appeared repelled by Trump: His corruption and self-dealing finally became an albatross around his neck, with Democrats moving the issue to the top of the political agenda. “While the crook president and his crook family rake in billions from around the world, you pay more for everything,” Senator Jon Ossoff told Georgia voters as part of a scorched-earth campaign that saw the Democrat—a potential 2028 presidential contender—finish with 59 percent of the vote.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a key campaigner along with Sanders for progressives across the country, drew thunderous applause on election eve when she argued against “playing nice with people who are committed to the destruction of our democracy” and declared: “There must be accountability for crimes that have been committed and wrongs that have been done against the country and the people of the United States of America.”
To do that, Democrats need smart accountability strategies—such as those of Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the presumptive chair of the House Appropriations Committee—that follow the money and connect the costs of the self-dealing by Trump and his cronies to oligarchical wealth, the affordability crisis, and lousy healthcare. Accountability and affordability can go hand in hand, but it will happen only if Democrats make a true break with the rotten status quo. A failure to reject Trump’s foreign policy—particularly when it comes to the war with Iran and his near-total support of Israel, two issues that Vice President JD Vance quickly identified as liabilities for the GOP—will send exactly the wrong message to voters. And pulling punches on economic issues will only raise questions about whether Democrats are sufficiently distinct from Republicans.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Democrats need to recognize that seeking facile compromises with Trump, who vows that he’ll be “Mr. Veto” on the issues that matter, is a fool’s mission—and voters who are hungry for change will not accept half-measures.
Unfortunately, some Democrats still don’t get it. Before the election, Hawaii Senator Brian Schatz suggested that Democrats should avoid “aspirational” agendas. “I do not think it is time to propose things that the president of the United States is guaranteed to veto,” Schatz said.
That’s the wrong take.
Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar of Texas has wisely warned, “We cannot be the party of nervous lawyers who just tinker around the edges.” Casar was spot-on when he said that Democrats “have to show we’re more than anti-Trump. That starts with cracking down on corporate greed to bring down the cost of health care, housing, child care, groceries, and gas…. If Donald Trump chooses to veto our popular, pro-affordability policies, the fight is far from over. We’ll run on them in 2028 and pass them in 2029.”
Democrats must counter Trump’s self-enriching schemes, crude abuses of power, and ugly theatrics with big ideas and clarity about how to implement them. Where to begin?
take on big money
The 2026 midterms saw record election spending—roughly $12 billion, according to OpenSecrets. Close to a half-billion dollars came from Musk alone. Republicans had an overwhelming money advantage. Democrats beat the money this time, but the party needs a comprehensive legal, legislative, and state-based strategy to address the crisis.
regulate ai
Democrats should follow the lead of Peggy Flanagan, who proposed an independent federal body to provide AI regulation and oversight. They should also encourage states to lead as “laboratories of democracy”: Polls show that 80 percent of Americans favor laws that choose humanity over machinery.
let abdul el-sayed lead on medicare for all
When Barack Obama campaigned in Michigan, he said that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American.” Yes! El-Sayed proposes to “finish the job” by “[expanding] Medicare to cover all necessary healthcare, including vision, dental, and hearing, and extend it to every single American from cradle to grave without premiums, copays, or deductibles.” El-Sayed is the right leader to join Sanders, who is expected to head the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, in fighting for an agenda that—as the midterm results make clear—is seen by the electorate as radical common sense. It is high time to ignore the establishment’s hand-wringing over the populist energy that was key to winning the midterms, to reject Trump’s corruption and his billionaire allies and declare, as Troy Jackson did at the finish of his campaign: “We’re not from the left, we’re not from the right, we’re from the bottom, and we’re rising!”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Budapest exhibition explores Van Gogh and Gauguin's artistic excursion to Montpellier
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
After Paul Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888 to stay with his friend Van Gogh, the two artists would go out to paint together and then socialise and discuss art in the evenings over a glass of wine. Their very different personalities, however, soon led to tensions. Living together in the confines of the Yellow House and sharing a small room as a studio, they began to row. As winter approached, and the weather made it impossible to work outside, the situation only worsened.
In mid-December, in an attempt to clear the air, Gauguin suggested that they should make a trip to Montpellier, 70 km west of Arles. Their goal was to visit the Musée Fabre, renowned for its fine collection of paintings.
The artistic result of this trip forms a central part of a major exhibition on Gauguin which opened this week at Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts. Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin: The Circles of Post-Impressionists and Symbolists (until 28 February 2027) provides a wide-ranging exploration of the art of Gauguin and his associates. The show’s title comes from a key painting by the artist inspired by the Montpellier visit, Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889).
Van Gogh and Gauguin travelled from Arles to Montpellier by train, which took around four hours. Although it has long been assumed that they made a day trip on either 16 or 17 December 1888, it is arguably more likely that they spent the night there and stayed for both days. The Musée Fabre had over 800 paintings on display, so they would surely have wanted time to savour the works. Many of the finest pictures were French, given by Alfred Bruyas, a local collector and patron of Gustave Courbet.
For Gauguin, the highlight of the museum was Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854). This landscape composition includes the figure of Courbet himself, laden with his equipment and holding a walking pole. He is greeting Bruyas, who is accompanied by a bowing servant.
Gauguin, who was impressed with the Courbet, painted a work in response, a year later, in the Brittany fishing village of Le Pouldu. The main figure in this work is Gauguin himself, facing a Breton woman on the other side of a gate.
Superficially, the Gauguin painting bears little resemblance to the Courbet. Stylistically, Courbet’s smoothly painted picture contrasts with Gauguin’s rough brushwork. The compositions appear to have little in common, other than showing an artist encountering other people—and being greeted with a “good day” (and, incidentally, both scenes also include a dog).
The moods seem very different. Courbet appears thrilled to greet his patron and friend. Gauguin’s encounter with the Breton woman, however, is fleeting, as they happen to pass each other at a gate. The Budapest exhibition’s lead curator, Judit Geskó, sees the Gauguin picture as representing “the artist as a solitary wanderer”.
But despite the differences, Gauguin’s decision to entitle his work as he did shows that he was directly acknowledging the source of his inspiration, the Courbet. Gauguin’s title is actually inscribed on the painting, in the lower-left corner.
Gauguin made two versions of his composition: the one on loan to Budapest from the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and the other (which was unavailable for borrowing) at the National Gallery in Prague. The Hammer picture, which was the original, was created to display on the dining room door in the small inn where he was staying in Le Pouldu.
As for Van Gogh, the Dutchman was particularly struck in the Musée Fabre by the portraits by Courbet. These included a self-portrait, The Man with the Pipe (around 1849), which may well have inspired Van Gogh one month later to paint his Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe (January 1889).
Bruyas was depicted by a range of artists and these portraits were also much admired by Van Gogh in the Montpellier museum. Vincent described Bruyas’ appearance to his brother Theo as “a gentleman with a beard, red hair, who looks damnably like you or me”.
Electric discussions
Both Gauguin and Van Gogh were great admirers of Courbet, who was very well represented in the Musée Fabre. Although they agreed about Courbet, their tastes for other artists were often rather different. Vincent wrote to Theo that their artistic discussions in Montpellier had been “excessively electric”. He explained: “We sometimes emerge from it with tired minds, like an electric battery after it’s run down.”
Despite these animated discussions, the inspirational visit seemed a success. Vincent reported back to Theo the day after their return that in the museum they had been “right in the midst of magic”. He added: “Gauguin said to me this morning, when I asked him how he felt: ‘that he could feel his old self coming back’, which gave me great pleasure.”
Sadly, the reconciliation did not last long: just four days later Van Gogh severely mutilated his ear. Although the trigger was probably news he had just received that Theo had become engaged (which Vincent feared would threaten his brother’s support), tensions with Gauguin were also a contributing factor.
Van Gogh in the Gauguin show
Budapest’s Gauguin exhibition is ambitious, with 80 works by the French master and 70 by other artists. Although financial valuations for exhibitions are rarely revealed, The Art Newspaper can report that its total insurance value is €1.5bn.
The show includes three works by Van Gogh: the landscape painting Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) and two rarely-displayed drawings from the collection of the Budapest museum, The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888).
The Budapest exhibition has two Gauguin paintings dating from his stay with Van Gogh in Arles: the landscape Les Alyscamps (October 1888, Musée d’Orsay, Paris) and the portrait Madame Roulin (November-December 1888, Saint Louis Art Museum). Both of these subjects were also tackled by Van Gogh.
Among the other Gauguin highlights in the show is Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901, Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich). This is one of four still-life paintings inspired by Van Gogh’s favourite motif—sunflowers. Gauguin painted these in the Marquesas Islands (north of Tahiti), with flowers grown from seeds he was sent by a friend from Paris.
The museum estimates that the Gauguin exhibition could see up to 350,000 visitors, a huge number for a medium-sized European capital. However, even this won’t match Geskó's Van Gogh show in 2006, which attracted 486,000 people to the museum to see the Dutch painter's works.

https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.title: Amtrak's Penn Station plan could funnel taxpayer money to new venue for James Dolan
https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.text:
Amtrak’s proposal to rebuild Penn Station could lead to heaps of taxpayer money being used to subsidize a new entertainment venue for the Madison Square Garden Company.
The plan to overhaul the station calls for Amtrak to purchase the Infosys Theater at MSG, demolish it and convert the site into a grand light-filled entrance on Eighth Avenue. Previous estimates have put the cost of purchasing the theater at hundreds of millions of dollars.
During an investor’s call Wednesday, MSG’s chief financial executive David Collins fielded questions about the potential sale of the theater, which has a capacity for roughly 5,600 people. He noted the move would take away a revenue source for the company — but said the money from the sale could be used to fund a new venue, potentially in the five boroughs.
“The primary way for us to minimize the tax leakage would be to reinvest all of the potential proceeds in another domestic venue. … I would say that we are not limited to just the New York City market,” Collins said. “However, I would also say that New York City is our core operating market and with us having one less theater here, we would definitely most likely look to the New York market first.”
He did not say whether the Garden would look to buy an existing venue or build a new one.
In recent years James Dolan, the billionaire owner of MSG and the New York Knicks, has struck gold with his Las Vegas Sphere. That cutting-edge venue has a capacity for 20,000 people and has been so successful that Dolan is building another sphere at National Harbor on the Potomac River, just outside of Washington, D.C.
Amtrak special adviser Andy Byford, who is leading the redesign effort of Penn Station, has repeatedly said that the national railroad is looking to get us much money in federal grants and before potentially seeking funding from New York and New Jersey. That means if Amtrak's plan goes through, taxpayers would likely be on the hook to purchase the Infosys Theater — and in turn to fund MSG’s new theater elsewhere.
Representatives for MSG and Amtrak did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
MTA Chair Janno Lieber has repeatedly criticized Amtrak’s plan and has declined to sign on as an official partner for the rebuild, stating the work could interrupt Long Island Rail Road service at the station. Lieber has said Amtrak has refused to disclose the full details of its plan unless the New York transit agency agrees to join the project.
The MTA was planning its own rebuild of Penn Station — which is owned by Amtrak — until President Donald Trump took over the project last year. Lieber in 2023 said he did not want taxpayer money to be used to purchase the theater, saying he thought “the Dolans have gotten a pretty good deal from New Yorkers so far.”
While the MTA’s plan was under consideration that year, a private developer with ASTM Group estimated at a public hearing that the cost of purchasing Infosys was “substantially less” than $1 billion. The estimate came from Peter Cipriano, who is now CEO of Penn Transformation Partners, which was selected by the federal government to redevelop the rail hub.
Dolan supported Trump’s 2024 election campaign and this year backed Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, who lost this week to Gov. Kathy Hochul.
MSG’s latest Securities and Exchange Commission filing lists the redevelopment of Penn Station as having a potential impact on its financial outlook, including the “potential transfer” of the Infosys Theater.
The Trump administration has set a tight deadline to begin work on the redevelopment of Penn Station. Officials said they expect shovels in the ground by the end of 2027.
Collins said during MSG’s investor call that executives “expect ample time to determine the appropriate path forward” on selling the theater.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.title: Republicans Are Desperate to Pretend They Never Supported the War With Iran
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.author: Alain Stephens
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.text:
Alain Stephens is an investigative reporter covering gun violence, arms trafficking, and federal law enforcement.
To say that Americans were pissed off is an understatement.
On Tuesday, Democrats didn’t just seize control of both houses of Congress. They redrew the American political map, capturing offices that had remained reliably Republican for generations, from the Deep South to Kansas and Texas. The Lone Star State alone, with its 40 Electoral College votes, now raises the possibility of a seismic shift in the calculus of future presidential elections.
The sheer scale of the historic Democratic surge delivered an unmistakable rebuke to America’s supposedly populist president. The message was clear and simple: We do not like you.
Much of Americans’ rapid disillusionment with the Trump administration can be traced to a single word — Iran — and the cascading economic hardships Americans have endured as the war has dragged on.
For the GOP, the threat is existential. The war has gone from a Republican loyalty test to a political albatross for many of its former supporters, one that many Republicans are now jettisoning themselves away from to salvage their own political futures.
By Wednesday, it had become the chief explanation for the party’s sweeping electoral defeat, with Vice President JD Vance declaring unequivocally on X that “the reason we lost is the war.”
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he wrote. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Coming from Trump’s own vice president, it was a striking about-face.
The tirade also raised an awkward question ahead of the 2028 presidential race: How does a potential successor to the MAGA mantle campaign against a war waged by his own administration?
Trump, however, has not gone nearly as far as his VP. Although the president acknowledged the war hurt Republicans, he still defended it on its merits. Speaking with reporters Wednesday after expounding at length about his White House ballroom, Trump said, “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it.”
Where Did All the Warmongers Go?
But on the campaign trail, Republicans were not completely oblivious to Americans’ collective frustration with the Iran war.
In September, ABC News identified 17 Republican lawmakers and candidates who had called for ending the war through public statements or votes. Much of the pressure came in competitive midterms races, as the conflict’s effects on oil, diesel, and fertilizer prices reached American households.
In Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson called for a “successful and immediate end” to the war in September, warning that voters were paying the price at gas pumps and grocery stores. Yet she voted six times against House measures directing Trump to halt the attacks. During an October 25 ABC interview, Hinson said she would not rule out a post-election U.S. offensive and said she trusted Trump and the military to choose the right timetable. Despite the president praising her weight loss at a recent rally, tepidly breaking with Trump wasn’t enough to get Hinson over the line, and she lost to Democrat Josh Turek by 4.5 percentage points.
Michigan also had its share of Iran backtrackers. Republican Senate hopeful Mike Rogers described Iran as an “imminent threat” when the bombing began on February 28. In May, he called the conflict a potential “win-win-win.” But with the midterms fast approaching, Rogers released a campaign ad declaring “the war with Iran needs to end” quickly and warned Michigan families could no longer afford the economic fallout.
Rep. John James, the Republican candidate for Michigan governor, likewise praised Trump’s use of force early in the war, saying the president “had the balls” to “assure the survival and success of liberty.” He voted against six House war-powers resolutions, including as recently as September. Days after that vote, he said the war needed to wrap up “quickly.” He went on to declare in an interview, “the position has always been, I hate war.”
Both Rogers and James lost their races.
Even Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a possible contender in the Republican Party’s next presidential contest who could reportedly be up for Pete Hegseth’s job, warned Monday that the war was a “big, big drag” on his party. Trump, DeSantis pointed out, campaigned against another Middle Eastern war. Now voters are dealing with higher fuel costs, and Republicans who refuse to acknowledge the connection are “gaslighting” them. But back in spring, DeSantis defended the strikes on Iranian leadership, describing its government as “a fanatical, apocalyptic, militant Islamist regime.”
The polling helps explain the Republican panic. An Associated Press poll found roughly 6 in 10 voters believed the U.S. made a “wrong decision” in attacking Iran. And it’s not as though Republicans weren’t warned. A handful within their own ranks, including Thomas Massie and Rand Paul, opposed the war from its earliest days and backed efforts to rein it in. But those criticisms seemed to fall on deaf ears.
A Hasty Retreat
With plenty of blame to go around, the criticism has gone beyond candidates and into the conservative media ecosystem.
During the network’s primetime Election Night coverage, Fox News host Sean Hannity told his colleague Bret Baier that the results would have been different without the Iran war. Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the war a betrayal of America First principles, demanded new Republican leadership, and labeled the conflict a “catastrophically stupid decision.”
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene called Trump breaking his promise not to start another foreign war his “biggest betrayal” and said “Americans are fed up with it.”
Other commentators placed the responsibility squarely on Trump himself for sucking his own party into a political quagmire. In The Federalist, senior editor John Daniel Davidson blamed the party’s collapse on Trump’s undermining of a GOP coalition built upon rejecting the interventionist politics of the George W. Bush era.
Some prominent Republican operatives are sure to be thrown under the bus by their own party in the retreat. The first to get the boot may be none other than Hegseth, America’s chief “warfighter,” who has been one of the war’s most enthusiastic, and public, cheerleaders. The defense secretary responded to the criticisms in a nearly six-minute-long video posted online on Thursday, in which he seemed to make the case for keeping his job, touting his elimination of the “Marxist ideology” of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and tarring transgender troops as having a “mental illness.”
“Regardless of how people care about the war, which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon, we need to continue, as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military,” he said. “This is not about me, but of course, the other side, in case you noticed, they’re obsessed.”
Already facing growing Republican dissatisfaction and a ballooning roster of disgruntled and ousted senior military officials, Hegseth now faces the prospect of investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress and an impeachment effort led by Massie. And while Trump has so far publicly defended his defense secretary, he has also reportedly consulted allies about whether to hit the ejector seat on Pete.
But while Republicans and Democrats read polls and calculate the political currency of war and economic hardship, the human cost cannot be measured in votes. At least 3,636 people had been killed in Iran as of early April, including 1,701 civilians and 254 children, according to human rights monitors. More fighting has followed and likely driven that number far higher.
At least 23 American service members have died in operations connected to the war, with almost 900 wounded by enemy fire. But these are estimates, and the Trump administration has worked to actively obfuscate the true casualty rates of the war. These are not electoral statistics. They are lives lost, families shattered, and consequences that will endure long after administrations swap office spaces.
For Republicans now scrambling to distance themselves from a deeply unpopular war, the political consequences may be harder to escape than their own voting records. Tuesday’s results show voters are increasingly willing to hold politicians accountable for needless wars, and the suffering inherited from them.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Whitney Museum selects a staff curator and a stage director to lead 2028 biennial
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Benjamin Sutton
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Whitney Museum of American Art has selected Meg Onli, a curator at the museum, and Zack Winokur, a choreographer and director for the stage, to curate the 2028 edition of the Whitney Biennial. It is due to open in March 2028.
“Every Whitney Biennial springs from a distinct curatorial alchemy,” Scott Rothkopf, the Whitney’s director, said in a statement. “Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art. Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial.”
The 2024 Whitney Biennial: our review
Onli is one of the Whitney’s star curators, having joined the institution as a curator-at-large in 2023, then as a curator in 2024. She co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, titled Even Better Than the Real Thing, with fellow Whitney curator Chrissie Iles. Most recently she co-curated the museum’s current Roy Lichtenstein retrospective (until 10 May 2027).
“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about,” Onli said in a statement. “I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead.”
Winokur’s work spans dance, music, visual art, opera and theatre. He is the co-founder and artistic director of the performing arts collective AMOC* (American Modern Opera Company), which last year staged a five-week takeover of the Lincoln Center campus on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. He was previously the artistic director of Little Island, a park and cultural event space designed by Heatherwick Studio and MNLA that rises out of the Hudson River not far from the Whitney. His projects for the stage and screen have included directing productions at Opera Philadelphia and the Santa Fe Opera, and working on the expanded version of The Wizard of Oz currently showing at Sphere in Las Vegas.
“I’m honoured to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur said in a statement. “Our shared desire to centre objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring. As an artist, what excites me most is being in service to other artists, and I’m delighted to have the opportunity to do so in the context of the Whitney.”
The 2026 Whitney Biennial, which was organised by staff curators Marcela Guerrero and Drew Sawyer, closed in October. It was seen by more than 550,000 visitors, according to the museum’s figures, around 75% of whom identified as either Millennials or Gen Z, making it the youngest audience since the Whitney started tracking visitors’ ages.
The exhibition’s 2026 edition was also remarkably controversy-free, though the exhibition is often a lightning rod for debates, protests and political statements. The 2019 edition was led by Whitney curators Jane Panetta and Rujeko Hockley, and came to be known colloquially as the “tear gas biennial” due to weekly protests and participating artists’ threatened withdrawals over the Whitney’s vice chairman at the time, Warren Kanders, who was the chief executive of Safariland, a defense and security contractor that manufactured tear gas canisters that had been deployed against asylum-seekers at the Mexico-US border, among other materials. Kanders eventually resigned from the museum’s board; he is currently the chairman and chief executive of Cadre Holdings, a Florida-based manufacturer of security and law-enforcement equipment.
The 2017 Whitney Biennial, which was co-curated by Christopher Y. Lew and Mia Locks, was largely overshadowed by the wide-ranging debate over a single painting in the exhibition: Dana Schutz’s Open Casket (2016), in which the artist portrayed the famous image from 1955 of 14-year-old Emmett Till lying in an open casket following his brutal abduction, mutilation and murder. The artist Hannah Black wrote an open letter criticising the work’s inclusion in the biennial and calling for its destruction, sparking protests inside and outside the museum and arguments about censorship, identity and cultural appropriation.
The 2028 Whitney Biennial will be the 83rd edition of the exhibition, which started out as a series of medium-specific exhibitions before becoming the Whitney Annual in 1937, then transitioning to its every-other-year format in 1973. It remains the most closely watched recurring exhibition of contemporary art in the Americas.

https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.title: New York Republicans Are Ripping Each Other to Shreds
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.author: Holly Pretsky
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.text:
New York City's Republican of the Moment Curtis Sliwa is DEFINITELY NOT demoralized by the absolute shellacking his party got on Tuesday.
"I view this complete tsunami, this blue tsunami, especially when it relates to the 62 counties of New York, as Liberation Day for Republicans who no longer feel that if they're not MAGA, they don't exist," Sliwa told Hell Gate. "You know, 'We're RINOs.' Well, guess what? I'm a proud RINO." (In case you've never seen Fox News, that's a Trumpworld pejorative that stands for "Republican In Name Only.")
The losses went far beyond GOP candidate Bruce Blakeman's double-digit defeat by Governor Kathy Hochul. Republicans lost at least six state Senate seats, at least seven Assembly seats, a major congressional seat in the Hudson Valley, all three statewide races by double-digit margins, and they barely hung onto a seat in the deep red North Country with a pretty embarrassing candidate.
Still, Sliwa's feeling…optimistic.
"This is a perfect opportunity for Republicans to organize and mobilize. The people united will never be defeated," he said. "That's a phrase that is very left-wing, very progressive. But this is what Republicans, if they want to save their party, must begin to do: Stop complaining, stop moaning and groaning. Your whole campaign was to basically call Zohran [Mamdani], you know, attaching him to Hochul, a communist, a socialist, a jihadist, and an Islamist. I don't even think they understand what a communist is. I don't think they understand what an Islamist is. But then again, they just attached it all together, and when all was said and done, Zohran helped Hochul, and Trump helped destroy Team Blakeman and other Republicans who were running under that MAGA mantra."
