https://jacobin.com/2026/11/finland-ai-g.title: In Finland, the Left Can Lead on Fair AI Policy
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/finland-ai-g.author: Mike Watson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/finland-ai-g.text:
In Finland, the Left Can Lead on Fair AI Policy
Finnish authorities have instructed Google to stop work on two data centers after the firm flouted environmental rules. Ahead of the country’s election, the Left is calling for a wider plan to ensure AI doesn’t cause further devastation.
Finland’s next general election has been set for next April 18, hopefully bringing an end to the National Coalition Party’s current slash-and-burn coalition, in which the far-right Finns Party plays a key role. Recent polls have, however, seen the latter worryingly rise to second position, becoming the main right-wing force for the first time ever. Trailing Antti Lindtman’s Social Democrats (SDP) by 6 percentage points, the Finns Party is placing its hope in polarizing the election over immigration. But as the SDP and other left-of-center parties like the Left Alliance and the Greens seek to fend off a far-right surge, a new key battleground has emerged: artificial intelligence.
Crossing over into the perennial issues of education, employment, and the environment, AI is already becoming a key issue for voters wherever elections are held globally. In Finland, a narrative is emerging that relates to the specific local terrain, culture, and economy. Unemployment is currently at 10 percent nationwide, the worst in the European Union, which makes the country particularly vulnerable to further AI-induced job loss. The Left Alliance’s leader Minja Koskela released a statement in October insisting that “The data center boom must be reflected in increasing tax revenues, jobs, and expertise, not in municipal residents’ electricity bills or the destruction of forest nature.” In doing so, she signaled that the Left Alliance, which has polled at over 12 percent for the first time ever, can be trusted to navigate the tricky terrain of ethical AI use.
This statement seems to have a major recent data center controversy in its sights. Google has been instructed by Finnish authorities to stop work on two data centers in Finland, located in Muhos and Kajaani. This followed news that the tech giant had flouted regulations by clearing hundreds of acres of forest across both sites prior to performing obligatory environmental impact assessments or ensuring that felled trees would be replaced. The extent of Google’s wrongdoing is still unclear, as recriminations pass between the firm and local authorities. In any case, the act has caused a media storm in a country defined by its relationship to nature, and particularly to its abundant forests, while drawing attention to the clear dangers AI poses for the environment. Public discontent led to a hundred protesters gathering outside Google’s Finnish headquarters in Helsinki on October 12 to demand environmental accountability. The protest signaled dismay at a foreign goliath hacking away at Finland’s natural resources.
Both conservative Prime Minister Petteri Orpo and Finns Party leader and Finance Minister Riikka Purra have welcomed Google’s €13 billion investment in the country, which will result in a total of four data centers (one already completed in Hamina, the two mentioned above and one more planned in Vaala). Yet they are walking a tightrope between seeking to embrace new and vital technology and disregarding the public interest in the name of profit. Finland’s right-wing parties universally caution — along with the Left — that assurances need to be made to prevent rising electricity consumption impacting energy costs. Yet the Finns Party’s nationalist rhetoric stands in stark contrast with its actions. As the second- biggest party in the governing coalition, it too must take some responsibility for permitting a foreign tech giant to run roughshod over Finnish sensibilities. They may as well have allowed Google to destroy Moominvalley, the fictional home of Finland’s much-loved unofficial mascot, the Moomins.
Juha-Matti Mustonen, a Left Alliance candidate in Oulu (the district where Muhos and Kajaani are situated, and where I live) wrote to me in email that, “It seems Google will face no sanctions for these logging activities. In fact, it appears the company will get away scot-free with the environmental devastation it has caused. An ordinary citizen would be heading straight to prison for such actions.” Police have since launched an investigation into Google’s actions, though the episode raises major questions about the governing parties’ seriousness in defending local interests, and it gets worse if we consider the actual financial benefits. As Mustonen continues: “The government was overjoyed by Google’s €13 billion investment. However, closer examination reveals that only a small fraction of the total investment will actually remain in Finland.” This latter point was backed up by Lassi Linnanen, professor of environmental economics and management at the Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology, on the national broadcaster’s politics show A-talk in mid-October. Linnanen stated that Finland offers land and infrastructure, while the profits will go elsewhere.
Left-Wing Solutions
Against this backdrop, AI will likely be a key election issue nationally, and particularly in Oulu. The Left will need to show it has the public interest at heart, while the Right merely pays lip service to the desire for a fair and equitable AI future. One politician who is well-placed to focus on this topic is the Oulu Left Alliance MP Jessi Jokelainen, who is running to maintain her parliamentary seat. This spring, Jokelainen published a policy paper called “Left-Wing Solutions to the Artificial-Intelligence Revolution,” arguing that AI productivity gains should be distributed to employees as shorter working hours instead of merely amounting to more profit for business owners.
Jokelainen also cites education as an area in need of overhaul, with lifelong learning necessary to ensure people aren’t left behind by AI advances. She argues for degree studies to be made more flexible for the unemployed. I am a teacher of academic writing in a Finnish university and can attest that AI is seen as an inevitability — for good and bad. It clearly brings great potential in the right hands. Yet it also brings considerable uncertainty for the sector. Finnish student numbers are in decline due to demographics. Along with the potential for the automation of teaching, this clearly threatens the sector, especially in nonvocational subjects. Lifelong training could breathe new life into Finland’s tertiary education sector.
What is clear is that tech giants see Finland as fertile ground for AI expansion. It is seen as the “Texas of Europe” for its level of data center investment and planning, and a pushover for capitalists: After all, the government recently proposed to cut corporate income tax from 20 to 18 percent, effective from early 2027. Given austerity measures, it might understandably be seen as gung ho in its courting of capitalist projects that have little consideration for the local environment or workers. Such austerity is arguably responsible for a slowdown of the economy through its negative impact on spending. Finland’s leaders mustn’t seek to compensate by giving hasty permissions for foreign AI companies who ignore ordinary Finns’ interests.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: The real race at the NYC Marathon is getting to the front of the toilet line
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
The New York City marathon was the culmination of months, or even years, of physical and mental preparation for more than 60,000 runners who dashed across the five boroughs on Sunday.
But before the run, participants had another important race to complete: the race to the bathroom.
Rows upon rows of purple, plastic portable toilets were stationed around the starting villages on Staten Island, where tens of thousands of runners waited for the race to begin. Doors constantly slammed shut as long lines of people in running shoes and cozy warm-up gear passed in and out of the stalls.
“It’s like the porta-potty company’s Super Bowl,” said Paola Yepez, 26, as she waited for the toilet before running her first marathon.
I was doing the same. My stomach twists in knots when I think about a half marathon I ran a few years ago. I needed the toilet before the race. But the line was so long I had to jump over the gates to get to the start. This time in the toilet line, I wanted to know how other runners were managing their uneasy stomachs and full bladders.
Using the facilities before the race is essential. Urinating or defecating outside of sanctioned toilets can lead to disqualification from the marathon and suspension from future races, according to New York Road Runners, which organizes the event.
One elite athlete went viral earlier this year when she kept competing after soiling herself at a HYROX race in Beijing, prompting outrage, disgust and vicarious humiliation. The pressure was on as runners queued up in front of the portable toilets on Sunday.
“We have a big responsibility on our plate,” said Angelo Martinez, CEO of John To Go, which provided more than 2,000 portable toilets and 46 hand washing stations for spectators and runners.
“When it's game time, [we’re] making sure that they can get ready to run the whole 26 miles and not have to worry about making a pit stop,” he said.
Martinez said John To Go started to prepare for the New York City marathon almost a year in advance. The company spent months investing in more toilets, making staffing plans and mapping out the transportation route. Deliveries started around 10 on Saturday night, he said.
“While the city's sleeping, we're delivering portable toilets and getting ready for the event, where it can be a seamless launch when they start running the race,” he said.
As a longtime runner, going to the bathroom before a race is one of the biggest sources of anxiety for me. I’m always paranoid that I’ll need to go mid-run and either suffer for miles or lose time using a toilet on the course.
As I waited with other runners, they told me about their training, their racing strategies, their goals and all the pre-race fuel sloshing around in their stomachs: gnocchi with pesto, pizza, coffee, bananas, sandwiches, sushi rice.
“After all the carb loading, I'm seriously considering going Keto, because I'm over it,” said Brian Dagliere, 36. “It sounds great, the carb load, but one way to describe it is, to me, it's disgusting. It's just a lot.”
Jodi Renert said her full bladder provided a welcome distraction.
“Waiting in the bathroom to pee is taking away my anxiety to run 26.2 miles,” she said, clutching a big bottle filled with a nutrition-packed drink and resisting the urge to cut to the front of the line.
“ I have to pee so bad,” Renert said. “Like, I shouldn't be drinking this, but it's got, like, all my carbs and electrolytes.”
The whole scene was a little ridiculous. While many New Yorkers were still in bed, we were lining up to flush the nerves — and the waste — out of our systems before we voluntarily ran an absurd distance.
The toilet line leaves a lot of time to marinate on every ache, pain and tummy rumble that could get in the way of achieving a hard-fought goal. Lisa Endrodi said she felt “awful.”
“Scared. Nervous. Yeah, all those emotions. Anxious,” she said.
Marathons have become a mid-life obsession for the 53-year-old, who traveled from the U.K. for her third 26.2-mile race.
“ My husband thinks I'm mad,” she said as she waited in line for the loo.
Going to the bathroom before a race is essential, she said.
“Especially for a female,” she said. “Most definitely. Yes.”
Running 26.2 miles is not a normal thing to put a body through. In my quiet moment of solitude inside the stinky stall, clutching my packet of tissues and bottle hand sanitizer, I remembered I was merely a human with basic biological needs that no amount of training could overcome.
Every person in the toilet line has their reason for running the race. Getting sober. Recovering from cancer. Checking a goal off the bucket list. I was there with my fiance, preparing to run my first marathon. We were racing together three weeks before our wedding, and we had committed to crossing the finish line together.
After multiple trips to the toilet, our starting time arrived, and we had to trust that our bodies were ready. Frank Sinatra’s “New York, New York” serenaded us as we ran side by side across the Verrazano Bridge. That’s when I began to lose a different fluid from my body: tears of joy.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘My reward for waiting in the cold was this painting-like view of the ghat’: Priya Ojha’s best phone picture
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Grace Holliday
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
When Priya Ojha first arrived at Yamuna Ghat in New Delhi, late in December 2021, she was disappointed. She had left her home at 5am especially to capture shots of one of the most sacred rivers in India, but had arrived in dense fog and almost complete silence.
“Visibility was so low that all I could do was wait in the cold,” Ojha recalls. “Around 8am, I heard a voice call out, ‘Dhoop aa gayi’ – the sunrays have come out. They were right. This place that had looked like a graveyard slowly became more lively as local priests started their daily routines and boat riders took out their craft for business.”
Ojha recalls that a young boy appeared at her side and said, “Help me make my first ride and I will show you the ghat.” She agreed: “And that’s how I came across this scene.
“The two boats layered between the foreground and the background give a sense of depth, which makes the photo feel more lively,” she adds. “I liked that I captured not just this majestic place and the hundreds of swirling seagulls, but people just like me who had come to experience its beauty, too.”
When she reflects on the photograph now, Ojha is reminded of her patience that morning. “My reward was this painting-like picture of the ghat,” she says. “Just what I had set out for.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.title: How a Socialist Can Govern a City Under the Thumb of the Trump Administration
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.text:
Socialists will soon govern three of the United States’ most influential cities: Los Angeles, New York City, and the District of Columbia.
Janeese Lewis George joins Zohran Mamdani and Nithya Raman as part of a new wave of socialist local executives. But unlike Mamdani and Raman, Lewis George will govern a city under federal rule.
D.C. is a “federal district,” subject to the whims and micromanagement of the president and Congress. If the federal government doesn’t like the city’s legislation, it can override it. This poses additional challenges if Lewis George wants to change how things are done in the nation’s capital.
Lewis George, a current D.C. city councilmember, has promised to usher in sweeping reforms centered around affordability, including stronger tenant protections, investments in affordable childcare, and long-sought-after reforms on the city’s restrictive zoning laws. She rose to political prominence as the first socialist on the city council, winning her seat on a platform of defunding the police in the wake of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor protests in 2020. (She has since called for hiring additional Metropolitan Police officers.)
For Lewis George to fulfill her campaign promises is “going to require Janeese to use her position and her longstanding reputation as an organizer to convince members of Congress that we can exercise Home Rule and that we deserve the dignity of any other collective body, like a state, in this country,” said Kurtis Hagans, chair of Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America, which endorsed Lewis George in the primary.
All local D.C. bills are required to go through a congressional review period of 30 working days for civil legislation and 60 working days for criminal bills. If Congress doesn’t like the bill, it can either decide to let that review period lapse, allowing the legislation to go into effect, or pass a joint disapproval resolution in both the House and the Senate. If they pass a disapproval resolution, it goes to the president’s desk, where they can choose to veto and let the new law stand or sign it and override the legislation.
Speaking to The Intercept on Election Day, voters said they supported Lewis George because they wanted to elect someone who would fight for everyday Washingtonians.
“I was certainly motivated by wanting really strong leadership for D.C. and people who are going to put D.C. first, in the sense of the residents and the community members and not solely as our role as the capital city,” said Izetta Mobley, a voter in Ward 4, where Lewis George serves as a councilmember.
For Mobley and other voters, that primarily means tackling issues of affordability. “Affordable housing and the rise in unhoused folks, and making sure that unhoused folks have support and city resources …those were very important to me,” said Mobley.
Although Democrats took both houses of Congress on Tuesday, paving a clearer path for the district to flex its autonomy, Lewis George will still have to contend with Democratic leaders like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, both moderates, who are likely to lead the Senate and the House next session. Schumer and Jeffries were often critical of Mamdani when he was running for mayor in their home state of New York, though they seized primarily on his stance on Israel.
Hagans pointed out that Lewis George has the longtime support of former at-large councilmember Robert White, who was elected as Washington’s non-voting delegate on Tuesday. But Hagans said the DC Metro DSA is also preparing to organize residents to put pressure on Congress, given ”the relative powerlessness of the district in the face of Congress.”
Governing Washington has other pitfalls. The district is hamstrung by the fact that the D.C. Council is required to pass a balanced budget and is prohibited from carrying it over into the following year. (Congress also gets to approve it.) The city is already struggling to close a $1.1 billion budget deficit for the upcoming fiscal year — caused by Congress.
In order to achieve her agenda, Lewis George has suggested raising taxes on businesses and the city’s wealthiest residents. For that, she’ll need the support of the city council.
Lewis George is aided by the fact that Tuesday also ushered in a record number of socialists on the city council, adding two, Aparna Raj and Oye Owolewa. “A big part of the vision for the district is to have these organizers on the council as well as an organizer-in-chief at the executive level,” said Hagans.
Aside from bold economic policies, many voters who spoke to The Intercept said they want the new administration to prioritize resistance to the federal takeover of Washington, D.C., and ending the scourge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “We’ve seen ICE raids in our neighborhood, literally where our kids used to go to school,” said Jason Cherkis, another Ward 4 voter. “That’s one reason we voted for Janeese for mayor because she was out front and speaking about ICE in a way our current mayor never did.”
Despite the restrictions placed on a D.C. mayor, immigrant advocacy and civil rights groups concerned about the incursion of ICE in the district are pushing for Lewis George to take a stand.
“We want to see the next mayor doing everything possible to protect these most vulnerable communities from continued attacks,” said Peggy Ramin, policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union of the District of Columbia. “Whether that is legislation or the mayor ensuring that the administration’s agencies are well educated as to what that means in terms of limiting cooperation and even prohibiting cooperation.”
In particular, Ramin said that her organization is calling on the D.C. council and Lewis George to pass legislation that would allow residents to sue any officer — local or federal — who violates constitutional rights.
Ramin is aware of the challenges facing the district to pass this type of legislation without incurring interference from Congress or President Donald Trump — who has personally vowed to oppose Lewis George.
“No matter what Congress ends up doing, whether it disapproves or passes a disapproval resolution or not, I think people here in D.C. are really demanding and asking our council to step up and pass this sort of legislation,” said Ramin.
Aside from federal immigration officials, residents also complained about the National Guard, whose presence was felt even on Election Day. “I have two boys, Black men,” said one voter, Tamika Jackson, “and the harassment is out of control.”
As evidenced by the record number of socialists winning power across the country, Hagans says it’s clear both D.C. and the nation are looking for fighters.
“Democrats have promised a lot for a long time, but they seem unwilling to stand up to Trumpism,” said Hagans. Voters are noticing “this new class of democratic socialists,” he said, concluding, “Maybe I don’t know what that means entirely, but let’s give it a shot.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.title: Texas’ School Voucher Program Could Be “Unrecognizable, If Not Extinct,” Says Democratic Lawmaker
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.author: Lexi Churchill, Jeremy Schwartz
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s vision for education was finally coming together.
This year, the state launched a voucher program that allowed roughly 110,000 of Texas’ more than 5 million schoolchildren to get a private education using taxpayer dollars. Abbott’s loyal appointee at the Texas Education Agency, Commissioner Mike Morath, was leading the state’s largest takeover of public schools in recent history. And the Texas State Board of Education, with Abbott’s support, helped pass a controversial new social studies curriculum that required teaching Bible stories and shifted away from world history to focus on Texas and the United States.
On Tuesday night, as Democrats clinched nearly every office in the state, it all began to unravel.
In a speech after denying Abbott a fourth term, Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa called for a reversal of his education agenda. She pledged to fire Morath and to end the public school takeovers.
Perhaps most significantly, she doubled down on a campaign promise to erase one of Abbott’s biggest accomplishments: school vouchers.
“We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam,” said Hinojosa, who did not respond to requests for an interview.
It is not clear how Hinojosa will deliver on that promise. While Democrats have the ability to restrict parts of the program, eliminating it would require legislative action.
But Hinojosa will have help.
Democrat Sarah Eckhardt, a former state senator who voted against vouchers and will now lead the state office charged with running the program, has said she will push changes to increase accountability and transparency.
Eckhardt, however, acknowledged the limitations of her office, saying that any big overhaul must come from lawmakers.
Democrats won back the Texas House for the first time in 24 years, but Republicans retained a majority in the Senate.
Rep. Diego Bernal, the Democratic vice chair of the House education committee, seemed confident that there is a path toward killing the program, at least as it now exists.
Bernal, whose district is in San Antonio, said some Republican colleagues previously told him privately that they had reservations about the voucher program, but were limited in what they could do because of pressure from leaders who have now been ousted.
“I guarantee that program is not going to be untouched, and it will be probably unrecognizable, if not extinct, by the time we’re done with it,” he said.
Rural Texas Pushes Back
Abbott spent years trying to pass a statewide voucher program. By 2024, he’d grown angry at rural Republicans who repeatedly blocked such legislation because, they argued, public schools were a vital part of their communities. So Abbott shelled out millions of dollars to oust them from office and elect pro-voucher Republicans instead.
He succeeded. And the following year, those Republicans helped pass the $1 billion state voucher program. This week, at least 13 Republicans who Abbott had previously endorsed or helped fund as part of his voucher push lost to Democrats or were trailing in close races.
Abbott’s office declined an interview request, referring ProPublica and The Texas Tribune to his campaign office, which did not respond.
His bullishness on vouchers turned off some Republican voters in rural communities that have historically been strongholds for his party, education experts and politicians said.
A Texas Tribune analysis found Democrats made striking gains in rural and semirural parts of the state, where concern over vouchers, along with issues like data centers, ran high. In rural counties, Abbott’s margin over Hinojosa fell 16 percentage points from his 2022 margin over former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke, and it fell 20 percentage points in exurban counties.
Former state Rep. Dewayne Burns, an anti-voucher Republican from a mostly rural district south of Fort Worth who was defeated by an Abbott-backed primary challenger in 2024, said many of his constituents felt betrayed by the governor’s push for vouchers. “That’s the first time that I think rural Texans really kind of stepped back and said, ‘Are you guys really supporting us?’” he said. “I think they overestimated the loyalty that Texans, especially rural Texans, had to the governor.”
Former state Rep. Steve Allison, who represented a suburban San Antonio district before he was unseated in the 2024 primary, said he remains convinced his constituents never wanted the voucher system. Pro-voucher groups targeted him in a series of ads that attacked him for issues like border security and property taxes but said little about school choice. Polls at the time showed Texans held complicated views on school choice, with one University of Houston poll showing that while two-thirds of Texans supported voucher legislation, an equal number believed that vouchers would funnel money away from already struggling public schools.
“I know what I saw when my staff took very careful notice of what phone calls were coming in and what emails and texts and visits were coming in,” he said in an interview. “It was clear that the overall district was opposed to vouchers.”
Concerns about vouchers became key in several rural and suburban Texas districts this year where Abbott’s selected candidates had won two years ago. One of those races was for Allison’s old seat, which pro-voucher candidate Marc LaHood won in 2024 after Abbott spent at least $700,000 supporting him.
Another was in Bell County in Central Texas. There, the Abbott-backed incumbent, Rep. Hillary Hickland, conceded a close race Wednesday morning. She did not respond to a request for an interview. Her Democratic opponent, Amelia Rabroker, a former teacher, said the Republicans’ heavy-handed push for vouchers spurred her to challenge Hickland.
“A lot of money was pushed into her campaign to make that happen, and she delivered on those vouchers, and it was very upsetting to the people of Central Texas,” Rabroker said. “I think it was a huge concern. The biggest.”
Similarly, LaHood, who did not respond to requests for comment, faced a flurry of questions over his support of vouchers at a candidate forum for the District 121 race in October. His opponent, Democrat Zack Dunn, said vouchers and public education were second only to affordability in the minds of voters he met. On Tuesday night, Dunn defeated LaHood with 54% of vote.
“Across the board, overwhelmingly the sentiment was, ‘We need to fully fund our public schools,’” Dunn said in an interview. “The voucher scam, the voucher scheme, the voucher vote that was taken is hurting us. It’s hurting us definitely across the state, but it’s hurting us in 121. Yes, we heard that over and over and over again.”
What’s Next?
Dunn said he would support measures that ensure more transparency in how taxpayer dollars are used for private schools.
Ultimately, though, he wants to see the program repealed.
Some changes can come through administrative actions by Eckhardt, the new state comptroller. In a news conference the day after her election, Eckhardt said she planned to rigorously audit how taxpayer money is spent and to release more information about the program to the public.
Under her Republican predecessors, the comptroller’s office shielded information that included data detailing how much state funding certain private schools received and how many students most public schools lost to the program. The office argued that it was protecting student privacy.
“As the comptroller, my job is to vigorously follow the money and report back to the Legislature if their investment is not panning out,” Eckhardt said. She added, “That is part of the vigorous audit and performance evaluation of this program that any comptroller should be doing, and I certainly will be doing.”
One key supporter of vouchers in the Senate, the last Republican bulwark in the state, is taking a more measured approach on the program’s future.
Houston Republican Sen. Paul Bettencourt, who led the effort to approve vouchers that had failed in prior years, said the Legislature will need to review the outcomes from the 2026-27 school year and assess the benefits and families’ concerns. He pointed to the fact that vouchers were returned by some parents whose children required special education services.
“I think that it has helped students in many other states,” Bettencourt said. “We need to look at what’s happened here with this first cohort, and we need to make sure that we’re debating not the emotionality prior to passage of a bill, but the facts of what happened after the passage of a bill.”
Scott Schneider, an attorney who represents private schools participating in the voucher program, said the midterm results shocked private school leaders. Some were counting on the state funding to support their business. He said private school leaders could start a lobbying effort to grandfather in the families already benefiting from the program, but schools are also planning for what they will do if the state funding goes away altogether.
“It’s going to be a hot mess,” Schneider said.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Strange, Empathetic Allure of Andy Beshear
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Grace Byron
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Strange, Empathetic Allure of Andy Beshear
The potential Democratic hopeful for president is not a socialist. But he has a folksy demeanor and moral compass.
Ever since I moved to New York, I’ve become accustomed to watching people’s eyes glaze over when I tell them I went to Indiana University. Many of these East Coast dilettantes who went to Yale or NYU, even some of my friends, cannot point to Indiana on a map. I’ve learned that New Yorkers all have a very different idea of what constitutes the Midwest. My home state borders Kentucky to the south and has plenty of cultural similarities with the Commonwealth. Fried chicken, gravy, and corn are staples throughout Indiana, but especially when you drive south through the hills. I grew up in Mike Pence’s Indiana; I was very aware of what it meant to live in a “red state.” Of course, I had a complicated upbringing, but I tell people they can’t talk shit about the Midwest unless they’ve lived there; These states are diverse. Many kinds of people call the region home.
For Governor Andy Beshear, this is familiar territory. He’s won big in Kentucky, a Republican-majority state, multiple times, rising through the ranks to become a potential Democratic presidential nominee for 2028. He’s yet to announce—and he’s not the only in the area running on an anti-Trump agenda—JB Pritzker seems potentially poised to run too. It’s a crowded race, and there’s a divide between the far and center left. Who will pull the party further? Alexandria O’Casio Cortez seems to be entertaining a run, and it seems Kamala Harris may try her luck again, despite the previous failure of her last-minute entry during the war on Gaza. Gavin Newsom remains a front-runner too. Early as it is, Andy Beshear, a lesser-known candidate who has only recently entered the spotlight, has released his memoir-cum-platform, too, called Go and Do Likewise.
Beshear lies somewhere in the middle among his fellow Democratic hopefuls. He may admire Zohran Mamdani, but he’s not a socialist. He may believe in liberal ideals like accessible healthcare for all and minority rights, but he has some critiques for mainstream MSNBC-loving liberals whose rhetoric abandons the working class. “Not thinking about health care as essential to rural America is not understanding how the economy works,” Beshear told The New Republic last year, before emphasizing affordability as the defining issue that concerned his rural constituents. He believes in protections against climate change, but thinks it is just as important to create new jobs in rural Kentucky and protect farmers from tariffs. He wants a ceasefire in Gaza, but believes Israel is a “critical ally” to the United States and has yet to use the term “genocide” to describe what’s going in Palestine. The author of a profile on Beshear put it this way while reflecting on his Christian faith for Vogue: “But as devout as Beshear is, I note an equally fervent faith in the power of pragmatism.” While some more provocative ideologues like Jennifer Welch and Hasan Piker have become spokespeople for the left, the path seems clear for a more stringent liberal like Beshear. He emphasizes social rights while still appealing to some mainstream Democrats. His local wins have already shown how Democrats can win votes “anywhere.” His upset victory has been heralded as a way forward for the left to win red states and seats—even if he barely won. Sometimes squeaking by is the only option.
Sometime last year, Beshear started receiving the profile treatment in the mold of a Kennedy. It was the black-and-white photos in Vogue that first caught my attention. He seemed like he was trying to seem like a Real American Man, relatable and folksy, with a clear, calm, empathetic, rational plan for the country. In an interview with Tyler Foggatt for The New Yorker’s Political Scene podcast, he spoke about red-state electability and the economy. Now, as Beshear returns for a new press cycle, he’s going after Trump: “He doesn’t give a damn about the Constitution,” he told MS NOW.
While Beshear wants the Democrats to be more than the party of #resistance, his memoir spends a fair amount of time differentiating his faith and politics from the current president’s crass, hawkish version of Christianity. He even nicknames his political foe Matt Bevin “Trump Lite.” According to Beshear, Bevin practices “Us” and “Them” politics and would rather die than admit he’s wrong. In short, he’s a bully—like Trump himself. In Go and Do Likewise, this tactic stands out. Trump is front and center by page two, scrunched between Bible verses and the Parable of the Good Samaritan. Later, Beshear points out that “Trump throws Gatsby parties with his billionaire friends, while Jesus hung out with the exact opposite.” He implies that “Now go and do likewise,” the command at the end of Jesus’s story, “means treating all people as people of God—not dividing the country by party, race, ethnicity, or even sexual orientation.” Empathy, he argues, is “neither liberal nor conservative.” They “certainly aren’t woke—a word that has become a pejorative to some people.” Moving beyond the lingo while still embracing its zeitgeist, he extolls us to “Make America Kind Again.”
For Beshear, the truth is that community is all around us. We don’t have to like our neighbor to care about them. Go and Do Likewise is full of Good Samaritans who don’t ask about pronouns in the face of a flood; they just get to helping their neighbors. It’s a value he sees everywhere he travels in Kentucky. “This is what our faith should teach us—that our own comfort does not have to come at another’s expense,” he writes.
This was not the version of faith that I grew up with; I am more familiar with JD Vance’s vision of the world—preaching one thing and practicing another all with a stern grip on right and wrong. Beshear notes that many Republicans cast faith in “militaristic terms,” rather than as the work of a beloved community. His brand of Christianity is not to make a Christian nation but to inspire through his faith. “God-talk is easy,” he says. “Living it out consistently is tough.”
As the former attorney general of Kentucky, Beshear fought for the rights of the many rather than the few. Even when it wasn’t politically expedient. He wanted everyone to be able to get healthcare and vaccines—including those with preexisting conditions and in rural, underserved areas. Beshear slowly unspools these victories over the course of the book: his achievements as a lawyer, his father’s own legal wins and political aspirations. As attorney general, Beshear took on opioid companies, winning settlements for those who had become addicted to pain pills. When talking about such cases, he likes to be clear. He doesn’t like to use the phrase “substance abuse disorder” but “addiction.” For Beshear, it’s important to use the language of his constituents. He wants to be the kind of candidate you can envision yourself having a beer with and shooting the shit. He’s certainly easier to imagine having a gab session with than Newsom or Harris.
“Candidates don’t sound like normal human beings when they use terms like ‘food insecurity’ when they should say people are hungry,” he writes. “I talked to people, not down to them.” He prefers to say why he is doing something rather than merely use empty rhetoric. Of course, that’s much easier on a state level than a national one, even if Beshear has already faced intense criticism from Republicans for his pro-choice and pro-trans stances. He even took a picture with the infamous drag group Ladies of Perpetual Indulgence at a Pride event. Unlike Newsom, who has consistently folded on trans issues, Beshear has defended trans women in sports, calling the restrictions just plain mean. This folksy, simple down-home talk of right and wrong and acceptance strikes me as a similar recipe to Dolly Parton’s anti-politics politics. She wanted everyone to get along and have a chance at a happy life. The Golden Rule was more important than partisan divides.
Beshear includes plenty of stories about other people in his book, including a Democratic senator from Louisville whose trans son took his own life. “The response? No compassion. No empathy,” he writes in anger. He vetoed the bill that sought to keep trans people out of sports, something he continually gets flak for to this day even as he’s instead sought to move the conversation to things like jobs and affordability. “Don’t tell me the Democratic Party should stop fighting for the rights of all people. Just explain your authentic why, and then get back to focusing on the issues that touch all our lives on a daily basis.” I can’t imagine a Democrat in Indiana saying something like during my teen years: “The moment we fail to see our shared humanity is the moment we let people fall through the cracks.”
It does seem, by and large, that Beshear is walking the walk as much as any politician can in his position. He helps everyone after tornados and floods, not just those who voted for him or adhered to strict Covid protocols. He is comfortable partnering with YouTube maverick and provocateur Mr. Beast for disaster relief fundraising as he is giving a speech at the Martin & Coretta King Unity Breakfast. From healthcare to racial justice, the back half of God and Do Likewise is a chapter-by-chapter breakdown of his more tightly held political beliefs. The “dream is nonpartisan,” he says, and admits that Democrats too make mistakes. Some critics have pointed out he’s a bit cautious when it comes to taking on Republicans like Mitch McConnell. He may be less compromising than someone like Gavin Newsom, but that doesn’t mean he can’t be timid about challenging the Republican establishment. It’s a classic paradox. Everyone has to pick their battles.
The personal stories that Beshear shares—from a friend who died in a mass shooting to a woman who got an abortion after her father sexually abused and raped her—inform his public ideology. He uses these parables to explain his positions. It is difficult to believe any politician fully, but there do seem to be a lot of genuinely held beliefs in Go and Do Likewise. There are a lot of natural disasters stateside, but foreign policy is largely absent—unlike in many other political hopeful’s books. Often, these publications are vanity projects—business cards for those trying to get in the game and do the press circuit. It’s a policy book sprinkled with faith rather than the other way around. JD Vance’s book, on the other hand, Communion, is a book instrumentalizes faith as a back door into his cruel beliefs about immigration and minorities.
Whether or not the kind of empathy Beshear champions takes root, it’s clear that the Democrats need a new strategy. They’re struggling to decide what that means. There are signs the midterms could be a win for liberals, but that hardly guarantees a certain victory. A politics of empathy, that grounds those often betrayed by the establishment—the poor and the downtrodden, people of color and queer people—would be a decisive refutation of mean-spirited MAGA politics. I’m not sure America is ready to become kind again. For many, I worry it is too late. I want to believe that we can still find connection, but in the isolation, misinformation, and division, many seem afraid to befriend anyone who doesn’t look like them. As the public sphere shrinks, we become more terrified than ever to engage with the other. For some, like Andy Beshear, the face of the other inspires compassion. For others, it merely inspires fear.

Texas Chose the Willie Nelson Slate
The country singer was an enthusiastic supporter of the Democrats who won every major statewide race in Texas.
There are many factors behind Tuesday’s great-big, Texas-size victories for Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa—and for the rest of the long-beleaguered Texas Democratic Party, which swept the GOP out of power in races up and down the ballot.
Donald Trump won the Lone Star State in 2024 by more than 1.5 million votes and carried 242 of the state’s 254 counties. But by 2026, Texas, like every other corner of the United States, had soured on the president. And this year’s Republican slate was uninspired, not just because of the many scandals associated with Trump-imposed Senate nominee Ken Paxton, but also because once-popular GOP stalwarts, such as Governor Greg Abbott, had messy records on everything from public education to immigration policy to data centers. Clearly, this was fertile territory for a Democratic rout.
But Talarico and Hinojosa also had the advantage of having been vetted by the man who invariably ranks at or near the top of lists of influential, and beloved, Texans.
That would be Willie Nelson.
The 93-year-old country singer has released more than 100 studio albums, won a dozen Grammys (having been nominated 59 times in seven different genres) and continues an endless tour that still fills arenas on his own and with a crowd of outlaw country players, folkies, rockers and rappers. It’s fair to say he has achieved “national treasure” status, as the songwriter who gave us “On the Road Again,” “Always On My Mind,” “Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain” and “Whiskey River.”
Nelson is a savvy longtime observer of the politics of his state and nation. And he speaks up.
Last month, the singer shared a video in which he announced, “I’ve gotten to know James Talarico. He’s a good man who will be a good senator for the state of Texas. Please vote and vote for James Talarico.” The two had indeed gotten to know one another; Talarico joined Nelson at his Austin show celebrating the nation’s 250th birthday, posting a photo of the pair and the message: “Happy Fourth of July from Willie and me!”
On the same day, Hinojosa shared a photo of her with the singer-songwriter and wrote: “Texas in our souls Willie Nelson.”
Nelson formally endorsed Hinojosa on October 3, along with a widely circulated message that urged viewers to visit her campaign website. Hinojosa responded, “We’re one month out from Election Day. Listen to Willie. Vote for change this year.”
As with the Talarico endorsement, Nelson’s Hinojosa backing was covered all over Texas media—along with endorsements of Democrats by other musicians with Texas ties, such as Don Henley of the Eagles and the members of the Chicks.
Nelson also went down ballot, endorsing Texan Vikki Goodwin for the powerful post of lieutenant governor—telling voters, “We need her!”
Nelson is not new to progressive politics. He was an active supporter of former US Representative Dennis Kucinich’s anti-war presidential bid in 2004, and has backed a number of Texas Democrats along the way—in particular Beto O’Rourke, who mounted serious bids for the US Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022. O’Rourke lost to Republican Ted Cruz in the Senate race and, this fall, Cruz snarkily announced, “Willie’s music is great, but historically, this has been the beginning of the end for Democrat campaigns in Texas.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Cruz got it wrong.
Democrats swept statewide contests on Tuesday, producing an epic political shift.
Goodwin beat longtime Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick on Tuesday, and will become the first Democratic lieutenant governor of the state in almost three decades.
Hinojosa will be the first Democratic governor since Ann Richards was defeated in 1994.
And Talarico became the first Democrat to win an election for a Texas US Senate seat since 1998—with 55 percent support and a margin of almost 1.2 million votes over Paxton.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-arrests-.title: NYPD arrests and charges city schools employee in murder of Brooklyn jogger
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-arrests-.author: Kaya Laterman
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-arrests-.text:
A current employee of the Department of Education was arrested and charged with murder Saturday in the death of Brooklyn jogger last month, the NYPD said.
Police officials said they arrested Sayed Mohassib, 27, and charged him with murder.
Katie Suarez, 28, was stabbed in the neck as she was running on the path on Shore Parkway near Bay 17th Street on Oct. 30.
It's unclear if Mohassib had a relationship to the victim, but police said previously they believed the attack to be random. His attorney information was not immediately available.
The city Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
On the night of the attack, Suarez was doing her usual routine, Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny told reporters during a recent briefing.
She left work at a nearby bank around 6:35 p.m., changed into athletic gear, met up with her mother who took her work outfit, and then set off for her run, he said.
Her father had also just left work and was planning to meet up with both of them at a nearby Wendy’s restaurant and give them a ride home after Suarez finished her jog, according to Kenny.
At 7:56 p.m., her father called Suarez to find out when she would arrive, and she told him she was about half a mile away and would be there soon. Kenny said when she didn’t arrive on time, the father set off to look for her on the path and at 8:16 p.m. he found her unconscious under a tree, bleeding from the neck.
The path where she was attacked is a stretch of running and biking trail that is not covered by surveillance cameras, Kenny added. The path runs along the water from a pier in Bay Ridge to a large shopping center in Bath Beach. It’s often crowded with runners, bikers and fishermen.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-optio.title: Enough With the “Public Option” Already
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-optio.author: John Canham-Clyne
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-optio.text:
Enough With the “Public Option” Already
The public option sounds like a step toward universal health care, but it’s really a delay tactic. The latest versions would force public plans to mimic private insurers, while the fight over the arcane details buys the industry another decade or two.
The difference between a vampire and a bad health care policy idea is that vampires jump out of their coffins and drink blood at sunset. Undead health care proposals emerge from think tank closets and suck the life out of useful ideas when the sun rises on a national health care debate. As public fury at exploding costs and deadly corporate claims denials boils over into historic Democratic election gains, can someone please find a wooden stake for the public option?
Improved and expanded Medicare for All would give everyone full coverage at much lower cost than the combined private premiums, taxes, and out-of-pocket payments that are eating up family income today. But it violates a cardinal rule of federal politics: never do anything that causes corporations or the ultrawealthy any pain.
Instead, corporate Democrats wanting to be seen “doing something” about the imploding US health care system have long peddled a vague public option notion because it sounds like the marriage of a big noncorporate vision (it’s public!) with competition and freedom of choice (it’s an option!). Liberal nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and pundits revived its rotting corpse in response to pro–Medicare for All candidates’ primary victories and Tuesday night’s stunning results.
It’s a perfect nonsolution to our three-headed crisis of health care cost, access, and quality. Nobody knows what a “public option” is because there’s no common definition and nothing like it has ever been seen in the wild, so it can be anything weaselly politicians want it to be. It needs to be put out of our misery.
The “Right” Path
There’s danger in chasing the content of various “public options.” The concept is designed as a distraction. Wasting years on policy rabbit holes is the point. But killing it requires some analysis, so it’s worth pointing out that every one of its shape-shifting forms withers under cursory scrutiny.
Rising Democratic Senate star Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) says she “wouldn’t say no forever” to a White House run if “there’s not anyone else who’s on the right path.” Slotkin’s favored path leads to one of the sillier public option proposals. In January, Slotkin, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) introduced the Affordable Consumer Health Options and Insurance Competition Enhancement (CHOICE) Act, or the Affordable CHOICE Act (“ACA” — get it?). The CHOICE Act would get the federal government into the business of selling crummy insurance to almost nobody by allowing the feds to market their own versions of “bronze,” “silver,” and “gold” plans on the Obamacare exchanges.
Even at record enrollment, the Affordable Care Act exchanges covered less than 7 percent of Americans. Nearly everyone with insurance has Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance through a job. Three-quarters of US working-age adults are eligible for job-based coverage, nearly all of which is considered legally “affordable” by ACA rules. That means almost all workers are barred from receiving ACA premium subsidies. Presumably they could buy a Slotkinized plan by paying the full premium cost if they really wanted one. Nice option.
Subsidized or not, Slotkinized plans would cover only between 58 and 82 percent of the actual cost of health care after premiums, depending on the “metal” label attached to the plan.
CHOICE Act public option plans would have to play the same failed “cost control” game as private insurers, building their own private provider networks and trading privileged access to their patients for discounts off market price from providers who join those networks. So, Senator Slotkin’s options will come loaded with the copays, coinsurance, and deductibles that private insurance corporations use to coerce patients into accepting in-network doctors and hospitals. It’s a mockery of “affordability” for patients and would offer neither better nor worse provider payments than UnitedHealth, Aetna, or Cigna.
The contrast between Senator Slotkin and the winner of Michigan’s other Senate seat couldn’t be clearer. At his victory celebration, Abdul El-Sayed turned his three-line slogan into a roaring call and response, with Medicare for All as the closer: “Money out of . . . POLITICS! Money in your . . . POCKET! Medicare for . . . ALL!” Corporate Democrats are still trying to paint Medicare for All as too radical and urge progressive winners toward “moderation,” torturing voting data into arguments about electability. The facts: In 2024, Elissa Slotkin defeated Mike Rogers by a 0.3 percent margin. With unlimited American Israel Public Affairs Committee and corporate cash arrayed against him and in the face of nakedly racist opposition, El-Sayed beat Rogers by a full 7 percent.
Wait, Not That Public Option
Criticize one slippery idea and the optionites will just say, “Hey, I didn’t mean that public option.” In two recent posts, economist Paul Krugman hyped a Medicare “buy-in” version to “allow individuals, and possibly more important, employers, to sign up for Medicare benefits, paying actuarially fair premiums to Medicare reflecting the health status of their workers” (emphasis added). Krugman insists that “many people and many employers would surely take it.”
Surely many who need it the most wouldn’t. The US health care system is so broken in part because we’ve asked six million separate employers who don’t know and shouldn’t be expected to know much about health care to buy it for most of us. But even they know that premiums reflecting the health status of workers would immediately price employers who most need an affordable option — those with high-cost employees — out of any “buy-in.”
The Krugmanite option violates a core Medicare precept. Of course, individual Medicare premiums shouldn’t exist at all. Paying taxes should buy your health care. Even so, except for a few high-income people, everyone pays the same Medicare premiums right now. “Actuarially fair premiums” tailored to health risks contradict the basic notions of solidarity at the heart of public benefits and the very idea of insurance, which is supposed to pool risk across groups of people, not segregate it.
Offering existing original Medicare as a standalone option for employers and nondisabled individuals younger than sixty-five to “buy” is an idea only a Nobel-winning trade economist dabbling in health care could love. Original Medicare’s cost-sharing has already driven most eligible people into Medicare Advantage plans run by the very companies that Krugman dismissed as “parasites.”
So, to fully cover their workers, employers would have to — you guessed it — buy supplemental insurance from the private insurance industry. Never underestimate the power of Nancy Pelosi’s Iron Law of Democratic Health Policy: Congress shall make no law respecting expansion of health care access that does not subsidize the private health insurance industry, and all gestures to the contrary shall be performance art.
False Equivalence
Some people may actually take these ideas seriously, but the essence of public optionism is a bully’s taunt.
Virtually every economic analysis of the issue has concluded that a single-payer system would generate large savings to fund both expanding coverage to everyone and dramatically improving existing coverage. Two key sources of those savings are huge, useless administrative costs: the insurance industry’s skim, and the massive bureaucracies that providers have to build just to get paid by thousands of private insurance plans whose terms and members constantly change.
Original Medicare is far more efficient than private insurance, spending 97 to 98 percent of revenue on actual health care, while private plans capture more than 10 percent of our premiums as overhead and profit.
If public insurance is so darned efficient, the argument goes, a public option should outcompete private insurance. That would have the dual benefit of giving people cheaper, better coverage, and proving to a socialism-averse public that something like Medicare for All could work. So prove it, lefties!
The problem, of course, is that operating in existing markets under rules that will force public options to behave like private insurers strips these plans of the permanence and power that make Medicare and truly “public” insurance relatively efficient.
Medicare controls prices because it permanently covers everyone in the largest group of people who use a lot of health care. When you turn sixty-five and enroll, you’re in for life. If hospitals want to treat the group of people most likely to need their services, they have to take Medicare prices.
The CHOICE Act makes a head fake in that direction. The bill instructs the Health and Human Services secretary to create a provider network and set hospital and physician prices “through a negotiated agreement with health care providers,” without naming which providers or how they’ll negotiate. In the absence of successful negotiations, CHOICE Act plans can just pay any claim at existing Medicare prices. That may sound like a little public muscle flexing to hold prices down, but the CHOICE Act also allows hospitals and doctors to opt out of the public options’ networks, turning Medicare prices into a backstop that applies only to out-of-network claims.
Having a guaranteed right to impose low prices on out-of-network care would give public option plans a little pricing leverage. But in the end, the Slotkinized plans would likely wind up creating networks and setting prices in a manner similar to private plans, whose tussles with hospitals are based entirely on market power. Having surrendered the power that allows Medicare to set its own prices and competing as start-ups with private insurance to entice “covered lives” to enroll, the public options would soon find themselves face-to-face with massively powerful regional health systems affiliated with Ivy League schools or the Catholic Church. Have fun.
To persuade the necessary “covered lives” to enroll, CHOICE Act plans will have to ape private plans by constantly marketing themselves and enrolling and disenrolling clients. Alongside the headache of managing networks, that work requires skimming billions in premium dollars off the top, just like private insurers.
Slotkin, Krugman, and their optional pals have also managed the remarkable feat of finding an idea that would add a little more bureaucracy to the already bloated administrative expenses that choke US hospitals. The CHOICE Act doesn’t create an option. It envisions hundreds of local public option plans with premiums set geographically — ACA plans are offered on a county-by-county basis. Viewed from a hospital’s business office, that means at least three separate local plans, one per “metal,” with each becoming just another payer with its own unique prices, networks, utilization review, and patient cost-sharing to follow, track, bill, and sue when payments don’t show up.
Finally, should policymakers and regulators fool themselves into thinking that these options will be efficient because, you know, they’re “public” and offer below-market premiums, the plans face a potential flood of high-risk sign-ups (the “adverse selection” problem). As Jim Kahn and Hank Abrons point out in Health Justice Monitor, even the more-expansive-than-Krugman version offered by The American Prospect is particularly vulnerable on this question. Being stuck with disproportionately high-cost patients wouldn’t be good for plans trying to prove the efficiency of public insurance, but it would be great for politicians seeking to prove that the government really can’t do health care.
We could go on forever about the details, but the content doesn’t really matter. These ideas are little more than lumps of lead over which political alchemists like Slotkin and Krugman chant their two magic words to dazzle us into believing they’re creating gold. Public options aren’t incremental reforms toward universal coverage. They’re increments of nothing that enable the status quo.
This fantasy nonidea endures because fighting for it achieves a critical bipartisan goal: buying time for corporate control of the rest of the health care system. A legislative timeline would likely look like this: two years until the Democrats have a shot at the White House, followed by a year or two of GOP panic about “communism.” Throw in two to three years to write the regulationss, then five or ten years to roll out the plans and watch them fail. Presto! A decade or two of corporate looting passes, with trillions of dollars squandered and another million or two preventable deaths.
There are plenty of meaningful steps on the way to a publicly financed universal health care system that ensures everyone gets the care they need without facing personal bankruptcy or fighting off bloodthirsty private bureaucrats. Politicians who want to improve access or cost control could jump on a few of these sample bandwagons. Don’t expect a rush, though. Most of these ideas take a bite out of the industry’s hide, and letting poor people who make an extra penny keep their health care will give alleged conservatives apoplexy. But here they are:
- Set fair hospital prices by regulation for all payers, to stop the gouging of employers and patients and end the episodic waves of terror that engulf communities when big insurance companies and hospitals threaten patients with loss of access during local rate negotiations.
- Lower the age at which everyone becomes eligible for Medicare to fifty or fifty-five.
- Eliminate the extreme cost-sharing in the original Medicare program.
- Abolish the Medicare Advantage privatization scheme that lets private insurance companies overcharge the federal government tens of billions of dollars a year, and use the savings to fund said elimination of original Medicare cost-sharing.
- Buck Washington, DC’s current antitrust fad by lifting restrictions on employers who want to join together to bargain for health care and administer benefits. Look, employer control of health care makes no sense. But if corporate politicians fantasize that it’s a route to better benefits and lower costs, let bosses gather the power to control prices and administrative costs, as long as they do it themselves without the insurance industry, and as long as they’re willing to pay the price of offering uniform plans across their cartel — no more tiny tweaks to networks or boutique cost-sharing provisions for each employer.
- Dramatically expand the time people can stay on Medicaid. Medicaid’s constant means-testing makes it an unreliable source of coverage. California applied for a waiver to keep kids enrolled through the first five years of their lives instead of making their parents reapply every year. Do more of that and for longer.
The worst thing about public optionism is enduring smug lectures that Medicare for All is a political fantasy that could never happen from people promoting a vague, unworkable idea now enjoying its twenty-third year of politically viable nonexistence. Yet The American Prospect casually assumes that a series of essential Medicare for All elements against which the industry will fight like rabid dogs can easily be grafted onto a public option.
Health care is a public good. Pretending that having government act like a health insurance corporation will do anything useful is absurd. Let’s kill this putrefying political monster right now.

https://gothamist.com/news/work-is-under.title: Work is underway to replace deteriorating Newark Bay Bridge, a major NY-NJ route
https://gothamist.com/news/work-is-under.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/work-is-under.text:
Work is underway to replace the outdated Newark Bay Bridge, which carries the New Jersey Turnpike extension into Hudson County and serves as one of the main connecting roads between the Garden State and New York City.
That bridge, also known as the Casciano Memorial Bridge, opened in 1956 and carries about 95,000 cars and trucks daily. The New Jersey Turnpike Authority has warned that it is at the end of its usable life. The project to replace it is scheduled to be complete in 2031. Officials say there will be no disruption for commuters and minimal impact to local residents during construction, as the existing bridge will remain open during construction.
“All that traffic brings wear and tear,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill said at a groundbreaking ceremony Thursday. “After 70 years of service, the bridge is in dire need of replacement.”
The new cable-stayed bridge will be built just north of the existing bridge across Newark Bay. It will have two lanes for traffic in both directions as well as full shoulders, addressing a safety concern plaguing the existing bridge.
“Because of the constant repair work on it, we have to shut down the shoulder routinely. Or if there is a downed vehicle, that shuts off a lane and we have to use the shoulder,” Sherrill said. “We can't get safety vehicles on the bridge.”
It cost about $40 million to build the existing bridge in the 1950s, said Kris Kolluri, the executive director of the New Jersey Turnpike Authority. That figure works out to be a little shy of $500 million in 2026 dollars.
The new bridge is expected to cost more than $6.7 billion, making it the most expensive single effort pursued by the Turnpike Authority. It’ll be paid for with toll revenue. Turnpike tolls have increased 3% annually since 2020. Sherrill did not directly say whether or not those annual increases will continue.
"We are going to make sure that we're not kicking the can down the road on anything,” Sherrill said. “So we'll be ensuring that we have the funding to continue to invest in infrastructure, which over time is going to ensure that every tax dollar is spent wisely.”
Kolluri noted that work in the river has already begun, with temporary construction trestles expected to be finished by the end of this year. The Turnpike Authority expects to award a contract for the actual bridge construction in March.
Sherrill compared the bridge to a pair of other major projects underway in the state — the new Hudson River rail tunnels currently being dug, and the new Portal Bridge currently being completed.
“ Unfortunately, in too many cases, it has been politically expedient for people to kick the can down the road, to do little patchwork repairs and not actually make sure we are making sound structural improvements,” Sherrill said. “So we are taking this on at every level, and making sure we're building for the future, and that New Jersey, once again, will be the crown jewel in infrastructure and improvement.”
The new Newark Bay Bridge will be a scaled back version of a $10.7 billion proposal, advanced by then-Gov. Phil Murphy’s administration, that called for building two new bridges and widening the part of the extension that weaves through Jersey City to the Holland Tunnel.
That original plan drew fierce pushback from environmentalists and Jersey City community groups, who warned it would bring unnecessary air and noise pollution to already overburdened neighborhoods.
Murphy later walked back the extension widening in Jersey City, but still pushed for a two-bridge replacement. Sherrill announced in March that the extra lanes would be dropped from the plan. Her decision was praised by the mayors of Newark and Jersey City and environmental advocates.
The groundbreaking for the new bridge was held on the 75th anniversary of the New Jersey Turnpike opening. Mid-century Gov. Alfred Driscoll championed the turnpike, Kolluri said, with a vision of an efficient system for moving freight and passengers without burdening local roads in a growing state.
Kolluri said the whole turnpike system now serves about 260 million vehicles annually.
“That is a volume that I don't think even Gov. Driscoll thought was possible,” Kolluri said.
