https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: New York’s Pension Funds Soared in the AI Boom — and Could Crash With the AI Bubble
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg David
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The city’s five pension funds — which cover city employees and currently provide benefits to some 160,000 retirees — climbed by about 23% in their last two fiscal years, as tech stocks and artificial intelligence-related investments skyrocketed. As a result, the city anticipated that its pension fund contributions could decline by about $8 billion over the next five years — while still meeting its obligations to retired city workers.
It’s a similar story for the state’s pension funds, which grew by about 17% over its last two fiscal years. They cover all state and municipal workers outside of New York City and currently make payments to more than 500,000 retirees.
But with the sharp drop in tech stocks last week and growing fears that the unprecedented surge in AI investments will not pay off, both the city and state now face the possibility of sharp declines in pension fund values. 
And that would require them to boost the amount they direct to pension funds each year to meet their commitments.
That, in turn, could crowd out other budget priorities — like expanded childcare or new investments in housing.
“AI is touching us everywhere in the pension funds,” City Comptroller Mark Levine told The City Reporter. “It is a massive component of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Our private equity investments are heavily in AI-related companies. We have gone big into private credit. And who is it being lent out to? AI.”
Markets plunged last week after the midterm elections, in part because winning Democratic candidates have pledged to slow the construction of data centers, without which the largest AI companies won’t be able to achieve the kind of growth they have promised investors.
The benchmark S&P 500 fell almost 3% for the week. The Nasdaq composite index declined 10% from its previous peak on Thursday, a drop called a correction, before slightly recovering on Friday to end the week down 6%. The Wall Street Journal reported that Anthropic, which is expected to launch its initial public offering before Thanksgiving, has been told by potential investors that it would have to reduce its expected valuation by at least 25%.
The city’s pension funds control $326 billion and the state’s funds are now at $310 billion, making them the third- and fourth-largest public pension funds in the country. The investment strategies for both are similar.
About a third of the assets are invested in U.S. stocks, with most of that in index funds that simply track key measures of the market.
International stocks — which have soared in the last year, primarily because of huge gains among South Korean companies providing chips for AI — bring the total equity investments up to 40%. Those gains are now endangered as well by an AI bubble bursting.
The index strategy, while regarded as the most prudent form of investing for individuals and pension funds, means the city has huge stakes in AI-centered companies, including chipmakers like Nvidia, Elon Musk’s SpaceX and older tech companies pushing aggressively into AI, like Meta (Facebook), Alphabet (Google) and Microsoft.
Bonds account for about a quarter of all funds, and AI companies have been issuing billions in corporate bonds this year. AI is also a growing part of stakes in real estate, private equity, pools of capital that are used to buy, fix up and sell companies, and private credit, a relatively new area in which firms lend money instead of a bank. So the city and state pensions funds’ investments outside of stocks also bring wide exposure to an AI bubble.
The city’s pension funds will not immediately buy shares in Anthropic if it goes public this month, the comptroller’s office says. But it will own Anthropic shares once the company is added to the Russell 3000 index, which tracks the 3,000 largest publicly held companies in the country and is expected to add Anthropic almost immediately. It will own more shares if, as expected, Anthropic is added to the S&P 500 about a year after its initial public offering.
“We don’t want to be overconcentrated in AI,” Levine said. He recently decided not to invest in a private-equity deal involving an AI company even though the proposal met the fund’s investment standards.
State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli, who decisively won his fourth term last week and is the sole trustee and makes all investment decisions for the state pension funds, was not available to comment last week.
Levine’s office is beginning a major reevaluation of the pension funds’ investments, something the office conducts every three to five years. Exposure to AI will be one of the top priorities, Levine notes, with the results expected within five months.
In the meantime, there is a role for AI in the city comptroller’s office.
“AI will help us by giving us new tools to assess risk,” he said.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Lost Rubens sketches return to German castle after 80 years
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Five oil sketches by Peter Paul Rubens will be shown together at the Ducal Museum in Gotha, Germany, for the first time since they were lost more than 80 years ago.
The five works depicting saints were part of a group of 22 sketches that Rubens painted on wood in 1620 and 1621 as preparation for the ceiling paintings of the Jesuit church in Antwerp, which was the biggest commission he had received by that time. The sketches are particularly important because the ceiling paintings, which were famous in the 17th century, are no longer in existence. The church was hit by a lightning bolt in 1718 and burned down.
The sketches were among the most valuable works in the collections at Schloss Friedenstein in Gotha, where they had been since at least the early 19th century; one had been there for three centuries. But by the end of the Second World War, all five had disappeared.
Three were taken by representatives of the ducal family—which had not been their owners since 1918. They returned to the castle as American and Soviet forces closed in on Gotha and, according to experts, removed truckloads of art in the last weeks of the war. Three sketches were transported to the city of Coburg for protection and from there, they were illicitly sold and ended up on the US art market. The two remaining studies were looted by the Red Army and were restituted to Gotha in 1959.
For many decades the three sold by the ducal family remained lost. Then in 2024, one of them, St. Gregory of Nazianzus, was returned by a museum in Buffalo, New York, with help from Christie’s. Now a fourth, The Prophet Elijah in the Golden Chariot, which ended up in a private US collection, has been recovered in a private settlement mediated by the Paris auction house Cabinet Turquin. The recovery was funded by the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation, which frequently acquires art for German museums.
Martin Hoernes, the secretary general of the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation, said a “figure in the low millions” had been agreed, below the market price. “No one wanted to criminalise the current owners,” he said, describing their acquisition of the sketch as a “good-faith purchase”.
The fifth sketch, showing St. Augustine, belongs to the Foundation E. G. Bührle Collection, which is on display in the Kunsthaus Zurich. The Bührle Foundation has agreed to loan it to Gotha’s Ducal Museum so that it can be shown alongside the other four for an exhibition, which opens today (9 November) and marks the 450th anniversary of Rubens’ birth next year.
“It is nothing short of a miracle that Peter Paul Rubens’ five oil studies can now be seen together at the Ducal Museum,” Tobias Pfeifer-Helke, the director of the Friedenstein Foundation Gotha, said in a statement. “They are not only five unique masterpieces by the Flemish painter and the jewels of the Gotha art collection, but also bear witness to European and international history.”

https://gothamist.com/news/will-voters-b.title: Will voters' ‘blue tsunami’ mean a reset on healthcare for NY?
https://gothamist.com/news/will-voters-b.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/will-voters-b.text:
With Democrats poised to take control of the House and Senate in January, some New Yorkers have big expectations for a healthcare policy reset — even reversing the funding cuts to Medicaid and other safety net programs that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans pushed through.
“Tuesday's election results were a lifeline to those in the healthcare community,” said Kenneth Raske, president of the Greater New York Hospital Association. “We will move from a position of despair to a position of hope for the future.”
Policy experts expect Democrats to advance new healthcare affordability legislation, and to try to at least partially undo healthcare spending cuts that would strip insurance from millions of people nationwide. But the experts also caution that the new Democratic majorities in Congress will still face roadblocks with Trump in office.
The stakes are high for healthcare consumers and providers in New York.
Cuts included in last year’s H.R. 1 domestic policy bill have already resulted in hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers losing coverage they held through the low-cost public insurance program known as the Essential Plan.
Many consumers are now staring down high costs for private plans on the Affordable Care Act marketplace, which increased after Republicans allowed enhanced federal insurance subsidies to expire last year.
Starting in January, many of the more than 6 million New Yorkers statewide who are insured through Medicaid will also face new requirements to maintain their health insurance. New York hospitals and clinics have raised concerns that more uninsured patients will result in revenue losses that could affect their services.
“It’s certainly possible for Democrats in both the House and the Senate to pass legislation that would roll back most or all the healthcare cuts in H.R. 1 and restore the enhanced premium tax credits,” said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan policy think tank.
But, he said, it would be far more challenging for that legislation to become law without a change of administration. “It requires a signature from President Trump and I think it's very likely that he would veto that type of legislation,” Fiedler said.
Despite last week’s "blue tsunami," Democrats still won’t have the supermajorities needed in both houses to override presidential vetoes — and Fiedler noted that some of the more moderate Republicans who might have been persuaded to vote with Democrats on healthcare legislation just got voted out of office.
Larry Levitt, the executive vice president for healthcare policy at the nonprofit KFF, echoed Fiedler’s sentiments. But he added that Trump can also be unpredictable and Democrats might be able to play some “3-D chess” to get healthcare concessions.
For instance, he said, Democrats in Congress could try to get a signature on legislation restoring more robust federal subsidies for ACA health plans by offering to include a measure Trump wants, such as an expansion of health savings accounts.
Or, he said, Democrats could try to use their power to hold up “ must-pass” legislation such as government funding bills to get what they want.
A brewing rift over Medicare for All
Policy experts and healthcare reform advocates said the Democrats’ gains not only set the stage for a potential reversal of healthcare cuts but also for Democrats to lay out a proactive vision for the future. That could include a renewed push for Medicare for All, a form of universal, federal health coverage.
“Everything’s on the table,” said Elisabeth Benjamin, vice president of health initiatives at the Community Service Society of New York, a nonprofit that advocates for access to affordable healthcare.
Though denounced by some critics as a far-left idea, Medicare for All is supported by a growing share of the electorate. Two-thirds of U.S. adults said they either strongly or somewhat favored having a national health plan in an October poll conducted by KFF. About 85% of Democrats polled supported such a plan, compared with about a third of Republicans.
But it’s also a point on which Democrats in Congress — including the New York delegation — are divided.
The current version of the Medicare for All legislation in Congress is sponsored by New York Democrats including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rep. Ritchie Torres.
But it has not been sponsored by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries or Sen. Chuck Schumer, who could be House speaker and Senate majority leader next year, respectively. The two New Yorkers are the current minority leaders in their chambers.
Schumer and Jeffries did not respond to requests for interviews on their healthcare priorities. But Jeffries told NBC in August he had reversed his previous stance in support of Medicare for All and now opposes it.
“I do support the notion we have to find a path forward to fix our broken health care system and make healthcare affordable for every single American,” Jeffries said.
Grace Mausser, cochair of the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, said she was optimistic about the the midterm elections creating new momentum for progressive initiatives, including Medicare for All, even if many of the Democrats elected are more moderate.
She said she was hopeful there could be incremental advancements with Trump still in office in preparation for the possibility of having a Democrat in the White House in 2029.
“ We would love to see Medicare For All go through committee markup,” Mausser said, keeping her expectations in check.
Democrats could also try to pass more incremental reforms such as lowering the age for Medicare eligibility from 65 to 55, Benjamin said.
Even if getting Trump’s signature on some of these proposals is unlikely, the next two years will be the time to lay the groundwork for future change, said Fiedler of the Brookings Institution.
He noted that a version of the Medicaid work requirements Republicans included in H.R. 1 were initially laid out in legislation that passed the House during the Biden administration.
“Just because something doesn't become law doesn't mean that important health policy work isn't happening over the next couple of years,” Fiedler said.

https://www.propublica.org/article/post-.title: Lawyers in This State Are Allowed to Ghost Clients for Years. Why Don’t More Judges Stop Them?
https://www.propublica.org/article/post-.author: Samantha Melamed
https://www.propublica.org/article/post-.text:
One morning in July 2025, I was the lone spectator in Judge Frank Palumbo’s courtroom in Philadelphia, watching prosecutors and public defenders haggle over the fates of defendants.
Palumbo paused the proceedings to talk to a lawyer he’d appointed to help a prisoner who had ineptly challenged his conviction. The lawyer profusely thanked the judge for the job. Then, Palumbo offered a bit of guidance: “I think I know where this is going to go. I don’t want to make it overly complicated. It’s real simple.”
The judge said he’d pass along a brief that a different lawyer had filed arguing that there was no merit to the man’s claims in a related case. “I’m not saying plagiarize,” the judge said.
The attorney told the judge he got the message. “So it’s called a Finley letter,” he said, using the common legal term for that no-merit brief, in which an attorney can argue against the client’s claims and ask to withdraw from the case.
“It’s looking like it’s going to be a Finley dismissal,” the judge agreed after a bit more discussion, “but every option is open.”
I’ve spent years covering criminal justice in Pennsylvania, including the post-conviction system that allows people to argue that their lawyer had mishandled their case or to raise newly discovered evidence. That day, I left the courtroom wondering how what I’d observed squared with the state’s promise of effective legal representation in cases like this.
That question sent me on a yearlong reporting odyssey, during which I read hundreds of Finley letters, tracked down court financial records from all 67 Pennsylvania counties, interviewed dozens of lawyers and analyzed thousands of court dockets. What I wanted to know was: Why has it become the norm for Pennsylvania’s lawyers to argue against their own clients? And who is this system serving?
I found that lax rules, low pay and heavy caseloads have compromised legal representation under the state’s Post Conviction Relief Act. Over the past year, I’ve reported on how lawyers, working under fee structures banned in other states, fell years behind on their cases. I spoke with prisoners who’d waited nearly a decade for their lawyers to file anything and others whose lawyers filed Finley letters despite compelling evidence of innocence. I also looked at three years’ worth of invoices and found that, three quarters of the time, Philly lawyers who wrote Finley letters had never spoken with their clients, contacted the trial lawyer or obtained available police files before deciding their claims had no merit.
None of those seemingly basic steps, I was surprised to learn, is required under the law. In fact, dozens of lawyers I spoke to expressed sharply divided opinions about the extent of their obligations to these clients.
But court-appointed lawyers are not working unsupervised. Judges are largely in charge of appointing them to cases, and those same judges are supposed to make sure they’re doing a timely and diligent job.
I noticed that judges continued to assign lawyers more cases even after appeals courts flagged serious issues with their work. And when it came to Finley letters, judges accepted almost all of them over the three years of cases I reviewed, despite the lawyers’ minimal investigative efforts. Some of the letters they approved contained obvious factual errors or even named the wrong client.
Last fall, after Palumbo gave the lawyer a copy of a Finley letter, the lawyer followed the template. His no-merit brief said that his client’s claim could not be considered because he’d missed his filing deadline. The bulk of the document was, in fact, identical to the other lawyer’s brief.
Palumbo, who didn’t respond to my requests for comment, accepted the Finley letter anyway, let the lawyer drop the client and dismissed the claim.
Who Judges Judges?
I thought a fair way to evaluate judges would be to look at the rulings of the Pennsylvania’s Superior Court, the state’s appeals court that hears hundreds of challenges to judges’ rulings on post-conviction matters each year.
And boy, did the Superior Court have thoughts on how judges are handling post-conviction cases.
In one withering opinion, a judge bemoaned an “embarrassing saga” of deficient lawyering that a Berks County judge had tolerated. Another derided a Philly judge and the five attorneys she’d appointed who all missed appeals deadlines, writing, “As Hall of Fame manager Casey Stengel said of the hapless 1962 New York Mets, ‘Can’t anybody here play this game?’”
After logging hundreds of rebukes laid out in Superior Court opinions by hand, I asked some colleagues with data skills to help identify as many of these cases as possible across the last 14 years, the time frame for which opinions were reliably posted online.
We found that the appeals court flagged more than 250 cases in which judges didn’t intervene as lawyers provided what the court labeled ineffective representation: “sandbagging” a client at a hearing, stonewalling a petitioner who’d mailed two dozen letters to the lawyer’s office or filing boilerplate appeals so vague that they doomed their clients’ cases. In hundreds more cases, judges failed to appoint a lawyer at all, held hearings where petitioners went unrepresented or allowed a lawyer to drop a case, leaving the client stranded on appeal. More than 200 times, they oversaw lawyers who abandoned clients, tanking their appeals or stalling their cases for years.
“Judges are in a terrific position to be able to prevent these kinds of injustices,” said Marissa Boyers Bluestine, a longtime post-conviction lawyer who now works at the University of Pennsylvania’s law school.
The scathing reversals aside, the Superior Court affirms about 80% of lower-court rulings. That’s expected given the strict deadlines and complicated rules about how appeals must be filed. The appeals court is also required to defer to the lower court’s factual decisions. And when it reverses due to an error, the recourse is generally limited to ordering a do-over or, on rare occasions, instructing the lower court to explore sanctions. In one opinion, the court resorted to using boldface to call out an egregious failure: “The PCRA court did nothing in this case for 20 years.” Then, it told the lower court to try again.
Judges do have the authority — and, in fact, an obligation under state rules — to make disciplinary referrals. Because complaints are confidential, there is no way to know how often they do so. But only six lawyers in the last decade have been publicly sanctioned for work on court-appointed post-conviction cases.
Judicial discipline is even rarer. No lower-court judge in at least a decade has been publicly disciplined for mishandling a post-trial matter. Judges who, according to the Superior Court, exhibited biases, imposed vindictive sentences or improperly denied recusal requests remained on the bench.
Even after the Superior Court raised alarms, more than 100 cases ricocheted between the appeals court and county judges two, three, four or more times, as judges repeated errors or reappointed lawyers to cases they’d already mishandled.
One such case played out after Jefferson County’s only judge, John Foradora, sentenced a woman to up to 22 years in prison for passing two narcotics pills in prison. Her lawyer failed to object to or appeal the lengthy sentence. After she filed a PCRA, the Superior Court found that her lawyers’ inaction enabled the “unduly harsh and clearly unreasonable” punishment to stand. But each time the Superior Court reversed, Foradora again imposed a lengthy term. After three such reversals, the woman wound up serving more than eight years. Foradora said through a court spokesperson that he was unable to comment.
Shannon McDonald, an attorney in the Philly suburbs, said that “some judges don’t consider PCRA a priority.”
She described waiting as a petition languished on a Delaware County judge’s desk for two years, until her client had finished his sentence and been released from prison. Then, the judge finally ruled, dismissing the claim.
The Finley Problem
Like lawyers, judges I’ve spoken with seem to be divided on their obligations, especially when it comes to the no-merit letters known as Finley letters. The state Supreme Court says that when a lawyer submits a Finley letter, the judge needs to conduct a review of the merits of the case.
Attorney Rob Perkins, who leads the nonprofit Allegheny Lawyers Initiative for Justice, told me that while he’s encountered some judges who take post-conviction matters seriously, others seem to view them as a nuisance. He said several lawyers told him that they were afraid that if they litigated cases too aggressively, judges would withhold future assignments. The no-merit letter becomes the simplest path forward: “When a judge is handed a no-merit letter that sounds good, I think their inclination is to accept that the attorney did their job.”
Superior Court opinions reflect this pattern as well. In my review, I found hundreds of cases overruling lower-court judges who accepted flawed Finley letters. The appeals court noted that lawyers claimed, incorrectly, that their clients had missed filing deadlines, rejected legitimate claims as meritless or failed to notice that their clients were serving illegal sentences.
In dozens of cases, judges approved defective Finley letters that did not fulfill basic rules, such as including a notification to the client or addressing all the claims the client wanted to raise.
Several judges told me that Finley letters serve an important purpose, in shutting down frivolous challenges that waste resources.
“Not all [claims] have merit,” Judge John J. Mead of Erie said. “A lot of them initially you could look at and make a determination [as to] whether or not it’s going to require a hearing.”
I’ve noticed that the system makes accepting Finley letters the simplest choice for judges. A judge who rejects a Finley letter must either find a new lawyer willing to take the case, or force the same lawyer to pursue a matter they previously deemed meritless.
Judges who take that path risk pitting a lawyer against his own client, the Superior Court wrote in one recent case, finding the judge’s actions resulted in the denial of a man’s right to counsel. His lawyer, forced to handle a hearing after writing a Finley letter, treated it “more like a cross-examination of a witness that [he] does not believe than a direct examination of his client.”
Jon Auritt, who retired after more than 50 years as a lawyer in Delaware County, said that these failures stem from a common cause: Instead of working independently, lawyers are beholden to the local judges who appoint them.
Even if judges are not as explicit as Palumbo was with their instructions, Auritt said, their message is often clear: “The judges are never incentivized to appoint a lawyer who might earnestly find a reason to overturn the conviction.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Russia’s Last Independent Newspaper Is Going Dark
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Russia’s Last Independent Newspaper Is Going Dark
Novaya Gazeta’s closing marks the end of what little press freedom remained in Putin’s Russia.
Russia’s Last Independent Newspaper Is Going Dark
The closing of “Novaya Gazeta” marks the end of what little press freedom remained in Putin’s Russia.
Novaya Gazeta—one of Russia’s last bastions of independent journalism—will publish a final issue and shut down next week.
The paper has faced mounting institutional pressures: It was evicted from its office space and labeled a foreign agent by the Kremlin, and banks have refused Novaya their services. Its reader-supported funding platform was also shut down.
The fact that the publication survived for this long is a testament to its reporters’ extraordinary bravery. Since its founding in 1993, Novaya has earned international acclaim for reporting in areas including human rights violations during the second Chechen War, the persecution of Chechnya’s LGBT community, and abuse inside Russian prisons. Over its years of courageous muckraking, six Novaya journalists were killed, including the crusading reporter Anna Politkovskaya.
After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the free-speech crackdown that followed, much of the paper’s staff fled to Latvia, where they launched Novaya Gazeta Europe. This outlet is expected to continue operations—but its website is blocked in Russia.
However, while the original paper will soon cease publication, readers and historians can still access its work. Kronika, a project from PEN America and Bard College dedicated to preserving journalism at risk of suppression, is digitizing the newspaper’s entire archive. In doing so, the project is keeping Novaya’s ideals and principles alive.
Novaya cofounder and former editor in chief Dmitrii Muratov told Columbia Journalism Review that, if not for the archive, decades of Russia’s historical memory could vanish. And if such a public record were lost, he said, “we would not know how dictatorships take shape.”
To mark the legacy of this singular newspaper, The Nation is republishing the piece below, which I originally wrote when Muratov and the Filipino American journalist Maria Ressa were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021.
In the Nobel lecture he delivered later that year, Muratov saluted his colleagues, who risked their lives to hold those in power to account and promote the public interest.
“We are the prerequisite for progress,” he said. “We are the antidote against tyranny.”
The following was originally published in The Nation, October 8, 2021.
A Courageous Voice for Press Freedom and Independence in Russia
As the Nobel Prize committee recognized with today’s award to Dmitrii Muratov, independent journalism and media freedom in Russia confront growing threats.
katrina vanden heuvel
I and my late husband, Stephen Cohen, first met Dmitrii Muratov in 1993. He and a few other colleagues had gathered in the basement cafeteria of Moscow News—then a bold newspaper of the glasnost era—to plan the launch of Novaya Gazeta. Survival was on their minds at that time; they were beginning the paper with two computers, one printer, two rooms—and no money for salaries. A few months later, an initial boost of support came from President Mikhail Gorbachev, who contributed part of his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize money to buy the newspaper its first computers.
Nearly 30 years later, the newspaper has another Nobel in its history. On October 8, Muratov was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize with Filipina journalist Maria Ressa “for their efforts to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace.”
I knew in 1993 that “Dima” was a bold and creative editor. What I did not foresee was that he would become such a vital defender and advocate of press freedom in Russia. The newspaper, which continues to publish against great odds, has paid a heavy price for its crusading investigations into Putin’s and other high-level officials’ corruption, human rights violations, the persecution of the LGBT community in Chechnya, right-wing nationalist extremism, and abuses of power. The paper has also spent decades carefully tracing Stalin’s crimes in newly opened archives.
Six of its courageous reporters—among them Anna Politkovskaya, who was killed exactly 15 years ago—have been murdered for their unflinching investigations. (Fewer than half the killings have been solved.) “When Anya was killed, I called an emergency editorial meeting and wanted to close down the paper,” Muratov told me once. “I told my staff no story is worth dying for. But they wouldn’t let me do it.… I knew we had to go on.”
Muratov is not afraid to publish dissenting, oppositionist views on Crimea, Donbas, Syria, and growing poverty and the abuse of civil liberties in Russia. He handles at least 10 lawsuits a month—filed by official organs. It is remarkable that amid the escalating crackdown on press freedom, he has managed to preserve a sense of humor and visibly enjoy mentoring a new generation of investigative journalists—and readers. Elena Milashina, who started at Novaya in her late 20s, is one of those journalists; since the publication of her article in March documenting the murders of LGBT people and reporting on the cold-blooded murders instigated by Chechnya’s leader Ramzan Kadyrov, she has faced physical threats and death threats.
Indeed, most of the journalists working at the paper are like Milashina: the same age as, or a few years older than, the publication itself. Younger generations may not read the print edition, but Novaya’s print circulation as of October 2021 is 90,000, social-media traffic is 30 million a month, and its website receives 8 million to 11 million monthly page views.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The paper’s founding independence was boosted by the fact that, until 2006, Novaya journalists owned 100 percent of its stock. In 2006, to secure a capital infusion, Muratov persuaded his staff to sell 49 percent of their stock to Gorbachev (10 percent) and a partner, mini-oligarch Aleksandr Lebedev (39 percent). Lebedev invested nearly $4 million to raise staff salaries, upgrade the paper’s offices, and turn Novaya into a paper with national reach. (In 2015, Lebedev stopped funding Novaya, revealing in a Guardian interview that he had ceased because of the expense and also the strain.)
Fifteen years after Politkovskaya’s murder, nearly 30 years after Novaya was founded, independent journalism and media freedom in Russia confront growing threats. An array of media regulations and laws, the labeling of independent media outlets as “foreign agents,” and increasingly restrictive regulation of the Internet are all deeply troubling. Some Russian media analysts and journalists believe that many of these new restrictions are fueled by the West’s anti-Russian sanctions, increasing political tensions, and a deepening and dangerous cold war. In such times, the already narrow space for diversity of views and freedom of speech shrinks. Many analysts also see the culture of impunity—the ongoing failure to hold accountable those who threaten, attack, or kill journalists—as posing a grave threat to media freedom and democracy itself.
How Dmitrii Muratov has navigated for decades the dangerous waters of Russian politics—he has friends across all levels of Russian society, including top politicians—often irritates members of Russia’s more hard-core opposition and some Western observers, who think he has sold out to the Kremlin. As I ventured onto Twitter this morning to post a congratulatory note, a cat lover named Svetlana posted: “With tremendous respect to Dmitry—in Russia there is a saying, ‘If he’s still alive, he’s working for them.’ I admire his courage. And so did Peskov [Putin’s press secretary]. Where does it leave us? Thank you.”
Muratov has used his influence and connections not for his personal ambitions, nor to enrich himself, but to keep alive one of the last havens of investigative journalism inside Russia. The Nobel Prize will likely give Novaya and Muratov domestic protection, but may well also earn Muratov more enemies among the Putin elite, who will allege that he has betrayed the country for awards and foreign funds. What matters, as Muratov said on learning of Oslo’s call, are “Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya, Stas Markelov, Nastya Baburova—these are the people who won the Nobel Prize today.”
Today’s prize will be wind at the back for all Russian investigative journalists.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: E-Bike Battery Fires Hit Record in NYC, But Solutions Remain Elusive
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
It’s a record. Already in 2026, New York City has suffered 406 lithium-ion battery fires, sparked by the electric cells that power an ever-growing fleet of e-bikes and electric scooters.
Since 2019, when the Fire Department first started keeping these stats, such blazes have resulted in 46 deaths and 628 injuries.
All this occurred despite an aggressive effort to end this grim but persistent trend. Laws were passed. Policies changed. The FDNY warned people again and again not to charge off-label batteries without safety certification.
And yet last month, four tenants of a Bronx public housing development perished in a fast-moving fire triggered by a battery charging inside their apartment.
Then last week, six people died in a Sunset Park blaze. A cause has not been officially released, but FDNY officials noted two charred lithium-ion battery-powered devices were removed from the scene. Not counting the victims of the most recent Brooklyn fire, that’s nine battery-fire deaths already this year.
And once again, elected officials are calling for reforms.
Last week, the City Council announced it will hold an emergency hearing on this issue on Nov. 20. And on Friday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters his administration is focusing on finding a solution, “whether it’s exploring additional legislation or it’s exploring additional policy that we can make at the administrative angle.”
Dwindling Enforcement
The solutions may not be so simple.
Workers who rely on e-bikes continue to buy and charge unsafe, off-label batteries, which are less expensive. Retailers and on-line outlets continue to sell them.
At times, the city bureaucracy has struggled to respond, even when they’re clearly warned of potential danger. In February 2023, journalist Fazil Khan perished in a raging fire in Harlem that erupted in an apartment below him where tenants were charging multiple batteries. Callers to 311 had warned the city weeks earlier, but there was no response.
That same year, the City Council took the first major step to confronting this issue, passing a law banning the sale of lithium-ion batteries that were not safety certified. This was a crucial step: Fire officials say batteries that are certified by the Underwriters Laboratory (UL) or aren’t charged via their manufacturer’s approved charger are vulnerable to bursting into flame. The resulting chemical fire is difficult to extinguish — and spreads quickly.
Since then, however, enforcement of the ban has wavered, according to Department of Consumer & Worker Protection (DCWP) records obtained by The City Reporter.
The law went into effect Sept. 1, 2023, while Eric Adams was mayor, and in the first four months his DCWP launched a wave of inspections citywide, issuing summons to 105 retailers at a rate of more than 26 per month.
In 2024 the agency issued summons to 108 businesses over 12 months, which dropped the rate to nine per month. Then in 2025, the last year of the Adams administration, enforcement fell even further, with summons issued to just 46 sellers all year for a rate of less than four per month.
In 2026, the first year of the Mamdani administration, enforcement got off to a slow start. By the beginning of August, DCWP had issued summons to just 26 sellers, but in August and September the city launched a sweep, bringing the total to 68 retailers hit with summons by last week. That was still a rate of just under seven per month.
And records show some of these retailers broke the law again and again, with some being hit with multiple summons for selling unsafe batteries since the law went into effect.
DCWP spokesperson Stephany Vasquez Sanchez said the agency “focuses on bringing businesses that remained in violation of (the law) into compliance,” and the agency’s tactics of shutting down repeat offenders “have improved compliance.”
“We’ve found that the majority of businesses stay in compliance once they learned to sell safe and certified devices,” she said. “We will continue our work to ensure compliance in this industry, especially to hold recidivist businesses accountable with our full authority.”
Another effort to get the delivery drivers who rely on e-bikes to stop using non-certified batteries kicked off in June 2025 under a law sponsored by then-Councilmember Keith Powers. The law created an exchange program for eligible drivers to turn in their unsafe batteries for those that were UL listed.
But the exchange program expired in 2025.
Last week after the Sunset Park catastrophe, Powers, now a state assemblymember, took to social media to call on the Mamdani administration to “resume that program and save lives.”
What Can Washington Do?
Another elected official who’s tried to staunch the sale of unsafe batteries is Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-The Bronx), whose district includes the Patterson Houses where a battery fire last month killed four tenants, including an 11-year-old boy, two teenage boys and a 33-year-old woman.
In 2024, and then again in 2025, Torres sponsored a bill that would require the Consumer Product Safety Commission to establish a safety standard for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in micromobility devices such as electric scooters and bikes. Nationally retailers would be barred from selling batteries that don’t meet those standards. In both years, an overwhelming and bipartisan House majority voted for it.
The bill, nevertheless, has been unable to get to the floor of the Senate, where Torres said it would also be overwhelmingly supported. The obstacle, he says, is Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky), who’s employed a tactic that allows a single senator to block a bill from getting to the floor, without explanation.
Torres is marginally optimistic that the Democratic wave gave control of Congress to his party “would improve the prospects” of the bill seeing the light of day.
But, Torres added, “a Republican minority in the Senate could remain an obstacle.”
“I see it as a matter of life and death,” the congressman said. “Poorly manufactured lithium ion batteries are literally ticking time-bombs and it’s communities like the Bronx that are hardest hit.”
Finally the deadly fire in the Patterson Houses in The Bronx last month cast a spotlight on another attempt to prevent more of these fires from costing lives.
In 2023, the same year the council passed the law barring the sale of uncertified batteries, the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) was considering prohibiting the charging of e-bike batteries, certified or not, on all public housing property. That September they dropped that plan and instead adopted a compromise: households could charge one battery per unit, as long as it was safety-certified and the charging could not block any exit from the apartment.
Since then, that compromise solution has been followed by no fewer than 53 e-bike battery fires in NYCHA apartments. In the Patterson Houses blaze, the residents were charging the battery in the kitchen, in a place that blocked the family from escaping.

https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-wo.title: Gov. Hochul won with a mandate from voters. But what was the message?
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-wo.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-wo.text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul scored the type of political victory on Election Day that typically comes with a mandate — but what message voters were trying to send depends on who you ask.
The Democratic governor topped her Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman by about 20 percentage points, or 1.2 million votes, tripling her margin of victory from the last time she ran in 2022. She increased her vote share in every single one of New York’s 62 counties, in red and blue areas alike, and won eight counties she lost four years ago — including Nassau, where Blakeman is county executive.
But what, exactly, does that result tell us about what voters are expecting from Hochul in her second full term? Everyone seems to have a different answer.
Christina Greer, a Fordham University political science professor, said the blue wave that swept the nation on Election Day — which saw Democrats win key races in traditionally Republican states — makes a New York-specific mandate difficult to define.
“I'm not sure if the governor has a mandate, and I think this goes for not just Kathy Hochul, but a lot of the Democrats who were successful on Tuesday,” she said. “I think we need to be careful as to: Is it a vote for Kathy Hochul, or is it a vote against Donald Trump?”
Hochul ran a campaign revolving around the cost of living.
She ran advertisements that touted the state’s free school meal program, her moratorium on data center construction and a round of energy rebate checks, which resulted in millions of payments of up to $200 landing in voters’ mailboxes shortly before Election Day.
Hochul’s campaign also focused on tying Blakeman to Trump, his friend and ally who headlined a rally in Syracuse just before voters started casting their ballots. Her ads frequently included a clip of Blakeman saying he would “never be disloyal” to the Republican president.
More than 60% of voters in New York view the president unfavorably, according to recent public opinion polls. Many voters blamed Trump for raising the price of gas through the war in Iran.
“ The Democrat message last night was basically, ’We’re not him,’” said Republican political consultant Mike Dawidziak. “And that message worked last night, but it’s not gonna work in two years.”
In 2018, the last midterm election with Trump in office, then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo, a Democrat, defeated Republican Marc Molinaro by 23 percentage points.
A Marist University poll last month showed Trump was clearly on voters’ minds when they headed to the polls this time, too.
Among likely voters in New York, 47% said their vote in their local congressional race was mostly a vote against Trump, while 18% said it was mostly a vote for Trump. About a third of voters said Trump wasn’t much of a factor at all.
In that same poll, 41% of likely voters said they had a favorable impression of Hochul, compared to 51% unfavorable. (A Siena University poll the same week was more favorable to Hochul, with 51% saying they had a favorable view of her.)
Hochul said she believes her huge margin of victory says more about her than it does the Republican president.
At an annual post-election conference in Puerto Rico on Friday, the governor said the takeaway from her huge margin of victory is simple: New York voters support her policies and want her to continue on.
“They want me to keep fighting to deliver affordability for New Yorkers,” she said. “They want me to keep building more housing. They want me to focus on energy resiliency and focus on the threat of climate change. And the other major one is childcare.”
Hochul, a centrist, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist whose 2025 victory marked a win for the left wing of the Democratic Party, have jointly implemented a major expansion of childcare in New York City and state that will persist into 2027.
Hochul endorsed Mamdani after he won the mayoral primary last year, and Mamdani, in turn, hit the campaign trail for Hochul, urging his supporters — many of whom are younger than Hochul’s base — to hit the polls.
Grace Mausser, cochair of the NYC Democratic Socialists of America, said Mamdani’s support of Hochul clearly paid off for the governor. She pointed to increased voter turnout in parts of Brooklyn and Queens that heavily supported the mayor in 2025.
She said Hochul would be wise to remember that when lawmakers return to the state Capitol in January. The governor will face renewed pressure from the left to raise income taxes on the wealthy — a move the governor has resisted.
“Taxing the rich isn’t just a DSA position, it’s a centrist position, too,” Mausser said, pointing to polls that have shown broad support for the issue.
Liz Benjamin, managing director of New York public affairs for the consulting firm Marathon Strategies, wrote an op-ed making the case that Hochul’s victory is a mandate to continue her brand of moderate politics and governing, rather than tack left.
She said Hochul’s margin shows that her win wasn’t a matter of progressive voters “holding their nose and voting for her.”
“I just don't think that that's in fact the case,” Benjamin said in an interview. “I think that this is because she actually made a viable argument to people and had a record of accomplishment and grew into the role.”
Bryan Lesswing, a former senior adviser to Hochul who now is a senior vice president at consulting firm SKDK, said the governor’s campaign excelled in appealing to voters with varying viewpoints.
“Her performance really shows, I think, a playbook for Democrats on the big tent politics that we're all talking about here that we need to shift toward, especially in the wake of [Trump’s win in] 2024,” he said.
Includes reporting by Walter Wuthmann

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.title: Mamdani says more help is coming to homeless New Yorkers living outside this winter
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.text:
The Mamdani administration will deploy more nurses and add warming buses and beds across the city this winter, to better protect New Yorkers sleeping on the street from extreme cold.
The city announced the sweeping changes to its Code Blue policy Monday, as well as $25 million in new funding for it. Code Blue is triggered when temperatures drop below 32 degrees Fahrenheit. The new measures include deploying another 300 canvassers to reach out to homeless residents, 800 more beds to keep New Yorkers warm and hiring additional nurses who can provide care on site.
Last winter, more than two dozen people died outdoors or in their homes during a brutal stretch of freezing temperatures.
“We have spent the past year preparing for any challenge winter throws our way. We have trained our workers, readied our equipment and strengthened our protocols because keeping New Yorkers safe can’t begin when the first storm hits,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.
“This winter, we’re doing things differently — we’re expanding Code Blue to reach more New Yorkers in need, equipping New York’s Strongest to clear snow and ice faster and leaving no stone unturned when it comes to protecting our neighbors from the cold. No New Yorker should face the dangers of winter alone, and no part of our city should be left behind.”
This winter, street canvassers will reach out to every homeless person they meet, rather than focusing on a list of at-risk individuals. More than 50 mobile vans run by the city’s public hospital system will provide medical care and transportation to warming facilities.
The Department of Homeless Services will also open four additional warming centers and deploy 20 warming buses.
City officials also announced improvements to its snow clearing efforts, putting a priority on keeping sidewalks clear for older adults and New Yorkers with disabilities. The city’s sanitation department will include more snow clearing routes on Staten Island and upgrade snow plows to more effectively clear roads. It also purchased the agency’s first snow blowers to clear bus stops and crosswalks faster.
New Yorkers can sign up for emergency alerts about extreme weather and emergency resources by texting NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 or download the app. Those interested can also sign up to be a snow shoveler earning $30 an hour.

https://hyperallergic.com/mona-chalabi-p.title: Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
https://hyperallergic.com/mona-chalabi-p.author: Lakshmi Rivera Amin
https://hyperallergic.com/mona-chalabi-p.text:
Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallegic about her first book, “Ten Lives.”
“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026).
When I met her in the West Village in September, she’d just come from recording its accompanying audiobook, a delicate process given the visuals on its pages. Chalabi organized meticulous interviews conducted with anonymous subjects across income levels over the course of six years into 10 vividly fleshed-out characters. Each represents a particular economic class, illustrated in her signature hand-drawn style and punctuated by reflections on her own financial struggles as a young journalist and, more recently, in the wake of her mother’s illness. Chalabi carries a long tradition of data visualization — W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes comes to mind — into her refreshing candor about class and the stifling silence around it, particularly in journalism and the art world.
That insistence on specificity and honesty in her reporting goes hand-in-hand with her political advocacy; Chalabi donated her $15,000 Pulitzer Prize award to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate and has been fighting for Palestinian rights since she was a teenager. Her drive to seek out and represent truth, in Ten Lives and in her social media posts, is anchored in a sensitivity and profound sense of responsibility. In this way, she restores some of the humanity and dignity to the statistics that capture the brutality of genocide, exploitation, and economic inequality, one brushstroke at a time. In an interview, we spoke about the financial realities of journalism, the value of collaboration in an era of isolation, and the art and literature that sustains her. Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length.
Hyperallergic: In the intro to Ten Lives, you recall getting scolded for not observing “the etiquette of looking away” as a child. And it’s so striking that you have made a career of doing the opposite. How did you decide to make class, something we’re taught to overlook from a young age, the subject of this book?
Mona Chalabi: The first line of the original manuscript said, “I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it.”
H: Ha!
MC: And my editor was like, “Yeah, you can't do that. No one's gonna want to read a book that you wrote simply for money.” But I also knew that this was a commercial idea, and that did inform it. I have been quite shameless about the fact that I want my work to reach a wide audience. That has always, always mattered to me. It was the beginning of the pandemic, and part of the way that I pitched it was this idea that there's gonna be a big financial crisis and the dynamics are more nuanced than simply talking about the one percent. There's this idea of a coming economic collapse or a coming financial crisis. But as soon as we're in it, it's not this cyclical model. The crisis is the system that we're in that is so broken.
H: That gradation of class that usually doesn't get talked about is such a crucial contribution of this book. What led you to stratify these stories based on subcategories that often just get collapsed into “working class, middle class, upper class”?
MC: Class is really informative about who I am and how I move through the world and my relationships. And I felt like it was really, really lacking in our discourse. I feel a bit hesitant to use the word “discourse,” but it's just true. And it's not just about discourse, it's more mundane than that. It's the way that someone like me can say, “I'm an Arab, cis, heterosexual woman,” with total ease, but class doesn't really come into it. There's a dishonesty there. Actually, class is really, really important. And many of us aren't really talking about that in accurate and fruitful ways.

https://gothamist.com/news/digital-skill.title: Digital skills are an increasing requirement in NYC jobs beyond tech, report finds
https://gothamist.com/news/digital-skill.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/digital-skill.text:
A new report finds that nearly half of all job postings in New York City now seek digital skills, including home health care, construction and retail jobs.
Forty-four percent of job postings in the city now seek applicants proficient with things like productivity software and AI, compared to 35% a decade ago, according to a study released earlier this month by the Center for an Urban Future, an independent think tank.
“ These are jobs that have long provided a foothold in the economy, and they're becoming harder to access,” said Eli Dvorkin, the center’s editorial and policy director. “The danger is that there is a new barrier to opportunity for New Yorkers who are already struggling, in many cases, to get ahead.”
Researchers analyzed hundreds of thousands of public job postings between 2015 and 2025. The report found that the share of job listings asking for digital skills increased in nearly every sector the study tracked.
For home health care services, where over half of workers have a high school diploma as their highest level of education, the report found nearly a quarter of job listings now ask applicants for digital proficiency.
“For years as a city, we've thought about the digital divide largely in terms of who has a computer or an internet connection,” Dvorkin said. “Those things still matter, but the new digital divide is about who has the skills to succeed in an increasingly digital economy.”
Data shows the top five in-demand digital skills were Microsoft Office, Data Analysis, Python coding language, Microsoft Outlook and familiarity with AI software.
The report also found roles that required electronic proficiency correlated with higher wages. Full-time job postings asking for at least one digital skill had a median salary of $110,000, compared to $87,900 for those that did not seek digital skills, according to the report.
The report authors argue the city needs to put more resources toward workforce development programs, educational institutions and libraries to better train potential applicants.
“ If Mayor Mamdani is to succeed in making New York more affordable, it's not going to be enough to only focus on lowering the cost of living. Policymakers are also going to need to help more New Yorkers qualify for better-paying jobs and building digital skills across our economy,” Dvorkin said.
A City Hall spokesperson said they’re bolstering their workforce development efforts through programs like CUNY Tech Futures, which teaches students AI and data skills.
“The City is committed to supporting its homegrown talent with hands-on fluency with the technologies they’ll be using on the job,” Matthew Beller, spokesperson for the NYC Office of Talent and Workforce Development, said.
The city's Economic Development Corporation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
This story has been updated with comment from Matthew Beller, spokesperson for the NYC Office of Talent and Workforce Development.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Canada’s proposed federal budget includes tax breaks for artists and $554m funding boost for museums
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Hadani Ditmars
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The proposed budget Canada’s Liberal government released on 5 November offers the country’s artists a lifeline, recommending new tax measures and funding channels. In a post on X, shortly after finance minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled the budget, the Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote that “if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to $45,000” ($31,800) of income from their creative work.
Much remains unknown about how this tax exemption and other measures would be implemented. The budget released last week only proposes a tax credit and the federal government has yet to set its cost, start date or eligibility rules. Ottawa says its planned consultations with Canadians and the cultural sector will be announced in the spring 2027 economic update.
The proposed budget also includes C$783.1m ($554m) over five years going toward the National Arts Centre, Library and Archives Canada, the National Battlefields Commission and national museums, according to The Canadian Press. It also promises free entry to national museums for visitors under age 25, funded through a subsidy of C$46.3m ($32.8m) over five years, then C$11.5m ($8.1m) per year. The budget also calls for increasing funding to the Canada Council for the Arts with a new investment of C$20m ($14.1m) over three years.
“This funding falls far short of what is actually needed: permanent, stable funding at a scale that enables impactful support for Canadian artists and institutions,” Jenna Faye Powell, the interim national executive director of Carfac (Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le Front des Artistes Canadiens), tells The Art Newspaper.
In addition to funding boosts and tax breaks for artists, the budget reiterates support for the long-promised adoption of artist’s resale rights in Canada, which would provide artists with royalties from secondary-market sales of their work. In the 2025 Budget, the government announced its intent to amend the Copyright Act to create an artist’s resale right in Canada, but the legislation never materialised.
Adopting an artist’s resale right “would provide creators of original visual artworks with a royalty each time their work is resold through an eligible sale, creating an additional source of income”, Carfac and the Regroupement des Artistes en Arts Visuels (RAAV) wrote in a joint statement. More than 100 countries around the world have artist’s resale right laws on the books, although neither Canada nor the United States has adopted such a policy despite multiple attempts.
“As a sector, we still have a lot of questions, while many artists need relief now,” Powell says. “Especially those still grappling with tariffs. Carfac will certainly push to be a part of that consultation process.”
For the Vancouver-based artist and pioneer of photo-conceptualism Ian Wallace, the proposed budget’s measures for supporting artists and the arts sector are welcome news. “Generous support of Canadian museums allowing them to build their collections by purchasing the work of emerging artists” is an important part of development of contemporary Canadian art history, he says, as is academic research and discourse around contemporary Canadian art.
Wallace adds that the tax credit is a “generous one”, although he says that “most Canadian artists are not selling more than C$45,000 a year in any case” and their yearly taxable income fluctuates wildly.
“When Canadian artists are doing their, work it’s not just to get by and pay the rent,” Wallace says. “It’s to contribute something to the overall culture. That’s the value of it: to show that there is a valuable cultural history in Canada that we are proud of and can articulate.” He adds: “I’m happy to see that artists and what they’re doing is respected and supported in the federal budget.”
As for the artist’s resale right legislation, Wallace has a more nuanced outlook. The law would apply to secondary-market sales that occur “outside of the normal sale structure that happens through a gallery that represents the artist”, he says. “In that sense, suddenly there’s another legal structure to deal with that might or might not be work well. I’m obviously for anything that supports the artist, but I can see some more bureaucratic and financial complications coming up with the artist’s resale right.” But, he adds, that is “more of a problem for collectors and institutions than artists”.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-dont-just.title: Opinion: Don’t Just Celebrate the City’s Seniors—Hire Them
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dont-just.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dont-just.text:
Share This Article
“Elected officials are right to value older adults as engaged citizens and active participants in our democracy. But if government recognizes the value of older adults at the ballot box, it should also recognize their value in the workplace.”
Last year, while attending City & State New York’s annual New York Aging Summit, I listened as Ryan A. Murray, executive deputy commissioner and chief program officer of the New York City Department for the Aging, posed a simple question to the audience.
He first asked how many organizations offered internship programs. Nearly every hand in the room went up. He then explained what a “returnship” program was—a structured, paid program that helps experienced professionals return to the workforce after an extended absence—and asked how many organizations offered one.
Not a single hand was raised.
The silence in that room said more than any speech could have.
Although Executive Deputy Commissioner Murray directed his question to representatives of nonprofit and community organizations that advocate for older adults, there was one additional audience I wish had been asked the same question: elected officials.
Every year, elected officials honor older adults through proclamations, appreciation luncheons, awards, and speeches celebrating their lifetime of service. Those gestures are meaningful and appreciated. But they do little to address one of the greatest challenges many older New Yorkers face: finding meaningful employment.
After the celebrations end, many of those same older adults continue struggling to reenter the workforce because of age discrimination, outdated hiring practices, and the mistaken belief that experience has an expiration date.
If government truly values the wisdom, experience, and contributions of older New Yorkers, it should do more than celebrate them once a year.
Government shouldn’t just celebrate seniors—it should hire them.
This attention is understandable. Older adults are among the nation’s most civically engaged citizens. According to AARP, Americans age 65 and older have had the highest voter turnout of any age group for decades, while voters age 50 and older routinely account for more than half of the electorate.
Elected officials are right to value older adults as engaged citizens and active participants in our democracy. But if government recognizes the value of older adults at the ballot box, it should also recognize their value in the workplace.
Unfortunately, experienced workers age 45 and older often encounter significant barriers when attempting to return to the workforce despite decades of valuable experience.
Although laws such as the Age Discrimination in Employment Act prohibit age discrimination, many older workers continue to face hiring decisions influenced by outdated assumptions about technology, adaptability, or career longevity.
This isn’t just a perception. According to AARP, older workers historically remain unemployed longer after a job loss than younger workers, underscoring the need for innovative pathways back into the workforce.
Government is not immune from this challenge. Legislative offices, like many other employers, often have relatively few experienced workers despite the institutional knowledge, professional expertise, and life perspective they can bring to public service.
So what can elected officials do to better connect experienced workers with employment opportunities?
Some have already taken meaningful steps. In October 2025, for example, State Sen. Cordell Cleare hosted a job fair in Harlem specifically for job seekers age 50 and older. Initiatives like Sen. Cleare’s deserve recognition because they acknowledge the unique employment challenges experienced by older workers and provide valuable opportunities to connect them with prospective employers.
But job fairs, by their nature, depend on private employers to do the hiring. Government can go one step further by becoming part of the solution itself.
Rather than simply connecting experienced workers with employers, elected officials can establish returnship programs within government.
Imagine a six-month paid legislative returnship where experienced professionals work alongside elected officials assisting with constituent services, casework, community outreach, scheduling, communications, and legislative research while updating their professional skills and rebuilding their résumés.
Rather than asking the private sector alone to solve the problem, government should lead by example.
On the legislative side, Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie and Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins could establish a pilot returnship program by providing participating legislators with additional funding—for example, enough to support two temporary or part-time legislative aide positions during the January through June legislative session. Similarly, Gov. Kathy Hochul could establish pilot returnship programs within state agencies through an executive order or budget initiative.
New York already has experience creating innovative public-sector workforce programs. New York City’s Silver Star program, for example, allows retired city employees to return to part-time, project-based work without jeopardizing their pensions. While Silver Star serves retirees rather than unemployed job seekers, it demonstrates that government can successfully design flexible employment programs that tap into the experience of older adults. A statewide returnship program would build upon that concept by helping experienced professionals reenter the workforce.
To ensure the program remains focused on its intended purpose, several safeguards should accompany any pilot initiative. The New York State Department of Labor should centrally administer the application process and refer pre-screened candidates to participating offices for interviews and final hiring decisions.
Priority should be given to applicants age 45 and older who are unemployed, underemployed, returning to the workforce after caregiving responsibilities, retired individuals seeking to resume public service, or military veterans transitioning into civilian employment.
Participating offices should also submit an annual public report summarizing the number of applicants, interviews conducted, participants hired, program completion rates, demographic information, and the number of participants who later secured permanent employment. Public reporting would promote transparency, discourage favoritism, and provide lawmakers with data to evaluate whether the pilot should be expanded.
Although this proposal focuses on New York State government, the same concept could be adopted by county governments, municipalities, Congress, and even private employers seeking to benefit from the experience of older workers.
New York has no shortage of ceremonies honoring older adults. What it needs are more opportunities to put that experience back to work.
If government truly believes older New Yorkers still have valuable skills to contribute, it should prove it—not with another proclamation, but with a job offer.
Don’t just celebrate seniors. Hire them.
Leon Tulton is a Bronx community advocate and former legislative staff member.

https://hellgatenyc.com/deadly-fires-rag.title: While Deadly Fires Rage, the City Says No New E-Bike Battery Charging Stations Until 2028
https://hellgatenyc.com/deadly-fires-rag.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/deadly-fires-rag.text:
Back in early 2024, Eric Adams's Department of Transportation launched a pilot to prevent the steady increase of deadly fires caused by lithium ion batteries used to power e-bikes. The year before, 18 New Yorkers had been killed in the blazes, which start when batteries malfunction and explode—often in the homes of the delivery workers who rely on them. 
So the DOT installed five public charging cabinets in locations around the city, where delivery workers could pay a small fee to drop off depleted e-bike batteries, safely charge them, and take another one from the cabinet for use. 
The stations were a hit: the DOT facilitated 12,000 battery swaps in over six months, and reduced at-home charging among participants by more than a third. When the pilot wrapped up at the end of that year, the DOT recommended a citywide expansion of the program, which eventually grew to 25 new charging stations installed where deliveristas work the most—Midtown Manhattan, the Upper East Side, and the Upper West Side.
Two years later, the Mamdani administration has installed just one more public charging cabinet—a small cabinet at the deliverista hub next to City Hall—and says there won't be any more until 2028. Public comment about the proposed 25-site launch wrapped up this August, but the City has yet to announce which sites it has decided it will move forward with for the project's design phase.
The administration's inaction comes as nine and possibly as many as 15 New Yorkers have died this year due to fires believed to be started by e-bike batteries. The FDNY has already responded to 406 of these types of fires in 2026 so far, up from the 241 that were reported over the same period of 2025.
Both fire safety experts and advocates for delivery cyclists agree that this timeframe is unacceptable.
