https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-data-cent.title: An Effective AI Pushback Has to Go Beyond the Local
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-data-cent.author: Aziz Huq
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-data-cent.text:
An Effective AI Pushback Has to Go Beyond the Local
The midterms made clear that Americans are angry about the headlong rush into artificial intelligence. We are blocked from needed federal action for now, but states and localities have options that can move us toward eventual national regulation.
Last week’s election returns embodied a broad, national, and bipartisan reaction against data centers. In forty-six of the forty-seven local referenda held across some thirteen states, voters rejected new data center construction. Public opposition reflects local concerns about water usage, grid sustainability, and noise pollution. This opposition is also bubbling up at a moment when most of the public distrusts artificial intelligence (AI) in general, when two-thirds of Americans hold negative views of AI firms and their close ties to the Trump administration, and when fears about AI rank high among Americans’ leading worries.
This confluence of AI-adjacent fears is no accident. Each anxious spark leaps from a different facet of a single Silicon Valley strategy for hyperscaling AI. If this strategy works, it would induce a dramatic decline in labor’s income share of income. If it fails, it would saddle the state with crushing mountains of debt.
Voters, to be sure, likely perceive this dilemma only weakly. Yet their vivid fears create a chance for the Left to articulate a comprehensive diagnosis of hyperscale AI’s manifold problems — one that not only affirms the public’s fears but also articulates a coherent response. And just as the Silicon Valley strategy runs on a logic of scale, so too an effectual pushback must escalate beyond the local.
Heads, AI Wins. Tails, You Lose.
Generative AI is being developed by a small handful of firms. They are taking on massive amounts of debt to build computing power on which costly new tools can be offered at scale. Given the size of these investments, the firms are commercially viable only if they sell their wares at scale. This means either tapping hidden wellsprings of productivity growth (unlikely) or being used as a low-marginal-cost substitute for white-collar labor (more likely).
The ensuing debt-fueled displacement of white-collar labor, if successful, will induce a massive shift of income from labor to capital, as even the AI firms concede. The ruination of ecosystems and acceleration of the climate crisis are mere side effects. There is strong historical evidence of technology’s corrosive effect on the labor share: recent data from Europe suggests that AI, no less than other recent tech leaps, causes losses to labor and corresponding gains to capital. Worse, because most democracies tax capital at lower rates than labor, that shift will constrict the state, diminishing its fiscal capacity to cushion job losses and declining wages. In effect, hyperscale AI creates a distributional crisis and robs the state of tools to address it.
Of course, this strategy might not work. AI might not be transformative as its boosters claim. Markets may lose their nerve before profits can be reaped. But if the AI strategy isn’t successful, the leading firms now dominant in public equity markets (and hence our pensions and 401[k]s), will almost certainly demand a “rescue” akin to the 2008–9 federal financial-crisis interventions.
As of August, hyperscale AI firms had accrued more than $500 million in debt from private equity, banks, and institutional investors such as Blackrock and Pimco. If that debt sours, the repercussions of the crisis, as in 2008–9, would likely force the government’s hand. If that happens, a massive transfer of risk to public balance sheets will follow. This is capitalism as a “heads I win, tails you lose” proposition.
Whether or not it founders, hyperscale AI capitalism will cleave open immense lost opportunities for society at large. On one estimate, US AI investments will add up to some $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032, or an average of 3.63 percent of US gross domestic product per year. This is $10 trillion that will not and cannot be spend on maternal care, pre-K education, cancer treatment, environmental mitigation, or any other social programs and planetary reparative work we desperately need. It is, by any measure, a staggering divergence of investment away from areas of urgent moral priority.
No wonder, then, that the American public has such profound anxieties. The data center build-outs are simply the most apparent of the many economic, political, fiscal, and environmental crises that hyperscale AI is inducing.
Building Toward a National Response
What then might be an effectual response? Except in Harwood, North Dakota, voters have pushed back at a local level by denying construction permission, or in Perry, Ohio, demanding that firms post a bond as insurance against the risk of fiscal implosion. Localities’ responses are circumscribed, though, by their limited powers and their small geographic reach. Cities and counties can do little about the labor market effects or fiscal risk. Many environmental costs associated with new demands on the electric grid are out of their reach. Some cities such as Austin and San Antonio own and operate their own electrical utilities, giving them a lever that doesn’t exist elsewhere in the country. But these are exceptions. Solely local responses are usually tightly constrained.
Since the effects of hyperscale AI capitalism emerge at the national level, it would ideally be the federal government that drives a comprehensive response. Pessimism about the prospect of federal action is wise for now. After Tuesday’s election, Trump reiterated his belief that data centers are “gold . . . only foolish leadership will say NO.” His December 2025 executive order, barring states from regulating AI, remains in force, although the legal theories upon which it rests are flawed. Even if a Democratic-controlled House and Senate can overcome his veto, any resulting AI legislation will likely be weak thanks to the need to assemble supermajorities to ensure bills’ passage.
The difficulty of federal action, however, does not mean that progressives should give up addressing hyperscale AI capitalism. They still have ways to use both their control at the state level and at the regional level to highlight its costsand offer the beginnings of a commensurate response — indeed, one that might be fully nationalized in two years.
In January, Democrats will have “trifectas” in twenty-two states and hold the governor’s office in seven more (Kansas and Alaska are still not called as I write). This is a first platform for action. To date, states’ responses have been reactive and purely negative: New York’s and Oregon’s governors paused data center construction, while laws imposing moratoria have been introduced but not passed in sixteen states. Advocates of successful local ballot initiatives have indicated that they plan to turn to bans in their states.
Yet a pause is not a policy. It does nothing to communicate the complex and interconnected harms of hyperscale AI capitalism. So it leaves the field open for AI’s advocates to advance their tall tales of illimitable gain. Nor does it prevent the building of data centers elsewhere in the nation and so does nothing to rein in its fiscal and labor costs.
An alternate approach would be for states to force tech firms to not just account for the local effects of data centers but also recognize and take responsibility for all the social costs of their hyperscale strategy. It would seek to channel economic development into less costly, more decent forms. Bans, however, are a badly formed tool to this subtle end.
As a start, states could recognize their own complicity in hyperscale AI. In forty states, data centers benefit from exemptions from the sales and use taxes that would ordinarily accrue on building materials, machinery, and equipment. The nominal justification for such exemptions is the jobs new builds purportedly bring. But a data center at best tends to create only two or three hundred jobs, with no long-term effect on wages. Where a landlord like Equinix, Data Realty, or CyrusOne rents computing power to remote clients, even that meager gain goes unrealized.
States’ and localities’ ensuing revenue loss is hard to measure, because only some of the states with these tax exemptions report their fiscal effect. Texas, however, lost some $1 billion in FY2025; in 2024, Illinois lost $370 million; and Arizona lost $19 million. A simple first step is terminating all these tax exemptions on the ground that the local benefits from data centers have been illusory, following Maine’s example. That might also prompt states to reconsider more generally their blind pursuit of corporate investments through tax relief.
Having withdrawn their reckless subsidies, states should follow Perry, Ohio’s lead by forcing tech firms to bear the social costs of their speculative investments. New construction, for example, might be conditioned on bonds tied to the environmental and state-level labor market effects of their business models. Firms would first be required to report not only on expected environmental harms (including from increased energy demand) but also address whether a data center’s expected uses will displace human labor or otherwise have wage-suppressive effects (as a leading study has already found). It would then have to post bonds sufficient to pay for state investments to buffer those effects.
The law might impel an AI-funded guarantee fund to sustain state unemployment payouts and retraining costs generated by AI. States could also require that data center investments be backed by sufficient nondebt financing to mitigate any risk of catastrophic fiscal events. And even if data centers are not fully banned, states might simply target specific uses as verboten — say, the large-scale automation of American jobs. Firms that flout this would see their centers shut down.
At the same time, states need not act alone. An underappreciated part of the American constitutional order is groups of states’ latent authority to enter into binding “compacts.” These are treaty-like agreements, often created without Congress’s approval, to coordinate regulation between a pool of states. Existing compacts address drivers’ licenses, insurance coverage, and medical practice. They allow states to set uniform standards and realize regulation at scale, even if the national government is AWOL.
Imagine Texas, Virginia, California, Pennsylvania, and New York forging an interstate compact on AI and data centers. No firm would be permitted to operate data centers in any state unless they agreed to meet certain environmental standards and avoid use cases that threatened serious job loss. The compacting states could require a common set of disclosures — not only about the data centers themselves but also about the fiscal and labor market risks associated with AI more generally, and perhaps about other AI-related harms.
Unlike simple bans, this arrangement is more likely to be politically self-sustaining. Firms would, in effect, have to document on an ongoing basis the knot of harms that flow from hyperscale AI — hence supplying the grounds for their own regulation. And they could not simply blame states for quashing economic growth. A race to the bottom as firms tried to pit states against each other would be more difficult.
It is true that hyperscale AI capitalists are likely to flee from compacting states. But notice that the creation of a robust compact would limit their flight options, at least within the United States. To see this, consider the political costs to a red state governor who welcomes fleeing data centers that decline to comply with environmental and labor market protections. Recall that some 89 percent of Americans oppose data center siting near them. Isn’t it likely that the governor will meet the same fate as other erstwhile champions of AI, such as outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott? Compacting to clarify AI’s harms makes it politically more difficult for noncompacting states to embrace the industry.
No doubt, these solutions are incomplete. But they offer a pathway for dealing with not just the local but also the national harms of hyperscale AI in a politically durable way. They not only signal clearly that voters’ concerns have been heard but also help build virtuous circles of disclosure, action, and revenue so the perils of hyperscale AI can be enduringly addressed — a groundwork that offers a foundation for national action when the time is right.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/w.title: Winter Is Coming: Will Mamdani Do A Better Job For Bus Riders And Citi Bikers This Year?
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/w.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/w.text:
Mayor Mamdani (seen not holding a shovel at all but merely represented as such by our graphics team) vowed a better winter for New Yorkers trying to get around. The Streetsblog Photoshop Desk
It’s a winter wonder-land.
Mayor Mamdani is overhauling the city’s emergency response to better address the needs of homeless New Yorkers and others after last year’s extreme weather killed 18 people — but the portion of the plan related to transportation is light on details, and would rely on cooperation from the private companies that operate and maintain the Citi Bike docks and bus shelters on which thousands of New Yorkers rely.
On Monday, Hizzoner announced a number of improvements to, and investments in, the city’s winter weather protocols — a reaction to the harrowing winter that tested his fledgling team’s emergency response just weeks into his mayoralty. This includes a $25-million investment into the city’s “code blue” response to get vulnerable New Yorkers inside on the worst nights. The city will deploy 300 more outreach workers, use mobile warming vans, open city hospitals as warming centers and open more beds to homeless New Yorkers who need a place to stay.
But pedestrians, cyclists and bus riders who bore the brunt of the mobility dysfunction last winter will still have a blizzard of questions about this winter’s plan.
For instance, the mayor’s announcement said that the city had “established new protocols with JCDecaux and Citi Bike to clear bus stops, bike-share infrastructure and other priority transit areas faster” — but when Streetsblog inquired further about what exactly these new protocols entailed, a City Hall spokesperson said that conversations are ongoing, but include clearer expectations for the companies.
Lyft, which operates Citi Bike, has already committed to do better this winter, its spokesperson said.
“Lyft and the city share a commitment to keeping Citi Bike running throughout the winter,” said spokesperson CJ Macklin. “We’re working with the mayor’s office and DOT on updated protocols to prepare for winter weather and keep bikes and stations available for the New Yorkers who rely on them year-round.”
Last year, Citi Bike docks remained snowed in for weeks, bus riders traversed snowbanks and waited in the middle of the street for their ride, and pedestrians shuffled single file through narrow paths in the accumulated ice and slush. But the clarity of the expectations isn’t really the problem.
The city subcontracts with the advertising firm JCDecaux to operate bus shelters at 3,400 stops, meaning that the company, not the city, is responsible for clearing those bus stops after a storm. But private property owners are still responsible for the more than 10,000 bus stops not maintained by JCDecaux.
For Citi Bike the situation is similar. Lyft, the company that operates Citi Bike and owns the bikes and the docks, is clearly responsible for clearing them out in the event of snow. The company’s contract with the city has strict Service Level Agreements that are meant to keep the system operable for paid members. Lyft must remove snow within 12 hours of the end of the storm and must maintain parallel paths for pedestrians perpendicular to and parallel to the stations. The penalty is $50 per station, per 12-hour period.
But, these agreements are largely suspended during winter weather whenever alternate-side parking regulations are also suspended, making it impossible for the city to even fine Lyft for failing to clear out the docks, according to Lyft’s contract with the city that Streetsblog obtained through a records request.
It is unclear if any of these systems are actually changing, and City Hall would not say.
On the plus side, the city has purchased 120 snow blowers to help public workers clear areas that can’t be reached by typical plows. The Mamdani administration has added an unspecified number of small snow plows for the city’s protected bike infrastructure, a brigade that now numbers 47.
Last year, major protected bike lanes remained unplowed days after major snowfall forcing commuting cyclists and delivery workers into traffic.
And last year’s twin storms — which also came during prolonged stretches of cold weather that prevented melting — revealed existing flaws in the city’s approach to clearing crosswalks and sidewalks. The Mamdani administration says it is addressing those flaws by formally incorporating bus stops and crosswalks into official snow removal routes. In practice, property owners will remain responsible for clearing the sidewalks, but the Sanitation Department will now use an internal dashboard to identify areas for the city to step in.
“The Department of Sanitation will now be monitoring unsheltered bus stops and crosswalks in high-volume corridors and other pedestrian infrastructure via an internal dashboard and will dispatch Emergency Snow Shovelers as needed to ensure the safety of all New Yorkers,” said agency spokesperson Vincent Gragnani.
This winter is expected to be very different than last year. Meteorologists don’t expect long cold stretches that keep snowfall and ice on the street. Instead a strong El Niño will cause warmer weather. This will bring heavier, wetter snow, which, followed by short cold snaps, can create slippery ice, emergency management officials said at Monday’s press conference.
Last year, the city implemented its so-called “winter plan” for 50 consecutive days. DSNY workers laid one billion pounds of salt, cleared 135,000 crosswalks and plowed 6,300 miles of streets. On typical years the plan is only in place for around 10 days per winter, officials said. Officials promised that all New Yorkers’ transportation needs would be taken care of this winter.

On November 5, U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation declaring the White House’s Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument—a designation that protects the spaces from major alterations in the future.
The proclamation, which is not legally binding, does not prohibit any forthcoming president from redecorating, adding new furniture, or making security and operational modifications, as long as they do not affect the monument’s architectural and historic character. The proclamation was accompanied by a fact sheet that noted that the Oval Office deserves greater recognition and protection. The White House and its grounds are already a National Historic Landmark administered by the National Park Service, having been designated as such in 1960.
Trump told the New York Times that he wants “to make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.” The proclamation followed a midterm election where Trump’s Republican Party suffered historic losses in both houses of Congress. Trump’s first interaction with reporters after receiving election results was during a visit to the construction site of the new 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom, built on the former site of the East Wing.
In his second term, Trump has commenced several renovation and building projects in the White House: paving over the Rose Garden; gilding the Oval Office; and the controversial demolition of the East Wing to make way for a new ballroom.
He has also undertaken similar ventures across Washington D.C., including the botched repair of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the contested remodeling of the Kennedy Center, and a planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch. These projects are estimated to cost over $1 billion in total, with funds collected from both public and private sources.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/impe.title: Impeachment Vote Looms for Hegseth
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/impe.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/impe.text:
Calls for self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ouster have grown louder on Capitol Hill as a possible impeachment vote looms this week. At the same time, Hegseth has shored up support at the White House and among MAGA faithful, according to dismayed Pentagon officials.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor Monday afternoon, charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Top Democrats have indicated a desire to join Massie’s effort since their midterm election landslide. “I am a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to be the next House speaker, told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday. Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., the current House Oversight Committee chair, told Newsmax on Friday it is “very possible” the votes exist to impeach Hegseth.
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment, agreed. “I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” she told The Intercept of Massie’s effort. In April, Ansari filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violations of the law of armed conflict and targeting of civilians, abuse of power, and obstructing congressional oversight. She called for a floor vote on his ouster this week.
“Hegseth has demonstrated that he is wholly incompetent. He’s committed what I believe to be war crimes in Iran and the Caribbean and he is ill-equipped for the job,” said Ansari. “My reason for introducing the articles of impeachment back in April had a lot to do with his conduct and the war crimes in Iran, including the bombing of the children’s school. But it’s refreshing to see that since then, more and more Republicans are also recognizing that his leadership has failed and that he’s putting all of us in danger.”
In the wake of a devastating election rout of the GOP that handed Democrats firm control of the House and the Senate, Congress begins a five-week lame-duck session on Monday. With dozens of Republican lawmakers ending their tenure in the House, it’s unclear how many will even show up for votes. Such absences, as well as outright defections in the GOP ranks, make it increasingly likely that Massie’s measure will pass, staffers on Capitol Hill told The Intercept.
On Sunday, GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas left open the possibility of backing the measure. “I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president,” he said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.” Outgoing House speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., did not answer when asked by Politico if GOP leaders would whip the Hegseth impeachment vote. House leaders must take up the matter within two legislative days; opponents could table the resolution or refer it to committee instead of voting directly on impeachment.
After narrowly being confirmed by the Senate, which required Vice President JD Vance to break a 50-50 tie, Hegseth’s tenure has been marked by fiascos and failures beginning with Signal-gate, the sharing of secret war plans in a chat group with a journalist. In that case, according to the Pentagon’s own inspector general, “Hegseth violated security protocols and endangered U.S. troops and objectives.” Since then, Hegseth has been under perpetual fire for the unsuccessful Iran war in 2026, specifically a strike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 150 civilians, most of them children. He faces pressure over his campaign of extrajudicial killings in attacks on so-called drug boats in the waters off Latin America. And questions continue to mount about his purge of top military leaders — many of them women and minorities.
“The fact that many career officials from the department have left citing his leadership, I think, is very telling,” said Ansari. Last week, The Intercept published an exposé quoting six current and former defense officials who currently serve or served under Hegseth and called for his ouster. “He is conducting state terrorism. He is 100 percent a war criminal. He needs to be prosecuted,” said Wes J. Bryant, one of those officials and, until last year, a senior targeting adviser and policy analyst at the Pentagon who was pushed out of his job for blowing the whistle on Hegseth’s efforts to undermine protections for civilians.
As calls for his ouster have grown louder, Hegseth launched a desperate bid to whip up support at the White House, including a nakedly obsequious video seeking Trump’s support that he posted on X. It was accompanied by a coordinated campaign of social media posts by Pentagon underlings tying Hegseth’s fortunes to the president with the text “STAND. FIGHT. DEFEND THE REPUBLIC.”
Hegseth’s hand was strengthened on Friday when Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles stepped down and was replaced by his hard-line domestic policy adviser, raging xenophobe, and illegal boat strike proponent Stephen Miller, according to two Pentagon officials. The embattled war chief was quick to offer “Huge CONGRATS” to Miller on X, and posted a photo of himself alongside Trump’s new consigliere. The same coterie of Hegseth devotees at the Pentagon followed with similar posts featuring Miller.
Wiles had reportedly soured on Hegseth, blaming his woeful management of the Iran war for flagging Republican fortunes. A senior Trump administration official also told MS Now that Miller and Hegseth “have been extremely close since the beginning of the administration.”
If the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate — a high bar, even when Democrats take control of the chamber in January. Neither of the two Cabinet secretaries impeached by the House — William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024 — were convicted by the Senate.
An Armed Services Committee staffer who spoke with The Intercept was skeptical that Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., would bring the measure to a vote. Ansari held out hope. “Thune is very much aligned in terms of his view that Hegseth is not fit for the job,” she said, adding, “I do think that the resounding victories on Tuesday night will impact the way Republicans operate moving forward.”
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring at the end of the year, has said for months that he regrets his vote to confirm Hegseth and rebuked the war chief for his desperate video address aimed at Trump. “[C]abinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way,” he wrote on X on Friday, also laying into Hegseth for “the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.” Tillis had also previously said Hegseth “needs to go.”
Massie suggested his impeachment resolution is the legislative equivalent of a mercy killing, calling it “a much gentler version” of what Democrats will do when they take control of Congress in January. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, and Ansari said that if Hegseth survives this year’s impeachment push, there were “many ways” for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session, specifically compelling him to testify before the American people. “I would be surprised to see him last the next two years in this administration,” she told The Intercept. “I think that he is not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration, but also the most unpopular — and it’s on a bipartisan basis. So the pressure will continue to grow for there to be some change at the Pentagon.”
Trump expressed mild “confidence” in Hegseth in a “60 Minutes” interview taped on Friday, touting the U.S. victory over Venezuela, but stopped short of praising his Pentagon chief for it. Asked if he credited Hegseth for what he considers a major victory, Trump replied: “No, but he was a part of it.” On Saturday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that calls for impeachment of administration officials amounted to “extortion at the highest level” and ordered the Justice Department to investigate those making the push.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, himself a potential target of impeachment, said on Sunday that the Justice Department would represent Hegseth during any impeachment proceedings. He added that he “would be very worried” if he were a Democrat threatening to investigate administration officials. Asked if he considered those threats to be a crime, Blanche said, “It depends on what’s said. So yes, there could be.”
The White House did not respond to questions about Trump’s support for Hegseth.
Update: November 9, 2026, 2:50 p.m. ET
The article has been updated to note that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against War Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday afternoon.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

Notes From the Blue Star State
Texas is predominantly and pragmatically populist. If the national Democratic Party wishes to conquer the Electoral College for a generation, it will follow the lead of the voters.
From the standpoint of The New York Times, Gina Hinojosa is the “first Hispanic” governor-elect of Texas, while James Talarico is a moderate from a “deeply conservative” state—and therefore likely to join the incumbent Senate leadership against challenges from what the Times calls the “far left.”
That’s not the way it looks from here. Hinojosa—a labor lawyer!—self-identifies as a “populist” in the grand farmer-labor tradition of the late 19th century (you can read about it in a book by Tom Frank). She rejects the “culture wars” of the “liberal-progressives” in the Democratic Party. Her issues are about the power of money and the price of power. Talarico, too, focused on billionaires, oligarchs, elections bought by AIPAC, and a message of basic human decency, motivated by faith.
According to the Times, the election was primarily a repudiation of Donald Trump. But in Texas, the campaign turned on Elon Musk, data centers, public schools, and the dark atmosphere of repression that had settled over this state as the local ruling class grew old. It was about the price of gas, the price of food, the soaring rents, and about whether abundant electricity would continue to underpin life in Texas. Ultimately, it was about who was in charge.
Foreign policy influenced the outcome only through Trump’s war on Iran. Oil was $65 a barrel in February and about $100 on Election Day. Texas produces oil, and those prices brought good money to the Permian Basin. But most of that flowed to refiners and to private equity—not to the urban commuters who vote here. The gas price measured Trump’s fealty to Netanyahu and, behind that, the catastrophe visited on Palestinians in Gaza. No other foreign issue mattered much. A colleague, taking the broad view, wrote that voters were offended by how Trump treated Zelensky. There weren’t 10 votes in Texas that turned on Ukraine.
The Democratic majorities that will ride to Washington in January will be fractious. The party is still dominated by Big Money, and those who campaigned against the Republican oligarchy will shortly have to confront its Democratic twin. The campaign-industrial complex that spent $1.5 billion on Kamala Harris two years ago is still in control. It is trying to keep the focus on Trump, to spin the victories in identity terms—a Black here, a Hispanic there, and many women, of course—and to keep the narrative away from the power of money and that despised label, “populism.”
Texas populism is not “democratic socialism.” The DSA is a rebellious force in solidly Democratic states; there, it can appeal to a narrow and concentrated base. Texas is not New York City or Los Angeles or Seattle, and after 30 years of Republican hegemony, there was no Democratic establishment to overcome. Texas populism is a form of Christian community socialism—dare I use that word?—which has always enjoyed latent appeal around here. That is why Talarico and Hinojosa (and Goodwin, Johnson, Eckhardt, and every other down-ballot Democrat) won votes previously cast for Trump. Given that Texas is a resource state, Texas populism also understands the realities of the energy system as coastal city dwellers often do not.
“Affordability” was the watchword of 2026. The next phase, within the Democratic Party, will separate those for whom it is just a question of talking points from those who feel the need to deliver. Higher wages. Lower prices. Stable rents. Good public schools. Healthcare that doesn’t break the bank. Electricity that becomes, once again, cheap and abundant. Housing that is decent and, well, affordable. Roads, bridges, rails, and water systems that are built to last.
To deliver affordability means stepping on toes and breaking taboos. Not least, the economists’ cartel with its aversion to rent and price controls. Not least, the health insurance industry and the pharmaceutical companies. Not least, the private-equity energy mafia. Not least, the budget and resource drain that is our distended, obsolete military. And not least, the shibboleth that interest rates are the sole domain of the Federal Reserve, to be raised—crushing housing while enriching the banks—on the empty pretext of “fighting inflation.” A comprehensive national affordability plan remains to be written. When it is, the Democratic donor class will be shocked.
Then there is the question of what to do about Trump. Those who tried to destroy him legally in the Biden interregnum will be back. To take up that cudgel again would be stupid. As a political force, Trump is already destroyed. His administration is breaking apart. He is also an old man in the last phase of his power. The Texas message, I believe, is to let him fade away, bring the cycle of personal political vengeance to an end—and focus on the problems of the people.
To those like Talarico, heading to Washington for the first time, the overseas trifecta—Russia, China, and Iran/Israel—will loom large. The foreign policy establishment is waiting. It will urge hectoring China, financing Ukraine, and sending bombs to Israel, come what may. The new group will have to figure out for itself that China is immune to American pressure. That Russia cannot be defeated—not on the battlefield, as US military intelligence has always known, and also not by sanctions. And that Iran, having won the war, will dictate terms in the Middle East—including on key matters to the Israelis. These facts are locked down, and the Obama-Biden foreign policy era is now over. The peace to come—which must come—will have to respect the realities of the world as it is.
At the national level, the wedge of Texas populism will be thin. It may be absorbed by the national leadership. It may be overshadowed by the all-or-nothing politics of the sectarian left. Or by a wave of scorched-earth revanchism from the Obama-Biden crowd. In the smog of elite Washington, it may have trouble discovering the realities of the larger world, and even more difficulty making its discoveries heard. The consultants and donors and experts will be on the newcomers—on Talarico, also on El-Sayed and any others inclined to think for themselves—like flies on honey.
Nevertheless, Texas has flipped. The state is no longer “deeply conservative.” It is predominantly and pragmatically populist. And Texas is still a very big state. If the national Democratic Party wishes to conquer the Electoral College for a generation, it will follow the lead of the voters here, of the new state government here, and of the new Texans in Washington.
I doubt that this is possible. But then, who expected Tuesday’s election result?

https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.title: Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out.
https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.author: Katie Nixdorf, Debbie Cenziper, Megan Rose, Brandon Roberts
https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.text:
These days, we know where almost everything comes from. Everyday items like food, clothes and pens all carry labels listing where things are grown, manufactured or even designed.
So why is it so hard to find where prescription drugs are made?
That question set off a 14-month investigation into where our medications are made, how the FDA polices drug manufacturers and what happens when inspectors report issues inside factories.
The vast majority of prescriptions filled in the United States are for generic drugs, which are often far cheaper than brand-name alternatives. 
For years, Congress, doctors and watchdog groups have questioned the quality of generic drugs made overseas. India produces about half of all generics used in the U.S., but the labels on pill bottles often don’t list where a drug is manufactured. Inspection reports describe unsafe manufacturing conditions at generic drug factories, but the Food and Drug Administration redacts the names of the medications made in those factories. That means if drugs made in errant factories wind up in your medicine cabinet, you’d have no way of knowing.
To better understand how the FDA regulates the generic drug industry, Debbie Cenziper and Megan Rose interviewed current and former factory inspectors, tested medications in a lab and sued the federal government for critical documents.
Here’s what they found:
- Birds defecated on boxes of sterile equipment. Inspectors reported finding dirty labs, mold and foul water at factories. Records referenced vials of medication that were “blackish” from contamination. Inspectors found what appeared to be metal shavings on equipment.
- Drug manufacturers manipulated and destroyed drug-testing records. At one factory, an analyst poured acid on records stuffed in a trash bin. At another, inspectors said in a report that records were “routinely manipulated” to cover up the presence of particulate matter —  which could include glass, fiber or other contaminants — in generic drugs.
- A lifesaving generic drug contained a lower amount of a key ingredient. We worked with an independent lab to test generic versions of tacrolimus, used to prevent organ rejection. We found some pills contained a lower amount of the key ingredient in the drug. Doctors and experts said that underdosing can leave patients vulnerable to organ rejection.
- The FDA allowed generic drug imports from banned factories — and didn’t inform the public. The agency gave some manufacturers a special pass to continue to ship drugs made in factories whose manufacturing practices were so bad they had been banned from the U.S. Over a dozen years, the FDA exempted at least 150 drugs or their ingredients from banned factories.
- A transplant patient’s lungs failed after she took generic versions of tacrolimus. Hannah Goetz had a double-lung transplant as a teenager and had to take tacrolimus twice a day. Her lungs failed in 2023, and she died at 21 years old, after years of relying on the generic drug made by two manufacturers with documented problems. Lawyers told Goetz’s mother that it was impossible to draw a straight line from Hannah’s death to a generic manufacturer, but her mother said she wonders if her daughter would still be alive if she took a different brand of tacrolimus.
In a response to ProPublica, a spokesperson for the FDA said in a statement that the exemptions given to banned factories are “thoroughly evaluated through a multi-disciplinary approach” but declined to say exactly what those evaluations entailed. The agency also said it requires manufacturers to conduct additional quality checks with third-party oversight before sending drugs to the U.S. The agency did not respond to questions about how it can know that generics are safe without a more robust testing program.
In statements to ProPublica, drug companies said that they take patient safety seriously, adhere to quality standards and are committed to working with the FDA on any regulatory issues.
ProPublica’s investigation, which went on to be a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting, published in 2025. 
Use our tool to find where your prescription drugs were made.
ProPublica’s Brandon Roberts and a team of data journalists made a tool called Rx Inspector that will show you the facility that manufactured your generic prescription drugs and any inspection reports, warning letters and import bans we have from the FDA. 
The data isn’t perfect; it’s possible the FDA hasn’t published everything it knows about a given facility, for example. Also, one company may have acquired another or moved the factory somewhere else. This tool also isn’t meant to provide you with medical advice: If you find something troubling, it doesn’t necessarily mean that your drug is compromised. Doctors and pharmacists advise that you not stop taking your medications. Instead, you should talk to your healthcare provider about any concerns.
Step 1: Enter the name of your prescription drug, as well as the company name found on your pill bottle or drug label.
Step 2: If there are multiple matches in our database, you can narrow your search using the markings found on a pill, for example.
Step 3: When you click on a drug, we’ll show you any manufacturing facilities we’ve been able to connect to it. Click on a facility to see any information we have from the FDA.
FDA inspections come with compliance outcomes, such as import alerts or warning letters. The best possible outcome of an inspection is “acceptable state,” which means the FDA took no compliance action and ProPublica found no issues documented by inspectors. Search your prescription here.
ProPublica described Rx Inspector and the methodology used to build it to the FDA, which did not comment. The agency previously told ProPublica that it doesn’t reveal where drugs are made on inspection reports to protect what it deemed to be confidential commercial information.
Read more of Cenziper, Rose and Roberts’ reporting from their series Rx Roulette or watch their video explainer.

https://hyperallergic.com/clouds-were-on.title: Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge
https://hyperallergic.com/clouds-were-on.author: Julia Curl
https://hyperallergic.com/clouds-were-on.text:
Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge
The Met Museum’s “Chasing Clouds” is a pleasing romp through the technical problem of capturing clouds at photography’s beginning.
The original 1996 Windows XP default background is arguably the most viewed photo of all time; its cumulus puffs drifting across a way-too-blue sky are seared into my and countless others’ Y2K childhoods. Such images of fluffy clouds are so ubiquitous that it’s hard to believe they once presented one of photography’s greatest technological challenges. The Met exhibition Chasing Clouds is a pleasing romp through the history of this problem through a union of art and science, spanning the early 1800s to 1929 — roughly photography’s first century. While the medium showed promise as “the pencil of nature,” its first processes were overly sensitive to blue light, registering the sky as a blank white space, impossibly overexposed.
While this lent some images a minimalist mystique, like John Beasley Greene’s “The Nile in Front of the Theban Hills” (1853–54), other photographers resorted to painting clouds into their landscapes by hand. An initial breakthrough came when French photographer Gustave Le Gray figured out how to stitch together two pictures — one calibrated to sky, and the other to land and sea. (Photographic fakery is as old as the medium itself.)
Though the exhibition begins with painted cloud studies and ends with photographic modernism, visual discoveries unfold in a dialogue between painting and technology rather than as a scientific march from one to the other. This makes for a much more interesting story; obsolescence is often a capitalist public relations trick.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-calls.title: Mamdani calls for investigation on how a man charged for jogger's murder was hired by DOE
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-calls.author: Carol Chen, Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-calls.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has ordered a probe into how the man charged with killing Brooklyn jogger Katie Suarez got a job in the city's public school system despite a documented history of psychiatric issues.
"I have directed my team to conduct a full review into this matter," Mamdani said at a press conference on Monday. The city’s department of education has suspended Sayed Mohassib, 27, the mayor said, and the city is offering counseling to students and families at P.S. 200 in Bath Beach, where Mohassib worked as a paraprofessional.
Mohassib was arrested on Saturday and charged with murder, tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon.
Suarez, a 28-year-old TD Bank employee, was stabbed in the neck on Oct. 30 while running on the Shore Parkway Greenway. She died several days later. According to news reports, Mohassib returned to work in the days after the alleged murder.
The case has drawn attention from elected officials and community members, who voiced concerns about how the city screens public school employees.
“I think to myself, ‘Just imagine what could have happened there with the children,’” said Cristina Romero, 47, who has two children at the school. “Why was that person there? Why wasn’t that person evaluated? Why were our children put in danger?”
City payroll records show Mohassib was employed by the DOE starting in April 2019. The department paid him as an hourly support staff through the 2023 fiscal year, then listed him as a paraprofessional in fiscal years 2024 and 2025. The DOE has not confirmed the specific responsibilities of his job at P.S. 200.
But during that same period, questions were raised about Mohassib’s mental fitness, according to a statement from the local elected officials and an NYPD spokesman.
In the fall of 2022, Mohassib was placed on military leave after a brief assignment with the NYPD, the police spokesman said. But, according to elected officials, Mohassib was discharged from the Marines for psychiatric reasons soon after. The Marines did not respond to Gothamist’s request for comment.
On Jan. 11, 2023, Mohassib asked to be reinstated to the NYPD. But several supervisors noted that he “appeared disheveled” and was behaving in a concerning way, the police spokesman said. The NYPD denied his request and he was taken to Bellevue Hospital.
“If the NYPD deemed him unfit, why would he then be deemed fit to serve in a classroom of children?” said City Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso, whose district includes the school where Mohassib worked, adding that the DOE needs to “take a hard look at how he was able to pass through DOE screening.”
DOE applicants are subject to criminal records searches, but there is no assessment of their psychiatric history and issues that come up during their employment might be missed, said Jennifer Weber, an education policy fellow at the Manhattan Institute.
"Once you're kind of in the system, they're not necessarily reevaluating your role in the system or reevaluating your records in the system," she said.
Jay Brown, president of Community Education Council 21, which borders the district that includes P.S. 200, said the case represented a systemic failure.
"We don't demonize people who are navigating mental illness," Brown said. "But in this case, there were warning signs."
State Sen. Andrew Gounardes, one of the elected officials who issued the joint statement, said that he wants Mamdani's review to determine how the DOE can work with other city agencies that have “orange flags or red flags about applicants."
Nicole Brownstein, a spokesperson for the DOE, said student safety is “our very top priority.”
“We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed,” Brownstein said.
The mayor's office has not said who will lead the review or when it will finish.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New centre for contemporary Indigenous art launches in upstate New York
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Branchline, a new 10,000-sq.-ft arts centre focused on championing contemporary Native American art, opened its main gallery to the public on Saturday (7 November). Located in the town of Katonah in New York’s Westchester County, Branchline is an initiative of the Gochman Family Collection (GFC), a private lending collection established in 2021 by the philanthropist Becky Gochman, who has a longstanding interest in Native art, and the former gallerist Zach Feuer.
Branchline is located steps from the Katonah station on the Metro-North Railroad, around 45 miles from Manhattan, and takes its name from a term for points where railroad tracks diverge and begin. When it is fully completed next year, the complex will span three adjoining buildings—including multiple galleries, a ceramics studio, two apartments, a deck filled with sculptures and a café.
Laura Phipps, a former associate curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art, was appointed director of the GFC earlier this year. She is working alongside the creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) and several other curatorial consultants at Branchline.
“Branchline builds on an extension of the ethos and the experience of the GFC, which is centring artists, supporting artists and sharing their work,” Phipps said at a preview of the centre on 5 November. “We were excited about all the ideas that Branchline conjures, both thinking about the metaphor of the train, the metaphor of trees, and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”
Organisers seek to explore innovative ways of activating the space in dialogue with the collection. The inaugural programme features a site-specific installation on the exterior of the main gallery building by the artist Matthew Kirk (Diné). The four-panel mixed-media work We Start To Think We’ve Got Someplace To Go (2026) features traditional Diné motifs made with construction materials.
The opening exhibition, Line Break, is curated by Branchline’s assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee/Diné) with the collection associate Nicole van Brugge. It explores the concept of lines and borders figuratively and metaphorically through nearly 30 works by 18 artists—including Sara Flores, Jeffrey Gibson, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, Kay WalkingStick, Marie Watt and Emmi Whitehorse.
A centrepiece of the opening show is the Diné artist Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021-24). It consists of abstracted musical scores that reference traditional Diné weavings while also evoking the sounds made by drones. The work is accompanied by isolated recordings Chacon captured of drones that hovered above the Standing Rock encampments during the Dakota Access Pipeline protests in 2016, with the lines in the work referencing the oscillating sonic waves of their erratic flight patterns.
Before establishing a dedicated exhibition space, some of the GFC’s holdings—totalling around 800 works—were displayed in private residences on Manhattan’s Upper East Side and in West Palm Beach, Florida. The GFC has loaned art to more than 100 exhibitions worldwide, with 260 works loaned to date.
Gochman and Feuer previously co-founded the Forge Project in 2021, an initiative similarly dedicated to the advancement of contemporary Native art and located around 70m north in Taghkanic, New York. That space also offers year-round exhibitions, artist residencies and workshops. It was converted from a private organisation into a Native-led nonprofit in 2024, when Gochman withdrew from the project. Candice Hopkins (Carcross/Tagish First Nation) is its current executive director and chief curator.
“We started Branchline and the Forge Project for social-justice reasons, and we are now separate from Forge, but we got the bug to collect Native art,” Gochman said at the preview. “The Branchline space functions as a free public space, which is a new concept for us. We are consistent, though, with the philosophy that artists and art come first, because we wouldn’t be here without them.”

https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.title: La cultura taína sigue viva: exposición en el Bronx celebra legado de Bobby González
https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.text:
Share This Article
Una nueva exposición en el Museum of Bronx History explora la vida del poeta, narrador y educador puertorriqueño que dedicó casi cuatro décadas a preservar la cultura indígena y desafiar los estereotipos sobre el sur del Bronx.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 4 de noviembre. Traducido por Jacob Velez. Read the English version here.
Para Bobby González, la preservación de la historia indígena comenzó cerca de casa: en la bodega de su familia, ubicada en el sur del Bronx.
Mientras crecía cerca de las viviendas públicas Melrose Houses, González conoció a personas de diferentes comunidades indígenas que visitaban el negocio de sus padres. Esas conversaciones lo ayudaron a comprender mejor su propia herencia taína y despertaron en él un compromiso de por vida con la enseñanza de la historia indígena.
Ahora, tres años después de su fallecimiento, su trabajo es recordado en una nueva exposición en el Museum of Bronx History (Museo de Historia del Bronx).
La exposición, titulada “From the South Bronx Reservation: Bobby González, Taíno Indian” (“Desde la reserva del sur del Bronx: Bobby González, indígena taíno”), inaugurada el 8 de octubre y abierta hasta marzo de 2027, explora la vida del poeta, narrador y educador puertorriqueño que dedicó casi cuatro décadas a preservar la cultura indígena y desafiar los estereotipos sobre el sur del Bronx.
Nacido en 1951, González creció en una familia puertorriqueña cuyos padres emigraron a Nueva York después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Su padre trabajó como cocinero antes de abrir una bodega en la década de 1970, donde González y sus hermanos ayudaban a administrar el negocio familiar.
Según Stephen Payne, director de la Sociedad Histórica del condado del Bronx, la bodega desempeñó un papel importante en la formación de la identidad de González.
Entre los visitantes había personas de ascendencia cherokee, quechua, lenape y de otras comunidades indígenas. Sus conversaciones motivaron a González a aprender más sobre las comunidades indígenas de América y a explorar su propia ascendencia.
Esa experiencia influyó posteriormente en la expresión “South Bronx Reservation” (“Reserva del sur del Bronx”), que González utilizaba para describir la presencia indígena en su vecindario.
Payne explicó que la expresión también reflejaba similitudes entre el sur del Bronx y algunas reservas indígenas de Estados Unidos, incluidos problemas relacionados con la contaminación y la falta de recursos.
Para González, el vecindario era mucho más que el lugar donde había crecido. Se convirtió en la base de sus escritos, su poesía y su activismo cultural.
Su viuda, María Aponte González, lo recordó como alguien que siempre mantuvo una profunda conexión con su comunidad.
“Era una persona de espíritu muy amable”, dijo. “Nunca gritaba, nunca levantaba la voz”.
Describió a su difunto esposo como una persona accesible y tranquila, a quien los miembros de la comunidad acudían frecuentemente en busca de consejos.
González cofundó la organización cultural Taíno del Norte, organizó el festival anual Bronx Native American Festival y escribió varios libros, entre ellos The Last Puerto Rican Indian (“El último indígena puertorriqueño”). También viajó por todo el país para ofrecer charlas en escuelas, universidades y museos sobre la historia indígena.
Su misión era desafiar la creencia de que los taínos, un pueblo indígena que habitaba originalmente el Caribe, incluido Puerto Rico, habían desaparecido siglos atrás.
“Somos taínos, todavía estamos aquí”, dijo Payne, al recordar una frase utilizada por la organización que González ayudó a establecer.
Payne explicó que la exposición destaca cómo la identidad indígena continúa formando parte de las comunidades puertorriqueñas, particularmente en el Bronx, donde González se convirtió en una figura importante del movimiento de revitalización cultural taína.
La exposición también llega en un momento en que el Bronx atraviesa cambios demográficos. Payne señaló el aumento del costo de vida y cómo ha contribuido a que los residentes puertorriqueños abandonen el distrito o la ciudad, lo que resalta la importancia de que los miembros de la comunidad compartan sus historias.
“Es muy importante preservar esa parte de la historia mientras todavía haya personas en la comunidad que puedan hablar de ella”, dijo.
La exposición reúne pertenencias personales, escritos y otros materiales que González conservó a lo largo de su vida.
Aponte González, quien fue cocuradora de la exposición junto con el documentalista Edwin Pagán, seleccionó los objetos de su hogar.
“Todo lo que van a ver en la exposición es obra de Bobby”, dijo.
En lugar de centrarse en cómo otras personas describían a su esposo, quiere que los visitantes conozcan su legado a través de los materiales que él mismo había creado.
Entre sus contribuciones se encontraban talleres de poesía, incluida una serie de poesía recitada que ayudaba a poetas emergentes a desarrollar sus propias voces. También utilizaba títeres y narraciones para enseñar a los niños sobre la historia indígena y sus tradiciones culturales.
Aponte González puso en marcha el Proyecto Legado de Bobby González en 2024, después de conversaciones que había mantenido con su esposo sobre la preservación de su trabajo antes de que enfermara gravemente.
Describió la exposición como un proyecto que tardó dos años en desarrollarse, con el apoyo de Pagán y el Museum of Bronx History.
Para Payne, la exposición también refleja un desafío más amplio que enfrentan las instituciones históricas: preservar las experiencias de las comunidades trabajadoras, cuyos documentos y pertenencias personales suelen perderse debido a la inestabilidad de vivienda o la falta de recursos económicos.
Explicó que las familias que han sufrido desalojos o mudanzas frecuentes pueden haber perdido fotografías, documentos y otros materiales que ayudan a contar sus historias. En esos casos, las instituciones suelen recurrir a testimonios orales e investigaciones de archivo para recuperar historias que, de otro modo, podrían desaparecer.
La colección de González ofreció una oportunidad diferente, ya que él había conservado gran parte de su propio trabajo, que su viuda ha puesto a disposición a través del Proyecto Legado.
Más allá de celebrar sus logros, tanto Aponte González como Payne esperan que la exposición anime a las generaciones más jóvenes a conocer sus raíces culturales.
“Los jóvenes necesitan hacer espacio en sus mentes y estar abiertos a aprender”, dijo Aponte González.
Para Payne, el mensaje principal es que la historia indígena no debe entenderse únicamente como algo que pertenece a un pasado lejano.
Espera que los visitantes reconozcan que las comunidades indígenas continúan preservando, recuperando y desarrollando sus tradiciones culturales en la actualidad.
A través de los escritos, las narraciones y el activismo de González, la exposición ofrece a los visitantes la oportunidad de explorar esa historia viva mediante las experiencias de un hombre que dedicó su vida a compartirla.
La exposición estará abierta al público en el Museum of Bronx History, en 3266 de Bainbridge Avenue, en el Bronx, hasta marzo de 2027.

https://hellgatenyc.com/the-new-museums-.title: The New Museum’s New Director: Art Is Not a Lubricant
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-new-museums-.author: Julianne Escobedo Shepherd
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-new-museums-.text:
This March, the New Museum reopened its 60,000-square-foot expansion with "New Humans: Memories of the Future," a sprawling meditation on the technological past, present, and future that included eerie floating jellyfish-drones, World War I prosthetics, and a video installation of a deepfake Kim Kardashian describing war in Sri Lanka. After that exhibit closed this fall, the New Museum put up the multidisciplinary artist Arthur Jafa's first museum survey in the United States, including huge video installations and photographic collage that interrogate and reframe the way Black lives are depicted in images.
Both of these must-see exhibitions share a probing, sharply current perspective that urge the viewer to question the cultural and technological mores that shape the world. Both were projects of Massimiliano Gioni, the Italian visionary who, in July, was announced as the New Museum's new director—only the third in its 49-year history—taking over for Lisa Phillips, who spent 26 years at the helm. Gioni, 52, has spent much of his celebrated career at the New Museum, joining in 2003 as director of special exhibitions before becoming its artistic director in 2014. He's a longtime East Village resident, but he has a global perspective too, as a former curator of biennales around the world, including in Venice, Gwangju, and Berlin.
Hell Gate videochatted with Gioni on an evening in late October about his perspective on art, his youth as a graffiti writer, and the polemical mission of the New Museum. "The New Museum is a place where, yes we show great art and artists, but as vehicles to understand the world we're in," he said. "There is less art for art's sake in our building than in others, I think."
This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Hell Gate: You've been in New York for exactly 20 years, is that correct?
Massimiliano Gioni: Actually, longer, because I came at the end of '99 and then I lived here until 2003. But the accent doesn't wash out.
I read in the Arthur Jafa exhibition catalog that you were a graffiti writer. What type of graffiti were you doing?
I was an aspiring graffiti artist in Italy and I even got arrested—I must say I was lucky that I got arrested in Italy, not in New York, much rougher—and I was still underage when that happened. Fortunately it didn't go down on my permanent record as they say. It was all Keith Haring's and Rammellzee's and even Basquiat's fault. The funny story is, graffiti art had an early exposure in Italy of all places. Not many people know that Jean-Michel Basquiat's first gallery show happened actually in the city of Modena at Emilio Mazzoli before it even happened in New York at Annina Nosei's. Probably the first museum show for graffiti art happened in Italy in the early '80s. It was called Arte di Frontiera, Frontier Art. I was too young to have seen the actual show, but the catalog of that show was my bible for growing up as a kid.
It was very much connected to certain fantasies I had about New York, probably, and also being born outside of a big city. I probably kind of identified with a slightly outsider's position. But that book with all the photos of, you know, A-One and Lee Quiñones and Crash and Lady Pink and all those guys. And then, of course, early SAMO was very inspiring. And then Keith Haring was, you know, for as many kids of my age, a kind of gateway drug. It was like the surrealists, and then Keith Haring.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Veering From Campaign Pledge, Mamdani Brings Back NYC Property Lien Sale for 2027
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned on a promise to end New York City’s practice of selling property owners’ municipal debts to investors, but his administration says it is bringing back what is known as the lien sale, one more time.
The city will hold a lien sale in mid-2027 before its authorization to do so expires under a local law the following year, City Hall confirmed. Administration officials said they want to collect overdue taxes while also contacting delinquent owners early so they have a chance to pay what they owe and avoid potential foreclosure.
“A consistent and standardized property tax enforcement system is critical for our city’s revenue and to be able to enforce the property tax in a fair way,” Cea Weaver, director of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants and one of Mamdani’s closest housing advisors, said in an interview. “Continuing to push off the lien sale would just mean that homeowners who really need help are digging themselves even further into a hole that we would then have to dig them out of.”
As a mayoral candidate, Mamdani vowed to “stop the tax lien sale on Day One,” if elected. He suspended the sale in March to complete a six-month review of the program. Officials said they concluded a lien sale with more outreach to homeowners would be more appropriate than ending it right away. Property taxes are the city’s largest source of revenue.
The city Department of Finance puts liens, or legal claims, on properties for unpaid property taxes and water bills. When the debt gets to a certain amount depending on the type of property — typically $5,000 for taxes three years overdue — the city can sell the liens at a discount to privately managed trusts, some of which issue bonds to investors. The trusts attempt to collect the debt and have the power to initiate foreclosure.
The city will issue a 90-day notice list of tax-delinquent property owners who may be eligible for the 2027 lien sale in late February or early March, according to DOF Commissioner Richard Lee. Outreach by the Mayor’s Public Engagement Unit and nonprofit organizations will begin before the list goes out to give owners a heads-up and allow them to start a payment plan or take other action to avoid the sale, City Hall said.
Some elected officials and community advocates have for years pushed to end the lien sale and find a different way for the city to do tax enforcement, arguing the practice disproportionately affects homeowners of color and tenants. City laws enacted earlier this year end the current lien sale process by 2029 and stipulate the city may transfer debts to an entity known as a land bank, which an official group is in the process of setting up.
“The important thing is that we have a tax system in which individuals are compliant,” Lee said in an interview. “We want to provide all the resources that we can in order to achieve that.”
Disproportionate Impacts on Homeowners of Color
Then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani created the lien sale in 1996 to address property abandonment and collect unpaid taxes. Since then, the lien sale has been a source of revenue for the city, with about $80 million raised on average each year.
But the sale has had harmful effects for some property owners, who often must pay more fees and interest on top of what they already owe — which sends them further into debt and can result in foreclosure, with owners losing their homes.
Elected officials and community advocates have long criticized the tax lien sale for targeting homes in majority-Black and -Hispanic neighborhoods, where most liens were sold in the two most recent lien sales. Critics also argue the lien sale strips the city of control over its debt, and thus the opportunity to steer the future of distressed properties.
In policy materials, Mamdani’s campaign echoed those criticisms, slamming the lien sale for “racism” and pointing to the negative effects on working-class homeowners and homeowners of color. The campaign also promised a Mamdani administration would work with the City Council to “permanently abolish the system,” calling it “a relic of the Giuliani era that has been a blight on our city for decades.”
Jakob Kendall Schneider, senior program manager of research and policy with the East New York Community Land Trust and a member of the Abolish the Tax Lien Coalition, said the group was reviewing the specifics of the 2027 sale, but emphasized holding the sale at all falls short of the group’s demand.
“Our goal is to abolish trust-based lien sales. That has not changed,” he said.
Referring to Mamdani’s campaign pledge, Schneider said, “It’s past Day One and there’s going to be a lien sale.”
The city’s last lien sale was in 2025 during the administration of Mayor Eric Adams. More than 4,500 liens were sold for $220 million, with hundreds of millions of dollars more collected from homeowners’ debt payments during the notice period, according to the city’s Independent Budget Office. Last year, 85% of eligible property owners avoided inclusion in the sale.
Adams also came out against the sale and as a candidate vowed to end it “for good.” The 2025 lien sale included exemptions and off-ramps for certain homeowners to offer greater protection.
‘Very High Bar for Lien Sale’
City officials said outreach for the forthcoming sale will include an increase in text and email notifications, getting in touch with homeowners in advance of the 90-day list, and engaging more with those who remain on the list within 10 days of the sale.
The process will feature new measures making it harder for some owners to become eligible for the sale in the first place and have their homes foreclosed on later.
To be eligible, two-and three-family homes must have $5,000 of water and sewer debt overdue by at least a year — an increase from $3,000 in the past. And a property can be foreclosed on only a year after the lien sale and if the value of the lien reaches $70,000 or 15% of the property value, whichever is less, as per the recent law.
“There is a very, very, very high bar to reach for the lien sale at this point to lead to a loss of equity in your home,” said Weaver, who is a member of the land bank group. “So given that very high bar that is in place and the significant outreach mechanisms that we have in place and that our administration is known for, we are clear that we think it’s appropriate to proceed with a lien sale.”
City Councilmember Sandy Nurse (D-Brooklyn) said the changes align with the reforms the City Council passed to eliminate the lien sale’s predatory elements and keep people in their homes.
“This builds in more of a human touch, it builds in more guardrails, it builds more offerings for people to not have a lien placed on their property and the lien not to be sold to these service providers,” she said. “I think with the reality of our financial situation and with the legislation that we passed and with the land bank coming online, we’re in a place where there are a lot of protections, and ultimately, we do need to collect municipal debt.”
It’s not the first time Mamdani’s actions as mayor have veered from his campaign promises, particularly when it comes to housing and staring down a challenging city budget forecast.
While campaigning, Mamdani said he’d implement an expanded version of a costly city-funded housing voucher program called CityFHEPS, based on laws the City Council had passed. But faced with a multibillion-dollar budget gap once in office, he didn’t follow through, and instead agreed to a more limited program that would operate in addition to CityFHEPS. His administration is currently rolling out that program, which will benefit about 5,600 New Yorkers living in shelters or facing eviction from rent-stabilized apartments.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/health-insur.title: End the Private Health Insurance Tax: Pass Medicare for All
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/health-insur.author: Tim Higginbotham
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/health-insur.text:
End the Private Health Insurance Tax: Pass Medicare for All
Make no mistake: the thousands of dollars that come out of your paycheck each year to pay for health insurance is a tax, just one paid to a private insurer rather than the federal government. Medicare for All would actually lower your taxes.
Every other Monday, I arrive at work bleary-eyed, still finishing my coffee, and settle into the workweek by reviewing my latest pay stub. I’m looking for miscounted hours, abnormal deductions — the sorts of mistakes that never happen but could.
This morning was different. I spent the weekend fixating on the sorry state of health insurance in this country, roused in large part by Democrats’ comprehensive midterm victory, including wins by supporters of Medicare for All like Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed. I arrived at my desk alert and reviewed my pay stub, focusing specifically on health care contributions.
When we look at our pay stubs, employer and employee health insurance contributions combine into a number we numbly accept as we focus on our take-home pay. In my case, the biweekly total is $1,267. That adds up to about $33,000 over the year, higher than the average employer-sponsored family plan cost of $28,303. Single-coverage plans average about $9,000, while workers buying on the marketplace pay upward of $7,500 annually ($12,000 in my home state of Alaska).
These figures represent real, consequential lost wages. And they get higher every year.
Health Insurance Premiums Are a Tax
I have a stable union job with my local municipal government. My health insurance leaves a lot to be desired, often burdening my family with out-of-pocket costs (a reality brought home just last week during an emergency room visit for our daughter, who thankfully is fine). Still, it is better than what most American workers have. I am meant to feel lucky for it.
Look at the alternatives: I could have a lesser plan with higher deductibles and out-of-pocket limits. I could have no insurance at all, like roughly 10 percent of Americans. Or scarier still, I could be forced to pay taxes into a single-payer system that removes health care from the workplace and covers everyone equally.
But staring at a pay stub leaves us to wonder: What are health insurance premiums if not a tax? They’re compulsory; we can’t opt out. And even if we could, we would never expose ourselves to such catastrophic risk. The deduction is listed separately from federal taxes on the pay stub, but what makes it different?
The answer is who gets the money. Our health care premiums are nothing other than a compulsory tax paid to private insurance companies instead of the federal government. When included with our other taxes, they make the United States one of the highest-taxed countries in the world — higher even than the Nordic states.
The United States spends roughly 18 percent of its GDP on health care, double that of peer nations with universal health care systems. The oft-stated benefit of our system is that it saves us from taxes, but in fact it taxes us at a premium and sends the excess to insurers as profit. Worse, it burdens us with impossible out-of-pocket costs at our times of greatest need.
Our paychecks suffer from this waste. Rising premiums help keep our wages stuck as employers weigh insurance and wages against the same bottom line. Every dollar diverted to surging premiums is a dollar stolen from our wages and benefits. All the while, workers shoulder ever-increasing deductibles and contribution shares.
Your Paycheck Under Medicare for All
You have heard, of course, that single-payer health insurance — Medicare for All — will cost trillions of dollars. It will raise your taxes. It will take away your hard-won and much-beloved employer-sponsored insurance.
It’s tempting to argue the obvious: yes, Medicare for All will raise your taxes, but the increase in your taxes will be significantly lower than your current premiums and out-of-pocket costs, which will disappear.
Looking at my pay stub, however, I don’t even want to concede that it will raise taxes. Again, payroll insurance contributions are a compulsory, unavoidable tax on your wages. Under Bernie Sanders’s Medicare for All proposal, my employer (a budget-strapped municipal government) would pay $260 per paycheck through a 7.5 percent payroll tax, and I would pay $94 via a 4 percent income tax after standard deductions. The combined total of $354 represents $913 in savings — $23,738 over a year.
Medicare for All will reconfigure your taxes, sure. But it won’t raise them. It will lower them.
The $24,000 newly freed from my paycheck would land on the bargaining table in negotiations over my union’s next contract. Some of this will go directly to wage increases. Some will go to benefits. Some will stay with the municipal government. For all future negotiations, though, we will not have to tackle the albatross of rising insurance premiums.
What Is Health Insurance For?
Health care is expensive, costing trillions per year no matter who pays. Currently, it’s paid for in a convoluted, wasteful scheme: private insurers act as payers using funds taken from our wages, while the government covers its share in Medicare and Medicaid. The rest is paid out-of-pocket by patients in times of need.
The effect is to chain us to our jobs, suppress our wages, and burden our negotiations.
We all know this is not what health insurance is for. Health insurance is meant to minimize risk, minimize costs, and mitigate catastrophes. This can only be accomplished with a single, government payer. A true tax should fund a public good to benefit society, not drain your wages to benefit profiteers.
With an overwhelming mandate and the policy still popular, Democrats ought to run a Medicare for All supporter in 2028 and make it their first priority in the new Congress. The policy will save up to a trillion dollars annually in overall spending. You can look at your pay stub to see where those savings will land.
