The Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto, has announced September 25, 2027, as the date it will open its forthcoming Dani Reiss Contemporary and Modern Gallery to the public. Begun in 2022, the project is being collaboratively overseen by Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, and Two Row Architect. Indigenous leaders and communities were also involved in the development of the wing. It is named for Dani Reiss, the CEO and chair of Canada Goose, who supplied $35 million in funding, with private donors and the governments of Ontario and Canada supplying the rest.
The new wing marks the gallery’s seventh expansion since opening in 1900. It will comprise 40,000 square feet distributed across five floors overlooking Grange Park and connecting to the museum’s Frank Gehry–renovated main building. Featuring 5,000-square-foot galleries with 23-foot-high ceilings, it will increase the institution’s gallery space by 30 percent. When completed, it will display nearly four hundred works from AGO’s collection of contemporary and modern art, with a focus on works by Canadian and Indigenous artists, as well as their international counterparts.
Of note, the building is designed to operate without burning fossil fuel and has received CAGBC Zero Carbon Building Design certification.
“The Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery is more than an expansion project—it is Toronto and Canada announcing its global position,” said AGO director and CEO Stephan Jost in a statement. “When this gallery opens in September 2027, the world will be made aware of the strength of the AGO collection and the degree to which it has evolved to be truly global.”
Jost will not be around to christen the new wing: He announced his departure from the institution earlier this year.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Stephen Miller Is the Real President Now
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Stephen Miller Is the Real President Now
Trump just promoted his worst, most dangerous adviser. Get ready for a constitutional crisis.
If Donald Trump were a normal president, the devastating defeat he and his party suffered in the midterms last week would cause him to moderate his policies. After all, the sheer scale of Republican losses dwarfs any rout suffered by a governing party in the midterms since at least 1974. As of this writing, Democrats have won the national vote in the House of Representatives races by nearly 13 percent—and that number could climb higher as more votes from slow-counting, Democrat-dominated California come in.
By contrast, Republicans won the national vote by 6.8 percent in the 1994 and 2010 midterms— both considered epochal wave elections—and Democrats beat the GOP by 8 percent in their 2006 “thumping” of George W. Bush.
And Democrats didn’t just win big—they won everywhere, making inroads into deep-red states that had been beyond their reach for decades, like South Carolina, Kansas, Mississippi (assuming, as seems likely, that Scott Colom wins his Senate race there), and, of course, Texas.
Previous presidents made dramatic changes after their midterm setbacks. After 1994, Bill Clinton famously adopted the policy of triangulation, co-opting GOP policies such as welfare reform and declaring that “the era of big government is over.” In the immediate wake of the 2006 loss, George W. Bush fired Donald Rumsfeld, one of the major architects of the disastrous war in Iraq.
Trump’s thrashing far exceeds either Bush’s or Clinton’s, but you wouldn’t know it from the way he’s reacted. True, he’s made some vague, seemingly chastened comments about working with Democrats and pulling back on some of his most toxic policies. In an interview with Ross Douthat on Sunday’s 60 Minutes, Trump said that his persecution of immigrants might have been too “tough,” and expressed a desire to strike a grand “deal” with the Democrats to allow migrants who have committed no crime to stay in the United States—in effect, an amnesty program of the type signed by Ronald Reagan, which subsequent presidents such as George W. Bush and Barack Obama also worked toward.
But Trump’s actions, not surprisingly, point in a totally different direction. He remains the same intransigent and extremist autocrat, one who is keen to double down on deeply unpopular and destructive policies. And nothing symbolizes that like the first big decision he made post-midterms—firing his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and replacing her with Stephen Miller, the architect of his anti-immigrant terror campaign and perhaps the most zealous white nationalist in his entire administration.
Trump’s decision to make Miller chief of staff makes clear that the president’s gestures toward a grand bargain on immigration are blather. If your goal is compromise, you don’t strengthen the power of a dangerous extremist like Miller.
Miller is far and away the most strident xenophobe in Trump’s inner circle. He was the architect of the family separation policy in Trump’s first term, and, as The New York Times notes, has been at the core of some of the most authoritarian, lawless policies of Trump’s second term:
In addition to helping oversee the militarized crackdown of the U.S.-Mexico border, [Miller] set in motion the suspension of U.S. refugee programs and the deadly deportation crackdowns on American streets.
But his influence during Mr. Trump’s second term has extended beyond immigration policy. He also pushed Mr. Trump’s lethal strikes on civilian boats in the Caribbean that the administration claimed were carrying drugs. He helped use the powers of the federal government to target political opponents and universities, and oversaw the federal crackdown in the District of Columbia.
To say that this clashes with the way Trump spoke on 60 Minutes is an understatement. He told Douthat that he had been politically “hurt” for implementing a harsh deportation policy that harmed migrants who had contributed to the well-being of the country: “For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that— that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.
“Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there’s a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company, or workin’ in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes.”
Trump acknowledged that immigration was a tough issue since there were people on the “pretty far right that would like everybody taken out.” Quite reasonably, Douthat asked, “Do any of those people work in your administration? Are they in the building with us right now?” Trump said yes. He’s right about that, obviously—but rather than dispense with those people, he just gave one of them the most important job in his administration.
All of this points to a president determined to learn nothing from his mistakes. On X, former representative Marjorie Taylor Greene noted that Miller “was kind of already running the White House in so many ways, so you can expect more of the same from the White House that you were probably already pissed off and frustrated about.” Greene added that the fact that Wiles was being shifted to Trump’s political team was a sign that Trump wants to play a major role in selecting his successor. This also suggests that Trump’s defeat in the midterms has not subdued his desire to dominate the political landscape.
Sarah Matthews, who worked with Miller in the White House during Trump’s first term, told The Bulwark that she expects the new chief of staff will be the “de facto president” while Trump focuses on his late-life passion for redecorating national monuments. If Matthews is right, we could be heading for an even more dangerous situation, with Trump remaining as a babbling figurehead while an empowered Miller pursues an extremist agenda even in the face of a hostile Congress. Given this reality, the United States is heading toward a constitutional crisis much larger than the impeachment battles of Trump’s first term.

https://hyperallergic.com/is-sexy-art-ba.title: Is Sexy Art Back, or Is It Just Me?
https://hyperallergic.com/is-sexy-art-ba.author: Lori Waxman
https://hyperallergic.com/is-sexy-art-ba.text:
Is Sexy Art Back, or Is It Just Me?
From Willem de Kooning’s miserable nudes to Alexandra Barth’s hot and bothered architecture, sex is in the air in Chicago.
CHICAGO — I see a lot of exhibitions in Chicago, and lately, I have been noticing more than a few that feel almost ridiculously erotic. I mean, I get it, there's always been plenty of eros in art, but I haven't observed it much lately at the school where I teach nor in the shows that I view. Is sex back? Or it could just be me. I turned 50 this past year, and popular culture suggests that this might be what happens around my age, à la Sharon Horgan's Youth and Olivia Colman's Wicker, both recent screen-based explorations of lusty midlife ladyhood.
For those who have never had one or maybe never will, female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100. It is not an easy ride. Shifting from one state to the other causes severe whiplash for driver and passengers alike. That’s based on an admittedly minuscule survey, though fear not, this will not be a personal essay about my own sexuality or that of my acquaintances. God, no. Maybe after everyone’s dead. What proceeds, instead, is a round-up of exhibitions that, for me, have a strong connecting thread, obviously red, and not discussed much if at all in the various associated didactics.
What shows? Last spring, Alice Tippit’s sly, meticulous paintings at the DePaul Art Museum had me thinking I probably needed to start talking to a therapist again, because what was going on in my head was not articulated anywhere in the otherwise delightful catalogue. Not even close. During the summer, SHADOW at tête-à-tête-à-tête, a wicked little curatorial project of Shannon Stratton, included Holly Murkerson’s sensuous photographs of a stone passageway worth entering and two dark leather-and-wood stools by David Sprecher and Neiva Mulhearn that required straddling and peering into.
What wasn’t a turn-on was the Art Institute of Chicago’s summer blockbuster, Willem de Kooning Drawing. You wouldn’t know from the glowing reviews or polite museum text that miserable naked women filled the walls. I like a good nude as much as anyone, but at some point, maybe it was the third room — definitely by the time I got to the giant rowboat charcoals of the mid-60s — de Kooning’s subjects started to look like crime victims.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-students-w.title: NY students will still have to take Regents exams, even as graduation rules change
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-students-w.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-students-w.text:
Students across the state will no longer need to pass Regents exams to graduate, but most students will still need to take them.
State education officials on Monday said high school students will still need to take assessments in four subjects to meet federal testing requirements.
The New York Board of Regents nixed passing the exams — which assess students' knowledge of English, math, social studies and science — as a graduation requirement earlier this year, creating uncertainty about how the changes would play out.
Passing the exams will no longer be required to graduate starting in the 2027-2028 school year. State officials have said the tests can be obstacles to graduation for students with disabilities, different learning styles or limited English proficiency.
But during a Board of Regents meeting on Monday, education officials said students would still need to take Regents exams or approved alternatives in each of the four subjects to satisfy statewide testing requirements under federal law.
The state will continue administering the Regents exams as it works on a new assessment system it aims to introduce in spring 2030.
Education advocates have raised concerns about the changes. In a June 2024 statement, EdTrust-New York warned that eliminating Regents exams as a graduation requirement could lead to inconsistent academic standards across school districts and make it harder to determine whether students are prepared for college and careers.
The group also raised concerns that the changes could worsen educational inequities, particularly for students of color and those from low-income backgrounds.
The New York State Education Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Swedish museums restitute objects to Nigeria and Bolivia
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Senay Boztas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Swedish museums last week began returning dozens of statues stolen by British troops from the Kingdom of Benin as well as sacred objects looted by grave robbers in the 1970s in Bolivia.
Three years after the Swedish government—at the time backed by the far-right Sweden Democrats—agreed to two restitution requests, the National Museums of World Culture (SMVK) began the final phases of enacting them.
At a ceremony in Lagos, 39 Benin objects were formally restituted to Nigeria, while according to Swedish media, 77 objects from the Niño Korin village—including the skull of a Kallawaya healer— were taken from storage in Gothenburg to be transported to the National Museum of Archaeology in La Paz.
The Bolivian objects, dating to around 600 to 1000 AD, the Tiwanku period, were looted by locals in grave robberies in the 1970s and were later sold to the museum, according to the SMVK website.
The African objects are some of thousands that were violently looted by British troops in 1897 from the Edo people in the old Kingdom of Benin, located in what is now Nigeria. They were later acquired by the former Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm. Six will remain in Sweden as part of a ten-year loan.
The restitution process began, according to the SMVK, after “clear signals from the Nigerian authority, the National Commission for Museums and Monuments, that they would welcome the return of all objects.”
Michael Barrett, the curator for Africa at SMVK, was in Lagos for the ceremonial signing-over of the 39 cultural objects, known as Emwin Arre. “I hope [this] is part of a broader shift in how our museums relate to the world around us,” he tells The Art Newspaper on his return.
“For too long colonial legacies of violence, theft, and exploitation have stood in the way of museum practices that are more responsive to a wider set of stakeholders, not least communities who have cultural and historical ties to our collections. Returning violently looted belongings to their communities of origin is a necessary first step.”
The process, he adds, is also part of earning the trust of modern audiences. “A focus on these relationships must be a central part of our practice going forward,” he adds. “At least if museums with ‘world collections’ are ever to live up to their potential [as] places where visitors may learn about humanity’s cultural achievements and many ways of being- in-the-world, in an environment defined by respect, empathy and curiosity.”
The Swedish restitutions follow a trend among European countries to return art and objects looted or obtained unethically from around the world. In 2022, Germany handed over a substantial collection of Benin bronzes to Nigeria. The Netherlands returned 119 similar objects in 2025 and the Dutch Museum de Fundatie returned an additional Benin bronze plaque last month.
While Cambridge University returned legal ownership of its collection of 116 objects to Nigeria in February, the British Museum last year ruled out the imminent restitution of stolen treasures, suggesting “collaboration” instead.
Staffan Lundén, researcher at the University of Gothenburg’s School of Global Studies, has studied the topic of “dealing with difficult pasts” and the British Museum’s collection of objects looted in Benin City. He says, by contrast, these restitutions were largely depoliticised in Sweden. “The decision was taken by the right-wing government,” he points out. “It is seen as common sense, moral justice and in line with the Swedish self-perception of being a progressive country which takes international responsibility.”

https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.title: NYC to Expand Homeless Outreach This Winter Following Last Year’s Deadly Cold
https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.text:
Share This Article
The city is earmarking an extra $25 million to hire 300 additional outreach workers and open more low-barrier shelter beds, officials announced Friday. It comes after a brutal freeze killed 18 New Yorkers last winter.
The city will spend an extra $25 million to expand its homeless outreach efforts when temperatures drop this winter—hoping to avoid a repeat of last year, when a brutal stretch of historically cold weather killed 18 New Yorkers, many of them unhoused.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the additional funding at a press conference on Monday, part of a sweeping package of winter preparedness reforms that will also include “supercharged” plows and new snow blowers.
The $25 million will go to beefing up the Department of Homeless Services’ “Code Blue” operations, which kick in when temperatures dip below 32 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.
It’ll pay for 300 additional outreach workers, including nurses, to canvas city streets and implore people to come indoors. It will also open more public warming facilities, including heated buses and vans, and to creating another 800 “low barrier” shelter beds—sites with fewer entry requirements and less stringent rules than typical city shelters.
Those beds will be in single- and double-occupancy rooms, officials said, offering greater privacy than crowded—and sometimes, dangerous—group facilities that many street homeless New Yorkers are reluctant to enter.
“When we speak to homeless New Yorkers, we will hear that if only there was a low barrier single room bed, they would then be willing to go,” the mayor said.
Mamdani was newly inaugurated when last winter’s emergency cold conditions hit—what officials say included the city’s first blizzard in a decade as well nine consecutive days of below-freezing temperatures.
The cold killed at least 18 people, including several unhoused residents.
“I wasn’t here in the heart of last winter, but I’ve reviewed it, and I know how it went, and I learned a lot from it,” said Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton, who oversees the Department of Homeless Services (DHS). Mamdani appointed her to lead the agency in February.
Dalton said DHS will be making key changes to its cold weather response this year, including having its street outreach teams adopt a “broad geographic canvassing approach.”
This breaks from previous winters in which homeless outreach teams focused their efforts on a list of about 350 known street homeless New Yorkers, visiting their usual spots and urging them to take shelter. On most nights, the city was only able to locate about 15 percent of the people on that list, Dalton said.
She added that workers are already engaging with those folks before very cold weather sets in, but that “an approach built around a vulnerable list leaves way too many people in the street that aren’t known to us, and only covers a small portion of people.”
Instead, Dalton says, outreach teams will “walk the streets, encampments, parks, and subway steps where we know the vast majority of people experiencing homelessness stay,” and “engage every vulnerable person along the routes.”
The commissioner said DHS tested this broader canvassing approach over the summer during heat waves, and were able to reach far more people—”more than 20 times as many as on a given day” compared to the summer before.
While homeless advocates applauded the additional resources, they said many of the changes are long overdue.
“These are smart responses that will save lives. But these are also well-known action steps that have been called for for years,” VOCAL-NY, a grassroots group that organizes low-income and systems impacted New Yorkers, said in a statement Monday.
VOCAL leaders called on the city to invest more in permanent solutions to getting New Yorkers off the streets, like with additional city-funded rental vouchers and supportive affordable housing.
“That’s kind of the the ideal. It’s moving people into permanent housing,” Charles King, the CEO of the homeless nonprofit Housing Works, told City Limits last week, when the organization held a funeral mass for nine of the unhoused New Yorkers who died of hypothermia in last winter’s extreme cold.
“At the end of the day, giving a person a decent place to live is what all of us need.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/doc-nyc-returns-.title: The Films We Can’t Wait to See at DOC NYC
https://hellgatenyc.com/doc-nyc-returns-.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/doc-nyc-returns-.text:
Is the success of "You Can See Everything" a harbinger of a new Golden Age of Documentary Filmmaking? Probably not! But this week, New Yorkers have the chance to see tons of very good documentaries at the DOC NYC festival before they fall into the abyss of never securing a distribution or streaming deal. 
We cannot tell you how many wonderful independent films we've seen at DOC NYC that have never resurfaced online or on the independent film circuit, betrayed by either lack of archival or music rights, or just the general shittiness of the film industry. So try to see as many as you can! Support independent journalism! (And if you're reading this before noon, definitely take advantage of DOC NYC's $5 film deal!) 
DOC NYC starts Wednesday and runs through the end of the month. The country's "largest documentary film festival" will spread out across three of our favorite venues in Lower Manhattan (SVA Theatre, IFC Center, and the Village East) with an online streaming option for many films. We're especially enamored with the new "Archival Storytelling Competition," because we cannot get enough of old, lush film reporting. 
Here are some of the films that we're not going to miss this year. 
"Kenny: The Marxist Who Would Be Mayor"
For some reason, radical mayors are on our mind, and on the mind of much of the country these days, so this documentary, pulling from archival footage about Detroit lawyer and politician Ken Cockrel Sr. stands out. None of the issues Cockrel railed against have been resolved (even by his son, who did eventually become Detroit mayor), but this makes us pine for local politicians who could speak clearly and plainly about policing in their cities. 
"The Newsreel: Characterization of Subversive Organization"
Every successful social movement needs some well-made propaganda, and this documentary follows the Newsreel, a filmmaking collective that spread out across cities and campuses across the United States in the 1960s, capturing activism and protest with an experimental approach that shaped modern documentary filmmaking.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ufcw-local-c.title: California UFCW Leaders Really Don’t Want Union Elections
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ufcw-local-c.author: Lisa Xu
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ufcw-local-c.text:
California UFCW Leaders Really Don’t Want Union Elections
United Food and Commercial Workers Local 8–Golden State has been headed by one family since 1984. Reform candidates say union staff are using intimidation tactics to prevent a competitive election this year.
In a union that has been headed by one family with no competitive elections since 1984, a group of grocery workers is organizing for change. But last week, they say, union staff who back the incumbent administration went to outrageous lengths in an attempt to make sure there’s no election this year either.
On the afternoon of Monday, November 2, Eric Marcuz, a veteran Northern California Safeway worker, stopped at the union office to pick up blank petitions to get on the ballot in the union’s upcoming election. Marcuz is running for president on the At What Cost slate in the 23,000-member United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8–Golden State (8-GS), one of the largest locals in the union.
To get on the ballot, Marcuz and his slate-mates have to collect 443 petition signatures — 2 percent of the local’s active members — by mid-November. If they don’t get enough signatures, no election will be held.
After Marcuz picked up the petitions from the local’s Roseville office, he got in his car to drive three hours south to Fresno, to start collecting signatures with another candidate on his slate at a Save Mart store there. (The local spans a ten-hour stretch from Bakersfield up to the Oregon border.)
When Marcuz stopped for gas, he said he noticed that a black Dodge Ram pickup stopped as well. When he got back on the freeway, so did the truck.
At the next gas stop, Marcuz spoke to the man driving the truck. It was Jeff Berns, a staff representative for Local 8-GS. His brother, Mark, is also on staff at the union — and the local’s election chair, responsible for overseeing the election.
Marcuz asked Jeff Berns why he was following him. According to Marcuz, Berns said he wanted to make sure that all the members got the “accurate information” that Marcuz’s slate was going to “divide” the union. He said he was going to follow him the entire time Marcuz was out, all the way back to Marcuz’s house in Redding, several hours north. Marcuz jokingly asked him if he needed a place to stay. Berns said he didn’t — because he’d been staying a lot in the Redding area lately himself, which Marcuz said he thought was “creepy” because that’s where Marcuz lives with his family (and is not where Berns lives).
Berns would live up to his promise — following Marcuz for the next three hundred miles, through every stop, exit, and U-turn. He even followed him inside the Fresno Save Mart and camped out for an hour with another union rep while Marcuz ate dinner at a supporter’s house one hundred miles north in Modesto.
No Competitive Elections
At the gas station, Berns repeated the mantra, “Solidarity works!” That’s the motto of the incumbent president, Jacques Loveall, who is heading the Solidarity Works Team slate in this election.
Loveall was appointed to lead the union in 2004, when his father, Jack Loveall, stepped down. The elder Loveall had held the top office since 1984; when he retired he was one of the highest-paid union officers in the country, earning the equivalent of $1 million today. (The Contra Costa Times reported that he had a $28,000-a-year country club membership and “two pilots on staff to chauffeur him in a private jet.”) Neither father nor son has ever faced a competitive election in the local.
Back on the freeway, Marcuz called a Department of Labor agent whom he had already been in touch with. They had previously spoken about the local’s apparent attempt to cancel the election by merging with a mysterious organization called the Staffing Agencies Federated Employees, an entity that listed one of Loveall’s relatives as its president on its initial filing. The agent told him to report the intimidation to the election chair and tell him to get the rep to back off.
Marcuz then called Mark Berns, the election chair, who he said told him he would talk to staff about acting in a professional manner.
More Reps
However, when Marcuz arrived at the Save Mart store in Fresno to begin collecting petition signatures, he and another slatemate, Mike Romero, said that three union reps were waiting for them, including Jeff Berns. One of the others was John Micheletti, a longtime Local 8 vice president. Far from being called off, they said, the intimidation had actually intensified.
Marcuz and Romero said the reps interfered with every conversation they attempted to have with workers about signing their nomination petition. The very first worker they engaged about signing, a longtime acquaintance of Romero’s, fled once a rep entered the conversation and became confrontational. The worker did not sign the petition.
“They were everywhere inside the store,” said Marcuz. At least one of the interactions was filmed on a phone.
Marcuz said that Berns told him, “I’m going to make sure everyone knows who you are and not to sign that.” And additionally, “We’re going to invalidate every single signature that you get.”
It is illegal for union staff and officers to campaign on union time. Berns said he was on vacation.
Romero, who has worked at Save Mart for thirty years, said, “This is the most I’ve seen of union staff in six months.” He said a fourth rep turned up after Marcuz left.
Seen This Before
These tactics — following opposition candidates and invalidating signatures — have both been alleged by previous members of the local who attempted to challenge the Lovealls.
A Contra Costa Times article published in 2004 reported that supporters of Loveall’s father got members to rescind their signatures to keep dissident candidate Jack Nordby off the ballot in 1997. A book written by then Local 588 reform activist Doug Slaydon states that as many as 150 signatures were removed. (Local 588 merged with another local to form Local 8-GS in 2006 — postponing a potential competitive election that year.)
Nordby also alleged that he was tailed by a pickup truck while collecting ballot signatures, followed around by union reps in stores, and once chased in his car while driving his wife and two daughters to church.
The Contra Costa Times also reported allegations that Local 588 staffers staked out the home of a member of UFCW Local 1179 who had led a successful rank-and-file opposition campaign to an attempted merger of the two locals and “tailed him in union cars.” “In June 1994,” reported the Times, the member, Michael Ross-Smith, “was rear-ended in Walnut Creek by three UFCW 588 business agents following him too closely in a white 1993 Ford Thunderbird leased to the union, according to a traffic collision report from the Walnut Creek police department.”
Tailed for Seven Hours
Marcuz and Romero said they quickly realized that they wouldn’t be able to collect petition signatures with this level of interference. Marcuz’s next stop was going to be to drop off petition forms with a supporter at the Turlock Safeway, over an hour to the north, but he made plans to meet the supporter at their house in Modesto instead.
When Marcuz left the parking lot of the Fresno store, Romero said three vehicles followed him. Romero also realized that one of the reps had stayed behind, and he became worried that he would be followed as well. He drove around for a long time before going home, to make sure he wasn’t followed.
Marcuz, meanwhile, said that Berns and Micheletti followed him for ninety miles, all the way to Modesto. They stayed parked outside the house while Marcuz ate burritos with the supporter — finally leaving after an hour, after 8 p.m.
“It’s crazy that they would literally go two hours out of their way to make sure nobody else can talk to the employees,” Romero said.
Marcuz said he almost canceled his plans to stay alone in a hotel in Roseville overnight, worried he would be tailed there, and contemplated driving for four more hours home to Redding. In total, he estimates he was followed for seven hours, over a distance of three hundred miles.
Scare Tactics
Section 610 of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA) forbids the threat or use of force or violence to restrain, coerce, or intimidate union members from exercising their right to nominate candidates or to vote in union officer elections, while Section 401(e) bars “improper interference” in the rights of union members to run for and support candidates for local union office.
“It makes me think of everyone that has known there’s been a need for change in the past and has been scared away from pursuing it,” Marcuz said. While Marcuz and his slate are standing strong, he said, “this might work. They might intimidate and scare enough people out of participating.”
In the morning, Marcuz filed a police report with the Roseville Police Department alleging stalking and harassment, citing the time and distance he was followed and the behavior he encountered in the Fresno store.
Local 8 did not respond to requests for comment.
Petition signatures are due November 17, and ballots will be mailed November 21.

Sheldon and Marianne Lubar have committed $10 million to the Milwaukee Art Museum to establish the Lubar Family Center for Drawings and Prints. The gift provides long-term support for researching and maintaining works on paper, which comprise more than half of the museum’s collection of some 35,000 objects.
Both Sheldon and Marianne Lubar serve as “Life Trustees” of the museum, and have been involved with the administration of the institution for more than fifty years. Previously, Sheldon has served as president of the museum’s board, and spearheaded the fundraising campaign that helped complete funding for the Santiago Calatrava-designed Quadracci Pavilion, which opened in 2001. Their daughter Joan is also a trustee.
“Great cities need great institutions,” Sheldon Lubar said in a statement. “We’re proud to support the Milwaukee Art Museum as Milwaukee’s great institution!”
The gift also endows several positions at the museum—the Lubar Family Curator of Drawings and Prints, the Lubar Family Paper Conservator, and the Lubar Family Fellow in Drawings and Prints—as well as the Lubar Family Drawings and Prints Exhibition Program.
“Behind every exhibition are people who study the art, care for it, and help us see it in new ways,” said Susan Lubar. “It’s exciting to support that work and to know this collection will continue to be a source of discovery for Milwaukee.”
Chicago Gallery News reports that Nikki Otten will lead the center as the Lubar Family Curator. She joined the museum in 2018 and is an expert in drawings and prints.
“Because works on paper are sensitive to light, they can only be on view for limited periods before returning to storage to rest,” Otten said. “Each exhibition offers an opportunity to share different selections and explore new connections across the collection. This gift supports the research and specialized care that make those experiences possible.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries Are Not Meeting the Moment
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elizabeth Spiers
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries Are Not Meeting the Moment
The Democrats’ congressional leaders have been handed an enormous mandate they have no interest in carrying out.
The big driver of turnout in the 2026 midterms was anger. For Republicans who voted for Democrats or decided to stay home, it was anger about affordability. Everything is too expensive and getting more so the longer the United States continues its needless war in Iran, maintains economically damaging tariff schemes, and fails to address rising healthcare costs.
Democrats shared in the broad outrage over affordability, but that was only part of the story. They were also angry that the Trump regime has worked to destroy the lives of immigrants, women who need reproductive health care, and LGBTQ people seeking basic protections of their civil rights, while financing a genocide in Gaza. Democrats were angry that the Trump administration has been wildly corrupt, staffed by incompetent, soulless Trump toadies like Pete Hegseth, Kash Patel, and Linda McMahon who have irrevocably harmed their agencies. Beyond the Beltway, meanwhile, Republicans have kowtowed to the interests of tech oligarchs who are determined to pursue a maximalist and accelerationist approach to AI that may end up killing us all, while allowing white Christian nationalists to dictate priorities for public education and science funding in a way that is wildly destructive to both. They were angry that Republicans have pursued and hoarded power via lies, broken laws and norms, and completely—indeed, gleefully—neglected their responsibility to serve all of America’s citizens, and not just the ones who are white, male, Christian, straight, and Republican.
Thanks to all of this anger at the governing status quo, Democrats routed Republicans on Tuesday on a scale that even the most optimistic of us didn’t anticipate. Anger is a powerful motivator, especially when the reasons to be angry continue to multiply. Yet when they were charged with grasping and communicating the stunning new mandate they were entrusted with, Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries—respectively the front-runners to serve as Senate majority leader and House speaker in the next Congress—behaved as if affordability were the only thing voters cared about, and the only thing that mattered. For Republicans who voted for Democrats, that might be true. But for the rest of us, the Democrats who have always voted for Democrats—or, to put it another way, actual Democrats—this seems like a willful refusal to hear what voters are telling them.
It also follows a dismaying penchant on the part of both Democratic leaders to act as though cultural and political disagreements inhabit different spheres. Their fetishistic belief in “kitchen-table issues” as the mystic, all-explanatory force in American politics hinges on the luxurious assumption that culture warfare can be dismissed as a distraction—a supposition that rests in turn on a mythical privileging of ideological consensus over pluralism and tolerance, and a set of policy agendas composed solely of safe things and sure things.
That, as Tuesday’s results demonstrated, is not the world we live in; it’s a fantasy world in which Schumer and Jeffries do not have to take risks, can always avoid confrontation, will continue appeasing the whims of tech oligarchs and their corporate donors in the healthcare industry, and won’t have to send back their AIPAC donations. In this well-appointed moneyed reverie, Democratic leaders won’t be forced to to take a stand on civil rights issues that by definition won’t lend themselves to consensus as a starting point. Most especially, they will be insulated from demands to cede or share power with the progressive wing of the party, which is in their view is a fringe movement led by naïve young people—even though a majority of Democrats have indicated over and over and over again in polls that they support Medicare for All, want a reset of our relationship with Israel, and believe that their wealthy friends should pay more taxes. In other words, Schumer and Jeffries cannot behave as if their personal politics are synonymous with what voters want, nor can they assume that what voters want is the same thing voters wanted 10, 20, or 30 years ago.
They also cannot lump everything that they consider economically important under the amorphous heading of “kitchen-table issues” and pretend that everything else is culture-war nonsense. Any politician who doesn’t understand that what constitutes a kitchen-table issue depends on whose kitchen table you’re sitting at is mentally stuck in an era when the only people at the kitchen table who counted were white middle-class homeowners. You cannot build a party around that constituency; the people whose interests the party should serve are too diverse and their needs too multivalent to be addressed solely by targeted tax credits or incremental clawbacks of Obamacare premiums.
Most of all, though, Schumer and Jeffrey cannot ignore, as has been their frequent wont, that voters believe, overwhelmingly, that the serial abuses and predations of the Trump administration must be met with accountability—meaning real consequences for the legions of bad actors in its orbit, and not just strongly worded letters. Schumer and Jeffries may want to just move on, but voters do not.
Both men had plenty of opportunities to use the outcome of the midterms to signal an aggressive program for righting the Trump administration’s wrongs. Instead, they chose to ignore virtually everything voters told them that presented itself as too much of a chore, or too great a departure from the status quo—from pursuit of progressive social agenda items to legal consequences for corrupt lawbreaking Republicans to a more aggressive posture toward the opposition party both in tactics and style. Their joint refrain was that what voters wanted was, conveniently, what they wanted: to move forward without any uncomfortable litigation of all of the horrors of the past couple of years.
“The American people don’t want us to get even. They want us to get things done on their behalf,” Jeffries told MS NOW, shortly after the returns were announced. “We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it’s our job to govern on affordability.” This understandably enraged a lot of voters—even centrists who otherwise are aligned with Jeffries politically—because it insultingly implied that the electorate’s desire for accountability is about petty revenge.
Jeffries’s claim, like so many Democratic extenuations of Trump-era abuses, confuses a politics of manners for a politics of morality. I always thought that Michelle Obama’s 2016 dictum, “When they go low, we go high,” counseled Democrats to uphold principled values in the face of corrupting forces. But in the hands of figures like Jeffries and Schumer, it’s become a mantra conveying disdain for the messy and often antagonistic nature of politics—especially when attaining and keeping power involves conflict, or God forbid, being rude. It childishly assumes that a healthy civil society is defined primarily by a rigorous sense of decorum. We don’t want to get even, it says; that sort of thing is beneath us.
This is stupendously wrongheaded; or to put it more bluntly, fuck you, and the decorum you rode in on. First and foremost, a desire for justice is not about getting even. Neither Jeffries nor Schumer would argue that if someone steals your car, you should just move on and hope everyone behaves better in the future. Nor should you naïvely assume that all car thieves, after some reflection, get in touch with their better angels for the good of society. Car thieves should be disciplined, and in some way held accountable for their actions.
But the corporate Democratic class that’s enlisted Schumer and Jeffries as its retainers takes a fundamentally different view of wrongdoing from on high, insisting that elites are different. Under this backward reasoning, violators of the law can and should be given a free pass if they’re rich enough, polished enough, and powerful enough. If Democrats of this persuasion are unwilling to go after Donald Trump, Elon Musk, or the other MAGA figures who’ve been responsible for the most egregious and immoral harms of the last few years, it tells elites that the law simply doesn’t matter—at least not for them. And it tells voters that their leaders will let elites continue to get away with murder—both literally and figuratively—and cannot be trusted to protect their interests against those of the right billionaire.
The Schumer and Jeffries brand of tolerance for elite impunity depicts the Democrats’ long-standing posture of learned helplessness as a kind of pragmatism rather than what it is: cowardice, or—what amounts to the same thing—an unwillingness to risk failure on any terms. This pantomime is so effective that just days after the Democrats’ stunning midterm victory, a certain kind of savvy centrist commentator can be found posting away on social media that there’s no use in focusing on ambitious legislation because the numbers might not quite be there, or Trump might veto it. Some people have been brainwashed into a fatalism that says nothing that can’t be done perfectly and safely is worth trying.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
This procedural purism seemingly mandates that Democrats avoid employing tactics that Republicans used successfully against them during this term and Trump’s last. When asked about a potential Supreme Court vacancy, Schumer has refused to say whether he’d hold the seat open until after the 2028 election. He told the AP that he’s “not going to allow any crappy nominees” or “right-wingers”—but given that any Trump nominee would be both, what’s the risk in committing? There isn’t any—Schumer and his allies just think it’s unseemly to hold up the process for partisan reasons. That, of course, never stopped Mitch McConnell from doing it, and it shouldn’t stop Democrats, either.
Democratic leaders also shouldn’t forgo legislation on the basis that Trump could veto it. One of the strangest ideas in politics is that if you try to legislate aggressively and fail, you cannot attack the same issue again later. Instead of understanding abortive legislating as a key element of coalition building, the faux-savvy orthodoxies of Schumer and Jeffries teach that failure is unacceptable and leaves a permanent residue. In 1992, Hillary Clinton tried to fix healthcare in her capacity as first lady, an incredible ambition for even a sitting president, and failed for all of the obvious reasons. That didn’t cause the electorate to decide healthcare was no longer broken and give up demanding any chance to the system—yet for the next two decades, the stigma of “we tried it before” stunted the necessary momentum to learn from past mistakes and build more permanent coalitions around universal healthcare, to the point that the final Democratic version of healthcare reform was the piecemeal, inadequate, market-driven model adapted from Republican proposals under the rubric of Obamacare.
In reality, voters want their leaders to get caught trying to improve the lives of ordinary people, and to fight important battles they know they might lose in the short run. Even as Trump responded to the debacle of the midterms by threatening widespread use of his veto power, he hasn’t actually wielded it as aggressively as he could have, out of his characteristic lack of interest in the work of legislating and policymaking. He might reverse course now, but it seems unlikely—he’s probably going to spend much of his remaining time in office shitposting and contemplating ballroom interior decoration. Yet there’s no political downside to forcing his hand—indeed, quite the opposite. If Democrats manage to pass legislation that voters actively want and the chief obstacle is Trump and his party, it’ll be easier to run against that party after he leaves office. Schumer and Jeffries have to demonstrate that they’re up for that kind of fight–or any kind of fight at all.
Many progressives (including me) were frustrated by their failures to use everything at their disposal against Trump and his apparatchiks when Democrats were in the minority. They also dismissed, and if the last few days are any indication, continue to dismiss, progressive anger as youthful naïveté—something that Democrats won in spite of and not because of. (This even though the best Democratic communicator about affordability in recent history—far better than Schumer or Jeffries—has been the young DSA mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani.) But those were bottom-up wins, not top-down wins. And both Schumer and Jeffries failed repeatedly to read the room when it came to picking candidates—Schumer repeatedly betting on the wrong horse in the primaries, and Jeffries refusing to endorse the overwhelmingly popular Democratic nominee in the New York City’s mayoral race. They are accustomed to an old system of power, whereby seniority matters more than what voters want and leadership can dictate priorities even if voters disagree with them.
If the leaders of the congressional Democratic Party cannot listen to voters, and refuse to deliver both accountability and legislation, voters will do what they did in many races that the candidates won despite a lack of support or outright hostility from leadership: They will work around them. Affordability is important, of course. But focusing only on the one thing Republicans want too—the lowest bar imaginable—is not enough.

The Zen Mona Lisa
A review of an ancient Chinese ink painting takes an art critic on a journey through his own past.
Editor’s Note: The following article is a chapter titled “Six Persimmons” that has been excerpted from From Darkness to Darkness by Will Heinrich, published by Thousand Horsemen Press in the summer of 2026 and available online and through independent booksellers. (Copyright © 2026 by Will Heinrich. Published by permission. All rights reserved.)
Every summer Jonah compiled a list of about a hundred upcoming museum shows for the newspaper’s special fall preview section. The first time he did it they were visiting Nadia’s college friend at her parents’ house in Pasadena, where he had to share a queen-size bed with Nadia and eight-month-old Orly. Fording hundreds of press releases, making decisions, and writing one-to-two-sentence synopses of complex shows he hadn’t seen while exhausted and sleepless was a trial. But the next year found him more confident, and ultimately the process became so automatic that it made no impression on him at all. If someone asked him in August, after he had filed his piece, what fall shows he was looking forward to, he would have to refer back to the document to come up with an answer.
One exhibit that did stick in his mind, though, the year Orly was six, was of a famous Chinese ink painting, a still life of persimmons, making a brief visit to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. It would be coming from the Japanese monastery which had acquired it when it was already nearly 300 years old and which had then kept it mostly rolled up and hidden away since the early 1500s. Jonah mentioned the show to his editor as one he’d like to cover, emphasising how unprecedented it was for the piece to travel and reminding her that he was her only freelancer with any affinity for, or knowledge of, Asian art.
She was amenable to his writing about it, she told him, but said that, because of the expense of covering the war in Ukraine, the art section had no travel budget left for the year.
“Do you really have to see it in person?” she asked.
Jonah hesitated.
“I mean,” he said, “for a review.”
Then cannily, or guilelessly, he added that he planned to go see it regardless. He figured that after more than a decade as an art critic, it was time to admit that art was important to him, and that so long as she did pay him to write something, he would at least break even on the experience. She offered to pay for a night in a hotel and he replied that he was planning to stay with his cousin.
“Well,” she said noncommittally, “see if you can find a cheap flight.”
Using credit card points, he found one for a couple of hundred dollars. He checked with his cousin and made plans to stay for two nights; it would be the longest he had been alone since Orly was born. Then he forgot about it, mostly. But he would mention his upcoming trip now and then to this or that person, amused to cut the figure of an adult whose job let him travel. Downtown to take notes about a conceptual art show, he met his father for coffee.
“Wow!” Alan exclaimed when Jonah told him about the ink painting. “I always wanted to see that but your mother and I were never in Kyoto on the right day.”
When the time came to go and Jonah found himself alone with a backpack on the E train, bound for Kennedy Airport, he was bemused again. As a younger man, he had travelled to escape his ordinary life, to fling himself without boundaries into unfamiliar locales. His last visit to San Francisco had been to visit a girl he’d briefly dated in New York, and he could still summon up the Pacific smell of the air when he first stepped out of the airport, the dark luxury of the apartment she was borrowing, the softness of her freckled, paper-white skin as they made love and fell asleep in a narrow guest-room bed. She had reminded him of a doe. Now, as he passed through the airport security line in New York, endured a two-hour delay caused by San Francisco air traffic related to the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference, read the London Review of Books, crammed himself into an economy seat, watched half a movie on his iPad, and took a cab, at his cousin’s suggestion, to Bernal Heights, it all felt more like an errand, albeit a pleasant one, than an adventure. The air smelled of nothing. His own company felt like a childhood friend he was glad to see again, but with whom, because it had been so long, he felt shy.
First thing the following morning, Jonah accompanied his cousin, an accomplished video game designer, as he walked his dog in a nearby park. They hadn’t met in years, and Jonah felt shy with him, too — as well as rebuked in his own aimless financial irresponsibility by the cousin’s comfortably furnished 3-bedroom house with basement rental apartment attached. Looking for something to talk about, he asked whether there had been many protests about Israel’s response to the attacks of October 7.
“Not really,” his cousin said. “I did drive past one group of people with signs that said ‘Stop the Genocide.’”
His tone made clear what he thought of the protestors’ use of the word “genocide.” Not seeing any benefit in starting an argument with his host at 7:30 in the morning, Jonah changed the subject. He went and climbed a nearby hill for its view of the city; returned to the house, where his cousin fed him breakfast; and rode the bus to a still awakening Chinatown to see a show someone had told him about, work by an artist he liked at a gallery he had encountered at art fairs but never visited in person. He chatted with the young man behind the desk, asking what else there was to see in the neighbourhood and sharing his concern that the artist, a Native American ceramicist who had gotten very popular, might get boxed into grinding out the same thing over and over. Because the young man asked, Jonah also shared his name. There was a photography gallery a few blocks away, another one Jonah knew by reputation; walking there he saw a large protest of the summit that had delayed his flight.
He got past the desk and into the show — tasteful, boring photography by a successful Japanese artist, what he privately thought of as “rich people art” — with only a brief hello, but then turned around, just when he would have walked out again, to see that the gallery founder and two directors had emerged to greet him.
“They told us you were coming,” explained one of the directors, a pretty young woman in a severe business suit. Once the founder had shaken his hand and gone back to his office, Jonah let the pretty young director show him around the exhibit he’d already dismissed as well as the gallery’s back office and viewing room. He took his usual approach in such situations, making small talk as if at a cocktail party and biding his time. He admired the unique design of the display racks in the viewing room. He inquired after her family and asked where she liked to eat in the neighbourhood. As soon as he could he slipped out and hurried over to City Lights, where he bought two paperbacks by the Sicilian writer Leonardo Sciascia, whom he’d never read before.
The restaurant she recommended turned out to be an ornate Szechuan spot, deserted at that hour, whose prices he could not possibly afford. Slinking out again after looking at the menu he felt foolish to have expected anything else. Fortunately he’d overheard the clerk at City Lights mention another place, an old-school Hunanese lunch counter where there was a television playing the local news and they did not offend Jonah’s sensibilities by charging for tea. Later he rode out to the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive to see the exhibition of a grad school friend, another conceptual artist who made work about North American settler colonialism; the next morning, he visited a sculptor who had gone to college with Nadia and had just spent six months carving the impurities out of an enormous chunk of quartz salvaged from a commercial rock quarry.
This sculptor’s New York gallery had just closed and he had a new baby in a carrier on his chest. Jonah’s heart was in his mouth every time the sculptor leaned over his opus, bringing the baby’s head within an inch of a corner; he remembered the dirty looks he used to get from old women in Jackson Heights when they saw him carrying his own newborn infant under one arm like a football. He and the sculptor went out for dim sum and to a bookstore and the sculptor shared the advice another artist had given him about making money.
“‘Use archival material,’” he said, “‘and get used to doing the same thing over and over.’”
Then Jonah walked a mile and a half to the Asian Art Museum, which had been closed to the public to host a grand lunch for the spouses of the heads of state in town for APEC.
“Jill Biden was standing right here two hours ago,” the museum’s press chief told him, grinning and squeezing his arm, once he’d gotten past security and been led into the dim and empty gallery. “I’ll leave you alone.”
Publicists liked to talk, and curators liked to lecture, but Jonah had learned to be forthright about his need for solitude. This time they had agreed ahead of time that he would have 45 minutes to himself before the curator arrived to explain what he was supposed to think of the painting. When he was starting out, he had sometimes spent many hours over multiple days confronting a work that perplexed him. In this case, having already seen many images of what turned out to be a very easily photographed black and white art work, and having already begun to write down ideas earlier in the day, he could probably have made do with a glance. He was unlikely to experience any transcendence in such a tightly choreographed encounter, anyway. He was just too contrary. But showing up felt like a matter of principle, and after all, it couldn’t hurt.
When the press contact, a former dancer type who later surprised Jonah by mentioning his wife and two children, returned with the curator, a trim older woman in an embroidered jacket, Jonah prepared to joust. She was perfectly nice and had interesting things to say. But he needed her to understand that he was no mere journalist, to whom the Zen esthetic was news, while she, as an academic, had to demonstrate her mastery of the material. Once he felt they had both made their points, he looked at his watch, and they continued next door to a Japanese pop art exhibit. Then the curator excused herself, but the former dancer offered Jonah a tour of the rest of the museum, and Jonah couldn’t see how to refuse, even though his feet hurt and his eyes were exhausted. He hadn’t ever been there before and, as the dancer pointed out, there was no way of knowing if he’d ever be back.
When finally he left, with many thanks and professions of good will, he got on a train to a gentrified section of Oakland for dinner with a close college friend who had, after an interval in academia, become a corporate lawyer. Jonah held the friend’s new baby and then, leaving the baby and his older brother with either the night nurse or the mother in law — she wasn’t introduced — he, his friend, and his friend’s wife, also a corporate lawyer, walked to a nearby French restaurant. Jonah had been surprised, because his friend always seemed worried about money, by how nice his house was, but he supposed it made sense. The first thing his friend said, once they had been seated and had ordered some appetizers, was, “Flying across the country to see one painting is completely ridiculous.”
Jonah wasn’t sure whether he was meant to litigate this question, for entertainment’s sake, or to agree that he had wandered into an unbelievable life. He suspected the latter, but either way he didn’t feel up to it.
“Well,” he said mildly, “art is important to some people.”
“No, of course,” his friend replied, and Jonah stopped listening. In the morning he discovered that a train ran directly to the airport from quite close to his cousin’s house. There had been no reason to take a cab when he arrived. He began transcribing his notes on the airplane, and then began writing, and when this flight, too, was delayed, and they were all forced to deplane for several hours, he was delighted. The airline gave them food vouchers, there was a decent enough sushi counter, and this way he could finish his piece and finish watching Parasite on his iPad before returning to family life. It was a beautiful experience. He was engaged in what he was doing, but with something deeper than his anxious ordinary mind; he could feel himself pirouette around the ink painting’s formal qualities and Buddhist subtext like an ice skater. “The point of this minimalism isn’t to make anything simple,” he concluded, after about 1000 words, “but to cut away distractions and reveal how complicated the world actually is.”
He filed that evening from Kennedy Airport, and when there was no reply the following day, he wondered if he should call. But then the assistant art editor sent an edit, and he dared hope he could get through the whole process without talking on the phone at all. He did end up speaking to the assistant editor, because she would need a synopsis of his piece for a meeting the following week and called to ask him to write one for her. In the course of their exchange, he mentioned that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa.” She suggested putting this phrase in the subheadline, and to make this intelligible, he agreed to add the fact that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa” to his story.
When the piece was published, he got vastly more response than he usually did, which is to say that as many as three or four people emailed him about it. One was a former college professor, who said that he wasn’t sure either of them had brought their best to the class they had shared, but that he congratulated Jonah on conserving his energies for such top-flight art writing. The next week Jonah went to Chinatown to visit an artist he might profile for a museum catalogue, a renowned older Japanese woman who had lived like a squatter in an unfurnished loft for 40 years. The gallerist who would be paying him for this, if she decided to spend what he was asking, sat between them as they chatted, interrupting their rapport from time to time to underline the parts of the artist’s life that she felt were important art historically. When she got up to use the bathroom, the artist followed her with her eyes.
“She’s okay,” the artist said. “But I think something weird about her. Like whenever we travel, she insist on getting one room with king size bed.”
“To share?” Jonah exclaimed.
On his way to Tribeca, where he was meeting his father for coffee, Jonah ran into a different art dealer, the one whose conceptual art show he had just reviewed, and she invited him into her office for a chat. They talked about marriage and their children, as they usually did, and she thanked him for the review, which he shrugged off.
“No,” she said, “it’s huge.”
She had worked at a mega gallery before opening her own space, and she told him that reviews in his paper had been the only ones the mega gallerist cared about. They appeared in sales presentations. They played a key role in what she called the mega gallerist’s “ongoing pissing contest” with his peers.
“Yeah,” Jonah laughed, “and then I get $250.”
The dealer’s jaw dropped, and he in turn stared right back at her. He couldn’t remember having ever surprised her before.
“Yeah,” he repeated. “Two-fifty for the short ones.”
“But you have so much power!” she exclaimed.
He didn’t know what to say.
“How was the piece?” Alan asked him, once they were sitting side by side in the little cafe that now occupied the former boarding house where Frederick Douglass had first slept when he came to New York.
“To be honest,” Jonah said, “I think it comes through pretty well in reproduction.” He made a deprecating gesture. “You know, it’s black and white.”
“It’s still good you went,” Alan said.
“Oh, yeah, no,” Jonah said, “it was a great trip. I’m glad I went.”
He walked Alan back to the loft and went upstairs to say hello to his mother, to whom he couldn’t help boasting that he’d gotten some nice emails about his latest review.
“Oh, I’m so glad!” she exclaimed. “Because I saw someone on Facebook making fun of you for calling it the Zen Mona Lisa.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-fire-deat.title: NYC fire deaths nearly double in 2026 as deadly Brooklyn blaze’s victims are identified
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-fire-deat.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-fire-deat.text:
Fire deaths in New York City have nearly doubled this year, the FDNY says, as police identified three of the six people killed in a house fire on 58th Street in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, last week.
Eighty-seven people have died in fires in the city so far in 2026, compared with 45 during the same period last year, according to the FDNY. The count includes two people who died this year from injuries sustained in fires in 2023 and 2025.
Police identified three of the people killed in Thursday’s fire as Lin Cheng Zong, 47; Weixiu Zeng, 52; and Li Sun Zhu, 21, all of whom lived in the house. The other three victims were badly burned and will require additional steps to be positively identified, police said.
Before the fire, city building inspectors had tried four times to get inside the two-story home, most recently less than three months before the blaze.
Inspectors went to the house on Sept. 9 and Oct. 22, 2025, and on Feb. 13 and Aug. 10, 2026, in response to 311 complaints made in the summer of 2025. No one let them in, the Department of Buildings said in a statement last week.
One complaint, in August 2025, reported illegal apartment conversions in the basement and on the first and second floors, city records show.
Inspectors left a notice on the door each time, then closed out the complaints under the agency’s standard procedures, the department said. It added that inspectors have no legal authority to force their way into a building.
Records kept by the city and the state attorney general list Wei Wang as the property’s owner. Wang, a doctor at Total Care Medical Center, a low-cost clinic serving the neighborhood’s Chinese community about 100 feet from the house, declined to answer Gothamist’s questions on Thursday.
“My lawyer said not to talk,” Wang said last week.
He declined to give his lawyer’s name. Messages left Monday were not returned.
Fire marshals are still investigating the cause, the FDNY said. Officials said Thursday that a lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but that it was too early to tell whether it started the fire, which also injured nine people, including five first responders.
Fires caused by lithium-ion batteries have also increased across the city, according to FDNY data: 276 between Jan. 1 and Sept. 7 this year, up 42% from 195 during the same period in 2025.
The Sunset Park fire came less than a week after four members of a Bronx family, including 11-year-old Zion Maine, died when a lithium-ion battery caught fire.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: The Big Review: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ★★★★½
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Linda Yablonsky
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Total star rating: ★★★★½
The works: ★★★★★
The show: ★★★★
He was Jack the Dripper. She was The Wife. That is how it went for artist couples in gender-coded mid-century America (and elsewhere). Yet, Lee Krasner (1908-84) played more than a supporting role in her decade-long marriage to Jackson Pollock (1912-56). When his work eclipsed hers, she remained as committed to her own painting as she was to every aspect of his life—except his infidelity and the alcoholism that in 1956 drove him to his death. Even then, she put her devotion to consequential use in securing his legacy. Now the time has come to fully appreciate hers.
Signature Pollocks ricochet off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa
That is the organising principle behind Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, the gorgeous and largely convincing blockbuster at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. While other US museums have previously surveyed the artists separately and in tandem, for the Met curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, none gave Krasner, a first-generation Abstract Expressionist, a fair shake.
Their exhibition strives to give a primacy to Krasner’s work that parallels Pollock’s. Note whose name comes first in the show’s title. Its subtitle likewise derives from a Krasner at the she-who-laughs-last finale. What’s more, a dramatically lit, black box of a gallery starts it off with a bracing presentation of six vertical abstractions that Krasner made in the 1950s by collaging cuttings from her unsold paintings with pieces of canvas and bits of Pollock’s drawings punctuated by slashes of pink and orange.
Nonetheless, the eye keeps moving to a window-like opening that functions as a proscenium for the theatre of Pollock’s Convergence: No. 10 (1952), an immense and riveting painting of black paint skeins shot with explosions of colour. Mounted on an angled, freestanding wall in another room, the sight offers viewers a taste of what is in store: signature Pollocks ricocheting off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa.
If only the curators did not show Krasner still riding his coattails. Pollock’s name remains the bigger draw. Ultimately, he still comes off as the bigger trailblazer, and she, his foremost champion, more willing to risk failure to experiment and invent. As Breslin speculated during the press preview: “I don’t think we would have a Jackson Pollock if it weren’t for what Krasner did to support his work.”
There is no way to test that theory, but if Krasner and Pollock proves anything, it is that the artists’ relationship was so codependent that the reverse may be just as true. Yet, today her influence and market value pale before his. Krasner’s auction record, set at Sotheby’s in 2019, is $11.7m for The Eye is the First Circle (1960), one of her larger canvases in the show. That is not chump change, but this year Christie’s sold Pollock’s Number 7A (1948) for $181.2m, an eye-watering price but still short of the reported $200m that financier Ken Griffin paid David Geffen, in 2016, for Number 17A (also 1948).
She was better-known
Krasner and Pollock met in 1942, when she was better-known to the Abstract Expressionist crowd in New York and Pollock the only unfamiliar name in a show of American and European Modernists (partially recreated at the Met) that the painter John Graham organised and included works by both. By linking their small, vibrant abstractions with works by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Henri Matisse, Amadeo Modigliani, Giorgio de Chirico and Willem de Kooning, the show virtually jumpstarted their careers. It also made them a couple.
Krasner introduced herself in a spontaneous visit to Pollock’s studio and was so dazzled that she hit a creative block. That did not stop them from dating. He was a Midwestern former student of Thomas Hart Benton in thrall to Picasso and Mexican muralists. She was inspired by Arshile Gorky’s abstractions and Matisse’s cut-outs. Soon he was importing a Matissean palette to his painting and showing at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of this Century gallery. Sales were not brisk. Pollock’s drinking was more prodigious. Krasner insisted they marry and move to Springs, in East Hampton—to protect him from himself—and persuaded Guggenheim to cover the downpayment.
Relocating did the trick for three unusually sober years—long enough for Pollock to produce his breakthrough drip paintings and achieve lasting fame, before settling, intermittently, into new bouts of alcoholism and depression; a creative paralysis set in. Krasner’s career took off, with a confident 1955 solo show at New York’s Stable Gallery.
Breslin and Kumar take care not to place the artists’ works close together, so Krasner’s modestly-scaled paintings can hook the eye without being overwhelmed by Pollock’s volatile monumentalism. Until she was widowed and took over Pollock’s now-famous barn, Krasner worked in their kitchen and he in an upstairs bedroom. Two contiguous galleries, both painted black, approximate the size of the artists’ studios and distill the show’s thesis with luminous economy, leading viewers from the lyrical, early choreography of his pours, drips and stains to her smaller but exquisite Little Images—mosaic-like geometries painted with a palette knife.
From these sepulchral chambers the show opens to a large, high-ceilinged gallery flooded with daylight from newly revealed windows on Central Park. Here, Convergence hangs, backed with the Met’s prize Pollock, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950). The operatic shift in tone and scale drives home the outsize renown Pollock achieved after a 1949 feature in Life magazine posed the question, “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?”
In the same gallery, tellingly, the eight collage paintings Krasner showed at Stable Gallery turn from the Pollocks to face each other like the stones of Stonehenge and look just as ritualistic, if more elated. After that, it’s back to black for a segment titled Re:Echo (after a Krasner), where Pollock’s arabesque, later works hang near her Robert Motherwell-like abstractions of the same period.
The rest of the show is all Krasner, but she outlived Pollock by 28 years. The swirling, abstracted floral landscapes became monumental, but appear in a few too many galleries, homogenizing their visual impact. The point—that no full understanding of one artist can come without the other—has already been made, capped by the one side-by-side juxtaposition: The Deep (1953), a chilling canvas where Pollock nearly obliterated a dark biomorph in clouds of white, and Birth (1956), an image of interlocking pink and black forms that Krasner painted the year he died. That pairing said it all.
Will this show correct a historic imbalance? Probably not market-wise, but a reputational correction seems both necessary and likely.
- Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, until 31 January 2027
- Curators: David Breslin and Brinda Kumar
- Tickets: $30 (concessions available)
What the other critics said
The New York Times’s Holland Cotter describes the exhibition as an “exercise of art-historical reset”, and calls its installation of Pollocks “an entrancing sight”, while exulting in the “distinctive impression of personal joy” in Krasner’s post-Pollock work. In The Wall Street Journal, Karen Wilkin applauds the curators for encouraging “concentration on their work, rather than the mythology attached to both painters”, and on her Instagram, Jasper Johns’s biographer Deborah Solomon raves: “It’s like holding two opposed thoughts in your brain at the same time and wondering if your head will explode from the exhilaration of it all.”

City Limits rounds up the latest housing and land use-related events and public hearings, plus affordable housing lotteries that are ending soon.
Welcome to City Limits’ NYC Housing Calendar, a weekly feature where we round up the latest housing and land use-related events and hearings, as well as affordable housing lotteries that are ending soon.
Know of an event we should include in next week’s calendar? Email us.
Upcoming housing and land use-related events:
- Monday, Nov. 9 at 6 p.m.: The Department of City Planning will hold an information session on its plans for a new city-wide system for assigning new addresses and verifying existing addresses. More here.
- Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 9 a.m.: The Landmarks Preservation Commission will meet regarding multiple applications. More here.
- Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 11 a.m.: The NYC Council’s Subcommittee on Zoning and Franchises will meet regarding the following land use applications: 108-05 68th Road Rezoning, 100-12 Queens Boulevard Rezoning, South Richmond Designated Open Space Amendment, and the Studio 54 Rehabilitation and Text Amendment. More here.
- Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 12 p.m.: The NYC Council’s Committee on Land Use will meet regarding the following land use applications: 108-05 68th Road Rezoning, 100-12 Queens Boulevard Rezoning, South Richmond Designated Open Space Amendment, and the Studio 54 Rehabilitation and Text Amendment. More here.
- Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 6:30 p.m.: The Department of Transportation will hold an in-person meeting in Brooklyn to get public comment on plans to rehabilitate the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE). More here.
- Thursday, Nov. 12 at 10 a.m.: The NYC Council’s Committee on Veterans will meeting regarding several bills, including one that would require an annual report from the Department of Housing Preservation and Development on the number of veterans applying for and benefiting from housing in city-run Mitchell-Lama developments. More here.
- Thursday, Nov. 12 at 6:30 p.m.: GrowHouse Design and Development Group, Inc. will host a hands-on workshop invites to people to learn more about Community Land Trusts. More here.
- Thursday, Nov. 12 at 6:30 p.m.: The Department of Transportation will hold a virtual meeting to get public comment on plans to rehabilitate the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE). More here.
- Friday, Nov. 13 at 11 a.m.: Believe New York will host the Affordable Housing Resource Conference to provide information and resources to New Yorkers in need fo affordable or supportive housing. More here.
- Saturday, Nov. 14, 1 to 4 p.m.: The Department of City Planning will lead a walking tour of the area south of Prospect Park in Brooklyn, which officials are eyeing for a rezoning. More here.
- Monday, Nov. 16 at 11 a.m.: The Department of Buildings will hold a hearing on proposed rules for a new city law that requires the installation of natural gas detecting devices in residential buildings. More here.
- Monday, Nov. 16 at 1 p.m.: The City Planning Commission will hold a public review session; the agenda has not yet been posted. More here.
