https://jacobin.com/2026/11/conservative.title: Reactionary Feminists Offer Bad Solutions to Real Problems
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/conservative.author: Kaja Kröger
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/conservative.text:
Reactionary Feminists Offer Bad Solutions to Real Problems
Reactionary feminist writers Mary Harrington and Louise Perry dress up arguments for marriage and sexual restraint in Marxist rhetoric. But they also point to the limits of liberal feminism — limits that the Left needs to grapple with.
To more and more people, the promises of sex-positive liberal feminism feel empty. The sexual ideas that have dominated feminism in the last two decades — including that sexual liberation always serves women’s interests, that consent is the only relevant sexual ethic, and that consuming porn and buying sex are benign practices like any other — are beginning to ring hollow.
In this context, an emergent theoretical strand with the pointed, self-chosen name “reactionary feminism” has drawn considerable attention. It calls into question the liberal assertion that every form of sexual morality is anti-feminist — a view the Left has absorbed in recent decades. Although they work to maintain an appearance of ideological ambivalence, reactionary feminists are aligned with the post-liberal right, and they are finding success in attracting to that project women who are disenchanted with feminism’s wholesale embrace of sexual openness for its own sake. Their prescriptions are often at odds with what many feminists would consider emancipatory, but they are identifying real flaws in liberal feminism, and the Left should take notice.
At the forefront of this new conservative feminism are British authors Mary Harrington and Louise Perry. Both have written popular books on how postwar sexual liberation in the West has failed women.
In her 2022 book The Case Against the Sexual Revolution, Perry argues that shifting cultural norms around casual sex have led to a hookup culture that frustrates many women — even if they endorse these norms politically. In Perry’s telling, this is no wonder: as rigid sexual morality has receded, a liberal feminist paradigm has taken its place, one that de-exceptionalizes sex and portrays it as inconsequential. With contraception and a sexual culture in which casual sex doesn’t require emotional commitments, why would we need to have special guardrails around sex? For straight women on the dating market, this often manifests as feeling simultaneously sexually pursued and emotionally neglected.
Many liberal women are responding to this dilemma with heteropessimism, or a bleak outlook on male-female pairings altogether. While reactionary feminism indulges its own form of gender fatalism (I return to this below), Perry is suggesting that these disappointed women look elsewhere: the problem is not heterosexuality but a culture of sexual casualness pursued erroneously in the name of progress.
By making implicit liberal assumptions about casual sex and social progress explicit, Perry taps into intuitions most people share: for instance, that the expectation of emotional commitment after having sex is not too much to ask, or that sex can be a site of exceptional vulnerability and risk. Her willingness to say these things aloud has earned her an audience eager to hear something more nuanced than slogans about sexual autonomy.
Frustration With Liberal Sexual Culture
In academic feminism, sex is often presented as a banal activity, like going on a walk together. What happens in the course of sex is equivalent to deciding to go down this path or climb up this hill — with both people able to say at any time that they would like to turn around and go back home.
This neutralized view of sex might appear emancipatory, promising as it does to overturn the sexual scripts and social stigmas that hold up the status quo. But unfortunately, it doesn’t align with actual experience. The vulnerability and boundary crossing involved in sex can have far-reaching consequences if someone takes advantage of them. For most people, the stakes of sex going well or poorly are thus much higher than those of going on a walk, even when people consider it casual.
The broad Left’s consensus on this view of sex poses a dilemma for many women. If I’m expecting emotional engagement from a man after a hookup, does that secretly make me “trad” and a conservative? If monogamy fosters moralism and possessiveness in sexuality, does that not make nonmonogamy far more feminist? The success of Perry’s book, which came out when #MeToo was still relatively fresh, and there was cultural space to consider the potential downsides of sexual liberalism, suggested that many women had been privately entertaining these questions for years. Perry shined a light on the gap between political endorsement of goals like sexual freedom and conflicted attitudes about what that actually looks like in real life.
There is no doubt that being “sexually liberated” — expressed, for instance, by engaging in nonmonogamy and kink or BDSM — has accrued social status and moral value among progressive feminists. Countless self-help books and articles about ethical nonmonogamy have come out in recent years. It seems simply cool to be chill enough to have an open relationship and not to really want someone to commit only to you. The alternative of wanting a committed romantic partner is, by contrast, conservative and uncool. Last year, writer Chanté Joseph went viral with a Vogue article that aptly captured this dynamic and asked, “Is having a boyfriend embarrassing now?” One of the women Joseph quotes says that having a boyfriend feels “Republican.” A hard blow for romantics.
At the same time, it has also become cool to enjoy more physically violent sex. We can see this most evidently in the mainstreaming of “kinky sex” in popular culture since Fifty Shades of Grey. Data backs this up. If you’re a woman under twenty-four, the chance that your partner choked you during your last sexual encounter is about one in three, according to a representative survey by Indiana University researcher Debby Herbenick. Among millennial women (age twenty-five to thirty-nine), the figure was only 11 percent, and for women above the age of forty, it was 3 percent. This is an immense shift in sexual behavior across a single generation.
In interviews with psychologist Nicola Gavey, young women who experienced such “rough sex” said they felt pressured by current sexual norms to make themselves want it in order not to seem boring or prudish. The reality of these parallel cultural developments is what makes Perry’s critique of liberal sexual culture more complicated than closed-minded conservative moralism.
Marxist Rhetoric
Reactionary feminists are not hesitant to offer women well-established conservative solutions for sexual liberalism’s discontents: refrain from casual sex, don’t get drunk with strange men around, get married. But they wrap these solutions in new leftist rhetoric.
For many liberal and leftist feminists, marriage is a historically sexist institution aimed at controlling women and property. For Mary Harrington, by contrast, marriage enables “radical solidarity between the sexes.” It acts “as the smallest possible unit of resistance to overwhelming economic, cultural and political pressure to be lone atoms in a market,” as she writes in her 2023 book Feminism Against Progress. Rather than striving to be a girlboss or buying yourself flowers, Harrington proposes an attractive vision of monogamous marriage as radical solidarity. Who wants to be a lone atom in the market?
In her book, Harrington argues that the belief in progress has led feminism astray: toward individual freedom, away from solidarity and care for others. For Harrington, this has to do with extending the concepts of freedom and trade from the economy to human relationships. But this “logic of individual profit” goes against our human nature as social animals. Harrington therefore wants to defend the relational interests of humans against “the market’s power to liquefy, to commodify and to alienate.”
The concepts of commodification and alienation are laden with the Marxist critique that capitalism is not the right way to organize work and production. From a Marxist perspective, commodification and alienation are wrong because they thwart what is most distinctive about being human: free conscious activity (you could call that human nature).
In the reactionary feminist view, things are not as clear. The cases of commodification they focus on are surrogacy, prostitution, and paying another woman to take care of one’s children.
Reactionary feminists are quick to use leftist rhetoric in their critiques, but they remain vague about why surrogacy and prostitution are wrong. Is it because no one should divert women’s bodies from their “proper” use — reproductive sex within heterosexual marriage? Or is it because of the exceptional nature of exploitation involved in renting a woman’s womb or circumventing the mutuality of sexual attraction with money? We can find indications for both lines of argument in Harrington and Perry.
Struggle of Interests
For Perry, it is no wonder that men and women have had very different experiences in this liberated sexual culture. She argues that men and women have fundamentally opposing interests in the “sexual marketplace,” as she calls it, a contention that revolves around divergent proclivities and vulnerabilities rooted in biological reality. Women may be choosier about mates, for example, because women are uniquely vulnerable to becoming pregnant and bearing children after a sexual encounter, whereas men’s reproductive imperatives may motivate them toward sexual novelty and variety. For Perry, drawing on a concept that the Marxist radical feminist Shulamith Firestone first introduced, women thus constitute a “sex class,” which is locked in conflict with an opposing class, even while heterosexual men and women are oriented toward each other.
If women and men simply have different interests by nature, then the possible political solutions seem reassuringly simple. One can become a revolutionary to overthrow nature (Firestone wanted to outsource pregnancy to artificial wombs) or become fatalistic about sexual relationships between men and women. While reactionary feminists tend to push back against heteropessimism, they are guilty of a version of it themselves. To them, women and men can never fully overcome their fundamental struggle of interests. We must all instead make peace with them and tame them through institutions like marriage, which they argue contains the excesses of an unchecked sexual marketplace.
The problem with proclaiming an eternal struggle of interests between women and men is that it obscures the forces of socialization on gender relations and sexual violence. It takes women’s submission and men’s aggression to be natural facts.
For Perry in particular, each notable difference in men and women’s behavior ultimately comes down to how women and men are simply wired differently and always have been. Although she is a critical thinker in other regards, Perry is captivated by evolutionary psychology and very keen to incorporate every “just-so” story that emanates from the field. Feminists have often disputed and criticized this science for naturalizing what is inherently social: gender roles.
In the status quo, then, Perry might be right that women and men have different interests in the “sexual marketplace.” But when we take gender roles into account — and resist being satisfied by speculative stories that neatly explain how each gender stereotype has a deep root in our prehistory — we can begin to see that it needn’t be this way forever.
Conservative Materialism
With their Marxist rhetoric, reactionary feminists pick up, in a new and more explicit way, a well-established materialist thread in conservative argument: washing machines did more for the advancement of women than equal rights ever could. Conservative crusader Phyllis Schlafly declared as much in the 1970s. If we step back from the obvious political function of Schlafly’s assertion — cementing the view that homemaking is women’s true nature — we can see a materialist argument. Schlafly claims that what changed women’s lives and work most profoundly was not equal rights but electricity, mass food production, and household appliances.
Harrington argues in a similar albeit more sophisticated vein that “the story of feminism is one of economic transitions — and particularly of the Industrial Revolution.” What enabled feminism’s fight for women’s equal rights was that women went from being producers in the agrarian household to wage workers and consumers.
Harrington holds that as capitalism made work “more centralised, more mechanised and less agrarian, the resulting split between ‘work’ and ‘home’ drove women increasingly into a domestic-only role.” In the reactionary feminist view, then, the core of feminist politics is less a question of moral progress than of material conditions.
This sounds eerily similar to a Marxist feminist perspective. And it also seems at odds with propagating women’s and men’s eternal struggle of interests. But Harrington and Perry see the biologistic opposition of interests as part of the material conditions of women’s lives. In doing so, they muddle the concerns of those radical feminists who are hyperfocused on women’s biology, with those of Marxist feminists, who look at economic and structural reasons for women’s situation.
Reactionary feminists use ideological ambivalence as a strategy in their political project. As Harrington told The Atlantic about her book: “There are a great many conservatives who haven’t noticed quite how much Marxism I’ve smuggled in.” But she is also candid about the mission of reactionary feminists to build conservative and, if need be, “illiberal” institutions.
Why the Left Should Care
Reactionary feminists aim to convince us that, given the persistence of sexual violence and disrespect of women in liberal sexual culture, monogamous marriage is our best choice. They assert gendered behavior and preferences to be natural facts that we can only passively defer to — women and men will allegedly always have antagonistic interests due to their supposedly ingrained and static biological imperatives. Although they use Marxist rhetoric, their concept of women’s interests lacks a clear class analysis. While they acknowledge that not all women have the same interests, they never address class antagonism in capitalism but rather talk solely of the cultural expressions of “liberalism” and “market society.”
That said, the Left needs to take seriously the offer reactionary feminists make to women dissatisfied with liberal feminism: a clear-cut judgment that what flies under the banner of sexual freedom is not always good for women. The rapidly rising number of women who are choked during sex, often enough against their will, is just one telling example of a sexual culture in which women still experience a lot of harm. This harm persists even though rigid sexual moralism has considerably lessened or fallen away.
Adherents of sex-positive feminism have little to say about this — for fear of moralism — and understandably so. But that fear has created a void in which it is difficult to talk about what sex should and should not look like. A substantive feminist vision of sexuality and of what the good life for a woman is could fill this void. Instead, conservative women have mostly filled it with their gender fatalism.
Many on the Left mistakenly think of all feminist cultural critiques as moralism that distracts from the real concern: economic interests. As the Russian revolutionary Alexandra Kollontai argued more than a century ago, even under socialism, people still need morality to guide gender relations and sexuality. Sexual violence does not disappear through economic reorganization.
Thus women also have a material interest in something that is difficult to grasp in purely economic terms: comradely men. But the feminist left rarely taps into this moral critique. There seems to be a larger focus on poses of political radicalism (like abolishing the family) that can be hard to relate to for the majority of people.
Reactionary feminists are right that it does women no favors when enjoying “rough sex” becomes a marker of being liberated. They are right that the sexual revolution’s promise of freedom has left many women feeling unsatisfied and vulnerable. But they are wrong in proclaiming women’s perpetual vulnerability for biological reasons.
What they ignore is that women’s vulnerability is socially made and culturally scaffolded, and that there can be a society in which biological sex does not make women vulnerable. However, such a world requires not only a widely shared vision of gender equality but also the willingness to proclaim some sex practices as bad for those involved. Even if it’s a hard pill to swallow for those for whom feminist politics means radicalizing liberalism, such a world will require some degree of sexual morality.

Five oil sketches by Peter Paul Rubens were removed from Ducal Museum in Gotha, Germany, during World War II. Three were returned since then, and now the remaining two have been recovered and restituted to the museum. All will go on view together for the first since in eighty years.
The Art Newspaper reports that the five sketches are part of a group of twenty-two that Rubens composed on wood between 1620 and 1621 as studies for his commission to paint the ceiling of the newly built Jesuit Church in Antwerp (now Saint Charles Borromeo’s Church). Rubens created thirty-nine paintings for the ceiling, in what was then his largest commission; the upper level focused on stories from the Old and New Testaments, and the lower level depicted saints.
The preparatory sketches are particularly significant because the paintings themselves were destroyed in a fire that swept through the church in 1718, caused by a lightning-bolt strike. According to The Art Newspaper, the sketches were among the most valuable works in the collections at the museum, whose holdings once belonged to the former Duchy of Saxe-Gotha. Representatives of the duchy, which hadn’t owned the work since 1918, removed a considerable amount of art from the castle in the closing weeks of World War II.
Two of the sketches were looted by the Soviet army but were returned to the museum in 1959. Three others ended up in Coburg, were illegally sold, and turned up in the US market. In 2024, one of them was returned by a museum in Buffalo, New York. Now a fourth has been located in a private collection in the US and returned through private settlement, funded by the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation.
The fifth sketch resides in the Foundation E. G. Bührle Collection at the Kunsthaus Zurich. The foundation has agreed to loan the work to the Ducal Museum for an exhibition of the complete series.
Tobias Pfeifer-Helke, the director of the Friedenstein Foundation Gotha, called the reassembled works “nothing short of a miracle.” He added, “They are not only five unique masterpieces by the Flemish painter and the jewels of the Gotha art collection, but also bear witness to European and international history.”

https://gothamist.com/news/t-mobile-slow.title: T-Mobile slowed Internet to a crawl for NY low-income users, AG says
https://gothamist.com/news/t-mobile-slow.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/t-mobile-slow.text:
T-Mobile has agreed to improve the home internet service it provides to low-income New Yorkers after the New York Attorney General’s office found it drastically capped speeds for participants in a state-mandated affordable service program, and made the plans difficult to find.
The Affordable Broadband Act mandates home internet providers offer high-speed broadband plans at reduced costs to qualifying households. The service can cost no more than $15 per month for download speeds of 25 Mbps, or $20 per month for speeds of at least 200 Mbps. It’s open to households that receive government benefits including Medicaid, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits and Home Energy Assistance Program benefits.
Just 15 households statewide were enrolled in T-Mobile’s Affordable Broadband Act plans, a spokesperson for Attorney General Letitia James said. Her office said the company coded its website so that information about the plans wouldn't appear in search engine results, despite the law's requirement that internet service providers make an effort to promote their affordable broadband plans.
James said customers in the program saw their speeds reduced more than 97%, to just 650 kilobits per second, after using 50 gigabytes of data in a month — a limit her office estimated a typical user would hit after four days of service.
“Reliable and affordable internet service is a basic need for all New Yorkers, but T-Mobile flouted the law designed to help vulnerable New Yorkers access it,” James said. “My office is committed to seeing the Affordable Broadband Act realize its goal of ensuring that New Yorkers in need are not denied access to affordable home internet. I encourage all eligible New Yorkers to enroll in a low-cost home internet plan through the ABA.”
James’ office said T-Mobile has agreed to remove the data caps for Affordable Broadband Act plan subscribers, and deliver the download speeds in compliance with the law. The company also agreed to expand its ABA offerings to more areas in the state, and make it easier for eligible New Yorkers to find and sign up for the plans, according to the attorney general’s office.
A spokesperson for T-Mobile said the agreement provides more clarity around the company’s offering and makes the plan available to more customers.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Getty to help conserve art-filled 17th-century church in Peruvian Andes
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
An art-filled 17th-century church in the Andes mountains will soon begin five years of conservation work. The project will strengthen the building and preserve its collection of 330 historical objects—including eight paintings by the artist Bernardo Bitti (1548-1610), an Italian Jesuit priest who introduced Mannerism to the Viceroyalty of Peru in the 16th century.
Getty will work with the Peruvian Ministry of Culture to conserve the Church of Santo Tomás de Aquino, also known as the Church of Rondocan—named for the town in the Cusco region where it was built. The project will include seismic stabilisation using local materials; located 3,400m above sea level, the 340-sq.-m church is in an area prone to earthquakes.
“We provide all the advanced conservation techniques available, and we handle the structural design of the project,” Claudia Cancino, a principal project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute (GCI), tells The Art Newspaper. The Peruvian government will finance the work, which will cost $5m and start in 2027. Like other churches in the Andean highlands, Rondocan has adobe walls (1.2m thick), buttresses and a wooden truss roof.
“The project is not only about the temple and its walls. It’s about the cultural and spiritual heritage of the church,” says César Ccorimanya Mayta, the parish priest at Rondocan for the past 17 years.
Involving the community as caretakers of the temple is part of the conservation process. Cancino and her team completed a similar project at the Church of Santiago Apóstol in the nearby town of Kuñotambo in 2019. As part of that initiative, they showed locals how best to take care of the building—including deceptively simple tasks, like cleaning the floors.
“You have to understand how to sweep the church and with what, because if you stir up too much dust it sticks to the murals,” Cancino says. “All this training was done with the community of Kuñotambo. We even have a manual in Quechua,” the local Indigenous language.
Through the work in Kuñotambo, the GCI became familiar with the Church of Rondocan. “The community asked for our support so that they could request the Archdiocese of Cusco and the Ministry of Culture to work on their church,” Cancino says.
“This church is much more than a historic building. It is part of the community’s memory, identity and everyday life,” Fernando López Sánchez, Peru’s vice minister of cultural heritage, said in a statement.
As part of the conservation project, a Bitti painting will travel to Los Angeles for scientific analysis and conservation on the Getty campus.
Bitti arrived in Peru in 1575, creating paintings for churches in Lima and Cusco. When the Jesuits were expelled from the Americas by the Spanish Crown in 1767, their works were sold. It is believed that the parish priest at Rondocan at that time bought Bitti’s paintings in Cusco and had them transferred to the church. The discovery, less than two decades ago, of the only complete series of eight Bitti canvases has sparked renewed interest in the study of his work.
In addition to the paintings, the church’s collection includes sculptures from the viceroyalty era, manuscripts and silver liturgical objects. “The art collection in this small town in the middle of nowhere is breathtaking,” Cancino says.

A conversation with the artist on his series of high school-inspired photos from Artforum's October 2000 issue
For Artforum’s October 2000 issue, Dennis Cooper interviewed Mike Kelley at the start of his “Extracurricular Activity Projective Reconstruction” series, a twelve-year project in which Kelley re-created found images of Halloween costumes, religious events, and oddball student portraits from high school yearbooks. These facsimiles of mundane extracurricular activity were shown as diptychs along with their original referent, and presented alongside intricately designed sets replicating the surroundings of the pupils in the photos.
In their conversation, Kelley speaks with Cooper about Extracurricular Activity Projective Reconstruction #1 (A Domestic Scene), 2000, a work that transformed a photo of a haunting “Tennessee Williams kind” of high school play into a “full-scale production” comprising a “crudely furnished studio apartment” stage set and “a twenty-two-minute video documenting a one-act play performed on that set.” After nearly twenty years of feeling that the critical response to his work primarily focused on themes of “nostalgia and trauma,” Kelley “gave the people what they want,” and leaned into a multiyear psychodrama dredging the American high school experience.
The sculptural element of the “EAPR” works was of increased importance to Kelley, who constructed them to be inspected in “close proximity,” inverting the tradition of shoddily built stage props meant to be seen by faraway audiences. This, along with Kelley’s concern for the “conundrum” of translating an image into a physical object, then back into a reproduction of the initial image, foregrounded a formalism that Kelley saw as otherwise underrecognized in his work. Speaking on his worries that the recorded play would outshine his set, Kelley lamented that people “always glom right on to [my work’s] abject nature, or blah blah blah blah . . . I’ve been typecast as some kind of mindfucker or something.”
Read “Trauma Club: Dennis Cooper Talks with Mike Kelley” in Artforum’s October 2000 issue.
–Theo Belci

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-curbs-sp.title: NYPD curbs spitting and idling tickets amid complaints about quality-of-life crackdown
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-curbs-sp.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-curbs-sp.text:
The NYPD is telling officers to stop giving out tickets for spitting, except in the transit system, and vehicle idling, except in response to specific complaints, according to internal NYPD guidance issued Friday that was reviewed by Gothamist.
The directive also cautioned officers not to issue summonses for jaywalking, which has not been a criminal offense since 2024.
It follows criticism by some New Yorkers over an increase in so-called quality of life enforcement by the NYPD. In October, a video circulated on social media that showed an NYPD officer forcefully arresting someone they had stopped for spitting in Brownsville, Brooklyn. Days later, City Councilmember Chris Banks announced that he would introduce a bill striking spitting from the city’s litter ordinance.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has faced criticism over his handling of policing issues on a number of fronts. After his election, Mamdani retained NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch who began the quality of life crackdown under Mayor Eric Adams. As a candidate for mayor, Mamdani said he would take a community-based approach to public safety and ask police officers to focus on solving serious crimes.
Residents who spoke to Gothamist for a number of stories about the low-level enforcement had mixed opinions about such summonses, with some supportive of the enforcement, and others critical.
An NYPD spokesperson characterized the guidance issued Friday as a routine reminder to officers about enforcement rules and expectations. The spokesperson said it was not done in response to Gothamist reporting.
Last week, NYPD spokesperson Bradley Weekes said officers are writing quality of life summonses because of an increased number of 311 complaints from residents. “People are asking the NYPD for help, and we are responding to what the community is asking us to do,” Weekes said in a statement.
City Hall declined to comment about the guidance issued Friday.
549 Summonses
In the last fiscal year, which ended at the end of June, NYPD officers wrote 549 civil summonses for spitting violations, according to Marisa Senigo, a spokesperson for the city’s hearing and trials office. NYPD officers wrote 222 civil tickets for engine idling in the same time period, she added.
After the video of the arrest in Brownsville, Councilmember Chris Banks told Gothamist in October that he was unhappy about how the arrest happened.
“We all want clean and safe and orderly neighborhoods, but we want to make sure that it's not at the expense of people's dignity,” Banks told Gothamist at the time. “And it can't be an excuse for the unnecessary or disproportionate confrontations that we're seeing.”
“We’ve seen how interactions between young Black and brown men particularly have become a death sentence for them or has got them involved in the criminal justice system,” Banks added.
Jaywalking has not been a criminal offense since 2024, when the City Council passed a bill that legalized the practice and then-Mayor Eric Adams did not veto the legislation.
The NYPD has not issued summonses for that offense since the law change, but has continued to enforce a similar violation called “pedestrian in the roadway.”
So far this year, NYPD officers have written dozens of criminal tickets for that offense, with most of the violations written by officers in a single precinct on Staten Island, according to a data analysis by the Data Collaborative for Justice at John Jay College.
Tickets tossed
Critics of the department’s quality-of-life enforcement have argued the process is a waste of police resources, and New Yorkers’ time.
In the last fiscal year, NYPD officers wrote more than 98,000 civil tickets for infractions like open containers and public urination. But nearly half of those summons were dismissed by hearing officers because they were defectively written or did not properly identify who received it.
“These summonses still force New Yorkers to spend time navigating the legal system and appearing at hearings, often over cases that should never have proceeded,” Amanda Jack, the policy director of criminal law reform at the Legal Aid Society told Gothamist at the time. “A dismissal rate this staggering only underscores how little justification there is for subjecting so many New Yorkers to this process at all.”
Weekes, the NYPD spokesperson, said at the time that the civil tickets were dismissed “based on technicalities” and that officers were identifying unlawful behavior and taking the correct action.
Criminal tickets issued by officers are dismissed at a similar rate, according to another analysis by the Data Collaborative for Justice.
In 2024, judges who presided over criminal summons cases threw out more than 65% of the cases because the tickets were not written properly or they did not correctly state what law had been broken.
Just 9% of criminal summonses issued that year ended in a conviction, the research concluded. The authors determined the process itself was the punishment for the New Yorkers given the tickets because they were forced to spend time fighting it in court and navigating the legal system.
If the recipient of a criminal summons does not pay the fine or fight to dismiss the ticket, a warrant for their arrest will be issued. In response to the quality-of-life enforcement, the Brooklyn district attorney’s office held an event last month to clear residents’ outstanding warrants that were triggered by unpaid criminal summonses.
In an interview with Gothamist at the time, District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said people with outstanding warrants for small infractions may be less likely to help law enforcement.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Art Gallery of Ontario sets opening date for $73m new wing
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Larry Humber
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO) in Toronto has announced that its new five-storey, C$100m ($73.4m), Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery, which will display around 400 modern and contemporary works, will open to the public on 25 September 2027. The expansion project was first made public in April 2022.
“The Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery is more than an expansion project—it is Toronto and Canada announcing its global position,” Stephan Jost, the AGO’s outgoing director and chief executive, said in a statement. “When this gallery opens in September 2027, the world will be made aware of the strength of the AGO collection and the degree to which it has evolved to be truly global.”
The new building is the result of a collaboration between three architecture firms: the Toronto-headquartered firm Diamond Schmitt (known for its revamp of Emily Carr University of Art + Design in Vancouver and the forthcoming New Brunswick Museum in Saint John); the New York-based firm Selldorf Architects (of the recent renovations of the National Gallery in London and the Frick Collection in Manhattan); and Two Row Architect, headquartered in Ohsweken, Ontario (known for the Perry Centre for Native American Art at the Shelburne Museum in Vermont).
“It’s not a small project,” Jost said at the time of the launch in 2022. The 40,000-sq.-ft expansion, which overlooks downtown Toronto’s Grange Park, increases the AGO’s display space by around 30%, including 5,000 sq. ft of gallery spaces with 23ft-tall ceilings.
The gallery is certainly in need of additional space for its collection of modern and contemporary work, which has grown by around 18,000 pieces in the past decade. In 2024 it received a gift of 37 works from the estate of the telecoms executive Philip B. Lind, including pieces by Laurie Simmons, Stan Douglas, Jeff Wall, Ai Weiwei, William Kentridge, Rodney Graham, Philip Guston and others. Last year, the gallery acquired more than 200 photographs by Peter Hujar and received more than 450 works from the late collectors Carol and Morton Rapp—among them works by Robert Rauschenberg, Claes Oldenburg, Kara Walker, Rachel Whiteread, Jasper Johns, Roy Lichtenstein, Lee Bontecoue, David Hockney and others. (The gallery also found itself at the centre of a culture war debate after opting not to acquire a work by the US photo-based artist and activist Nan Goldin.)
The AGO also boasts the largest public collection of Henry Moore’s work outside the UK—so much so that two years ago, to mark the 50th anniversary of the gallery’s Henry Moore Sculpture Centre, the city of Toronto declared 13 November to be Henry Moore Day.
The project of building a new wing was sparked by a lead gift of C$35m ($25.7m) from Dani Reiss, an art collector, chairman and chief executive of Canada Goose and member of the Order of Canada. The Reiss Gallery project is now fully funded, thanks to contributions from a community of supporters and the governments of Ontario and Canada.
Speaking on behalf of the federal government, Gregor Robertson, the minister of housing and infrastructure, said: “The federal government is proud to support this sustainable, state-of-the-art gallery that will host some of the world’s best modern and contemporary art for generations to come.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Hundreds protest US Senate bill that would gut key section of National Historic Preservation Act
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Emma Cieslik
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
On Monday (9 November), hundreds of protesters gathered on the West Lawn of the US Capitol in Washington, DC, to protest the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA, or senate bill S.5653), which would gut a key section of the National Historic Preservation Act. Representatives from more than 100 tribal nations, members of congress, leaders from the Association of African American Museums, the DC Preservation League, the American Institute of Architects and the Archaeological Institute of America gathered to protest a bill that would remove the requirement for federal agencies to notify and consult with the public and tribal nations about potential harms to historic sites, as stipulated in Section 106, Title III of the National Historic Preservation Act.
The BAAJA, described by New Mexico congresswoman Melanie Stansbury at the protest as a “dirty deal”, was created without tribal consultation or public input. According to California representative Jared Huffman, the 500 new pages of legislative text, which he described as “the most sweeping legislation we’ve seen on energy and environmental policy in decades”, was released just 48 hours before the Senate was set to vote on it Monday evening.
“They scheduled this vote for tonight to try to prevent something like this,” Huffman told protesters gathered on the Capitol lawn; organisers estimated around 800 people attended. “To try to prevent the American people from having a say, from looking under the hood of this sweeping legislation and understanding what’s actually it, but you came anyway.” Holding signs with illustrations of President Donald Trump’s planned Triumphal Arch in flames and “Nix 106”, protesters gathered for over two hours to listen to more than 15 speakers who argued that BAAJA would seriously threaten US history.
Greg Werkheiser, a leader of the Section 106 Coalition and co-founder of Cultural Heritage Partners, kicked off the protest. “We gather at the seat of American democracy, where the laws of this nation are written, to affirm one simple principle: the people deserve a voice in decisions that affect the places that we love,” he said. “That is the promise we have come here today to defend.”
Along with removing the requirement for federal agencies to engage with the public, the BAAJA would also make consultation with tribal nations optional, narrow what types of activity trigger a federal historic preservation review, restrict the definition of what constitutes a historic site, and remove any consideration of sensory, indirect and cumulative effects of changes to historic and sacred sites, essentially allowing federal agencies to take over tribal and state historic preservation offices that do not abide by limits and deadlines that the new bill would set. The BAAJA would even restrict what legal action people and organisations can take against the destruction of historic and sacred sites.
“For tribal nations,” Arizona congresswoman Adelita Grijalva said, “the fight is more than historic preservation. It’s about sovereignty. It’s about self-determination. It’s about the fundamental right to protect our ancestral homelands, culturally significant sites, and traditions that have existed since time immemorial.”
In its current form, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act requires federal agencies to consider the impact of federally funded building projects and requires that people receiving federal funds or permits consult with tribal nations. If passed, S. 5653 would make that consultation—the requirement that tribal nations participate in decision-making—optional.
“Our sacred places are living places of prayer, our responsibilities to them do not end at the reservation boundary,” Harry Antonio Jr, the governor of the Pueblo of Laguna in New Mexico, said at the rally. “You do not have to share our prayers to understand why those places deserve respect. Section 106 gives our governments a way to bring those concerns into federal decisions.”
Senators in favour of the bill have argued that its passage would lead to more economic opportunities. Articulating a position held by most rally attendees, Grijalva said: “Economic development does not require sacrificing our history, our culture or our sovereignty. We can create jobs without destroying sacred places. We can create jobs without sacrificing Mother Earth, our land, our water.”
Rashida Tlaib, the congresswoman from Michigan, said the bill would be used to fast-track projects with severe environmental consequences, including data centres and gas pipelines. “This bill strips away what little tools we already have to defend ourselves from corporate polluters,” she said.
The senate’s vote on the BAAJA coincides with Trump’s push to build a 250ft-tall arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. On 5 November, protesters gathered at its proposed site and spoke against it during a National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) meeting. Although the NCPC voted to approve the arch, a Washington, DC judge then immediately blocked construction for 14 days.
“The court orders stopping construction of those projects would not be possible if this BAAJA legislation becomes law,” Huffman said. “If this becomes law, the administration will use that in those pending court cases to make it much, much harder to stop Trump from advancing those and other vanity projects.”
Speakers urged protesters to call their senators, and implored senators to vote down the bill or to table a vote until the newly elected members of congress are sworn in in January.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.title: Man charged with murder after woman found stabbed to death in Queens, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.author: Phil Corso
https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.text:
A 54-year-old man has been charged with murder in connection with the fatal stabbing of a woman inside a building in Flushing, Queens, last week, police said Monday.
The NYPD identified the man as Zhordrack Blodywon, 54, who police said is homeless. He was arrested Monday evening and charged with murder, robbery and criminal possession of a weapon. His attorney information was not immediately available.
Police said officers responding to a 911 call around 4:30 p.m. Friday found an unidentified woman unconscious and unresponsive inside a building at 3617 164th St. The woman had multiple stab wounds and was pronounced dead at the scene by emergency medical workers, according to police.
The city's Office of Chief Medical Examiner ruled the death a homicide, police said.
Authorities have not released the woman's identity or age. Police have also not disclosed what led to the stabbing or whether Blodywon knew the victim.
Authorities said the investigation remains ongoing.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-civil-libe.title: NY civil liberties groups push for 48-hour limit on police retaining Flock camera data
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-civil-libe.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-civil-libe.text:
New York law enforcement officials say the data collected by Flock cameras and similar license plate readers can be invaluable in solving crimes, such as carjackings.
But civil liberties groups are pushing back, arguing that the mass information collected from the devices amounts to an unwarranted invasion of privacy. They say that safeguards must be put in place, including forcing law enforcement agencies to delete the data within 48 hours.
The dueling arguments were made at a state Assembly hearing on Tuesday, as New York lawmakers consider bills that would place limits on the controversial technology.
Automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, have been the subject of controversy, with critics raising concerns about privacy and mass surveillance. The biggest network of readers is maintained by Flock Safety, a company whose cameras — which have been frequently vandalized — feed data on vehicle location into a nationwide database that can be accessed by a wide variety of law-enforcement agencies.
“The argument that we should keep the data just in case it becomes useful is precisely the logic of mass surveillance and incongruent with any democratic society,” Daniel Schwarz, senior privacy and technology strategist for the New York Civil Liberties Union, told lawmakers.
The “longer location records are kept, the more ways they can be misused,” Schwarz said.
Suffolk County District Attorney Raymond Tierney, who serves as president of the state District Attorneys Association, told lawmakers that the license plate readers are “a critical tool in investigating, solving, and preventing crime.”
He used the example of a bystander spotting a particular make and model of a vehicle fleeing a crime scene.
“We'll look at the license plate reader technology,” Tierney said. “If we see a car that matches that description, we'll continue our investigation.”
Albany County Sheriff Craig Apple testified that a 48-hour retention period for data would be too short since tips often come in after days, weeks or even months. Deleting the data after two days, or even a month, would harm law enforcement’s ability to investigate them, he said.
”Look — 24 hours, 48 hours I think is just unrealistic and you might as well just get rid of the cameras altogether,” said Apple, who is president of the New York State Sheriffs Association.
A representative from New York Attorney General Letitia James’ office expressed support for limiting how long the data could be held, but didn’t offer a specific retention period.
“I think establishing limits on the amount of time data can be held is probably the best security that the data won't be misused,” said Tyler Nims, chief of the AG’s Enforcement Misconduct Investigative Office.
In New York City, the New York Police Department uses license plate readers manufactured by the company Leonardo Elsag, according to the agency’s use policy. Brad Weekes, a spokesperson for the NYPD, said the city has its own infrastructure for the readers — meaning the NYPD controls access to the data, which is not fed into a national database.
The NYPD has access to a national database maintained by Vigilant Technologies, but does not feed its data into it, the spokesperson said. The city does not contract with Flock.
Kevin Kane, Flock’s director of government affairs, said in written testimony to the Assembly that the company welcomes a statewide policy that sets safeguards.
“Flock’s view is that privacy and public safety are not opposing goals,” Kane wrote. “Legislation should preserve timely, case-specific investigative leads while establishing a framework for the collection, access, retention, and sharing of data.”
Assemblymember Nily Rozic, a Queens Democrat who heads the Assembly’s consumer affairs committee, said she believes there are “legitimate benefits to this technology.”
“But as the technology becomes more widespread, we also need to take a closer look at how it operates, what information is being collected, who has access to it, how long it is retained and with whom it is shared,” she said.
A previous version of this story misstated the name of NYPD spokesman Brad Weekes.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-denied-st.title: Man denied stabbing Brooklyn jogger but described being covered in blood, complaint says
https://gothamist.com/news/man-denied-st.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/man-denied-st.text:
The man accused of fatally stabbing a Brooklyn jogger last month told police he came to the bike path with a knife because “people were going to come to kill his family,” according to a criminal complaint.
Sayed Mohassib, a 27-year-old Department of Education employee with documented mental health issues, was arrested and charged with murder Saturday in connection with the killing of 28-year-old Katie Suarez.
Suarez was stabbed in the neck as she was running on the path on Shore Parkway near Bay 17th Street on Oct. 30, and died at a local hospital days later, officials have said.
The criminal complaint states Mohassib told investigators that he went along the bike path to the Verrazzano Bridge, then came back, sat on a bench, and “became covered in blood” on his jacket, pants and clothes. But he denied stabbing anyone and did not mention crossing paths with Suarez, the complaint states.
NYPD detectives previously said they believed it was a random attack.
The complaint also states that surveillance video captured him running away from the scene, returning to his apartment, and then emerging in his underwear about 15 minutes later to throw things into the garbage chute.
Despite denying stabbing anyone, Mohassib told police that he got rid of his bloody clothing and the knife, and tried to clean blood off his hands and off the walls of his apartment, the complaint states. Detectives who visited his apartment observed a reddish stain on the wall that later tested positive as blood, according to the complaint. Mohassib also identified himself in the surveillance video, the complaint states.
Besides the murder charge, Mohassib is also accused of tampering with physical evidence and criminal weapons possession, according to the documents. A Brooklyn judge ordered him held without bail as the case proceeds, and his attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Local lawmakers on Saturday demanded a full investigation into Mohassib’s hiring by the city’s Department of Education. They said he’d previously been discharged by the U.S. Marine Corps for psychiatric issues and had a brief stint at the NYPD before being hired by the city schools in 2024. City payroll records show he was working as a "substitute school aide.”
Mohassib is due back in court on Tuesday.

https://gothamist.com/news/nj-gov-sherri.title: NJ Gov. Sherrill announces her new lieutenant governor pick
https://gothamist.com/news/nj-gov-sherri.author: Mike Hayes, Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/nj-gov-sherri.text:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Monday she has selected Shirley Emehelu, a former prosecutor currently serving as New Jersey’s acting secretary of state, as her new lieutenant governor.
The appointment marks a historical milestone and follows big electoral gains for Democrats in last week’s midterm elections. For the first time in New Jersey, the two highest executive offices in state government are now held by women. Democrats will also send a record number of women to Congress, including Rebecca Bennett, a first-time candidate who ousted a well-known New Jersey Republican in the House of Representatives.
The governor said Emehelu’s leadership of the state’s midterm election amid “attacks” by the Trump administration was a reason she selected her for the role.
“That was pretty impressive,” the governor said. “She worked around the clock.”
Sherrill said selecting a woman for the roll was not a priority for her.
“I did not go into the process thinking we had to have a certain gender in the role,” she said, adding that Emehelu, a Nigerian-American, is the first immigrant to hold the lieutenant governor position.
Emehelu said it was a “profound honor” to make history with Sherrill. She was sworn in as her family and Sherrill looked on.
Her appointment follows the September resignation of former Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell.
Sherrill had demanded Caldwell, her running mate in last year’s election, step down after an internal investigation determined he had sexually harassed female staff in his office and committed ethics violations.
Caldwell has challenged the investigation’s findings. He has not been charged with any crime.
The investigation into his behavior dovetailed with a voter registration scandal that rocked New Jersey ahead of this year’s mid-term elections.
State law requires that the Lieutenant Governor hold a cabinet office as well. Caldwell served as secretary of state, making him New Jersey’s top elections official.
Emehelu, who originally joined the Sherrill administration as the acting state comptroller, was tapped to become acting secretary of state on the day he resigned.
Caldwell, a Black pastor who had served as the president of Centenary University, boosted Sherrill’s standing with the Black community during her campaign. On the day he resigned, Sherrill commended Caldwell for his commitment to advancing policies aimed at improving the lives of Black New Jerseyans. Influential Black politicians and community leaders around the state publicly urged Sherrill to continue that commitment after Caldwell’s departure.
Democrats secured an 11-1 advantage in the state’s congressional delegation. The party flipped two Republican seats in New Jersey.
In North Jersey, Bennett defeated Rep. Tom Kean in the state’s 7th Congressional District. In South Jersey, Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock denied Rep. Jeff Van Drew a fifth term in congress. Sherrill and other prominent Democrats in the state hit the campaign trail for both candidates.
This story has been updated with comment from Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Lt. Gov. Shirley Emehelu.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Aros museum in Aarhus, Denmark acquires sun-like Olafur Eliasson sculpture in new partnership with the artist
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Aros Aarhus Art Museum in eastern Denmark will acquire a major piece by the high-profile Danish-Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson—a crowd-pleasing vast glowing yellow sphere that appears to hover in space (Presence, 2025)—as part of a new long-term partnership.
The initiative between the artist and the museum, called “Shared Futures”, also encompasses Thin Ice, a solo exhibition to open autumn 2027. “This exhibition presents key works from recent decades alongside new projects reflecting Eliasson’s growing engagement with the climate, ecology, and humanity’s relationship with its surroundings,” says a statement.
A new site-specific version of Eliasson’s installation Waterfall (2004) will meanwhile be installed on Aros’s Art Square from 9 October next year; Studio Olafur Eliasson will also create a publicly accessible library collection of books on Eliasson’s artistic production at Aros under the plans. In addition, the partnership includes a dedicated postdoctoral research position in collaboration with Aarhus University.
Eliasson says in a statement: “Aros has supported my work in Denmark for many years, so it felt natural to make my online archive and library available there… the ambition is to show that museums can offer depth and focus for engaging with an artist’s practice in a more detailed, granular way.” The museum is also home to Eliasson’s rainbow rooftop walkway Your Rainbow Panorama (2011).
Rebecca Matthews, the museum's director, tells The Art Newspaper: “I first met Olafur Eliasson when I was chief executive of the European Capital of Culture in 2017, when he created an extraordinary stage design for the performance Tree of Codes. We were supposed to have our photograph taken together, but it was pouring with rain, so we ended up standing in a colonnade, talking. I remember thinking: If I ever get to lead a museum, he will be the first person I call.” Matthews became director of Aros in 2022.
In December 2025, Eliasson appeared on The Art Newspaper podcast A brush with…. with Ben Luke. “His works can be deceptively simple or enormously complex, but often share a rigorous and reductive geometry, which may conversely produce expansive and multifarious perceptual, sensory and embodied effects,” wrote Luke.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.title: Literatur | Ilse Aichinger wollte sich ihre Renitenz bewahren
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.author: Thekla Sickinger
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.text:
- Kultur
- Literatur
Ilse Aichinger wollte sich ihre Renitenz bewahren
Wo die Wirklichkeit versagt, beginnt das Schreiben: »Kontern« war das Motto von Ilse Aichinger, die vor zehn Jahren in Wien starb.
Am 11. November 2016 stirbt Ilse Aichinger in Wien. Die österreichisch-jüdische Schriftstellerin wurde 95 Jahre alt. »Ich gebrauche jetzt die besseren Wörter nicht mehr«, beginnt der schmale, 1976 erschienene Band »Schlechte Wörter«, der manchen als Höhepunkt ihres Werkes gilt. Lapidar erteilt der Eröffnungstext guten, besseren oder gar besten Redewendungen eine Absage, um sich stattdessen zu zweit-, drittbesseren oder eben »schlechten« Wörtern zu bekennen. Die Begründung: »Das Beste ist geboten.« Aber: »Gebote jagen mir Angst ein.«
Aichinger wurde 1921 in Wien geboren und erlebt dort den Aufstieg der Nationalsozialisten. Sie hat allen Grund, Gebote zu fürchten. Nach dem »Anschluss« Österreichs im März 1938 wird die Mutter, die als eine der ersten Frauen in Österreich Medizin studiert hat, gemäß den Nürnberger Gesetzen als »Volljude« deklariert, entlassen und zwangsumquartiert.
Aichinger, die wegen ihres »deutschblütigen« Vaters als »Mischling 1. Grades« gilt, darf nicht studieren und muss Zwangsarbeit leisten. Ihrer Zwillingsschwester, die später bildende Künstlerin wird, gelingt mit einem der letzten Kindertransporte im Juli 1939 die Flucht nach England. Die zurückgebliebene Familie kann nach Kriegsbeginn nicht mehr ausreisen. Aichinger, deren »Mischling«-Status der Mutter vorübergehend Schutz bietet, muss im Mai 1942 die Deportation ihrer geliebten Großmutter, ihres Onkels und einer Tante mitansehen.
Der Widerstand, auch der Widerstand gegen sprachliche Normen, der sich als roter Faden durch Aichingers Schreiben zieht, ist biografisch motiviert. Aichinger hat erlebt, was im äußersten Fall passieren kann, wenn Worte zu starren Bedeutungen gerinnen, die diejenigen, die damit bezeichnet werden, fixieren. Ihre Kritik an der Welt ist immer auch Sprachkritik: Kritik an einer Sprache, die unbedacht benennt und einteilt oder, wie in der Nachkriegszeit, Tradiertes fortführt, ohne unhintergehbare Brüche anzuerkennen.
Mit ihrem Gedicht »Winterantwort« schreibt sie 1963 den Höhepunkt des Rotkäppchen-Märchens, einen der bekanntesten deutschen Texte, neu, um an den Zivilisationsbruch der Judenvernichtung zu erinnern: »Großmutter, wo sind deine Lippen hin, / um die Gräser zu schmecken«.
Schon in ihrem Roman »Die größere Hoffnung«, der als eine der ersten literarischen Auseinandersetzungen mit der Judenverfolgung gilt, heißt es: »Großmutter, warum hast du so kalte Hände?« Auch das vermag Literatur: Das Kind kann in der Fiktion der Sterbenden die Hände halten. In der Realität sieht Aichinger ihre in das Vernichtungslager Maly Trostinec bei Minsk verschleppten Verwandten niemals wieder. Vergeblich wartet sie noch lange nach Kriegsende auf deren Rückkehr.
Wo die Wirklichkeit versagt, beginnt das Schreiben. Aichingers Werkherausgeber, der früh verstorbene Journalist Richard Reichensperger, bezeichnet die Literatur der Autorin als »Bergung der Opfer in der Sprache«. Wo Menschen vernichtet wurden, setzt Aichingers Sprache ein Denkmal, das sich gegen das von den Nationalsozialisten intendierte Vergessen stemmt. »Ich erinnere mich der Küche meiner Großmutter«, fängt der Titeltext des 1987 veröffentlichten Buches »Kleist, Moos, Fasane« an, der in das späte Werk vorausweist, in dem Aichinger die ihrem Schreiben zugrunde liegenden Erlebnisse explizit benennt.
Im Spätwerk, das sich großteils aus Zeitungskolumnen zusammensetzt, die ab 2001 in Buchform erscheinen, taucht etwa wieder eine »Brücke« auf, wie sie zum Schluss des frühen Romans symbolisch am Ort des Suizids der Protagonistin steht. In den späten Texten handelt es sich um die Schwedenbrücke, also die Stelle in Wien, die Innenstadt und Leopoldstadt verbindet: In der Leopoldstadt befindet sich im 17. Jahrhundert das Ghetto, von dort fahren 1942 mit Menschen beladene Viehwagen zu den Deportationszügen.
Aichingers Texte des frühen und mittleren Werkes, ihre Prosastücke, Szenen, Hörspiele, Gedichte, die bis in die 90er Jahre erscheinen, werden mehrfach als hermetisch, unverständlich, gar esoterisch tituliert, auch wenn sie der Autorin zahlreiche Literaturpreise einbringen. Aichingers sporadische Interviews, ihr Rückzug aufs Land nach dem Erfolg der »Spiegelgeschichte«, für die sie 1952 Preis der Gruppe 47 bekommt, und der Heirat mit Günter Eich, verfestigen den Ruf der stillen, schwer zugänglichen Schriftstellerin.
Erst nach dem Tod Eichs 1972, mehreren Umzügen und Jahren ohne Publikationen tritt Aichinger im achten und neunten Lebensjahrzehnt verstärkt in die Öffentlichkeit: Sie spricht in Interviews über ihr Leben, das ihrer Verwandten und Freunde und verflicht in Zeitungsbeiträgen Beobachtungen aus dem Kaffeehaus oder einem der mehrmals täglich frequentierten Wiener Kinos mit Erinnerungen zu einer eigenen Art Autobiografie.
Ihr Antrieb bleibt, Realität und Sprache zu »kontern«. Noch im letzten großen Interview aus dem Jahr 2005 spricht sie von ihrem »Zorn über die Welt«, von ihrer Freude am »Anarchischen« und der Notwendigkeit von Rebellion.

https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ca.title: Manhattan's Canal Street is getting a face-lift, but it'll take a while
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ca.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ca.text:
There’s a long road ahead for Canal Street in Manhattan.
The downtown thoroughfare, known for its mercilessly crammed sidewalks and vendors hawking designer-ish handbags, watches and other goods, is getting a much-anticipated face-lift, but it isn’t going to happen quickly.
The Department of Transportation told a local community board committee meeting that much of the construction it planned for the west side of Canal Street will be delayed until 2027.
“Anything involving concrete work is going to be pushed to the next year,” said Lauren Rennée, a deputy commissioner for the Department of Transportation.
“We would have loved to do more,” she added.
The Department of Transportation has split the Reimagining Canal Street project into two phases. The first phase, which was scheduled for this fall, entails improving west Canal Street, where, according to the transportation department, vehicle traffic is the biggest concern.
The second phase targets east Canal Street, where concerns about walkability are paramount. Specific plans for improvements to the eastern side of the street have yet to be announced, but that work is scheduled for 2027.
East Canal, where most of the vendors are stationed, is where collisions happen the most. According to data from the department, 190 people were injured on East Canal St. between 2020 and 2024, and two were killed in a car crash. New Yorkers have been anticipating wider sidewalks for decades.
The west side improvements include adding new crosswalks, two-lane bike lanes, pedestrian areas lined with planters and concrete blocks, and painted curb extensions from the West Side Highway to Broadway.
The only undertaking that has been executed this fall is painted curb extensions — essentially extending the pedestrian area into the shoulder — at five different sites near west Canal, Rennée told the community board meeting.
Signs about the construction project are plastered across the area, but there is little sign of any major work.
The transportation department contends that the project is still on schedule, and that more work will be done in the coming weeks, including the installation of planters. Any remaining work, Renée said, will be picked up next year.
The project is an important step in making sure New Yorkers have safe streets, said Mona Bruno, a spokesperson for the transportation department, in a statement.
“We began installing Canal Street West this fall as promised and substantial progress has been made as we work around the clock to deliver these upgrades to enhance safety," Bruno said in a statement.

Mona Chalabi on Money and Art
An interview with the Pulitzer Prize winner, Lori Waxman on bringing sexy back in Chicago, stolen Picasso prints found, and the problem with clouds.
“I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it,” Mona Chalabi says in her new book Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are — or tried to, anyway, before her editor stopped her. The Iraqi-British, Pulitzer-winning artist and illustrator has made a career saying what nobody else can, or will — calling out fellow journalists for their refusal to report on Palestine, for instance. Today, she talks to Associate Editor Laskhmi Rivera Amin about her data-driven, hand-drawn process, as well as how class and inequality shape journalism, art, and our lives.
Funny — as an editor, my favorite thing is not stopping my writers. That’s precisely how Lori Waxman’s piece on the return of sexy art in Chicago was born. No, this is not a personal essay about her or her acquaintances’ sexuality (“Maybe after everyone’s dead,” she says). It’s much better — loaded with art historical judgments (has anyone referred to Willem de Kooning’s drawings as “slasher sketches” before? We ought to); discussion of glory holes and sexy architecture; and gems about life (“female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100”). God, I love my job.
—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor
Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026). | Lakshmi Rivera Amin
