https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘I’m looking for faces which surprise me’: how Richard Avedon photographed the soul of his subjects
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Richard Avedon had only taken a couple of frames when he accidentally hit his head on a light being held above him. The Dalai Lama burst into laughter. That was when Avedon snapped two more frames and announced: “Oh, I got it!”
Avedon’s assistant, Sebastian Kim, was baffled. “I was like, what the hell happened? There’s only four frames out of a roll of 12 frames,” he recalls in a phone interview. “I realised he knew at that moment that something had happened, a mistake had happened: he hit his head and the Dalai Lama lit up.”
Kim, 52, now an eminent photographer in his own right, is among the interviewees who feature in a new documentary, Avedon, directed by Oscar winner Ron Howard, which premiered at the Cannes film festival and is released on Netflix this week.
The film explores the six-decade career of the fashion and portrait photographer renowned for white backgrounds that stripped away distractions and for capturing figures ranging from Marilyn Monroe and Charlie Chaplin to civil rights activists, anti-war protesters and working-class Americans.
Avedon was raised in New York City. His father, Jacob Avedon, co-founded a specialty store on Fifth Avenue, which was lost overnight during the Great Depression. Avedon struggled academically, flunking out of high school despite winning a citywide poetry prize.
He once said: “My father wanted me to be strongly educated, strong physically, and to make a living. But I always felt that I flunked. I grew up thinking I was certifiably stupid. I couldn’t graduate high school. I flunked everything.”
In the second world war, Avedon joined the Merchant Marine. Assigned to the photographic unit, he took more than 100,000 ID card photos and performed autopsy documentation. Observing endless faces against white backdrops taught him that no two faces are alike.
At the New School’s Design Laboratory, Harper’s Bazaar art director Alexey Brodovitch provided Avedon’s foundational philosophy: “Astonish me.” When Avedon struggled to design a neon sign using traditional media, Brodovitch suggested using pipe cleaners or spaghetti, teaching Avedon never to be blocked by technical limitations.
Commissioned by Harper’s Bazaar magazine, Avedon brought theatricality to fashion. Observing Christian Dior’s 1947 The New Look collection, Avedon captured models moving, swirling and laughing across Paris streets, transforming fashion photography from static posing into dynamic visual storytelling.
His approach to portraiture was no less distinctive. Avedon’s studio aesthetic relied on a stark, seamless white paper backdrop, bounded by a bold black film border. He once explained: “It’s the existential white. The only thing you see is the geography of the face. One of the functions of art is to eliminate in order to make more powerful or stronger what the artist wants to get across.
“I remember once that I fasted for three days. I fasted with a friend. And she and I decided after the fast, how will we break the fast? We decided on a peach. I never tasted anything like that peach in my life. Because everything, because of the fast, becomes so precious. That’s a little bit about getting rid of the background.”
For his picture of Monroe in 1957, Avedon waited through hours of joyful posing until the actor collapsed into quiet exhaustion. Monroe slumped into a corner, allowing Avedon to capture her unguarded melancholy – a portrait often called Sad Marilyn.
He believed that models were active creative collaborators rather than decorative props. He once said: “I know perfectly well what I want before I leave the house in the morning but if the girl doesn’t feel that she’s part of it, if she feels that she is someone that’s hired for an hour, a stick of wood that’s going to be told to stand over there and do that, that’s exactly what you get out of her.”
By engaging sitters through conversation, music and playfulness, he created an atmosphere of mutual trust. Models like Penelope Tree and Lauren Hutton recall in the film that working with him was liberating, allowing them to drop their guards and express vulnerability in front of the lens.
Dallas Brennan Rexer, 54, one of the film’s producers, said: “He was trying to get into their head and into their soul, in a way, through his photos. It was the same process for him regardless, and the models that we interviewed spoke about how they weren’t treated as a model who was just there to hold the clothes on.
“They were a human that he connected to and he asked them questions and he tried to understand what they were thinking about and what they were feeling and tried to help get something out of them that radiated and gave them an energy. That’s what made the photos special. It wasn’t just that they were pretty and their clothing looked nice.”
Avedon photographed the Duke and Duchess of Windsor in their hotel suite. Aware of their polished public persona, he broke through their guard by claiming his taxi had run over a dog.
Rexer elaborates: “He knew how he felt about their politics and he didn’t want to allow himself to be used to make another polite pretty picture of them. He wanted to say something much more pointed and important. He used the photograph in a very clever and specific way. He captured the moment that he thinks said everything that needed to be said about them.”
Though Avedon achieved commercial success – directing television campaigns for Calvin Klein – he channelled his resources into politically charged documentary work.
In 1963, Avedon reconnected with his high school friend James Baldwin, with whom he had co-edited a school magazine. Together they published Nothing Personal, combining Avedon’s portraits of civil rights leaders and mental asylum patients with Baldwin’s rich prose.
Rexer explains: “Dick was at a place in his life where he was ready to get involved in something political and he wanted to do something meaningful on civil rights. Nothing Personal is a phenomenal book. The text that James Baldwin wrote is poetic and beautiful, but it also is so resonant today.”
Avedon’s asylum photographs were deeply personal, influenced by his sister Louise, who suffered from severe mental illness. He said: “I photographed things that frightened me so that I could understand them.”
But when Nothing Personal received a withering review in the New York Review of Books, Avedon was crushed. He admitted: “That review simply stopped me from working for about a year because I began to question myself as an artist.”
Yet Avedon continued his political involvement. During the civil rights movement, he quietly supported activists. Rexer notes: “In the background very quietly, Dick was sending film down to SNCC [the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee] because they were using photography to keep people accountable to what was going on in the south. Then they would send the film back, and he would take it to the lab and process it for them, quietly on the side to just keep the movement going.”
These efforts culminated in In the American West (1979–1984), commissioned by the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas. Over five summers, Avedon photographed working-class Americans against white paper. Avedon stated of the project: “I’m looking for faces which surprise me. I’m looking for a face that will hold the wall.”
In 1992, at age 69, Avedon became the first staff photographer in the history of the New Yorker magazine, hired by editor Tina Brown. He produced portraits of global figures and controversial fashion essays, such as the Mr and Mrs Comfort portfolio.
In a statement provided by Netflix, Howard observed: “He had to learn to bridge his commercial success and his creative endeavors, using his own resources to underwrite far riskier projects. He figured out how to lean into the popular to make space for the unusual ... In many ways, Avedon defied the idea that there must be a division between art and commerce, highbrow and lowbrow, beauty and brutality.”
Avedon’s internal contradictions are at the heart of Howard’s documentary, which draws from unprecedented access to personal archives held by the Richard Avedon Foundation, including hundreds of thousands of negatives, contact sheets and behind-the-lens footage.
Rexer says: “The archive is daunting at first because there were 16,000 sittings, and that can only mean hundreds of thousands of images, and so it’s a bit overwhelming in the first couple of months.”
Among the production team’s most extraordinary discoveries was a cache of casual audio tapes recorded inside Avedon’s studio during the 1960s and 1970s with collaborators like Marvin Israel and Doon Arbus.
Rexer says: “They would put a recorder on the table and hit record and forget about it. So you could be a fly on the wall. He was working out a lot of questions about truth and identity and self and all of the big things like beauty. They would have these wonderful lunches with these abstract conversations about it but then he could turn that into something concrete.”
Despite all the success, the workaholic Avedon lived in a constant state of anxiety and self-doubt. His son, John Avedon, says in the film: “He had a bull-like confidence in himself. At the same time, he was totally insecure. He absolutely suffered from performance anxiety, but then he absolutely performed. I think he had to be anxious in order to perform.”
For Rexer, this is the key to unlocking much of Avedon’s work. She explains: “You need to have the confidence to walk up to Henry Kissinger and say: ‘I’m taking your portrait right now and no, we’re going to do it this way and put your hands down and look into my lens.’
“But also the insecurity or the lack of know-it-allness to be able to ask questions and connect with his subjects and explore and make people feel comfortable too. It didn’t just come in big in the room. He made space for the people he was photographing. That’s beautiful.”
Avedon suffered a cerebral hemorrhage and died in 2004, aged 81, while in San Antonio shooting a project titled Democracy for the New Yorker.
For Kim, his influence remains profound. He says: “I credit him for making me the person that I am. The way that he shaped the person that I am, the photographer that I am. He has had such an impact on so many people. It was difficult, but I look back and it’s the discipline that creates character.”
- Avedon is available on Netflix on 11 November

https://www.propublica.org/article/bill-.title: The Garbage Man: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills
https://www.propublica.org/article/bill-.author: Alex Cuadros
https://www.propublica.org/article/bill-.text:
Reporting Highlights
- A Little-Known Investment: Bill Gates has quietly accumulated a $29 billion stake in America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services.
- Climate Pollution: EPA inspectors have repeatedly found methane — a highly potent greenhouse gas — escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits.
- Undermining Climate Policies: Republic has lobbied against regulations that could make the waste industry cleaner, including by keeping organic garbage out of landfills in the first place.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates.
Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort.
For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change.
“If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air, to name just a few.
With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion.
Bill Gates’ Stake in Republic Services, a Landfill Operator, Now Exceeds a Fifth of His Net Worth
While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.
One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions, and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.
Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place.
“It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.
As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.”
Gates’ Climate Awakening
Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows.
In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year. He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.
A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.
Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga, had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation.
It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that Gates started to grasp the potentially “catastrophic” effects of greenhouse gases, he later wrote. But he also saw that the poorest people in the world needed more energy to improve their lot. The solution, he concluded, was something climate activists often underplay: innovation that could make clean energy cheap enough to naturally displace fossil fuels. That was the idea behind Breakthrough Energy, the initiative he launched in Paris in 2015.
Around the same time, methane began to emerge as a focus of climate action. The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it’s responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.
In speeches and interviews, Gates has sometimes warned about methane, but usually from agricultural sources (“cow farts,” in his words). He has rarely mentioned landfills, even after Larson — who still runs Gates’ investment office, Cascade Asset Management — joined Republic’s board in 2009. Gates’ stake in the company, though, was a relatively small portion of his own net worth until fairly recently. And as Larson put it to Fortune, “I’ll call Bill about something I’m buying if he needs to know, but Bill might not have any idea what Cascade owns.” (Gates’ Republic holdings are publicly disclosed in securities filings.)
Elsewhere in Gatesworld, people started to home in on the climate threat posed by landfills. The root of the issue is that landfills store buried trash — and when organic waste decomposes underground, in the absence of oxygen, it generates methane. The Gates Foundation has funded research and advocacy aimed at solving that problem, and Breakthrough has backed at least two early-stage companies developing their own solutions. One, Windfall Bio, uses microbes to digest methane into fertilizer. Its product was actually tested last year at a Republic landfill in California, where the pink liquid was sprinkled on the soil covering the top layer of trash.
Windfall said the test worked, substantially reducing emissions, but the startup reportedly ceased operations after a Department of Energy grant was canceled. (Windfall didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.)
On the surface, Republic has pursued a path consistent with Gates’ mission. In 2019, it became the first U.S. landfill operator to sign up for the Science Based Targets Initiative, promising to cut its emissions by 35% by 2030. Not that this was charity. Republic’s “climate leadership” became part of its pitch for garbage-collection contracts in progressive cities and counties. The company also won placements on stock indexes for businesses that meet certain environmental, social and governance criteria, attracting sustainability-minded investors.
Still, a fundamental tension remained — one at the heart of Gates’ vision. As Republic’s then-CEO Donald Slager put it on a 2017 call with investors, “You can’t have sustainability without profitability.”
A Not-So-Model Landfill
Each day, Americans throw away melon rinds, salmon skins and half-eaten drumsticks, paper towels, cheese that was too funky and eggs a day past their sell-by date. They discard greasy pizza boxes with crusts still rattling around inside and unthinkable amounts of leftover Chinese takeout. Not to mention the occasional dead pet.
Most of that trash — 240 million tons a year, enough to bury Manhattan under 100 feet of refuse — is hauled to one of the country’s 1,400 active landfills, where hulking vehicles with spiked wheels crush it into thin layers. At the end of each day, bulldozers typically spread soil on top, and for almost everyone who produced that trash, it will forever remain out of sight and out of mind.
People who live near landfills, though, describe smelling rotten cabbage, rotten eggs and rotten fish, as well as ammonia and skunk. Or as a neighbor to one Republic landfill put it: “I started smelling this stench like burning diapers. … It was foul.” Some describe burning throats, burning eyes, headaches and nausea. And while methane itself has no scent, those odors indicate that the gas is being released, studies show.
Still, modern landfills are an undeniable improvement over what came before. Open dumping and burning remained widespread until the 1970s. It was only in the ’90s that federal regulators started requiring operators to collect leachate (garbage juice, which can contaminate groundwater) and, at larger facilities, landfill gas (which is typically about half methane and half carbon dioxide but can also contain carcinogens like benzene).
Industry experts often compare landfills to living, breathing creatures. Underground trash inevitably shifts and settles, making it difficult to keep that gas from escaping. Managing such a beast is costly, which helps to explain why smaller operations have increasingly given way to corporations like Republic, which can turn a profit through economies of scale.
Republic declined to make executives available for interviews or to allow ProPublica to visit a landfill. But in May 2022 — around the same time Gates was lobbying for the passage of President Joe Biden’s historic climate bill — the company invited the Houston Chronicle to its local McCarty Road Landfill. Opened a half century earlier, the facility had passed through two corporate owners before being swallowed up by Republic, and now it was the site of a very Gatesian kind of project.
On the day of the visit, gulls circled hungrily as workers in neon vests gave a tour of the gas-collection system. Like at most other large landfills in the country, wells had been drilled deep into the trash below — five hundred of them in total. The top of each well sprouted from the grassy slopes in the form of a stubby black pipe fitted with a valve for adjusting the flow of underground gas. The workers also showed off large, bright blue, snail-shaped “blowers” — machines that suck that gas into a network of pipelines, then push it to the clanking, humming on-site plant that turns it into a salable product.
Most landfills that are required to collect gas simply burn it off. But they can also process it into “renewable natural gas,” which is functionally equivalent to the version pumped by oil companies. In part because this reuses the carbon from decomposing waste, it’s generally considered more climate-friendly. It also turns an environmental liability into a source of revenue — exactly the kind of win-win that Gates has long championed.
Yet the technology is no guarantee that the climate is being protected. In fact, it may be just the opposite.
In September 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency issued an “enforcement alert” saying that landfills across the country were “violating monitoring and maintenance requirements.” While the EPA didn’t name the operators, ProPublica obtained the corresponding spreadsheet through a public records request, and a fifth of the facilities targeted belong to Republic.
McCarty, far from being a model landfill, was among the worst offenders. It would soon earn Republic a formal “finding of violation” for allegedly failing to detect “exceedances” — methane escaping at levels above federal limits — for years on end. The EPA also noted repeated failures to address flooded wells, gullies formed by erosion and trash peeking through the surface of the landfill. Despite Republic’s economic incentive to capture methane, EPA inspectors found evidence of “poor maintenance” and “careless operation” of the gas-collection system as well.
And McCarty is hardly an outlier. Recent studies suggest that landfills with renewable natural gas facilities can actually emit more methane than those that only burn off the gas or use it to generate electricity. One possible explanation is that methane concentrations can vary across different parts of a landfill. According to researchers at Carbon Mapper, a NASA partner that measures emissions from various industries, some operators may prioritize collecting gas with higher methane content, which is cheaper to process — allowing more of the remaining methane to leak out.
Republic spokesperson Rob Litt declined to comment on whether that happened at McCarty, but said in a statement, “We employ hundreds of environmental managers and engineers. … If issues are identified, we work to resolve them.”
“Protecting the environment is part of Republic Services’ business,” he added.
The issues aren’t exclusive to landfills with natural gas facilities. Since 2020, EPA inspectors have used handheld methane detectors to sweep at least 39 of Republic’s roughly 200 landfills, according to inspection reports obtained by ProPublica. Including the issues at McCarty, they documented more than 1,400 problem spots — ranging from animal burrows to choked-off wells — spewing excessive amounts of methane.
In some cases, methane could be seen bubbling up through dark, fetid leachate pools. In others, so much methane was being released — with concentrations between 100 and 300 times the federal limit — that it was an explosion hazard.
Methane Bubbles at a Republic Services Landfill
What the Satellites Saw
Around the time of the Houston Chronicle visit, Republic’s CEO, a former McKinsey consultant named Jon Vander Ark, was promoting a new slogan: “Sustainability in action.” Meanwhile, though, Republic was quietly shying away from true climate leadership.
In 2021, two years after Republic signed on to the Science Based Targets Initiative, the SBTI made its minimum climate goal much more ambitious. Waste Management (where the Gates Foundation owns a small minority of the shares) would soon adopt it.
This was just months after Gates published “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” in which he exhorted private companies “to embrace the harder steps” toward solving global warming. Republic staff calculated that the new SBTI target could require more than $1 billion in additional spending on gas wells and other improvements, according to a former employee. Though that is less than half of what Republic has spent on dividends for Gates alone, it would leave less money for the company to redistribute to him and other shareholders. Republic has also spent more than $8 billion buying its own stock in the open market, ProPublica’s analysis shows, likely boosting the value of shares held by investors.
The matter was finally presented to the board around the second half of 2024, this person said. By then the board included Larson, Gates’ longtime investment manager — whose “insight into sustainability issues” is cited in company filings — and three other people with business ties to Gates (one has since left). While that is only four board members among a total of 13, Gates’ dominant shareholding means that, “as a practical matter, on any matter that gets voted on, he will almost certainly control the outcome,” said Lipton, the corporate-governance expert.
Republic never made the leap, and now it walks an awkward line. It continues to tout its affiliation with the SBTI while saying, in a note buried deep in one of its many sustainability reports, that the more ambitious target is “not an immediate strategic priority.”
Per SBTI rules, Republic has until the end of this year to submit an updated target. But when ProPublica asked if it would, the spokesperson said only, “We are reviewing our goals.” He declined to comment on the estimated cost or the board discussions.
There is, though, an even larger issue with Republic’s climate claims.
In line with its existing SBTI goal, Republic says it has already cut its landfill emissions by 20% since 2017. But that figure isn’t based on actual measurements of methane escaping from its facilities. According to the method cited in its sustainability reports, Republic instead typically measures the methane collected by its wells. Then it extrapolates how much it’s failing to collect — and how much is being emitted — based on the characteristics of each facility.
This method is based on an industry study that, as the EPA has noted, excluded data from gas-collection systems that were “not working well.” The EPA’s own reporting rules allow the same basic approach, which can cause companies collecting less gas due to a “malfunction or inefficiency” to “erroneously report decreasing emissions,” according to a 2025 study using satellite data by researchers at Harvard, NASA and Carbon Mapper. The researchers specifically examined two Republic landfills, and at one of them, the company reported declining emissions to the EPA even though satellite measurements showed they had risen over a four-year period.
The reporting gaps can be enormous. A study led by Hannah Nesser, now at Georgetown, found Republic facilities to be the No. 1 and No. 2 emitters among the roughly 70 large U.S. landfills the researchers observed over the course of 2019. The first, the National Serv-All Landfill in Indiana, was found to be releasing an astounding 13 times as much methane as what the company reported to the EPA. And that pattern repeated to varying degrees across three-quarters of the Republic landfills in the study. (McCarty wasn’t in the study, but according to measurements by Carbon Mapper, it emits more than twice what the company has reported.)
In response to questions about these studies, the Republic spokesperson said, “We stand by the sustainability results we’ve achieved.”
He also pointed to a letter from the National Waste and Recycling Association, a major trade group, questioning the accuracy of satellite measurements. It is a tactic from the playbook of another major climate polluter, the oil and gas industry, said Katherine Blauvelt of Full Circle Future, which advocates for cleaning up landfills.
“Satellites, peer-reviewed research studies and EPA inspectors on the ground all keep finding the same thing: unchecked and underreported methane emissions,” she said. “There’s a fire alarm going off and instead of getting out the extinguisher, the waste industry is blaming the smoke detector.”
Quietly Fighting Climate Policies
Last year, Gates published a blog post criticizing the “doomsday view” of global warming — a striking shift for someone who’d once warned of the failing ecosystems, mass migration and soaring mortality that could result from hotter temperatures. That led climate skeptics, including President Donald Trump, to say that Gates had admitted he was wrong. But Gates called that a “gigantic misreading.” While he believed more lives could be saved by improving global health, where he’d decided to shift his resources, he remained a “climate activist,” he told one audience.
Gates has tried to lead by example. In 2019, he sold his shares in oil and gas companies because, he later wrote, “I don’t want to profit if their stock prices go up because we don’t develop zero-carbon alternatives.” He kept flying by private jet, but he “offset” those emissions by buying credits from a company that removes carbon from the air. He has also called on other business leaders to “make sure that they’re not holding back” climate policies, even if those policies could cut into profits.
Republic has actively worked against such policies — and yet Gates, according to securities filings, has never sold a share.
In the final year of the Biden administration, the EPA announced a plan to update its landfill gas rules, which have changed little since the ’90s. Among other potential changes, the agency asked for comments on the newer technologies, such as satellites and drones, that research has found to be effective in monitoring and controlling methane pollution.
Some landfill operators were already experimenting with these innovations. But they wanted almost all of it to remain voluntary, according to a joint statement from the National Waste and Recycling Association and the Solid Waste Association of North America, both of which have Republic executives on their boards.
“We do not believe that any of these technologies are sufficiently developed,” the industry groups said, adding that the various innovations were “not cost-effective,” “reliable” or “transparent.”
The Republic spokesperson declined to comment on whether that lobbying goes against its climate commitments.
“A lot of the issue comes down to the profit of the corporate landfill operators and their resistance to do things that will eat into that,” said Darin Schroeder of the Clean Air Task Force, a climate advocacy group.
Gates’ press representatives didn’t respond to questions about whether he’s aware of the issues at Republic — or whether he has independently investigated the source of a fifth of his fortune. But ProPublica interviewed multiple former employees at Breakthrough Energy, Gates’ clean-tech investment arm, who all spoke on condition of anonymity. They each said they hadn’t even heard about his landfill holdings.
“I agree there’s a bit of a conundrum there,” said one high-ranking staffer who was laid off last year. But this person added, “Based on my time with him, I think he’s very serious about climate change. This isn’t a vanity thing for him.”
“My theory is that he probably doesn’t have much involvement in those investments,” said another laid-off staffer.
Gates’ investment managers, at least, can’t claim total ignorance. Larson and Thomas Handley, a Cascade senior adviser, both participate actively in Republic’s board discussions, according to a fellow director who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share details of those private discussions. The board also receives regular management briefings, including “high level” reports on the company’s lobbying and litigation over “practices we could do better,” this director said. (Larson didn’t return phone messages left by ProPublica at his office, and Cascade didn’t respond to a question about his and Handley’s involvement in Republic.)
It’s unclear if Gates himself ever learned of those reports. But he appears to have an even larger blind spot on the issue. The waste industry doesn’t fit neatly into his view of climate change as a problem to be solved mainly through technological breakthroughs. Innovations can help, but the root of the problem is the inescapable fact that, when organic waste decomposes in the absence of oxygen, methane is produced.
Properly managing the waste we’ve already buried is only the first step, said Riley Duren, the former NASA engineer who founded Carbon Mapper. “In parallel,” he said, “reduce food waste. Full stop. Then divert organic waste away from landfills to prevent future emissions.”
This isn’t a utopian fantasy. Germany started phasing out the landfilling of biodegradable waste in 1993, and its landfill methane emissions have plunged by more than 90%. (That compares to a decline of 40% in the U.S. over roughly the same period.) Within the U.S., California now requires food scraps and yard trimmings to be collected for composting or other uses, and state regulators found that the economic, climate and health benefits would ultimately outweigh the costs.
In its glossy sustainability reports, Republic says that “organics recycling plays an important role in our operations.” And in California, with its mandatory collection rules, the company processed close to a million tons of organic waste last year, much of that at composting facilities.
But that remains a small fraction of its business. Speaking to a different kind of audience — investors — Republic has described landfilling, along with dumpster collection, as its most profitable segments. So when the EPA floated a federal organics-diversion policy in 2024, the company, along with the rest of the landfill industry, opposed this, too. Their response invoked an argument often used by opponents to regulation: It should be left to the states to decide.
“It’s like you’ve got a mousetrap, and it catches mice,” said Robert Bullard, a Texas Southern University professor widely seen as the father of the environmental justice movement. “You’ve got a landfill, and it makes money — big money. So why tinker with it?”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Union Hits Local News Giant With Federal Labor Complaint After Reporter Is Fired
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The union representing editorial staff at the city’s biggest local newspaper chain says in a federal complaint that a reporter was fired in retaliation for union organizing, as the two sides head into their first bargaining session this week.
Renee DeLorenzo, who most recently covered business features and cultural issues at local news site QNS, was dismissed from her job on Oct. 29, the same day that Schneps Media acquired a competing Queens paper.
Schneps Union, which represents editorial staff at amNewYork and other neighborhood papers across the five boroughs and Long Island, filed a complaint with the National Labor Relations Board accusing Schneps Media of failing to inform the union of its decision to dismiss DeLorenzo and refusing the union’s attempts to discuss the matter further.
In a complaint submitted last week, Schneps Union suggested DeLorenzo’s firing was linked to her union activism: “Renee was an outspoken proponent of the Union during the unit’s recent organizing campaign, a fact the Employer knew.”
At her firing, DeLorenzo was told that she was being laid off as a result of the company’s acquisition of the Queens Chronicle, a competitor. But she told The City Reporter that as she became more involved in the union, appearing in two Instagram videos promoting their campaign, management retaliated, first reassigning her from a beat covering politics, and then firing her last month.
Schneps Media CEO Josh Schneps told The City Reporter “it would be inappropriate to comment on an issue now currently under review by the NLRB.”
Approximately 30 Schneps Media reporters voted to join Local 1096 of the NewsGuild of New York in July. Since then, they’ve accused Schneps of stonewalling negotiations for better wages, benefits and working conditions. The two sides are scheduled to meet for their first bargaining session on Thursday. Starting salaries for reporters range between $40,000 and $50,000 a year.
DeLorenzo said she was “in shock” and started “panicking” when she learned of her dismissal.
MORE: Follow The City Reporter’s Award-Winning Labor Coverage
Union leaders said they were blindsided by Schneps’ announcement last month that it had purchased a competitor, the Queens Chronicle, the same day the company laid off DeLorenzo, who had been working at QNS for about a year.
Schneps Media is owned by Victoria and Josh Schneps, a mother-son duo who jointly operate dozens of hyperlocal newspapers in New York City and Long Island. The company boasts 2 million weekly readers across its brands and formidable advertising prowess among its network of community papers.
The company has faced criticism for cozying up to the centers of political power in New York: for years it distributed a free, semi-regular paper, boosting then-Brooklyn Borough President Eric Adams to about 140,000 households in the borough. Postage for that paper, One Brooklyn, was paid for by taxpayers while Schneps collected advertising revenue.
Victoria Schneps founded the company in 1985 with the Queens Courier from her Bayside home “with four children, a dream and a prayer and $250,” she told the New York Times in 2017. She slowly pieced together a media empire including the Gay City News, Brooklyn Paper, the Bronx Times, the Long Island Press and others. In 2019, Schneps acquired and merged two free citywide papers, amNewYork and Metro New York, in a major coup for the company that led to layoffs at those papers.
The company fiercely resisted its staff’s union effort, first rejecting its request for voluntary recognition, forcing an election overseen by the NLRB, and then trying to toss six of its members out of the union by challenging their eligibility. Schneps hired Bond, Schoeneck & King, a notorious union-busting law firm.
Since launching its organizing push, Schneps Union has mounted escalating actions to move the company to bargain on a first contract. Last month, its members rallied outside a company gala celebrating Queens business leaders; the union also took credit for the company’s last-minute cancellation of a September gala celebrating labor leaders where the union also planned to protest.
MORE: Welcome to Hotel RAV4: The Brutal Commute of New Yorkers Priced Out to the Poconos
The union sometimes poked fun at management. In late July the union published a video on its Instagram page, starring DeLorenzo, where a cartoonish voice narrates portions of an email that Victoria Schneps sent to staff in the lead-up to the union election that month.
“Vote NO to the union. Give us a chance to address your concerns without a third party,” wrote Schneps.
DeLorenzo was hired a year ago as a general assignment reporter at QNS, an online publication covering Queens, where she worked on politics, elections and other stories. But this summer — around the same time she appeared in two pro-union Instagram videos — she was asked to cover arts and culture instead.
On Oct. 29, she was preparing to work on stories about street safety and the New York City Marathon when she received a message asking to meet immediately with her boss and the company’s HR director. Anticipating her firing, DeLorenzo said she twice and without success requested that a union representative be present for the meeting. She said she rejected an offer of two weeks’ severance because she would not sign a separation agreement she believed “would have signed away my right to speak about what happened.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/l.title: Lower Manhattanites Call for Parking Placard Purge
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/l.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/l.text:
New York City’s government-parking placard system needs to be torn down and rebuilt from first principles, starting in the illegal parking epicenter of Lower Manhattan, the Community Board 1 transportation committee charged last week.
“What exists today is not a rules-based permit program that is occasionally abused, but a culture of illegal parking in which a placard, vest, or badge on the dashboard signals that the law does not apply,” the committee wrote in a 10-page resolution [PDF] passed last Wednesday. “Such a system cannot be repaired — it must be replaced.”
Parking placards effectively give drivers carte blanche to dump their vehicles wherever they want — particularly in areas with a lot of municipal buildings, like the Financial District, which sits entirely within the area represented by Manhattan CB1.
“There are a lot of people with placards, and there are a lot of people who won’t enforce against placards as a courtesy,” said CB1 Transportation Co-Chair Betty Kay. “It ends up incredibly non-functional and pedestrians feel very unsafe.”
The CB1 committee endorsed a slate of prior efforts to rein in the seemingly immovable problem of placard parking. The full board will vote on the resolution on Nov. 24.
The list of measures backed by the resolution included state legislation authorizing automated camera parking enforcement and a City Council bill allowing citizen reporting of illegal parking. The city to should also follow the 11 recommendations laid out in a bombshell 2024 Department of Investigation report, the resolution said, such as eliminating NYPD’s so-called self-enforcement zones around precinct station houses, and replacing physical placards with a single digital system that ties each permit to a license plate.
Placard corruption complicates attempts by Mayor Mamdani to remake the streets to be the “envy of the world,” with bike lanes and bus lanes across the city routinely spoiled by unchecked illegal parking. 
“If we can’t take on that issue, we’re just not going to be able to do anything with our open space,” Jess Coleman, Kay’s co-chair, told Streetsblog. “The scale of the problem is just enormous.”
The civic push comes as Department of Transportation leaders have been looking into automating enforcement of parking in FiDi, after a complete abdication by the Police Department to rein in the illegal driving habits. 
The board members hope the new mayor will finally take on the placard class. 
“It just keeps getting worse and worse, and originally with the new mayor — who looked like he would make some new movement — there was some hope, but we haven’t seen any,” said Kay.
There are upwards of 100,000 official placards in circulation, issued by three agencies: NYPD, the Department of Transportation and the Department of Education. The permits technically only allow holders to park in No Parking areas, loading zones, metered spots without having to pay and zones signed for agency parking, according to city rules.
There is no publicly available database of who has these parking perks, and the NYPD recently rejected a Streetsblog request under Freedom Information Law to release its list of roughly 35,000 placards.
Streetsblog has documented how drivers with the permits have a disproportionately unsafe record on the road, including NYPD officers, city marshals and non-profits workers. 
“Leadership at the agencies and the elected officials are out of excuses and need to take action to finally clean this corruption off of our streets,” the anonymous yeomen behind the social media watchdog @placardabuse said in response to an emailed request for comment. “Deliberate failure and open fraud can no longer be an option in New York City.”
The placard abuse issue has flared up in FiDi repeatedly over the years. Illegal parking exacerbates the lack of space on the narrow and windy street grid that dates back to the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam.
Business leaders and politicos have urged Mamdani to make good on his campaign promise to reclaim space from cars in Manhattan’s oldest neighborhood. 
The mayor in the spring said he would tackle the city’s curb management with a dedicated office at DOT. The agency has since hired Laura MacNeil, who previously led a similar division at the U.S. Department of Transportation to head the New York City curb office, along with more than 30 employees and additional hiring “underway,” according to an agency rep. 
“Creating streets that are the envy of the world starts at the curb, because the curb lane is critical to a street’s success — if it isn’t working, the whole street isn’t working,” said DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn in a statement. “New York City’s curb regulations have not evolved quickly enough since 1950, when overnight street parking was legalized. The result is a curb that too often feels chaotic and unsafe, and our Office of Curb Management will lead the charge on modernizing how we use curb space.”
The agency did not respond to a separate request for comment about the CB1 placard resolution, and neither did City Hall, NYPD or DOE.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: White supremacist Nick Fuentes linked to college Republican group, records show
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jason Wilson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A college Republican coalition claiming 31 affiliated student groups in 14 states that attacked the Trump administration from the right routed its email through the same Microsoft 365 account as a company controlled by white nationalist Nick Fuentes.
Until Monday morning, Microsoft’s public sign-in records put the College Republican Patriot Coalition (CRPC)’s web domain in an account registered to NJF LLC, a Fuentes-managed company that also runs his personal website and online store.
By Monday evening, hours after the Guardian sent questions to Fuentes and the coalition, the domain no longer appeared in that account, and a Microsoft verification code had been deleted from its settings. Fuentes’s own domains remained in the account.
The organization has hinted at ties with Fuentes in the past, but no operational link has been definitively shown until now.
The revelation of an operational link between Fuentes and the highlights the inroads that Fuentes and his white nationalist “Groyper” movement have made among younger Republican activists and student organizations.
“[Fuentes] advises his young followers to join organizations that are closer to the conservative establishment, and he tells them to ‘hide their power level’ and maybe downplay their kind of most radical ideas,” said Ben Lorber, a senior research analyst at Political Research Associates, a non-profit that researches extremist groups.
The CRPC has not publicly named its leaders and is not associated with any known registered legal or organizational entity.
The Guardian contacted Nick Fuentes and the CRPC for comment.
In social media posts on Wednesday, CRPC blamed Tuesday’s midterm defeats on the Trump administration and the Republican party, saying young voters had received “a war on behalf of Israel, stunted deportations, and a flailing economy”. The statement listed 31 college Republicans groups, including chapters at the University of Florida, Clemson and Iowa State University, and state-level federations in Georgia, Maryland, New York, Tennessee and Virginia.
The coalition’s post-election messaging echoed attacks Fuentes made on Donald Trump before the vote. Fuentes posted on 26 October that Trump had “started a war with Iran that we are not only losing but which also destroyed the economy”. He also reportedly accused Trump of starting the war at Benjamin Netanyahu’s bidding, criticised his failure to deport millions and told viewers of his stream: “Normies don’t like war with Iran. Normies don’t like 3.7% inflation!”
But the group has never admitted the apparent affiliation with the far-right podcaster disclosed by the email link. Simon Dickerman, a former Fuentes associate, said in a 2022 live stream that the coalition “has to pretend like it has nothing to do with Nick Fuentes because Nick has made himself so radioactive to other people”, but the shared Microsoft account is the first confirmed operational link between Fuentes and the coalition.
The Guardian contacted Simon Dickerson for comment.
Many of the groups on the CRPC statement also belong to College Republicans of America (CRA), which is seeking recognition as the Republican party’s official student wing and has publicly contended with the more established College Republican National Committee over who should represent college activists. CRA’s political director, Kai Schwemmer, appears in the coalition’s Instagram posts this year.
The Guardian reported on Schwemmer’s appointment and his history of bigoted statements on live streams in March. (He claims he has abandoned his extremist views.)
The Guardian contacted CRA and Schwemmer for comment on CPRC’s shared email infrastructure with Fuentes’ company.
Lorber, the extremism expert, said of Fuentes’s so-called “America first” movement: “From the very beginning, Fuentes positioned America First as an alternative to Turning Point USA, and so it makes sense that he has a toehold in alternative campus conservative groups that position themselves as more radical than the mainstream GOP campus groups”.
‘A recent antisemitic gesture’
Student groups closely affiliated to CRPC have encountered local controversies, often over their promotion of white nationalist ideas, links to white nationalist activists, and endorsement of political candidates who have themselves voiced views similar to Fuentes’s.
The University of Florida’s College Republicans chapter has co-authored eight Instagram posts with CRPC this year, and was deactivated by the university in March after photographs reportedly appeared to show members flashing Nazi salutes and posing with Fuentes and Myron Gaines, the antisemitic influencer and podcaster.
The university said on social media that the Florida Federation of College Republicans had told it that the state group had “disbanded the local chapter of College Republicans”. The Guardian reported in March that the chapter’s state leadership had cited “a pattern of conduct that violated its rules and values, including a recent antisemitic gesture”.
The chapter sued for reinstatement, and was represented by Anthony Sabatini, the lawyer and former Republican state representative. A federal judge dismissed the Florida case in June after a bench trial, and the CRPC reportedly co-hosted the chapter’s first meeting after the ruling.
Sabatini, a Lake county commissioner who served in the Florida House from 2018 to 2022, headlined a 2022 conference in Tampa that was reportedly organized by former members of Fuentes’s America First Foundation, and reportedly called for a moratorium on immigration, the abolition of the Juneteenth national holiday that celebrates the end of slavery, and telling the crowd: “God bless the nationalist populist movement.”
The Guardian contacted Sabatini, UF College Republicans and the Florida Federation of College Republicans for comment.
‘Who cares about the lying media?’
The Florida chapter’s complaint argued that the university had acted in part because they had hosted the Republican “gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, a critic of Israel”. In a post co-authored with the CRPC, the chapter had called the Fishback event the “Largest Candidate event at UF in almost 10 years”.
Fishback, a 31-year-old investor, finished third in August’s Republican primary for governor. His campaign was peppered with controversies arising from his racist remarks.
He repeatedly referred to Byron Donalds, the Republican congressman who on Tuesday was elected Florida’s first Black governor, as a “slave”. In July, he wrote in a statement that a dispute had led Donalds “to chimp out on a 5’0 blonde woman in a Naples grocery store”, using a slur that likens Black people to apes. Fishback has reportedly said he was “not aware of the history” of the comparison.
On 28 October, Fishback floated a run for president in 2028. The College Republican chapters at Clemson and Georgia State, both on the CRPC’s list, hosted him on 29 and 30 October. On Wednesday, Fishback quote-posted the coalition’s election statement with the words “Great statement”.
The Guardian contacted Fishback for comment.
At the chapter’s first meeting after its return, the speakers included Marshall Rawson, the Republican nominee for a north Florida seat in the state house, who reportedly marched with the neo-Confederate League of the South at the 2017 Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. In a statement, Rawson said he had been “very active defending historical monuments” throughout his adult life.
“Who cares about the lying media when the largest and most active College Republican chapter in the United States is behind you!” Rawson posted on X that week, alongside a photo of himself with chapter members. The chapter’s post about the meeting, co-authored with the coalition, also thanked Tim Marden, the chair of the Alachua county Republican party and mayor of Newberry, who has publicly backed Rawson.
The Guardian contacted Rawson for comment.
In an email, Marden wrote: “I prefer to use my relationships as an opportunity to influence people in what I believe is a more positive direction. Life is not an all or nothing scenario.”
‘A non-English-speaking hellscape’
The Maryland Federation of College Republicans, which is on the coalition’s list and co-authored the Instagram version of Wednesday’s statement, invited the white nationalist Jared Taylor to speak at Salisbury University this spring.
Salisbury postponed the talk in March “based on public safety considerations”, saying that anticipated attendance, “counter-demonstrations, and related security needs” had “increased significantly”. It noted that the federation was “not an SU organization” but an outside group renting space on campus. The university’s College Democrats group had planned a protest for the day of the talk. The chair of the Maryland Republican party, Nicole Beus Harris, reportedly said the party had not been involved and condemned “the advertised event and the speaker’s despicable views”.
The talk went ahead on 29 April under heavy security, as dozens of protesters gathered outside at a demonstration organised by the Salisbury College Democrats. Taylor reportedly called the protesters “a bunch of big babies”.
The federation’s then chair, Colin McEvers, at that time a Salisbury student, reportedly introduced Taylor as someone who might have the key to “save our country, to keep it from becoming a non-English-speaking hellscape where white people are spit at, despised and persecuted”. College Republicans of America, which the Maryland federation joined in 2025, said it “did not endorse or sanction the Maryland event”, the Guardian reported in July.
A Facebook account with McEvers’ name in its URL now posts under the name Maryland White Republican Council. On Wednesday, it said: “It is time for the pro-White flank of the right wing that has been censored, suppressed, and cast aside by the establishment to legitimately take the reins of the GOP.”
The Guardian contacted the Maryland Federation of College Republicans for comment.
Asked about his call for “white advocacy” in the Republican party, McEvers responded in an email that despite a failed effort from the Maryland GOP to censure him, he was able “to secure the Republican nomination for Delegate in Maryland Legislative District 32, become a member of the Anne Arundel County Republican Central Committee, and there have been many people within the party, of all age groups, who have come to accept that White advocacy is both acceptable and necessary for Republican success”.
On the Maryland White Republican Council page, he wrote: “White people of all age groups failed to show up for the GOP this year, mostly among young voters. This proves that White people, namely young White men, are a legitimate voting bloc that the Republican Party must explicity advocate for; hence, the White Republican Council, which fundamentally promotes White Advocacy within the GOP in order to get Whites out to vote Republican.”
He denied any direct relationship with the CRPC.
‘A spectacular failure and a disaster’
One of the main public outlets for CRPC is its Instagram account, which features photos of faceless members carrying out flyer drops around the country, memes including racist depictions of Trump administration officials, and retrospective albums of face-to-face meet-ups, many of which redact the faces of members who presumably do not wish to be identified as adherents of Fuentes’s movement.
On the blacked-out faces, Political Research Associates’ Lorber said: “It makes it clear that they [are] associated with a radical right politics that they don’t necessarily want traced to their names and faces right now.”
Fuentes dropped out of Boston University after he was seen at the 2017 Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and built a following of young men, known as “Groypers,” through his livestreamed show, America First.
He was present at the riot at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021, though he did not enter the building, and in 2022 dined with Trump and the rapper Kanye West at Mar-a-Lago. Trump later said he did not know who Fuentes was.
After being banned from YouTube and many other platforms for hate speech, Fuentes was allowed back on X by Elon Musk in 2024. In October 2025 his podcast briefly became the highest-trending on Spotify, and Tucker Carlson gave him a friendly two-hour interview that the Guardian reported in November had set off “a bitter and widening civil war within the American right”. The president of the Heritage Foundation, Kevin Roberts, apologized after initially defending Carlson’s interview.
Fuentes backed Trump in 2016 and 2020, but has increasingly attacked him from the right over Israel and what he sees as the insufficient radicalism of the Republican party, especially on immigration.
Growing disillusionment has seen Fuentes urge his followers in recent months to disengage from elections or even to vote for Democrats. In February he reportedly told his audience: “Do not vote in the midterms. The Republicans have to lose.” When Trump went to war with Iran, Fuentes condemned the war and mocked people who had voted for Trump believing he represented a break with US foreign policy. On election day he posted: “Get out and vote Democrat today.” On election night, he reportedly said: “This is literally the worst case scenario for Republicans playing out tonight. And honestly, I could not be happier.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ‘I’m lucky to have grown up around artists’: Cora Sheibani on her path to becoming a jeweller
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Caroline Roux
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The jeweller Cora Sheibani lives in London and works from a small studio in Mayfair. She was raised in the art world—her father was the celebrated Swiss dealer Bruno Bischofberger, who collaborated with artists including Jean-Michel Basquiat, Andy Warhol and Francesco Clemente. As a dyslexic, Cora did not embrace reading as a child, but now she explains why it is her window on the world.
For me, luxury is about having time. As you get older, and as the world gets faster, there’s never enough of it. In an ideal world I would travel more, both for work and for pleasure; and visit exhibitions, galleries and museums. But I also have a son who needs a lot of my attention—he is very autistic, with severe ADHD—and so I travel through books, and reading has become a way to experience culture, art and creativity.
I’m lucky to have grown up around artists and people who didn’t follow the conventional path. Francesco Clemente is a close family friend, and his daughters are more like my cousins. We’re close to the Schnabel family; Jean Tinguely was my sister’s godfather. So even though I barely read as a child—it was just too hard—I made myself study liberal arts before I became a jeweller. Only after university I started reading German literature. It’s my mother language, after all.
Gold, the friendly metal
I’ve always loved jewellery. When I was 15, I worked in my parents’ gallery over the summer, and spent half my earnings on two rings, both bronze, one Greek, one Roman. Now I work primarily with gold: at first it was because yellow is my favourite colour, but you also learn that gold is the friendliest metal to handle.
It was hard to be taken seriously as a jeweller at the beginning. People thought it was a hobby, and I really had to be patient and persevere—that’s something I can do, that dyslexia taught me. Now I’m incredibly proud of my work and how successful the business has become.
Jewellery books and especially exhibition catalogues are a real inspiration. An essay by Amin Jaffer in the catalogue for Joyaux Dynastiques, a show at the Hôtel de la Marine in Paris last year of royal jewels, explained the meaning of a particular kind of nine-gem Indian jewel. It really helped me with a commission I’d just received from a client for a piece using nine different coloured stones.
Collector’s treat
I buy some early editions from Shapero Rare Books in Mayfair—I pass it every time I go from the gym to the studio and can’t resist taking a look. I just finished reading Crime and Punishment by Fyodor Dostoyevsky in its first English translation by Frederick Whishaw. It’s very rare, a real collector’s item. It’s generally thought that translations have improved, but there’s something special about reading a contemporaneous one. It’s a rich experience that takes you back in time.
Once a month, I get together with my book club. There’s only three of us, and we don’t all have to read the same book. Instead, we talk about what we are each reading. We meet, usually on a Friday morning, at Daria Buchman’s house, and have a breakfast of scrambled eggs. Daria, with her husband Dimitry, sponsors the International Booker Prize, so she is really on top of every new novel. She hadn’t read Beloved by Toni Morrison, though. I’d read three works that talked about slavery from different regional angles—Beloved, Crooked Plow by Itamar Vieira Junior and Ben Okri’s The Last Gift of the Master Artists—and recommended to my group they did the same. You begin to understand a bit better how the lives of people from one continent evolved in such different (and at times similar) ways. On the other hand, Daria made me read the wonderful Wuthering Heights. I wouldn’t have done it if she hadn’t insisted.

https://gothamist.com/news/emerald.title: Rent-stabilized buildings hit auction block, despite Mamdani’s efforts to intervene
https://gothamist.com/news/emerald.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/emerald.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s effort to steer the sale of crumbling apartment buildings to tenant-approved owners has suffered another setback. Dozens of deteriorating properties in East Harlem that City Hall tried to deliver into the hands of an affordable housing developer are instead heading to the auction block in Manhattan starting Tuesday afternoon.
Mamdani administration officials had supported a bid by the firm Spatial Equity to purchase the 38-building portfolio before its lenders auctioned it off. The properties were previously owned by bankrupt real estate investment firm Emerald Equities Group and contain a combined 850 mostly rent-stabilized apartments.
But tenants and attorneys involved in the potential deal say negotiations fell through, and the banks and other financial institutions that control roughly $250 million in mortgage loans will proceed with foreclosure sales for each individual building over the course of three auction days.
Cara Polte, a resident of one of the buildings on East 103rd Street and the co-founder of the East Harlem Tenant Union, said tenants will continue advocating for a new buyer committed to resolving thousands of housing code violations that have plagued the buildings for decades,
“We’re definitely not stopping,” Polte said. “But this obscures the pathway a little.”
Mayor's Office to Protect Tenants Director Cea Weaver said the foreclosure sale isn't the end of the city's effort to force owners to improve conditions in the building.
"The Mayor's Office is proud to support the tenants of the East Harlem Tenants Union as they organize for better living conditions and more control over the future of their homes," Weaver said in a written statement.
The stalled negotiations mark a new obstacle to the Mamdani administration's efforts to influence transactions involving financially distressed and derelict buildings – a priority he described on his first day in office.
Hours after his inauguration, Mamdani announced that he had directed city lawyers to attempt to block an unrelated bankruptcy sale of nearly 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments. That unprecedented intervention ultimately failed to stop the transaction, but it did help compel the new buyer to commit to resolving hundreds of outstanding violations in the buildings.
Mamdani has also championed other policies meant to help nonprofits and some private developers acquire buildings, including a measure known as the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act that would give some groups a head start on buying financially distressed properties before they hit the open market. His predecessor, Mayor Eric Adams, vetoed a previous version of the legislation before the City Council approved a revised measure last month.
Polte said the auction complicates the tenants’ goal of turning her building and four others along East 103rd Street into a “community land trust” – a form of nonprofit ownership that gives tenant groups power over housing decisions or allows residents to purchase their units at permanently affordable rates.
“I don't think anyone has a clear vision about what comes next because the lender was not willing to play ball with negotiations,” Polte said.
Spatial Equity had attempted to purchase the buildings but had its initial $68 million bid – roughly a quarter of the debt – for the portfolio rejected, City Limits reported in July.
Polte said the lenders also rejected a $110 million offer from Spatial Equity last month and have not communicated about the amount they would accept.
“It’s been difficult to try to negotiate or even hear what would get them to say yes,” she said.
The mortgage loans are controlled by a trust managed by a variety of banks, as well as the lender Sabal Investment Holdings. The loans were partially insured by Freddie Mac.
Sabal executives did not respond to requests for comment on Monday.
Spatial Equity principal Teg Sethi declined to comment on the failed purchase.
Roughly 1,600 buildings with rent-stabilized apartments are facing financial distress, meaning their expenses outpace revenue from rent, according to data published by the city’s Rent Guidelines Board earlier this year. Landlord groups say sharp restrictions on rental increases, exacerbated by the board’s recent two-year rent freeze, have made ownership untenable and have warned of a dramatic rise in foreclosures.
Tenant advocates counter that many property owners facing financial problems, like Emerald Equities, took on too much debt with a plan to pay it back by raising rents before new laws limited their ability to do so.
The East Harlem efforts hint at the complexity of housing deals that involve those rent-regulated buildings now at risk of foreclosure.
“These things are very complicated,” said David Lebenstein, an executive managing director specializing in nonprofit purchases at Cushman & Wakefield. “Every deal has to be analyzed given the cash flow, the rent rolls and the occupancy levels.”
Lebenstein said lenders of rent-stabilized apartment buildings are often willing to wipe away debt if it means salvaging some value.
“They recognize they’re underwater,” he said. “If they’re owed $100 million and they get $70 million, that’s a victory.”
That does not appear to be the case with the former Emerald portfolio.
The upcoming foreclosure auction is the latest twist in the tangled history of the East Harlem apartment buildings.
Emerald Equities acquired the 38 buildings for $350 million in 2016 and began raising rents on the stabilized apartments to increase the company’s revenue and pay off its debts – a strategy allowed by state law at the time and common in gentrifying sections of the city.
Emerald took out another $180 million loan on the buildings in December 2018, just six months before state lawmakers passed a package of tenant protection measures that outlawed many of the tactics Emerald used to increase rents.
Lenders foreclosed on the properties in 2024, and Emerald filed for bankruptcy a year later. An investigation by the New York Attorney General’s Office and the state’s Division of Homes and Community Renewal found the company had also illegally lifted 21 apartments out of the rent stabilization system.
A previous owner, British investment firm Dawnay Day Group, had pursued a similar strategy for deregulating apartments and raising rents nearly a decade earlier before it too declared bankruptcy in 2009.
The procession of owners has left the buildings in disrepair. A retaining wall collapsed in the rear of buildings on East 103rd St. earlier this year, days before Mamdani and Cea Weaver, the head of his tenant protection office, visited to meet with tenants in March.
When Gothamist toured the buildings in April, a single boiler serviced three of the properties and one first-floor tenant covered a gaping hole in his kitchen with rotting plywood.
Attorney Matthew Latterner said conditions have only worsened for renters. He said he and tenants “appreciate that the Mamdani administration is intervening,” even if the efforts have so far failed to influence the lenders.
He said he would immediately sue whoever takes over the buildings following the foreclosure sales to demand they improve conditions at buildings that totaled more than 2,300 housing code violations in April.
“Our number one priority has been to fight for these tenants and we’re going to keep doing that no matter who the owner of the buildings are,” Latterner said. “Whoever the new owners are, we’re prepared to sue the living bejeezus out of them on day one to make sure tenants get the repairs they need and keep their families safe.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/s.title: ‘Sociopaths’ Illegally Blow Safety Redesign Outside Greenpoint School
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/s.author: Sam Brule
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/s.text:
A crossing guard and a stone are all that prevents drivers from blowing off the city's new traffic diverter in front of a school on Driggs Avenue. Photos: Sam Brule (main), Noel Hidalgo (inset)
The newly redesigned low-traffic intersection in front of a Greenpoint school is mostly successful — except for some “sociopaths,” that is.
That’s how one local activist referred to the drivers who still plow through the city Department of Transportation’s traffic diverter that, at least on paper and in plastic, prevents drivers from using Driggs Avenue as a neighborhood cut-through. The diverter is an increasingly common tool for reducing car traffic in residential communities, especially near schools like PS 110.
But neighbors are still noticing broken plastic most mornings, the result of some drivers who simply won’t play by the new rules.
“You can’t prevent someone who’s just that much of a sociopath,” said Carrie Hill, a school parent and advocate.
Despite the few drivers who cut through, Hill said the redesign, which was installed last month, was mostly successful.
“It’s slowing traffic down,” she’s aid. “I’m hoping that after a couple times of someone making this error and being like, ‘Oh, this isn’t a cut-through anymore,’ they will just use the suggested route.”
For now, though, some of Hill’s “sociopaths” have been driving over (and around) the flexible bollards to save time. Streetsblog checked out the scene on Monday and, as if on cue, a westbound Tesla driver drove onto the sidewalk to continue straight on Driggs, now an illegal move.
This reporter was so shocked by the driver’s high-speed move that he didn’t have time to get an in-focus photo of the offender. Not one minute later, a class of young children from P.S. 110 took that same path after an outing at the nearby McGolrick Park.
One local said the diverter makes the roadway a bit “more chaotic” for now, but thinks it’s just a matter of time before drivers become accustomed to the changes (just as they did on the 39th Avenue bike boulevard in Queens).
“Right now it looks like, at the very least, people have not gotten used to it,” said Liam McCormick of Little Dokebi.
The DOT says the diverter will reduce cut-through traffic in the neighborhood, which then makes streets safer.
“The traffic diverter at Driggs Avenue and Monitor Street puts the safety of students, pedestrians, and cyclists first by limiting cut through traffic while maintaining necessary local access,” a DOT spokesperson said.
But the agency offered no comment about the psychology of drivers who are abusing the new road design, but said it will add planters and granite blocks to further encourage drivers to obey the new traffic pattern.
The diverter and other improvements nearby were a long time coming. In 2021, beloved PS 110 teacher Matthew Jensen was killed by a hit-and-run driver on McGuinness Boulevard, just blocks from the school. Days after, then-Mayor Bill de Blasio promised extensive safety improvements, which were initially blocked by his successor, but reinstated by Mayor Mamdani.
In 2023, tragedy in the form of a driver struck and killed cyclist Teddy Orzechowski, 73, at Monitor and Driggs right outside the school.
Since 2024, there have been 36 reported crashes on just the eight blocks of Driggs Avenue between Meeker and McGuinness, according to city stats, injuring 11 people.
The killings emboldened activists and city officials to take on the entrenched car culture as well as the Adams administration, which took bribes from a local business owner to stall the safety improvements, according to law enforcement authorities.
“This neighborhood has been a victim of Robert Moses since the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway was put in,” said Noel Hidalgo, a resident of the neighborhood who has been tracking reckless drivers at the diverter. “These are neighborhood streets and they should be for neighborhood vehicles.
Hidalgo said the changes are largely working. “This weekend was one of the most peaceful in the neighborhood,” he said.
One thing everyone could agree on, was that the intersection was a good first step to a true low-traffic neighborhood. The other steps? The DOT closed slip lanes from high-speed Meeker Avenue onto Engert Avenue and from McGuinness Boulevard onto Newton Street.
Some drivers still complain that they need to find different routes, but none of the changes are permanent. Besides, drivers can access every location that they previously could access, just from another direction.
“People get way too wrapped up in like, ‘What if it’s going to be terrible?'” Hill said. “Try it. If it works, it works. If it doesn’t, it doesn’t. And we try something else.”
The only thing that’s permanent, after all, is road violence, but that, too, could change.
Sam Brule is a senior at The New School. He’s previously worked at the New School Free Press, the Sopris Sun in Colorado, and most recently amNY. When he’s not writing, he works as a bike messenger.
