https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | People mock Renoir, but painting joy is no easy feat
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ben Luke
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
“These young people are enjoying life, the beautiful weather, the morning sun shining through the foliage; what do they care about the rest of humanity?” So wrote Georges Rivière, writer and champion of Pierre-Auguste Renoir, of the French painter’s Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876), one of the highlights of Renoir and Love at London’s National Gallery (until 31 January 2027). “They are happy,” Rivière added, “and these are the words that come to mind of all who see this charming painting. None has given me more pleasure than this one.”
“Beautiful”, “happy”, “pleasure”—these terms sit uncomfortably with what John Elderfield, former curator at New York’s Museum of Modern Art, described to the painter Howard Hodgkin as “the modern attraction to difficulty”. Paul Perrin, co-curator of the Renoir show, writes in its catalogue that the “blissful couples and air of happiness” in Renoir’s 1860s to 1880s paintings have made them “immensely popular” yet also prompted “contempt for their apparent lack of complexity and depth”. His assessment was newly confirmed by the critic Eddy Frankel, writing recently in The Guardian: “I’ve hated his work for decades.” For him, Renoir only appeals “when his nudes look like a super-psychedelic, ultra-horny version of Rubens”.
Renoir himself understood that milder emotions irked critics. “It’s hard to get people to admit that a painting can be great painting and still be happy,” he wrote. But love, as framed in this show, has multiple forms, among them empathy. Specialists suggest that Renoir was not ignorant of the “anguished or miserable” elements of life that Perrin describes as being essential to many conceptions of modernity. When Rivière wrote about young people dancing in ignorance of the rest of humanity, he didn’t need to add that happiness can be fleeting and is often most intensely felt at its briefest.
The writings of Baudelaire, and the paintings of Renoir’s peers like Degas and Manet, tell us how visible hardship would have been at the time. And Renoir, unlike those two peers, grew up in working-class Paris, so had lived experience that gave him, as Rivière wrote, “a keen sense of pity” for the poverty of “Montmartre families”. But Renoir clearly felt that if he did want to create great, happy art, he had to avoid troubling subject matter: “There are enough annoying things in life for us not to make more of them,” he said.
Rococo pleasures
Another factor in Renoir’s commitment to joy and play was his deep admiration for what he saw as the golden age of French painting: the Rococo. As Mary Morton writes in the Renoir and Love catalogue, the work of artists like Jean-Antoine Watteau and Jean-Honoré Fragonard “embodied graceful pleasure and a harmonious relationship between the human figure and nature”.
Renoir shares this infatuation with Rococo with a contemporary artist who I think has come closer than anyone else to creating a great art of happiness: Ragnar Kjartansson, whose exhibition Weekdays in Arcadia opens at the Goodwood Art Foundation in Chichester this month (26 November-12 April 2027). Kjartansson told me in 2017 that his fascination with the period lies in the “contrast of really intellectual minds and… silly-billy nothingness”. At Goodwood, he will show No Tomorrow (2022), a video installation that extends his 2017 dance collaboration with choreographer Margrét Bjarnadóttir and composer Bryce Dessner. When I saw the original ballet, in which a group of female performers dressed in jeans and white T-shirts dance with acoustic guitars for the duration of the piece, one moment made me instantly grin: arranged in a grid, every other dancer would take it in turns to leap into the air while the performer next to them stood still, prompting a joyous effect of corporeal effervescence. Kjartansson told me he and Bjarnadóttir felt No Tomorrow was “a Watteau painting in disguise”.
Kjartansson’s most famous piece, The Visitors (2012), a video installation in which he and his friends perform a song in different rooms of a half-derelict mansion in New York State, provokes a similarly ecstatic response from its viewers. But Kjartansson was conscious, perhaps with the reputation of artists like Renoir and of the Rococo period in mind, that he was “in danger of becoming the feel-good artist”. And indeed, part of what makes him such a compelling figure is that the light of his work always comes with copious amounts of shade. At Goodwood, he is interested in “the idea of encountering monuments to sorrow and shakiness in the woodlands”. And yet, I suspect he will find ways to make us smile amid the melancholy.
Achieving joy in art is difficult. Perhaps the most perceptive observer of this fact is one of Renoir’s artistic heirs, Henri Matisse, who spoke of the anguish behind the pleasure in his work: “this happiness, this light and this serene wisdom that [have] seemingly become mine are sometimes earned through the harshness of adversity”. Matisse and, I think, Renoir—like Kjartansson—knew that achieving happiness is a deadly serious business.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Artist Sun Xun’s new animated film was made over a decade from thousands of artworks
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Mark Asch
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A phrase cinephiles sometimes use to describe a visually beautiful movie is “every frame a painting”, but that is rarely more true than in Magic Atlas, a feature-length animation film by the Chinese painter Sun Xun, which was awarded a Special Jury Prize at the recently concluded Tokyo International Film Festival.
Sun spent ten years, on and off, working on the film, which he largely self-financed; rather than employ professional animators, he employed hundreds of art students (in one interview, he says 500 over the course of production) to produce individual frames, in a sort of supersized workshop model. Each frame has its own tactile quality, particularly in the sequences made in the unconventional animation medium of woodcut. When a shaft of line streams through a high window, piercing the blackness of an otherwise dark room, you can see the individual carving marks scored into the wood, which across several dozen frames dance and shimmer like the scales of a carp moving through a clear pond.
Magic Atlas is a visual artist’s film, and as a storyteller, Sun thinks like a visual artist, proceeding by association, symbolism and dream logic. The magic atlas of the film’s title is a map to the mystic realms traversed by an explorer in a steampunk flying contraption. After the kaleidoscopic imagery of the film’s opening overture, he spends most of the film in one such world, a coal-mining kingdom called Luocha, where he is imprisoned on the eve of a magic festival. Maps are illegal in Luocha, as are memories. The authoritarian logic of the film is definitely allegorical, but the allegory is hard to pin down; the land’s emperor speaks of forced labour and industrial quotas, in perhaps a Maoist register, but the power behind the throne is an Orwellian cabal of anthropomorphised talking animals, who smoke cigars like colonial lords, and the state’s surveillance protocol is carried out by an army of mosquitos with cameras for heads—a swarm, if not a flock (or Flock).
In a manner similar to Chinese cinema’s emerging mystic-virtuoso Bi Gan, Sun is applying poetic ideas derived from Eastern spirituality about the oneness of all things, the many stories that are all one story. The film opens with a quote from Avatamsaka Sutra invoking “the past, the present, the future lying in the present”, and ends with a lengthy monologue, voiced by Sun himself, delivered by a hieroglyphic eagle. Its ideas about the transmigration of souls are mirrored in the mix of animation styles—the film spends most of its time in Luocha, which is rendered in monumental black-and-white woodcuts and illustrations reminiscent of Rockwell Kent, but also jumps at times to different styles that are each a world in and of themselves.
There are homages to Salvador Dalí and Pieter Bruegel the Elder; a segment in riotous pastels with the Jazz Age voluptuousness of Reginald Marsh and a segment animated in crayon and magic marker by Sun’s Instagram followers during the Covid-19 pandemic; and segments informed by Sun’s own research into different styles of traditional Chinese art, including, he said in a post-screening interview, Dunhuang murals, Song dynasty painting, and multiple styles of calligraphy.
Exhibitions of Magic Atlas materials including woodcuts and concept art have shown at the Times Museum of Guangdong, and additional shows are planned in the United States (where Sun is represented by Sean Kelly Gallery). Sun received initial seed funding from Judith Neilson, the Australian philanthropist and founder of the Asian-focused White Rabbit Gallery, whose current show, up through November 15, includes Magic of Atlas – Luocha: An Infinite Journey, an 8ft-high, 52ft- long, 13-panel woodcut relief depicting images from the story in a scroll that can be stopped and started by the eyes of the viewer passing across the work—a static form of visual narrative that can be traced back to antiquity, long before still and moving images diverged.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump-era lawlessness must be prosecuted. Our new group is working to end the impunity | Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The Democrats’ midterm victory was resounding, but it will not be enough to re-establish the rule of law in the United States.
The basic principle that even the president and his officials and cronies are subject to the law has been profoundly undermined by Donald Trump through unchecked ICE violence, apparently large-scale official corruption, and frequent defiance of the law.
Democratic-run congressional committees can investigate and expose lawlessness but cannot prosecute the criminality they uncover. More is needed.
Many people equate democracy with elections, but they are not enough. A president can be elected, his policies can be publicized by the media and debated by the public, his legislative proposals can require the assent of a majority of lawmakers, but if the president holds himself above the law, a nation ceases to be a democracy. That is what has been at stake in Trump’s second term.
The American system delegates many of the responsibilities for upholding the rule of law to an independent judiciary. If a president violates our rights, we can file a civil suit in court and hope a judge orders the president to stop.
But if the president or his allies engage in criminality, the American system has a built-in weakness. Some countries empower prosecutors to be independent, akin to a judge. But in the United States, the prosecutor for any federal crime is an employee of the Department of Justice. It is headed by the attorney general, who is nominated by and serves at the pleasure of the president.
In other words, the president can decide which criminal conduct in his administration will be prosecuted – and which will not.
Because the president’s ability to control the Department of Justice could put him and his friends above the law, presidents traditionally have exercised that power with restraint. While setting broad priorities, most presidents deferred to the judgment of their attorney general. But not Trump.
Trump has weaponized his justice department, pursuing his perceived political enemies while neglecting crimes by his allies, who have often enjoyed effective impunity. They have little to fear from Trump’s politicized prosecutors.
The result has been increasingly brazen behavior – seemingly corrupt deals that few past officials would have dared to make, and arbitrary violence by ICE and others that is excused rather than investigated.
The Rule of Law Project, a new civic group of which I am a founding board member, seeks to end that impunity. We are hiring former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to investigate allegations of corruption and abuse by government officials and their accomplices that the current justice department is ignoring.
We have attracted an extraordinary set of past public servants. Many have served in the justice department, which has been decimated in the second Trump administration. We don’t know their political views and haven’t asked. What we know is that they are eager to continue their work in a different capacity.
The Rule of Law Project operates from the premise that criminal cases are more likely to be pursued if a prosecutor can be handed a case file that is largely ready for action. We will do the legwork of interviewing witnesses, collecting documents, and analyzing the results, with the aim of putting cases together while the evidence is fresh.
We won’t have subpoena power, wiretaps, or a grand jury, but many cases can be built with witnesses who voluntarily cooperate. Indeed, in the most sensitive cases, cooperating witnesses are essential.
Until we have a president and attorney general who believe in the rule of law, we plan to present these ready-made cases to state and local prosecutors, who are not subject to federal control. Many would like to uphold the law but lack the investigative resources to take on these cases on their own.
I have seen the power of such investigations in my global work. For the mass atrocities under Syria’s former president Bashar al-Assad, for example, the international criminal court did not have jurisdiction, and Syrian prosecutors took instructions from the dictator.
The only option was national courts around the world exercising what is known as universal jurisdiction. But a typical prosecutor there would have no clue about how to prosecute torture, executions, or forced disappearances in Syria, let alone the resources to advance such a case.
That’s why, with the encouragement of Human Rights Watch, the UN general assembly established the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism (IIIM) for Syria. A similar mechanism has been established to address atrocities by the military junta in Myanmar.
The IIIM, based in Geneva, is essentially a prosecutorial team without a court. They have no capacity to bring prosecutions, but they prepare them. That way, when an abusive Syrian official shows up in a national jurisdiction, local prosecutors have a place to turn for the evidence they need.
That happened in the German city of Koblenz, where a former Syrian intelligence officer was convicted of crimes against humanity for overseeing a detention facility where torture was pervasive. He was sentenced to life in prison. The IIIM has contributed to 269 distinct investigations and prosecutions in 16 different jurisdictions, including in France, Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the United States.
The Rule of Law Project will play a similar role in the United States. It will develop the prosecution-ready cases that make it harder for available prosecutors to say they are too busy to take on Trump officials’ illegality.
The project will also make it harder to look forward, not back, as Barack Obama erroneously did with respect to the torture and abuse of the George W Bush administration’s “war on terrorism”. In May 2009, I met with Obama to make the case that the failure to hold perpetrators accountable would lead to future abuses. He thought it would be too divisive.
Sadly, that precedent of impunity is contributing to Trump’s lawlessness today, such as the summary execution of people in alleged drug boats that he has ordered in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
This is not a vindictive exercise. The project seeks not to even scores but to uphold the law. It will apply an “ordinary times” test – what would a prosecutor do, regardless of the party holding the White House, if they simply analyzed the facts and applied the law free of the politicized limitations of the Trump administration?
What if Trump pardons the culpable before he steps down? That is unlikely to save his accomplices, because the president’s pardon power does not extend to state crimes. Much of the criminality that merits investigation can be characterized as an offense under either federal or state law.
It is extraordinary that the United States needs a group like the Rule of Law Project. But these are extraordinary, even unprecedented, times.
To salvage America’s democracy, it is not enough to vote out corrupt and abusive officials. They should also be prosecuted to re-establish the rule of law.
We cannot count on the federal government under Trump to perform this role. We as citizens must take it on.
- Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.title: Repression | Mexiko: Offensive gegen Zapatisten-Gemeinden
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.author: Luz Kerkeling
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.text:
- Politik
- Repression
Mexiko: Offensive gegen Zapatisten-Gemeinden
Der Staat und die Eliten versuchen, den indigenen Widerstand gegen die umstrittene Autobahn »Route der Maya-Kulturen« zu brechen.
Das renommierte Menschenrechtszentrum Fray Bartolomé de las Casas (Frayba) aus dem südmexikanischen Bundesstaat Chiapas schlägt Alarm: »Wir prangern öffentlich die schwerwiegende Gefahrensituation an, mit der Gemeinden von EZLN-Unterstützer*innen auf ihren wiedergewonnenen Territorien konfrontiert sind«, heißt in einem aktuellen Kommuniqué.
Mehrfach wurden in den vergangenen Tagen Basisgemeinden der sozialrevolutionären Bewegung um die Zapatistische Armee zur nationalen Befreiung (EZLN) bedroht und schikaniert. Teile ihrer Ländereien wurden okkupiert, gemeinschaftlich angebaute Maisfelder und Waldstücke zerstört sowie Rinder geraubt. Es kam auch zu Geldstrafen oder Verhaftungen von Personen, die ihre Kinder in die autonomen zapatistischen Schulen geschickt oder die das unabhängige Gesundheitssystem der EZLN genutzt haben.
All diese Praktiken stehen laut Frayba »im Widerspruch zur Regierungsrhetorik, da es sich um eine Reihe von Maßnahmen zur Aufstandsbekämpfung handelt, die zu einem schwerwiegenden Vorfall wie dem Massaker von Acteal führen könnten.« 1997 wurden in diesem Dorf 45 – explizit pazifistische – pro-zapatistische Bewohner*innen von paramilitärischen Kräften ermordet. Sie hatten direkte Kontakte zu Bundesarmee und -polizei. Die in Sichtweite stationierten staatlichen Sicherheitskräfte griffen nicht ein.
Regierung will freie Bahn für die Autobahn
»Diese Angriffe implizieren eine direkte Bedrohung der Unversehrtheit der Gemeinden, ihres Territoriums und der Ausübung ihrer Autonomie«, so das Zentrum weiter. Sie »finden im Kontext des voranschreitenden Baus der Autobahn San Cristóbal-Palenque – offiziell bekannt als ›Route der Maya-Kulturen‹ – statt, sowie im Zusammenhang mit den fortwährenden Angriffen, die bereits die Vollversammlung der Kollektive der zapatistischen autonomen Regierungen (ACGAZ) öffentlich gemacht haben«.
Aktuell liegen Berichte vor, nach denen der Bau dieser auf Tourismus und Extraktivismus ausgelegten Schnellstraßentrasse intakten Regenwald zerstört und den kleinbäuerlichen Gemeinden durch Korruption, Desinformation und Gewaltandrohung aufgezwungen wird. Selbst eigene staatliche Umweltgesetze wurden laut Frayba nicht ausreichend befolgt. Auch die von Mexiko unterzeichnete ILO-Konvention 169 über indigene Rechte wird demnach permanent verletzt. Vermessungs- und Bauarbeiten mit schwerem Gerät werden auch auf Flächen der Zapatistas weitergeführt.
Spiel mit dem Feuer
Für diese sind das Provokationen der Eliten in einem größeren Kontext: »Dieses Jahr im Juli haben wir unsere Absicht bekanntgegeben, nach Mexiko-Stadt zu reisen, um uns mit den Gruppen, Kollektiven oder Gruppenlosen aus den suchenden Familien zu treffen. Um ihrer Geschichte und der Geschichte ihrer Vermissten zuzuhören: Gruppe für Gruppe, Familie für Familie.«
In ihrem Kommuniqué vom 3. November stellt die Vollversammlung der Zapatistischen Autonomen Regierungen ACGAZ klar: »Die Regierenden spielen mit dem Feuer. Wir wollen keinen Aufruhr machen, wir können es aber. Diese Provokationen zwingen uns nicht, die Reise abzusagen.«
Die Zapatistas werfen der Regierung vor, die Menschenrechtsverletzungen zu dulden und teilweise sogar zu protegieren: »Diejenigen, die provozieren, sind Mitglieder des Kartells um Mario Delgado, Staatsminister für öffentliche Bildung. Der Haupt-Auftragskiller ist Eusebio Cruz Ruiz, der sich als Lehrer präsentiert und sagt, er erhält von Delgado direkte Anordnungen.«
Die »Reise für das Leben« geht weiter
Frayba fordert angesichts der Ereignisse von der Regierung die sofortige Einstellung aller Angriffe auf die zapatistischen Gemeinden sowie die uneingeschränkte Achtung ihres Rechts auf Autonomie und Selbstbestimmung. Ein klares Zeichen für die Bedeutung der aktuellen Mobilisierung der EZLN ist die Solidarität der unabhängigen Gewerkschaft »Nationalkoordination der Bildungsarbeiter*innen« (CNTE) mit »unseren Geschwistern Zapatistas«. In der CNTE sind rund 500.000 Aktivist*innen, hauptsächlich Lehrkräfte, organisiert.
Bei den geplanten zapatistischen Aktivitäten handelt es sich um die zweite Etappe der »Reise für das Leben«, das »Kapitel Mexiko«. Im Rahmen des »ersten Kapitels« der »Reise für das Leben« hatten 2021 über 170 Delegierte der EZLN und des Nationalen Indigenen Kongresses CNI über 250 Städte im »widerständigen Europa« besucht und sich intensiv mit anti-systemischen linken Gruppen ausgetauscht. Zum aktuellen Vorhaben in Mexiko-Stadt ab Dezember stellte Subcomandante Moisés von der EZLN klar: »Wir werden kommen, ob sie es wollen oder nicht.«
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: This small Alaska town is swamped by cruise ship visitors every summer. But what happens when they all go home?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Molly McCluskey in Skagway, Alaska
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
October comes to the small Alaska coastal town of Skagway like a sigh. The shops that were bustling throughout the crazed tourist season are reducing their opening hours or beginning to close. The hordes of employees sleeping in overcrowded bunkhouses are leaving or have left.
The crowds of cruise passengers who have filled the streets since April, wearing lanyards emblazoned with the names of their ships, have dwindled to a trickle. Soon, they will all be gone. Snow is visible on the nearby mountains.
What is left after the season has ended and the last ship has disappeared from sight is a year-round community of about 1,100 people – on paper, at least – and the concern that, as the demands of the cruise ship industry grow, life in this small town is becoming more and more difficult.
“The year-round economy, the year-round population is one of my bigger concerns as someone who lives here,” says Skagway’s mayor, Orion Hanson. “What does Skagway do without a coffee shop to congregate in or without a restaurant open all the time? We don’t have a diner any more.”
Two local restaurants stay open, albeit with limited hours outside the cruise ship season. But the Sweet Tooth cafe, once a longstanding year-round diner, is gone. It is now a storefront for Diamonds International, a tax-free jewellery store that partners with cruise lines for onboard retail and shops in ports that open seasonally.
At the height of the Klondike gold rush, Skagway was the largest town in Alaska, with a population of about 10,000 people. In 1900, it became Alaska’s first official city. But by 1910, as the gold rush subsided, the population had dwindled to about 600 people.
It took a decade for that dramatic swing. Now, as one of the most popular cruise ship destinations in the world, it can happen in a single day, when thousands can flood on to Skagway’s streets from cruise ships, only to leave again when the sun sets. The most recent figures available show that more than 1.35 million tourists arrived in Skagway by cruise ship in 2025, alongside more than half a million crew – and the numbers are growing each year.
That means housing, services and infrastructure designed for a town of about 1,000 people having to accommodate an influx of thousands of workers who arrive in late winter and stay until early autumn.
“Part of the complication of Skagway is that you have such a boom in the summer and such a lull in the winter,” says Hanson. “In terms of revenue that’s not directly related to cruise ships there is not a lot.
“As we saw during the pandemic, we’re at risk,” he says. “If all your eggs are in one basket, it leaves you very vulnerable.”
Like many tourist towns, Skagway has a housing shortage. Unlike other towns, however, it is squeezed into a narrow valley set at the northern end of Alaska’s Inside Passage, a 500-mile maritime route that hugs the coast along Alaska and British Columbia. It is known for its rugged mountains, forests, glaciers and abundant wildlife; there are no realistic commuting options and no room to expand – the only road leads to Canada.
The Skagway Development Corporation commissioned a report in 2023 that found there were 644 housing units in town. In the years since, more have been added, but not enough for the town to accommodate the cruise ship industry and the businesses that support it, its permanent residents, seasonal employees and the workers and families who keep Skagway’s essential services running.
As a result, everything from warehouses to single-family homes, from tents to recreational vehicles or motorhomes, are accommodating the increasing numbers of seasonal workers each year.
“There’s a lot of congregate living and couch surfing,” says Al Wall, director of the town’s Dahl Memorial Clinic. “There are quite a few people that sleep in hammocks in the woods. And frankly, some would prefer to sleep in a hammock in a tree than stay in a crowded place with a bunch of people.”
In years past, many seasonal workers slept in camp sites. But a change in the town’s law forbidding season-long camping pushed them into traditional homes that previously housed the town’s established population.
Janilyn Heger, a longtime Skagwegian, owns the town’s distillery, Skagway Spirits. She and her husband Gary, who owns a construction company, once managed the town-owned camp sites.
“The city made the decision for whatever reason to abandon that type of housing, and that created a domino effect that has been a disaster for the community,” she says.
“Employers started buying buildings and displacing year-round housing and so now we’re at an absolute standstill. There’s none to be had.”
Skagway’s housing shortage has become so severe that many of the town’s limited hotels have been converted into accommodation for seasonal employees.
Longtime resident Mike Healy bought Sergeant Preston’s hotel from friends when he was unable to find land to build enough employee housing to meet his businesses’ needs.
“I didn’t want to purchase Sergeant Preston’s … I approached the city and said, hey, Municipality of Skagway, I am going to purchase the only year-round hotel in this community if you don’t free up some land for housing.”
Healy, not receiving an answer, duly converted the hotel into seasonal housing, part of a portfolio that provides off-season accommodation to visiting workers and contractors.
Jonathan Hillis, a town assembly member who owns the local Mountain Shop outdoor gear store, says that pattern is playing out across town.
“We have very few places now for independent travellers to stay, which is fostering this kind of cycle of more and more cruise ship tourists and fewer independent travellers.”
The scale of cruise tourism is a frequent topic of debate in towns throughout the Inside Passage. As the 2026 season winds down, these towns are consulting the docking schedules for 2027 and 2028, making note of the projected increase in tourism, and asking how much they can realistically handle.
One hundred miles south of Skagway in Alaska’s capital, Juneau, there have been repeated attempts to limit cruise ship tourism. After a ballot measure for “ship-free Saturdays” failed in 2024, the city introduced a voluntary limit on the number of ships that could dock daily.
Farther south in the Inside Passage, Ketchikan has reported more ships as a result of cruises adhering to Juneau’s limitations, while Sitka, also on the cruise ship destination trail, is reviewing its agreements with the industry after an anticipated increase in visitor numbers in 2027.
A survey conducted by Oregon State University reveals a nuanced position when it comes to the cruise sector in Skagway. Just over 40% of people who responded thought that the benefits of tourism outweighed the costs, compared with 25% who put it the other way round. Another 33% viewed the relationship as roughly balanced.
Whatever the sentiment, for a small town that is economically dependent on one industry for its livelihood, options are limited.
“There’s only so much we can do, even if we wanted to,” Hanson says. “We need to be incredibly careful about not rocking the boat.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: ‘The many v the money’ should frame the next US Congress
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Naomi Klein
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Judd Legum shined a spotlight on the role of dark money in US elections. Today’s edition was written by Naomi Klein, Guardian US columnist and author of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor.
To see the battle lines of the post-midterm era in sharp relief, look to Texas.
Just two days after her earthquake victory as the governor-elect, Gina informed reporters that she had already asked the parks and wildlife department to freeze a proposal to sell 1,300 acres (525 hectares) in a state park to SpaceX until she is sworn into her new office. The department complied with her request.
The Boca Chica state park is next door to Starbase, Elon Musk’s rocket launch facility and company town. That makes the park’s beaches and protected lands – a refuge for shore birds and sea turtles – the ideal location for SpaceX to expand.
“These are our beaches we’re talking about. I mean, selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “It’s unacceptable. Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas.”
This was not about shutting down “Elon Musk and his companies”, she went on, “but it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas. And that’s what changes now that I will be governor.”
When Hinojosa’s clips circulated on X, she was roundly mocked by Musk’s many fans: imagine valuing some “empty beaches” more than the need for ocean-front launchpads to the stars! Imagine caring more about some lowly birds than Musk’s hulking, phallic, silver rockets! She must be a [insert vomitorium of misogynistic, racist and ableist slurs here]. Musk, his boys and bots predicted, will just pick up his expensive toys and move them to still-Republican Louisiana or Florida, leaving economic carnage in his wake.
So far, Hinojosa seems unmoved. In Texas, she and Senator-elect James Talarico shaped their campaigns as battles of the many v the money, a vertical struggle pitting the vast majority of Texans, struggling to get by, against the increasingly concentrated wealth at the top – perfectly embodied by the man flooding their democracy with cash. As Talarico reminded an audience of supporters in Austin last month: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.”
The richest man in the world didn’t get his senator, or his governor, as the early clash over Boca Chica state park makes clear. What he did get – or rather, help produce – is an America polarized around a new political axis. On one side are ultrarich tech oligarchs, whose wealth is tethered to dreams of merging with machines and becoming multiplanetary, no matter the cost to our multispecies planet. On the other side are regular people, with human needs for things such as clean air, fresh water and healthcare – maybe even a day off at a public park – and who increasingly find themselves competing over these basics with sprawling datacentres and rocket launchers.
The oligarchs in this battle have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth, thus the threats that Musk will soon ditch Texas if its newly elected representatives dare to keep their promises to voters (just as he dumped California and Canada before that). If all else fails, maybe he will join his friend Peter Thiel in Argentina, which Javier Milei is rapidly turning into techno-libertarian laboratory (Interestingly, Tesla just launched an Argentine division.)
 The oligarchs in this battle seem to have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth.
In sharp contrast, the masses of people in this battle, regardless of their political leanings, tend to be attached to where they live – to its cities, towns, public lands and to the only planet that we know of suited to human life. This is as true in Texas as it is in Tirana, Albania, where, under the banner of the “flamingo revolution” citizens have been in revolt for months against a different set of oligarchs who laid claim to a different beloved wildlife refuge for their private benefit.
In our book End Times Fascism, Astra Taylor and I characterize these as fights between “the leavers v the stayers” – and we make the case that they increasingly define our age. You can see these fault lines running through a great many of the hot-button issues that animated and energized this election cycle. There were the many ballot measures to tax the super-rich to pay for basic services, and entirely predictable tantrums from billionaires who threatened to pick and leave rather than pay up. There was the muscular, national backlash against artificial intelligence and datacenters, which focused on the ways this latest (final?) capitalist stage is devouring art, literature, incomes, lands, energy and wellbeing. (As the Guardian reported, “Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total.”)
The commitment to place, and to one another, was equally evident in the rage at the US war-of-choice in Iran, and at Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with many winning candidates including Abdul El-Sayed consistently stressing that the money being spent to kill children far away should be used to care for children at home, and that all children are equally deserving of life and opportunities.
Similar dynamics were there, too, in the revolt against ICE: As Minnesota’s Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said in her victory speech, the movement that lifted her to power all began when Minnesotans decided to stand up to “masked goons shooting our neighbors”. And the faultlines were clearest of all in the white-hot anger at the legalized corruption at the heart of the US political system, now widely understood as the wellspring producing all the other depravities.
Writing in this space one month ago, Rebecca Solnit astutely characterized the midterms as “a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve”. Well, the results are in and they could scarcely be more decisive. The complicating factor, however, is that it is not only the GOP that is aligned with the tech overlords and their anti-human, anti-Earth agenda. Plenty of powerful Democrats have chosen to underwrite their political campaigns and their personal wealth portfolios by entangling themselves with the very individuals and corporations their voters just roundly and unequivocally rejected.
Shamefully, the campaign to defeat a California ballot measure that would have imposed a much-needed, one-time 5% tax on billionaires – one of few places where tech oligarchs clocked a victory last week – was only successful because powerful Democrats including outgoing governor (and presidential hopeful) Gavin Newsom sided with the billionaires (as did the incoming governor). Meanwhile, several Senate Democrats have joined with Republicans to push through a sweeping bill in the current lame-duck Congress that would dismantle a host of environmental protections and be a bonanza for fossil fuel companies and the datacentres that burn them.
This kind of betrayal is the surest path for Democrats to turn their historic midterm victories into entirely predictable defeats before the highly consequential 2028 presidential election.
In Texas, Hinojosa is showing a better way. By picking an early fight pitting public beaches against Musk’s private rockets, she is telling voters which side she is on – the side of life, not machines; the side of staying, not leaving. That is how the Democrats just won, and it is their path to continue winning.
Want to hear more from our contributors?
Follow them on Substack and elsewhere: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum, Wajahat Ali, Margaret Sullivan and Charles Blow.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/mouvemen.title: « Le rapport de force est de notre côté, il faut continuer » : après avoir claqué la porte de Matignon, lycéens et étudiants dans la rue ce mardi
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/mouvemen.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/mouvemen.text:
Lycéens, étudiants et enseignants appellent à une nouvelle journée de mobilisation et de manifestations ce mardi 10 novembre. La veille, les organisations de jeunesses ont claqué la porte du comité de réforme de Parcoursup pour dénoncer la présence de l’extrême droite alors que, de son côté, le gouvernement n’avait rien de neuf à mettre sur la table.
Pas plus que les syndicats de travailleurs (avec son maigre « coup de pouce » au Smic), Sébastien Lecornu n’a convaincu les lycéens et étudiants qu’ils recevaient lundi, dans la foulée de la Conférence sociale. Face à l’absence de réponses du gouvernement à la hauteur des exigences défendues depuis bientôt deux mois, leurs différentes organisations – de même qu’une intersyndicale de l’Éducation nationale – appellent à redescendre dans la rue dès ce mardi 10 novembre.
« Le rapport de force est de notre côté, il faut continuer. Je ne dis pas qu’on a des victoires, mais je dis qu’on tient le bon bout », a jugé lundi soir Ryad Rani, président de l’Union syndicale lycéenne (USL), après la rencontre avec le premier ministre.
Après avoir rencontré le locataire de Matignon, étudiants et lycéens ont claqué la porte du comité de réforme de Parcoursup en raison de la présence de l’extrême droite (des membres de l’Uni et du RN) et du Medef. Tous sont cependant restés assez longtemps pour constater que le gouvernement n’avait rien de neuf à leur annoncer. La transformation progressive de Parcoursup dès 2027, avant son remplacement complet en 2028, déjà promise il y a 15 jours, a tout du ripolinage.
« C’est le moment d’amplifier la mobilisation »
« Le gouvernement ne prend toujours pas au sérieux nos revendications. Ce ne sont pas des annonces sur la transparence des algorithmes locaux et sur la lisibilité de Parcoursup grâce à des vidéos faites par l’IA pour mieux expliquer comment on est sélectionnés entre le lycée et l’université qui vont répondre à nos revendications », a dénoncé auprès du Monde Éloïse Lefebvre-Milon, secrétaire générale de l’Union étudiante.
Seule innovation de la journée : « des cours de rattrapage » qui pourront être organisés pendant les vacances scolaires, « en février » ou « à Pâques », selon le ministre de l’Éducation nationale qui n’a pas précisé quels moyens seraient dégagés pour les mettre en place. Édouard Geffray a, en revanche, de nouveau menacé de sanctions les élèves mobilisés sur les blocages – faute de répondre à leurs revendications.
Face à l’inertie savamment entretenue de l’exécutif, « l’idée, c’est d’avoir une journée de mobilisation au sens large, avec des grèves, des manifestations et des rassemblements » pour « offrir un rebond à la mobilisation de la jeunesse avec des cortèges encadrés, sécurisés alors que devant les lycées, ça commence à pas mal se tendre », a de son côté expliqué à l’AFP Sophie Vénétitay, secrétaire générale du Snes-FSU, premier syndicat dans le second degré.
« C’est le moment d’amplifier la mobilisation en continuant à mettre le gouvernement sous pression », avait fait valoir dans un communiqué l’intersyndicale CGT, FSU, FO, Solidaires, Union syndicale lycéenne, Unef, Union étudiante, Fage et FSE, après le 5 novembre où 1,6 million de personnes ont manifesté.
Dans l’Éducation nationale, la grève « s’annonce suivie à certains endroits », a estimé la responsable syndicale, tout en reconnaissant que la mobilisation devrait être moins importante que celle du 5 novembre, où près de 16 % des enseignants s’étaient mis en grève selon le ministère. Des manifestations sont prévues dans la plupart des grandes villes de France. À Paris, un cortège partira à 14 heures de Panthéon en direction de la Place d’Italie.
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Policial, gay e petista: deputado eleito em Goiás quer aproximar segurança pública e esquerda
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: João Palhares
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Entre 66 deputados estaduais, federais, senadores e governo eleitos em Goiás neste ano, Fabrício Rosa (PT) é a única pessoa que se declarou LGBT+ para a Justiça Eleitoral. Pela primeira vez, um homem gay faz parte do grupo de 41 pessoas com mandato para a próxima legislatura na Assembleia Legislativa de Goiás (Alego). Policial rodoviário federal, professor e doutor em Direitos Humanos, Fabrício se prepara para assumir uma cadeira que nunca foi ocupada por uma pessoa assumidamente LGBT+.
Sem discrição, Fabrício foi eleito com 81.540 votos e ocupou a votação como segundo deputado estadual mais votado do estado, atrás apenas de Carol do Amiltinho (MDB). Dois anos antes, em 2024, havia conquistado uma cadeira na Câmara Municipal de Goiânia com 7.216 votos, como o terceiro candidato do PT eleito ao cargo. À época, Fabrício já se declarava LGBT+ e se tornou o primeiro vereador assumidamente gay eleito na capital.
Natural de Goiânia, Fabrício atua em pautas como saúde pública, moradia, cultura, igualdade racial e direitos da população LGBT+. É um dos fundadores do movimento nacional Policiais Antifascismo e diretor da Rede Nacional de Policiais LGBTQIA+ (Renosp), e propõe uma reformulação profunda do modelo de segurança pública do estado. Em abril, foi preso pela Polícia Militar durante um ato do MST em Santa Helena de Goiás, em memória dos 30 anos do Massacre de Eldorado dos Carajás. Em julho, a Justiça arquivou o caso após o Ministério Público de Goiás (MP-GO) concluir que não havia justa causa para uma ação penal.
Ao olhar para o cenário de disputas nas eleições de 2026, o resultado tem um peso significativo para os corpos dissidentes no estado. Segundo dados do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), das 595 candidaturas a deputado estadual em Goiás, 332 informaram a orientação sexual. Desse número, 321 se declararam heterossexuais e apenas 11 informaram outra orientação, entre quatro gays, dois bissexuais, duas lésbicas, dois assexuais e um pansexual. “Ser o primeiro também significa enfrentar muitos ataques, ameaças e tentativas de silenciamento. Espero que as próximas pessoas LGBTQIA+ que chegarem à política não precisem enfrentar a mesma violência que nós enfrentamos”, conta Fabrício.
Na conversa a seguir, Fabrício comenta o que explica o salto de 20 mil, nas eleições que concorreu em 2022 ao mesmo cargo, para 81 mil votos; como pretende enfrentar a bancada conservadora na Alego; a disputa pela presidência da Casa e os planos para levar o mandato aos 246 municípios goianos.
Confira a entrevista na íntegra
Brasil de Fato DF – Você é policial há mais de 20 anos, e em abril foi preso pela própria PM num ato do MST em Santa Helena. Como foi viver uma abordagem desse outro lado? O que aquele dia te mostrou sobre a polícia, que você não tinha visto de dentro da corporação, e como isso pretende guiar seu trabalho na Alego?
Fabrício Rosa – Sou policial rodoviário federal há 26 anos, mas também sou militante dos direitos humanos e da reforma agrária. Não vejo contradição entre essas duas condições. Pelo contrário, acredito que a polícia deveria existir para proteger os direitos da população, inclusive o direito de manifestação e de luta por justiça social. O Brasil é um país profundamente desigual na distribuição de terras, e a reforma agrária é uma questão de justiça social.
A minha prisão não revelou uma realidade que eu desconhecia. Sou militante LGBTQIA+, antiproibicionista, defensor da legalização da maconha e há muitos anos denuncio a violência policial. Mas viver pessoalmente essa repressão reforça a gravidade do problema.
Goiás tem uma das polícias mais letais do Brasil. Aproximadamente três em cada dez mortes violentas intencionais no estado decorrem de intervenções policiais. É um número alarmante, que exige uma transformação profunda na nossa política de segurança.
Na Assembleia Legislativa, quero defender um modelo de polícia mais democrático, humanizado e cidadão, com câmeras corporais, mecanismos de controle da atividade policial, valorização dos profissionais e formação em direitos humanos. Não queremos uma polícia fraca, mas uma polícia forte para proteger a sociedade, e não para violar os direitos da população.
Você já cobrou da esquerda uma aproximação com os trabalhadores da segurança pública. Ao mesmo tempo, é um homem gay dentro de uma instituição policial. Em qual desses dois espaços foi mais difícil ser aceito?
São duas experiências diferentes, mas ambas apresentam dificuldades. Ser um homem gay dentro de uma instituição historicamente marcada pelo machismo, pelo conservadorismo e por uma cultura de masculinidade autoritária nunca foi simples. Por outro lado, ser policial dentro dos movimentos sociais também exige construir confiança. E compreendo essa desconfiança, porque muitos militantes tiveram suas histórias marcadas pela repressão e pela violência policial.
Mas acredito que minha trajetória demonstra que essas identidades não são incompatíveis. É possível ser policial, gay, socialista, antiproibicionista e defensor dos direitos humanos. Uma das minhas principais tarefas políticas é construir pontes entre esses dois mundos. Sempre cobrei da esquerda uma aproximação maior com os profissionais da segurança pública, porque policiais também são trabalhadores, enfrentam problemas salariais, adoecimento mental e condições difíceis de trabalho.
Se a esquerda desistir de dialogar com os policiais, estará entregando milhares de trabalhadores ao discurso autoritário da extrema direita. Precisamos disputar politicamente essas instituições e construir uma segurança pública comprometida com a democracia.
Você foi o primeiro LGBT+ da Câmara de Goiânia e agora chega à Alego com essa mesma marca. O que você pretende fazer para que deixe de ser o único?
Ser o primeiro é uma conquista histórica, mas também uma responsabilidade enorme. Eu costumo dizer que quem chega primeiro precisa abrir a porta para que muitas outras pessoas possam entrar. Quero que nosso mandato seja um espaço de formação e fortalecimento de novas lideranças LGBTQIA+, especialmente travestis, mulheres trans e homens trans, que enfrentam barreiras ainda maiores para acessar a política institucional.
Na Câmara de Goiânia, apresentamos e aprovamos projetos de enfrentamento ao preconceito, realizamos audiências públicas, atividades educativas nas escolas e destinamos uma parcela importante das nossas emendas parlamentares às demandas da comunidade LGBTQIA+. Também temos incentivado a filiação de pessoas LGBTQIA+ ao Partido dos Trabalhadores, fortalecido sua participação nos movimentos sociais e aberto espaços para novas lideranças dentro do nosso mandato.
Ser o primeiro também significa enfrentar muitos ataques, ameaças e tentativas de silenciamento. Espero que as próximas pessoas LGBTQIA+ que chegarem à política não precisem enfrentar a mesma violência que nós enfrentamos. Não quero continuar sendo o único. Quero ajudar a construir uma geração inteira de lideranças LGBTQIA+ ocupando os espaços de poder em Goiás.
Você saiu de 20 mil votos em 2022 para mais de 81 mil agora, num estado em que a direita é maioria. O que explica isso hoje para você?
Acredito que nosso crescimento eleitoral pode ser explicado por alguns fatores. O primeiro foi a comunicação. Apostamos nas redes sociais, numa linguagem jovem, criativa e conectada com os problemas reais da população. Investimos em vídeos, cartilhas, adesivos e numa comunicação muito próxima das pessoas. O segundo foi o diálogo com a juventude, que representa uma parcela importante do nosso eleitorado. Conseguimos construir uma identificação com jovens que procuram novas formas de participação política e novas lideranças.
O terceiro fator foi não abrir mão das nossas convicções. Continuamos defendendo os direitos LGBTQIA+, os direitos humanos, a legalização da maconha, a reforma agrária e o enfrentamento à violência policial. Não escondemos nossas pautas para tentar agradar setores conservadores. Também acredito que estamos vivendo um momento de busca por novas lideranças políticas, com autenticidade, coragem e capacidade de dialogar com as transformações da sociedade.
E houve muito trabalho. Fizemos uma campanha com poucos recursos, percorremos mais de 50 cidades e começamos nossa mobilização ainda em fevereiro. Além disso, as pessoas acompanharam nosso mandato combativo na Câmara de Goiânia.
Nossa eleição demonstra que Goiás é muito mais diverso do que o discurso conservador costuma fazer parecer. Mostramos que não é preciso abandonar nossas bandeiras para ampliar nosso eleitorado. Pelo contrário, muitas pessoas votaram em nós justamente porque nunca abandonamos essas bandeiras.
Sua audiência pública sobre a saúde de crianças e adolescentes trans foi cancelada no plenário e atacada do lado de fora, mesmo tendo sido um pedido das famílias. Na Alego, muitos deputados se elegem dizendo que vão proteger as crianças, como é o caso de Amauri Ribeiro, que já esteve em vários embates. Como você pretende fazer esse debate lá dentro?
Pretendo fazer exatamente o que fizemos na Câmara de Goiânia: enfrentar o preconceito com conhecimento, mobilização social e coragem política. Aquela audiência pública nasceu de uma demanda das próprias famílias, de mães e pais preocupados com a saúde e a dignidade de seus filhos. Infelizmente, setores conservadores tentam transformar a vida de crianças e adolescentes trans em instrumento de disputa ideológica.
Vamos continuar ouvindo as famílias, os movimentos sociais, profissionais de saúde, pesquisadores, a Defensoria Pública e o Ministério Público. Precisamos discutir políticas públicas com base em evidências científicas e no princípio da proteção integral de crianças e adolescentes. Quando tentaram impedir nosso debate dentro da Câmara, não nos calamos. Levamos a discussão para outros espaços, mobilizamos os movimentos sociais e transformamos a indignação em luta.
Na Assembleia Legislativa, teremos uma tribuna ainda maior para enfrentar esse preconceito. Não podemos aceitar que a defesa das crianças seja utilizada como justificativa para produzir violência contra crianças. Nenhuma criança pode ser abandonada pelo Estado porque sua existência contraria as convicções religiosas ou ideológicas de um parlamentar. Nossa responsabilidade é garantir saúde, educação, acolhimento e dignidade para todas elas.
Você defende que o PT lance candidatura própria à presidência da Alego, tendo quatro deputados em 41. O que o partido consegue negociar a partir disso? E o que, para você, não entra na negociação?
Defendo que o Partido dos Trabalhadores tenha a audácia de apresentar uma candidatura própria à presidência da Assembleia Legislativa, mesmo contando com apenas quatro deputados entre os 41 parlamentares. Neste momento, existem várias candidaturas sendo articuladas por setores de centro e centro-direita. Por que a esquerda não pode apresentar também um nome?
Temos quadros extremamente qualificados, como Antônio Gomide, que foi prefeito de Anápolis por duas vezes e tem uma trajetória respeitada na política goiana. É um parlamentar experiente, com capacidade de diálogo e acúmulo político para disputar a presidência da Casa. Uma candidatura do PT poderia reunir setores da centro-esquerda e dialogar com parlamentares de centro que desejam uma Assembleia mais independente e plural.
Evidentemente, sabemos fazer política. Não temos problema em negociar ou até retirar uma eventual candidatura, desde que existam compromissos concretos com nossas pautas, estrutura institucional para nossos mandatos e participação nos espaços de decisão. Mas existem limites muito claros. Nossa autonomia parlamentar não está em negociação. Ninguém vai decidir como devemos votar, quais pautas podemos defender ou quais denúncias podemos fazer.
Também não aceitaremos a submissão do Legislativo ao Executivo. A Assembleia Legislativa não pode ser um puxadinho do governo Daniel Vilela. Precisa ter independência para fiscalizar, investigar e, quando necessário, enfrentar o governo estadual. Estamos abertos ao diálogo, mas não à submissão.
Na campanha, você falou em levar suas pautas aos 246 municípios. No interior, o poder costuma estar na usina, no frigorífico e na igreja. Como é fazer política sendo um homem gay diante dessa realidade, sobretudo em Goiás?
Percorri boa parte de Goiás durante a campanha e percebi que o interior é muito mais diverso do que muitas pessoas imaginam. É claro que existe uma estrutura de poder concentrada, marcada pela influência econômica do agronegócio, de grandes empresas, de grupos políticos tradicionais e de instituições religiosas. Mas o interior também é formado por trabalhadores rurais, professores, estudantes, artistas, comunidades LGBTQIA+ e movimentos sociais que precisam ter voz.
Nosso desafio é construir um mandato verdadeiramente estadual, que não fique restrito à capital. Queremos criar plataformas permanentes de participação popular, com reuniões virtuais envolvendo lideranças de todas as regiões, especialmente produtores culturais, militantes LGBTQIA+, professores, trabalhadores da educação e movimentos sociais ligados à reforma agrária e à reforma urbana.
Também queremos organizar uma Caravana dos Direitos Humanos, percorrendo as principais cidades-polo de Goiás, com um calendário de encontros presenciais, escutas populares e articulações regionais. Além disso, vamos construir uma rede de lideranças e assessores distribuídos pelas diferentes regiões. Não queremos um mandato que visite o interior apenas em períodos eleitorais, mas que mantenha uma presença permanente.
E sobre fazer política sendo um homem gay em Goiás, acredito que nossa eleição já demonstra que podemos romper barreiras. Não pretendo esconder quem sou para dialogar com o interior. Quero mostrar que um homem gay pode defender os trabalhadores do campo, a agricultura familiar, os professores, a saúde, a cultura e o desenvolvimento regional.
Os direitos humanos não são uma pauta exclusiva das capitais. A dignidade de uma pessoa LGBTQIA+ que vive numa pequena cidade do interior vale exatamente o mesmo que a dignidade de alguém que vive em Goiânia. Queremos chegar aos 246 municípios não apenas levando nossas pautas, mas ouvindo as pessoas e construindo coletivamente as prioridades do nosso mandato.

https://gothamist.com/news/study-links-a.title: Study links ADHD to NYC’s deadly subway surfing trend
https://gothamist.com/news/study-links-a.author: Ramsey Khalifeh, Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/study-links-a.text:
People killed “surfing” on top of New York City subway trains tend to be teen boys diagnosed with ADHD, according to a new study published this week.
The trend of young people subway surfing has persisted in recent years, despite at least 12 people being killed riding on the outside of trains since the start of 2024.
The study, which was conducted by researchers from NYU-Langone and the city hospital system, analyzed records of 43 patients under the age of 21 who were taken to Bellevue Hospital between 2018 and 2025 with some form of subway-related trauma.
The research, which was published in the Journal of Adolescent Health, is the first of its kind that looks into subway surfing in the United States. The study identified 10 patients who were injured from subway surfing. All of those surfers were male teenagers who had “markedly higher rates of ADHD” compared to the rest of the group.
“The most striking finding in our series is the overrepresentation of ADHD; 60% of surfers carried the diagnosis versus 6.1% of nonsurfers,” the study said. “This association has not been previously described in the train surfing literature and is among the most notable findings of our study.”
Researchers behind the study acknowledged the sample size is too small to make a sweeping generalization of all young people in New York City who ride on top of trains. The analysis doesn’t include two young girls, 12-year-old Zemfira Mukhtarov and 13-year-old Ebba Morina, who died while riding on top of a J train in Williamsburg in Oct. 2025.
Eveline Teresa Hidalgo, senior author of the study and pediatric neurosurgeon at NYU and Bellevue, said the subway surfers diagnosed with ADHD had also been treated for the disorder.
“We don't know what this means exactly, and it's not that ADHD causes them to subway surf, but it means that it's something that we need to investigate further,” said Hidalgo. ”It could be associated with some attention-seeking behavior. It could be associated with the thrill-seeking behavior, and it's a typical teenage behavior.”
Hidalgo said the study shows how subway surfing can cause life-altering injuries among people who don’t die after falling from trains. Some patients they studied at Bellevue suffered injuries to their brains and spine, and some had their limbs amputated.
Both the MTA and NYPD have attempted to prevent subway surfing in recent years.
The transit agency has teamed up with city officials to lobby social media giants like Meta and TikTok to ban or censor videos of teens subway surfing in New York City. The MTA has also piloted installing barriers between subway cars on the 7 line — where subway surfing is prevalent as the line is mostly elevated — to prevent people climbing on top of cars. The NYPD has also deployed drones to monitor elevated train tracks to spot and catch surfers.
NYPD data shows 185 people have been arrested for subway surfing so far this year, a 12% increase compared to the same period last year.
The study compared New York City’s subway surfing wave to a similar trend in Berlin in the 1990s. After 18 people died subway surfing over a six-year period in the German capital, the city’s S-Bahn transit system slowly decommissioned a fleet of train cars after finding they were easier for riders to climb.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.title: Actor Says He Removed His Mother’s Art from Venice Biennale Installation as a Pro-Israel Protest
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.text:
Actor Eric Rasmussen revealed this week that he had removed his contribution to an installation by Denniston Hill in the main exhibition of the Venice Biennale because the residency program appeared to support the “eradication” of Israel, in Rasmussen’s view.
In an op-ed published by the Jewish Journal on Monday, Rasmussen wrote that he had combined two drawings by his mother of Adolf Hitler drawn from a notebook she kept during her childhood. The resulting work, transferred to an acetate panel, was included Denniston Hill’s installation, an exquisite corpse–style work titled Chimera (2026) that is located in the Giardini section of Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition.
The piece features contributions by dozens of past residents at Denniston Hill, which was cofounded by artists kara lynch, Julie Mehretu, Paul Pfeiffer, and Jessica Rankin, along with art historian Lawrence Chua and curator Beth Stryker, and is located in Upstate New York. Rasmussen was a resident at Denniston Hill in 2019 through the DPAA Workshop.
Rasmussen said his submission to Chimera was a 1943 drawing by his mother that he had previously enlisted in a performance staged during his Denniston Hill residency. The piece is a drawing of a mustachioed man and some numbers, along with text reading, “Mister Hitler is invaded and his spitting.” For the Venice Biennale, he added a caption in red: “Mom’s childhood drawing 1943. The Toxicity of the Past?”
“I felt like the piece reflected the work I did at Denniston Hill while, at the same time, gesturing toward our current moment,” Rasmussen writes. “Neither the ‘toxicity’ of authoritarian leaders nor the rabid antisemitism called to mind by Hitler’s image remain in the past.”
ARTnews was able to confirm that the drawing did make it on view in time for the Biennale’s opening in May by examining installation shots of Chimera disseminated by the exhibition, which closes later this month.
It appears to have been taken away by Rasmussen at some point after mid-May, when, he wrote, Denniston Hill sent an email noting that the organization was more than 70 Biennale participants who had signed an open letter that objected to the Biennale’s claims of political neutrality. The signatories said this conflicted with the controversial decision this year to host pavilions for Israel, Russia, and the United States, all of which are “current regimes committing war crimes,” the letter said.
Moreover, according to Rasmussen, Denniston Hill wrote that it was “aligning with ANGA,” or the Art Not Genocide Alliance, a group that has repeatedly protested Israel’s presence at the Biennale while also noting that Palestine has no official pavilion in the show, and never has. (Palestine is not considered a state in Italy; only countries viewed as states by Italy’s government can have national pavilions at the Biennale, per the exhibition.)
“ANGA clearly considers all of Israel to be occupied Palestine and its goal is not to oppose policies of the government of Israel but to destroy the nation,” Rasmussen claimed in his Jewish Journal essay, which alleged that Denniston Hill has “no problem blithely aligning itself with an organization that seeks that nation’s eradication without even asking for the opinions of its artists.”
His essay also labeled anti-Zionism “an assault on not only the Jewish state and Jewish history, but also on language itself,” and claimed that linking “Zionism with racism, colonialism and apartheid” was akin to “Cold War KGB propaganda.”
Without stating a precise date for the work’s removal, Rasmussen said he “wrote a lengthy email” to Denniston Hill seeking the return of the drawing. Denniston Hill obliged the request and gave back the drawing, he said.
Representatives for Denniston Hill and the Biennale did not respond to requests for comment.

https://citylimits.org/after-a-decade-ny.title: After a Decade, NYC Opened Its Waitlist for General Street Vendor Permits. Here’s What You Need to Know.
https://citylimits.org/after-a-decade-ny.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/after-a-decade-ny.text:
Share This Article
The city is adding 10,500 new merchandise vending permits next year—which grant vendors the right to legally sell goods, rather than food—after capping the number at just 853 for decades. “I said, ‘Oh my God, this thing is really happening,'” said Calvin Baker, a longtime Harlem vendor who was among the first to apply.
Some opportunities come along only once a decade.
For New Yorkers who earn their living as street vendors—an industry predominantly represented by immigrants, including many Latinos—that includes getting on the waitlist for a coveted city license.
For the first time in a decade, the city opened its waitlist last week for street vendor merchandise licenses, which grant vendors the right to legally sell goods, like jewelry, toys and clothing, rather than food.
“I said, ‘Oh my God, this thing is really happening,'” said Calvin Baker, a longtime Harlem vendor, describing how he felt when he was finally able to apply last week.
For decades, he and other vendors have fought against the city’s rigid 853-capped license limit, set in 1979. Since then, these licenses for non-veteran general vendors became available only when an existing license holder gave theirs up, leading to thousands of people selling merchandise on the streets without one—risking costly fines and potential criminal charges as a result.
Earlier this year, the City Council overrode former Mayor Eric Adams’ veto to pass a bill creating 10,500 new merchandise vending permits, and started taking applicants for a new waitlist last week.
“It was so good to see people that were on the line, on the struggle with me in the streets, fighting to get these licenses, sitting down there waiting for their turn to go fill out the application,” said Baker, 64, who sells hats, gloves and other apparel. “It was a blessing for me, man. I felt the peace of God. I felt satisfied.”
Previously, once a license became available, the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) would contact applicants from the existing waitlist, which closed in 2016.
But under the new law, the city will add another 10,500 licenses—including 3,478 Citywide General Vendor or called “white,” licenses, which allow for vending anywhere in the city, and 7,875 outer borough or “green” licenses—which will become available early next year.
“It is extremely difficult to predict, but it is fair to say that we estimate that thousands of people will apply,” said Mohamed Attia, director of the Street Vendor Project, the advocacy group behind the license expansion.
In August, DCWP started giving priority to applicants who were already on the 2016 waitlist, and began contacting them, sending them letters describing the next steps. They had until Oct. 29 to submit a license application, a DCWP spokesperson explained.
After that, the new 2026 waitlist opened on Nov. 2, and will close on Dec. 16. Vendors have to submit an application to join the list, and then wait for DCWP to tell them where they stand and what they need to do next. 
Baker was among the first applicants last Monday.
“It’s like you run the New York Marathon and you say, ‘Lord, how am I gonna do it? Can I finish this race?’ But then you get in it, and you finish it. The satisfaction that you feel from doing that. That’s the satisfaction I felt from filling out the application,” Baker described.
A DCWP spokesperson didn’t specify how many people have applied so far.
“DCWP is working hard to ensure the rollout of new general vendor licenses proceeds in a clear, orderly, and accessible manner,” a spokesperson said. “We know that street vendors are community fixtures—and we are proud to support these small businesses through best-in-class licensing services, proactive business education, and reforms to cut red tape.”
Where and how can a street vendor apply?
If you’re not already on the 2016 waitlist, you can apply to the new one online or by mail, and in very limited circumstances, such as “hardship cases,” in person.
Vendors can apply for either a white or green license, or both, in one application.
If you need help with your application, you can connect with the Office of Street Vendor Services at the Department of Small Business Services (SBS) by calling 888-SBS-4NYC (888-727-4692).
You can also get assistance in person by visiting NYC Business Solutions Centers during office hours (Monday to Friday, 9 a.m.- 5 p.m) at the following locations:
- The Bronx: 400 East Fordham Rd., 7th Floor, Bronx, NY 10458
- Brooklyn: 9 Bond St., 5th Floor, Brooklyn, NY 11201
- Lower Manhattan: 14 Wall St., 17th Floor, New York, NY 10005
- Upper Manhattan: 361 West 125th St., 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10027
- Washington Heights: 560 West 181st St., 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10033
- Queens: 90-27 Sutphin Blvd., 4th Floor, Jamaica, NY 11435
- Staten Island: 120 Stuyvesant Pl., 3rd Floor, Staten Island, NY 10301
Applicants can also make an appointment with the Street Vendor Project via email or phone (646-602-5679).
“There is a lot of misinformation and a lot of confusion about what this license is,” Attia explained.
“This license allows people to sell merchandise products out of the streets, the public sidewalks, out of a table, and there are so many rules around it,” he added. “So, if you are a food vendor, this license is not for you. If you have a retail business and you want to expand to some private events, some pop-up markets, this license is not for you.”
What are the requirements for applying?
The information requested from applicants is basic personal information, such as their name, address, phone number, and email. Additionally, it asks if a person has been selling general merchandise from January 2025 to Nov. 2, 2026.
Although most of the city’s street vendors are immigrants from different parts of the world, the application is only available in English. SVP said it is assisting applicants in seven languages.
The form also requires the submission of a photo ID, which may be a driver’s license, permits issued by a government agency, passport, or municipal ID card, among others.
One ironic feature of the process: previous civil or criminal summonses issued to the applicant can serve as proof of their vending experience (in addition to pictures showing the person vending, receipts for merchandise purchases, or a letter from an elected official, community leader, or nonprofit organization stating past vending activity).
SVP advocates see this as an acknowledgement that the prior system left many people without a way to sell legally, and as a reminder of how difficult it was to obtain a license under the old cap.
“The application was very easy,” Baker said. “”t took 10 minutes.”
Then what?
The waitlist application is separate from the license application, so joining the waitlist does not automatically result in a license.
DCWP will review the applications, assign each one a number, and contact applicants with information about next steps starting in February 2027.
“I’m looking for the ultimate. I’m looking for my license,” Baker said. “I will feel a lot better. I won’t have to always look around and worry about the NYPD running down on me, and just tossing my stuff any kind of way they want to without even having respect for your stuff.”
