Call for Proposals: Roman Witt Residency at the University of Michigan
This residency at the U-M Stamps School, in partnership with the U-M Museum of Art (UMMA), offers artists a $20,000 honorarium, housing, studio space, and a culminating exhibition in UMMA’s prominent Stenn Gallery.
The mission of the Roman J. Witt Residency Program is to support the production of new works of art at the University of Michigan. Open to both established and emerging artists and designers, the program awards one residency each academic year.
The 2027-28 Witt Residency is organized in partnership with the University of Michigan Museum of Art (UMMA). The residency will culminate in an exhibition at UMMA’s Irving Stenn, Jr. Family Gallery, opening in March 2028.
The 1,200-square-foot Stenn Gallery is a glass-walled, street-facing space on UMMA’s ground floor. Its location and glass frontage offer opportunities for projects that consider public visibility, the movement of people through campus, or the relationship between the museum and its surroundings.
The Witt Residency is open to established artists and designers. Proposals may address any subject or take any artistic or design approach, and should explain how the project would respond to the Stenn Gallery’s setting and scale. During the Witt Residency, it is expected that the resident actively engages with the students, faculty, and public of the broader Stamps, UMMA, and U-M communities, through student engagement and public programs connected to the project. Applicants should identify campus connections or resources at the University of Michigan that could support their project, and explain how these might inform its development.
The residency period runs from September 2027 through June 2028. During this period, the selected resident will complete the project with UMMA and Stamps, spending up to twelve weeks in Ann Arbor. Together, the resident and U-M staff will determine the residency schedule, checklist details, installation approach, and programming.
Recent Witt artists-in-residence include:
- Conrad Egyir, 2027 (in partnership with the U-M Institute for the Humanities)
- Holly Bass, 2026 (in partnership with UMMA)
- Stacey Kirby, 2025 (in partnership with Stamps Gallery)
- Machine Dazzle, 2024 (in partnership with UMMA)
Proposals for the 2027-28 Witt Residency Program can be submitted through January 25, 2027. The Witt Residency program’s application process is conducted using the online review system SlideRoom. A nominal $15 submission fee applies, which goes directly to SlideRoom for providing hosting services.
For more information, visit stamps.umich.edu.

https://hellgatenyc.com/michael-bloomber.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/michael-bloomber.text:
He was a billionaire politician who is maybe not so politically relevant; she was his girlfriend of 26 years, a financial executive, whatever that means. Can we make it any more obvious? 
That's right: Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his longtime partner Diana Taylor finally tied the knot on Monday after more than a quarter century together. And what a quarter century it's been! 
"Twenty-six years after a chance seating assignment, Mike Bloomberg and Diana Taylor have married," a spokesperson for Bloomberg posted on the ex-mayor's X account. "The longtime couple exchanged vows today in a small, private ceremony at their home on the Upper East Side, joined by family, including his daughters, Emma and Georgina. The two first crossed paths when they sat next to each other at a Citizens Budget Commission meeting while he was first running for Mayor."
Extremely romantic origin story aside (we always thought it was strange that the Citizens Budget Commission only meets by candlelight at that cute hole-in-the-wall Italian spot down the block), Bloomberg and Taylor have been through a lot together over the last two and a half decades.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Bringing Billionaires to Account at the Ballot Box
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Futrelle
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Bringing Billionaires to Account at the Ballot Box
Last week’s midterms were a powerful repudiation of MAGA, but the fight against oligarchy will be a longer struggle.
The midterms were more than just a victory for Democrats—they were also a critical blow for democracy, as well as a powerful repudiation of President Donald Trump’s crass authoritarianism and of the Republicans who have enabled his worst impulses. But if we want to enable our still-fragile democracy to thrive again, we need not only to purge it of the baleful influence of MAGA but also to confront directly another dire, and continuing, threat to self-rule: that of the billionaires who are increasingly using their wealth and power to try to override the will of the people. In some cases, our moneyed oligarchy quietly (or not so quietly) bankrolls the worst among the Republicans; in others, it puts considerable rightward pressure on the Democrats it supports.
Do we the people have a chance against billionaire money? We just might, as two case studies from the midterms make clear: James Talarico’s successful Senate candidacy in Texas, and the failed campaign for a billionaire wealth tax in California.
On the surface, the two campaigns seem to offer radically different lessons. In Texas, Talarico was able to overcome some $200 million in spending from Elon Musk and deliver a decisive victory, one that Talarico touted as proof “that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”
But it was more than simply people power that enabled Talarico to win; he also responded to Musk’s intervention in the race with a certain shrewdness, ultimately recognizing that in many ways Musk and his money were more formidable opponents than the corrupt and uncharismatic Ken Paxton. (Even Trump, Paxton’s key political supporter, jokingly referred to him as a “pain in the ass” who didn’t know how to dress, or talk, properly.) Given that Talarico was essentially running against a tag team of Paxton and Musk, he made the world’s richest man one of his primary foils in the campaign—thereby turning the millions that Musk directed into the coffers of the Paxton campaign into a political liability. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon,” Talarico said on the campaign trail. “If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon, too.” Musk, Talarico said, clearly “wants his very own personal United States senator,” one who would do Musk’s bidding in the state where he lives in exchange for purchasing his office.
All in all, Musk spent close to half a billion dollars in the midterms and got close to zero return. Six of his seven Senate picks went down in defeat (with one race still too close to call), and only a small handful of the 43 House candidates he supported prevailed. But it was the Texas race that marked his most significant defeat. Talarico, not surprisingly, sees his victory as a major blow in the battle against billionaires in politics. “We’ve just sent a message to every millionaire mega donor, to every trillionaire mega donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system,” he declared in his victory speech.
In California, the lesson seemed to be of a rather different sort. The backers of Proposition 40—the voter initiative to ratify a billionaire wealth tax—were unable to fend off a “no” campaign backed by billionaire money. One top staffer of the SEIU–United Healthcare Workers West, the union behind the ballot initiative, blamed the campaign’s likely defeat on “billionaire-funded propaganda” that misled voters.
There was indeed a torrent of such propaganda coursing through California’s airwaves. After the billionaire tax was first put forward by Dave Regan of the SEIU-UHW, a number of the state’s wealthiest residents began strategizing how to defeat it in a secret Signal group chat. Google cofounder Sergey Brin, worth a cool $219 billion even after the dip in Big Tech stock values last week, led the charge, cofounding an innocuously named group called Building a Better California. Brin’s outfit quickly amassed a $333 million war chest, plumped up considerably by a $102 million donation from Brin himself. The group quickly realized that its biggest backers could ill afford becoming the face of the campaign; its own polling showed that “billionaires are seen as having a net negative impact across issues,” as internal documents seen by The New York Times put it. (Ya think?) And so their “billionaire-funded propaganda” starred not Brin himself but an assortment of non-billionaire opponents of the measure, Anti-Prop 40 ads thus featured doctors, carpenters, firefighters, and teachers, and even the Democratic governor of California, Gavin Newsom.
As the casting decisions for these ads suggest, the story of Prop 40’s defeat was far more complicated than a simple blame-the-billionaires narrative would suggest. Regan is a divisive figure, to put it mildly—a publicity-hungry activist who’s considered something of an asshole not only by tech billionaires but also by some Democratic politicians; he has also, more significantly, been credibly accused of bullying and worse by union officials. He pushed the referendum largely on his own, without first making much of an attempt to build a coalition. He also sidestepped (some would say stepped on) an already existing campaign by the California Teachers Association (CTA) for another ballot proposition calling to make permanent an increased income tax on the wealthy (happily, despite all the confusion, this measure has passed). Prop 40 would have directed almost all of the proceeds of the wealth tax toward healthcare—a provision that alienated some union leaders who felt that at least some of the money should have gone to support their members as well. As a result, several leading unions, including CTA and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, came out against the tax.
In the end, the SEIU-UHW spent most of the $34 million it raised on gathering signatures, according to The New York Times, leaving only a small fraction of money on hand to counter the massive ad spending from Brin’s group. That enabled the “no” voices to define the terms of the debate. Weirdly, the union spent some of its paltry ad money on perplexing campaigns directed at Planned Parenthood, which had come out against the bill, and Newsom himself. (The anti-Newsom message was featured in ads that didn’t even run in California.) Why they went this way instead of pulling a Talarico and going directly after Brin I don’t know. When you’re fighting billionaires, you need to fight billionaires—not just in general but with great specificity, by name.
It didn’t help that Regan was not himself the best face for the Prop 40 campaign. The controversial and often volatile activist has long had a reputation as a bully. The issue came to a head in September when the press got hold of two investigative reports on his behavior sponsored by SEIU’s national union and its California council that substantiated accusations of threats and bullying of union officials by Regan—and a 2009 physical assault on a woman who was then SEIU California’s executive director. One of the reports concluded that Regan has a “propensity for bullying women and women of color.” (Regan dismisses the allegations as “politically motivated,” ginned up by opponents of Prop 40. A union hearing is set for December.)
And then in the final week of the campaign, as a sort of dysfunctional cherry on top, some 230 of SEIU-UHW’s own staffers went on strike, saying that the union wasn’t negotiating with them in good faith over a raise, derailing the union’s attempts to seal the deal with voters.
In the end, Prop 40 was defeated by more than all this internal dysfunction and a well-funded pro-billionaire agitprop offensive. Voters also appear likely to have passed a poison-pill measure bankrolled by the billionaire’s coalition, Prop 42, that bars future wealth taxes in California. Prop 42’s passage would leave proponents of a California wealth tax in worse shape than if the initiative had never been put forward in the first place. “What a waste of resources and what a squandering of an opportunity,” one prominent supporter of Prop 40 told Politico. “There was no coalition, they pissed off everyone, and so many of those natural allies that would’ve supported it refused.” Billionaires, in California and elsewhere, emerged from the fight not only with their wealth intact but feeling empowered. The apparent lesson for them was that they can win any future battles over wealth taxes by simply sacrificing a small sliver of that wealth to political donations.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But the ongoing struggle to contain the damage wrought by the superrich is hardly as hopeless as Prop 40’s defeat might make it seem. Talarico’s win shows that even the world’s richest man can lose to a charismatic politician who knows how to mobilize the disgust most Americans feel toward the excessive power of money in politics. In Talarico’s case, it certainly didn’t hurt that Musk himself is an odious, cringey edgelord who has almost completely squandered whatever goodwill he once had as a supposed tech wunderkind; his favorability rating, as measured by recent polls, is in the 30s, right alongside Donald Trump’s. But the thing is, most Americans seem to have grown profoundly tired of our billionaire class as a whole; they’re not just sick of Musk. If you start looking at our other billionaires, particularly of the tech variety, you’ll find that some are as widely despised as Musk, if not more so. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from last year, Amazon’s bald, newly buff Jeff Bezos had a 29 percent favorability rating; Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg garnered a pathetic 26 percent.
In other words, the people, if not the billionaires, are on our side here. According to the most recent Harris Poll Americans and Billionaires survey, more than half of all Americans think billionaires are a threat to democracy. And they want something done about it: 69 percent say the ultra-wealthy should have less influence in politics, 71 percent think wealth taxes should be imposed on the rich and 53 percent that there should be actual caps on wealth. They’re right on all counts, of course. We just need to do a better job of convincing them to vote as if these opinions matter.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Justiça Federal desiste de R$ 209 mi extra para pagar penduricalhos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Felipe Pontes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente do Conselho da Justiça Federal (CJF), ministro Luís Felipe Salomão, que também preside o Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ), desistiu formalmente, nesta terça-feira (10), de solicitar crédito extra de R$ 208,9 milhões com o objetivo de pagar penduricalhos — como são conhecidas as verbas indenizatórias e outras gratificações que se somam aos vencimentos dos juízes.
Em ofício enviado à Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), Salomão informou não haver mais a necessidade de suplementação orçamentária, devido ao surgimento de novas receitas que permitem ao Judiciário fazer os pagamentos com verbas próprias.
“Surgiram fatos novos com aportes de receitas e adequações orçamentárias, típicas desta época de final de ano, com empenhos e despesas não efetuados, ensejando consequente reanálise das contas. Por isso cessou, no âmbito da Justiça Federal, a necessidade então identificada”, justificou o ministro.
A desistência ocorre após repercutir na imprensa o pedido por mais recursos feito pelo Judiciário e pelo Ministério Público da União (MPU), que, por sua vez, disse precisar de mais R$ 324 milhões para o pagamento dos penduricalhos. Somadas, as solicitações de recursos chegavam a R$ 533 milhões.
A solicitação de suplementação orçamentária foi alvo de pedido de esclarecimentos feito pela AGU junto ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), no âmbito de três ações diretas de inconstitucionalidade (ADIs) que tratam do pagamento de penduricalhos a juízes e membros do Ministério Público.
De acordo com a AGU, a falta de recursos poderia comprometer, por exemplo, o pagamento da parcela de valorização por tempo de antiguidade na carreira (PVTAC), equivalente à soma de 5% do salário de juízes e promotores a cada cinco anos de trabalho, limitada a 35% do salário.
Diante da falta de previsão orçamentária, a AGU pediu que o Supremo decida qual procedimento deverá ser adotado para cumprir a decisão da Corte que autorizou o pagamento do benefício.
“Afigura-se imprescindível a orientação desse Supremo Tribunal Federal quanto ao modo pelo qual deve ser dado o escorreito cumprimento ao julgado”, solicitou o órgão.
Penduricalhos
No dia 25 de março deste ano, por unanimidade, os ministros decidiram que as indenizações adicionais, gratificações e auxílios deverão ser limitados a 35% do valor do salário dos integrantes da Corte, que tem o teto como referência e é equivalente a R$ 46,3 mil.
Contudo, a soma do salário e benefícios ainda pode chegar a R$ 78,8 mil mensais para quem recebe o adicional tempo de serviço, benefício que foi mantido pelo STF. O adicional prevê o acréscimo de 5% ao salário por ano trabalhado e pode ser somado a outros penduricalhos.

https://gothamist.com/news/central-park-.title: Central Park rape suspect taken into custody at Miami Burger King, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/central-park-.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/central-park-.text:
A man accused of raping a woman in Central Park last month was taken into custody Tuesday while working at a Burger King in Miami, police said, adding that he will also be charged in two earlier rapes in the park.
In a social media post, police identified the man as Dereck Rivera-Deleon and said the earlier attacks happened in 2021 and 2023.
The department did not say how investigators linked him to those attacks or release any details about either. Several days after the attack on Oct. 24, the NYPD released images of a man in his 30s wearing a black hoodie.
The most recent attack happened near East 66th Street and Fifth Avenue around 8:30 p.m., police said at the time. The victim, a 39-year-old woman, was taken to a hospital, and the man fled, according to police.
NYPD detectives assigned to a U.S. Marshals regional fugitive task force took Rivera-Deleon into custody with help from the U.S. Marshals Service, officials said on X.
Police did not say what charges he faces in the October attack or when he will be brought back to New York.
It was not immediately clear whether Rivera-Deleon has a lawyer.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/am.title: American Alliance of Museums Makes Case for Policy Proposals Following Democrats’ Landslide Election Win
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/am.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/am.text:
Since President Donald Trump returned to office last year, his administration has made reining in the cultural sphere a core plank of his agenda.
Those efforts have included slashing federal funding for the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) and the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA); attempting to remake the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., in his image; and unleashing a relentless barrage of executive orders, attempted firings, and investigations targeting the Smithsonian Institution and its affiliated museums. The campaign reached a fever pitch in July, when the White House released a 162-page report detailing supposed “ideological capture” at the National Museum of American History. Two congressional hearings followed, in which lawmakers grilled the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, over her perceived failure to uphold the institution’s mission.
The American Alliance of Museums (AAM), a leading industry group for museums, has steadfastly defended cultural institutions facing Trump’s wrath, rebuking the administration’s efforts in public statements.
Now, with the political winds shifting and Democrats having secured their biggest midterm election victory in decades, AAM isn’t wasting time. In a statement released November 4, the day after the election, the organization said it plans to push the newly elected Congress to restore or increase funding for the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS), as well as for the NEA and NEH. (Trump’s proposed 2025 budget would have decimated IMLS, but following an advocacy campaign led by AAM, and legal challenges from the American Library Association and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, its budget was largely restored.) AAM also called for lifting the House Appropriations Committee’s current ban on earmark funding for museums.
Asked about the organization’s priorities for the incoming Congress, an AAM spokesperson told ARTnews, “We’re focused on continuing to build strong bipartisan support for museums, protecting federal funding for museums, and ensuring museums can fulfill their educational missions without political interference which is an important part of the conversation for the entire field.”
AAM did not offer details on how Congress might prevent political interference in the museum field. In late September, a group of Democratic lawmakers led by Representative Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico introduced a bill to protect the independence of the Smithsonian Institution, a measure AAM endorsed. At the time, Devon Akmon, chair of AAM’s board, said of the bill, “Protecting the Smithsonian’s scholarly independence honors that public trust and affirms a principle fundamental to all museums: scholarship and interpretation must be guided by evidence, expertise, and professional standards, not political influence.” The bill has not advanced since its introduction and will need to be reintroduced when the new Congress convenes in January.
On December 2, AAM will host a live webinar with Brandy Dillingham, its director of advocacy, and Nichole Westin, its senior director of government and field relations, on how the election results may affect museums.

https://taz.de/Wurde-Nvidia-Tech-Bro-Jen.title: Honeytrapping und Midlifecrisis: Jensen Huang verstehen
https://taz.de/Wurde-Nvidia-Tech-Bro-Jen.author: Uli Hannemann
https://taz.de/Wurde-Nvidia-Tech-Bro-Jen.text:
Honeytrapping und Midlifecrisis : Jensen Huang verstehen
Wurde Tech Bro Jensen Huang am Cockring durch die Manege gezogen? Oder reden wir mal wieder zu wenig über Gefühle? Gebüßt wird jedenfalls fleißig.
D ie Kacke ist am Dampfen. Jensen Huang, 63, Mitgründer von Nvidia, einem der führenden US-Chipentwickler im Bereich KI, ist mit beiden Füßen in eine sogenannte Honey Trap gelatscht. Dort klebt er nun.
Honeytrapping ist ein uraltes Geschäft. Brutus und Cäsar, Mata Hari und die alliierten Generäle. Es gibt Liebe und Sex für die eine, Informationen politischer, militärischer oder wirtschaftlicher Natur für die andere Seite. Eine Win-win-Situation, so lange, bis alles rauskommt. Zum Beispiel durch Erpressung, denn oft geht es auch schlicht um Geld.
Der Honeypot, in dem nun der Tech Bro landete, heißt Alice Huang. Die 42-jährige Chief Executive des Computing-Unternehmens Megaspeed aus Singapur hatte eine Affäre mit dem Nvidia-Chef. Im Netz kursieren Bilder von Huang und Huang – nicht verwandt und nicht verschwägert – auf einem Sofa in Taipei im Rahmen der IT-Messe Computex. Er hat den Arm um sie gelegt, sie drückt ihm ein Küsschen auf die Wange. Allerliebst sieht das aus, nur ein Unhold will solchen Menschen Böses: „Uh uh uh uh, wir waren so glücklich …“ (Trio: „Nur ein Traum“).
In diesem Fall schlugen jedoch US-Geheimdienste Alarm. Denn, und darin liegt nun eben der Verdacht des Honeytrappings, Alice Huang wird unbewiesen unterstellt, den Intimkontakt benutzt zu haben, um – ein No-go im umkämpften KI-Markt – über Megaspeed Hochleistungschips von Nvidia nach China weiterzuverkaufen. Was von beiden Firmen bestritten wird. Bekannt ist allerdings, dass Jensen Huang für mehr technologischen Austausch auch mit China plädierte. Ob als am Cockring durch die Manege gezogene, verliebte Marionette der Chinesen oder aus eigenem Denken? Wer weiß das schon?
Dritte Midlife-Crisis
Die chinesische Regierung ist offenbar romantischer veranlagt. Das ehrt sie. So viel Wärme und Empathie hätten wir ihr gar nicht zugetraut. Schützend hält sie die Hand über unsere zwei Turteltäubchen und deren hehre Motive. Sie glaubt noch an die reine und wahre Liebe (oder zumindest an den Rausch des Crushs) und weist sämtliche Spionagevorwürfe brüsk von sich. Wo Zweifel an der Liebe aufkommen, schlagen die Emotionen erfahrungsgemäß hohe Wellen.
Wir halten es eher mit den Chinesen. Denn wir verstehen Jensen Huang. Dreiundsechzig gilt ja als ganz schwieriges Alter, die dritte und letzte Midlife-Crisis, „die fünfte Pubertät“, „der Tod des Clowns“. Wider die insgeheim bessere Einsicht möchte man sich noch nicht darauf beschränken, diesen Lebensabschnitt bis zum Tod im langweiligen, aber bequemen Ohrensessel der gealterten Leidenschaft zu verbringen, dem ungefähr gleichaltrigen Ehegespons freundlich die Füßchen massierend.
Wir wissen nicht, was Jensen Huang mit seiner Frau vereinbart hat, aber seine öffentlichen Entschuldigungsbeteuerungen legen nahe, dass eine Affäre mit der Spitzenmanagerin eines anderen Konzerns nicht Teil dieser Vereinbarung gewesen sein dürfte. Wenn Libertinage im Hause Huang – so schließen wir aus den gewinselten „Ich war meiner Frau untreu“ –, dann sicher nur mit stark gebremstem Schaum.
In einem Milieu zugedrogter Vergewaltiger und misogyner Maskulinisten mit übersteigertem Selbstbewusstsein wirkt der zerknirschte Kniefall nicht unsympathisch. Ein verknallter Brillennerd, ein armes, dummes Sünderlein – da können wir Normalos, die diesbezüglich schon mal Scheiße gebaut haben, mit einem Blick in den Spiegel wunderbar andocken.
Und er muss ja auch büßen. Wir wissen nicht, ob er nun die Reisetasche packt, natürlich fürs Luxushotel, und nicht wie wir, um bei einem Kumpel auf dem Sofa zu pennen.
Aber die Aktie von Nvidia stürzt ab, und auch die persönliche Aktie von Jensen Huang erlebt ihren schwarzen Freitag. Denn er steht in vielerlei Hinsicht vor einem Scherbenhaufen. Mutti schimpft, sein Job wackelt, und die Sicherheitsbehörden stehen ihm auf den Füßen. Doch das Schlimmste ist der Abschied aus dem Wunderland. Sollte seine Alice ihn nur benutzt haben; war das alles nur ein Traum?
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. Hundreds gathered around Anish Kapoor’s iconic Cloud Gate, knows as the “Bean,” in Chicago’s Millennium Park on Sunday in an attempt to shift the sculpture seven inches to the left. Despite the crowd’s best efforts, the silver 110-ton stainless steel sculpture could not be moved.
ARTnews reports that the stunt was based on a viral online joke, which holds that a man is trapped inside the 66-foot-long, 33-foot-high, kidney bean–shaped sculpture. An unknown party created a Partiful event invitation announcing that “new findings suggest that there might be [a] latch door under the right side of the bean. If we move the bean about 7 inches to the left we might be able to access that door and give the man inside the bean resources.”
Alderman Brendan Reilly, who represents the ward that includes Millennium Park, told Book Club Chicago that his office received multiple calls about the rumor last summer. “I am happy to confirm that a man has not been trapped inside ‘Cloud Gate’ (a.k.a ‘the Bean’) for the past 21 years,” he wrote in a statement.
On July 31, 2025, a group dressed in black gathered near the Bean with signs calling for the release of “the man in the Bean.” A video of that event went viral on Instagram and TikTok, resulting in the flood of calls to the alderman’s office.
The Instagram account @thingstodoinchicago posted a video of Sunday’s mob, capturing the group surrounding one end of the sculpture and appearing to give a concerted push. “What started as a viral internet joke turned into a real-life gathering,” the post reads, “proving once again that Chicago has a sense of humor like no other.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.title: Arizona Town’s Probe on Sex Abuse Claims Could Block Prison Firm Building New ICE Camp
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.author: John Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.text:
This story was published in partnership with LOOKOUT News.
An official from Marana, Arizona, is seeking clarification from the private prison giant Management and Training Corporation about its handling of sexual abuse allegations at the former state prison in the town, following an investigation from LOOKOUT and The Intercept.
In an October 28 letter, reviewed by LOOKOUT and The Intercept, Marana Finance Director and License Inspector Yiannis Kalaitzidis asked MTC Senior Vice President Mary Calvin for a written explanation of what the town official called an “apparent inconsistency” between state records and the facility’s 2023 Prison Rape Elimination Act, or PREA, audit, a report required by the federal law.
The request is part of the town’s review of MTC’s October 1 application for a business license to “Operate Marana Detention Facility.” The company ran a former Arizona state prison in Marana and plans to reopen it imminently as a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention camp.
The letter cites a September 29 LOOKOUT and Intercept investigation about how state records reference three allegations of sexual misconduct at the prison in 2022 and 2023.
PREA audits — which are required for jails, prisons, and detention centers at least once every three years — must record all allegations of sexual misconduct at detention facilities, whether they are substantiated or not. Certified in December 2023, MTC’s report for the Marana prison, however, recorded none.
Kalaitzidis noted in his letter that the audit says the finding of zero incidents was verified by the warden, chief of security, PREA compliance manager, and internal investigator. He also wrote that, despite the apparent reviews by several company officials, the report “does not appear to be certified or signed by any MTC personnel.”
The letter says the town of Marana is requesting the explanation as part of an investigation into whether MTC “made a material false statement in conducting the business” of the state prison facility, which would be grounds for denial of a business license according to the town’s code.
“The Town of Marana is currently reviewing MTC’s business license application,” said Andrea De La Cruz, the assistant town manager, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept by email. “As part of our review process and due diligence, the Town has contacted MTC to request additional information. The application remains under review, and no final determination has been made at this time.”
MTC did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Changing Political Context
Local residents and officials say the state, the federal government, and MTC left them out of meaningful discussions about reopening the prison as an ICE camp, LOOKOUT and The Intercept previously reported.
For now, a town business license is among the few levers local officials have.
In an October 2 letter from the local group Pima Resists ICE, or PRICE, to a Marana official who specialized in licensure, organizers cited not only the discrepancies between state investigations into sexual abuse and the PREA audit, but also alleged violations involving an escape from an MTC prison in Kingman, Arizona, in 2010, as well as abuses in a New Mexico immigration camp run by MTC as revealed in a 2017 DHS Office of Inspector General report.
The inquiry comes as Arizona’s political landscape is shifting. The midterm election gave Democrats control of both chambers of the state legislature as well as the governor’s office — a historic change in state power. Republicans will be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years.
That has Democratic lawmakers talking about taking on one of the most contentious laws in recent Arizona history. Following protests across the state, Democrats took up the cause of repealing a controversial 2010 anti-immigrant law known as Senate Bill 1070. In 2012, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down three of its provisions, leaving a requirement that police check the immigration status of people they stop under certain circumstances.
“I would absolutely love to see a repeal of SB1070,” state Sen. Analise Ortiz, a Democrat from Glendale, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept. “There are still parts of that law on the books that are enabling cities to collaborate with ICE to rip families apart, and that needs to stop.”
State Rep. Betty Villegas, D-Tucson, echoed Ortiz: “We already have bills aligned to focus on what other states have done to control ICE from coming into private property.”
Following the lead of neighboring New Mexico’s prohibition on local jurisdictions entering into contracts with ICE for immigrant detention camps, Villegas said Democrats in Arizona see an appetite for doing something similar in their own state.
Ortiz agreed, saying there is “likely an appetite” for something similar in Arizona, and that the Latino Caucus would address the issue.
Local nonprofits said lawmakers should also conduct a review of no-bid contracts like the one inked between the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, and MTC.
“This was literally handed to them with no review and no public input,” said Caroline Isaacs, the executive director of Just Communities Arizona, a nonprofit working on criminal justice reform. “We do not want the Democrats to wait until things get bad to investigate conditions.”
“We want them to do this now, before people get hurt.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/vance-maga-t.title: Trump’s Midterm Rout Didn’t End the Threat From J. D. Vance
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/vance-maga-t.author: Gilbert Achcar
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/vance-maga-t.text:
Trump’s Midterm Rout Didn’t End the Threat From J. D. Vance
President Trump’s midterm debacle has weakened the entire MAGA camp. But J. D. Vance, a more disciplined and more ideological far-right figure, is already positioning himself to inherit the movement in 2028.
Donald Trump may have foreseen another reversal of his political fortunes when he chose J. D. Vance as his running mate. For who would want to remove Trump if the result were Vance at the helm of US executive? After all, Trump is the ultimate opportunist, a man who can smile and shake hands with Zohran Mamdani while hurling outrageous anti-socialist and Islamophobic slanders at him; a man who can pose as a dove while acting as a hawk, and who is so obsessed with his own ego that he is ultimately his own most effective enemy — as he proved brilliantly in bringing about the Republicans’ midterms debacle. Vance, on the other hand, is a consummate far-right ideologist. True, he does not lack opportunism either. As Compact magazine’s editor Matthew Schmitz recently reminded readers in a New York Times op-ed: “He made his way from the Rust Belt to Yale Law, and from saying Mr. Trump might be ‘America’s Hitler’ to serving as his vice president.”
Yet this is closer to the cold-blooded careerism so common on the far right than to Trump’s crude, crowd-pleasing demagogy. Moreover, as The Washington Post’s George F. Will, a traditional conservative and longtime Trump critic, put it: “Trump’s deepening weirdness (e.g., repeatedly proclaiming his admiration for various men’s and women’s body parts) suggests he is residing in the suburbs of dotage. Vance has no such excuse.” Unlike Trump, Vance harbors intellectual pretensions and has been cultivating his own wing of the MAGA movement with close, personal ties to other far-right ideologues such as Steve Bannon and Tucker Carlson. In that sense, he would be an even more dangerous president than Trump. However, the resounding rebuke Trump suffered in the recent elections has also damaged his entire camp, including the ideological far right that Vance represents. Schmitz concludes: “Perhaps he can complete another unlikely journey, to the presidency. But he now seems farther from that office than he did just one week ago.” That is fair enough, but no one should assume that the vice president too has become a lame duck.
Vance’s Post-Mortem
Vance was visibly stunned by the scale of the electorate’s repudiation of Trump — which is also a repudiation of the MAGA craze by a clear majority of voters. Like a rat fleeing a sinking ship, the vice president hurried to disclaim responsibility for the debacle and distance himself from the president. His reaction is revealing, for it indicates what his ideological campaign will center on in the next two years, as he plainly seeks to become the next MAGA presidential candidate. On the afternoon of November 4, once the Republican rout was largely confirmed, he posted his break with Trump on X. Citing an unnamed pollster, “one of the smartest people I know in politics,” he listed what he described as the four main issues behind the rout — and, by implication, his four priorities for the next two years: “1) End the war; 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation; 3) Put America First; 4) Change our relationship to Israel.”
Let us consider these four points and what they leave unsaid. Trump’s war on Iran has obviously not gone down well with the US public. Not only did it flatly contradict the pacifist-sounding promises of Trump during his presidential campaigns — promises that, to be sure, reflected no real love of peace, only an appeal to the old far-right isolationist legacy long embodied by Pat Buchanan. More importantly, while Trump assumed that the US public would barely feel the consequences of the war, it came home to roost in the form of an inflationary surge fueled by gas prices. Yet the war accounts for only part of this surge, which — under the name of “affordability” — loomed far larger than war itself in the campaign. Hence, Vance’s second point on the cost of living. But he keeps mum about the squeeze’s root causes, above all Trump’s outrageously pro-rich budget and his ultranationalistic, wildly erratic tariffs. Vance would not say a word about these for the very good reason that he fully endorsed them, unlike the war on Iran, from which he tried, albeit timidly, to distance himself.
The Same Old Scapegoats
Then comes the old far-right refrain of “America First,” dear to Trump and the MAGA crowd. This hollow slogan serves only to stoke the basest ultranationalist sentiments among mostly poor white social layers that tend to interpret their economic hardship in a highly skewed, xenophobic, often racist way. It is a slogan whose clearest translation is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). And one that obscures all the real problems that the US working class is facing, offering tariff fetishism as a universal panacea instead. For the section of the far right to which Vance belongs, and which he hopes to lead, this jingoism has typically gone hand in hand with antisemitism. It is their way of perverting the massive — and entirely legitimate — rise in popular antipathy toward Israel caused by the appalling genocidal war it has waged in Gaza with full US support, from Joe Biden to Trump: diverting it into a “blame it on Israel” stratagem. The aim is, of course, to deflect attention from the reality of US imperialism, including, in this case, the deeply corrupt interests of the Trump syndicate and its cronies, by resorting to the oldest of far-right scapegoating tricks.
As for Vance’s fourth point, his phrasing — “Change our relationship to Israel” — is deliberately vague, a far cry from the increasingly popular and unambiguous calls to end all US military support for Israel. The key issue is certainly not the $3.8 billion that Washington grants Israel every year under a memorandum of understanding concluded by the Obama administration. In a classic case of US taxpayers’ money being funneled to the US military-industrial complex, these funds were earmarked for Israeli purchases of US weaponry. The mercenary logic governing Trump’s foreign policy — which, by gutting the United States Agency for International Development, has inflicted severe damage on several countries of the Global South — had already led him to cut off the much larger US funding of Ukraine’s purchases of US military hardware, forcing Kyiv’s European backers to foot the bill themselves. Now Israel will have to pay for its deadly US imports on its own — hardly a big deal for the Zionist state. Trump presented the move as agreed upon with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who confirmed it, even boasting of what he portrayed as a shift in Israel’s relationship with its US godfather from dependence into equal partnership.
Peter Thiel’s Godson
That said, the most glaring blind spot in Vance’s account of the rout is his total silence on one of the issues that decided the elections: Big Tech, AI, and data centers. “There’s no question about how voters feel about data centers after Election Day, with restrictive measures across 10 states going 43–1 at the ballot box. The margins weren’t close, with an average of 75% of people favoring restrictions,” wrote Maria Curi of Axios. “America turns on Donald Trump’s tech cheerleaders,” declared a Financial Times headline in the elections’ wake. Polls indicate that public resentment of what is perceived as a Big Tech mafia has become one of the main channels through which Americans register the immense social inequality of their society, far greater than in any other economically advanced country. On this, of course, Vance — the political godson of Peter Thiel, who, along with Elon Musk, is the farthest right of the Big Tech tycoons — would not utter a single word, even though some of his most populist MAGA allies, such as Steve Bannon, have joined the anti–Big Tech chorus, which fits neatly with the anti-elitist rhetoric characteristic of their brand of far-right ideology.
Vance is being built up as the standard-bearer of MAGA continuity. While many expected a reshuffle that would oust the ultramasculinist, hyperarrogant “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth, one of the administration’s most unpopular liabilities, Trump instead promoted his éminence grise, Stephen Miller — a sinister far-right ideologue, rabidly antimigrant (Mr ICE par excellence) and Islamophobic — to the key post of White House chief of staff. Vance immediately hailed the promotion on X: “Stephen Miller is an amazing patriot and will do great things.” Backed by Thiel, Donald Trump Jr, and others of their ilk, Vance is already poising himself to lead the MAGA current into the 2028 presidential election. It is vital not to underestimate the threat he represents, and to make the fight against this chief embodiment of the US far right as one of the priorities of the coming period.
Vance might have once been thought of as “Trump lite.” But it’s abundantly clear now that, if he somehow made it to the White House, he could possibly be even worse that the godfather of MAGA himself.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.author: Jana Frielinghaus
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.text:
- Politik
- Patricia Schlesinger
Patricia Schlesinger: Mitnahmementalität einer Spitzenverdienerin
In Berlin hat ein Untreue-Prozess gegen die Ex-Intendantin des RBB und weitere ehemalige Mitglieder der Leitung des Senders begonnen.
Ihr Fall dürfte für viele Kritiker das Paradebeispiel für Filz und Vetternwirtschaft auf der Führungsebene des Öffentlich-Rechtlichen Rundfunks, aber auch für Mitnahmementalität und Verschwendung der »Zwangsgebühr« sein: Patricia Schlesinger, im August 2022 fristlos entlassene Intendantin des Rundfunks Berlin-Brandenburg (RBB). Zumal der Journalistin und Ex-ÖRR-Funktionärin offenkundig jegliches Unrechtsbewusstsein fehlt.
Am Dienstag hat vor dem Landgericht Berlin der Prozess wegen Untreue gegen die 65-Jährige begonnen. Laut Anklage müssen sie und weitere frühere RBB-Führungsmitglieder sich wegen zahlreicher Fälle von Untreue verantworten. Sie haben dem Sender demnach einen Schaden im Umfang von 1,7 Millionen Euro zugefügt. Im Kern geht es um ein mutmaßlich von den Angeklagten etabliertes Vergütungs- und Zulagensystem, von dem Schlesinger und andere Mitglieder der Geschäftsleitung ohne sachlich gerechtfertigten Grund profitierten. Es ging um üppige Boni, die sie sich genehmigten – zusätzlich zum Gehalt, das im Fall von Schlesinger mehr als 25.000 Euro monatlich betrug. Trotzdem dinierte und verreiste die Dame laut Anklage zusätzlich privat auf Senderkosten.
Laut Anklage flossen zwischen April 2019 und Juli 2022 rund 933.500 Euro an variablen Vergütungen an Schlesinger, den Verwaltungsdirektor, die juristische Direktorin und weitere Mitglieder der Geschäftsleitung. Mit rund 223.700 Euro bekam Schlesinger demnach die größte Summe für »erreichte Zielvereinbarungen«. Einen sachlichen Grund für diese Sonderzahlungen gab es aus Sicht der Generalstaatsanwaltschaft nicht. Ziel von Schlesinger und dem früheren Vorsitzenden des RBB-Verwaltungsrats sei es gewesen, sich durch die Einführung der variablen Vergütung eine zusätzliche Einnahmequelle zu verschaffen, sagte Oberstaatsanwältin Judith Kohlstedt-Mansouri bei der Anklageverlesung. Mehrleistungen hätten sie dafür nicht erbracht. Außerdem sei ihnen bewusst gewesen, dass sie dadurch die Überwachungspflichten des Verwaltungsrats »faktisch außer Kraft« gesetzt hätten. Und für die Abendessen mit wichtigen Leuten in ihrer Privatwohnung auf Kosten des RBB hätten »keine konkreten Anlässe« bestanden, so Kohlstedt-Mansouri.
Schlesingers Verteidiger Oliver Sahan erklärte dazu, Auftrag seiner Mandantin sei es gewesen, aus dem RBB einen »ernstzunehmenden Hauptstadtsender« zu machen, veraltete Strukturen aufzubrechen und die Digitalisierung voranzubringen. Paradoxerweise stehe sie nun »öffentlich am Pranger«, weil sie diese Aufgaben erfüllt habe. Die Reform habe den Interessen des RBB gedient, indem konkrete Unternehmensziele festgelegt und »Anreize für höhere Effizienz« gesetzt worden seien. Zudem sei die Reform auch gegenüber dem Verwaltungsrat offen kommuniziert worden. Und die beim RBB abgerechnete private Reise nach London habe der Vorbereitung auf die Übernahme des ARD-Vorsitzes gedient, sagte der Anwalt. Es sei um einen Erfahrungsaustausch mit der BBC zum »Umgang mit öffentlicher Kritik« gegangen.
Schlesinger war von Juli 2016 bis zu ihrem Rücktritt im August 2022 RBB-Intendantin. Zudem hatte sie 2022 sieben Monate lang den ARD-Vorsitz inne. Die fristlose Kündigung schob der RBB-Verwaltungsrat nach. Ermittlungen der Generalstaatsanwaltschaft begannen unmittelbar danach. Dass der Prozess erst jetzt beginnen konnte, lag nach Angaben der Behörde unter anderem an der enormen Menge auszuwertender Dokumente und Informationen. Bislang sind 56 Verhandlungstermine bis zum 29. Juni 2027 angesetzt.
Parallel zu dem Strafprozess läuft ein Zivilverfahren, in dem Schlesinger und der RBB gegenseitig Ansprüche geltend machen. Die Ex-Intendantin fordert ein sogenanntes Ruhegeld in Höhe von 18.300 Euro monatlich und erzielte diesbezüglich bereits im Juli 2025 einen Teilerfolg. Der Sender wirft ihr Pflichtverletzungen vor und verlangt insgesamt rund 1,8 Millionen Euro von ihr zurück.
Claus Kleber, langjähriger Moderator des ZDF-»heute journals«, war einer von mehreren prominenten Journalisten und ÖRR-Vertretern, die zum Verhandlungsauftakt erschienen waren. Er erklärte am Rande des Prozesses, sie wollten diesen als »Freunde und ehemalige Kollegen« beobachten. »Diese Sache ist in der Öffentlichkeit größer geworden, als sie strafrechtlich ist. Es ist zu einer Art Scherbengericht über den ganzen Öffentlich-Rechtlichen Rundfunk aufgerufen worden«, beklagte Kleber.
Wie wäre es angesichts dessen, die Vergütungs- und Ruhestandsregelungen für Führungskräfte allgemein zu reformieren und vor allem die vielen prekär beschäftigten Mitarbeiter*innen im ÖRR besser zu bezahlen? Schließlich kassieren viele Ex-Führungskräfte ganz legal riesige Ruhegehälter – selbst wenn sie bestens dotierte Folgejobs haben.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Tate Britain spotlights Bloomsbury artists Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant for the first time since 1999
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Andrew Pulver
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Bloomsbury Group seems to have been ever-present in UK culture since its inception in the early 20th century, just before the First World War. Lytton Strachey, John Maynard Keynes, Virginia Woolf, E.M. Forster, Vanessa Bell, Duncan Grant—their names are legion as representatives of a flowering of British intellectualism across the full spectrum of literary and artistic endeavours. While Roger Fry was arguably Bloomsbury’s most influential art-world voice, as the critic who essentially introduced European Post-Impressionism to Britain with a celebrated exhibition at the Grafton Galleries in 1910, Bell and Grant were the group’s most active and high-profile painters. The pair’s bracketing together for a new Tate Britain exhibition is also a result, no doubt, of their 40-year open relationship that saw them live and paint together—and each other—over many decades.
The Bloomsbury Group has largely retained its high profile over the decades, with feature films on many of its protagonists and even a BBC mini-series in 2015 called Life in Squares, named for the supposed Dorothy Parker gag that the group “lived in squares, painted in circles and loved in triangles”. Bell and Grant’s former home Charleston, near Lewes in East Sussex, has maintained a near-constant programme of exhibitions to keep the flame alive, the latest of which, Mad Bloomsbury (4 November-11 April 2027) examines the group’s engagement with mental health issues.
But the Tate show marks the first Bloomsbury-focused show at the national home for British art for over a quarter of a century. Thomas Kennedy, the curator of Modern British art at Tate Britain, thinks it is about time. “That means an entire generation of visitors have not seen an exhibition on Vanessa or Duncan’s work at Tate, and we felt that it was important for us to revisit their practices again after so long,” Kennedy says. “I don’t believe there’s ever been a major exhibition on Vanessa and Duncan together, and it’s so fascinating to see the ways they differ. We should recognise their individual accomplishments of course, but also the works they made together and how they influenced each other. We know about their relationship—she was married and he was gay—but this exhibition explores what that really meant in their artworks and in their life.”
Out of fashion
Looking back at that previous 1999 show, the cuttings files reveal that the turn of the millennium clearly marked a low point in critical opinion of the Bloomsbury artists; outright abuse might be the best description of some of the responses. The Guardian art critic Adrian Searle called them “a bit crap”, “lightweights” and “third rate”, while for the novelist Philip Hensher writing in The Independent, these “no-hopers” and their “rubbish” inspired simple “rage and loathing”.
But Kennedy is not having it. Bell and Grant, he says, “started experimenting with art in unique ways that hadn’t really been seen in Britain before”. He adds: “They created some of the first abstract works in Britain, which is sometimes very much overlooked. And they were creating these works together, and talking about art all day, every day, breaking the distinction between fine and decorative art with the Omega Workshops. What they were doing was really special.”
Bell, whose sister Virginia Woolf was even more celebrated in her field, is perhaps now the slightly more recognisable name of the two painters, though, as Kennedy points out, both Bell and Grant were considered leading figures during their lifetimes. Their close physical proximity, from when they moved to Charleston in 1918 to Bell’s death in 1961, meant their styles were often similarly adjacent, though Kennedy is clear on the differences. “Vanessa’s painting is more deliberate with very considered blocks of colour and very strong outlines, whereas Duncan’s is scratchier, more impulsive and it feels like he is experimenting more with more expressive techniques,” he says.
Kennedy adds: “However, later on, when they’re working on the Famous Women dinner service [a collection of 50 hand-painted plates], their styles are completely the same: the authorship has very much broken down and we can’t tell who did what. So much so that Roger Fry told them to paint in different studios to reassess their own way of making. It’s fascinating to see that push and pull between what they were taking from each other.”
In the end, it might be that the very thing that seemed to diminish the Bloomsbury Group for previous generations—their complex, near-incestuous love lives—is what is powering their current revival: to contemporary perspectives they now look like pioneers of unrepentantly queer lifestyles. Bell married fellow painter Clive Bell in 1907, then had a long relationship with Fry and had a daughter, Angelica, with Grant in 1918. Grant, for his part, had a string of male lovers while maintaining his domestic relationship with Bell. “They were looking towards non-monogamous relationships and accepting queer relationships. The latter, as you know, was illegal in the UK at the time,” Kennedy says. “Within the Bloomsbury Group they felt freedom—both artistically and the way they lived.”
• Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, Tate Britain, London, 12 November-11 April 2027

Fall 2026 Art and Architecture Books from Yale University Press
The Bayeux tapestry, a new biography of Edward Hopper, The Met's exhibition catalogue on Krasner and Pollock, what architecture is, and more
The Fall 2026 lineup of art and architecture books from Yale University Press has both beauty and erudition. Exhibition catalogues from our museum publishing partners include Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous (The Metropolitan Museum of Art), Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism (Art Institute of Chicago), Roy Lichtenstein: Like New (Whitney Museum of American Art), and The Bayeux Tapestry (British Museum).
Owen Davies explores the Art of Divination across time and geography; Witold Rybczynski is characteristically eloquent on What Architecture Is; Neil Levine analyzes The Sculpture of Donald Judd; and Louis Shadwick gives us a brilliant new biography of Edward Hopper.
To learn more, visit yalebooks.yale.edu.
The Art of Divination
By Owen Davies
In this captivating book, Owen Davies explores the global history of divination practices from tea leaves and tarot cards to pyromancy and palmistry that seek to answer questions that range from the philosophical and metaphysical to the romantic and personal. Organized into six thematic groups—observing the natural world; making patterns; communicating with gods and spirits; signs from the human body and mind; looking to the heavens; and chance and calculation—Art of Divination allows readers to see connections between different ages and places.
The Bayeux Tapestry
By Owen Davies
The Bayeux Tapestry is an iconic artwork, almost seventy meters long, which tells the story of the events leading to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066 by William, Duke of Normandy. Featuring a full-color reproduction of the Tapestry and all-new photography, this beautiful book allows the reader to follow the visual narrative—with a scene-by-scene transliteration and English translation of the Tapestry’s Latin—while texts from international experts unpick the importance of the work in understanding this pivotal point in European history.
Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
By David Breslin and Brinda Kumar
The book surveys two icons of Abstract Expressionism that examines their distinct but connected careers and artistic legacies.
Edward Hopper: A Life
By Louis Shadwick
Edward Hopper: A Life reexamines the standard view of this renowned artist by interweaving his life and work and vividly reconstructing the personal, cultural, historical, and political contexts of his time. Using major new archives and a wealth of newly discovered sources, Louis Shadwick presents the richest and most complete story of Hopper’s life and art to date, revealing new dimensions to an artist whose carefully wrought identity has never been fully unraveled.
Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism
By Art Institute of Chicago
Mary Cassatt (1844–1926) was a trailblazing artist who worked across media, manipulated materials, transformed subjects through series and scale, and marketed and exhibited her artwork in novel ways. In Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism, scholars highlight Cassatt’s daring, ingenuity, and ceaselessly independent vision—both in her artistic technique and choice of subject matter—and consider the lasting impact of her aesthetic breakthroughs and significant legacy.
Roy Lichtenstein: Like New
By Alex Da Corte and Meg Onli
Contributions by Dan Nadel, Marshall N Price and Carmen Winant
A career-spanning look at the methods, influences, motivations, and continuing relevance of one of America’s foremost Pop artists.
The Sculpture of Donald Judd
By Neil Levine
The Sculpture of Donald Judd is the first chronological study of the artist’s pathbreaking and enormously influential work beginning with his turn from painting to sculpture in 1961–62 until his death in 1994. The analyses of the work, often considered the foundation of Minimalism, are based on close readings, highly attentive to detail and informed by a friendship with the artist.
What Architecture Is
By Witold Rybczynski
What is it about architecture that distinguishes it from ordinary building? Frustrated with the many cookie-cutter buildings going up around his home in downtown Philadelphia, eminent architectural historian and critic Witold Rybczynski offers an immersive meditation on the question in this extended essay, an insightful and opinionated reflection on the essential qualities of architecture both historical and modern. Witty, personal, and engaging, this cri de coeur from an esteemed critic takes on the age-old question of what elevates a mere building into an art form.
To learn more, visit yalebooks.yale.edu.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Câmara Legislativa do DF aprova mudança que abre caminho para terceiro mandato de Wellington Luiz na Presidência
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Cruz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Câmara Legislativa do Distrito Federal (CLDF) aprovou, nesta terça-feira (10), em segundo turno, a Proposta de Emenda à Lei Orgânica (Pelo) que altera as regras de reeleição dos integrantes da Mesa Diretora. O texto recebeu 15 votos favoráveis e um contrário e abre caminho para que o atual presidente da Casa, Wellington Luiz (MDB), dispute um terceiro mandato consecutivo à frente do Legislativo distrital, no biênio 2027-2028.
A mudança também beneficia outros sete integrantes da atual Mesa Diretora que foram reeleitos deputados distritais em outubro e poderão disputar novamente os mesmos cargos. Ao todo, oito dos nove integrantes da atual direção da Casa poderão concorrer à recondução.
A proposta permite a reeleição para o mesmo cargo na passagem de uma legislatura para outra, mas mantém a proibição de recondução dentro da mesma legislatura. Na prática, um deputado eleito para a Mesa em janeiro de 2027 não poderá disputar novamente a mesma função em 2029. Caso seja reeleito deputado distrital em 2030, poderá concorrer ao cargo novamente em janeiro de 2031.
Durante a sessão, o deputado distrital Chico Vigilante (PT) defendeu a aprovação da proposta e afirmou que a votação demonstrou a autonomia do Legislativo distrital em relação ao Executivo. “Não é questão de direita ou de esquerda, é questão do Parlamento do Distrito Federal. Nós estamos mostrando que esse poder aqui é independente. São os deputados e as deputadas que mandam aqui”, afirmou o deputado.
Chico também defendeu a mudança como uma forma de evitar a permanência prolongada de um mesmo parlamentar na Presidência da Casa. “Na próxima legislatura, qualquer um de nós terá direito a um mandato. Eu particularmente trabalhei para que a gente votasse essa emenda e quero dizer que não serei candidato a presidente. Não tenho vontade nem disposição. Mas é preciso que nesta Casa tenha pessoas que respeitem os deputados e as deputadas”, declarou.
Defesa da mudança
Entre os parlamentares favoráveis, Paula Belmonte (PSDB) afirmou que considera equivocada a regra anterior e defendeu a possibilidade de os deputados da próxima legislatura escolherem novamente os integrantes da Mesa. “Quando eu cheguei aqui nesse parlamento, eu achava muito estranho nós termos uma reeleição nos dois mandatos, numa legislatura. Eu confesso que achava um erro dessa Casa Legislativa e hoje nós estamos reparando esse erro”, afirmou.
Wellington Luiz, por sua vez, reconheceu que a aprovação da proposta não garante sua permanência na Presidência e afirmou que ainda há questões jurídicas a serem discutidas. “Essa aprovação hoje não garante a eleição de nenhum parlamentar, incluindo eu. Eu tenho questões jurídicas ainda a discutir. […] O que precisa haver entre nós é respeito”, declarou o presidente da casa.
Com a aprovação em segundo turno, a proposta será promulgada pela própria CLDF, sem necessidade de sanção do Governo do Distrito Federal (GDF). A eleição da nova Mesa Diretora está prevista para janeiro de 2027.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-indicted-.title: Man indicted in stabbing murder of Brooklyn runner Katie Suarez
https://gothamist.com/news/man-indicted-.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/man-indicted-.text:
A Brooklyn grand jury Tuesday voted to indict Sayed Mohassib, 27, on second degree murder charges in the killing of jogger Katie Suarez last month, the Brooklyn district attorney’s office said in a statement.
Mohassib was arrested Saturday and charged with killing Suarez along a bike and running path in Bath Beach on Oct. 30.
“Katie Suarez was a young woman with her whole life ahead of her, brutally taken from her loved ones in a senseless act of violence,” District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said in a statement. “Today’s indictment marks an important step toward securing justice and I commend the NYPD for its swift and thorough investigation.”
Mohassib, who worked for the city Department of Education, denied killing Suarez but told investigators that he was sitting on a bench along the path and became “covered in blood,” according to the criminal complaint against him after his arrest.
Police say there is surveillance footage of Mohassib running away from the scene of the stabbing, entering his apartment building and then walking out about 15 minutes later to throw items in the garbage, the complaint said.
He later told police that he got rid of his clothing and the knife and tried to wipe his hands and the wall of his apartment clean of blood, according to the complaint. Detectives investigating the case saw a reddish stain on a wall in his apartment that was later identified as blood, the complaint states.
Mohassib's attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Tuesday.
Prior to his employment with the Department of Education, Mohassib served briefly as an NYPD officer and in the U.S. Marine Corps, but was thrown out due to psychiatric issues.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said the city will investigate how he was allowed to work in the education department despite that history.
Prior to Mohassib’s arrest, NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny told reporters that Suarez’s killing was believed to be a random attack.
Suarez, who worked at a nearby bank, was doing her usual routine of going on a late afternoon run along the path, which runs along the waterfront in Southern Brooklyn.
Her mother and father were waiting nearby to drive home with her when she finished her run. When she didn’t arrive on time, Suarez’s father walked the path, looking for her. He ended up discovering her lifeless body near the path where she collapsed after being stabbed.
Mohassib was ordered held without bail after his arraignment on the charges from the criminal complaint. He will be arraigned on the indictment in the coming days, but the hearing has not yet been scheduled.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.title: The Secret Handshake’s Latest Statue Mocks President Trump for Toe-Related Deferment to Avoid Vietnam War Draft
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.text:
One of the five deferments President Donald Trump received to avoid being drafted for the Vietnam War is now the subject of a new statue mocking him by the Secret Handshake, an anonymous artist collective. On Monday, a gold statue appeared on the National Mall depicting Trump sitting down and holding his right foot, reports the Washington Post.
The plaque at the base of the statue says, “We honor the service and sacrifice of our Commander in Chief, Donald J. Trump. He’s a soldier in spirit, who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs,” a reference to the deferment in question.
The inscription adds, “We salute a leader who knows you can’t spell sacrifice without ‘I,’ and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you’re called to stand up, it’s best to just sit down and rest your feet.” The statue has been named The Foot Soldier.
The statue was accompanied by a mascot, a masked individual in a big-toe costume that had nine hairs and their name “TOEY” printed in block letters. “I’m the biggest toe. The hugest toe. Huge. Hugest toe. Largest toe that anyone’s ever seen,” says Toey, concealing their identity and repeating things such as “Draft dodger? I hardly know her.”
In a statement on Monday responding to the work’s installation, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said, “Trump Derangement Syndrome is a sick and incurable disease that has rotted the brains of these Democrat activists. President Trump will never waver in fighting for and protecting the American people.” During the Vietnam War, Trump received deferments, four of them being for his studies in college.
The Foot Soldier is the latest work by the Secret Handshake, whose work has been taunting the president since 2024. They include a pile of feces; an 8-foot-tall sculpture of a gold-painted hand squashing the green crown of the Statue of Liberty; and a statue of Trump holding hands with disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, which has repeatedly been reinstalled throughout D.C.
On Monday, the group said that as Trump “continues to wage a war and threaten new ones, it’s time to harken back to a time when Donald Trump would do whatever it takes to stay out of combat.”

Regierunsgchef Netanjahu : Das Ende in Sicht
Die Koalitionsverhandlungen sind zäh in Israel. Aber es zeichnet sich ab, dass sich der Ministerpräsident gerade selbst ins Aus befördert.
E s geht in die heiße Phase: In Israel haben ernsthafte Koalitionsgespräche begonnen, nachdem Präsident Herzog Oppositionsführer Gadi Eisenkot mit der Bildung eines neuen Kabinetts beauftragt hat. Eisenkots Block braucht für eine Mehrheit weitere 13 Sitze – es sei denn, er setzt auf eine Minderheitsregierung mit Unterstützung der arabischen Parteien. Allerdings wird eine solche Minderheitsregierung von der zionistischen Partei Israel Beitenu nicht mitgetragen. Wenn alles so bleibt, ist sie daher so gut wie ausgeschlossen, denn eine ein „Nein“ von Yisrael Beiteinus würde für das Eisenkot-Lager ein Loch von weiteren sieben Sitzen bedeuten.
Mögliche Koalitionspartner wären die ultraorthodoxen Parteien. Mit diesen liebäugelt gerade Liberman, Eisenkot ist nach Medienberichten ebenfalls ebenfalls nicht abgeneigt. Die Ultraorthodoxen könnten durchaus Interesse an einer Regierungskoalition mit der Opposition haben, schließlich ist Netanjahu auch daran gescheitert, eine dauerhafte Befreiung Ultraorthodoxer Männer vom Wehrdienst durchzusetzen. Allerdings bleibt die religiöse Schas-Partei erst einmal in Netanjahus Lager – und die Partei „Vereinigtes Thora-Judentum“ hat lediglich sieben Sitze im Parlament.
In dieser unklaren Situation ist momentan nur eines sicher: Die Ära Netanjahus könnte tatsächlich bald zu Ende gehen. Kürzlich nannte Netanjahu die arabischen Parteien „Hamas-Unterstützer“, obwohl er selbst vor Jahren versucht hatte, die Vereinigte Arabische Liste auf seine Seite zu ziehen, und für eine Einheitsregierung warb.

Artnet reports that the nonprofit printmaking organization Print Center New York (PCNY) has announced the appointment of Yukiko Yamagata as executive director. She began the role on November 9 and succeeds Judy Hecker, who led Print Center for a decade.
“Leading Print Center is truly a dream role,” Yamagata told Artnet. “I’m really driven by a strong belief that a society in which creativity and free expression thrive is the cornerstone of democracy.”
Yamagata came to PCNY from Creative Time, where she served as deputy director, then as interim executive director, over a twenty-two-month period. She also spent sixteen years at Open Society Foundations as curatorial and deputy director for culture and art and oversaw a $15.8 million program providing fellowships and grants to socially-engaged artists around the globe. She has also held positions at the New York Public Library’s Schomberg Center for Research in Black Culture and the Whitney Museum of American Art.
“Yukiko brings to Print Center a unique combination of leadership experience in the arts, philanthropy and organizational development, alongside a clear and inspiring vision for how Print Center can be best positioned in this next chapter of the organization’s growth,” Board Chair David Sabel said in a press release.
Yamagata told Artnet that an exhibition of Susan Meiselas’s photographs at the Whitney in 2000 fundamentally shaped her approach to public curation. Meiselas, she said, “views photography not as an isolated object, but as a starting point that expands a circle of knowledge and connection and engagement.” She added, “That concept has really shaped my career in the arts, throughout photography, socially engaged art, and public art.”
Anne Coffin founded International Print Center New York in 1995 as an alternative space for exploring the possibilities of the print medium. The organization changed its name to Print Center New York in 2022.
