https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.title: Kalshi Is Cozy With Trump — But It’s Ramping Up Dem Hires and Campaign Spending
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.text:
Since the start of the year, the prediction betting site Kalshi has two hired former officials from Joe Biden’s White House as a policy adviser and a top lobbyist.
The company’s co-founders have also spent nearly $1 million on donations to federal candidates, with more than a third, or $377,000, going to Democrats like Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., according to a new report.
Kalshi’s spending spree shows how much prediction market sites have ratcheted up their presence in Washington as regulators craft rules for the industry. While the sites’ close relationship with the Trump administration has drawn headlines, the report from the progressive group Demand Progress details how the industry’s influence operation crosses party lines.
The push for bipartisan relationships began months ago, but it could pay dividends as Democrats take over both chambers of a Congress, said Ella Fanger, the corporate power policy adviser for Demand Progress. A betting market critic, Fanger predicted that the companies will keep trying to win allies on both sides of the aisle.
“They’ve been hopeful that they can have Democratic champions for their policy agenda,” she said, “and not just have Trump’s cronies sticking out their necks for them.”
The hiring spree of former Biden officials and spending on Democratic candidates come as prediction markets are facing increasing scrutiny over betting on elections and a spate of suspicious trades from Washington about policy moves and even military action.
On Tuesday, Democrats on Capitol Hill called for Trump to bar White House staffers from using the betting sites and, with Democrats taking Congress, many observers expect investigations into their use in Washington.
In a statement, Kalshi said it was willing to work “across the ideological spectrum.”
“Kalshi has had substantive conversations with policymakers over the past year regarding legislation that protects consumers, keeps minors off our platform, makes insider trading bans standard across the industry, and ensures the CFTC” — the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — “has the resources they need,” said the company’s head of government relations, John Bivona, a former Democratic congressional staffer and Biden White House official.
“We’ve come out in support of legislation introduced by members across the ideological spectrum,” Bivona said, “and we’ve worked with dozens of lawmakers from both parties on these priorities.”
Hiring Republicans — and Dems
Kalshi and its rival Polymarket are the dominant players in the prediction market industry, which has flourished since Donald Trump became president thanks to his administration’s hands-off approach to regulation.
The ties between the prediction betting sites and Trumpworld go all the way to the president’s inner circle, as evidenced by Donald Trump Jr.’s financial stakes at both competitors.
Polymarket has also hired as a lobbyist a Republican former top official at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The federal regulatory body has, under the Trump administration, sued states for trying to regulate sports betting as gambling.
The Demand Progress report covers Trump Jr.’s ties to the industry, but it also shines a light on the role of former Democratic congressional and executive branch staffers.
Kalshi’s hires have tended toward establishment Democrats. Among them are Stephanie Cutter, a political strategist whose work spanned the Obama and Biden administrations as well as Kamala Harris’s campaign for president. Cutter was tapped as a policy adviser for Kalshi in April. Bivona was hired by Kalshi as its head of government relations in January.
Tripled Lobbying Spend
Overall, Kalshi has spent $1.8 million on lobbying in the first half of 2026, compared to $615,000 in all of 2025, according to the Demand Progress report.
Polymarket spent a relatively meager $180,000 during the same period this year, compared to $360,000 last year.
Fanger, whose group is critical of the prediction markets’ attempts to neutralize state sports gambling regulators, said she is worried that a pliant Congress could approve the Trump administration’s favorable regulations.
“The concern is basically just that we could get legislation that would codify the rulemaking that the CFTC has already begun,” she said, referring to the agency’s efforts to formally exercise jurisdiction over sports, political, cultural, and weather betting contracts. “And we think that it’s important for states to be able to regulate this industry as gambling, which is what it is.”
The industry may need all the lobbyists it can get if progressives gain power in the next Congress. Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., who is angling to chair the House Financial Services Committee, said in a letter last week that she wants to “rein in predatory lending and predatory platforms, including prediction markets, so that our constituents keep more of their hard-earned dollars in their pockets.”
Waters is also a longtime foil to the crypto industry. Crypto currency interests alienated Democrats by spending tens of millions of campaign dollars on Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who lost his seat to Democrat Sherrod Brown in the midterm election.
While crypto has lavished money on campaign spending through a super PAC, the prediction market industry has opted for a quieter campaign of smaller donations routed through more traditional channels.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/bande-de-g.title: Génocide à Gaza : Lewis Hamilton en visite symbolique à Rafah
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/bande-de-g.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/bande-de-g.text:
Le pilote britannique, septuple champion du monde de Formule 1 s’est rendu au poste-frontière égyptien et point de passage vers l’enclave palestinienne de Gaza ce 10 novembre. Un geste fort, alors que le territoire reste occupé par l’armée israélienne et l’aide humanitaire acheminée au compte-goutte.
Le septuple champion du monde de Formule 1, Lewis Hamilton s’est rendu, ce mardi 10 novembre, au poste-frontière égyptien de Rafah, porte d’entrée vers la bande de Gaza. Malgré l’accord de paix présenté par Donald Trump en octobre 2025, l’enclave palestinienne essuie toujours des attaques de l’armée israélienne qui commet un génocide depuis octobre 2023.
Sur place, le pilote britannique a rencontré des organisations humanitaires qui acheminent de l’aide vers le territoire palestinien occupé, dont les entrepôts du Croissant-Rouge égyptien (ERC). Le nombre de camions transportant des produits de premières nécessités et d’autres besoins pour les populations reste bien en deçà du minimum convenu de 600 par jour.
« J’espère sincèrement que nous parviendrons un jour à instaurer la paix »
Cette visite n’a rien d’un hasard. Le sportif a régulièrement publié des messages sur les réseaux sociaux concernant les enfants tués lors des frappes aériennes israéliennes à Gaza et a appelé à un cessez-le-feu. En octobre, Lewis Hamilton a affirmé : « Je pense que nous devons veiller à faire pression pour libérer le Congo, libérer le Soudan, libérer la Syrie, libérer la Palestine. J’espère sincèrement que nous parviendrons un jour à instaurer la paix ».
Deuxième pilote de formule 1 à avoir pris le départ de 400 courses, Lewis Hamilton a pris le temps de saluer les travailleurs et de s’entretenir avec les responsables des organisations humanitaires. L’armée israélienne ne s’est toujours pas retirée de Gaza et étend son contrôle sur 60 % du territoire palestinien, a indiqué le mois dernier une commission indépendante d’experts de l’ONU.
Pour une information libre sur la Palestine
Nous avons été l’un des premiers médias français à défendre le droit des Palestiniens à disposer d’un État viable dans le respect des résolutions de l’ONU. Et nous avons inlassablement défendu la paix au Proche-Orient. Aidez-nous à continuer de vous informer sur ce qui se passe là-bas. Grâce à vos dons.
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-wild-.title: Wild Horse Nine Skewers the Dangerous Fools Behind US Empire
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-wild-.author: Eileen Jones
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-wild-.text:
Wild Horse Nine Skewers the Dangerous Fools Behind US Empire
Wild Horse Nine is an irreverent portrait of the dopes who traffic in violence against democracy around the world, all in the service of US empire. But the connection between human callousness and evil has flown over the heads of some critics.
The climactic speech of Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy Wild Horse Nine is the “Kill ’em” monologue, delivered by an old Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) operative named Chris Carlisle (John Malkovich), who’s dying of cancer and whose mind is also starting to go. But after decades of habitual lying for professional reasons, he’s pledged to tell the truth to a Chilean college student and leftist organizer named Monica (Mariana di Girolamo) in what becomes an unlikely end-of-life friendship.
When Chris finally does tell her the truth as he knows it, after a life spent doing the worst, sickeningly violent, and incalculably harmful dirty work for US empire, it’s so terrible that it brings tears to her eyes. It’s about what you’d have to do to really achieve widespread democracy and human flourishing: eradicate those forces that are always going to support fascism, that will always be dedicated to upholding the power of dictatorial, money-grubbing, and colonizing monsters for all the typical reasons.
Chris includes himself in the roster of people who should be killed, or should’ve been, long before he could make this cold assessment of his own life’s work: “I’m a big shot at the CIA. A veteran of Guatemala 1954 — success. The Congo 1960 — success. The Bay of Pigs 1961 — less successful. Dallas 1963 . . . ”
It seems Chris played a key role in the John F. Kennedy assassination and is talking more and more freely about it, even including it in the memoir he’s dictating into a tape recorder. You may recall another CIA agent being evoked in Wild Horse Nine, also wonderfully played by Malkovich, who’s writing a memoir — or as Osborne Cox calls it in the Coen brothers’ comedy Burn After Reading (2008), a “mem-wah.” Malkovich has had a whole history of playing CIA agents experiencing various degrees of career turmoil and mental instability. He was the rogue assassin Booth, seeking to kill the current president in In the Line of Fire (1993) and tormenting Clint Eastwood’s aging Secret Service agent for failing to prevent the assassination of JFK.
In Wild Horse Nine, Chris has become such a loose cannon that his superior, MJ (Steve Buscemi), a CIA bureau chief overseeing South American operations, decides they can’t wait for Chris’s death by natural causes, no matter how imminent it might be.
The “kill ’em” speech alone is so powerful, though it’s delivered with such perfectly shocking casualness that it would probably get John Malkovich another Best Actor Oscar, except that his costar, Sam Rockwell, is equally fantastic as Chris’s only friend, the irascible longtime CIA protégé Lee Chesterfield. In all likelihood they’ll both be nominated and then split the Academy Award vote and lose.
They play old cronies in 1973 Santiago, Chile, who’ve just finished destabilizing the government of democratically elected President Salvador Allende, to the point that Chris can predict the exact time the coup d’etat by Augusto Pinochet’s military forces will occur, after which the roundup, torture, and murder of leftists will begin. Lee has agreed to a trip to the Chilean territory of Easter Island so that Chris can see the “big heads,” his last goal before he dies.
There’s no sugarcoating the fact that Chris is a hopelessly corrupt old spook, but the process of dying, plus his Catholic fear of going to hell for his innumerable mortal sins, has given him a certain melancholy sweetness and has also made him want to reckon, very loudly and publicly, with his god-awful past. Lee has been assigned by MJ to keep Chris in line and, if he can’t do that, to kill him on the island. Chris, who in his lucid moments knows this, carries a scrap of paper around reminding himself, “Don’t trust Lee!”
Chris also periodically forgets that he’s arranged to have Lee ease him out of life in a mercy killing on the island. The code word is “Arkansas.” As Chris reasons, he’d never casually say “Arkansas” because “no one wants to go to Arkansas.”
If you know Martin McDonagh’s film work at all, most famously In Bruges (2008) and The Banshees of Inisherin (2022), you recognize the elements of McDonagh’s favorite designs. They include, most prominently, two male friends bickering and bonding and betraying in shades of light humor and dark antipathy. Then there’s the heartbreakingly beautiful setting that creates the ironic backdrop to human viciousness, making the viewer wonder once again what the hell is wrong with us as a species. It’s always in an earthly paradise where people turn on each other and the shooting starts.
The title Wild Horse Nine is one that McDonagh shrugs off as far as any deep meaning, saying “I like numbers and I like horses.” But there’s no question that wild horses roaming free on gorgeously shot Rapa Nui are a key element of the film, especially the one particular horse with the distinctive white stripe on his forehead that keeps approaching Chris. “Are you a cancer-sniffing horse?” Chris asks.
The haunting attentions of the horse, like the odd, poignant friendship with Monica, takes on outsize importance as Chris tries to reckon with his own grim legacy. “I should’ve shot fewer people and spent more time with horses,” is one awkward, emotionally stunted conclusion drawn.
Wild Horse Nine doesn’t fail to include the almost nonexistent personal lives of Chris and Lee. McDonagh favorite Tom Waits gives a one-scene performance as Chris’s reclusive and estranged brother, a crusty old wreck who lives in a hut near Monument Valley — John Ford’s Monument Valley in Utah, where he shot all those celebrated Westerns — which serves to demonstrate how few and tenuous Chris’s links to life are anyway. And Lee is frequently on the phone with his wife Marge, played by Parker Posey. She’s an emotionally erratic alcoholic who has a very active sex life during Lee’s long absences from home. When Lee asks after the kids, Marge squawks, “The kids? Who cares!”
The message is pretty clear — what Chris and Lee have, personally, is each other, and that relationship, built on professional barbarism, is coming to a necessary end.
In an interview with Seth Myers, Malkovich called the two main characters “American jackasses,” just much more lethal than most.
The point is they’re still typical, on a continuum between ordinary chuckleheads and the dangerous chuckleheads in positions of power. If we find some of these jackasses dangerously likable, well, of course we do — we were raised with them, they’re our relatives, our neighbors, our old college pals we gave a pass to for a while before their malevolence became clear. And obviously McDonagh wants to connect these ordinary people with a harsh look at the United States and the simpleminded attitude of hero worship that’s been inculcated in the Western world since World War II:
The film explores a time when, seemingly, America’s place in the world was as the good guy, which is what most kids in the West — not just in the U.S. but in the U.K. and Ireland, Western Europe — are brought up to feel. The C.I.A. are the good guys and the K.G.B. are the bad guys; America is the good guy and Russia is the bad. But the more I read about what the C.I.A. were up to throughout the end of the last century, and particularly in Chile — to destabilize and help overthrow a democratically elected government, which ended up in fascist horrors for 15 years — it makes you think that you’re not being told the truth about the West and its moral outlook.
To those on the Left, this probably seems like a far too mild agenda. But we’ve got to keep in mind the extraordinary level of delusion that still prevails in the United States. For every leftist that knows all about what the CIA did in Chile in 1973, there are a hundred Americans who either don’t know about it or refuse to acknowledge the fact of it or what the fact means. There’s a reason McDonagh includes documentary footage of Chile ’73 in Wild Horse Nine, as well as actual footage of the capture of Patrice Lumumba, prime minister of the First Congolese Republic after having played a significant role in overthrowing the region’s Belgian colonizers. He was also taken out through a CIA-engineered coup — tortured, executed, body dissolved in acid.
In Wild Horse Nine, Chris claims blandly that “I liked Patrice.” When Lumumba told him the CIA would be responsible for the end of democracy in the Congo for at least a generation, Chris replied in tones of sympathetic reasonableness that of course it would. That was the whole point.
It’s interesting to note that among the many excellent reviews the film is getting, it’s also racking up a few prominent bad reviews from sites like NPR and the New Yorker. But what’s not mentioned in these reviews are such gutting interludes as the Lumumba footage. Instead the critics carp about the “tiresome bickering-and-bantering routine” of the two lead characters and McDonagh’s irreverent attitude, not making any attempt to consider the relationship between the two, the blandly callous rhetoric about horrors, the crude joking around, the hideous incongruence that we encounter every single day in the United States in the forms of blithering government edicts and banally evil pronouncements of the tech lords and brainwashed media commentary and sociopathic online f-ckery of all sorts.
We live among American jackasses, and there are big consequences that arise from the way they flourish here and around the world.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.author: Moritz Eltmann
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.text:
- Kommentare
- Kalifornien
Vermögensteuer jetzt erst recht
Die Niederlage in Kalifornien zeigt, wie groß die Widerstände gegen eine progressive Steuerpolitk sind. Daraus lernen lässt sich dennoch. Ein Kommentar.
Quälend lange hat es gedauert, bis in Kalifornien, das sich sonst für seine High-Tech-Industrie rühmt, das Ergebnis einer wichtigen Volksabstimmung feststand: Die von einem Gewerkschaftsbündnis geforderte, fünfprozentige Sonderabgabe für die rund 200 Milliardäre zur Finanzierung von Gesundheitsprogrammen für Arme ist knapp durchgefallen. Dabei gilt gerade der bevölkerungsreichste US-Bundesstaat sonst als offen für progressive Ideen, und die blaue Welle bei den Midterms war hier besonders groß.
Die Unterstützer führen ihre Niederlage darauf zurück, dass einige konservative Milliardäre riesige Summen in Anti-Werbung über alle Kanäle steckten. Der Frust darüber, mit ungleichen Mitteln kämpfen zu müssen, ist verständlich, doch als alleinige Erklärung greift das zu kurz. Potenzielle Unterstützer wandten sich ab, da sie die konkrete Verwendung der Einnahmen einseitig fanden und zum Beispiel Schulen weitgehend leer ausgegangen wären. Auch die Form einer einmaligen Abgabe statt einer dauerhaften Steuer stieß nicht überall auf Begeisterung.
Die Ablehnung verweist aber auch auf ein ganz grundsätzliches Problem: In Zeiten eines schädlichen Standortwettbewerbs ist gerade die Nähe zu den Milliardären und ihren Unternehmen ein Nachteil. Eine fortschrittliche Steuerpolitik kann in Zeiten flexibler Kapitalbewegungen zur Flucht führen. Führende demokratische Politiker, aber auch Beschäftigte aus dem Silicon Valley befürchteten angesichts der Drohungen der Milliardäre, ihre Luxuszelte woanders aufzuschlagen, dass auch Teile der Unternehmen in andere Bundesstaaten verlegt würden. Das wäre wirtschaftlich und daher auch für die öffentlichen Finanzen schädlich.
Die Kalifornien-Schlappe lehrt, dass es erfolgversprechender ist, eine echte Vermögensteuer auf nationaler Ebene zu fordern oder noch besser international wie aktuell im Rahmen der brasilianischen Initiative in der G20-Industrie- und Schwellenländer-Gruppe. Eine höhere Besteuerung der ganz großen Vermögen ist und bleibt die mit großem Abstand wichtigste finanz- und wirtschaftspolitische Forderung von Linken. Vermögensteuern könnten für anderweitig dringend benötigte öffentliche Mittel sorgen, es gibt laut Umfragen vielerorts klare Mehrheiten dafür, und sie machen grundsätzlich deutlich, wie Umverteilung für mehr soziale Gerechtigkeit sorgen könnte. Natürlich sind die Widerstände dagegen auf allen Ebenen stark und konnten echte Fortschritte bislang verhindern. Mit der Krise der Staatsfinanzen dürfte sich das früher oder später ändern. Nach der Niederlage in Kalifornien gilt: Der Kampf für eine progressive Finanzpolitik muss jetzt erst recht weitergehen.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: London’s Photographers’ Gallery to launch exhibition programme for emerging voices
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Simon Bainbridge
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Photographers’ Gallery in London is launching a 10-year programme to platform emerging talent through a series of biennial exhibitions. The initiative has been made possible by what the not-for-profit gallery describes as “a very generous grant” from the UK-based John Kobal Foundation.
Shoair Mavlian, the director of the Photographers’ Gallery, declined to specify how much the grant is worth, but she tells The Art Newspaper that it will cover all the costs of staging the shows in its second-floor space, newly named the John Kobal Foundation Gallery.
The initiative will see one artist selected every two years for an exhibition. The first solo exhibition will be announced later this year and will run from 23 June to 26 September 2027.
“The whole idea of the programme is based around giving an opportunity to someone who hasn’t had an institutional solo show before,” she says. “The Photographers’ Gallery is in a similar situation to all other museums in the UK in that we are pressured into having to always do blockbuster shows [to generate revenue]. And what this programme allows us to do is to take risks.”
The gallery received a renewed three-year grant from Arts Council England in 2023, as one of the funding body’s national portfolio organisations (NPO). This grant represents around 20% of the gallery’s revenue, says Mavlian, however, it has remained the same throughout years of rising operational costs and high inflation, and so like other UK arts organisations, the gallery has become more reliant on other sources of income. Its accounts for the year ending 31 March 2025 report £620,573 in admissions income, which is more than two thirds the value of its NPO grant over a single year.
“We are under this constant pressure to sell tickets and bring people through the door—which, of course, is important. But what that means is we then don’t always see the full breadth of photography that is being made today. We are often looking at things that are historic rather than looking at the contemporary.”
The John Kobal Foundation was established in 1990 a year before the death of the eponymous film historian and photography collector “to advance the public appreciation and awareness of photography”.
“We are delighted to support this important new initiative," says Michael Mack, the co-chair of the John Kobal Foundation, “which honours John’s vision of nurturing creativity and innovation in photography.”

https://hyperallergic.com/how-miles-gree.title: How Miles Greenberg Got “WAR” Past the Censors
https://hyperallergic.com/how-miles-gree.author: Phillip Pyle
https://hyperallergic.com/how-miles-gree.text:
How Miles Greenberg Got “WAR” Past the Censors
“There was not a single outlet, institution, or gallery that wanted to get behind this thing,” the artist told Hyperallergic about his new, six-hour performance piece.
Miles Greenberg’s mother took him to see Marina Abramović perform The Artist Is Present at the Museum of Modern Art when he was just 12 years old. The experience would serve as the zero point for the New York-based Canadian artist’s own performance-based practice, and the birth of his unyielding desire to “see [his] work at a museum, where it would be approached as a sculpture.” Later training under playwright Robert Wilson, choreographer Édouard Lock, and the very “grandmother of performance art” who spurred his interest in the medium, Greenberg began developing works that ironically share more with the histories of painting and sculpture than a lineage of performance. He has stood on plinths as the tortured satyr Marsyas from Greek mythology, the arrow-pierced Christian martyr Saint Sebastian, and in original statuesque poses that recall the Baroque ecstasy of a Bernini sculpture.
On October 29, the artist presented “WAR” (2026), a six-hour durational performance organized by Performa and curated by Zoe Lukov. More than 40 performers walked on treadmills in the vacant site of the former 86th Street Cinema in New York to a trance-like score by artist Chino Amobi. Greenberg spoke with Hyperallergic about the difficulties of securing a venue for the work amid Israel's genocide on Palestine, the limitations of endurance, and performance as a “gateway into a state that is difficult to reach.”
Hyperallergic: You often reference martyrs, saints, warriors, and other archetypes across history dedicated to either heroic causes or beliefs beyond themselves. Why are you interested in these figures? Do they resonate with you besides their art-historical or imagistic qualities?
Miles Greenberg: The West has canonized these stories as a means of cutting right to a series of moralistic teachings that have been central to Western societies writ large for the last several millennia. They're represented in different ways, but there's this longstanding tradition of just about every artist from the Renaissance up until contemporary times — though, maybe to a lesser extent — regurgitating these art-historical figures, characters, stories, and fables over and over again.
With performance, which continues to be niche and sit around the edges of art history, people’s minds go more to the shock value of it, which I’m not particularly seduced or interested by, rather than what it is that we mean or wish to convey. So it’s really a strategic play on my behalf to choreograph or rein in their imagination and channel it in the right direction. I think of these works as portraits more than I wish to identify with the figures. There can be some crossover. Saint Sebastian is a notable example I have some personal investment in as a queer person.
I also think situating myself centrally in that tradition helps to quite simply attribute value and clarity and define my practice within that canon and lineage of art history, rather than somehow adjacent or parallel to it as a young queer Black performance-based person. I’m not interested in marginality as a destination, and I don’t see any reason not to put me in conversation with the canon. I was raised by the canon, so I’m going to make like the canon.
H: What led you to turn to the subject of war with this particular work?

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: How Mona Chalabi Explains Income Inequality
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Naomi Elias
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
How Mona Chalabi Explains Income Inequality
An interview with the data journalist about how she uses numbers and design to illustrate how class weighs on the lives of Americans.
Iraqi British journalist Mona Chalabi is trying to convince the world that data visualization is cool—and it’s working. She has amassed a significant social following with her whimsically hand-drawn and boldly color-blocked figures that foreground what she calls data’s “human aspect” and make it more legible and engaging. Chalabi—who was formerly a data editor at The Guardian and is presently a lecturer of graphic design at Al-Quds Bard in Palestine—has come to be known for using these tools to make social issues the center of her work. The data journalist was awarded the 2023 Pulitzer Prize in Illustrated Reporting and Commentary for her New York Times series depicting the staggering wealth gap between Jeff Bezos and average Americans.
In her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, she again turns her pen to the problem of money in America by mapping the country’s “economic universe”—i.e., the financial lives of 10 representative Americans of different income deciles. These include a woman working as a birth surrogate for supplementary income, a recent divorcée, a Gen Z rideshare driver recovering from gambling addiction, and a veteran conflicted about his need for disability assistance. She explores how much people have and don’t have, where it comes from, its relationship to their health and sense of identity, all with her trademark visual flair. (One figure from the book depicting mortgage denial rates by the race or ethnicity of applicants replaces the usual bars in a bar graph with upturned middle fingers that get progressively larger). She also weaves her own financial portrait with theirs, showing remarkable transparency about her career earnings and family history in recognition of how we’re all implicated in each others’ universes. The book reflects Chalabi’s personal commitment to not participating in the harmful but normalized practice of looking away from social inequities. Below, she talks to The Nation about the journalistic rules she’s happy to break, and how data can help reveal, and potentially overthrow, unfair systems.
—Naomi Elias
Naomi Elias:  Why did you land on money as the subject for your first book?
Mona Chalabi: At the start of Covid, when I was worrying about money, and I was thinking about the forces that had shaped my life. I mentioned in the book how on the one hand I felt precarious, but also I was not precarious at all, which is kind of a theme throughout the whole book, people feeling precarious even despite not necessarily being. I lived on the third floor of a Brooklyn brownstone at that point, and I remember seeing some of my neighbors, the people who owned their full brownstones, descending and climbing into their Range Rovers and just disappearing upstate. The streets literally emptied. And those of us that were left behind had a different kind of exposure to the pandemic because of class. And at the same time, we were also far less exposed than the people working in Amazon, for example, who were delivering our goods, the people who were stocking the shelves in the supermarket while we wandered around with our masks on. It was really clear to me that class really, really mattered.
NE: Why the focus on income and not wealth?
MC: Partly pragmatism. It would be really hard to extract that data from the people that I was interviewing, because sometimes their wealth actually isn’t even known to them. There are instances where people don’t exactly understand how much money their partner might have. And, for reasons I talk about in the book, I really focus on the household rather than the individual.
It also requires a different kind of honesty. I already found it so remarkable that people would just sit down for hours and hours detailing their finances to me. If I would have started to get into how much they were going to inherit from their parents, I don’t know if I could have relied on the same kind of honesty from them. And more importantly, the fact-checking would have been harder. It’s one thing to gain consent from them to tell me the story, but it’s another thing to then contact their parents and be like, “So, how much wealth exactly do you have?”
NE: When you narrowed down the responses to your questionnaire, in order to find “ten representative Americans,” what sort of demographics were on your mind?
MC: There were groups that I wanted to see represented, that I didn’t hear from. For example, I think it’s a failing of the book that I don’t have anybody who’s Native American in there. It’s not perfectly representative. I did know that I didn’t want these 10 people to be white; I didn’t want them to live on the two coasts. I did find that just because of the nature of my Instagram following—and by the way, obviously I didn’t find everyone through Instagram—but a lot of the people who responded were between 20 and let’s say early 40s, and I wanted a bigger age range than that. I did want to have some gender representation. I definitely wanted to include some disability representation. There were so many different boxes that I wanted to check, and what happened was that certain themes that I knew that I wanted to explore—like gambling addiction, like surrogacy—meant that I just set aside whoever was responding to me, and I went out looking for those people by going through nonprofits or through chat forums or whatever it might be to find someone who was navigating that particular world.
NE: Over the course of the years you worked on this book, subjects’ financial circumstances changed sometimes dramatically, which created really interesting storylines, as in the case of you meeting Chris Smalls before he became president of the Amazon Labor Union. How did that evolving data affect the story you were telling?
MC: That definitely wasn’t the plan. When I first sold the book, I was like, “Yeah, I’m going to have this written for you in 18 months.” Completely delusional and arrogant. And in a way that was actually a blessing, because if I just did three interviews with each person, a snapshot of their lives, I wouldn’t have seen that evolution. It’s because I struggled so much to find those 10 people, and each interview just led to so many more questions for me to understand them. Their lives did change. I mean, Chris’s a really dramatic one, but all of them. It’s depressing to me that when I met Tiffany [a 46-year-old Black goat farmer in Ohio representing the book’s poorest decile], one of the first times we spoke, she was like, “God, I would hate to be working in Burger King.” And then on one of our calls she’s like, “Yeah, I had to start working at McDonald’s.” So, yeah, their lives did change quite dramatically, as did mine. I think the book is stronger for it, and it changed the nature of our conversations. If I had done that snapshot approach, I don’t think there would have been that same kind of emotional investigation. There’s a vulnerability in disclosing numbers, and there’s also a vulnerability in admitting to working in Burger King when it’s the very thing that you said you never ever wanted to do.
NE: I’m interested in how you view hand drawing as a way of visualizing imprecision and why you think that’s important in data visualization.
MC: It’s fundamentally more honest. Many of the data sets that I’m looking at, the underlying information actually does have quite a big margin of error. So to present in these really clean charts is fundamentally a bit misleading. I was working with data that did have that degree of precision, but even then I want people to be able to see the respective scale of these bars as opposed to things with decimal places. Including these wobbly lines, the idea is that you see that the underlying data is imprecise, and it reminds me of this human aspect of the data, like, a human was responsible for choosing which variables to gather, what time period. It’s also about what is in vogue in terms of data collection. There’s so much bias that is involved. I hope that by presenting information in this way, I’m not hiding from that. It’s a bit more explicit: Here’s my hand and my pen and where my bias lies as I’m presenting this to you.
NE: All journalistic mediums (editorial, broadcast) are dealing with the attention span issue in their audiences. How does that influence your artistic choices?
MC: I’m much more familiar with how to navigate that on social media. I will often present an extremely simplified version of the statistics and then kind of gradually complicate it. And that’s obviously a really difficult line. You never want someone to have walked away with a version that is so simplified and abstract that it’s wrong, basically. And so, it’ll be a case of when I’m saying breaking it down into pieces, it might be that the title gives you the most simple takeaway, and then there’ll be one asterisk in the graphic and then another one. I’m trying to kind of guide where your eye goes in terms of how you’re consuming that information. I call that iterative storytelling. If you imagine on Instagram, it’s like each swipe is a different part of the story and I guess in a way, each chapter here is like another swipe and another complication.
NE: You break with some journalistic practices in this book by paying your interviewees and including yourself and your financial history in the story. What was behind that choice?
MC: I actually did more than that. Another practice that I broke with was I sent them the chapters prior to publication, which you don’t normally do. That felt really important to me, and I said that I would do that right from the start, even though nobody asked. And obviously the consequence of that was that not everyone was super happy with their chapter. Some of that actually did result in a little bit of a negotiation, which is why I did it. I’m willing to make a little sacrifice so that you don’t feel bad about this project.

Then to speak a little bit to the other principles that you mentioned that I parted with, disclosing my personal circumstances was really unpleasant, and it’s the reason why I’m very, very anxious about talking to you right now, why I’m anxious about the book coming out. I’ve done work in the past that has been a bit revealing, but this feels really different. I felt like there was no way I could make this argument that many of us are navigating shame about our finances and a lot of us are dishonest, and that actually we need to have much more frank conversation about class.… How could I do all of that without actually walking the walk? And because so much of the book is actually claiming a very important way to address inequality is redistribution, hoarding up all of the assets that I got from the book felt wrong. Look, I know it’s really complicated if we just change the journalistic norm and everyone can be paid for participating in journalism, but to write a book about class and to interview people who literally, in some cases, were really struggling, and to just take those stories and make money from writing those stories without paying them money, I kind of think it’s indefensible.
NE: You express a desire for this book to encourage people to make “collective economic demands on government that are more specific and more powerful than ‘tax the rich,’” which I found interesting because you once said data journalism is not suited to a radical agenda “because all it can do is show you the consequences of the system and not how it operates.” Do you still believe that and how does your work address that issue?
MC: I do think in a way the book is still showing you a lot of the consequences of how the system is operating. At least the charts are doing that. A lot more of the back and forth, the actual transcripts, are revealing more of the how. I still do think that there’s a lot of truth in that. I hope that this book is not solely a work of data journalism, because if it were just that, I don’t think it would be a radical book. I don’t even know if it’s radical. It’s funny, I was approached about writing a book for a few years before I undertook this and a lot of them were conversations about basically publishing a collection of my graphics, and that was so uninteresting to me. I have no desire to do a coffee-table book of my illustrations. I was really clear about this when we were really figuring out the design, but the illustrations and the charts are in service of the text. I still believe that data journalism alone is never going to assure a radical agenda, because when it’s done badly it can have this silencing effect on individual voices.
NE: And when done correctly?
MC: I just did a silly little chart yesterday about intergenerational mobility. It was about the percentage of people that earn less than their parents. And a few people said, “This makes me feel better.” I think really good data journalism actually galvanizes people to become more radical because it lets you know that there’s this tendency to internalize many things and assume that it’s our individual shortcomings.
I spoke to one of my closest friends this morning, she was my French professor, and one of the things that we have spoken about in the past is the fact that in France it’s illegal to collect data on religion. That’s because of the French concept of secularism, which they’re obsessed with, which I understand in theory, but what it means is that it’s virtually impossible to prove, on a systematic basis, Islamophobia in France. Now, Muslims in France aren’t like, “Oh, I don’t know if Islamophobia exists. I haven’t seen the data or I haven’t seen the chart.” They are well aware of the fact that Islamophobia exists, that anti-Arab racism exists. And I understand the arguments that some French people will make to me, that what does it do to let’s say a 17-year-old boy who is the child of North African immigrants, to see what his chances are of going to college? Is that massively demoralizing? Or does it contextualize their struggle and let them know that it’s not them? I think really good data journalism does reveal some of these systems.
I wrote an article for The Guardian ages and ages ago, and they never ended up publishing it. As soon as Trump took office, I went around and interviewed a bunch of people who worked at the Census Bureau, including the former Census Bureau director. And I was like, “Things are about to get bad, aren’t they?” And everyone was very clear on like, “Yeah, they’re about to get bad.” I think the fact that Trump, as is the playbook of authoritarian regimes, is interested in dismantling the data sets that reveal discrimination on a systematic basis means that it’s not for me to be sitting there pondering about the efficacy of these things. If he believes that those numbers matter, then I fucking believe they matter.
Like, this might feel like a stretch, but it’s something I’ve been thinking about. I wanted to create a chart on suicide rates in the Israeli military, and they stopped publishing those statistics a few years ago. And I’m like, OK, if you believe that those statistics are harmful, then I want them even more. I really, really want to understand what’s going on. I hope I’m communicating both that, yes, I believe that these data sets matter, that it matters to see.… One of the data sets that [Trump’s] stopping is the one that shows employment discrimination. I want that data set to continue to be able to see racial patterns in employment discrimination. And I don’t believe that relentlessly collecting that data, documenting that data, publishing the data is sufficient to overturn the systems that we have. So it’s both things. It’s not blind faith and adoration of numbers at all.

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: CCJ aprova projeto que prevê cannabis medicinal gratuita pelo SUS no RS
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O projeto que prevê o fornecimento gratuito de medicamentos à base de cannabis pelo Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) no Rio Grande do Sul foi aprovado por unanimidade na Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) da Assembleia Legislativa nesta terça-feira (10). De autoria do deputado estadual Leonel Radde (PT), a proposta também busca incentivar pesquisas sobre o uso medicinal da planta.
Apresentado em 2023, o Projeto de Lei (PL) 19/2023 propõe criar uma política estadual de uso e fornecimento gratuito de medicamentos à base de canabinoides, substâncias presentes na cannabis, como o canabidiol (CBD) e o tetrahidrocanabinol (THC). O texto prevê a oferta pelo sistema público estadual de saúde, em caráter excepcional, para pacientes que possam ter sintomas e outros efeitos das doenças reduzidos com esses tratamentos, conforme as evidências científicas disponíveis.
Além do acesso aos medicamentos, a iniciativa prevê orientação a pacientes e familiares, divulgação de informações científicas e formação de profissionais e gestores da saúde. Também incentiva parcerias com instituições de pesquisa e associações de pacientes que atuam com cannabis medicinal, de acordo com as exigências legais e sanitárias.
Radde comemorou a aprovação e defendeu que a proposta seja votada pelos deputados ainda em 2026. “São 16 estados no Brasil que já fazem a distribuição de medicamentos à base de cannabis. A aprovação na CCJ por unanimidade é muito importante, agora espero que a tramitação até a votação em plenário seja breve para que seja votado ainda este ano”, afirmou.
Segundo o parlamentar, cerca de 70 mil pessoas utilizam medicamentos à base de cannabis no Rio Grande do Sul. Na avaliação dele, a política estadual poderá beneficiar essa população ao ampliar o acesso aos tratamentos.
A justificativa do projeto aponta o custo dos medicamentos como uma barreira para famílias que não têm condições de pagar pelo tratamento. A proposta busca reduzir essa dificuldade e estimular pesquisas que orientem o uso medicinal dos canabinoides, com atenção à qualidade dos produtos, às doses e às necessidades de cada paciente.
A aprovação na CCJ é uma etapa da tramitação e ainda não torna a proposta lei. O texto ainda precisa ser votado no plenário da Assembleia Legislativa.
O que mudou nas regras nacionais
No Brasil, o acesso medicinal à cannabis passou por mudanças ao longo da última década. Em 2015, a Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa) autorizou a importação de produtos à base de canabidiol para tratamento de saúde. Em 2019, estabeleceu regras para a fabricação, a importação e a venda de produtos de cannabis em farmácias, mediante prescrição.
Uma nova etapa ocorreu em janeiro de 2026, quando a agência aprovou normas para a produção de cannabis medicinal no país. A medida cumpriu uma decisão do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ), de novembro de 2024, que reconheceu a possibilidade de produção para fins medicinais e farmacêuticos, sob regulamentação.
As regras de cultivo entraram em vigor em agosto deste ano. Elas permitem a atividade por empresas e instituições autorizadas pela Anvisa, que devem cumprir exigências de segurança, controle de qualidade e acompanhamento da origem e do destino da produção. Para o cultivo destinado à produção medicinal e farmacêutica, as variedades devem ter até 0,3% de THC. Há regras específicas para o cultivo voltado à pesquisa científica.
A regulamentação também criou um modelo experimental para associações de pacientes sem fins lucrativos. A participação depende da seleção de projetos pela Anvisa, com limites de produção e de pacientes atendidos, além de acompanhamento da qualidade e da segurança dos produtos.
Já as regras atualizadas para fabricação e importação de produtos de cannabis para uso medicinal estão em vigor desde maio. Essas autorizações sanitárias, porém, não garantem automaticamente a oferta gratuita pelo SUS, que depende de decisões e políticas específicas de acesso aos tratamentos.

https://gothamist.com/food/its-cold-in-n.title: It's cold in New York. Soup season in the city has begun.
https://gothamist.com/food/its-cold-in-n.author: Robert Sietsema
https://gothamist.com/food/its-cold-in-n.text:
Sure, soup can be eaten all year round. But what can be better for a light lunch in early November than a bowl of Manhattan clam chowder with a handful of oyster crackers? As the days get colder, we search for heartier soups, or a bowl to warm ourselves with soups as a prelude to a main course. Soups are also an easy way to eat vegetarian, and even save some calories.
So, welcome to soup season! Here are 10 of the most diverse, exciting bowls in the city we could find, including some that will be familiar, and others that will make you slurp with surprise. This is an international group, and they are arranged in no particular order.
White and red clam chowder
The perpetual battle rages on between chowder lovers: red or white? The white c was carried by Bretons to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and thence to New England. The red originated here in New York, presumably among those of Italian descent. The white is creamy and soothing, with a jolt of flavor from the shellfish; while the red is more aggressive, and loaded with vegetables. Why not get a bowl of both for slightly over $12 each at Grand Central Oyster Bar, in one of the city’s most dramatic restaurant settings? Grand Central Terminal, 89 East 42nd St.
Pickle soup
Poland is a soup-intensive country, and scanning the menu of any Polish restaurant you’ll find red borscht and white borscht, tomato, tripe, chicken noodle and split pea, but also some with unexpected ingredients like sauerkraut, sorrel, duck blood and cucumber pickles. The latter is a frequent offering at Retro as a daily soup ($8.50). It’s more mellow than you might expect with pickle juice as its base. Sour cream does the trick to neutralize, along with potatoes and fistfuls of dill. 853 Manhattan Ave., Greenpoint
Sancocho
Every culture has its “everything but the kitchen sink” soup, with an infinitely expandable roster of ingredients. Sancocho is a fine example, a soup found in every Dominican restaurant in town, including Don Emilio Diner in Castle Hill, where on the day we tried it, the soup ($8) contained pork ribs, chicken, plantain, and yuca in a broth of disintegrated pumpkin, propelled by the pungent flavors of oregano and garlic. 1315 Castle Hill Ave., Bronx
Assam laksa
Want a soup that bombards you with strong flavors, leaving you reeling from the taste? Such a soup is the Malaysian assam laksa found at the venerable Taste Good. Just look at its partial catalog of ingredients: fermented shrimp paste, funky and fishy mackerel, sweet pineapple, fresh lemongrass, chiles and mint. Fortunately, the bulbous rice noodles are as bland as can be. 82-18 45th Ave., Elmhurst
Matzoh ball soup
After that bowl of assam laksa, what stands at the opposite end of the pungent-bland spectrum? Matzoh ball soup, that’s what! At newly reopened Carnegie Deli, the broth is unimpeachable in its soothing plainness, the matzoh balls more bouncy than usual, with plenty of fortifying veggies minced into the broth. The totality ($16, with noodles added) is wonderful in its savory subtlety. 834 7th Ave., Midtown
Luosifen
Stall #19 at the new 99 Ranch Market basement food court, known as Luo Xiao Du, specializes in luosifen soup in a half-dozen varieties. The pottage hails from Guanxi, an autonomous coastal region between Hong Kong and Hanoi, and employs a broth famously made from snails. This version ($11) has a few snails dropped in for visual effect, along with bamboo shoots, a boiled egg, chili oil, peanuts, and a half dozen other things, for a very rich and fortifying bowl, but one that will leave you fanning your mouth. 37-11 Main Street, Flushing
French onion soup
French onion soup as we know it was supposedly invented in the Les Halles Market in Paris to feed workers using ingredients common in the market: onions, butter, cheese and stale bread. Today, it is found in nearly every French bistro, including Bar Six in the Village, where a powerful caramelized onion broth buoys up a raft of gruyere, and conceals a thick slice of bread in its depths ($15). Your only challenge is how, exactly, to eat it, since the cheese clings mightily to the spoon. 502 6th Ave., Greenwich Village
Cow foot soup
Soups made from the long-boiled feet of cows are common throughout the Caribbean, and evidence of the “everything but the squeal” approach that makes those cuisines more eco-friendly through their use of the entire animal. The swatches of trotter at the Trinidadian Bake & Things in the soup ($8) are pleasantly rubbery and gelatinous, and potatoes are mixed into the mellow yellow broth. Every bite is a sunny delight with lots of chewing involved, and the collagen and gelatin are bound to help your skin. 1489 Flatbush Ave., Flatbush
Lagman
Lagman is the signature soup of Uyghur cuisine, a soup indispensable to the menus of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, as well as the Xinjiang autonomous region of northwestern China. At its heart are irregular handmade wheat noodles in a rich beef broth flavored with dill and cilantro. In the version found at Shashlik Uz N1 in Ditmas Park, the soup ($11.99) also contains colorful bell peppers, fennel, celery, onions, green beans, and giant wads of fresh dill, tasting of the stockyard and the meadows. 115 Ditmas Ave., Kensington
Scandinavian fish and shellfish bisque
Located on the ground floor of the Scandinavia House, Bjork Café & Bistro offers a full range of Scandinavian specialties, from Swedish meatballs to preserved fish platters to the open face sandwiches known as smorrebrod. Several soups are offered, including a fish and shellfish bisque ($19) featuring cod, gray shrimp and mussels bobbing in a yellow broth of surpassing mellowness, with shredded leeks and carrots waving like seaweed in tidal pools along the shoreline. 58 Park Ave., Murray Hill

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/zo.title: Zohran Mamdani Visited MoMA’s West African Modern Architecture Survey and Loved It
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/zo.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/zo.text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has continued his social media campaign to stump for exhibitions staged by the city’s museums, this time focusing on a survey of West African modernist architecture at the Museum of Modern Art, whose praises he sang on Instagram early this morning.
Titled “Architects of Liberation: Modernism in Western Africa,” the 400-work show surveys architectural projects in Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, and Cameroon produced during a period of decolonization that began in some countries in the late 1950s. Curated by Martino Stierli and Ikem Stanley Okoye, the show features architectural models and archival imagery, as well as some contemporary artworks.
“visited @themuseumofmodernart this weekend and am still thinking about their exhibition ‘architects of liberation: modernism in western africa,’” wrote Mamdani in his post.
He specifically singled out Kader Attia’s 2014 sculpture Indépendence Tchao, a sculpture composed of rows of rusting index card boxes that the Algerian French artist obtained from a French colonial police headquarters. They are topped with a sign reading “HOTEL INDÉPENDENCE,” a reference to a similarly named hotel in Dakar, Senegal.
Mamdani wrote that the sculpture asks the question: “to what extent were the visions of the independence era achieved?”
It’s the second museum presentation Mamdani has posted about in the past month. In October, to celebrate his birthday, Mamdani visited the Studio Museum in Harlem, where he took in Taylor Simmons’s painting The Hypnotist (2026). Mamdani called the work by Simmons, a current participant in the museum’s storied artists-in-residence program, “just incredible.”

https://taz.de/Nach-der-Parlamentswahl-i.title: Nach der Parlamentswahl in Israel: Der Anfang vom Ende?
https://taz.de/Nach-der-Parlamentswahl-i.author: Marina Klimchuk
https://taz.de/Nach-der-Parlamentswahl-i.text:
Nach der Parlamentswahl in Israel: Der Anfang vom Ende?
Die neue israelische Knesset tritt zum ersten Mal zusammen. Eine Regierung ist noch nicht gebildet, doch handlungsunfähig ist die Opposition nicht.
Es könnte das sein, worauf viele Israelis kaum noch zu hoffen wagen: der Anfang vom Ende der Ära Netanjahu. Oder auch ein weiterer vergeblicher Versuch, den Regierungschef abzulösen, der seit 2009 mit nur einer Unterbrechung an der Macht ist. Am Sonntag hat Israels Präsident Itzhak Herzog den Chef des Oppositionsblocks, Gadi Eisenkot, mit der Regierungsbildung beauftragt. Dafür hat er zunächst 28 Tage Zeit. Am Dienstag ist nun die 26. Knesset, das neu gewählte israelische Parlament, zu ihrer konstituierenden Sitzung zusammengekommen.
46 der 120 Abgeordneten ziehen erstmals ins Parlament ein. Viele dieser Neuen haben eine direkte Verbindung zum Massaker des 7. Oktobers 2023 – als Angehörige von Opfern oder Armeereservist:innen etwa. Mehr als drei Jahre danach prägt dieser Tag die israelische Gesellschaft und Politik.
Zwar gibt es in der neuen Knesset eine Mehrheit gegen Netanjahu. Doch die Parteien, die ihn ablösen wollen, müssen sich erst auf eine gemeinsame Regierung einigen. Scheitert die Regierungsbildung, könnten erneut Wahlen anstehen. Und Neuwahlen, das lehrt die Geschichte, enden fast immer mit Netanjahus Machterhalt.
Auch ohne neue Regierung ist die Knesset jedoch handlungsfähig. Sie kann Ausschüsse bilden und Gesetze verabschieden, während Netanjahus bisherige Regierung die Amtsgeschäfte weiterführt.
Erster Amtsakt der Opposition: Knesset-Sprecher ablösen
Der oppositionelle Block des Wandels will den bisherigen Knesset-Sprechers Amir Ohana ablösen. Ohana ist ein enger Verbündeter Netanjahus. In die Kritik geriet er unter anderem wegen seines erniedrigenden Umgangs mit Angehörigen der Opfer des 7. Oktobers. 2025 hinderten Parlamentswachen Angehörige gewaltsam am Zugang zur Besuchertribüne. Ohana entschuldigte sich anschließend bei den Betroffenen.
Am Dienstag gab das Oppositionsbündnis seinen Kandidaten für Ohanas Nachfolge bekannt: Matan Kahana von Eisenkots Partei Jaschar. Der Einigung gingen tagelange Verhandlungen voraus. Nach einem Bericht des israelischen Nachrichtenportals Ynet soll Kahana das Amt zunächst während der Regierungsbildung übernehmen.
Die Wahl des Knesset-Sprechers ist die erste Bewährungsprobe für die Zusammenarbeit der Opposition. Auch deshalb ist dieser Posten so umkämpft. Wer ihn besetzt, bestimmt Tagesordnung und Ausschussbesetzung, kann Gesetzesinitiativen vorantreiben und aufhalten.
Kahana ist 54 Jahre alt. Schon in frühen Jahren schloss er sich als Jugendbetreuer der nationalreligiösen Bewegung Bnei Akiva an. Vor seiner politischen Karriere diente er in einer Spezialeinheit und als Kampfpilot der Luftwaffe. 2019 zog er für das rechte Bündnis Jamina in die Knesset ein. In der großen Koalition unter der Führung von Naftali Bennett und Yair Lapid, die nur ein Jahr hielt, von 2021 bis 2022, war er Religionsminister. Später wechselte er zu Benny Gantz’ Nationaler Einheit; 2025 verließ es die Knesset. Jetzt kehrt er zurück.
Kreative Wege zur Koalition
Weder Netanjahus Bündnis noch Eisenkots Block verfügt allein über eine Mehrheit. Gemeinsam mit der arabisch geführten Gemeinsamen Liste und der Partei Ra’am käme Eisenkots Bündnis jedoch auf 67 Sitze – genug, um einen Nachfolger für Ohana zu wählen. Beide unterstützen seine Ablösung. Für die Gemeinsame Liste sagte Ahmad Tibi heute zu, für Kahana zu stimmen. Ob Eisenkots Bündnis sich auf eine Koalition mit den mehrheitlich arabisch geprägten Parteien einlässt, ist allerdings fraglich. Als weitere Option steht eine Koalition mit der Partei Vereinigtes Torah-Judentum im Raum.
Netanjahu klammert sich derweil wie an ein sinkendes Boot an die Erzählung, die Wahl sei von den arabischen Parteien „gestohlen“ worden. Er ruft zu einer großen Koalition auf. Mit einer solchen würde Gadi Eisenkot gegen sein Wahlversprechen, Bibi abzulösen, verstoßen.
Auch auf Kandidaten für weitere Schlüsselposten hat sich das Eisenkot-Bündnis derweil verständigt: Der rechte und säkulare Avigdor Liberman soll den Außen- und Verteidigungsausschuss leiten, Liran Avisar Ben-Horin von B’Yachad den Finanzausschuss und Roy Folkman von Jaschar den vorläufigen Organisationsausschuss. Mit den Nominierungen demonstriert das Bündnis: Wir können auch ohne fertige Regierung handeln.
Innenpolitisch brodelt es in Israel. Eine zentrale politische Priorität der Wähler:innen ist das Versprechen der Opposition, eine unabhängige, staatliche Untersuchungskommission zu den Versäumnissen rund um den 7. Oktober 2023 einzurichten, die Netanjahu bisher ablehnt.
