https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-housin.title: On Strike for a Different Spain
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-housin.author: Mario Arguiriano, Chris Mills Rodrigo
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-housin.text:
On Strike for a Different Spain
Spain will see a general strike on Wednesday, following mass protests around housing. A member of Marxist group Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista discusses how these protests have cohered a militant class-based movement for more sweeping change.
- Interview by
- Chris Mills Rodrigo
Spain’s streets and town squares have been flooded with protesters this fall, since the brutal eviction and subsequent death of eighty-seven-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen. This September, she was removed from her Madrid apartment of some seventy years, after an investment fund quintupled her rent.
The marches and encampments, first called by Madrid’s tenants’ union, have primarily focused on Spain’s housing crisis. The situation has intensified over the last decade as rents have nearly doubled while wages have remained largely stagnant. The protests have already triggered a general strike this Wednesday, November 11, and snap elections called by Pedro Sánchez’s center-left Partido Socialista (PSOE) for November 29.
The promise of a strike and elections did not quell the protests. The encampment in Puerta del Sol in Madrid that kicked off this cycle remained active until police tore it down last week. Spin-off strikes focused on disinvestment in public education have closed down major motorways.
Comparisons to the Indignados protests (also known as 15-M) of 2011 come easily. Both kicked off with encampments in the center of Madrid and centered on housing affordability. And yet things are markedly different this time around. While 15-M aimed to include everyone regardless of class position and was organizationally anarchic, today’s protesters are speaking much more openly of class struggle and organizing themselves into people’s assemblies.
The prominent presence of the Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista (CJS, Socialist Youth Coordination) in the current protest movement is both emblematic of those changes and critical to understanding them. CJS is a Marxist revolutionary organization and part of the broader Movimiento Socialista (MS), a communist current that originated in the Basque Country in a 2018 split from the local left-nationalist front. Since its national inception in 2024, CJS has grown to over a thousand members all across Spain. It has been the most visible organization in the recent protests apart from the tenants’ unions and represents a militant left-wing flank not satisfied with letting this moment of upheaval be tranquilized by elections or tepid strikes.
Ahead of November 11, CJS has organized over a hundred youth strike committees aimed at ensuring the demonstration will be a class-based action that challenges rent-seeking, the current government, and capitalism itself. In an interview for Jacobin, Chris Mills Rodrigo spoke with a member of CJS, Mario Arguiriano, about the organization’s role in the recent protests and how it hopes to direct the anger and energy of the Spanish public into structural change. This interview was translated from Spanish by the author and lightly edited for length and clarity.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Let’s start with the immediate context of what’s happening in Spain. Who was Maricarmen?
- Mario Arguiriano Maricarmen was a sick eighty-seven-year-old woman who had rented an apartment in the center of Madrid for seventy years. Not very long ago, the apartment was bought by a Spanish company called Urbagestión that basically wanted to kick her out to make money. It tried to raise her rent by 500 percent, which she could not afford living on a modest pension, and a judge ordered an eviction. Maricarmen’s eviction was a brutal one in which over two hundred police participated. There was a lot of violence toward the people there defending her. It makes sense that Maricarmen has become a symbol of a fight that confronts the public’s needs with the needs of the housing market and the minority of parasites that live off of speculation and extracting ever more of workers’ salaries.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Why did her eviction provoke such a visceral response?
- Mario Arguiriano I believe that there exists and has been forming for years among the working class, especially among the youth of the working class, a wide dissatisfaction — with housing conditions, salaries, rising military spending, the genocide in Palestine, the authoritarianism of capitalist states, and also a dissatisfaction with [Pedro Sánchez’s] so-called progressive government. That dissatisfaction has taken on various forms when it comes to protests. Last year, there were massive solidarity protests with Palestine in Spain. We could call Maricarmen’s eviction the spark that lit the prairie of dissatisfaction. After that, it was a good decision to steer the protests toward a more permanent form in the shape of encampments, which have allowed for the accumulation of strength and energy in the context of the fight for housing, which also goes further than housing to a more general indictment of the system.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Housing has been a major focus of the protests and their coverage. But it sounds like your analysis is broader. How do you all understand the current conjuncture for the Spanish working class?
- Mario Arguiriano For us, the housing problem is an expression of both the functioning of capitalism and the crisis of capitalism in decline. We have low interest rates, which creates the conditions for overaccumulation of capital, causing idle capital to tend toward speculation on things like housing. The current “progressive” government in Spain is very comfortable targeting vulture funds, but if you look at the data, vulture funds represent a small portion of the housing market. What we have instead is a bourgeoisie and also a petty bourgeoisie, so to speak, that has found housing to be a comparatively lucrative investment and a way to suck the blood of those who need it. The housing market under capitalism generally has an inflationary tendency because it’s based on a logic of rent extraction in which the best way to make the most profit is to have prices rise constantly. And, without grand historical struggles, that’s the way the market normally functions. Today the market around housing is stimulated by governments exactly because it offers opportunities for business to a portion of capital that would otherwise be idle. These days in Spain — although this happens practically everywhere — basically any rich person you can think of owns fifty, one hundred, two hundred homes. [Diego] “Cholo” Simeone, the coach of Atlético Madrid, for example, owns more than 180 apartments. Amancio Ortega, the richest man in Spain, has a ridiculous number of apartments. It’s a general practice that can’t be reduced to vulture funds. On the other hand, I’d say that the housing problem is also the problem of salaries. Salaries in Spain have been stagnant for decades, and, in fact, low salaries have been a structural element of Spain’s capitalist model forever. One of the primary elements that Spain offers international capital, at least since [Francisco] Franco’s time, is a structurally precarious labor market with low wages. We have had unending housing price increases like other European countries — especially in the last eight years with the progressive government. Even after it approved housing laws that it promised were historic, nothing has changed. The problem of housing is also a problem of the authoritarian character of capitalist states. Without going too deep into it, the housing movement in Spain is one of the primary victims of the repressive laws that were passed by the last right-wing government and maintained by the progressive one. The Ley Mordaza (Gag Law) has permitted an increase in police power and fines. The housing movement has had to pay millions and millions of euros in fines over the last ten years based on this law that the PSOE and Podemos governments have maintained. So, as you see, if you start pulling on the thread of housing, you end up coming to more structural questions. In fact, in the final instance, the problem of housing is the problem of capitalism and the capitalist form of the state. A government of workers could resolve the problem of housing quickly via measures like nationalizing land or other proposals we’ve made like expropriating speculators, prohibition of speculation on housing, and planning and distribution of housing geared toward social needs. That would solve the problem of housing and has happened in other countries starting with worse conditions. But those solutions aren’t accessible, aren’t feasible, at least not fully, under the capitalist form of the state. It’s important to fight for short-term improvements without selling smoke to the public and without pretending that the resolution to these problems is simple, because while in the short term that can generate excitement, in the medium term it can generate demobilization, disengagement, and disenchantment.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo I’d like to hear a little more about what infrastructure CJS developed before the protests and how you put it into action.
- Mario Arguiriano CJS has had a brief existence, yet from the start we have insisted that our goal is to generate a mass communist organization, based on militancy and discipline. We’re radically opposed to forms of political parties opposed to what the working class needs, like the parties that keep popping up in Spain, formed of four famous people with wide media presence but lacking militant bases. So, from early on we have made clear that our objective, and the only route the working class has to reach revolutionary objectives and build strategic strength, is permanent, disciplined, and constant work out of the spotlight, out of the daily trends. This type of organization can later act appropriately in moments of rupture. I think we’ve had a strategy of patience and slow accumulation of strength aimed at building a revolutionary project. We believe that recent events have shown that our model works — that an organization with clear strategic objectives, strong messaging, and a hardworking and disciplined membership that remains tactically flexible can make good use of big protest moments to share its message, reinforce itself organizationally, and reinforce the movement in general. We have presence in the majority of cities in Spain and are looking to reinforce our reserves in those cities and others where we don’t have a presence, in villages, and ultimately in all environments and spaces.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo What’s your relationship with the tenants’ unions that have also played a big role in these protests?
- Mario Arguiriano The tenants’ unions were the ones who organized against Maricarmen’s eviction, who initiated the protests, and even led on the creation of the encampments. We have never hidden that we have strategic differences with the tenants’ unions, which are a project more oriented toward reform than revolution. We have insisted to them that reform is important and we don’t reject it, but it’s important to orient them toward a revolutionary, emancipatory, or socialist project. However, it’s clear that despite these differences, there’s space for joint work and unity of action in terms of protest and mobilization for worker interests. We’ve seen that these past days, and not just with tenants but also with many other actors. We have differences and strategic debates, but we can and should work toward basic common objectives without obscuring those differences, maintaining debate, and with liberty for everyone to espouse their own analysis and lift up their own projects.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo I’ve seen a lot of comparisons to 15-M. In what ways is that comparison accurate, and how is this movement distinct?
- Mario Arguiriano During the first few days of the encampments, the comparisons with 15-M were everywhere, but over time they started to disappear. Even the mass media, which is normally a medium of organized idiocy, has realized that this is something different, or at least that there are important differences. I believe that the key social and historical difference is that in the last fifteen years we’ve seen a change in the composition of classes, or a change in class relations, that has essentially been a process of proletarianization of a sector of the middle class, especially in the sector that remains prominent in the protests: young people, normally with college degrees, that are part of, in their working conditions and in their relationships with capital, the working class. In 2011, although we experienced a difficult crisis, the generation that led 15-M still lived accustomed to a period of expansion of the middle class and expansion of certain expectations. The best way to illustrate it is to say that during 15-M people protested not being able to buy a house, and today people protest not being able to rent a room. It’s normal that that difference generates a different political consciousness. So in the current protests we see a much more positive opinion toward organization, working-class consciousness, the concept of the working class, and socialism. We’ve seen the normalization of red flags, chants like “Socialism or Barbarism,” and radical critiques of capitalism. This would have been unthinkable during 15-M. Communism was frowned upon, and there was broad skepticism toward the concept of organization. There was also a much more interclass and less politically developed consciousness, without wanting to exaggerate the consciousness of the current encampments and protests — which remain a pluralistic space where many sectors, different organizations, and different levels of consciousness coexist. There are notable differences [with respect to 15-M] that even the smartest bourgeois thinkers are acknowledging.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo One impact of the protests is that there will now be general elections in November. How is CJS approaching those?
- Mario Arguiriano We will not participate in the elections, and we maintain a critical perspective on existing parties. We insist on the need to keep constructing a party of workers, and that none of the existing parties represent the interest of workers or are at the level needed to confront a capitalism that is increasingly catastrophic, linked to wars, genocides, and ecological crisis.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Before the elections, there will be a general strike. How are you preparing for that day, and what are your objectives?
- Mario Arguiriano The general strike that has been called, which we will support with all our resources, is one where there will be two models of strike in dispute. One is the government’s strike, which is the model being pushed by the major unions — the Comisiones Obreras (CCOO) and the Unión General de Trabajadores (UGT) — which work like transmission cables for the state and the government. That is a strike against the political opposition and is part of a political campaign. We believe that that model is an embarrassment, an insult to the concept of a general strike. Instead what should be created, by all organizations with a focus on class, is a class-based strike against the whole capitalist government. Strikes are spaces for working-class struggle against capital and capitalist states. That’s a general strike. Any model that supports one or another capitalist government is a farce and an insult to the Spanish working class. We want to insist on that in all kinds of spaces. Right now, you have to put in a lot of effort to impose a baseline of rationality in Spanish public debate, because we’re living through a process of the dumbing down of the public via crude lies. Maricarmen was evicted with a PSOE law, under a PSOE government, by police under the PSOE, and it’s talked about like the [conservative] opposition killed her. This is not true. Any party in charge of the capitalist state will enact evictions because all of them reinforce the model of housing as a market, and we’re not going to let any of them off the hook. A few years ago, Podemos, which now presents itself as a left-wing party, argued that the current housing law was a panacea, that it had practically saved the working-class public of Spain with it. It’s delirious that it now wants us to forget that. This strike by itself will not impose major demands. This strike should serve to build class power with the aim of an independent project and to stimulate fights for housing, improved salaries, and against the authoritarianism of capitalist states. Within the strike, CJS will push the need to construct an alternative political structure for workers — not just strong unions but a party for workers. To achieve that, we will participate in broad committees and promote strike youth committees open to whomever.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo What’s the role of unions in the Spanish working-class struggle? I understand that the major unions are quite linked to the government, but is there a future where unions can be part of the fight that you’re starting?
- Mario Arguiriano Of course, there are numerous unions in Spain that have a focus on class and are engaged in righteous struggles for workers’ rights. And even in the membership of major unions like the CCOO, there are people who fight daily for workers. We criticize the leadership of unions, which doesn’t represent the needs of workers. Unions are very important in working-class struggle; they should be organs for that and not for collaboration between classes. The leader of CCOO, Unai Sordo, wrote an article about the strike that is essentially apologia for the PSOE’s economic policy. How is it that you are going to go on a strike defending the government and its economic policies? We can’t accept this; it’s essentially an insult. That’s how we approach the question of unions. We don’t denounce or disregard union work. In fact, we will work with class-focused unions to try to drive mobilizations separate from the mobilizations that will be apologia for the government, or that might even include government ministers. The idea that there could be ministers protesting against their own government could make anyone go nuts.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo When the protests and the encampments end, what’s the plan to keep the critiques that have been levied going?
- Mario Arguiriano In Movimiento Socialista, we plan to work around two axes. The first is to strengthen the working-class movement, collaborating with other actors like labor unions and tenants’ unions toward shared objectives. For example, it’s very important for us to create a wide front for political rights capable of confronting the state, its authoritarianism, militarism, and new repressive laws. Our other axis of work, complementary with the first, is to keep working to build a mass revolutionary party, not only in Spain but across Europe and, ultimately, around the world. That requires diversified work: exposition of strategies, development of different tactics, and the production of a revolutionary political program in favor of a different form of state, a different mode of production, and a different way to live that the working class can coalesce around. We believe that is absolutely urgent. We have to fight at all levels, which includes the political. We have to counter-propose a workers’ program, a socialist program, against the program of capital.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.title: Ernährungsmedizin | Mangelernährung als unterschätztes Problem
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.author: Ulrike Henning
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Ernährungsmedizin
Mangelernährung als unterschätztes Problem
Im Rahmen von Therapien kann es unbeabsichtigt zum Fehlen von Nährstoffen kommen – sowohl in der Klinik als auch ambulant.
Mangelernährung in Zusammenhang mit Krankheiten ist nicht nur ein Problem von Krankenhauspatienten. Auch nach einem stationären Aufenthalt, etwa bei fortlaufender Therapie mit Medikamenten, kann sie auftreten. Und es gibt einige Patientengruppen, bei denen Ärzte besonders aufmerksam sein müssen. Die Thematik Mangelernährung ist Gegenstand einer Aktionswoche, die von der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Ernährungsmedizin (DGEM) mit neun Partnern veranstaltet wird, darunter Krebsmediziner, Diabetologen und Ernährungsfachleute mit ihren Verbänden.
Grundsätzlich bis zu 30 Prozent aller stationären und bis zu fünf Prozent aller älteren ambulanten Patienten sind laut dem in Berlin niedergelassenen Internisten und Ernährungsmediziner Matthias Pirlich betroffen. In der Folge werden Muskeln abgebaut, das Immunsystem wird geschwächt. Behandlungskomplikationen und Pflegebedürftigkeit nehmen zu, am Ende steigt die Sterblichkeit. Andererseits verbessert zielgerichtete Behandlung auch die Prognose: Unter anderen sinken Komplikationsraten und Kliniksterblichkeit deutlich, stationäre Wiederaufnahmen werden seltener.
Bislang fehlt es unter anderem an systematischem Screening der besonders gefährdeten Patienten. Das liegt auch an der veralteten Version des noch verwendeten Diagnosesystems ICD-10. Laut Pirlich sind die Diagnosekriterien zu diesem Thema im klinischen Alltag »unbrauchbar«. Jedenfalls erlauben sie nicht, Betroffene einfach oder sicher zu erfassen. Das führte auch zu Abrechnungsstreitigkeiten zwischen Kliniken und Krankenkassen. Im neuen ICD-11, das ab 2027 in Kraft tritt, wurden aber die Diagnosekriterien geändert. Erfasst werden nunmehr niedriges Körpergewicht, Gewichtsverlust und niedrige Muskelmasse sowie verminderte Nahrungsaufnahme. Diese und weitere Kriterien gehen zurück auf eine internationale Experten-Initative von 2019. Inzwischen belegen über 900 wissenschaftliche Publikationen, dass die Kriterien aussagekräftig sind. In Deutschland soll es bis Ende 2027 eine gemeinsame Richtlinie zur besseren Diagnostik und Behandlung geben, erarbeitet vom Gemeinsamen Bundesausschuss für das Gesundheitswesen. Damit sollen bisherige Versorgungslücken geschlossen werden.
Dabei zeigt sich Mangelernährung nicht unbedingt eindeutig und für Laien klar erkennbar. Jutta Hübner, Internistin mit onkologischen Schwerpunkten und einer Professur am Universitätsklinikum Jena, beschreibt die alltägliche Lage vieler Krebspatienten: »Man isst allein zu Hause, in der Familie, man isst etwas weniger, geht früher von Feiern weg. Niemand merkt, was los ist, man redet nicht darüber.« Wegen moderner Krebstherapien, oft mit einer Tablette täglich erledigt, gibt es zum Beispiel keinen Haarverlust oder andere offensichtliche Signale.
Trotzdem verursachen die Medikamente laut Hübner »Unwohlsein, leichte Übelkeit und Schwäche«. Es werde weniger gegessen, es gebe etwas Durchfall, etwas Verstopfung. »Auf Dauer führt das zu Mangelernährung – auch bei Übergewichtigen. Die Schleimhäute in Mund und Darm werden immer empfindlicher.« In solchen Fällen sei eine qualifizierte Ernährungsberatung nötig, vor allem für die ambulanten Patienten. Dabei müssten auch die Begleiterkrankungen und Lebensphasen (wie die Menopause bei Frauen) mitgedacht werden.
Die Beratung könnte vom behandelnden Onkologen oder vom Hausarzt kommen, der eben auch die anderen Krankheiten des Patienten kennt. Aber nicht immer geht das auf: Ansprechpartner bei der Suche nach geeigneten Spezialisten könnte dann die jeweilige Landeskrebsgesellschaft sein.
Zu den Risikogruppen gehören laut Jürgen M. Bauer Menschen mit Adipositas und Diabetes, insbesondere wenn sie über 65 Jahre alt sind. Auch sie können GLP1-Rezeptoren (geläufig als Abnehmspritzen beziehungsweise neuerdings auch in Tablettenform) verordnet bekommen. Doch Bauer, ärztlicher Leiter der Geriatrie am Universitätsklinikum Heidelberg, warnt: »Diese Personengruppe war nicht in die Zulassungsstudien eingeschlossen.« Zu beachten sei hier, dass in der Therapie nicht nur Fett verloren gehe, sondern auch Muskelmasse. Damit könnten eben auch Muskelkraft und -funktion abnehmen.
Auf jeden Fall sollte vor Beginn der Verordnung der Ernährungsstatus geprüft werden, ebenso wie kognitive und muskuläre Funktionen. Auch wenn es im Therapieverlauf zu Einbußen komme, »dann ist das der falsche Patient«. Es sei zu vermeiden, dass altersbedingte Gebrechlichkeit hier quasi unbeabsichtigt durch eine medikamentöse Appetitsteuerung herbeigeführt werde. Für diese Zusammenhänge fehle zurzeit noch das Bewusstsein, vor allem dann, »wenn die Zahl auf der Waage das Wichtigste ist«, gibt Bauer zu bedenken.
Während der Therapie mit den GLP1-Agonisten sei für eine ausreichende Eiweißzufuhr zu sorgen, zwischen 1,2 bis 1,6 Gramm pro Kilogramm Zielgewicht, empfiehlt etwa eine US-amerikanische Fachgesellschaft. Laut Bauer ist das eine anspruchsvolle Aufgabe, wenn sich die Nahrungsmenge aufgrund der Medikamentenwirkung verringert. Zur Erhaltung von Muskelmasse und -funktion sei außerdem regelmäßiges Krafttraining die wirksamste Maßnahme. Gerade bei dieser älteren Patientengruppe sollen die GLP-1-Agonisten weder aus dem Internet bezogen noch ohne ärztliche Begleitung eingenommen werden.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: How Did New York Become So Unequal?
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Joshua B. Freeman
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
A Tale of Two Cities
How did New York go from a center of social-democratic experiment to one of neoliberal devastation?
How Did New York Become So Unequal?
A new history of New York examines how it went from a center of social-democratic experiment to one of neoliberal devastation.
In 2013, Mason B. Williams published City of Ambition, in which he told the story of New York’s transformation during the New Deal era, when federal dollars from Washington powered Fiorello La Guardia’s expansive vision for the role of municipal government in everyday life. La Guardia’s alliance with Franklin D. Roosevelt, supported by an expanding labor movement and a network of left and liberal organizations, laid the basis for the New York I grew up in. Federal funds allowed the city to build the high school I attended, the subway lines I spent a lifetime riding, the highways, bridges, and tunnels that whisked me around the city and sometimes congealed me in traffic jams, the innumerable parks, playgrounds, beaches, swimming pools, and health clinics, and the public-housing system that currently has more than a half-million residents.
Books in review
City of Fortune: Inequality and the Making of Contemporary New York
Buy this book
Williams’s new book, City of Fortune, chronicles a transformation just as profound: the post-1970s-fiscal-crisis replacement of the local New Deal order with a New York version of neoliberalism. Williams shows in devastating detail how, over the past half-century, the city’s economy and municipal capacity for governance have grown at the same time that it has developed levels of poverty and inequality unprecedented in its modern history. It is the relationship between these trends—how “the systems that made [the city] work for some imposed costs and violence on others”—that is the central focus of his book.
Williams has digested the vast literature on modern New York, of which these trends are only a part. To it, he has added a massive research effort of his own, in scores of archival collections and publications, giving his volume an authoritative quality. His wide-ranging knowledge might bring to mind comparisons to the late historian Mike Wallace—and they would not be entirely unjust. But unlike Wallace’s encyclopedic accounts of life and change in New York, City of Fortune focuses on three particular issues to tell its story: policing, education, and housing. All three profoundly affected the lives of New Yorkers; all three were political flash points; and all three were intertwined with changes in both material conditions and ideological assumptions.
Like many other American cities in the 1960s and ’70s, New York suffered a massive increase in crime and the sense of danger and disorder that came with it. By the mid-1970s, the New York Police Department had been diminished by cuts in funding and personnel and seemed utterly ineffective in countering the trend. (Those of us who had cars stolen or apartments broken into during those years can remember how the police considered the idea of investigating such crimes laughable.)
But starting under Mayor Ed Koch, a new generation of police leaders and new crime-fighting strategies, many coming out of the academic world, reshaped police activity and remade life for millions of New Yorkers, especially men of color. Pursuing various iterations of “community policing” and “broken windows” theory, the NYPD aggressively combated even minor acts of disorder in neighborhoods targeted as centers of drug activity and crime, arguing that doing so would allow the natural mechanisms of community self-regulation to reemerge.
In the early 1990s, the crime rate in New York began to fall, and it would continue to do so until Covid-19 hit in 2020. How much police strategy had to do with this is unclear, since crime would soon decrease in other cities as well. Still, the NYPD doubled down on its intense policing in high-crime areas, which tended to be neighborhoods with large African American or Latino populations. “Stop-and-frisk” became the favored mode of policing, a practice both deeply racist in disproportionately targeting non-white men for searches without legitimate cause and a clear violation of the Fourth Amendment. Even as crime continued to drop, the city refused to reduce the pressure: In 2011, it recorded an astounding 685,724 stops.
In some precincts, there were more stops than residents. If you were young and Black, the relentless harassment could lead to jail time for petty offenses, job loss, or far worse. The swagger and sense of omnipotence that came with the official veneration of aggressive policing resulted in a series of tragic murders of innocent people by police officers that tore the city apart. Yet, Williams notes, the NYPD would only become more “impervious to reform.”
****In education, the city faced two massive challenges: the extreme racial segregation in its schools (among the worst in the nation) and their failure to provide huge swaths of students with a decent education. Rather than confronting segregation head-on—a politically difficult approach—the city began experimenting with “magnet schools” to draw students from both white and non-white communities to superior schools with superior resources. At roughly the same time, progressive educators like Deborah Meier began creating public schools that broke from the older, more rigid and hierarchical approaches to pedagogy and drew interested students from across relatively broad areas to alternative learning communities.
The idea of school choice, which encompassed both developments, proved ideologically promiscuous: It soon became a favored approach of leftists, liberals, and free-market conservatives. By the early 1990s, it was also the official policy of the New York City Board of Education. New schools (some dubbed “academies”) popped up like mushrooms, both within the regular public-school system and as charter schools, supported by foundation as well as taxpayer money.
Some of these new schools proved to be excellent, although they often created conflicts as they took over the buildings of older schools the way hermit crabs take over the shells of other creatures. They also helped keep middle-class white students in the public-school system—an explicit goal of city leaders. But in doing so, critics argued, they siphoned away resources as well as many of the best teachers and students from the rest of the system and left behind those who could not (or didn’t know how to) get into selective schools. Regardless of the reasons it was initiated, Williams notes, school choice often ended up reinforcing and deepening segregation and inequality.
New York’s housing market was plagued by segregation and inequality as well. “Nothing animated the city’s business community quite like rent regulation,” Williams observes, framing his discussion of housing around the never-ending contest over whether to expand, diminish, or eliminate rent control.
These limits on rent increases—a legacy of federal price controls during World War II—helped preserve a city made up largely of working- and middle-class renters during the postwar years, when America’s other major cities mostly shrank in size and vitality. In 1970, 1.3 million apartments in New York City built before 1947 were covered by the state’s strict rent-control law, while another 375,000 units built later were regulated by a looser rent-stabilization system the city set up in 1968. Rent regulations, by design, limited landlords’ profits and challenged the idea that owners of property had the right to do whatever they wanted with it. Landlords knew there was little point in arguing that they should be allowed to make more money—but the claim that rent control made it impossible to properly maintain their existing buildings and discouraged new construction carried more weight.
In 1971, with the support of Governor Nelson Rockefeller, the New York State Legislature instituted “vacancy decontrol,” which removed the limits on what a landlord could charge for a previously rent-controlled apartment after the former tenant had vacated it. The backlash against this victory for building owners was so intense that, three years later, the Legislature required that apartments leaving the rent-control system be placed, after a onetime opportunity to hike the rent, under rent stabilization, gradually shifting housing from the older regulatory system to the newer one. But rather than ending the battle, the decision simply changed the terrain on which it has continued.
For one thing, the mayor-appointed Rent Guidelines Board, which determines each year how much stabilized rents can be raised, became the object of intense lobbying by tenants and landlords, with hearings that are famously epic, unruly affairs. For another, real estate interests continued to chip away at the system, eventually winning laws that removed apartments whose rent was above a certain cap or whose tenants made more than a certain income (“luxury decontrol”). In 1997, Governor George Pataki and Republicans in the Legislature were set to gut the system beyond recognition, until a massive mobilization of tenants, backed by organized labor, largely forced them to retreat.
Despite how heroically tenants and their organizations have dug their heels in to maintain these restrictions on rent, the housing-affordability crisis in the city has only worsened. The removal of hundreds of thousands of apartments from the rent-regulation system, the failure to build enough new housing, and a growing population have combined to accelerate gentrification and make finding a place to live a nightmare for all but the well-off. “By 2011,” Williams writes, “for the first time in the city’s modern history, the median New York rental household was officially rent-burdened, paying more than 30 percent of its income in rent—and a third of households paid more than half.”
The three stories that form the spine of City of Fortune will be familiar to longtime New York residents, if not to outsiders, but Williams tells them with an impressive combination of lucidity and granular detail. He also makes two very important points about their dynamics that are not often brought out.
The first is the centrality of state politics to what happens in New York City. The system of rent regulation, for example, comes primarily from state law, though city ordinances are involved too. Its fate has remained in the hands of a Legislature made up mostly of people elected outside of the city and governors who looked to the suburbs for swing votes to keep them in office. The mayor may press the Rent Guidelines Board to limit increases on regulated units, but the state, if it chooses, could get rid of the entire system. Tax-abatement programs to encourage housing construction likewise come from Albany, not City Hall. So do charter-school authorizations and many of the regulations (including the testing regime) that shape the city’s school system. More broadly, the ability of the city government to create and maintain programs of all kinds, from policing to transit to healthcare access, depends on legal and financial relationships with the state and federal governments. The city cannot even change its income-tax rates, which are controlled by the state, to the frustration of the current mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Even with a DSA-led campaign to “Tax the Rich,” he failed to win state approval for a higher income tax on wealthy residents or a boost in corporate tax rates, ultimately settling for a modest surcharge on real estate taxes on expensive second homes.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The second point that Williams stresses is the continuity of public policy across parties and mayors. Though packaged and sold differently from administration to administration, practices like aggressive community policing (including stop-and-frisk) and school choice have proved remarkably durable, even with the mayor’s office occupied by such seemingly dissimilar characters as Ed Koch, David Dinkins, Rudy Giuliani, Michael Bloomberg, and Bill de Blasio. Williams never steps back enough to ask why this is so, though he does mention some factors in passing, including the power of institutional interests like the NYPD and the continuing influence of various lobbies and advocacy organizations.
Williams’s concentration on particular policy areas allows us to see the expanding impact of neoliberalism on everyday life, but it also limits his portrayal of the larger structures of economic and political power that shaped the evolution of the city. For example, the post-fiscal-crisis New York economy is quite different from its earlier incarnation, with the virtual disappearance of manufacturing—once a mainstay—and the increased importance of services, finance, and real estate. The new robber barons in the city, though they may be extracting wealth from across the globe and bringing it into New York, are also more attentive to municipal matters than their predecessors. And they are much more ideologically engaged: Issues like charter schools and school choice have become vehicles for delegitimizing the state and promoting free-market ideas (though when it comes to policing, the same folks are all for strong government).
The 1975 fiscal crisis, widely interpreted by politicians, business leaders, and the press as a verdict on the flaws of expansive egalitarian government, led to years of austerity. It also laid the basis for a consensus on the importance of attracting and catering to wealthy companies and individuals and maintaining an orderly city that would not offend them. This became the new common sense, the hegemonic idea sustaining the power of New York’s financial and real-estate elite. In myriad ways, it shaped public policy no matter who headed City Hall.
What did not happen in the years after the post-crisis recovery is as revealing as what did. While billions of public dollars were devoted to subsidizing high-end office construction, not a single new unit of public housing has been built in the past 35 years. During the same period, cities all over the world have built mass-transit lines or whole new systems; New York added only four subway stops, all serving wealthy Manhattan neighborhoods. As economic inequality and homelessness soared, with nearly one in seven public-school pupils homeless, the government failed to build the housing and provide the services needed for the displaced and resourceless.
City of Fortune is shocking not only for the details it recounts but also for its disturbing picture of the moral and political failures of New York’s leaders. How can a city like New York, with a landscape now punctuated by palaces for the ultra-wealthy—such as the $238 million penthouse that billionaire Ken Griffin counts as a second home—have 420,000 children living below the poverty line? How can a society go so wrong so quickly?
Williams sees some hope in the future and gives us a hint of what that future might look like. Ending his book on an upbeat note, he recounts an October 2019 rally in the Long Island City neighborhood of Queens, where Bernie Sanders, after suffering a heart attack, relaunched his presidential campaign with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at his side. In the crowd listening to Sanders’s moving appeal for solidarity across racial, religious, and national lines, Williams writes, was Zohran Mamdani, who had just launched his own campaign for the State Assembly.
Mamdani’s astounding election as mayor and his first months in office suggest that a new era might be beginning in New York. Unlike his opponents, Mamdani has a gut feel for the changes that took place in the city during the years Williams examines: the massive growth of inequality; the daily struggle of so many New Yorkers just to get by; the precarity of even young professionals in fields like higher education, culture, and the arts; and the extraordinary diversity of a city in which over 37 percent of the population was born outside the country (compared with 18 percent in 1970).
For progressives and ordinary New Yorkers, Mamdani is a breath of fresh air. Like Fiorello La Guardia, he is everywhere, filling potholes, shoveling snow, rallying with striking nurses, sharing iftar with city workers, riding his bike with Brooklyn parents taking their kids to school, and sitting in the nosebleed section of Madison Square Garden watching the Knicks. So far, he has been largely successful in avoiding pitfalls and inching toward fulfilling his campaign promises, which included freezing regulated rents, universal childcare, and free buses. But Williams’s account is a cautionary tale about the obstacles he faces: the limited power of the city in such crucial areas as tax policy and education; the fiscal challenges in an era when, unlike La Guardia’s, the federal government is determined to undermine blue-state cities rather than partner with them to better the lives of their residents; and the enormous power of the self-serving financial and real estate interests. It is too early to say if Mamdani and the movement that helped him win office will be able to break the link between the city’s growth and the grotesque inequality that Williams so ably chronicles. At stake is what it means to be a civilized society.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: MP denuncia Milton Leite, o ex-presidente da SPTrans na gestão Nunes e mais 12 por ligação com PCC no transporte público
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O ex-vereador paulistano Milton Leite (União Brasil) foi denunciado pelo Ministério Público Estadual junto a outros 13 suspeitos de integrar e promover a atual da facção criminosa Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) no transporte público da capital paulista e outras cidades.
Leite está preso desde o dia 18 de setembro, quando se entregou na sede da Delegacia de Investigações sobre Entorpecentes, em Mogi das Cruzes, região metropolitana de São Paulo (SP). A investigação aponta que ele seria o verdadeiro dono da empresa Transwolff, que atuou em linhas de ônibus da capital paulista, e que os sócios dela estariam subordinados ao ex-vereador.
A defesa do ex-vereador afirmou que está tomando conhecimento da denúncia e, por enquanto, não irá se manifestar.
Além de Leite, foi apresentada denúncia contra Levi dos Santos Oliveira, ex-presidente da SPTrans, órgão que gerencia o transporte público da capital paulista, no governo de Bruno Covas (PSDB), ex-secretário municipal de Mobilidade e Trânsito e novamente presidente da SPTrans no governo de Ricardo Nunes (MDB).
Contra Oliveira, pesa a acusação de que ele teria conhecimento da atuação do crime organizado nas empresas de ônibus e de que promoveu pessoalmente a facção. Trocas de mensagens entre ele e suspeitos de integrar o PCC foram encontradas pelos investigadores.
Também foram denunciados: Danilo Morgado, candidato do PL à prefeitura de Praia Grande em 2024 e a deputado estadual em 2026, derrotado em ambos os pleitos; Carla de Paula Muller e Paulo Sirqueira Korek Farias, empresários do ramo de transportes; e José Daniel Satilite, apontado como integrante do PCC e sócio de fachada de uma empresa de ônibus e de uma refinaria de petróleo.
Promotores e investigadores acusam o grupo de agir para infiltrar o crime organizado no transporte coletivo de ônibus de municípios paulistas, corromper funcionários públicos e financiar campanhas políticas na região de Praia Grande, no litoral.
A denúncia, assinada por três promotores do Grupo de Atuação Especial de Combate ao Crime Organizado (Gaeco) regional do ABC Paulista, foi oferecida na noite de segunda-feira (9), três dias após a Polícia Civil apresentar o relatório final de investigação, com 104 páginas.
Promotores do Gaeco acusam o grupo de articular a infiltração do crime organizado no transporte coletivo de ônibus na capital e outros municípios paulistas, além de corromper funcionários públicos e financiar campanhas políticas na região de Praia Grande, no litoral.
As defesas dos demais acusados ainda não haviam se manifestado, mas, durante as investigações, todos alegaram inocência.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ju.title: Julia Stoschek Collection to Celebrate 20 Years with ‘Selfish in Bed’ Exhibition and Düsseldorf Reopening
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ju.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ju.text:
Sarah Lucas doesn’t appear particularly apologetic in her 2000 self-portrait Selfish in Bed II. Standing with her hands on her hips, the British artist wears a black T-shirt with the words “SELFISH IN BED” printed across the front. Next April, that cheeky photograph will set the tone for a major group exhibition celebrating the 20th anniversary of the Julia Stoschek Collection in Düsseldorf, Germany.
Aptly titled Selfish in Bed, the exhibition opens on April 10, 2027, and will bring together 52 works by 43 artists, including Tracey Emin, Bill Viola, Wolfgang Tillmans, and Bruce Nauman. Selfish in Bed marks the inaugural exhibition of the reopened Julia Stoschek Foundation’s Düsseldorf headquarters, which closed for renovations in April 2025.
Curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, the director of Finland’s EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art and former director of Berlin’s KW Institute for Contemporary Art, the show looks at how we construct our identities, express our sexuality, and present ourselves to the world.
The exhibition takes the bed as its starting point. It’s a place increasingly of contradictions: It’s private and vulnerable, yet inter-connected, where we spend hours scrolling through the images and opinions that shape how we see ourselves. The show explores that tension through works spanning the late 1960s to the present, including several that the foundation has never exhibited before.
There are more than a few highlights. Emin’s Why I Never Became a Dancer (1995), Simon Fujiwara‘s Joanne (2016/2018), and Hannah Wilke’s Through the Large Glass (1976), all explore women’s relationships with their bodies, sexuality, and public image. Meanwhile Monica Bonvicini‘s Destroy She Said (1998) challenges traditional domestic roles, and Ed Atkins’s Us Dead Talk Love (2012) examines questions of identity and authenticity in the digital age.
The exhibition is set to span two floors, and include video projections, mirrored surfaces, glass walls, and television monitors creating an immersive environment. Works by Viola, Tillmans, and Rosemarie Trockel will be presented together in a grouping that explores the human experience from birth onward.
For Stoschek, whose collection now includes more than 1,000 works by over 300 artists, the anniversary is also an opportunity to reflect on two decades of collecting.
“I am a very emotional collector,” Stoschek said in a statement. “An artwork has to get under my skin. I need images that stay with me.”
The Düsseldorf headquarters, housed in a converted industrial building dating to 1907, has undergone an extensive renovation by Berlin architecture firm Kuehn Malvezzi, which originally adapted the space for exhibitions in 2007. In Berlin, the foundation closed its exhibition space at the end of October after a decade of programming, shifting its attention toward Düsseldorf and international projects.
A publication marking the collection’s 20th anniversary will accompany the exhibition, with contributions from writers and critics including Rachel Cusk, Chris Kraus, Dean Kissick, and McKenzie Wark.
Selfish in Bed will run from April 10 through December 19, 2027, with an opening reception on April 9.

https://taz.de/Ansturm-auf-Elektroautos/.title: Ansturm auf Elektroautos: Mehr Förderung und längere Förderzeiten
https://taz.de/Ansturm-auf-Elektroautos/.author: Bernward Janzing
https://taz.de/Ansturm-auf-Elektroautos/.text:
Ansturm auf Elektroautos: Mehr Förderung und längere Förderzeiten
Der Bund will nächstes Jahr mehr Geld für die Förderung der Elektromobilität geben. Ein spezieller Fördertopf ist bereits leer.
Die hohen Spritpreise zeigen Wirkung: Immer mehr Menschen wollen ein E-Auto haben, die Hersteller kommen deswegen mit der Produktion nicht mehr nach. Im Oktober waren 37 Prozent aller Neuzulassungen von Pkws in Deutschland reine Elektroautos. Zählt man die Hybrid-Modelle noch hinzu, hatten im Oktober sogar 75 Prozent der Neufahrzeuge Elektroantrieb.
Die Nachfrage nach Elektroautos sei so groß, dass es „bei einzelnen Modellen aktuell zu einer Verlängerung der Lieferzeiten“ kommen könne, räumt auch der Verband der Automobilindustrie ein. Die Unternehmen passten aber „ihre Produktionskapazitäten entsprechend der Nachfrage an, um Lieferzeiten möglichst gering zu halten“. Das Branchenportal Carwow benennt Lieferzeiten, die bei einzelnen Modellen bei einem Jahr und mehr liegen.
Angesichts der unerwartet hohen Nachfrage will die Bundesregierung nach einem Bericht der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters im kommenden Jahr deutlich mehr Geld für die Förderung von Elektroautos bereitstellen als ursprünglich geplant. Statt der vorgesehenen 803 Millionen Euro sollen nun für die Kaufprämie im Jahr 2027 sogar 1,72 Milliarden Euro veranschlagt werden.
Das gesamte Programmvolumen soll aber offenbar nicht erhöht werden. Das kann dazu führen, dass der vorgesehene Etat deutlich vor dem geplanten Ende 2029 ausgeschöpft ist. Seit dem Programmstart im Mai wurden bisher im Mittel rund 4.400 Euro pro Fahrzeug bezahlt. Bei einer angesetzten Fördersumme von 3 Milliarden Euro dürfte das Geld somit für rund 680.000 Fahrzeuge reichen. Zum 1. Oktober waren bereits fast 98.000 Zuschussanträge bewilligt und 432 Millionen Euro ausbezahlt, davon gut 200 Millionen allein im vorangegangenen Monat.
Tesla Model Y am häufigsten gefördert
Laut Zahlen des Bundesamts für Wirtschaft und Ausfuhrkontrolle entfielen die meisten Förderzusagen auf Modelle des Volkswagen-Konzerns, gefolgt von Stellantis und Tesla. Betrachtet man die Marken der Konzerne separat – also zum Beispiel VW und Audi –, steht Tesla an der Spitze der geförderten Hersteller. Der Tesla Model Y ist mit fast 8.300 geförderten Exemplaren das beliebteste Modell überhaupt.
Zugleich boomte der Bau von geförderten Ladeboxen. Die entsprechenden Fördermittel sind deswegen bereits ausgeschöpft. Am Dienstag schloss das Bundesverkehrsministerium das Programm „Ladeinfrastruktur in und an Mehrparteienhäusern“. Für Wohnungseigentümergemeinschaften war das Programm bereits am 2. November beendet worden.
Auslöser des Elektrofahrzeug-Booms sind neben der staatlichen Förderung und der ausgeweiteten Modellpalette – allein von deutschen Herstellern gibt es inzwischen mehr als 110 Modelle – die hohen Treibstoffpreise. Diese lagen nach Zahlen des Wirtschaftsverbands Fuels und Energie im September für Benzin bei durchschnittlich 2,31 Euro und für Diesel bei 2,37 Euro. Andererseits ist das Laden eines E-Fahrzeugs auch nicht jederzeit günstig: Kunden, die für ihre heimische Ladesäule einen dynamischen Strompreis gebucht haben, bezahlten in diesen Tagen in der Spitze fast 1 Euro pro Kilowattstunde – in jenen Stunden nämlich, in denen bei fehlender Sonne und wenig Wind ein Drittel der deutschen Stromerzeugung aus Erdgas stammte.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/abu-dhabi/.author: Vadim Kamenka
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/abu-dhabi/.text:
À Abu Dhabi, les négociations ont débuté ce mardi 10 novembre entre les États-Unis, la Russie et l’Ukraine pour tenter d’avancer sur un processus diplomatique. Si certains évoquent la possibilité de cessez-le-feu locaux, la bataille autour du nombre de morts se poursuit. Des groupes de hackers évoquent un bilan de 400 000 morts russes entre février 2022 et l’été 2026.
En pleine négociation diplomatique à Abu Dhabi, entre Washington, Kiev et Moscou, un chiffre met en avant la réalité de la guerre. Plus de 400 000 Russes auraient trouvé la mort au combat en Ukraine depuis l’invasion, le 24 février 2022. Ces informations ont été obtenues par le groupe de hackers biélorusse « Cyber Partisans », lié à l’opposition, et par le collectif ukrainien « Silent Crow », qui ont piraté l’agence nationale des statistiques Rosstat le 1er novembre.
Ils ont eu « accès à plus de 11 millions d’actes de décès, comprenant notamment l’âge des défunts, leur lieu de résidence et le lieu de leur décès », explique le journal du Guardian qui a récupéré une partie des données.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120378.title: Nations League | Niclas Füllkrug im DFB-Team: »Verantwortung in anderen Räumen«
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120378.author: Frank Hellmann, Herzogenaurach
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120378.text:
- Sport
- Nations League
Niclas Füllkrug im DFB-Team: »Verantwortung in anderen Räumen«
Der 33-jährige Stürmer soll seine positive Attitüde bei den Spielen gegen Serbien und die Niederlande nun wieder in die Nationalmannschaft tragen.
Als ob Niclas Füllkrug nie weg gewesen wäre, grüßte er bei seiner Rückkehr in die deutsche Nationalmannschaft mit einem einfachen »Moin« vom Podium. Und ja, einerseits fühlte es sich für den 33-Jährigen in Herzogenaurach gleich wieder vertraut an, andererseits spürte der Mittelstürmer auch »eine krasse Veränderung«, weil er in so viele »frische Gesichter« schaue.
Dass Füllkrug für die Spiele in der Nations League am Freitag in Belgrad gegen Serbien und drei Tage später gegen die Niederlande in Berlin von Jürgen Klopp eine Nominierung erhielt, erfreue ihn auch deshalb, weil er »unter einer der größten Persönlichkeiten im deutschen Fußball« vorspielen könne.
Mit einem aufgeräumten und ausgeruhten Auftritt nährte der beim SV Werder Bremen wieder aufgeglühte Torjäger bei der ersten Pressekonferenz im Quartier des DFB, dass alle Seiten vom Comeback profitieren. Er vereint, was jeder Mannschaft hilft: Torinstinkt, Teamgeist und Realitätssinn. Dazu kommt die positive Ausstrahlung. Aus seinem Naturell sind Publikumslieblinge geschnitzt.
Erfahrung und Form
Der Bedarf für Füllkrugs Berufung war aber sportlicher Natur: Tim Kleindienst ist seit einer halben Ewigkeit verletzt, Nick Woltemade fast ebenso lange aus der Spur und Younes Ebnoutalib noch etwas unfertig. Und weil es bei den ersten vier Länderspielen unter dem neuen Bundestrainer eben nur drei Tore gab, musste auch Klopp das Faustpfand der Erfahrung in Kombination mit der aktuellen Form berücksichtigen. Insofern konnte der 59-Jährige gar nicht anders, als den besten Bundesliga-Torschützen zu berufen, der zurzeit sogar treffsicherer als Weltfußballer Harry Kane ist.
Die Brücke zum englischen Weltklassestürmer baute Füllkrug gleich selbst. »Anspielbar sein, Bälle festmachen und Verantwortung in anderen Räumen übernehmen«, das sei genau wie bei Kane auch seine Aufgabe. »Es ist leicht, Stürmer nur über Tore zu definieren.« Zuletzt im Auswärtsspiel beim verlorenen Bundesligaspiel in Stuttgart habe er 77 Ballkontakte gesammelt, denn bei Werder suchten und fänden ihn die Mitspieler ständig. Im Nationalteam werde es »dann vielleicht etwas mehr der Abschlussspieler sein«.
Das Alter spiele bei alldem keine Rolle: Es brauche auf dieser Position »Erfahrung, Timing, Routine« – und weniger den Sprintertypen. Füllkrug erinnerte an sein früheres Vorbild Miroslav Klose, der mit 36 Jahren noch Weltmeister wurde und erst mit 38 die Karriere beendete. »Alter ist für mich kein Thema. Ich muss mich selbst über mich erschrecken – ich fühle mich nicht wie 33!« Und wie sagte gerade Sportdirektor Rudi Völler, der mit 34 noch die WM 1994 spielte? »Es ist eine Frage der Fitness.«
Wohlfühloase Werder
Dass in Füllkrugs Zeit bei West Ham United und AC Mailand immer mal wieder der Körper streikte, ist jedoch Fakt. Der Familienvater brauchte mit einer weiteren Luftveränderung im Sommer erst die Wohlfühloase an der Weser, um wieder in beste Verfassung zu gelangen. Werder sei nun einmal seit dem 14. Lebensjahr ein fußballerisches Zuhause. Dazu sagte er selbst: »Im eigenen Bett schläft man am besten.«
Über seine Rolle beim Nationalteam wollte und konnte Füllkrug nicht viel sagen. Klopp findet grundsätzlich, dass Kai Havertz alle Anlagen zu einem Weltklasseangreifer mitbringt, weshalb der Offensivallrounder vom FC Arsenal erneut beginnen dürfte. Füllkrug bekommt die Rolle als Joker, die ihm mit dem Adler auf der Brust gut bekannt ist. In seinen 24 Länderspielen – das letzte im Juni 2025 bei der Nations-League-Finalrunde gegen Frankreich – schoss Füllkrug immerhin 14 Tore, obwohl er nur achtmal in der Startelf stand.
Insbesondere bei der Heim-EM 2024 betätigte sich Füllkrug als gut gelaunter Teilzeitarbeiter, der alles dem Erfolg unterordnete. Am Dienstag erinnerte er sich dann nicht nur an die schönen Momente nach den ersten EM-Siegen, sondern auch den Abend, als das unglückliche Viertelfinal-Aus gegen Spanien zu beklagen war. In jener Nacht ahnte Füllkrug sicher nicht, dass er nun vom selben Ort aus um die Teilnahme an der EM 2028 in Großbritannien spielt.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Country Repudiated Bigotry in This Election. Will the Sports World Follow?
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Dave Zirin
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The Country Repudiated Bigotry in This Election. Will the Sports World Follow?
If we follow the lead of billionaire team owners, toxic cable news channels, and misguided athletes, it’s a resounding no. That just means we need to forge our own path.
The confetti had not even been swept up after last week’s historic electoral repudiation of Donald Trump when Democratic Party leadership made it clear that they would not try to, in the words of incoming Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries, “get even” with the assorted criminals that have been stripping this country for parts. But people don’t want to “get even,” as if this were all some childish tit-for-tat. They want justice.
The electorate voted for a reckoning, but the current Democratic leadership—including Jeffries and incumbent leader of the newly flipped Senate Chuck Schumer—are utterly unequal to the task. Their inadequacy is a huge liability. If they fail to live up to voters’ expectations, that avalanche of young people we just saw go to the polls might stay home in 2028 out of disgust, potentially sweeping into power a shrewder generation of racist authoritarians bleating about Democratic “broken promises.” It’s a movie we’ve seen before.
Concerns about their total absence of spines goes beyond squandering electoral gains, though. If they fail to provide the kind of reckoning voters went to the polls to endorse, they’re also signaling to the public that they accept the kind of racist political rhetoric we saw germinate over the past several months. From Trump on down, these midterms contained a measure of anti-Islamic bigotry that was beyond the pale. And while it face-planted electorally, that does not mean it didn’t also change the boundaries of how politicians feel like they get to speak and act toward our Muslim neighbors.
This has even infected our national pastime. After the election, Toronto Blue Jays player Anthony Santander posted anti-Muslim screeds on social media, including graphic memes—since taken down—that included the phrase, “America voted for Sharia Last Night!” overlaid on an image of Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and “Islam is not peaceful.” In response, the Blue Jays issued a milquetoast statement that read, “Baseball is for everyone and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization’s values and beliefs.”
This is not nearly good enough. Shireen Ahmed, senior contributor to CBC sports and cohost of the Burn It All Down podcast, pointed out that the Blue Jays have a track record of diversity celebrations and a significant Muslim fanbase, which makes the response all the more disappointing. “The Blue Jays play in one of the most multicultural cities in the world,” she wrote. “According to a 2024 report from Statistics Canada, up to 57 per cent of Toronto’s population is racialized. The Blue Jays as an organization celebrate this diversity with cultural events and heritage themes throughout the season including Pride Night and Caribbean Carnival night.”
It’s true that the sports world may be one of the last to actually show some backbone and reflect the popular will: The conservative billionaire team owners and the news networks they watch (or own) love to mewl about the mythical—coded as white male—right-wing sports fan, whom they fear alienating above all. And it’s also true that the politics of the owner’s box, which is overwhelmingly reactionary, will always matter more than the political ideas of fans or players. Even so, it’s time for these institutions, which have cowered in the face of Trump’s poisonous white supremacy, to show where they stand in the wake of last week’s overwhelming repudiation.
There was a beautiful—and tragic—moment at the end of a recent game between the San Antonio Spurs and Dallas Mavericks. Spurs star Victor Wembenyama was caught on video whispering into Dallas Mavericks guard Kyrie Irving’s ear, “Free Palestine, my brother. I’m proud of you.” Irving, long a supporter of a free Palestine, has been wearing keffiyehs, Palestinian colors, and political shirts and bracelets to represent his solidarity since Israel launched a total war on the people of Gaza in 2023. That a star of Wembenyama’s stature feels he has to furtively whisper such a sentiment speaks volumes. It speaks to a sports world in 2026 where players are policed by right-wing blowhards on behalf of team owners, where outspoken athletes feel like they must hide in shadows, even when opposing a genocide.
Anti-Arab and anti-Islamic racism just got muzzled at the polls, but the dangerous rhetoric that produced such a backlash is now off the leash. It will be a collective task to make racists afraid again to speak their bile and sports owners to see that it doesn’t pay to be the great underwriters of the white revanchism that has scarred the political landscape for too long.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Brasil pressiona pelo fim dos combustíveis fósseis com entrega de Mapa do Caminho na COP31, na Turquia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A ideia de um Mapa do Caminho para o Fim dos Combustíveis Fósseis surgiu no ano passado, durante a 30ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP30), em Belém do Pará, e foi oficializada pelo Brasil nesta terça-feira (10), no início da COP31, em Antália, na Turquia, em uma cerimônia concorrida.
O documento, anunciado há algumas semanas pela Presidência da COP30, traz uma série de procedimentos, classificações e cronogramas para os países planejarem sua transição energética. Boa parte do conteúdo foi discutida por cerca de 60 países em Santa Marta, na Colômbia, no início do ano, em um evento preparatório.
A proposta, no entanto, não é mandatória e precisa da adesão de todos os países. O tema ficou de fora do texto final da COP30 por causa da resistência de países grandes produtores de petróleo, como a Arábia Saudita, à sua inclusão. Mesmo com a resistência, as autoridades esperam manter a discussão, mesmo que fora da agenda oficial. Entre as medidas, está, por exemplo, uma diminuição gradual dos subsídios aos combustíveis fósseis, que, em 2025, representavam mais que o dobro dos incentivos às energias renováveis no Brasil.
O secretário-geral da ONU, António Guterres, solicitou que cada nação elabore seu próprio plano nacional de abandono a estes hidrocarbonetos. “Os países importadores devem reduzir sua exposição, ampliando o acesso a energias limpas. Os países produtores devem diversificar suas economias”, e cada plano nacional “precisa de cronogramas, responsabilidades e financiamento”, enumerou Guterres.
“Precisamos sair da dependência do uso de combustível fóssil, porque é isso que está aquecendo a temperatura da Terra. Qual é o caminho que se pode fazer isso? Planejar de forma justa para que todos possam fazer suas transições”, disse a deputada federal e ex-ministra do Meio Ambiente e Mudança Climática, Marina Silva.
Além do fim dos combustíveis fósseis, o Brasil apresentou também o Mapa do Caminho para o Desmatamento Zero. O secretário-executivo da Convenção do Clima (UNFCCC), Simon Stiell, lembrou que a elaboração do documento contou com mais de 180 contribuições de países e organizações. “Precisamos avançar mais e mais rápido. Nesta era de implementação, isso significa transformar os compromissos existentes em resultados na economia real e na vida das pessoas”, afirmou.
O diretor de Mudança do Clima do Programa das Nações Unidas para o Meio Ambiente (Pnuma), Martin Krauss, lembrou a importância do financiamento: “Para cada dólar gasto em florestas, quase cinco dólares são destinados a subsídios agrícolas que podem prejudicá-las. Não estamos apenas financiando pouco as florestas: estamos pagando para perdê-las.”
O ministro dos Povos Indígenas do Brasil, Eloy Terena, defendeu que o financiamento climático chegue diretamente aos territórios indígenas, que desempenham um papel fundamental na proteção das florestas.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/co.title: Contemporary Stained-Glass Windows Installed in Notre-Dame, Spanish Man Awarded $1.12 M. for Renaissance Door Discovery, and More: Morning Links for November 10, 2026
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/co.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/co.text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.
Good Morning!
- New stained-glass windows by French artist Claire Tabouret have been quietly installed in the Notre-Dame de Paris cathedral and will be unveiled to the public on December 7.
- Canada has just proposed a federal budget that exempts artists from paying taxes on C$45,000 ($38,000) of their earnings.
- The 1963 handwritten final draft of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr’s historic “I Have a Dream” speech is being offered for sale at Christie’s New York.
The Headlines
WINDOW OF OPPORTUNITY. New stained-glass windows by French artist Claire Tabouret have been quietly installed in the Notre-Dame de Paris cathedral and will be unveiled to the public on December 7, reports Le Figaro. The project, backed by French President Emmanuel Macron, has faced controversy, but has moved forward against all odds, overcoming one legal challenge while still facing another. The six new windows feature a color-rich, figurative telling of the story of the Pentecost and have been placed along the nave’s southern aisle. The windows were made with the Simon-Marq workshop in Reims and for now, they are reportedly hidden behind red curtains. Meanwhile, heritage groups have opposed the project because it requires the removal of existing 19th-century stained-glass windows designed by Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc, who intended them as part of a cohesive homage to Gothic architecture.
BRINGING HOME THE CANADIAN BACON. Things are looking up for Canadian artists who are still grappling with US tariffs. The country has just proposed a federal budget that exempts artists from paying taxes on C$45,000 ($38,000) of their earnings, reports The Art Newspaper. “In Budget 2026, we’re backing the Canadian artists who tell our stories,” wrote Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in a November 5 social media post. “That means if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to C$45,000 of income derived from your creative work,” he added. And that’s not all; the proposed budget also pledges C$783.1 million ($554 million) over five years to the National Arts Centre, Library and Archives Canada, the National Battlefields Commission and national museums. Visitors under 25 will also get free entry to national museums, thanks to C$46.3 million ($32.8 million) in subsidies for the same five years, followed by C$11.5 million ($8.1 million) per year. Not to be forgotten, the Canada Council for the Arts will get C$20 million ($14.1 million) over three years. However, some tell TAN the funding is still short of what is needed. “As a sector, we still have a lot of questions, while many artists need relief now,” said Jenna Faye Powell, interim national executive director of Carfac (Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le Front des Artistes Canadiens).
The Digest
The 4 a.m., August 28, 1963, handwritten final draft of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr’s historic “I Have a Dream” speech is being offered for sale at Christie’s New York to benefit charity on January 22, 2027. [ArtDependence]
In an open letter appealing to the Nuremberg City Council, a contemporary arts association has warned of the possible closure of the 1967-founded Kunsthalle Nürnberg amid a strained public budget. [Monopol Magazine]
Artist Olafur Eliasson is partnering with ARoS Aarhus Art Museum in Denmark to create a publicly accessible study space and library containing research materials about Eliasson’s practice, opening alongside a major solo exhibition dedicated to him, plus newly installed artwork and more. [Ocula]
Artist Ryan Gander dishes on the YBA’s “egocentric, attention-seeking, shallow kind of art.” Plus, the act of drawing and painting being “futile and dumb,” despite including several of his own new paintings in his latest show, “Maybe: Ryan Gander” at Towner gallery in Eastbourne. [The Guardian]
The Kicker
WHEN ONE DOOR CLOSES … A decade after, Juan Francisco León Catena, a resident of Úbeda in southern Spain, chanced upon a magnificent Renaissance doorway hidden behind the walls of his property under renovation—he will be awarded a €1 million prize ($1.12 million) for his trouble, reports El País. Following a long legal battle, León Catena is poised to receive the award, granted by the Spanish Historical Heritage Law for chance, significant artistic finds. In this case, that find is a 15th-century portal from a former hospital church designed by Spanish Renaissance architect Andrés de Vandelvira. Discovered in excellent condition, experts deemed it of “great aesthetic value” and a unique Renaissance artwork. However, the local Andalusian Regional Government initially refused to pay up in a case that made its way to the High Court of Justice of Andalusia, which ultimately rejected their arguments. Now, León Catena is in talks with the city of Úbeda on how to best promote the heritage site, and there is the additional question of surrounding, city-owned buildings that also house the relic but are in dire need of restoration and risk collapse.

https://taz.de/Geplatzter-Diesel-Deal/!6.title: Geplatzter Diesel-Deal: Trump erleidet Schiffbruch
https://taz.de/Geplatzter-Diesel-Deal/!6.author: Mathias Brüggmann
https://taz.de/Geplatzter-Diesel-Deal/!6.text:
Geplatzter Diesel-Deal: Trump erleidet Schiffbruch
Während in Abu Dhabi über ein Ende des Krieges in der Ukraine verhandelt wird, ist Donald Trumps großes Energiegeschäft mit Moskau gescheitert.
Erstmals seit mehr als neun Monaten sitzen Unterhändler der USA, der Ukraine und Russlands wieder am selben Tisch – vermittelt von Donald Trumps Schwiegersohn Jared Kushner und dem Sondergesandten Steve Witkoff. Der US-Präsident hatte im Vorfeld ein „großes, schönes Abkommen“, das „ganz Europa“ betreffen könnte, versprochen. Doch sein vorheriger „Deal“ war wieder einmal gescheitert.
Vier Tanker voll Diesel hatte Russland vom Hafen Primorsk bei Sankt Petersburg vom 20. Oktober an durch die Ostsee in Richtung US-Ostküste geschickt. Doch inzwischen funkt die für einen griechischen Reeder unter der Flagge Maltas fahrende „Agoi Fanendes“ über seinen Transponder statt „Ziel: New York“ nun „For Orders“, also frei zum Verkauf.
Die anderen drei Tanker, alle unter westlichen Sanktionen stehend, drehten auch ab: Die russische „Talisman“ dümpelt mit 324.000 Barrel Russen-Diesel im Bauch sogar vor Algerien. Die „Leruo“ unter der Flagge Sierra Leones mit Eigner in Hongkong ist seit dem 2. November – einen Tag vor den Midterms-Wahlen in den USA – gen Brasilien unterwegs.
Russland leugnet diese Fakten: Putins Sonderbeauftragter Kirill Dmitrijew nannte die Berichte über umgeleitete Tanker auf „X“ schlicht: „Fake. Die Tanker in Richtung USA sind weiter auf Kurs.“ Putins Sprecher Dmitrij Peskow erklärte, Details der Lieferungen seien „Geschäftsgeheimnisse“, aber „der gesamte Diesel wird seine Käufer finden“. Der Kreml bestritt auch jeden Zusammenhang mit den US-Wahlen.
Warnung vom US-Senat
Trump hatte am 9. Oktober mit Kremlchef Wladimir Putin telefonisch einen Diesel-Deal vereinbart: Russland liefert bis Jahresende rund zwei Millionen Tonnen in die USA und dafür hebt Washington bis April 2027 die Energiesanktionen gegen Moskau auf. Russland kann damit ohne Probleme Öl und Treibstoff nach China, Indien, in die Türkei und anderswohin verkaufen.
„Niedrigere Preise für Amerikaner, vor allem unsere Farmer, Rancher und Trucker, sind meine größte Priorität“, schrieb Trump auf seiner Plattform Truth Social. Der vor den Zwischenwahlen arrangierte Deal sollte die infolge von Trumps Irankrieg stark gestiegenen Dieselpreise senken. Dass er nun nicht zum Tragen kommt, liegt an der Isolation des US-Präsidenten: Schon vor den Midterms liefen US-Senatoren beider Parteien Sturm gegen Trumps Dieselplan.
Zwölf Senatoren von US-Demokraten und US-Republikanern nannten den Deal einen „Verrat“ und forderten in einem Brief an Trump seine Rücknahme. Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj sprach von einem „Geschenk an Putin“, der mit dem Geld den Krieg finanziere.
Trump beschimpfte Selenskyj daraufhin wüst: „Die Ukraine braucht einen neuen Anführer“. Er verlangte indes, dass die ukrainische Armee ihre Angriffe auf russische Raffinerien einstelle, da damit die weltweite Öl- und Treibstoffversorgung gestört werde. Die EU stufte die vereinbarten Diesel-Mengen als makroökonomisch bedeutungslos ein.
AfD will auch
New Jerseys Gouverneurin Mikie Sherrill (Demokraten) warnte zwölf Hafen- und Terminalbetreiber am 2. November, jeden Tanker mit russischem Diesel abzuweisen. Sonst würden Millionenstrafen verhängt. Käufer für den Russen-Diesel hatten sich in den USA schon zuvor nicht gefunden, da demokratische Abgeordnete gewarnt hatten, Abnehmer würden mit Sanktionen belegt.
In Russland kam die Spritversorgung zwischenzeitlich wieder ins Lot. Nun haben russische Tankstellenbetreiber seit der Wiederaufnahme der ukrainischen Drohnenangriffe auf Raffinerien am Wochenende wieder Abgabebeschränkungen für Diesel und Benzin verhängt. Die ukrainische Armee hat durch Drohnenangriffe rund ein Drittel der Raffineriekapazitäten in Russland zerstört.
Inzwischen will die AfD-Fraktion im Bundestag eine ähnliche Lieferoption: Der Antrag „Diesel-Abkommen für Deutschland – Energiesicherheit nach US-Vorbild in Kooperation mit Russland gewährleisten“ wurde am Donnerstag in erster Lesung ins Parlament eingebracht.

Les mouvements de grève s’intensifient dans le cœur industriel de l’Allemagne face au blocage du patronat qui voudrait imposer des baisses du salaire réel dans les négociations collectives, dans le droit fil des réformes antisociales programmées par le gouvernement du chancelier Merz
Entamés le 1er novembre, les mouvements de grève dans la métallurgie et l’électro-industrie continuent de s’étendre en Allemagne. Toutes les grandes entreprises de ce qui constitue le cœur industriel du pays, de Mercedes Benz à Audi en passant par Airbus, Thyssen Krupp ou Bosch, ont tour à tour cessé le travail. Près de 430 000 salariés sur plus de 2000 sites sont entrés dans le mouvement, selon le syndicat IG Metall. Le conflit porte sur les négociations tarifaires (l’équivalent des conventions collectives françaises) des quelque 3,7 millions de salariés du secteur.

‘All I can do is hug my children and cry’: Palestinians in Gaza face deadly winter floods
On MEE Live, Palestinian journalist Nada Nabil spoke to MEE journalist James Schneider about how heavy rains and flooding are worsening conditions for displaced families in Gaza, where many are living in tents and damaged homes.
Nabil said people who would normally welcome the rain are now afraid of it. She recounted how one mother told her that all she could do was hug her children, cry and promise them better days when the sun returned.
The flooding comes as Palestinians in Gaza continue to face the consequences of Israel’s restrictions on humanitarian aid entering Gaza.
Despite the ceasefire, Israel continues to obstruct the entry of essential supplies, including tents, blankets and materials needed to repair damaged infrastructure.
