Billionaire Les Wexner’s name will remain on Ohio State University’s Wexner Center for the Arts, even though the school received hundreds of requests to remove it owing to his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, the Columbus Dispatch reports. More than five hundred requests sought to remove the name from the campus’s arts center, medical center, and football complex in Columbus. The decision to keep it was made by OSU interim provost Trevor Brown, who on November 6 rejected an advisory committee’s recommendation that the school look into the mogul’s relationship with the late pedophile and that it review allegations of sexual misconduct by Wexner and abusive employment practices at his businesses.
Wexner, the founder of clothing brand The Limited, a cofounder of Bath & Body Works, and a former principal of lingerie retailer Victoria’s Secret, is OSU’s biggest donor, having gifted the school more than $200 million to date, according to the New York Times. He was mentioned more than one thousand times in the Epstein files released by the US Department of Justice earlier this year.
Brown, in a letter to the advisory committee, noted that Wexner had not been charged with or convicted of any crime, further stating that the committee had never been meant to serve as an investigative organ. Though he affirmed that the university would revisit the matter if new evidence became available, this was cold comfort to the members of Wex Workers United, the arts center’s union, which had campaigned to have the name removed.
“Workers will bear the brunt of this decision, fielding angry and hostile comments from the public and having the work we do questioned for its association with the Wexner name,” a representative of WWU told Hyperallergic.
The release of the Epstein files has reverberated throughout the worlds of art and education, with School of Visual Arts chair David A. Ross and L’Institut du Monde Arabe president Jack Lang among those who vacated their roles after being named in them.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: Kiev à beira do colapso e Trump pressionado favorecem acordo para fim da guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: O Estrangeiro
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
Desde que os Estados Unidos, junto com Israel, atacaram o Irã, as negociações para colocar fim ao conflito entre Rússia e Ucrânia — que em fevereiro do ano que vem completará cinco anos — ficaram para segundo plano. Agora, uma mesa de negociação trilateral acontece em Abu Dhabi, nos Emirados Árabes, com a participação da Rússia, Ucrânia e dos próprios Estados Unidos.
A reunião à porta fechada durou quase quatro horas desta terça-feira (10), com um breve intervalo. No início das negociações, o chefe da delegação russa, o assessor presidencial Vladimir Medinsky, expressou a esperança de que elas levassem a progressos rumo a uma solução pacífica.
Para o jornalista Serguei Monin, correspondente do Brasil de Fato em Moscou, ainda é preciso que informações dessas conversas venham a público para compreender quais são os interesses colocados na mesa e o que cada país envolvido no diálogo estaria disposto a ceder ou não. Em participação no podcast O Estrangeiro, Monin destaca como uma boa notícia o fato de o tema principal para os três países ser a segurança.
“A gente vê a delegação russa, a delegação ucraniana e os Estados Unidos falando que o formato, a arquitetura de segurança internacional, as garantias de segurança da Rússia e da Ucrânia são prioritárias. Quando a gente fala de segurança, é basicamente quais são as condições de resolução da guerra: quais são as delimitações fronteiriças, porque tem territórios em disputa, e quais são os formatos de acordos que podem ser plausíveis para ambas as partes”, explica, salientando que é justamente esse o ponto mais conflitante, já que há muitas divergências.
Os aspectos humanitários, segundo o jornalista, são de maior facilidade de resolução, tanto que, após a reunião desta terça-feira, a única sinalização concreta veio na direção da troca de prisioneiros. Serguei Monin relata que, apesar da ausência da Europa, delegações da Organização do Tratado do Atlântico Norte (Otan) compareceram em grande número, e isso está sendo avaliado “como um sinal de seriedade das negociações”.
O analista geopolítico Marco Fernandes analisa que atualmente há condições mais favoráveis do que nas outras dezenas de tentativas de um acordo de paz. Ele explica que a Ucrânia vive uma situação de extrema fragilidade neste momento. “A indústria siderúrgica da Ucrânia acabou, não existe mais. Na prática, a eletricidade está muito afetada. Ontem mesmo [segunda-feira (9)], havia entre 400 mil e 500 mil pessoas em Kiev sem luz. A Rússia vem atacando também outras usinas de eletricidade no país. Então, de fato, a Ucrânia acho que está à beira do colapso e, por isso, aceitou uma negociação”, pontua.
Fernandes considera que há um terceiro elemento nessa história, que é a pressão dos EUA por uma resolução no conflito após a derrota de Trump nas midterms. “O Trump precisa entregar alguma coisa. Até agora, ele só entregou derrota: prometeu acabar com a guerra da Ucrânia em 24 horas, já faz dois anos e nada aconteceu. Ele achou que fosse acabar com o Irã em três dias, como aconteceu com a Venezuela, e isso não aconteceu. Pelo contrário. Eu acho que também isso pode se aplicar ao Irã. Ontem, [segunda-feira], inclusive, teve rumores de que estariam próximos de um acordo. O Trump tem agora dois meses ainda antes que os democratas assumam para tentar entregar pelo menos essas duas vitórias”, avalia.
Para o analista, a Europa, que teve a participação nas reuniões rejeitada pela Rússia, é um dos principais obstáculos para a paz. “A Europa continua a enviar muita ajuda para a Ucrânia. Inclusive, tem uma coisa muito grave que foi anunciada essa semana, que a Europa vai pela primeira vez colocar tropas de treinamento que eram feitas na Europa para a Ucrânia, e que agora vai ser no território ucraniano”, alerta.
Os analistas concordam que, além do impasse territorial, o ponto central é a questão da construção da arquitetura de segurança que contemple os dois países envolvidos. Marco Fernandes observa que a Ucrânia avalia a concessão de parcelas territoriais, mas sinaliza que deverá exigir, como contrapartida, o que está previsto no Artigo 5º da Otan para desencorajar futuras agressões. “É aquele artigo que diz que qualquer país da Otan que seja atacado, os outros, em princípio, teriam que responder, ainda que isso não seja automático”, conta.
Por outro lado, a diplomacia russa exige a contenção do avanço militar ocidental, demandando a ausência de tropas e armamentos da Otan próximos às suas fronteiras, além da consolidação do controle sobre as regiões sob sua burocracia. Diante dessas posições divergentes, questão crucial a ser resolvida é como desenhar um modelo de fronteira e de diálogo institucional, como a eventual reativação de uma mesa permanente entre Otan e Rússia, que atenda às garantias exigidas por Moscou sem violar a soberania regional, assegurando uma convivência organizada que evite o reacendimento do conflito em poucos anos.
“E parece que os Estados Unidos estão bancando essa solução. Porque isso, na verdade, era uma mesa permanente [que aconteceu entre 2002 e 2014, quando houve a anexação da Criméia] em que não é que a Rússia sentava com o chefe da Otan. A Rússia sentava com 20 países da Otan e, nesse sentido, a Rússia era um a mais. E isso seria um canal permanente de diálogo a partir de agora para evitar escalar tensão, para evitar provocações. Então isso poderia ser uma arquitetura”, exemplifica Fernandes.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘Everything and everyone we love is at stake’: Thunberg slams COP31 talks
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
‘Everything and everyone we love is at stake’: Thunberg slams COP31 talks
Climate activist urges world leaders to put people and planet before profit as she arrives at UN climate talks.
Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has condemned the United Nations climate talks as hypocritical and urged world leaders to put people and planet ahead of profits and power.
Thunberg made the comments on Tuesday as she arrived at the COP31 conference in the Turkish resort city of Antalya.
“It’s a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo,” Thunberg said.
“Our political and economic systems that have become incompatible with human nature.”
The talks follow a year of deadly climate-related disasters, including heatwaves and floods, and another energy shock caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.
COP31 co-hosts Turkiye and Australia are promoting renewable energy and rooftop solar installations, but both still rely heavily on fossil fuels, especially coal, to generate electricity. Previous hosts, including Brazil, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan, are major oil producers.
Climate change is “threatening everything”, Thunberg said, warning that “everything and everyone we love is at stake”.
“We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she said.
Thunberg rose to prominence in 2018 as a 15-year-old, when she began a solitary “School Strike for Climate” outside the Swedish parliament.
The Antalya summit is the first she has attended since the 2021 talks in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed world leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah”.
She has also campaigned for other causes, including the Free Palestine movement, and more recently backed French students protesting for more school resources.
Her arrival in Antalya has created excitement among many of the youth climate activists at COP31 who are demanding more climate finance.
“I hope that Greta’s presence here reminds us of why we started this work in the first place: to push for meaningful change, hold decision-makers accountable, and work towards a better future for all of humanity,” Amber Turner, a 26-year-old fellow with the Alliance of Small Island States, told The Associated Press news agency.
Qiyun Woo, a youth environmentalist from Singapore, said Thunberg’s “powerful” presence “adds to calls from a generation that inherits the consequences of these negotiations”.
COP31 runs in Antalya until November 20.
Next year’s edition, COP32, is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.title: Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.author: Matt Sledge, Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.text:
Self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment Tuesday night, as solidarity from House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Though Democrats overwhelmingly joined Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide, the House voted 211 to 204 to refer the charges to a committee, allowing Republicans to slow the process. With 11 Democrats absent, they lacked the numbers. Massie, however, dismissed the impact of Democratic absences to The Intercept. “No, there were enough Republicans to rally to get here,” he said.
The procedural vote spared Republicans a more difficult vote on whether to impeach Hegseth on Massie’s eight charges, including waging wars without Congressional authorization and undercutting measures to prevent civilian casualties. It followed a week of increasingly desperate efforts by the Pentagon chief to shore up Congressional and White House support, including a campaign-style video intended to influence Trump, a social media campaign by underlings, and a rare appearance by Hegseth himself before the Pentagon press corps.
Over half an hour on Tuesday morning, Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight charges. He claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.” That, too, turned out to be false as 203 members of Congress voted with Massie.
On Tuesday, a coalition of more than 40 civil society organizations – including Oxfam America, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Common Defense, Demand Progress, MoveOn, and the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft – sent a letter calling on all House members to vote for every article of impeachment filed against Hegseth.
“Pete Hegseth’s time at the Pentagon has done grievous harm to the nation and to the Constitution,” said Demand Progress Senior Policy Advisor Cavan Kharrazian. “This is a man who ignored the will of Congress to execute an illegal war in Iran, kidnapped a foreign leader for oil, restarted war on Yemen, sent missiles to kill suspected drug traffickers and weaponized the Pentagon against a political enemy.”
The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. In neither case did the Senate vote to convict.
After the vote, Massie called out the display of inaction from his Republican colleagues.
“They diagnosed why they lost the election,” Massie said of fellow Republicans following the vote on Tuesday night. “But tonight they were paralyzed to do anything about it. And that’s the story of Congress.”
Absent from the vote were Democratic Reps. Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi, of California, Laura Gillen of New York, Steven Horsford of Nevada, Jonathan Jackson of Illinois, Brittany Pettersen of Colorado, Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico, Haley Stevens of Michigan, Marilyn Strickland of Washington, and Frederica Wilson of Florida. The absent Republicans were Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Neal Dunn of Florida, Russell Fry of South Carolina, Julia Letlow of Louisiana, Tom Tiffany and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin, and Rudy Yakym of Indiana.
A senior Congressional staffer predicted that Hegseth would face a very rough road if he survived impeachment. “Oversight is going to come crashing down on his head,” that staffer said. “Will Hegseth continue to obstruct? Yes. But wait until the subpoenas start.”
Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, who will head the House Armed Services Committee in the next Congress, said Hegseth and Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg would be first on the list to testify.
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment, told The Intercept there were “many ways” for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session, specifically compelling him to testify before the American people. “I would be surprised to see him last the next two years in this administration,” she told The Intercept. “I think that he is not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration, but also the most unpopular — and it’s on a bipartisan basis. So the pressure will continue to grow for there to be some change at the Pentagon.”
Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., told The Intercept that the incoming Democrats have Hegseth in their sights. “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached. I want him prosecuted, They murdered people in the Caribbean. And we killed 163 little girls in Iran,” he said. “Everybody in my class is ready for him to go. We tried it, It didn’t work. Well do it again.”
In a Truth Social post, President Donald Trump celebrated the outcome while expressing confusion over the vote. Trump called it the “Democrats’ attempt to impeach” Hegseth, despite the fact the effort was introduced by Massie, a Republican, who he called “a major LOSER.” He claimed it was an “EXONERATION” of Hegseth and added: “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: House Republicans block effort to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
House Republicans on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, rejecting allegations that the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of the Iran war and other conflicts globally.
The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.
Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman who lost his primary after breaking with the president, had proposed impeaching Hegseth in September, alleging an array of illegal acts, including killing civilians in Iran, launching unauthorized operations in Venezuela and Yemen, and retaliating against a Democratic senator.
Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Their motion succeeded on Tuesday, by a 211-204 vote, largely along party lines. Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the motion, along with all Democrats.
Trump, who was twice impeached, celebrated what he hailed as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot’ and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote.
“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump said on Truth Social. “They must be stopped!”
The Pentagon, meanwhile, declared “total victory”.
“The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House judiciary committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” Sean Parnell, a department spokesperson, wrote in a social media post.
Tuesday’s vote is unlikely to be the final word on efforts to remove Hegseth from office, after Democrats won decisive majorities in the November midterm elections. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take control of the chamber in January, has backed the push to impeach Hegseth, accusing the embattled secretary of having “undermined America’s national security”.
The resolution’s downfall took place hours after Hegseth held a defiant press conference at the Pentagon, where he dismissed the impeachment effort as a “political spectacle” orchestrated by the ousted Kentucky congressman.
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.
The conflict with Iran has proven divisive with Republicans, and ahead of the midterms, small but growing numbers voted with Democrats on war powers resolutions intended to force Trump to bring the hostilities to a close. Warren Davidson, one of the House Republicans who voted for such resolutions, said he nonetheless rejected the idea of impeaching Hegseth.
“It’s an effort to blame-shift on to Hegseth Congress’s failure and President Trump’s decision,” Davidson said in an interview.
“I think Hegseth has been incredibly effective at restoring morale for the active-duty force, restoring the warrior ethos, the proper focus to the military that they exist to fight and win wars.”
The defense secretary, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer, has been one of the most pugnacious members of Trump’s second term cabinet, and taken an unusually heavy handed approach to managing the US military. Hegseth has orchestrated the departure of top generals, blocked the promotions of scores of officers, many of them women and people of color, and implemented new rules that prompted much of the press corps to leave the Pentagon.
He has also become the public face of some of the administration’s most politically costly policies, particularly the Iran war, which has dragged on for months while putting upward pressure on petroleum prices and played into Democrats’s hands in last week’s midterms.
Massie’s resolution outlined eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, including attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and spurning a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict.
It also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary.
The final two impeachment articles target Hegseth’s involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House.
Had the impeachment resolution passed, it would have had to be approved by the Senate, which Republicans control by a 53-seat margin. It is unclear if it would have had enough votes to pass, or if the Republican leader John Thune would have even put it up for consideration.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/bi.title: Museum Organizations Call Bipartisan Infrastruture Bill a ‘Sweeping Assault’ on Historic and Sacred Places
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/bi.author: Brian Boucher
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/bi.text:
Some historic preservationists are alarmed at the potential effects of a bipartisan bill whose sponsors say it aims to cut red tape for infrastructure and energy production projects.
On Monday, the US Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (S.5653), introduced by Senator Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican, by a vote of 73–25. The bill is cosponsored by Senators Mike Lee, a Utah Republican; Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat; and Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat. (The current session of the Republican-controlled Senate runs through December 18; new senators will be sworn in on January 3.)
Crucially, the act would narrow the scope of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), in part by limiting which types of projects trigger review.
Speaking on the Senate floor Monday, Capito said that “for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.” Data from the National Association of Manufacturers, she said, “shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.”
According to the Art Newspaper, about 800 protesters gathered on the West Lawn of the US Capitol, among them leaders from the Association of African American Museums, the DC Preservation League, the American Institute of Architects, and the Archaeological Institute of America. Representative Melanie Stansbury, a New Mexico Democrat, called the act a “dirty deal.” Critics cited by the paper noted that the senators introduced the 500-page bill just 48 hours before the Senate vote was scheduled.
S.5653 targets Section 106 of the NHPA, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of federally funded building projects and requires those receiving federal funds or permits to consult with tribal nations. According to the Art Newspaper, the new bill would make consultation with tribal nations optional and remove the requirement that federal agencies notify and consult with the public and tribal nations about potential harm to historic sites. It would also narrow the definition of what constitutes a historic site.
On November 6, the 106 Strong Coalition, which includes more than 1,200 organizations, tribal nations, and advocates, sent a letter to Congress calling for the defeat of S.5653. Signatories include the American Alliance of Museums, numerous state museum associations, and many individual museums. The letter calls the bill “a sweeping assault on the protections Congress enacted sixty years ago to ensure that federal agencies consider the consequences of their decisions for America’s historic and sacred places.”

https://hyperallergic.com/brokies-this-m.title: Brokies, This Met Gala Is for You
https://hyperallergic.com/brokies-this-m.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/brokies-this-m.text:
Brokies, This Met Gala Is for You
T-shirts revolutionize the Costume Institute’s programming, the sociability of MoMA’s Brancusi exhibit, and the curators of the 2028 Whitney Biennial announced.
A saturated blue sky and cascades of complementary golden-yellow foliage laid the foundation for a vibrant, picturesque Diwali weekend in the suburbs. It wasn’t the most festive Diwali for me — instead of lighting diyas and playing with sparklers, I spent a majority of the weekend hand-feeding a friendly yard squirrel while wearing some bullshit pajamas extracted from the depths of my childhood closet.
Think I’m slumming it? Well, think again! Because those dilapidated pajamas are almost certainly what inspired the theme for next year’s Met Gala and related Costume Institute exhibit: extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday, a program “devoted to the undersung beauty and allure of quotidian garments.” (That’s code for jeans.)
(And t-shirts. And raincoats. Maybe pajamas, but also maybe not.)
It’s an exasperated, last-minute pivot after controversial British fashion designer John Galliano, who was central to the Costume Institute’s original program for 2027, withdrew from participating entirely this August in response to the public backlash toward his racist behavior in the past. Between “elevating” daily wear into runway fashion and exploring how “humble, even ‘disposable’ materials” like paper and aluminum can become wearable, this enormous exercise in putting a positive spin on gentrifying economic recession is at odds with NYC residents who are buckling from profound unaffordability as the city speedruns its transformation into a private equity playground.
I guess I can’t really say which is worse — the current standard of celebrities in bespoke, extravagant garments from elite fashion houses hanging off their GLP-1 frames, or the notion that a Met Gala dress code calling for aluminum foil pants, a shrunken tee, and maybe a jacket made from hole-punched plastic circles is what’ll push people to consider everyday wear in a different light.
However, before we get too pressed, we have to acknowledge that this is a big moment for the Bad Bunny x Zara collection! On the plus side, it might make it easier for some ~lowly civs~ to sneak in and eat all the cheese cubes. Dress for the job you want, right?
Speaking of jobs — Whitney Museum curator Meg Onli returns as a co-curator for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, sharing the stage with director and dancer Zack Winokur, who co-founded the interdisciplinary American Modern Opera Company in 2017. I found the 2026 Biennial to be a textbook case of the whole being less than the sum of its parts. Let’s see how Winokur’s hand in artistic performance direction manifests in this curatorial behemoth; I’m sure he’s used to working with a lot of moving parts.
Back to the here and now, I’m long overdue for multiple museum visits at the peak of the season. The days keep slipping through my fingers before I’ve had a chance to visit the Krasner Pollock show at The Met or the Architects of Liberation at the MoMA. Mayor Mamdani actually paid a visit to the MoMA show before I did, and he’s significantly busier than I am, so there’s really no excuse!
In another nudge for me to make the journey uptown, MoMA recently opened its Brancusi exhibition. With a replica of Brancusi’s studio and a selection of rare media documenting his work environment and the social atmosphere he cultivated between his sculptures and his guests alike, the exhibition spotlights the artist’s labor-intensive process as an art form in itself.
Critic Aruna D’Souza noted that the “sculptures seem to be maintaining COVID-era social distancing protocols,” and chalked that awkward dynamic up to the MoMA’s renovated gallery layout, recalling the previously approachable setup’s capacity to “allow for art objects to talk to each other.”
On Sunday, I bore witness to a conversation that made me think about Brancusi’s glinting buffed bronzes and smooth marbles. The chatter between a yellowing tree branch, an overturned recycling bin, and the white picket fence behind them might have been too maximalist compared to the Romanian sculptor’s sleek, pared-down modernism. Nevertheless, I pulled over to eavesdrop.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Peruvian senator calls for removal of large-scale replicas of Moche erotic sculptures from public park
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.
“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.
The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.
Known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.
“It’s a complicated issue,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”
The Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva says. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”
One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.
The Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.
Jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”

https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.title: Nuevo grupo de demócratas latinos busca ampliar su influencia política en los cinco condados de Nueva York
https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.text:
Share This Article
La organización busca aumentar la representación latina en la política local, formar futuros líderes y fortalecer la participación comunitaria en toda la ciudad de Nueva York, según su fundadora, Jamey Battle.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 4 de noviembre. Traducido por Jacob Velez. Read the English version here.
Después de años de participar en clubes demócratas, organizaciones de mujeres y redes profesionales, Jamey Battle dijo que se hacía constantemente la misma pregunta.
“Pensaba: ¿dónde están los demás latinos?”, dijo Battle, quien antes trabajó en la Asamblea Estatal de Nueva York y en una compañía haciendo lobby. “¿Cómo puedo incorporarlos a este espacio? ¿Cómo podemos involucrarnos en este movimiento político?”.
En lugar de seguir buscando representación latina dentro de las organizaciones políticas existentes, Battle decidió ayudar a crear un espacio propio, centrado en las voces y experiencias de la comunidad latina.
El mes pasado, Latino Democrats of New York City (LDNYC por sus siglas en inglés) celebró su lanzamiento oficial como organización 501(c)(4). Fundada en octubre de 2025 como un grupo de organización voluntaria, LDNYC cuenta actualmente con casi 200 miembros, según un comunicado de prensa.
La organización busca aumentar la representación latina en la política local, formar futuros líderes y fortalecer la participación comunitaria en los cinco condados de la ciudad de Nueva York.
“Se me ocurrió la idea de Latino Democrats hace aproximadamente un año. Le envié un mensaje de texto a mi vicepresidenta, Evelin Vazquez, y nos comunicamos con personas de nuestra red que compartían dos valores: la integridad y el compromiso de poner a la comunidad en el centro”, dijo Battle, presidenta de la organización.
“Finalmente me di cuenta de algo: ¿por qué estoy dedicando tanto tiempo a intentar que los latinos encajen en un espacio que nunca fue creado para nosotros, que no está dirigido por nosotros ni para nosotros y que tampoco responde a nuestras necesidades?”.
El grupo celebró su reconocimiento como organización sin fines de lucro el 21 de octubre con una recepción inaugural llamada “Primera Noche”, realizada en Lighthouse Rooftop, en Long Island City, Queens.
La velada reunió a funcionarios electos, líderes comunitarios, organizadores y simpatizantes en una celebración que incluyó discursos, entregas de reconocimientos y conversaciones sobre la participación política latina.
Entre los asistentes estuvieron Claire Valdez, quien asumirá su cargo en el Congreso en enero para representar al Distrito 7 de Brooklyn y Queens; Brian Romero, recientemente elegido para representar a Woodside y Jackson Heights en la Asamblea estatal; además de los asambleístas de Queens Catalina Cruz y Steven Raga, entre otros.
Durante la recepción, los oradores compartieron historias personales sobre sus familias, sus trayectorias profesionales y las experiencias que los llevaron a involucrarse en el servicio público.
Uno de los participantes recordó haber crecido con una madre salvadoreña que llegó a los Estados Unidos sin documentos migratorios a los 12 años. También relató las historias familiares que escuchaba sobre explotación laboral, robo de salarios, prácticas policiales y operativos de las autoridades migratorias, experiencias que, según explicó, continúan influyendo en su manera de defender a la comunidad.
En el estado de Nueva York, los latinos representan 2.2 millones de votantes elegibles, lo que los convierte en el grupo racial o étnico más numeroso después de los votantes blancos, según el Pew Research Center.
Para Battle, el lanzamiento de la organización representa una oportunidad para incorporar a más neoyorquinos latinos a los espacios políticos y desarrollar una red más sólida de líderes comunitarios.
El lanzamiento ocurre mientras los demócratas celebran amplias victorias en todo el país en las elecciones de mitad de mandato del martes, incluidos los triunfos de varios candidatos respaldados por Latino Democrats NYC.
“Estoy muy emocionada por los próximos años, por la oportunidad de movilizar y entusiasmar a la comunidad latina de Nueva York y de construir poder político para todas las comunidades latinas de la ciudad”, dijo Battle.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Student Homelessness Declines but Remains Stubbornly High, Report Finds
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Amy Zimmer, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
One in eight New York City public school students experienced homelessness last school year, according to a report released Tuesday by the nonprofit Advocates for Children.
That meant more than 138,000 children lived in temporary housing, whether in shelters or “doubled up” with family or friends. The total dropped 10% from the previous school year — largely driven by a decline in the number of families living in shelters. Still, the figure remained staggeringly high, roughly equivalent to the population of Albany, and marked the 11th straight year the number topped 100,000, the report said.
Of those students, 37% lived in shelters, while 58% shared housing with other families because of economic hardship, the report said.
Students who are homeless, particularly those living in shelters, tend to fare worse academically than their peers in permanent housing. In 2025, about 27% of students living in shelters in grades 3-8 were proficient in reading, less than half the rate of students in permanent housing, according to state test results. About 59% graduated on time, compared with the citywide rate of 81%, and 14% dropped out of school, about triple the dropout rate of their peers.
A major factor contributing to these poor outcomes is that simply getting to school can be a challenge.
Nearly half of students in temporary housing and 63% of those living in shelters were chronically absent, meaning they missed at least 10% of the 2024-25 school year. That compares to about a third of students citywide. And 1 in 5 students in shelters transferred schools at least once during the year, more than four times the rate for their peers.
Jennifer Pringle, director of Advocates for Children’s Learners in Temporary Housing Project, said the city must do more to address these challenges, warning that people without a high school diploma are 4.5 times more likely to experience homelessness as young adults.
“Unfortunately, for too many families, being in shelter derails their education,” Pringle said. “I know this is the long game, but if we really want to address family homelessness, we have to focus on education now.”
Far-Flung Shelter Placements Keep Children Out of School, Advocates Say
While the Department of Homeless Services tries to place families in the borough where the youngest child attends school, that’s not always the case. About 37% of families in shelters are placed in a different borough from where their children attend school, Pringle said.
Because of that, many children in shelters rely on school buses, but Pringle said it typically takes more than a month to get assigned to a route. Even then, families can face delays and buses that fail to show up.
“The city has a lot of control over these systems,” Pringle said. “New York City Public Schools does not control where the Department of Homeless Services places families in shelters. But the Department of Homeless Services’ practices about shelter placements makes a tremendous difference to whether or not a child can be stably educated.”
Once a family is placed in a shelter, there is no mechanism to revisit that placement, Pringle said. She suggested that shelter case managers check in with families a week after they arrive to see whether they want to transfer closer to their children’s school.
Families remain in shelters for an average of 14 months, she added. For parents spending several hours a day getting their children to and from school, that leaves less time to work or look for permanent housing.
“It may be unrealistic to expect that the city can place all families close to kids’ schools. But let’s at least design a process that you know takes this into consideration and makes it a greater priority,” she said.
The city has been working to improve attendance strategies and has expanded Every Child and Family is Known, a program that pairs homeless students and their families with designated school staffers who build relationships and connect them with support and resources.
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said the Education Department has worked with other city agencies in recent years to improve policies for families, including eliminating a requirement that children attend all housing meetings and expanding community schools offering wraparound services such as eye care and housing support in districts with high concentrations of shelters.
“Supporting these students is both a priority and shared responsibility,” Samuels said in a statement. “As this report shows, this work is far from over, and we’ll continue to work in partnership to bolster resources, address ongoing challenges and ensure that our most vulnerable students have the support they need to receive a rigorous, high-quality education.”
Department of Homeless Services Commissioner Erin Dalton also pointed to declines in chronic absenteeism among students living in shelters and said the agency was expanding outreach to children who frequently miss school and working to help families transition to more stable housing.
Bronx Leads NYC in Student Homelessness Rates
The Bronx continued to have the highest rate of student homelessness, with nearly 1 in 6 students experiencing homelessness in the 2025-26 school year.
Manhattan had the next-highest rate, at 1 in 7 students, but saw the biggest year-over-year drop, at 18%, largely because fewer students enrolled in the borough’s schools were living in shelters. Staten Island had the lowest rate, with about 1 in 20 students experiencing homelessness.
At the school district level, the highest rates were in the South Bronx’s District 9, Brownsville’s District 23 and Bushwick’s District 32. More than 1 in 5 students in those districts experienced homelessness last year.
At the other end of the spectrum, fewer than 5% of students in District 26, which spans Queens neighborhoods including Bayside, Fresh Meadows and Jamaica Estates, experienced homelessness.
Amy Zimmer is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat New York. Contact Amy at azimmer@chalkbeat.org.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bars-and-.title: NYC bars and restaurants say they're struggling and may raise prices
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bars-and-.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bars-and-.text:
New York City bars and restaurants are struggling to keep up financially amid rising operating costs and uneven customer spending, according to a survey by trade association NYC Hospitality Alliance.
Many bars, restaurants and nightlife establishments are considering raising menu prices or reducing staff, if they haven’t already, according to the NYC Hospitality Alliance’s quarterly survey. It found that among the 275 establishments represented in replies to the survey, half said they were breaking even or operating at a loss in the third quarter of this year. About the same amount said their sales were below expectations.
It was a dip in performance after a strong second quarter, in which operators received a boost from World Cup and Knicks game watchers, said Andrew Rigie, executive director of the New York City Hospitality Alliance. The group represents more than 3,000 restaurants in the city.
“These big events gave a lot of small businesses a big boost, he said. “Unfortunately, it seems that it was short-lived.”
According to the survey, 61% of restaurant operators said they had or were considering raising menu prices, and 57% reported reducing or considering reducing employee hours or staffing levels. Almost half of operators surveyed, or 45%, identified labor costs as a leading business concern. Other major issues cited were inflation and tariffs, liability insurance and commercial rents, according to the survey.
Rigie said the numbers speak to how widespread challenges like labor costs and rising cost of goods are in the industry, and a need for policymakers to step in to address them. He said one area of concern should be the city’s affordability crisis, which beyond affecting individual New Yorkers, also affects restaurant sales when people spend less money.
“The cost to purchase goods continues to go up, has stayed high, and there's really only so much that restaurants can pass the cost on to their customers in the form of increased menu prices,” Rigie said. “When you start to increase menu prices, you can deter customers from coming to the restaurant and spending money. Often, they will order differently. They'll order less. So even some restaurants that have experienced increased overall sales, they've reported decreased profitability. So it's a complex issue that's going on.”

https://taz.de/Verhandlungen-in-Abu-Dhab.title: Verhandlungen in Abu Dhabi: Europa am Katzentisch
https://taz.de/Verhandlungen-in-Abu-Dhab.author: Tanja Tricarico
https://taz.de/Verhandlungen-in-Abu-Dhab.text:
Verhandlungen in Abu Dhabi: Europa am Katzentisch
Über ein Kriegsende in der Ukraine und die Sicherheitsordnung in Europa verhandeln seit Dienstag die USA, Russland und die Ukraine. Ergebnisse erwartet niemand.
Nach monatelangem Stillstand kommen die Verhandlungen um einen möglichen Waffenstillstand im Ukrainekrieg wieder in Gang. Auf Initiative der US-Regierung unter Donald Trump sprechen derzeit Delegationen der Ukraine und aus Russland in Abu Dhabi. Die Hoffnung: ein Waffenstillstand in der Ukraine, möglichst bald, noch bevor der Winter eintritt.
Teil der Verhandlungen sind wie auch immer geartete Sicherheitsgarantien, die vor allem die Europäer gewährleisten sollen. „Die Anspannung ist groß“, sagte Jared Kushner, Trump-Schwiegersohn und einer der Verhandlungsführer für die USA. Ähnlich äußerte sich der US-Sondergesandte Steve Witkoff.
Die USA verfolgen bei den Verhandlungen nicht so sehr humanitäre Interessen, sondern wollen verstärkt in wirtschaftliche Beziehungen mit Russland einsteigen. Die Strategie des Kreml, zivile Infrastruktur in der Ukraine anzugreifen und somit der Bevölkerung kurz vor Winterbeginn das Leben schwer zu machen, geht derzeit auf. Während gesprochen wird, halten die Angriffe der russischen Armee auf die Ukraine unvermindert an.
Immerhin melden ukrainische Medien eine Einigung „auf einen großen Austausch von Kriegsgefangenen in naher Zukunft“ zu einigen“ und berufen sich damit auf Quellen in der ukrainischen Verhandlungsgruppe.
Zugleich muss die Ukraine um weitere militärische wie finanzielle Hilfen aus Europa ringen. Seit Montag hält die sogenannte Koalition der Willigen unter Führung Großbritanniens ein Manöver in Polen ab. Rund zwei Wochen soll das Ganze dauern. Es geht um die Vorbereitungen für den Fall, wenn es zu einem Waffenstillstand kommen sollte und wie dieser dann abgesichert werden könnte. Die Armeen aus 11 Ländern der Koalition üben also schon mal.
Meloni ist sauer
Am Verhandlungstisch in Abu Dhabi sitzen derweil nur Russland, die Ukraine und die USA – die Europäer müssen zuschauen. Eine Gruppe bestehend aus der EU, der Nato, Italien, Großbritannien, Frankreich, Deutschland, der Ukraine und den USA veröffentlichten im Vorfeld ein gemeinsames Statement. Darin machten sie klar, dass auf einer bestehenden Sicherheitsarchitektur aufgebaut werden müsse. Ohne die Europäer könne eine dauerhafte Stabilität nicht gewährleistet werden.
Sie wollen also mitsprechen. Aber wie genau das funktionieren kann ist bisher unklar. In dieser Woche wird die Europäische Politische Gemeinschaft in Dublin zusammenkommen, am Tag danach soll es einen informellen EU-Gipfel ebenfalls in Dublin geben. Die italienische Ministerpräsidentin Giorgia Meloni hatte in der vergangenen Woche einen Wutbrief an EU-Ratspräsident António Costa geschickt – und darin „dringend“ um Klarheit gebeten.
Melonis Initiative ist sicher auch innenpolitisch motiviert, adressiert aber tatsächlich eine Lücke, die die EU-Mitgliedstaaten nach mehr als viereinhalb Jahren Krieg noch nicht geschlossen haben.
Irland hat derzeit die EU-Ratspräsidentschaft inne und lädt daher in die irische Hauptstadt ein. Spätestens zum EU-Gipfel kurz vor Weihnachten in Brüssel wollen die 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten zu einer gemeinsamen Haltung kommen und vor allem entscheiden, wer eigentlich für die EU beim Thema Ukrainekrieg sprechen soll.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-isra.title: « Ils avaient l’intention de lancer des pierres » : un adolescent de 14 ans assassiné par l’armée israélienne en Cisjordanie pour un soupçon
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-isra.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/armee-isra.text:
Un jeune Palestinien de 14 ans a été tué lundi 9 novembre par l’armée israélienne à côté de Naplouse. Ce nouveau crime traduit une nouvelle fois une politique de nettoyage ethnique de la part des autorités israéliennes et des colons. Ces derniers ont également agressé une vingtaine de militants pacifistes.
En Cisjordanie, l’armée israélienne a encore tué. Un adolescent de 14 ans a été assassiné ce lundi 9 novembre au cours de la soirée à Burqa. Les militaires ont affirmé avoir riposté à des jets de pierres. « Selon des informations locales, les forces israéliennes ont mené un raid à Burqa et ouvert le feu sur des habitants », constate le quotidien Haaretz.
De son côté, le Croissant-Rouge palestinien a indiqué avoir pris en charge deux blessés par balle et les avoir évacués vers l’hôpital, précisant que les forces israéliennes avaient empêché ses équipes d’accéder à un troisième blessé et arrêté trois secouristes bénévoles. Il s’agirait d’un adolescent de 17 ans qui a été blessé à l’abdomen et un jeune homme de 19 ans qui a reçu des soins au niveau de la main.
Les colons continuent leurs attaques
Interrogée par l’AFP, l’armée a affirmé ce mardi 10 novembre que « les soldats ont identifié plusieurs terroristes qui avaient l’intention de lancer des pierres sur une route empruntée par des véhicules israéliens ». « Les soldats ont riposté en tirant dans leur direction afin d’éliminer la menace », a-t-elle ajouté. La Commission des affaires civiles de l’Autorité palestinienne a précisé que le corps de Moutaz Eyad Daghlas était détenu par l’armée israélienne.
Ce nouveau drame confirme des violences croissantes de l’armée et des colons sur l’ensemble du territoire occupé. Ces dernières heures, une vingtaine de colons israéliens ont attaqué une quarantaine de militants de l’organisation « Protective Presence », qui aidaient des agriculteurs palestiniens à récolter des olives dans le village de Qusra, en Cisjordanie.
Selon Haaretz, six personnes ont été blessées, dont quatre bénévoles israéliens de l’organisation « Rabbis for Human Rights », un journaliste et un habitant palestinien. Une femme a également été hospitalisée pour une blessure à la tête, tandis que les autres ont subi des blessures légères et ont été pris en charge par le Croissant-Rouge palestinien.
Les militants ont déclaré avoir appelé la police après avoir aperçu des colons se rassembler sur une colline voisine, mais les affrontements ont éclaté après l’arrivée des soldats israéliens sur les lieux. Les soldats ont dispersé les assaillants à l’aide de gaz lacrymogènes, mais les colons ont tenté de lancer une nouvelle attaque depuis une autre direction, contraignant les militants à évacuer les lieux.
241 mineurs palestiniens tués
Selon l’ONG israélienne de défense des droits humains, B’Tselem, au moins 241 mineurs palestiniens ont été tués par l’armée dans ce territoire depuis le 7 octobre 2023 jusqu’au début de l’été.
Au total, près de 1116 Palestiniens ont été tués en Cisjordanie depuis octobre 2023, en majorité par des soldats israéliens, selon un décompte de l’AFP établi à partir de données du ministère palestinien de la Santé. Une enquête des Nations unies, datée de juin, a révélé que les attaques, parfois meurtrières et quasi quotidiennes, perpétrées par les colons, ont augmenté de 130 % en trois ans.
« La participation croissante des forces de sécurité israéliennes aux attaques menées par des colons équivaut à un effondrement de facto de la distinction entre colons et soldats », tranche le rapport.
Pour une information libre sur la Palestine
Nous avons été l’un des premiers médias français à défendre le droit des Palestiniens à disposer d’un État viable dans le respect des résolutions de l’ONU. Et nous avons inlassablement défendu la paix au Proche-Orient. Aidez-nous à continuer de vous informer sur ce qui se passe là-bas. Grâce à vos dons.
Je veux en savoir plus !

This is an entry from: Live: US Republicans derail bid to impeach Pentagon chief over Iran war
US Republicans derail bid to impeach Pentagon chief
10 November 2026 23:51 GMT
Republicans in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, handing President Donald Trump a victory days after his party's crushing midterm election defeat.
The House voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively derailing a planned vote Wednesday on whether to bring formal charges against the embattled Pentagon chief.
The resolution was introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, a Trump critic who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural maneuver, according to US media.

The organizers of the Liverpool Biennial have revealed the theme and artists for the event’s fourteenth iteration, cocurated by Aimee Harrison and Lucía Sanromán and slated to run June 5–September 12, 2027. Titled “The Age of Magical Thinking,” the exhibition takes as its starting point psychologist Jean Piaget’s theory of cognitive development, which is based on the idea that an individual’s imagination is especially fertile during a specific period of childhood. To that end, the biennial will center the experience of childhood as it pertains to past, present and future.
“I think of childhood and youth as a period of constant transition, of change and possibility, but also a time that demands and requires the urgency to question the present,” said Sanromán in a statement. “Artists in the exhibition give us insights into the imagination of childhood, spurring us to boldly ask for a better future. The exhibition responds to the loud demands by young people throughout the world to be taken seriously in how political decisions are made, and for whom.”
Among the twenty-five participating artists are British Argentine artist Amalia Pica, who explores communication through installations, sculptures, and collages; the Kosovo-born Petrit Halilaj who investigates topics including cultural identity, nationhood, and heritage; and Dutch photographer Rineke Dijkstra, known for her starkly intimate portraits of adolescents.
The biennial will take place across multiple venues, including Bluecoat, Exhibition Research Lab at Liverpool John Moores University, FACT Liverpool, Open Eye Gallery, Victoria Gallery &
Museum, and Walker Art Gallery, with more to be announced.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Lula e presidente da Turquia se reúnem e falam de comércio bilateral
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Marcelo Brandão
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Em visita à Turquia para participar da 31ª Conferência sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31), a partir de amanhã (11), o presidente brasileiro Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva se encontrou com o presidente anfitrião Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Na reunião, os dois líderes demonstraram interesse em fortalecer as relações e o comércio entre Brasil e Turquia.
“Conversamos sobre o avanço do nosso comércio bilateral, que já chegou a 5,9 bilhões de dólares, e observamos que é possível ampliar esse valor rapidamente. Destaquei o interesse de estabelecer parceria mais robusta na área de defesa com a Turquia”, disse Lula em postagem na rede social X.
Lula também relatou os cumprimentos dados por Erdogan pela vitória nas eleições presidenciais de outubro. Segundo o presidente brasileiro, seu homólogo destacou “a expressiva mobilização que tomou conta das ruas no Brasil” por conta da disputa eleitoral.
COP 31
Lula e Erdogan também conversaram sobre o evento global de mudanças climáticas.
O presidente brasileiro lembrou da última edição da conferência, realizada na cidade de Belém, no Pará, e colocou-se à disposição para “trabalhar pelo êxito” da COP31. E também citou a recente iniciativa de seu governo de criar um conselho para debater a gestão federal dos minerais críticos e terras raras.
“Ressaltei que a COP31 representa oportunidade de levar adiante as iniciativas que lançamos na COP30, em Belém, e me coloquei à disposição para trabalhar pelo êxito da conferência. Mencionei a criação de conselho vinculado à Presidência da República para definir políticas nacionais sobre minerais críticos e promover seu processamento em território brasileiro. E aventei a possibilidade de cooperação com a Turquia nessa área”.
Participação na COP31
Lula participará da Cúpula de Líderes, segmento da COP que reúne os chefes de Estado dos países participantes, nos dias 11 e 12. Lá, ele deverá discursar duas vezes. A primeira fala, durante a cerimônia de abertura, será reservada a poucos chefes de Estado, entre eles, o presidente brasileiro.
Para integrantes do Itamaraty, esse é um sinal do prestígio do Brasil na agenda ambiental. Além de ter sediado a última COP, em Belém, o Brasil tem números positivos a apresentar. E esse deverá ser o tom do primeiro discurso de Lula na cidade turca de Antália, sede dessa edição da conferência.
Além do discurso durante a abertura, Lula deverá fazer uma fala mais curta, de até três minutos, na parte aberta a todos os países participantes, e participar de uma reunião sobre florestas e financiamento para o Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre (TFFF, na sigla em inglês).

https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2026.title: Maybe it’s a new tagline. Maybe it’s more punctuation. Maybelline’s 35-year-old slogan has an update
https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2026.author: Alyx Gorman explains it to Emma Joyce
https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2026.text:
Alyx, I hear a certain makeup brand has updated its tagline. Why is this a big deal?
The jingle that has been burned into the minds of women around the world since its Christy Turlington-helmed debut in 1991, “Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline”, has received what has being described as a “modernisation”. In a new campaign with Miley Cyrus, the “she’s” will be replaced with “we’re”, which both changes the observer’s perspective to something a little more self-directed and makes it more inclusive. But it’s a punctuation change that is raising eyebrows.
Replacing “she” with “we” feels like a positive move. So what’s turning heads?
They’ve replaced a single comma with a pair of full stops. The slogan is now: “Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline.”
Maybe. That’s. A. Bit. Confusing?
Not according to Sandrine Jolly, global brand president of Maybelline New York. She told WWD that, previously, “the jingle was giving ambiguity – it was more of a question”. Now: “The ‘maybe’ is not a doubt or a hesitation any more. ‘Maybe’, period, is a statement of possibility, and that is what we want to be for women.”
A statement of possibility?
Maybe. That’s what you say when you’re too polite to say no.
What has been the response from the public so far?
“Running to the comments to find the other Virgos with an eye twitching at these misplaced periods,” according to one remark on WWD’s Instgram post about the change. Or, more bluntly: “Terrible grammatical choices.”
Was it written by AI? Or is this proof it’s 100% human-made?
I think it might have been written by the screenwriters of Succession. It’s very We Here For You.
Maybe.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/re.title: Man Who Discovered Renaissance Church Facade Hidden in His House to Receive €1 M. Reward
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/re.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/re.text:
When Juan Francisco León Catena bought an old house in southern Spain, he expected that a planned renovation would incur costs. What he came to learn was that a Renaissance church facade was hidden behind the walls—and that it came with a reward worth more than €1 million ($1.2 million).
The discovery dates to November 2016, when León Catena and his father began tearing down interior walls in a property he’d purchased in Úbeda, a historic town in Andalusia that, together with neighboring Baeza, was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. Behind the plaster and partitions, they found an enormous stone facade measuring roughly 49 feet wide and 36 feet tall.
The stonework turned out to be part of the chapel of the former Hospital of San Jorge, also known as the Hospital of Pero Almindes, which was founded in 1347. The surviving facade includes Renaissance additions attributed to Andrés de Vandelvira, the 16th-century architect responsible for some of the region’s most celebrated buildings.
According to El País, heritage officials who examined the discovery praised its remarkable state of preservation and artistic value, describing it as a rare example of Renaissance funerary chapel architecture.
The discovery also brought León Catena’s renovation plans to a halt. Under Spanish heritage law, the facade is protected, meaning any alterations to the property are subject to strict restrictions. But the same legislation, passed in 1985, also provides financial rewards for people who accidentally discover historically significant objects or structures during construction or demolition work.
Getting that reward proved more complicated than finding the facade.
The regional government initially refused to pay, setting off a legal battle that dragged on for years. Spain’s Supreme Court has now settled the dispute in León Catena’s favor. Now, nearly a decade after the discovery, an Andalusian government valuation committee has determined that León is entitled to more than €1 million. He has yet to receive the money.
The monument itself, meanwhile, remains in limbo. León Catena has been negotiating with local officials over a plan to expose the facade to the street, allowing residents and tourists to see it. In exchange, he has proposed that the city cover the cost of renovating the four-story building.
But time may be running out. A conservation report commissioned by the regional government warned that leaking roofs in adjoining municipal properties have caused water damage, rotting wooden beams, and mold. The deterioration, officials said, could eventually lead to a structural collapse.
“Every month that passes without action increases the concern,” León Catena told El País, adding that the authorities have been warned about the risks but have yet to agree on a solution.
For now, the facade is cordoned off, essentially as it was when León Catena discovered it in 2016. He and his family, who had originally hoped to make the building their home, have since moved into another building on the same street.
“Too much time has passed,” León Catena said. His priority now, he added, is to make the long-hidden monument accessible to the public.

https://hyperallergic.com/gochman-collec.title: Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester
https://hyperallergic.com/gochman-collec.author: Petala Ironcloud
https://hyperallergic.com/gochman-collec.text:
Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester
The private collection opened its Branchline location in Katonah as a way to bring Native art into public view, though questions linger about its engagement with the local Lenape community.
KATONAH, NY — In 1680, English colonists bought the land that would become Bedford, New York, from a Munsee Lenape sachem named Katonah, meaning “great hill.” Today, his name belongs to a Westchester village that is now home to Branchline, the Gochman Family Collection’s (GFC) new gallery and studio space, which opened to the public on November 6 with Line Break, an exhibition of works drawn primarily from its holdings of contemporary Native American art.
Since its founding in 2021, GFC has collected over 800 works with support from Native and non-Native gallerists, artists, and curators alike, including Creative Director and Curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít), curator and Hyperallergic contributor Shándíín Brown (Diné), and Director Laura Phipps, who also serves as Branchline’s director. Designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, the new space occupies two historic storefronts steps from Katonah’s Metro-North station, with free-admission galleries, skylit artist studios, a community ceramics studio, and apartments for invited artists.
Branchline makes a public home for what has essentially been a lending operation: According to GFC, more than 260 of its works have appeared in over 100 exhibitions at institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and The Broad, and it charges no loan fees. That model speaks to a known problem with private collecting, explained Joseph Pierce (Cherokee), professor and founding director of the Native American and Indigenous Studies Initiative at Stony Brook University. “Just because you collect something doesn’t mean you’re going to show it,” Pierce told Hyperallergic. “The risk is that it doesn’t circulate.”

https://gothamist.com/news/jersey-city-m.title: Jersey City mayor names new public safety director, police chief
https://gothamist.com/news/jersey-city-m.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/jersey-city-m.text:
Jersey City is getting new public safety brass next year, with a pair of new leaders that Mayor James Solomon said will continue the progress police have made over the past year.
Jocelyn Roldan will become the city’s acting public safety director in January, while Travis Ragland will take over as police chief in February. Roldan and Ragland will replace Anthony Ambrose and Robert Kearns, the current public safety director and police chief, respectively. Solomon said the new leaders will continue to push reform efforts spearheaded by Ambrose.
Roldan is the first Latina to step into the role, city officials said. She joined the Jersey City police in 2009 and rose through the ranks, spending time as commander of the division’s internal affairs unit. She's most recently been working as Ambrose’s chief of staff.
“She has spent her career holding this department to the highest standards, and she will lead it the same way,” Solomon said.
Jersey City’s Department of Public Safety includes the police division, fire division and office of emergency management. Much of Ambrose’s work since starting in January had been focused on changing how Jersey City police operate. He eliminated the use of fixed patrols and returned cops to walking the beat, he resurrected the city’s motorcycle police unit for traffic enforcement and he implemented a data-driven program to track police performance in Jersey City, similar to New York City's CompStat.
Ambrose is the only person to have led the police departments in New Jersey’s two largest cities, having previously run Newark’s public safety department, earning a reputation as a reform-minded leader for guiding that city’s police division through a federal consent decree process. He had pledged a similar transformation in Jersey City earlier this year.
“The Stone Age of the Jersey City Police Department is moving, starting today,” Ambrose said when he first started in March. “We are doing things differently. We're changing the way we do business.”
The early numbers on Ambrose’s Jersey City report card are promising. Crime has dropped across a number of categories so far this year compared to the same time period last year, according to city data. That includes a 40% drop in shots fired and a 47% decline in car break-ins.
“We've done a lot of good things,” Ambrose said.
Solomon praised Ambrose as having “delivered genuine change.”
“We were extremely lucky to have his leadership, his experience, and he was able to really create transformational change in a short period of time,” Solomon said.
Ambrose said he had only intended to be in Jersey City for three months; he said he stayed longer because he enjoyed the challenge and he liked the people he worked with in the city.
Current police chief Kearns announced he will step down in February. Kearns has served as chief since 2023.
“I'd like to think that I left Jersey City PD a little bit better than when I got it,” Kearns said, his voice cracking with emotion.
Ambrose praised Kearns for working with him on making changes to the city’s police.
“It's kind of hard when you want to move the furniture in the house you owned for a long time, and you have to move the furniture the way I was asking him to move it,” Ambrose said. “And he agreed, and he moved it, and he became a partner instantly.”
Ragland, the incoming chief replacing Kearns, became a cop in the city in 2005; he most recently served as the commander of the division’s traffic unit.
Ragland will be the city's second Black police chief, and its first since Walter Adams was appointed to the position in 1988.
Both Roldan and Ragland are Jersey City natives. City Council President Denise Ridley said she’s optimistic that their connections to the community will make them more effective leaders.
“Being a Jersey City native, growing up here, knowing the community, having community members recognize you and feel that they can trust you is an important part of this job,” Ridley said. “It helps to bridge that gap between community and our public safety department, and that is something that we truly need to make sure that we are focusing on.”
City Councilmember Michael Griffin echoed that.
“These are children of Jersey City,” Griffin said of Roldan and Ragland. “They grew up in these golden neighborhoods and now they're going to protect them, like they've done in the past.”
Solomon, Roldan and Ragland said they were committed to continuing the reform policies instituted under Ambrose, and making further changes to advance the same goals.
Roldan said she plans to grow the size of Jersey City’s police force, from its current size of 773 officers to around 900. Solomon said he supported that goal, and was committed to working with the city council to find the money for that growth even as the city faces a deep fiscal crisis.
Police staffing is a challenge in Jersey City, as new cops increasingly seek out departments that offer better starting pay and veteran officers leave the force. Ambrose estimated that over 100 officers will retire from Jersey City over the next three years.
Roldan and Ragland also said they planned to create new specialized units, similar to a dedicated domestic violence unit established under Ambrose.
“Acting Chief Ragland and I have discussed a robbery squad within the first 90 days, as well as an auto theft task force so that we can target specific crimes that are starting to plague the community,” Roldan said.
The new leadership is set to take over as the city starts to negotiate new contracts with police and fire unions, which have been out of contract for years.
Jack Collins, president of IAFF Local 1066, said the first round of contract talks are scheduled for this week. He said he’s optimistic that city leadership will come to the table in good faith.
The shakeup of public safety leadership comes after a string of high-profile exits from the Solomon administration. Jersey City’s finance director, deputy mayor for housing and corporation counsel all stepped down last month.
