https://taz.de/Verhandlungen-in-Abu-Dhab.title: Verhandlungen in Abu Dhabi: Hoffnungen auf einen Getreide-Deal
https://taz.de/Verhandlungen-in-Abu-Dhab.author: Mathias Brüggmann
https://taz.de/Verhandlungen-in-Abu-Dhab.text:
Verhandlungen in Abu Dhabi: Hoffnungen auf einen Getreide-Deal
Die Erwartungen an die Gespräche zwischen Russland und der Ukraine sind niedrig. Aber wenigstens ein Getreide-Abkommen könnte dabei herausspringen.
Auf den Gleisen bei der ukrainischen Grenzstadt Tschop stauen sich Hunderte Waggons voll mit Mais und Weizen und Zisternen mit Sonnenblumenöl. Die Ladungen warten tagelang auf ihre Passage über die Grenze in die Slowakei. An anderen Grenzstationen der Ukraine zu den angrenzenden EU-Staaten sieht es nicht anders aus. Die Abfertigung verläuft sichtlich schleppend.
Und diese Nadelöhre an den Grenzen werden zunehmend zu einem gewaltigen Problem. Denn seit Sommer haben sich Russland und die Ukraine gegenseitig mit Drohnen- und Raketenangriffen auf Hafenanlagen und Frachter im und am Schwarzen Meer paralysiert. Fast ein Fünftel des weltweit gehandelten Getreides sitzt fest, wegen der De-facto-Blockade des Schwarzen Meeres für von oder nach Russland oder der Ukraine fahrende Frachter.
Seit der russischen Invasion 2022 sind nach ukrainischen Regierungsangaben etwa 1.100 Objekte der ukrainischen Hafeninfrastruktur angegriffen und teilweise zerstört worden: sowohl Getreidesilos als auch Verladeeinrichtungen. Inzwischen attackiert Russland auch vor den Küsten Bulgariens und Rumäniens Schiffe, die in die Ukraine fahren.
Auf der russischen Seite warnt der Gouverneur der Region Rostow, Jurij Sljusar, in einem Interview mit dem TV-Sender Rossija 24: „Wenn wir dem Agrarsektor nicht radikal helfen, werden wir ihn verlieren.“ Denn: „In allen drei unserer Häfen – in Rostow, Taganrog und Asow – ist der Betrieb praktisch eingestellt“, so Sljusar. Viele russische Betriebe, die schon jetzt unter massivem Dieselmangel aufgrund ukrainischer Angriffe auf Raffinerien litten, stünden vor dem Bankrott.
Ukraine könnte Hälfte ihrer Getreideexporte verlieren
In der Ukraine ist die Lage inzwischen so dramatisch, dass das Land nach Angaben von Agrarminister Taras Wysozkyj in diesem Jahr die Hälfte seiner Getreide-, Ölsaaten- und Speiseöl-Exporte einbüßen könnte. Schon jetzt seien Export-Erlöse im Wert von 3 Milliarden US-Dollar verloren.
Über Häfen an der Donau, die von Russland inzwischen ebenfalls angegriffen werden, oder mit der Bahn oder in Lkws könnten nicht einmal die Hälfte der sonst über die Schwarzmeerhäfen verschifften Ladungen ins Ausland transportiert werden. Um einen großen, 60.000 Tonnen fassenden Getreidefrachter zu ersetzen, wären mehr als 2.000 große Lkw nötig.
Am Ende könnte eine katastrophale Ernte stehen: Man werde den Mais wohl auf den Feldern stehen lassen, da die nötige Trocknung nach der Ernte mehr koste, als für den Mais am Ende aktuell erlöst werden könnte, heißt es bei der ukrainischen Agroholding HarvEast. Zudem seien alternative Transportrouten zu teuer und es gebe gar nicht genug Lagerkapazitäten. Viele Silos sind durch Luftangriffe zerstört, in anderen lagern noch Teile der Ernte der Vorsaison, die wegen des Beschusses von Frachtern nicht abtransportiert werden konnten.
So rechnet das ukrainische Agrarministerium mit 17 Prozent weniger Aussaat von Weizen, beim Mais sogar mit einer Halbierung. Wirtschaftsminister Oleksander Krawtschenko rechnet damit, dass die De-facto-Blockade zusammen mit den russischen Angriffen auf die Infrastruktur das Land in diesem Jahr 1,5 Prozentpunkte des BIP kosten und die Exporteinnahmen in Höhe von 40 Milliarden Dollar gefährden wird.
Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj, der Russland mehrfach zum Stopp der gegenseitigen Angriffe am Schwarzen Meer aufgerufen hat, spricht bereits davon, die Lage sei „so schlimm wie um die Straße von Hormus, nur für den Agrarsektor und nicht die Ölindustrie“.
Nun hofft er darauf, dass eine Lösung für die Schwarzmeer-Blockade bei den gerade laufenden Verhandlungen zwischen Russland und der Ukraine unter US-Vermittlung in Abu Dhabi gefunden wird. Russland indes versucht, seine Getreideexporte jetzt über die Ostsee umzuleiten: Neben russischen Häfen auch über den litauischen Hafen Klaipėda.
Litauen hat kein eigenes Labor
Litauens Regierung hat verfügt, dort aus Russland oder Belarus ankommenden Weizen, Gerste, Sonnenblumenkerne und Mais erst zu verladen, wenn Herkunftstests abgeschlossen sind. Damit soll verhindert werden, dass die Agrarprodukte aus den besetzten Gebieten der Ukraine stammen.
Da es in Litauen kein Labor für die erforderlichen Analysen gebe, müsse deren Auswertung im Ausland erfolgen und dauere mindestens zwei Monate, sagte ein Vertreter des litauischen Landwirtschaftsministeriums. Die Exporteure müssten alle Kosten für Lagerung, Tests, Rücksendung oder Vernichtung tragen.
Unterdessen ist laut der US-Behörde USDA die Getreideproduktion der sieben größten Weizenanbauländer dieses Jahr wegen Dürren und Missernten um 11 Prozent gesunken. Die US-Ernte ist die kleinste seit 1970. In der Folge ist der Weizenpreis schon jetzt gegenüber dem Vorjahr um 11,9 Prozent auf 6,75 Dollar pro Bushel (der Maßeinheit für Weizen an US-Börsen) gestiegen.
Die Welt stehe vor einer Krise, die „jahrelange Fortschritte bei der Hungerbekämpfung zunichtemachen und Millionen in akute Ernährungsunsicherheit stürzen“ könnte, heißt es in einer Analyse des Think Tanks Council on Foreign Relations.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.title: Solstice Sonnet
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Zeina Hashem Beck
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
Poems
                                        
                                    
                                     / 
                                                                            November 10, 2026
                                    
                
        
                            
                
                                
    
The Litani banks fill with phosphorus.
Here, the cricket repeats, somewhere, somewhere,
with its dark wings, its five eyes, its toothed legs.
Don’t mistake me for a recovered heart,
fascinated by the longest sunsets.
I am a green permanent resident,
which rings more eternal than citizen.
The summer solstice is about distance,
angles. Pulsing with airports & amens
under the fog, I give up on endings.
You point, articulate: Ta-mal-pa-is.
Try mountains if you’re searching for soul. Break—
but don’t trust me on this. Most days, I don’t
venture out in twilight like hungry deer.
Venture out in twilight like hungry deer!
But don’t trust me on this. Most days, I don’t
try mountains. If you’re searching for soul, break.
You point: articulate Tamalpais
under the fog. I give up on endings,
angles. Pulsing with airports & amens,
the summer solstice is about distance
which rings. More eternal than citizen,
I am a green permanent resident,
fascinated by the longest sunsets.
Don’t mistake me for a recovered heart
with its dark wings, its five eyes, its toothed legs.
Here, the cricket repeats, somewhere, somewhere—
a litany. Banks fill with phosphorus.
    
    
        
     
            
                            
                    
                                        
                        Zeina Hashem Beck is the author of the mirror sonnet collection This Was Supposed to Be About Beauty (Penguin, March 2027) and Sublingual: Failing in an Other’s Language (Haymarket, fall 2027), her debut nonfiction book. Her collection O (Penguin) won the 2023 Arab American Book Award for Poetry and was named a best book of the year by Literary Hub and the New York Public Library. She’s also the author of Louder than Hearts and To Live in Autumn, as well as the chapbooks 3arabi Song and There Was and How Much There Was. Her work has appeared in LARB, Lit Hub, Poetry, and elsewhere. She grew up in Lebanon and currently resides in the Bay Area.

The top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, is all but certain to become the next Speaker of the House, despite dissatisfaction among some freshman lawmakers and their progressive colleagues in the chamber, sources have told Middle East Eye.
There simply is no alternative leader in the running.

The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts has named Franklin Sirmans as chair of the board. Three other board members have also been named: Cheryl Finley, Candice Hopkins, and Suzi Kwon Cohen.
Since 2015, Sirmans has been the Sandra and Tony Tamer Director of the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). During his tenure, he has overseen the acquisition of over a thousand works of art, both by donation and purchase. Prior to joining PAMM, Sirmans was the department head and curator of contemporary art at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA). He was also the Artistic Director of the 2014 Prospect New Orleans biennial. At LACMA, he oversaw major retrospectives by Glenn Ligon and Blinky Palermo and curated “Noah Purifoy: Junk Dada” and “Fútbol: The Beautiful Game.” Sirmans is the former U.S. editor of Flash Art and editor in chief of ArtAsiaPacific.
The Foundation’s board is composed of 18 individuals across the arts. Sirmans succeeds Deborah Willis, while Naomi Beckwith and Cary Davis will also leave the board. “Our new board members bring valuable expertise and fresh perspectives that will deepen the Foundation’s commitment to artists and the visual arts field,” said Joel Wachs, President of the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, in a press release. “Together with Franklin Sirmans’ leadership, their knowledge, insight, and experience will help us advance our mission and meet the evolving needs of artists and the organizations that support them.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Quando a terra vira lar, dignidade e futuro
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Leilianne Gurgel
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
No dia 4 de novembro de 2026, a Superintendência Regional do Incra no Médio São Francisco completou dois anos de sua recriação. A data representa muito mais do que a retomada de uma estrutura administrativa: marca o fortalecimento da presença do Estado em uma região estratégica, onde a política de reforma agrária tem um papel fundamental na vida de milhares de famílias e no desenvolvimento dos territórios.
Ao longo desses dois anos, temos trabalhado para aproximar a instituição das comunidades, ampliar o acesso às políticas públicas e transformar direitos em oportunidades concretas. Porque falar de reforma agrária é, antes de tudo, falar de gente e de famílias que sonham com um pedaço de terra onde possam viver, trabalhar, produzir e criar seus filhos com dignidade.
Democratizar o acesso a terra vai muito além da distribuição de hectares. Significa garantir condições para que as famílias possam permanecer em seus territórios, construir autonomia, gerar renda e participar do desenvolvimento da região. É compreender que a terra não é apenas um espaço de produção, mas também um lugar de pertencimento, identidade e construção de histórias.
Foi com esse sentimento que vivenciamos, em agosto, um momento muito especial no Território Quilombola Conceição das Crioulas, em Salgueiro, no Sertão de Pernambuco. A entrega de 44 novas moradias mostrou, na prática, que uma casa representa muito mais do que paredes e um teto. Representa segurança, dignidade, pertencimento e a possibilidade de construir um futuro com mais tranquilidade.
Para quem acompanha de perto a realidade dessas comunidades, é impossível olhar para uma entrega como essa sem perceber o que ela significa na vida das pessoas. Uma moradia transforma a rotina de uma família, oferece proteção às crianças, proporciona mais segurança às mulheres e fortalece os laços de uma comunidade com seu território.
Talvez exista também uma dimensão ainda mais especial nessa missão quando se trabalha por essas políticas no lugar onde a própria história começou. Depois de quase quatro décadas vivendo no Rio Grande do Norte, retornar às minhas raízes no Médio São Francisco trouxe, junto com o reencontro com a minha terra, uma responsabilidade ainda maior: contribuir, por meio do trabalho no Incra, para que a política de reforma agrária alcance cada vez mais famílias deste território.
Como mulher, mãe e assistente social, carrego comigo a compreensão de que nenhuma política pública se realiza plenamente se não alcançar as pessoas em sua realidade cotidiana. Por trás de cada processo administrativo existe uma história, uma expectativa, uma família que espera. É no contato com as comunidades, na escuta, no diálogo e na busca por soluções que compreendemos a dimensão humana do trabalho que realizamos.
E os resultados desses dois anos demonstram a importância estratégica do Incra para o desenvolvimento do Médio São Francisco. Nesse período, foram aproximadamente R$ 29 milhões destinados a créditos produtivos, criando condições para que famílias assentadas invistam em suas atividades, fortaleçam a produção e ampliem suas possibilidades de geração de renda. Outros R$ 47,5 milhões em crédito habitacional representam investimentos que chegam diretamente à vida das famílias, contribuindo para a construção de moradias e para a melhoria das condições de vida no campo.
Somam-se a esses resultados a emissão de 6.814 Contratos de Concessão de Uso (CCUs) e a regularização de mais de 2 mil novas famílias, ampliando o acesso a direitos e fortalecendo a segurança das famílias em seus territórios.
Esses números revelam que a atuação do Incra não se limita à regularização fundiária ou à destinação de terras. A autarquia exerce um papel estratégico na articulação de políticas públicas que envolvem moradia, produção, inclusão social, desenvolvimento econômico e garantia de direitos.
Sua presença no Médio São Francisco é fundamental para que os investimentos públicos cheguem a quem historicamente mais precisa deles e para que o desenvolvimento regional também aconteça a partir do campo, dos assentamentos e das comunidades quilombolas.
Mas os números, sozinhos, não contam toda essa história. Para quem olha apenas para os dados, são casas, contratos, créditos e investimentos. Para quem acompanha de perto, são famílias que passam a ter mais segurança, agricultores que encontram condições para produzir, mulheres que conquistam mais autonomia, crianças que crescem com melhores perspectivas e comunidades que fortalecem seus vínculos com a terra e preservam sua memória.
E talvez seja esse o sentido mais profundo de voltar para casa: reencontrar as próprias raízes e poder contribuir para que outras pessoas também encontrem na sua terra um lugar de pertencimento, trabalho, dignidade e futuro.
Porque a terra não é só patrimônio. Para milhares de famílias, terra é identidade, memória, sustento, proteção e esperança. E é nesse encontro entre território, pessoas e políticas públicas que a reforma agrária ganha seu verdadeiro significado.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Fire contained on platform in Iran’s South Pars gas field
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Fire contained on platform in Iran’s South Pars gas field
Iranian authorities have contained a fire that broke out on a platform in South Pars gas field, the world’s largest offshore natural gas field.
The Pars Oil and Gas Company said the fire broke out on Tuesday on a gas platform in Phase 14 of the South Pars field and was extinguished immediately, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported.
“During the incident, 17 workers jumped into the sea to save their lives; rescue operations for them are currently underway,” Kourosh Dehghan, Bushehr Province’s director general of crisis management, told Fars.
“Further details regarding the scale of the incident and the condition of the workers will be announced later,” Dehghan added.
Bushehr’s crisis management office later said all 17 workers were in good condition after boarding lifeboats and rescue craft, and that three heavy rescue vessels had been sent to the platform to bring them back.
Officials are considering a gas leak or an operational mishap as possible causes for the fire, Fars said.
The news agency added that the platform accounts for only 14.5 million cubic metres of South Pars’s total daily production of more than 700 million cubic metres of gas.
Iran shares the reservoir with major gas exporter Qatar, which calls its portion the North Dome.
The reservoir contains an estimated 1,800 trillion cubic feet (51 trillion cubic metres) of usable gas, enough to supply the world’s needs for 13 years.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pi.title: Oxford University Museum Returns 39 Sets of Ancestral Remains to Naga People of India
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pi.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pi.text:
At a ceremony held on November 9, the Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University in the UK formally returned 39 sets of ancestral remains to the Naga people of India. The remains, primarily human skulls, were taken during the British colonial rule of India and Burma (now Myanmar) and have been in the museum’s collection for more than a century. A delegation of almost 30 community members from Nagaland, an Indian state bordering Myanmar, traveled to Britain for the handover.
The Pitt Rivers claims to hold the largest collection of Naga artifacts in the world, most of which were acquired by John Henry Hutton, an anthropologist and colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service, and a second administrator/anthropologist, James Philip Mills, between 1910 and 1940. Within that collection, 219 items are listed as Naga human remains, including 39 ancestral human remains and 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. (The current return concerns only the 39 ancestors.)
On its website, the museum notes that colonial “collecting” was “often bound up with the structures of colonial violence; remains and objects were frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given.” Mills, who wrote three monographs on Naga culture and practice, refers to at least one armed expedition to demand “headhunting trophies” from Pangsha village, remarking that the Pitt Rivers would thus “get some fine specimens.”
While the Naga people practiced headhunting at the time, taking the severed heads of enemies as trophies, they also kept and cared for the heads of their own chiefs. According to anthropologist Dolly Kikon (a member of Nagaland’s Lotha-Naga community, now at the University of California, Santa Cruz) one of the remains being returned is a chief’s skull.
The Pitt Rivers removed all human remains, including those of Naga people, from display in 2020. Sensing an opening, Kikon contacted the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven and offered to connect her with the Naga community. The return is the culmination of the museum’s work with Naga partners, including the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR) together with tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities.
Naga tribal leaders plan to bury the remains together in a joint memorial park. “They’ve been here in a foreign land for more than a century,” said Dr Vihuto Asumi, President of the Sumî Hoho Naga tribe. “We believe that their spirits are still not at rest, so by doing this, we believe it will bring spiritual healing, not only to the ancestral remains here but to everyone who died during the headhunting days.”

https://hyperallergic.com/mamdani-begins.title: Mamdani Begins Reconstruction of Historic Chinatown Building Decimated in 2020 Fire
https://hyperallergic.com/mamdani-begins.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/mamdani-begins.text:
Mamdani Begins Reconstruction of Historic Chinatown Building Decimated in 2020 Fire
Some $184 million will go toward the revival of 70 Mulberry Street, which once housed community-based organizations.
On Monday, November 9, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, along with the commissioners for the departments of design and construction, citywide administrative services, and cultural affairs, commenced the $184 million reconstruction project of 70 Mulberry Street, a historically significant building that sustained severe damage from a fire in 2020.
Upon the project's expected completion in 2030, 70 Mulberry Street will house or provide additional space for the five community organizations that operated there before the fire, including the Museum of Chinese in America (MOCA). The new building will include artist Jennifer Wen Ma's "Wings of Everchange 易之翼," a permanent, three-part art installation commissioned by the Department of Cultural Affairs’ (DCLA) Percent for Art program.
Working between Beijing and New York City, Ma has produced varied interdisciplinary media ranging from "cleansing walks," which appear like one-person funerary processions, to collections of plants coated in Chinese ink.
Designed by Grimshaw Architects, the new building retains architectural traces of the 1892 building, while expanding to include six community rooms, multipurpose areas, outdoor spaces, and several modern accommodations. The renovated building is expected to provide approximately 30% more public space than the original facility and will extend three floors higher.
Founded and constructed in 1892 as Public School 23, the building was repurposed into a community hub in the mid-1970s. After the fire devastated much of the building's structure in 2020, the five organizations operating there relocated to nearby venues. While MOCA had moved to its 215 Centre Street flagship in 2009, it retained the old gallery space at 70 Mulberry Street as an archival space and research library for the museum's 85,000-item collection, most of which was salvaged from the fire.
Since accepting a $35 million city capital grant tied to the construction of a Chinatown jail in 2019, MOCA has come under intense scrutiny. In July, protesters condemned museum leaders for accepting the so-called "jail money" in exchange for their complicity in the jail's construction and the possible devastation to Chinatown's communities.
Ma's public installation touches upon much of the Mulberry Street site's historical record and its role in Chinatown in three capacities.
The central sculpture in the building's atrium will be modeled after the graceful brushstrokes of Chinese calligraphy and incorporates salvaged materials from the 2020 fire. Within the sculpture, glass orbs serve as time capsules dedicated to certain individuals or groups touched by 70 Mulberry Street. Ma also plans to launch a publicly accessible website and app with oral testimonies from 70 community members about the building. The third part of the installation extends to the historic spiral stairwell, where ink paintings on glass panels snake up several floors along the inner stair tower.
The New York City Public Design Commission unanimously approved Ma's design in January 2024 as part of the Percent for Art program, which mandates that 1% of eligible funds for city-backed construction projects be spent on public artworks.
"Our community has gone through so many challenges and changes," Ma said in a statement. "I set out to make a work that would embrace these changes, honoring our history, anchoring us in the present and taking us soaring into the future.”

https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-ke.title: Gov. Hochul keeps the door open to redrawing New York’s congressional map
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-ke.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-ke.text:
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she remains open to a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for Democrats to redraw New York’s congressional districts as soon as 2028.
The Democratic governor told reporters Tuesday that major Democratic wins across the country in last week’s elections wouldn’t necessarily derail her party’s push to change the state constitution to allow for mid-decade redistricting in the Empire State.
But Hochul also didn’t commit to moving ahead with the plan, which was first put into motion last year as Republicans in Texas, North Carolina and other states began redrawing congressional districts to benefit their party.
The Republican efforts — backed by President Donald Trump — either backfired or didn’t matter, with Democrats easily picking up enough seats across the country to take control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
“Those newly drawn lines [in other states] are still there,” Hochul said at her Manhattan office. “And while it didn’t have an effect on this year’s election, there’s always another election every two years.”
The governor continued: “You can't assume that there's going to be the same outcomes every two years, and so I want to look at it long-term.”
In New York, the state constitution requires a bipartisan panel to redraw congressional lines after each once-a-decade Census, with lawmakers getting final approval. But it doesn’t provide a mechanism to change the districts during the intervening years.
That hasn’t stopped Democrats from trying.
In March, the U.S. Supreme Court halted a lower court’s order that would’ve required redrawing New York’s 11th congressional district, a Republican stronghold that includes all of Staten Island and parts of Brooklyn. The order was spurred by a Democrat-led lawsuit that argued the current district disenfranchised Black and Hispanic voters. Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, a Republican who has held the district since 2021, was re-elected last Tuesday.
In June, state lawmakers gave preliminary approval to a constitutional amendment that would open the door to mid-decade redistricting. The amendment would also remove a prohibition on gerrymandering — drawing district lines to benefit a particular party or candidate — and make it easier for the Democrat-dominated Legislature to make changes to the map on its own.
But a constitutional amendment has to be passed by consecutively-elected legislatures before it goes to voters for final approval. So lawmakers would have to approve the amendment again next year to have any chance of drawing new lines by 2028.
If lawmakers do approve it again, it would set up a statewide referendum on the ballot as soon as November 2027.
Former Rep. John Faso, a Hudson Valley Republican who has helped fight the Democratic redistricting effort, said Democrats would be making a “big mistake” by going ahead with the amendment in New York.
Faso noted voters approved the current redistricting process in 2014 and roundly rejected a prior Democrat-led effort to make changes in 2021. The state Court of Appeals also rejected a Democrat-drawn map in 2022 for violating the anti-gerrymandering provision.
“It’s a terrible affront to the voters of our state,” he said of the proposed amendment. “It basically is attempting to rig the districts to benefit one party over the other, and I don't think the voters will go for it.”
Hochul has no formal role in the amendment process. But she pushed for the change as the de facto head of the state Democratic Party, with support from Brooklyn Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next House speaker.
State Sen. Shelley Mayer, a Yonkers Democrat who heads Senate Democrats’ reelection efforts, said it’s “premature” to say whether lawmakers will take up the amendment again next year.
“ I do think it's clear that the efforts that Republicans [in other states] made were a fool's errand, because we won many of the seats that they sought to redistrict to their advantage,” Mayer said. “That being said, there's a lot in this amendment that we should review that goes beyond mid-Census redistricting, and I think we need to have a thoughtful conversation about it.”
Rep. Joseph Morelle, a Rochester-area Democrat who serves as Jeffries’ point man on New York redistricting efforts, told POLITICO he will urge state lawmakers to move ahead with the amendment.
Hochul acknowledged that the “political landscape has changed” since lawmakers first approved the constitutional amendment earlier this year.
“I’m going to take that into account,” she said. “I'm going to talk to Leader Jeffries, and I'm going to talk to the two [state] legislative leaders about where we want to go with this.”
The state Legislature is set to return to the Capitol in January. Democrats will have a two-thirds supermajority in both the Senate and Assembly when they begin the 2027 legislative session, which runs through June.

Amtsenthebungsverfahren gegen Hegseth : Klare öffentliche Meinung
Mit einem Ja zu einem Impeachment-Verfahren würden sich die Republikaner einen großen Gefallen tun. Die Frage ist, ob sie das Rückgrat dazu haben.
D er Antrag für ein Amtsenthebungsverfahren gegen Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth kommt zu einem denkbar ungünstigen Zeitpunkt in der US-Politik, nämlich dem Zeitraum nach einer Wahl und vor der Konstituierung des neuen Kongresses im Januar. Doch dies darf kein Grund dafür sein, dass eine völlig unqualifizierte Person weiterhin die Kontrolle über das mächtigste Militär der Welt behält.
Dass der Antrag überhaupt erst jetzt zur Debatte steht, liegt vor allem daran, dass die Republikaner in den vergangenen knapp zwei Jahren die politische Agenda von Donald Trump ohne große Widerrede einfach durchgewunken haben. Sich gegen ihn zu stellen, bedeutete für viele das politische Aus. Die Quittung dafür gab es vergangene Woche an den Wahlurnen. Der scheidende republikanische Abgeordnete Thomas Massie hat mit seinem jetzigen Vorstoß seiner Partei jedoch eine Chance zur Wiedergutmachung gegeben.
Die Frage ist, ob die bei den Zwischenwahlen so schwer abgestraften republikanischen Abgeordneten die Chance ergreifen werden und Hegseth tatsächlich zur Rechenschaft ziehen – oder ob sie erneut das tun, was Trump von ihnen verlangt, und ihre schützende Hand über Hegseth halten.

Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Insgesamt acht Anklagepunkte führt Massie in seinem Antrag an, die verdeutlichen, dass Hegseth in der Ausübung seines Amtes klar gegen Gesetze verstoßen und amerikanische Soldaten in Gefahr gebracht hat.
Ob Republikaner Massies Steilpass annehmen werden, wird sich in den kommenden Tagen zeigen. Die öffentliche Meinung zu Hegseth ist jedoch klar: Er soll weg. Er steht für den Irankrieg, den die Bevölkerung nicht will. Vor allem wollen die Amerikaner:innen nicht die wirtschaftlichen Auswirkungen, die das Leben in den vergangenen Monaten deutlich teurer gemacht haben. Doch auch wenn der jetzige Antrag scheitern sollte, die Tage von Hegseth an der Spitze des Pentagon dürften gezählt zu sein.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/ile-de-f.title: Ce que l’on sait de l’élue régionale victime d’un jet de bouteille remplie d’essence devant un lycée à Chelles
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/ile-de-f.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/ile-de-f.text:
Une élue régionale a reçu une bouteille remplie d’essence ce mardi 10 novembre devant un lycée de Chelles (Seine-et-Marne). Si les circonstances précises restent à déterminer, l’incident a suscité une volée de réactions au sein de LR et du gouvernement.
Que s’est-il réellement passé ce mardi 10 novembre au matin devant le lycée Gaston-Bachelard de Chelles (Seine-et-Marne) ? Une conseillère régionale LR d’Île-de-France dit avoir été visée par une bouteille remplie d’essence alors qu’elle se trouvait devant l’établissement, en compagnie de parents d’élèves « pour essayer de permettre que les cours reprennent », selon les mots de Valérie Pécresse, présidente LR de la région Île-de-France.
L’élue, Angela Avond, « complètement sous le choc », selon Valérie Pécresse qui comptait se rendre sur place, a porté plainte pour « tentative de meurtre ». « Ce déferlement de violence doit cesser », a ajouté la présidente de région qui gère les 468 lycées franciliens.
Le maire de la ville, Brice Rabaste (LR), qui s’est rendu sur place après l’événement, raconte qu’elle a reçu « une bouteille d’essence sur la poitrine qui a arrosé tout son manteau ». Le caractère intentionnel reste encore, à ce stade, à déterminer. Une enquête a néanmoins été ouverte pour « tentative d’homicide volontaire », a précisé le parquet de Meaux.
« Aucune goutte d’essence n’est tombée sur elle »
« Aucune goutte d’essence n’est tombée sur elle, la bouteille est restée fermée même après avoir été lancée », assure une lycéenne interrogée par BFMTV, « et d’ailleurs nous l’avons aidée à se relever. Ce n’était pas intentionnel ». L’élue LR, régulièrement présente devant le lycée depuis le début des blocus pour qu’ils soient levés, aurait voulu s’interposer entre un groupe d’élèves et quelques poubelles placées par des lycéens au milieu d’un parking à distance des bâtiments scolaires.
Les élèves savaient-ils qu’il s’agissait d’une conseillère régionale, également maire adjointe en charge de la jeunesse ? Pour Valérie Pécresse, « si elle n’avait pas été élue, ce ne serait pas moins grave ». C’est toutefois bien parce qu’elle le soit, puisque l’incident a suscité une volée de réactions au sein de LR et du gouvernement.
« Je condamne l’agression d’une conseillère régionale, adjointe au maire de Chelles, par un élève lui ayant jeté une bouteille d’essence au niveau du torse, devant un lycée », a réagi sur X le ministre de l’Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez. « Nous ne sommes plus ici dans le cadre d’un mouvement lycéen, ce sont des violences urbaines, qui appellent la réponse la plus ferme et déterminée », a-t-il ajouté.
La présidente de l’Assemblée nationale, Yaël Braun-Pivet a fait de même et « condamne cet acte avec la plus grande fermeté, l’auteur devra être jugé à la hauteur de la gravité des faits. » En visite dans un collège du 10e arrondissement de Paris, le ministre de l’Éducation nationale, Édouard Geffray, a condamné « un comportement qui s’appelle un crime ». L’élue « doit évidemment avoir le soutien de toute la société, de toute la communauté politique », a-t-il poursuivi devant la presse.
Trois jeunes lycéens de 15 à 17 ans ont été placés en garde à vue dans la journée, pour des faits d’attroupement et dégradation par moyen incendiaire, a priori sans rapport direct avec l’incident, ajoute le procureur. La personne qui a jeté la bouteille n’a pas encore été identifiée, selon les précisions apportées par le parquet à la mi-journée, et est toujours recherchée.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Do Socialists Even Believe in Socialism Anymore?
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Mike Beggs, Ben Burgis, Bhaskar Sunkara
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Do Socialists Even Believe in Socialism Anymore?
The American left has a growing list of victories—and an unfinished argument about the society it wants to build.
We’ve all seen the cover. some of us even have a copy of it hanging in our living room: “The Red Apple.” The New York Post marked Zohran Mamdani’s November 2025 election with a Soviet-inspired cover that featured the incoming mayor carrying a hammer and sickle high above his head.
It was an image that those of us who grew up in New York during the Rudy Giuliani or Michael Bloomberg era couldn’t have imagined. The larger global context made it even more remarkable, demonstrating socialism’s advance in the United States even as it’s in retreat in much of Europe and Latin America. And since last year, Mamdani’s election has helped catalyze a string of socialist victories in congressional races. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has surged to over 120,000 members, and with the midterm results, the movement’s small congressional contingent is set to become dramatically larger.
What does socialism mean, though, to the socialists of our era? Their predecessors in early-20th-century socialist parties liked to talk about a “minimum program” of reforms within capitalism and a “maximum program” of reforms that go beyond capitalism entirely. Some even theorized a “transitional program” to bridge the gap between the two.
The “minimum program,” at least, is easy enough to see today. Socialist candidates for office talk about Medicare for All, jobs programs, and ending America’s wars overseas. In New York, Mamdani has conducted hearings on the misdeeds of negligent landlords, frozen the rent for millions of New Yorkers in rent-stabilized apartments, and established a Mayor’s Office of Worker Power to help people organize their workplaces. He’s worked to expand free childcare and taken the first steps to build public grocery stores in each of the city’s five boroughs. And through it all, the city’s economy has continued to boom.
To progressive allies of the DSA, these reforms are proof of the movement’s inherent pragmatism—in deeds, if not always in words. But others can reasonably ask if this generation’s socialists still believe in socialism at all.
When the leading DSA-affiliated politicians like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are asked to define socialism, they tend to talk about mitigating income inequality and giving everyone a dignified life. While these are certainly goals close to the heart of any socialist, it’s hard to see how they add up to socialism as a system, since they avoid the question at the core of socialism: the ownership of the means of production. Similarly, while the radicalism of some clauses of the DSA’s national platform—including the calls to abolish the Senate and to dismantle the carceral state—has been a lightning rod for criticism from the right, the document offers little detail about how a world beyond capitalism would work.
The DSA platform calls for public ownership of the largest corporations and essential industries. That would be a major transformation, but it could still leave much of the economy organized around private employers and wage labor. Even the section titled “Democracy at Work” is about trade unions, not who owns the means of production. And although the DSA declares a classless society its goal, it offers little explanation of how its demands for change within capitalism would get us there.
This blurriness about the “maximum program” can’t be chalked up to a lack of radical commitment or to strategic coyness. It reflects a real problem. On the one hand, capitalism is a brutally unequal system in which many struggle to take care of their families and spend much of their waking lives in jobs they despise. There are many good reasons to find it abhorrent. On the other hand, especially after the failures of state socialism in the Eastern bloc, many people who are deeply critical of capitalism aren’t entirely sure what an economically viable alternative to it would look like.
In light of that uncertainty, many progressives, and surely many readers of The Nation, wonder if it’s better to drop the socialism talk entirely. Politicians like Zohran Mamdani should abandon the historical baggage associated with socialism, their thinking goes, and just embrace social democracy and the great effort to tame, rather than replace, capitalism.
On one level, it’s easy to see their point. Social democracies like Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Finland really were, at their peak, the most livable societies that human beings ever built. If the United States adopted the Nordic model in the coming years, it would be the greatest triumph of the American left since the Civil War and Reconstruction. That much should be obvious to anyone with progressive values. What might be less obvious is that it would still be a woefully insufficient response to growing levels of inequality and discontent.
Admittedly, one reason that socialists like ourselves stubbornly refuse to limit our horizons to social democracy is purely ideological. Even in the most expansive social-democratic welfare states, like Sweden in the 1970s, most of the working-age population worked for capitalist employers. Democracy stopped at the factory and office doors.
In the places where most adults spend their working days, we do not interact with each other as equals. The working-class majority have to do what they’re told by bosses or risk becoming unemployed. Often, workers’ best recourse against unreasonable demands is the power of exit. But even if they’re able to exercise that option, they will still have to find a new boss to submit to. They can choose their masters, but they can’t choose not to have a master. Meanwhile, some of their fellow citizens, due to nothing but accidents of birth, can live off trust funds without having to work at all.
For egalitarians, this is a deep injustice, and one that remains even when extensive public provision and a powerful labor movement have sanded off some of the system’s worst effects.
Even if we were willing to swallow this imbalance of power at the heart of the economy, though, there’s also a practical objection to stopping at social democracy. Thinking that’s as far as we can go sounds realistic, but it’s far from clear that capitalism as it exists in the third decade of the 21st century can sustain ambitious pro-labor policies and deep welfare-state commitments that would enable full employment and the truly comprehensive provision of public goods.
Michał Kalecki identified the underlying problem decades before it came to the fore. In his 1943 essay “Political Aspects of Full Employment,” Kalecki argued that while sustained full employment might be economically achievable under capitalism, it was politically unstable. Individual capitalists might occasionally welcome state policies to these ends in the short term to help restore demand for their products, but over time they would come to resist them. Tight labor markets weaken workplace discipline, strengthen workers’ bargaining power, and erode employers’ social authority—an environment, the business leaders feared, that would undermine capital accumulation.
Much of today’s progressive discourse ignores this lesson entirely. Full employment, expansive fiscal policy, and ambitious state investment are often presented by American progressives as stable end points within capitalism. Yet these policies will be bitterly contested by capital and, inevitably, will provoke crises.
Governments, for their part, can sometimes sustain such policies against the immediate wishes of business, especially when public order is at stake. But this autonomy is limited, since states remain dependent on private investment for growth, employment, and tax revenues. In an era of intensified global competition, and with aging populations already threatening the existing welfare states, it’s unclear that the Golden Age advances of the middle 20th century, when both labor and capital grew stronger, can return.
All this, of course, might sound like the case for an even more moderate reform program, one that avoids burdening capitalist job creators with excessive interference from labor but rewards workers with reasonable wages and protections in return. We draw the opposite conclusion. We think that people have the right to both the security of a welfare state and a voice in their workplaces. Precisely for that reason, socialists must not shy away from maximal demands: doing away with capitalism altogether.
The socialism of central planning and administrative allocation was a failure in the Soviet Union and similar societies. Learning from that history requires rethinking how egalitarian production and distribution can actually work.
If we need market mechanisms in at least some sectors of the economy, it doesn’t follow that we need capitalist property relations and the deep inequalities of power that go with them. We know that worker-owned and democratically governed firms can operate efficiently. Spain’s Mondragon Corporation, a federation of dozens of autonomous cooperatives, employs around 70,000 people. Its worker-members elect their governing bodies and participate in strategic decisions. If we could have a market sector where every company worked that way—where it was all Mondragons and no Amazons—we could have a prosperous modern economy without workplace authoritarianism and labor exploitation.
One reason cooperatives are rare under capitalism is that even relatively well-off workers who could pool their resources to start a business would be making a risky bet. It’s not rational for people with very limited resources to put all their financial eggs in the single basket of a venture that could go belly-up and leave them with nothing. Apologists for capitalism conclude that capitalist employment relations are morally innocent and mutually beneficial. Capitalists assume the risk and get the power, while workers surrender their power but get the security of a biweekly paycheck. We think that a better society would offer workers better options than the choice between economic insecurity and economic oppression.
In our vision of socialism, a large state sector provides universal public services such as education and healthcare, while a regulated market sector composed of democratic, worker-controlled firms produces ordinary goods and services in response to consumer demand. This means that workers do not have to risk their personal savings; public banks finance the companies, which must pay their members regular wages that meet minimum benchmarks. Worker-members also share any profits remaining after wages and other obligations have been paid.
Our model retains markets because prices, competition, and consumer choice solve real coordination problems. But it rejects capitalism on egalitarian and democratic grounds: A dynamic economy doesn’t require a separate class of owners with authority over production, investment, and the lives of ordinary workers.
This is no utopia. It wouldn’t automatically eliminate all forms of inequality, and it certainly wouldn’t eliminate all sources of political conflict. It would, however, be the first dominant form of human social organization since the Neolithic Revolution that did not divide society into a class of subordinated producers and a class of rulers living off the fruits of those producers’ labor. That’s the North Star that past generations of socialists understood themselves to be striving toward. It’s the vision that many of them died for, whether killed by strikebreaking Pinkertons or fighting as internationalist volunteers in the Spanish Civil War. We still think humanity has a chance to achieve that future.
DSA founder Michael Harrington used to say that radicals had to “walk a perilous tightrope.” We had to “be true to the socialist vision of a new society” and also “bring that vision into contact with the actual movements fighting not to transform the system, but to gain some little increment of dignity or even just a piece of bread.”
Harrington is not often invoked in DSA circles nowadays, but almost every socialist in the country is still trying to walk that tightrope, judging reforms both by the relief they bring and by the strength they give working people to fight for more. Universal healthcare would weaken workers’ dependence on employers for medical coverage. More public housing would reduce tenants’ dependence on private landlords. Stronger unions would give workers more power over their jobs. But turning these gains into steps toward socialism requires organizing and political agitation. That transformation won’t follow automatically from a popular mayor or a well-run sanitation department.
The New York Post cover was meant to be a warning about the society that Mamdani wants to build. We owe its readers a clearer picture of that society than a hammer and sickle can provide.

A campanha presidencial do segundo turno de 2026 levou uma multidão de pessoas a tentar ocupar as redes sociais com informação de qualidade para ajudar os indecisos a optarem num voto por Lula e pela democracia. O engajamento foi tanto que o termo “psicose política” se popularizou para definir aquela pessoa que via as eleições até em sonhos.
O momento escancarou ainda a manipulação das big techs. A Meta foi uma das peças centrais, com documentos e dados mostrando um favorecimento dos perfis ligados ao então candidato e senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ).
Neste cenário, é possível ter uma relação saudável com as plataformas como ferramenta de circulação de informações de interesse público?
No BdF Entrevista, o criador de conteúdo Thiago Guimarães, do canal Ora Thiago, avalia que é necessário diminuir a opacidade das plataformas digitais e a dependência que temos desse ambiente digital.
As semanas que antecederam o segundo turno demonstraram o tamanho do desafio. Milhares de pessoas, de uma hora para outra, mesmo aquelas que não eram propriamente produtoras de conteúdo, dedicaram horas diárias à tarefa de disseminar dados, combater notícias falsas e conversar diretamente com eleitores em dúvida, convertendo perfis pessoais em verdadeiras centrais de comunicação democrática.
“Esse nível extremo de imersão afetou diretamente a rotina e o estado emocional dos militantes digitais. Quando a preservação da democracia é percebida como um dever individual urgente, o indivíduo entra em estado de alerta ininterrupto”, avalia. “A chamada ‘psicose política’ reflete esse fenômeno em que a fronteira entre a vida privada e o debate público se dissolve, levando o eleitor a sentir que cada mensagem enviada pode definir o futuro do país.”
Ao comentar o tema da regulação das big techs, além da já citada necessidade de transparência, Thiago Guimarães também afirma que é preciso superar o que ele definiu como “grandes muralhas na frente de um horizonte democrático”. Para ele, a maioria das pessoas relaciona internet com “meia dúzia de plataformas” controladas pelas já conhecidas gigantes da tecnologia.
“A internet é gigantesca”, pontua, ao defender uma disputa da vida digital e uma menor dependência desse ecossistema. “A gente pode disputar uma vida digital mais ampla, mais diversa. Uma vida digital em que a gente tem múltiplas possibilidades de existir online. Hoje a gente não consegue fazer isso. Qualquer profissional hoje precisa ter uma conta nessas determinadas plataformas, senão ele não tem acesso à vida econômica, ao consumo, a clientes para o negócio que ele precisa construir”, pondera.
Guimarães explica que a lógica da produtividade para o algoritmo é a essência do ecossistema digital e que também pressiona quem trabalha e ganha a vida com conteúdo na internet. “Quando uma marca decide me contratar, uma das coisas que pedem é o print dos analytics dessas plataformas para elas entenderem qual é o desempenho do meu canal, como é que o meu canal tem performado com um determinado tipo de audiência”, exemplifica.
O criador de conteúdo pondera que há muito poder e pouca transparência nesse gerenciamento de dados. Ele compara à mensuração de audiência da TV tradicional, que é feita por um terceiro independente, no caso, o Ibope. “A plataforma e o sistema dela, essa infraestrutura que mantém aquilo possível, são parte central de toda uma economia de atenção. A gente chama de economia de atenção, em que o grande fator determinante são os dados que as plataformas fornecem”, afirma. “E tudo isso termina por definir o debate público. É um sistema nebuloso”, reforça.
Por essa razão, o youtuber avalia que conseguir um equilíbrio entre a economia da atenção e o interesse público não é impossível, porém é bastante desafiador. “Não é de interesse para o Instagram, YouTube, para qualquer uma dessas plataformas, que a informação que circula ali seja a informação de interesse público. Existe informação de interesse público que circula nessa plataforma, mas é mais porque a gente não tem outra escolha, a não ser fazer a informação circular por meio dessas plataformas. Mas a prioridade dessas plataformas é o modelo de negócio delas”, resume.

https://hyperallergic.com/mrs-gallery-ma.title: Mrs. Gallery Marks 10 Years of Getting Art Collectors to Queens
https://hyperallergic.com/mrs-gallery-ma.author: Aaron Short
https://hyperallergic.com/mrs-gallery-ma.text:
Mrs. Gallery Marks 10 Years of Getting Art Collectors to Queens
A decade since Sara Maria Salamone and Tyler Lafreniere found their storefront space on Craigslist, the gallery presents a rotating anniversary show that channels its evolving nature.
Maspeth has not traditionally been thought of as an arts hub like Bushwick or the East Village, but one gallery has thrived by drawing collectors from all over the world to Western Queens.
“We’ve had people stop here on the way to the airport and end up buying something,” Mrs. Associate Director Lily Frances Pendery told Hyperallergic. “We had an advisor who recently spent an hour and a half with us. Anyone who comes in the door is serious about what their visit is for.”
From its leafy one-way street near the Long Island Expressway, Mrs. has worked with dozens of emerging artists, held 72 shows, and traveled to art fairs in Paris, South Korea, and across the country. This fall, the gallery is celebrating its anniversary with DECENNIUM: Ten Years at Mrs., a rotating exhibition of 30 works by 23 artists.

https://gothamist.com/news/rikers-detain.title: Rikers detainee's death is at least the 9th in corrections department custody this year
https://gothamist.com/news/rikers-detain.author: Ryan Kost
https://gothamist.com/news/rikers-detain.text:
A 36-year-old man died on Rikers Island early Tuesday, according to the city’s Department of Correction.
A correction officer found the man in his bed at the Robert N. Davoren Center, according to the department. Staff called a medical emergency and he was pronounced dead just after 6 a.m. The department did not release a cause of death.
The department and court records identified the man as Cesar Mederocuret, though the Legal Aid Society, which represented him, identified him as Cesar Gabriel Medero Curet in a statement. Gothamist has reached out to the group and city officials for clarification.
He is at least the ninth person to die in the department’s custody this year and at least the second man to die in that particular facility. He had pleaded not guilty to charges of attempted second-degree murder, attempted first-degree assault and third-degree assault.
Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards said in a statement that “this profound loss weighs heavily on us all.”
The department said it will investigate the man’s death in coordination with city and state authorities.
The department said it had notified the court-appointed officials who are overseeing reforms on the island, as well as other state and local officials.
The Legal Aid Society said in its statement it had no information about the circumstances of the man’s death or what happened in his final moments. The group called for a swift, independent and impartial investigation into his death.

https://taz.de/Regisseur-Martin-McDonagh.title: Martin McDonagh über „Wild Horse Nine“: „Das ist mir beim Käseessen eingefallen“
https://taz.de/Regisseur-Martin-McDonagh.author: Jenni Zylka
https://taz.de/Regisseur-Martin-McDonagh.text:
Martin McDonagh über „Wild Horse Nine“: „Das ist mir beim Käseessen eingefallen“
Martin McDonaghs „Wild Horse Nine“ ist ein Spätagentenfilm. Der Regisseur spricht über Schuld und Reue und das Grün von Irland und der Osterinsel.
Der irische Regisseur und Dramatiker Martin McDonagh schreibt seit den 90er Jahren Theaterstücke. Sein 2004 entstandener Debütkurzfilm mit Brendan Gleeson wurde mit dem Kurzfilm-Oscar ausgezeichnet, mit Gleeson drehte er vier Jahre später auch sein Langfilmdebüt „Brügge sehen … und sterben?“ und 2022 „The Banshees of Inisherin“. McDonaghs vielfach ausgezeichnete schwarze Tragikomödie „Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri“ beschäftigte sich 2017 mit Gerechtigkeit und Protestformen in öffentlichen Räumen: Es geht darin um eine Frau, die angesichts des Mordes an ihrer Tochter ihre Kritik am Handeln des lokalen Polizeichefs auf Plakatwänden äußert. „Wild Horse Nine“ erzählt von den CIA-Agenten Chris und Lee, die kurz vor dem Militärputsch in Chile 1973 nach Rapa Nui entsandt werden. Der todkranke Chris schert sich dabei weder um Geheimhaltung noch um Konventionen, äußert sich gegenüber vermeintlichen Studentinnen lautstark über die Taktiken der CIA und begegnet seinem restlichen Leben mit galligem Humor.
taz: Herr McDonagh, in „Wild Horse Nine“ spielt John Malkovich den zynischen Chris, dem seine Loyalität und das Verdecken von beruflichem Fehlverhalten ebenso egal geworden ist wie das Befinden anderer Menschen. Was interessiert Sie an der Figur?
Der Film
„Wild Horse Nine“. Regie: Martin McDonagh. Mit John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell u. a. Vereinigtes Königreich/USA/Chile 2026, 118 Min.
Martin McDonagh: Wahrscheinlich hängt das mit meiner Angst zusammen, irgendwann mal selbst ein bisschen so wie Chris zu werden. Vor allem mag ich seine Unverschämtheit – als Drehbuchautor ist das durchaus befreiend, eine Figur zu schreiben, die meinen eigenen Gedanken und Gefühlen diametral entgegengesetzt ist. Man kann sie Dinge tun und sagen lassen, die man im echten Leben nie sagen würde, weil man ja dieser Figur treu bleiben muss. Sie dabei nicht zu bewerten, ist die Herausforderung.
taz: Woher stammt die Bitterkeit dieses Charakters?
McDonagh: Aus einer Enttäuschung – tief in Chris steckt ein stark empfindender Mann, in dessen ruhigen Momenten man diese Gefühle hoffentlich auch wahrnehmen kann. Der Film soll im Grunde eine Abhandlung über Schuld und Reue sein, darüber, dass jemand am Ende seines Lebens weiß, dass er nicht alles richtig machen konnte. Es bringt mir komischerweise Freude, so etwas zu schreiben.
taz: Malkovich und Sam Rockwell spielen Kollegen und enge Freunde. In Ihren Filmen gibt es oft Darstellungen von Männerfreundschaften – wie wichtig ist Freundschaft für Sie?
McDonagh: Das stimmt, schon seit „Brügge sehen … und sterben?“ erzähle ich von Männerfreundschaften. Ich glaube, das stammt aus meiner eigenen Erfahrung, ich fühle mich dabei sicher. In Hollywoodfilmen ist die Beschäftigung mit Männerfreundschaften eher unterrepräsentiert, da zeigt man lieber entweder oberflächliche „Buddys“ oder Konkurrenten. Aber tiefer in die männliche Psyche einzusteigen, diese Art von Männlichkeit darzustellen, das fasziniert mich. Sowohl in „Brügge“ als auch in „Wild Horse Nine“ grenzt die Freundschaft an eine Liebesbeziehung zwischen Männern. Und in meinem Film „The Banshees of Inisherin“ ging es quasi um das Ende einer solchen Männer-Liebesbeziehung.
taz: Kann ein desillusionierter Charakter wie Chris in einer generell nicht besonders hoffnungsvollen Zeit voller Gewalt und Misogynie denn dabei helfen, wieder an etwas zu glauben?
McDonagh: Das hoffe ich. Auch wenn beide Männer keine Helden sind, wahrscheinlich sind sie sogar selbst misogyn und politisch auf der dunklen Seite, haben sie etwas Anständiges – die Machenschaften der CIA bekanntzumachen, ist richtig. Und die Freundschaft zwischen den beiden ist real, das zu zeigen, war mir wichtig.
taz: Chris analysiert in einer Szene die Völker der Erde anhand ihrer Käsesorten – Länder mit offen schwulen Menschen produzieren demnach besseren Käse. Woher kommt das?
McDonagh: Das ist mir tatsächlich beim Käseessen eingefallen. Und da ist doch etwas Wahres dran – um guten Käse zu produzieren, muss man zufrieden sein.
wurde 1970 in London geboren. Er begann in den neunziger Jahren als Dramatiker zu arbeiten. Sein erster Spielfilm war „Brügge sehen … und sterben?“ (2008). „Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri“ lief 2017 im Wettbewerb von Venedig, wo auch „The Banshees of Inisherin“ 2022 Premiere feierte.
taz: Wofür steht Sam Rockwells Figur des Lee?
McDonagh: In der Beziehung steht sie für den sorgenden, liebevollen Teil, in dem ich persönlich mich eher wiederfinde. Er sollte natürlich den Gegenpart zu John bilden. Aber Johns Draufgängertum ist ohnehin nur gespielt – seine sanften Momente überwiegen zum Ende des Films.
taz: Malkovich hat im Film eine spezielle Art zu sprechen, die gleichzeitig gekünstelt und distanziert, dennoch überzeugend wirkt – haben Sie die gemeinsam entwickelt?
McDonagh: Die Zeilen selbst stehen alle so im Skript – Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich und ich haben allerdings vor dem Dreh ein oder zwei Wochen lang zusammen geprobt. John ist ein sehr geschickter Schauspieler, der alles naturalistisch klingen lassen kann, was man schreibt – beide haben einen Theaterhintergrund, sie können jeden Text so sprechen, als ob er ihnen gerade eingefallen ist.
Empfohlener externer Inhalt
Wir würden Ihnen hier gerne einen externen Inhalt zeigen. Sie entscheiden, ob Sie dieses Element auch sehen wollen:
Trailer „Wild Horse Nine“
Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung
taz: Wieso lassen Sie die Geschichte auf Rapa Nui, der Osterinsel, spielen?
McDonagh: Vor 15 Jahren reiste ich zum ersten Mal nach Rapa Nui, weil ich hoffte, die Insel als Figur in einer Geschichte nutzen zu können. Ich hatte mir verschiedene Plots überlegt, die alle nicht funktionierten – bis die Idee mit der US-Intervention in Chile durch die CIA dazukam, die die Wahl Allendes zum Staatspräsidenten verhindern wollte. Diese unerhörte Geschichte beschäftigt mich schon seit meinen Teenagerzeiten. Die beiden Dinge zusammenzubringen, war der Beginn des Films. Ursprünglich sollten es allerdings ein todkranker Vater und ein Sohn sein, die zusammen eine letzte Reise auf die Osterinsel machen – davon sind auch noch ein paar Merkmale in den Charakteren von Rockwell und Malkovich zu finden.
taz: Das Setting war also vor der Story vorhanden?
McDonagh: Ja, ich mochte das Geheimnis, das die Skulpturen, die Moai umgibt, und die Insel als solche ist ohnehin sehr hübsch mit ihrem vulkanischen Gestein und dem satten Grün, das mich an die irischen Arainn-Inseln erinnert. Am meisten haben mich aber die wilden Pferde überrascht, die sich frei auf der Insel bewegen – die habe ich darum mit eingebaut.
taz: Wie sind Sie dem konservatorischen Risiko begegnet, in der Nähe dieser historischen Figuren einen Film zu drehen?
McDonagh: Wir haben eng mit der Gemeinde dort zusammengearbeitet, hatten ihnen auch vorher das Drehbuch vorgelegt und erklärt, wie wir die Figuren filmen wollen, wo im Bild sie zu sehen sind. Um sicherzugehen, dass die Moai respektiert werden, dass ihnen nichts passiert, haben wir aufgepasst, dass wir nicht zu nahe an sie herankommen, man musste immer mindestens einen Meter entfernt von ihnen sein, darf sie ohnehin nicht anfassen.
taz: Das schwerwiegend unrechtmäßige Verhalten der CIA in Chile ist mehr oder weniger bekannt, gab es dennoch eine Reaktion der CIA auf Ihren Film?
McDonagh: Bislang nicht – und mich interessiert auch nicht wirklich, wie man den Film dort findet. Man weiß ja eh nicht, ob die CIA gerade mithört. Ich bin nicht mal sicher, ob es solche Menschen, die am Ende ihres Lebens Schuld und Reue für ihre politisch motivierten, falschen Aktivitäten empfinden, dort tatsächlich gibt. Manchmal wundere ich mich, dass man so etwas nicht öfter hört – wo bleiben etwa öffentliche Aussagen von Ex-CIA-Agenten, die sich schuldig fühlen, die ihr Verhalten oder das ihrer Behörde bereuen? Dieser Teil meiner Geschichte beruht tatsächlich auf reiner Erfindung.
taz: Sind CIA-Mitarbeiter in Ihren Augen böse Menschen?
McDonagh: Na ja, ich glaube schon, dass das vor allem Menschen sind. Aber ich will ihnen nicht vergeben. Und ich würde mich ehrlich freuen, mehr über ihre Zweifel und ihr Bedauern zu hören.

Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. https://www.humanite.fr/monde/afrique/se.title: Sénégal : des dizaines de familles de migrants affligées après le naufrage meurtrier
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/afrique/se.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/afrique/se.text:
Sur la côte de Thieppe au nord-est du Sénégal, trente-neuf corps d’aspirants à l’exil ont été retrouvés sur la plage. L’embarcation, qui a fait naufrage vendredi 6 novembre, pourrait avoir transporté au moins 150 personnes. Sur place, les familles des disparus dénoncent la migration irrégulière et son lot de tragédies.
Sur l’immense plage près de la commune de Thieppe, au nord-est du Sénégal, Ibrahima Diaw confie son incompréhension en contemplant la pirogue brisée à bord de laquelle son fils a embarqué en espérant rejoindre l’Europe, avant d’y perdre la vie. « La mer est un mystère pour moi », souffle le vieil homme.
Les secours ont repêché 39 corps sans vie sur ces plages de sable fin depuis le naufrage de cette embarcation vendredi 6 novembre. Un bilan provisoire qui est déjà l’un des plus élevés de ces dernières années. Cet énième drame de l’exil endeuille une nouvelle fois ce pays ouest-africain, où de nombreux jeunes tentent régulièrement de rejoindre l’archipel espagnol des Canaries par la dangereuse route atlantique.

https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Mahmoud Darwish
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
I Am Yusuf, My Father
I am Yusuf, my father. My brothers do not love me,
Father, do not want me among them. They attack me,
pelting me with stones and words. They want me to
die, that they may say my eulogy. In my face they’ve
shut your door, and from the field they’ve driven me.
They’ve poisoned my grapes, Father. They’ve smashed
my playthings, Father. When the breeze blew and
ruffled my hair, jealous, they rose up against me, and
against you. But what have I done to them, Father?
Butterflies alighted on my shoulders, ears of grain
bent toward me, birds perched upon my hands. So
what have I done, Father? Why me? You named me
Yusuf, and they cast me into the well, but blamed the
wolf. The wolf is more merciful than my brothers…
oh, my father! Did I wrong anyone when I said that:
I saw eleven stars, saw the sun, and the moon, saw
them prostrate before me?
(Translated from the Arabic by Barbara Romaine)

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ho.title: US House Democrat leader Jeffries will retain position despite opposition, sources say
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ho.author: Yasmine El-Sabawi
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ho.text:
US House Democrat leader Jeffries will retain position despite opposition, sources say
The top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, is all but certain to become the next Speaker of the House, despite dissatisfaction among some freshman lawmakers and their progressive colleagues in the chamber, sources have told Middle East Eye.
There simply is no alternative leader in the running.
"It's a cost to go against someone who will eventually be the leader of the caucus. There's not enough people who are willing to do that," one source said.
This comes as many voters have expressed their desire to see Jeffries vacate the position, accusing him of being out of step with the party's growing leftist progressive wing, which wants to see money out of politics, and a stop to the transfer of weapons to Israel.
New lawmakers are looking to work with him instead, three sources familiar with the internal process on Capitol Hill confirmed to MEE.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The 56-year-old Jeffries is backed by pro-Israel lobbying groups and has made it clear he is an avowed protector of Israel. He has also received substantial financial support from a litany of big corporations, including tech and weapons manufacturers.
Perhaps most importantly, his candidacy in his New York district and his leadership bid were endorsed by progressive kingmaker and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani - much to the chagrin of Mamdani's own supporters.
Mamdani is largely credited with setting off a wave of young Democratic Socialists launching campaigns for office.
Just before the 3 November midterm elections, Redbox Research's polling showed only 19 percent of Democratic voters want to keep Jeffries as their leader in Congress.
A Change.org petition last week already had one million signatures calling for him to step aside.
The Speaker of the House is second in line to the US presidency, after the vice president. Jeffries, in particular, would also become the first Black lawmaker to ever assume the role.
"I would suspect most Democrats will think twice about about blocking that historic achievement - even if they have other concerns about Jeffries," Chris Edelson, a constitutional scholar and political science lecturer at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst, told MEE on Tuesday.
'Undecided'
The vote, which is done through secret ballot, is set for next week. The 120th Congress will be sworn in on 3 January 2027.
Speaking to reporters during their new member onboarding session this week, some of the most progressive, pro-Palestine, political novices made it clear they are willing to work with anyone who shares their goal of delivering for voters - even though they were specifically asked about whether they would back Jeffries.
"This was a historic class [of new lawmakers], one that has a lot of firsts," Colorado Representative-elect Melat Kiros said.
"We might have different ideas about how to accomplish certain things, but we all agree that we have to reduce costs for families. We all agree that we have to root out corruption in government. We all agree that our foreign policy has to actually reflect our values. In order for us to be able to do that, we need an agenda that's bold enough to meet that vision," she said.
"And so what we're demanding is an agenda. It's not about the individual. It's about what kind of priorities, what kind of floor votes, what kind of plan do we have to actually fight."
New Jersey Representative-elect Adam Hamawy maintained the group is "undecided".
"We're not going to rubber stamp anything. We want to sit and have a conversation about the issues and what's the plan going forward. And I think that's what the American people elected us to do, is to have these conversations," he said.
Ohio Representative-elect Don Leonard, however, posted a video on Instagram on Monday, making it clear he'd been told there would be consequences for not voting for Jeffries.
"I met with... senior members of the Democratic House, who told me in no uncertain terms that the decision as to whether or not I support Jeffries, regardless of his willingness to speak with me and meet the interests of my constituents on a couple of key issues... would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next two years here in Washington, as well as being sure to lose my election in two years," he said.
Those key issues, he explained, were getting corporate money out of politics, and ending US support for Israel and its wars in the region.
"The big 'D' Democratic Party needs some little 'd' democracy," Leonard added.
On Tuesday, Republicans came together to declare Trump loyalist and Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan as their leader in the House for the next session, and to keep South Dakota Senator John Thune as the minority leader in the Senate.
Senate tussle
Indeed, ensuring that party members get in line is, in effect, the job of the leader.
Building personal relationships is critical in the corridors of power, Neil Sroka, a former progressive strategist, told MEE on Tuesday.
"It's not just ideological [matters] that drive decision-making behind who's a [Senate] Majority Leader and who's a Speaker of the House. There are regional concerns, there are state delegation concerns, and so the politics of it are very complicated, and I don't envy any member of Congress or a member of the US Senate who are trying to figure out how to navigate those complicated waters, and especially in an ideologically complicated result as in this election."
If someone's leadership bid is potentially threatened, it could be the top Democrat in the Senate, the 75-year-old Chuck Schumer, sources told MEE. At the very least, his support base would be eroded even if he retains his post, and he would have to make room for the left-wing flank to bring their issues to the floor.
He is even more unpopular among Democratic voters than Jeffries, polling at just 11 percent favourability.
'Schumer’s foreign policy record is a serious liability for his continued leadership'
- Cavan Kharrazian, senior policy adviser, Demand Progress
The New York senator is also backed by corporate interests and is a staunch supporter of Israel, as well as a hawk on Iran, even if he didn't like the way President Donald Trump himself carried out a seemingly endless war.
"Politics matters to some extent, but it also matters who a senator is going to see in the Senate gym," Sroka explained. "That's what we recalled back from the 2018 race - even though there might have been some agita about Leader Schumer and whether or not he was really in line with the rest of the Senate, he had everyone on speed dial. Everyone knew him really well, and it was very hard to step outside of that lane."
On Tuesday, anti-war activists from Code Pink, among other groups, staged a protest outside Schumer's office after being locked out by his staff, they said.
They were specifically protesting against the $1.5 trillion budget requested by the Trump administration for the Department of War, which will have to go through the Senate.
The bill also includes a provision that would permanently integrate US and Israeli military tech advancements in a way that would - as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put it - turn Israel from a foreign aid recipient to a full-scale partner.
Only one senator with some limited backing to be speaker has emerged as a vocal advocate of such a move: Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen. He is perhaps the Senate's most visible progressive voice on foreign policy, after Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders.
Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has already said for months he would like to see Van Hollen elected as the top Democrat in the Senate, even though the senator had not shown interest in the position.
"I have said that I am in listening mode," Van Hollen told a reporter on Capitol Hill this week. "There are clearly lots of people around the country, and a number of our members, quite a few of our members, who want to have this discussion, and so I'm in active listening mode... I haven't closed the door."
Cavan Kharrazian, a senior policy adviser with the group Demand Progress, told MEE that Schumer's record comes into sharper focus now that Van Hollen has emerged as a possibility.
"Van Hollen has been at the forefront in the Senate of challenging unconditional support for Israel and has made clear he will oppose funding legislation in the lame duck [session]," he said. "That puts real pressure on Schumer to take a firm stand against war funding... and explain how he can lead his caucus in the direction voters are demanding after spending so much of his career resisting it."
Schumer has long been criticised as being too soft on Trump since his first term from 2016-2020, and the backlash against the current administration in the midterm elections has, if anything, shown that Democrats want fighters to represent them.
“Schumer’s foreign policy record is a serious liability for his continued leadership," Kharrazian said. "The midterms underscored the need for leaders who will confront Trump’s reckless wars and forge a new foreign policy grounded in diplomacy, human rights, and people’s needs at home," Kharrazian added.
