https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: DF é o único estado do país não habilitado para receber novos recursos da Política Nacional Aldir Blanc
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Distrito Federal (DF) é o único estado do país que não foi habilitado para receber os novos recursos da Política Nacional Aldir Blanc de Fomento à Cultura. A informação foi divulgada na tarde desta terça-feira (10) pelo Ministério da Cultura (MinC). De acordo com o órgão, foram habilitados 26 estados, em aferição no dia 30 de outubro, que atingiram o percentual mínimo de 60% de execução exigido para cumprir o requisito da continuidade dos repasses.
O MinC observou que o Distrito Federal recebe recursos da Aldir Blanc tanto na condição de estado quanto na de município. Dos R$ 15,79 milhões destinados ao DF, foram executados apenas 5,78%, o equivalente a R$ 912 mil. Já na condição de município, o DF recebeu R$ 17,3 milhões e gastou R$ 515 mil, o que representa 2,97%. Os dados estão disponíveis no Painel de Dados da política, disponível no site do MinC.
Embora não tenha alcançado o percentual mínimo de 60% na avaliação estadual de outubro, o DF ainda poderá atingir o índice exigido para a parcela municipal, cuja aferição está prevista para 14 de dezembro de 2026.
Segundo o ministério, a aferição verifica a execução de, no mínimo, 60% dos recursos considerados no cálculo, conforme as regras da Portaria MinC nº 243/2025, atualizada pela Portaria nº 319/2026. No levantamento, os estados habilitados apresentaram percentuais iguais ou superiores ao limite estabelecido. A habilitação por execução financeira representa o cumprimento de uma das condições para o próximo repasse, que depende ainda dos demais requisitos previstos na regulamentação.
Consulta e prazo para recurso
O Distrito Federal pode apresentar recurso no prazo de 20 dias após a publicação do comunicado no Diário Oficial da União (DOU), realizado no dia 9 de novembro.
Caso não consiga reverter a situação, o DF não receberá a parcela correspondente no exercício financeiro. O repasse poderá ser solicitado no exercício seguinte, mediante cumprimento dos requisitos, sem possibilidade de acumular parcelas.
Em comunicado, a Secretaria de Cultura do DF informou que existem quatro processos seletivos em andamento, que somam R$ 28,84 milhões: o Edital nº 15/2026 – Produções Audiovisuais e Produções Culturais (R$ 23,05 milhões); o Edital nº 19/2026 – Pontos de Cultura (R$ 3,6 milhões); o Edital nº 20/2026 – Premiação de Pontos e Pontões de Cultura (R$ 900 mil); e o Edital nº 21/2026 – Pontões de Cultura (R$ 1,29 milhão).
Segundo a pasta, o Edital nº 15/2026, que concentra a maior parte dos recursos, já se encontra na fase de recursos contra o resultado da análise de mérito, com previsão de pagamento aos agentes culturais contemplados na primeira semana de dezembro. A conclusão desse processo permitirá ao Distrito Federal alcançar os percentuais superiores ao mínimo de 60% de execução dos recursos recebidos nas modalidades Estado e Município.
A Secec também apontou que “mantém diálogo com o Ministério da Cultura para alinhar os procedimentos de execução e aferição das metas. Em 29 de outubro de 2026, foi encaminhado ofício ao Ministério, disponibilizado na íntegra a seguir, apresentando as particularidades do modelo adotado pelo DF e solicitando tratamento compatível com seu regime jurídico-constitucional próprio”.
A pasta garantiu o compromisso com a execução da política e assegura que “os percentuais mínimos de 60%, tanto dos recursos estaduais quanto dos municipais, serão alcançados até a primeira quinzena de dezembro de 2026, possibilitando a destinação dos recursos ao fomento cultural e aos agentes culturais do DF”.
Aldir Blanc
Criada pela Lei nº 14.399/2022, a Política Nacional Aldir Blanc estabelece o financiamento contínuo de ações culturais em todo o país, por meio da transferência de recursos federais para estados, Distrito Federal e municípios. A previsão é de R$ 15 bilhões ao longo de cinco repasses, em dois ciclos, com parcelas de até R$ 3 bilhões. No primeiro ciclo foram repassados R$ 3 bilhões e, na primeira parcela do segundo ciclo, foram repassados aproximadamente R$ 2,5 bi aos entes federativos.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: French far-right author Zemmour launches second bid for 2027 presidency
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
French far-right author Zemmour launches second bid for 2027 presidency
Zemmour wants to kick out ‘foreign unemployed people’ after last month’s violent protests.
French far-right Eric Zemmour, known for his anti-Islam and anti-immigrant stance, says he’ll be standing in next year’s presidential election.
“I can confirm to you that I will indeed be a candidate in the presidential election”, Zemmour told TF1 TV, adding that he was running to “keep a France that is French”.
Zemmour, a 68-year-old Jewish author and veteran television commentator, finished fourth in the 2022 presidential election.
This time, he says he wants to expel foreign offenders who are in prison, as well as “foreign unemployed people who have been out of work for more than six months”, even if they are legal residents.
He says he wants “two million fewer immigrants” in France, who are seen by many among the far right as key instigators of violence during last month’s student-led cost of living protests.
Last month’s violence has led to the soaring popularity of frontrunner Marine Le Pen, with whom Zemmour will be competing against in April 2027.
Le Pen, who is the leader of the far-right National Rally party, is widely projected to win the election to replace Emmanuel Macron, who will end his term as president of France.
Meanwhile, far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, who has been accused of encouraging the unrest, unveiled his programme on Saturday to some 17,000 supporters.

https://hyperallergic.com/mexican-duo-ro.title: Mexican Duo RojoNegro Installs Colossal Work on UC San Diego Campus
https://hyperallergic.com/mexican-duo-ro.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/mexican-duo-ro.text:
Mexican Duo RojoNegro Installs Colossal Work on UC San Diego Campus
María Sosa and Noé Martínez, the Michoacán artists representing Mexico at the Venice Biennale, hand-painted 260 ceramic tiles for the installation.
Sometimes, the best lessons are taught outside the classroom. Though still embedded on a college campus, a new artwork in San Diego brings a wealth of Mesoamerican history to the public commons, imparting ancient customs and knowledge that resisted colonial extinction efforts to the next generation.
A permanent outdoor artwork by RojoNegro, the duo representing Mexico at the 61st Venice Biennale, was recently unveiled on the University of California, San Diego (UCSD) campus. Comprising 260 unique, hand-painted ceramic tiles mounted on four tree-like panels, “La asamblea del barro” (2026) probes the transmission of cultural memory across generations by drawing on the relationship between Mesoamerican and Western knowledge that is inextricably connected through colonialism.
Hailing from Michoacán and based in Mexico City, RojoNegro artists and life partners María Sosa, who has Purépecha roots, and Noé Martínez, whose family origins trace back to Mexico's Huasteca region, use their multidisciplinary practice to bring Indigenous ways of being to the foreground. Together, they disrupt dominant colonial narratives and legacies by invoking the ancestral knowledge imbued in materials and practices that have endured four centuries of violent erasure.
“In 'La asamblea del barro,' we include the four cosmic trees that sustain the universe in Mesoamerican thought, an idea that lives on among our Indigenous peoples and bears witness to a cultural and ideological resistance that reveals the profound relationship between the body, its surroundings, and the forces of nature,” RojoNegro explained in a statement on the artwork.

https://taz.de/Die-umstrittene-Linken-Po.text:
Debatte um Linkspartei-Politikerin Emde : Ihr wird zu viel Bedeutung beigemessen
Die umstrittene Vanessa Emde aus Berlin-Neukölln wird viel zu wichtig genommen. Es kann nicht sei, dass von ihr Rot-Grün-Rot abhängt.
T raut man der medialen Aufregung der vergangenen Wochen, dann hängen Wohl und Wehe der deutschen Hauptstadt an einer einzigen Frau. Wird Vanessa Emde im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus in der Linksfraktion Platz nehmen oder nicht? Das ist im Grunde eine Provinzposse. Doch SPD und Grüne haben sie, von hyperventilierenden Medien getrieben, zu einer Schicksalsfrage von nationaler Tragweite aufgeblasen. Berlins SPD-Chef Steffen Krach hat es sogar zur Bedingung für eine Koalition mit der Linken erklärt, dass sie Emde aus ihrer Fraktion ausschließt. Das ist absurd.
Ja, manche Aussagen von Emde sind streitbar. Strategisch klug und solidarisch von ihr war es auch nicht, sich in einem Instagram-Video von einer Erklärung zu distanzieren, die sie erst kurz zuvor mit allen Abgeordneten ihrer Fraktion unterschrieben hatte. Und es mutet etwas bizarr an, vor dem Parteitag der Linken in Berlin gegen die eigene Partei zu demonstrieren, statt sich im Saal für die eigene Person starkzumachen. Aber die Aufregung um Emde trägt Züge einer Hexenjagd. „Offener Antisemitismus“, wie manche ihr vorwerfen, sieht jedenfalls anders aus. Und hat die Hauptstadt sonst keine Probleme?
Emde wird zu viel Bedeutung beigemessen, von allen Seiten. Dass es nun so wirkt, als könnte ihre Fraktion sie vor allem aufgrund äußeren Drucks ausschließen, ist fatal. Die Linke erweckt damit den Eindruck, sie werde von ihren Koalitionspartnern in spe getrieben. Dabei ist es allein ihre Sache, wie sie mit ihrer Abgeordneten umgeht.
Von Emde allein hängt aber auch nicht die Zukunft der Palästinasolidarität in der Partei ab. Es wäre ja schon ein Fortschritt, wenn die Berliner Polizei damit aufhören würde, Demonstranten zu verprügeln, die gegen Israels Kriege demonstrieren, und sie nicht mehr jede Bagatelle mit aller Härte verfolgen würde. Eine linke Bürgermeisterin könnte das ändern.

https://www.humanite.fr/medias/assemblee.title: Pétition contre CNews : l’Assemblée nationale classe (une nouvelle fois) sans suite l’expression légitime de la colère des citoyens
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/assemblee.author: Caroline Constant
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/assemblee.text:
Après la mise aux oubliettes de la pétition sur la loi Duplomb (2 millions de signatures), puis sur « le permis de tuer » pour les policiers (732 000), c’est au tour de la pétition contre CNews (1 066 880 signatures à cette heure) de servir de paillasson à la droite, le tout sous couvert de liberté d’expression. Un comble.
Ça s’est joué à un cheveu, ou plus précisément à trois voix près : l’Assemblée Nationale ne discutera pas de la très problématique chaîne CNews, malgré 1 066 880 signatures de citoyens recueillies en un temps record depuis l’attentat de Trappes, le 23 novembre dernier. 28 députés de la commission des affaires culturelles ont voté pour le classement de la pétition, et 25 contre.
Pour Alexandre Porter, son président (LR), la pétition est « en dehors des compétences de notre commission ». Il a proposé « l’organisation d’un grand débat, en séance publique, sur l’avenir de la presse, la liberté d’expression, la régulation des médias, la lutte contre les ingérences étrangères et l’influence des réseaux sociaux ». Ce sera à la conférence des présidents, qui réunit les onze présidents de groupe, de décider de la tenue ou pas d’un débat de cette nature.
« Une fréquence, ça se mérite, ça ne souille pas »
La pétition avait été lancée en juin dernier par Lucas Massoni, un citoyen ulcéré des digues toujours franchies en matière de racisme par CNews. Il demandait notamment la suppression du Canal TNT de la chaîne de Vincent Bolloré. « Une fréquence, ça se mérite, ça ne se souille pas », a-t-il notamment indiqué.
Or, ces fréquences appartiennent à l’État, elles sous louées aux chaînes, et donc sous contrat. Il avait énuméré les manquements à ce contrat de CNews (27 rappels à l’ordre par l’Arcom depuis 2019), 52 sanctions contre la défunte C98 et CNews, dont 16 pour la seule année 2024, ainsi qu’une longue liste d’amendes.
C’est à l’Arcom, successeur du CSA et gendarme de l’audiovisuel, de se prononcer sur ce genre de sujet, mais l’Arcom manque de moyens et a les mains liées. Surtout, le débat lancé par cette pétition dépasse l’Arcom, et pose la question des limites, posées par la loi, de la liberté d’expression, et de leur respect, sous peine de pourrir le débat démocratique. Visiblement, respecter la loi du 13 juillet 1990, dite loi Gayssot, c’est trop demander aux députés.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Rethinking the Early History of North America
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Ned Blackhawk
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Zones of Encounter
Rethinking the early history of North America
Rethinking the Early History of North America
Peter Mancall’s new book reframes the history of the American continent as a zone of encounters between Native peoples, European empires, and African societies.
On October 12, 1992, the commemorations for the 500th anniversary of Columbus’s landfall were uneven. Urban gatherings were moderately sized, but the mood was often less than celebratory. In Columbus, Ohio, the city’s $95 million floral and garden exposition drew roughly half the expected number of visitors. In Berkeley, California, the city defiantly reclaimed the date as Indigenous People’s Day, while in Nevada, an antinuclear gathering took place at a US Department of Energy test site, co-organized by Western Shoshone activists. Few festive events marked the quincentenary; fewer still generated national attention. By contrast, a century earlier, the 400th anniversary of Columbus’s arrival served as an occasion to celebrate—so much so that one of the country’s largest fairs ever was held in its honor, Chicago’s Columbian Exposition. But not so in 1992, when Columbus Day largely came and went.
Another date that has seen a dramatic shift in how it has been memorialized is 1776. Synonymous with the founding of the United States, 1776 has been treated by generations of Americans as part of a broader civilizational story: the westward expansion of European peoples, institutions, and political traditions. Within that framework, national commemorations form essential chapters in a single narrative linking European arrival to nationhood, thus blurring the distinction between the history of Europeans in what would become North America and the history of the United States itself.
Books in review
Contested Continent: The Struggle for North America, c. 1000-1680
Buy this book
But over the past 40 or so years, a remarkable shift has occurred. More recent interpretations attempt to disentangle the history of colonization from that of the US Constitution. In this view, the United States is understood less as the political expression of European settlement than as a particular constitutional project: one grounded in republican government, in the institutions and philosophies articulated in the Declaration and then codified in the Constitution. Such interpretations do not deny the centrality of European colonization to the nation; rather, they critically reexamine North American and US history to foreground the peoples excluded, displaced, or subordinated by it. Native nations, enslaved Africans, and non-Anglo populations claimed as well as rejected the United States. In this interpretive framework, the history of the United States is not reducible to the history of Europeans in North America, even if European settlement formed its precondition.
The 12-hour PBS series The American Revolution reflects this interpretive shift. Its opening episodes foreground historians of Native America, seeking to widen the traditional narrative beyond a familiar story of colonial resistance to Britain. In doing so, the series implicitly asks whether 1776 should be remembered primarily as the triumph of a particular people in its struggle toward self-government, or as the beginning of a contingent experiment in such government. With more than half a dozen historians of Native America foregrounding the latter, the series details how the republic was founded, witnessed, and carried forward by a range of peoples and perspectives—peoples and perspectives that became more diverse with continental expansion.
Into this interpretive fray comes the latest offering in the venerable Oxford History of the United States, a now 10-volume series that, in the words of its publisher, “blends social, political, economic, cultural, diplomatic, and military history into coherent and vividly written narrative.” Initiated under the coeditorship of C. Vann Woodward and Richard Hofstadter in the 1960s, the series has become in many ways the Cadillac of US historical production: tomes written by master craftsmen without a female or minority author among them (yet). The books are not necessarily flashy but instead reflect the boxy and somewhat stodgy assumptions of the postwar historiography from which the series was born: sweeping national narratives organized around the development of the United States as a political, constitutional, and national project.
Peter Mancall’s Contested Continent joins these celebrated studies while also subtly unsettling the framework on which the series was built. Covering the period from 1000 to 1680, Mancall’s book offers the broadest chronological and geographic coverage of any of the volumes to date, stretching across a vast Atlantic world that encompasses Native peoples, European empires, African societies, and the unstable zones of encounter connecting them. Rather than treating the United States as the inevitable center of the narrative, Mancall uses these landscapes to frame a history in continental rather than national terms: a far-reaching “struggle for North America.”
That shift in scale and perspective mirrors the broader changes in historical interpretation that are now shaping commemorative debates. Earlier volumes in the series generally operated within the gravitational pull of the nation-state. Their organizing assumption was that US history could be narrated as the development of a single political society that moved, however unevenly and even hypocritically, toward national consolidation. Mancall’s study instead reflects the growing influence of Atlantic history, Native history, and borderlands scholarship, all of which have challenged nation-centered narratives. Such studies emphasize movement, contingency, competing sovereignty, and the permeability of imperial borders. The result is a history less concerned with national origins than with the larger continental and imperial processes out of which the United States emerged.
In so doing, Mancall draws on a remarkable range of sources, an impressive command of the field, and a clear narrative style. Unlike many comparable works, Contested Continent is exceedingly well referenced. Sources are used so extensively that Mancall reveals how laborious an undertaking it is to tackle this bewildering, not exactly global, not exactly continental, not exactly national history—a notoriously vast undertaking that ranges across geographies, times, and climes. Nowhere do eventual national borders and boundaries offer analytical comfort.
To give structure to this seemingly boundless inquiry, Mancall leans on the political constructions and material limits of the time—charting the development of European empires across the natural limits that land and sea then imposed for the movement of peoples, flora, and fauna. Starting with the introduction of maize in Native America, and then venturing to the Nordic expansions across the North Atlantic before settling into the more familiar Atlantic empires, Contested Continent captures the forces of technological and human movement that wove together the four continents that became forever conjoined after 1492. This Atlantic world has defined the modern era. Its histories of exploration, settlement, missionization, plantation economics, and racial formation generated the eventual origins of what would become North America and the United States, doing so empire by empire, peoples by peoples, and ultimately death by death.
While its nearly 700-page narrative doesn’t reach 1776, Contested Continent illuminates the tensions between writing the history of the Atlantic world and attempting to connect that project to national history. Notably, the 400-year history of North America before 1492 is condensed into a single chapter. By contrast, Columbus receives such extended coverage in the second chapter that readers might forget Mancall’s earlier insistence that American history extends deep into the pre-Columbian world. Twenty pages aim to yet again reinterpret the famous mariner whose 1493 letter saw quick publication “in Strasbourg, Valladolid, Florence, Heidelberg, Augsburg, Nuremberg, Venice, Pavia, Lübeck, Ferrara, Bologna, Burgos, Brescia, and Milan, as well as continuing to appear in printers’ works from Rome and Basel.” The first European images of the Western Hemisphere also accompanied his writings, several of which are included to illustrate the seismic recalibrations unleashed after his first voyage. Although Columbus may no longer be celebrated as the “discoverer” of North America, Contested Continent squarely positions him as a central hand in writing the resulting history.
Though brief, the book’s opening chapter does set the analytical framework for interrogating the more traditional national histories that follow. One of Mancall’s most significant methodological moves is that he develops the book’s narrative within a frame of confrontation and conflict. Violence, gritty and repugnant, is a central if not defining force in Contested Continent.
If you’re unfamiliar with the loss of life after 1492, brace yourself. Taking a less deterministic and epidemiological perspective than Jared Diamond does in Guns, Germs, and Steel, Mancall examines European expeditions alongside studies of Indigenous history and culture. Chilling conclusions abound: From the Andes to the St. Lawrence and from Puerto Rico to the Mississippi, European explorers rushed across the hemisphere with a ferocity often forgotten by subsequent historians, particularly those in the United States. In this sense, Contested Continent stands apart from the other volumes in the Oxford series—despite many calls to broaden US history, too few view that history apart from its eventual or current territorial form. By immersing the reader in a nearly global history of the post-Columbian world, Contested Continent reveals the ubiquitous violence and suffering at its core.
Although it may be surprising to those who were raised on the celebratory Cold War version of US history, contemporaneous studies of early America remain as sobering as they are compelling. Slavery, Indigenous holocaust, and violent social relations characterize works in the field, especially those on the 17th-century world of exploration, settlement, and fracture. Several of Mancall’s concluding chapter titles convey such an emphasis—for example, “Enslavement” and “An Empire for Extraction.”
A second analytical contribution of Contested Continent lies in its treatment of imperial governance as inseparable from the intellectual, political, and legal resistance that it provoked. While specialists can point to comparable works, Mancall assembles hundreds of discrete studies into broader forms and then keeps on going, both chronologically and interpretively. By synthesizing the historical literature in this way, he demonstrates how instantly European imperialism became not only a global phenomenon but also a governing project formed in the face of open and reasoned resistance. Close studies of the writings of the Andean author Guamán Poma de Ayala, the Mexica scribes of the Florentine Codex, and (most indelibly) the 16th-century works of Bartolomé de Las Casas cement this effort, offering vivid contemporary accounts of European expansion and, ultimately, genocide. “To Las Casas,” Mancall observes, “writing a history was a form of bearing witness.” His Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies was among the 43 volumes published in Seville alone by 1552. The everyday ubiquity of the printing revolution, Mancall notes, became one of 1492’s most immediate legacies: “Once printers started spreading stories about the Western Hemisphere, they never stopped.” Las Casas’s text “would soon become the most influential European published work about the Western Hemisphere since the 1493 publication of Columbus.”
Read together, these anti-colonial writings—old and new—recast the violence of conquest not as an unfortunate by-product of cultural collision but as the result of deliberate choices made by imperial powers in full view of contemporary critique. As Greg Grandin has similarly suggested in America, América, Las Casas’s writings and his conversion from colonizer to priest and from participant to advocate offered what should be understood as the first condemnation of global colonialism. Such condemnation both preceded English colonization and was understood across Europe.
Another fierce critic of this emerging order was Guamán Poma. As he toured the Viceroyalty of Peru, Mancall writes, Guamán Poma was inspired to offer a bracing account of “the tragedy that had unfolded over the course of his own life.” Like Las Casas, he had witnessed cruelties and indignities. In his eventual but long-unpublished epic work, El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (The First New Chronicle and Good Government), Guamán Poma lamented how “all the demons of hell had come forth in order to trouble the poor of Jesus Christ.” Andean leaders were routinely assaulted, whipped, beaten, and hanged. Urbanization and exile followed: Lima had become “full of Indians who had abandoned their communities and African slaves who had escaped from their masters and become servants, even officials.” Such heterogeneity took a particular toll on Indigenous women, often forced into economies of sexual exploitation that filled the vacuum left in the conquest’s wake. Violence shaped the foundations of the family as Indigenous women became, in Guamán Poma’s words, “loaded down with mestizo and mulatto children.” One wonders when the sexual violence against Indigenous women so evident on these pages will find a more central place in the history of the Americas.
Mancall ultimately carries the analytical frames of imperialism, violence, and disruption into the English colonial world, connecting the national narrative to the continental, imperial, and even interpersonal dynamics that produced it. In English plantation societies, indentured servants drawn from colonies closer to home, such as Ireland, supplied much of the earliest generations of laborers. From Virginia to Barbados, the demand in Europe inspired the introduction of new export products, particularly tobacco and sugar. Harsh disciplinary regimes followed. “I have seen such cruelty there done to Servants, as I did not think one Christian could have done to another,” reported an early writer on Irish laborers in Barbados. By 1660, Mancall writes, sugar had so revolutionized the island’s economy that English leaders “concluded that they could not attract sufficient indentured labor across Britain’s current colonies. The most reliable source of labor, the king believed, was captive Africans.” Only after 1492, then, did institutions of human enslavement begin to structure North America and the United States thereafter.
Deftly capturing large-scale economic and social dynamics, Mancall also remains attentive to everyday forms of resistance, particularly in the late 1600s, when multiple imperial regimes either fell or were challenged by social and anti-colonial revolts. He ends with the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 and highlights the fractures of empires rather than their totalizing outcomes. By 1680, along the Rio Grande, dozens of Pueblo Indian villages had endured generations of Spanish violence, religious persecution, and labor drafts. What at the time were—and still remain today—the oldest continually inhabited human societies in what would become the United States, Pueblo nations organized and revolted against the yoke of colonization, destroying Spanish colonial churches, symbols, and archives. It is within this dialectical encounter between cultures and communities that Mancall locates what would become North America: “Nowadays,” he writes, “scholars recognize that, even if most of the written evidence emphasized Europeans’ actions, Indigenous Americans and Africans, even those brutalized by enslavement, retained agency as well.” However violent, however fractious and agonistic, “Indigenous, Africans, and Europeans together created a new world.”
In certain respects, Contested Continent perfectly prepares the way for the rediscovery of this knowledge and a new American history to be written thereafter. Throughout his sweeping account, Mancall demonstrates that the continent was never a wilderness awaiting European discovery. It was a world of competing sovereignties, economies, and cosmologies that Europeans entered into unevenly and often precariously. By tracing the contingencies of conquest, diplomacy, migration, and survivance across the continent, he helps challenge the triumphalist narratives that still frame the United States as the inevitable product of an Anglo-American political tradition alone. In this way, Contested Continent’s strongest contribution lies less in proposing a revised commemorative framework than in revealing the instability of older ones.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
At the same time, the book stops short of fully resolving the problem it so clearly identifies: If the North American continent and, with it, the republic that emerged rely on competing historical claims, then the question is not merely how historians recover neglected voices but also how those recoveries intervene in the broader scholarly and public conversations. Contested Continent gestures toward this challenge without entirely articulating what a rediscovered national story might finally look like. After chronicling more than 600 years of history, perhaps Mancall felt that he had covered enough, but he concludes somewhat abruptly in 1680, thereby ceding much of the telling of this story to the older volumes in the series. Because the interventions of Contested Continent are so persuasive, the book gives rise to the question of what a new history of the United States that begins with Mancall’s volume might look like—and it also raises the question of whether, in fact, the Oxford series, which began publishing in 1982, might be in need of a reset.
What would be the central themes and preoccupations of this new series of US histories? First, there would be a shift away from viewing the United States as a linear extension of European settlement and republican ideology and toward a more rigorous understanding of North America as a site of encounter among many peoples whose collective interactions shaped the continent’s subsequent development. Native nations, enslaved Africans, imperial rivals, missionaries, merchants, and migrants would no longer be peripheral actors in this new rendering of American history. Instead, they would be constitutive agents initiating the processes from which the nation emerged.
Second, there would be a more sustained focus on the contested nature of sovereignty in the development of the United States, thereby correcting the current, overly familiar accounts of state formation that portray US expansion as coherent, consensual, or inevitable. Empires and nations would be front and center, but so too would be the many who challenged and resisted them: local, Native, colonial, African American, all engaged in their own ongoing experiments in government.
Finally, this new account of US history would integrate the authoritarian dynamics of empire into the story of American modernity itself. Imprinted upon the globe in so many places—from the Philippines to Puerto Rico, Alaska to Hawai’i—unbridled US authority has governed millions of non-subject populations, often through force. Rooted in the suppression of Native resistance, the legacies of such anti-democratic practices are becoming more evident, and they inform current efforts to extend US authority into new colonial settings, from Venezuela to Greenland.
Histories of struggle and survival thus become essential means through which to understand our modern American life. Deep, immersive histories like Mancall’s offer contrasts with those that view modernity as the achievement of a unified liberal republic or the fulfillment of Enlightenment philosophies and capitalist economics.
Such a rediscovered American history would not dissolve the national history into fragmentation. Instead, it would recast the nation as a perpetually unfinished project, a “more perfect union” whose legitimacy depends on recognizing the many peoples who have sustained that experiment over time. In this light, the uneasy commemorations of the recent past would reveal less a collapse of national mythologies than a transformation in historical consciousness. The celebratory confidence that animated the Columbian Exposition of 1893 was undergirded by a presumption that establishing the nation was itself the accomplishment of progress, rather than marking these founding moments as the birth of experiments whose causes and consequences were yet to be determined.
Ultimately, Contested Continent suggests that moments of “discovery” and “founding” should not lend themselves easily to uncritical celebration. The American Revolution gave rise to an unprecedented experiment in government in North America, an experiment that has yielded many successes worth celebrating: the formal abolition of human enslavement, the extension of political rights regardless of gender, and the tenuous but exceptional, government-to-government relationship that exists between Native nations and the United States.
Perhaps, in the end, new histories, textbooks, and syntheses may reveal how the nation’s significant achievements did not emerge from the presumed certainty or righteousness of its beginnings, but from the continuing struggle to engage in that experiment. A global and Indigenous cast has played an immense historical role in that experiment, doing so in order to pursue visions of happiness and the good on a continent that many have long called home.

Fire breaks out on platform in Iran’s South Pars field
10 November 2026 22:23 GMT
A fire has broken out on a platform in Iran’s South Pars gas field, but the situation is fully under control, Iran’s Fars news agency reported, citing the deputy oil minister.
The platform accounts for only 14.5 million cubic metres of South Pars’s total daily production of over 700 million cubic metres of gas, the news agency said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘É a educação racista do apartheid sendo exportada’, afirma presidente da Fepal após agressões por turistas israelenses na Bahia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A população de Itacaré, cidade no sul da Bahia, tem denunciado, há alguns dias, o vandalismo feito por turistas israelenses na cidade contra um mural em solidariedade às vítimas palestinas do genocídio em Gaza. A região tem sido bastante escolhida por grupos de jovens israelenses que tiram férias depois de concluir a prestação de serviço obrigatória ao Exército.
A intervenção artística havia sido realizada em 30 de outubro, nas paredes do Casarão Azul, imóvel histórico localizado no centro da cidade. Após as ações dos turistas contra o local, o proprietário solicitou que os autores da homenagem removessem a pintura.
Além do episódio específico, moradores da região afirmam que casos de intolerância e até assédio contra mulheres por parte desses israelenses têm se tornado comuns. A população tem cobrado posicionamento do governador Jerônimo Rodrigues (PT) e também do presidente Lula (PT). A deputada federal Erika Hilton (Psol-SP) tem defendido a proibição de ingresso no país de turistas que recentemente passaram pelo serviço militar de Israel.
No Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, o presidente da Federação Árabe-Palestina (Fepal), Ualid Rabah, considera a proposta uma medida necessária e avalia que ela atingiria a quase totalidade desses grupos, visto que o serviço militar é obrigatório em Israel e envolve a participação direta nas zonas palestinas ocupadas. “Estamos falando de 100% daqueles que servem nas zonas palestinas ocupadas, participando do apartheid, do genocídio, do desterro, das humilhações diárias, ofender o direito internacional todos os dias.”
Rabah afirma que as agressões não são novidade e que há casos de desrespeito praticados por grupos de jovens israelenses em vários países do mundo. “Aqui no Brasil, além de Itacaré, aconteceu em Morro de São Paulo, em Santa Catarina e mais recentemente no Rio de Janeiro. É violência contra os brasileiros, racismo, assédio sexual contra as mulheres, depredação de patrimônio histórico”, ressalta.
O presidente da Fepal também explica que o turismo israelense tem sido importante para a região e representa, atualmente, cerca de 20% dessa economia para a cidade. E isso se dá, entre outros fatores, porque houve uma série ou telenovela gravada em Morro de São Paulo e que fez sucesso em Israel anos atrás, atraindo esse interesse. “Então eles entram no serviço militar, servem em Gaza, ao genocídio, e vêm passar férias, dar uma descansada, dar uma desestressada do genocídio da Palestina”, critica.
“Existe uma educação racista que o regime de apartheid impõe à sua sociedade e que acaba sendo transportada por esses turistas”, resume.
Ualida Rabah alerta que esse tipo de comportamento pode, infelizmente, contribuir para preconceitos contra os judeus e o judaísmo. “Ao Israel promover e criar esse tipo de gente, ressuscita um ódio mouco aos judeus. E é por isso que muitos judeus antissionistas têm acusado Israel e o sionismo como o pior perigo para o judaísmo desde o nazismo”, relata.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump’s FCC nominee avoids questions from Democrats on Carr’s ‘censorship agenda’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
During a contentious Tuesday hearing on her nomination by Donald Trump to serve as a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) commissioner, Senate Democrats hammered Danielle Thumann about recent actions taken by the Brendan Carr-led regulator that have been criticized as hostile to press freedom.
Thumann, who serves as senior counsel to Carr, is expected to be approved as commissioner, with Republicans in charge of the US Senate and House. But Ben Ray Luján, a senator of New Mexico, assured her that the commission’s actions will be under close scrutiny when Democrats take charge of the chamber in January.
Luján asked Thumann repeatedly whether she agrees with actions taken by Carr’s FCC, including a nearly unprecedented order in late April forcing ABC to apply early to renew its local station licenses, a move that immediately followed criticism of one of the network’s biggest stars, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, by the president and Melania Trump, the first lady. Carr was also accused of pressuring ABC affiliates to drop Kimmel’s show the previous fall.
“Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airways?” Luján asked.
“I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues, and I’m not familiar with all of the details regarding the investigation of ABC or the early license renewal of their licenses,” Thumann responded. “And I haven’t been involved in any of those conversations regarding any of their practices or regarding Jimmy Kimmel.”
Luján pressed Thumann to name an issue she has disagreed with Carr on, and she demurred. He also asked her whether it was “appropriate for the FCC to call up Disney’s broadcast license for early renewal”.
Several of Luján’s Democratic colleagues also took turns pressuring Thumann on the FCC’s actions toward television networks, with Ed Markey, the Massachusetts senator, grilling her on “Chairman Carr’s FCC censorship agenda”. “Ms Thumann, does the FCC have the authority to punish a broadcaster because the president disagrees with its news coverage?”
Pushing back on her response, Markey said: “Again, this should be a straightforward constitutional limitation, because the FCC cannot punish a broadcaster simply because the president doesn’t like his coverage. Yet Chairman Carr, your boss right now, has threatened to do exactly that.”
Markey accused her of choosing to “evade” his questions, saying that “anyone seeking a seat on the Federal Communications Commission must be willing to stand up to such threats and to defend the first amendment, and you are not willing to do so here in your confirmation hearing.”
Senator Tammy Duckworth also asked Thumann about whether she would yield to political pressure to punish disfavored networks. While Thumann said the commission has to deal with complaints against networks it regulates, she acknowledged that “editorial decision-making is protected by the first amendment for broadcasters”, and added: “I don’t think that a decision [about a station’s license] should be based purely on someone’s discontent with the content that’s being aired.”
Several Senate Democrats said it was inappropriate for the commerce committee to hold the confirmation hearing, and that if Republicans were going to nominate another member of the party to the commission, they should follow past precedent and nominate a Democrat as well. The FCC currently has one commissioner nominated by a Democratic president, Anna M Gomez, but her term has already technically expired.
At the end of the hearing, Luján issued a warning to Carr. “Mr Carr, if you’re listening now, know you’re going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions, and you don’t have the protection of the gavel any longer,” he said. “Subpoena authorities that you have to respond to so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place.”

https://hyperallergic.com/trump-proclaim.title: Trump Proclaims Gold-Studded Oval Office a National Monument
https://hyperallergic.com/trump-proclaim.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/trump-proclaim.text:
Trump Proclaims Gold-Studded Oval Office a National Monument
"It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody,” Trump said, which is flatly not true, as anyone can reverse the proclamation.
Apparently scrambling to secure his legacy after the blue tsunami of midterm triumphs for Democrats, President Donald Trump proclaimed the White House's Oval Office, Outer Oval Office, and Cabinet Room a joint national monument on Thursday, November 3. The proclamation rests on the same historic preservation law the president invoked to significantly diminish two cultural sites in Utah earlier this year.
The proclamation is not legally binding, meaning a future president could simply reverse it. Trump has outfitted the Oval Office with gold frames and trim, Mar-a-Lago maximalism, and his approximations of Louis XIV's Palace of Versailles in an aesthetic that former President Barack Obama said looked like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” The president issued the proclamation under the Antiquities Act of 1906, a law that lets presidents designate national monuments and protects archaeological and historical sites on federal lands.
While the Antiquities Act does not give presidents the authority to reduce, alter, or raze national monuments, Trump invoked the law in 2017 to shrink the boundaries of the Grand Staircase-Escalante and Bears Ears, two national monuments in Southern Utah that encompass culturally significant Indigenous lands. President Joe Biden restored the national monuments to their original size, though Trump doubled down in his second presidential term by reducing both sites by approximately 90% each this July.

https://taz.de/Gentrifizierung-in-NYC/!6.title: Gentrifizierung in NYC: New Yorks letzte Runde?
https://taz.de/Gentrifizierung-in-NYC/!6.author: Ruth Lang Fuentes
https://taz.de/Gentrifizierung-in-NYC/!6.text:
Gentrifizierung in NYC: New Yorks letzte Runde?
„Jimmy’s Corner“ ist eine der wenigen verbliebenen Kneipen am Times Square. Das Stammpublikum kommt seit Jahrzehnten. Doch das könnte bald vorbei sein.
Es ist irgendwas Soulig-Bluesiges zwischen Muddy Waters und Sam Cooke, was durch das Stimmengewirr zu uns durchdringt, als wir „Jimmy’s Corner“ betreten. Die Musik kommt tatsächlich von einer richtigen CD-Juke-Box, aber um dorthin zu gelangen, führt der Weg durch den engen Schlauch zwischen ewig langem Tresen und Wand. Jetzt verstehe ich, warum diese Art von Kneipe hier „dive bar“ heißt. Man muss regelrecht eintauchen, in und durch die Menge an schwitzenden, plappernden, saufenden, lachenden Menschen hindurch, die am Tresen stehen, weil sie gerade bestellen wollen oder schon auf ihre Drinks warten oder einfach nur mit der Barkeeperin reden wollen.
Wendy heißt sie, wie wir wenig später erfahren, und sie hat heute wirklich keinen Bock, viel zu plaudern. Sie sind nur zu zweit im Service und es gibt viel Bier zu zapfen, Geld zu kassieren und leere Flaschen und Gläser einzusammeln. Über unser Trinkgeld beschwert sie sich dann trotzdem: „Bei Drei-Dollar-Bieren nur ein Dollar Trinkgeld?“ Ich erkläre, wir kämen aus Europa, bei den nächsten zwei Bieren legen wir gleich vier Dollar obendrauf. „Ihr seid doch diese Journalistinnen, die letztens schon mal hier waren“, sagt sie dann deutlich zufriedener.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Wenige Tage zuvor hatten wir uns an den mit Boxkampfpostern zutapezierten Wänden und der funky Musik erfreut und vor allem am bezahlbaren Bier. Uns war gar nicht bewusst gewesen, wie besonders diese Bar in der 44. Straße mitten in Manhattan ist. Bis ein Typ erzählte, dass er seit 40 Jahren hierherkomme. Und der Mann auf den vielen Fotos mit lauter Boxgrößen Jimmy sei, der Gründer dieser Bar, der vor knapp sechs Jahren verstorben ist. Auch, dass der Kneipe die Räumung drohe, was Wendy bestätigt.
Elder Statesman des New Yorker Boxsports
Jimmy’s Corner liegt wie ein Relikt aus einer anderen Zeit eine Seitenstraße entfernt von den blinkenden Lichtern und Werbetafeln des Times Square. Vor 55 Jahren, 1971, eröffnete Jimmy Lee Glenn das Lokal zusammen mit seiner Frau Swietlana „Swannie“ Garbarska. Ihr Sohn Adam, der zehn Jahre später zur Welt kam und mittlerweile der Kneipenchef ist, erzählt am Telefon – er ist gerade nicht in der Stadt –, dass Jimmy zwei Straßen weiter zudem ein Boxstudio betrieb. Er sei so etwas wie der Elder Statesman des New Yorker Boxsports gewesen.
75 Jahre sei er im Boxsport in verschiedenen Rollen tätig gewesen. Alle hätten ihn gekannt und respektiert: Muhammad Ali und Mike Tyson kamen gerne mal vorbei. In der Kneipe hängen gemeinsam aufgenommene Fotos. Es war eine Zeit, in der die Gegend geprägt war von Sexshops, Prostitution, Freiern, Drogen, illegalen Geschäften, eine Zeit und eine Gegend mit dem rauen Charme eines Martin-Scorsese-Films. So klingt es jedenfalls, wenn Adam von seinem Aufwachsen dort erzählt.
Sein Vater Jimmy habe bis zu seinem Tod im Alter von fast 90 Jahren täglich in seiner Kneipe gestanden und mit den Gästen gesprochen. Egal ob arm oder reich, welche Hautfarbe, aus welchem Land, ob Stammgäste oder Touris – alle seien sie willkommen gewesen in Jimmy’s Corner. Und so sei es noch heute. „Genau das macht New York aus“, sagt Adam. Hunderte Fotos erzählen Geschichten von den Abenden und Nächten, die das Lokal schon erlebt hat. Auf Dollarscheinen haben Gäste Grußnachrichten und Liebesbekundungen hinterlassen.
Aber die Zeiten am Times Square haben sich längst geändert. Große Marken haben heute hier ihre Geschäfte, es gibt überteuerte Restaurants und Hotels. Längst dominiert der Kommerz rund um Jimmy’s Corner. Währenddessen beträgt die Miete des Lokals weiterhin nur 5.000 Dollar, dabei könnte sie in dieser Umgebung locker das Dreifache kosten. Das weiß auch Adams Vermieter, ein großer Immobilienkonzern namens Durst Organization.
Vergangenen Dezember habe der Immobilienkonzern versucht, den Mietvertrag zu kündigen und die Räumung beantragt, erzählt Adam. Aber er wäre nicht der Sohn eines ehemaligen Boxers und Boxtrainers, wenn er einfach klein beigegeben hätte. Stattdessen entscheidet er sich dafür, in die Offensive zu gehen, in den Kampf. Und reicht eine Klage beim obersten Gerichtshof von New York ein.
Einige Punkte im Mietvertrag seien juristisch anfechtbar, erklärt Adam. „Der Mietvertrag enthält nämlich eine Klausel, die besagt, dass sie uns rauswerfen können, wenn mein Vater stirbt. Meiner Meinung nach ist das rechtswidrig. Mein Vater dachte, es handele sich um einen ganz normalen Standardmietvertrag“, sagt er. Und fügt hinzu: „Ich verstehe, dass es ums Geschäft geht, aber das bedeutet nicht, dass das auf hässliche Weise geschehen muss. Es hätte bestimmt auch einen anderen Weg geben können.“ Im Laufe des Gesprächs stellt sich heraus, dass sowohl Adam als auch seine Frau Anwälte sind, er mit Abschluss in Harvard. Das sei natürlich von Vorteil, meint Adam, aber auch traurig. „Denn die meisten kleinen Unternehmen wären nicht in der Lage, sich so zu wehren.“
Die Zukunft einer der kultigsten Spelunken New York Citys – der damalige Bürgermeister Eric Adams erklärte 2022 den 18. August sogar zum „Jimmy Glenn Day“ – ist also ungewiss. Mindestens sechs Monate werde er noch bleiben können, schätzt Adam, hofft aber auf mehr. Offiziell läuft der Mietvertrag bis 2029. Für ihn bedeute die Bar alles. „Es ist der Ort auf der Welt, an dem ich mich am allermeisten zu Hause fühle“, sagt er.
Jimmy’s Corner steht für so viele Orte, die immer mehr aus den großen Städten verschwinden, denke ich traurig, während ich durch das ganze Bud Light langsam betrunken werde und wir von verschiedenen Seiten zugetextet werden. Es geht um Basketball, um Jobs, um irgendwelche Orte, die ich nicht kenne, um die Liebe. Jeder scheint hier seine Geschichte erzählen zu wollen. Über dem Tresen hängt eine einzige Regel: „Lasst uns hier nicht über Politik sprechen.“
„Es muss ein Gleichgewicht geben zwischen echten New Yorker Orten mit Charakter und den großen Läden“, hat Adam noch zum Abschluss unseres Telefonats gesagt. Schließlich sei das Großartige an New York, dass es ein Ort ist, an dem alle möglichen Menschen aufeinandertreffen und miteinander zurechtkommen müssten. So wie bei Jimmy’s eben. „Nicht jeder mag solche Spelunken wie Jimmy’s, aber wenn es einem gefällt, kommt man wieder.“ Ich hoffe sehr, dass ich wiederkommen kann.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Mike McMahon
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Political Power of Seniors
In places like Wisconsin, campaigns can’t win without seniors. They are the second-largest, fastest-growing, and most reliable group of voters.
It feels so good to see: college students marching to the polls after their campus voting sites were shut down, young men and women dancing at El-Sayed’s watch party, 18-year-olds taking selfies with “Just Voted” stickers.
This midterm election, young voters swung dramatically toward more progressive candidates, helping fuel the midterm sweep. But young and first-time voters make up a critical but small portion of the electorate, with voters under 30 casting only one in 10 votes.
A much slower, less dramatic but promising trend is emerging among the most reliable voters in the country—senior citizens. Seniors always show up. Two out of three seniors vote in midterms, and even more vote in presidential elections. And the much-maligned “boomers” have been steadily trending left since 2016.
Progressives shouldn’t be wary of seniors. On the contrary, they should seek them out, explicitly lay out a progressive senior agenda, and engage them in their campaigns.
I’ve spent the last three years organizing with older adults in Wisconsin. I’ve sat in community meetings, talked with them in their homes, shared meals at church, and had hundreds of conversations about aging, caregiving, and politics. Here’s what I’ve learned: For candidates who want to put people over corporations, transform healthcare, fund public transportation, and raise wages for working people—especially care workers—seniors will help lead the way.
In places like Wisconsin, campaigns can’t win without seniors. They are the second-largest, fastest-growing, and most reliable group of voters. That’s serious political power.
Every election cycle, progressives work hard to generate new voters, engage young people, and promote new leaders and voices. This is necessary and smart. Yet if candidates and campaigns aren’t engaging seniors on the issues that matter most to them, in most times and places, it won’t be enough.
Wisconsin saw this during the Democratic primary this year. Progressive Francesca Hong was making headlines by leading in the polls. But a dramatic last-minute shift narrowly handed David Crowley the win. Had the polls failed again?
The polls weren’t wrong so much as misunderstood. Wisconsin’s gold standard, the Marquette Law School Poll, accurately measured Hong’s support but also identified the race’s wild card: a large share of undecided voters.
The poll found that 46 percent of voters age 60 and older remained undecided less than two weeks before the Democratic primary. In other words, seniors decided that primary at the last minute.
I believe Hong could have won their votes, but her message hadn’t reached them. As one senior voter told me: “The only thing I know about her is from the negative TV ads her opponents are running.”
Hong ran an inspiring campaign, and she was the first candidate to commit to the Small Town and Rural Seniors (STARS) candidate forum in July. For an hour, gubernatorial candidates answered questions from the elders who organized the event: What would you do about the caregiver shortage in our state? How would you support transportation for seniors in rural areas? How can we protect seniors from online and phone scammers?
Seniors in attendance sat in a tight semicircle around Hong and the other candidates, listening intently. As rural seniors posed questions, Hong’s answers became stronger, clearer, and more confident. You could see her realize she didn’t need to persuade people to support her progressive agenda; she needed to show them she could deliver it.
When asked about a manufactured homes bill of rights midway through the forum, she stated with conviction that she aimed to make Wisconsin hostile to private equity. The 70-to-80-year-olds in the room interrupted her with applause.
Hong’s responses impressed many seniors in that room. But Wisconsin has over a million seniors, hundreds of thousands of whom hadn’t heard her message.
When senior voters hear about—and are included in—progressive politics, they listen. In the Texas Senate race, voters 65 and older moved away from Trump and toward Talarico by nine points. It wasn’t the biggest swing in the midterm elections, but in a state where seniors make up 29 percent of voters, that’s a critical number of votes.
Back in Wisconsin, Representative-elect Rebecca Cooke’s campaign is a good example. She expanded her appeal in Wisconsin’s rural Third Congressional District by making aging with dignity a priority in her campaign, helping her seal her victory on election night. I suspect we’ll see this slow but steady senior impact everywhere as we continue to crunch the numbers from the midterms.

The seniors I organize with have been proving for years that elevating senior issues can move local elections, especially in rural areas. They have been organizing there to protect publicly owned nursing homes from sale to private buyers. Many have turned these local organizing campaigns into electoral victories. This spring, Sauk County seniors helped recruit candidates who opposed selling their county nursing home and won eight of nine contested races. In Lincoln County, nursing home supporters were inspired to run for office and won.
When candidates address senior issues, seniors turn out. And it’s not just nursing homes. In rural Walworth County, seniors have won investments in public transportation and are leading the charge for multigenerational care (senior care and childcare). Others are campaigning for reforms to protect manufactured housing from private-equity predators. These, too, can be winning issues for campaigns.
Seniors may or may not call themselves progressive, but the issues they care about and the solutions they favor often are. Seniors are strong proponents of government investment, even across party lines.
A 2024 Hart Research poll found that older voters in Wisconsin believe the government should do more to ensure access to quality, affordable long-term care. Majorities of Democrats, independents, and Republicans support policies including higher wages to attract and retain long-term care workers in smaller towns and rural communities, and expanded access to Medicaid.
I’ve learned a lot working with senior citizens. My assumptions have been challenged, and I’ve become clear-eyed that they are an important, even crucial, part of a progressive coalition. And perhaps most importantly, they are eager to hear from us.
The bottom line: Candidates who directly engage seniors and support a progressive senior agenda will win votes, and in aging states like Wisconsin, Michigan, and beyond, senior votes can push them over the finish line.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Deputados da base obstruem votação na Câmara Legislativa do DF por falta de pagamento de emendas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Cruz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A falta de pagamento das emendas parlamentares provocou um impasse entre deputados distritais durante a sessão ordinária da Câmara Legislativa do Distrito Federal (CLDF), nesta terça-feira (10). Parlamentares da base do governo obstruíram a votação e contribuíram para o encerramento da sessão em meio à cobrança pela liberação dos recursos indicados pelos deputados.
A discussão começou com o deputado Jorge Vianna (Democrata), que questionou o atraso no pagamento das emendas parlamentares. A insatisfação também foi manifestada por outros integrantes da base governista, que pressionaram o Executivo pela execução dos recursos.
Durante a discussão, o deputado distrital Hermeto (MDB) relatou uma conversa que teve, na segunda-feira (9), com o secretário de Economia do DF, Valdivino José de Oliveira. O encontro tinha como objetivo tratar da liberação de emendas de sua autoria destinadas à Companhia Urbanizadora da Nova Capital (Novacap) e ao Programa de Descentralização Administrativa e Financeira (Pedaf).
“Ele me contou uma história tão triste para eu liberar minhas emendas que eu quase peguei meu dinheiro e fiz um empréstimo para o GDF”, declarou. Em seguida, resumiu sua reação ao cenário apresentado pelo secretário: “Se eu pudesse, eu doava para o GDF para ajudar no caixa”.
Emendas impositivas
Durante o debate, o deputado distrital Max Maciel (Psol) comentou a cobrança e destacou que parte das emendas parlamentares tem execução obrigatória, conforme previsto na Lei Orgânica do Distrito Federal. “Se eles estão reclamando que não estão executando as emendas deles no governo, a oposição aqui não vai nem querer ter uma questão de ordem nesse momento. Mas é importante dizer o seguinte: parte dessas emendas são impositivas, que regem a nossa Lei Orgânica”, afirmou o deputado.
O deputado Chico Vigilante (PT) também cobrou o cumprimento das regras orçamentárias e mencionou uma decisão do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), atribuída ao ministro Flávio Dino, sobre a destinação de metade do valor das emendas parlamentares para a saúde.
Vigilante defendeu a convocação do secretário de Economia, Valdivino José de Oliveira, para prestar esclarecimentos aos deputados sobre a falta de execução dos recursos. “Eu acho importante convocar o secretário de economia aqui na Câmara Legislativa para explicar isso. Uma vez não cumprido, a própria Câmara tem o dever e a obrigação de entrar na defesa do mandato dos parlamentares, para que seja cumprido o que determina a Constituição e a Lei Orgânica do Distrito Federal”, afirmou o distrital.
Antes da discussão sobre as emendas, os deputados apreciaram projetos previstos na pauta da sessão, entre eles a proposta de alteração da Lei Orgânica do DF que permite a reeleição dos integrantes da Mesa Diretora da CLDF entre legislaturas. A proposta foi aprovada em segundo turno, com 15 votos favoráveis e um contrário, abrindo caminho para que o atual presidente da Casa, Wellington Luiz (MDB), possa disputar um terceiro mandato.

https://hyperallergic.com/susan-siltons-.title: Susan Silton's Loud and Proud Whistle
https://hyperallergic.com/susan-siltons-.author: David S. Rubin
https://hyperallergic.com/susan-siltons-.text:
Susan Silton's Loud and Proud Whistle
A Los Angeles exhibition surveys the groundbreaking queer artist's multi-decade career, including her memorable work on the politics of vocal expression.
LOS ANGELES — Susan Silton’s four-decade retrospective at the Los Angeles Municipal Art Gallery documents her multifaceted investigations into queerness, illness, the environment, and the politics that surround these topics. As a conceptual artist, she works in multiple media, including prints, photography, video, installation, and performance. Focused on inclusivity and community engagement, her projects are often collaborative and participatory.
Silton was already an established graphic designer when she produced the political print “Target” (1991), which superimposes labels denoting gender, nationality, and sexual orientation onto an image of a man with a target on his back. Critical of a culture that reduces people to identity categories rather than recognizing their shared humanity, Silton later created an innovative series of self-portraits by moving her face across an active scanner. In “Self Portrait #4” (1995), she distorted her physiognomy to resemble a malleable substance, a metaphor for her belief that queerness is only one of many aspects of a person’s identity, and that it can be fluid. In a related move, she scanned and manipulated images of early 20th-century bird illustrations to create the series Aviate (1998-2000), resulting in sublime, colorful, linear abstractions that symbolize birds flying freely, no longer defined solely by their behavior or physical characteristics.

https://taz.de/Album-von-Endless-Wellnes.title: Album von Endless Wellness aus Wien: Vielleicht ist das Internet schuld?
https://taz.de/Album-von-Endless-Wellnes.author: Karoline Gebhardt
https://taz.de/Album-von-Endless-Wellnes.text:
Album von Endless Wellness aus Wien: Vielleicht ist das Internet schuld?
Die Wiener Band Endless Wellness arbeitet sich auf dem Album „Domino Days“ am Sound der Hamburger Schule ab. Eigenständig klingt das trotzdem.
Wer die Welt nicht versteht, kann immerhin Musik darüber machen. So wie die Wiener Band Endless Wellness das tut. In den Songs ihres neuen zweiten Albums „Domino Days“ erklären sie die Gegenwart zwar nicht, durchleben sie aber intensiv: mit trotzigem Gesang, Gitarrenhooklines zwischen Indiepop, Punk und Texten, die von Versäumnissen, Zeugnisflecken und einer Welt aus Plastik handeln.
Beim Sound von „Domino Days“ braucht man als Hörerin einen Moment, um sich zu sortieren, wird dann aber überzeugt. Zwischen dem Debüt „Was für ein Glück“ und seinem Nachfolger liegen zwei Jahre und viel Entwicklung.
Endless Wellness klingen nun selbstbewusster. Zwei der vier Bandmitglieder singen. Der stellenweise deklamatorische Gesang von Philipp Auer wirkt zunächst gewöhnungsbedürftig, beim Auftaktsong „Züge“ sticht dann eine pointierte Beobachtungsgabe hervor.
Endless Wellness
Endless Wellness: „Domino Days“ (Buback/Indigo). Live: 25. 11. 2026 „Technikum“ München, 26. 11. 2026 „Dieselstraße“ Esslingen, 27. 11. 2026 „Gebäude 9“ Köln; wird fortgesetzt
Wie bei vielen deutschsprachigen Indiebands stellen sich mitunter Assoziationen an die frühen Tocotronic ein. Bei „Niemand darf uns sagen, was wir sollen“ erinnern Endless Wellness an den Gestus der Hamburger Schule, wo bekanntlich die Symbiose aus Trotz und Poesie in den 1990ern mehrheitsfähig wurde.
Trotziges Schreddern
„Zange, Stange, fassen, lassen, Nächte und Tage“, nach wenigen Songs lässt die Band Paar- und Kreuzreime hinter sich und gewinnt auch sprachlich an Eigenständigkeit. In „Züge“ schreddert die Gitarre von Adele Ischia rotzig. Ein schöner Gegensatz zum ausgeglicheneren Sound von „Platanen“, bei dem Bassistin Milena Klien erstmals den Gesang übernimmt. Violine und Vibrafon unterstreichen ihre ausgeglichene Stimme.
Bei allem klanglichen Zucker geht es textlich kritisch zu, wenn Klien singt, dass „das Internet keinen Arm hat, der mich halten kann in meiner Festung aus Plastik und Papier“. Melancholisch untermalt die Geigenmelodie das ermüdende Gefühl einer Generation, die sich mit emotionalem Fallenlassen schwertut. Vielleicht ist das Internet schuld. Vielleicht die Boomer.
Melodisch vielschichtig bieten Endless Wellness ein Kaleidoskop gegenwärtiger Popstile. Wenn Auer Zeilen wie „In feuchten Händen hielt ich mein Zeugnis/Das Protokoll der Versäumnis“ dazu mit einem Hauch zu viel Theatralik vorträgt, spielt er hörbar mit seiner Stimme. Auch sein bissiger Humor schiebt die Songs an.
Im Titelsong „Domino Days“ atmet Sänger Philipp Auer endlich durch. Statt seiner sonst trotzigen Stimme murmelt er nur ins Mikrofon und legt die operettenhafte Attitüde ab. Dazu spielt ein minimalistisches Schlagzeug, schlicht, aber effektiv. Besonders mitreißend ist „Nie mehr sicher“, das rhythmisch Gesellschafts- und Allerweltskritik mit Esprit mischt.
Überlastete Gesellschaft
Kontrastreich und punkig geht’s weiter. Wenn Klien singt, schafft Ischias Gitarre Platz, laut sägend im Viervierteltakt. „Ambiguitätstoleranz“ kreischt die Bassistin – ironischerweise bezeichnet der Begriff die Fähigkeit, Ungewissheit auszuhalten, ohne ungehalten oder von Sorgen überrollt zu werden. „Domino Days“ von Endless Wellness ist ein Album gegen kollektive Unsicherheit und Überlastung, das Gegensätze, Widersprüche und gesellschaftliche Fliehkräfte zu Kernthemen macht und zugleich die Hand zur Flucht aus der modernen Tristesse reicht.
Das liegt an der inhaltlichen Bandbreite, am Humor, am Trotz, der Trauer und Wut über eine Welt am Abgrund in amüsante Songtexte verwandelt. Und an durchaus unerwarteten Brüchen, wenn etwa in „Die Katze“ eine repetitive Gitarre abrupt verstummt und stattdessen ein von Adele Ischia gespieltes Klavier dazwischenfunkt, als säße man in einem Saloon.
Das Intro von „Happy and you know it“ klingt, als leite es szenisch in einen Film. Textlich wird mit Egozentrik abgerechnet, während Ischias Klavier die Melancholie zum Spazierengang einlädt und sich das Schlagzeug jazziger Rhythmen bedient. Selbst das Outro überrascht, indem der Song in Pixies-Gefilde abbiegt.
Unprätentiös und sinnreich
Leicht depressiv, cool und gegensätzlich, sodass man es nicht kommen sieht. Das Erwartbare macht Musik vielleicht manchmal langweilig, dafür aber auch leicht verdaulich. Endless Wellness schaffen es, Unvorhersehbarkeit konsumierbar zu machen. Ein Talent, das der Steigerung ihres Bekanntheitsgrades zuträglich ist.
Anklänge an die frühen Tocotronic und andere rebellische Pop-Werke über die Unerträglichkeiten der Welt und jugendliche Wut über kleinbürgerliches Allerlei sind nicht zu leugnen. „Domino Days“ kommt textlich nicht ganz so raffiniert rüber, dafür aufgeweckt, unprätentiös und sinnreich.
Das Album schließt mit „So allein sollen wir nie wieder sein“. Vielleicht schaffen es die Protagonisten der Songs also doch, sich auf das emotionale Wagnis einzulassen. Eine stellenweise sperrige, dabei aber tröstlich nachdenkliche Gegenwartsdiagnose.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. La révélation de violences sexuelles et physiques faites aux enfants dans le périscolaire suscite depuis plusieurs mois une indignation légitime, ainsi que des tentatives d’esquisser les pistes pour construire un espace renouvelé d’accueil en périphérie de l’école.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Voters Who Saved Democracy Are Being Written Out of the Story
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Tim Wise, Kimberlé Williams Crenshaw
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Voters Who Saved Democracy Are Being Written Out of the Story
The media downplayed the importance of Black voters for Democratic victories.
Here are some media headlines and hot takes after last week’s Democratic midterm victories. See if you can catch what’s missing from their framing.
First, CNN ran an exit-poll explainer under the headline “Women, young voters and independents: See where Democrats made inroads.” Time said the “distinct gains came from young, rural, and Hispanic voters.” The Washington Post told readers, “Democrats have a surprising group of voters to thank”: namely, rural voters in Republican strongholds. And Reuters reported, “Latinos drive Democratic gains.”
While those shifts were real, and the shift among Latinos was critical to Democratic fortunes in Texas, what each outlet neglected to mention is the centrality of Black voters to the party’s wins. And yet, these voters were the most crucial part of the story.
In Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio, Michigan, and Mississippi—where Scott Colom appears set to become the first Black senator since Reconstruction—only the Black vote secured Democratic victories and flipped the Senate. In each of those states, exit polls show that white voters supported Republicans and would have gladly kept the chamber in GOP hands.
Even in Texas, although Latinos are the largest group of voters of color, at 25 percent of the total, with only 72 percent voting for James Talarico, and only 39 percent of white voters doing so, he needed the 12 percent of the electorate that was Black to turn out big, and they did, with 91 percent of their vote.
The extent to which the media downplayed the importance of Black voters to Democratic victories was stunning. For instance, Newsweek highlighted rural voters breaking for Democrats in South Carolina, while only noting farther down in the story that those rural voters were Black, while white rural folks mostly stayed home.
And The Washington Post, rather than crediting Black voters for Annie Andrews’s win there, ran a graphic highlighting the “significant improvements” Democrats made with less-educated whites, as if to suggest that had powered her victory. But this “improvement” moved these only voters from a 42-point Republican margin to a 21-point margin—hardly the key to Andrews’s victory, since this group still overwhelmingly rejected her.
The New York Times followed the same pattern, running a story proclaiming “White, Working-Class Voters Shifted Left,” noting, almost as an afterthought, that they still rejected Democrats by nearly 20 points.
And it wasn’t only in Senate races where the Black vote made the difference. In House races, white voters mostly supported Republicans nationally, meaning that here too, African American voters led the way, however much the media appears to have missed it.
This is no minor mistake, but rather anti-Blackness that refuses to give credit where it’s due. To the political press, those who drift away and come back are a story. Those who never left are like humidity in New Orleans, always there and not worth a headline. That tendency punishes Black Americans for being right first, seeing what Trumpism was in 2016, and voting against it consistently for a decade.
And when we see Black movement in the numbers, as with increased turnout, they still struggle to get credit. During an interview in which he was crediting every other possible constituency for the Democrats’ victories, a Vox interviewer asked Democratic political consultant David Shor about Black turnout. Only then did Shor acknowledge that the Black share of the electorate had risen four points in Georgia compared with the 2022 midterms. But even then, he immediately changed the subject back to the Latino vote in Texas, which wasn’t what the interviewer had asked about, and which also ignored the importance of Black turnout in that state.
This kind of erasure also harms those who did swing, because it hides who their allies are. Working-class whites who voted for Democrats spent years hearing that their problems were caused by “Black crime,” “DEI,” or government handouts to Black communities. In the end, they got nothing from those who offered them scapegoats without solutions. When they finally woke up, they joined a coalition that Black voters had been holding down the whole time.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But if the coverage never says so, these new arrivals may fail to realize that the people they were taught to fear are the ones who kept the door open for them. Black voters are the base of any coalition that can beat authoritarianism. Leaving that out of the story is how the right keeps working people divided.
Perhaps the most dangerous effect of erasing the importance of the Black vote is on Democratic priorities. Parties respond to stories about why they won. If the official story is that white rural voters or independents delivered the majority, the party will cater to them and, once again, treat the concerns of its most loyal voters as something that can wait.
But Black voters cannot afford to wait. In April, the Supreme Court gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has dismantled much of the federal civil rights apparatus, and the Justice Department’s Voting Rights Section has been hollowed out.
Restoring the Voting Rights Act is the Democratic Party’s best strategy for concretizing its gains. It won Senate seats in three (and likely four) Southern states, flipped House seats throughout the region, and held on to others, despite Republican attempts to gerrymander them away. A South where Black citizens can vote freely, in fairly drawn districts, is a South where those gains can last. And a South that is competitive for Democrats, where the promises of Reconstruction can finally be realized, is the recipe for lasting multiracial democracy.
Yes, President Trump will veto a new Voting Rights Act. But Democrats should pass it anyway, and they should make the veto a central issue in 2028.
But that won’t happen if the party believes the media framing about their victories. In state after state, Black voters didn’t just save the Democratic Party; they saved democracy. The least we owe them is the courage to tell the truth about that, and perhaps a thank you.

Petition opposing Hakeem Jeffries as US House Speaker passes one million signatures
More than a million people have signed a petition urging Democrats to reject Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the US House of Representatives, as growing opposition to his leadership puts his support for Israel and US foreign policy under renewed scrutiny.
Jeffries, who currently leads the House Democrats, is expected to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress convenes in January, after the Democrats' sweeping midterm victories on 3 November.
But Jeffries is not the speaker-elect yet. He confirmed his candidacy last week, but his colleagues must elect him later this month. Jeffries stands currently uncontested, with no other Democratic lawmaker throwing their hat in the ring for the position.
While no one in the party has come forward to run against Jeffries, several newly elected lawmakers have voiced reservations about his policy positions, casting doubt on whether or not they will endorse him.
Some voters and influencers have mobilised, with dozens of viral videos urging citizens to call their representatives and sign the petition against Jeffries.
